messages.content:
Read this:

Vaibhav: "Gurpreet, how was school?"
Gurpreet: "Fine."
Vaibhav: "And the fractions test next week? Are you ready?"
Gurpreet: (long pause) "I don't get fractions, Papa."
Vaibhav: "Since when?"
Gurpreet: "Since the first class. Everyone else understood."
Vaibhav: "Did you ask your teacher?"
Gurpreet: "No! Everyone would laugh. Aman already says I'm slow."
Vaibhav: "So you've been sitting there confused for two weeks?"
Gurpreet: (nods, eyes wet)
Vaibhav: "That sounds lonely. Thank you for telling me now. Shall we do one sum together tonight?"
Gurpreet: "Just one?"
Vaibhav: "Just one. And tomorrow, can you ask the teacher one question after class, when no one is around?"
Gurpreet: "Maybe."

For how long had Gurpreet been confused about fractions?
Gurpreet had been confused for two weeks, since the first class.
Why hadn't Gurpreet asked the teacher?
Gurpreet was afraid that everyone would laugh, especially since Aman already called Gurpreet slow.
What did Vaibhav do to help, and why could it work?
He thanked Gurpreet, offered one sum together and suggested asking the teacher privately after class, which makes asking feel safe.
What is it like for Vaibhav to learn of the two weeks of silence?
Vaibhav seems concerned and gentle, recognising how lonely it must have been and choosing warmth over a lecture.

metadata.subtype: Child too shy or proud to ask [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Swati, five, had given up her bottle months ago. But when the fever came, she dug the old sippy bottle out of the kitchen drawer in their Bengaluru flat and held it out to Sharmila. "Amma, milk in this. Pwease." Her visiting cousin giggled. "Baby talk!" Swati's lip wobbled. Sharmila filled the bottle, then turned to the cousin. "When we're poorly, we all want to be little again. It's okay." That night Swati slept curled in her parents' bed. Once the fever was gone, she announced the bottle was "for babies" and put it back in the drawer herself.

Where did Swati find the old bottle?
In the kitchen drawer.
Why did Swati's lip wobble?
She felt embarrassed and hurt when her cousin laughed at her baby talk while she felt poorly.
What did Sharmila get right?
She filled the bottle without shaming Swati and explained to the cousin that wanting to be little when ill is okay.
How might the cousin see the bottle after Sharmila's words?
The cousin might see it as comfort for a sick child rather than something to laugh at.

Read this:

Two days before Christmas, the Bandra playschool split the children into Team Star and Team Bell for decorating. Thomas got a star sticker. Within minutes, Star was the best team in the world. When Vijay from Team Bell asked for the red ribbon, Thomas hid it behind his back. "Bell team is bad. They cheat." Nobody had cheated. At home, Thomas told his mother that Bell children were naughty. "Isn't Vijay your friend from the bus?" she asked. "Yes." "Is he naughty?" "...He shares his crayons." Next morning, Thomas gave Vijay the red ribbon.

What did Thomas hide behind his back?
The red ribbon.
Why did Thomas say the Bell team was bad?
He felt excited and loyal to his new Star team, so the other team quickly felt like the bad ones, though nobody had cheated.
What question helped Thomas, and how could a parent use it again?
His mother asked whether Vijay from the bus was naughty; parents can ask about a real friend on the other team to break the us-and-them feeling.
What was the decorating game like for Vijay?
Vijay was left out of the ribbon and called bad, which likely felt confusing and unfair from a friend.

metadata.subtype: My friends are the good ones [Actor]

messages.content: Why can good friends disagree even when they like each other very much?

Liking someone does not make people think alike, so even good friends disagree. Because each person has different wishes and opinions, disagreements will happen, and talking about them calmly can even make a friendship stronger.

Read this:

I'm Jyoti, and last quarter I watched our small team in Gurugram get it exactly backwards. Rajni spent forty minutes choosing the font for an internal memo only four people would read. She made a comparison chart. Meanwhile Tushar signed a year-long contract with a new courier firm after one friendly phone call. "Good vibe," he said. I wasn't the manager, just the person sitting between them. So at lunch, I tried something. I drew a quick grid on a napkin: small or big, familiar or new. "Memo font: small, familiar. Two minutes, max." Rajni laughed, relieved. "Courier contract: big, new, hard to undo." Tushar went quiet. "Want to look at it together tomorrow?" I asked. He did. We found a cancellation fee he'd missed. Rajni now sends memos in whatever font opens first.

How long did Rajni spend choosing the memo font?
Forty minutes.
Why might Jyoti have felt uneasy sitting between Rajni and Tushar?
Jyoti felt concerned watching one colleague waste effort on a tiny choice while another rushed a big one, but was not the manager and had to find a gentle way to help.
What tool did Jyoti use, and why did it help both colleagues?
A simple napkin grid of small or big, familiar or new, which showed each person how much thinking their choice deserved.
How might Tushar feel when the cancellation fee turned up?
He might feel embarrassed but also relieved that someone helped him catch it before it cost the team more.
I'd like an invitation to my grandmother's eightieth birthday lunch: relatives only, vegetarian menu, a small garden near our house, 12:30 pm. 35 words. Signed the Nair family.

Dear relatives,
We invite you to my grandmother's eightieth birthday lunch. It will be held in a small garden near our house at 12:30 pm. The menu will be vegetarian.
The Nair family

Read this:

The school bus was leaving in ten minutes and the power had gone out. In the half-dark, Amandeep's mother called from the kitchen, "Take your lunch, your water bottle, the permission slip, your library book, your jersey for PT, and don't forget to give Ma'am the money for the trip!"

Amandeep, eight, nodded and ran around the flat. Her little sister Leela was crying about her own shoes. The torch flickered.

When the bus came, Amandeep had her lunch and the library book. The slip, the jersey and the money were still on the table.

That evening her mother sat with her. "That was too many things at once, wasn't it?" Together they drew a little checklist with five pictures and stuck it by the door.

What did Amandeep leave on the table?
The slip, the jersey and the money.
How might Amandeep have felt running around the dark flat?
She probably felt flustered and rushed, trying to hold too many things in her head at once.
How did Amandeep's mother fix the problem, and why might it work?
They drew a checklist with pictures by the door, so Amandeep doesn't have to remember everything in her head.
What might it have been like for Leela that morning?
Leela was crying about her shoes, so she probably felt upset and left out in the rush.

Read this:

Monsoon, first day: Avni pointed at the window. "Look, rain!" Irfan, fifteen months, stared at her face, not the window.
Four days later: Avni pointed again and said, "Rain, Irfan!" His eyes followed her finger to the glass. He squealed and slapped the pane.
Next week: Irfan pointed at a crow on the wet railing, then turned to check Avni was looking. She laughed. "Yes! A crow!" He grinned, pointing again and again.

What did Irfan point at in the last beat?
A crow on the wet railing.
How did Irfan feel when Avni said "Yes! A crow!"?
He felt delighted and pleased, grinning and pointing again and again.
How can Avni keep building this shared attention?
Keep pointing at interesting things, naming them, and responding warmly when Irfan points.
What is it like for Avni when Irfan checks she is looking?
Avni feels happy and connected, laughing because he now shares what he sees with her.
What does "turn over a new leaf" mean?

It means to change your behaviour and start acting in a better way.
Example: Sanjay turned over a new leaf and now goes for a walk every morning instead of sleeping late.

Read this:

"Kamal, we'll be late for the Diwali show!"
"I do it myself, Mumma!"
Kamal sat on the step with his new shoes. He pushed his foot in. It went in sideways.
"Let me help."
"No! Myself!"
Binita took a breath and crouched beside him. "Okay. You do it. I'll hold the other shoe."
He pulled. He wriggled. His tongue poked out. At last the foot slid in.
"I did it!"
"You did," said Binita, smiling, and picked up the second shoe for him to try.

What did Kamal say when Binita offered to help?
He said, "No! Myself!"
How did Kamal feel when his foot finally slid in?
He felt proud and happy, shouting "I did it!"
What did Binita do well even though they were late?
She took a breath, let Kamal do it himself, and helped only by holding the other shoe.
What might Binita have been feeling as they ran late?
Binita was probably a little anxious about the time, but chose patience.

Read this:

Devika could not sleep. At a dinner she had let slip that Sarita was laid off in March, something Sarita had told her in confidence, and it was already spreading. She rang Sarita before anyone else could. "I repeated your secret to people at dinner. I am sorry. No excuses. If you need distance, I will give it."

Sarita's ears burned, humiliation and rage in equal parts. "That was mine to tell," she said. "When Aditi asked about my job hunt I felt exposed." Then she stopped and waited. Devika did not argue. She wrote to each person she had told, asked them to let it go, and stayed quietly available for two weeks. Sarita watched the repair, not the excuses, and it decided her. A month later they met for tea.

Meanwhile Siddharth confided over coffee that he was seeing someone behind his partner's back. Sarita's chest tightened. "I won't lie for you, and I think you should tell her yourself," she said. She did not post about it or cut him off.

And an old flatmate who rang only when short of cash or needing a sofa got a different answer that month: "I can lend this once, but not again soon." Sarita hung up without a long explanation, knowing a friendship with no care running both ways stays thin.

When had Sarita been laid off?
Sarita was laid off in March.
How did Devika's and Sarita's handling of the leaked secret compare with Sarita's handling of Siddharth's confidence?

Devika told Sarita first, apologised without excuses and offered distance, and Sarita said clearly how it felt and judged by the repair. When Siddharth confided, Sarita refused to lie for him and told him honestly what she thought, without exposing him or cutting him off.
How did Sarita feel when Aditi asked about her job hunt?
She felt exposed, humiliated and full of rage.
What did Sarita do about the old flatmate who rang only when in need?
She offered to lend once, said no to more without a long explanation, and did not pretend the friendship was close.

Read this:

Kaito had spent months saying "da" for everything in the Madrid flat. On Tuesday he stood at the fridge, slapped the door, and said, "Milk." Lucia, his mother, froze with the kettle in her hand. "Milk? You want milk?" "Milk. Cup. Blue cup." She poured it into the blue cup. Kaito drank, set it down, and said, "More," very firmly, as if he had always been able to.

What did Kaito ask for at the fridge?
Milk, in the blue cup.
Why did Lucia freeze with the kettle in her hand?
She was surprised and thrilled to hear Kaito use real words after months of only saying "da". 😊
How could Lucia build on this moment?
Give him what he asks for when he uses words and repeat them back in short phrases, like "milk in the blue cup".
What is it like for Kaito when his words finally get him what he wants?
It likely feels powerful and satisfying, which is why he said "More" so firmly.
Write a letter of about 120 words to my grandfather in the village, telling him about my new school.

Dear Dadaji,
I hope you are well and that your knees are not troubling you much this winter. I have some news. I started at my new school last Monday. It is much bigger than my old one, with three floors and a huge playground. On the first day I felt nervous, but a boy called Samuel showed me around, and now we sit together. My favourite subject is science, because our teacher lets us do experiments every Friday. The canteen samosas are good, but not as good as Dadi's. I miss our evening walks to the fields. Please write back and tell me about the new calf.
Your loving grandson,
Abhay

Read this:

Gargi: new girl at work update
Nirmala: the "weak" one?
Gargi: yes. today she forgot to cc the manager. classic
Nirmala: didn't you say she fixed the client's data issue yesterday
Gargi: she got lucky. anyone could have fixed that
Nirmala: you said nobody in your team could figure it out for a week
Gargi: ok but she also asked me a question she should know
Nirmala: gargi. what did you think of her on day one
Gargi: that she seemed lost
Nirmala: and has anything since changed your mind?
Gargi: ...the data thing
Nirmala: 🤔
Gargi: fine. maybe i made my mind up too fast

What did the new colleague forget today?
To cc the manager.
Why did the data fix feel like luck to Gargi?
Gargi had decided on day one that the new colleague seemed lost, so good work felt like a fluke while small slips felt like proof, which seemed reasonable.
How does Nirmala help Gargi test the judgement?
Nirmala asks what Gargi thought on day one and whether anything changed it, helping Gargi see the first impression steering everything.
How might the new colleague feel if Gargi keeps this view?
She might feel undervalued and anxious, doing good work that goes unnoticed.

Read this:

Wei and Tuan started as summer interns at the same Hanoi engineering firm on the same Monday. By the second week, the difference was clear. Ms Lan stopped by Wei's desk every afternoon: "Try the drainage plan for Block B. I'll mark it up tomorrow, and I'll be honest." Her red notes were long and sometimes stung.
Tuan, seated at the far end of the office, was asked to scan old drawings and order lunch. Nobody checked his work, because nobody expected much. By August, Wei was presenting a section at the client meeting. Tuan had learned where every file was and little else.
On the last day he told his mother, "I think I'm just not an engineer." He never found out that Ms Lan had simply decided, on day one, which of them looked keen.

What did Ms Lan ask Wei to try?
The drainage plan for Block B.
What was Tuan feeling when he said he's "just not an engineer"?
He felt discouraged and small, having taken the lack of challenge as a verdict on his ability.
What could Tuan have asked for early on to change things?
He could ask Ms Lan directly for a real task and honest feedback, like Wei's, instead of waiting to be noticed.
How did Ms Lan's red notes affect Wei?
They sometimes stung, but the honest feedback pushed Wei to improve until presenting at the client meeting.

metadata.subtype: Boss expects excellence or expects nothing [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Zainab, you think your team's rule is unfair? Let me tell you about my hockey days. Our coach once benched the whole team for a match because one girl came late. We lost badly. Afterwards I asked him, 'Should eleven people pay for one person's mistake?' He was quiet. The next season he made new rules: the late person runs extra laps, not the whole team. Nobody complained. Fairness means the consequence fits the mistake and the person." Aditi Phuphi sipped her tea. "Now, what's happening in your team?"

Why did Aditi's coach bench the whole team?
Because one girl came late.
What might Aditi have been feeling when she asked the coach her question?
She likely felt the punishment was unfair and was frustrated by losing.
What lesson does Aditi share about fair consequences?
That a consequence should fit the mistake and fall on the person who made it.
How might the late girl have felt about the whole team being benched?
She probably felt guilty that everyone paid for her mistake.

Read this:

In the small government school outside Nashik where Eshaan had started teaching, the headmaster pinned the district scholarship notice for young teachers on the board. Eshaan read it three times and walked away.

That week he had written a wrong answer on the blackboard in a maths lesson, and a sharp girl in the front row had pointed it out. The children giggled. Eshaan had felt like the floor opened. That night he redid every lesson plan for the month, until the lamp oil ran low.

Bhavna, who taught the fourth standard, found him in the staff room at seven, red-eyed. "You didn't sleep. Over one sum?" He nodded. "And now you won't apply for the scholarship?"

"What if I fail at that too?"

"Then you'll learn something. Like the girl who corrected you."

He laughed, a little. That afternoon, he told the headmaster about the blackboard mistake, and asked for the scholarship form.

Who pointed out the wrong answer on the blackboard?
A sharp girl in the front row pointed it out.
What was Eshaan feeling after the blackboard mistake?
Eshaan felt humiliated and anxious, as if the floor had opened, which is why he redid every lesson plan overnight.
What went wrong in Eshaan's reaction, and what fixed it?
He overworked and avoided the scholarship out of fear; talking to Bhavna, admitting the mistake to the headmaster and applying fixed it.
How might the girl who corrected Eshaan see the moment?
She probably felt proud of spotting the error, and may learn from Eshaan that mistakes can be corrected calmly.

Read this:

Wednesday night
Day 6 of trying the ten-minute sitting thing Sarita taught me. Honestly? Most of it was thinking about lunch, my presentation, whether I left the geyser on. Sarita says that's normal, you just keep coming back to the breath. It feels like training a puppy. 🙂
But today something different happened. In the middle of the lab, when the experiment failed again, I noticed my chest getting tight. And I just... breathed. Slowly. Three times. Didn't throw the beaker. Didn't cry in the washroom like last week.
Also I've stopped eating with my phone. Food tastes better? Weird.
Going to keep going. Tomorrow: sit before class, not after.
Aadhya

How long is the sitting practice Sarita taught Aadhya?
It is ten minutes.
What does Aadhya's noticing the tight chest in the lab show about Aadhya's progress?
It shows Aadhya is becoming aware of stress as it rises, which made it possible to calm down with breaths instead of reacting.
What is Aadhya doing that supports focus?
Aadhya practises daily, keeps coming back to the breath, and has cut small multitasking habits like eating with the phone out.
How might Sarita feel hearing about the lab moment?
Sarita would probably feel happy and encouraged that the suggestion is helping Aadhya in real situations.

Read this:

Neelam, you said no to the canteen group again today; I saw. Let Trisha-aunty tell you a small thing. My first job was at a bank branch in Pune, forty years ago. A colleague named Rosy asked me to lunch on my second day. I said I'd brought tiffin. She asked the next week; I said I was tired. She asked a third time; I said maybe tomorrow, and hid in the record room. After a month she stopped asking. I ate alone for most of that year. Then one Friday I was so tired I nearly said no again, but I said yes just to stop myself. We ate vada pav on the steps. Rosy became the friend who carried my wedding sari and held my first baby. All from one tired yes. So tomorrow, when they ask, say yes, Neelam.

What did Trisha and Rosy eat on the steps?
They ate vada pav on the steps.
How might young Trisha have felt hiding in the record room?
Trisha was likely shy and anxious, avoiding the lunch even though it left her eating alone.
What turning point in the story changed Trisha's first year?
Saying yes to Rosy on a tired Friday, which began a lifelong friendship.
What might it have been like for Rosy when Trisha kept saying no?
Rosy may have felt turned away and unsure whether Trisha wanted company, which is why she stopped asking after a month.

Read this:

"Naveen-da, how did you know Ritu was the one?"
"Ramesh, that's a film question."
"I'm serious. Ma keeps sending profiles. One girl seems nice, but I don't know."
"What don't you know?"
"If we want the same things. She wants to live abroad. I want to stay near Ma."
"Did you ask her about it?"
"Not directly. It felt too early."
"Too early is better than too late. Ritu and I talked about money, kids, where to live, even who cooks. Before the engagement."
"Wasn't that awkward?"
"Very. We fought once. But after that I trusted her more."
"So I should just ask."
"Ask. And listen. Maybe she has good reasons."

Where does the girl Ramesh is considering want to live?
She wants to live abroad.
What is Ramesh worried about?
Ramesh is worried that the girl and Ramesh may want different things, since she wants to live abroad and Ramesh wants to stay near Ma.
What advice does Naveen give Ramesh?
Ask her directly about big things like money, children and where to live, and really listen to her reasons.
How did talking early affect Naveen's relationship with Ritu?
It was awkward and led to a fight, but afterwards Naveen trusted Ritu more.
Welcome verse of six lines for baby Zoya, with real rhymes, 35 words.

Welcome, Zoya, little one,
Your life has only just begun.
Our hearts are full, our smiles are wide,
We welcome you with joy and pride.
Sleep sweetly now, our little star,
We love you just the way you are.

Summarize this reply in two sentences.

"Indeed, your example is an unfortunate one for your argument," said Holmes, taking the paper and glancing his eye down it. "This is the Dundas separation case, and, as it happens, I was engaged in clearing up some small points in connection with it. The husband was a teetotaler, there was no other woman, and the conduct complained of was that he had drifted into the habit of winding up every meal by taking out his false teeth and hurling them at his wife, which, you will allow, is not an action likely to occur to the imagination of the average story-teller. Take a pinch of snuff, Doctor, and acknowledge that I have scored over you in your example."

Holmes says the newspaper case is a poor example, because he has worked on it and knows that the husband was sober and faithful. The complaint was that he threw his false teeth at his wife after meals, which no ordinary storyteller would invent.

Read this:

Tenzin: payal can u finish the robot code by tonight
Payal: i already did the sensor part yesterday
Tenzin: i know ur the best. i'll mention you to the judges i promise
Payal: you said that last time too
Payal: can i ask something clearly
Tenzin: ok
Payal: whose name is on the entry form
Tenzin: mine, but it's a team thing
Payal: am i on the team list
Tenzin: …not officially
Payal: then i don't think i should keep writing the code
Tenzin: wow ok. i was going to help you get into the senior club
Payal: you keep saying that. it never happens
Payal: i'm going to ask Mr Das if i can enter the junior category myself
Tenzin: fine
Payal: good luck tonight

What part of the code did Payal already finish?
The sensor part.
How does Payal feel about Tenzin's promise?
Payal feels doubtful and used, since the same promise was made last time and never kept.
What did Payal do that was wise?
Payal asked clear questions about names on the form, stopped doing unpaid work, and turned to Mr Das to enter solo.
How might Tenzin see Payal's questions?
Tenzin seems defensive and annoyed, perhaps because the questions expose how one-sided the arrangement was.

Read this:

Last spring our firm brought in an AI tool to summarise contracts, and I loved it. What used to take me a morning took twenty minutes. By summer I had stopped reading the full documents at all. Then my senior, Mridul, asked, 'Eshaan, what does the indemnity clause say?' It was in a supplier contract I had 'reviewed'. The summary had skipped it. I hadn't read it. I remember the silence on that call. Nothing bad had happened yet, but it could have, and my name was on the review, not the tool's. Since then I use the summary as a map, not the territory: I read every clause it flags and spot-check the ones it doesn't. Once a week I review one contract fully by hand, so I don't lose the skill. Mridul calls it my gym day. I'm slower than I was in summer. I'm also better.

What did the AI summary skip?
An indemnity clause in a supplier contract.
What did Eshaan feel during the silence on that call?
Embarrassed and alarmed, realising Eshaan's name was on a review that had not really been done.
How does Eshaan now use the tool responsibly?
Eshaan treats summaries as a map, reads the flagged clauses, spot-checks the rest, and reviews one contract fully by hand each week to keep the skill.
How might Mridul see Eshaan's weekly 'gym day'?
As a sensible habit that keeps the junior sharp and accountable, which is why Mridul jokes about it approvingly.
Could I have a peace of cake? Is the word right?

Could I have a piece of cake?
Why: "Piece" means a part of something. "Peace" means calm and quiet.

Read this:

"Pankaj Mama, which way to the temple?"
Pankaj Mama stuck his thumb out over his shoulder.
Kavitha looked at the thumb. "Is that a thumbs-up? Like, it's good?"
"No, no! That way. Behind me."
"Oh. In Chennai we'd point with a finger."
"Here we use the thumb or whole hand. Pointing one finger at someone is rude for the old people."
"Really? I pointed at the priest this morning."
Mama laughed. "He'll forgive you. Next time, use the whole hand."
"So the temple is behind you, past the pond?"
"Yes. Past the pond, left at the banyan tree."
Kavitha nodded. "Words are safer."

Where was the temple, according to Pankaj Mama?
Past the pond, left at the banyan tree.
What was Kavitha feeling when she saw the thumb?
Kavitha felt confused and unsure, thinking the thumb might mean "good" rather than a direction.
What did Kavitha do that helped?
She asked for the directions in words and checked the route, pairing the gesture with clear language.
How might the priest have seen Kavitha's pointing?
The priest might have felt it was a bit rude, but probably understood she was from somewhere else.

Read this:

Peer mentor's note, first-year block, written by Bidisha.
Rajni has been one of the liveliest people on our floor. Since the statistics results came out and she failed, she's changed. She's skipped every stats class for two weeks, and when anyone mentions the re-exam, she changes the subject or leaves. She stays in her room with the door shut. I didn't lecture her. Yesterday I knocked and said, "Want to go to the canteen? No stats talk, just samosas." She came. At the end, I said, "If you want, I'll walk with you to the stats professor's office hour on Thursday. You don't have to say anything; I'll just be there." She was quiet for a while. Then she said, "Okay. Just Thursday." What I'll do next: knock on her door at 3 on Thursday.

Which subject did Rajni fail?
Statistics.
Why did Bidisha offer samosas without stats talk first?
Bidisha felt concerned but sensed that lectures would push Rajni away, so a relaxed outing felt like a safer way to reconnect.
What makes Bidisha's offer about Thursday a good first step?
It is small and concrete, just walking together to the office hour, and it offers company rather than pressure.
How might Rajni feel agreeing to "Just Thursday"?
Rajni probably feels nervous but a bit relieved, with one small, manageable step and someone beside her.
Prudent means what?

Prudent means sensible and careful, especially when thinking about the future. It is an adjective.
Example: It is prudent to keep a little cash when you travel to small villages.

Read this:

Emeka was halfway through shading a giraffe's neck when his mother called from the kitchen. "Emeka, run to the corner shop for bread, please."
"Not now!" he snapped, and the pencil skidded across the table. His eyes stung.
Zanele looked at the giraffe, then at his face. "It's hard to stop when you're in the middle of something," she said. "Take a minute."
He sat without speaking. The next Saturday she said, "Five minutes, then bread, all right?" Emeka finished the neck, capped his pencil, and reached for his shoes, whistling.

What did Emeka's mother ask him to buy?
She asked him to run to the corner shop for bread.
What was Emeka feeling when he snapped 'Not now!'?
He was upset and a bit heartbroken at losing his drawing flow. His stinging eyes show it was real hurt, not just rudeness.
What made the difference the next Saturday?
Zanele gave a five-minute warning, so Emeka could finish the giraffe's neck and go without anger.
How might Zanele have felt about the first snap, and what did she do with it?
She may have been surprised, but she looked at his face, named how hard stopping is and gave him a minute rather than scolding.

Read this:

Kavitha's pay from the garment unit in Tiruppur covered her younger brother's college fees and most of the rent since Appa's accident. So when the floor supervisor, Harish, called her 'slow cow' in front of the line, she swallowed it. The other women said, 'That's just how supervisors are.' For a while she repeated it to herself too. Then one night, eating cold rice after a twelve-hour shift, she caught herself thinking she deserved it. That frightened her more than Harish did. She couldn't quit; that was simply true. But she could stop calling it normal. She started eating lunch outside, away from the line, even for ten minutes. She wrote Harish's words in a small notebook with dates. On Sundays she went to the tailoring class at the church hall, three hours of learning a skill that might one day be her own shop.

Where did Kavitha go on Sundays?
Kavitha went to the tailoring class at the church hall.
What did Kavitha feel when she caught herself thinking she deserved it?
Kavitha felt frightened, because it meant she was starting to accept the abuse as normal.
What small ways did Kavitha protect her dignity while staying?
Eating lunch outside away from the line, noting Harish's words with dates, and learning tailoring on Sundays as a way out.
How do the other women on the line see Harish's behaviour?
They see it as just how supervisors are, which makes it harder for Kavitha to name it as wrong.

Read this:

"Some of us were up till one making slides," Kavitha said, dropping her bag on the library table.
"Wow, dedicated," Vikas said. "I slept at ten. Best sleep of my life."
Kavitha stared at him. "Must be nice."
"It was!"
She opened the laptop. "Some people's names are on this project too, you know."
"Yeah, it's looking great." He gave a thumbs up.
Kavitha closed her eyes for a second. Then she turned to face him.
"Vikas, I'm going to say this clearly, because hints aren't working. I've done the research and the slides. I need you to do the conclusion and the references tonight."
Vikas's face fell. "Wait. You were saying that before?"
"Three times."
"I honestly thought you were just tired. Sorry. I'll do the conclusion and references tonight, and send them by nine."

How late was Kavitha up making slides?
Kavitha was up till one making slides.
What was Kavitha feeling as Vikas missed each hint?
Kavitha felt resentful and exasperated, closing her eyes for a second because her unfair share of work was going unnoticed.
What would you advise someone in Kavitha's place from the start?
State the problem and the request clearly, as she finally did, instead of hinting and hoping it lands.
How did Vikas read Kavitha's hints?
Vikas read them as tiredness or small talk, not as a complaint about the work, which is why he was surprised.

Read this:

"Rashmi, you brought your phone?" Mehak whispered on the picnic bus.

"No. We all agreed, no phones this picnic."

"But Tanu brought hers."

"That's Tanu's choice. We voted."

At the lake, Tanu spent the whole time on her phone. Rashmi, Mehak and the others played frisbee and caught tadpoles.

On the way back, Ma'am said, "Thank you to everyone who kept our promise."

Rashmi sat up straighter. "See? It felt good to keep it."

Mehak nodded. "Even if Tanu didn't."

What did the class agree about phones?
They agreed no phones this picnic.
How did Rashmi feel when Ma'am thanked the class?
Rashmi felt proud and good about keeping the shared promise.
How could Ma'am build on this feeling?
She could involve children in making rules together, so they value keeping them.
How might Tanu feel when Ma'am thanked the others?
Tanu might feel a bit left out or embarrassed.

Read this:

So here's the thing I'm a bit embarrassed about. At the college fest committee, Ramesh was reading out the budget, and I laughed and said, "Say it again in your village accent, it sounds so cute." People giggled. After the meeting, Ramesh stopped me on the stairs, very quietly. "Zeenat, I know you didn't mean anything. But the accent jokes follow me everywhere. That one stung." My first feeling? Defensive. I wanted to say, "It was a compliment!" I wanted him to say it was fine. My ears were burning. But I made myself stop. I said, "You're right. I'm sorry it came across like that. I won't do it again." And then I left it there. I didn't make him reassure me. That part was hard.

Where did Ramesh stop Zeenat?
On the stairs.
What was Zeenat's first feeling when Ramesh spoke to her?
Zeenat felt defensive and embarrassed, wanting to insist it was a compliment and wanting Ramesh to say it was fine.
Which choice worked, and why?
Apologising for how it came across and not asking Ramesh for reassurance worked, because it respected his hurt instead of shifting attention to Zeenat's feelings.
How might Ramesh feel after Zeenat's apology?
Ramesh might feel relieved and respected, glad that speaking up quietly was heard without a fight.

metadata.subtype: Being told about an unintended slight [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Gargi, you and your brother were fighting over the tablet again, so let your Dida Bidisha tell you something. When I was nine, my brother Tapan and I fought about everything: the window seat, the last rasgulla, who Ma loved best. Once we didn't speak for three days over a comic. But one evening at the para football ground, the bigger boys started calling Tapan "Scarecrow" and pulled his shirt. I ran over, stood in front of him and said, "Leave my brother alone or I'm calling Ma." They left. Walking home, Tapan said, "You still owe me that comic." I laughed so hard. We fought all our lives, and we stood up for each other all our lives too.

What did the bigger boys call Tapan?
They called Tapan "Scarecrow."
What was Bidisha feeling when she ran to stand in front of Tapan?
Bidisha felt protective and angry at the bigger boys, even though she and Tapan fought at home.
Which choice in the story showed loyalty, and why did it matter?
Standing in front of Tapan and threatening to call Ma showed that home fights didn't stop her defending him outside.
How might Tapan have felt when he said "You still owe me that comic"?
Tapan probably felt grateful and relieved, and joked to show things were normal between them again 🙂

Read this:

Ammi held out the spoon. "Bhindi, Zeenat?" Zeenat, two, clamped her lips and turned her face into the chair. "No." Across the mat, her cousin Dilnaz, four, crunched a piece loudly. "Mmm! Crispy!" Zeenat stared. Dilnaz took another and grinned, green bits on her chin. "More, Khala, please." Zeenat pointed at Dilnaz's plate. "That." "The same bhindi?" Ammi asked, smiling. Zeenat opened her mouth, chewed slowly, then held out her hand for more.

What vegetable did Ammi offer Zeenat?
Bhindi.
What does Zeenat's long stare at Dilnaz suggest?
Zeenat seems curious and less wary; watching Dilnaz enjoy the bhindi made the strange food look safe to try.
What changed Zeenat's mind, and how could Ammi use that at the next meal?
Seeing Dilnaz eat happily was the turning point, so Ammi could seat Zeenat beside a child enjoying a new food instead of pushing the spoon. 🙂
How might Dilnaz feel about being watched and copied?
Dilnaz is simply enjoying the snack, but being copied may feel nice, like being the big cousin who shows the way.

1) How should I prepare for a school debate?
2) what did the principal announce this morning
3) Why is it better to carry an umbrella than to stand under a tree in a storm?
4) What's the meaning of the word jealousy?
5) Is there a mistake here? The man whom I met him was kind.

1. Learn both sides of the topic, and note two or three strong points. Practise answering the opposite side calmly.
2. I don't know, because I can't hear your school announcements. Ask a classmate or check the notice board.
3. Standing under a tree is risky. Because lightning tends to strike tall objects, and the current can pass through the tree to people near it. An umbrella does not protect you from lightning either, so go indoors.
4. "Jealousy" is a noun. It means an unhappy feeling that you get when someone has what you want.
5. Corrected: The man whom I met was kind. Why: "whom" already stands for the man, so we do not add "him" after the verb.

Read this:

Lokesh still remembered the sting from his first job in Hyderabad: a manager presenting his research as "our findings" without a glance in his direction. So when Zainab, the new analyst on his team, spent her weekend cleaning up the messy survey data, he didn't wait. On Monday at ten, before the client report went out, he posted in the team group: "Before this goes to the client: Zainab rebuilt the survey dataset over the weekend and caught 312 duplicate responses. Without that, our main finding would have been wrong. Thank you, Zainab." He copied their director, Mrs. Rao. Zainab replied with a small 🙏 and nothing else. But at lunch she came over. "In my last job, nobody ever named who did what," she said. "I didn't know it could feel like this." Mrs. Rao asked Zainab to present the data section to the client that Friday.

How many duplicate responses did Zainab catch?
312 duplicate responses.
What was Zainab feeling when she spoke to Lokesh at lunch?
Zainab felt appreciated and moved, surprised by how good it felt to be named for her work, unlike in her last job.
What made Lokesh's credit strong?
It was timely, before the report went out, public in the team group with the director copied, and specific about what Zainab did and why it mattered.
How did Mrs. Rao respond to the message?
Mrs. Rao took notice and asked Zainab to present the data section to the client that Friday.

Read this:

Monday: After their fight about his job move, Nitin went silent. Jahnavi followed him from the kitchen to the balcony. "Talk to me! Why do you always do this?" He put on his headphones and went for a walk. She sent nine messages. No reply till midnight.
Thursday: At the next disagreement, she tried something different. "I can see you're shutting down. I need us to finish this. Can we pick it up on Sunday evening, after dinner?" He blinked, then nodded.
Sunday: At eight he came to the table, a bit stiff, and talked for twenty minutes. When he began drifting off again, Jahnavi said calmly, "It's okay to pause. It's not okay to vanish for days. That's my limit." He sat back down.

How many messages did Jahnavi send on Monday?
She sent nine messages.
What was Jahnavi feeling on Monday when she followed Nitin, and what shows it?
She felt shut out and desperate; she followed him from room to room and asked why he always does this.
What changed on Thursday, and why did it work better?
She calmly named his shutting down and asked to continue at a set time, which gave him space without dropping her need.
How might Nitin experience a calm request compared with being chased?
Being chased probably made him feel cornered, so he left; a calm, timed request felt manageable, so he came back.
Should I write "a well known author" or "a well-known author"?

Use a hyphen before a noun: "a well-known author". When the phrase comes after the noun, you usually leave the hyphen out, as in "The author is well known."
Examples: She is a well-known author. The author is well known.

Read this:

"Mummy, listen to this," Hemant said, holding up his laptop. "A guy called Omkar wrote under my article. Very polite. He says my chart has the wrong year for the rainfall data."
"Wrong? You checked it three times."
"I know. That's why my face is hot." He scrolled. "But he's right. I typed 2019 instead of 2018."
"So write back and say he's mistaken."
"Mummy, no. He isn't mistaken. He took the time to check my work." Hemant typed: "Thank you, Omkar, you're right. Fixed, and I've added a correction note at the top 🙏"
"Now everybody will see you made an error."
"Better they see me fix it than see me argue." He pressed publish and let out a breath.

What error did Omkar point out in Hemant's article?
Omkar said the chart had the wrong year, 2019 instead of 2018.
Why did Hemant thank Omkar even though his face felt hot?
The mistake stung, but Hemant saw that Omkar was polite, was right, and had taken the time to check the work.
What made Hemant's response a sensible way to handle the mistake?
He thanked the critic, fixed the chart and added a visible correction note. Owning the error openly is more credible than arguing.
How might Mummy see Hemant's decision to publish a correction?
She seems to worry that everyone will see the error, so she probably sees it as embarrassing. She may see it differently once she notices he stays calm.

Read this:

“Come here, my little Zoya, and I'll tell you about Mr Anand,” said Nani Salma. “When I was ten, our teacher was Mr Anand, and our class had a girl called Meena who read very slowly. One day a boy began copying her, and the room laughed. Mr Anand did not shout. He walked to the back, stood beside Meena's desk and said, 'In this room everyone gets the time they need. Meena, please begin again.' We waited. Meena finished, red in the face, and he said, 'Thank you. Well read.' Next day my bench-mate Hafsa told a shy boy, 'Take your time.' I heard myself say it too. We had copied him without knowing.”

Where did Mr Anand stand when he spoke to the class about Meena?
Mr Anand stood beside Meena's desk at the back of the room.
What might Meena have felt while the class waited for her to finish?
Meena probably felt nervous and exposed but also supported, since Meena finished red in the face and was thanked for reading well.
What could a teacher do today when a child is mocked for reading slowly?
A teacher could stop it calmly, stand near the child, give the child time to read and thank them for it, as Mr Anand did.
How might the boy who copied Meena have felt when the teacher spoke?
The boy may have felt caught and ashamed, since the room stopped laughing and the teacher's calm words made the copying look unwelcome.
"Mujhe bhookh lagi hai, kuch halka khane ko milega?" English mein bolo.
In English: "I am hungry. Can I get something light to eat?" The word "light" here means a small, easy meal.

Read this:

Hi Zainab,
It's 4:40 and the flat is so quiet I can hear the fridge. Mumma's shift ends at eight, Papa's at nine. I can eat what I want, watch what I want, and nobody asks about homework. Sounds great, right? For a week it was. Now I scroll videos till my eyes hurt, just so there's some noise. Remember your Dadi shouting at us to wash our hands before her pakoras? I miss that so much. Nobody here even knows I got the part in the school play yet. Maybe I'll tell them at dinner, if they aren't too tired.
Write back soon, okay? 🙂
Kashish

What time does Mumma's shift end?
Mumma's shift ends at eight.
What is Kashish feeling while writing about the quiet flat?
Kashish feels lonely, even though the freedom is real; the videos are mostly there to fill the silence.
What small step could help Kashish feel less alone after school?
Tell Mumma and Papa about the play and the quiet afternoons, and set up regular calls with Zainab or join an after-school activity.
How might Kashish's parents feel if they learned about the lonely afternoons?
They would likely feel sad and a little guilty, and might look for ways to connect, like a quick call from work or a shared dinner ritual.
Describe a school bag in one sentence, with at least three items inside it.
My school bag holds a notebook, a water bottle and a box of colour pencils.

Question time:
My teacher used the word "rehearsal". What is it?
Meaning of "hit the nail on the head"?
Which is correct, "sandwhich" or "sandwich"?

1. As a noun, "rehearsal" means a practice of a play or show before the real performance.
2. It means to say or do exactly the right thing. For example: your answer hit the nail on the head.
3. It is "sandwich". There is no "h" after the "w".

Read this:

The wedding hall was loud and lunch was late. Manjula Aunty put one jalebi on Shreya's leaf. "If it's still there when I come back from greeting the bride, you get two." Shreya stared at the jalebi. Drums boomed, cousins ran past, and Aunty took a long time. Shreya sat on her hands. She turned her whole body toward the band and counted the drummers aloud, "One, two, three, four!" Then she counted balloons. When Manjula Aunty came back, the jalebi was still there, sticky from the heat. "Two!" Shreya shouted, holding up two fingers.

What did Shreya count first while she waited?
She counted the drummers aloud.
Why did Shreya turn her whole body toward the band?
She wanted the second jalebi, and not seeing the sweet made the wait easier; looking at the drummers kept her hands and mind busy.
Which part of Shreya's waiting worked best, and why?
Counting drummers and balloons; thinking about something else carried her through the long, noisy delay better than staring at the jalebi and trying hard.
How might Manjula Aunty feel on coming back to the leaf?
Manjula Aunty finds an untouched jalebi and a proud child holding up two fingers, and is likely delighted that Shreya waited so long in all that noise 😊
What is one teaching note for Raga Marwa?
No Pa; komal Re and tivra Ma create tension.

Read this:

Monday: Usha, five, came home from the zoo trip. "Monkey! And ice cream! And the bus!" Bhupen smiled, confused. "Which came first?"

Wednesday: At bedtime he asked about her day. Usha frowned, thinking. "First assembly. Then drawing. Then... lunch. Then I fell."

Saturday: Usha told Nani on the phone about the zoo trip. "First we went on the bus. Then we saw the monkeys. Then we got ice cream. At the end I slept in the bus." Nani laughed. "What a story!" Usha looked at Bhupen, proud.

What did Usha say happened at the end of the zoo trip?
She said she slept in the bus at the end.
Why did Usha look at Bhupen proudly at the end?
She felt pleased with herself because she had told the story in order and Nani enjoyed it.
What small step helped Usha learn to tell events in order?
Bhupen asking "Which came first?" and inviting her to describe her day gave her practice putting events in sequence.
How might Nani feel hearing Usha's story?
She seemed delighted and entertained, laughing and calling it a great story.

Read this:

Anders came back from the toilet to find his rocket drawing torn in two. Emil stood beside it, chewing his sleeve. Heat rushed through Anders's whole body and he punched Emil's arm. Emil yelled and hit back, and both boys were crying when Mamma came in. "Hands are not for hitting. Tell Emil with words." Anders gulped. "You tore my rocket and I am so mad!" "I did not mean to," Emil sniffed. Mamma fetched the tape while both boys sat glaring, a bit red-eyed.

What did Anders find torn in two?
He found his rocket drawing torn in two.
What was Anders feeling when he punched Emil's arm?
He was furious. The anger rushed through his whole body and he lashed out before words came.
What worked better than hitting once Mamma came in?
Saying with words, "You tore my rocket and I am so mad," got a hearing, and Mamma fetched tape to fix it. Hitting only made Emil angry and he hit back.
How might Emil see the torn drawing and Anders's punch?
Emil says he did not mean to, so he may feel guilty and hurt at being hit. He hit back because he was scared and upset too.

They dispersed about the room, reminding me, by the lightness and buoyancy of their movements, of a flock of white plumy birds. Some of them threw themselves in half-reclining positions on the sofas and ottomans: some bent over the tables and examined the flowers and books: the rest gathered in a group round the fire: all talked in a low but clear tone which seemed habitual to them. I knew their names afterwards, and may as well mention them now.

Question: What do the people do after they scatter about the room?
Some half recline on sofas and ottomans, some bend over the tables to look at flowers and books, and the rest gather round the fire. All talk in a low but clear tone.

Read this:

Eshaan: Try something. Imagine it's five years from now. Which choice would you regret most?
Pema: Ok. If I turn down Gangtok I'd regret not trying. But honestly? What I'd regret most is us being bitter about it.
Eshaan: Same. If we move and you're miserable, I'd regret it. If we stay and I've turned you down, I'd regret that too.
Pema: So distance isn't the scary part.
Eshaan: No. It's resentment. Distance we can plan around.
Pema: Then let's plan. Maybe two years, then decide again?
Eshaan: Yes. Let's write what each of us needs from the two years 🙂
Pema: And what we won't put up with. Deal 🙂

What did Eshaan ask Pema to imagine?
Eshaan asked Pema to imagine being five years on and to say which choice would bring the most regret.
What does Pema dread more than distance, and what does that reveal about Pema's feelings?
Pema dreads bitterness and resentment more than distance, which shows Pema cares most about how the couple feels together.
What could Eshaan and Pema do with their two-year idea?
They could each write what they need from the two years and agree when and how to decide again, so the plan can be trusted.
How might Eshaan have felt hearing Pema's answer?
Eshaan probably felt relieved to hear the same fear, and reassured that they were on the same side.

messages.content:
Read this:

Thursday
I don't even know how to write this. Hafsa, my ex, sent screenshots of our private messages to her friends. The ones where I said I get nervous before exams and cried after Nana died. Now they're in a group of thirty people. Someone added laughing faces.
I wanted to disappear. I thought about not going back to school, ever.
But I remembered what the cyber-safety talk said: save everything first. So I took screenshots of the group, the names, the times.
Then I told Papa when he got home. He read everything, sat down next to me and said, "Chaitanya, this is not your fault. What she did is wrong, and serious." He wrote to the principal tonight. Tomorrow we're going to school together, and on Saturday we'll go to the police cyber cell to file a complaint.
I still feel sick. But I'm not holding it alone.

How many people were in the group with the screenshots?
Thirty people.
What was Chaitanya feeling after the messages were shared?
Chaitanya felt humiliated and sick, wanting to disappear and never go back to school.
Which steps did Chaitanya and Papa take, and why do they matter?
Saving evidence, telling Papa the same day, emailing the principal, and planning a cyber cell complaint mean adults can act and Chaitanya isn't alone.
How does Papa respond when he reads the messages?
Papa sits beside Chaitanya, says clearly it isn't Chaitanya's fault and that the sharing was wrong and serious, and acts that same night.

Read this:

Monday: In the team meeting at the clinic's admin office, Mridul sat silent while the manager asked for ideas about the waiting-room queue. Lakshmi remembered how he had proposed a token system twice last year, and both times been talked over.
Wednesday: Over lunch, Lakshmi asked him, "What would you change about the queue, if it was your call?" He shrugged. "Doesn't matter what I think." She waited. He mentioned the token idea again, quietly.
The next Monday: Lakshmi said in the meeting, "Mridul has a token plan. Could he run a one-week trial at the front desk?" The manager agreed. Mridul spent the afternoon drawing up the numbers, sleeves rolled up.

What system had Mridul proposed twice?
A token system.
What was Lakshmi thinking while Mridul sat silent?
She felt concerned, remembering he had been talked over twice and suspecting he had learned to give up.
What steps did Lakshmi take to restore Mridul's agency?
She asked for his view privately, waited, then proposed a real trial he could run.
How does Mridul seem to feel by the next Monday afternoon?
Mridul seems energised and engaged, rolling up his sleeves to work on the plan.
Make this apology sound sincere: Sorry about that.
I am really sorry about that.

Read this:

Saturday, 11:30 pm
Riya's birthday party. Someone brought a bottle and hid it in the terrace water tank room. Divyansh drank way too much. By nine he was slumped against the wall, eyes half closed, mumbling.
I looked around. Everyone was laughing, dancing, taking videos. Nobody looked scared. So I thought, okay, he's just being dramatic, it's fine. I even laughed.
At ten, Riya's mother came up, took one look and her face went white. She turned the music off, put him on his side, called his parents and a doctor friend. His father came in ten minutes.
I keep thinking: I saw him first. I looked at everyone's calm faces and decided nothing was wrong. Why did I trust their faces more than my own eyes?

Where was the bottle hidden?
It was hidden in the terrace water tank room.
How does the diary writer feel now about the party?
The writer feels guilty and shaken, realising that calm faces were trusted over what was clearly wrong.
What did Riya's mother do, and what could the writer do next time?
She stopped the music, put Divyansh on his side and called his parents and a doctor friend; next time the writer could fetch an adult straight away.
How might Divyansh's father have felt arriving at the party?
He was probably frightened and upset, rushing over after the call about his son.

Read this:

Hi Suraj,
I owe you an apology. During the group study on Thursday I saw you staring out of the window and giving one-word answers, and I told Manoj you were bored and didn't care about the project. I only had your face and your voice, and I filled in the rest myself. Then Kavya said you seemed lost, and I finally asked you outright. You said you hadn't understood the second section and felt awkward saying so. That was very different from what I'd guessed. I'm sorry for calling you bored behind your back. Can we go through the section on Saturday? I'll bring the notes.
Naveen

What did Naveen see Suraj doing during the group study?
Naveen saw Suraj staring out of the window and giving one-word answers.
What was Suraj actually feeling during the study session?
Suraj was confused about the second section and awkward about saying so, which was different from the boredom Naveen guessed.
What could Naveen do differently next time Naveen isn't sure about someone's attention?
Naveen could ask directly and kindly straight away, instead of guessing and telling others.
How might Naveen have felt on learning what Suraj was really feeling?
Naveen felt sorry for guessing and saying it behind Suraj's back, and wanted to make up for it by going through the section together on Saturday.

metadata.subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

In class eleven, Kamal had a Hindi essay due, and he did not write a line. Every evening he found a better task: sharpening pencils, rearranging shelves. Somewhere underneath he believed that if the essay came out weak, Vijay Sir would see that he was not as capable as everyone assumed. On the last night he scribbled a rushed page and handed in something much thinner than he could have written. Vijay Sir returned it with a single line of comment about effort.
At twenty, Kamal had a thesis chapter to begin and felt the same heavy dread. This time his friend Abhinav said, "Come to the library. Set a timer for twenty minutes. Write the ugliest paragraph you can." Kamal laughed, sat down and typed a messy opening that made no sense. The timer beeped. Abhinav peered at the page. "See? It's a start." Kamal hadn't planned to keep going, but he wrote another paragraph and then a third, and then the library lights blinked for closing.

How long was the timer that Abhinav told Kamal to set?
Abhinav told him to set a timer for twenty minutes.
How does Kamal's way of starting at twenty differ from his approach to the Hindi essay?

For the Hindi essay Kamal put it off every evening, afraid Vijay Sir would see he was not capable, and handed in something thin. At twenty he set a timer for twenty minutes in the library beside Abhinav and wrote the ugliest paragraph, and that messy start took away the dread so he kept writing.
What was Kamal feeling as he put off the Hindi essay?
He was afraid and anxious about being judged, and busy tasks helped him avoid that uncomfortable feeling.
What could Kamal try if the dread comes back before a big task?
He can set a short timer, work near a friend or in a library, and allow himself a messy first paragraph before he polishes anything.
Group email about a lost brown wallet near the park on Sunday morning, asking anyone who finds it to contact Dhruv. Subject, around 40 words, signed Dhruv.

Subject: Lost brown wallet near the park

Dear all,
I lost a brown wallet near the park on Sunday morning. If anyone finds it, please contact me. I would be very grateful for any help, and thank you for looking out for it.
Dhruv

Read this:

On his way back from the town college admission office, Lokesh stopped at the old primary school in Chandpur. Usha teacher was still there, grey now, marking copies under the neem tree.
She had been the strictest teacher in the village. She made him rewrite every sum until it was perfect. She'd once kept him back till dark over one wrong answer. He'd hated her for it.
Now he'd got into the science stream with the highest maths marks in the block.
"Teacher, I came to say thank you," he said, touching her feet. "You pushed me when I wanted to give up."
Usha teacher smiled, her eyes wet.
Walking home, Lokesh passed his little brother's school, where a teacher was shouting at a small boy and twisting his ear. Lokesh stopped. Usha teacher had been strict. She had never been cruel. That was different, and he'd make sure his brother knew it.

Where was Usha teacher marking copies?
Under the neem tree.
How did Lokesh feel about Usha teacher when he was younger?
He resented her strictness and felt angry, especially at being kept back till dark over one wrong answer.
What did Lokesh understand when he passed his brother's school?
That strictness and cruelty are different, so harshness is not good just because Usha teacher's strictness helped him.
How might Usha teacher feel when Lokesh thanks her?
She seems deeply moved and proud, her eyes wet, to see her strictness had helped him.

Read this:

Monday. The inter-school short film contest wanted a three-minute film by Saturday. Rashmi pictured it all: film on Thursday after school, edit on Friday night, submit Saturday morning. "Two evenings, easy," she told her friend Bhupen. She didn't think of the last time, when a two-minute class video had taken a week.
Thursday. Rain. The park where she wanted to film was flooded. Bhupen had tuition till six. When they finally shot indoors at seven, the phone memory filled up after four scenes. They deleted old photos and shot again. The light was bad.
Saturday. Rashmi edited from midnight to 4 a.m. The music didn't match the scenes. The export failed twice. She submitted at 11:52, eight minutes before the deadline, with a jump in the sound she had no time to fix.
On the form, it asked, "How long did this take?" She laughed tiredly and wrote, "Longer than I imagined."

By when did the contest want the film?
By Saturday.
How did Rashmi feel as she typed on the form?
Rashmi felt exhausted and a little rueful, laughing tiredly at how wrong the two-evening estimate had been.
What could Rashmi have done when she first estimated the time?
Rashmi could have remembered the class video that took a week and started filming earlier, with extra time for weather and technical problems.
How might Bhupen have seen Rashmi's "Two evenings, easy"?
Bhupen may have believed it at first, but by Thursday night Bhupen would have seen how much the plan ignored real problems.

Read this:

Sahil: Ravi was glaring at me all through PE
Sahil: then he stood in the corridor door and wouldn't let me pass. said "watch yourself after school"
Deepak: wait what. did he touch you?
Sahil: no. just blocked me and did that sneer thing. my legs are still shaky tbh
Deepak: ok. don't go back at him. not worth it
Sahil: part of me wants to. he's done this to 3 people
Deepak: that's exactly why. stay where people are. where are you now?
Sahil: canteen
Deepak: stay there, I'm coming. then we go to Mr Khan together before last bell
Sahil: ok
(40 minutes later)

messages.content: For a teen magazine, write under 90 words about how it's okay not to be good at everything.

Nobody is good at everything, and nobody needs to be. You might be brilliant at drawing but hopeless at maths, or great at football but terrible at singing. That is completely normal. Every person has a different set of strengths. Trying new things is wonderful, even if you are bad at them, because the fun is in the learning. So be patient with yourself. The old neem tree at the end of Station Road had given shade for sixty years. One Monday, a notice appeared on its trunk: it would be cut down to widen the road. messages.content: Does "settle in" mean to sit down?

Why does a cycle tyre become hard when we pump air into it?
Packed-in air pushes harder on the rubber. Because more and more air is squeezed into the same space, its push on the inside of the rubber grows and the tyre stiffens.

Sticky notes everywhere, eighty tabs open, phone buzzing through every meeting. I once forgot to book an ambulance transfer because a group chat about cake distracted me.
That scared me. So I changed four things. Everything goes into one list the second it comes in. Big jobs, like the new staff rota, get broken into steps so small they're almost silly. All app notifications are off, except the hospital pager. And I take a real break outside twice a day, even when I think I can't.

Which of Nazia's changes protects the important work best?
Turning off all notifications except the pager, because it stops small interruptions from stealing attention from patient transfers.
How might patients and families feel the difference in Nazia's work?
Their transfers now get her full attention, so things are less likely to slip, which means fewer delays and more trust.

So, you asked on the podcast about the best congratulations I ever gave. I'm Madhuri, and honestly I learnt it by getting it wrong first. When my flatmate Jahnavi got her job offer from the Chennai firm, I burst into her room with a party popper and a speaker blasting dance music. She smiled, but it was a thin smile. She said thanks and went back to her laptop. Later I saw her on the balcony, very quiet. The job meant leaving her mother alone in Nagpur, and she was proud and sad at the same time. There's a long line of ants going up our wall every morning. Where are they going?
They're probably following a scent trail to a food source. Worker ants leave a chemical track, and others follow it to bring food back to the nest.
How do they find it?
One ant finds the food, then returns to the nest leaving a trail. Others follow it, add to the trail and strengthen it. If there's no food left, the trail fades.

Yes. Wipe the area and store sweets in closed boxes, and the ants will move on.

Gautam sighed loudly. "It's obvious. The three means fifteen." Usha's lip wobbled. "You said it's three!"
He threw up his hands. "She's not even trying, Nani."
I asked him, "Do you remember not knowing this?" He said no.
What I did next: I gave them a paper plate and crayons. Gautam made a clock with Usha, one hand at a time, starting with just the hours. By the end she could say "three o'clock", and they were both grinning.

What did Gautam say the long hand shows?
Gautam said the long hand is minutes.
Why did Gautam get frustrated with Usha?
Gautam felt impatient and frustrated, because the clock seemed obvious to him and he couldn't remember not knowing it.
Why did the paper-plate clock work better?
Making the clock one hand at a time, starting with hours, gave Usha the small steps Gautam had skipped.
What was the lesson like for Usha?
Usha felt lost and close to tears, confused by 'quarter' and a three that meant fifteen, until the steps got smaller.

In the canteen, Ganga leaned over her tea. "Promise you won't tell anyone, but Naveen didn't clear the placement round." Vasudha's eyes widened, and Ganga felt the small glow of being the one who knew. By evening the glow had gone sour. Someone in the hostel corridor said, "Sorry about placements, Naveen." Ganga's stomach dropped when she saw his face.

Naveen had told only one person. His ears rang, he felt suddenly naked in the corridor, and for an hour he was so angry that he typed out a list of things Ganga had once said to him in private. His thumb hovered, then he deleted every line. He wrote, "Can we talk somewhere quiet?"

Ganga came before he could change his mind. She did not wait for him to speak. "I told Vasudha. I wanted to seem important, and that was wrong. I have no excuse. You can be angry." Naveen kept his arms folded. "I need some space, and I'll decide what's left between us." Ganga nodded and did not argue. The next week she noticed that she thought twice before repeating anything at all.

What did Ganga tell Vasudha in the canteen?
She told Vasudha that Naveen had not cleared the placement round.
How did Ganga's and Naveen's views of the same leak differ, and what did each do about it?

Ganga felt the glow of knowing then a sinking stomach, so she owned it and apologised with no excuse. Naveen felt exposed and furious, held back from leaking her secrets, and asked to talk privately, then asked for space.
What was Naveen feeling in the corridor when he heard the sorry about placements?
He felt exposed and furious, as though everyone had seen something private.
What could Ganga do in the weeks after Naveen asked for space?
She could give him the distance he asked for without pressing, and be more careful with what others tell her.

Vandana had been the top student in her village school, with Amma waking her at five and teachers checking every notebook. Now, three months into college in the district town, her hostel cupboard was a heap of loose pages. She had missed the exam form deadline by a day and paid the late fine from her food money. At night she lay awake, mind jumping from song to song.
Farhan, from her class, found her crying in the reading room. 'You're the sharpest one in our batch,' he said. 'What's going on?'
'I can't hold anything together without someone reminding me.'
He helped her buy a cheap wall planner and a file with coloured tabs. Then he said, 'The college has a visiting counsellor on Wednesdays. Might be worth asking about the sleep and focus. My cousin went. It helped.'
On Wednesday, Vandana went.

What did Vandana pay the late fine from?
Her food money.
What does Vandana mean by 'I can't hold anything together without someone reminding me'?
She means that without Amma and teachers structuring things, she feels lost and overwhelmed managing on her own.
What choices helped Vandana start to cope?
Using a wall planner and a tabbed file, and going to the visiting counsellor on Wednesday about sleep and focus.
How might Farhan feel when he sees Vandana go to the counsellor?
Farhan may feel glad the suggestion helped and relieved that his classmate is getting support.

In the university library in Accra, Kofi had noticed a pattern: he'd sit down after dinner, check messages 'quickly', and forty minutes later still be reading group chats.
So on Sunday he made a rule and told his friend Vera: 'When I sit down in the library after dinner, I open my first task before I look at anything else. Phone goes in the backpack, zipped.'
Vera raised an eyebrow. 'That's it?'
'That's it. Once the first task is open, I usually keep going.'
On Monday he sat down at 7:10, put the phone in the backpack, and opened his economics reading at the marked page. He read twelve pages before he even remembered the phone. On Wednesday he slipped and checked first; it cost him half an hour. On Thursday he was back to the rule.
By Friday Vera was sitting next to him, her phone zipped into her own bag.

How many pages did Kofi read on Monday before remembering the phone?
Twelve pages.
How might Kofi have felt after slipping on Wednesday?
He probably felt annoyed with himself about the lost half hour, but determined enough to return to the rule the next day.
What else could Kofi add to the rule for harder evenings?
Prepare the first task the night before, with the page marked, so opening it takes no thought.
How does Vera's view change over the week?
Vera is doubtful at first but by Friday is using the same rule beside him.

Read this:

Last month, my friends and I were at the mall when someone said, "Let's skip tuition and go bowling." Everyone was laughing, and before I even thought, I said, "Yes!"

At home that night, alone, I thought about it. My board exams are in three months. Tuition was the class I needed most. Why did I say yes so fast?

I think it's because when my friends are all around me and everyone's excited, my brain just goes quick. When I'm calm, I think things through.

The next day my cousin Rukmini said, "Try saying 'let me think' when you're with them." I tried it the next week. It worked.

I'm Rafiq. I still say yes sometimes. But now I notice.

What did Rafiq's friends suggest doing instead of tuition?
Going bowling.
Why did Rafiq say yes so quickly at the mall?
Rafiq felt excited with everyone laughing, so the group's energy pushed a snap choice before thinking.
What did Rukmini suggest, and why did it help?
Saying "let me think" when with the group, which gives time for careful reasoning to catch up.
How might Rukmini feel on hearing the suggestion worked?
Rukmini probably feels pleased and proud to have helped.

Wednesday. At break, I saw Jatin sitting alone under the neem tree with his lunchbox closed. Everyone else was playing. I walked over. “Can I sit with you?” He shrugged, but he made room. I didn't say much. I opened my lunch and offered him a piece of my paratha. After a while, he said, “I miss my old school.” I said, “That sounds hard.” Then a group of boys came by and said something mean about his accent. I stood up and said, “Leave him alone.” They walked away, and I told Mrs. Rao what happened. Jatin looked at me and said thanks. Amandeep.

Where was Jatin sitting alone?
Under the neem tree.
What was Jatin probably feeling when he sat with his lunchbox closed?
He was probably lonely and missing his old school, which he said aloud after Amandeep sat with him.
What did Amandeep do when the boys said something mean?
Amandeep said “Leave him alone” and then told Mrs. Rao, so an adult knew.
How might Amandeep have felt when the boys said something mean about Jatin's accent?
Amandeep was probably protective of Jatin, standing up to say, "Leave him alone," and then telling Mrs. Rao.

Abhinav: ya what's up

The third time this week.

Dear Amandeep,
Thanks for the tips after my first internship interview. I told you eye contact makes my skin prickle. Since Tuesday I've tried what you suggested: looking at the eyebrows or the bridge of the nose, then glancing away at the notepad while I think. It felt less like a staring match. The panel didn't seem to mind. The interviewer even said I was a very good listener. But on a date on Friday, my usual steady gaze made the other person go quiet, which was odd, because I thought they'd like it. I've decided to soften it there too, glancing away when I laugh. It's a bit of a puzzle, but I'm getting there.
Chandrika

What did Chandrika try looking at in the interview?
Chandrika tried looking at the eyebrows or the bridge of the nose.
What was Chandrika feeling about eye contact?
Chandrika finds it uncomfortable, since it makes the skin prickle, and wants to seem confident without it feeling like a staring match.

Chandrika decided to soften it by glancing away while laughing, because the usual steady gaze had made the other person go quiet.
How might the interviewer have seen Chandrika's glances away?
They may have seen a thoughtful, attentive listener, as they said Chandrika was a very good listener, and not someone avoiding them.

The market lane was empty by nine, and Anand and Anjali, married three years, were still in the tailoring shop, shutters half down, quarrelling about whether to take on the wedding order.
"Say something!" Anand said, louder. "You just stand there!"
Anjali stood with arms crossed, eyes on the floor. The louder Anand got, the smaller Anjali's answers became, until there were none. Anand hit the counter with a palm.
Then Anjali tapped the counter twice, the sign they had once joked about. "Pause," Anjali said, voice thin. "I am too full. Give me half an hour, then ask me everything."
Anand breathed out. "Half an hour. I will get tea."

What did Anand and Anjali quarrel about in the tailoring shop?
They quarrelled about whether to take on the wedding order.
What was Anand feeling as Anjali stood with arms crossed and said nothing?
Anand felt shut out and frustrated. The louder voice and the palm on the counter show that the silence was making Anand more upset.
What helped when Anjali tapped the counter twice and said "Pause"?
The tap and the word gave Anjali a way to ask for a break instead of going silent. Anand agreed to half an hour and went for tea, so the fight stopped rising.
What might Anjali have been going through as the answers became smaller?
Anjali was probably overwhelmed, with too much said too quickly to answer. The thin voice and the request for half an hour suggest Anjali needed time, not to punish Anand.

Akash,
You asked why I left the call centre. Honestly, I saw the writing on the wall. Our team went from forty to twelve in a year. The chatbot now answers most questions, and we only get the angry ones.
I'm twenty-five. I didn't want to wait to be let go. So I looked at what's growing where we live: rooftop solar. Every other building in our area is putting panels up, and the installers are always busy.
I did a government-certified course for solar technicians, three months, evenings and weekends. My hands were clumsy at first. I felt stupid next to eighteen-year-olds who'd done wiring since school. But I kept going, and now I'm apprenticed to an installer.
The pay is lower for now. Some days I miss the air conditioning. But I'm learning something no chatbot can do on a roof.
If you want, I'll send you the course details.
Kamal

How long was Kamal's solar technician course?
Three months, evenings and weekends.
How did Kamal feel next to the eighteen-year-olds in the course?
Kamal felt clumsy and stupid at first, but determined to keep going.
What made Kamal's career change deliberate?
Kamal noticed the trend early, chose a growing local field, took a certified course and started an apprenticeship.
How might Akash respond to Kamal's letter?
Akash might feel worried about Akash's own job and curious enough to ask for the course details.

Read this:

"Sit, Reena, and listen, because your notice reminds me of mine," said Joseph. "I was twenty-five, newly working, and a letter came about my filing. I was terrified. In the corridor outside the office, a man in a neat shirt said, 'Give me five thousand in cash, no receipt, and this file disappears.' I wanted to say yes so badly.

"But something felt wrong. Why no receipt? I asked, and he laughed and said receipts were for fools. So I walked away. My uncle sent me to a chartered accountant, who filed the reply on the official portal and handed me a proper receipt.

"That man would have owned me. Next year he would have come for more, and I would have had nothing to show I was honest. Keep every receipt, beta."

What did the man in the corridor ask Joseph to hand over?
The man asked for five thousand in cash, with no receipt.
What made Joseph hesitate even though Joseph badly wanted to say yes?
Something felt wrong to Joseph, especially that there would be no receipt, so Joseph asked about it and then walked away.
What should Reena do about the notice, based on Joseph's story?
Go to a certified professional, reply through the official portal, and ask for a receipt for everything.
How might the man in the corridor have seen the young Joseph?
The man probably saw a frightened newcomer who would keep paying to make the problem vanish, an easy person to hold power over.

Family counselling note, Thursday.
Usha came in about her son Pankaj, who joined a meditation "family" eight months ago. She described the changes: he no longer argues or questions anything; he calls his old friends "lower-energy people" and has stopped seeing them; most sentences now include the group's words, such as "surrender" and "the Source". He moved into the group's house in March.
In April his father gave him an ultimatum: "Them or us." Pankaj left the dinner table and did not call for six weeks. Usha said, "We pushed him right into their arms."
We talked about staying steady instead: short, warm messages without arguments, his favourite food on Sundays, no insults about the group, and a clear line that home is always open. Usha agreed to try, and to bring her husband next time.
Yesterday Usha sent Pankaj a photo of the mango tree in the yard. He replied with a heart.

What did Pankaj's father say in April?
He said, “Them or us.”
How does Usha feel about the ultimatum now?
Usha feels regretful and sad, believing the family pushed Pankaj right into the group's arms.
What plan did Usha agree to try?
Short, warm messages without arguments, his favourite food on Sundays, no insults about the group, a clear message that home is open, and bringing her husband next time.
How might Pankaj have experienced the ultimatum?
Pankaj probably felt attacked and forced to choose, which made the group seem like the only place that accepted him, so he stayed away six weeks.
