Himani: hey, can I ask how you ended up in urban planning? You never said
Shalini: long story lol
Himani: I've got time. Did you always want it?
Shalini: no, I studied accounts. Then I spent a year helping my aunt's cooperative map water pipes and got hooked
Himani: what was the first thing that hooked you?
Shalini: standing in a lane with an old man who showed me where the water used to flow before the road was built
Himani: that sounds like a real moment
Shalini: it was. most people ask about the salary 😅
Himani: I'm more curious what you'd tell the younger you
Shalini: to not be embarrassed about the detour. thanks for asking 🙂

What did Shalini study before urban planning?
Shalini studied accounts.
What was Himani feeling while asking these questions?
Himani was curious and warm, wanting to know about Shalini's path without judging it.
What kind of follow-up question worked best in this chat?
Open questions about a moment, like what first hooked Shalini, invited a story. Himani listened and did not offer advice or compare.
How might Shalini have felt about being asked instead of being asked about the salary?
Shalini probably felt seen and pleased, since most people ask about the salary and this question invited a real story about the detour. 🙂

Dear Diary, Thursday.
Weird thing today. Someone messaged me on the gaming app saying they'd give me free game coins if I sent them the OTP that just came to my phone. Then another message: "Quick, it expires in 2 min!" My thumb was literally on the screen. Then I remembered Jasleen didi's rule: "If someone is rushing you about money, stop." So I put the phone down. The OTP message said it was for a payment from our family account.
I showed Jasleen didi. She said I'd just saved Papa's money, and we told Papa together. He called the bank and blocked the number.
I feel a bit shaky still. But proud I stopped.
Jomon

How long did the message say the offer would last?
It expires in 2 min.
How does Jomon feel after stopping?
Jomon feels a bit shaky but proud of stopping.
What rule helped Jomon, and why does it work?
If someone is rushing you about money, stop; scams depend on urgency, so pausing breaks them.
How might Jasleen didi feel when Jomon shows the message?
Jasleen didi likely felt relieved and proud that the rule worked and Jomon didn't share the OTP.

Indu beta, you think I don't see you going quiet every time your husband sends money to his parents? I was the same. Let your Dilnaz phuphi tell you. At twenty-four I was earning more than your phupha. Every month he sent money home to his mother in Lucknow, and I said nothing. But I kept a list in my head. Every sari I didn't buy. Every trip we didn't take. Every time his mother phoned and didn't ask about me.

The list got long. I got cold. He didn't know why.

One night I said it aloud, gently: "I feel resentful when money goes to your mother without us deciding together. I don't want to feel that. Can we decide as a team?"

He was hurt at first. Then he said, "I didn't know it felt like that." We started deciding together, every month, over tea. The list in my head stopped growing.

Where did Dilnaz's husband send money every month?
He sent money home to his mother in Lucknow.
How did young Dilnaz feel while keeping a list in her head?
Young Dilnaz felt quietly resentful and grew cold, while her husband didn't know why.
What choice inside the story stopped the silent ledger from growing?
Dilnaz said her resentment aloud gently and asked to decide about the money together as a team.
How did Dilnaz's husband react when she spoke up?
He was hurt at first, then realised he hadn't known how she felt, and agreed to decide together.

Jin had been promoted to lead designer at the Cape Town studio in under two years. Zanele, the junior on her team, always said "Well done, you" with a smile that stopped before her eyes.
Jin chose not to take the bait. She walked Zanele through her client-presentation template and let her present the second half of the Harbour project pitch. When Zanele mixed up two sets of floor plans in front of the client, Jin quietly said, "Let me take this bit," and later fixed it without a word in the team chat.
But on Friday, Jin learned that the client's revised brief had sat in Zanele's inbox for three days, unforwarded, while Jin worked on the old version.
She asked for a quick walk outside. "I need client emails forwarded the same day. If it happens again, I'll have to bring our manager in. I'd rather not."
Zanele looked at the pavement. "Understood."

How long had the client's revised brief sat unforwarded?
Three days, in Zanele's inbox.
What does Zanele's smile that stops before her eyes suggest?
It suggests she feels envious and resentful of Jin's fast promotion, hiding it behind polite words.
What did Jin do after the unforwarded brief?
She spoke privately, set a clear same-day rule for client emails, and named the manager as the next step if it happened again.
How might Zanele have felt when Jin quietly fixed the floor-plan mix-up?
Zanele may have felt embarrassed yet relieved not to be humiliated in front of the client or the team.

The dairy cooperative in Anand was about to switch cattle-feed suppliers, and Disha, the young manager, was sure the new supplier was better. It was cheaper and the samples looked good. But before signing, during the Holi holidays when the office was half empty, she sat down and wrote a question in her notebook: what would change my mind? She wrote: if the milk yield drops in the trial, if the farmers complain, if the supplier missed deliveries elsewhere. Then she called Vishal, the oldest vet in the district, who she knew disliked new suppliers. "Tell me every reason this is a bad idea." He talked for twenty minutes. Two points stung. She didn't argue. She wrote them down. Then she asked the supplier for a two-month trial with ten farmers first. Vishal grunted. "Sensible."

Who did Disha call before signing?
Vishal, the oldest vet in the district.
How did Disha feel when two of Vishal's points stung?
She felt uncomfortable but stayed curious instead of defensive, writing them down rather than arguing.
Which of Disha's steps made her decision stronger?
Writing what would change her mind, asking a smart critic for the best case against, and running a trial before committing.
How does Vishal seem to see Disha's approach?
Vishal seems grudgingly impressed, calling the trial sensible even though he dislikes new suppliers.

Imran, you asked how to encourage the weaker ones in your class. Let me tell you about a girl called Pinki, from my first year teaching in Nagpur, when the children called me Usha teacher. She was nine and she hated long division. One day I watched her try it the book way and fail, then try splitting the number into hundreds and tens and fail, then try guessing and checking, and get it right. Before, I'd have said "good girl, clever girl". That day I said, "Pinki, you tried three ways and didn't give up. That's how you got it." She looked at me as if no one had ever said that to her. The next week she asked for the hard sums. Praise what they did, beta, not what they are.

What three ways did Pinki try for long division?
The book way, splitting the number into hundreds and tens, and guessing and checking.
Why did Pinki look at Usha teacher as if no one had ever said that?
She was surprised and moved to be praised for her persistence rather than her cleverness; it showed her that her effort mattered.
What choice does Usha urge Imran to make in class?
To praise what the children do, their methods and persistence, rather than what they are, so they reach for harder work.
How might Imran use this story with the weaker students?
Imran might watch for a child trying different approaches and name it aloud, helping that child see progress as something they can build.

"Can I have some crayons?" Yamini asked.

Sangeeta pulled the box close. "No. I won't share with you. You're not my friend."

Yamini, five, felt a sting in her chest. Her eyes went watery. "That makes me sad," she said quietly.

Then she walked over to the clay table.

The teacher had heard. She came over with a second box. "Yamini, asking was fine. Sangeeta, we take turns with class crayons. Five minutes each."

Where did Yamini go after Sangeeta refused?
Yamini walked over to the clay table.
What was Yamini feeling when her eyes went watery?
Yamini felt hurt and sad, stung by Sangeeta's words.
What did Yamini do that helped her?
She said how she felt in words and went to play somewhere else instead of fighting.
How does the teacher see Yamini's request?
The teacher sees it as fair to ask, and helps set turns, making clear Yamini wasn't wrong to want a share.

Hana was planning the team retreat for her design studio in Kyoto. Her first thought was a mountain hike and hot springs; she loved both, and surely everyone did. She almost booked it. Then she caught herself. Did she actually know? She sent a short, anonymous survey to all twelve people. Before looking at the answers, she wrote down her guess: ten would want the hike. Then she went further. She asked Ada, the newest member, from Lisbon, and the two oldest designers what they'd enjoy. The results surprised her. Only four wanted the hike. Three had knee problems. Most wanted a cooking class and a museum. Hana laughed at her own guess. "Ten!" she said to Ada. "I was so sure." Ada smiled. "Thanks for asking. I'd never have said anything."

How many people wanted the hike in the survey?
Only four wanted the hike.
What was Hana feeling when she saw the results?
She felt surprised and a little amused at herself, laughing at how sure she had been.
What did Hana do that others could copy?
She wrote down her guess, sent an anonymous survey, and asked people unlike herself before deciding, treating her surprise as a lesson.
How might Ada feel about being asked?
Ada seemed grateful and relieved, since she would never have spoken up on her own.

"Hafsa, you've been staring at that page for ten minutes."
"Noor apa, Mrs Kapoor gave me four out of ten on the essay. But she added up the rubric wrong. I told her, and she said, 'Object again and I'll make sure you fail the term.'"
"She said that? In those words?"
"Yes. Everyone heard."
"And what did you feel?"
"My hands went cold. I just said sorry. Now I feel like a coward."
"Being afraid to speak isn't weakness. Did you keep the paper?"
"Yes."
"Good. Write down the date and her words tonight. Then we tell Ammi. The school has a grievance process, and you use it."
Hafsa took a breath and slid the page into a folder.

What did Mrs Kapoor say she would do if Hafsa objected again?
She said she would make sure Hafsa fails the term.
What was Hafsa feeling after she said sorry to Mrs Kapoor, and what shows it?
Fear and some shame about giving in. Her hands went cold and she called herself a coward.
What steps does Noor suggest Hafsa take?
Keep the paper, write down the date and Mrs Kapoor's words tonight, tell Ammi, and use the school's grievance process.
How might Noor see Hafsa's silence in class?
As understandable, not cowardly. She tells Hafsa that being afraid to speak is not weakness, and helps her find a safe way to be heard.

First of the month. Indu received two hundred rupees and set three jars on the shelf. "One for a treat, one for the book I want, one for giving," she said. Eighty into the first, ninety into the second, thirty into the third.
Second Saturday. She took twenty from the treat jar for jalebis. Her cousin Vishal had lost his lunch money, so she dropped ten rupees from the giving jar into his hand.
Last day. The book jar held ninety, and the book cost more. Indu shrugged. Next month it would fit.

How many jars did Indu use?
Indu used three jars.
What was Indu feeling as she saw the book jar was still short?
Calm and patient, since she shrugged and knew it would fit the next month.
What could Indu do if she wants the book sooner, and why?
She could take a little more from the treat jar for a month or earn a few rupees with small jobs at home, so the book jar fills faster.
How might Vishal have felt when Indu gave him the ten rupees?
Grateful and relieved, since he had lost his lunch money.

"Imran, can I tell you something weird I noticed about myself?"

"Always, Binita."

"Every morning for three years, I open my email first thing. I spend the best two hours of my day replying to small stuff. Then I'm tired when the real work starts."

"So stop?"

"I kept saying I can't. Clients expect quick replies. What if I miss something important?"

"Have you tested that?"

"That's the thing. I asked myself: if I were starting this job today, would I choose email first? No. I'd do the hard thinking first."

"So what's stopping you?"

"Fear. And it's just what I've always done."

"Try it for a week?"

"I did. Last week. First ninety minutes, no email. Then replies."

"And?"

"Nobody complained. Not one client. And I finished the proposal that's been stuck for a month."

"So the feared disaster..."

"Never showed up. I'm keeping it."

What did Binita finish during the test week?
The proposal that's been stuck for a month.
Why had Binita kept opening email first for three years?
Binita felt afraid of missing something important and upsetting clients, and it was simply the habit Binita had always had.
How did Binita question the default, and what did the test show?
Binita asked what she'd choose if starting the job today, then tested ninety email-free minutes for a week; nobody complained.
How might Imran see Binita's experiment?
Imran seems encouraging and curious, and might be tempted to try a similar test with Imran's own habits.
Maine dost se kaha "I'll give you a missed call." Foreigner samajh nahi paya. Kya bolun?

A "missed call" is a call that rings and is not answered. In India people use it as a signal, but many foreigners do not know this habit. You can say: "I'll ring once and hang up, then you can call me back."

Pooja, sit. You look worried about that group chat. Let me tell you something from when I was your age.
We didn't have phones, but we had a notebook that went round the back benches. One day someone drew a cartoon of Sebastian, the new boy, with huge ears and a joke about his old shirts. Everyone added something. When it came to me, I felt a flash of fear. If I didn't write something, would I be next?
So I wrote a joke. Everybody laughed. I felt big for one minute.
That evening I saw Sebastian at the bus stop, alone, rubbing his eyes. I felt sick. That was the turning point.
The next morning I tore that page out and gave it to him, along with a note: "I'm sorry I wrote on this. It was cruel. Want to sit with me at lunch?"
He did. He became one of my best friends. Your Francis Uncle still remembers how easy it was to be cruel.

What did the back-bench notebook show about Sebastian?
A cartoon with huge ears and a joke about his old shirts.
Why did young Francis join in the mocking?
He felt a flash of fear that if he didn't write something, he would be the next target.
What was the turning point, and what did Francis do next?
Seeing Sebastian alone at the bus stop made Francis feel sick; the next morning he tore out the page, apologised and invited Sebastian to lunch.
How might Sebastian have felt seeing the notebook page?
Sebastian likely felt humiliated and alone, being new and mocked by the whole back bench.

Mehak was standing at the Dadar bus stop when the HR executive called. "Just letting you know, your joining location will be Chennai, not Mumbai." It was said so casually that Mehak almost said okay. Instead she asked, "Could you please send that to me in writing, with the reason and whether it's permanent?" That evening, over pav bhaji with her friend Ira, she opened the email. It confirmed Chennai, for at least the whole first year. "So?" Ira asked. Mehak took out her notebook. She had chosen this company over another Mumbai offer partly because of home: no rent, Aai's cooking, her little brother's exams. With Chennai, that part had changed. "I'm not going to ignore it," she said. "I'm not going to panic either. I'll compare again, honestly, with the new facts." She drew two columns and started.

Where was Mehak when HR called?
At the Dadar bus stop.
How did Mehak feel on reading the written confirmation?
Mehak was unsettled but calm, determined neither to ignore it nor to panic.
What else could Mehak do while comparing again?
Mehak could ask HR whether a move back to Mumbai is possible later, and check whether the other Mumbai offer is still open, before deciding.
How might Ira see Mehak's reaction?
Ira sees Mehak handle surprising news steadily, getting it in writing and planning to decide with the new facts.

Tuesday. Simran showed Maria the fake posts about her. Maria's first words were, "Don't reply. Let's save them." They screenshotted each one, with dates, into a folder.
Thursday. After school, with Maria beside her, Simran knocked on Mrs D'Souza's door. Her hands were shaking. Mrs D'Souza closed the door, listened without interrupting, and said, "Thank you for telling me. None of this is your fault." She called Simran's father before Simran reached home.
The following Monday. Simran was still in her usual seat, with her phone, and no one had asked her to stay home. The posts were gone. In the corridor she passed Maria and smiled, a real one this time.

Who did Simran knock on the door of on Thursday?
She knocked on Mrs D'Souza's door.
What does Simran's real smile on Monday suggest?
It suggests she feels safer and relieved, now that she was believed and the posts are gone.
What did the adults do right after Simran reported it?
Mrs D'Souza listened, said it was not her fault, called her father the same day and acted without taking away Simran's seat or phone.
How might Maria feel about the part Maria played?
Maria likely feels glad and proud that helping save the evidence and staying beside Simran made a real difference. 😊

At the school assembly hall, the principal asked the children to write about "the most exciting day of your life." Bhupen, eleven, wrote fast.

"It was the day my baby brother was born. I was in class, maths period, when Papa came to the door. I saw his big smile. Dhruv sir let me go early."

After school, he showed his teacher, Dhruv sir.

Dhruv sir smiled. "I remember that day too. But you were in PT on the field, not maths. I came to tell you your father was at the gate."

Bhupen frowned. He could see the maths classroom so clearly, the blackboard, the door. "Are you sure, sir?"

"Quite sure. But what matters is the smile, right?" Bhupen nodded, still puzzled.

Where was Bhupen really, according to Dhruv sir?
In PT on the field, not maths.
Why was Bhupen puzzled after Dhruv sir spoke?
He felt confused, because the memory of the maths classroom was so vivid that he was sure it was true.
What did Dhruv sir's last words help Bhupen understand?
That the important feeling of the day, the smile, is real even if some details are mixed up.
How might Dhruv sir feel reading Bhupen's story?
Dhruv sir probably felt warm and touched to remember the day with Bhupen.

At Teej the whole village hung swings from the neem trees, and Vasudha and Ishita had planned it for weeks: matching green bangles, one swing, taking turns, just the two of them. They had even linked little fingers and sworn to be best friends forever. But on the day, a new girl from the city, Rhea, arrived with shiny mehendi cones, and Ishita went straight to her. By afternoon the two were on the swing together, laughing, and when Vasudha came up, Ishita said, 'There's no room.' Vasudha stood there in her green bangles until her eyes stung, then walked home alone along the canal. She didn't touch her ghevar. When her mother asked, she only said, 'I'm never having a best friend again.'

What did Vasudha and Ishita wear to match?
Matching green bangles.
How did Vasudha feel standing by the swing?
Vasudha felt hurt and betrayed, her eyes stinging, after being told there was no room.
How could Vasudha's mother help her that evening?
She could listen to what happened and let Vasudha be sad, then gently say that one hurt doesn't mean every friendship ends this way.
What might Ishita be feeling on the swing with Rhea?
Ishita is probably excited by the new girl and her mehendi, perhaps not thinking about how Vasudha feels.

In their Noida flat, Divyansh had been going to four coaching classes since March. By August he had headaches most afternoons. He shouted at his sister Sangeeta for using his charger. He felt sick every evening before the maths batch.

"You should tell Mummy," Sangeeta said.

"And say what? That I'm weak?" He took his bag and went.

He kept going. The headaches became normal. He started lying awake. He told himself real students didn't complain.

Then, in the week of his mid-terms, he sat at his desk and felt nothing. Not tired, not stressed. Just empty. He opened his notes and stared at them for an hour. The next day, the same.

He wrote the chemistry paper without remembering half of it. When the results came, he didn't even feel surprised.

Sangeeta found him on the balcony that evening and sat beside him. "Come," she said softly. "Let's tell Mummy together, now." This time he went.

Since when had Divyansh been going to four coaching classes?
Since March.
How did Divyansh feel in the week of his mid-terms?
He felt empty and numb, unable to focus on his notes at all.
What could Divyansh do now to recover?
He could tell his parents and the school counsellor how he has been feeling, reduce the coaching load with them, and see a doctor about the headaches if they keep going.
How might Sangeeta have felt sitting beside him on the balcony?
Sangeeta was probably worried and sad for him, having warned him earlier, and this time she made sure he told their mother that evening.

When is the chemistry test?
The chemistry test is on Friday.
How does Avni feel about the goal of becoming a doctor?
Avni feels inspired and moved, but also restless, since “study everything” gives no clear place to start.
What step helped turn the dream into action?
Planning one hour of organic chemistry tonight for Friday's test, a near step that guides daily action.

Zubin is supportive but practical, gently pushing Avni to think about this week, not only the distant dream.

Day one, three weeks before boards: Rajni made a timetable with every subject crammed in, but on the first evening she spent forty minutes answering messages. She went to bed feeling sick and behind.

Day ten: Her friend Tejas showed her his trick: phone in the kitchen, twenty-five minutes of work, five minutes of walking around. Rajni tried it with chemistry. It was hard to sit still for the first two blocks, and she almost went for her phone. By the fourth, she had finished a whole chapter of questions.

The morning of the exam: Her hands were cold. She breathed slowly, read all the questions first, and started with the ones she knew. She finished with ten minutes to check.

Where did Tejas keep his phone while studying?
He kept his phone in the kitchen.
How did Rajni feel after the first evening of her timetable?
She felt sick and behind, since forty minutes of messages had eaten her study time and made her doubt her plan.
Which part of Rajni's exam morning approach worked, and why?
Reading all the questions first and starting with ones she knew calmed her nerves and saved time, so she had ten minutes left to check.
How might Tejas feel seeing Rajni use his trick?
He might feel glad and a bit proud that his simple method helped a friend, and it may make them study partners.

Hansa signed for a desk at the glass-walled co-working space in Bengaluru the same week she read that a rival startup had one. She hired a part-time designer, and put money into paid ads, because that was what the rival did. Kamal, the founder at the next desk, noticed her ad dashboard flickering. "Do you know how much they raised?" he asked. "About ten times what you have." Hansa shrugged. But in the second month she was checking her bank balance in the corridor by the coffee machine, where nobody could see her face. She could afford the designer for only another week. The rival kept going, because their cash could absorb it. Hansa's could not.

Which three things did Hansa copy from the rival?
A desk at the co-working space, a part-time designer and paid ads.
What was Hansa feeling in the second month, and how can you tell?
Hansa was anxious, shown by checking her balance in the corridor where nobody could see her face.
What could Hansa do instead of copying the rival?
Hansa could spend only on what brings the first customers and match her spending to her own cash.
How might Kamal have felt watching Hansa's spending?
Kamal was probably concerned, as the question about how much the rival raised suggests.

Dear Nirmala ma'am,
I wanted you to hear it from me first: we're shutting down the millet-snack venture at the end of this month. Two years ago you told me to sell a hundred packets before building anything bigger, and I'm glad I listened; it's why the loss is small. We did reach real customers, around four hundred regulars in Ludhiana and Chandigarh, and the money from my uncle's friend kept us going for eighteen months. But our cost per packet never came down enough, and the big stores wanted margins we couldn't give. I cried for two days, honestly. Then I wrote down everything I'd do differently: price for profit from the first batch, talk to store buyers before designing packaging. I'll repay our investor as much as I can and take a job for a while. I'm not done with building things.
Gratefully,
Gurpreet

How many regular customers did Gurpreet's venture reach?
Around four hundred regulars in Ludhiana and Chandigarh.
How did Gurpreet feel about shutting down, and what shows it?
Deeply sad, since Gurpreet cried for two days, but also determined, as the line 'I'm not done with building things' shows.
What lessons did Gurpreet take from the shutdown?
Price for profit from the first batch, and talk to store buyers early before spending on things like packaging.
How might Nirmala feel reading this letter?
Sad for Gurpreet but proud that Gurpreet tested small first, learned honestly and still wants to build.

The school bus was stuck in traffic for an hour, and everyone was hot and cranky. Shreya and Nikita were arguing about the window seat. Then Nikita snapped, "At least I don't still sleep with a teddy bear, Shreya!"
The whole bus laughed. Shreya went scarlet and turned to the window.
Nikita's stomach dropped. That was the secret Shreya had told her in Class 3.
When the bus finally reached school, Nikita caught up with her. "I'm really sorry. There's no excuse. I was angry, but that's my fault, not yours."
Shreya didn't look at her. "I need some time."
"Okay. I'll wait."

What secret did Nikita shout on the bus?
That Shreya still sleeps with a teddy bear.
How did Nikita feel after she let the secret out?
She felt awful and guilty, her stomach dropping.
What did Nikita do right in her apology?
She said sorry with no excuses, took responsibility and accepted that Shreya needed time.
How might Shreya feel after Nikita apologises?
Shreya is still hurt and embarrassed, needing time before trusting Nikita again.

Three sentences, no more: shorten this.

The lemon-and-spoon race at the Bhatpara fair was over in a minute. Sharmila's lemon rolled into the dust just before the line, and three girls ran past her. She stood still, then burst into loud, angry tears. Her aunt Minakshi pushed through the crowd and knelt beside her. She didn't say "don't cry." She held Sharmila's dusty hands and said, "You were so fast. That's why it hurts so much." Sharmila cried into her aunt's shoulder until her breathing slowed. They shared a paper cone of roasted chana. When the teacher called for the second heat, Sharmila looked up. "Can I go again?" Minakshi wiped her face with the end of her dupatta. "Hold the spoon a little lower this time." Sharmila ran. She finished fourth, grinning.

At the Bhatpara fair, Sharmila's lemon rolled into the dust just before the line and three girls ran past her, so she burst into loud, angry tears. Her aunt Minakshi knelt beside her, held her dusty hands and said she had been so fast, which was why it hurt so much, and Sharmila cried into her shoulder until her breathing slowed. After they shared a paper cone of roasted chana, Sharmila asked to go again in the second heat, and with Minakshi's advice to hold the spoon a little lower, she ran and finished fourth, grinning.

Sunday, late. I've been sick with fever all week, and today was the first day I went to school. Everything felt heavy, even my bag. I walked so slowly that Parveen had to wait at the gate twice. In the class my eyes kept closing and when Rohit asked me for my ruler, I snapped, "Get your own!" I felt bad right after. Amma says I need lots of sleep and no big homework for a few days. She made khichdi and let me lie on the sofa. I feel a little better now. If I'm still this tired next week, Amma says we'll ask the doctor. — Imran

Who waited at the gate twice for Imran?
Parveen waited at the gate twice.
Why did Imran snap at Rohit, and what does Imran say about feeling afterwards?
Imran was worn out after being ill, so snapped easily. Imran felt bad right after, which shows the snap was tiredness and not meanness.
What could Imran's family do to help Imran recover?
Give Imran rest and low demands, as Amma does, and check with the doctor if the tiredness goes on.
How might Parveen feel about waiting for Imran?
Parveen waited at the gate twice, so is probably patient and caring, and might also be worried about how slow and heavy Imran looks.

At the temple fair in their village near Hubli, Avni, five, stood with her walker and watched her cousins race round the banyan tree. 'Amma, why can't my legs run like theirs?' Bhavna knelt beside her. 'Your legs work differently, kanna. The muscles need help, so you have your walker, like I need my glasses.' Avni frowned at the running children. 'I want to run.' 'I know.' Bhavna squeezed her hand. 'But guess who climbed all the temple steps by herself this morning?' Avni's face lifted. 'Me!' 'You. Every single step.' Avni straightened up. 'Let's go tell Ajji.'

What did Avni use at the fair?
Her walker.
What was Avni feeling as she watched her cousins run?
She felt sad and left out, wishing she could run like them.
What made Bhavna's answer helpful?
It was honest and simple, compared the walker to glasses, and then reminded Avni of something she was proud of.
How might Ajji feel when Avni tells her about the steps?
Ajji is likely to feel proud and delighted with her granddaughter.
Mom is turning fifty and keeps saying she wants "no fuss." Should we still do something?

You can respect "no fuss" and still make the day feel special. A quiet breakfast she doesn't have to cook, a handwritten card from each family member, or her favourite meal for dinner are all low-key ways to celebrate.
Can we invite her sisters?

That might be lovely, but check what "no fuss" means to her first. You could ask her lightly if she'd like to see her sisters that week. If she seems happy, invite them for a small tea instead of a big party.

Sunday night
Neelam's pain flared this morning, the kind that keeps her in the dark with the curtains shut. The old me would have hovered at the door, asking if she was sure she needed nothing, or worse, whether it was really that bad. Today I knocked once. "What would help today?" "Quiet. And warm water." I brought it and left. At lunch she snapped when I clattered a pan, and I felt the old sting, as if she didn't want me around. I reminded myself: that's the pain talking, not her. In the evening she came out, pale, and said sorry. I said there was nothing to forgive. Then I went for my walk by the lake, because when I skip my own rest, I start keeping score. Came back calmer and made dal. She ate a little.
Bhupen

What did Neelam ask for?
Quiet, and warm water.
What did Bhupen feel when Neelam snapped over the pan?
Bhupen felt the old sting of rejection, as if not wanted around, before remembering it was the pain talking.
Why does Bhupen's evening walk matter?
It protects Bhupen's own rest, so caring does not turn into keeping score and resentment.
How might the day have felt for Neelam if Bhupen had hovered and questioned the pain?
She would have felt doubted and crowded on a painful day, instead of believed and given the quiet she asked for.

Dear Swati,
I saw what happened in the bus today, when those girls kept laughing at your shoes and calling you "chappal-queen." I was two seats behind. I didn't know what to say, so I didn't say anything to them. But I'm sorry I didn't come and sit with you. I should have.
Tomorrow I'll save you the seat next to me. We don't have to talk about it if you don't want to.
I also told Ma'am after school what I saw. She said she'd talk to the girls and call your mother this evening, so don't be surprised.
You're not alone.
Jasleen

What were the girls calling Swati?
They were calling Swati "chappal-queen."
How does Jasleen feel about not acting on the bus?
Jasleen feels sorry and a little guilty for not sitting with Swati at the time.
Which of Jasleen's steps show quiet solidarity?
Offering Swati a seat, not forcing any talk, and telling Ma'am the same day, without lecturing the girls.
How might Swati feel reading the letter?
Swati might feel comforted and less alone, knowing someone saw and cares.

"The Holy One said, 'Behold, O son of Pritha, my forms by hundreds and thousands, various, divine, diverse in hue and shape. Behold the Adityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Aswins, and the Maruts. Behold, O Bharata, innumerable marvels unseen before (by thee). Behold, O thou of curly hair, the entire universe of mobiles and immobiles, collected together in this body of mine, whatever else thou mayst wish to see. Thou art, however, not competent to behold me with this eye of thine. I give thee celestial sight. Behold my sovereign mystic nature.'"

Answer from the text. What does the Holy One give, and why?

The Holy One says the listener cannot see the divine forms with ordinary eyes, so the Holy One gives heavenly sight. The listener can then see the many forms, the gods and the whole universe gathered in the Holy One's body.

At the first harvest, Omkar Dada carried the first bundle of wheat to the edge of the field and placed it under the neem tree with a lamp. Ira watched, holding her mother's hand. “Why are you giving wheat to the tree, Dada?” He knelt. “It's our way of saying thank you, to the earth and the rain, before we eat.” Ira thought. “Like saying thank you for food?” “Exactly.” Ira picked up a single grain and put it next to the bundle. “My thank you.”

Where did Dada place the first bundle of wheat?
Under the neem tree, with a lamp.
What was Ira feeling when she added her own grain?
She felt proud and included, wanting to give her own thank you after understanding the ritual.
What did Dada do that helped the ritual mean more than imitation?
He explained simply that it was a way of saying thank you to the earth and rain, linking it to something Ira knew.
How might Dada feel when Ira adds her grain?
He likely feels moved and happy that she understood and joined in.

It was Diwali week, and the whole flat smelled of ghee sweets. Deepika and her brother Yash sat on the floor with the ludo board.
"I need a six," Deepika said. She cupped the dice, blew on it three times and squeezed her eyes shut. "Six, six, six."
It rolled a two.
"I didn't blow hard enough," she decided, and on her next turn she blew five times.
Six!
"See?" Deepika bounced on her knees. "I made it!"
Yash opened his mouth, then just smiled and moved his green token.

How many times did Deepika blow on the dice the first time?
Deepika blew on the dice three times.
Why did Deepika feel so happy when the six came?
Deepika felt proud and in charge, believing her five hard blows made the dice give a six.
How could Yash gently help Deepika another day?
Yash could play a round where nobody blows on the dice and count the sixes together, so Deepika sees sixes still come.
How does Yash see Deepika's dice ritual?
Yash seems to find it sweet and chooses not to argue, letting Deepika enjoy feeling in charge.

In the reception hall's office, the manager laid out the floor plan, the menu list and the deposit form. Kavitha's father asked, "Is this all right with you two?" Kavitha and Jeevan glanced at each other. "Do whatever you think, Uncle," Jeevan said. Kavitha nodded, to avoid any argument. Three weeks later they arrived for the tasting. The hall was vast and echoing, and the menu was almost all sweets and rich gravies. They had wanted a small garden lunch. The deposit was not refundable. "We can adjust the menu a little," the manager said kindly, "but the hall is fixed." Kavitha swallowed and looked at Jeevan. Neither spoke.

What did Jeevan say when asked if the plan was all right?
Jeevan said, "Do whatever you think, Uncle."
Why did Kavitha nod when Jeevan said that?
Kavitha wanted to avoid an argument, and now feels dismayed and stuck at the tasting.
What could Kavitha and Jeevan have done at the office, and why?
They could have said what they wanted, such as a small garden lunch, and asked to see options, because choices are easy to change before a deposit is paid.
How might Kavitha's father have felt on hearing the couple was unhappy?
Kavitha's father would probably feel surprised and sorry, having believed the couple was content when they said to do whatever the father thought.

Darshan, you'll laugh, but for my whole first semester I called Amma every single night. From the hostel corridor, in my nightie, crying like a six-year-old. Especially in exam week. I'd ask her to tell me what she cooked, what the neighbour's cat did, anything. Once I made her sing the Bengali lullaby she used to sing when I was small. Twenty minutes of that, and then I could study. My roommate thought I was homesick-mad. Maybe I was. But Amma never said "grow up". She'd just say, "Urmila, eat something, then call me back if you need to." In second semester I noticed I was calling every other day. Now it's Sundays, mostly to tell her about the lab. I still ask for the lullaby before finals, though. One verse.

What did Urmila once ask Amma to sing?
The Bengali lullaby she used to sing when Urmila was small.
Why did the nightly calls help Urmila during first-semester exams?
Far from home and stressed, she needed to feel looked after, and Amma's voice and small stories soothed her enough to study.
Which choice of Amma's helped Urmila grow steadier rather than more dependent?
Never saying 'grow up', just comforting her and adding 'eat something, then call me back', which met the need while pointing her gently back to her own day.
How might Urmila's roommate have seen the nightly calls?
The roommate thought Urmila was 'homesick-mad', perhaps without realising the calls were helping her cope.

Squeeze this excerpt into two sentences.

I arrived at Geneva. My father and Ernest yet lived, but the former sunk under the tidings that I bore. I see him now, excellent and venerable old man! His eyes wandered in vacancy, for they had lost their charm and their delight—his Elizabeth, his more than daughter, whom he doted on with all that affection which a man feels, who in the decline of life, having few affections, clings more earnestly to those that remain. Cursed, cursed be the fiend that brought misery on his grey hairs and doomed him to waste in wretchedness! He could not live under the horrors that were accumulated around him; the springs of existence suddenly gave way; he was unable to rise from his bed, and in a few days he died in my arms.

The narrator arrives at Geneva, where the father and Ernest are still alive, but the father sinks under the news. His eyes are blank because he has lost Elizabeth, whom he loved like a daughter, and within days he dies in the narrator's arms.

Madhuri, twenty, was helping the panchayat clerk list families for the new water-tank connections in her village near Nashik. The rule was clear: households nearest the dry end first.
That evening her aunt Chandrika came to the verandah. "Put our name up, beti. You're family. Who'll know?"
Madhuri's stomach tightened. She loved Chandrika Kaki. Kaki had fed her every summer as a child.
But she thought of old Sakharam Kaka at the dry end, carrying pots up the slope every morning at seventy.
"Kaki, I can't jump the list," she said slowly. "But your house is next in line after the dry end. I'll make sure the form is ready so there's no delay."
Chandrika's face went stiff. She left without tea.
Madhuri sat on the step a long time, feeling like she had done right and wrong at once.

Which households were to get connections first?
Households nearest the dry end.
What was Madhuri feeling as she sat on the step?
She felt torn and uneasy, sure she had been fair but sad at hurting her aunt.
How did Madhuri work through the conflict?
She refused to jump the list but helped her aunt's form be ready for her turn, holding fairness while still caring for family.
How might Chandrika Kaki see Madhuri's answer?
She seems hurt and offended, feeling family loyalty should come first.
