messages.content:
Read this:

Vandana, you asked how I got interested in politics. It wasn't the TV debates. They just made me angry.
At seventeen, our municipal councillor held an open meeting about the broken drains in our ward. My mother dragged me along. I'm Gautam, and I expected shouting.
Instead, I saw how things actually work. The councillor explained which money comes from the state and which from the city. An engineer showed the plan. Residents asked hard questions. The councillor promised a date, and wrote it on a board.
Three months later, the drains were done. I went back to the next meeting on my own.
Now I read two newspapers that disagree with each other every morning. I don't trust any single one.

What was the open meeting about?
The broken drains in their ward.
How did Gautam feel about TV debates?
Gautam felt angry and put off by them.
What did Gautam learn from the meeting, and how does it shape Gautam's news habits?
How local government actually works, which led Gautam to read two newspapers that disagree, instead of trusting one.
How might the councillor feel seeing Gautam return to the next meeting?
The councillor may feel encouraged that a young person is taking an interest.

Read this:

Rafiq: chai at 4? the stall downstairs has fresh samosas
Sarita: busy today, thanks
Rafiq: no worries 👍
(next day)
Rafiq: walking to the post office at lunch, want to come? 10 mins
Sarita: need to finish the report
Rafiq: cool
(Friday)
Rafiq: getting cutting chai, want one brought up?
Sarita: ...ok. ginger if they have
Rafiq: done
(Monday)
Sarita: is the 4 pm chai thing still on
Rafiq: always
Sarita: fair warning i'm not good at talking
Rafiq: that's fine. i'm good at eating samosas
(Monday, 4:20 pm)
Sarita: thanks for not asking a hundred questions
Rafiq: anytime. same time tomorrow?
Sarita: maybe. probably yes 🙂

What did Sarita ask for on Friday?
Ginger chai, if they had it.
How does Rafiq seem to feel when Sarita keeps saying no?
Rafiq seems patient and unbothered, replying 'no worries' and 'cool', and keeps offering without pressure.
Why did bringing chai up on Friday work when the other invites didn't?
It asked almost nothing of Sarita, no walking out and no talking, so saying yes felt safe.
What might Sarita feel by Monday?
Sarita feels a little safer and grateful, enough to ask about the chai first, though still nervous about talking.

- How can I stay focused while studying at home?
- What does incompetent mean?

1. Keep your phone in another room and study in short blocks with a break in between. A tidy desk also helps.
2. Incompetent is an adjective that means not having the skill to do a job well.

Read this:

Raghav had been chatting with Harish for three weeks on a gaming forum, mostly after eleven, when his parents were asleep. Tonight Harish wrote: don't tell anyone we talk, they wouldn't get it. Also, what area do you live in? Something twisted in Raghav's stomach. Then he thought, that's silly, he's just being friendly. Everybody has odd rules online. He typed his neighbourhood and the school bus stop. Exams were five days away, and the chat was the only thing that made him forget. The next night Harish asked for a photo of his house and told him to come alone to the park. Raghav shut the laptop, hands cold, and realised he had ignored his own alarm for three weeks. He went straight to his mother's room and showed her the screen. She held him, said he wasn't in trouble, and they blocked the account together.

What did Harish ask for the next night?
Harish asked for a photo of Raghav's house and told Raghav to come alone to the park.
What feeling did Raghav push aside?
Raghav pushed aside his unease, since something twisted in his stomach, but he called it silly.
What could Raghav have done when Harish asked for secrecy?
Raghav could have ended the chat and told a parent at once, since asking for secrecy is a warning sign.
How might Raghav's mother have felt?
Raghav's mother was probably frightened but protective, since she held him, said he wasn't in trouble and blocked the account with him.
The chairman spoke eloquently, says the newspaper. What kind of speaking is that?

Eloquently means in a clear, flowing and persuasive way. It is an adverb.
Example: The girl spoke eloquently about why the library should stay open.

Read this:

In the two-room flat in Seelampur, the TV, the pressure cooker and his little sisters' skipping song all ran at once. Sahil read the same line of his chemistry notes four times, then slammed the book and snapped at his youngest sister for touching his pen. She cried; his mother glared. That night his cousin Amandeep, who shared his mattress, said, 'Yaar, you're not angry at Pinky. You've got no corner.' Together they cleared the loft over the kitchen door, hung a bedsheet, and put a torch and a cushion up there. Sahil's mother agreed to keep the TV off from seven to eight. By Friday he had stopped snapping.

What did Sahil and Amandeep put in the loft?
A torch and a cushion, behind a hung bedsheet.
Why did Sahil snap at his youngest sister over a pen?
He felt frustrated and irritated after reading the same line four times in the noise; the anger came from having no quiet space, not from the pen.
Which change helped most, and why?
A small private corner and an agreed quiet hour gave Sahil room to think, so small things stopped setting him off.
How might Sahil's mother have seen his snapping before the loft was set up?
She may have seen only a rude son making his sister cry, not the constant noise wearing him down.

Read this:

On the balcony of their Lucknow flat, Hafsa had a bucket of water and a pile of paper boats. Dhruv from next door watched.
"This one is tall," Hafsa said, and dropped it in. It fell on its side.
"This one is long." It floated, then tipped.
"This one is fat at the bottom." It floated and stayed straight, even when Dhruv blew on it.
Hafsa pointed. "Fat one wins. Fat bottom doesn't fall."
Next day, when Dhruv asked her to make him a boat, she folded the wide one straight away, without trying the others.

What happened to the tall boat?
It fell on its side.
How did Hafsa feel when the fat boat stayed straight even when Dhruv blew on it?
She felt proud and sure of herself, pointing and declaring that the fat one wins.
What could Hafsa test next, now that she knows the wide base works?
She could try different papers with the wide fold, since changing one thing at a time will show what else keeps it steady.
How might Dhruv see Hafsa's boats the next day?
Dhruv may be impressed that she knows exactly which boat to fold, and happy to get one that floats straight.

metadata.subtype: Approach: tests several options and remembers which worked [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

At dusk, walking home from the fields, Vaibhav stopped dead by the old banyan tree. "Amma, there's a bhoot up there. I heard it whoosh."
Indu didn't laugh. She crouched beside him. "You heard a whoosh? That sounds scary. Shall we be detectives and look?"
They stood still. Whoosh. A dark shape swooped out of the branches.
"That's a bat," Indu said. "Bats wake up in the evening to catch insects. They're shy. They won't come to us."
Vaibhav held her hand tighter. "Detective bat-watchers?"
"Detective bat-watchers," she agreed. He counted three more bats all the way home.

What swooped out of the banyan tree?
A dark shape, which Indu said was a bat.
Why did Vaibhav stop dead by the tree?
He heard a whoosh and imagined a bhoot, so he felt scared.
Which of Indu's choices helped Vaibhav most?
She took his fear seriously, made it a detective game, and gave a simple true explanation about bats instead of laughing or adding scary stories.
What would change if Indu had said, 'Yes, bhoots live there, so hurry home'?
Vaibhav would likely become more frightened of the tree and the dark, perhaps for a long time.

Read this:

Oskar was halfway through a friend's holiday photos when he caught himself sighing at his own Berlin flat: the one radiator, the crooked shelf, the view of the tram depot. Beach in Portugal. Rooftop dinner. New car. His thumb kept moving. He put the phone face down on the table. Elif, his flatmate, looked up from her laptop. 'You've got the face again.' 'Yeah.' He tried something his old football coach used to say: compare yourself with who you were. Two years ago he had been sleeping on his brother's sofa in Hamburg, with no contract. Now he had a job he liked and a room with a door. 'Honestly,' he said, 'this flat is fine. It's not a beach. It isn't meant to be.' Elif grinned and pushed the biscuit tin towards him.

Where had Oskar been sleeping two years earlier?
On his brother's sofa in Hamburg.
What was Oskar feeling while scrolling the holiday photos?
Oskar felt dissatisfied and a bit envious, sighing at his flat's single radiator and crooked shelf.
What small step broke the spell of the photos for Oskar?
Putting the phone face down and comparing his life with his own past, not with friends' best moments.
How does Elif see Oskar's change of mood?
Elif spots 'the face again' and is glad to see him settle; pushing the biscuit tin over shows warmth and relief.

Read this:

At the school sports day in Mysuru, Leela, ten, finished her ice candy and tossed the stick onto the grass near the track. Half the parents in the stands had done the same.
Hemant Sir, the PE teacher, was walking past. He bent down, picked up her stick, then two plastic cups nearby, and slipped them into his tracksuit pocket.
Leela watched, cheeks hot. "Sir, I'll take it."
He smiled. "Thank you, Leela. The ground's our classroom too."
He didn't say more. But after the relay, Leela saw him still carrying a pocketful of wrappers to the bin.
At the prize-giving, she noticed her own mother drop a juice box. Leela picked it up and held it out. "Amma, pocket."
Her mother laughed, embarrassed, and took it.

Where did Hemant Sir put the trash?
He slipped it into his tracksuit pocket.
What was Leela feeling when her cheeks went hot?
Leela felt embarrassed and a little ashamed, realising she had littered like the grown-ups.
Why did Hemant Sir's action work better than a lecture?
He quietly showed what to do by pocketing the trash, so Leela learned by copying him.
How might Leela's mother feel when Leela hands her the juice box?
Her mother seems embarrassed but amused, surprised to be corrected by her daughter.

Read this:

At the municipal pool in Valencia, Yosef watched Santiago and two others dare each other at the edge. "Bet you won't jump in the deep end," Santiago said. The coach had gone inside for a whistle. Yosef, who could only manage the shallow lanes, took a breath and jumped. The cold closed over his head. He kicked, swallowed a mouthful of water and could not find the bottom. Santiago shouted for help. The lifeguard dived in and hauled him to the wall while he coughed. Later, wrapped in a towel, Yosef listened as the coach spoke to the whole group. His legs still shook. He had wanted to look brave; now he only wanted to learn properly.

Where did Yosef jump?
He jumped into the deep end of the pool.
What was Yosef feeling as he sat wrapped in the towel?
Shaky and scared, and a little ashamed, since he wanted to look brave but now only wants to learn properly.
What could Yosef have done when Santiago dared him?
He could have said no and asked the coach for a lesson, because being brave can mean choosing to learn safely.
How might the lifeguard see what happened?
The lifeguard sees a child in trouble in water too deep for his skill and acts at once, so the focus is on getting him out safely.

metadata.subtype: Approach: jumping into the deep end to prove he is brave [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

My name is Madhuri, and I'm the one in our family who notices things. Jagdish Chacha visits us every Diwali but never stays the night. When he comes, Dadi gets up and goes to her room. Papa talks to him in a too-cheerful voice, and the photo album with the old Kanpur house is always put away before he arrives. This year he held my little brother on his lap, and his hands shook a bit. When I asked Mummy why Dadi leaves, she said, 'Grown-up matters.' Since then I've invented a dozen stories: prison, a fight about land, something worse. I watch Chacha's face at dinner, and I can't tell if he is sad, or ashamed, or just tired.

What happens to the photo album before Jagdish Chacha arrives?
The album with the old Kanpur house is always put away.
What is Madhuri feeling after Mummy says 'Grown-up matters'?
Madhuri feels anxious and restless with curiosity, inventing a dozen stories, some of them frightening, like prison.
What small step could Madhuri's parents take?
Share a simple, honest version of the story, so Madhuri isn't left imagining something worse than the truth.
What might it be like for Jagdish Chacha during these visits?
He may feel unwelcome and uneasy, with Dadi leaving the room and Papa's voice too cheerful; his shaking hands hint that he feels it.

Read this:

By Wednesday of release week, Joseph noticed the pattern. He had snapped at the tester on Monday; by Tuesday the whole team was snapping at each other, and Aditi, usually the first to flag a bug, had gone silent in the standups, her camera off. That evening he scrolled back through the team chat and saw his own message: 'Why is this STILL broken?' He winced. On Thursday, before walking into the glass meeting room on the fourth floor of the Koramangala office, he stood by the water cooler and took three slow breaths. 'Okay,' he began, keeping his voice low. 'This release is tight, and I've been short with all of you. That's on me, not you. Let's just list what's stuck.' There was a pause. Then Aditi spoke. 'The payment screen crashes on older phones. I found it on Monday. I didn't want to be the one to say it.'

What message of his own did Joseph find in the team chat?
He found 'Why is this STILL broken?'
Why did Joseph wince when he read his own message?
He felt ashamed and uneasy, seeing that his irritation had spread through the team and made people like Aditi stop speaking up.
Which of Joseph's steps settled the room, and why?
Taking slow breaths, speaking low and naming both the pressure and his own shortness; owning the tension made it feel safe for others to talk 👍
What was it like for Aditi during the snappish days?
Aditi felt it wasn't safe to bring bad news, so she sat on a crash she had found on Monday until Joseph's calm made speaking up possible.

metadata.subtype: Setting the tone of a team [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Vikas here, from the room opposite Sunaina's in our PG in Gurugram. In first semester her light was on till three most nights, and I'd see her at noon in the corridor eating instant noodles straight from the packet. She missed a lot of morning lectures. I don't know exactly what changed; maybe the week she was sick, maybe just exams. Around January she started going to bed at roughly the same time, and I'd hear her alarm at seven every day, even Sundays. On Sunday afternoons she began cooking a big pot of dal and rice in the shared kitchen and packing it into boxes for the week. Now and then she knocks to ask if I want to walk to the park. Honestly, she looks less grey. I've started copying the dal plan.

What does Sunaina cook on Sunday afternoons?
A big pot of dal and rice, packed into boxes for the week.
Why is Vikas unsure what made Sunaina change?
He only sees her from outside, her light, her alarm and her cooking, so he can guess at her reasons but cannot know them.
What makes Sunaina's new routine likely to last?
It is simple and regular: a steady bedtime, the same alarm every day and one weekly cooking session instead of daily effort.
How has Sunaina's change affected Vikas?
He notices she looks less grey, enjoys the walks to the park, and has started copying her dal plan himself.

Read this:

Akash, you think you can study with that chat pinging? Let your Harish chacha tell you about the nineties. At sixteen, I had a small radio on my desk and a friend, Mukesh, next door. Every time a wicket fell in the commentary, Mukesh shouted the score over the wall and I shouted back. I thought I was studying chemistry the whole evening. I'd look up and an hour had gone, and I had read four pages and couldn't tell you one equation. My elder sister watched me once and said, "You're not studying and listening. You're doing a little of one, then a little of the other, and losing time in between." One night, before the half-yearly, she took the radio away for two hours. I finished a whole chapter. I was furious, and then grateful.

What did Mukesh shout over the wall?
The score, every time a wicket fell.
How did young Harish feel when his sister took the radio away, and afterwards?
He felt furious at first, then grateful when he finished a whole chapter.
What was the turning point in Chacha's story?
His sister taking the radio away for two hours before the half-yearly, which let him finish a chapter and see how much the switching had cost.
How did Harish's sister see his studying?
She saw that he was doing a little of each and losing time in between, not studying and listening at once.

Read this:

Every morning Charu took the 8:12 bus from Marathahalli, sat in the same seat and plugged in the same earphones. At the office she fixed the same kind of bugs, drank the same vending-machine coffee and ate lunch at her desk. She wasn't sad, exactly. Everything was just grey, like a photo left in the sun.
Evenings blurred: order food, scroll, one more episode, another, sleep at one. Her colleague Ramesh mentioned he'd started evening pottery. "You should come, Charu."
"Maybe," she said, already opening her phone. That night she watched four episodes of a show she didn't even like. When the screen asked, "Are you still watching?", she clicked yes.

What time is Charu's bus?
The 8:12 bus from Marathahalli.
How does Charu feel about her days?
She feels grey and tired of the sameness, not exactly sad but dulled.
What small change could Charu try?
Say yes to Ramesh's pottery class, or change one part of the routine instead of adding screen time.
How might Ramesh feel when Charu says "Maybe"?
Ramesh might feel a little disappointed but hopeful she will come someday.

Read this:

Dear Simran,
You asked how the product launch went. Short answer: I still don't know what all the applause meant.
When I finished the demo, the front rows clapped loudly and fast; a few even stood. That felt like real approval. At the back, the sales team clapped politely, three or four claps, eyes on their phones. Courtesy, I think.
And then, when everyone else stopped, one man near the door kept going. Slow. Clap... clap... clap. People turned. Was he mocking me? The pricing slide had gone badly.
Afterwards I found him at the tea counter. He was a senior engineer from the Chennai office. He laughed and said he claps slowly when he's thinking, and my pricing slide had given him an idea. I'd spent twenty minutes feeling mocked.
Same sound, three meanings. I'm learning to look at the room, not just listen.
Shankar

Where did Shankar find the man who kept clapping?
At the tea counter.
How did Shankar feel when the slow clapping continued?
Shankar felt anxious and humiliated, fearing the man was mocking the launch after the pricing slide went badly.
What did Shankar do to find out what the slow clap meant?
He found the man at the tea counter and talked to him instead of just assuming mockery. 🙂
What did the slow clap mean to the senior engineer?
For the engineer it was a thinking habit; he was forming an idea from the pricing slide, not mocking.

Read this:

Lavanya: Are you up?
Sarika: Always. What's happening?
Lavanya: It's festival week and my mother's house smells like lamp oil and jasmine. I stood in the doorway and almost cried.
Lavanya: I stopped believing the way I did a few years ago. But I miss the singing. The aunties. Sitting in a row with everyone.
Sarika: That makes sense. That was a whole world.
Lavanya: It feels silly to grieve something I walked away from.
Sarika: It's not silly. You lost something, even if you chose it.
Lavanya: I don't want to pretend it didn't matter. Or pretend I still believe.
Sarika: You don't have to do either. Come Saturday? We're serving lunch at the shelter. There's a lot of singing in that kitchen.
Lavanya: Yes. I'd like that.
Sarika: I'll save you a spot at the chopping board.

What does Lavanya's mother's house smell of during festival week?
It smells of lamp oil and jasmine.
Why does Lavanya feel it is silly to grieve?
Lavanya walked away from the belief, so missing it feels wrong, even though the loss feels real.
What new source of meaning could Lavanya try?
Serving lunch at the shelter with Sarika, where there is singing, or other service, art, reflection or time with friends.
How does Sarika see Lavanya's grief?
As real: Sarika says it isn't silly and that Lavanya lost something even if Lavanya chose it.

Read this:

Every afternoon after lunch, the flat in Pune went quiet for a while. Five-year-old Eshaan used to hate it. 'Boring!' he'd moan, rolling on the rug. His father Tenzin didn't argue. He simply lay on the sofa with his own book while soft flute music played. One day Eshaan dragged his crayons over and drew a whole train, carriage by carriage. When the music ended he looked up, surprised. 'Papa, can quiet time be longer tomorrow?'

What did Eshaan draw during quiet time?
A whole train, carriage by carriage.
How did Eshaan feel about quiet time at first?
He felt bored and fed up, moaning 'Boring!' and rolling on the rug.
Why did Tenzin's approach work better than arguing?
By resting with his own book and music, Tenzin showed quiet time was worth having, so Eshaan found his own calm activity.
How might Tenzin see quiet time?
Tenzin seems to see it as real rest, not laziness, which is why he joins in himself.
He gave a good speach at the farewell party. Check the spelling.

He gave a good speech at the farewell party.
Why: The noun is spelled "speech", with "ee".

Read this:

Playgroup note, Thursday. Tarun screamed twice this morning, and they were very different. On the swing, he screamed at the top of the arc, face bright and eyes shining, and asked for "more!" Later, in the sandpit, his shoe came off, and he screamed again with a red, scrunched face, stamping his foot. I pushed the swing higher the first time and helped with the shoe the second. Dhruv, playgroup teacher

What came off in the sandpit?
Tarun's shoe.
How did Dhruv tell what each of Tarun's screams meant?
By reading his face and the setting: a bright face on the swing meant joy and excitement, while a red, scrunched face and stamping in the sandpit meant frustration.
What would you advise a new helper about Tarun's screams?
Look at his face and at what just happened before reacting, since the same scream can mean joy or frustration.
How might Tarun's parents feel reading this note?
They would likely feel reassured that Dhruv understands Tarun's loud sounds and responds to each one properly.

metadata.subtype: Screaming and shrieking in play or upset [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the small town of Kurukshetra, Mehak had noticed things about her brother Ujjwal for weeks. Money missing from the kitchen tin. His moods swinging from cheerful to snappish. The smell on his jacket that he blamed on "the dhaba". Excuses that didn't quite match.
Her first instinct was to shout, or to tell their father everything at dinner. Instead she waited until he was alone on the roof.
"Ujjwal, I've seen three things. Money gone from the tin. You came home at two on Tuesday. And you've stopped going to cricket. I'm not angry. I'm worried about you."
Ujjwal looked at the fields for a long time. "It's not that bad," he said. But he didn't walk away.

Where did Mehak talk to Ujjwal?
On the roof, when he was alone.
What was Mehak feeling when she chose to wait instead of shouting?
Mehak felt worried and angry at first, but chose calm because she cared more about being heard.
Which part of Mehak's approach made it easier for Ujjwal to listen?
She named three specific things calmly and said she was worried, not angry, without accusing or lecturing.
What is it like for Ujjwal when he doesn't walk away?
He seems defensive, minimising it, but perhaps relieved that his sister noticed without attacking him.
"Ye kitaab kal tak lauta dena." Translate karo.
It is: "Please return this book by tomorrow."
"By tomorrow" aur "till tomorrow" mein kya farak hai?
"By tomorrow" means no later than tomorrow. "Till tomorrow" means up to tomorrow and then stop, so it fits an activity that goes on, like "I will stay here till tomorrow."

Read this:

The rain was so loud on the tin roof that Avni Ma'am had to raise her voice. Bhupen, five, kept trying to write his name. The B kept tipping over.

Avni Ma'am knelt beside him. "You've written it four times. Well done, you kept trying!" She drew a star on his hand.

Bhupen felt tall and happy. He wrote it once more, slowly. The B stood up straight.

What did Avni Ma'am draw on Bhupen's hand?
Avni Ma'am drew a star on his hand.
What was Bhupen feeling when he got the star?
Bhupen felt proud and happy.
Why was Avni Ma'am's praise helpful?
She praised his effort in trying again, which made him keep trying instead of fearing mistakes.
How might Avni Ma'am feel when the B stands up straight?
She likely feels glad that her praise encouraged him.
Pin a reminder on the fridge for my brother Sahil: take out the rubbish before he leaves and lock the door. About 30 words, from Maya.

Sahil,
Please take out the rubbish before you leave today. Don't forget to lock the door behind you. Thank you for remembering.
Maya

Read this:

Week one: Noor wanted the big paintbox at the stationery shop, the one with twenty-four colours. She had eleven rupees. Her brother Pranav spent his coins on toffees every day and waved the wrappers at her. She nearly gave in on Friday. Instead she dropped her coins into an old tea tin and wrote the price on the lid.
Week three: The tin rattled heavier. At Pranav's birthday party she took one sweet instead of five, and didn't complain when her turn at the carrom board came last.
Week five: Noor tipped out the tin and counted twice. Enough. She carried the paintbox home against her chest like a trophy. 'I waited for this,' she told Pranav. 'All by myself.'

Where did Noor keep her coins?
In an old tea tin, with the price written on the lid.
How did Noor feel carrying the paintbox home, and what shows it?
She felt proud; she held it against her chest like a trophy and said she had waited all by herself.
What choice in week one set up Noor's success?
Instead of giving in on Friday, she put her coins in the tea tin and wrote the price on the lid, making her goal visible.
How might Pranav see Noor's paintbox after watching her save?
Pranav might be impressed, or a little envious, seeing that her waiting brought something bigger than his daily toffees.

Hafsa, fifteen, sat in her room in Hyderabad, scrolling through the class group. Nobody had replied to her message about the project. She read it as: nobody cares.

She'd been feeling this way for a while. She kept remembering the bad times: the dance performance where she tripped, the friend who stopped calling. It felt like facts, not feelings.

Her uncle Zubin, visiting for the week, knocked on her door. "You've been quiet for days. Can I sit?"

Hafsa shrugged. He sat and waited. Slowly she told him.

"That sounds really heavy," he said. "Feeling low for this long isn't something you should carry alone. Let's tell your mum tonight, and find someone good you can talk to." Hafsa nodded, eyes wet.

Who knocked on Hafsa's door?
Her uncle Zubin, visiting for the week.
Why did Hafsa read the silence in the class group as "nobody cares"?
Her long low mood made neutral silence feel like rejection and pulled up memories of failures, which felt like facts.
What did Zubin do that was helpful?
He sat and listened, took her feelings seriously, and planned to tell her mum that night and find a professional to talk to.
How might Hafsa's classmates see the unanswered message?
They may not have noticed it or were busy, not meaning any rejection at all.

On the third day of his internship, just before the big client presentation, Kiran felt his heart pounding so hard he could hear it. His jaw was clamped shut, his neck was rigid and his stomach was in knots.
"You okay?" asked Eshaan from the next desk. "You're grinding your teeth."
"I think I'm having a heart problem," Kiran whispered.
Eshaan didn't laugh. He walked Kiran to the office nurse on the ground floor. The nurse checked his pulse, asked some questions and said, "This looks like stress. Your body is reacting to pressure, and that's real. But please book a proper check-up with your doctor to rule out anything else."
Kiran sat for a while, breathing slowly. Knowing what it probably was made his heart settle a little. He booked the check-up that evening, and got through the presentation with shaky hands but a clear voice.

What did Eshaan notice Kiran doing?
He noticed Kiran grinding his teeth.
What was Kiran afraid of before the presentation?
He was afraid he was having a heart problem.
What did Kiran do that helped both his fear and his health?
He accepted help to see the nurse, learned it was probably stress, and still booked a proper check-up to rule out other causes.
How might Eshaan have felt when Kiran whispered about a heart problem?
Eshaan was probably concerned and took it seriously, which is why he walked Kiran to the nurse instead of laughing.

In their Nairobi flat, Wanjiru, who was five, finished her sweet and held out her hand for another. "No more today," Mama said, putting the tin on the high shelf. Wanjiru's face went hot. Her friend Selin, visiting, still had half of hers. "It's not fair!" Wanjiru stamped both feet so hard the cups rattled. "I hate you!" she shouted, then burst into tears and stamped again.

Where did Mama put the tin?
On the high shelf.
What was Wanjiru feeling when she shouted 'I hate you'?
She felt angry and that it was unfair, especially with Selin still eating, and her body reacted before her words could.
What could Mama say next that keeps the limit?
Something calm like, 'You're really angry. The answer is still no more today,' without shouting back or giving in.
How might Selin feel watching this?
Selin may feel awkward or a little scared, holding her half-eaten sweet while Wanjiru stamps and cries.

Gurleen, before you walk into that salary talk, let your Rukmini Aunty tell you how I nearly lost my best job. I was twenty-six, a pharmacist moving to a hospital chain in Pune. Someone had told me, "Always ask for more." So when they made the offer, I said, "Double it or I'm not coming." No reasons, no numbers. The HR head, a calm woman called Mrs Deshpande, went silent, then said, "Then perhaps we're not the right place." My stomach fell through the floor. I cried that night and called her back the next day. I apologised, and this time I came with reasons: my years at the old hospital, my night-shift experience, what others in the role earned. I asked for something specific and asked what flexibility she had. We met in the middle. We worked together fifteen years. So ask, Gurleen. But ask with reasons, and leave the door open.

What did young Rukmini first demand?
Double it or I'm not coming.
What was Rukmini feeling when Mrs Deshpande said they might not be the right place?
Rukmini felt shocked and afraid, stomach falling, realising the ultimatum might cost the job.
What was the turning point, and why did it repair things?
Calling back to apologise and returning with reasons and a specific ask, which showed respect and gave Mrs Deshpande something to work with.
How might Mrs Deshpande have felt during the two calls?
She was probably put off by the ultimatum, then pleasantly surprised by the apology and reasons, enough to meet in the middle.

Chetan: not coming to the pool party
Ira: why?? you love swimming
Chetan: I can't take my shirt off. I look like a stick next to those gym guys online
Ira: those pics are edited and posed. you know that
Chetan: yeah but I still compare. I check the mirror like 20 times a day. every time I feel worse
Ira: that sounds exhausting
Chetan: it's all I think about now honestly. even in class
Ira: then maybe it's time to talk to someone. the counsellor at school is actually nice
Chetan: feels embarrassing
Ira: lots of people feel bad about their bodies. getting help isn't embarrassing
Chetan: ok. maybe I'll go monday

What event is Chetan skipping?
Chetan is skipping the pool party.
How does Chetan feel when comparing to the images online?
Chetan feels inadequate and worse each time, so much that it fills the whole day.
Why does Ira suggest the counsellor?
Because Chetan's body thoughts have taken over the day, even in class, which is a sign to get help.
How might Ira feel reading that Chetan checks the mirror so often?
Ira may feel worried and caring, wanting Chetan to get support rather than suffer alone.

What does Alice say to her feet? Sum it up in a line or two.

"Curiouser and curiouser!" cried Alice (she was so much surprised, that for the moment she quite forgot how to speak good English); "now I'm opening out like the largest telescope that ever was! Good-bye, feet!" (for when she looked down at her feet, they seemed to be almost out of sight, they were getting so far off). "Oh, my poor little feet, I wonder who will put on your shoes and stockings for you now, dears? I'm sure I shan't be able! I shall be a great deal too far off to trouble myself about you: you must manage the best way you can;—but I must be kind to them," thought Alice, "or perhaps they won't walk the way I want to go! Let me see: I'll give them a new pair of boots every Christmas."
As Alice suddenly grows very tall, she says goodbye to her far-away feet, worries about who will put their shoes on, and jokes about sending them new boots every Christmas.

The chairs at the Thursday caregivers' circle in the community centre were set in a ring, and it was Vaibhav's turn. He started steady: his mother's stroke in March, learning to cook her soft meals, the night shifts he had swapped at work. Then he tried to say that last week she had said his name clearly for the first time since, and his lips began to shake. The words wouldn't come. He pressed his palms flat on his knees. Nandini, who ran the circle, didn't fill the silence. She said only, "Take your time. We're here." Vaibhav breathed out slowly, took two more breaths and looked at the floor tiles. "She said 'Vaibhav,'" he managed. "Like before." Across the ring, an older man was nodding, his eyes wet.

On which day did the caregivers' circle meet?
It met on Thursday.
Why did Vaibhav's lips begin to shake?
He was overwhelmed with relief and love, recalling his mother saying his name clearly; the shaking may also carry the exhaustion and fear of the months since March.
How did Nandini support Vaibhav, and why did it help?
She didn't fill the silence and simply told him to take his time, which let him breathe slowly and finish in his own way.
What might it be like for the older man listening across the ring?
He may feel moved and connected, perhaps recognising his own caregiving struggles in Vaibhav's words.

Read this:

Team note. Jagdish, design team manager.
Last quarter, my team of six spent most of the day in chat and meetings. Shreya, 25, our youngest designer, came to me with a proposal: two "deep work" afternoons a week, no meetings, chat on "do not disturb", urgent issues by phone only.
She'd tracked her own week: fifty-two chat interruptions a day, the longest focus stretch twenty minutes. She looked nervous presenting it, as if I might think she was lazy.
We tried it for a month. At first people felt anxious about missing messages. By week three, two designers finished projects that had dragged for months. Shreya also suggested we move project updates to a written weekly note instead of a meeting.
Not everyone loved it. Our sales liaison grumbled. But we've kept it, and I've asked Shreya to present the idea to other teams.

How many chat interruptions a day did Shreya track?
Fifty-two chat interruptions a day.
How did Shreya seem to feel while presenting her proposal?
Shreya seemed nervous, worried the manager might think she was lazy.
What made Shreya's proposal persuasive?
She brought data from her own week, suggested a clear, limited experiment, and offered a simple replacement for status meetings.
How might the sales liaison see the new afternoons?
The sales liaison may feel frustrated at slower replies, and might need a clear way to reach the team urgently.

Gautam planted a sunflower seed in the pot beside our stairs on Monday. On Thursday morning I found him kneeling there with his fingers deep in the soil. "Just checking if it's growing," he said. He lifted the seed out, and I saw a thin white thread coming from it, so small. He set it back, pressed the soil down and looked pleased. The next week nothing came up. Gautam dug again and found the seed brown and soft. He looked at it for a long time and said, "I should have waited." I couldn't tell if he was sad or just surprised. - Deepika

How many days after planting did Gautam dig up the seed?
Gautam dug up the seed on Thursday morning, after planting it on Monday.
What might Gautam have been feeling when he found the brown seed?
Sad and regretful, though Deepika could not tell whether he was sad or just surprised.
What could Gautam do instead of digging while he waits, and why?
He could water gently and mark days on a calendar, or grow a second seed in a clear cup to watch, so he can look without disturbing it.
How does Deepika see what happened to Gautam's seed?
Deepika is sympathetic and cannot tell what Gautam felt, but notes how long he looked at the seed.

The big wheel at the Pushkar fair creaked and glittered. Gautam, five, held his father's hand tightly. 'Papa, my tummy's funny. Like something's flapping inside.' Kamal crouched. 'Flapping? That sounds like butterflies. Lots of people get butterflies in their tummy when they're nervous or excited.' Gautam thought. 'Both?' 'Maybe both.' Kamal put Gautam's hand on his chest. 'Is your heart going fast too?' Gautam nodded. 'That's your body telling you, this is a big thing.' Gautam looked up at the wheel. 'Can we go on the small swings first?' 'Good idea.' On the swings, Gautam laughed, and said, 'The butterflies are flying away.'

What did Gautam say was flapping inside?
Something in his tummy.
What was Gautam feeling as he looked at the big wheel?
He felt nervous and excited, with butterflies in his tummy and a fast heart.
What did Kamal do to help Gautam understand his body?
He named the flapping feeling as butterflies and linked it to feeling nervous or excited.
How might Kamal have felt when Gautam chose the small swings?
He was probably pleased that Gautam listened to his body and chose a smaller step.

The argument with her flatmate Leila started over the dishes and slid into everything: the late-night calls, the borrowed jacket, the time Zanele forgot to pay her share of the gas. Zanele felt her jaw lock and her face go hot. Her hands were shaking. She knew the next thing she said would be unkind. 'Leila, I need a break. I'm too angry to talk well. Twenty minutes, then I'll come back.' She walked round the block in the Cape Town wind, hands in her pockets, until her breathing slowed. When she came back, Leila was at the table, arms crossed. Zanele sat down. 'I'm back. I want to sort this, not win it. Can we pick one thing?' They started with the dishes, and made a rota before bed.

How long a break did Zanele ask for?
Twenty minutes.
What was Zanele feeling as the argument grew?
She was very angry, with a locked jaw, hot face and shaking hands.
What makes Zanele's break different from avoiding the problem?
She said when she would return and came back to talk calmly, focusing on solving one thing rather than winning.
How might Leila have felt when Zanele walked out?
She may have felt annoyed or worried Zanele was avoiding it, and relieved when Zanele came back as promised.

Amandeep had been head of the hospital's admin department for six months. In every weekly meeting, he'd share a plan, and everyone would nod. No questions. No objections.

At first he thought the plans were good. Then a new billing process he'd pushed failed badly. Afterwards, Anand, one of the clerks, admitted quietly, "We all thought it wouldn't work, sir. Nobody wanted to say."

Amandeep felt a chill. His title was silencing people.

At the next meeting, he tried something new. Before sharing his own view, he asked, "What problems do you see with this idea? I want to hear them first."

Silence. Then Anand spoke, carefully. Then two others.

After the meeting, Amandeep found Anand. "Thank you for speaking up. That's exactly what I need."

Over the next month, he thanked people publicly whenever they brought bad news early. The meetings got louder. And the plans got better.

How long had Amandeep been head of the admin department?
For six months.
What did Amandeep feel when Anand admitted nobody wanted to speak?
Amandeep felt a chill of alarm and some shame, realising his title was silencing his staff.
What changes did Amandeep make, and why did they work?
He asked for problems before sharing his view and thanked people who brought bad news, making disagreement feel safe.
How might Anand have felt speaking first at the next meeting?
Anand probably felt nervous but encouraged, since Amandeep had invited problems first.

On his first day at a Bengaluru school, Gautam wrote the area of a circle as 2πr on the board. A girl in the front row put up her hand. 'Sir, isn't that the circumference?' The class went still, waiting to see what he'd do. Gautam looked, laughed at himself and said, 'Good catch. It's π r squared. Keep checking me.' Twenty minutes later, Tanvir, known as the class topper, started talking over a classmate's answer. Gautam said evenly, 'Tanvir, let Deepti finish, then you're next.' The class exchanged glances; the old teachers had let Tanvir say anything. At the end of the week, Gautam sent the same note home for two talkers: Tanvir and a boy from the back row. Some students grumbled that the new sir was strict. But hands went up more often.

What did Gautam wrongly write on the board?
2πr as the area of a circle.
Why did the class go still after the girl's question?
They were curious and a little nervous, waiting to see if the new teacher would be embarrassed or angry at being corrected.
Which of Gautam's choices set a fair tone?
Owning the mistake openly, and applying the same rule to the topper as to a boy from the back row.
How might Tanvir experience the new teacher?
Tanvir, used to being allowed to say anything, may feel surprised and a bit put out at being told to wait.

The elective form was due at nine the next morning, and the power had gone out in Farhan's neighbourhood. He sat by candlelight with his phone at nineteen percent, scrolling another article comparing economics and psychology. He had already asked four teachers, two seniors and his cousin. He messaged his friend Akash: "Which one has fewer risks?" Akash replied: "Bro, you've asked everyone. Both are fine." Farhan kept scrolling. Each article said something new, and each new thing made him more nervous. Eleven percent. He thought: "If I read one more, maybe I'll be sure." At four percent, he realised he'd been looking for a choice with no downside, and there wasn't one. He ticked psychology, the one he'd liked first, and the phone went dark.

How many teachers had Farhan asked?
Four teachers, plus two seniors and his cousin.
What was Farhan feeling as he kept scrolling?
He felt more and more nervous, each new article adding worry instead of certainty.
What would you advise Farhan the next time he faces a choice like this?
Set a time limit for gathering views, then pick the option that fits best, knowing no choice is risk-free.
How does Akash see Farhan's search?
Akash thinks Farhan has asked enough, and seems a little exasperated but kind.

I'm Yogesh, and I've shared a study table with Sachin in the hostel common room all semester. In September he did everything in one long block from two to midnight, and I watched him stare at the same maths problem for an hour after lunch, yawning.
In October something changed. One morning at seven I came down and found him already at the table, working through control systems problems, fast. He said, 'I've figured out my brain works best before lunch. After lunch it's porridge.'
Now his day has a pattern. Mornings till twelve: the hard problems. After lunch: copying lab data, formatting reports, emails. Evenings: light revision.
I can't know how he actually feels inside, but in the mid-sems he topped control systems, and he's stopped yawning at his books after lunch.

What does Sachin now do after lunch?
Copying lab data, formatting reports, emails.
What does Sachin's 'After lunch it's porridge' suggest about how he feels?
It suggests he feels dull and sleepy after lunch, and more confident now that hard work sits in his sharp mornings.
What else could Sachin do if the evening revision starts slipping?
Move part of it to a short morning slot, since that is when he thinks best, or keep evenings only for light review.
How does Sachin's new routine look to Yogesh?
Yogesh sees him working fast in the mornings, no longer yawning after lunch, and topping control systems.

A crate of mangoes tumbled off a handcart near the colony gate, and five-year-old Sonali watched the vendor chase the rolling fruit. That evening her uncle Saurabh asked, "Was the man wearing a red cap?" Sonali thought for a moment, then nodded. "Red," she said. Next morning she told her friend all about the mango man in the red cap, and at school she drew him with one, coloured in hard with her crayon. Her mother had been at the gate too. She remembered a bare head and a grey towel over his shoulder. Sonali was sure about the cap.

What fell off the handcart near the colony gate?
A crate of mangoes tumbled off the handcart near the colony gate.
Why did Sonali feel so sure about the red cap the next morning?
Uncle Saurabh's question had slipped the red cap into Sonali's picture of the vendor, so it now felt like something she had seen herself. She even drew it and coloured it in hard.
At which moment could Uncle Saurabh have asked differently, and what could he have said?
When he first asked about the vendor that evening. An open question like "What did the man look like?" would have let Sonali describe him without a cap being suggested.
How might Sonali's mother see the red cap story?
Her mother remembers a bare head and a grey towel, so she may realise the cap came from Uncle Saurabh's question and not from the gate.

At the tuition class in a Kolkata flat, Sir was angry. Chandrika had forgotten her homework for the second time.
"Shankar, you're the monitor," Sir said. "Take her mat to the back. She sits alone today. And tell her she's letting the whole class down."
Shankar froze. Chandrika sat next to him every day and shared her erasers. But Sir was the teacher. Teachers knew what was right, didn't they? And Sir had said it, not him.
He carried the mat to the back. "You're letting the class down," he mumbled, not looking at her.
Chandrika sat alone by the shoe rack all evening. On the way home, Shankar kicked a stone the whole length of the lane.

Where did Shankar carry Chandrika's mat?
He carried the mat to the back.
Why did Shankar do what Sir said, even though Chandrika was his friend?
He felt uneasy but believed the teacher must know what was right, and that the blame would be on Sir, not on him.
What could Shankar do the next day?
He could say sorry to Chandrika and, if asked again, tell Sir quietly that he didn't want to scold a friend.
How might Chandrika feel sitting alone by the shoe rack?
Chandrika would feel ashamed and lonely, and hurt that her friend repeated the scolding.

Coaching note, Thursday.
In today's project review, Sahil interrupted Eshaan's update in front of eleven people: 'You're hiding the delay from the client, and everyone knows it.' He had no slide, no dates, nothing on paper. Eshaan went red, said the delay had been agreed with the client last week, and the next forty minutes became an argument about tone instead of the schedule. Two people left early. Afterwards Eshaan asked me whether Sahil was 'out to get' him.
The concern may still be real; I don't know yet. But the way it was raised made it harder to examine. I met Sahil at five. He was shaken and a bit defiant. We agreed he would write down what he saw with dates and talk to Eshaan privately first, with me present if he wanted.
Mentor, delivery team

How many people were in the room when Sahil interrupted?
Eleven people.
How was Sahil feeling when the mentor met him at five?
He was shaken and a bit defiant, probably still sure of his concern but aware the meeting had gone badly.
What other approach would have made Sahil's concern easier to examine?
Writing down what he saw with dates and raising it privately with Eshaan or a manager first, so the facts could be checked without an audience.
How did the meeting feel for Eshaan?
Eshaan felt attacked in front of the team, went red and even wondered whether Sahil was out to get him.

Darshan: so which pricing did you pick? the team is still split
Mohit: monthly plan at the lower price
Darshan: sales will be mad, they wanted yearly only
Mohit: I know. but nobody can prove which works. we've argued 3 weeks
Mohit: so I picked the one we can undo cheaply. it's a settings change, not a rebuild
Darshan: and if it tanks?
Mohit: review date is 15 March. I've shared the numbers that would make us switch: if sign-ups don't rise 10% or cancellations go above 8%, we go back to yearly
Darshan: everyone saw that?
Mohit: posted in the team channel with the dashboard link 📊
Darshan: ok that's actually hard to argue with
Mohit: that's the idea. we stop debating and start measuring

When is the review date?
15 March.
How does Mohit seem to feel about picking one option?
Mohit seems calm and confident, not because the choice is certain, but because it can be undone cheaply.
What else could Mohit do to make the review fair?
Mohit could ask sales to agree the switch numbers in advance, so no one argues about the result on 15 March.
How might the sales team see this decision?
Sales may be unhappy at first, but a clear review date and switch numbers show their preference could still win.

I'm Uday. In Class 5, a new boy called Joel joined our section. He hummed while he worked and flapped his hands when he got excited about trains. My friends thought he was weird. Urmila said, "If anyone sits with Joel, they can't sit with us." Everyone agreed. I agreed too, out loud. Inside I felt sick and scared. I didn't want to be alone at lunch.
But Joel knew every train route in the country, and I wanted to hear about them.
So I did small things. I said hi at the gate. I lent him my blue pen. In library period, where Urmila couldn't see, I sat with him, and he showed me a map of the Konkan line.
After a month, Urmila caught us. I waited for trouble. Instead she sat down and asked, "Which is the longest route?"

What did Joel show Uday in library period?
A map of the Konkan line.
Why did Uday agree out loud with Urmila?
Uday was scared of being alone at lunch, even though agreeing felt sick inside.
What small brave steps did Uday take?
Saying hi at the gate, lending the blue pen and sitting with Joel in library period.
How might Joel have experienced Uday's small kindnesses?
As one friendly face in a class that was shutting him out; he happily shared his train maps.

The loan camp at Kheda's panchayat hall ran from ten till four, and by the end sixty-two farmers had their crop-loan forms checked and signed. Not one had to come back.
On the bus back to the branch, Damini, the branch manager, turned round in her seat. 'Tanvir, that was the smoothest camp we've had in three years. Your checklist at the door saved hours.'
Tanvir smiled and looked out at the cotton fields. 'The sarpanch had told everyone what to bring, ma'am. And you did the planning. Honestly, it was an easy village.'
Damini frowned slightly but let it go.
That night, going over the register, he found he'd written one farmer's survey number with two digits reversed. His stomach dropped. He corrected it, then sat staring at the page. There, he thought. That's the real me. The camp was luck.

How many farmers had their crop-loan forms checked and signed?
Sixty-two farmers had their crop-loan forms checked and signed.
What does Tanvir's thought 'That's the real me' reveal about how he sees himself?
He believes his success was luck and that one small mistake is the true proof he isn't good enough.
What could Tanvir try the next time Damini praises his work?
He could simply say thank you and write down what he actually did, like the checklist, instead of giving the credit away.
How might Damini see Tanvir's answer on the bus?
Damini may feel puzzled or a bit frustrated that her honest praise was brushed aside, since she saw his checklist make the difference.

Tuesday: Sharmila and Ganga, both five, fought over the one purple crayon in their class, and Ganga snapped it in half. Both cried. Thursday: their teacher gave them a sand timer. "Two turns each," she said. They took turns, watching the sand run, and argued only once. The next Monday: when Ganga reached for the purple, she stopped. "Sorry about the broken one," she told Sharmila. "You go first."

What did Ganga do to the purple crayon on Tuesday?
She snapped it in half.
What does Ganga stopping and apologising on Monday suggest?
She felt sorry about the broken crayon and wanted things to be fair with Sharmila.
Why did the sand timer help?
It made turns clear and fair, so the girls didn't have to argue about who had it longer.
How might Sharmila feel when Ganga offers her the first turn?
Surprised and pleased, and more willing to share in return.

'Go without me,' Hemant called through the bathroom door. 'My face is all puffy and this shirt looks terrible.'
'It's the final. We need our goalkeeper,' Asif said.
'I look like a balloon today.'
'You played the semi with a cold and saved two penalties.'
Silence. Hemant stood at the mirror, jaw tight. Then, almost to himself: 'If you'd said this about yourself, what would I tell you?'
'What?'
'I'd tell you it's one bad day. That your face doesn't catch the ball. That you're allowed to feel a bit rubbish and still show up.'
'...That's actually decent advice.'
Hemant breathed out slowly. 'I don't have to like how I look today. It can just be okay.'
He opened the door, gloves already in his hand.
'Ready?'
'Ready enough. Let's go.'

What position does Hemant play for the team?
He is the goalkeeper.
What was Hemant feeling as he stood at the mirror with his jaw tight?
He felt self-conscious and low about his puffy face, tempted to skip the final.
What small step helped Hemant move on with his plans?
He asked what he'd tell a friend in his place, spoke to himself that kindly, and settled for 'okay' instead of perfect.
How does Asif see Hemant's bad body day?
He sees his goalkeeper, not a balloon, and just wants his friend on the pitch for the final 👍

I'm Pranav, and I live on the third floor of the hostel. Our floor had fights about everything: music at night, the fridge, bathroom cleaning. Gautam, our floor rep, could have just written rules and pinned them up. Instead, one evening, he knocked on all twelve doors and said, "Common room, eight o'clock, everyone." I asked him later why he didn't just decide. He said, "If I make the rules alone, nobody will follow them. Everyone uses the floor, so everyone has to agree." At the meeting people argued, laughed and voted. Quiet hours after eleven. Fridge cleaned Sundays. A cleaning rota by room. It took ninety minutes. Six weeks later, the rules on the notice board are still being followed.

How many doors did Gautam knock on?
All twelve doors.
What was Gautam thinking when he called a meeting instead of deciding alone?
He felt sure rules made alone wouldn't be followed, and hoped a shared decision would stick.
Why did a group meeting suit this problem?
Everyone shares the floor, so rules everyone helped make are more likely to be accepted and followed.
How might the other residents see the meeting?
They likely felt heard and more willing to follow rules they had voted on.

"Pradeep, the college called Papa. They say you haven't paid the second-term fee."
"It's fine, Reena. The form's just late. It'll sort itself out."
"They also said your attendance is low."
"Everyone's attendance is low."
"The counsellor emailed you twice."
"I'll read it."
"When?"
"Soon."
"Pradeep. When did you last open your college email?"
He was quiet. "A month? Maybe more."
"Why?"
"Because every time I think about it, I feel sick."
"So you don't look."
"So I don't look."
Reena sat beside him. "Let's open it together. Right now. Then we call the counsellor tomorrow morning, first thing."

How long since Pradeep last opened his college email?
A month, maybe more.
Why doesn't Pradeep look at his email?
Every time he thinks about it he feels sick with dread, so not looking keeps the feeling away.
What does Reena suggest?
Open the email together right now, then call the counsellor first thing tomorrow morning.
How might Papa have felt after the college called?
Probably worried and surprised, hearing about the fee and attendance for the first time.

Monday. Madhuri sat with her notes for the term exam and a message from the lake-protection group. A permit had been granted for a peaceful walk on Friday. Her friend Sudha said, “I’m going. Come with me?” Madhuri’s stomach twisted.
Thursday. She told her parents about it. They worried aloud, and she promised to stay near the organisers and leave if things turned tense.
Friday. The crowd was bigger than she expected. Her heart pounded, but organisers with armbands walked along the line and reminded people to stay calm. A stranger smiled and passed her a water bottle.
Saturday, she was back at her desk, tired and glad.

What kind of event was Madhuri considering on Friday?
It was a peaceful walk for the lake-protection group, and a permit had been granted.
What was Madhuri feeling at the start of the walk?
Madhuri was scared, with her heart pounding, and also proud to be there. The organisers' reminders and the stranger's kindness helped steady her.
What choices did Madhuri make to balance the cause against the risks?
She told her parents, promised to stay near the organisers and to leave if it turned tense. She also went with a friend to a permitted event.
How might Sudha have felt when Madhuri said yes?
Sudha was probably glad and reassured to have company. Sudha had invited Madhuri directly, so it mattered to her.

Madhav's kabaddi raid had been perfect: two touches, a dive, a clean escape back over the line. His cousin filmed it behind the Barsana bus stand, and Madhav posted it that evening with loud music. Next morning, on the way to school, he checked the phone every thirty seconds. Eighteen likes. Then nineteen. By lunch he was proud and sick at the same time, because a boy from the next village had three thousand for a scooter wheelie. Madhav stopped talking during games period. Sarika ma'am, the PT teacher, noticed him sitting on the steps staring at the screen. She sat down with her whistle still around her neck. "Show me." He showed her. "Nice ankle hold," she said. "Now show me the part where you lost the last raid." He laughed despite himself. "Tomorrow," she said, "you teach the juniors that escape." He did.

Where did Madhav's cousin film the kabaddi raid?
Behind the Barsana bus stand.
How was Madhav feeling by lunch, and why?
He felt proud and sick at once, pleased with his raid but deflated because another boy's video had thousands more likes.
How did Sarika ma'am support Madhav?
She looked at the actual skill, joked about the lost raid, and gave him a real task, teaching juniors, that showed his worth outside the likes.
What is it like for Sarika ma'am to see Madhav on the steps staring at his phone?
She probably felt concerned, seeing a usually lively player go quiet, and wanted to steer him back to what he is actually good at.

On the veranda of Nani's house, Karthik sat with the wooden shape box. He picked up the round red block and pushed it at the square hole. It stuck. He turned it and pushed harder. Stuck.
He banged it once and looked at cousin Eshaan.
Eshaan just watched.
Karthik moved his hand. Round block, round hole. Plop! It dropped inside.
He peered in, then grabbed the next block.

What colour was the round block?
The round block was red.
How might Karthik have felt when the block kept sticking?
He was probably frustrated, which is why he banged it once and looked at Eshaan.
What could Eshaan do if Karthik gets very upset next time?
Eshaan could point gently at the right hole or show one block, but still let Karthik push it in himself.
How might Eshaan see Karthik's plop moment?
Eshaan may feel pleased and amused, seeing Karthik work it out without any help.

messages.content:
She was not one that would have disturbed the house much on her own account. Every object she saw, the moment she crossed the threshold, appeared to delight her; and every circumstance that took place about her: except the preparing for the burial, and the presence of the mourners. I thought she was half silly, from her behaviour while that went on: she ran into her chamber, and made me come with her, though I should have been dressing the children: and there she sat shivering and clasping her hands, and asking repeatedly—"Are they gone yet?" Then she began describing with hysterical emotion the effect it produced on her to see black; and started, and trembled, and, at last, fell a-weeping—and when I asked what was the matter, answered, she didn't know; but she felt so afraid of dying! I imagined her as little likely to die as myself. She was rather thin, but young, and fresh-complexioned, and her eyes sparkled as bright as diamonds. I did remark, to be sure, that mounting the stairs made her breathe very quick; that the least sudden noise set her all in a quiver, and that she coughed troublesomely sometimes: but I knew nothing of what these symptoms portended, and had no impulse to sympathise with her. We don't in general take to foreigners here, Mr. Lockwood, unless they take to us first.

In about three sentences, what does Nelly say about this woman?

Nelly describes the young wife as easily delighted by everything in the house except the funeral. During it, she hid in her room, trembling and crying that she was afraid of dying. Nelly noticed her cough and quick breathing but did not understand them or feel sorry for her.

Wednesday, 2 am feed done
Our daughter Mishti is three weeks old and my phone won't stop buzzing. My wife Parveen's mausi sent a voice note about a gang stealing newborns from hospitals, and now the whole family group is sure it's happening in our city. Ma wants us to keep the curtains shut all day. I felt my own chest tighten listening to it. But then, standing at the counter warming the bottle, I saw the kettle's cord hanging within reach of the baby bouncer, and the gas knob we keep forgetting to turn off. Nobody sends voice notes about those. Tomorrow I'll ask Ma, kindly, how many babies she actually knows were taken. And I'll tape the cord up.
Ujjwal

What did Parveen's mausi send?
She sent a voice note about a gang stealing newborns from hospitals.
How can you tell Ujjwal felt the fear too?
Ujjwal writes that their own chest tightened listening to it, which shows the rumour reached him even though he later questions it.
What small steps does Ujjwal plan, and why are they wise?
Ujjwal plans to ask Ma kindly how many babies she knows were actually taken and to tape up the kettle cord; this checks the scary story against reality and fixes a real hazard.
How might Ma see the curtains-shut idea?
Ma probably sees it as protecting her grandchild; the rumour feels urgent to her, so keeping the curtains shut feels like love, not panic.

I'm Shreya, and I was in the second row of the audience when my classmate Harsha danced at the school cultural fest. Everything was perfect until the third song. Then Harsha raised the wrong arm, and the girl beside her bumped into her. I saw it clearly. Harsha's eyes went wide for a second. I don't know what she was thinking. But then she smiled, took a little step to find the beat, and swung into the next turn with everyone. The lady beside me whispered, "Lovely," and hadn't noticed anything at all. Afterwards I told Harsha, "You covered that so well," and she said, "Which bit?" Then she laughed. So maybe she did notice.

Which song did the mistake happen in?
It happened in the third song.
What might Harsha have felt when her eyes went wide?
She may have felt a quick jolt of panic, though Shreya can't be sure, before calmly getting back into the dance.
Which part of Harsha's recovery worked best, and why?
The smile and the small step to find the beat worked best, because they let her rejoin without drawing attention.
How did the slip look to the lady next to Shreya?
The lady didn't notice it at all and found the dance lovely.

I'm Darshan, Tarun's cousin. Yesterday Tarun was telling Nani about the zoo. “We saw… a… um… the big… the… the grey one with the…” He waved his arm like a trunk. I wanted to shout “Elephant!” but his mother put a hand on my arm and just waited, looking at Tarun. Nani waited too. Tarun frowned, then said, “Elephant! And it sprayed water!” He went on and on after that. I'm not sure if he was shy or just finding the word, but waiting worked.

What animal was Tarun trying to name?
The elephant.
What might Tarun have been feeling as he searched for the word?
He may have felt a bit frustrated or shy while searching for the word. When he found it, he seemed excited to keep talking.
Why was waiting better than finishing the sentence for Tarun?
It let him find the word himself, which gave him confidence to keep telling the story.
How did waiting feel for Darshan?
It was hard for Darshan, who wanted to shout the answer, until it was clear that waiting worked.

Read this:

Dear Diary,
Today was a GOOD day. It rained all week and we were stuck indoors, and I was so grumpy I fought with Imran over the TV remote three times. Last night I couldn't even sleep properly. Today the sun came out and Ammi sent us to the park. Imran and I raced to the big tree ten times, played catch and rolled down the grassy slope till we were dizzy. When we came home I did all my maths without a single fight. Ammi said, 'See what running does?' Even Imran was nice. Tomorrow Ms Pinto wants to keep us in at games time to finish our project. I'm going to ask her if we can finish it after school instead.
Reena

How many times did Reena and Imran race to the big tree?
Ten times.
How did Reena feel after the week stuck indoors?
Reena felt grumpy and restless, fighting with Imran and sleeping badly.
Why is it sensible for Reena to ask Ms Pinto to keep games time?
Physical play helps Reena's mood and focus, so taking it away could make work and behaviour worse, not better.
How might Ammi see the change after the park?
Ammi likely felt pleased and relieved, seeing running bring back peace and focus.

Read this:

Ishita, you're worried about your friend and that group online? Sit. Let your Ganga Masi tell you something from when I was sixteen.

My closest friend then was Pinky. We did everything together. Then she found a chat forum, some group that said people like her were being wronged by people like our neighbours. Within months she changed. She stopped laughing at my jokes. She called our old friends traitors.

I wanted to shout at her. I wanted to mock the forum. But my mother said, "If you mock it, you push her further in." So I kept walking home with her. I asked her what she read and why it mattered. I listened more than I argued.

Then one evening she said the group wanted her to leave home and "join them properly." That night I told my mother everything. My mother went to Pinky's mother the same night.

It was hard. Pinky didn't speak to me for months. But she came back. Friendship and a trusted adult, together, that's what did it.

What did Pinky call her old friends?
Pinky called them traitors.
What was young Ganga feeling as Pinky changed?
Ganga felt hurt and frustrated, wanting to shout and mock the forum, but also deeply worried about losing her friend.
What was the key choice in Ganga Masi's story, and why did it work?
Telling her mother the same night Pinky spoke of leaving home was key, because a trusted adult could protect Pinky while Ganga stayed her friend.
What was it like for Pinky's mother to hear the news?
Pinky's mother was likely shocked and frightened, but able to act that night because Ganga's mother came to her.

The three of them were picked for the inter-school quiz team. Vishal went to the organiser and came back with news: questions on science, sports and everyday knowledge, plus buzzer rounds where the fastest hand wins. Now he knew what to study and how fast the answers must come.

Vidya read the kids' page in the paper every morning and a book of general knowledge before sleep, and copied down fresh facts on cities, famous people and world records in a notebook with a marbled cover.

Jomon announced he would learn the whole thick encyclopedia. By the second week his eyes were red, the facts had blurred together, and he could not say which chapters mattered or where he was weak.

Then the team sat a mock round. Jomon, Vishal and Vidya all missed the questions about rivers and capitals. They spent the next week with an atlas and a wall map, quizzing each other at the dining table. In the next mock, their score jumped.

What did Vishal find out from the organiser?
That there were questions on science, sports and everyday knowledge, plus buzzer rounds.
Why did Jomon's approach leave him confused while Vidya's notebook and the team's later plan worked?
Jomon tried to learn everything and could not tell which facts mattered, while Vidya kept a notebook of new facts and the team used the mock round to find rivers and capitals as the weak spot.
How was Jomon feeling by the second week?
Tired and overwhelmed, since his eyes were red and the facts had blurred together.
What could Jomon do differently?
He could ask the organiser or teacher which topics matter, study a little each day, and use a mock round to spot weak areas.

Thursday night
Today Kamal wasn't at the morning meeting, and by eleven the whole team was lost. Nobody knew the client's new file names; nobody had the vendor's number. Kamal always has these. He's the one who sends the checklist the night before, catches the typo in the invoice, quietly books the meeting room none of us remembered. We just assume it happens. At lunch Priti said he had messaged in, exhausted, taking two days off. I felt a bit sick thinking how long it's been since anyone said thanks, me included. I'm writing down three things I can take over from him on Monday, and I'll say thank you before I forget again.
Yash

What did nobody have when Kamal was absent?
Nobody had the vendor's number.
What was Yash feeling after hearing Kamal was exhausted?
Yash felt a bit sick and guilty, realising how long it had been since anyone thanked Kamal.
What choice does Yash make for Monday?
Yash plans to take over three of Kamal's tasks and to thank Kamal before forgetting again.
What might months of quiet fixing have been like for Kamal?
He may have felt relied on but unseen, carrying everyone's gaps without thanks until he was worn out.

Tuesday night.
Posted about the hostel curfew again. The calm version last week, with the survey numbers, got 14 likes. Tonight I wrote "the admin treats us like cattle" and it crossed 600 by dinner. Strangers sharing it. My phone buzzing on the mess table like it was alive. I felt amazing for about an hour. Then Sabina read it over my shoulder and said, "Warden ma'am isn't herding cattle, yaar. She fought for the late library pass." I snapped at her. Now it's 1 a.m. and I'm scrolling my own old posts. They get sharper every week. I don't even think the warden is the villain. I just know the angry lines get clapped. When did I start writing for the clapping?
Ankita

How many likes did the calm post with the survey numbers get?
The calm version got 14 likes.
What was Ankita feeling at 1 a.m. while scrolling old posts?
Ankita felt uneasy and a little ashamed, seeing the posts grow sharper and realising they were written for the clapping, not from real belief.
What could Ankita try before the next post?
Write what is actually believed, like the survey numbers, ask whether a line is there for truth or for likes, and make things right with Sabina.
How might Sabina have felt when Ankita snapped?
Sabina probably felt hurt, having only stood up for a warden who fought for the late library pass.

Dear Rehana,
I'm writing because I didn't handle Friday well. When your phone rang during the test and I said, in front of everyone, 'Some people clearly don't care about their future,' I shamed you. I'm sorry. I found out afterwards that it was your mother calling from the hospital.
Today I spoke to the class. I didn't mention you. I said that our rule about phones stays, but that none of us, me included, gets to embarrass anyone in front of others. We agreed that anyone expecting an urgent call can tell me before a test.
If you'd like to talk, I'm in the staffroom after sixth period. You're welcome to bring a friend.
Yogesh Kulkarni
Physics

Who was calling when Rehana's phone rang?
Rehana's mother, calling from the hospital.
What might Rehana have felt after Friday's comment?
Rehana likely felt humiliated and hurt, shamed in front of the class while already worried about the call from the hospital.
What did Yogesh do to repair things?
Apologised privately in writing, then spoke to the class about not embarrassing anyone without naming Rehana, and set a fair rule for urgent calls.
How might the rest of the class see the new urgent-call agreement?
They may feel it is fairer and safer, knowing even the teacher won't embarrass them and they can explain in advance.

Check my English: "This is the boy whom helped me."
Oh, and I don't understand "outcast". Can you help?
One more thing: what does "walk on eggshells" mean?
Then, is it "desert" or "dessert" for a sweet after a meal?

1. Corrected: This is the boy who helped me. Why: "who" is the subject of "helped", and "whom" is for the object.
2. Outcast is a noun that means a person whom others have pushed away.
3. It means to be very careful not to upset someone. For example: we walked on eggshells around Dad when he was angry.
4. It is "dessert", with a double "s". The "desert" has one "s".

In a café in Madrid, Alejandro had a spreadsheet of twenty-four master's programmes: Lisbon, Utrecht, Lyon, Milan. Columns for fees, rankings, weather, even distance to the sea. His friend Freya watched him add another row.
"You said you'd decide in March," Freya said. "It's May."
"I just want to be sure."
In June he finally picked Utrecht and sent the form. That evening, instead of celebrating, he scrolled through the Lyon course page again. "Lyon had that river," he murmured.
Freya put down the cup. "Last time you had three options and chose your bachelor's in ten minutes. You loved it."
Alejandro shrugged and kept scrolling.

Which programme did Alejandro finally pick?
In June he finally picked Utrecht and sent the form.
What does Alejandro's scrolling on the Lyon page suggest he feels after choosing?
It suggests he still feels unsure and slightly regretful, as if one of the other twenty-three options might have been the right one.
What could Alejandro learn from how he chose his bachelor's?
He could narrow to a few options that meet his key needs and decide quickly, as he did with three options before and ended up loving it.
How does Freya see Alejandro's months of comparing?
Freya sees him stuck and unhappy, and remembers that fewer choices once made him quick and content.

"Dolma, you're from Ladakh, na? Is it true you all drink butter tea the whole day?"
"Some of us. I prefer coffee."
"Do all Ladakhis..."
"Rakesh, I can only tell you about me."
Rakesh laughed and wandered off. Dolma turned back to her circuit diagram, jaw tight.
Uday, who shared her lab table, pulled up his chair. "That's the third time today, isn't it?"
"Fourth. The warden wants me to say something about my culture at Freshers' Night. As if I'm a brochure."
"Do you want to?"
"No. I want to talk about the robot arm."
"Then talk about the robot arm. I'll tell the warden you're busy with the tech fest." Uday leaned over the diagram. "Why did you put the motor there?"
For twenty minutes Dolma explained torque and forgot to feel watched.

What did the warden want Dolma to do at Freshers' Night?
To say something about her culture.
What does Dolma's tight jaw after Rakesh's question suggest?
It suggests she was tired and irritated at being treated as an example of her whole region rather than as herself.
What did Uday do that let Dolma be an individual?
He asked what she wanted, offered to handle the warden, and asked about her robot arm, treating her as a fellow engineer.
How might Rakesh see his questions compared with how they felt to Dolma?
Rakesh probably thinks the questions are just curiosity, not realising the repeated questions make Dolma carry a whole region on her shoulders.
