Read this:

Avni, you say your team goes cold on you and you can't tell why. Let me, your old Ojas Chacha, tell you about the shop. When I was twenty-five, Bauji handed me the cloth shop, and my cousin Mohan kept working the counter. Mohan was ten years older. Suddenly he started calling me "boss" with a funny twist, doing exactly what I said and nothing more. When I changed the display, he said, "As you command." It made my skin crawl. I wanted to shout. Instead one evening, after we pulled the shutter down, I sat on the step and said, "Mohan bhai, I think I've missed something. Say it straight, I won't be angry." He was quiet a long time. Then: "You never once asked me. I've run this counter for eight years." After that I asked him before every change. The "boss" jokes stopped within a month.

What did Mohan say when Ojas changed the display?
He said, "As you command."
How did Mohan feel about Ojas taking over the shop, going by what he finally said?
Mohan felt hurt and overlooked, because he had run the counter for eight years and was never once asked.
What choice by Ojas turned the story around?
Instead of shouting, he sat on the step after closing and invited Mohan to say it straight, promising not to be angry.
What would have changed if Ojas had shouted at Mohan?
Mohan would probably have kept his hurt hidden behind more jokes, and the tension at the counter would have grown.
"Aap yahin ruko" - polite aur casual?
Polite: "Could you wait here for a moment, please?" Casual: "Wait here, okay?"

Please go through this passage with me.

"'Oh,' returned the fairy, 'that does not signify! Here is a talisman will remove all difficulties;' and she held out a pretty gold ring. 'Put it,' she said, 'on the fourth finger of my left hand, and I am yours, and you are mine; and we shall leave earth, and make our own heaven yonder.' She nodded again at the moon. The ring, Adele, is in my breeches-pocket, under the disguise of a sovereign: but I mean soon to change it to a ring again."

What does the fairy offer, and what does the ring do?
She offers a pretty gold ring as a charm that removes all difficulties. If it is put on the fourth finger of her left hand, they will belong to each other and leave earth to make their own heaven.

You want to know my biggest early mistake as a manager? Siddharth. He'd sit in every sprint planning, nod, and say, "Yep, doable." Then the week would end and his tasks would be untouched. Not late by a day. Untouched. I thought he was lazy, honestly. I nearly wrote him up.
Then a colleague said, "Manoj, have you ever seen anyone say no in your meetings?" I thought about it. Nobody had. I'd built a room where "yes" was the only safe word.
So I started ending planning with, "Okay, what here do you think is a bad idea?" and then waiting, awkwardly long. The third time, Siddharth said, "The API migration. It's going to break the billing system." He was right. We rescheduled it. His tasks started getting done.

What did Siddharth say about the API migration?
"It's going to break the billing system."
Why might Siddharth have said 'Yep, doable' while leaving tasks untouched?
In a room where only yes felt safe, he likely couldn't voice his disagreement, so it came out as quiet non-delivery.
What change did Manoj make, and why did it work?
Ending planning by asking what was a bad idea and then waiting, which made 'no' safe and let Siddharth raise the real risk. 🤔
How might the colleague have seen Manoj's meetings?
As a place where everyone nodded along, which is why the colleague asked whether anyone had ever said no.

messages.content:
Read this:

Parul had the slides ready: car-free Sunday mornings on the lake road in Kukatpally. She was sure. But on Friday evening, in the noisy municipal office, she turned to Ojas and asked, "Who will hate this most?" "The shop owners," he said. "Harish from their association wrote us a long letter." Parul printed all six pages and read them on the bus home, pen in hand. Some points were weak. One was not: the vegetable vendors' delivery vans came only on Sunday mornings. In her notebook she wrote, "If deliveries can't work, I rethink this." On Saturday she called Harish. "What would make this workable for you?" By Monday her plan had a delivery lane until nine.

How many pages was the association's letter?
The letter from Harish's association was six pages long.
Why did Parul ask Ojas who would hate the plan most?
Parul felt confident in the plan but was eager to find its weak spot before committing, so she treated the strongest opposition as useful information rather than a threat.
What could other planners learn from Parul's weekend?
They could read the opposing letter in full, call its writer with an open question, and let the one strong point reshape the plan instead of defending the original.
How might Harish see the municipal office after Parul's call?
Harish would probably feel heard, since the association's letter led to a real change, and may trust the office more in future talks.

They walked on without knowing in what direction. There was too much to be thought, and felt, and said, for attention to any other objects. She soon learnt that they were indebted for their present good understanding to the efforts of his aunt, who did call on him in her return through London, and there relate her journey to Longbourn, its motive, and the substance of her conversation with Elizabeth; dwelling emphatically on every expression of the latter, which, in her Ladyship's apprehension, peculiarly denoted her perverseness and assurance, in the belief that such a relation must assist her endeavours to obtain that promise from her nephew which she had refused to give. But, unluckily for her Ladyship, its effect had been exactly contrariwise.

I need this paragraph summarised in three sentences.

Two people walk on without noticing where they go, because there is so much to think, feel and say. She learns that their good understanding is owed to his aunt, who told him in London about her talk with Elizabeth. The aunt hoped to win a promise from her nephew, but it had the opposite effect.

Parveen Aunty put down her knitting when her nephew said his team would just add one more feature. "Let me tell you what Chaitanya and I did in our twenties. We built software for small printing presses. Two years we worked on it. When nobody bought, we told ourselves the problem was missing features. So we added a billing module. Then a stock module. Then a module for wedding-card designs. Each one took months and cost money we had saved for our own weddings. Sales didn't move. But stopping felt like saying those two years were wasted, and neither of us could bear to say it. In the end the money ran out and we stopped anyway, with even more wasted. On the day we shut it, Chaitanya said to me, 'We could have stopped a year ago and lost less.' I've never forgotten that."

Please give a three-sentence recap of this piece.

Parveen Aunty tells her nephew that she and Chaitanya spent two years on printing-press software and kept adding features when nobody bought it. Stopping felt like calling the two years wasted, so they went on until the money ran out. Chaitanya then said they could have stopped a year earlier and lost less.

On the path to the well in their village near Nashik, Mahima, two, would not stop asking. "What that?" She pointed at a goat.

"Bakri," said Jyoti Mausi.

"Bakri!" Then she pointed at a cart, a bucket, a red flower. "What that? What that?" Each new word she repeated loudly.

At the well a dog barked and she hid behind Jyoti's legs. "Scared," she whispered, a new word. Jyoti crouched. "Yes, you felt scared. He's just saying hello."

What was the first thing Mahima pointed at on the path?
She pointed at a goat, and Jyoti Mausi named it bakri.
How did Mahima feel when the dog barked, and how did she show it?
She felt scared, hiding behind Jyoti's legs and whispering the new word "scared."
What did Jyoti do well when Mahima named her fear?
She crouched down, repeated the feeling word back and gently explained the dog, helping Mahima connect words to both things and feelings.
What is it like for Jyoti Mausi to answer "What that?" again and again?
It might be a little tiring, but she seems patient and pleased by how quickly Mahima is learning words.

"Parul, come fast, everyone's jumping off the canal bridge!" Parveen shouted from the gate.
Parul grabbed her slippers. "Wait, how deep is it?"
"Who cares, it's so hot! Everyone's doing it."
Parul's heart was already racing. She could hear the shrieks from the road. Her feet wanted to run.
"Parveen, stop. Did anyone check the water after last week's rain?"
"Stop being boring."
Parul stood still, breathing. "Let's go and look first. If it's too fast, we sit on the bank and eat mangoes. I'm not jumping blind."
At the bridge the water was brown and fast. Two boys were already coughing on the bank. Parul called her uncle, who came and told everyone to get out, and the kids moved to the shallow steps.

What was everyone doing at the canal?
Jumping off the canal bridge.
How did Parul feel when she first heard the shouts?
She felt excited and tempted; her heart raced and her feet wanted to run.
What helped Parul make a cooler choice?
She stopped, breathed and asked about the water, then went to look before deciding, and called her uncle when it was unsafe.
How might Parveen feel after seeing the coughing boys?
Parveen may feel shaken and relieved that Parul slowed them down.

Read this:

In the Class 6 science club, Rehana ma'am played a short video of students passing a basketball. "Count how many times the white-shirt team passes. Carefully." Gurleen leaned forward, lips moving. Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen. When the video ended, she shot up her hand. "Fifteen!" "Correct," said Rehana ma'am. "And did anyone see the tiger?" Half the room burst out laughing. Gurleen frowned. What tiger? Rehana ma'am played it again. Right in the middle, a person in a tiger costume walked slowly through the players, waved at the camera and walked off. Gurleen's jaw dropped. "That wasn't there!" "It was," said Rehana ma'am. "Your eyes saw it. Your attention didn't."

How many passes did Gurleen count?
Fifteen.
Why did Gurleen insist 'That wasn't there!'?
Gurleen felt shocked and puzzled, because her attention was so fixed on counting passes that the tiger never registered.
What does this experiment teach Gurleen about noticing things?
That attention decides what we see, so when focused on one task, it helps to look again or ask others what they noticed.
How might the children who saw the tiger feel?
They probably felt amused and a bit proud, laughing that anyone could miss something so strange.
Explain how to cut a mango in four numbered steps. Keep each step under eight words.

1. Wash the mango well.
2. Stand it on a board.
3. Slice off each side.
4. Scoop out the flesh with a spoon.

Read this:

Wasim, sixteen, had turned the balcony of their Hyderabad flat into a small recovery corner for injured street dogs, with his mother's permission and a local vet's number stuck to the wall. He spent his pocket money on bandages and dog food. He made posters, ran an online group of forty volunteers, and once argued with the society secretary for an hour to let a limping puppy stay a week. His sister Minakshi teased him: "You'll marry a dog." But when a frightened mother dog finally let Wasim touch her, Minakshi saw his face, soft and fierce at once, and stopped teasing. At night he still sat up with the group chat, planning.

How many volunteers were in Wasim's online group?
Forty volunteers.
What does Wasim's face, soft and fierce at once, suggest he felt when the mother dog let him touch her?
Deep care and determination, showing how much this cause means to him.
How could Wasim keep his passion from wearing him out?
Share tasks with his volunteers and set some hours when he is off the group chat.
How did Minakshi's view change?
She moved from teasing him to respecting how much the cause meant to him.

Read this:

The bank's employee counselling room had a box of tissues and a window onto the car park. Reena had used six already.
"Eight months," she said. "Shankar sat next to me for eight months. He brought me tea. He told me about his mother's operation and the hospital bills. I gave him sixty thousand, a bit at a time."
Last week HR had found out that he'd told four other people the same story. His mother was fine. He'd resigned and stopped answering calls.
"I'm a credit officer," Reena said. "I check people's stories for a living. How did I not see it?"
The counsellor said, "People who do this are practised. They study what makes someone kind, and they use that. Being fooled by a skilled liar is not a failing in you. It says he was good at lying, not that you are foolish."
Reena looked at the car park for a long time.

How much money did Reena give Shankar?
Reena gave Shankar sixty thousand, a bit at a time.
Why does Reena feel so ashamed?
Reena checks people's stories for a living, so being fooled for eight months makes her question her own judgement and feel foolish.
What does the counsellor say that could help Reena?
The counsellor explains that practised liars study and use people's kindness, so being fooled says Shankar was skilled at lying, not that Reena is foolish.
How might the four other people HR found be feeling?
They are probably feeling the same shame and self-doubt as Reena, each thinking they alone should have seen through the story.

Read this:

In the physiotherapy department of the city hospital, the junior staff kept a whiteboard of who had handled the most patients. Ojas was always near the bottom, and it gnawed at him. One quiet afternoon he took out his first-month logbook. Back then he had needed help with every patient. Now he took his own cases and even trained the interns. He smiled for the first time in weeks. That night he left the staff group that posted rankings every day. He kept one colleague, Tejas, close, the calmest person in the department, and asked if he could watch how he explained exercises to older patients. Tejas said yes. Ojas made a note: check logbook monthly, ask Tejas, ignore the board.

Where did the junior staff track who handled the most patients?
On a whiteboard.
How was Ojas feeling before he looked at his logbook?
He felt low and anxious, gnawed at by always being near the bottom of the board.
What did Ojas do to keep comparison helpful?
He compared himself with his first month, left the ranking group, and chose Tejas as someone to learn from.
How might Tejas see Ojas's request?
Tejas would likely feel respected and glad to help a colleague improve.

Read this:

Last month Nitin trapped me by the water cooler. He kept grabbing my lunch box and laughing, and his friends blocked the way out. My heart was banging so hard I could hear it, and my face went hot. Then I shoved him hard. Later I sat in the office feeling sick with shame. I kept thinking, I'm not a pusher. I'm Dilnaz, the quiet one. Ms Rao, the counsellor, didn't shout. She asked what my body did first. I told her about my heart and hot face. "That's your body getting ready to fight," she said. "It doesn't make you a bad person." She said she would speak to Nitin's class teacher too. We practised what to do next time: step back and call a teacher.

Where did Nitin trap Dilnaz?
Nitin trapped Dilnaz by the water cooler.
How did Dilnaz feel sitting in the office afterwards?
Dilnaz felt sick with shame and confused, thinking "I'm not a pusher".
How did Ms Rao's question about the body help Dilnaz?
By asking what Dilnaz's body did first, Ms Rao helped Dilnaz see the shove as a fight reaction to being trapped, and they planned a safer step for next time.
How might Ms Rao see the shove differently from how Dilnaz first saw it?
Ms Rao sees it as a body reacting to being cornered, while Dilnaz first took it as proof of being a bad person.

Read this:

"The Berlin team replied," Mohit said, not looking up from his laptop. "They want a second interview."
"Oh. That's great." Sudha folded a kurta very carefully. "When?"
"Next Thursday."
"Great."
"You keep saying great."
"It is great. For you."
"For us, I hoped."
Sudha put the kurta down. "Mohit, my parents are getting older. Papa's knee. I told you I wanted to stay in Jaipur."
"I know. I just thought, maybe for two years..."
"Let's talk about it after the interview. No point before."
"Yeah. After."
He went back to the laptop. She went back to folding. Neither of them said what both were thinking: that "after" had been the answer for four months now.

When is Mohit's second interview?
It's next Thursday.
What does Sudha's repeated 'great' suggest about how she feels?
It suggests Sudha is hiding worry and hurt behind politeness, because the Berlin job pulls away from the life near family she wants.
What could Mohit and Sudha do instead of saying 'after' again?
They could set a real time before the interview to talk openly about Berlin, Jaipur and what each of them needs, even if it's uncomfortable.
What might Sudha's parents feel if they knew about the Berlin plan?
Sudha's parents might worry about losing her nearby support as they grow older, adding to the pressure she already feels.

Read this:

In Madrid, Lucia's C chord sounded muffled every time, like a pillow over the strings. Her teacher Santiago tapped her hand. "Your third finger is touching the second string. See? Slow down." At home that night she propped a mirror against the wall and played one note at a time, watching her fingertips. A tiny curve of the knuckle lifted the finger just clear. She strummed. The chord rang. She played it ten times more, then grinned at her reflection.

Where did Lucia watch her hand while she practised?
She watched her fingertips in a mirror propped against the wall.
What was Lucia feeling when the chord finally rang?
Delighted and proud, which is why she grinned at her reflection.
What else could Lucia do to keep the chord clear, and why?
She could check her finger position slowly at the start of each practice, so the habit stays right.
How does Santiago see Lucia's problem?
Santiago sees a small fixable finger position, not a lack of talent, and simply points to it.

metadata.subtype: Approach: using a teacher's feedback to correct errors [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Class teacher's note, Monday. At the lockers I overheard a boy ask Amandeep, "Nice book. Whose grandad did it belong to?" Others laughed. Amandeep's cheeks reddened, but he answered calmly, "It was my cousin's, and it still has every page." Then he went quiet for the rest of the break.
I asked him to stay after class. He said it was fine, and that he didn't want a fuss. I told him a book or a uniform says nothing about a person's worth, and that he should come to me if it keeps happening. I spoke to the boy privately and changed the seating.
Chandrika, who has a second-hand set herself, sat with Amandeep at lunch.
Mr. Dsouza

What did the boy ask Amandeep about his book?
He asked whose grandad the book had belonged to.
What might Amandeep be feeling after the remark, even though he replied calmly?
He is probably hurt and embarrassed: his cheeks reddened and he went quiet for the rest of the break.
What could Amandeep do if the teasing keeps happening?
He can keep answering calmly and tell Mr. Dsouza again, remembering that a book or uniform says nothing about his worth.
How might Chandrika have felt seeing this?
Since Chandrika has a second-hand set too, she probably understood the sting, and sitting with Amandeep at lunch shows her support.

Read this:

Hostel mentor's note: first-year check-ins, Block C. Ramesh, room 214.
In September Ramesh's laundry pile was a running joke; his friend Jahnavi from the next block once pinned a sign on it. Today his side of the room was the tidiest on the floor, and he had been to the campus gym four times this week.
When I asked what changed, he grinned and held up his earphones. There is a crime podcast he loves, and he only lets himself listen while washing clothes or on the treadmill. "If I want to know who did it, I have to be scrubbing socks." He said he cheated twice in the first week, then made it a real rule.
Jahnavi, passing by, said he now volunteers for his floor's laundry run.
Next check-in: October.

When does Ramesh let himself listen to the crime podcast?
Only while washing clothes or on the treadmill.
What does Ramesh's grin suggest about how he feels now?
Ramesh seems pleased and a bit proud; chores that used to pile up now come with something he looks forward to.
Why does Ramesh's rule work?
Linking a podcast he loves to dull tasks gives them pull, and keeping it strictly reserved after two early slips keeps that pull strong.
How might Jahnavi see the change in Ramesh?
Jahnavi, who once pinned a sign on his laundry pile, seems amused and impressed that he now volunteers for the laundry run.

metadata.subtype: Pairing a treat with a chore [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the playground of their Bengaluru apartment block, Thomas grabbed Ramesh's toy truck and ran off. Ramesh sat down and wailed.
Thomas's mother knelt beside him. "Ramesh is crying. He was playing with that. Can you give it back and say sorry?"
Thomas stared at Ramesh. Then he walked over, held out the truck, and gave him a clumsy hug round the neck. Ramesh stopped crying and took the truck.

What did Thomas grab from Ramesh?
Ramesh's toy truck.
What might Thomas have been feeling when he stared at Ramesh?
He may have been puzzled or a little uneasy seeing Ramesh cry, without fully understanding it was his fault.
What did Thomas's mother do that helped repair the moment?
She explained simply what happened and prompted him to give the truck back and say sorry.
How might Ramesh feel about the clumsy hug?
Ramesh probably felt comforted and less upset once he had the truck and the hug.

Read this:

At the anganwadi in the small town, Rehana yelled "I WANT THE RED BLOCKS!" across the room.

Dolma Teacher put one hand flat on top of her head, their signal. Rehana saw it, put her own hand on her head and said, much more quietly, "I want the red blocks, please."

"That's a lovely indoor voice. Thank you for trying," Dolma Teacher said, and handed them over.

At playtime in the field, Rehana screamed happily while being chased. Dolma Teacher only smiled. Outside, screaming for fun was fine.

What was the signal Dolma Teacher used?
She put one hand flat on top of her head.
What was Rehana feeling when she yelled for the red blocks?
She was probably eager and a bit impatient to get the blocks. Copying the signal shows she wanted to get it right once reminded, and she likely felt pleased at the praise.
What small step helped Rehana switch to an indoor voice?
The shared hand-on-head signal reminded her without a scolding, and praise for trying made her want to do it again. 👍
How does Dolma Teacher see Rehana's screaming in the field?
She sees it as fine and just smiles, because outside, screaming for fun is allowed.
Should "occured" have two r's?

Yes. The correct spelling is "occurred", with a double c and a double r. The final r doubles when you add -ed.
Example: The accident occurred near the school gate.
Exactly what length is the tunnel under the hill near the station?
I don't know the exact length, and I won't guess. The railway or highway authority publishes such figures.

Read this:

Harish, twenty-five, had been sent to run the new cold-storage unit outside Shahjahanpur, and on the first day he saw the problem. Workers from Rampur sat on the left, workers from Khera on the right, and the two villages had quarrelled over canal water for years. At lunch someone mimicked the Khera accent and got a laugh. Harish didn't laugh. "Not here. Anyone does that again, they explain it to me." Then he redrew the shifts. Every crew had two people from each village, rotating as loader, counter and checker, and all crews shared one target: the potato stock in by Holi without a single spoiled sack. Imran from Khera and old Bhola from Rampur were put on the same crew and argued for a week. By the third week Harish found them sharing tea on the loading dock, arguing about cricket instead.

What target did all the crews share?
The potato stock in by Holi without a single spoiled sack.
Why did Harish refuse to laugh at the mimicry?
He felt concerned that mocking one village would deepen the old quarrel, and was determined to show that mockery had no place in his unit.
Which of Harish's steps did most to soften attitudes, and why?
Mixing each crew with equal, rotating roles and one shared target, because working together as equals changes views more than a lecture.
What is it like for Imran and Bhola to be on the same crew?
At first it is uncomfortable and they argue for a week, but shared work slowly turns it into easy company over tea and cricket.

The writer joked about another way the whale could have carried Jonah. What was it, and why does he reject it?

But was there no other way for the whale to land the prophet within that short distance of Nineveh? Yes. He might have carried him round by the way of the Cape of Good Hope. But not to speak of the passage through the whole length of the Mediterranean, and another passage up the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, such a supposition would involve the complete circumnavigation of all Africa in three days, not to speak of the Tigris waters, near the site of Nineveh, being too shallow for any whale to swim in. Besides, this idea of Jonah's weathering the Cape of Good Hope at so early a day would wrest the honor of the discovery of that great headland from Bartholomew Diaz, its reputed discoverer, and so make modern history a liar.
The whale might have gone round the Cape of Good Hope. The writer rejects it because it would mean sailing all around Africa in three days, and the Tigris near Nineveh is too shallow for a whale.

Read this:

Tuesday night
The Singapore offer came today. Big job, new city, the freedom I've wanted since college. I'm Sahil, twenty-six, and I've spent six hours pacing. Papa's heart surgery was only in March. Ma can't manage the hospital runs alone. And Diwali without me would break her. So I made the list I always make. Freedom: huge. Security for them: huge. Tradition, being the son at home: smaller than they think, bigger than I admit. This time, security for them comes first. Not forever. I'll ask for the offer to be held a year. Dolma took her Berlin job last month and left her parents with her brother. I don't think she's wrong. Her family, her ranking. Mine is this, for now.

When was Papa's heart surgery?
Only in March.
How does Sahil feel about turning down freedom for now?
Sahil feels torn, pacing for hours, but settles on the choice with a kind of clarity after making the list.
What does Sahil do well in deciding, and what is the key choice?
Sahil names each value, decides that security for the family ranks first this time, and asks to hold the offer a year instead of giving up freedom forever.
How might Ma feel if Sahil stays home for the year?
Ma would likely feel relieved and supported, since she can't manage Papa's hospital runs alone and Diwali without Sahil would break her.

messages.content:
Read this:

Arnab, sulking because the guests finished the fish fry? Sit. Let your Lavanya Paati tell you about the payasam.

When I was ten, in Thanjavur, important guests came to see my elder sister. Amma made me wear my stiff silk skirt, sit on the mat with my knees together, and not say one word. Guests ate first, of course.

I watched them finish the whole vessel of payasam. My favourite. I smiled on the outside and burned on the inside.

After they left, I cried to Appa that the house was a stage and I was a doll on it.

He didn't scold. He scraped the vessel and gave me the last spoonful. "Outside face for guests, inside face for us," he said. "Both are true. Now eat."

What did the guests finish?
They finished the whole vessel of payasam.
What was young Lavanya feeling as she watched the guests eat?
She felt resentful and hurt, smiling on the outside while burning inside at losing her favourite dish.
What turning point helped young Lavanya accept the guest rules?
Appa didn't scold her; he gave her the last spoonful and explained that the house has an outside face and an inside face, both true.
How might Appa have seen Lavanya's tears?
Appa saw a child who had held herself together all evening, and wanted to comfort her rather than punish her.

Read this:

In the Jubilee Hills office of the event company, Avni stared at the photos from last night's wedding: orange marigolds everywhere, when the bride's family had asked for white. The family was furious. Avni had trusted Shreya, her new coordinator, with the entire décor order.

Avni felt let down, and then worse: foolish. Maybe she just couldn't hand things over.

Before saying anything to Shreya, she scrolled back through their chats. Her own instruction had been a two-minute voice note, recorded in a car, saying "the same flowers as the Reddy wedding." The Reddy wedding had been orange.

Avni closed her eyes. That was on her too.

She called Shreya in. "The flowers were wrong, and part of that is my unclear brief. From now on, every order gets a written sheet with colours and quantities, and you'll send me a photo of the sample before we confirm."

The next wedding, Shreya's sample photo came in two days early. The flowers were perfect.

What colour marigolds had the bride's family asked for?
They had asked for white.
How did Avni feel after seeing the wedding photos?
Avni felt let down and then foolish, doubting whether she could hand things over.
What did Avni do before blaming Shreya, and why did it help?
She checked her own instructions and found them unclear, so she could fix the process with written sheets and sample check-ins instead of taking the work back.
How might Shreya have felt when Avni admitted her brief was unclear?
Shreya probably felt relieved and more trusted, not solely blamed for the mistake.

Read this:

The colony water tank had a rusty ladder, and Yogesh was already halfway up. "Come on, Keerthana! Everyone's done it!"
Keerthana, ten, looked at the ladder. The third rung was bent. Her stomach felt tight.
"Chicken!" Yogesh shouted. The others started flapping their arms and clucking.
Her face went hot. If she didn't climb, they might not call her for cricket tomorrow. They might laugh about it at school.
She put one hand on the cold rail. Then she remembered Amma saying the tank was locked for a reason.
"I'll keep score for cricket instead," she said, her voice small.
Some of them kept clucking. Keerthana walked to the bench anyway, heart thumping, and didn't look back.

What was bent on the ladder?
The third rung was bent.
What was Keerthana worried about when they called her chicken?
She worried they would not call her for cricket tomorrow and would laugh about it at school.
Which choice at the ladder showed good judgement?
Remembering Amma's warning and offering to keep score instead kept her safe while still trying to stay part of the group.
What would change if one other child had also refused to climb?
Keerthana would feel less alone, the clucking might stop, and it would be easier for others to say no too.

Read this:

Santiago had worked at an investment bank in Madrid for three years. He was good at it. He also spent weekends volunteering with a river clean-up group and felt a pang every time he helped finance a new coal-linked project on Monday.
His friend Kwame, an engineer, said over tapas, "You talk about the river like it's your real life and the bank like it's a costume."
It stung because it was true.
Santiago didn't quit. He asked his manager about the bank's new sustainable finance team. He took an evening course on green bonds. He told his parents, who'd been proud of the "serious job," that he might earn a bit less.
Six months later he moved teams. The work was still finance; it was still hard. But on Monday mornings he no longer felt he was leaving himself at the door.

What did Santiago volunteer with at weekends?
A river clean-up group.
Why did Kwame's comment sting Santiago?
Santiago felt uncomfortable and exposed, because the comment named a split he already felt.
What did Santiago do to bring his work and values together?
He looked for a role inside the bank that matched his values, took a relevant course, and talked honestly with his parents.
How might Santiago's parents feel about the move?
His parents might worry about the lower pay but feel proud he found work he believes in.

Read this:

The park would close in fifteen minutes, and Dilnaz wanted a game. She looked at Arohi, who was on the swings. If she says no, I'll ask the twins by the slide, Dilnaz thought. "Arohi, want to play catch?" "Not now." Dilnaz didn't wait. She ran to the slide. "Want to play catch?" The twins nodded. They played till the whistle blew.

How long until the park closed?
Fifteen minutes.
What was Dilnaz thinking before she asked Arohi?
She felt ready and hopeful, with a backup plan in case Arohi said no.
What else could Dilnaz try if the twins also said no?
She could ask to join what they are already playing, since that might be easier.
How might Arohi feel seeing Dilnaz play with the twins?
Arohi might feel fine, since she wanted to swing, or a little left out.

Read this:

Day one. Minakshi, two months into the team, posted in the project chat: "What if we sent reminders by voice call for older customers?" Tushar read it on the metro and thought, that's good. That's really good. Then: why didn't I think of it?
Day three. The client call. The director asked for fresh ideas. Tushar's mouth was dry. Two seniors had been let go last quarter. He heard himself say, "I was thinking we could try voice-call reminders for older customers." The director nodded. "Great, Tushar, lead that."
Minakshi said nothing. On the way out Tushar told himself, it's a team, ideas belong to the team.
Day ten. Minakshi hadn't posted in the chat since. Tushar noticed. Every time he opened the project folder, his stomach turned slightly, like he'd borrowed something and hadn't returned it.

What did the director say after Tushar spoke on the call?
The director said, "Great, Tushar, lead that."
What was Tushar afraid of when he spoke on the client call?
Tushar was afraid of being let go like the two seniors and wanted recognition, so fear pushed him to present Minakshi's idea as his own.
At which moment could Tushar still have put things right?
On the call, or on Day ten when he noticed the silence, Tushar could have said the idea was Minakshi's and handed Minakshi the lead.
How has Minakshi been affected by what happened on the call?
Minakshi has stopped posting in the chat, which suggests Minakshi no longer feels safe sharing ideas with the team.

Read this:

The staff room of the government school in Nashik was quiet after the last bell. Shalini, twenty-four, was marking copies when her phone lit up: Kavitha, her college friend. "Last chance! Join my start-up. Double your salary, if we take off." Shalini looked at the steady line of her payslip taped inside her diary, and the list next to it: Appa's pension shortfall, her brother's fees, a small amount saved each month. She typed, "I'm staying. I need to know the rent will be paid." Her shoulders relaxed as she sent it. Then a little worry crept in. What if Kavitha succeeded and she'd missed it? She let the thought sit, then went back to marking. Certainty felt like enough, for now.

What did Shalini have taped inside her diary?
The steady line of her payslip.
What mixed feelings did Shalini have after she sent the message?
She felt relief as her shoulders relaxed, and then a small worry that she might be missing something if Kavitha succeeded.
What was Shalini's key choice, and what guided it?
She chose to stay in the steady school job because her family's needs, like her brother's fees, made certainty matter most to her.
How might Kavitha feel about Shalini's reply?
Kavitha may be disappointed to lose a friend on Kavitha's team, but may also understand Shalini's family responsibilities.

Read this:

At the college incubator in Kochi, Jomon's desk had a sign: 'Farm-to-canteen, fresh daily.' His venture supplied vegetables from nearby farms to three hostel canteens. The incubator mentor, Lokesh, asked him to present his numbers at the monthly review. Jomon's hands were shaking when he showed the slide. Spoilage was eating most of his profit. Two canteens paid late. "I think I should shut it," he said quietly. Lokesh didn't rush to comfort him. He asked, "What did you learn that the next version needs?" Jomon listed three things: cold storage, payment terms in writing, and fewer customers who pay reliably. He closed the venture that term. The next year he helped a new student team avoid the same mistakes.

How many hostel canteens did Jomon's venture supply?
It supplied three hostel canteens.
Why were Jomon's hands shaking during his presentation?
He was nervous and probably ashamed to show that his venture was losing money.
How did Lokesh's question help Jomon?
It turned a painful failure into a list of lessons, so the closure became useful rather than only a loss.
How might the new student team see Jomon's past failure?
They would see it as valuable experience that could save them from making the same mistakes.
Write an apology to a neighbour for noise last night. Keep it to three sentences and make the last one a promise starting with "I will".
I am sorry for the noise from our house last night. We had guests and forgot how late it was. I will keep the volume low from now on.

Retell this from Binita's point of view, in the first person.

At her sixth birthday in the society clubhouse, the lights went off and everyone started singing. Shalini had been racing around with Binita all evening. Now twenty grown-ups and children stood in a ring around her, every face looking her way. The candles glowed. Shalini's cheeks went hot. She pulled her frock over her knees, ducked her head below the table edge and whispered, "Stop singing." Binita crouched beside her. "Blow fast and it finishes," she whispered back. Shalini blew, then hid her face in Binita's shoulder, grinning.

At Shalini's sixth birthday in the society clubhouse, the lights went off and everyone started singing. Shalini and I had been racing around all evening. Now twenty grown-ups and children stood in a ring around her, every face looking her way. The candles glowed. Her cheeks went hot. She pulled her frock over her knees, ducked her head below the table edge and whispered, "Stop singing." I crouched beside her. "Blow fast and it finishes," I whispered back. Shalini blew, then hid her face in my shoulder, grinning.

Read this:

I'm Zeenat. Last Saturday I lost in the second round of the school chess tournament.

I moved my knight without looking and Amandeep took my queen. When we shook hands my eyes went blurry and I ran to the corridor.

Ms Pereira came out. She didn't say "don't cry". She sat on the bench next to me and said, "That hurts, doesn't it?" I nodded and cried properly. She just waited.

Then she asked, "Want to see what happened?" We set up the board and she showed me the knight move. "You'll never do that one again," she said.

After lunch there was a friendly game for everyone who was out. I almost didn't go, but I did. I lost that one too, but not because of my knight.

Who took Zeenat's queen?
Amandeep took Zeenat's queen.
What was Zeenat feeling after shaking hands with Amandeep?
Zeenat felt upset and disappointed, with eyes going blurry, and ran to the corridor to cry.
What did Ms Pereira do that another adult could copy?
Ms Pereira named the hurt, waited while Zeenat cried, then looked at the mistake calmly, which made trying again feel safe.
How might Amandeep have felt when Zeenat ran to the corridor?
Amandeep may have felt happy about winning but also awkward or sorry to see Zeenat upset.

This is from an old detective story. Rewrite it in everyday English.

One morning, at a little before seven o'clock, I was awakened by the maid tapping at the door to announce that two men had come from Paddington and were waiting in the consulting-room. I dressed hurriedly, for I knew by experience that railway cases were seldom trivial, and hastened downstairs. As I descended, my old ally, the guard, came out of the room and closed the door tightly behind him.

One morning, just before seven, the maid knocked on my door to wake me. She said two men had come from Paddington and were waiting in the consulting room. I dressed quickly, because I knew from experience that railway cases were rarely small matters, and hurried downstairs. As I went down, my old friend the guard came out of the room and shut the door firmly behind him.

"Amma, Ganga Masi has fever again and she's alone in Pune."
"I know, Nitin. I sent her a message this morning."
"What did you write?"
"Take rest, drink water, call if needed."
"She'll read that and feel lonelier."
"What else can we do from here?"
"Let me send a voice note. She always says our voices sound like the old house."
"Go on, then."
"Masi, it's Nitin. I'm sitting in the kitchen, Amma is frying pakodas and scolding me for eating them hot. Can you hear the oil? We'll save you some when you visit. Get well soon, Masi, please call when you wake."
Twenty minutes later the phone rang. Ganga Masi's voice was hoarse.
"Nitin! I heard the oil and your Amma scolding. I felt I was in the kitchen with you. Play me that again, na?"
"Masi, I'll send you a new one every evening."

What was Amma frying while Nitin recorded?
Amma was frying pakodas.
Why did Nitin think the typed message was not enough?
Nitin was worried that Ganga Masi, sick and alone in Pune, would read the short message and feel lonelier.
What made Nitin's voice note comforting?
Nitin brought Masi into the moment with kitchen sounds, Amma's scolding and a promise to save pakodas, so she felt part of home.
How did Ganga Masi experience the voice note?
Ganga Masi felt comforted and less lonely, as if she were in the kitchen with them, and wanted to hear it again.

Salma Apa, you know your Asif. Put me in a crowded room and I light up. Cricket after school, chai at the corner, the group call till midnight, I say yes to all of it. When everyone goes home and the house goes quiet, I feel flat, like a phone at two percent. Last Saturday some older boys from tuition said they were riding to the highway dhaba at night, three to a bike, no helmets. Everyone said yes, so I said yes too, before I'd even thought. Halfway there I felt sick about it and made them drop me at the petrol pump. I called Abbu to fetch me. He didn't shout; he just said, "Next time, call before." I think I say yes because I'm scared of the quiet, not because I want to go.

Where did the older boys say they were riding at night?
To the highway dhaba, three to a bike, no helmets.
What does Asif think lies behind saying yes to every plan?
Asif thinks the yeses come from being scared of the quiet, not from really wanting to go.
What choice did Asif make halfway to the dhaba?
Asif asked to be dropped at the petrol pump and called Abbu, stepping out of a risky plan.
How might Abbu have felt when that call came?
He was probably worried but relieved; he stayed calm and only asked to be called earlier next time.

Trisha, you're chewing your nails over this band audition, so let your Deepika Maasi tell you something.

When I was fifteen, our school started a band. They needed a drummer. I had been drumming on every tiffin box and table in Pune for years. Everyone told me to go.

And I said, very calmly, "I'll fail." I could see it: my sticks slipping, the music teacher frowning, the older boys smirking at a girl on drums. It didn't feel like a fear. It felt like I already knew, the way you know tomorrow is Tuesday.

So I didn't go. I sat at home and polished my shoes, of all things.

Two years later, at my farewell, the music teacher said, "Why didn't you ever try for the band? We never found a decent drummer."

I never found out if I'd fail. That's the part that still pinches. The forecast was the only thing that actually stopped me.

What did Deepika do at home instead of going to the audition?
She sat at home and polished her shoes.
Why did "I'll fail" feel like knowledge to fifteen-year-old Deepika?
She could picture the whole scene so clearly, the sticks slipping and the frowns, that it felt as certain as the day of the week. Picturing it vividly made the guess feel like a fact.
What turning point is Deepika Maasi hoping Trisha will choose differently?
Deepika is hoping Trisha goes to the audition despite the forecast, since staying home is the only way to be sure of never finding out. Going gives the prediction a chance to be proved wrong.
How might the music teacher's words at the farewell have felt to Deepika?
They probably stung, showing that the chance had been real all along. Hearing the band never found a decent drummer turned the old forecast into a regret.

Beta, sit. You're worried about your friend, so let me tell you about Wasim. I'm your Suraj Chacha; you know he was my closest friend. In 1998 the floods ruined his cloth shop in Bhagalpur. He was twenty-four. He sat on my verandah and said, 'It's over, Suraj. I'm finished.' I wanted to say, 'Don't talk like that.' But I didn't. I let him talk for an hour. He talked about the stock, his father's name on the board, his fear of facing the lenders. When he was quiet, I took a notebook. 'What can't we change?' The stock was gone. The season was lost. 'And what can?' He knew the weavers. He had customers who trusted him. 'One thing for tomorrow,' I said. He chose: visit the weaver in Nathnagar. That's all. He didn't cheer up that day. But he went. You can't order a man to hope, beta. You can only walk beside him.

What happened to Wasim's shop in 1998?
The floods ruined his cloth shop in Bhagalpur.
Why did Suraj Chacha hold back from saying 'Don't talk like that'?
He felt concern for Wasim and wanted him to feel heard, so he listened for an hour rather than brush aside Wasim's despair.
Which turning point helped Wasim move, and what can the listener learn for their own friend?
Splitting what couldn't change from what could, and then choosing one thing for tomorrow, gave Wasim a real step; the listener could do the same after first listening.
How might Wasim have felt being allowed to talk for an hour?
Wasim may have felt heard and less alone, which made it easier to think about what he could still do.

Monday. In the class chat Tejas wrote, "Yes, you can post my dance photo in the fest album, Hrithik." Hrithik did.
Thursday. Tejas opened his phone and saw the same photo in a big group of strangers, with a joke caption. His face went warm. He messaged Hrithik: "I said yes to the fest album, not this. Please take it down." For an hour there was no reply, and Tejas felt his chest tighten.
Saturday. Hrithik wrote, "Deleted it. I thought a yes was a yes for everything. Sorry." Tejas replied, "Ask each time, okay?" Hrithik sent a thumbs-up, and this time he added, "Can I share the fest photo on my page?" Tejas said, "Not today."

On which day did Tejas say Hrithik could post the photo?
He said so on Monday, in the class chat.
What was Tejas feeling on Thursday when he saw the photo in the big group?
He felt embarrassed and anxious, shown by his warm face and tight chest. He might also have felt betrayed, since he had agreed only to the fest album.
What should Tejas do if someone pressured or threatened him about sharing more pictures?
Not give in, keep the messages, and tell a trusted adult or report it to the school or platform.
How might Hrithik have understood the first yes?
He may honestly have thought one yes covered any sharing, until Tejas explained that it did not.

Jasleen, sit a minute. Twice this week you've told me you might be coming down with something before Thursday's board meeting. Let me tell you about Rakesh.
When I was twenty-five, at the insurance office in Chandigarh, Rakesh sat beside me. Clever man. And every time he had to present to the regional head, the day before there'd be a headache, or his mother visiting, or 'I've had no time at all.' I'll admit I resented it a little; I was presenting too, and I had no excuses.
Then one evening I said to him, 'Rakesh, if you try your best and it's ordinary, that's allowed. We'll still sit together at lunch.' He laughed at me: 'Alka, you sound like my mother.' But the next time, no headache. His talk was a bit dull, and he was fine.
So, Jasleen. Try fully. Ordinary is allowed.

Where did Alka work at twenty-five?
At the insurance office in Chandigarh.
How did young Alka feel about Rakesh's excuses, and why?
Alka resented them a little, because Alka was presenting too and had no excuses to lean on.
What did Alka choose to say to Rakesh, and why did it help?
That trying his best and being ordinary was allowed, and they would still sit together at lunch; it made an imperfect result safe, so the excuse was no longer needed.
How might Jasleen hear this story, given the week's talk of coming down with something?
Jasleen may feel gently caught out on recognising the pattern, but also relieved that an ordinary, honest try at Thursday's meeting would be welcome.

The career counselling room at the Jaipur school had a poster of a tree with branches labelled with jobs. Yash, fifteen, sat opposite Aadhya Ma'am with his aptitude report. 'Language and social reasoning, very high,' she said. 'Numerical, average.' Yash looked at his shoes. 'Papa wants me to take science. Everyone in the family did.' 'And you?' 'I like history. And I write for the school paper.' 'Hmm. What do you imagine doing at twenty-five?' He hesitated. 'Maybe journalism. Or law?' 'Both fit your strengths. Shall we invite your father for a meeting? You can show him this report, and I'll explain the options in humanities.' Yash let out a breath. 'Will you be there?' 'Of course.'

What were Yash's strongest areas in the aptitude report?
Language and social reasoning.
Why did Yash look at his shoes when talking about his father?
He was worried about disappointing his father and the family tradition of science.
What step did Aadhya Ma'am suggest to handle the family expectation?
A meeting with his father where Yash could share his report and she could explain humanities options.
How might Yash's father feel at the meeting?
He might be surprised or anxious at first, but seeing the evidence could help him support Yash's choice.

Indu had woken Zubin at one, three and five, each time with the same dream about the lift getting stuck. That afternoon in their Dadar flat, she held up a drawing. "Pappa, look, it's you!" "Indu, I'm on a call, stop pestering!" Her face crumpled. Zubin ended the call, knelt, and looked properly: a man with huge eyebrows and a smile. "I'm sorry. I'm so tired my brain is broken." That evening he asked Indu's Nani to keep Indu on Saturday night so he could sleep. Indu packed her own toothbrush, delighted.

What was Indu's dream about?
The lift getting stuck.
What was Indu feeling when her face crumpled?
She felt hurt and pushed away, having wanted to share her drawing and getting a snap instead.
What was a wise step Zubin took after apologising?
He asked Nani to keep Indu on Saturday night so he could get real sleep, rather than just trying harder.
How might Zubin feel after snapping at Indu?
He probably feels guilty and foggy, aware that his own sleep debt, not the drawing, caused the snap.

Irawati's email to the department coordinator, Siddharth, said only: "Sir, regarding the form. Please check. Thanks." She pressed send and felt done. Two days later there was no reply. She met Siddharth in the corridor, and he said, "Which form? Check what? I get sixty emails a day." Her cheeks burned. That night she wrote again. Subject: "Internship form: signature needed by 12 October." First line: "Could you please sign the attached internship form by 12 October?" Then two lines on why. Siddharth replied the next afternoon: "Signed. Collect it from the office."

What did Irawati's first email say?
It said: "Sir, regarding the form. Please check. Thanks."
How did Irawati feel when the coordinator asked "Which form? Check what?"
Embarrassed, since her cheeks burned.
What change to the second email made it work?
A specific subject line, the request in the first line and a deadline date.
How does Siddharth's inbox explain the missing reply?
He gets sixty emails a day, so a vague message with no clear request is hard to act on and easy to skip.

In the school counsellor's office, Rashmi sat stiffly, handbag on her knees. "Pihu is just rude now. She shouts at me, locks her door, won't eat with us. I'm tired of it." Vandana, the counsellor, nodded. "That sounds exhausting. Can I tell you what Pihu's teachers see? She's gone very quiet in class, stopped art club and sits alone." Rashmi's face changed. "She loved art." "Sometimes when teenagers pull away and snap, it's a sign they're struggling, not attitude. What if tonight you just say you're worried and listen?" That evening Rashmi knocked, sat on the edge of Pihu's bed and said, "I'm worried about you, not angry." Pihu cried for a long time. The next day Rashmi booked the doctor's appointment Vandana had suggested.

What club did Pihu stop going to?
She stopped going to art club.
How was Rashmi feeling when she first sat in the office?
She felt tired and angry, seeing Pihu's behaviour only as rudeness.
What helped Rashmi approach Pihu differently?
The counsellor shared what teachers saw and suggested speaking with concern, not blame, so Rashmi said she was worried, listened and then booked a doctor.
How might Pihu have felt when her mother said she was worried, not angry?
Pihu may have felt relieved and finally safe enough to let her sadness out, which is why she cried.

Pradeep, you asked why I looked so miserable after the district debate. So here's the thing. The judges give you a feedback card, right? Mine had ten lines. I've read it maybe thirty times, so I know it by heart. 'Strong opening.' 'Excellent rebuttal.' 'Good eye contact.' 'Well-researched.' Five more like that. And one: 'Spoke too fast in the closing.' And I swear, the only line I could hear was that last one. Too fast. I walked out of the hall thinking I'd embarrassed the whole school. My mother said, 'Indu, how did it go?' and I said, 'They said I talk too fast.' That's it. That's all I told her. Only today, reading it out to you, did I notice I'm holding a card that mostly says I was good.

What did the one critical line on the card say?
It said, 'Spoke too fast in the closing.'
Why did that one line stick so hard for Indu?
Indu felt hurt and embarrassed by the criticism, so attention locked onto that one line and the nine pieces of praise faded into the background.
What could Indu try when the next feedback card arrives?
Read the whole card aloud, count the good lines as well as the critical one, and then pick the closing speed as the one thing to practise.
What would change if Indu's mother had read the card?
She would likely have seen mostly praise and felt proud, instead of hearing only that her child talks too fast.

Siddharth: hey, you ok? you sighed about twenty times at robotics practice 😅
Pankaj: sorry. just a lot
Siddharth: you skipped mess lunch again too. third day
Pankaj: no time. lab record due fri, TA duty, cousin's wedding calls every night
Pankaj: and I forgot to order the motor driver for the robot. that one's on me
Siddharth: no lecture, promise. what can I take off your plate?

Siddharth: I'll place the parts order tonight. and I'll bring you a plate from the mess tomorrow at 1

Pankaj: the order list is in the team folder
Siddharth: found it. order placed. go sleep 🙂

How many days in a row had Pankaj skipped mess lunch?
Three days; Siddharth says it is the third day.
What does Siddharth's "no lecture, promise" suggest about how Siddharth feels?
Siddharth is concerned and caring, and wants Pankaj to feel safe admitting the slip instead of feeling judged.
Why was asking what to take off Pankaj's plate more useful than advice?
It removed real work, the parts order and the lunch trip, instead of adding one more thing for Pankaj to think about.
What is it like for Pankaj to get this offer?
Pankaj is surprised at first ("...seriously?") and then relieved, since one task is lifted and someone has noticed without scolding.

"She cancelled again?" Asif asked, handing Raghav a glass of chai on the hostel terrace.
"Her train got delayed. Third time." Raghav stared at his phone. "Ishani says next month for sure."
"Five months, man. Not one video call?"
"She's shy on camera. I told you."
Asif hesitated, then turned his own phone around. "Someone in my class got the same messages. Same poems, same shy on camera, from a different name. The pictures are a model's."
Raghav read it. His jaw worked. "I told her about my dad's surgery. I told her things I haven't told you."
"I know."
"I'm such an idiot."
"You're not. You were honest with someone who wasn't. That's on them."
Raghav put the chai down. "It still feels like someone died."
"Then it's okay to feel that," Asif said, and sat down beside him.

Where are Raghav and Asif talking?
They are talking on the hostel terrace, over chai.
What does Raghav mean when he says it feels like someone died?
He feels real grief for the person he believed in, even though she never existed as he knew her.
What could Raghav do now that he knows?
He could stop replying, report the profile, send nothing more, and keep talking to Asif or a counsellor about the hurt and shame.
What was it like for Asif to show Raghav the proof?
Asif hesitated, likely dreading the hurt it would cause, but chose honesty and then stayed beside Raghav instead of mocking him.

"You're pacing. Is it the Monday meeting?" Ganga asked from the sofa.
"The boss walks in with that face and I forget every word. Last week I said nothing about the delayed vendor file."
"Did it get sorted?"
"No. It's still stuck. If I say so, the boss will snap."
"Maybe the face has nothing to do with you. Write it down. Two lines: what is stuck and what you need."
"In an email? Before the meeting?"
"Then it's on record, and you don't have to fight the mood in the room."
Tushar stopped pacing. "Okay. I'll send it tonight. And I'll stop guessing what the face means."
"Good. Now sit. Your tea has gone cold."

What was stuck at Tushar's office?
The vendor file was delayed and still stuck.
Why does Tushar stay silent about the vendor file?
Tushar fears the boss will snap, and the boss's face makes every word vanish from Tushar's mind.
What could Tushar try so the problem does not blow up later?
Send a short email with what is stuck and what is needed before the meeting, so the issue is on record without facing the mood.
How might the boss see receiving that email?
The boss would likely see a clear, early warning they can act on, rather than a surprise later.

Sunaina: the pop-up flopped. sold 20 cakes out of 80. it's all my fault
Shalini: ok. before "all", let's do the pie chart thing

How many cakes did Sunaina sell out of 80?
Sunaina sold 20 cakes out of 80.
How did Sunaina feel right after the pop-up, and how did that change?
Sunaina felt it was all Sunaina's fault and was discouraged, then calmer and more balanced after slicing the causes.
Why is the pie chart useful here?
It lets Sunaina own a 25% share with concrete fixes, pricing and earlier posts, without carrying the rain and the back lane too.
How might Shalini feel about Sunaina's new plan?
Shalini seems pleased and supportive, joking about a tent to keep things light.

Dear Vinita di,
Ammi must have told you I topped the second-semester statistics paper. Please don't make a big deal of it when you call. It genuinely means nothing. The paper was easy, everyone says so, and half the questions were from last year. If it had been hard, I'd have been in the middle like always.
You'll say I'm doing the thing again. Maybe. When I failed the programming practical in first year, I told you it proved I wasn't cut out for engineering. I still think that. So I know it looks odd that the failure counts and this doesn't. But the practical was real. This was a fluke.
Anyway, how is Pune? Is the new flat warm enough?
Rafiq

Which paper did Rafiq top?
Rafiq topped the second-semester statistics paper.
Why does Rafiq insist that topping the paper 'means nothing'?
Accepting the success would challenge Rafiq's belief about not being cut out for engineering, so calling the paper easy keeps that belief safe.
What question could Vinita di ask to help Rafiq see the pattern?
Vinita di could ask why the failed practical counts as 'real' but the topped paper is a 'fluke', and whether both results might count as evidence.
How might Vinita di feel reading 'Please don't make a big deal of it'?
Vinita di may feel proud but also sad, seeing Rafiq unable to enjoy a real achievement and quick to change the subject.

Class 5, Monday. Teacher's note.
Vandana's new bicycle was stolen from the school stand on Friday. This morning Pranav told his group, "It happened because she's always talking in class. God punished her." Vandana heard it and went very quiet.
I asked Pranav to stay back. "Do you think only naughty people lose things?" He said yes, because that is fair. I asked if he remembered when his own tiffin was stolen last year. He did. "Were you naughty?" He shook his head, looking unsure.
We talked about how bad things can happen to good people, and that thinking otherwise can hurt them twice. I've also informed the principal about the theft and asked for a lock at the stand. Tomorrow, circle time on this.

What happened to Vandana's new bicycle?
It was stolen from the school stand on Friday.
Why does Pranav believe Vandana deserved the theft?
He feels that the world should be fair, so it seems to him that only naughty people lose things, which feels safer to believe.
How did the teacher respond, and why is it a good approach?
The teacher reminded Pranav of his own stolen tiffin, talked about bad things happening to good people, and asked for a lock, protecting Vandana and teaching fairness.
How might Vandana feel hearing Pranav's comment?
Vandana probably feels hurt and ashamed, blamed on top of losing her new bicycle.

Kaito and Nadia were sitting on the swings in the park behind their block in Osaka, their school bags in the sand, when Nadia said, "Can I tell you something? You can't laugh."

"I won't."

"My parents are separating. Dad's moving out next month. I've known since summer." She pulled at a thread on her sleeve. "I haven't told anyone."

Kaito felt proud she had picked him, and scared he would say the wrong thing. He almost made a joke about the loud neighbours to lighten it, then stopped. "That sounds really hard. Thanks for telling me."

They swung slowly for a while.

"Please don't tell the others at school."

"I won't. It's yours to tell." He paused. "Have you talked to any adult about how you're feeling? Like your aunt, or Ms Tanaka?"

"Not really."

"Maybe your aunt? You said she's easy to talk to."

Nadia nodded. "I'll call her tonight."

Where were Kaito and Nadia sitting?
They were sitting on the swings in the park behind their block in Osaka.
What two feelings did Kaito have when Nadia confided in him?
Kaito felt honoured that she chose him, and scared of saying the wrong thing.
What did Kaito do well in this conversation?
He listened, held back a joke, kept the secret private, and gently encouraged Nadia to talk to a trusted adult like her aunt.
What is it like for Nadia to share this after keeping it since summer?
Nadia may feel nervous but relieved to stop carrying it alone, especially when Kaito does not laugh. 🤍

At the tractor dealer's tent at the Sonpur fair, the salesman slid a form across the table. "Only for fair days, Yogesh-bhai. Sign today and the rotavator comes free." Yogesh turned the pen over in his fingers. The man was friendly and the machine was shiny, but half the terms were printed so small he'd need Usha's reading glasses. "Give me all the terms in writing," he said. "I'll come back tomorrow." The salesman's smile thinned. "Tomorrow maybe the offer is gone." "Then it wasn't much of an offer." That night, under the lantern, Usha read every line aloud. The interest was higher than he'd been told, and the free rotavator had a charge buried on page three. Next morning they went to the cooperative society office and to another dealer at the far end of the fair, and compared. Yogesh walked past the first tent without stopping. The salesman called out a new, lower price. Yogesh just waved.

What did the salesman say would come free if Yogesh signed today?
The rotavator.
What was Yogesh feeling as he turned the pen in his fingers?
Yogesh felt tempted by the shiny machine but uneasy and cautious about the tiny print he couldn't read.
Which steps protected Yogesh?
Asking for all the terms in writing, waiting a night, having Usha read every line, and comparing with the cooperative and another dealer before deciding.
What does the salesman's new, lower price suggest?
It suggests the fair-days deadline was pressure rather than a real limit, and that the salesman still wanted the sale.

Monday. A stranger messaged Tenzin in a game chat. "You are so mature for your age. Not like the other kids." Tenzin felt his cheeks warm and sat a little taller. Wednesday. The stranger wrote again. "Our chats are special. Don't tell anyone, not even your parents." Tenzin's stomach went tight. He remembered a school talk about secrets that make you uneasy. Friday. He stopped replying and told Binita Ma'am, his class teacher, at the end of the day. She stayed with him and said, "This is not your fault. You have done nothing wrong. Thank you for telling me." She told the school safeguarding lead and helped him tell his parents that evening.

On which day did Tenzin tell Binita Ma'am?
He told her on Friday.
What did Tenzin feel on Monday, and what changed by Wednesday?
On Monday he felt flattered, his cheeks warm and sitting taller; by Wednesday the request to keep it secret made his stomach go tight and uneasy.
What should a child do when a stranger flatters them and asks for secrecy?
Stop replying and tell a parent or teacher, as Tenzin did with Binita Ma'am 🤍.
How might Binita Ma'am see Tenzin's decision to tell her?
As a brave and sensible step: she stayed with him, said it was not his fault, told the safeguarding lead and helped him tell his parents that same evening.

Vishal, you're asking whether to keep Nishant home from the school trip. Let me tell you what I did with you. At nine you were scared of swimming lessons. First I shouted, "Just jump in," and pushed you to the edge. You shook so hard you were sick. So then I stopped the lessons completely. No pool, no worry. But your fear only grew; soon you wouldn't even walk past the pool. Your Amma said, "Neither way is working, Madhav." So we tried small steps. One day, only sitting by the pool. Then feet in the water. Then the shallow end, me beside you, saying, "You're scared, and you're doing it." It took the whole summer. By Diwali you swam a length and grinned at me.

What was Vishal scared of at nine?
Vishal was scared of swimming lessons.
What did Madhav want when the lessons were stopped completely?
Madhav wanted to shield Vishal from worry after the pushing went badly; the feeling behind it was an anxious protectiveness.
What was the turning point in Madhav's story?
When Amma said neither way was working, Madhav switched to small steps with warm encouragement beside the pool.
How did young Vishal experience the small steps compared with being pushed?
Being pushed made Vishal shake and be sick, while small steps with Madhav alongside let Vishal face the pool and finally grin after swimming a length.

"That paragraph doesn't make sense," Minakshi said, tapping Bhavna's essay. "Which part?" Bhavna asked, gripping her pencil. "The second line. I can't tell who 'they' is." Bhavna groaned. "I'm so bad at this." Minakshi shook her head. "You're not. I'm saying that line is unclear, not that you are. Should I read it aloud so we can hear it?" Bhavna nodded. As Minakshi read, Bhavna said, "Oh, I meant the villagers. I wrote 'they' too early." She fixed it. Then she added, "Can you tell me when something works too? I only hear the bad parts." Minakshi laughed. "The last paragraph made me smile."

What did Minakshi say was unclear?
Minakshi said the second line was unclear, because it was hard to tell who 'they' is.
Why did Bhavna say she was bad at writing?
She seemed to feel stung and to take the comment about the line as being about her, which is a common reaction to criticism. Her tight grip on her pencil shows her tension.
What did Minakshi do that made her feedback easier to use?
Minakshi pointed to one line, said the line was unclear and not Bhavna, and offered to read it aloud together.
What would you advise Bhavna to do when she hears feedback next time?
Ask which part it refers to, as she did, and ask for what works too.

Before: On the first day of the Puja holidays, Bidisha sat in her Didima's front room doing the lighthouse jigsaw. She had finished it three times already. When her cousin Gargi opened a new box of tangram shapes, Bidisha shook her head. "Those are boring."
During: On Ashtami, while the aunties went to the pandal, Gargi spread the shapes on the floor and made a swan, then a running man. Bidisha did the lighthouse again. Once, when nobody was looking, she picked up a triangle, turned it, could not see where it went, and put it straight back.
After: On Dashami, Gargi showed everyone a boat she had built herself. The uncles clapped. Bidisha hugged the lighthouse box to her chest and said she did not like new puzzles anyway.

How many times had Bidisha already finished the lighthouse jigsaw?
She had finished it three times already.
Why does Bidisha put the triangle straight back?
She feels nervous and a little embarrassed when she cannot see where it goes, and going back to the lighthouse feels safe because she already knows she can do it.
How could an adult help Bidisha try the tangram shapes?
An adult could sit with her and make a silly, wrong shape on purpose, laughing at it, so that not knowing feels normal and she can try one small piece at a time.
How might Gargi see Bidisha during the holidays?
Gargi may think Bidisha is just bored or stubborn, not seeing that Bidisha is afraid of getting it wrong and is missing out on learning something new.

Week 1, Monday: Ojas, twenty-one, bought two lottery tickets at the counter near the station, same as every morning. Nothing again. "Twenty-three days without even a small prize," he told Trisha. "It has to hit soon."
Week 3, Thursday: He was buying ten a day now, with part of his stipend. "The longer it goes, the closer I am," he said. Trisha frowned. "Each draw starts from zero, Ojas. It doesn't know about the other days."
Week 5, Saturday: Ojas skipped their movie night, saying he was short of cash. When Trisha borrowed a pen from his bag, a thick bundle of losing tickets slid out. She sat down next to him. "Can we talk about this? I'm not angry. I'm worried."

How many tickets a day was Ojas buying by week 3?
He was buying ten a day.
Why does 'the longer it goes, the closer I am' feel true to Ojas?
Ojas feels hopeful that each loss is a step toward a win that is owed, so buying more seems like making sure he is there when it finally comes.
Why was Trisha's 'I'm not angry. I'm worried.' a good choice?
It lets Ojas talk without feeling judged, which is more likely to help him stop than a lecture.
What are the five weeks like from Trisha's side?
Trisha watches a friend drift from a small habit to skipping plans, and the bundle of tickets turns her unease into real worry.

Disha, you want Ammi to pack your bag every night? Let your Rehana Dadi tell you about your Abbu, Arif. When he was nine, I packed his bag every single night. He never once looked at the timetable. Then my cousin's wedding came, in Hyderabad, and I was away three days. The first morning, Arif packed alone. He put in Monday's books on a Thursday, because Monday was the only day he remembered. No science book, no English notebook. His teacher sent a note home with 'unprepared again' underlined twice. When I came back, he was waiting at the door, not to hug me, but to ask, 'Ammi, how do I read the timetable?'

How long was Rehana away for the wedding?
Three days.
How might young Arif have felt when the teacher's note came home?
He probably felt embarrassed and helpless, having never learned to read the timetable himself.
What choice in the story could have prevented Arif's trouble?
Arif learning to pack from the timetable himself, with his Ammi checking at first, instead of her doing it every night.
How did Arif's teacher see those days?
The teacher only saw a boy arriving without the right books and underlined 'unprepared again', not knowing his mother usually packed for him.

messages.content: Explain this to a four-year-old, please: The moon looks different each night because we see different amounts of its sunlit side.
The moon looks different on different nights. The sun shines on one half of the moon. Each night we can see a little more or a little less of that bright half.
Reception pe poochna hai ki report kab milegi. Kaise puchun?
Ask: "Excuse me, when will my report be ready?" If you want to ask about the day, say: "Could you tell me when I can collect my report?"

Rewrite in formal English:

The lift's broken again, so you'll have to take the stairs till they fix it.
The lift is out of order again, so please use the stairs until it has been repaired.

Monday. Deepika stared at x² + 5x + 6 = 0 for twenty minutes. The textbook's steps might as well have been in another language. She was close to tears when her brother Eshaan said, “Ask the AI to explain it like you're twelve.” She did, and it broke the steps into small pieces: find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5.
Wednesday. She asked for five practice questions and solved them all on paper before looking at the answers. Three right, two wrong. She asked why the wrong ones were wrong.
Saturday. Class test. Deepika solved four equations with no phone in sight and got three right. She told Eshaan, “It didn't do it for me. It sat next to me while I did it.”

How many practice questions did Deepika ask for?
Deepika asked for five practice questions.
How did Deepika feel on Monday?
Deepika felt frustrated and close to tears after twenty minutes with no progress.
What could Deepika do if the tool's explanation is still unclear?
Deepika could ask her teacher or ask the tool to explain in a different way, since another route may click when the first does not.
How might Eshaan see her progress?
Eshaan is probably pleased, since his suggestion helped, and her sentence about the tool sitting next to her shows she did the work.

At Farhan Bhai's bag shop, Madhav held up the blue bag with the rocket on it. "I like this one better. Please?"

Farhan Bhai named the price. Mummy winced; it was almost double the plain grey one, and the electricity bill was due. "Madhav, I can't do this one this month."

"But the grey one looks like an old man's bag! And the rocket one has a bottle pocket. Mine always leaks on my books."

Mummy thought. "The pocket is a fair reason. Farhan Bhai, does any cheaper bag have a bottle pocket?"

Farhan Bhai pulled down a green one with a side pocket. No rocket. Madhav frowned, then grinned. "Can I draw a rocket on it myself?"
"Deal."

What did the green bag have?
A side pocket.
What was Madhav feeling when Mummy said she couldn't buy the rocket bag this month?
Disappointed and a bit frustrated, which is why he pushed back with reasons like the leaking bottle.
How did Mummy keep Madhav's trust while saying no?
She explained the limit honestly, took his bottle-pocket reason seriously and found a cheaper bag that met that need.
How might Farhan Bhai see the negotiation?
Farhan Bhai likely sees a family watching its spending and helps by bringing out a cheaper bag with a pocket instead of pushing the dearer one.

Evening in the village, and Sharmila had just come back from the fields, her feet dusty and her back aching. Before she could sit, Minakshi ran up. "Amma! Madhu broke the pot at the well and he fell in the mud, he looked so silly!" She laughed and flapped her arms like him falling. "And he didn't do his homework!" Madhu stood behind the door, his face red. Sharmila closed her eyes. "Minakshi, enough." Minakshi's smile faded. She had expected Amma to say, good girl for telling. Madhu glared at her and went to the back of the house. He didn't call her for their usual game of stones that night.

What did Minakshi say Madhu broke?
She said he broke the pot at the well.
What did Minakshi expect when she told Amma?
She hoped Amma would praise her as a good girl for telling, so she felt let down when Amma said 'enough' and her smile faded.
What went wrong, and what could fix it?
Mocking and reporting Madhu only tired Amma and hurt Madhu; Minakshi could say sorry to Madhu, and Amma could later talk to each child calmly and separately.
How does Madhu feel after being mocked in front of Amma?
He feels humiliated and angry, so he glares at his sister and skips their usual game of stones.
