At five, Madhav flopped on the floor ten minutes into a rainy afternoon. "I'm bored. What now?" Papa Vijay pulled out a big cloth, some clothes pegs and a torch. Madhav grumbled, then built a cave, and the afternoon was gone.
At fifteen, Madhav had begun building a small robot arm for the school fair in March. It was October. The first weeks were exciting. By December, he found the wiring dull and the arm still barely moved. One evening he pushed the tools aside. "This is so boring. I'll never finish." His friend Wasim looked at the pile. "You've done more than you think. Remember how it looked in October?" Madhav remembered the cave and how he had turned a flat afternoon into something he liked. He split the work into a small weekly goal, played music while he soldered, and stuck a photo of the first version above his desk. His science teacher stopped by. "Show me on Friday whatever you have." Madhav picked up the screwdriver and began again.

In which month was the school fair for which Madhav was building the robot arm?
It was in March.
How does Madhav's way of meeting boredom at fifteen connect to what he did at five?

At five he turned a flat afternoon into a cave with a cloth, pegs and a torch. At fifteen, during a months-long project, he met boredom with the same inventiveness, using small weekly goals and music, and kept going despite setbacks.
What was Madhav feeling when he pushed the tools aside and said it was so boring?
He felt discouraged and doubtful about finishing, with the boredom of the wiring making the goal seem far away.
What could Madhav do if progress on the robot arm slows down again?
He can review his old photo and weekly goals, ask Wasim or the science teacher for a check-in, and take a short break before starting again.

Every one knows that by the peculiar cunning of their gills, the finny tribes in general breathe the air which at all times is combined with the element in which they swim; hence, a herring or a cod might live a century, and never once raise its head above the surface. But owing to his marked internal structure which gives him regular lungs, like a human being's, the whale can only live by inhaling the disengaged air in the open atmosphere.

Why must a whale come up to the surface when a fish need not?
A fish breathes through gills, taking air from the water. A whale has lungs like a person, so it can only breathe the open air above the sea.

I posted a short video about how my college's fest threw away trays of food every night. I thought I was being honest. By morning it had been shared by pages I'd never heard of, and there were over five hundred comments calling me ungrateful, attention-seeking, a liar.
My thumbs were already typing. I had a whole reply ready, full of capital letters. Charu, my roommate, just said, "Read it again tomorrow. If you still want to post it then, post it."
I sat on the bed and argued with myself. Right now I'm angry. Anything I write now, they'll screenshot. Tomorrow I'll still be right, if I'm right. So I saved the draft and put the phone in Charu's cupboard.
The next day I read the draft and cringed. I deleted it. The comments slowed on their own by evening. I'm Salma, and waiting was the smartest thing I did that week.

How many comments were there by morning?
There were over five hundred comments.
What was Salma feeling while the reply was being typed?
Salma was angry and hurt, typing a reply full of capital letters after being called ungrateful and a liar.
What else could Salma have done during that waiting day?
Salma could have talked it through with Charu or another trusted person, which would help sort the fair comments from the cruel ones.
How might Charu have felt holding the phone in the cupboard?
Charu may have felt protective and a bit anxious, wanting to help without taking over Salma's choice about replying.

Irawati's diary. Bengaluru. Late.

Papa fell in the bathroom in Indore this morning. He's fine, only a bruise, but I heard it from Kamal-uncle next door, not from Papa. Papa said on the phone, "Why worry you for nothing?"

I sat at my desk after the call and cried. I'm six hundred kilometres away building a career while my parents get older without me. Should I quit and go home? I love this job. I love them more. It feels like choosing.

But crying at my desk isn't helping them.

So tonight I made a list. Video call every evening at eight, not just Sundays. Book a trip home for Diwali now, not "sometime." Ask Kamal-uncle if he'd check on them each morning, and pay a local helper to come in daily. Tell Papa honestly that I'd rather know about small falls than find out later.

Love can travel, I think. It just needs a timetable.

Who told Irawati about Papa's fall?
Kamal-uncle next door.
What was Irawati feeling after the call with Papa?
Irawati felt guilty and torn between loving the job and loving the parents more, crying at the desk.
What did Irawati decide to do, and why is it wise?
Irawati planned daily calls, booked a Diwali trip, arranged a morning check and a helper, and asked Papa for honesty, turning guilt into action.
How might Papa see Irawati's request to hear about small falls?
Papa may have hidden it to protect Irawati from worry, so the request could feel both loving and a little uncomfortable.

I'm Jyoti, and I was sitting opposite Vishal in our university canteen in Manila, three weeks into the exchange. He wanted more water, so he lifted his hand, palm up, and curled one finger at the server. She came, but her face had gone flat, and she set the jug down harder than needed. Vishal didn't seem to notice, or maybe he did; he rubbed the back of his neck afterwards. Our classmate Marites leaned over and said quietly that many people here use that sign only for dogs. Vishal went red. Marites showed us how she calls someone: palm down, fingers scooping towards herself, exactly like my grandmother does back home. The next day I saw Vishal raise his hand, palm down, scoop gently and smile at the same server. She smiled back.

How did Marites show she calls someone?
Palm down, fingers scooping towards herself.
What might Vishal have been feeling when Marites explained the sign?
He went red, which suggests he felt embarrassed; rubbing his neck earlier may mean he already sensed something was off, or it may have been nothing.
What did Vishal do well the next day?
He used the palm-down scoop Marites showed and added a smile, which showed respect for how people there call someone.
How did the server seem to see Vishal's finger beckon?
Her flat face and the jug set down hard suggest she felt treated rudely, as if called like a dog.

Meaning of invention, please.
what does "make up your mind" mean
How old is my neighbour?
Can you fix my sentence? She doesn't has a car.

1. Invention means a new thing that someone has made or thought of. It is a noun.
2. It means to decide. For example: please make up your mind about the colour of the cake.
3. I don't know, because I can't see your neighbour's details. If you wish to know, you could politely ask.
4. Corrected: She doesn't have a car. Why: after "doesn't", use the base form "have".

My name is Nikita. In Class Five I got a low mark in the maths test, and I put the paper at the bottom of my bag. The paper needed my mother Arohi's signature. Every evening I told myself, "Tomorrow." At dinner I talked very loudly about anything else. The paper felt heavier each day, like a stone I had to carry to school and home again. On the fifth day, my mother stopped stirring the dal and said, "You've been quiet in a strange way. Is something on your mind?" My voice shook. I took out the paper. She said, "Thank you for showing me. Let's look at it together," and I cried a little.

Where did Nikita put the maths paper?
At the bottom of the bag.
What was Nikita feeling every evening while saying "Tomorrow"?
Afraid and burdened. The paper felt heavier each day, like a stone Nikita had to carry.
What made the first admission easier for Nikita?
Arohi stopped stirring, asked calmly what was on Nikita's mind, and then said "Thank you for showing me. Let's look at it together."
How might Arohi have felt watching Nikita talk loudly about anything else?
Concerned and puzzled. Arohi noticed the strange quiet and gave Nikita a calm chance to say what was wrong.

Vinita, I have to tell someone, so it's you. I'm Payal, and three weeks ago I did something I'm not proud of.
My manager asked me to put an earlier date on a supplier contract, so it looked signed before the audit period. I said, 'Okay, sir.' That's it. Two words. I was so scared of being the new girl who makes trouble, of losing the job I waited a year for. So I changed it, printed it, filed it. I told no one.
Since then I can't sleep properly. Every time the audit team walks past, my stomach drops. It's my initials on the file, not his.
And yesterday he came to my desk again. Another contract. 'Same as last time, na?' As if it's normal now. As if I'm the person who does that.
I said I'd do it after lunch. I didn't. It's still on my desk.
So that's why I called you, Vinita. I don't know how to undo it. I only know I can't do it again.

What did Payal's manager ask her to do?
Put an earlier date on a supplier contract.
What is Payal feeling now?
Guilty and frightened, losing sleep and dreading the audit team, especially since her initials are on the file.
What could Payal do now about both contracts?
Leave the second one unchanged, write down both requests, and talk to a trusted senior, HR or the ethics channel about correcting the first.
How might Vinita feel hearing this?
Worried for Payal but glad she spoke up, and likely keen to help her find the right person to tell.

You're asking me if it's okay to change your mind, Shalini? I changed mine in the middle of Class 11. Let me tell you how.

I'm Parul. I'd wanted to be a doctor since I was eight. My whole family was proud. So in Class 11, I studied chemistry every single evening. Two hours. Tuition on Saturdays. And my tests came back 40, 42, 39. Not because I was lazy. I just wasn't getting it.

One day I cried in the washroom after a test and my class teacher sent me to the counsellor. I was ashamed to say it out loud, but I did: "Maybe medicine isn't for me."

She didn't argue. She asked what I liked. Statistics, I said. The one chapter in maths I always finished first. She showed me data science programmes. I'd been avoiding that idea for a year because it felt like giving up.

It wasn't giving up. It was steering.

What were Parul's chemistry test scores?
How did Parul feel admitting "Maybe medicine isn't for me"?
Parul felt ashamed saying it aloud, after crying in the washroom, but it also opened the way forward.
What else could Parul do while switching paths?
Parul could explain the change to the family with what the counsellor showed, so the pride they felt can move to the new plan.
How might the counsellor see Parul's shift?
The counsellor likely feels glad Parul spoke honestly, and sees the change as a sensible response to clear feedback.

messages.content: How do I make a jug of lemonade? Use exactly five numbered steps and keep each step under ten words.

1. Squeeze two lemons into a jug.
2. Add four spoons of sugar.
3. Pour in a litre of cold water.
4. Stir until the sugar dissolves.
5. Add ice and serve in glasses.

Deepak was clearing his cupboard in the flat when a small keychain fell out from under his old geometry box. It was the plastic turtle Mahima had given him. He waited for the familiar clench in his chest, the heat behind his eyes, the speeches he used to rehearse in the shower. It didn't come. Only a kind of tiredness, as if he'd been carrying a heavy bucket for months and just noticed his arm ached. She had not apologised. She probably never would. He wasn't letting go because she deserved it. He was tired. He dropped the turtle into the donation bag, felt lighter, and went to help his mother in the kitchen. He did not text Mahima. The door was closed, and that was fine.

What fell out from under Deepak's geometry box?
A plastic turtle keychain that Mahima had given him fell out.
What did Deepak feel when he held the turtle?
Tiredness rather than anger. He compares it to carrying a heavy bucket for months and finally noticing his arm ached.
What did Deepak do that shows healthy letting go?
He put the turtle in the donation bag and did not text Mahima, so he released the anger without reopening the door.
How might Mahima see this if she knew?
She might not realise, since she never apologised, and letting go for Deepak is about his own peace, not about her earning it.

In the small town of Kottayam, Joseph worked as an accounts clerk at a rubber cooperative and wanted to become a web developer. For a year he'd bought random online courses and finished none.
One evening at his friend Sahil's phone repair shop, he borrowed a notebook. "I'm going backwards this time," he said. He had printed ten job ads for junior web developers from the district town and the city.
He read them aloud and tallied. "Ten want basic web languages. Eight want one framework. Six want a portfolio site. Four want some database work." Then he wrote what he already had: "Spreadsheets. Some database from the cooperative's stock system. That's it."
Sahil leaned over. "So what's first?"
"The basics, then the framework they all mention, then a portfolio. The database I half have." Joseph crossed out three of the random courses on his phone. "The ads decide. Not me guessing."

How many ads wanted a portfolio site?
Six ads wanted a portfolio site.
What does Joseph's crossing out of courses suggest he is feeling?
It suggests he feels clearer and more determined, relieved to stop guessing after a year of unfinished courses.
What else could Joseph do with the list of gaps?
He could set a rough order and timeframe for each gap and check it with a working developer, so the plan stays realistic.
How might Sahil see Joseph's new approach?
Sahil seems curious and supportive, asking what comes first and watching his friend finally make a clear plan.

In the Edinburgh flat, Mina sat opposite Nkechi at the table. Dinner was ready and the candles were lit for their anniversary. Nkechi's laptop was open beside the plate, and every few minutes Nkechi's eyes slid to it. “Sorry, one second,” Nkechi said, typing. Mina watched the noodles go cold. Once, Mina said, “How was your day?” and the answer was, “Fine, busy,” without a glance. Mina cleared the plates alone, said, “It's fine,” and went to bed early. It wasn't quite fine. It was the fourth time this month that Mina had felt like the last item on a very long list. Nkechi didn't notice, and Mina said nothing.

What was the occasion for the dinner?
The candles were lit for their anniversary.
What did Mina feel while saying “It's fine” and going to bed early?
Mina felt hurt and lonely, like the last item on a long list, but kept it unspoken.
What could Mina say or do the next day to be heard without a big argument?
Mina could tell Nkechi calmly that dinner time matters, and suggest a laptop-free hour that evening.
How might Nkechi see the evening?
Nkechi probably sees a busy day and a short delay, and does not realise how absent Nkechi seemed to Mina.

Night fell over the paddy fields. Sangeeta, the neighbour, carried Irfan to the edge of the field, where hundreds of tiny lights were blinking in the grass.
Irfan went quiet. Then, in a soft, breathy voice, he said, "Ooh... light." He pointed, and whispered again, "Light."
Sangeeta whispered back, "Fireflies." Irfan didn't take his eyes off them.

Where did Sangeeta carry Irfan?
To the edge of the paddy field.
What was Irfan feeling when he whispered "Ooh... light"?
He was full of awe and wonder at the blinking fireflies, which made his voice soft and breathy.
What did Sangeeta do that matched Irfan's mood?
She whispered back and named the fireflies, keeping the moment quiet and shared.
What would change if Sangeeta had spoken loudly?
The quiet wonder might have been broken, and Irfan could have lost that moment of awe.

- Quick one: why do birds fly south or to warmer places in winter?
- How can I stay safe while using the internet?

1. They go where food is easier to find. Because insects and plants become scarce in the cold, while warmer places still have enough to eat.
2. Do not share your address, school or passwords with strangers. Tell a trusted adult if something online makes you uncomfortable.

Financial literacy counsellor's note, community centre, Saturday.
Sunaina, 25, came with her mother, Ganga. Sunaina has been paying her mother's rent, her younger sister's school fees and her uncle's hospital bills since her father's death two years ago. She has no savings and said, "I feel guilty if I say no to anyone."
Ganga looked surprised. "I didn't know she was paying for my brother too."
We did not decide amounts for them. We listed every expense, what Sunaina earns, and what she wants for her own future. They agreed on a fixed monthly amount for rent and fees, for the next three years, until her sister finishes school. Sunaina will keep a small savings every month. Ganga will speak to her brother's sons about his bills.
Sunaina said, "It's the first time it feels like a plan, not a hole."
Next step: review in six months.

How long has Sunaina been paying the family's costs?
Since her father's death two years ago.
What does Sunaina feeling guilty if she says no suggest?
It suggests she felt pressured and overwhelmed, unable to set limits, with no savings of her own.
Why did the counsellor not decide amounts for them?
Letting Sunaina and Ganga decide together, with clear figures in front of them, makes the plan their own and more likely to feel fair and guilt-free.
How might Ganga feel learning Sunaina was paying for her brother too?
Ganga seems surprised and perhaps sorry, realising how much her daughter had been carrying alone.

Thursday
Mock exam tomorrow and my brain is already saying the usual thing: you always freeze. Every single time.
Himani told me to test it instead of believing it. So here goes. Times I froze: the Class 12 physics board paper, the first-year maths mid-sem, the viva in March.
Times I did NOT freeze: the chemistry mid-sem (got 38/40), the English presentation, the second maths test, the lab exam in April.
Huh. That's four against three. So "always" is wrong.
What was different when I didn't freeze? I'd slept properly. I'd done a full practice paper under a timer. And I started with the question I knew best, not question one.
When I froze, I'd stayed up late and started with question one no matter what.
So tomorrow: sleep by 11. Start with the easiest question.
Tarun

What did Tarun score in the chemistry mid-sem?
Tarun got 38/40.
How does Tarun feel about the mock exam at first, and what shifts that?
Tarun feels anxious, with the old voice saying "you always freeze", and becomes steadier after finding four times of not freezing.
What did listing the counter-examples show Tarun to work on?
That sleep, timed practice and starting with the easiest question made a difference, so those became tomorrow's plan.
How might Himani feel on seeing this list?
Himani would probably feel pleased and encouraged that testing the belief worked better than just believing it.

Monday of winter sports week. The kho-kho captains picked teams in the school ground. Raghav was picked last. He walked to his team with his hands in his pockets.
Wednesday. At the park, his cousin Kashish called, "Come play cricket!" Raghav stayed on the swing. "Nobody ever chooses me. I never win anything. Why bother?" Kashish said, "You won the chess thing last month." "That doesn't count."
The next Saturday. At the Lohri gathering, the older cousins were picking teams for tug-of-war. Kashish was a captain. "Raghav!" she called first. Raghav blinked. His team lost, but he laughed so hard he fell in the grass. On the way home he said, "Maybe it's not never. Maybe it was just Monday."

What game were the captains picking teams for on Monday?
They were picking teams for kho-kho in the school ground.
Why did Raghav stay on the swing on Wednesday?
Raghav felt hurt and discouraged after being picked last once, and had stretched it into a rule that nobody ever chooses him.
What did Kashish do that helped break the rule?
Kashish reminded him of the chess win and later picked him first, giving real evidence against "never".
How might Kashish have felt when Raghav said the chess win didn't count?
Kashish was probably puzzled and a bit sad, seeing her cousin ignore a clear win.

In the school hall in Rotterdam, the poetry prize was the last thing announced before the holidays. Elif, eleven, had written about her grandmother's garden. Her best friend Vera had written about the sea. When Mr Jansen said, "The winner is Vera Kowalczyk!" Elif was the first on her feet, clapping and whistling, which she'd only just learned to do. Vera went bright red. Elif felt warm all over; she'd heard Vera read that poem aloud on the tram and knew it was good. Then, as Vera walked up for the book token, Elif thought of her own poem, still folded in her bag, and a small ache came and sat quietly beside the warmth. On the way out, she hugged Vera anyway. "Read it to me again on the tram?"

What did Vera's winning poem describe?
Vera wrote about the sea.
What shows that Elif feels real warmth for Vera, even with the small ache?
She's first on her feet, whistling, and hugs Vera afterwards asking to hear the poem again; the ache sits beside the warmth rather than replacing it.
What small step could Elif take with her own folded poem?
She could share it with Vera on the tram too, or ask Mr Jansen for feedback, turning her wish into her next try.
How might Vera feel hearing Elif's whistle first?
Vera probably feels embarrassed but delighted, knowing her best friend is proud of her.

"So, two months on the testing team," Rajni said, closing her laptop. "How was it, honestly?"
Jeevan took a breath. "Better than before. I actually learned the automation tools. But I'm still doing a lot of manual checks, and my pay hasn't moved since I joined."
"Are you telling me you're leaving?"
"No. I'm telling you I'd like to stay six more months, with it written down." He slid a page across. "By March: I write automated tests for two full modules on my own. And we discuss a pay revision at the March review."
Rajni read it twice. "That's fair. I'll put a review in both our calendars for 15 March."
"Thanks." He hesitated. "And if it doesn't happen, I'll be honest with you then."
"Meaning you'll have a plan?"
"Meaning I'll already have one." He smiled a little. "My CV's updated. It's just sitting in a folder."

What date did Rajni set for the review?
She set the review for 15 March.
How does Jeevan seem to feel when he slides the page across?
He seems nervous but determined, taking a breath before speaking and hesitating once, yet asking clearly for the written goal.
What else could Jeevan do to make the March review go well?
He could keep a short monthly note of the tests he writes, so the review rests on clear evidence of the goal.
How does the plan look to Rajni as his manager?
Rajni sees a fair, clear request instead of a sudden resignation, and knows what to support so he stays.

Give me the gist of this meeting at Pemberley.

She had instinctively turned away; but stopping on his approach, received his compliments with an embarrassment impossible to be overcome. Had his first appearance, or his resemblance to the picture they had just been examining, been insufficient to assure the other two that they now saw Mr. Darcy, the gardener's expression of surprise, on beholding his master, must immediately have told it. They stood a little aloof while he was talking to their niece, who, astonished and confused, scarcely dared lift her eyes to his face, and knew not what answer she returned to his civil inquiries after her family. Amazed at the alteration of his manner since they last parted, every sentence that he uttered was increasing her embarrassment; and every idea of the impropriety of her being found there recurring to her mind, the few minutes in which they continued together were some of the most uncomfortable of her life. Nor did he seem much more at ease; when he spoke, his accent had none of its usual sedateness; and he repeated his inquiries as to the time of her having left Longbourn, and of her stay in Derbyshire, so often, and in so hurried a way, as plainly spoke the distraction of his thoughts.

Elizabeth meets Darcy unexpectedly in the grounds of his house. He is polite and asks after her family, but both are embarrassed, and he keeps repeating his questions. Elizabeth is confused by his changed manner and feels very uncomfortable.

Diary, Friday night
I've been hiding something all week. A person in my game chat called Tigerclaw asked where I study, and I TOLD them. We chatted every night after that. Mumma had said no chatting with strangers. My tummy has hurt for days.
Tonight Bidisha didi found me crying in the bathroom. She said, "Whatever it is, Mumma will help. Come."
I told Mumma with my eyes on the floor. I waited for shouting. Instead she held my face and said, "Thank you for telling me. We are on your side, always." We blocked Tigerclaw together, and Papa wrote to the school so they know.
I feel so much lighter. I wish I had said it on the first day.
Yash

What did Yash tell Tigerclaw?
Where Yash studies.
Why did Yash hide the chats all week?
Yash felt ashamed and scared of being shouted at for breaking Mumma's rule.
What made telling Mumma easier, and what could Yash do sooner next time?
Bidisha didi's push helped; next time Yash could tell on the first day, since Mumma was on Yash's side.
How did Mumma see Yash's confession?
Mumma was grateful to be told and saw it as a reason to protect Yash, not to punish.
What does comments mean in 'please leave comments below the video'?

Comments are short remarks or opinions that people write about something. It is a noun, in the plural here.
Example: Several viewers left kind comments below the video about the dance.

Centre or center: which is correct?

Both are correct. "Centre" is British, and "center" is American. Indian English usually follows the British spelling.
Example: The shopping centre is next to the bus stand.

Why does Jane cry while she studies?

One day I had come to my studies in lower spirits than usual; the ebb was occasioned by a poignantly felt disappointment. Hannah had told me in the morning there was a letter for me, and when I went down to take it, almost certain that the long-looked for tidings were vouchsafed me at last, I found only an unimportant note from Mr. Briggs on business. The bitter check had wrung from me some tears; and now, as I sat poring over the crabbed characters and flourishing tropes of an Indian scribe, my eyes filled again.
She had hoped a letter would bring news she had waited a long time for. It was only an unimportant business note from Mr. Briggs, and the disappointment made her cry.

Teacher's note - Suraj, Class 8 science, Thursday
During group work, I assigned Kishore to Aarush's table. Aarush looked at Kishore, rolled his eyes and said, "Ugh. Not him," in a voice meant for everyone. His lip curled as Kishore sat down.
Kishore went very still. Then he said, calmly, "That's not a nice way to talk to me." He picked up his notebook and moved to the empty chair at the next table.
I was impressed. He didn't shout or trade insults, even though his hands were shaking.
After class I spoke to Aarush privately about how contempt, even without swear words, damages trust in a group and hurts people. He muttered that he "didn't mean anything." I told him his face had said plenty.
I checked in with Kishore at lunch. He said, "I just didn't want to sit where someone thinks I'm nothing." I'm keeping an eye on the pair.

What did Aarush say when Kishore was assigned to his table?
"Ugh. Not him."
What was Kishore feeling when Aarush curled his lip?
Kishore felt hurt and humiliated, his hands shaking, sensing that Aarush thought he was beneath him.
What did Kishore do that was wise?
He named the effect calmly and moved to another table, instead of retaliating.
How might Aarush have seen his reaction?
He claimed he "didn't mean anything," perhaps not noticing how much his eye-roll and tone said.

Monday: Dhruv told Chinmay his family was keeping Paryushan, and that on the last day everyone asks forgiveness. A classmate sniggered, "Jain rules are so weird." Chinmay laughed along, then felt uneasy.
Saturday: Dhruv invited him to the Jain temple near their Ahmedabad pol. Chinmay took off his shoes, kept quiet, and whispered questions. "Why does your family eat before sunset?" "So fewer tiny creatures are harmed," Dhruv's Dada explained, and told him that on the last day people say "Michhami Dukkadam", forgive me if I hurt you.
Sunday: Dhruv folded his hands. "Michhami Dukkadam, Chinmay." Chinmay folded his too. Next day, when the classmate said "weird" again, Chinmay said, "It's not weird. Ask Dhruv. He'll explain."

What did Dhruv's Dada say Michhami Dukkadam means?
It means forgive me if I hurt you.
Why did Chinmay feel uneasy after laughing along?
Chinmay felt uneasy and a little guilty, sensing the "weird" comment was unfair to his friend's faith.
What did Chinmay do that shows curiosity and respect?
He took off his shoes, kept quiet in the temple, asked questions, and later answered the classmate instead of laughing along.
How might Dhruv see Chinmay folding his hands?
Dhruv likely feels respected and happy that his friend joined the forgiveness ritual 🙏

In the office pantry, Uday was complaining. "My bonus vanished again. And my salary account is always empty by the 25th. How are you never broke?"
Yogesh opened a spreadsheet on his phone. "One sheet. Everything I have and everything I owe, once a month. And every rupee coming in and going out, whatever it's called: salary, bonus, a gift from my aunt. To me, it's all one pool."
"But you have those labelled savings pots too. Trip, Laptop, Emergency."
"Those are just tools. They help me remember what the money is for. But when I decide anything, I look at the whole sheet first."
Uday frowned. "So the bonus doesn't feel like free money?"
"It feels nice. But it goes on the same sheet as the rent."
Uday took a photo of the column headings. "Can you show me this on Saturday?"

When does Uday's salary account run empty?
Uday's salary account is always empty by the 25th.
How does Yogesh seem to feel about money decisions?
Yogesh seems calm and steady, because one sheet shows the whole picture before any decision.
How does Yogesh use labelled pots without letting them mislead?
The pots remind Yogesh what money is for, but every decision starts with the whole sheet, where a bonus sits beside the rent.
How does Uday feel by the end?
Uday feels curious and hopeful, asking Yogesh to show the sheet on Saturday.

It was his sister Mahima's birthday, and Jagdish, twenty-four, had promised to be home by seven. At five, his team lead messaged: a client wanted changes to the report by tomorrow morning. The office was emptying. His phone buzzed with a photo of the cake. Jagdish felt the old reflex: stay late, say yes, prove himself. Then he opened the report. Most of the changes were small. He estimated two hours. He messaged his lead: "I'll finish the main edits by 6:30 and the rest by 9 a.m. tomorrow. Is that okay?" The reply came: "Fine." He worked fast, logged off at 6:30 and caught the bus. At home, Mahima was blowing out candles when he walked in. She threw a cushion at him. "You came!"

What time had Jagdish promised to be home?
By seven.
What did Jagdish feel pulled to do when the client's request came, and why?
He felt pressured by the old urge to stay late and say yes to prove himself, even at the cost of his promise.
Why was Jagdish's message to his lead a good way to set a boundary?
It offered a clear, realistic plan that met the client's needs without giving up his evening, so both sides were respected.
How might Mahima have felt if he hadn't come?
She'd likely have been hurt and disappointed, since it was her birthday and he had promised.
Report this without quotation marks: Mother said to Ravi, "Wash your hands."
Mother told Ravi to wash his hands.

Sunday night. Dear diary, today I dropped an easy catch in the last over and we lost the match. I wanted to dig a hole in the ground. Nitin muttered, "Great job," and looked away. My eyes stung all the way to the bus. Then Diya sat next to me and said, "Everyone drops one. I dropped two last week." She shared her orange slices. My chest felt looser. If everyone was like Nitin, I would be scared to even hold a ball. Tomorrow I will go to practice and take catches. Maybe.

- Varun

What did Diya say to Varun on the bus?
She said, "Everyone drops one. I dropped two last week."
How did Varun feel after Diya spoke, and what does it change for Varun?
Varun felt relieved and less alone, as Varun's chest felt looser, and Varun now plans to go to practice and take catches.
How could Varun get that confidence back at practice?
By taking catches one at a time with kind teammates like Diya close by. 🙂
What might Diya be trying to do when she says she dropped two last week?
Show that dropping a catch is normal, so Varun does not feel alone or scared to play.

Rewrite this dialogue as a short paragraph with no quotation marks. Aparna is the one asking the riddle.

"Okay, riddle. Three friends ate lunch: one had rice, one had roti, one had noodles. Charu didn't have rice. Aparna didn't have roti or noodles. Who had noodles?"
Charu scratched her head. "Wait. Aparna didn't have roti or noodles."
"So?"
"So Aparna had rice!"
"And?"
"I didn't have rice... so I had roti or noodles. The third friend?"
"Didn't have roti."
"Then I had roti, and the third friend had noodles!"
Aparna clapped. "Step by step."

Aparna gave Charu a riddle. Three friends ate lunch: one had rice, one had roti and one had noodles. Charu didn't have rice, and Aparna didn't have roti or noodles. Who had noodles? Charu scratched her head and worked it out. Since Aparna didn't have roti or noodles, Aparna had rice. Charu didn't have rice, so she had roti or noodles. The third friend didn't have roti. So Charu had roti, and the third friend had noodles. Aparna clapped and praised her for going step by step.

Having descended the hill the general after whom Pierre was galloping turned sharply to the left, and Pierre, losing sight of him, galloped in among some ranks of infantry marching ahead of him. He tried to pass either in front of them or to the right or left, but there were soldiers everywhere, all with the same preoccupied expression and busy with some unseen but evidently important task. They all gazed with the same dissatisfied and inquiring expression at this stout man in a white hat, who for some unknown reason threatened to trample them under his horse's hoofs.

What does Pierre try to do after he loses sight of the general, and how do the soldiers look at him?
He gallops in among the infantry and tries to pass in front of them or to the right or left, but there are soldiers everywhere. They all gaze at him with a dissatisfied, inquiring look.

The client wanted the revised floor plans by six, and the office generator kept tripping in the heat. Madhuri had drawn the staircase three ways already. Each time, a message from Pankaj popped up: 'Send me what you have.' 'Why that width?' 'Wait, let me look first.' By two o'clock she noticed she had stopped choosing anything. She sent even the door swings to him and sat staring at the frozen screen, waiting. When the power came back, she walked to his desk. 'Pankaj, I know the deadline's tight. But when every step goes past you, I stop trusting my own eye, and we lose time. Can we check in at three and at five, and I decide in between?' He rubbed his neck. 'Fair. Three and five.' She finished the staircase by half past four.

Two sentences, please: what is this passage about?

Pankaj keeps asking Madhuri to send him every drawing detail, until she stops trusting her own eye and waits for him. She asks him to check in only at three and five, he agrees, and she finishes the staircase by half past four.

After tuition, Jagdish walked slower than usual so that Sonal would reach the bus stop first. She didn't; she waited for him under the neem tree.
"You didn't call last night," she said.
"Tired," he said, which was partly true. What he couldn't say was that their nightly calls had started to feel like homework he had never chosen. On Saturday he had hinted, "Maybe we both need more time with friends?" and she had laughed and texted him twice as often.
Now she held out a keychain she had made with his initials. "For your bag."
He took it, said "Nice," and felt worse.
His friend Omkar, who had watched from the tea stall, asked later, "Are you two okay?"
Jagdish shrugged. "She's too much these days."
Omkar looked at him for a moment. "Or are you just not saying something?"

What did Sonal give Jagdish at the bus stop?
She gave him a keychain she had made with his initials, for his bag.
What was Jagdish feeling when he took the keychain and said 'Nice'?
He felt guilty and trapped, because the calls had come to feel like unchosen homework, yet he could not bring himself to say so.
What could help break this cycle of hints and clinging?
Jagdish could say plainly and kindly what he feels instead of hinting about more time with friends, so Sonal is not left guessing and holding on harder.
What is it like for Sonal when Jagdish goes quiet and slow?
Sonal senses a change without knowing what it is, so she waits, asks about the missed call and makes him a gift, trying to hold on.

Board exams were a week away, and Arnab was supposed to be revising. Instead, stuck at home during a heatwave with the power flickering, he spent an hour scrolling edited photos of models and influencers. Smooth skin. Perfect teeth. Studio light.
When he caught his reflection in the dark phone screen, he felt plain, almost ugly. He couldn't focus on his notes at all.
The next day at the school's revision class, it was hot and crowded. Vasudha had a pimple on her chin. Someone's shirt was untucked. Everyone looked tired and real. Arnab realised he felt fine. Normal. Like one of the group.
Walking home, he thought: my face didn't change overnight. What I was comparing it to did. That evening he left his phone in the kitchen while he revised.

Where did Arnab catch his reflection?
He caught his reflection in the dark phone screen.
What was Arnab feeling after an hour of scrolling edited photos?
He felt plain, almost ugly, and too unsettled to focus on his notes.
What choice did Arnab make that evening, and why does it help?
He left his phone in the kitchen while he revised, which cut down the edited images he kept comparing himself with.
How might Vasudha see the revision class compared with Arnab's night of scrolling?
Vasudha probably saw an ordinary hot, tired class, not knowing it helped Arnab feel normal again.

At the playgroup in Durban, Nour fell off the little slide and cried. Zanele toddled over and patted her back, pat, pat, pat, exactly the way her own mother patted her at bedtime. Nour kept crying. Zanele patted harder, then looked round for a grown-up.
By home time, Zanele was worn out. She dragged her blanket to her mother, held it up and whined until she was wrapped in it and lifted.

Where did Nour fall from?
The little slide.
What was Zanele feeling when she held up her blanket at home time?
She was tired and wanted comfort, so she asked to be wrapped up and lifted.
How could the grown-ups support Zanele's patting?
Notice it warmly and then step in to comfort Nour properly, since Zanele is copying care but can't fully soothe a friend yet.
How might Nour experience Zanele's patting?
Nour might feel a little less alone, though she keeps crying and needs an adult too.

Naveen spent twenty minutes at the bathroom mirror of their Chennai flat, staring at the pimple on his chin. At the school annual day, he was sure every head in the hall turned toward it. He kept his hand over his face during the prize list. Afterwards his friend Harish slapped his back. "Why were you hiding? Nobody's looking at you, machan. They're looking at their own phones." Naveen didn't believe him. That night he typed in his notes: "No one understands. Nobody has ever felt this stupid." The next morning, his older cousin, visiting from Bengaluru, laughed at breakfast about her own "volcano chin" at sixteen. Naveen looked up, surprised.

Where did Naveen spend twenty minutes?
At the bathroom mirror of their Chennai flat.
Why did Naveen keep his hand over his face during the prize list?
He felt self-conscious and embarrassed, sure every head in the hall was turned toward his pimple.
What could help Naveen feel less alone?
Hearing stories like his cousin's and talking with friends, which show that others have felt exactly the same.
How does Harish see the situation?
Harish thinks nobody was looking and finds the hiding a bit funny, not realising how exposed Naveen feels.

The plan I wrote for the dance society app was beautiful: event calendar, ticket booking, member profiles and a photo gallery, all in ten days. I'm Sudha, and I had only just started learning the app framework.
By day four I had a calendar that crashed if two events fell on one date, and nothing else. That evening Vidya, the society secretary, asked if we could still use it for the fest. I heard myself say 'maybe' and knew that meant no.
So I sat on the hostel stairs with my plan and asked one question: what does the fest actually need? A calendar, and a way to see who is performing when. I crossed out booking and the gallery. Profiles became a plain list.
For the next six days I only fixed and polished the calendar. It went live two days before the fest. Nobody asked about the gallery.

What happened on day four when two events fell on one date?
The calendar crashed if two events fell on one date.
What did Sudha feel after answering Vidya with 'maybe'?
Sudha felt uneasy and a bit ashamed, knowing 'maybe' really meant no, and that pushed a rethink of the plan.
Which approach would have suited Sudha better from the start?
Planning just the calendar first and adding booking or a gallery only once it worked would have avoided losing four days.
How does the app look to Vidya and the dance society at the fest?
For them it works and does what they need; they can see who is performing when and do not miss the extras.

Shreya, you're going to laugh. When I was twenty, your Samir chacha got dumped by a girl named Farah, in the college library of all places. And what did I do? I went home and drew a flow chart. Farah's family, my exams, the distance between our hostels, some theory about "secure" and "insecure" people from a psychology book. Three pages, with arrows. I showed it to my roommate Joseph and said, "You see? This was never going to work."

Joseph read it all and said, "Nice arrows. You haven't cried once."

I was furious with him. But that night I went for a walk by the river and, finally, it came. All of it. The chart was right about some things. It just wasn't the point.

Where was Samir dumped?
Samir was dumped in the college library.
Why did drawing the flow chart feel reasonable to young Samir?
Young Samir was hurt, and turning the breakup into arrows and theory felt clever and safe, keeping the pain at a distance.
What turning point in the story let Samir finally feel it?
Joseph's remark, "You haven't cried once," stung, and that night's walk by the river let the feelings come.
How might Joseph have felt reading the three pages?
Joseph was likely concerned, seeing a friend hide hurt behind neat theory, so he spoke honestly.

Monday: Four boys in Jeevan's lane turned up for evening football in the same shiny sports shoes with a famous logo. Jeevan looked at his old rubber ones, split at the toe, and said he had homework. He watched from the window instead.
Tuesday: At dinner he blurted, "Amma, everyone has those shoes except me." Amma put down her spoon. "Thank you for telling me straight. We can't buy them this month. Let's talk again at Diwali. But are your friends your friends because of shoes?"
Jeevan didn't answer.
Friday: Vinita from next door banged on the gate. "We're one player short! Come on!" Nobody looked at his feet. He scored twice. Walking home muddy, he realised he hadn't thought about shoes once.

What was wrong with Jeevan's old shoes?
They were split at the toe.
Why did Jeevan say he had homework on Monday?
He felt left out and ashamed of his old shoes, so he avoided the game.
What did Jeevan do that helped, and how did Amma respond?
He told Amma honestly how he felt; she thanked him, said they would talk again at Diwali and asked whether friendship depends on shoes.
How do Vinita and the players see Jeevan on Friday?
As the extra player they need; nobody even looks at his feet.

School counsellor's note, Class 10, by Chinmay
Sarita came to see me today, very angry. Her parents had booked a family trip for the same weekend as her friend's birthday. "They should know it matters to me. I shouldn't have to tell them." I asked if she had told them. She said, "They should just know." Then she talked about her friends. Two of them couldn't come to her dance show last month. "Real friends make time for things like that. Always." She has been silent at home for three days.
I asked, "What happens when people don't do what they should?" She said, "I get angry and stop talking to them." "Does that get you what you want?" She was quiet.
What I did next: we practised one sentence she could say to her parents tonight: "This birthday matters to me. Can we talk about the dates?"

What did Sarita's parents book?
They booked a family trip for the same weekend as her friend's birthday.
Why is Sarita so angry at her parents and friends?
Sarita feels resentful because she believes they should understand and always be free without being told, and they fell short.
What practical step did Chinmay offer?
Chinmay helped Sarita practise one clear sentence to say to her parents tonight, so she could ask instead of expecting them to know.
How might Sarita's parents see the three days of silence?
They are probably confused and worried, not knowing that the birthday matters so much to her.

Vikas had been Kamal's flatmate in Andheri for a month, and he still hadn't worked out how to join the others.

Kamal's college friends came over every Friday: the same four, the same order of seats on the sofa, the same takeaway biryani split five ways. They finished each other's stories. They had nicknames for everyone. Vikas liked watching them; it looked warm.

One Friday Kamal mentioned that a colleague had invited him to a pottery class on Saturdays.

"Pottery?" said one of them. "Since when are you an artist?"

"You'll miss our Saturday cricket," said another.

Kamal laughed it off. "I'm not going anyway."

But later, while clearing plates, Vikas saw Kamal look at the class brochure for a long moment before putting it in the drawer.

What did Kamal's friends eat every Friday?
Takeaway biryani split five ways.
What does Kamal's long look at the brochure suggest?
It suggests he feels disappointed and torn, wanting to try the pottery class but pressured by the group to stay.
What small step could Kamal take?
He could tell his friends that he'll try the pottery class for a few weeks and still join Saturday cricket when he can, so both are possible.
How does Vikas see the group from outside?
Vikas finds it warm and a little hard to enter, and notices the quiet pressure on Kamal that the group itself may not see.

Freya had spent last spring checking Emre's phone in their Berlin flat, and hating herself for it.

This autumn things were different. She'd started climbing on Tuesdays with her friend Elif, and was, to her surprise, good at it. She'd picked her cello back up. And when the jealousy spiked badly in September, she had booked a few sessions with a counsellor at the student centre instead of waiting it out.

Emre had changed too. He told her about his plans without being asked. He left his phone on the table and didn't flinch when she walked past it.

On Saturday he went to a colleague's birthday. Freya felt the familiar tug of worry. Then she texted Elif: "Climbing tomorrow?" and practised a hard piece until her fingers ached.

When Emre came home, she realised she hadn't checked the time once.

What did Freya start doing on Tuesdays?
Climbing, with her friend Elif.
How did Freya handle the tug of worry on Saturday?
She felt the old worry but stayed steady, texting Elif and practising cello rather than checking on Emre.
What role did the counsellor play in Freya's progress?
When the jealousy spiked badly despite reassurance, the counsellor gave Freya support to work on it rather than waiting it out.
What is it like for Emre when Freya no longer checks?
He likely feels trusted and relieved, and more relaxed about being open.

“Practice at six, boys,” Tanuja called across the community-centre yard, coach of the youth football group. “And before you ask, yes, we are still the best team in the colony.”
“Best,” chorused the others.
Mohit lingered at the back. “Tanuja didi, can I say something? I'm skipping Saturday film night. I'd rather go to my dance class.”
Someone snorted. “Dance?”
Tanuja looked around. “Anyone else have a problem with that?” Nobody spoke. “Mohit is on the team, and he's here at six every day. Film night is optional.”
Mohit let out a long breath. “Thanks.” A younger boy whispered, “Can you show me some moves?”

Where does the football group practise at six?
They practise in the community-centre yard.
What was Mohit feeling when Mohit lingered at the back and asked, “can I say something?”
Mohit was nervous about being teased but wanted to be honest about a different interest.
What did Tanuja's response do for the group?
Tanuja backed Mohit as a team member, said film night was optional and let the group see that belonging does not need sameness.
What might the younger boy who asked for moves have been feeling?
The younger boy may have felt curious and relieved that a different interest was accepted, and wanted to try it too.

Read this:

You know what happened yesterday, Tarun? I'd been at the library since eight. Twelve hours. Choosing which topics first, which notes to trust, whether to redo the mock test.
By the time I walked out, I was done. Home had texted: "Nilesh, dinner at home or tiffin from the canteen?" I didn't even answer. I bought a huge packet of spicy chips and a cold drink from the stall and ate them on the bus.
Then the teacher's email about choosing a project partner came, and I just replied "whatever works". Now I'm stuck with the one person who never shows up.
Honestly, it wasn't a decision. It was like my brain handed the wheel to whoever was nearest.

How long had Nilesh been at the library?
Twelve hours, since eight in the morning.
What does 'my brain handed the wheel to whoever was nearest' suggest about how Nilesh felt?
Nilesh felt too drained to steer anything, so the easiest option simply won, whether chips on the bus or 'whatever works'.
What small step could stop Nilesh's worst choices on long study days?
Nilesh could delay any reply that matters, like the partner email, until the next morning, and carry a proper dinner plan so the bus stall isn't the default.
What was it like for the person at home who texted about dinner?
They got no answer at all, so they may have waited, cooked for nothing, or worried about where Nilesh was.
What is a wise saying about patience? Make it one sentence of exactly eight words.
Patience turns many small steps into long journeys.

Read this:

Pankaj: ok new rule, tell me if it's silly
Jasleen: go on
Pankaj: after dinner I go to the library. before I read a single message, I open the first task on my list
Jasleen: and the phone?
Pankaj: goes into my bag, zip closed, under the desk
Jasleen: what if someone needs you urgently?
Pankaj: then they'll call and I'll hear it, but I'll only check the bag at the ten o'clock break
Jasleen: hmm, ok 🙂 that's clear
Pankaj: it worked tonight. I did the first problem set before the break and my brain felt lighter
Jasleen: so the rule is: dinner, library, task, then phone
Pankaj: exactly. no deciding, just doing

Where does Pankaj put the phone during study time?
Pankaj puts the phone into the bag, zip closed, under the desk.
What does Pankaj want from the new rule?
Pankaj wants to remove the daily choice about starting, and feels lighter after finishing the problem set before the break.
What could Pankaj try if the bag rule fails on a stressful day, and why?
Pankaj could tell Jasleen the plan each evening so there is someone to check in with, because a small promise to someone helps a habit hold.
How might Jasleen feel about the rule at first?
Jasleen is careful and asks about urgent calls, which shows a sensible worry, but is reassured once the plan is clear. 🙂

messages.content:
Read this:

"Wasim, you asked how I finally cleared anatomy. Honestly? I stopped rereading. In first year I'd read the same chapter five times, highlight everything, feel great, and forget it by the test.
This year I split each topic across the week. Monday I'd study the bones of the hand. Wednesday I'd close the book and write down every bone I could remember, then check what I'd missed. Saturday, again, just as it was getting fuzzy. The next week, once more.
It felt awful. Rereading feels smooth; testing yourself feels like pushing a cart uphill. I kept thinking I was bad at it because I got so many wrong on Wednesdays.
But in the exam, I just knew them. So yes, it's harder, and yes, it works. That's Raghav's secret, and now it's yours."

What did Raghav do on Wednesdays?
Closed the book, wrote down every bone that could be remembered, then checked what was missed.
Why did testing feel so bad to Raghav at first?
Getting so many wrong on Wednesdays left Raghav discouraged, as if bad at it, while rereading had felt smooth and comforting.
What could Wasim take from Raghav's method?
Spread each topic across the week, recall it without looking, and come back to it just as it starts to fade.
How might Wasim react to hearing that the better method feels worse?
Wasim may be surprised or doubtful, since smooth rereading feels like learning, but might try it after hearing how the exam went.
The bell rang before I finished my test paper, and I left two questions blank.
That's frustrating. Do you think you could have finished with a better plan?
I spent too long on one hard question.
Next time, try a first pass through the paper and answer the easy ones first. Mark the hard ones and return to them if you have time.
I'll try that. Should I tell the teacher what happened?
You can mention it kindly if you wish, but the main thing is to learn from it. A time check halfway through the test is a useful habit.

Read this:

Dear Anand,
Remember I said I'd read about other philosophies over the holidays? I did.
I read a bit about Stoicism: focus on what you can control, accept what you can't. Then about Buddhism: attachment causes suffering. And then I reread the Gita that Ajji gave me: do your duty without clinging to results.
It surprised me how similar some ideas are, though the reasons are different. Stoics talk about reason, Buddhists about suffering, the Gita about dharma.
I also read an atheist writer who says we can build ethics just on human wellbeing. I didn't agree with all of it, but it made me think.
I'm not changing my beliefs. But I think I understand them better, and others too.
Write back. You still owe me your views on free will.
Karthik

Who gave Karthik the Gita?
Ajji.
What was Karthik feeling when noticing the similarities?
Karthik felt surprised and curious about how different traditions share ideas.
What approach did Karthik take that others could learn from?
Karthik read several worldviews, compared their reasons, and stayed open even when disagreeing.
How might Anand respond to this letter?
Anand might feel interested and ready to share Anand's own thoughts on free will.
Give three reminders for keeping a desk tidy, numbered, each under eight words.

1. Put pens back in the box.
2. Stack your books neatly.
3. Throw away old paper.

Read this:

I'm Avni, and I was in the passenger seat when it happened. A bike cut in front of Lokesh at the signal and scraped the side of our car with a long screech. Two years ago, I know exactly what he'd have done: jumped out and shouted. This time he gripped the steering wheel, and I watched his jaw tighten. He breathed out through his nose, slowly. Then he rolled down the window. The biker was already apologising, scared. Lokesh just said, 'Are you hurt?' The boy shook his head. 'Then go slower, okay?' The signal turned green and we drove off. Later I asked him how he stayed calm. He shrugged. 'I wasn't calm. I just didn't need to act on it.' I'm still not sure what he was feeling.

What did the bike scrape?
The side of their car.
What might Lokesh's tightened jaw and grip on the wheel suggest?
They suggest he felt a surge of anger he was holding in, rather than real calm.
What did Lokesh's pause make possible?
It let him see the biker was scared and apologising, so he checked on him instead of starting a fight.
How might the biker have experienced Lokesh's response?
Relieved and perhaps ashamed, expecting shouting but getting concern instead.

Read this:

The lights went out just as Devika's phone buzzed with the tuition group's results. "Battery's almost gone," she said, squinting. "Hemant, science quiz... two wrong." Hemant dropped onto the mattress and pulled the sheet over his head. "I'm useless at science." Devika scrolled with the last of the battery. "Wait, it also says eight out of ten. That's good!" The sheet came off. "Really? Eight?" He was grinning in the candlelight. Then he frowned. "But you said two wrong." "Same thing," Devika said. The phone died. Hemant lay there in the dark, counting on his fingers, eight and two, eight and two, puzzled why one had felt like a slap and the other like a sweet.

What did Devika first read out about Hemant's science quiz?
She read out "two wrong."
What was Hemant feeling when he pulled the sheet over his head?
He felt discouraged and ashamed, calling himself useless at science because "two wrong" sounded like failure.
What could Devika say next time she shares a result?
She could give both sides at once, eight right and two wrong, so the wording doesn't swing his mood.
How might Devika see Hemant's sudden change of mood?
She seems surprised, since to her "two wrong" and "eight out of ten" are simply the same thing.

Read this:

In their kitchen in Sydney, Yuki, two, shook her head at the peas and flung a spoonful onto the floor. "No!" Her mother, Olga, did not raise her voice. She held up two small bowls. "Peas or carrot today?" Yuki pointed at the carrot, squashed a piece between her fingers, then put it in her mouth. Olga wiped the floor later and went on eating her own dinner.

What did Yuki fling onto the floor?
Yuki flung a spoonful of peas onto the floor.
What does Yuki's shaking head and "No!" suggest she wants at that moment?
She may be testing what it is like to choose and have some control, rather than trying to be defiant.
What could Olga do if Yuki refuses both bowls another day?
Stay calm, let the meal end without a fight, and offer food again at the next mealtime.
How might Olga feel about the flung peas?
She may feel worn out and a little exasperated, but her calm voice and small choices show she is choosing not to fight over each bite.

Read this:

In the student kitchen in Berlin, Felix was showing the new exchange student, Rafael, how things worked.
“Professor Weber is tough, but she marks fairly. Dr Lang loses assignments, so always email him a copy. And be careful lending money to Jonas on the second floor. He's borrowed from three of us and never paid back.”
Rafael nodded. “Is he, like, a bad guy?”
Felix paused. He could have said a lot. Jonas's messy room, his weird girlfriend, the time he cried at a party. The others would have laughed.
Instead he said, “No. Just don't lend him money. That's all I know for sure.”
Later, Rafael politely refused when Jonas asked for twenty euros. Jonas shrugged and asked someone else.

Who does Felix say loses assignments?
Dr Lang loses assignments.
What was Felix feeling when he paused before answering?
He felt tempted to share juicy stories but uneasy about it, choosing to stick to what was true and useful.
What makes Felix's warning about Jonas useful rather than cruel?
It's accurate, limited to what Felix knows, and meant to protect Rafael, not to entertain others.
How might Jonas be affected if Felix had shared the other stories?
He could have been mocked and judged for private things that had nothing to do with money.

Read this:

Jasleen's phone had a cracked screen and nine percent battery when she sat down in the hospital corridor to make the rota. Her mother would be in for at least another week, the power had been going off at home every evening, and her final-term assignments were due Friday.
She drew seven boxes in her notebook. Nights at the hospital, medicine pickup, cooking for Nani, who lived with them.
Then she used the battery carefully. She called her brother Harman first: "You take Monday, Wednesday and Friday nights." Then Masi: "Can you cook Tuesdays and Thursdays?" Masi said yes before she finished. Her last call was to Dilnaz aunty from the flat below: "Could you pick up medicines on Saturday mornings?"
The phone died after the third call. Jasleen tore out the page and taped it to the nurses' notice board for the family to photograph. That night, for the first time in a week, she slept at home.

How much battery did Jasleen's phone have when she started?
It had nine percent battery.
What was Jasleen likely feeling when she began making the rota?
She was likely exhausted and pressured, with her mother in hospital, power cuts at home and assignments due Friday.
What else could Jasleen do if one person drops a slot?
She could name a back-up for each task on the same page, so one missed day doesn't fall back on her alone.
How might Masi feel being asked to cook?
Masi seems glad to help, saying yes before Jasleen even finished, perhaps relieved to have a clear way to be useful.

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Neel, their cousin, and I was staying at Kiran and Salma's flat over Diwali. Salma had just cleared the civil services prelims, and the whole family kept saying "Our Salma" every few minutes.

Kiran laughed and passed the sweets round, but I saw Kiran leave the room twice and stand on the balcony. Later, in the kitchen, Kiran said something short to Salma: "Everything is about you this week." Salma looked shocked. "I didn't ask for it. It's hard for me too." Kiran didn't apologise, but sat down.

The next day I heard Kiran tell their mother, "It stings when you introduce Salma first." Their mother went quiet, then said she hadn't realised.

I can't say what Kiran feels inside, but the trips to the balcony stopped.

What had Salma just cleared?
The civil services prelims.
What might Kiran's trips to the balcony suggest, and how sure can Neel be?
They may suggest a stinging sense of being overlooked, but Neel only saw behaviour and cannot be sure of Kiran's inner state.
What did Kiran do that helped with the envy?
Kiran said how it felt, first to Salma and then to their mother, instead of competing for approval.
How might Salma have felt about the attention that week?
Uncomfortable or pressured. Salma says "I didn't ask for it. It's hard for me too."

Read this:

Farida's rule sat in a note on her phone, written two years earlier with help from Amandeep, a friend who was a registered adviser: "Target 60% shares, 40% debt funds. If shares drift below 55% or above 65%, move back to 60. Only on the first working day of a quarter."
On 1 April the market had fallen hard, and her share portion had slipped to 52 percent. The complication: Farida was at a client site in rural Odisha for two weeks, with one bar of signal and a laptop that kept dying.
She could have waited until she got back, when things looked calmer. Instead, at 6 am, standing on the guest-house roof where the signal was best, she moved enough from her debt fund into shares to bring it back to 60. It took twenty minutes and three dropped connections.
She didn't look at the market again until July.

What share of her money did Farida's rule target for shares?
60% shares.
What might Farida have felt on the guest-house roof at 6 am?
She may have felt uneasy moving money into a falling market, but determined to follow the rule set when she was calm.
What made Farida's rule easy to follow even in a crisis?
It was written in advance with clear numbers and a fixed date, so she didn't have to make an emotional judgement.
How might Amandeep see Farida's choice?
Amandeep, who helped write the rule, would likely be glad she followed it despite the crash and the poor signal.

Read this:

I've shared an office with Manoj for two years, and I've watched him handle arguments about memory in a way I didn't expect.

Last week our colleague Wasim insisted Manoj had promised him the Friday off during a meeting. Manoj didn't remember that. I thought he'd deny it straight away.

Instead he said, "I don't remember saying that, Wasim, but you might. Let's check the meeting notes." The notes showed the Friday off had been discussed, but not settled.

Manoj said, "So we were both partly right. Let's sort it now." Wasim relaxed.

I don't know what went on in Manoj's head. But he didn't call anyone a liar, and the problem was fixed in ten minutes.

What did the meeting notes show?
The Friday off had been discussed, but not settled.
What does Manoj's calm reply suggest about how he felt?
It suggests he felt steady and open, not threatened, and willing to accept his memory might be incomplete.
Why did Manoj's approach work so quickly?
He checked the record, admitted each side could be partly right and didn't call Wasim a liar, which lowered tension.
How might Wasim have felt when Manoj suggested checking the notes?
Wasim probably felt respected and relieved, which is why he relaxed.

Read this:

Come and sit, and I will tell you how Samir and I bought our flat, because we nearly got it wrong. I am Nirmala, and back then I was twenty-five and sure a spreadsheet could tell me everything. Samir said, "Let's live it first." So for three months we moved the loan instalment we would owe into a separate account each month and lived on whatever was left. I remember thinking that if it felt tight now, it would feel worse later. The sums held. But we cancelled the trip to the hills we had planned, and I sulked about it. The test showed us the budget was workable, with hardly any room for travel. We signed, and ate a lot of home-cooked meals for years. I am glad we practised first.

How long did Nirmala and Samir practise living on the smaller amount?
They practised for three months.
What was Nirmala feeling about the cancelled trip to the hills?
Nirmala felt disappointed, and admits to sulking about it.
What wise choice did the couple make before signing, and why did it help?
They lived on the reduced income for three months first, which showed whether the loan was manageable before they were committed.
How did Samir seem to see the trial?
Samir saw it as a sensible way to check the plan by living it, as the words "Let's live it first" show.

Read this:

I remember the evening Kunal finally apologised properly. We were sitting by the college lake.
He said, "I told everyone your secret because I wanted to look interesting. It made you feel betrayed. I'm sorry."
It was a good apology. I could feel that. But my chest still hurt.
I said, "Thanks for saying that. I need a little time."
He nodded. He didn't argue or look annoyed. He just said, "Okay. Whenever you're ready."
For two weeks, he didn't push. No sad messages, no sulking in class. He just said hi, normally.
I'm Rajni, and I think that waiting did more for us than the apology itself.

Where were Rajni and Kunal sitting when he apologised?
By the college lake.
What was Rajni feeling after Kunal's apology?
Rajni felt grateful for the apology but still hurt, which is why Rajni asked for a little time.
What made the waiting period work?
Kunal accepted Rajni's need for time without pushing or sulking, just saying hi normally for two weeks.
What might Kunal have been experiencing during those two weeks?
He was probably anxious and hopeful, but he held back from pushing, respecting that forgiveness was not owed on schedule.

Read this:

Vishal had already typed three paragraphs to his manager, Usha, explaining why he should not present the quarterly review to the client. The client deserved a senior voice. His numbers needed another week. The team would benefit from hearing someone new. In the office pantry, waiting for the kettle, he peeled off a sticky note and wrote the reason without polish: I'm scared I'll freeze in front of them. Seven words. He reread the email and asked himself: if his friend Rohit sent him this, would he buy it? He could hear his own reply: "You're nervous, yaar, just say so." Vishal deleted two paragraphs, then the third. The new message was one line: "Honestly, I'm nervous about presenting. Could we do a practice run first?" Usha answered in ten minutes; she had already booked the small conference room for Thursday. "Of course. 4 pm. 🙂"

What did Vishal write on the sticky note?
I'm scared I'll freeze in front of them.
Why did the three-paragraph email feel reasonable to Vishal while he was writing it?
Every reason sounded mature and focused on the client and the team, so it let him avoid the less flattering truth that he was afraid of freezing.
Which choice turned things around for Vishal, and why did it work?
Asking whether he would accept the same email from Rohit; he knew he wouldn't, so he sent the honest one-line version and got the practice run he actually needed.
What might Usha have done if she had received the original three paragraphs?
She might simply have handed the presentation to someone else, never learning that Vishal was nervous or that a practice run could help him.

Read this:

At the school library, Preeti wanted a book from the top shelf. She stretched and stretched. "If I try hard, my arms will get long," she said. Keerthana watched. "They won't." Preeti stretched until her fingers shook. The book stayed up. The librarian came over. "Shall I get it?" Preeti nodded, arms aching.

What did Preeti want?
A book from the top shelf.
What was Preeti feeling when her fingers shook?
She was tired and frustrated, still hoping her arms would grow.
What else could Preeti have tried sooner?
Ask the librarian right away, since stretching couldn't close the gap.
How does Preeti's stretching look to Keerthana?
Keerthana sees it won't work and isn't convinced by the idea.

Read this:

Parveen, sit here with your old Irawati Nani. You told me some boys laughed at a girl in your class. Let me tell you what I did when I was fifteen. It was the monsoon, and a new girl, Latika, came to school with a torn umbrella and cheap slippers. The rich girls in our row mocked her every day. "Here comes the flood!" I said nothing. I was scared of them. Then one lunchtime I just picked up my tiffin and sat beside her. I didn't give them a speech. I shared my aloo. The next day, another girl joined us. Within a week, the teasing had nearly stopped. Latika and I wrote letters for fifty years.

What did the rich girls shout at Latika?
"Here comes the flood!"
What was Irawati feeling before she sat beside Latika?
She was scared of the girls who were mocking Latika, which is why she had said nothing at first.
What turning point in the story changed things?
Irawati picked up her tiffin and sat beside Latika without a speech, and the next day another girl joined them.
What might sitting together have meant to Latika?
Latika likely felt less alone and safer, knowing at least one person was on her side.

Read this:

Rosa was halfway through her first results presentation at the lab in Seville when Dr. Elif Aydın grunted: a short, low "hmph" from the back row. Rosa's mouth went dry. Was the data wrong? She clicked to the next slide. Another grunt, then a throat-clear. Her palms started to sweat. She could keep going and hope, or she could ask. She stopped. "Dr. Aydın, is there something on this slide you'd like to raise?" Elif blinked, then smiled. "No, no. Sorry. I grunt when I'm thinking. A bad habit. Actually, I was thinking this curve is very clean." A couple of postdocs laughed; clearly this was well known. "Oh," Rosa said, relieved. "Good. I'll keep going." Afterwards one of the postdocs whispered to her, "Her grunts scared all of us in our first year too."

What did Elif say she was thinking about the curve?
That the curve is very clean.
What was Rosa feeling when Elif grunted?
Rosa felt anxious, mouth dry and palms sweating, fearing the grunts meant the data was wrong.
Why was stopping to ask a good choice?
A grunt is a weak cue, and asking whether Elif had something to raise replaced a scary guess with the real meaning, letting Rosa continue relieved.
How had the postdocs experienced Elif's grunts?
They had been scared by them in their first year too, which is why they laughed knowingly.
I bought a umbrella yesterday. Correct it, is it fine?
No. The correct sentence is: "I bought an umbrella yesterday." Why: "umbrella" begins with a vowel sound, so we use "an", not "a".
Describe a mango-eating session with my cousins in summer, about 80 words, for a memory journal.

Every May, my cousins and I sat on the back steps of Nani's house with a bucket of cold water full of mangoes. We didn't use knives or plates. We squeezed each mango until it was soft, bit off the top and sucked out the sweet, golden juice. It ran down our chins and elbows. The seeds were thrown into the garden, in the hope that they would grow. By the end, we were sticky from head to toe, and nobody cared at all.

Read this:

Note for the staff room, Monday. Thomas, Nursery B. During tidy-up I told Mahima to “pull your socks up” because she was slow. She stopped, bent down and carefully pulled up both socks, then looked at me, waiting. A few children laughed. Mahima's eyes filled. She had done exactly what I said. I knelt and told her, “You're right, you did it. I used a grown-up saying. I meant: please tidy faster.” She nodded and picked up the blocks. Note to self and team: at this age, say what we mean in plain words.

What did Mahima do when told to pull her socks up?
She bent down and carefully pulled up both socks.
Why did Mahima's eyes fill when the children laughed?
She probably felt confused and embarrassed, because she had done exactly what she was told and could not see what was funny.
What did Thomas do to repair the mix-up?
Thomas admitted using a grown-up saying and restated it in plain words, so Mahima knew what was meant and felt right, not silly.
How did the laughing children see Mahima's socks?
They saw a funny mistake, perhaps because they already knew the saying, without seeing that Mahima had listened carefully.

Read this:

Preeti: how's your cousin doing?
Pradeep: not great. still in the night shelter, working day labour
Pradeep: I keep telling him to apply for the government training course and he just doesn't
Preeti: is he sleeping ok?
Pradeep: no. shelter's noisy. he eats once a day
Preeti: then honestly I'm not surprised. when you're hungry and tired every day, your brain is busy just getting through
Pradeep: I thought he was being lazy
Preeti: it's not laziness. it's no room left
Pradeep: ok. what do I do
Preeti: help with the basics first. food, a quieter place to sleep. then the course
Pradeep: my friend has a spare room for a month. I'll ask
Pradeep: and I'll stop nagging
Preeti: 🙏

Where is Pradeep's cousin staying?
In the night shelter.
How does Pradeep feel after Preeti's explanation?
Pradeep feels a bit guilty for having thought the cousin lazy, and more willing to help.
What does Preeti suggest, and why?
Help with the basics first, food and a quieter place to sleep, because a mind busy surviving has no room for planning.
How might Pradeep's cousin feel if he gets the spare room?
The cousin would likely feel relieved and calmer, with more mental space to think about the course.
