messages.content:
Read this:

Subject: Two weeks in — how's the handover working?

Hi Ayesha,

It's been two weeks since you and Bhavesh started the new handover note between the morning and night shifts at the lab. I asked Bhavesh the same question yesterday, and now I'd like your honest view too.

He told me the note is useful but takes almost twenty minutes to fill in, so he sometimes skips parts. If you're finding the same, let's cut it down. I'm thinking just three boxes: samples pending, machines needing attention, anything urgent.

Could you tell me by Friday which parts you actually read? After that, I'd like to keep a quick fifteen-minute check-in with each of you on the first Monday of every month, just to see it's still working.

Thanks for sticking with this.

Deepika

How long did Bhavesh say the note takes to fill in?
He said it takes almost twenty minutes to fill in.
What does Deepika's email suggest Deepika wants from Ayesha?
Deepika seems eager for an honest opinion and a little concerned the note has become a chore, hoping Ayesha will say which parts truly help.
What else could Deepika try if shortening the note still didn't work?
Deepika could bring Ayesha and Bhavesh together for a short talk about the handover itself, so they design the note together.
How is Bhavesh affected by Deepika's check-in?
His complaint about the long note is taken seriously, so he can expect a shorter form and may feel less pressured to skip parts.

metadata.subtype: Approach: follow-up check-ins and adjusting the arrangement [Revision]

messages.content: Describe my grandfather's armchair and the corner of the house where he sits, in about 70 words. He reads the newspaper there every morning.

In the corner of the house stands my grandfather's armchair, where he sits and reads the newspaper every morning. The seat has taken the shape of him after so many mornings, and the arms are worn smooth. The corner is quiet, and the rustle of newspaper pages is the only sound. Nobody else sits in the chair. It feels like a quiet throne in the middle of our busy home.
My group's science project was delayed because I forgot to bring my part to school. Write a sorry message to my group mates, about 50 words.

Hi everyone,
I am really sorry that I forgot to bring my part of the project. It slowed all of us down, and that was my mistake. I will bring it as soon as I can, and I will help finish the rest. Thank you for being patient.
Your group mate

Read this:

Monday. Ujjwal, two, pointed at the moon. "Chanda... moon!" At home they speak Hindi and Punjabi, and nursery sings in English. Amandeep smiled. Wednesday. "Doodh! More milk!" Ujjwal said, holding out the cup. Amandeep filled it. Saturday. Ujjwal told his Nani "moon" and told his Nana "chanda", pointing at the sky each time, checking who understood.

What did Ujjwal point at on Monday?
Ujjwal pointed at the moon.
What might Ujjwal be feeling or wanting when he says "moon" to Nani and "chanda" to Nana?
Ujjwal is trying words out and checking who understands, with curiosity and pleasure, not confusion.
What choice did Amandeep make when Ujjwal mixed the words, and why is it wise?
Amandeep smiled and filled the cup without correcting, which lets Ujjwal keep exploring the sounds and words from all the languages.
How might Nani have felt when Ujjwal said "moon" to her?
Probably delighted, since the toddler was sharing a word and looking for a reply from her.

"If it were not such a very wild night," he said, "I would send Hannah down to keep you company: you look too desperately miserable to be left alone. But Hannah, poor woman! could not stride the drifts so well as I: her legs are not quite so long: so I must e'en leave you to your sorrows. Good-night."

Why does he not send Hannah to keep her company?
He would like her to have company on such a wild night. But Hannah cannot stride through the snowdrifts as well as he can, so he says good night and leaves her alone with her sorrows.

Read this:

In the village near Muzaffarpur, Ganga, nineteen, ran a small tailoring stall from the front of the house. Her elder brother Kiran had started drinking country liquor with the other men in the evenings. Now it was most nights. He came home loud, slept past noon and asked her for money. At the well, the women whispered, and Ganga walked home with her face burning. She lay awake worrying he'd hurt himself on the road, then felt furious at him in the morning. She was exhausted. One day she went to the women's self-help group and told them. They listened. The leader said, 'You can't stop him. But you can stop paying for it, and you can look after yourself.' That evening, when Kiran asked for money, Ganga said, 'No. I love you, but no.'

What did Ganga run from the front of the house?
A small tailoring stall.
What was Ganga feeling as the women whispered at the well?
She felt ashamed, with her face burning, and also worried and exhausted.
What limit did Ganga set, and why is it wise?
She stopped giving Kiran money, which protects her and stops her from paying for his drinking.
How might Kiran react to Ganga's no?
He may be angry or surprised at first, but it shows him his drinking has consequences.

metadata.subtype: Family or friends affected by someone's use [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Mahima, you've scratched your head about fifty times," Shreya whispered across their shared desk.
"Have I?"
"And now you're rubbing your forehead. Stuck on the worksheet?"
"Not stuck. Itchy! Amma oiled my hair last night, and now my whole head's crawling."
"Eww. Okay."
"And I slept really late because of my cousin's wedding. My brain feels like cotton."
"So not confused, just itchy and tired?"
Mahima looked at the page again. "Well… number six is a bit confusing."
"Want to do it together?"
"Yes, please. But don't lean on my oily head."

What had Amma done the night before?
Amma oiled Mahima's hair last night.
Why did Mahima keep scratching and rubbing her forehead?
Mostly because her oiled head itched and she felt tired after a late night; only a little because she felt confused by number six.
What did Shreya do that worked better than guessing?
She asked a friendly "Stuck on the worksheet?", which uncovered the real reasons and still led to help with number six.
What would change if Shreya had told the teacher that Mahima didn't understand anything?
Mahima would feel embarrassed and misjudged, since the scratching was mostly itching and tiredness.

metadata.subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

Sudha, I'll be honest about how it felt. When he speaks, my chest lifts. I'm Mohit, and I've watched every speech since I was seventeen. It felt like he was talking straight to people like me.

Then my cousin said his promise on jobs hadn't been kept. My face went hot. It felt like she'd called me stupid, not him. I nearly shouted.

That night I looked at the numbers myself. Some were good, some were not. I still support most of what he does. But I realised I had never once said out loud what I disagree with.

Now I can say, "I'm proud of this policy and worried about that one." Pride and criticism can share a chest. My cousin and I even talk about it over tea.

Since what age has Mohit watched every speech?
Mohit has watched every speech since the age of seventeen.
Why did Mohit's face go hot when his cousin spoke?
It felt as if the cousin had called Mohit stupid, not the leader, so criticism of the leader landed as an attack on Mohit.
What did Mohit do that keeps admiration healthy?
Mohit checked the numbers himself, kept supporting what works, and learned to say what he disagrees with, so pride and criticism sit together. 🙂
How might the cousin have felt when Mohit nearly shouted?
The cousin was probably surprised and defensive, since a fair point about jobs got a fierce reaction, and the later talk over tea may have felt like relief.

Read this:

"Deepak, my cousin's wedding is on Saturday. Come with me. There'll be food and a DJ."
"I'll pass."
"Why? You love food."
"I won't know anyone. I'll stand in a corner. Your relatives will ask who I am and I'll say something stupid. It'll be so awkward."
"You don't know that."
"Harsha, I know exactly how it'll go. I've been to weddings."
"With me?"
"No."
"Then you don't know. My cousins are nice. My Nani will feed you until you can't move."
"They won't like me."
"You've met none of them."
"That's why. It's safer not to go."
"Safer from what?"
He shrugged. "From standing there feeling stupid."
"And what about sitting at home feeling stupid?"
Deepak opened his mouth, then closed it.
"I'll be at your door at seven," said Harsha. "You can leave at nine if it's awful."
"...Fine. Nine."

Whose wedding is on Saturday?
Harsha's cousin's wedding is on Saturday.
What is Deepak afraid of, and why does staying home feel safer?
Deepak is afraid of feeling awkward and embarrassed among strangers, so avoiding the wedding feels like protection from that feeling.
What did Harsha offer that made saying yes easier?
Harsha offered to come at seven and let Deepak leave at nine if it's awful, making it a small, safe test.
How might Harsha feel if Deepak had said no again?
Harsha might feel disappointed and a bit hurt, having wanted Deepak to meet the family.

metadata.subtype: Sure that the date will go badly [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the church in Beirut, Sami, eight, stood in the line of children in white, his new shoes pinching. His grandmother had pressed his shirt twice. His cousin Tariq, who had made his first communion the year before, winked from the pew.

Sami's stomach fluttered. Everyone was watching: his parents, both grandmothers, the neighbours from the third floor.

When his turn came he remembered to fold his hands, and he didn't trip. Afterwards the family took eleven photos on the steps.

At lunch he whispered to Tariq, "What was supposed to feel different?"

Tariq shrugged. "Teta says it means you're bigger now in church. You take part properly."

Sami chewed on that with his almond cake. He felt proud. He also still didn't quite know what had changed.

How many photos did the family take on the steps?
The family took eleven photos on the steps.
What mixed feelings did Sami have after the ceremony?
Sami felt proud of doing it right, yet confused about what was supposed to feel different.
What would help Sami understand the rite?
An adult, perhaps Teta or the priest, sitting with him to explain what the step means and what he now takes part in.
How might Tariq see Sami's question?
Tariq takes it lightly, sharing Teta's simple explanation, maybe because he wondered the same last year.

Read this:

Hansa, you want to cycle to the lake with your friends and your mother says no? Let me tell you how your Disha Masi got her cycle.
When I was sixteen, in Nagpur, I wanted to ride to school alone. My father said no, every time. I argued, I sulked, and once I even took the cycle without asking. Big mistake. He locked it for a month.
So I tried a different way. I wrote down a plan. Same road every day, the main one, not the shortcut. I'd call from the school phone when I reached. And we'd try it for two weeks. If I missed one call, the cycle went back in the shed.
I showed it to him after dinner, calmly, no crying. He read it twice. "Two weeks," he said.
I didn't miss a single call. After two weeks he said, "Take the shortcut if you like."

How long was the trial period in Disha's plan?
They'd try it for two weeks.
What was Disha's father likely feeling when he read the plan twice?
He was probably cautious but reassured, since the calm, written plan showed he could trust Disha after the earlier sneaking.
What was the turning point in Disha Masi's story?
Switching from arguing and sneaking to a calm, written plan with a two-week trial and daily calls, which built trust.
How might Disha's father have felt when she took the cycle without asking?
He probably felt worried and betrayed, which is why he locked it away for a month.

Read this:

Kishore, you asked how my tutoring thing went. So, I'm Aadhya, and every Saturday I help Class 6 kids with maths at the community centre.
First week, there was this boy, Ronak, who frowned the whole time. Arms crossed, eyes narrowed. I thought, great, he's bored. He hates me. So I talked faster to get it over with.
Next week, same frown. So I stopped and just asked, "Ronak, are you bored, or is something confusing?"
He looked shocked. "Confusing! The fractions part. I didn't want to say."
I'd read his frown completely wrong. It was concentration, and confusion. Not boredom at all.
Meanwhile the girl next to him, who smiled and nodded the whole time? She'd understood nothing either. Her smile was politeness.
So now I don't trust faces. I ask one question every ten minutes. "Still with me?"

Where does Aadhya help Class 6 kids with maths?
At the community centre.
What was Aadhya thinking when Ronak frowned the first week?
Aadhya felt discouraged and assumed Ronak was bored and disliked the tutoring, so rushed through the lesson.
What did Aadhya change after learning the frown meant confusion?
Aadhya now asks a quick "Still with me?" every ten minutes instead of trusting faces.
How was Ronak feeling during those sessions?
Ronak was confused by the fractions and too shy to say so, which his frown hid.

metadata.subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

Saurabh: how did the client talk go??
Pankaj: really well 🙂
Pankaj: I rehearsed it aloud twice in the meeting room last night and timed it. twelve minutes
Saurabh: and the slides?
Pankaj: six slides, one message each. main message: we can cut delivery time by two days
Saurabh: any hard questions?
Pankaj: one about the cost of overtime. I said "I don't have that figure, I'll send it by tomorrow noon"
Saurabh: you didn't bluff?
Pankaj: no, and they seemed to trust me more. I sent the number this morning ✅
Saurabh: proud of you. I'd have made something up 😅

How long did Pankaj's timed rehearsal take?
The timed rehearsal took twelve minutes.
Why did Pankaj say "I don't have that figure" instead of guessing?
Pankaj felt steady and secure, because preparation had calmed the nerves, and guessing would have risked trust.
What steps prepared Pankaj for the talk?
Pankaj rehearsed aloud twice, timed it, kept six slides with one message each and knew the main message.
How does Saurabh feel about Pankaj admitting not knowing the figure?
Saurabh is impressed and a little self-aware, saying "I'd have made something up".

Read this:

January. Leela, in her first job in London, set up a standing order with her bank: the day her salary landed, a fixed slice would move into a savings pot she named "Ammamma, Kochi". She printed a photo of her grandmother on the veranda and stuck it by the door.
April. Elizabeth, her flatmate, dragged her to a shoe sale. Leela tried on a pair, looked at them and put them back. "I've unsubscribed from all the shop emails," she said. "If I don't see it, I don't want it as much." Elizabeth bought two pairs and laughed at her.
September. Leela showed Elizabeth the pot on her phone, then the plane ticket. "Kochi. Three weeks. Ammamma doesn't know yet."
Elizabeth looked at the photo by the door. "Okay," she said. "That's better than shoes."

What did Leela name the savings pot?
Leela named it 'Ammamma, Kochi'.
Why did Leela put the shoes back at the sale?
Leela felt tempted but steady, keeping the trip to Ammamma in mind, and having removed shop emails made the wanting weaker.
Which steps helped Leela's future self?
A standing order on payday, unsubscribing from shop emails and the photo of Ammamma by the door made the goal automatic and concrete.
How does Elizabeth's view change by September?
Elizabeth laughed at Leela in April, but by September feels impressed and agrees the trip is better than shoes.

Read this:

When his mother Rajni left for two weeks to look after his grandmother, Vikas, nineteen, had their house in the kasba to himself for the first time. The first morning he burned the rotis and ate them anyway, standing by the stove. By day three he had found a rhythm: fill the water drums before the supply stopped at eight, soak the clothes while the rice cooked, hang them on the roof before the sun got fierce. When the kitchen tap started leaking, he didn't call the plumber from the market; he watched the neighbour uncle do it once and changed the washer himself. On the phone, his mother asked if he was eating. 'Dal, rice, bhindi,' he said, a little proud. 'The rotis are still shaped like maps.'

By what time did the water supply stop?
At eight.
What does 'a little proud' in Vikas's reply suggest?
He felt pleased with himself for running the house alone, while being honest about his rotis.
What could Vikas do to keep improving before his mother returns?
He could practise rotis daily and write down the routine that works, so it lasts after she is back.
How might Rajni feel hearing his reply on the phone?
Relieved he is eating properly and amused by his joke, maybe proud of how he is coping. 😊

Read this:

At five, Vasudha loved her biscuit until her big sister Leela was handed a bigger one. Then her lip wobbled and she pushed the small one away, crying, although a minute earlier it had been the best thing all afternoon. At ten, she brought home twenty-six out of forty in a spelling test and stared at the floor. Her friend Rehana had scored full marks. Vasudha's stomach felt heavy all evening, until Leela said at dinner, "My whole class averaged fourteen on the same test last year. Maybe yours was hard." At school next morning she heard that the class average was thirteen. She walked in almost skipping. Five years later, Vasudha spent a long Saturday afternoon scrolling smooth, glowing faces on her phone. She held it above her and thought her own nose looked wrong. Then she went to a cousin's birthday and sat with four classmates, laughing over cold samosas. Nobody's skin looked like the pictures, and she forgot her nose entirely, humming as she walked back home.

How many marks did Vasudha score out of forty on the spelling test?
She scored twenty-six out of forty.
How does Vasudha's biscuit at five compare with her spelling test at ten and her phone at fifteen?

In each case the same thing felt big or small depending on what she compared it with: the biscuit beside Leela's bigger one, twenty-six marks beside Rehana's full marks and then a class average of thirteen, and her face beside glowing faces and then beside classmates. What changed was the comparison, not the biscuit, the marks or the face.
What was Vasudha feeling when she stared at the floor after the spelling test?
She felt disappointed and low, because her marks looked small next to Rehana's full marks.
What could Vasudha try after a long scroll through polished pictures?
She could put the phone down and spend time with real people, or remind herself that the pictures are a carefully chosen, polished set. 🙂

Read this:

In their small flat in Copenhagen, Emil sat on the floor while his sister Noa pushed a wooden train into a cardboard tunnel. Emil's eyes followed it right to the tunnel's mouth. When it vanished, he didn't look at Noa's hand. He turned his head to the far end and waited, mouth open. The train rolled out. Emil shrieked and slapped the rug. "Again!" Noa laughed. "He knows where it comes out now," she called to their dad.

What did Noa push into the cardboard tunnel?
She pushed a wooden train into the cardboard tunnel.
Why did Emil turn his head to the far end of the tunnel?
He expected the train to come out there and waited eagerly; when it did, he was delighted.
What game could Emil's dad try next to build on this?
He could roll a ball behind the sofa and let Emil guess which side it will come out.
What is it like for Noa to watch Emil wait at the far end?
Noa is amused and a little proud, noticing that her little brother has learned something new and wanting their dad to see it.

Quick one: why does a crowd get noisy when many people talk at once?
How many followers does my friend have online?
What does "let sleeping dogs lie" mean?
What is wrong with this sentence? "I enjoyed very much the film."
"desirable" - what does that mean?

1. Each person raises their voice to be heard, which makes everyone louder. Because one group's noise forces the next group to speak up, the volume keeps climbing.
2. I don't know that. I can't see anyone's accounts. Ask your friend, or look at their profile if they have shared it.
3. It means do not bring up an old problem that is best left alone. For example: the fight is over, so let sleeping dogs lie.
4. Say it this way: I enjoyed the film very much. Why: the object "the film" must come right after the verb, and the adverb phrase goes after it.
5. "Desirable" is an adjective. It means worth wanting.

Read this:

I'm Meena from next door, and on Saturday I watched Jahnavi and Harish turn their living room into a quiz hall. Harish's father read out questions from a card, and Jahnavi's mother held up a steel spoon. "First to grab the spoon answers!" Harish grabbed it three times in a row. Jahnavi got the science questions, and Harish the sports ones. By the end, they had a small tally on the wall. "I am slow on history," Jahnavi admitted. "And I miss geography," said Harish. They wrote both on a sticky note. I had thought it was just a game, but I saw it was a test with a purpose.

What did the parents use as a buzzer?
They used a steel spoon as a buzzer.
What did Jahnavi and Harish feel about their weak topics, and what shows it?
They seemed comfortable and honest, not embarrassed, admitting history and geography aloud and writing both on a sticky note.
What alternative approach could the pair use to prepare, and why?
They could split the subjects between them and each become the expert. That would save time and reduce clashes over answers.
How does Meena see the mock quiz?
Meena thought it was just a game and then saw it was a purposeful test, so Meena's view changed to respect for how seriously the two were preparing.

metadata.subtype: Approach: practising with a partner using mock rounds [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dolma, you're scared of the canteen food because of what your friends say? Let your Pala, your father, tell you something. I'm Jagdish. When I was sixteen, in the Dehradun hostel, a rumour went round that the Thursday rajma made people sick.
Every Thursday, I'd sit in front of my plate and my stomach would start turning. Before the first bite! Once I felt so sick I went back to my room without eating.
Then one Thursday, the cook changed the day. Rajma came on Tuesday instead, and nobody knew. I ate two plates and felt fine.
When I found out, I laughed. The rumour had made me sick, not the rajma.

Which day was the rajma said to make people sick?
The Thursday rajma.
Why did Jagdish's stomach start turning before the first bite?
Jagdish felt anxious about the rumour, and expecting to feel sick brought on real nausea.
What was the turning point in Jagdish's story?
Eating rajma on Tuesday without knowing and feeling fine, which showed the rumour, not the food, was making him sick.
How might the cook have felt about the rumour?
The cook may have felt hurt or frustrated that people blamed the rajma without cause.

Read this:

Vishal, you asked me to talk about placement season for your college radio show, so here's the honest version. I'm Rekha. Two months before placements, I'd wake up at 4 a.m. with my heart racing. Half of me was hopeful: I'd worked hard, my projects were good. The other half was pure dread: what if nobody picks me, what if I freeze, what will Papa say? The dread was vague and huge. So I did something my senior Meenal suggested. I wrote the dread down as a list. "Freeze in interviews" became "do three mock interviews". "No company picks me" became "apply to twelve, not four". "Papa" became "talk to Papa this Sunday". I went to my faculty mentor with the list, and she helped me pick which companies suited me. Each small step made the dread smaller. I still felt nervous on the day. But it was nervous with a plan.

How many companies did Rekha decide to apply to?
Twelve, not four.
What was Rekha feeling in the two months before placements?
Rekha felt both hopeful about the hard work and full of dread about freezing or not being picked, waking at 4 a.m. with a racing heart.
What helped Rekha turn dread into action?
Writing the fears as a list, turning each into a small step, and going to the faculty mentor for help choosing companies.
How did Meenal's suggestion help?
Meenal's idea of writing the dread down as a list gave Rekha a way to break vague fear into manageable steps.

metadata.subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]

messages.content:
Read this:

Student council note. Teacher adviser: Manoj Deshmukh.
This week the council discussed a case: a Class 6 boy broke a window while playing cricket at break. Some members wanted him suspended for a week.
Vikas (twelve) disagreed. He said suspension was too big for an accident, and wouldn't fix the window. He suggested the boy help the caretaker repair it and write an apology.
Others argued that rules need strong punishments. Vikas listened, then asked, “Does the punishment fit what happened?”
The council voted for Vikas's idea. The headmistress agreed.
Next step: I've asked Vikas to help draft a fairer list of consequences.

What did some council members want for the boy?
They wanted him suspended for a week.
How did Vikas feel about the suspension idea?
He felt uneasy that it was unfair and too big for an accident.
What did Vikas suggest, and why was it fairer?
Helping the caretaker repair the window and writing an apology, because it matched the accident and fixed the harm.
How might the boy who broke the window feel about the council's decision?
He may feel relieved and more willing to put things right.

- Help me correct this: He is the taller boy in the team.
- What does "rain check" mean in "Can I take a rain check?"
- Why do we feel cold when we step out of a swimming pool?
- Quick one: what is "stammer"?
- How can I thank a teacher who helped me a lot?

1. Write it as: He is the tallest boy in the team. Why: use the superlative "tallest" when comparing one with many.
2. It means you cannot come now but would like to do it another time. For example: I am busy today, so can I take a rain check on the film?
3. The water on our skin evaporates and takes heat with it. Because evaporation needs heat, it draws that heat from our body.
4. As a verb, "stammer" means to speak with pauses or by repeating sounds.
5. Tell her plainly what she helped you with and how it made a difference. A short handwritten note is a kind way to do it.
Why do flower pots need small holes at the bottom?
The holes let extra water drain out. Because roots need air as well as water, and soil that stays soggy leaves no room for air, roots in a pot without holes can start to rot.

Read this:

I'm Nirmala, and I was sitting with Jahnavi on the school bus when the comment came in under her dance video: “lol who told you that you can dance.” I saw her face drop. Her thumbs were already moving to reply.
Then she stopped, locked the phone and put it in her bag. “Not now,” she said, mostly to herself. “An hour.”
She talked to me about the maths test for the rest of the ride, though she kept glancing at the bag. At home, about an hour later, she messaged me: “Checked again. Not replying. It's someone I don't even know.” She had deleted the comment and blocked the account.
That evening she called me, just to talk. She asked if I thought the video was bad. I said no, and meant it. She laughed a little and said she would post the next one anyway.
I don't know what she'd have typed on the bus. I'm glad she didn't.

What did the comment say?
lol who told you that you can dance.
How did Jahnavi feel when she first saw the comment?
Jahnavi was hurt, her face dropping, and her first urge was to fire back a reply.
What else could Jahnavi do if more mean comments come?
Keep the same pause, delete and block, and tell a parent or teacher if it turns into repeated targeting.
What was it like for Nirmala to get that evening call?
Nirmala felt trusted to reassure a friend, and meant it when saying the video wasn't bad.

metadata.subtype: Approach: handling a negative comment by pausing [Revision]

messages.content:
- Can you correct this for me? "He is more taller than his sister."
- What is the meaning of hostility?

1. Write it as: He is taller than his sister. Why: "taller" is already a comparative, so "more" is not added.
2. Hostility is a noun that means angry and unfriendly feeling toward someone.

Read this:

Karthik's diary, 11 p.m.

Amma's chemo day again. I took Pooja to school, then went straight to the hospital, then the lab. I reached the circuits practical twenty minutes late and the examiner would not let me start. So that's a fail on paper.

Fees are due on the 15th and Appa's shop has been shut most of this month.

I sat on the hostel steps for a long time. Dilnaz came out with two cups of tea and didn't ask anything for ages. Then she said, "You know the department has a re-test rule for medical emergencies at home, right?" I didn't. She showed me the circular on her phone.

Tomorrow: 9 a.m., HoD's office, hospital letter in hand. Then the scholarship desk. Writing it here so I can't pretend I forgot.

I still feel like I'm juggling knives. But at least I've put two of them down on the table.

Why did the examiner not let Karthik start the circuits practical?
Karthik reached the circuits practical twenty minutes late.
How was Karthik feeling while sitting on the hostel steps?
Karthik felt overwhelmed and defeated, with a sick Amma, a failed practical and fees all at once, and later a little steadier once there was a plan.
What small step helped Karthik start seeking help, and what else could help?
Writing down a fixed time for the HoD's office and the scholarship desk turned worry into action; Karthik could also tell a teacher about home so future clashes are planned for.
What was it like for Dilnaz to sit with Karthik on the steps?
Dilnaz probably felt concerned and chose to wait quietly before speaking, so that Karthik would not feel pushed, then offered one useful fact.

metadata.subtype: Academic Setback, Financial Stress & Family Illness

messages.content:
Read this:

Last winter I, Harsha, started closing my bedroom door. Not slamming, just closing. I had a notebook with a lock where I drew comics, and I didn't want Amma reading them. When she knocked, I said, "Wait!" and pushed it under my pillow. My big sister Gargi told everyone her little brother was getting "too grown-up." Then in February I got a high fever. I felt tiny and hot and scared, and I called for Amma three times in the night. She sat on my bed with a wet cloth, and I held the end of her sari like when I was little. Nobody mentioned the notebook. When I got better, I closed the door again. But now I leave it open a crack.

What did Harsha keep in the notebook with a lock?
The comics he drew.
Why did Harsha call for Amma three times during the fever?
He felt tiny, hot and scared, and wanted her close for comfort, even though he wanted privacy at other times.
What did Amma do well when she sat with Harsha?
She comforted him and didn't bring up the notebook, respecting his privacy while still being there.
How might Amma feel seeing the door left open a crack?
She may feel glad he still wants her near, even as he keeps some things to himself.

metadata.subtype: Wanting privacy but still needing comfort [Actor]

messages.content: My grandmother is learning Ludo from me, and she keeps asking if she can move backwards.
Ha, she is playing by her own rules already. In the usual game, pieces only move forward around the board, so you can explain that gently.
She gets upset when I cut her piece.
Cutting is part of the game, but in a family game you can agree on a softer rule, such as sending the piece back without any fuss. Say it with a smile.
She says I'm being too fast with my moves.
Slow down and say aloud what you're doing, like, 'I rolled a four, so I'll move this piece.' It helps her follow the game and makes it feel more relaxed.
She won a round! She's very proud.
Then she deserves a celebration. A cup of tea and a small cheer are in order, and you can tell the family that she beat you fair and square.
She wants a rematch tomorrow. I think she's hooked.
That's the best sign. Keep the rules friendly, and you may find yourself with a regular Ludo partner.

Read this:

The board results came out, and everyone in Kakrala village seemed to know Saurabh had got eighty-eight percent. Ojas, his older brother, had scraped through last year.
At the chai stall Ojas said, loud enough for the others, "Maybe the examiner felt sorry for him." At home: "Our topper doesn't carry water buckets now?"
Saurabh felt the words land. He had a sharp answer ready about last year's results. He didn't use it.
When the headmaster visited to offer sweets, Saurabh didn't go on about the marks. "Ojas bhaiya taught me to use the diagrams in geography," he said. It was true.
That night, Ojas was studying for his repeat accounts exam by lantern. Saurabh sat beside him with his own old notes. "These might help. I made them easy." Ojas grunted, but he pulled the notebook closer.

What percentage did Saurabh get?
Eighty-eight percent.
What was Saurabh feeling when Ojas mocked him at the chai stall?
He felt hurt and tempted to hit back about last year's results, but held it in.
Which choices kept the peace between the brothers?
Saurabh avoided boasting, gave Ojas credit for the geography diagrams, and shared his notes for the repeat exam.
How might Ojas see his younger brother's success?
Ojas probably feels jealous and embarrassed, since he scraped through, which is why he needles Saurabh in front of others.

Read this:

When Vidya joined our section in August, I thought she was being rude. Somebody said Mr Pai's surprise test was "very season two", the whole row groaned in agreement, and Vidya just said, "Harish, what does that even mean?" It's from a web series everyone watched last year, where season two ruined everything. You say it when something good turns bad. I explained it, feeling like an old man. Two weeks later I called her drawing "mid", meaning it was good, the way my group uses it. She went silent for the rest of biology. Turns out at her old school in Chennai, "mid" meant boring, basically an insult. I had to explain myself again, this time with my ears burning. Now we keep a list on the back page of her rough book: our words, her words, and what they meant last month. Half of them are already out of date.

What does 'very season two' mean in Harish's class?
You say it when something good turns bad, after a web series where season two ruined everything.
How did Harish feel explaining 'mid' the second time?
Harish felt embarrassed, ears burning, and probably a little guilty for hurting Vidya with a word meant as praise.
What could someone do when a newcomer misses group slang?
Explain it plainly without teasing, and check what words mean where the other person comes from, like the list on the back page of the rough book.
What was it like for Vidya to hear 'very season two' in her first days?
Vidya was left outside a joke the whole row shared, so all she could do was ask what it meant while everyone else groaned together.

The school bus left in six minutes, and the card swap on the back benches was ending. Uday, eleven, held up his silver goalkeeper card. "Fifty rupees, or five cards." His classmate Harsha laughed. "Those are twenty. I'll give you twenty." "Twenty? It's mine. I've had it since Class 4." "It's the same card the stationery shop sells." The driver honked. Two more boys offered fifteen and twenty. "You're all cheating," Uday said, face hot. Harsha shrugged and got on the bus. Uday climbed on last, card in hand. Halfway home he thought: if it were Harsha's card, would I pay fifty? He didn't like the answer. He put the card in his pencil box and said nothing.

How much did Harsha offer for the silver goalkeeper card?
I'll give you twenty.
Why did Uday feel the others were cheating him?
He had owned the card since Class 4, so it felt worth much more to him. The buyers only saw an ordinary shop card, and he took their lower offers as unfair.
What question did Uday ask himself on the bus, and how could it help him next time?
Whether he would pay fifty if it were Harsha's card. Asking this before setting a price could help him see the gap between what owners and buyers think.
How might Harsha see Uday calling everyone cheats?
Harsha probably thinks it's a bit unfair and silly, since twenty is the normal price, and just shrugs it off rather than arguing.

I'm Tanuja, from the house opposite. During the Pongal holidays our lane was covered in kolams, and Harsha, who is almost two, spent the whole week trying to cross them. On the first day he crawled right through the rice flour. By the third day he was stepping carefully between the lines, arms out, stopping to wobble. On the last morning he ran the length of the lane to his grandmother. Maybe he was proud; I only know he didn't look down once.

What covered the lane during the Pongal holidays?
Kolams covered the lane.
What might Harsha have been feeling when he ran the length of the lane?
Probably confident and pleased with himself, though Tanuja can only guess from how he never looked down.
How could Harsha's family support his walking during a festival week like this?
They could give him space to practise on the open lane while guiding him around fresh kolams, rather than carrying him everywhere.
How does Tanuja see the change across the week?
Tanuja notices him move from crawling through the flour to stepping between lines and then running, a clear gain in balance and control.

"Madhuri! The alarm! Madhuri, come!"
"Harsha bhaiya... I can't..."
"What do you mean, you can't? You know the rules!"
"I know them. My legs won't go."
"Give me your hand. Low, like this. Door. Stairs. Go."
Outside, on the pavement, their mother wrapped Madhuri in a shawl. It had only been smoke from burnt toast, and Papa had already opened every window.
"I knew what to do," Madhuri sobbed. "I said it in class. But I just stood there."
"Knowing it isn't the same as doing it," Harsha said. "You've only ever heard it. Tomorrow we'll do it for real. Ten times, if you want."

What had caused the smoke?
Burnt toast.
How did Madhuri feel when she said her legs wouldn't go?
She felt frozen with fear and later upset and ashamed that she knew the rules but couldn't act.
What else could help Madhuri besides practising at home?
She could ask her school to include a surprise drill, so she practises moving when she isn't expecting it.
How does the moment look to Harsha?
Harsha is scared and impatient at first, then understanding, offering to practise with her as many times as she wants.

When the email came through that their grant had been approved, the whole lab in São Paulo cheered. Yara smiled too, but Beatriz noticed that her voice when she said "Great news" was tight and high, and her hands were gripping her coffee cup. Beatriz couldn't tell what was underneath. Nerves about leading it? Something at home? Later, when the others had gone to lunch, Beatriz sat down beside her. "You seemed a bit tense when the grant came in. I might be reading it wrong. How are you feeling about it?" Yara let out a breath. "Happy. And terrified. It means four months of fieldwork in Manaus, and my father's been unwell. I don't know how to tell my mother." Beatriz nodded. "That's a lot at once. Do you want to talk it through, or just sit for a bit?" "Talk. Please." They skipped lunch.

How long will Yara's fieldwork in Manaus last?
Four months.
What was Yara feeling about the grant?
Yara felt happy and terrified at once, worried about leaving for fieldwork while her father was unwell.
What made Beatriz's check-in careful?
She waited for a private moment, described the tense cue while admitting she might be wrong, asked how Yara felt, then offered talk or quiet.
How did the rest of the lab react to the grant?
The rest of the lab cheered, reading only good news, unaware of Yara's mixed feelings.

messages.content:
Read this:

Divyansh: new manager update. she wants a status message every 2 hours
Varun: every 2 hours??
Divyansh: and she rewrites every email I draft before I can send it
Divyansh: yesterday she told me which font to use in a spreadsheet only I use
Varun: that's intense
Divyansh: I used to stay late fixing things nobody asked me to. now I do exactly what's on the list and log off at 6
Varun: you sound tired
Divyansh: drained. like there's no point thinking if she'll redo it anyway
Varun: have you told her?
Divyansh: I'm scared she'll think I'm difficult
Varun: what if you ask for the goal, not the steps? like "tell me what done looks like, and let me figure out how"
Divyansh: ...that's actually a good line
[Two weeks later]
Divyansh: update. she agreed to a Friday check-in instead of 2-hourly
Divyansh: I fixed the report template on my own this week. felt like me again 🙂

How often did the manager want a status message?
Every 2 hours.
How does Divyansh feel under the constant checking?
Divyansh feels drained and discouraged, seeing no point in thinking when the manager will redo it anyway.
What line did Varun suggest, and why did it help?
Asking the manager to say what "done" looks like and leave the method to Divyansh, which gave room for judgement and brought initiative back.
How might the manager see Divyansh after the change?
The manager probably sees Divyansh taking initiative again, fixing the report template independently.

Rain hammered the station roof and the night train was two hours late. On the crowded platform Eshaan's phone buzzed with a forwarded message: “A woman is carrying off someone's child from the waiting hall.” Below it was a photo of Ira, taken from behind, a sleeping girl on her shoulder.

Within minutes a ring of men had gathered. “Where are you taking her?” “Show us the ticket!” Ira clutched the child, eyes wide, trying to speak over the voices. Nobody had waited for facts.

Eshaan looked at the message again: no name, no sender, nothing checkable. Eshaan walked to the railway guard. “There's a crowd around a woman with a child. Please come.” The guard arrived and asked calmly whether someone could be called for the child. Ten minutes later a woman ran in, dripping wet. “That's my sister! She's been holding my daughter while I bought tickets.”

What did the forwarded message claim?
The message claimed a woman was carrying off someone's child from the waiting hall.
What was Ira feeling, clutching the child with wide eyes?
Ira was frightened and helpless, trying to speak while a ring of men shouted, and nobody waited for facts.
What choice did Eshaan make instead of joining the crowd?
Eshaan noticed the message had no name or sender and asked the railway guard to come, rather than confronting Ira.
What might it have been like for Ira when the woman ran in and said the child was her daughter?
Ira likely felt huge relief but also shaken and humiliated, since strangers had accused Ira before checking anything.

Friday, a week before Suraj's wedding: Tejas told himself, as he often did, 'My name goes with me.' He had started saying it after a college night he still regretted.
The wedding night: the baraat danced through the Jaipur lane, drums thundering, forty cousins in pink turbans. Someone knocked over a fruit seller's cart and the crowd laughed and kept dancing, stepping on oranges. Suraj's cousins started throwing the fruit at each other. The old seller stood frozen. Tejas felt the pull to keep dancing, one pink turban among forty. He stopped. He stepped out of the procession, knelt and began picking up oranges. Suraj saw and came over. They paid the seller for the damage, apologised and rejoined the baraat.
Two days later: the seller turned up at the reception with a basket of fresh oranges as a gift. Suraj hugged Tejas. 'You saved my wedding's name.'

How many cousins were in pink turbans?
Forty cousins.
What did Tejas feel as the crowd laughed at the cart?
Tejas felt the pull to keep dancing along, but also uneasy, remembering that his name went with him.
What did Tejas do that others could copy?
He stepped out of the crowd, helped the seller and brought the groom along to repair the harm.
How might the fruit seller have felt when Tejas knelt to help?
The seller likely felt relieved and respected after standing frozen while the crowd laughed.

In the government school at Nandgaon, Madam asked Tanuja to read the Hindi lesson aloud. Tanuja stood up, and the words on the page seemed to jump. "The farmer... the far... the fra..." Someone giggled. Tanuja crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and said in a deep voice, "The farmer has lost his reading glasses!" The whole class burst out laughing, and so did she. Madam smiled but didn't move on to the next reader.
After the bell, Madam called her over. "You made them laugh very well. Was the reading hard today?" Tanuja shrugged and pulled another face. Her friend Zeenat, waiting by the door, noticed Tanuja's fingers twisting the end of her plait.

What did Tanuja say in a deep voice?
"The farmer has lost his reading glasses!"
Why did Tanuja pull a funny face instead of trying the word again?
She was embarrassed as the words jumped and someone giggled; the joke let her take charge so the class laughed with her, not at her.
What choice did Madam make after the bell, and why is it wise?
She praised the joke but gently asked if the reading was hard, which looks past the clowning to the worry underneath.
What might Zeenat have understood from Tanuja's twisting fingers?
Zeenat may have sensed that Tanuja was more worried than her funny faces showed.

"Pradeep bhaiya, what's that?"
"My packing card, Swati. Look. Pencil box, ruler, bottle, tiffin, sports shoes."
"There are no words."
"Words are boring. I drew them. I see the shoe, I pack the shoe."
"Why is the tiffin smiling?"
"So I don't forget it. Last week I forgot it."
"Can you make me one?"
"You make it. What do you need for nursery?"
"Crayons. Napkin. My water bottle. Teddy."
"Teddy's not allowed."
"Teddy's allowed on Friday."
"Fine. Draw a teddy with an F on it."
Next morning Swati packed her bag first and waved the card at him.

Why did Pradeep draw the tiffin smiling?
He drew it smiling so he wouldn't forget it, since he forgot it last week.
How did Swati feel when she waved her card at Pradeep the next morning?
She felt proud and pleased, because she had packed her bag first using her own picture card.
What else could Pradeep do to help Swati use her card?
He could check her bag with her against the card for the first few days, until the habit is hers.
How does the picture card look to Swati?
Swati, who likes the smiling tiffin, sees it as fun and easy, and wants one of her own.

Raghav, before your exam, let your Hemant Dadu tell you something. When I was eleven, in our town in Satara, I had a rule. Before every test I touched the school gate three times with my left hand, then walked in without stepping on the shadow of the flagpole. Every single time. My friends laughed. I laughed too, a bit, because I knew a gate can't give marks. But the one morning I forgot, I sat in the maths test sweating, sure I'd fail. I didn't fail, by the way. I got my usual marks. Still, next time, three taps. For years. Even now, before the doctor's appointments, I sometimes tap the doorframe. So if you have your lucky pencil, keep it, beta. Just make sure you've also opened the book.

How many times did Dadu touch the school gate before each test?
Three times, with his left hand.
Why did Dadu keep tapping the gate even though he knew it couldn't give marks?
It made him feel safer and calmer before tests, and the one time he forgot, he felt anxious, so the ritual stayed.
What balance does Dadu suggest for Raghav's lucky pencil?
He suggests keeping the pencil for comfort but making sure he also studies, so the ritual never replaces the work.
How might Dadu's friends have seen his gate-tapping back then?
They laughed at it, finding it funny, though they may not have known how nervous he felt without it.

Saturday morning in the Irfan household meant a chore chart on the fridge, covered in gold stars. Six stars meant ice cream.
Irfan was folding laundry when he asked Ankita to fetch the socks from the balcony.
“How many stars?” she asked immediately.
He paused. “For bringing socks?”
“Yes. How many?”
Irfan looked at the chart. Every box was a transaction now. Last week she had refused to help Nani carry vegetables because “it's not on the chart.”
That night he took the chart down. The next morning, when Ankita set the table without being asked, he didn't give a star. He said, “You remembered Nani's spoon. That's thoughtful.”
Ankita looked at him, surprised, then smiled shyly. She went back and straightened the spoon.

How many stars meant ice cream on the chart?
Six stars meant ice cream.
Why did Irfan pause when Ankita asked for stars for bringing socks?
He felt uneasy and disappointed that every small task had become a transaction, especially after she refused to help Nani.
What step did Irfan take, and why is it a wise one?
He took the chart down and began noticing Ankita's thoughtfulness instead, so she helps because it matters, not for stars.
How might Ankita feel when her father notices Nani's spoon?
Ankita seems surprised and quietly proud, feeling seen for being thoughtful.
Who jilted Miss Havisham?
Compeyson, a smooth swindler, took money from her and never came on the wedding day. He was also Magwitch's old partner in crime.

Sum up this in a single sentence.

By the quantity of provision which I had consumed, I should guess that I had passed three weeks in this journey; and the continual protraction of hope, returning back upon the heart, often wrung bitter drops of despondency and grief from my eyes. Despair had indeed almost secured her prey, and I should soon have sunk beneath this misery. Once, after the poor animals that conveyed me had with incredible toil gained the summit of a sloping ice mountain, and one, sinking under his fatigue, died, I viewed the expanse before me with anguish, when suddenly my eye caught a dark speck upon the dusky plain. I strained my sight to discover what it could be and uttered a wild cry of ecstasy when I distinguished a sledge and the distorted proportions of a well-known form within. Oh! With what a burning gush did hope revisit my heart! Warm tears filled my eyes, which I hastily wiped away, that they might not intercept the view I had of the daemon; but still my sight was dimmed by the burning drops, until, giving way to the emotions that oppressed me, I wept aloud.
After three weeks of hard travel and despair, the narrator spots a sledge with a well-known figure and weeps as hope returns.
"Hum log pichhle hafte nani ke ghar gaye the." English?
It is: "We went to our grandmother's house last week." Use the simple past because the time, "last week", is finished.

Make this easy for a child in two sentences.

"Let me see," said Holmes, standing at the corner and glancing along the line, "I should like just to remember the order of the houses here. It is a hobby of mine to have an exact knowledge of London. There is Mortimer's, the tobacconist, the little newspaper shop, the Coburg branch of the City and Suburban Bank, the Vegetarian Restaurant, and McFarlane's carriage-building depot. That carries us right on to the other block. And now, Doctor, we've done our work, so it's time we had some play. A sandwich and a cup of coffee, and then off to violin-land, where all is sweetness and delicacy and harmony, and there are no red-headed clients to vex us with their conundrums."
Holmes stops at a street corner and names the shops in order, because knowing London exactly is a hobby. Holmes then says the work is done and suggests a sandwich, a coffee and some violin music.

In Berlin, the course choices for the upper school were due Friday. Elif, sixteen, sat at the kitchen table with the form while her father cut apples. 'Biology and chemistry, of course,' he said. 'Doctor. Stable life.' Elif's pen hovered. Her sketchbooks, full of redesigned bus stops and chairs, lay on the windowsill. The aptitude test at school had said she was strong in spatial thinking. Ms Vera, the careers advisor, had said, 'Talk to him with your evidence, not just your feelings.' So Elif opened her sketchbook. 'Baba, I'm good at science, but I lose track of time when I design. Architecture needs both maths and art.' He looked at the bus stops for a long while. 'Show me the test results too.'

What did Elif's sketchbooks contain?
Redesigned bus stops and chairs.
What might Elif have been feeling as her pen hovered over the form?
She felt torn between her father's hopes for medicine and her own interest in design.
Why was Ms Vera's advice useful for Elif?
Bringing her sketchbooks and test results gave her father concrete evidence of her strengths, not just a wish.
How might Elif's father see the choice after looking at the sketchbooks?
He might begin to see architecture as a serious path that uses her abilities, while still wanting stability for her.

Tuesday. In maths I asked Miss Aditi, “Should I subtract before I carry? Is that right?” and I said her steps back to her. Some kids looked at me like I was being annoying, but Miss said, “Yes, that's a careful way to check.” Then she told me exactly which step was right and which one to fix. I liked that she didn't just say “good.” Mama says I ask a lot of questions, but I think asking is how I learn. Tomorrow I will do the same again when I don't understand fractions. Zainab.

Who did the writer ask about subtraction?
Miss Aditi.
How did Zainab feel about checking the steps with Miss Aditi, even when some kids looked annoyed?
Zainab felt confident and pleased, liking that Miss didn't just say "good" and believing that asking is how to learn.
What made Miss Aditi's reply helpful?
She named which step was right and which to fix, rather than just saying good.
How might the classmates who looked annoyed be feeling?
They may be impatient or curious, but Zainab's careful checking may help them notice what they too are unsure about.
Why should a group going on a trek keep together?
Everyone is safer in a group. Because someone who falls behind might get lost or hurt without anyone noticing, staying close lets everyone help each other.

Everyone in the Malmö office agreed Oskar had come back strong after his grandmother's funeral. He answered emails fast, joined every meeting, and when asked, said, "I'm fine, thanks, really." He didn't want to be the sad one in the room.
But at lunch he ate at his desk, and once Mina saw him staring at his screen for ten minutes without typing.
On Friday she brought two coffees to his desk. "Oskar, your grandmother, Ingrid, she was the one who knitted, right? You showed us that ugly Christmas jumper."
He laughed, surprised, and then his eyes filled. "It was terrible. She made one every year. I have eleven."
"Eleven?"
"Eleven." He took a breath. "Honestly, I'm not fine. I'm angry that I didn't visit more."
Mina pulled up a chair. "Tell me about the jumpers."

How many jumpers does Oskar have?
Oskar has eleven.
Why did Oskar keep saying he was fine?
Oskar didn't want to be the sad one in the room and feared burdening others, while inside he was angry and grieving.
What worked about Mina's approach?
She brought coffee, named his grandmother Ingrid and a real memory, which let Oskar laugh, cry and finally admit what he felt.
How did Mina likely see Oskar before Friday?
Mina likely felt concerned, noticing he ate alone and stared at his screen, and suspected he wasn't as fine as he said.

Every evening after the buffaloes were fed, Hemant, sixteen, climbed onto the flat roof of their house with his books and a solar lamp. Below, the village went dark early; above, the stars came out. He wanted to be an IAS officer.
His father needed him on the farm, especially now that the loan for the pump was due. Hemant didn't argue. He fed the animals at five a.m., went to school, came back, worked, then studied until his eyes watered.
One day, Shankar Guruji, the retired schoolteacher, saw him reading on the roof. He climbed up, puffing. "Hemant, you're studying the wrong books for that exam."
He came back the next day with a bag of old newspapers, maps and his own notes. "Two evenings a week, my veranda. Bring questions."
Hemant's father saw the bag. He said nothing, but that night he told Hemant to sleep an hour later and skip the morning milking.

Where did Hemant study every evening?
He studied on the flat roof of their house with his books and a solar lamp.
What was Hemant's father feeling when he told Hemant to skip the morning milking?
His father probably felt proud and moved, seeing a respected teacher invest in his son, and wanted to give him a little more rest to study.
How did Shankar Guruji help Hemant's dream?
He corrected Hemant's books, gave him newspapers, maps and notes, and offered regular sessions, filling the coaching gap as a local mentor.
What is it like for Hemant to balance farm work and study?
It is exhausting; he works from five a.m. and studies until his eyes water, but he stays determined.

The train was two hours late, the platform was hot and crowded, and Rehana was tired. “I want waterrrr!” she whined, pulling at Saurabh's sleeve. “Now! Give!” Saurabh was tired too, but he crouched. “I hear you're thirsty. Can you ask in your asking voice?” Rehana scowled, then said in a small voice, “Papa, can I have water, please?” “Of course.” He handed her the bottle straight away. She drank, then sighed. “Thank you.” She leaned on his leg while they waited.

How late was the train?
Two hours late.
What was Rehana feeling when she whined and pulled at Saurabh's sleeve?
She was tired, hot and thirsty, and her frustration came out as whining and demanding.
Which choice by Saurabh worked, and why?
He stayed calm, named her thirst and asked for her asking voice, then responded at once to the polite request.
What was the wait like for Saurabh?
He was tired too, but chose to coach gently instead of snapping.

Subject: re: how's the new job
Hi Anjali,
Work is intense but fine! We launch the new water filter next month. There's a small known limitation with the seal, it can wear out early in hard-water areas, so we're just not highlighting it in the leaflet. Management calls it 'managing the message'. Honestly, if we delayed the launch, the factory team in Pune could lose shifts, so it's kind of the responsible thing?
Anyway, my manager says I'm great at 'customer-friendly' copy. I rewrote 'leaks after six months' as 'performance may vary with local water conditions'. Pretty neat, right?
I just read that line back and it looks a bit weird written down. Probably just tired.
Tell me about your trip!
Elizabeth

How did Elizabeth rewrite 'leaks after six months'?
Elizabeth rewrote it as 'performance may vary with local water conditions'.
What does Elizabeth's remark that the line 'looks a bit weird written down' suggest?
It suggests part of Elizabeth senses the soft words are hiding a real defect, though the feeling is brushed off as tiredness.
What turning point is available to Elizabeth now?
Elizabeth could name the problem plainly, a seal that leaks, and push for it to be fixed or disclosed instead of accepting 'managing the message' and the jobs story.
How might a customer in a hard-water area be affected?
They could buy the filter trusting the leaflet and then face leaks the company knew about, feeling misled.

Before Saturday, can we try something? Imagine it's Sunday evening and we lost. Why? I wrote down two big reasons. One: the venue's internet is patchy, and our model needs a download. 'Nikita? It's past eleven.' Gautam stood in the doorway.
'I can't sleep, Papa. What if I blank in the chemistry exam? What if everyone else gets science and I don't?'
He came and sat on the chair. 'That's a big worry. Where do you feel it?'
'Chest. Tight.'
'Okay. That tightness is a signal to slow down, not proof the worst will happen. Try this: write every what-if on this page, then close the notebook.'
She wrote four. He read them without laughing.
'Tomorrow, before school, walk with me to the milk booth. Moving helps.'
'That's it?'
'Not quite. You've had this tight chest most nights for a month now. That's too long to carry alone. On Saturday we'll talk to the school counsellor, together.'
Nikita looked at the closed notebook. 'Okay.' Her shoulders came down a little.

Where does Nikita feel the worry?
In her chest, which feels tight.
What was Nikita worried about?
She was anxious that she would blank in the chemistry exam and not get science.
Which of Gautam's steps help tonight, and which address the longer pattern?
Writing down the what-ifs and a morning walk help tonight; seeing the school counsellor on Saturday addresses a worry that has lasted a month.
How might Gautam feel reading her four what-ifs?
He was probably worried but calm, reading them seriously without laughing so that she felt heard.

Hi Neelam,
You asked how I finally started practising the tabla again. It wasn't willpower. I've tried willpower. It lasts a week.
This time I did three things. First, I made it tiny: five minutes. Second, I tied it to my commute. I get home at seven, drop my bag, and play before I even change. Third, I took the tabla out of its case and left it on the mat in the living room. No case, no excuse.
Some days I play for forty minutes. Some days just five. But it's been two months.
Try it with your sketching?
Samir

How long does Samir practise at minimum?
Five minutes.
What was Samir feeling about willpower?
Samir felt frustrated with willpower, which only ever lasted a week.
Which of Samir's three changes do you think matters most, and why?
Leaving the tabla out of its case, because removing friction makes starting almost effortless.
How might Neelam feel reading this letter?
Neelam may feel encouraged and curious to try the same setup with Neelam's own sketching.

Ammi called Parveen four times before noon, as she did most days now. Had Parveen reached work? Was the gas off at home? Had Nadeem's train arrived safely? On the crowded station platform, Parveen could barely hear her over the announcements. Ammi's voice was thin and fast, and she said she hadn't slept properly since Abbu's operation. Parveen felt her chest tighten. Somewhere in the last year she had started parenting her own mother, and it frightened her. She also felt guilty for being irritated by the calls. That night she texted her brother Nadeem: "Ammi isn't okay. I've been handling it alone and I can't. Can we both talk to her on Sunday?" On Sunday, squeezed onto Ammi's bed, they held her hands. "Ammi, we love you. This much worry is hard on your health. Will you come with us to Dr Mathew?" Ammi cried, then nodded. Nadeem booked the visit; Parveen promised to come too.

How many times did Ammi call before noon?
Four times.
What two feelings did Parveen have about Ammi's calls?
Fear at having started to parent her own mother, and guilt at feeling irritated by the calls.
Which choice changed things, and why?
Parveen stopped handling it alone and asked Nadeem to talk to Ammi together, so the load was shared and Ammi was gently steered to a doctor.
How might Ammi feel when both children held her hands?
She may feel loved and seen rather than scolded, which is why she cried and then agreed to see Dr Mathew.

metadata.subtype: Adult child seeing a parent low or anxious [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

At five, Tanvir slid off his chair and announced, "I'm bored. What can I do? Can I have the tablet?" His mother handed him a roll of masking tape and some cardboard tubes. "Build something." He grumbled, then taped a very long telescope and spent the afternoon spotting imaginary ships.

At nine, Tanvir sat at the back of the classroom with his chin in his hand and his body sunk low in the chair. The teacher, also named Payal, saw it and thought, "He looks bored." She stopped beside his desk. "Tanvir, are you with us? Tell me what you're working on." He straightened a little. "I stayed up late finishing my model. And I was thinking about the answer. I think it's twelve." He was right.

His friend Hrithik whispered after class, "I thought you were asleep." Tanvir grinned. "I think better slumped." The teacher smiled and added, "Next time I'll ask first and assume later."

What did Tanvir's mother give him when he said he was bored at five?
She gave him a roll of masking tape and some cardboard tubes.
How do Tanvir's boredom at five and his slouching at nine differ in what they show?

At five Tanvir's boredom is real and settled by simple materials, while at nine his slumped posture looks like boredom to the teacher but actually comes from tiredness and thinking, so posture is a clue and not proof.
What was Tanvir probably feeling when he said he was thinking about the answer?
Tanvir felt sleepy but engaged, comfortable slumped in a way that helped him think.
What did the teacher do that was wiser than assuming?
The teacher stopped at his desk and asked him about his work instead of deciding from his posture that he was bored.

In the small town of Aldona in Goa, Nazia had learned everything about baking from Maria aunty: how to feel when dough was ready, how to fold butter for puffs. For three years she worked in Maria's bakery at dawn.

Then Nazia started making cakes on her own for weddings, and people began asking for her by name. Maria aunty grew quiet. She told a customer that Nazia's cakes "look nice but taste of nothing". She stopped lending her the big oven.

Nazia didn't understand. Hadn't Maria wanted her to be good?

She cried one evening at her cousin's house, confused and hurt. Her cousin said, "She taught you well. Now you're good enough to scare her."

Nazia did not stop baking. She went to Mrs. Lobo, who ran the church catering, to learn about large orders. She still took Maria aunty her favourite coconut sweets at Christmas and thanked her for the puffs. But she took the wedding orders.

What did Maria aunty say about Nazia's cakes?
She said they "look nice but taste of nothing".
How did Nazia feel when Maria aunty turned cold?
Nazia felt confused and hurt, crying at her cousin's house.
What did Nazia do that was wise?
She kept respecting and thanking Maria aunty, found another guide in Mrs. Lobo, and kept taking wedding orders instead of shrinking.
How might Maria aunty feel as customers ask for Nazia by name?
Maria aunty probably feels threatened and envious, which shows in her comments and in taking back the oven.

Read this:

Last winter my older sister Kiran coughed through the nights in the room we share in Ludhiana. She'd laugh it off: "Winter throat." I tried pressure first. I forwarded her scary articles, and once I told her in front of Mummy that she was being stupid. She just coughed more quietly, into her pillow, and stopped mentioning it. That frightened me more than the cough. So one evening I changed tack. "I'm going to the clinic on Thursday for my own check-up. Come with me? Kulfi after." She was quiet, then nodded. In the waiting room she held my hand like when we were kids. The doctor listened properly and gave her a plan to follow. What helped wasn't my arguing. It was sitting beside her. I'm Baljeet, and I'm still learning that.

What did Kiran call her cough?
Winter throat.
Why did Kiran start coughing more quietly into her pillow?
The pressure made her feel judged and scared, so she hid the cough rather than face it or be argued with.
What turning point does Baljeet describe, and why did it work?
Inviting Kiran along to a shared clinic visit with kulfi after; gentle company felt safe, while arguing had only pushed her to hide it.
What was that waiting room like for Kiran?
She was probably frightened, holding Baljeet's hand like a child, but comforted not to face the doctor alone 🤍

At the village tea stall in Nashik district, Maria handed over her exam results slip and admitted she'd got the algebra section wrong again. Dilnaz, stirring the pot, let out a low, satisfied chortle. Maria's stomach dropped. Was Dilnaz laughing at her? But Dilnaz's shoulders were loose and her eyes were on the tea, not on Maria. Then Dilnaz said, "Same mistake I made in my first year. I thought only I did that." She slid a hot glass across the counter. Maria laughed with her, the tight feeling in her chest loosening. The same chortle, she thought, could have felt so different if it had come with a pointing finger.

Where did Maria hand over the exam results slip?
Maria handed it over at the village tea stall in Nashik district.
What did Maria feel when she first heard the chortle?
Maria's stomach dropped and she feared being laughed at over the wrong algebra. Dilnaz's loose shoulders and lowered eyes pointed to shared amusement, but Maria had to hear the words to be sure.
What could Maria do if a chuckle after a mistake still feels unclear?
Ask kindly what the laugh meant, or watch whether the person's body and words are warm, as Dilnaz's were.
How might Dilnaz have felt when saying 'same mistake I made'?
Dilnaz probably felt fellow-feeling and some relief at not being alone in making the mistake, which is why the chortle came out soft.

The overnight train to Kochi was packed and noisy, and Thomas, twenty-six, had his five-year-old son Chinmay tucked beside him on the lower berth. When the ticket checker smiled and asked, 'What's your name, little one?' Thomas answered, 'Chinmay. He's the shy one, he won't talk.' Chinmay pressed into his father's side. Across the aisle, three children were playing snap. 'Want to play?' a girl called. 'He doesn't like joining in,' Thomas said. Then his office phone rang, and it was his boss, and the connection kept dropping. He went to the door end of the coach to hear. It took twenty minutes. When he came back, Chinmay was sitting cross-legged in the middle of the other berth, slapping cards down. 'I'm Chinmay! I won two!' Thomas stood in the aisle holding his phone, suddenly unsure which of them had been shy.

What did Thomas tell the ticket checker?
Thomas said, 'Chinmay. He's the shy one, he won't talk.'
What was Thomas feeling when he came back and saw Chinmay playing?
He felt surprised and unsure, starting to wonder whether the 'shy one' label was really about Chinmay or about his own belief.
What could Thomas try the next time someone asks Chinmay a question?
He could wait and let Chinmay answer for himself, and let him decide whether to join games, instead of saying no for him.
How might the girl who invited Chinmay see him now?
She probably sees him as a fun, chatty player who likes winning at snap, not a shy child at all.

messages.content: Stationary or stationery: which one is pens and paper?

"Stationery" means pens, paper and envelopes. "Stationary" means not moving. A memory trick: stationery has an e for envelope.
Examples: Amara bought stationery for the new term. The bus was stationary at the signal.
Should I take a gap year before my master's?
It depends on what you'd do with the year. A gap year can be valuable if you work, travel or build skills. What are you thinking of doing?
I'd like to work for a year first.
That can help in many ways. Work experience can strengthen your application and help you choose the right course. Keep in touch with your professors so they can still write references.
My parents worry I won't go back to studying.
That's a fair worry. You could share a clear plan with them: when you'll apply, which courses you're looking at and how the job fits in. A plan on paper often helps parents feel calmer.

Last Eid, when I was nine, I kept a list in my head all day. Simran had carried the plates. I had stirred the seviyan. Our cousin Ayaan had done nothing except eat raisins. When Khala handed out the nankhatai biscuits, she gave me five and Simran three, because I'd been in the kitchen longest. I should have been happy. Instead I shouted, "That's not FAIR! Four and four!" Everyone stared. Khala laughed. "Zainab, you're complaining about getting MORE?" I was. It felt wrong in my tummy. Then I told Khala that Ayaan should get only one because he did nothing, and nobody laughed at that. Now I think fair is a bit more wobbly than I thought.

How many biscuits did Khala give Simran?
Three.
Why did Zainab shout "That's not FAIR" about getting more?
Zainab felt uncomfortable and upset, with a wrong feeling in the tummy, because an unequal split seemed unfair even with the extra coming to Zainab.
What could Khala say to help Zainab think about fairness?
Khala could praise Zainab's care for fairness and talk gently about how sharing can be kind, not only exact, so Ayaan isn't cut down to one biscuit.
How might Ayaan feel about Zainab's one-biscuit idea?
Ayaan might feel hurt and left out, since eating raisins at a festival hardly seems a crime to a small cousin.

Teaching assistant's note, chemistry lab, Week 9.
I have noticed a change in Jaya, a second-year student. She has forgotten to record data twice this week, which is unlike her careful work earlier in the term. She sighs often and I saw her skip the lunch break to finish another course's worksheet. She mentioned a part-time job and a family function. I did not want to lecture her about time management; I think she knows. Instead I asked, "Is there something here I can take off your plate?" She asked if the lab report deadline could move by three days. I agreed and informed the professor, Ujjwal sir. I will check in with Jaya next week.

How many times did Jaya forget to record data this week?
She forgot to record data twice this week.
How does the teaching assistant seem to feel about Jaya?
The teaching assistant seems concerned and caring, noticing the change and choosing not to lecture.
What did the teaching assistant do, and why did it help?
They asked what could be taken off Jaya's plate and moved the lab report deadline by three days, easing one real demand.
How might Jaya feel when the deadline is moved?
Jaya would likely feel relieved and grateful, with one less thing pressing on an overloaded week.

"Eight weeks," Shalini said, holding up eight fingers. "Eight weeks and my chit hasn't come out once. This Monday it's me for sure."
"You want to read the news at assembly?" Chinmay asked.
"No! That's the point. I'm betting you a chocolate it's me. I haven't practised, so obviously it'll be me."
"There are forty chits in that box every week."
"Forty chits, but mine's been waiting. It's my turn. The box has to even out."
"Does Ma'am take your chit out when it isn't picked?"
"...No."
"So every Monday it's one in forty. Same as last week. Same as the first week."
Shalini frowned at her fingers. "It feels like it's saved up."
"Feelings don't shake the box," Chinmay said. "Practise anyway. Then you're fine either way."

How many chits are in the box every week?
There are forty chits in the box every week.
Why does Shalini feel her name is sure to come out this Monday?
Shalini feels anxious and sure it is her turn, as though eight weeks of waiting had saved up extra chance.
What advice does Chinmay give, and why is it sensible?
Practise anyway, because each Monday is one in forty whatever happened before, so being ready works either way.
How does Chinmay see Shalini's bet?
Chinmay sees it as a feeling, not maths, and patiently points out that the box has no memory.

I was folding laundry in the next room on Saturday, so I heard most of it. Indu's cousin Payal, seventeen, had come over with one question: "Indu didi, should I do engineering?" Indu didn't announce an answer. She asked what Payal liked doing on a free afternoon, and Payal said drawing and repairing the family's ceiling fan. Indu said her own route, accounts and then logistics, was mostly detours, and she wasn't sure she'd pick it again. Then she called through the wall, "Ritu, do you still have that alumni contact for the design course?" I passed it over. I can't say whether Indu felt nervous about giving advice, but she kept asking, "What do you think?" Payal left with two names to contact.

What did Payal say she liked doing on a free afternoon?
Payal said drawing and repairing the family's ceiling fan.
What did Indu seem to want when she kept asking "What do you think?"
Indu seemed to want to hear Payal's own preferences rather than push the cousin toward a single path, though Ritu admits it is impossible to know whether Indu felt nervous.
What could Payal do next?
Reach out to the two contacts, including the design-course alumnus, and compare what Payal enjoys with what each path involves before deciding.
How might Payal have felt when Indu admitted her own route was mostly detours?
Payal may have felt relieved that there is no single correct path, which fits Payal leaving with two contacts instead of one verdict.

The rain was heavy and the temple doors would close in ten minutes. Jyoti Dadi hurried Jahnavi up the wet steps. At the door, Jahnavi stopped, folded her hands and bent to touch the step with her fingers, then her forehead, as Dadi had taught her. Dadi waited though they were late. On the way back, a monk in a maroon robe stood at the bus shelter. Jahnavi pressed her palms together and gave a small bow, the way her friend Dolkar greeted monks. The monk smiled and bowed back.

What colour robe was the monk wearing?
Maroon.
What was Jahnavi feeling when she stopped at the temple door despite the rush?
She felt it was important and respectful to greet the temple properly, and seemed calm and sure of what to do.
Why was Dadi right to wait even though they were late?
Waiting let Jahnavi finish her greeting, showing her that respect matters more than rushing.
How might the monk see Jahnavi's small bow?
He likely felt respected and touched that a small child greeted him in a way familiar to him.

Read this:

Shreya, you're worried because your college friends have scattered. Your old Farhan uncle has been through this, thirty years ago.

When I was your age there were three of us in Lucknow: me, Anil, and Rehana. Then everything happened at once. I got a job in Bombay. Anil fell for a girl and vanished into her family. Rehana's father fell ill, and she had to run his shop and had no time or money for trips.

We wrote letters at first. Then postcards. Then a line at New Year. Every New Year I thought, I should visit Rehana, and every year I didn't. I felt guilty, and I later learned she felt the same about me.

The turning point came when I finally took a train to Lucknow, unannounced. Rehana opened the door and burst out laughing.

What did Rehana have to do after her father fell ill?
Run his shop.
How did Farhan feel every New Year when he didn't visit?
Farhan felt guilty, and later learned Rehana felt guilty too.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
Farhan finally took the train to Lucknow unannounced; it broke the cycle where both felt guilty but neither acted.
How might Rehana have felt when she opened the door and saw Farhan?
She probably felt surprised and delighted, and maybe relieved after years of her own guilt.
