Hi Gopika Akka,
Remember at Diwali you said I was "always on my phone" and I said no I'm not? I checked. My phone keeps a usage report, so I looked at the whole last week. Short videos: 2 hours 58 minutes a day. Three hours. Every day. I honestly thought it was forty minutes. Sunday was over four. I added it up: that's more than twenty hours a week, more than all my tuition classes put together. Nobody had to tell me anything; the number did it. So I've set a one-hour limit on the app and moved it off the first screen. I'll check the report again next Sunday and send you the number, even if it's bad.
Your little brother,
Harsha

How much time a day did Harsha spend on short videos?
2 hours 58 minutes a day.
How did Harsha feel seeing the report?
Harsha was shocked and a bit embarrassed, having guessed only forty minutes.
What could make Harsha's plan stick?
Checking the report every Sunday as promised, so he can see whether the one-hour limit is working and adjust it.
How might Gopika Akka feel reading the email?
She may feel pleased and relieved that he saw it for himself, and touched that he'll share the number even if it's bad 🙂.

messages.content: Tell a story of about 80 words about a rooster who forgets how to crow, and a little girl who helps him remember. End with the sun rising on cue.

Every morning, the rooster crowed to wake up the village. But one day he opened his beak, and nothing came out. He felt so ashamed that he hid in the barn. A little girl found him there. "Don't worry," she said gently. "Try again." She stood beside him and crowed softly herself. The rooster stretched his neck, took a deep breath and let out a loud, proud cock-a-doodle-doo! At that very moment, the sun rose over the hills.

The principal's inspection was the next morning, and the chemistry lab was a mess. Raghav had been asked to lock it on Friday. He forgot. Now two beakers and a thermometer were missing.
Noor found him hiding in the library behind the atlas shelf.
"Everyone's looking for you."
"I'm the worst," he said. "I always mess things up. I'm useless. I can't go back there."
Noor sat down. "You forgot to lock a door. That's a thing you did. It's not what you are."
Raghav didn't answer, but he stopped pulling at his sleeve.
"What would fix it?" she asked.
He thought. "Tell Ma'am. Help her count what's missing. Maybe the cleaners moved them."
They went together. Mrs Pinto listened and said, "Thank you for coming to me, Raghav. Mistakes happen. Let's check the store." The beakers were in the store cupboard. Only the thermometer was really gone.

What was missing from the chemistry lab?
Two beakers and a thermometer.
What was Raghav feeling while hiding behind the atlas shelf?
Raghav felt ashamed and useless, as if he were a bad person, which made him want to hide.
How did Noor help turn shame into something useful?
She separated the act from the person and asked what would fix it, which helped him move from hiding to repair.
How did Mrs Pinto respond, and why did it matter?
She thanked Raghav and calmly helped search, responding to him with care, which made it easier for him to face the mistake.

In the market town of Karad, Vijay had been invited by his cousin Alka to a "rural uplift" group. They met in a rented room above the cloth shop and spoke movingly about helping farmers.
At the third meeting, Vijay raised his hand. "Where does the money from the membership go? Who's the head of the organisation? Can I meet someone who was in it before?"
The room went quiet. The speaker said, "Questions like that show a lack of faith." A few people shook their heads at Vijay.
That night he sat in the cyber cafe near the bus stand and searched the group's name. He found a local news report about a complaint filed against its founders and a thread where former members said they'd been shouted at for asking about accounts.
He showed Alka the next day. She read it twice. "They never told us any of this."
"They didn't want us asking," Vijay said.

Where did Vijay search for the group's name?
At the cyber cafe near the bus stand.
How did Vijay feel when the room went quiet after his questions?
He likely felt uncomfortable and suspicious, especially when people shook their heads at him.
What else could Vijay and Alka do with what they found?
They could share the news report with others in the group and talk to a trusted elder or local official before anyone pays more.
How might Alka feel after reading the news report?
Alka seems shaken and perhaps betrayed, saying they were never told any of it.

Jasleen: Kiran, you look tired. I thought you had started the new job?

Kiran: I did. In week two of being laid off I took the first offer that came.

Jasleen: Did you ask about the terms?

Kiran: No. I was scared of the gap. Lower pay than before, and the role isn't even what I trained for.

Jasleen: And now?

Kiran: Three months in and I am applying again. I've wasted the months and lost the pay.

Jasleen: Did you compare it with anything?

Kiran: No. I said yes to the first phone call. I'd have said yes to anything.

Jasleen: That's what fear does.

Kiran: I know. I should have asked for a day.

How many months into the new job was Kiran when applying again?
Kiran was three months into the job and applying again.
What was Kiran feeling when accepting the first offer?
Kiran felt scared of the gap without a job, and the fear made Kiran say yes without asking about terms.
What could Kiran do differently with the next offer, and why?
Kiran could ask for a day to read the terms and compare the role, because a short pause protects against a poor fit.
How might Jasleen see Kiran's situation?
Jasleen looks sympathetic and gently points out that fear made the decision, so probably feels concerned for Kiran.

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear diary, Harsha here.

I copied Himani's maths homework on the bus today. All ten sums. It's not a big deal. Literally everyone copies. Neeraj copies every day and nobody says anything.

And Mrs Pinto gives SO much homework. Ten sums a night is too many for anyone. If she gave less, I wouldn't have had to.

Also I understood most of it anyway. I just didn't have time because of cricket. So it's basically like I did it.

Himani looked at me a bit funny when I gave her notebook back. Whatever.

I'm still a good student. I always get A's. One copy doesn't change that.

I'm going to sleep now. I don't feel bad. Much.

How many sums did Harsha copy?
All ten sums.
Why does Harsha keep listing reasons after copying?
Harsha feels a little guilty and wants to keep feeling like a good student, so the reasons arrive after the act to ease that uncomfortable feeling.
What could Harsha try next time there's no time for homework?
Harsha could tell Mrs Pinto honestly about the cricket clash and ask for help or a little extra time, instead of copying.
How might Himani feel after lending the notebook?
Himani seems uneasy, looking at Harsha a bit funny, maybe unhappy to have her work copied.

Read this:

Sunday night

Eleven months of flat-hunting. Shalini and I were both exhausted, and last night we snapped at each other over a parking space in a flat we hadn't even bought.
Today my brother Lokesh came for lunch and asked, "What exactly are you looking for?" We rattled off the list: near Shalini's office, two bedrooms, a school nearby, a lift, within budget.
"And have you seen flats with all of that?"
"Yes, maybe five."
"Then why are you still looking?"
We had no answer. So we made a rule, right there at the table: from now on, the first flat that meets every must-have and is within budget, we take. No "one more viewing".
Next Saturday we'll go back to the list and look at what's open.
Writing this, I feel lighter than I have in months.
— Yogesh

What did Lokesh ask at lunch?
He asked, "What exactly are you looking for?"
How does Yogesh feel after making the rule?
Yogesh feels lighter and relieved after months of exhausting searching.
What else could Yogesh and Shalini add to their rule?
They could set a deadline, such as deciding within a month, so the rule is backed by a clear end point.
How might Shalini be affected by the new rule?
Shalini may feel relieved too, since fewer viewings mean less tension and fewer arguments.

metadata.subtype: Approach: satisficing with a clear stopping rule [Revision]

'Tanvir, it's Sunday. Why are you ironing your formal shirt at nine?'
'Thought I'd go to the library.'
'You finished the assignment last night.'
'I know. But if I sit around, I feel like a loser. Everyone's doing internships.'
'You sat around yesterday for ten minutes and kept checking your phone for emails.'
'That's the thing. Even when I rest, I'm not resting. My chest feels tight.'
'Come to the lake with me. No phone. Two hours.'
'And then?'
'Then you study tonight with a brain that works.'
At the lake Tanvir kept reaching for his pocket. By the second hour he was skimming stones and laughing at Amandeep's terrible throws.

Where did Amandeep invite Tanvir to go?
To the lake, with no phone, for two hours.
Why does Tanvir feel like a loser when he rests?
He feels anxious and guilty, as if resting means falling behind everyone doing internships.
What did Amandeep suggest, and why might it help?
Two phone-free hours at the lake, so Tanvir's rest is real and his brain works better when he studies later.
How might Amandeep see Tanvir ironing a shirt on Sunday?
Amandeep probably finds it worrying and a bit sad to see a friend who cannot switch off.

Read this:

Saturday: At Dadi's house in Jaipur, Vijay bent and touched her feet the moment he came in. Dadi pressed his head. "Jeete raho." He felt the old warm feeling from every summer he'd spent there.

Monday: Back home in Pune, Devika Aunty from the flat below was locking her door. Vijay pressed his palms together. "Namaste, Devika Aunty-ji." She laughed. "Aunty is enough, beta. But thank you." He grinned; in this building, "Aunty" already meant respect.

Thursday: At his friend Imtiaz's house, Imtiaz's grandfather sat by the window. Vijay started to bend, then saw Imtiaz touch his hand to his forehead. "Adaab, Dadajaan." Vijay copied him carefully. The old man smiled and waved them in.

What did Dadi say when Vijay touched her feet?
"Jeete raho."
What was Vijay feeling when he touched Dadi's feet on Saturday?
Warm and nostalgic, feeling the old comfort of every summer spent at Dadi's house.
What did Vijay do that was wise on Thursday?
He paused and watched Imtiaz, then copied the adaab greeting, fitting his respect to that family's custom.
How did Devika Aunty react to "Aunty-ji"?
She was amused and touched, laughing that "Aunty" is enough while thanking him for the respect.

Read this:

Irawati's phone buzzed for the fourth time before lunch: an unknown number, the loan app's recovery team. Her stomach tightened. "Pay today or we will message your contacts," said the latest voicemail.

In the office pantry she whispered to her colleague Asif, "I keep thinking of taking a loan from a different app to clear this one."

"Don't," Asif said. "That's how it stacks up." He suggested she save every call log and voicemail, note the times, and go to her bank about a repayment plan. "And threats like that are harassment, Irawati. It can be reported."

She opened a notes file and began listing the date, the number and what was said. Her hands slowed. She would ask the bank for an appointment first thing tomorrow.

What did the latest voicemail threaten?
It said that if she did not pay today they would message her contacts.
What was Irawati tempted to do, and what does it show about her state?
She was tempted to take a loan from a different app to clear this one, which shows how anxious and cornered she felt.
What should Irawati do next?
Save the call logs and voicemails, note dates and times, talk to the bank about a repayment plan, and report the harassment.
How does Asif see the idea of a second loan?
Asif sees it as a trap, since that is how debt stacks up.

Read this:

Dear Eshaan,
You asked how the new routine is going. Well, I've read every interview with the three founders I admire, and I'm copying their habits. Up at five like the first one. Same black T-shirt every day like the second, to save "decision energy." No lectures after lunch, because the third one said college slows you down. Cold showers, a gratitude journal, no weekend outings.
I'm three weeks in. My marks in the mid-sem dipped, but that's temporary. They all struggled before they made it.
Mamu asked me, his only nephew, an odd question on the phone yesterday: how many people wake at five, wear the same T-shirt and skip lectures, and never become founders? I said that's not the point. But I haven't stopped thinking about it.
Anyway, how's your placement prep?
Chinmay

What time does Chinmay now wake up?
He wakes up at five, like the first founder.
Why does copying these habits feel like a sensible plan to Chinmay?
He admires the three founders and believes their habits caused their success, so repeating them feels like the surest way to follow them, even as his marks dip.
What could Chinmay do with Mamu's question before continuing the routine?
He could honestly think about the many people with the same habits who never became founders, and keep only the habits that actually help him, like protecting his lectures.
How might Eshaan react reading about the skipped lectures?
Eshaan might be worried about the dipped marks and wonder whether the black T-shirt and cold showers are really what made those founders succeed.
Tell me 13 to the power of 13.
I'm not sure of the value, as a number this big is easy to get wrong. A scientific calculator will show it.
What do "i.e." and "e.g." stand for?

"I.e." means "that is" and restates or explains something. "E.g." means "for example" and introduces examples.
Example: Bring a fruit, e.g. an apple or a banana, and meet at the main gate, i.e. the one near the library.
Dukaandaar se bolna hai "Isse chhota size hai kya?"
Say: "Do you have this in a smaller size?"

"Pranav, test me again. B-E-A-U-T-I-F-U-L?"
"Correct. Next, necessary."
"N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y."
"Correct! Jagdish, you've got all twenty."
"Not 'separate.' I always get it wrong."
Pranav yawned. "Isn't the test on Friday? Just hope for the best."
"Hoping doesn't spell anything," Jagdish said. "Miss Rego said the trick is 'there's a rat in sepARATe.' Let me write it ten times."
He wrote it, lips moving. Then he looked up. "I think I can get twenty out of twenty this time."
"You're really into this."
"Last test I got fourteen. I practised every night this week. I actually think I can do it." He grinned. "Test me on 'separate' again."

What did Jagdish get on the last test?
He got fourteen.
How does Jagdish feel about Friday's test, and why?
He feels hopeful and fairly confident, because he has practised every night and has a trick for 'separate'.
What small step helped Jagdish most with 'separate'?
Using Miss Rego's 'rat in sepARATe' trick and writing the word ten times gave his hope a clear path.
How is Pranav's view of the test different?
Pranav thinks you should just hope for the best, while Jagdish sees that hoping without practice won't spell anything.
Can you tell me who has wrote this poem? Is it good English?

Can you tell me who wrote this poem?
Why: "Has wrote" mixes two forms. Use the past simple "wrote", or "has written" with the past participle.

This happened the winter I was eleven. Papa's shop closed, and I decided the best thing was not to ask. If anyone mentioned it, I said, "We're fine." I said it so often I almost believed it.
But I kept waking at three in the morning with my heart thumping. At school, when my friend Imran borrowed my eraser without asking, I yelled at him in front of everyone. He looked at me as if I were a stranger.
That evening I finally asked Papa, "Is it bad?" He told me the truth, in small pieces. It was hard to hear. But after that, I slept.
— Usha

At what time did Usha keep waking up?
At three in the morning.
Why did Usha decide the best thing was not to ask?
Not knowing felt safer than hearing bad news about Papa's shop, so saying "We're fine" kept the fear at arm's length.
What turning point helped Usha sleep again?
Finally asking Papa "Is it bad?" and hearing the truth in small pieces; facing it eased the worry that had been leaking out.
How might Imran have felt being yelled at over an eraser?
Imran was probably shocked and hurt, since the anger was far bigger than a borrowed eraser and he couldn't know about the shop.

Shrink this extract to three sentences.

Vaibhav, you say your first version is "just a landing page". Let your Chetan Chacha tell you about my furniture-rental idea when I was twenty-five. I wanted to rent furniture to students who move every year. I was told, start small. So I made a website with our name, a nice photo of a sofa, and a button that said "Coming soon, leave your email." Two hundred people left their emails. I was thrilled. Then I asked them for feedback. Everyone said the same thing: what does it cost, what can I rent, how long, who delivers? I had learned nothing about whether students actually wanted to rent. I'd only learned that people will type an email into a box. Next time, I rented out five real beds to five real students for one month. That taught me more in four weeks than that website did in four months.

Chetan Chacha tells Vaibhav that his first furniture-rental website, with a sofa photo and a coming-soon button, got two hundred emails. But feedback showed he had learned only that people will type an email, not whether students wanted to rent. Next time he rented five real beds to five students for a month, which taught him far more.

Monday. Vinita's mother handed her a printout: Raghav, twenty-four, six feet, government job, same community. "Perfect on paper," her mother said. Vinita folded it into her notebook and felt nothing at all.
Two weeks later, a Sunday. Vinita and Raghav walked around the lake for three hours. She asked how his family argued. He said, "Loudly, then we eat together." She told him she hated loud rooms. He paused. "Then I'd need to learn to argue softer. Could you teach me?" She laughed, surprised.
A month later, a Friday evening. Her mother asked, "So? Height, job, everything matches, na?" Vinita shook her head. "None of that is why I said yes to a fourth meeting, Ma. It's that he asked me to teach him something."

How long did Vinita and Raghav walk around the lake?
Vinita and Raghav walked around the lake for three hours.
Why did Vinita feel nothing at all when she read the printout?
The printout listed only height, job and community, so she felt bored and unmoved; none of it told her who Raghav really was.
What went right in the Sunday walk, and why did it matter?
Vinita asked about how his family handled arguments, and Raghav answered honestly and offered to change; that revealed his temperament and willingness to learn, which a printout can't show.
How might Vinita's mother see the match differently from Vinita?
Her mother sees the matching height, job and community as the main reasons, while Vinita values the respect and openness she found in their talks.

After the meeting where the regional head announced that the delayed shipment was "Chinmay's oversight", Chinmay sat at his desk staring at nothing. The delay had been a warehouse fault, and he had emailed about it twice. Eshaan, two desks away, stayed back after everyone left and slid a printout onto his desk: the forwarded warnings, highlighted. "I sent the same thing to the regional head. Said I'd seen it myself." "They'll notice you," Chinmay said. "Let them." Chinmay swallowed. Next morning he told the head that any follow-up should come to him first, not Eshaan, since he had been the one on the account. At lunch he set a tiffin box on Eshaan's desk. "I owe you more than this." Eshaan grinned. "Then remember it."

What was highlighted on the printout Eshaan gave Chinmay?
The forwarded warnings were highlighted.
How did Chinmay feel about Eshaan's support, and how can you tell?
Chinmay was moved and grateful: he swallowed, tried to shield Eshaan by asking that follow-up come to him first, and said he owed more than a tiffin box.
How did Chinmay try to protect Eshaan and honour the debt?
He asked the head to send any follow-up to him first and set a tiffin box on Eshaan's desk, saying he owed more than that.
How might Eshaan see the risk taken?
Eshaan seems aware of being noticed and says "Let them", which suggests standing up for fairness mattered more than staying safe.

Site supervisor's note, warehouse project, Pune, 14 March
Indu, our junior engineer, came to my cabin after lunch. On Monday she had noticed that the back fire exit was blocked by cement bags stored by the civil team. It wasn't her area, and for two days she said nothing.
She told me what changed her mind. She had asked herself how she would feel if she had stacked those bags there herself. "Then I'd move them in five minutes," she said. "Walking past them every day is also something I'm choosing."
She was nervous and kept apologising for "interfering". I told her this is exactly the kind of interfering we need.
Action: bags moved today, exit marked, and the safety officer will check every exit on Friday.
Vaibhav

What was blocking the back fire exit?
The back fire exit was blocked by cement bags stored by the civil team.
Why did Indu keep apologising for "interfering"?
She felt nervous stepping outside her own area and worried she might seem to be overstepping, even though she knew the blocked exit mattered.
Which question helped Indu act, and why does it work?
She asked how she would feel if she had stacked the bags herself; it removes the comfort of "I didn't cause it" and shows that walking past is also a choice.
How does Vaibhav see Indu speaking up?
Vaibhav sees it as the right kind of interfering and acts at once, moving the bags and asking the safety officer to check every exit.

Mentor note, Friday demo prep. The campus notes team came in with a list of nine features. Indu wrote them on the board and asked the others one question: "With only two weeks, what does a student need on day one to bring a friend back?" Answers came out loud. "Somewhere to upload notes." "A way to find them." Someone asked about ratings, and Indu said, "Nice, but nobody rates what they cannot find yet." Profiles went the same way. The board ended with two lines under Launch and seven under Later, and the team spent the rest of the hour dividing upload and search between them. I said nothing during the reasoning and only asked when they would show it to a first-year student. They said Tuesday.

Tanuja, project mentor

How many lines ended up under Launch and under Later?
The board ended with two lines under Launch and seven under Later.
How might Indu have felt about the nine-feature list?
Indu seemed determined to cut the list down, wanting the team to focus on what a student needs on day one.
What could the team do if first-year students ask for ratings?
The team could move ratings up the Later list once real requests show that it matters.
How might a first-year student see a site with only upload and search?
A first-year student might find it simple and useful straight away, since finding notes is the main need.

At the district hospital's records office, Sarika had worked for four months with an interpreter, Mrs. Das, beside her at the weekly meeting. Sarika is Deaf and signs Indian Sign Language. Pradeep, the senior clerk, still spoke to Mrs. Das instead of to her: "Tell her the files need re-sorting." Every time, Sarika felt herself shrink a little, as if she were a parcel being discussed. On Monday she signed, and Mrs. Das voiced it: "Pradeep, please talk to me directly. Look at me. Mrs. Das will interpret; you don't need to say 'tell her'." Pradeep went red. "Sorry. I didn't know how." "Just talk to me like anyone else." The next week he faced her and said, "Sarika, can you take the orthopaedic files?" and waited while Mrs. Das signed. At the end he clumsily signed "thank you", which he'd learned from a video. Sarika smiled and signed it back slowly, so he could see it again.

How long had Sarika worked with an interpreter at the meeting?
Four months.
How did Sarika feel when Pradeep spoke to the interpreter instead of her?
Sarika felt diminished and ignored, as if she were a parcel being discussed rather than a colleague.
What did Sarika ask Pradeep to do, and why was it fair?
To look at her and talk to her directly while Mrs. Das interpreted, which gives her equal access and respect in meetings.
How did Pradeep respond over the next week?
Pradeep was embarrassed at first, then faced Sarika, asked her questions himself, and even learned to sign 'thank you'.

metadata.subtype: Sign language in workplaces and public life [Expressing]

messages.content: Can you make up a CHAI acrostic? Each line should open with the next letter.

Cups are warm in our hands
Hot steam curls into the air
A little ginger wakes the taste
In the evening we sit and talk

Read this:

You want to know why I stopped wearing that dupatta, Apa? Fine. I'm Zainab, and it's stupid, but here.

It was Ammi's old one, the orange one with a small burn mark near the edge. I liked it. I wore it to the school exhibition on Saturday.

I walked in, and Aditi leaned over to Gunjan and whispered something. Gunjan covered her mouth. That was all I needed. I knew what Aditi said. "Look, she's wearing a curtain." I could hear it in her exact voice, the one she uses for mocking.

I folded the dupatta into my bag in the washroom and spent the whole exhibition feeling cold and plain. I didn't look at them once.

Did I ask them? No. Why would I? I knew.

...Although Gunjan did come and ask me later where I got the colour. I said I didn't remember.

What mark was on Ammi's old dupatta?
A small burn mark near the edge.
Why did Zainab feel she didn't need to ask Aditi what she whispered?
Zainab was already a little unsure about the old dupatta, so the whisper seemed to confirm her fear. The imagined words felt as real as if she'd heard them.
What turning point did Zainab miss, and what could she do now?
When Gunjan asked where the colour came from, it was a chance to see the whisper might not have been mocking. Zainab could still ask Aditi or Gunjan directly, or just wear the dupatta again.
How might Gunjan feel after asking about the colour and getting "I don't remember"?
Gunjan may feel brushed off and confused, since the question sounded friendly. Gunjan might even wonder if Zainab is upset with her.
Personal or personnel department?

Say "personnel department". "Personnel" means the people who work for an organisation. "Personal" means belonging to one person or private.
Examples: The personnel department handles new staff. Please do not read my personal diary.

How can I speak English with more confidence?
Quick one: why do we wear light-coloured clothes in summer?
What is the full name of the shopkeeper at the corner store?
What does the word "inkling" mean?

1. Talk to a friend in English every day, even for a few minutes. Do not worry about small mistakes, and keep going.
2. Light colours keep us cooler. Because they reflect more sunlight, while dark colours take in more of it as heat.
3. I don't know; I can't see your neighbourhood. Ask the shopkeeper politely.
4. Inkling means a slight idea or feeling about something. It is a noun.

The break room at the accounts office was empty after six, the kettle ticking as it cooled. Vijay and Sarita, partners for two years, often waited here for the shared cab. Vijay had rehearsed a sentence all week and now it stuck in the throat. "There's a thing I've never told anyone," Vijay said. "In college I failed a year and told my family I was on an exchange. I still feel ashamed."

Vijay stared at the floor, waiting for the sigh, the joke, the pity.

Sarita set down the cup. "That sounds heavy to carry alone. Thank you for telling me." No lecture. After a moment, "Do you want to say more, or is that enough for today?"

Vijay let out a long breath. "That's enough for today. But it helped."

Where were Vijay and Sarita waiting?
In the break room at the accounts office, waiting for the shared cab.
What might Vijay be worried Sarita will think about the failed year?
That Sarita will sigh, joke or pity Vijay, since Vijay stares at the floor waiting for it and still feels ashamed of the old lie.
What did Vijay do that made it safer to open up?
Vijay shared one piece at a pace Vijay chose, then noticed whether Sarita held it with care, and Sarita's question about saying more or stopping gave Vijay control of the pace.
How might Sarita have felt receiving Vijay's confession?
Probably trusted and careful, since Sarita thanked Vijay, avoided any lecture and checked how much more Vijay wanted to say.
Dost ne likha "I will come tomorow." Is it right?
Not quite. It is: "I will come tomorrow." Why: "Tomorrow" is spelled with one m and a double r.

It was pouring, and the school bus was forty minutes late. Bidisha stood under the shed, not speaking to her little sister Nirmala. That morning Nirmala had spilled ink on Bidisha's homework, and Bidisha had shouted at her.
Two older girls from another school were waiting too. One grabbed Nirmala's umbrella. "Share, na." They laughed and held it out of reach.
Nirmala's lip trembled. She looked at Bidisha.
Bidisha was still angry. But she stepped forward. "Give it back. She's my sister." Her voice cracked, but she didn't move.
They dropped it. The bus came. Bidisha sat next to Nirmala and, without a word, held the umbrella over both of them to the door.

How late was the school bus?
The bus was forty minutes late.
What might Bidisha have been feeling when her voice cracked?
She was nervous and still a little angry, but her loyalty to Nirmala was stronger than her grudge.
What could Bidisha do if the older girls bother them again?
She could tell the bus conductor or a teacher, so an adult can stop the older girls.
What is it like for Nirmala when Bidisha steps forward?
Nirmala feels relieved and protected, even though her sister had been angry with her that morning.

I'm Indu, and I was in the playground when the PE teacher announced that only Class 7 could use the new football at lunch. Vaibhav had been waiting all week for that ball. He said, "Okay, Sir," but his lips were pressed thin and his ears had gone red. He didn't argue. I can't be sure what he was thinking, but he walked off very stiffly. Behind the canteen he kicked the old ball against the wall, hard, again and again, until he was out of breath. Then he sat down next to me and said, "It's not fair. We're good players too." I said maybe he could ask Sir about taking turns. The next day he did, politely, and Sir agreed to Class 6 on Fridays.

Which class could use the new football at lunch?
Only Class 7.
What might Vaibhav's thin lips and red ears suggest?
He was probably angry and disappointed at a rule that felt unfair, even while staying polite, though Indu can't be sure.
What gave Vaibhav's anger a safe outlet?
Kicking the old ball against the wall behind the canteen, talking it over with Indu, and the next day raising the fairness politely.
How might the PE teacher have seen Vaibhav's "Okay, Sir"?
The teacher might have thought Vaibhav accepted the rule calmly, missing the anger underneath until the polite request the next day.

Uday: papa's been taking that herbal powder for his BP for 3 weeks
Uday: the machine at home shows lower readings now. he wants to stop his tablets
Pallavi: wait, did anything else change in those 3 weeks?
Uday: hmm. he started walking after dinner. and he's cut down on pickles since Mummy's rule
Pallavi: so the powder, the walks and less salt all came together. no way to tell which one did it
Pallavi: and home readings go up and down from day to day anyway
Uday: true. but he's convinced
Pallavi: honestly the safest thing is that he doesn't stop anything without asking his doctor first. take the readings and the powder packet to the appointment
Uday: ok. i'll book it this week
Pallavi: good. and ask if there's proper research on the powder, not just someone's story

What else changed for Papa during those weeks?
He started walking after dinner and cut down on pickles since Mummy's rule.
What is Uday worried about?
That Papa wants to stop his tablets because of the lower readings, which feels risky to Uday even though Papa is convinced.
What does Pallavi advise, and why is it wise?
That Papa shouldn't stop anything without asking his doctor and should bring the readings and the powder packet, because several changes came together and only a doctor can judge safely.
How might Papa see the lower readings?
As proof the powder worked, since the readings dropped after he started it, without noticing the walks and the lower salt.

Yusuf's diary, Monday
Plan: homework at five. Reality: played cricket till seven. Then dinner. Then I was tired. My sister Farida saw my face and said, "Timer, little brother." We set it for twenty-five minutes. No talking. I did the English worksheet and half the maths. Then a five-minute break. Then the other half. Done by nine. I hate admitting it, but the timer works. Tomorrow I'm doing homework at five before cricket. I'll write in here if I actually do it.

How long did they set the timer for?
Twenty-five minutes.
What does Yusuf writing "I hate admitting it" suggest?
Yusuf felt a bit sheepish but relieved that the timer helped to stop the putting-off.
What small step would help Yusuf tomorrow?
Start the timer at five before going out, so cricket becomes the reward after homework.
How might Farida see Yusuf's evening?
Farida probably feels pleased that the timer idea helped Yusuf get it done.

Monday: A fire engine raced past the school gate while Tanvir, four, waited with his mother, Damini. He covered his ears and watched it go.
Wednesday: At dinner Tanvir told Papa, "A fire engine came, and the firemen were going to save a cat." Damini smiled; she had only said maybe they were going to help someone.
Saturday: At Nani's house, after a cartoon about firefighters, Tanvir said, "The fire engine stopped at my school, and a fireman gave me his hat, and I held the big hose!" He believed every word. Damini didn't argue. She just asked, "Which part do you remember with your own ears?" He thought. "The loud noise."

What did Tanvir do when the fire engine raced past on Monday?
He covered his ears and watched it go.
Why does Tanvir believe a fireman gave him a hat?
A cartoon and his mother's words mixed into his memory, and each retelling reshaped it until it felt as true as the loud noise.
What did Damini do on Saturday, and why was it a good choice?
She didn't argue but asked which part he remembered with his own ears, gently helping him find the real memory without shaming him.
How might Papa feel hearing about the cat on Wednesday?
Papa probably thought it was a sweet, exciting story, with no way of knowing the cat came from a guess and not from the day itself.

You want the real story, Wasim? Fine. I'm Harsha, I'm sixteen, and I'm not proud of that night.
So the class chat was busy after results, and someone posts, "Harsha topping the list… from the bottom 🥇." Everyone reacts. Like, instantly.
And the thing is, I'd already been thinking it. That maybe I'm just not a studying kind of person. Appa's been quiet all week about my marks. So that message didn't feel like a joke. It felt like someone reading my mind out loud.
My thumb just went. I wrote something really rude back, about his face. Didn't even reread it. Because if I stayed quiet, then everyone would think I agreed.

What did the message in the class chat say about Harsha?
It said "Harsha topping the list… from the bottom 🥇."
Why did the message feel like more than a joke to Harsha?
It hit a fear Harsha already had, that he was not a studying kind of person, so he felt exposed and ashamed, as if someone read his mind out loud.
What turning point was available to Harsha in that moment?
He could have waited and reread before replying, or messaged someone he trusts about how it hurt, rather than firing back in public.
What might Wasim be experiencing as Harsha tells this story?
Wasim is probably listening with concern, perhaps surprised to hear how much the joke hurt and how worried Harsha is about Appa's silence.

The Christmas concert had already started when Francis, five, discovered his angel wings were tied on backwards, and there was no time to fix them. He walked on stage anyway. The audience laughed kindly at the crooked wings. Francis turned red, stared at the floor, and stopped singing. Manoj Sir, at the piano, caught his eye, pointed at his own wonky tie, and winked. Francis gave a tiny smile. He sang the last verse softly, then ran off to hide behind the curtain.

What was wrong with Francis's wings?
They were tied on backwards.
What was Francis feeling when he turned red and stared at the floor?
Francis felt embarrassed by the unexpected laughter and attention.
How did Manoj Sir help Francis without drawing more attention?
He caught his eye, pointed at his own wonky tie and winked, showing that mistakes are okay.
How might the audience see Francis?
The audience probably found him sweet and didn't mean to embarrass him.

“Ma'am, ma'am, I know this one—” Noor blurted, half out of the seat, on Nandini's second day as a Class 8 teacher.
“Noor, I'm glad you know. Hand up, please, and I'll come to you next.” Noor sat down, red-faced, hand raised.
“Ma'am, yesterday you let Rohan shout out,” said a boy at the back.
Nandini paused. “You're right. That was unfair to you. From now on the rule is the same for everyone, including me.” A few children grinned. In the corner, Aditi, who had not spoken all week, lifted her hand halfway.
Nandini went to her first. “Yes, Aditi?”
“I didn't get the last step.”
“Thank you. Who else didn't?” Eight hands went up.

On which day of Nandini's teaching did Noor blurt out the answer?
It was Nandini's second day as a Class 8 teacher.
How did Nandini likely feel when the boy said she had let Rohan shout out?
She likely felt caught out and a little embarrassed, pausing before admitting the slip rather than protecting her image as the teacher.
What did Nandini's handling of the first interruption teach the class?
It taught that a hand up gets you a turn, that the rule is the same for everyone, and that saying you did not understand is welcome.
How might Aditi have felt when Nandini went to her first?
Aditi probably felt surprised and brave, since it was the first time Aditi had spoken all week, and safer when eight hands went up.

Ulla sat in the bike seat behind Lars, reciting as they rode through Copenhagen. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door."
"Five, six?" Lars prompted.
"Pick up sticks! Seven, eight, lay them straight!" She bounced to the rhythm.
At the red light she said it all again, faster. "I know it all, Pappa!"
"Tomorrow, the song about the moon?"

What was Ulla reciting on the bike?
She was reciting "One, two, buckle my shoe."
What does Ulla bouncing to the rhythm suggest?
It suggests she enjoys the beat of the rhyme and feels proud of knowing it.
How did Lars help Ulla remember the rhyme?
He prompted her with "Five, six?" and let her finish, then suggested a new song.
How might Lars feel hearing her say it faster?
He likely feels proud and pleased by her quick memory.

'Tushar, you told your mother "Dadi lets me," didn't you? Come, let your Deepika Nani tell you something. My own grandmother spoiled me rotten. Jalebis before dinner, no sweeping, stories till midnight. My mother had rules: homework first, one sweet only. Once I stamped my foot and said, "Ammamma says I don't have to!" in front of both of them. My grandmother's face fell. My mother went red. That night Ammamma told me, "My love is a holiday, kanna. Your mother's rules are your home. Don't make us fight." After that, I enjoyed my jalebis at her place and did my sweeping at home. Both of them loved me. They just loved me in different ways.'

What sweets did young Deepika get before dinner?
Jalebis.
What was young Deepika feeling when she stamped her foot?
Frustrated and defiant, wanting to use Ammamma's softness against her mother's rules.
What choice in the story fixed things?
Enjoying the treats at Ammamma's place while following her mother's rules at home, without setting them against each other.
How did Ammamma feel when Deepika used her against her mother?
Hurt and uncomfortable; her face fell, and later she asked Deepika not to make them fight.

The call centre in Buenos Aires had a new banner above the coffee machine: Embrace every challenge! Valentina, a team manager, had seen three new agents quit in two months.
She started watching Vera, the newest. Vera was bright and friendly, but she was put on live calls on day three with no practice. When she mixed up two billing codes, the floor supervisor marked it red on the public board. After that, Vera stopped trying new call types and passed every tricky customer to someone else.
Valentina thought: the banner says challenge, but everything here punishes it.
So she asked for Wednesday mornings off the phones for her team. They practised difficult calls with each other, recorded them and talked about what went well. Errors were discussed privately, and she took the red marks off the public board.
Two weeks later, Vera volunteered for the complaints line.

Where was the new banner placed?
It was placed above the coffee machine.
What did Valentina think when she watched Vera pass on tricky calls?
She felt concerned and saw the contradiction: the banner asks for challenge, but the workplace punishes mistakes, so Vera plays safe.
What did Valentina change, and why did it matter?
She got practice time off the phones, used recorded practice and feedback, and removed public red marks, which made learning safe and possible.
How might Vera feel volunteering for the complaints line?
Vera probably feels nervous but safer and more confident now that mistakes are treated as part of learning.

Saga Dawa month meant no meat in Tenzin's kitchen, the way it had been in Ama's house in Dharamshala. But tonight six friends were coming, Simran among them, the one who called any meal without chicken 'just a snack'. Then the rain knocked out the power, leaving one gas burner and a torch. Tenzin, twenty-five, made a big pot of vegetable thenthuk and, with the last of the phone battery, ordered a plate of chicken momos from the corner shop for anyone who wanted them, kept on a separate plate by the door. Simran arrived dripping, laughed at the torchlight, then went back for the thenthuk twice. 'Okay, this is not a snack.' Nobody teased anyone's plate. The momos disappeared too.

What did Tenzin cook in the big pot?
Vegetable thenthuk.
What was Tenzin probably feeling when the power went out with six friends on the way?
Tenzin was probably worried and under pressure, with one burner, a torch and guests coming, yet calm enough to plan.
How did Tenzin keep the custom and still welcome everyone, despite the power cut?
Tenzin kept the kitchen meat-free but offered chicken momos from outside on a separate plate, and nobody mocked anyone's choice.
How did Simran's view of a meatless meal change?
Simran moved from calling it 'just a snack' to going back twice and saying so, because it was offered warmly, without a lecture.

In the kasba market, Minakshi, twenty-one, set her basket of homemade mango pickle jars on Saurabh's shop counter. He picked one up and sniffed. "Good. But I can only pay this much." He named a price below what the oil and mangoes had cost her. Minakshi's jaw tightened. She had practised this with her mother. "Bhaiya, at that price I lose money. But if you take twenty jars a month instead of five, I can come down a little." Saurabh frowned. "And if they don't sell?" "Put them near the billing counter. If they're still here after a month, I'll take back what's left." He looked at the jars, then at her steady face. "Fine. Twenty jars. Your price minus a bit." She walked out, heart racing, grinning.

What did Minakshi sell to Saurabh's shop?
Homemade mango pickle jars.
What does Minakshi's tightened jaw suggest when she heard his first price?
She felt frustrated and firm, because his offer was below what the ingredients had cost her.
What made Minakshi's counter-offer work?
She traded a small price cut for a larger order and offered to take back unsold jars, easing his risk while protecting her income.
How might Saurabh see the deal afterwards?
He probably feels he got a fair price with little risk, and may respect Minakshi for negotiating calmly.

Read this:

Thursday, late.

All afternoon I was sure Seema wanted my project. She kept copying the director on my emails, asked for my client notes "just to read", and smiled too much in the review. I typed a sharp message to her twice and deleted it twice.

On the bus home I asked myself the annoying question: have I ever wanted her work? Yes. Last month, when she got the launch, I read her whole deck looking for mistakes. That is exactly what I was accusing her of.

Writing that down made my chest loosen. What I actually want is for the director to see my work, not to beat Seema. So tomorrow I'll ask the director for ten minutes, and I'll tell Seema plainly that I'd like my name on the client notes.

Vandana

How many times did Vandana type and delete a sharp message to Seema?
Vandana typed the sharp message twice and deleted it twice.
Why did Vandana feel so certain that Seema wanted the project?
Vandana was anxious about being overlooked and had once wanted Seema's launch too, so seeing that same wish in Seema felt obvious.
What small step cooled Vandana down, and what comes next?
Asking whether the same wish lived in Vandana took the heat out; next come a calm ten minutes with the director and a direct request to Seema about the notes.
How might Seema have experienced the next day if the sharp message had been sent?
Seema would likely feel accused and defensive over ordinary questions, and the two would argue instead of sorting out credit.

"Siddharth, bhai, listen. My friend's group doubles your money in six weeks."
"Doubles? Who pays for the doubling, Sahil?"
"The trading guy. He's got screenshots. Proof."
"Screenshots aren't proof. Anyone can make those."
"You're so boring."
"Maybe. I'm putting a small amount every month into a regular fund. It's slow."
"Slow is useless."
"It's not flashy. But it's spread across lots of companies, so one bad one doesn't sink it."
"And if my guy is real?"
"If it's real, why is he in a chat group begging for your pocket money?"
"..."
"Just ask someone who knows before you send anything. Please."
"Fine. But if I miss out, I'm blaming you."

How quickly did Sahil's friend's group claim to double money?
They claimed to double it in six weeks.
What does Sahil's 'You're so boring' suggest about how he feels?
He is excited by the idea of fast money and a bit irritated that Siddharth is questioning it.
What would you advise Sahil to do next?
Ask a trusted, knowledgeable adult or professional before sending any money, as Siddharth suggests.
How does Siddharth see his own small monthly investment?
He sees it as slow and unexciting but safer, because it is spread across many companies.
The tomatos are cheap at the market today. Check the spelling.

The tomatoes are cheap at the market today.
Why: Many nouns that end in -o after a consonant take -es in the plural, as in tomato and tomatoes.

Dear Deepika Ma'am,
I'm writing because of what you said after debate practice today, that I look "closed-off" when I fold my arms and that judges might mark me down. I've been thinking about it all evening. Honestly, there are three reasons I fold them. The auditorium AC is freezing and I always forget my sweater. Also, when I'm waiting to speak, holding my arms feels like holding myself together; it calms me. And only sometimes, like when Rohan interrupted me three times, it's me saying "stop". I didn't want you to think I was being rude to the team. I will try keeping my hands on the lectern when I speak. Could you tell me if I start looking closed-off again, so I can check which reason it is?
Thank you,
Wasim

Who interrupted Wasim three times?
Rohan.
How was Wasim feeling while writing the email?
Wasim felt worried and a little misunderstood, anxious that Deepika Ma'am thought the folded arms meant rudeness to the team.
What plan did Wasim suggest, and why is it sensible?
Keeping hands on the lectern while speaking and asking Ma'am to point out the folded arms, so they can check which reason it is rather than guess.
How might Deepika Ma'am read the email?
Deepika Ma'am may be surprised that the folded arms usually meant cold or self-calming, and glad Wasim explained instead of sulking.

messages.content:
Read this:

On the medical ward in Chennai, Vidya, a final-year student, spoke English to the consultants on rounds and Tamil to the patients' families. But with Lavanya, the ward attendant who had worked there twenty years, Vidya had slipped into rapid English, full of terms: "Please prep bed six for the NG tube, and do the I/O charting."
Lavanya nodded, then quietly asked another attendant what "I/O" meant.
Vidya saw it from the nursing station. Her stomach dropped. She hadn't meant to sound superior, but she had been enjoying sounding like a doctor.
After rounds she went over. "Akka, I spoke too fast earlier. I meant, keep a note of how much water he drinks and how much urine comes, for bed six. In Tamil, I should have said it."
Lavanya smiled. "Twenty years I've done that chart, ma. I just didn't know the English name."
Vidya laughed and asked her to teach her the ward's shortcuts.

Who did Vidya speak Tamil with?
Vidya spoke Tamil to the patients' families.
What was Vidya feeling when she saw Lavanya ask another attendant?
Vidya felt a drop in her stomach, embarrassed and uneasy that her rapid English had made Lavanya feel left out.
What small, kind step did Vidya take?
She went back, apologised for speaking too fast, explained the task in plain words and asked Lavanya to teach her the ward's shortcuts.
How did Lavanya see the situation?
Lavanya felt a little left out by the English term but not small, since she had done that chart for twenty years and simply didn't know its English name.

Read this:

At their flat in Koramangala, Dhruv mentioned, a little awkwardly, that Jeevan still owed him for the concert ticket. Jeevan laughed. "I paid you back that same night, in the auto. I remember doing it." He could picture it: the auto's yellow light, the phone screen, Dhruv saying thanks. Dhruv shrugged. "I don't think so, man." Jeevan, a bit offended, opened his payment app to prove it. He scrolled to that date. Nothing to Dhruv. He scrolled again. Nothing. There was a half-typed payment, never sent, and a message to Dhruv that said "sending now". Jeevan's face went hot. The auto, the screen, the thanks: he had rebuilt the whole scene around what he had meant to do. He sent the money at once, with a long apology.

What did Jeevan find in the payment app?
A half-typed payment, never sent, and a message to Dhruv saying 'sending now'.
How did Jeevan feel when the app showed nothing?
Jeevan felt embarrassed, his face going hot, because the vivid scene he remembered was built around what he had meant to do.
What did Jeevan do right once he saw the record?
He sent the money at once with a long apology, trusting the record over his confident memory.
How might Dhruv have felt raising the debt?
Dhruv felt awkward mentioning it, and was probably relieved when Jeevan checked and paid.

what does "a thorn in the side" mean?
One more thing: can you fix my sentence? The girls was singing a song in the hall.
And is "maternal" a hard word? What does it mean?

1. It means a constant source of annoyance. For example: the leaking tap was a thorn in his side.
2. Corrected: The girls were singing a song in the hall. Why: "girls" is plural, so it takes "were".
3. Maternal means connected with a mother. It is an adjective.
Is 2,718,281 a prime number?
I'm not sure if it is prime, as I can't test a number this size reliably. A prime-checking tool or a maths teacher can confirm.
Change to reported speech: My aunt said, "I am making payasam tonight."
My aunt said that she was making payasam that night.
I had "butterflies in my stomach" before my speech. Is that a stomach problem?

No. It describes the nervous, fluttering feeling you have when you are anxious or excited about something. It is not an illness.
Example: Ira had butterflies in her stomach before the first day of school.

Jomon: Reached home?
Anirban: Just now. Still thinking about what you said at dinner 🙂
Jomon: That I leave wet towels on the bed and you plan holidays till they stop being fun?
Anirban: That part too 😅
Anirban: No, the other part. That when we fought about my night shifts in March, we sat on the kitchen floor and talked till 2 am and nobody walked out.
Jomon: That's the part I trust most. Not the fireworks. The floor.
Anirban: I used to think love had to feel like the first month. It doesn't. It feels like this.
Jomon: Like a cold kitchen floor?
Anirban: Like knowing how we fix things.
Anirban: So yes. Let's tell both our families on Sunday. I'm choosing you, towels included.
Jomon: Choosing you too. Spreadsheet holidays and all ❤️

What did Anirban and Jomon do when they fought about the night shifts in March?
They sat on the kitchen floor and talked till 2 am, and nobody walked out.
What does Anirban's line 'It feels like this' suggest about Anirban's feelings?
Anirban feels calm and secure rather than dazzled, trusting the way they fix things more than the excitement of the first month.
Which choice makes this commitment likely to hold, and why?
They choose each other while naming real flaws, like wet towels and over-planned holidays, and they trust a way of repairing fights they have already tested.
If Jomon had hidden the annoyance about the holidays, what might change?
Anirban would be committing to an edited version of Jomon, and the unspoken irritation could surface later instead of being known and accepted now.

messages.content:
Read this:

Friday
Sarika came back to school today after her Nanaji's funeral. At lunch, Mehul said to her, "Well, at least your Nanaji was really old. He had a good long innings." He meant it kindly, I think. Then Tanya added, "Everything is part of God's plan."
I watched Sarika's face. She smiled, but her jaw went tight and she put her roti back in the box. She didn't say anything for the rest of lunch.
I didn't know what to say either. After school, walking to the gate, I just said, "Sarika, I'm so sorry about your Nanaji. I'm here if you want to talk, or not."
She stopped and hugged me. She said, "Thank you for not telling me it's fine."
I keep thinking about Mehul's face. He'll never know it hurt. Should I tell him? Maybe I will, gently.
Yash

What did Mehul say to Sarika at lunch?
He said, "Well, at least your Nanaji was really old. He had a good long innings."
What was Yash feeling while watching Sarika at lunch?
Yash felt uneasy and unsure, noticing Sarika's hurt but not knowing what to say.
Why did Yash's words work better than Mehul's and Tanya's?
Yash simply said sorry and offered to be there without explaining the death away, so Sarika didn't have to pretend it was fine.
How did Sarika experience Mehul's and Tanya's words?
Sarika felt hurt and alone, forcing a smile while her jaw tightened and she stopped eating.

Read this:

Karthik, you think your brother is Amma's favourite? Let me, your Vandana athai, tell you about my elder brother Sundar, your periyappa.
In Madurai, in the eighties, Sundar was the golden boy: first rank, cricket captain, our father's pride. I was twenty and doing my BSc, and I spent a whole year trying to beat him at everything. I learned chess because he played chess. I entered the essay competition he had once won. I lost at chess, won the essay, and nobody at home even noticed, because he'd just got into engineering.
One night I cried at him, angrily. "You get everything." And he said, "Vandana, Appa shouts at me every day about marks. I envy you. You get left alone."
After that we went to Appa together and told him how it felt. He didn't change overnight. But I stopped racing Sundar. I started racing only myself.
So, Karthik: talk to your brother before you decide he has it easy.

Which competition did Vandana enter?
The essay competition Sundar had once won.
How did Vandana feel during the year of trying to beat Sundar?
Envious and unnoticed, ending in angry tears when nobody at home noticed her win.
What was the turning point in Vandana's story?
Sundar saying he envied her; they then went to Appa together to say how it felt, and she stopped racing him.
How did Sundar see being the favourite?
As pressure, since Appa shouted at him daily about marks, and he envied Vandana's freedom.

Read this:

Gargi, you gave Ria a sticker today without saying sorry? Ha. Your Dhruv Dada did the same thing, long ago. My friend Mohan was slow at kho-kho, and one day I shouted, "Tortoise! You lost it for us!" in front of the whole team.

Next morning I brought him my best marble, the blue one with the white swirl. I just put it in his hand and talked about kites. He took it. We played. I thought that was the end of it.

But for weeks Mohan didn't sit next to me at lunch. Finally my mother asked, "Did you say sorry, or just give him a marble?" So I went and said it: "Sorry I called you tortoise. It was mean." Mohan grinned. "I know. Keep your marble next time. Just say it."

What did young Dhruv give Mohan?
Dhruv gave his best marble, the blue one with the white swirl.
Why did young Dhruv give the marble without mentioning the name-calling?
Young Dhruv felt guilty and wanted to cancel the harm quietly, hoping the gift would make it as if nothing had happened.
What turning point in the story finished the repair?
His mother's question led Dhruv to say an actual sorry, which Mohan had needed more than the marble.
How might Mohan have felt taking the marble without an apology?
Mohan was probably still hurt, which is why he stopped sitting next to Dhruv at lunch for weeks.

Read this:

It was the second week of the sprint when the client called the Bengaluru office and changed the payment screen completely: no more card form, a new login first, and a demo in five days.
Ishita, twenty-four, had written forty test cases for the old screen. Her teammate Avni groaned. “All that, wasted.”
Ishita didn't answer at once. She opened her test sheet, read down it, and started sorting: which cases still matter, which need rewriting, which can go. Of forty, eleven still fit. She wrote down what she didn't know yet and took it to the product lead in a list.
By the afternoon she had a new plan on the whiteboard. Avni came back from lunch and read it. “You're oddly calm.”
“I was annoyed for about an hour,” Ishita said. “Then it was just a new puzzle.”

How many of the forty test cases still fit?
Of forty, eleven still fit.
How did Ishita feel about the change, by her own account?
She says she was annoyed for about an hour, and then felt calm, treating it as a new puzzle.
What approach helped Ishita adapt so quickly?
She sorted her old work into keep, rewrite and drop, and listed her unknowns for the product lead instead of guessing.
How does Avni see the change compared with Ishita?
Avni first sees it as wasted work and is frustrated, while Ishita sees a new puzzle.

Read this:

On Diwali evening the community centre hall smelled of ghee. Anjali set a tray of besan laddoos on the long table and said good evening to each person coming in, even the two who never nodded on the stairs. Tejas, from the flat opposite, took one and said, "I never thanked you for carrying my shopping last month." Anjali laughed. "You can thank me by joining the phone list for emergencies." Tejas wrote a name and number on the sign-up sheet. Weeks later, when the shared water tank overflowed at midnight, that list brought five neighbours in ten minutes, and a small squabble about whose turn it was to mop was over in a shrug.

How long did it take five neighbours to arrive when the tank overflowed?
Five neighbours arrived in ten minutes.
Why did Anjali greet even the two who never nodded, and what did Anjali want?
To include everyone and build trust, hoping small warmth would open a connection.
What small step by Anjali prepared the lane for the midnight overflow?
Asking neighbours to join a phone list for emergencies.
How does Tejas see Anjali?
As a kind neighbour worth thanking; Tejas mentions the shopping and signs the list.

Read this:

"Nani, you gave me thirty and Nikhil twenty." Ankita, ten, held up the coins.
"You fetched the vegetables, beti."
"But Nikhil fetched the milk twice and the newspaper. That's three trips. I only did one."
Nikhil, eight, looked up hopefully. "She's right, Nani."
"Arrey, it's just pocket money."
"It's not fair if it's not counted." Ankita took out a sheet of paper. "I'm making a chart. Trips, sweeping, watering plants. Each gets five rupees."
"And who checks the chart?" Nani asked, amused.
"Me."
"And if I give you extra because you're my first grandchild?"
"Then I'll give it to Nikhil." Ankita slid ten rupees across the table.
Nani shook her head, smiling. "This girl will run a bank one day."
Nikhil pocketed the coins before anyone could change their mind.

What did Ankita fetch for Nani?
She fetched the vegetables.
What does Ankita's chart suggest about how she feels about fairness?
It suggests she is determined that fairness means counting exactly, even when counting leaves her with less.
How could Nani help Ankita keep fairness without making it rigid?
She could praise Ankita's honesty and also explain that small gifts of love don't always need to be counted like payments.
How does Nikhil see Ankita's rule?
Nikhil is happy and a bit surprised, since Ankita's strict counting gives Nikhil more money.

Read this:

In her small room in a Kolkata mess, Rekha had spent a month building a sculpture from old glass bangles: dozens of them, red and green, melted and fused into a twisted column. The bangles were her grandmother's; after Thakuma's death, the family had given them to Rekha. At the college exhibition, her classmate Usha stood in front of it for a long time. "It's so festive," Usha said. "Like a wedding." Rekha's throat tightened. "They were my grandmother's. She died in March." Usha's face fell. "Oh, Rekha. I'm sorry. I didn't know." Rekha shook her head. "No, don't be sorry. She wore them at every wedding in the family. Maybe that's in there too." Usha looked again, quieter. "It's grief and celebration, then." Rekha smiled for the first time that evening. "Yes. That's exactly what she was."

What was Rekha's sculpture made from?
Old glass bangles, red and green, melted and fused into a twisted column.
What was Rekha feeling when Usha called the sculpture festive?
Her throat tightened with grief, because the bangles were her grandmother's and she had died in March.
What did Rekha do that allowed both readings to stand?
She shared the story of the bangles but welcomed Usha's reading, since her grandmother wore them at every wedding.
How did Usha's view of the sculpture change?
She first saw it as festive like a wedding, then, after hearing Rekha, as grief and celebration together.

metadata.subtype: Sculpture as expression of inner states [Expressing]

messages.content: My history book calls it the freedom struggle. Does struggle mean having a hard time?

As a noun, a struggle can be a long, hard fight for a cause or a goal. As a verb, to struggle means to try very hard with difficulty.
Example: The book describes the struggle for the right to vote.

Read this:

I'm Manoj, and I used to think a scream was a joke. Siddharth and I would shriek across the field to scare each other, and everyone laughed. So when someone screamed near the back gate one evening, I rolled my eyes and kept kicking the ball. Siddharth stopped. "That didn't sound like a joke." We went to look, carefully, from the corner, and saw a younger boy on the ground, holding his knee. Siddharth ran to get the caretaker while I stayed with him. Since then I never use a scream as a prank, and I never ignore one.

Where did someone scream one evening?
Someone screamed near the back gate.
What was Manoj feeling when Manoj first heard the scream, and what changed?
Manoj assumed it was a joke and eye-rolled. After Siddharth said it didn't sound like one, Manoj felt worried enough to go and look.
What should someone do when they hear a scream that might be a prank?
Take it seriously, check safely and call for help. Ignoring it could leave someone hurt.
How might the younger boy on the ground have felt?
He was probably scared and in pain, and relieved when someone came. If everyone ignored screams, he would have had to wait.

metadata.subtype: Screams as alarm and help calls [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Sudha Aunty,
You told me to write when something happened that I didn't want to tell Ammi yet, so here it is. On Saturday some boys from my building were daring each other to race scooters down the flyover ramp without helmets. They'd filmed two already and everyone was screaming. It was my turn. My heart was banging and I actually had my hand on the handle. Then I remembered what you said about deciding things 'before the crowd arrives.' I'd already decided, weeks ago: no dares on roads. So I said, 'Not doing it. I'll film.' They called me scared. I was, a bit. But I'd rather be scared on the pavement. I'll tell Ammi this weekend.
Tanvir

What had Tanvir decided weeks ago?
No dares on roads.
What do Tanvir's banging heart and hand on the handle suggest Tanvir was feeling?
Tanvir was caught up in the excitement and pressure and was close to going along with it.
What lesson from this could help Tanvir in future heated moments?
Deciding limits calmly in advance, so Tanvir has a ready answer when the crowd and excitement hit.
How might Sudha Aunty feel reading the letter?
Relieved Tanvir was safe, proud that her advice helped, and glad Tanvir plans to tell Ammi. 🙏

Read this:

Mehak, you keep asking how I stay so calm at the dispensary. Honestly? I'm not calm. Since Nani fell in her kitchen in Nashik, and she still lives alone, I worry about her all the time. For a month I carried it behind the counter. I'd be counting tablets and suddenly picture her on the floor. Twice I had to recount a whole order.

So now I do this. When the worry shows up at work, I say to myself, "Not here, Disha. Seven o'clock." I even write it on the back of my hand sometimes. And at seven, on the bus home, I actually open it. I call Nani, I let myself feel scared, I message the neighbour aunty, I plan one thing for the weekend. Then I put it away till the next evening.

It isn't locking it up. It's giving it an appointment.

What did Disha have to do twice at the dispensary before trying the new habit?
Disha had to recount a whole order twice.
Why does saying "Not here, Disha. Seven o'clock" feel possible to Disha, when simply ignoring the worry did not?
Disha trusts that the worry will really get its turn at seven, so pausing it doesn't feel like abandoning Nani. The promise is kept every evening, which makes it believable.
What was the turning point that let Disha focus at work again?

The moment Disha stopped just carrying the worry all day and gave it a fixed time on the bus home, with real actions like calling Nani and the neighbour. Keeping that appointment every evening is what makes the daytime pause work.
How might Nani experience Disha's seven o'clock routine?
Nani likely gets a steady call every evening and knows the neighbour is in touch, so she may feel looked after rather than worried over in scattered bursts. The routine gives her something to expect.

messages.content: What was the print run of the first edition of a small poetry book from 1932?
I don't know the print run, because it is hard to confirm for old, small books. A library catalogue or a rare-book dealer may have it.

Two directors, one for operations and one for marketing, had argued for a month over whose customer list should be cleaned first. Yogesh tried separate chats, then a joint one, and both times the directors repeated the same points. On a Friday afternoon in the Chennai office, he noticed the talks were going in circles and his team sat idle. This was beyond what he could settle alone. He wrote one page: both positions in neutral words, what each would cost in time, and the date a choice was needed. He sent it to Reena, the executive sponsor, and asked for a ruling by Tuesday. Neither director liked being summarised so briefly, but each agreed the page was fair. Reena chose the operations list first, marketing's in April, and Yogesh told his team to start.

What did Yogesh ask Reena to do by Tuesday?
Yogesh asked Reena for a ruling by Tuesday.
What was Yogesh feeling as the talks went in circles?
Yogesh was probably frustrated and concerned about his idle team, which led him to see the matter as beyond what he could settle alone.
What could Yogesh have tried before going to Reena?
Yogesh could have asked both directors to agree on criteria such as customer impact and cost and score the two lists together, since it might settle the matter without a ruling.
How might the directors have felt about the one-page summary?
Neither liked being summarised so briefly, but both accepted the page as fair, which made it easier to accept the ruling.

messages.content:
Read this:

At the colony's monthly meeting, Dhruv had already decided which way Vidya from the far block would vote. She always objected, he thought. Then he caught himself and asked her outright, “What worries you about the parking plan?” Vidya blinked. “The lane behind B block floods. Nobody has asked us.” It was a fair point he had missed.

Later, three men near the tea table joked about the security guards, mimicking how they speak. Someone laughed. Dhruv put his cup down. “They've watched over our children's cycles for years. Could we not?” One man shrugged, another looked at his shoes, and the laughing stopped.

Dhruv still walked home with his own block friends, chatting as usual. He just no longer needed them to be the only ones who mattered.

What did Vidya say worries her about the parking plan?
Vidya said the lane behind B block floods and nobody has asked the far block.
Why did Dhruv ask Vidya outright about the parking plan?
Dhruv felt uneasy on catching himself assuming Vidya would object, and was curious to hear Vidya's real reasons instead of guessing.
What did Dhruv do when the joking about the guards began, and what happened next?
Dhruv put his cup down and asked them to stop, mentioning the guards' years of watching over the children's cycles, and the laughing stopped.
How might one of the guards feel if they had overheard the meeting that evening?
They might feel relieved and quietly respected that someone in the group spoke up on their behalf, though the mocking would still sting.

Please write a job application email, about 90 words, for the post of junior librarian at a public library. My name is Divya Nair and I have a library science diploma and two years of experience at a school library.

Subject: Application for the Post of Junior Librarian

Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing to apply for the post of junior librarian at your library. I hold a diploma in library science and have two years of experience working in a school library. I enjoy helping readers find the books they need and keeping the shelves in good order. I would be glad to attend an interview at your convenience. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Yours sincerely,
Divya Nair
I won a small trophy for the inter-house relay and I have to say a few words on stage.
Congratulations. What do you feel most grateful for?
My teammates, and our coach.
Then you already have your message. Thank the team, the coach and the people who cheered. Keep it to a few sentences.
I'm scared I'll forget what to say.
Write three points on a small card and glance at it if you need to. Practise it twice aloud, and you'll be calmer on stage.
What if my voice shakes?
A shaky voice is normal and the audience will be on your side. Take a slow breath before speaking and look at a friendly face in the crowd.
Should I add something funny?
A small, kind joke can be nice, such as how tired your legs were at the last baton change. Keep it light, and make sure it doesn't tease anyone.

Preeti: karthik can I tell you something weird
Karthik: ya
Preeti: someone keeps making fake accounts using my photos. posting that I cheated in the exam
Karthik: since when?
Preeti: like a month? I thought it would stop
Karthik: do you have screenshots
Preeti: some. I deleted a few bc I didn't want to see them
Karthik: don't delete. make a note with dates and what each post said. then it's proof, not just a bad feeling
Preeti: ok. doing it now

Karthik: that's a lot. you need to show an adult today, not later
Preeti: my mom's home. going

How many posts did Preeti count?
Preeti counted 14 posts from 5 accounts.
Why did Preeti delete some screenshots at first?
Preeti felt hurt and upset seeing them and wanted to avoid the pain, not realising they were evidence.
What else could Karthik do as a friend?
Karthik could stay in touch that evening and offer to tell the teacher what Karthik has seen, so Preeti does not feel alone.
How might Preeti's mother see the list her daughter made?
Her mother likely felt shocked and protective, but the dated list gave her something clear to report and show the teacher that same evening.
