messages.content:
Read this:

Bedtime notes for Farida
Bedtime was a battle all last week: bargaining, crying, running off. This week I kept the same steps every night. Warm bath at seven, lamp turned low, the 'chanda mama' song twice, then one long cuddle and her toy elephant. No scolding, no extra stories. On Monday she cried for a while. By Thursday she was yawning in the bath and pointing to the lamp herself. Tonight she was asleep before the second song ended.
Harsha

What song did Harsha sing?
The 'chanda mama' song, twice.
How did Farida seem to feel about bedtime by Thursday?
She seemed calm and safe, yawning in the bath and pointing to the lamp because she knew what came next.
Why did the same steps every night work better than bargaining?
The predictable routine told Farida's body that sleep was safe, so she stopped fighting it.
What would change if Harsha scolded or added extra stories?
Farida would be left guessing and upset, and bedtime would likely stay a battle.

Read this:

Neelam joined the Saturday "life mastery" sessions at a Pune co-working space because her classmate Sangeeta said they were friendly. They were: tea, hugs, clapping for anyone who shared.
By the fourth week, Neelam started noticing things. The leader said, "Your family keeps you small. Spend less time with them." A member who asked why the advanced course cost so much was called "weak" and "not ready", and nobody spoke to him at tea. Every session ended with a push to pay for the next level, and quickly.
On the bus home, Neelam made a list in her phone. Keeps me from family. Wants big money fast. Calls doubters weak. She stared at it. "Three for three," she murmured. "That's not self-improvement. That's control."
She didn't go the next Saturday. When Sangeeta messaged, Neelam wrote back: "I'd rather talk to you one-on-one. Can we get coffee?"

What was the member who questioned the cost called?
He was called 'weak' and 'not ready'.
What was Neelam feeling as she made the list on the bus?
She felt uneasy and suspicious, realising the friendly group showed three warning signs of control.
What else could Neelam do to help Sangeeta?
She could share her list with Sangeeta over coffee, gently, so Sangeeta can check the signs for herself.
How might the member who asked about cost have felt at tea?
He likely felt hurt and isolated when nobody spoke to him after he asked a fair question.

metadata.subtype: Approach: notice the warning signs of pressure and isolation [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Saturday
Second offer came today. A mid-sized logistics company in Pune, junior analyst, starting on the 1st.
Harsha asked if I'd keep interviewing for the bigger names. Two months ago I would have. But this month's PG rent is due in ten days, and Papa's retirement money isn't meant for me. Amma keeps saying "take your time" in the voice that means please don't.
So last week I set myself a bar: I'll take any role that's stable, where I'll actually learn something, and that pays on time. That's it. Not the best job in the country. Good enough.
This one: a team lead who says she trains freshers properly, salary on the last working day, and a real project in month one. Tick, tick, tick.
I emailed my acceptance at 6 pm and told the other two recruiters I'm withdrawing. My shoulders feel lighter.
Rashmi

When does the new job start?
It is starting on the 1st.
How does Rashmi feel after accepting?
Rashmi feels relieved, shoulders lighter, after weeks of pressure over rent and family expectations.
What else could Rashmi do to keep growing after joining?
Rashmi could agree learning goals with the team lead in the first month, so good enough keeps getting better.
How might Amma see Rashmi's decision?
Amma, who said take your time but sounded anxious, may feel relieved that a steady role with on-time pay is settled.

metadata.subtype: Approach: satisficing on the first acceptable offer [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the hot afternoon in their village near Bikaner, Parul, eleven, and her friend Ankita had two ice cubes from the shop fridge.
“Which will melt first,” said Parul, “in the clay pot or the steel glass?”
Ankita guessed steel. “Steel gets hot.” Parul guessed the same.
They put one cube in each and sat in the shade, checking every few minutes.
The steel one melted first. But the clay pot's outside was wet and cool when Parul touched it.
“Why is the pot sweating?” Ankita asked.
Parul took out her notebook. “Let's write it down and ask Sir tomorrow.”

Where did they put the ice cubes?
One in the clay pot and one in the steel glass.
How did the girls feel when the pot's outside was wet?
They felt curious and puzzled, wanting to know why the pot was sweating.
What did Parul do that shows good scientific thinking?
She wrote down what happened and planned to ask the teacher instead of guessing.
How might their teacher react to their question the next day?
The teacher may be pleased and use it to explain how clay pots keep things cool.

Read this:

Rohan, you cannot decide between commerce and computers? Let me tell you about a student I taught, Deepika. I am Chetan, her computer teacher. In the summer she signed up for a free coding course and a free beginner's accounting course, both online at home. Every week she wrote in a notebook which one she opened without being asked and which one she had to force herself to open. By the end of the holidays she had finished the accounting course, with all its small tests, and dropped coding at the third lesson. She showed me the notebook in July. It said what I could not have told her: she liked the ledgers. Her evidence was better than any advice I could have given.

Which course did Deepika finish?
Deepika finished the beginner's accounting course.
How did Deepika feel about each course, according to her notebook?
She opened accounting willingly and had to force herself to open coding, so she enjoyed accounting more.
What could Deepika do next with this evidence?
Talk to an accountant or try a harder accounting lesson, because a further trial shows whether the interest holds.
How might Chetan feel about the notebook?
Impressed and a little humbled, since Chetan says the evidence was better than any advice.

Read this:

At the music school in Porto Alegre, Paulo had practised the guitar four hours a day all summer. On the first day of term, a new student, Sofia, sat down and played a piece so clean and fast that the whole room went quiet. Paulo smiled and clapped with the others. Inside, something dropped. He walked home the long way, past the river, thinking: she's just born with it. I'll never get there. Four hours a day for nothing. When his teacher suggested he and Sofia practise duets, Paulo said he was too busy. He skipped the next ensemble class. That night he didn't pick up his guitar at all. Her playing kept looping in his head, and each time it felt like something was being taken from him.

How many hours a day had Paulo practised all summer?
Four hours a day.
Why did Sofia's playing make Paulo feel something dropped inside?
He felt threatened and envious, believing the gap was fixed and that her talent meant his work was for nothing.
What could Paulo try instead of avoiding Sofia?
He could accept the duet practice and watch how she works, treating her skill as something he can learn from.
How might Sofia feel when Paulo avoids the duet?
Sofia might feel confused or unwelcome as a new student, not knowing why he pulled away.

Read this:

Monday: Placement results were delayed again. Pallavi paced the hostel corridor, checking the portal twenty times, unable to eat. Her friend Jahnavi asked, "What can you actually do today?" Pallavi snapped, "Nothing. That's the problem."
Wednesday: Pallavi sat down with a notebook and split a page in two. Could change: polish the backup CV, apply to two small firms, call Mummy. Couldn't change: the company's timeline. She did the first three things and closed the portal.
The following Monday: Still no result. Pallavi noticed the tight feeling, named it, and went to badminton anyway. "Not knowing is awful," she told Jahnavi, "but I'm getting better at it."

How many times did Pallavi check the portal on Monday?
Twenty times.
How was Pallavi feeling on the first Monday?
She was anxious and frustrated, unable to eat and snapping at Jahnavi.
What changed on Wednesday, and why did it help?
Pallavi split what she could change from what she couldn't and acted on the first, which gave her some control and calm.
How might Jahnavi feel hearing "I'm getting better at it"?
Jahnavi likely feels glad and relieved that her question helped, even after being snapped at.

Read this:

"Where's Sahil?"

"On the sofa. His cousin called him a crybaby at lunch."

Papa went in. "Sahil? What happened? Who said it? Why didn't you tell me? Are you hurt?"

Sahil pulled his knees up, tucked his chin and turned his face into the cushion.

"Let him be for a bit," Sangeeta said softly. She sat at the other end of the sofa with her tea and didn't say anything else.

After a while, Sahil's foot slid over to touch her leg.

"I'm here," she said.

"He laughed at me," he whispered.

What did Sahil's cousin call him at lunch?
A crybaby.
What was Sahil feeling when he tucked his chin and turned his face into the cushion?
He was most likely hurt and ashamed after being teased, and wanted to hide. Papa's many questions may have made him feel even more crowded.
Which approach worked better, and why?
Sangeeta's quiet presence worked better than Papa's many questions, because it let Sahil come to her in his own time.
How does Papa probably feel when Sahil curls up?
Papa is likely worried and wants to fix things fast, which is why he asks so many questions at once.

Read this:

Jaya, you asked how old Jomon handles a team where one person does everything. Let me tell you about my first team, at a printing press in Kochi.
I was twenty-five, managing four people. Susan did the proofs, the layouts, the late-night fixes. Benny chatted with clients and somehow never had a finished page. For months I said nothing. Susan never complained, and Benny made everyone laugh.
Then one evening I found Susan asleep on the paper stacks at nine, and Benny's desk empty since four. That's when I saw it: by keeping quiet, I was paying for Benny's ease with Susan's health.
Next morning I took Benny out for tea, just the two of us. No shouting. I showed him the job sheet and asked, "What's getting in your way?" He went red, then admitted he was scared of the new layout software. Within a month he was doing his share, and Susan finally took her leave.

Where was Jomon's first team?
At a printing press in Kochi.
What did young Jomon feel on finding Susan asleep on the paper stacks?
Jomon felt a jolt of guilt and alarm, realising that months of silence had been costing Susan her health.
Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
Talking to Benny privately over tea with the job sheet and a real question; it uncovered the fear of the software without shaming him.
What might Benny have felt when shown the job sheet?
Benny was embarrassed, since he went red, but perhaps relieved to finally admit being scared of the software.

Read this:

Sharmila, you said you might join the student march next month, so let me tell you about mine. I'm Mahima. At sixteen, I joined a march for a cause I cared about. The organiser put us school kids in the front row "for the cameras". There was no water, no marshals, and no plan for what to do if things got rough. When the crowd surged, my knees went weak. I remembered that I could leave. I took two friends by the arm and slipped down a side street. The organiser never looked for us. Later I learned that people who lead well look after the young ones first.

Where did the organiser put the school students?
The organiser put the school students in the front row.
What did Mahima feel when the crowd surged, and what did Mahima remember?
Mahima felt frightened, with weak knees, and remembered that Mahima could leave.
What could Sharmila look for in a real leader before joining a march?
A plan for safety, water, marshals and an exit, and signs that the leaders protect the young.
How did the organiser seem to see the students?
As a crowd for the cameras rather than people to look after, since they were placed in front with no safety and nobody searched for them.
Dawat se jaldi jaana hai. Host ko kaise bolun?
Say: "I'm sorry, I have to leave early. Thank you so much for inviting me."
Find a single word for "very big": The station was very big.
The station was huge.

Read this:

In the residential school outside the town, lunch was always dal, rice and one sabzi. On Monday, Kamal leaned across the bench and whispered, "Don't eat the dal. Three boys from Class 9 got sick from it yesterday."
Manoj looked at his plate. Suddenly the smell seemed wrong. His stomach turned. He felt a wave of sickness rise before he had even lifted the spoon.
"I'm not hungry," he said, pushing the plate away. He sat through the period with a cold sweat on his neck.
At evening study, the warden announced that the Class 9 boys had eaten street pakoras on their outing; nothing to do with the mess. Manoj felt his stomach unknot almost at once. At dinner he ate two helpings of the same dal.

What had the Class 9 boys actually eaten, according to the warden?
They had eaten street pakoras on their outing.
Why did Manoj feel sick before even eating?
He felt anxious after Kamal's warning, and that fear made the smell seem wrong and created real sickness.
What could Manoj do next time he hears a rumour like this?
He could check with the warden or mess staff before believing it, and notice whether the feeling started with the rumour rather than the food.
How might Kamal feel after the warden's announcement?
Kamal might feel sheepish, realising the whispered rumour made Manoj miss lunch for nothing.

Read this:

"Irawati, you did it again."
"Did what?"
"The phone. I paused the movie to get the sweets, and in the four seconds before I stood up, it was already in your hand."
"I didn't even notice."
"I know. That's the scary part. You did it while the rangoli powder was drying. When Mausi went to answer the door. When the ad came on."
"I'm not even looking for anything. I just... scroll."
"What were you scrolling just now?"
"...I don't know. A video of a dog. Someone's new shoes."
"And?"
"And it's nice for a second. Something new."
"Try this. For the rest of Diwali, your phone goes in my bag when we're together. When you're bored, just tell me you're bored."
"That's embarrassing."
"Try it anyway, Iru."
"Okay, Devika. But you're holding it."

What was Irawati scrolling just now?
A video of a dog and someone's new shoes.
What does "I didn't even notice" suggest about Irawati?
Irawati seems startled and a little embarrassed; reaching for the phone has become automatic, set off by each pause rather than chosen.
Why might Devika's idea help?
Putting the phone in the bag breaks the easy grab, and saying "I'm bored" names the feeling that starts the loop, so Irawati can choose something else.
What is it like for Devika to watch this?
Devika seems worried, calling it the scary part, and maybe a little lonely, since Irawati drifts to the phone at every pause in their time together.

metadata.subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]

Read this:

With three hours left in the college hackathon and the Wi-Fi dropping every twenty minutes, Chandrika spread her hands over the table. "Here's how we win. We finish all four features, the live demo runs first try, the judge from the logistics company is on our panel, she loves the route-map idea, and she offers us internships on the spot."
Amandeep rubbed tired eyes. "Or: we get one feature working properly and show that."
"That's so flat. Mine actually feels like it'll happen. I can see her face when the map loads."
"Every bit of that has to work out. The Wi-Fi alone..."
The screen froze again. Chandrika stared at the spinning circle, then at her list of four features. "Okay," she muttered, "but mine's a better story."
"It's a better story," Amandeep agreed. "It's a worse plan."

What keeps interrupting the team during the hackathon?
The Wi-Fi keeps dropping every twenty minutes, and the screen froze again.
Why does Chandrika's plan feel more likely to her than Amandeep's?
She can picture it vividly, down to the judge's face when the map loads, and that detail makes it feel real even though each step adds another chance of failure.
What could Chandrika and Amandeep do with the three hours left?
Get one feature working properly first, keep a backup of the demo in case the Wi-Fi fails, and add more only if time allows.
How does Amandeep see the difference between the two plans?
Amandeep sees Chandrika's plan as a better story but a worse plan, because the dropping Wi-Fi alone could break it.
Please pick up him at the station at six. Is the word order right?

Please pick him up at the station at six.
Why: When the object of a phrasal verb is a pronoun, it goes between the verb and the particle: "pick him up".

Read this:

Sunday: Rehana's toes only reached the ground on tiptoe, and every time she tried to pedal she tipped over. Her brother Rafiq offered to push her. She shook her head.
Tuesday: "The pedals aren't the problem," she told Rafiq, pulling the seat down to the lowest notch. "Staying up is. If I can't stay up, pedalling just makes me fall faster." She walked the cycle along, then pushed with both feet and lifted them, gliding for two seconds. Then three.
Friday: She glided across the whole courtyard with her feet up, counting aloud to seven. "Now," she said, "now I'll try the pedals." The first push went round, then the second.

How far down did Rehana pull the seat?
She pulled it down to the lowest notch.
Why did Rehana shake her head when Rafiq offered to push?
She wanted to work it out herself; she seems determined and a little stubborn about finding her own way.
What else could Rehana try if gliding stops getting better, and why?
She could glide down a very gentle slope, because the extra speed makes balance easier to find.
How does Rehana's plan look to Rafiq?
Rafiq might be puzzled at first that she refuses a push, and then impressed when her gliding works.

metadata.subtype: Approach: gliding without pedals first to find balance [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Creche note, Friday. Sabina, eighteen months, hid behind her mother's legs when a visiting uncle, Bhupen, came in, and stared at him with one eye. He waved from the door and sat across the room without coming closer. I suggested her mother take Sabina on her lap. After a while Sabina held up her cup toward him from there. Nobody asked for a hug. Next time I will seat him at a distance again and let her decide.

How old is Sabina?
Sabina is eighteen months old.
What might Sabina have been feeling as she stared at Bhupen from behind her mother's legs?
She may have felt wary because his face was new to her, though a stare is only a cue and not proof of what she thought.
What did the adults do that let Sabina warm up?
They let her stay on her mother's lap, kept Bhupen at a distance and never asked for a hug.
How might Bhupen have felt about sitting across the room?
He may have wanted to be friendly and chose patience so Sabina would feel safe, and he probably felt glad when she held up her cup.

Read this:

Sunday night. Tanya's message came at eleven: "Saw a man selling roasted corn and thought of you. Miss you." Suraj sat up in bed. Eight months since the breakup. His chest ached with a sudden longing. He opened their old photos: Juhu beach, the scooter trip to Lonavala, her head on his shoulder. He fell asleep with the phone in his hand.

Wednesday. At lunch he told Imran, his oldest friend. "I think I should meet her." Imran put down his fork. "Remember the Lonavala trip? She didn't speak to you for two days because you were ten minutes late." Suraj had forgotten that. He'd also forgotten the jealous calls, the tears when he met his friends.

The next Monday. Suraj had thought about it all week. He missed being loved; he didn't miss being afraid of her moods. He replied: "I'm glad you're okay. I don't want to restart things, but I wish you well." Then he joined Imran's Saturday football team.

How many months had passed since the breakup?
Eight months had passed.
What was Suraj feeling on Sunday night?
Suraj felt a sudden ache of longing, falling asleep looking at old photos.
How did Imran help Suraj choose consciously?
Imran reminded him of the parts he'd edited out, like the silent treatment and jealous calls, so Suraj could see what he really missed.
How does Imran see Suraj's plan to meet Tanya?
Imran is worried, remembering how unhappy the relationship made Suraj.
Teacher said my essay is 'too verbose'. Mujhe ye shabd nahi pata.
"Verbose" means using more words than needed. Your teacher wants shorter, clearer sentences. Example: "His answer was verbose; he could have said it in two lines."

Read this:

Emil had a poster on volcanoes due Wednesday at his school in Stockholm. On Monday, Soo-ah asked if he wanted to work in the library after class. "No need," Emil said. "It's one poster. Ten minutes." He pictured it: print three photos, write a title, done. On Tuesday evening he sat down at the kitchen table. The printer was out of ink. His mother drove him to the shop in the snow. The facts he'd found didn't fit on the paper, so he rewrote them twice. At nine his father found him in tears over a glue stick that had dried out. Emil remembered, too late, the same thing had happened with the Viking poster in autumn. Soo-ah's poster, finished on Monday, had a paper volcano that popped out.

What was the printer out of on Tuesday evening?
The printer was out of ink.
What was Emil feeling at nine o'clock?
He was upset and overwhelmed, in tears over a dried-out glue stick after expecting the poster to take ten minutes.
What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
Emil pictured only the ideal path and forgot the Viking poster; next time he could plan for things going wrong and start on Monday like Soo-ah.
How might Emil's parents feel about Tuesday evening?
They were probably tired and a little frustrated, with a drive in the snow and a crying child late at night.

Read this:

I'm Salma, Nazia's older sister, and I watched this whole thing from our balcony in the new Hyderabad colony. When a Tamil-speaking family moved into B-block, some aunties said they were "different" and their children "rough". Nazia, nine, repeated it at dinner.
Then the colony cricket team got a new player: Gowri, from B-block, who bowled faster than any boy. Nazia kept wicket for her. I can't tell you what went on in my sister's head, but I saw them practise every evening, counting runs in two languages and swapping words. Last week Nazia came home with a steel box of lemon rice from Gowri's mother and ate every grain.
At dinner someone repeated the "rough" line. Nazia put her spoon down. "Gowri isn't rough. She just bowls fast."

What did Nazia bring home from Gowri's mother?
A steel box of lemon rice.
What might Nazia putting her spoon down at dinner suggest about her feelings?
It suggests she now feels protective of Gowri and no longer believes the fear she once repeated.
What helped Nazia's view change?
Playing on the same cricket team, keeping wicket for Gowri and practising together every evening, so knowing Gowri replaced the aunties' words.
How might Gowri have felt about the colony before joining the team?
Gowri may have felt unwelcome and watched, which is why having Nazia as a teammate and friend could matter a lot.

Read this:

"Dat?" Simran pointed at the pressure cooker whistling on the stove in their Chennai flat.
"Cooker," said her brother Saurabh, nine, not looking up from his homework.
"Coo-ker!" She pointed at the window. "Dat?"
"Crow."
"Kwo! Dat?"
"A light." Saurabh laughed and put his pencil down. "Is she going to ask about everything?"
Amma smiled from the doorway. "Last month she had ten words. Now I've stopped counting."
Simran pointed at Saurabh's face. "Sad?"
"I'm not sad, I'm doing maths."
"Maths sad," Simran decided.

How many words did Simran have last month?
Last month she had ten words.
What is Simran feeling as she points at everything?
She is curious and eager, excited to learn a name for everything she sees.
How could Saurabh help Simran's words keep growing?
He could keep naming things clearly, add a little more, like "a black crow", and answer her questions even when busy with homework.
How does Saurabh feel about all of Simran's questions?
Saurabh is a little distracted at first but then amused and fond, laughing and putting down his pencil to answer her.

Make this easier to read, in modern English.

When Bharat took his homeward road
Still Rama in the wood abode:
But soon he marked the fear and care
That darkened all the hermits there.
For all who dwelt before the hill
Were sad with dread of coming ill:
Each holy brow was lined by thought,
And Rama's side they often sought.
With gathering frowns the prince they eyed,
And then withdrew and talked aside.

When Bharat took the road home, Rama was still living in his forest hut. But soon he noticed fear and worry darkening all the hermits there. Everyone who lived in front of the hill was sad, dreading some coming trouble. Every holy forehead was lined with thought, and they often came to Rama's side. They eyed the prince with growing frowns, then withdrew and talked among themselves.

Make this simpler for a younger reader, with short sentences.

The next morning Harish went with Santosh to meet the principal and showed her everything. She listened, kept copies, and called in the students' parents that week. When one teacher suggested moving Santosh to another section "to avoid trouble," the principal said no: "He did nothing wrong. They're the ones who'll change."

The next morning, Harish went with his son Santosh to see the principal. He showed her everything. She listened and kept copies. That week she called in the other students' parents. One teacher wanted to move Santosh to another class to avoid trouble. The principal said no. "He did nothing wrong," she said. "They are the ones who will change."

Read this:

[Voice note, sent 11:40 pm]
"Deepak! It's Kalyani, obviously. Day four in Pune and I have to tell you everything. The hostel room is tiny but it has a window with a tree, and a crow that visits every morning. I've already been to three cafés, a bookshop that stays open till ten, and a street where they sell vada pav for fifteen rupees. Today we had orientation and I joined the drama club and the photography club, and I think the trekking club, I'm not sure, I signed so many sheets. Everyone is from somewhere different. There's a girl from Shillong on my floor who's already my best friend, probably. Mummy called twice and asked if I'm eating properly and I said yes, yes, bye, I was running to a quiz. I haven't cried once, can you believe it? Okay, I'm going to sleep. Actually, no, they're making instant noodles downstairs, gotta go!"

How many cafés has Kalyani been to?
Kalyani has already been to three cafés.
How does Kalyani seem to feel in her first days in Pune?
Kalyani feels thrilled and full of energy, so caught up in new things that there is no time to feel homesick.
What small step could help Kalyani later, when the excitement fades?
Kalyani could make time for proper calls with Mummy and keep one or two routines from home, so there is a base when the novelty wears off.
How might Mummy feel after being told yes, yes, bye?
Mummy may feel glad Kalyani is happy but also a little left out and worried whether Kalyani is really eating and resting.
Can you correct this? My aunt have two daughters and both of them is studying in Chennai.

My aunt has two daughters and both of them are studying in Chennai.
Why: "Aunt" is singular, so the verb is "has". "Both of them" is plural, so it needs "are".

Read this:

In their house in Rewari, Kashish, eighteen, had started doing something strange. Before bed she checked the gas knob, then the front door latch, then the gas again. She had never done that before her brother Sachin came home to study for his civil services prelims. Sachin checked everything twice, sometimes three times, and asked her whether she'd locked the scooter or switched off the geyser, in a tight, fast voice. The whole house had started to hum with it. One night their mother saw Kashish at the gas knob and sat them both down. She said plainly that Sachin was anxious about his exam, that it wasn't anyone's fault, and that there would be one routine now: Ma would lock up at ten, once, and nobody else would check. Sachin agreed to talk to a counsellor. Kashish slept better that week.

Who would lock up at ten under the new routine?
Ma, once, and nobody else would check.
Why had Kashish started checking the gas and the latch?
Sachin's tight, repeated questions filled the house with tension, and she picked up his alarm without deciding to.
Which choices by their mother lightened the house?
Naming Sachin's anxiety honestly and without blame, setting one clear locking routine, and Sachin agreeing to see a counsellor.
What was it like for Kashish living with Sachin's worry?
The house seemed to hum with tension, and she found herself copying his checking, until the new routine let her sleep better.

Read this:

Daycare note, Tuesday.

Nirmala, two, arrived watching videos on her grandfather Ramesh's phone. She stared, not blinking. When he took it, she screamed and hit the floor.

I offered sand and water play. At first she wailed. Then she dug.

I told Ramesh gently that short screen time, watched together, is kinder. He said he'd try more walks to the park instead.

What did Ramesh say he'd try instead of the phone?
Ramesh said he'd try more walks to the park.
What does Nirmala's screaming when the phone was taken suggest?
It suggests Nirmala felt upset and frustrated, her attention caught so strongly that losing the phone felt overwhelming.
What did the note-writer offer instead of the screen?
The note-writer offered hands-on sand and water play and advised shorter, shared screen time.
How might Ramesh see the phone after the talk?
Ramesh may now see it as something to limit and share, and look for outdoor time instead.

Read this:

Age fifteen: after three videos on electricity, Lokesh told the class, 'The teacher's wrong. Current doesn't get used up.' The teacher smiled. 'Then what does the bulb use?' Lokesh opened his mouth and found he had no answer. His ears went hot.

Age twenty: Urmila learned a project framework in a weekend workshop and felt like an expert. For three weeks she corrected her classmates. Then her team's real project hit a supplier delay, and the framework's neat boxes did not fit. Her confidence dropped, and she felt she knew nothing. She began asking the seniors detailed questions, and her skill began to grow.

Age twenty-five: Uma, a young engineer, solved bugs that stumped others in minutes. 'It's easy, anyone can do it,' she said, and privately wondered whether she belonged. A colleague said, 'It took me two days last week.' Uma blinked. She started noticing the gaps in her own knowledge, stopped brushing off what she did well, and began teaching the fix to others.

What question did the teacher ask Lokesh about the bulb?
'Then what does the bulb use?'
How does confidence relate to real skill at fifteen, twenty and twenty-five?

Lokesh felt like an expert after three videos but could not answer a basic question. Urmila felt expert after a workshop until a real project dropped her confidence before her skill grew, and Uma, truly skilled, assumed her fixes were easy and doubted herself.
What was Lokesh feeling as his ears went hot?
Embarrassed, as he realised he did not know as much as he had claimed.
What could Urmila do during the dip in confidence?
Keep asking the seniors detailed questions and treat the dip as a normal sign that she is learning.

Anjali had a rule: the cooking drama only at the gym, on her tablet, while she used the cross-trainer. It worked for a month. Then quarter-end hit her accounts team, and she was leaving the office after nine. The gym closed at ten. On the first late night she opened the tablet on the bus "just to see how the episode starts", telling herself she would save the rest. She got off with the episode finished and the gym already dark. By Friday she had watched four more on the bus and hadn't touched the cross-trainer. Joseph, her husband, noticed she was chatty about the show and oddly quiet about the gym. "Still gym-only, that drama?" he asked lightly. Anjali looked at the tablet. "More like bus-only now."

What time did the gym close?
At ten.
Why did opening the tablet on the bus seem fine to Anjali?
With late nights and no time for the gym, she told herself she would only watch the start; it felt like a small comfort rather than breaking the rule.
Given the quarter-end crunch, what could Anjali choose instead?
Pause the drama during busy weeks, or pair it with a short workout at home, rather than letting the bus become its new home.
How does Joseph read Anjali's mood about the show and the gym?
Joseph notices she is chatty about the drama but quiet about the gym and suspects the pairing has slipped, so he asks a light question instead of lecturing.

Mridul: you were smiling all day at the counter, good day? 🙂
Baljeet: lol that's my bank face
Baljeet: honestly, worst day this month. the system crashed twice and a customer shouted at me about his passbook
Mridul: wait what. you looked so cheerful
Baljeet: we're trained to keep the smile on. doesn't mean I'm happy, just means I'm polite
Mridul: I'm realising I read every smile at work as "all good"
Baljeet: most people do. the only real smile today was when the chai came at 4
Mridul: I'll learn the difference. want to grab dinner, no smiling required?
Baljeet: yes please. my face is tired
Mridul: I'll pick the place. you can frown the whole time

How many times did the system crash?
The system crashed twice.
What was Baljeet feeling behind the smile at the counter?
Baljeet was stressed and worn out after two crashes and a shouting customer; the raised mouth corners were trained politeness, not joy.
What did Mridul decide after the chat?
Mridul decided not to read every smile at work as 'all good', and offered a relaxed dinner where Baljeet wouldn't need to smile.
How did Baljeet's smile look to Mridul during the day?
To Mridul it looked cheerful, like a good day, so the stress came as a surprise.

"She sent the client file with the old logo again," Rehana said, dropping into the chair beside Faisal. "Told you on day one. Maria's not up to it."
"Again? That's the first time I've heard of it."
"Well, and last week she asked where the templates were."
"Everyone asks that. I asked that."
"And she took forty minutes for a ten-minute task."
Faisal frowned. "The audit summary? The client wrote back saying it was the clearest one they'd had."
"Luck. Or someone helped her."
"Rehana, who helped her?"
Rehana opened her mouth, then shut it. "I don't know. I just had a feeling about her from the interview. She seemed nervous."
"So you decided in the interview."
"I didn't decide anything." She stared at the logo on her screen. "Did I?"

What did the client say about the audit summary?
The client wrote back saying it was the clearest one they'd had.
Why does Rehana feel her view of Maria is fair?
Rehana feels sure and a little irritated, because each small slip seems to confirm the feeling from the interview, so it looks like evidence rather than a first impression.
What could Rehana try before judging Maria again?
She could write down Maria's good work, like the audit summary, next to the slips, and compare the slips with what other new staff usually do.
How might Maria be affected if Rehana's view goes unchecked?
Maria could be judged harshly for normal new-starter mistakes, and her strong work might never be credited.

Nilesh first heard it on Monday on the stairs of their Nagpur school: Harsha sir, the history teacher, was being transferred because the principal was angry with him. By Tuesday it was in the class group. By Wednesday the Class 9 kids were whispering it in the canteen, adding that he'd been 'caught' doing something, though nobody said what. Nilesh watched Harsha sir take attendance that Thursday. The class was quieter, stiffer. Two boys who usually argued with him about dates just stared at their desks. Harsha sir looked up, puzzled, and asked if everyone was feeling all right. Nilesh wanted to say, nobody even knows if it's true. But by now saying that felt strange, like questioning something everyone had already decided. He stayed silent, and hated that he did.

On which day did the rumour reach the class group?
On Tuesday.
How did Nilesh feel after staying silent?
Nilesh felt frustrated and ashamed, hating that he kept quiet when he doubted the rumour.
What small step could Nilesh take next time?
He could say quietly to a friend, 'Do we actually know this?', or refuse to pass it on, before a rumour hardens into 'fact'.
How might Harsha sir experience that Thursday class?
Harsha sir seems puzzled and a little worried, sensing the class has changed towards him without knowing why.

Losar morning in Dharamshala: Tenzin, two, wanted to put on his new boots himself, jammed his foot in sideways, and threw them across the room, roaring. His father Imran picked him up and held him. Two days later: Tenzin pulled at a boot again, grunted, then pushed it towards Imran and said, "Help." A week after Losar: he got one boot on alone, stamped, and yelled, "Me did it!"

What did Tenzin do with the boots on Losar morning?
He threw them across the room.
How can you tell Tenzin felt proud instead of angry by the end?
He stamped and yelled "Me did it!", showing he felt proud once he managed alone.
What could Imran do while Tenzin is learning to ask for help?
Praise him for saying "Help" and do only the tricky part, so Tenzin still feels in charge.
How might Imran feel as the week goes on?
Relieved that the roaring has turned into asking for help, and pleased by Tenzin's success.

School counsellor's note, Monday.

Imran, class eleven, came to see me today. He said he felt tired of everything: tuition, coaching, family expectations. He kept talking about when he was small. "Life was so easy. I just played cricket all day in the lane."

I asked about his early years. His sister Hafsa, who walked him here, said quietly, "You were scared of the neighbour's dog. You hated going to school."

Imran laughed a little, surprised. "I forgot that."

I explained that when we feel pressured, the past can seem golden. We talked about small ways to make now easier. I'll meet him weekly, and with his permission I called his parents this evening to talk about the pressure he's under.

What did Imran say he used to do all day when he was small?
He played cricket all day in the lane.
Why did Imran remember his childhood as easy?
He felt tired and pressured by tuition and expectations, so the past seemed golden and comforting.
What steps did the counsellor take?
The counsellor explained why the past looks golden, planned weekly meetings and called his parents that evening, with his permission.
How might Hafsa feel walking Imran to the counsellor?
Hafsa probably felt worried and caring, wanting her brother to get help.
What are the vadi and samvadi of Raga Darbari Kanada?
In this teaching table, the vadi of Raga Darbari Kanada is R, and the samvadi is P.

Under the neem tree in the lane, Manoj found his little brother Siddharth curled up, sobbing into his knees. Moti, their puppy, had died that morning. Manoj's own eyes stung, and he wanted to say, "Stop crying, it's okay," but he swallowed it and sat down beside him instead. "I miss him too," he said. Siddharth leaned into his shoulder. Manoj pulled Moti's old rope out of his pocket and put it in Siddharth's hand. "Come, let's go to the pond where he liked to splash." They sat on the bank for a long time. Somewhere in there Manoj's tears finally came, quietly, and neither of them minded.

What did Manoj put in Siddharth's hand?
He put Moti's old rope in Siddharth's hand.
What did Manoj want to say at first, and why did he not say it?
He wanted to say, "Stop crying, it's okay," but he seemed to sense that his brother needed company more than a quick fix, so he sat down beside him.
What small step helped both brothers with their sorrow?
Going together to the pond where Moti liked to splash and sitting there let them remember him and cry side by side.
What might it be like for Siddharth to have Manoj beside him?
He is not alone in his sadness, which is why he leans into Manoj's shoulder.

Ishita, beta, you say you'll start exercising "when life settles down"? Let your Sharmila Maasi tell you, life doesn't settle. When I was your age, a young bank officer in Nashik, I sat at a desk twelve hours a day. My back hurt, and I kept saying, "Next month." Then my friend at the branch made me a deal. Every evening at six, we would walk around the lake for twenty minutes, together. If one of us skipped, she had to bring the other one vada pav the next day. And I gave myself a reward right away: after each walk, I could read one chapter of the detective novels I loved. No walk, no chapter. The first month was hard. By the third, I was waiting for six o'clock. Forty years later, I still walk, and my back thanks me.

At what time did Sharmila Maasi and her friend walk around the lake?
Every evening at six.
What was young Sharmila feeling before the deal with her friend?
She felt stuck and in pain, her back hurting, always putting exercise off to next month.
Which choice in the story made the habit last?
The walking deal with a friend, the vada pav penalty and a chapter of a detective novel as an immediate reward, which made each walk pay off right away.
How might Sharmila's friend have benefited from the deal?
The friend also got a walking partner and a reason to keep going, so the deal helped both of them.
Reply dene mein deri ho gayi. Formal aur casual dono mein sorry kaise bolun?
Formal: "I apologise for the delay in replying." Casual: "Sorry for the late reply!"

Lucia had found the meditation centre in Lisbon during the worst year of her twenties, and the teacher's quiet voice had given her mornings a shape again.

Two years later she was there every evening. Her friend Emil noticed first.

"You missed my birthday dinner," he said over coffee. "And you told me you turned down the promotion so you could help at the centre more."

Lucia bristled. "The teacher says ambition is noise."

"Did the teacher tell you to turn it down?"

She paused. "No. I decided."

"Then that's yours to question," Emil said gently. "I'm glad it helps you. I just miss you."

That night Lucia sat on her bed feeling a mix of gratitude and unease. She wrote two lists: what the centre gave her, and what she had quietly handed over. The next day she emailed her boss to ask if the promotion was still open.

What did Lucia write that night?
Two lists: what the centre gave her, and what she had quietly handed over.
What did Lucia feel as she sat on her bed that night?
She felt grateful to the centre but also uneasy, sensing she had let her devotion push aside her own judgement.
What small step helped Lucia take her judgement back?
Writing the two lists and then emailing her boss about the promotion kept her work in her own hands.
How does Emil see the change in Lucia?
Emil is glad the centre helps her but misses her and worries she is giving up her job and friends for it.
Who signed the library guest register right after the founder?
I don't know that level of detail. The library's own old registers might hold the answer.

The only dhaba near the college in Sagar had four plastic tables, and Farhan's group took two every evening. Farhan, nineteen, always ordered first for Parul: plain dal, no onion, no garlic, roti kept away from the non-veg pan. He had learnt her Jain rules in the first week and never joked about them. His own Ammi's rule was halal only, so he stuck to paneer here.
One evening Deepak pulled his chair back when Ramu, the cleaner's son who studied with them, sat down. 'My family doesn't eat with—'
Farhan cut in, quietly. 'Parul's rule is about what's on her plate. Yours is about a person. That's different.'
Parul nodded and passed Ramu the pickle. Deepak looked away, but stayed.

What did Farhan order for Parul?
Plain dal, no onion, no garlic, and roti kept away from the non-veg pan.
What was Farhan feeling when Deepak pulled his chair back from Ramu?
He felt uneasy and quietly angry at the unfairness, yet calm enough to speak without shaming Deepak loudly.
How did Farhan balance respect for food rules with fairness?
He respected Parul's diet and his own family's rule, but pointed out that refusing to eat with a person is different and unfair.
How might Ramu have felt when Parul passed him the pickle?
Ramu probably felt accepted and relieved, seeing friends stand by him instead of letting Deepak's rule push him away.

'Noor, look! This headband helps you study. Marks go up in one week!' Hafsa held out the tablet. Noor, sixteen, put down her tea. 'Who says so?' 'The video. A lady with glasses.' 'Is she a scientist or is she selling it?' Hafsa paused. 'There's a buy button under her.' 'Hmm. Search it. Add the word review.' Hafsa typed. 'Some people say it just gives a headache. One says it's a nice hairband.' She giggled. 'And any real studies?' 'I can't find any. Only shops.' 'So what do we know?' Hafsa sighed. 'That she wants my pocket money.' 'And what helps marks?' 'Doing my maths,' Hafsa groaned, reaching for her notebook. 'Fine.'

What did Hafsa add to her search when Noor suggested it?
She added the word 'review' to her search.
What was Hafsa feeling when she first held out the tablet?
She was excited and hopeful, believing the headband could really raise her marks in one week.
What worked well in Noor's approach?
She asked questions instead of lecturing, so Hafsa found the buy button and the missing studies herself.
If you were Noor, why might you want Hafsa to reach the answer on her own?
Hafsa is more likely to remember to check who is selling something next time if she discovered it herself.

I share a flat with Ritu, and last month I watched her fight with bread.
She wanted to bake a proper loaf. The first one came out like a brick. She said, "I can't bake. I'm not a baking person," and nearly threw the flour away.
The next morning there was a sticky note on the fridge in her handwriting: I can't make bread YET. Below it, a list. Water too cold? Didn't knead long enough? Oven not hot enough?
I don't know what went on in her head. But she changed one thing each time. Warmer water. Longer kneading, with a timer. An oven thermometer she borrowed from me.
Loaf four was edible. Loaf six was actually good, and she gave me the heel with butter. The sticky note is still on the fridge. Someone, I think Ritu, has crossed out YET.

What did Ritu borrow from the narrator?
Ritu borrowed an oven thermometer.
What does the sticky note suggest about how Ritu felt after the first loaf?
It suggests she moved from feeling defeated to feeling hopeful, turning "I can't" into "I can't yet" and asking what to change.
Why did Ritu's approach work better than just baking again and again?
She changed one thing at a time, water, kneading and oven heat, so her effort was guided by a strategy and each loaf taught her something.
How does the narrator see Ritu's bread project?
The narrator watches with interest and some admiration, admitting not knowing what was in her head but enjoying the good loaf.
Is an accidental meeting a planned one? I'm checking what accidental means.

No. Accidental means happening by chance, not planned or meant. It is an adjective.
Example: Their accidental meeting at the bus stop led to a long friendship.

In Johannesburg, Lindiwe was folding baby clothes when Kofi's mother called from Kumasi. "Of course the naming ceremony will be here," she said. "Our church is waiting. People will ask what kind of family forgets its roots." Then, softer: "Your father's heart is not strong, you know."

Lindiwe hung up with her jaw tight. She and Kofi had already agreed on a small ceremony at home; the baby was six weeks old and neither of them could face a long flight.

When Kofi got back from work she showed him the call log. "I feel squeezed from every side."

"Then we answer together," he said.

On Sunday they video-called his parents side by side. Kofi spoke first. "We love you. The ceremony will be here in March, and we'll stream it so the whole church can watch." His mother sighed heavily. Lindiwe smiled, said thank you for caring, and did not repeat the reasons.

How old was the baby when Kofi's mother called?
The baby was six weeks old.
How did Lindiwe feel after the call from Kumasi?
Lindiwe felt squeezed and tense, her jaw tight from the guilt and hints.
Which choice helped the couple hold their ground?
Answering together on one video call, with Kofi speaking first and a warm but clear plan, kept the decision with them.
What is it like for Kofi's mother to hear the plan?
She is probably disappointed and worried about how her church and family will see it, which shows in her heavy sigh.

In their small flat in Osaka, Yuki had made one rule for herself: ask, don't guess. On bad mornings Noa's back locked so tight that getting out of bed took ten minutes. Yuki used to hover in the doorway, offering tea, heat packs, tips from articles. It made Noa snap, "Stop watching me!" and made Yuki feel useless. Now she asked once: "What would help today?" Today the answer was, "Just the heat pack, and no talking for an hour." Yuki handed it over and went to the kitchen without sulking. The sharpness was pain, not a verdict on her. At noon she laced up her running shoes. "I'm going to the river for an hour. My phone's on." Noa smiled for the first time that day. "Good. Go and breathe for both of us."

How long did getting out of bed take on bad mornings?
Ten minutes.
How did Yuki feel back when she used to hover?
Yuki felt useless, especially when Noa snapped, "Stop watching me!"
What makes Yuki's new approach supportive without hovering?
She asks once what would help, does exactly that, doesn't sulk at sharpness, and keeps her own run to recharge.
How might Noa feel when Yuki goes to the river?
Noa seems glad and relieved, smiling for the first time that day, perhaps less guilty about needing care.

Ojas: are you seeing the class group
Trisha: yeah. the thing about Deven's presentation
Ojas: 50 messages in 10 min
Trisha: someone made his face into a sticker
Ojas: this is bad

How many messages were posted in ten minutes?
There were 50 messages in 10 min.
Why hadn't Ojas said anything at first?
Ojas felt uneasy but assumed someone else in the big group would step in, so the responsibility felt shared and nobody, including Ojas, acted.
What made Ojas's message work?
It was calm, named that Deven was in the group and asked everyone to stop without starting a fight; Trisha backing it at once helped others join in.
How might Deven feel on getting Ojas's message afterwards?
Deven may feel less alone and relieved that at least some classmates saw the pile-on as wrong and stood up for him.

On a Sunday night in his Kolkata flat, Samir finally messaged Raghav Sen, a game designer whose talk he had watched three times. Then he opened his phone's reminders and set one for the following Sunday: 'If no reply, send one follow-up. After that, let it go.'
All week, between classes and his shift at the print shop, he felt the urge to check. The reminder helped; there was nothing to decide until Sunday.
Sunday came with no reply. Samir sent a short follow-up: 'Hi again, sharing this once more in case it slipped past. No worries at all if you're busy.' He noticed a small sour thought, he could at least say no, and let it pass. The plan said move on.
Three days later, Raghav replied: 'Sorry, I was away at a festival. Your question is a good one. Call on Friday?' Samir laughed out loud in the metro.

What did Samir's reminder say?
If no reply, send one follow-up. After that, let it go.
What was the small sour thought Samir noticed, and what does it show?
The thought that Raghav could at least say no shows a flash of resentment, which Samir noticed and let pass instead of acting on.
What would you advise Samir if the follow-up had also gone unanswered?
Move on as planned, without bitterness, and choose another designer to contact, keeping the same one-week rule.
How might Raghav feel on seeing the follow-up after the festival?
Raghav might feel grateful for the reminder and relieved that it was polite, which makes it easy to reply and suggest a call.
Our cat keeps scratching the sofa and my mother is getting angry.
Scratching is natural for cats. They do it to stretch, mark territory and keep their claws in shape. Giving the cat somewhere else to scratch usually helps.
What kind of thing works?
A sturdy scratching post, tall enough for the cat to stretch fully, placed near the sofa. Many cats prefer rough materials like rope or cardboard.
The cat ignores it.
Try moving it to a spot the cat likes more, or rubbing it with something the cat likes. Praise when the cat uses it. It can take a few weeks.
Should I punish the cat for scratching?
No. Punishment does not teach a cat and can make it afraid of you. Redirect the cat to the post and reward it instead.

Kaito, nine, wrote about his weekend for the class newsletter: "We went there and did it, and then we ate it. It was so good." In his head there was the lake, the paddle boat with a broken seat, and the rice balls his grandfather had packed. Felix, who sat next to him, read the page and frowned. "Went where? Did what? Ate what?" Kaito was puzzled. It was all so clear to him. He picked up his pencil and asked himself what Felix would need if Felix had not been there. He added the name of the lake, the paddle boat, and the rice balls his grandfather had packed. Felix read it again and grinned. "Now I can see it."

What did Kaito write first about his weekend?
Kaito wrote that they went there and did it, and then ate it, and it was so good.
What was Kaito feeling when Felix asked "Went where?"
Puzzled, because it all seemed clear in his head.
What did Kaito add that helped Felix understand?
Kaito added the name of the lake, the paddle boat and the rice balls his grandfather had packed.
How did Felix see the first page?
Felix found it confusing, since it did not say where, what or which food, and could picture it only after the details were added.

Hafsa, you're nervous about tomorrow's speech, so listen to your Baljeet Uncle. At sixteen I stood for house captain. I wrote my speech on the back of a calendar page. One promise: proper drainage so the ground would not flood during monsoon practice. One story: the day my shoes floated away in the middle of a football match. I read it to the mirror every night. Then I read it to my friend Gulshan, who timed me on his watch: three minutes ten. Too long. I cut every "as we all know" and "respected teachers and friends," and got it down to two minutes flat. On the day, the hall laughed at the shoes and remembered the drainage. I won by a small margin, and Gulshan claimed half the credit.

What was the one promise in Baljeet's speech?
The promise was proper drainage so the ground would not flood during monsoon practice.
How might Baljeet have felt while reading to the mirror each night, and what does it show?
Baljeet was probably nervous but determined, shown by the nightly practice and the willingness to be timed and corrected.
What choice in the story shortened the speech, and why did it help?
Cutting the filler phrases brought it to two minutes, because a shorter speech keeps the one promise and the story clear.
How did Gulshan help in the story?
Gulshan timed the speech on his watch and showed that it was too long at three minutes ten.

Rajni had eight hundred contacts and a phone that buzzed all day, yet most afternoons she ate lunch alone at her desk in the insurance office. On Friday she carried two cups of tea to the pantry, where Vishal was rinsing his lunchbox. They hadn't really spoken since she snapped at him in the client meeting. "I was rude," she said. "I'm sorry. I've had a rough month, and I took it out on you." Vishal dried his hands slowly. "It stung," he said. "But thanks." The silence was awkward. She stayed in it. "Would you want a Wednesday lunch? Just us, and maybe Ritu?" He took the tea. "Wednesdays work." Back at her desk, she muted three noisy group chats and set a reminder to call her college friend on Sunday.

How many contacts did Rajni have?
Eight hundred.
Why did Rajni stay in the awkward silence instead of leaving?
She wanted to repair the friendship for real and was willing to feel uncomfortable rather than escape it.
Which choice after the pantry shows Rajni moving from a crowd to depth?
She muted three noisy group chats and set a reminder to call her college friend, putting her energy into a few real people.
What might Vishal feel when Rajni admits she was rude?
He was hurt, as "It stung" shows, but her honest apology and mention of a rough month let him feel respected and willing to try again.

In their small town near Satara, Anjali had become Mahima's timetable. Wake at six. Study at seven. Library at four, to read the English books Mahima loved. Every hour, Anjali checked. "Have you started? Why are you on page twelve only?" On Wednesday at four, Anjali said, "Library time. Go." Mahima was already putting on her chappals, but she stopped. She sat back down. "I'm not going." "You love the library!" "Not today." Anjali stared at her. "You're being impossible." Mahima went to the terrace and sat with her knees up. She did love the library. She'd been halfway through a novel. But every step of her day had Anjali's voice on it, and saying no felt like the only thing that was hers. After an hour, Anjali came up with two cups of tea. "Maybe I push too much." Mahima took the cup. "Let me decide when I go. I'll still go."

What was Mahima halfway through at the library?
She'd been halfway through a novel.
Why did Mahima refuse to go to the library she loves?
Mahima felt controlled and resentful, and refusing was the only thing that felt like her own choice.
What did Mahima ask for, and why could it work?
To decide when she goes to the library herself, which gives back ownership so she'll want to go.
How might Anjali have felt on the terrace with the two cups of tea?
Anjali seemed sorry and a bit unsure, beginning to see she pushed too much.

On the first hot day of summer term at the Bhopal school, the canteen line buzzed with the same news: if you swallow a watermelon seed, a watermelon grows inside you. Lalit heard it from Binita in the morning. At recess three more children said it. By lunch, a boy in 6C swore his cousin had needed an operation. Lalit had laughed at breakfast. By the last bell, he was carefully spitting every seed out of his watermelon slice onto a napkin, and he felt a small wobble in his tummy whenever he thought about the one he'd swallowed last week. When the science teacher heard, she smiled and said, 'Seeds don't grow in stomachs.' Lalit nodded, but he still spat out the seeds.

What did the children say happens if you swallow a watermelon seed?
A watermelon grows inside you.
How did Lalit feel thinking about the seed he swallowed last week?
Lalit felt worried, with a small wobble in his tummy, because the story had started to feel true after hearing it so often.
What could Lalit ask himself the next time a 'fact' spreads?
Where it came from and who actually knows, instead of believing it because many people repeat it.
How might the science teacher see the children's worry?
The teacher finds it amusing but also sees how quickly a repeated story can feel true to children.

With the hostel closing in three days and monsoon rain flooding the road, Afreen stood under a shop awning while the broker held out his phone. "Jagdish-ji says no. He won't rent to your community. Sorry." He shrugged as if it were about the weather. Afreen's face burned. She was angry and, underneath, small, as though she had done something wrong by being herself. Then she reminded herself that a refusal like this shows what the landlord believes, not what she is. She opened her notes app and typed the date, the broker's words and the landlord's name. She rang Sana from the college legal aid clinic, who offered to explain her options. That evening Afreen's classmate said her cousin had a room going, and Afreen went to see it in the rain.

How many days were left before the hostel closed?
Three days.
What did Afreen feel beneath her anger after the refusal?
She felt small, as though she had done something wrong by being herself.
What did Afreen do that turned the refusal into action?
She noted the date, the broker's words and the landlord's name, contacted the legal aid clinic and followed a lead on another room.
How might Jagdish see his refusal?
He may see it as an ordinary decision about his property, though it rests on a prejudice that reflects on him, not on Afreen.

Monday. The client called at nine: the invoice Karthik sent had the wrong amount, by a lot. Amandeep apologised, fixed it, and by lunch had half-written an email moving Karthik off the account. She didn't send it. Something about how fast she'd written it bothered her.
Tuesday. She opened Karthik's work log for the whole year. Eleven months, forty-odd invoices, no errors. She also noticed the new billing tool had gone live last Thursday, and two other people had filed bug reports since.
Thursday. She sat with Karthik. "Walk me through Monday." He showed her the screen where the tool had pulled last year's rate. He had checked the total but not the rate line. "That part's on me," he said. Amandeep deleted the draft email. Instead they added a rate check to the team's list, and she asked the tool team to fix the bug.

How many months of Karthik's work log showed no errors?
Eleven months, with forty-odd invoices and no errors.
Why didn't Amandeep send the email on Monday?
She felt uneasy about how quickly she had written it, sensing that one error was colouring her whole view of Karthik.
Which choice worked, and why?
Reviewing Karthik's full year and the new tool's bugs before deciding, which showed one slip in context rather than a pattern.
How might Karthik have felt when asked to walk through Monday?
Karthik was probably nervous but relieved to be asked, and he felt able to own his part honestly.

Two months after her brother Manpreet died in the road accident, Gurpreet was back at school. At lunch in the canteen, Wasim did his funny impression of the PT teacher, and Gurpreet laughed out loud. Then she stopped, cheeks burning. How could she laugh?
In the counsellor's room that afternoon, she said it all. "Some days I'm so angry at him for riding in the rain. Then I feel guilty for being angry. And today I laughed."
Mrs D'Souza listened. "Grief comes in waves. Laughing doesn't mean you loved him less. It sounds like the sadness is still about Manpreet, and you still enjoy hockey and your friends."
Gurpreet nodded.
"If the sadness starts spreading to everything, or you feel worthless, come and tell me that same day. We'll keep meeting every Friday."

What was Wasim doing when Gurpreet laughed?
His funny impression of the PT teacher.
How did Gurpreet feel right after laughing?
She felt ashamed and guilty, her cheeks burning, as if laughing meant she didn't care about her brother.
What did Mrs D'Souza do that supported Gurpreet?
She listened, explained that grief comes in waves and laughter is okay, set regular meetings and told her what signs would need extra attention.
How might Wasim feel if he knew why Gurpreet stopped laughing?
He might feel awkward or worried he'd upset her, though he probably helped her by bringing a moment of lightness.

Dear Nirmala Ma'am,
You asked us to write to you about anything on our minds after the counselling session. Here goes.
At school I talk a lot, I run the drama club, I argue with teachers politely. At home, I say "hmm" and "okay". My parents think I'm a shy, quiet child. My friends think my parents are cool because I never mention them. I planned it this way: home is calm if I stay small, and school is fun if I stay big.
But last week was the drama club play. I didn't tell my parents. I played the lead. Everyone's families clapped in the front row, and I looked at the empty seats and felt strange, like half of me was missing.
Is it wrong to keep things separate? It stops fights. But I wonder if my parents would even like the loud me.
Keerthana, Class 10

What part did Keerthana play in the drama club play?
Keerthana played the lead.
How did Keerthana feel looking at the empty seats, and why?
Keerthana felt strange and lonely, like half was missing, because the parents who never hear about school were not there to see it.
What could Nirmala Ma'am suggest as a small first step?
Nirmala Ma'am could suggest sharing one small school story at home, like a single photo from the play, to see how it goes.
What would change if Keerthana's parents knew about the drama club?
They might see a side of Keerthana they never knew, and could come to the next play; the risk of a fight is real but so is being known.

messages.content: I lent my friend 500 rupees two months ago. Write a polite reminder message, about 40 words, that won't hurt our friendship.

Hey Kunal, hope you're doing well! Just a small reminder about the 500 rupees I lent you in August. No rush if things are tight, but could you send it back sometime this month? Thanks, and let's catch up soon.

By eleven, Ojas was kneeling on the mat in the village school, poking his slate, then poking the boy beside him. When Harish asked him to trace the letter, Ojas's lip shook and tears came. Harish opened his mouth to scold him, then stopped. Ojas walks from the fields at dawn, and his tiffin tin was empty on the shelf. Harish handed him the snack bag early: puffed rice and a banana. Ten minutes later Ojas was tracing slowly and humming. That evening Harish wrote in his register: 'Check the tiffins before calling anyone naughty.'

What was in the snack bag Harish handed to Ojas?
Puffed rice and a banana.
Why did Harish stop himself from scolding Ojas?
He noticed the empty tiffin tin and remembered Ojas walks from the fields at dawn, so he thought hunger, not naughtiness, was behind the poking and tears.
What small step could Harish take every morning after this?
He could check tiffins early and keep a snack ready, so a hungry child is fed before being judged for fidgeting.
How might the boy beside Ojas see things if Harish had scolded instead?
He would likely think Ojas was just a troublemaker, and Ojas would stay hungry, tearful and still poking him.

messages.content: Ask for quiet more politely: Be quiet after ten.
Could you please keep the noise down after ten?

When Lokesh's offer letter came from the famous IT company, his father distributed pedhas to the whole lane in their town near Sangli. Relatives called from three villages. Nobody asked what the job was, and Lokesh didn't either. The other offer, from a small agri-tech firm in Kolhapur that built soil-testing tools, he declined in one line. Six months later, home for Gudi Padwa, Lokesh sat on the verandah with his school friend Yogesh. "So, what do you do there?" Yogesh asked. Lokesh paused. "I watch server alerts. When one turns red, I raise a ticket for another team." "And then?" "Then the next one turns red." Yogesh was quiet. "The Kolhapur people came to our village last month. They're testing soil for my father's farm." Lokesh looked at the pedha in his hand and didn't eat it.

What did Lokesh's father distribute?
Pedhas to the whole lane.
What does Lokesh not eating the pedha suggest?
It suggests Lokesh felt regret and a quiet sadness, seeing that the famous name brought pride to others but dull work to Lokesh.
What would you change first if choosing again?
Ask each company exactly what the role involves day to day and what you would learn, before letting the name decide.
How might Yogesh see Lokesh's job?
Yogesh sees past the famous name to repetitive work, and his mention of the Kolhapur firm hints at what Lokesh gave up.

messages.content: The teacher wants to "nip it in the bud" when students copy each other. What will she do?

She will stop the problem early, before it grows bigger.
Example: The rumour is spreading, so let's nip it in the bud.

Turn all the dialogue into reported speech, with no quotation marks.

In the Friday planning meeting, Uma proposed that all the team's meetings go online. Six of the seven nodded. Jahnavi, the seventh, did not; she sat with her pen still.
"Can I say why I'm hesitant?" Jahnavi asked. "I think new joiners learn a lot by sitting in the room. But you're right that the commute takes up hours, and that's a real cost."
Uma tilted her head. "So, what would work?"
"Try it for a month with one in-person day for new people, and see how they feel. If the numbers show I'm wrong, I'll say so."
Uma smiled. "That works. Let's track it."

In the Friday planning meeting, Uma proposed that all the team's meetings go online. Six of the seven nodded, but Jahnavi, the seventh, did not and sat with her pen still. She asked if she could say why she was hesitant. She said that she thought new joiners learn a lot by sitting in the room, but that Uma was right that the commute takes up hours, which is a real cost. Uma tilted her head and asked what would work. Jahnavi suggested trying it for a month with one in-person day for new people, to see how they feel, and said that if the numbers showed she was wrong, she would say so. Uma smiled and said that worked, and that they should track it.

Tushar, you asked why I never scold you for eating your prasad at once. That winter I was eight, and we lived with my Tayaji. Every week he promised, "Wait, Jasleen, next Sunday I'll bring you a whole box of pinni." Sunday came, and nothing. Again and again.
So when the new teacher said, "One sweet now, or two if you wait till after lunch," I grabbed the one so fast the girl beside me laughed. Teacher frowned and called me greedy.
I wasn't greedy, beta. I had learned that "later" meant "never". Only when that teacher kept her word for a whole month did I start to wait too. That is why your Bibi keeps every small promise she makes you.

What did Tayaji promise to bring every week?
A whole box of pinni.
Why did young Jasleen grab the one sweet so fast?
Young Jasleen felt distrustful after so many broken promises; "later" meant "never", so taking the sweet at once felt sensible, not greedy.
What turned things around in the story?
The teacher keeping her word for a whole month showed Jasleen that waiting could actually pay off.
How might the teacher have seen young Jasleen at first?
The teacher first saw only greed and frowned, not knowing about the broken promises at home.

All summer, Chandrika's grandmother and three cousins were staying in their two-room house in Madurai, and there was never a quiet corner. 'I'll get better at maths this holiday,' Chandrika kept saying. By July she hadn't opened her maths book once. There was always noise, always something. Her mother, Vinita, found her sulking on the step. 'What does "better" mean?' Chandrika shrugged. 'Better.' 'How about five sums, right after your bath, on the terrace, before the cousins wake up?' 'Just five?' 'Just five. And you tick the calendar.' The next morning Chandrika did five sums on the terrace while a crow watched. She ticked the calendar. By the end of the holiday there were twenty-eight ticks, and she had finished the whole chapter on decimals.

Where did Chandrika do her five sums?
She did them on the terrace, right after her bath.
Why had Chandrika not opened her maths book by July?
Her wish to 'get better' was vague, and in a noisy house she felt stuck, with no clear place to start.
What made Vinita's suggestion work?
It set a small, specific target, five sums at a set time and place, with a tick to check, which was easy to start even in a busy house.
How might Vinita feel seeing twenty-eight ticks?
Vinita would likely feel pleased and proud that a small plan helped her daughter finish the decimals chapter.
Could you compose a haiku about a crow sitting on a wall?

A crow on the wall
Watches the street with sharp eyes
Then flies off at dusk

At the bakery near the university in Berlin, a customer squinted at Amara's name badge and said loudly, "Where are you from? Your German's surprisingly good for..." He trailed off. Amara was about to say, drily, "For a Berliner?" when Zeynep swept in from the ovens. "Excuse me! That is racist! You can't say that to her!" The whole queue turned. Zeynep kept talking: how she'd heard this all her life, how exhausting it was, how people like him never learn. The man left. Later Zeynep hugged Amara and showed her a long post she'd written about "what happened to my coworker today". Amara thanked her, and meant it. But in the post she was just "my coworker", and the story was Zeynep's. That night she texted: "Thank you for having my back. Next time, ask me first?"

What was Amara about to say to the customer?
"For a Berliner?"
Why did Amara feel uneasy about Zeynep's post even though she was thankful?
In the post she was only "my coworker", and the story had become Zeynep's, leaving Amara grateful but sidelined.
Was Amara's text a good way to handle it, and why?
Yes; it thanked Zeynep honestly while asking for one clear change, being asked first, so support can follow Amara's lead next time.
Why might Zeynep have reacted so strongly at the counter?
Zeynep said she'd heard remarks like that all her life, so the moment may have stirred her own hurt as much as concern for Amara.
Write a short question about the moon that begins with "Why" and ends with a question mark.
Why does the moon change shape through the month?

In their village near Amritsar, Gurleen, five, stood at the gate every evening. “Is Papa coming today?”
“Not today,” said Vandana. “The day after tomorrow.”
“Is that far?”
Vandana gave her two pebbles. “Throw one in the pot tonight, and one tomorrow night. Then Papa comes.”
That night Gurleen threw one. “Tomorrow, one more. Then Papa!”
She stopped waiting at the gate and went to feed the calf.

How many pebbles did Vandana give Gurleen?
She gave her two pebbles.
How was Gurleen feeling as she stood at the gate each evening?
She felt impatient and missed her Papa.
What did Vandana do that helped Gurleen understand?
She used pebbles to show the days, so Gurleen could see how long to wait.
How might Papa feel when he arrives and sees Gurleen?
He probably feels happy and loved, knowing she counted the days.
What does "fill up" mean? The driver said "let's fill up before the highway".

To fill up means to make something completely full, such as a car's fuel tank or a bottle.
Example: Please fill up the water bottle before we start the trek.
Write a message to my group project partners, about 35 words: we meet at the library at 4 pm on Wednesday, and everyone should bring a laptop. I'm Joseph.

Hi everyone,
Our group will meet at the library at 4 pm on Wednesday to work on our project. Please bring your laptops. Let me know if you cannot make it. Thank you!
Joseph

Vaisampayana continued, "O king, O lord of men, that slayer of hostile heroes, the Suta's son, said these words to Duryodhana, 'O Kaurava Duryodhana, do thou lay unto thy heart the words that I shall tell thee; and, O represser of foes, after having heard my words, it behoveth thee to act accordingly every way. Now, O best of monarchs, O hero, hath the earth been rid of foes. Do thou rule her even like the mighty-minded Sakra himself, having his foes destroyed."

Question: What does the Suta's son tell Duryodhana to do?
The Suta's son tells Duryodhana to lay the words to heart and act on them. Since the earth is now rid of foes, Duryodhana should rule it like Sakra himself, with his foes destroyed.
When do I use "please accept my apologies"?

Use it for a serious or formal apology, such as in a letter or an email to a customer or an older person. For small slips "I'm sorry" is enough.
Example: Please accept my apologies for missing the meeting.

I sit next to Madhav in Hindi class, so I see it up close. When the teacher says, "Madhav, read the next paragraph," his ears go red first, then his neck. His hand grips the book so tight the page crinkles. He reads the first line, stops, and stares at the words as if they've turned into another language. He sits down, and for the rest of the period he doesn't look up. Last month he stopped coming on Fridays, when we have recitation. I don't know what he's thinking; he never says. But this week the teacher started letting him read sitting down, one line, then two. On Friday he came. He read four lines. His ears were still red. He finished anyway.
Yusuf

What happens to Madhav's ears when he is asked to read?
His ears go red first, then his neck.
What might Madhav's staring at the words suggest he feels, given Yusuf can't be sure?
It suggests his mind has gone blank with fear, even though the words are familiar.
What change did the teacher make, and what happened?
The teacher let him read sitting down, one line then two, and on Friday he came and read four lines.
How might Yusuf feel watching Madhav finish four lines?
Yusuf may feel glad and quietly proud of him, having seen up close how hard it was.

The power went off just as Trisha and Dilnaz started their card-trading game. Trisha's mother lit a candle and called, "Ten minutes, then homework!"
They each had fifteen cards. The rule was to swap fairly, one for one. Whoever made the best set in ten minutes got the last packet of cards from the cupboard.
In the flickering light, Trisha saw she could slide a spare card under her knee. Dilnaz wouldn't see. And what if Dilnaz was already hiding one? Then Trisha would be the silly one who played fair.
Her hand moved toward her knee. Then Dilnaz laid all her cards face up. "See? Nothing hidden."
Trisha's cheeks went hot. She put the card back.

How many cards did each girl have?
They each had fifteen cards.
What was Trisha worried about when she thought of hiding a card?
She was afraid Dilnaz might already be cheating, and she did not want to be the silly one who played fair and lost.
What helped Trisha choose to play fair?
Dilnaz laid her cards face up, which showed she was not cheating and took away Trisha's fear.
What would change if Dilnaz had not shown her cards?
Trisha might have hidden the card out of fear, and the game could have turned into both of them cheating.
