At the play school, Rekha aunty tied red ribbons on half the children and yellow on the rest, just for relay teams.
By snack time, Anjali, a red ribbon on her wrist, had decided things. "Reds sit here. Yellows are slow." She pulled Tia away from Mira, a yellow, whom she had played with all week. "She's yellow," Anjali said, as if that explained everything.
Rekha aunty knelt down. "Yesterday you and Mira were best at swings. Is Mira different now?"
Anjali looked at her ribbon, then at Mira, and frowned.

What colour ribbon was on Anjali's wrist?
A red ribbon.
What does Anjali's frown at the end suggest?
Anjali seems puzzled and unsure, starting to notice that a ribbon made her treat a friend differently.
How did Rekha aunty help Anjali think again?
She knelt down and asked a gentle question about Mira and the swings, instead of scolding.
What was snack time like for Mira?
Mira probably felt hurt and confused when her playmate suddenly called her "yellow" and pulled Tia away.
Help me write a short message inviting my cousins to my first sitar recital next Sunday at 6 pm. About 50 words.

Hi everyone! After two years of practice, I'm finally giving my first sitar recital next Sunday at 6 pm at Kala Bhavan hall. I'll be playing two short pieces, so it won't be long, I promise. It would mean a lot to see your faces in the audience. Please come!

On Saturday night Nilesh laid a printed sheet on the table: fees for both colleges, entrance dates in April, average job outcomes for each path. “Ma, Papa, I'll appear for the engineering exam. In the evenings I'll also build a design portfolio, six pieces by December. If my rank is good and the portfolio is weak, I choose engineering. If it's the other way round, we sit down and talk again.” His mother, Nirmala, pushed her glasses up and read the sheet twice. “You're not just saying you don't want engineering?” “No, Ma. I'm giving both a fair chance.” Papa asked how he would learn design. “A free online course to begin with.” Papa nodded slowly. “Six pieces by December. We'll look at them together.”

By when does Nilesh plan to have six design pieces?
By December.
What might Nilesh be worried about while presenting the sheet?
That his parents will hear it as a rejection of engineering, so he shows that both paths get a fair chance.
What else could Nilesh do to strengthen the deal, and why?
Ask a working designer and an engineer to comment on his plan and portfolio, because outside views help his parents trust the arrangement.
How does the proposal look to Nirmala?
Nirmala sees facts and a deadline, and that her son's idea keeps engineering open, so she may feel reassured that he is not simply refusing.

The sports room still had sugarcane pieces from the Pongal celebration stacked in one corner when Coach pinned up the district basketball squad. Shreya ran her finger down the list twice. Tanuja, Grade 10. No Shreya.
Behind her, Tanuja, her best friend since Class 3, squeaked. "Shreya. Shreya, I'm in!"
Shreya turned and hugged her hard, and the gladness was real; she had watched Tanuja practise free throws alone every evening since June. "You deserve it. Totally."
Later, in the empty changing room, Shreya sat on the bench with one shoe on and let her eyes sting for a minute. She had wanted it too. Then she wiped her face, tied the lace, and went to buy Tanuja a celebration rose milk.

Since when had Tanuja practised free throws alone every evening?
Since June.
What was Shreya feeling alone in the changing room?
Shreya felt a quiet sadness at not being picked and let her eyes sting, even though her gladness for Tanuja was real.
What would you say to Shreya about feeling both glad and sad?
Both are real and allowed; taking a minute to feel the loss, as she did, can make the celebration with Tanuja sincere rather than forced.
How might Tanuja feel about Shreya's hug and the rose milk?
Tanuja probably feels deeply supported and relieved that the selection has not come between the two best friends.

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Kalyani Didi,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone. Here's the truth, since you're the one person I can say it to.
Last week in the hostel I couldn't sleep, and I imagined being sixty: still in the bank job Baba found for me, the tabla gathering dust under the bed, never having told Baba I don't want his life. It frightened me so much that I've done nothing since. I've started the music school form eleven times and closed it, because every answer seemed not good enough.
Writing this, I can see how silly that is. If I'm scared of a wasted life, staying frozen is exactly how I'd waste it.
So I'm sending the form tonight, imperfect. And when I'm home in October I'll talk to Baba, with you there, if you'll sit with me.
Your brother,
Arnab

How many times had Arnab started and closed the music school form?
He had started it eleven times and closed it.
What was Arnab afraid of when he imagined being sixty?
He feared still being in the bank job Baba found, the tabla unused, never having told Baba he doesn't want that life.
What realisation turned Arnab from frozen to acting?
He saw that staying frozen was itself how he would waste his life, so he chose to send the form imperfect and talk to Baba.
What might Kalyani Didi feel on reading this letter?
She may feel trusted and protective, and glad he asked her to sit with him when he talks to Baba.
Tell a six-word story about a missing sandal.
One sandal waited by the door.

"Ooh!" wailed the girl, pointing to the wing. "That's it, that was our lodging. You've burned to death, our treasure, Katie, my precious little missy! Ooh!" lamented Aniska, who at the sight of the fire felt that she too must give expression to her feelings.

What does Aniska lament when she sees the fire, and what does she feel she must do?
Aniska wails that the wing was their lodging and has burned, calling Katie 'our treasure' and 'my precious little missy'. At the sight of the fire she feels she must express her feelings too.

Saturday: The lake picnic Hemant had waited for all month was cancelled when the rain began at seven. He stomped to his room. "It's all ruined. I hate rain."
Sunday: It was still pouring. From his room he could hear his brother Anirban and their parents building a blanket tent in the hall, and smell khichdi and papad. Anirban knocked. "We're doing a torch picnic inside. Come." "It's stupid," Hemant said through the door.
Monday: At school, Anirban told his friends about the blanket tent and the ghost stories by torchlight. Hemant listened, saying nothing. That evening he asked his mother, "Can we do the tent again?" "Maybe next rainy day," she said.

What were Anirban and their parents building?
A blanket tent in the hall.
What might Hemant have felt listening to Anirban on Monday?
Left out and regretful that he had missed the fun by sulking.
What else could Hemant have done on Sunday?
Joined the torch picnic, and asked separately to reschedule the lake trip.
How did the rainy weekend feel for Anirban?
Anirban enjoyed the tent and ghost stories and happily told his friends about them.
Is it "scene" or "seen" in "Have you ___ my pen?"

Write "seen". "Seen" is the past participle of "see", and "scene" is a place where something happens or a part of a play.
Examples: Have you seen my pen? The first scene of the play takes place in a market.

You asked how I ended it with Hafsa. I'm Imran, and I'll be honest: it was the hardest phone call of my life.

We'd been together since the start of Class 11. By the end of the year, I knew I didn't feel the same. I delayed for weeks. Then I realised every day I waited, she was still planning things for us.

So I called her. Not a text. I said, "Hafsa, I care about you, but I don't feel the same anymore, and I don't want to mislead you." I didn't list her flaws. I didn't say "maybe someday."

She cried. I wanted to take it back, just to stop her crying. But I didn't. That would have been worse.

A month later she told her friend, and her friend told me, that she was glad I was clear. It still hurt her. But she didn't have to wonder.

What did Imran say to Hafsa on the call?
"Hafsa, I care about you, but I don't feel the same anymore, and I don't want to mislead you."
How did Imran feel when Hafsa cried?
Imran felt a strong urge to take it back to stop her crying, feeling guilty and pained, but held firm.
Why was not taking it back the right choice?
Taking it back would have given Hafsa false hope and more pain later; staying clear was a form of respect.
How did Hafsa come to see the ending, a month later?
She was glad Imran had been clear, even though it still hurt, because she didn't have to wonder.

In the school workshop in Da Nang, Tuan laid a sketch on the table: a bridge of wooden sticks with one tall arch and no side supports. "This will hold the most weight," he said, and everyone nodded. Nadia frowned at the arch, which looked thin at the base, but said nothing. Linh glanced at Nadia and bit her lip. On test day the arch bowed and cracked under the second weight. The team stared at the pile of sticks. "I thought it might," Nadia said at last. "So did I," said Linh. Tuan looked from one to the other. "Then why did nobody say so?" No one answered. Each of them had thought someone else would speak first.

Where was the bridge test held and what happened to the arch?
The arch bowed and cracked under the second weight on test day.
Why did Nadia stay silent when the plan was shown?
Nadia felt doubtful but hesitant to object, probably not wanting to be the only one to disagree with a confident plan.
What could the team do differently next time, and why?
They could ask each member for a concern before choosing a design, because that lets doubts be voiced without anyone standing alone.
How might Tuan feel when learning that two people had doubts?
Tuan probably feels surprised and a little hurt, since a concern could have saved the bridge.

At the playground in Berlin, Vera squirmed beside the swing, hopping from foot to foot while a bigger boy swung and swung. She reached for the chain.
"Not yet," said her father Felix, kneeling beside her. "Let's count his swings. Ten more, then it's yours."
"One, two..." Vera counted loudly, holding her own elbows to keep her hands still. By seven she was singing the numbers. When the boy hopped off she clapped and climbed on.
"That was a long wait," said Felix.
Vera nodded, pumping her legs.

What did Felix and Vera count while they waited?
They counted the bigger boy's swings.
What is Vera feeling as she squirms beside the swing?
Impatient and eager. She hops from foot to foot, reaches for the chain and has to hold her own elbows to keep her hands still.
What choice by Felix helped Vera wait?
He knelt beside her and turned the wait into a count, promising it was hers after ten more swings.
How might the bigger boy feel with Vera waiting beside the swing?
Perhaps a little watched, but Vera's counting shows the wait is fair and short, so he can finish his turn.

Monday. Sumit rode his scooter to his part-time job with one earphone in, taking calls from his manager at every signal. It felt efficient.
Wednesday. Near the school on Station Road, he was on a call about a delivery when a boy in a blue uniform stepped off the kerb. Sumit hadn't seen him at all, though the boy had been standing there in plain sight. He braked hard; the scooter skidded and stopped just short. The boy's mother pulled him back, shouting. Sumit's hands shook for an hour.
The following Monday. Sumit told his sister Rajni he had set his phone to reply 'Riding, will call back' automatically. He left the earphones at home. "I thought I could do both," he said. "I can't. Nobody can."

What colour was the boy's uniform?
Blue.
How did Sumit feel after braking near the school?
Sumit felt shaken and frightened, his hands shaking for an hour, realising he hadn't seen a boy standing in plain sight.
What rule did Sumit set, and why is it wise?
An automatic 'Riding, will call back' reply and no earphones, so calls can't pull his attention while riding.
How might the boy's mother have felt as she pulled him back?
She was probably terrified and angry, shouting at the rider who hadn't seen her son.

Read this:

The Sunday bazaar at the community centre was packed wall to wall, and Aparna lost her uncle Mohit somewhere near the pickle stalls. Her eyes filled. She wanted to run and look everywhere at once. Instead, she stepped back against the painted wall of the hall and put one hand flat on it. She breathed in slowly and out slowly, counting in her head. One. Two. Three. All the way to ten. The noise was the same, but she felt steadier. She looked at the stalls. The community centre's own desk had a lady with a badge and a microphone. Aparna walked over. "I'm lost. My uncle's name is Mohit." A minute later, his name boomed through the hall.

Where did Aparna stand to calm down?
Against the painted wall of the hall.
How did Aparna feel before she started counting?
She was frightened and close to tears, wanting to run everywhere at once.
What else could Aparna do if there were no desk with a microphone?
She could ask a stall-keeper in a fixed stall to call her uncle's number, staying in one place.
How does the announcement look to Mohit?
Mohit hears his name and learns that Aparna is safe at the desk, so he must feel relieved.

Read this:

In the clinic waiting room, Karthik, five, pressed against Asif's side. "Abbu, will the doctor's snake-thing hear my secrets?"
"The stethoscope? What secrets?"
"That I ate the biscuits."
Across the room a mother told her son, "Sit still or the doctor will give you ten injections." Karthik's eyes went huge.
Asif lowered his voice. "Nobody gets injections for fidgeting. The stethoscope only hears your heart going thump-thump. No secrets."
"Is it scary?"
"It's cold, like a spoon. That's all."
Karthik walked in holding Asif's finger, whispering, "Cold like a spoon."

What did Karthik call the stethoscope?
The doctor's snake-thing.
What was Karthik worried the stethoscope would do?
Hear his secrets, like eating the biscuits, so he would be found out.
How was Asif's approach different from the other parent's?
He gave simple true facts, that it hears heartbeats and feels cold, instead of scaring with a made-up threat about injections.
How might the boy across the room feel after his mother's warning?
He might become more frightened of the doctor and of injections, making the visit harder.

Read this:

Daniel's brother Yosef was waiting in the hallway of their Toronto apartment when Daniel came back from the award evening.
"Congratulations, Mum's perfect son," Yosef said. "Must be nice being the one they actually like." Then, quieter and worse: "I wish you'd never been born."
Daniel's face burned. He had a sharp answer ready: at least I'm not failing three subjects. He swallowed it.
He noticed Yosef's eyes were red. He remembered Dad at dinner saying, "Why can't you be more like Daniel?" twice that week.
"I didn't ask them to say that stuff," Daniel said. "It's not fair to you. I know."
Yosef slammed his door anyway.
Later Daniel found Mum and Dad in the kitchen. "You have to stop comparing us," he said. "Yosef hates me because of it, and honestly, I'd hate me too." Mum set down her tea. Dad started to argue, then stopped.

What did Daniel's parents do at dinner that week?
Dad said, "Why can't you be more like Daniel?" twice.
What was Daniel feeling when Yosef said the cruel words?
He felt hurt and angry, with a sharp reply ready, but he held it back once he noticed the pain in Yosef's red eyes.
What wise steps did Daniel take after the fight?
He chose not to retaliate, told Yosef he understood it was unfair, and asked his parents directly to stop comparing them.
How does Yosef see Daniel after the award evening?
Yosef sees Daniel as the preferred son who takes all the love, and his cruelty comes from feeling unwanted and compared.

Read this:

The fair was so crowded that Shankar lost Papa's hand near the giant wheel. A man with a shiny red balloon bent down and smiled. "Come with me, I'll find your papa." Shankar reached for the balloon. Then a woman in a plain khaki jacket stepped between them. "I'm Devika, from the lost-children desk." Her face was stern. Shankar burst into tears and tried to pull away. Devika knelt and stayed beside him. She called out his name on the loudspeaker, and told the fair police about the balloon man. Papa came running. Shankar still thought the balloon man was nicer.

What colour was the balloon the man held?
It was a shiny red balloon.
Why did Shankar reach for the balloon and cry when Devika came?
The shiny balloon and the smile made Shankar feel happy and safe, while Devika's stern face made him feel afraid, so his feelings pointed him the wrong way.
What could Papa tell Shankar after the fair?
Papa could say that helpers at the desk are safe to go to even if they look serious, and never to go with someone who just offers a treat.
How might Devika feel when a lost child cries at her?
She might feel sorry he is scared but stay calm, because she knows keeping him with her is what keeps him safe.

Read this:

Come, Vaibhav, sit. You're angry with your brother, I know. Let me tell you about my father.
When I, Irawati, was twenty, I married your Aajoba against Baba's wishes, and Baba did not speak to his only daughter for two years. Then one day he sent word through my aunt: tea, at the station canteen, Sunday.
I almost didn't go. When I sat down, he said, "Let us not open old files today." So we didn't. He told me one true thing: "I missed your laugh." I told him one: "I missed your stories." Then we drank our tea.
We never agreed about my marriage, beta. Not once. But we had tea every month after that until he died. Small steps, Vaibhav.

Where did Irawati and her father meet for tea?
At the station canteen, on Sunday.
What might young Irawati have been feeling when she almost didn't go?
She was likely nervous and hurt after two years of silence, afraid the meeting would reopen the fight.
In the story, what choice at the tea made the reunion possible?
Agreeing not to open old files that day and each saying one true thing, so they could start small.
How might Irawati's father have felt saying "I missed your laugh"?
He was probably vulnerable and relieved, finally letting his daughter see that he had missed her.

Read this:

I'm Dolma, and in my second year I decided I didn't believe in rebirth or anything else my grandmother taught me. It felt like taking off a heavy coat. I was relieved. I was also, if I'm honest, a little proud of myself, as if I had seen through something nobody else could. One evening in the hostel, Charu was keeping a fast for her fiancé, and I laughed and said, 'You know the moon doesn't care, right?' She didn't answer. Later I heard her on the phone, voice small, telling her mother she felt stupid. That stopped me. I had called myself rational and then been cruel. I knocked on her door and apologised. Now I try to live by things I can name: be truthful, don't harm, help when I can. I still light a butter lamp with my grandmother when I'm home, for her. I'm lonelier than I was. But I'm less proud, and kinder.

What did Dolma say to Charu about the fast?
Dolma said, 'You know the moon doesn't care, right?'
How did Dolma feel after deciding not to believe?
Dolma felt relieved, like taking off a heavy coat, and a little proud.
What did Dolma learn to do instead of mocking?
To apologise, respect Charu's practice, and live by named values like truthfulness and not harming.
How did Charu feel after Dolma's remark?
Charu felt small and stupid, telling her mother so on the phone.
The lift in our building is out of order again.
That is a nuisance. The first step is to report it to whoever manages the building, such as the maintenance staff or the residents' committee.
We've already reported it many times.
Then put it in writing, listing the dates of each failure, and send it to the committee. A written record is harder to ignore.
Who else could we go to?
If the building has a registered society, its office-bearers are responsible. Some places also have a lift inspection department, which you can find through the local authority.
Is there anything for people who can't use the stairs?
Raise it specifically in your complaint, because it can make the issue more urgent. Neighbours can also help one another with errands while it is repaired.

Read this:

Lab supervisor's note, Wednesday
During the titration practical, Sumit winked at Omkar across the bench when Omkar's flask turned bright pink too early. Omkar winked back and both grinned; it was clearly their private joke about Omkar always overshooting. A few minutes later, Sumit winked at Prachi when she asked to borrow his clamp. Prachi's face tightened; she took the clamp without a word and moved to the far bench. I don't think Sumit meant anything by it, but Prachi had no way of knowing that. After class I spoke to Sumit on his own. He looked surprised and said it was "just a thanks". I explained that a wink only works when the other person is in on the joke. He agreed to talk to Prachi, and before the end of the day I checked with her: he had apologised, and she said she was fine.

What happened to Omkar's flask during the titration?
It turned bright pink too early.
What did Prachi's tightened face suggest she was feeling?
Prachi likely felt uncomfortable and uneasy, perhaps reading the wink as flirting or mockery, since she wasn't in on any joke.
What steps did the supervisor take, and why did they help?
Speaking to Sumit privately, explaining when a wink works, and checking with Prachi the same day, so her discomfort was taken seriously.
Why might Sumit have been surprised by Prachi's reaction?
To Sumit it was 'just a thanks', like the friendly wink with Omkar, so he didn't expect it to land differently with Prachi.

metadata.subtype: Winking and eyelid flutter in social play [Mismatch]

messages.content:
Read this:

Elizabeth, you're waiting for someone to notice you. I did that too, for four years. Let your Sangeeta Ma'am tell you. At twenty-five I was the best coder on my floor at a bank in Chennai. I knew it; I thought everyone knew it. Promotion lists came out twice, and my name wasn't on either. I cried in the ladies' room and said nothing. Then an older colleague, Rebecca Joseph, found me there. She asked, "Who in the room speaks for you when you're not there?" Nobody, I realised. She offered to be that person. But she said, "You have to give me something to say." So I started asking for feedback every month, in writing. I volunteered for the project the director cared about. I told Rebecca plainly what I wanted: team lead within a year. Eleven months later I got it. So ask, Elizabeth. And find your Rebecca.

How many times did promotion lists come out without Sangeeta's name?
Twice.
What was young Sangeeta feeling in the ladies' room?
Sangeeta felt hurt and invisible, crying after being passed over twice.
What was the turning point in Sangeeta's story, and why did it work?
Rebecca's question about who speaks for her led to monthly written feedback, a visible project and a plainly stated goal, which gave her sponsor something to say.
How might Rebecca Joseph have seen the young Sangeeta?
Rebecca likely saw a talented but invisible colleague and felt moved to sponsor her, recognising the pattern.
Recast this sentence in the active voice: The old tree was struck by lightning.
Lightning struck the old tree.

Read this:

"If you loved me, you'd say yes," Anirban, Dolma's partner, said, arms folded in the doorway.

"It isn't about love. I'm just not comfortable with that."

"So I'm the bad one now? Maybe I should just leave. Everyone at my office says I'm too patient with you."

Dolma's throat went tight and the room seemed to shrink. There was fear, and under it a fog of confusion: was this normal? Was it Dolma's fault for saying no?

"I don't want you to leave," Dolma said slowly. "But my answer is still no. I'm not going to change it because I'm afraid."

Anirban went out and banged the door.

Dolma sat very still, then picked up the phone and called a friend from college. "Can I talk to you? Something isn't right."

Where was Anirban standing when saying "If you loved me, you'd say yes"?
In the doorway, with arms folded.
What was Dolma feeling when Anirban threatened to leave?
Fear and confusion: Dolma's throat went tight, the room seemed to shrink, and Dolma wondered whether it was normal or Dolma's fault.
What did Dolma do that was wise, and why does it matter?
Dolma kept the boundary without giving in to fear, then called a trusted friend soon after. This is not love and not Dolma's fault, and confiding early makes it easier to get support.
How might Anirban's leaving and the banged door affect what Dolma does next?
It shows that the pressure works through fear of being left, which is why Dolma reaching out to a friend rather than calming Anirban down matters.

Read this:

Okay, you want to know about the anonymous account? I'm Gargi. It started in February. An account with no photo, called "truthteller_x," sent me messages every night. "Everyone laughs at you." "Nobody wants you in the group." Stuff about my weight.

The worst part wasn't even the words. It was the guessing. I lay awake going through every name. Was it the girls from dance? My old best friend? I even started to suspect Gurleen, who has been nothing but kind to me. I was checking everyone's face at school for clues.

Gurleen noticed I was acting weird and asked. I told her, and I told her I'd suspected her. She wasn't even offended. She said, "Stop guessing. Let's give it to someone who can actually find out."

So we screenshotted every message, reported the account on the app, and that same day I showed my mother and our school counsellor. The account was taken down in a week.

I still don't know who it was. And I've decided I'm okay not knowing.

What was the anonymous account called?
It was called "truthteller_x."
What was Gargi feeling while guessing who was behind the account?
Gargi felt anxious and consumed, lying awake suspecting everyone, even kind friends like Gurleen.
What did Gargi and Gurleen do that was wise?
They saved screenshots, reported the account and told Gargi's mother and the school counsellor that same day, instead of guessing.
How did Gurleen react when she learned Gargi had suspected her?
Gurleen was not offended; she understood and helped Gargi stop guessing and get help.

Read this:

In Buenos Aires, Alejandro had two job offers: a stable bank job and a small start-up building farm software. He was twenty-five and had some savings.
His girlfriend Valentina suggested they write it down. What did he know? The bank's salary, the start-up's smaller pay with shares, that he loved the product. What didn't he know? Whether the start-up would survive.
"Guess," she said. "Out of ten start-ups like this, how many last three years?"
"Maybe three."
"And if it fails, what happens to you?"
"I'd have learned a lot, and I could find another job."
He took the start-up, with an agreement to review after one year. Eighteen months later it shut down. He was sad, but not bitter. "It was a good decision that turned out badly," he told Valentina. "Those aren't the same thing." He started at a bigger farm-tech firm a month later.

How many start-ups like this did Alejandro guess would last three years?
Maybe three out of ten.
How did Alejandro feel when the start-up shut down?
Alejandro felt sad, but not bitter, seeing the choice as sound even though it turned out badly.
What made Alejandro's decision process sound despite the uncertainty?
He listed what he knew and didn't, estimated the odds, checked what failure would cost him, and set a review point.
How might Valentina see Alejandro's reaction to the shutdown?
Valentina probably feels proud that he can separate a good decision from a bad outcome.

Read this:

In the empty classroom of the coaching institute, Kavitha sat staring at her mock paper: 38 out of 100, red circles everywhere. "Useless," she muttered. "You're useless. You'll never clear this." Francis, the senior who ran the evening doubt sessions, was stacking chairs. He stopped. "Would you say that to a friend who got this score?" Kavitha frowned. "No. I'd tell her one bad mock isn't the exam." "So tell yourself." She almost rolled her eyes. Instead she picked up a pencil and wrote on the back of the paper: I didn't finish the tax section because I spent too long on question 4. That's fixable. I'm tired, not stupid. Next week, timed practice, 20 minutes a section. Her shoulders came down a little. Francis nodded at the page. "That's the voice that passes exams."

What score did Kavitha get on her mock paper?
She got 38 out of 100.
What was Kavitha feeling when she first looked at her paper?
She felt ashamed and angry with herself, calling herself useless and sure she would never clear the exam.
What changed when Kavitha rewrote her self-talk?
It named the real mistake, too long on question 4, and set a practical plan, so it stayed accountable without the cruelty.
How does Francis see Kavitha's harsh words?
Francis sees them as unhelpful and gently challenges them by asking whether she would speak that way to a friend.

Read this:

I'm Lokesh, and last month I was meant to read the thought for the day in assembly. We had been standing in the sun for ages. When I walked to the mike, my ears started buzzing and the ground felt tilted. Sangeeta, who was next in line, whispered, "You've gone white! Are you that scared?" I didn't know. Maybe I was scared. Maybe it was the sun, or that I had skipped breakfast. Mr Menon saw my face and didn't wait to find out. He sat me down on the steps in the shade, gave me water and sent Sangeeta running for the school nurse. The nurse checked me and called home. Sangeeta read the thought for the day instead. I read it the next week.

What was Lokesh meant to read in assembly?
The thought for the day.
What was Lokesh feeling when Sangeeta asked about being scared?
Lokesh felt dizzy and confused, and honestly unsure whether the paleness came from fear, the sun or a skipped breakfast.
Why was Mr Menon right not to wait to find out the cause?
Sudden paleness with buzzing ears and a tilting feeling needs sitting down, water and adult help whatever the cause, so he acted and sent for the nurse.
How did Sangeeta read Lokesh's white face?
Sangeeta took it as stage fright, one possible reading, when heat or hunger might have caused it too.

Read this:

In the sandpit at the park in Berlin, Yosef was driving a shiny red digger. Tuan watched it go back and forth.
Then Tuan reached out and pulled it right out of Yosef's hands.
Yosef's mouth opened. He wailed, loud, tears running down.
Tuan stood very still, holding the digger. He looked at Yosef, then at his own hands. He gave a funny little laugh, then stopped.
Yosef's mum came hurrying over. "What happened?"
Tuan put the digger behind his back. "I didn't do it," he said.

What colour was the digger?
It was shiny red.
What does Tuan's funny little laugh suggest he was feeling?
He seemed confused and nervous; he wanted the digger, but Yosef's crying surprised him and he didn't know what to do.
How could an adult help Tuan at this moment?
An adult could crouch down calmly, name what happened and point to Yosef's tears, helping Tuan notice his friend's feelings without shaming him.
What is Yosef experiencing right now?
He is upset and shocked that his digger was snatched away, which is why he is wailing.

Read this:

Before (a hot April day): Samir Bhaiya put one jalebi on a plate. “Wait till I come back, Anirban, and you get two.” Anirban stared at it. He ate it in ten seconds.
During (a week later): Same jalebi, same plate. This time Anirban turned his chair to face the wall and hummed a song about a train. He sat on his hands. He counted his toes.
After (the next Sunday): Samir came back. The jalebi was still there.
“Two!” Anirban shouted, clapping. He ate both slowly, licking the syrup off his fingers.

How long did it take Anirban to eat the jalebi the first time?
He ate it in ten seconds.
How did Anirban feel when he got two jalebis?
He felt proud and delighted, shouting and clapping.
What helped Anirban wait the second time?
Turning away, humming a song, sitting on his hands and counting toes: distractions that made waiting easier than plain willpower.
How might Samir Bhaiya feel seeing the jalebi still there?
Samir Bhaiya probably felt surprised and proud of his little brother.

Read this:

Class note, Holi party. When the colour trays came out, Minakshi grabbed the whole green tray before anyone else could. Sahil reached for it too, and Minakshi pushed him, fast, without a word. Then she ran off to the slide, green hands and all. When I brought her back, she looked surprised, as if the grab and the push had happened on their own. We practised "freeze, breathe, ask" together, and she asked Sahil, "Can I have green after you?" He said yes. I told her mother at pickup, and we will play freezing games next week.

Which tray did Minakshi grab?
The whole green tray.
How did Minakshi seem when the teacher brought her back?
She looked surprised, as if the grab and the push had happened by themselves; she acted on her first impulse without thinking.
What helped Minakshi slow down?
Practising "freeze, breathe, ask" with the teacher, which led her to ask Sahil for a turn.
How might Sahil have felt when he was pushed?
Sahil was probably startled and upset, then pleased when she asked nicely and he could say yes.

Read this:

In the college chemistry lab, the four of them bent over the titration results. Ojas tapped the notebook. “Concentration is 0.5. Clear. Let's write it up.”
Lavanya looked at her burette readings again. She had got 0.3, twice. But Ojas sounded so sure, and Farah and Nitin were already nodding. They must know something I missed, she thought. She kept her notebook closed.
They submitted 0.5.
The next week the lab assistant returned the reports. “Correct value was 0.3,” he said. Ojas groaned. Farah said, “I got 0.3 too! I thought I'd done it wrong.” Nitin said, “Same.”
Lavanya stared at them. All three of them had been sitting on the same doubt.

What value did Ojas say the concentration was?
He said the concentration was 0.5.
Why did Lavanya keep her notebook closed?
She felt unsure of herself and assumed the others knew better, because Ojas sounded so certain and the others were nodding.
What could the group try before submitting next time?
Each person could read out their own result first, before anyone announces an answer, so different values come out.
How might Farah feel when she learned her 0.3 was right?
Farah might feel frustrated and a bit foolish for doubting that result, and relieved not to be the only one.
Meeting mein bolna hai "Kripya dobara bataiye." English?
Say: "Please say it again."

I determined to watch his movements. My heart invariably cleaved to the master's, in preference to Catherine's side: with reason I imagined, for he was kind, and trustful, and honourable; and she—she could not be called the opposite, yet she seemed to allow herself such wide latitude, that I had little faith in her principles, and still less sympathy for her feelings. I wanted something to happen which might have the effect of freeing both Wuthering Heights and the Grange of Mr. Heathcliff, quietly; leaving us as we had been prior to his advent. His visits were a continual nightmare to me; and, I suspected, to my master also. His abode at the Heights was an oppression past explaining. I felt that God had forsaken the stray sheep there to its own wicked wanderings, and an evil beast prowled between it and the fold, waiting his time to spring and destroy.

List the key points of this section as three bullets.

- The narrator decides to watch Mr. Heathcliff and sides with the kind, trusting master over Catherine, whose principles the narrator doubts.
- The narrator wishes something would quietly free both Wuthering Heights and the Grange of Mr. Heathcliff.
- Heathcliff's visits are a nightmare, and his life at the Heights feels like an evil beast stalking a stray sheep.

Read this:

Dear Rajni,

I'm writing this instead of saying it, because I'm a coward about saying it.

Last Friday, when the anonymous school confessions page posted the clip of you singing at the assembly, the comments were already crazy. Hundreds. Everyone was adding something. I scrolled for ten minutes and then I added one too, under a made-up name. It was mean. I won't repeat it.

I keep trying to explain how it felt. It didn't feel like me typing. You felt far away, like a picture, and everyone else was doing it, so it seemed like just one more drop in the rain. But it was my thumb. On Monday I saw you eat lunch alone in the library, and I knew which drop was mine.

I've deleted it. I'm sorry. Your high note was actually good.

Jasleen (the girl two rows behind you in maths)

Where did Jasleen see Rajni eating lunch on Monday?
Jasleen saw Rajni eat lunch alone in the library.
Why did posting the comment not feel like her own action to Jasleen at the time?
Rajni felt far away like a picture, the name was made up and everyone else was commenting, so it felt like one more drop in the rain.
What choice did Jasleen make after Monday, and what could she add to it?
She deleted the comment and wrote to apologise; she could also report the clip to a teacher so the page takes it down.
How might Rajni feel reading this letter?
Rajni may feel a mix of hurt and relief, hurt to know a classmate joined in, but glad someone admitted it and praised Rajni's high note.

metadata.subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Childminder's note, Maria D'Costa, holiday afternoons, Wednesday.
Simran (9) arrived after lunch and announced, "I'm bored," four times in the first twenty minutes. She lay on the floor, then on the sofa, then under the table. I didn't offer the tablet or a craft; I told her she could help me fold clothes or find her own thing. She groaned.
At about quarter to three, she went quiet. I found her at the dining table with scrap paper, a stapler and my old newspaper. She had started "The Colony Times": a report on the new stray kitten, an interview with the watchman (she went down and asked him three questions), and a weather forecast: "Hot. Still hot."
When her mother came, Simran made her buy a copy for one rupee.
Plan: leave the scrap-paper box out on Friday.

What did Simran name her newspaper?
"The Colony Times."
What does Simran's going quiet at about quarter to three suggest?
It suggests her boredom had turned into an idea, and she was absorbed in making something of her own.
What choice by Maria helped Simran's game appear, and why?
Not rushing to fill the boredom with the tablet or a craft left space for Simran to invent the newspaper herself.
How might the watchman feel about being interviewed by Simran?
He might feel amused and quite pleased to be asked questions and to appear in her paper.

metadata.subtype: Restless boredom on a long afternoon [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Joseph, you asked how I learned to lead. Sit down. I'm Dolma, and when I was twenty-five I ran the weaving centre in our town near Darjeeling. My first big order was two hundred shawls for a shop in Delhi. I was so frightened I wanted to weave them all myself. My old teacher said, "Give it to your weavers, but tell them everything." So I did. I told Pema and the others the buyer, why the order could save the centre, the date the truck would come, and exactly how tight the weave should be. Then I said, "We'll check the first ten together. After that, weave your way." The truck left on time.

How many shawls were in the order?
The order was two hundred shawls.
What did Dolma feel when the big order came?
Dolma felt frightened, wanting to weave all the shawls alone rather than hand them over.
Which choice in the story led to the truck leaving on time?
Telling the weavers the buyer, the reason, the date and the standard, checking the first ten together, then letting them weave their own way.
How might Pema and the other weavers have felt about the order?
They likely felt trusted and responsible, knowing why the order mattered and being free to weave their own way after the check.

Read this:

Irawati's journal, Sunday.
I've always said police in this city are useless or worse. After what happened to Ayesha's brother at the checkpoint last year, I meant it.
Today, in the crowd at the old market, a little boy, maybe four, stood by the fruit stalls screaming for his mother. People stared. A constable, a heavy man with a grey moustache, pushed through, knelt right down on the wet ground and gave the boy his whistle to hold. He asked the mother's name, then got the loudspeaker shop to announce it. He bought the boy a banana. Twenty minutes later the mother came running, crying, and he just nodded and went back to his post.
I don't know what to do with that. Ayesha's brother was treated badly. This man was kind. Both happened. Maybe I have to stop saying "all of them".

What did the constable give the boy to hold?
He gave the boy his whistle to hold.
What is Irawati feeling at the end of the entry?
Irawati feels unsettled and conflicted, holding both Ayesha's brother's bad experience and the constable's kindness.
What fairer way of judging is Irawati moving toward?
Judging officers one by one instead of saying "all of them", since both harsh and kind treatment really happened.
How might the boy's mother have felt when she found him?
She came running and crying, clearly terrified and then hugely relieved to find her son safe.

Read this:

Class note. Teacher: Sabina.
Nikita (five) asked me six times today, “Is it my birthday?” Her birthday is on Friday.
So I made a paper chain with three links. “Each morning, you tear one link. When there are no links, it's your birthday.”
She tore one today. “Yesterday I had four sleeps. Today three. Tomorrow two!” she said.
She didn't ask again all afternoon.
Next step: I'll use paper chains for the class trip next month.

How many times did Nikita ask if it was her birthday?
She asked six times today.
How did Nikita feel about waiting for her birthday?
She felt impatient and excited, asking again and again.
Why did the paper chain help Nikita wait?
It showed her the days in a way she could see and count, so waiting felt easier.
How might the teacher feel when Nikita stops asking?
The teacher probably feels relieved and pleased that the chain helped.

Read this:

In the school garden period, Mohit tripped over a hose and scraped his knee on the gravel. It was bleeding a bit and full of grit, and he was trying not to cry in front of everyone.
Akash remembered the first-aid talk from last week. "Don't touch it with dirty hands," he said. He helped Mohit to the tap and poured clean water over the scrape until the grit came out. Then he ran to Ms Kulkarni.
Ms Kulkarni brought the first-aid box, covered the knee with a clean dressing and phoned Mohit's mother.
"You knew what to do first," she said to Akash. "And if it had been bad, what number?"
"112," Akash said, "and tell them the school's name and address." She nodded.

How did Mohit scrape his knee?
Mohit tripped over a hose and scraped his knee on the gravel.
What was Mohit feeling after he fell?
Mohit was in pain and embarrassed, trying not to cry in front of everyone.
What would you advise a child who sees a classmate get a small scrape?
Rinse it with clean water if it's small, avoid dirty hands, and fetch an adult straight away, as Akash did.
How might Ms Kulkarni see Akash after the incident?
Ms Kulkarni probably felt reassured and pleased, seeing that the first-aid talk had actually stuck.
Make a chore chart with three lines in the form "Day: task", for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.

Monday: water the plants
Tuesday: sweep the floor
Wednesday: wash the dishes

Cut this to two sentences.

In the hill town of Kalimpong, Dolma and three girls from Class 6 called themselves the Kite Club. Every lunch break they sat on the same wall, flying paper kites and trading strings. They had a special three-tap handshake. When Gopika, new in school, wandered over holding a kite, Dolma said, 'This wall is only for the Club.' Gopika's face dropped. One of the girls whispered, 'She has a good kite, though.' Dolma hesitated, then said, 'Maybe tomorrow. We have to vote.' Gopika walked back slowly to the steps, still holding her kite.

In Kalimpong, Dolma and three Class 6 girls formed the Kite Club, flying paper kites on a wall at lunch and sharing a three-tap handshake. When new girl Gopika came over with a kite, Dolma said the wall was only for the Club but then hesitated and said maybe tomorrow, after a vote, and Gopika walked back slowly, still holding her kite.

Read this:

I'm Nazia. My little brother Asif had never seen bubbles before last week.
I blew the first one and it floated right past his nose. He gasped, eyes wide, and clapped his hands together, fast.
Then it popped, and he looked at me, mouth open.
So I blew another. Gasp, clap. Another. Gasp, clap, and this time a squeal.
We did it about twenty times. He never got bored.

About how many times did Nazia blow bubbles?
About twenty times.
What was Asif feeling when he gasped and clapped at the bubble?
He was surprised and delighted, a quick burst of pleased excitement at something new.
Why was blowing the bubbles again and again a good idea?
Repeating the fun let Asif enjoy the surprise safely, knowing another bubble would come.
What would change if Nazia had blown only one bubble?
Asif might have been left puzzled and disappointed when it popped, without the chance to enjoy the surprise again.

Read this:

In the market town of Moga, Gurleen ran a small tailoring shop. Across the square, Gautam's shop had started offering "stitching in 24 hours" at a higher price, and the queue outside was long. Gurleen's first thought was to do the same. That evening, sitting among the fabric rolls, she thought it through aloud to her sister. "Gautam has three tailors. I have one, and it's me. His customers are college girls who want outfits for tomorrow's function. Mine are older women who order wedding suits weeks ahead, and they care about fit, not speed." She tapped her notebook. "If I promise 24 hours, I'll ruin my own work." So she offered something different: "free second fitting" for wedding orders. By Diwali her order book was full.

How many tailors does Gautam have?
Three tailors.
How did Gurleen feel about copying Gautam at first, and later?
She was tempted at first, but grew cautious and clear, seeing that 24-hour stitching would ruin her own work.
What else could Gurleen ask before offering the free second fitting?
She could ask a few regular customers what they value most, to check the idea fits them.
How might Gurleen's older customers see the free second fitting?
They would probably feel valued and reassured, since fit matters more to them than speed.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asks why something worked for them and what is different here [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

In Class 5, I led the freeze-out of Jahnavi. I'm Chandrika. I'm not proud of it.
Jahnavi had joined our group of four. My best friend started sitting with her at lunch. I felt a cold fear: what if they left me out?
So I told the others Jahnavi had laughed at us behind our backs. It wasn't true. For two weeks, we didn't speak to her. When she sat down, we got up.
I felt strong. The others listened to me. And I kept telling myself she deserved it.
One day I saw her eating alone behind the water tank. She was crying and pretending she wasn't. I felt sick, but I still didn't stop.

Where did Chandrika see Jahnavi eating alone?
Chandrika saw her eating alone behind the water tank.
What made Chandrika start the freeze-out?
Chandrika felt a cold fear of being left out when the best friend started sitting with Jahnavi.
What could Chandrika have done when feeling that fear?
Chandrika could have talked to the best friend about feeling left out, or told a teacher, instead of turning the group against Jahnavi.
What was it like for Jahnavi during those two weeks?
Jahnavi felt lonely and hurt, eating alone and crying while pretending not to.

Read this:

Note, Saturday. Parveen, my former student, came to see me at the college about her future.

Her father wants her to join the family hardware shop in Bhopal. She has spent five years training as an architect and wants to design low-cost homes. She said, "Everyone makes it sound like I have to choose between being a good daughter and being an architect."

I asked her what she actually valued in each. She thought for a long time. The shop, she said, was about her father's pride and the customers who had trusted him for thirty years. Architecture was about making homes people could afford.

Then she laughed, surprised. "The shop sells building materials. Half its customers are building homes."

By the end she had a draft plan: work at a firm on weekdays, help at the shop on Saturdays, and start a small design desk inside the shop for local builders.

I told her to show her father the plan, not just the problem.

— Avni

Where is the family hardware shop?
The family hardware shop is in Bhopal.
How did Parveen feel when she noticed the shop sold building materials?
Parveen was surprised and happy, laughing as she saw that her two roles might fit together.
What could Parveen do when she talks to her father?
She could present the plan as a way to honour the shop and her training together, and invite him to shape the design desk with her.
How might Parveen's father see the plan?
He might feel relieved and proud that the shop and his customers stay part of her life, though he may worry about her time being split.
What are the vadi and samvadi of Raga Jog?
In this teaching table, the vadi of Raga Jog is M, and the samvadi is S.
What is the avaroha of Raga Darbari Kanada?
The avaroha of Raga Darbari Kanada is: S' n d P M g M R S.
I'd like a story of about 90 words about the moon visiting a small girl who cannot sleep. It should end with the girl falling asleep.

Mira lay awake, staring at the ceiling. Suddenly, a silver beam slipped through her window. It was the moon, who had come down to see why she was not asleep. "I am scared of the dark," whispered Mira. "But I am here," said the moon softly. "I light the night for everyone." She smiled and felt less afraid. The moon sat quietly beside her window, glowing. Mira closed her eyes and listened to the quiet, and soon, she was fast asleep.
Remind me to water the tulsi plant. Under ten words, as a command.
Water the tulsi plant before the sun gets strong.

Read this:

I'm Madhuri, and I work two desks from Gurpreet at a software firm in Toronto. In Gurpreet's first week I watched a small scene. Gurpreet asked a new teammate, cheerfully, "So how much do you earn, and are you married?" The teammate blinked, laughed politely and changed the subject. Later, in the lounge, Gurpreet took a call from home and spoke loudly; two people looked up. I can't know how Gurpreet felt about those glances. That afternoon I told Gurpreet quietly that back home those questions show interest, but here many people save them for close friends. Gurpreet nodded slowly and said, "Oh, I see." The next day Gurpreet asked the teammate about the weekend instead, and calls moved to the corridor.

Where does Madhuri work?
Madhuri works at a software firm in Toronto.
Why did Madhuri speak to Gurpreet quietly that afternoon?
To explain kindly without embarrassing Gurpreet, since the questions came from interest, not rudeness.
What did Gurpreet change afterwards?
Gurpreet asked the teammate about the weekend instead, and moved calls to the corridor.
How might Gurpreet have felt about the glances in the lounge?
Possibly puzzled or a little self-conscious, though Madhuri cannot know for sure.

Read this:

Monday night. "Avni, brush your teeth. Now." Avni, five, ran and hid behind the curtain. Nazia had to carry her to the sink, and both of them ended up cross.
Tuesday night. The same words, the same curtain, tears this time.
Thursday night. Nazia tried something different. She held out two toothbrushes. "Pink one or green one tonight? And do you want to start at the top or the bottom?" Avni came out from behind the curtain. "Green. Bottom!" She brushed by herself, making monster faces in the mirror.

Where did Avni hide on Monday night?
Behind the curtain.
Why did Avni hide when told to brush her teeth 'now'?
Avni felt bossed and defiant; the order made her want to show that she could decide.
What did Nazia change on Thursday, and why did it work?
Nazia offered two choices, which toothbrush and where to start, so Avni felt in control while still brushing.
What were Monday and Tuesday like for Nazia?
Nazia was probably tired and cross, carrying Avni to the sink and dealing with tears.

Read this:

Placement counsellor's note, 2 p.m.
Indu came in with her uncle Gautam, who did most of the talking. "Two offers. One pays more, in Chennai. Why is she even thinking about the other?"
Indu sat with her arms folded. When I asked her directly, she said the Chennai role meant night shifts in a call centre, and the other, at a Mysuru design studio, meant training in her real field. She added, quietly, that she had been ill last year after months of irregular sleep.
Mr Gautam was worried, I could see, about her mother's expenses since her father passed away. I told him his worry made sense. Then I asked Indu to list what each job would give her in three years, not only what it paid.
She chose to take a day. Mr Gautam shook my hand on the way out and said, "I just want her secure." Indu touched his arm. I will check in with her on Thursday.

What did the Chennai role involve?
Night shifts in a call centre.
How can you tell Indu felt pressured at the start?
She sat with her arms folded while her uncle did most of the talking, showing she felt uneasy and unheard.
How did the counsellor help Indu weigh the offers?
The counsellor validated Mr Gautam's worry and asked Indu to list what each job would give her in three years, beyond pay.
How might Mr Gautam see Indu's hesitation?
He is anxious about the family's expenses and wants her secure, so he may see the lower offer as a risk rather than a choice about growth and health.

Read this:

Sunday, 1 a.m.
Finally bought the laptop. After three weeks. I compared thirty-four models on a spreadsheet: processor, weight, battery, screen, reviews, price. Every time I thought I'd decided, another video said something else was better.
Binita bought hers in one afternoon. Three options at the shop, chose the middle one, done. She loves it.
Mine arrived today. It's good. It's actually great. But I keep thinking about model 17, the lighter one. And model 22 had a better screen. I'm sitting here with a great laptop, feeling like I lost.
Note to self for next time: pick three things that matter, pick three models, stop.
Bhupen

How many laptop models did Bhupen compare?
Bhupen compared thirty-four models on a spreadsheet.
Why does Bhupen feel like losing despite having a great laptop?
Bhupen feels dissatisfied and unsure, because comparing so many options leaves others, like models 17 and 22, still nagging.
What is Bhupen's note for next time, and why could it help?
Pick three things that matter and three models, then stop, so fewer options leave less room for regret.
How does Binita feel about her own laptop?
Binita loves it, having chosen from three options in one afternoon without second-guessing.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Thursday. Akash came in upset about an email from his lab supervisor, Jahnavi, that read only: "Send me the data. Now." He had taken it as anger and was rehearsing what to say to withdraw from the project. I asked what else could explain the message. He listed a few: she might be rushed, or on her phone, or in a meeting. We agreed the email itself did not tell us her tone. I suggested he reply briefly and ask, "Do you need the raw file or the summary, and by when?" That gives her something easy to answer. He did, and she answered within a minute: raw file, before her flight. Akash relaxed and said he should have checked first. I will note that his worry was understandable.

What did Jahnavi's email say?
It said, "Send me the data. Now."
What did Akash believe about the email at first, and what did the counsellor help him see?
He believed Jahnavi was angry, and the counsellor helped him see that the short wording could also mean she was rushed or busy.
What could Akash do in future when a message seems curt?
He could reply with a short, specific question, or call, to check what the sender needs instead of assuming anger.
How might Jahnavi have seen her own message?
She probably wrote it quickly because she was rushing to catch a flight, and may not have realised it could sound harsh.

metadata.subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

Hi Rafiq bhai,
You have to take this quiz. I did it at midnight and I've been thinking about it all day. My result was "The Quiet Visionary". It says: "You feel things more deeply than others realise. You are mature for your age, and sometimes misunderstood by those closest to you. You have hidden potential waiting to come out."
Bhai, that is SO me. Nobody at home gets that I'm not just the "moody one". I've put it as my profile caption so people finally understand.
Ammi says it's just a game. But how would a game know all that?
Send me your result. I bet yours is totally different.
Chandrika

What was Chandrika's quiz result called?
The Quiet Visionary.
Why does the result mean so much to Chandrika?
Chandrika feels misunderstood at home, so the flattering words bring relief and a longing to be seen, which makes them feel precise.
What could Chandrika do to test how personal the result is?
Compare it with Rafiq's and friends' results, or read the other result types, to see whether the same words fit everyone.
How might Ammi see the new profile caption?
Ammi may feel a little hurt or worried that Chandrika trusts a game more than the family to understand.

metadata.subtype: Online quiz result feels like being seen [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Ankita,
I'm writing because I couldn't say it on the phone.
You asked why I didn't come to the concert with everyone on Saturday. The truth is, Papa asked me to stay home with Dadi because she wasn't well. I wanted to come so much. I kept thinking you'd all say I'm boring, that I never do anything fun.
But I also couldn't stand the idea of Papa thinking I'm not a good son. He trusts me.
So I stayed. Then I spent the whole evening feeling like a bad friend instead.
I hate disappointing anyone. It's like I can't be both at once.
Are you angry with me?
Chetan

Why did Papa ask Chetan to stay home?
To stay home with Dadi because she wasn't well.
What did Chetan feel on Saturday evening?
He felt like a bad friend and worried his friends would think him boring, even though he chose to be a good son.
What could Chetan try so he isn't torn apart by wanting everyone's approval?
Tell friends honestly why he can't come, as he does now, and trust that real friends can understand without constant proof.
How might Ankita feel reading this letter?
Ankita would probably feel touched and understanding, maybe sorry that Chetan worried so much.

Read this:

Aadhya, you asked how I finished the project? Okay, don't judge. Two weeks, and I did nothing. Nothing. Then Thursday night, the deadline's Friday at ten, and I suddenly feel this fear, like ice in my stomach. And that fear is rocket fuel.
I made coffee, sat down at eleven, and just went. Slides, script, everything. By six a.m. it was done. I even got a good grade.
So I'm thinking, maybe this is just how I work, right?
Though, honestly, I slept through Saturday. I snapped at my mum. And there was one slide I knew was wrong. I just didn't have time to fix it.
I'm Sahil, and I'm the king of the last minute.

What time did Sahil sit down to work?
At eleven.
What did Sahil feel on Thursday night before starting?
Sahil felt fear, like ice in the stomach, which turned into a burst of energy.
What wrong lesson might Sahil take, and what does he ignore?
That this is just Sahil's way of working, while ignoring the lost Saturday, snapping at Mum and the wrong slide.
How might Aadhya respond to Sahil's story?
Aadhya may feel amused but also concerned, noticing the costs Sahil mentions but brushes aside.

Read this:

"Jomon, sorry, do you have fifteen minutes this week? For coffee?"
"Pallavi, right? From the analytics team?" He smiled. "Tomorrow, four o'clock, the canteen."
Next day Pallavi arrived early with a list on her phone.
"I've been here eight months and I don't know if I'm on a path or just doing tasks," she said. "Should I learn more coding? Move to product? Stay?"
"Good questions. What do you enjoy most on a normal Tuesday?"
"Cleaning messy data, honestly. Is that weird?"
"It's rare. And valuable." He tapped the table. "You'll be fine here, you know. People notice your work."
Pallavi's shoulders dropped. She realised that was the answer she'd most wanted, more than any course name.

How long had Pallavi been at the company?
Eight months.
What does Pallavi's shoulders dropping suggest?
She felt relieved and reassured, because hearing that someone experienced believed in her mattered more than the practical advice.
What could Pallavi do next to make the most of this first coffee?
Ask Jomon if they can meet again and pick one practical step, like a project with more messy data.
How might Jomon see Pallavi's list and questions?
He likely sees an anxious but serious junior and feels glad to be asked, noticing her work is valuable.

Summarize Jaya's study plan in two sentences.

In Jaya's village near Sirsi, the only good signal was on the roof, and the only quiet place was her grandmother's room. With board exams two months away, Jaya made a plan. Every evening from six to eight, she gave her phone to Ajji, who put it in the steel cupboard. On the small wooden desk she kept only that day's book and a pencil. Her cousin Yusuf laughed. "You'll go mad." For the first three days, she did. Her hand kept reaching for nothing. By the second week, she was finishing a full chapter each evening. She stopped scolding herself before bed, because there was nothing to scold.

With exams coming, Jaya gives her phone to her grandmother every evening and keeps only one book on her desk. It is hard at first, but within two weeks she finishes a chapter each night and stops scolding herself.

Read this:

The history exam was at eight the next morning, and at 1:40 a.m. Mahima, sixteen, was still scrolling.
She'd opened her phone “for five minutes” at eleven. Now her eyes stung and she remembered nothing from chapter six.
Her brother Siddharth knocked. “Your light's still on.”
“I know,” she snapped. Then, more quietly, “I can't stop.”
He held out his hand. “Give it. I'll put it on the fridge.”
She hesitated, then handed it over.
In the morning, tired but less foggy, she wrote on a sticky note: Phone on fridge at 10. Every night. She stuck it on her mirror.
She passed, barely. That night at ten, she walked the phone to the fridge herself.

What time was the history exam?
At eight the next morning.
How did Mahima feel when she said “I can't stop”?
She felt frustrated and helpless, aware she was stuck in scrolling.
What limit did Mahima set, and why might it work?
Putting the phone on the fridge at ten every night, because the phone is out of reach at bedtime.
How does Siddharth help his sister?
He notices the light, offers to take the phone and supports her without lecturing.
'Wo hamesha haar ke rota hai' matlab sore loser? Sahi word hai?
Yes. A "sore loser" is someone who gets upset or angry when they lose a game. Example: "Don't be a sore loser; shake hands and play again tomorrow."

Read this:

I'm Kalyani, Gurpreet's classmate. Since the monsoon, she has been different.
It started when a boy in our class who uses a wheelchair couldn't get to the new science lab on the second floor. Everyone felt bad for a day. Gurpreet didn't stop at a day.
She wrote a letter to the principal and got twenty signatures. When nothing happened, she measured the stairs, found out about ramps, and presented to the school council with photos.
Some people called her a show-off. She kept going, quietly. I don't know if she's doing it for him or for herself or both.
Last week the school moved his class's labs to the ground floor. Gurpreet just said, "Good," and went back to her book. But she was smiling at the page.

How many signatures did Gurpreet get?
Twenty signatures.
What does Gurpreet smiling at her book suggest about how she felt?
It suggests she felt quietly satisfied and relieved that the change finally happened.
What did Gurpreet do that made her effort work?
She kept going after the first letter failed, gathered facts and photos, and used the school council.
How does Kalyani see Gurpreet's campaign?
Kalyani admires the persistence but admits she isn't sure of Gurpreet's reasons.

In merchantmen, oil for the sailor is more scarce than the milk of queens. To dress in the dark, and eat in the dark, and stumble in darkness to his pallet, this is his usual lot. But the whaleman, as he seeks the food of light, so he lives in light. He makes his berth an Aladdin's lamp, and lays him down in it; so that in the pitchiest night the ship's black hull still houses an illumination.

Answer from the text. How does the passage contrast a merchant sailor with the whaleman?

The merchant sailor, short of oil, dresses, eats and stumbles to bed in the dark. The whaleman seeks the food of light and lives in light, making his berth an Aladdin's lamp, so even the blackest night finds the hull lit within.

Read this:

Afreen, put the phone down for a minute. You've checked it twenty times since dinner. Let your Farhan Mamu tell you something. When I was fifteen, there were no chats, just the landline in the corridor. I called my best friend Vinod on a Sunday about the cricket match, and his mother said he'd call back. He didn't. Monday, nothing. By Tuesday I had it all worked out: he was angry about the run-out, he'd told the whole team, they'd all laughed at me, and I would be dropped and friendless for the rest of school. I skipped practice so no one could say it to my face. On Wednesday Vinod turned up at our door, soaked. The rain had killed their phone line for three days. He'd been worried I was angry with him! Every step of my story had felt certain, and not one of them had happened.

Why had Vinod not called back?
The rain had killed their phone line for three days.
Why did Farhan feel sure the whole team was laughing at him?
He was anxious and hurt when Vinod didn't call, and each fearful guess, the run-out, the team, being dropped, felt like the next logical step, so fear passed for certainty.
What choice in the story made things worse, and what could have helped instead?
Skipping practice kept the fear untested; walking over to Vinod's house or asking a teammate would have shown the truth days sooner.
What was the silence like from Vinod's side?
Vinod was cut off by the dead line and was worried Farhan was angry with him, so he came over in the rain to check.

Read this:

Eshaan, it's your Mridul Chacha. I heard you haven't been sleeping since the fire at your office. Let me tell you something I've told very few people. At twenty-four I was on a train that derailed near Itarsi. I wasn't badly hurt, but I saw things I won't describe. For a year I pretended I was fine. I snapped at your aunt, avoided trains, couldn't bear the sound of metal scraping. I thought men were supposed to just get over things. Then my hands started shaking at work. Your aunt found a counsellor at the district hospital, and I went, grumbling. Talking about it slowly, in that small room, helped more than I believed it could. Later I joined a Sunday walking group; nobody there knew, and that was restful too. The memory is still there, beta. It just doesn't drive anymore. Please let someone help you with this.

Where did the train Mridul was on derail?
Near Itarsi.
How did Mridul feel during the year he pretended he was fine?
He was distressed and ashamed of it, believing men were supposed to just get over things, so he hid it and snapped at people.
What helped Mridul heal?
Seeing a counsellor and talking about it slowly, along with a Sunday walking group that gave him calm company.
How might Eshaan's aunt have experienced that year?
Hurt by his snapping and worried when his hands began shaking, which is why she found him a counsellor.

Read this:

14 April, Baisakhi
Everyone at home is at the gurdwara and then the mela. I said I had a headache. I didn't. I just kept looking at the result: FAIL, Organic Chemistry.
Why? Why did I fail when I studied? Was it the second half? Was it me? Maybe I'm just not a science person. Maybe Nitin was right that I only got into this course because of luck. No, he never actually said that. Did he?
Nitin texted: "Jasleen, the resit form closes Friday. Want to fill it together?" I read it three times and then went back to asking why.
It's nine at night now. I have written "why" in this diary eleven times. I have not opened the resit form. I feel worse than this morning.

When does the resit form close?
The resit form closes Friday.
What is Jasleen feeling after a whole day of asking why?
Jasleen feels low and stuck, even worse than in the morning, because asking why over and over hasn't led to any plan.
What small step could Jasleen take right now?
Jasleen could reply to Nitin and fill in the resit form together, then list which topics in the second half need work.
What is it like for Nitin when Jasleen doesn't answer?
Nitin reached out with a practical offer, so the silence might leave Nitin worried or unsure whether the help was welcome.

Read this:

I'm Irawati and I sit behind Sarika in Class 4. On Thursday I watched her best friend Nisha talking with the new girl, Pooja, by the water tank. Sarika stopped a few steps away and rubbed her sleeve. I can't say what she felt, but she stayed there for a moment.
Then she walked up. "Hi, Pooja. I'm Sarika." And to Nisha, quietly, "I like sitting with you, but a game is more fun with three. Want to play catch?"
Nisha grinned. Pooja nodded. They spent the whole break tossing the ball, all three laughing.

Where did Nisha talk with Pooja?
They talked by the water tank.
What might Sarika have been feeling when she stopped and rubbed her sleeve?
She may have felt a small pang or unsure, though Irawati says she cannot tell exactly what Sarika felt.
What did Sarika do that turned it into a game for three?
She said hi to Pooja, told Nisha honestly what she liked, and suggested catch for three.
How might Pooja have felt when Sarika came over?
She was probably glad to be included, since she nodded and joined the game.

Read this:

Week one: Kunal forgot his half of the group project slides, again. Swati was furious. 'Are you just lazy?' she snapped. His face went blank, and he didn't come to the next meeting.
Week two: Swati felt bad. This time she asked, 'What makes it hard?' Kunal shrugged. 'I start, then I lose track. I'm not trying to let you down.' So they tried something new: Swati set a shared reminder for the day before, and they worked side by side on a video call for an hour, each on their own slides.
Week four: Kunal finished his five slides a day early. Swati sent a thumbs-up and 'Proud of you.' He wrote back, 'First time ever. Same time next week?'

How many slides did Kunal finish a day early?
His five slides.
What did Kunal's blank face after 'Are you just lazy?' suggest?
It suggests he felt hurt and ashamed, which is why he stayed away from the next meeting.
What turning point changed how Swati helped Kunal?
Asking 'What makes it hard?' instead of calling him lazy led to shared reminders and working side by side on a video call.
How might Kunal feel reading 'Proud of you' from Swati?
He may feel encouraged and valued, which is why he suggested the same time next week.

"You think too much of your 'toilette,' Adele: but you may have a flower." And I took a rose from a vase and fastened it in her sash. She sighed a sigh of ineffable satisfaction, as if her cup of happiness were now full. I turned my face away to conceal a smile I could not suppress: there was something ludicrous as well as painful in the little Parisienne's earnest and innate devotion to matters of dress.

What does the narrator give Adele, and why does the narrator turn away?

The narrator tells Adele she thinks too much of her dress, then fastens a rose in her sash. Adele sighs with deep satisfaction, and the sight is so funny, as well as sad, that a smile must be hidden by turning away.
Do castles mean the same as forts?

They are similar. Castles are large, strong buildings where a king, queen or noble family lived, often with thick walls and towers. It is a noun. A fort is more of a military building.
Example: We saw two old castles on our trip through the hills.

Read this:

At the insurance office in Nagpur, the Friday target meeting had become almost cheerful. Madhuri watched Gurleen, from the next desk, tick the "site verified" box on a claim she had checked only by phone. "Virtual verification," Gurleen said, and a few people laughed. Six months ago, when Madhuri first saw someone do that, she had lain awake worrying about it. Now it was a running joke. There was even a sticker on the team's water cooler, a smiling face with the words "Verified-ish." Madhuri's own queue had forty claims and the deadline was four o'clock. She picked up the next file, called the garage owner, heard him say the car was repaired, and ticked the box too. Her stomach didn't even flutter this time. She noticed that, briefly, and then Gurleen passed her a biscuit and she forgot.

How many claims were in Madhuri's queue?
Madhuri's own queue had forty claims.
How has Madhuri's feeling about the ticked box changed over six months?
Six months ago she was worried enough to lie awake, but now she feels almost nothing, her unease faded because everyone jokes about it.
What turning point could Madhuri still take when she notices that her stomach doesn't flutter?
She could treat that moment as a warning, stop joking along, and raise the verification practice with a manager or compliance team.
What would change if one person in the team refused to laugh at the joke?
The shortcut would seem less normal, and others who still feel uneasy might feel brave enough to question it too.

Read this:

Suraj had known Chinmay since school, so he noticed every small change once Chinmay started dating Fatima.

At first it was little things. Chinmay, who used to eat anything, learned to order the vegetarian thali when they all went out, because Fatima didn't eat pork and he'd decided to make meals simpler for everyone. Fatima started coming to their Sunday cricket and cheering badly.

Then, one evening at Suraj's flat, Chinmay went quiet over dinner. "Mom asked me yesterday what Fatima's 'community' is. Just like that."

Fatima put down her spoon. "My father asked the same thing about you last week."

They looked at each other across the table. Suraj waited for someone to change the subject.

Instead Fatima said, "So we tell them together. Not separately." Chinmay nodded slowly.

Suraj realised they weren't just a couple anymore. They were a team facing something.

What did Chinmay's mom ask him?
What Fatima's "community" is.
How does Suraj feel when Chinmay and Fatima look at each other across the table?
Suraj feels a little tense and uncertain, waiting for someone to change the subject, and then quietly impressed that they face it together.
What choice did Chinmay and Fatima make, and why does it matter?
They decided to tell their families together, not separately, which tests and strengthens whether they can face the outside as a couple.
What might it be like for Fatima to hear Chinmay's mother's question?
She may feel hurt and wary, recognising the same worry her own father has, but also determined not to let it split them.

Read this:

"You turned down Mumbai?" Jahnavi stared at her cousin over the dinner table.
"I did," Devika said. "I'm staying at the school in Nashik."
"But the Mumbai firm pays double! And the city!"
"The city is expensive, the job's contract is only a year, and Aai's knee surgery is in March." Devika stirred her dal. "Here I have a permanent post, a pension, and I'm home."
"Don't you feel you're missing out?"
Devika was quiet. "Sometimes. When I see photos. My stomach twists." She shrugged. "But at night I sleep. I know what next year looks like. That matters to me more than excitement right now."
"And if you regret it?"
"Then I'll think again. But I chose what makes me feel safe."

When is Aai's knee surgery?
Aai's knee surgery is in March.
How does Devika feel when she sees photos of the city life she turned down?
Her stomach twists with a pang of missing out, though overall she feels calm and safe with her choice.
What might help Devika if doubts grow later?
Revisiting the choice honestly when things change, as she says she will, and talking it over with family she trusts.
How does Jahnavi see Devika's decision?
Jahnavi is surprised and puzzled, seeing mainly the double pay and the city, not the safety Devika values.

Read this:

Rafiq, you'll laugh. My second week in Chennai, my Tamil was about six words, and I needed a mop. At the hardware shop I told the owner, "Hello, I'm Payal, new in the building upstairs," and then I started acting. Hands gripping a stick, pushing it back and forth across the floor. He nodded, very confident, and brought me... a broom. I did it again, bigger, even made a squeezing motion for the bucket. He brought a bucket. Just a bucket.
Then I remembered my phone. I found a photo of a mop, held it up and said, "This one?" He laughed so hard, slapped his forehead, and said the Tamil word slowly for me, twice. Now I point, show a picture, and then check: "This? Yes?" It saves a lot of brooms.

What did the shop owner bring the first time Payal mimed?
He brought a broom.
How do you think Payal felt when the owner brought just a bucket?
Payal probably felt frustrated and a bit embarrassed, though the way the story is told suggests it also felt funny looking back. 😅
What does Payal do now to avoid mix-ups?
Point, show a picture on the phone, and then check with "This? Yes?" before buying.
How might the shop owner have seen the miming?
He seemed confident he understood each time, so the mime misled him until the photo made it clear, which is why he laughed and taught the word.

metadata.subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]

messages.content:
Read this:

Gurleen's shift at the Hyderabad call centre ran from eight at night to five in the morning, and it was Diwali. Back in Amritsar, the gurdwara would be glowing and her family would be lighting candles on the roof. She could see it all in the photos on her phone, between calls.

Her chest hurt every time she looked.

At midnight, on their break, her flatmate Pema, who worked the same shift, set a tiny clay diya on the canteen table and lit it. "I couldn't find more. One is still one."

Gurleen laughed and cried at once.
