At five in the morning she called Biji, who was already up. "Make kada prasad this Sunday," Biji said, "and give some to the girl who lit your lamp."

On Sunday Gurleen stirred the ghee and flour in their tiny kitchen, following Biji's voice on speaker, and Pema ate two bowls.

What did Pema set on the canteen table?
Pema set a tiny clay diya on the canteen table.
How did Gurleen feel looking at the photos between calls?
Gurleen felt a sharp ache of homesickness; her chest hurt every time she looked.
What eased Gurleen's Diwali away from home?
A friend's single diya, a dawn call to Biji, and cooking one family dish together, which comforted her without pretending the loss was small.
Why might Pema have lit the diya?
Pema probably noticed Gurleen's sadness and wanted to give her a small piece of the festival, even with only one lamp.
Write a short story for children, about 80 words, about a fisherman who finds a tiny fish in his net and decides to let it go.

Old Raghu cast his net into the sea every morning. One day, among the big fish, he found a tiny silver one. "You are too small to sell," he said. The little fish trembled. Raghu looked at it for a while, then gently lowered it back into the water. "Go and grow," he said. Years later, when his nets stayed empty during a storm, a huge shoal of silver fish swam in. Raghu smiled. He knew the sea remembered kindness.

Read this:

Monday: A wallet went missing in the boys' hostel wing. By dinner, the wing had decided it was Rafiq, the scholarship student whose shoes were always patched. Kashish heard three boys agreeing loudly. He said, calmly, “Did anyone see him take it?” Nobody had.
Wednesday: The wing group chat was full of jokes about Rafiq. Someone tagged Kashish to add one. He wrote, “I'm not joining this. There's no proof.” Two others stopped posting.
The following Monday: The wallet was found in the laundry, still in the owner's jeans. The owner went to Rafiq's room and apologised. Rafiq said, “Kashish was the only one who asked for proof.” He said it quietly, and shook Kashish's hand.

Where was the wallet found?
It was found in the laundry, still in the owner's jeans.
How did Kashish seem to feel when he asked "Did anyone see him take it?"
He seemed calm and steady, not angry, just firm about wanting facts.
What did Kashish's refusal on Wednesday achieve?
By refusing to join and pointing out there was no proof, he broke the group's unanimity, and two others stopped posting.
How might Rafiq have felt during that week?
He probably felt humiliated and alone, blamed because he was poorer, until Kashish's stand showed someone believed in fairness.

metadata.subtype: Standing up for the blamed person [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Ritu Didi,
I need your advice. You know Chachaji's factory hires every summer. He's asked me to help pick new workers, and he said, "Choose our village boys first, family and friends only."
But at the gate there's a woman, Sharda, who has come every morning for a week. She's more skilled than half the boys he named. She's from a different caste, and I heard someone say that's why she won't get in.
I love Chachaji. He paid my fees. But choosing only our own feels wrong when someone better is waiting.
I've been lying awake. I don't want to disrespect him, and I don't want to walk past her either.
I'm thinking of asking him to meet her with me. Is that too much?
Siddharth

How long has Sharda come to the factory gate?
She has come every morning for a week.
How does Siddharth feel about Chachaji's instruction?
Siddharth feels torn and uneasy, loving and owing Chachaji, yet feeling it is wrong to pass over someone more skilled.
Is asking Chachaji to meet Sharda a good way through the tension?
Yes; it respects Chachaji while giving a fair chance to a skilled worker, instead of either obeying blindly or defying him.
How might Ritu Didi respond to this letter?
She might feel proud of Siddharth's fairness and help plan a respectful talk with Chachaji.

metadata.subtype: Universal principle against loyalty to own circle [Actor]

messages.content: Explain indispensable in a sentence.

Indispensable means absolutely necessary, so that you cannot manage without it. It is an adjective.
Example: In the hills, a warm jacket is indispensable, even in summer.

Read this:

Hafsa taught science at the government school in a small town near Aligarh and watched the canal behind it fill with plastic every summer. At twenty-five, she started with her own home: a cloth bag for the vegetable market, steel tiffins instead of foil, and the ceiling fan instead of the cooler when the heat allowed. Her friend Pooja teased her. "One person won't save the canal." Hafsa shrugged. "Maybe not. But I can't teach it and not do it." When a well-paid job offer came from a packaging company, she hesitated for a week. She turned it down and applied instead to a solar-pump project for farmers. It paid less. Pooja stopped teasing and asked how to find one like it.

What did Hafsa start using at the vegetable market?
She started using a cloth bag.
Why did Hafsa hesitate for a week over the packaging company's offer?
She was tempted by the good pay but felt it clashed with what she believed about the environment.
What makes Hafsa's approach convincing to others?
She practises what she teaches in small daily choices and in her career, not just in words.
How did Pooja's view change over the story?
She moved from teasing Hafsa to asking how to find similar work herself.

Read this:

In the girls' group at the kasba school, everything went through Nazia. If she smiled at you in the morning, your whole day was warm. If she didn't, nobody else would either.
Bidisha had been inside the circle for a month. Monday: Nazia shared her aam papad with her. Tuesday: nothing, not even a glance. Wednesday: arm around her shoulders. Bidisha's stomach never stopped churning.
On Friday Nazia said, "If you're really my friend, you won't talk to Rupa any more. She thinks she's clever."
Rupa sat next to Bidisha on the tempo every morning. She had shared her maths notes when Bidisha was sick.
Bidisha went home and wrote the week in her notebook. Warm, cold, warm, test. Written down, it looked like a trick.
On Saturday on the tempo, she sat beside Rupa as usual. When Nazia's cousin glared, Bidisha simply smiled back. Her heart raced, but she stayed.

What did Nazia share with Bidisha on Monday?
Her aam papad.
How did Bidisha feel as Nazia switched from warm to cold?
She felt anxious and on edge, her stomach churning because she never knew which Nazia she would get.
What helped Bidisha break free of the pattern?
Writing the week down showed her the warm-cold trick, so she refused Nazia's loyalty test and stayed with steady, kind Rupa.
How might Rupa see Bidisha sitting beside her on Saturday?
Rupa probably feels relieved and valued, since their friendship is steady and she had helped Bidisha before.

Read this:

"Darshan, you say you're no good at swimming. Let me tell you something. I learned to swim at thirty-five. Thirty-five! In the village pond, all the children laughed at me. I swallowed so much water. I told myself, not good yet. Every morning I went back. First I floated, then I kicked, then one stroke, then two. It took months. Now look, I still swim every Sunday. So when you say you can't, just add 'yet' at the end." Thomas tapped his grandson's shoulder. "And practise."

At what age did Thomas learn to swim?
He learned to swim at thirty-five.
What might Thomas have felt when the children laughed at him?
He may have felt embarrassed, but he still chose to keep going.
What advice does Thomas give Darshan?
He tells him to add "yet" when he says he can't, and to practise.
How might Darshan see swimming after hearing this story?
He may feel more hopeful, knowing even his grandfather improved slowly with effort.

Read this:

The power went off in the fifth over, so Samir and his cousin Shankar crowded round Nana's old radio on the balcony, the commentary crackling. "Rajat Dev never fails," Samir announced. "Remember his century in March?" Shankar said nothing about the four ducks since. Then the radio hissed: Rajat Dev, caught behind for six. "That wasn't out! The umpire can't even see in this light," Samir shouted, though he could not see anything either. When the batsman who replaced Dev hit a fifty, Samir shrugged. "Lucky. The ball was old by then." Shankar grinned. "So when your man scores, it's talent, and when anyone else scores, it's luck?" Samir opened his mouth, closed it, and turned the radio up.

How was Rajat Dev out, according to the radio?
He was caught behind for six.
Why did Samir insist the umpire could not see?
He felt upset and protective of his hero, so blaming the umpire felt more believable to him than accepting a poor innings.
What could Samir try the next time his hero gets out cheaply?
He could use the same test for every player, asking whether he would call it bad luck if it happened to someone he didn't support.
How does Shankar see Samir's reasoning?
Shankar finds it funny and a bit unfair, noticing that Samir calls his hero's runs talent but another player's runs luck.
Can you split this long sentence into three? My cousin Aisha, who lives in Pune and works as a nurse, came to visit us last weekend and brought a box of homemade ladoos that my mother loved.
My cousin Aisha lives in Pune and works as a nurse. She came to visit us last weekend. She brought a box of homemade ladoos, and my mother loved them.

Read this:

The Pune train was delayed four hours, the station Wi-Fi was dead, and Zubin's phone had nothing to offer but its own gallery. Scrolling for something to do, Zubin landed in the folder from second year: Afreen and Zubin on the hostel roof, Afreen's birthday cake smeared on both their faces, the two of them asleep on a bus to Goa.
For months, whenever Afreen's name came up, Zubin had felt only fury about the rumours she had spread. Fury was easier. It had edges.
But on the cold bench, with the platform lights buzzing, the fury wouldn't come. Something heavier came instead. Zubin missed her. Missed the person in these photos, the one who had seemed safe.
Zubin cried quietly behind a pillar, for the first time since it happened, and felt oddly lighter afterwards.

How long was the Pune train delayed?
The train was delayed four hours.
Why was fury easier for Zubin than what came instead?
Fury had edges and felt strong, while underneath lay a painful grief for the friendship and for the person Afreen had seemed to be.
Why is crying behind the pillar a step forward?
Letting the sadness out instead of covering it with anger moves Zubin through the loss and brings some relief.
What would change if Zubin had kept holding only the fury?
The grief would stay buried, and Zubin would likely remain stuck in anger without the lightness that came after crying.

Read this:

In Yogesh's kasba, the panchayat school needed a new clerk. Seema, who had topped the typing test and kept the library register spotless as a volunteer for two years, applied. So did Monu, the sarpanch's nephew, who couldn't type. On Tuesday the notice went up on the panchayat wall: Monu. Yogesh, home from college for the holidays, stood reading it with a cup of tea going cold. He understood it, in a way. His own mother had once found his cousin a job at the sugar mill; family looks after family. That was the pull. But he also saw Seema at the bus stand, folding her typing certificate back into its plastic cover. That was the cost. He found he couldn't be simply angry, or simply understanding.

Who topped the typing test?
Seema.
Why couldn't Yogesh feel simply angry about the notice?
He felt torn, understanding the pull of family loyalty from his mother helping his cousin, yet troubled by the unfairness to Seema.
What could Yogesh do with what he saw?
He could calmly raise the need for open, test-based hiring at the next village meeting, without attacking the sarpanch's family.
What was it like for Seema at the bus stand?
It was likely a quiet, painful disappointment, folding away a certificate that had not counted against a family tie.

Read this:

In the Delhi colony's community room, Gurleen had been teasing little Ramesh all afternoon about losing at carrom. “Butterfingers! Even my Nani plays better!” At first he giggled and stuck his tongue out. Gurleen was two years older and the colony champion, and the older kids laughed every time she said it. By the fourth game, Ramesh wasn't giggling. His chin was down, and he flicked the striker without looking. When he missed again and Gurleen opened her mouth, she stopped. His eyes were wet. She put down her striker. “Hey. I've been going on too long. Sorry. Want me to show you the angle shot?” Ramesh sniffed and nodded.

Who was the colony carrom champion?
Gurleen was the colony champion.
What was Ramesh feeling by the fourth game?
Ramesh felt hurt and embarrassed, his chin down and eyes wet from the repeated teasing.
What did Gurleen notice, and what did she do about it?
She noticed his lowered chin and wet eyes, stopped teasing, apologised and offered to teach him the angle shot.
Why was the teasing harder for Ramesh to laugh off?
Gurleen was older and the champion, and the older kids kept laughing, so the teasing had an unequal power balance and kept repeating.

Read this:

First week of term. Vikas's hostel door was always open. He fixed Ramesh's laptop, lent notes to three people and stayed up till two listening to Usha cry about her breakup, then wrote half her lab report so she'd have one less worry.
Three weeks later. Vikas fell asleep in his own lab exam. When Usha texted "can u talk?? 😢" that night, he stared at the screen feeling tired and oddly angry, and didn't reply.
Next Saturday. He called Usha in daylight. "I care about you. I can listen for a bit, but I can't do your reports, and I think the hostel counsellor could help with the heavy stuff." She was quiet, then said, "Fair." They talked for twenty minutes. That night Vikas slept eight hours.

What happened to Vikas three weeks later?
He fell asleep in his own lab exam.
How did Vikas feel when Usha texted that night?
He felt exhausted and resentful, staring at the screen feeling tired and oddly angry, and he didn't reply.
Which change made Vikas's helping sustainable?
He kept caring and listening but stopped rescuing by doing her work, and pointed her to the hostel counsellor for the heavy problems.
How might Usha feel when Vikas sets his limit?
She might feel a little stung at first, then respected and supported, since he still listens and shows her where more help is.

Read this:

Seema Didi,
You asked how I'm doing since Priti and I broke up. Better, honestly. It's been two months.
At first I kept replaying it. Everyone thought we were perfect: same college, same jokes. But every time we talked about the future, it was a fight. She wanted a big city job and a life that moved fast. I want to come back to Nashik and help run Papa's workshop, and I want time. We kept pretending that didn't matter.
You told me to write down what I actually value. I did. Family close by. Honesty about money and plans. Kindness when tired. Priti had some of that, but we wanted different lives, and that's not a small thing.
I've stopped checking her profile. I'm playing cricket again on Sundays.
Next time, I'll talk about the future on the third date, not the third year.
Santosh

How long ago did Santosh and Priti break up?
Two months ago.
How does Santosh feel now about the breakup?
Santosh feels better and clearer, though at first Santosh felt stuck replaying it.
What would you advise Santosh before dating again?
Keep using the values list, and talk honestly about future plans early, so compatibility is tested before years pass.
How might Priti have experienced the fights about the future?
Priti may have felt frustrated and unheard too, wanting a fast city life while sensing Santosh didn't share it.

Read this:

Tejas, two, sat on his grandfather Hrithik's shoulders on the road to the bus stand. A buffalo stood by the roadside and Tejas pointed with a fat finger, looking down at Hrithik. “Bhains,” said Hrithik. “Big buffalo.” Tejas pointed again and said “Ba.” When the bus arrived and Hrithik's brother climbed on, Tejas waved his whole hand until the bus turned the corner.

What did Tejas point at by the roadside?
A buffalo.
What might Tejas have wanted when he pointed and looked down?
He probably wanted to share what he saw and get a name for it. He could also have been checking that Hrithik had noticed.
What could Hrithik do next to help Tejas learn more?
He could keep naming things Tejas points at and wait for him to try the words himself.
What might the brother on the bus feel when Tejas waves?
He may feel warmed by the wave and wave back, since the child is saying goodbye in his way.
Can you write a short message thanking my team for working late to finish the launch? About 50 words. I'm the manager.

Hi team,
Thank you for all the late evenings this week. Because of your hard work, we finished the launch on time, and the client is very happy. I know it wasn't easy, especially with the last-minute changes. Please take Friday afternoon off. You have earned it.
Gauri

Read this:

Jomon: passed the wiring practical!!! 🎉
Pankaj: bro!! the one you failed in March?
Jomon: that one. this time I practised the panel layout every evening for 6 weeks
Jomon: instructor said my joints were the neatest in the batch
Pankaj: from BA history to electrician, who saw that coming
Jomon: not me lol. but the history degree didn't get me a single interview
Jomon: this got me 2 calls already
Pankaj: how did you stay at it after March?
Jomon: nearly quit. then I watched the instructor find a short in 2 minutes and thought, I want hands that know stuff like that
Pankaj: proud of you man
Jomon: next is solar panel installation. 3 month course, starts Nov
Pankaj: you're gonna wire my house one day
Jomon: only if you pay 😄

How long did Jomon practise the panel layout?
Every evening for 6 weeks.
How does Jomon feel about passing the practical?
Jomon feels thrilled and proud, especially after failing it in March.
What helped Jomon master the skill this time?
Steady evening practice on one specific task, and a clear example to aim for in the instructor's skill, helped Jomon improve.
How does Pankaj see Jomon's change of path?
Pankaj is surprised by the switch from history to wiring but clearly proud and supportive.

Read this:

Subject: The list I've been making

Hi Nazia,

You asked last month why I've been so quiet. Here's the honest version.

I've been making a list. Late at night, mostly.

The Kathak diploma I dropped in Class 11 because Ma said dance was a hobby, not a future.
Rehaan, who asked me to come to Bengaluru with him, and I said no because I couldn't imagine telling my parents.
The gap year I wanted after graduation, which turned into a bank exam I didn't want and didn't clear.

What gets me is not that I chose wrong. It's that I don't think I chose at all. I chose whatever would make the least noise at home. I was scared, and I called it being sensible.

I'm not asking you to fix it. I just needed someone to read it who knew me back then.

Love,
Sonali

Why did Sonali drop the Kathak diploma?
Sonali dropped it because Ma said dance was a hobby, not a future.
How can you tell Sonali's regret is tangled up with feeling afraid?
Sonali writes that each choice was made to keep things quiet at home, and admits being scared and calling it being sensible.
What small step would help Sonali now?
Talking it through with Nazia, who knew Sonali back then, could help sort which of these lost chances can still be picked up in some form, like dance classes, and which need grieving.
If you were Nazia reading this, what would you want?
You might feel moved and a little sad for your friend, and you would want to call or meet soon to listen, since Sonali said this is not a request to fix things.

metadata.subtype: Stage 2: Counting the roads not taken [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Seema, Saurabh's didi. Since he turned fifteen, my brother has become a closed door. He writes in a notebook he takes everywhere, texts someone and smiles, won't say who. Mummy worries. I don't, much; I was fifteen once, and I kept a notebook too.
But Wednesday was different. He came home with his sleeve pulled over his wrist in the heat, and flinched when I bumped his arm. He said he'd fallen. He wouldn't look at me.
I sat down with him on the stairs and said, "Your notebook is yours. This isn't the same. Did someone hurt you?" After a long time he nodded: some older boys at the bus stop. I told him it wasn't his fault. We told Mummy together that evening, and she called the school straight away.

What did Saurabh say had happened to his arm?
He said he'd fallen.
What does Seema think about Saurabh's notebook and smiling at texts?
She thinks it's ordinary privacy, remembering she kept a notebook at fifteen too, so she isn't worried by it.
What did Seema do that helped once she noticed the wrist?
She sat with him, separated his private notebook from the injury, asked directly, said it wasn't his fault, and told Mummy with him that evening.
What might Saurabh have been feeling when he pulled his sleeve down and wouldn't look at Seema?
He was probably scared and ashamed, trying to hide the harm, and may have worried that telling would make things worse.

metadata.subtype: Private is not the same as hidden [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Yash. I was in the room when our college film club reviewed the screening that went wrong. I'll tell you what I saw.

The projector had failed halfway through, and people had walked out. At the review, everyone said Vaibhav, who organised it, should have known the auditorium projector was unreliable. "It was obvious."

Vaibhav sat very still. Then he took out his phone and read from the booking email. The auditorium staff had written: "Projector serviced last week, fully working." He'd also tested it the day before.

"So what should I have known?" he asked quietly. Nobody answered.

The club president finally said, "Okay. Next time, we ask what we actually knew when we decided." Then she added a backup projector to the checklist.

I don't know what Vaibhav felt exactly. But I noticed he stayed back to help clear up, and he looked a little lighter.

What did the auditorium staff write in the booking email?
Projector serviced last week, fully working.
What was Yash feeling as the room went quiet after Vaibhav's question?
Yash seemed uncomfortable and more aware, realising the blame had been unfair once the booking email was read.
What did the club president do that turned the review toward learning?
The president set the rule of asking what was actually known at the time, and added a backup projector instead of blaming.
How might Vaibhav have felt when everyone said it was obvious?
Vaibhav probably felt hurt and unfairly blamed, since he had checked the email and tested the projector.
Why is it kind to ask before taking someone's photograph?
Asking shows respect for the person in the picture. Because everyone has a right to decide how their face is shared, and some people may not want to be photographed, a question lets them choose.

Read this:

It was a hot Christmas afternoon in Durban, and Lindiwe clomped down the hallway in her father's big work boots, laces trailing. Thabo's reading glasses sat on the end of her nose.

"Class, sit down," she told her teddies, in his deep teacher voice. "Who has done their homework? Hmm?" She tapped the table twice, exactly like him.

Gogo Vera watched from the kitchen and called, "Mr Thabo, your lunch is ready."

Lindiwe nodded seriously. "After marking, Gogo."

What was Lindiwe wearing on the end of her nose?
Thabo's reading glasses sat on the end of her nose.
What does Lindiwe's deep teacher voice suggest she feels?
It suggests Lindiwe admires her father and feels big and confident by becoming like him.
What did Gogo Vera's reply get right?
Gogo Vera joined the game by calling her "Mr Thabo", treating the admiration warmly instead of telling her to take the boots off.
What might Thabo feel if he saw the teddy-bear class?
Thabo would probably feel touched and amused to see his own habits copied so carefully.

Cut this extract down to three sentences.

Divyansh, you failed one exam and now you say you'll drop out. Sit. Your Lakshmi Paati failed too, you know. In 1978, second year of chemistry at the women's college, I got 28 in organic. That night I wrote in my notebook, "I am not clever enough for science." My roommate, a practical girl, took the notebook and said, "Now write the proof under it." So I did. Proof I'm not clever: I failed organic. Proof I am: I topped physical chemistry. Other reasons I failed: I skipped the reaction charts to rehearse for the dance show. Suddenly it wasn't a verdict, it was a list. I made one change, one chart every night, and passed the supplementary easily. I didn't feel cheerful, kanna. I just felt accurate.

Lakshmi Paati tells Divyansh that she once failed organic chemistry and wrote that she was not clever enough for science. Her roommate said to write the proof, and the list showed she had topped physical chemistry but skipped reaction charts for a dance. She studied one chart every night and passed easily, feeling accurate rather than cheerful.

Read this:

Saturday night.
At the birthday party a gift went missing from the table, and my niece Chandrika had been sitting right there. Two aunties started asking her, "Was it the boy in the blue shirt? He was near the table, na?" I saw her face going blank, ready to agree.
So I took her to the balcony and asked, "What happened near the gift table?" She said a lady in a yellow dupatta moved the presents to the bedroom to make space. Nothing about a boy. I typed her exact words into my phone right then, with the time.
Later we found the gift on the bed. If I'd let the blue-shirt question stand, I think she'd have "remembered" him by tomorrow.
Zainab

Where was the missing gift found?
On the bed.
What was Zainab feeling watching Chandrika's face go blank?
Zainab felt worried that Chandrika was about to agree with the aunties rather than tell her own memory.
What did Zainab do that kept Chandrika's account her own?
Took her aside, asked an open question, and typed her exact words right away with the time.
How might the boy in the blue shirt have been affected?
He could have been wrongly blamed and embarrassed if Chandrika had agreed with the aunties.

'Mahima di, do you have five minutes?' Neelam asked, hovering by the desk.
'For you, ten. What happened?'
Neelam put her phone on the desk. 'I wrote this last night. Word for word.'
Mahima read it aloud. '"Tuesday, 5:40 p.m. Sir said: mark all twelve new joiners as having attended the safety induction on Monday. We'll do the session later. Just sign as trainer."' She looked up. 'Did the session happen?'
'No. It's scheduled for next week.'
'Did you read the code of conduct?'
'Section six. False training records. It says to raise it with a senior or the compliance team.' Neelam swallowed. 'So I'm raising it with you. I don't want to get anyone in trouble. I just can't sign that.'
'You won't have to.' Mahima picked up her phone. 'I'm calling compliance now, and I'll ask them to move the induction to this week so the new joiners actually get it.'

How many new joiners were to be marked as having attended?
All twelve new joiners.
What does Neelam swallowing before speaking suggest?
She is nervous and a bit afraid of causing trouble, but determined not to sign a false record.
What made Neelam's approach effective?
Bringing an exact written note and the policy section to a trusted senior, so the response could be quick and factual.
How does Mahima see Neelam's concern?
Mahima takes it seriously at once, calling compliance and making sure the new joiners actually get the safety training.

metadata.subtype: Approach: document the request and check the code of conduct [Action]

It was the last day of the project handover, and the office in Bengaluru was chaos: two clients calling, a server down. Tejas's new manager, Ankita, who had just moved from the Berlin office, walked up to his desk. "Your report has three errors. Fix them by four." Then she walked off. Tejas sat stunned. At his previous team, a manager would have said, "Maybe we could look at a few small things?" This felt like a slap. He wanted to complain. With forty minutes left, he didn't have time to brood. He fixed the errors. Then he walked to her desk. "Ankita, can I ask something? When you said the report had errors, were you upset with me?" She looked surprised. "No! I was just saying what needed doing. In Berlin that's normal. Should I say it differently?" Tejas smiled. "Maybe add a 'please'. I'll get used to the directness." "Deal," she said.

By what time did Ankita want the errors fixed?
By four.
What was Tejas feeling when Ankita walked off?
He felt stunned and hurt, as if slapped, because he was used to softer, indirect feedback.
What did Tejas do that helped under time pressure?
He fixed the errors first, then kindly asked Ankita whether she was upset, instead of brooding or complaining.
How did Ankita see her own direct words?
She saw them as just saying what needed doing, normal where she came from, and she was willing to adjust.

metadata.subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]

messages.content:
Read this:

You asked about being head girl. Honestly? I'm Minakshi, seventeen, and it changed me faster than I'd like to admit. In the first month I loved it: teachers calling me by name, juniors going quiet when I walked in. I started telling people how to line up, what to wear for assemblies, even how to speak to me. When the Class 8 kids complained about losing their lunch-break football for my discipline drive, I told them to stop whining. I didn't notice I'd stopped asking anyone anything. Then my best friend Sangeeta said, in the canteen, 'You talk to us like we're files now.' That stung. I went home and read back my messages from that month. She was right. Every message was an order.

What did the Class 8 kids lose because of the discipline drive?
Their lunch-break football.
How did Minakshi feel when Sangeeta said 'You talk to us like we're files now'?
Minakshi felt stung and hurt, then uneasy on seeing the orders in the old messages.
What could Minakshi change after reading back the messages?
Start asking juniors for their views and give back the football break, so the role serves people rather than control.
How might the Class 8 kids see their head girl?
They likely see her as bossy and unfair, having their football taken and their complaints dismissed.

Santiago, twenty-six, had just joined a design studio in Buenos Aires, and Noa was the senior on his team. On his first project he shared all his sketches openly and helped Noa finish her deck at midnight. She thanked him and returned the favour a week later, covering his client call when his flight was delayed. Then, in a big meeting, Noa presented one of Santiago's layouts as her own. Santiago's face went hot. After the meeting he asked to talk. "That layout was mine. I'd like it credited." Noa looked away, then nodded. "You're right. I panicked." The next day she emailed the client, naming Santiago as lead on that page. Santiago didn't hold a grudge. Next project, he shared his sketches with her again, and this time watched as she said his name first.

What did Noa present as her own?
Noa presented one of Santiago's layouts as her own.
What was Santiago feeling when his face went hot?
Santiago felt angry and hurt, betrayed by Noa taking credit for his work.
What does Santiago's approach show about responding to defection?
He named the problem plainly but calmly, then forgave once Noa corrected it, which kept the partnership without inviting more exploitation.
How might Noa have felt when Santiago asked to talk?
Noa likely felt caught and ashamed, looking away before admitting she had panicked.

Looking back at Class Ten, I think I was tired for a whole year. My day was an hour on the school bus, a classroom with fifty-five of us, then tuition until eight, then homework. I hardly saw the sky except through a bus window. At night I scrolled through pictures of other people's marks and holidays and felt small. Payal, who sat two benches away, was the only one who noticed. One day Payal said, "You look like you haven't laughed in ages." I said I was fine. Then I cried. Payal didn't try to fix anything, just started walking with me to the small park behind school for fifteen minutes every afternoon. It doesn't sound like much, but I began to feel like a person again. Vasudha

How many students were in Vasudha's classroom?
There were fifty-five of them in the classroom.
How did Vasudha feel when scrolling through other people's marks and holidays?
Vasudha felt small, tired and lonely, comparing the crowded days with everyone else's pictures.
Which choice by Payal helped Vasudha begin to feel better?
Payal noticed and asked, did not try to fix anything, and started walking with Vasudha to the small park behind school for fifteen minutes every afternoon.
What might Payal have been thinking when noticing that Vasudha had not laughed in ages?
Payal was probably concerned and caring, and noticed something the others missed.
Is it eigth or eighth?

The correct spelling is "eighth": it is "eight" plus the letter h.
Example: She finished eighth in the race.

I'm Ishita, and I shared a project group with Aditi and two others this semester. In week two, Karthik submitted his part of the market survey a day late. He said sorry in the group chat. Aditi didn't reply.
At the next meeting she divided the tasks on the whiteboard. Karthik's name had nothing beside it. "It's fine, I'll do the analysis myself," she said. "We can't risk another delay." When Karthik offered to draft the slides, she said she'd already started them.
By week six he'd stopped offering. At the final review, the professor asked him a question about the survey and he answered it better than any of us. Aditi looked surprised.
I don't know what was going on in her mind. From where I sat, it looked like that one late day had become the whole story of Karthik for her.

What did Karthik submit a day late in week two?
He submitted his part of the market survey a day late.
Why might giving Karthik nothing have felt sensible to Aditi?
She was worried about another delay hurting the project, so after one late submission it felt safer to take his work herself than to trust him again.
What went wrong in the group, and what could have fixed it?
One late day made Aditi stop giving Karthik any tasks, and he stopped offering; giving him a small task with a clear deadline would have let the group see what he could actually do.
How might Karthik have experienced weeks two to six?
Karthik probably felt pushed out after apologising, which may explain why he stopped offering, even though he understood the survey better than anyone.

Nandini, you're crying into your phone because it's your first Chhath away from Patna? Let your Ganga Mausi tell you about mine.

I was nineteen, in a nursing hostel in Mumbai. On Chhath evening I could almost smell the thekua frying at home and hear Maa singing at the ghat. I lay on my bed with my face to the wall. I didn't eat.

Then my roommate from Kerala, who knew nothing about Chhath, said, "Tell me what your mother does. Let's do one thing."

We had no ghat. So we bought sugarcane and bananas, went to Juhu beach at sunset, and found hundreds of families from Bihar already there, standing in the water. A woman I had never met made a place for me beside her.

I still missed Maa. But I didn't feel alone.

Go and find your one thing.

Where was Ganga's hostel?
Ganga was in a nursing hostel in Mumbai.
What was young Ganga feeling on Chhath evening before her roommate spoke?
She felt a sharp homesickness, lying with her face to the wall, too low to eat.
What turning point eased young Ganga's homesickness?
Her roommate asking her to do one thing her mother did, which led them to the beach where other families were celebrating.
What might the roommate have felt seeing Ganga face the wall?
The roommate likely felt concerned and caring, wanting to help even without knowing the festival.

Darshan, let me tell you about my brother Mohan and the television. We were always fighting. One Sunday I said, "Let's stop and think. What is fair?" We looked at the week. "Monday, Wednesday, Friday for me," I said, "and Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday for you." Mohan frowned. "But you have exams on Fridays." I thought about it. "Then I'll take a Saturday instead of a Friday, and you take Friday." We shook on it. Some weeks it did not suit one of us, and we changed a day, but the rule itself never broke. I'm Pooja, and I still remember how fair it felt.

Which days did the narrator first ask for?
Pooja first asked for Monday, Wednesday and Friday.
How did Mohan feel about the plan when pointing out that Pooja had exams on Fridays?
Mohan seemed doubtful about the plan, frowning and pointing out that Fridays would not suit Pooja's exams.
What choice in the story kept the plan fair, and why?
Swapping a Friday for a Saturday kept it fair, because the days matched each child's homework and both felt heard.
How did the plan look from Mohan's side?
Mohan got a say in changing the days and shook on it, so the plan probably felt fair and not something forced by an elder sibling.

For the campus radio's Honest Hour, this is Lakshmi. Last semester I got hooked on bad news. It started with one cyclone update. Then I'd wake at 3 a.m. and check: more storms, a bridge collapse, a post saying our generation has no future, a thread about layoffs. Every refresh felt like keeping watch, as if something would sneak up on me if I stopped. My roommate Sangeeta would ask, "Anything new?" and honestly, most nights, no. Same stories, new angry comments. But my heart would be racing and I'd skip breakfast. I told Sangeeta the world was ending. She asked what I'd do differently if it was. I had no answer. I just knew I felt terrible, and scrolling didn't make me know any more.

At what time would Lakshmi wake up and check the news?
At 3 a.m.
Why did scrolling feel like "keeping watch" to Lakshmi?
Lakshmi felt anxious that stopping would let something bad sneak up, so each refresh felt like protection and the checking felt necessary even though it brought no new information.
What could Lakshmi have done on those 3 a.m. nights?
Keep the phone out of reach at night, and if the worry stays heavy, talk to Sangeeta or the college counsellor.
What was it like for Sangeeta to share a room with Lakshmi then?
Sangeeta likely saw the racing heart and skipped breakfasts and felt worried, asking gentle questions to help Lakshmi notice nothing new was being learned.

You asked how married life is, Jyoti? Honest version. I'm Bhavna, and Pankaj is a wonderful salesman. I've seen him at the showroom: patient with every fussy customer, laughing at their jokes, remembering their kids' names.

Then he comes home at nine, and he's someone else. "Hmm." "Not now." "Can we not talk?" He eats looking at his phone. For the first few months I thought he'd stopped liking me.

Then one Sunday I watched him on a customer call from home. Warm, funny, forty minutes. When he hung up, he just sat there, empty, like a battery at one percent. That's when I understood. The kindness is real; it's just all spent before he reaches me.

So now we've agreed: for the first twenty minutes at home, he gets silence and tea. After that, we talk. It's better.

What time does Pankaj come home?
Pankaj comes home at nine.
What did Bhavna feel in the first few months?
Bhavna felt hurt and unsure, believing Pankaj had stopped liking Bhavna.
Why does the twenty-minute arrangement help?
It gives Pankaj time to recharge after spending his warmth on customers, so there is some left for real talk at home.
What is the day like for Pankaj by nine o'clock?
Pankaj is drained, like a battery at one percent, having spent his patience and charm on customers all day.

In the government school in Barabanki, Asif sir held up Farhan's essay on the village pond. "This is too good, Farhan. Did the computer write it?"

The whole class turned. Farhan's face burned. He had spent two evenings on it at the tea stall, under the bulb, while his father served customers.

He wanted to shout. Instead he took a breath. "No, sir. I wrote it. Can I show you?"

After class he opened his rough notebook: crossed-out lines, a sketch of the pond, a first draft with spelling mistakes. "This is from Tuesday. This from Wednesday."

Asif sir turned the pages slowly.

"One more thing, sir," Farhan said. "My cousin's phone has a chatbot app. I asked it for three words that mean 'dirty.' I used 'murky' from it. That's all."

Asif sir looked at him for a long moment. Then he nodded. "Thank you for telling me that. I'm sorry I said it in front of everyone." He returned the essay with a mark and a small tick beside "murky."

Where did Farhan write the essay?
Farhan wrote it at the tea stall, under the bulb, while his father served customers.
What was Farhan feeling when Asif sir questioned him in front of the class?
Farhan felt humiliated and angry, with a burning face, and wanted to shout.
What did Farhan do that was wise?
Farhan stayed calm, showed his dated drafts and sketches, and honestly admitted using the app for one word.
How does Asif sir seem to feel after seeing the notebook?
Asif sir seems convinced and a little regretful, apologising for accusing Farhan in front of everyone.

Last winter my flatmate Jaya asked me, for the fourth time, to come with her to an evening of Marathi stage songs at the old theatre in Dadar. I'd always said no. The singing sounded fussy to me, too many turns in every line. But that week I'd read somewhere that we often like things just because we know them, and it made me wonder about my playlist, which was the same film songs I'd had since school. So I made a deal with myself: three evenings, full attention, then decide. The first night I checked the time a lot. The second, one slow song stuck with me on the train home. By the third, I was waiting for a particular singer. I still don't love all of it. But I love her voice, and I wouldn't know that if I'd trusted my first no.
Uma

Where did Jaya take Uma for the stage songs?
To the old theatre in Dadar.
Why did Uma decide to give the stage songs three evenings?
Uma felt curious and a bit unsure about that first no, suspecting liking might just be familiarity, since the playlist was the same film songs from school.
Which part of Uma's plan made the decision fair, and why?
Promising full attention for three evenings before deciding gave the music a real chance beyond the first strange impression.
How might Jaya feel when Uma starts waiting for a particular singer?
Jaya would likely feel pleased and closer to Uma, after asking four times, to share something she loves.

The school trip to the hill fort went wrong from the start. The bus was an hour late, it drizzled all the way up, and Sonali left her new water bottle on the bus seat. At the top there was only thick white fog. She sat on the wall and sulked.
"Wait," said Imran Sir, the geography teacher. "Give it five minutes."
Then the wind moved. The fog tore open like a curtain, and there was the whole valley: green fields, a silver river twisting for miles, tiny villages, cloud shadows sliding over them.
Sonali forgot to breathe. She felt smaller than a stone on that wall, and a warm happiness spread through her chest. The bottle didn't matter at all. She stood beside Imran Sir in silence until the fog closed again.

What did Sonali leave on the bus?
Her new water bottle, on the bus seat.
What did Sonali feel when the fog tore open?
Sonali felt tiny but warmly happy, full of awe, and the lost bottle stopped mattering.
What did Imran Sir do that helped Sonali see the view?
He asked her to give it five minutes instead of giving up, and then stood beside her in silence.
How might Imran Sir have felt when the fog cleared?
He was probably glad and moved too, having waited for it and sharing the silence with Sonali.

There the son recognised not the sire, the sire (recognised not) the son of his loins, the brother (recognised not) the brother, the sister's son (recognised not) the maternal uncle. The maternal uncle (recognised not) the sister's son, the friend not the friend. The Pandavas and the Kurus fought as if they were possessed by demons.

How bad was the confusion in this battle?
So bad that fathers and sons, brothers, uncles and nephews, and even friends could not recognise each other.

At the company's Diwali mela, a tarot reader had set up a table between the food stalls. Arohi's colleague Sarika pushed her into the chair. The reader turned three cards. "You are independent, but sometimes you long for someone to lean on. A change in work is coming."
Sarika gasped. "That's you!"
Arohi smiled. "Would the opposite fit too? 'You like leaning on people but sometimes need to be alone'?" She thought about it. "Yes, honestly."
Then she asked the reader, "Which month? What kind of change?" The reader said only, "Soon."
Arohi thanked him, and said on the way out, "Fun to think about. But I'm not deciding the Hyderabad transfer on three cards."

Where had the tarot reader set up a table?
Between the food stalls at the company's Diwali mela.
What does Arohi's smile at Sarika's gasp suggest?
Arohi felt amused and curious rather than swept away, enjoying the moment while staying sceptical.
How did Arohi test the reading?
By checking whether the opposite line also fitted and asking for specifics like the month, which the reader couldn't give.
How did Sarika experience the reading differently?
Sarika was impressed and excited, taking the general lines as proof the reader really knew Arohi.

Elif turned her phone face down on the café table in Uppsala and let it buzz. Oskar again. Third call.
They had argued about his weekend trip with the climbing club. He hadn't asked before booking it, and she had wanted to say it made her feel like an afterthought, but the words stuck. Arguing out loud with Oskar always ended with her crying and him staying calm. Silence was easier. Silence she could win.
So for two days she read his messages and didn't answer. Are you okay? Did I do something? I'll cancel if you want.
That last one gave her a small, hot flicker of satisfaction. Then it faded, and something else crept in. He wasn't learning why she was hurt. He was only learning to fear her quiet.
She picked up the phone and began, slowly, to type the sentence she had swallowed.

Where was Elif when she let the phone buzz?
She was at a café table in Uppsala.
What did Elif feel when Oskar offered to cancel?
She felt a small, hot flicker of satisfaction, then unease as she saw he was only learning to fear her quiet.
What turning point is Elif reaching when she starts to type?
She chooses to say the swallowed sentence, that she felt like an afterthought, instead of using silence to make Oskar give in, which gives them a real problem to solve.
How might the two days of silence feel to Oskar?
He likely felt anxious and confused, guessing what he did wrong and ready to give up his trip just to end the silence.

The first year at the architecture firm, I treated every deadline like a college jury. All-nighters, cold coffee, drawings emailed at 3 a.m. I was proud of it, honestly. I thought that was what serious people did.

By March I was snapping at my mother on the phone and forgetting simple dimensions. One evening Vasudha, the senior designer, found me redrawing a staircase for the fourth time. She didn't lecture. She just said, "Shreya, the site doesn't open until Monday. Go home."

That weekend I did something small. I wrote my own closing time on a card, seven-thirty, and taped it under my monitor. Some weeks I break it. But now when I stay late, I choose to, and my drawings have fewer mistakes. I still miss the adrenaline sometimes, which surprised me.

What time did Shreya write on the card under her monitor?
She wrote seven-thirty as her own closing time.
How did Shreya feel about her all-nighters at first, and what changed?
She felt proud of them and saw them as what serious people do; later, after snapping at her mother and making mistakes, she realised they were wearing her down.
What went well in how Vasudha helped Shreya?
Vasudha gave a simple fact and a clear nudge to go home instead of a lecture, which let Shreya make her own decision about limits.
How might Shreya's mother have experienced the change?
She likely noticed Shreya was less irritable on calls once Shreya started leaving work at a set time.

I'm Urmila, and I sell vegetables at the Saturday market. That morning a little boy, Farhan, stood alone by my baskets. "Ab-bu?" he called, and his voice was shaking, choked, like a sob was stuck. I crouched down next to him. "We'll find Abbu. Stay with me." I didn't leave him. I called out loudly over the stalls. His father came running within a minute and scooped him up. Farhan buried his face and cried then, finally.

Where did Farhan stand alone?
By Urmila's vegetable baskets.
What was Farhan feeling when his voice shook?
He was frightened and distressed at losing sight of his father, close to crying.
What did Urmila do that was wise?
Urmila crouched beside him, stayed with him, and called out for his father rather than leaving him alone.
How might Farhan's father have felt when he came running?
He was likely terrified at first and hugely relieved to find him safe.

How can I share a room with my sibling peacefully?
Quick one: what is "intangible"?

1. Agree on a few simple rules, like keeping your things on your own side and lowering the noise at night. Talk calmly when something bothers you.
2. "Intangible" is an adjective. It means unable to be touched, like a feeling.

The results came out during a power cut, so the whole class crowded round the one notice board with phone torches. Nilesh found his name: Maths 96, English 58.

"Ninety-six! I'm brilliant at maths," he said loudly.

"And English?" asked his sister Kalyani, who'd come to pick him up.

"The teacher's biased. And the paper was too hard. Nobody could do the essay."

Kalyani checked the board with her torch. "Your friend Rehan got 84 in English."

"He's lucky. He got the topic he liked."

"And in maths, were you lucky?"

"No, that's skill."

Kalyani laughed. "So the good mark is you, and the bad mark is everyone else?"

Nilesh opened his mouth, then shut it. In the dark, it was harder to argue.

What marks did Nilesh get?
Maths 96, English 58.
Why did Nilesh blame the teacher and paper for his English mark?
Nilesh felt embarrassed and wanted to protect his proud self-image, so blaming others felt easier than looking at his own gaps.
What did Kalyani point out, and how could it help Nilesh?
Kalyani noted he credited himself for maths but blamed others for English; seeing that could help him learn where to improve.
How might Nilesh's English teacher feel hearing this?
The teacher might feel hurt and unfairly blamed.

'No way! Homework on weekends is torture,' Mahima said, slapping the desk during debate practice. 'Children need to play!'
'Okay, okay, you win,' Baljeet laughed. 'You should say this at home. Your Papa's always talking about extra tuition.'
'At home?' Mahima's voice dropped. 'I can't argue with Papa. Mummy says we don't answer back to elders.'
'But you're not being rude. You're just saying things.'
'It feels rude there. Here it's a game.'
'So you're two people?'
Mahima thought. 'No. One me. Two rooms.'
'Which one's the real you?'
'Both,' Mahima said. 'Maybe one day I'll say the tuition thing nicely. When Papa's in a good mood.'

What did Mahima slap during debate practice?
The desk.
Why does Mahima's voice drop when Baljeet mentions home?
Mahima feels uneasy, because arguing with Papa feels rude at home, where Mummy says you don't answer back to elders.
What choice does Mahima consider for raising the tuition topic at home?
Saying it nicely one day when Papa is in a good mood, which keeps Mahima's voice while respecting the home rules.
How might Baljeet see Mahima after this talk?
Baljeet may understand that the quiet Mahima at home and the loud one in debate are the same person in different rooms.

Rostov saw that it had been well considered by them. Sonya had already struck him by her beauty on the preceding day. Today, when he had caught a glimpse of her, she seemed still more lovely. She was a charming girl of sixteen, evidently passionately in love with him (he did not doubt that for an instant). Why should he not love her now, and even marry her, Rostov thought, but just now there were so many other pleasures and interests before him! "Yes, they have taken a wise decision," he thought, "I must remain free."

Question: Why does Rostov decide that he must remain free?
Although he finds Sonya lovely and thinks she loves him, he feels there are so many other pleasures and interests ahead of him just now.
Why does a metal spoon in hot soup get hot, but a wooden one does not?
Metal carries heat well and wood does not. Because heat passes easily through metal up to the handle, while wood slows it down, so a wooden handle stays cool.

I'm Indu. When I moved to Mumbai for my first job, the cheapest room I found was with a retired teacher, Usha aunty, in Virar. ₹5,000 a month, home food, very kind. I nearly said yes on the phone.
Then I lay in bed and walked through a whole Monday in my head. Office in Lower Parel at 9:30. The Virar local, then a change. Wake at five-thirty, leave at six-forty. Coming home, the seven o'clock trains are the worst. Home at maybe 9:30. Eat, sleep, repeat. Where was the time for anything else?
Still, it was only imagination, so I tested it. The Monday before I joined, I did the journey at rush hour. I couldn't even get into the first train. It took two hours and ten minutes one way.
I called Usha aunty and thanked her. I took a shared room in Dadar for ₹9,000 instead. More money, but three extra hours every day.

How much was the room with Usha aunty?
₹5,000 a month, home food.
How did Indu feel after the test journey?
Indu was probably drained and a bit shaken after not even getting into the first train, and clearer about the choice.
What else could Indu weigh besides time?
The extra ₹4,000 a month against the budget, and whether a middle option closer than Virar exists.
How might Usha aunty feel about the call?
Perhaps a little disappointed, but touched to be thanked and likely understanding about the long journey.

Read this:

Mentor note, Jaya.

Gautam came to my office at 8:30, hood up, eyes down. Someone had taken a photo at the farewell, catching Gautam mid-laugh with an open mouth, and turned it into a meme going round three class groups. Gautam said very quietly, "Everyone's seen it. I want to disappear." Gautam hadn't eaten breakfast.

I told Gautam plainly that the cruelty belongs to the people making the meme, not to Gautam. I stayed while we reported the posts and blocked the accounts, and I passed the matter to the college's student welfare lead that same morning. Two friends from Gautam's hostel wing offered to walk with Gautam to lunch.

I reminded Gautam that these things fade faster than they feel today. I will check in tomorrow.

Where was the photo taken?
The photo was taken at the farewell, catching Gautam mid-laugh with an open mouth.
What was Gautam feeling when saying "I want to disappear"?
Deep shame and exposure, shown by the hood up, the eyes down, the skipped breakfast and the wish to disappear.
What did Jaya do, and what else could help?
Jaya stayed with Gautam, reported the posts, blocked the accounts and told the welfare lead that morning; friends can keep walking with Gautam to meals and remind Gautam it fades.
How might the two hostel friends' offer affect Gautam?
Their offer to walk with Gautam to lunch shows the mockery is not everyone's view, which can make the shame feel less total.

"Tenzin, just look. Look at my returns." Sudha turned her phone around. "I put in ₹20,000 in March. It's ₹31,000 now."
"How?"
"It's an app. There's a group. The mentor says it's guaranteed. I even took some out, and it came to my account."
Tenzin felt the pull. Rent had just gone up. Everyone in the group looked so happy.
"What's the catch?"
"No catch! But there's a special round this week. Bigger deposit, bigger returns. It closes Sunday. Don't tell too many people, they want to keep it small."
"Why keep it small?"
"So it stays profitable. Come on, Tenzin. Don't be the one who missed out."
Tenzin hesitated. The words "guaranteed," "closes Sunday" and "don't tell" sat strangely together.
"Let me think till tomorrow," Tenzin said.
Sudha rolled her eyes. "By tomorrow it might be full."

How much had Sudha put in in March?
₹20,000 in March.
What was Tenzin feeling while Sudha talked?
Tenzin felt tempted and anxious about missing out, especially with rent going up, but also uneasy about the words used.
What would you advise Tenzin to do next?
Take the extra day, check with the official regulator whether the app is registered, and talk to someone independent before deciding.
How does Sudha see the scheme?
Sudha trusts it because it paid out once, and sees Tenzin's caution as missing a chance.

The metro was stuck between stations, lights flickering, and Kashish was already late for a client call. Then her phone buzzed: Uma, her batchmate, had been promoted to team lead. Congratulations poured in on the group.
Kashish felt her jaw tighten. Two years, same projects. Why Uma?
The train stayed still. She opened her notes app instead of the group chat. She typed: What do I have? A job I like. A manager who teaches. What did I have a year ago? No client calls. What can I control? My pitch today.
The lights came back on. She typed to Uma: "Well deserved. Coffee this week?"
She was still a little jealous. But the mood was hers again.

What was Uma promoted to?
Uma was promoted to team lead.
What does Kashish's tightening jaw suggest she felt?
It suggests she felt a sharp jolt of envy and resentment when she heard about Uma's promotion.
What did Kashish do well with her envy?
She wrote down what she has, compared with her own past and focused on what she can control, so envy did not set her mood.
How might Uma feel when she gets Kashish's message?
Uma would likely feel pleased and warm, taking it as real support from a batchmate.

The review meeting at the ward office ended, and Hemant sat back down with the composting report open. 'Total flop,' he muttered. Omkar, from the accounts desk, pulled up a chair. 'Flop out of ten, or flop out of what?' Hemant almost laughed. On the whiteboard he drew a line from 0 to 10. Collection from the two big colonies: steady every week, so maybe a 7. Bins in the market lane: broken twice, smelly, a 3. Volunteer turnout: strong for a month, then gone, a 4. He wrote two columns, Kept Going and Fell Apart, and the second was shorter than he expected. 'So it's a five, not a zero,' Omkar said. Hemant circled the market lane. 'And this is what the next round fixes first.'

Which part of the composting drive did Hemant give a 3?
The bins in the market lane, which broke twice and were smelly, got a 3.
Why did 'total flop' feel true to Hemant right after the review meeting?
Hemant was frustrated and discouraged after the meeting, so the problems filled his mind and one bad part seemed to stand for the whole drive.
What choice turned Hemant's review from a verdict into a plan?
Drawing a 0-to-10 line and making two columns let him score each part on its own, so he could see the colonies were working and pick the market lane as the first fix.
How might Omkar see Hemant's shift from 'flop' to 'five'?
Omkar likely finds this far more useful: a flat 'flop' gave the team nothing to act on, while a five with one clear first fix gives everyone a next step.
Aunt Shobha is my father's sister. What is her son to my father?
He is your father's nephew. Because a nephew is the son of a person's brother or sister, and Aunt Shobha is your father's sister.

The market was closing and Papa had only enough change left for the bus. Vasudha pointed at a shiny toy train. "Papa, buy it!" Deepak shook his head. "Not today, beta." Vasudha's face went hot. She felt Papa didn't love her at all. She opened her mouth to scream, the way she did when she wanted things. Then she saw the bus coming. She tugged Papa's sleeve instead. "Can I have it on my birthday?" Deepak squeezed her hand. "We'll ask for it then. Come, bus!" She looked back at the train, sighed and climbed on.

Why couldn't Deepak buy the train that evening?
Papa had only enough change left for the bus.
How can you tell Vasudha was furious at first?
Her face went hot, she felt Papa didn't love her, and she opened her mouth to scream the way she usually did.
What did Vasudha try instead of screaming, and why was it wise?
She asked if she could have the train on her birthday, which kept her wish alive without a fight.
What is it like for Deepak when Vasudha tugs his sleeve instead of screaming?
He feels relieved and proud; it lets him say yes to a plan even though he cannot say yes today.

At my first job, my manager Kiran had a word for everything. Staying till eleven was 'ownership'. Weekend calls were 'passion'. When Reshma cried in the washroom after a third late night, Kiran called it 'growth pains'. I went along with the words for months. Then one Friday Kiran announced, 'We're motivating the team with a stretch target: everyone stays till the release is done.' Something snapped into focus. I asked, 'What does that actually mean for people? How many hours, and who's covering Reshma's childcare?' The room went quiet. Kiran said, 'Eshaan, it's just a push.' I said, 'A push is fine. But if it means fourteen-hour days for two weeks, let's say that, and then decide if it's fair.' We ended up splitting the release into two phases. Reshma mouthed 'thank you' across the table. I realised how much the nice words had been doing our thinking for us.

What did Kiran call staying till eleven?
Kiran called it 'ownership'.
Why did something 'snap into focus' for Eshaan?
Eshaan felt uneasy and protective of teammates like Reshma, and the word 'motivating' finally seemed to be hiding exhausting, unfair hours.
What did naming it plainly lead to?
Saying 'fourteen-hour days for two weeks' let the team judge whether it was fair, and the release was split into two phases.
How did Reshma experience Eshaan's question?
Reshma seemed relieved and grateful, mouthing 'thank you', since Reshma's childcare had been ignored under the word 'push'.

I'm Pooja, and my brother Nakul is fifteen, so I get a front-row seat to his opinions. When Vasudha aunty moved into the flat above us, the first thing he heard about her, from the watchman, was that she'd complained about the building's cricket games. From that day she was "the grumpy one" to Nakul. Then she lent us her ladder. She fed our cat when we went to Nagpur. She clapped from her balcony when Nakul's team won the colony match. Each time he shrugged: "She's still grumpy, just being polite." I can't see inside his head, but it looks to me as if the watchman's sentence got there first and just sat down. Yesterday she brought him a slice of cake for his birthday. He said thank you without looking at her.

What did the watchman say about Vasudha aunty?
That she'd complained about the building's cricket games.
Why does Nakul keep calling Vasudha aunty grumpy?
Nakul has felt resentful since the watchman's comment, the first thing he heard about her, so her kind acts get explained away as politeness.
What could help Nakul update his view of Vasudha aunty?
Listing what she has actually done since moving in, the ladder, the cat, the clapping, and asking whether the watchman's story still fits.
How does Pooja see what is happening in Nakul's mind?
Pooja can't see inside his head, but thinks the watchman's sentence got there first and stayed, shaping everything after.
I missed a week of classes and now I'm behind.
That is stressful, but it can be fixed. Start by finding out what was covered.
How do I do that?
Ask a classmate for notes, check the college notice board or website, and see your teachers. Tell them honestly why you missed the week.
What if there's too much to catch up on?
Make a list of topics and tackle them in order of importance. Ask your teachers which are the key ones. It is better to catch up on the essentials than to try to do everything.
Will the teachers be angry?
Some may be disappointed, but most are helpful if you are honest and show that you are working to catch up. Go to them early, before exams.

Sunday
Diary, today Ammi said I have "Salma Apa's memory". Here's why.
At dinner I told Khalu about our trip to the lake when I was six. I said the boat nearly tipped over and a duck stole my biscuit. Salma Apa said, "Kiran, that was ME. You were asleep in the car." Ammi laughed and agreed!
But I REMEMBER it. I can see the duck's orange feet.
Then Apa said she has told that story so often that I must have heard it a hundred times. Maybe my brain just put me in it?
It's a bit creepy but also funny. Tomorrow I'm going to ask Abbu what he remembers and write it down before anyone else talks.
Kiran

What did Kiran say the duck stole?
Kiran said a duck stole the biscuit.
Why does Kiran still feel sure about the duck?
Kiran feels certain and a bit puzzled, because Kiran can picture the duck's orange feet, and hearing Salma Apa's story so often makes it feel like Kiran's own memory.
What does Kiran plan to do tomorrow, and why is it a smart check?
Kiran will ask Abbu what he remembers and write it down before anyone else talks, so no other version gets mixed in.
How might Salma Apa feel when Kiran tells her story as Kiran's own?
Salma may feel amused but a little protective of her memory, since she was the one near the duck while Kiran was asleep.

Dear Farhan,
You asked why I missed your birthday dinner. I owe you a proper answer.
For three months I've been working at the architecture firm all day and designing a café logo for a friend at night. Last week I fell asleep on the bus and ended up at the depot. On Thursday I burst into tears because the printer jammed. That's when I knew I wasn't thinking straight enough to decide whether to quit, which I'd been planning to do that week.
So I changed the plan. I've taken ten days' leave from Monday, approved and handed over. I told my friend I'm stepping back from the logo; she was kind about it. I'm not deciding anything about the job until I'm back and have slept properly.
Can I buy you a late birthday coffee when I return?
Lavanya

What did Lavanya step back from?
Lavanya stepped back from designing a café logo for a friend.
What moment made Lavanya realise something was wrong, and how did it feel?
Bursting into tears over a jammed printer made Lavanya see the exhaustion clearly, a feeling of being worn out and not thinking straight.
What else could Lavanya do during the ten days of leave?
Lavanya could keep the days light and restful, and write down questions about the job to look at only after returning.
How might Farhan feel reading this letter?
Farhan may feel less hurt about the missed dinner and more concerned and glad that Lavanya is taking care, and trusted with the honest reason.

messages.content: Please revert back to me soon. Is it good English?
Not quite. Say: "Please reply to me soon." Why: "Revert" means to go back to an earlier state, so it is not the usual word for replying, and "back" repeats the idea.
Can I say "trousers" in America, or is it "pants"?

American English says "pants" for the garment, but "trousers" is also understood. In British English "pants" usually means underwear, so be careful.
Example: He wore grey trousers to school.
Make this sound more casual: I would appreciate it if you could pass me your notes from the last lecture.
Can you pass me your notes from the last lecture?

Briefly, in two sentences, what is this passage about?

In Mahima's kasba, everyone knew when she was coming: loud laugh, bicycle bell, a bag of roasted peanuts to share. This week her whole calendar was the temple fair, the new film at the town's old cinema hall, and Friday's chaat trip with six friends. Her friends adored her; she made every plan feel like a festival. On Thursday, Bhavna stopped her at the school gate. "Mahi, the science project. It's due Monday. Have you started?" Mahima's smile faded. She hadn't even opened the book. She thought of the chaat trip, then of Sir's face on Monday. "Friday I'll go for one hour only," she said slowly. "And Saturday you come to my house and we do the project." Bhavna laughed. "One hour? You?"

Mahima, who makes every plan feel like a festival, has a busy week of a fair, a film and a chaat trip. When Bhavna reminds her the project is due Monday, Mahima cuts the chaat trip to one hour and will work on it with Bhavna on Saturday.

At the government school where Madhav taught Class 8 science, Mondays were hard. He'd sleep badly, the bus would be crowded, and some weeks he felt nothing for the lesson. Kashish, a first-year teacher, asked him in the staffroom how he always looked prepared. Madhav showed her his routine card: "7:45 arrive. 7:50 write today's aim on the board. 7:55 set out materials. 8:00 first question to class." "Even when you don't feel like it?" "Especially then. Once the aim is on the board, my hands know the rest." Kashish tried it the next Monday. By the second period she noticed she had forgotten to feel tired.

What does Madhav do at 7:50?
At 7:50 he writes today's aim on the board.
How did Kashish feel by the second period on Monday?
She felt more energetic, surprised to find she had forgotten to feel tired.
Why does Madhav's routine card help on flat days?
It removes the need to feel motivated first: each small fixed step leads to the next, so action builds the drive.
How might Madhav's students experience his routine on flat days?
They get a clear aim and a prepared lesson every day, without noticing whether their teacher felt like it.

The hackathon registration closed in an hour, and the canteen Wi-Fi kept dropping. Chetan pushed his laptop towards Minakshi. "Register. Please. You're the best coder I know."
"I'm not ready. My projects aren't polished."
"You said that about the internship too. And the coding contest."
Minakshi shrugged.
Chetan hesitated, then opened his own project folder. "Look at this. My first app. It crashed every five minutes. My code is a mess." He scrolled through ugly lines. "I still entered last year. I learned more than all semester."
Minakshi stared at the screen. "It really crashed?"
"Constantly. Register. I'll team with you."
She reached for the laptop.

How long until hackathon registration closed?
An hour.
What was Chetan feeling when he pushed his laptop towards Minakshi?
He felt frustrated and eager, sad to see her talent going unused out of fear.
What did Chetan do that helped Minakshi?
He showed his own messy, crashing first app and offered to team up, making imperfection feel normal.
What is it like for Minakshi to see Chetan's messy code?
Minakshi seems surprised and a little relieved, seeing that even good coders start with flawed work.

"Didi, am I ugly?"
Rashmi looked up from her book. "What? Who said that?"
"Mitali. She said I'm so dark I disappear at night. Everyone laughed."
Rashmi put the book down and pulled Bidisha onto the bed. "Bidi, listen. Your skin is lovely. Mitali's words show she's unkind. They don't say anything about you."
"But everyone laughed."
"Some people laugh because they're scared of being next. Did anyone not laugh?"
"...Suhana didn't. She gave me her eraser after."
"Then sit with Suhana. And we're telling Ma right now."
Ma came in from the kitchen, heard it all and knelt beside Bidisha. "Nobody gets to say that to you. Not ever." That evening she wrote to the class teacher, who replied that she would speak to Mitali and the class the next morning.

Who did not laugh at Bidisha?
Suhana.
What does Bidisha's question "Am I ugly?" reveal?
She felt deeply hurt and ashamed, and was starting to believe Mitali's cruel words.
What steps did Rashmi and Ma take?
Rashmi reassured her and suggested sitting with Suhana, then took her to Ma, who wrote to the class teacher that evening.
Why might some classmates have laughed along?
Rashmi suggests some laugh because they are scared of being teased next.

Didi, you're asking about Eshaan? Don't. I'm Chinmay, and I'm done with him.

You know what he did? We had a plan: Saturday, science model, his house. I carried my whole volcano on the bus. Paint, soda, everything. And when I got there, his mother said he'd gone to the cricket nets with the Class 10 boys.

So that's who he is. A fake. A loser who drops people for seniors. I don't care about anything else he's done.

What? Don't give me that look, I'm your brother, I know that look. Yes, he helped me with maths all of last term. So? And he sat with me when my grandfather died. That was then. Now I know the real Eshaan.

He's been messaging. Six times. I haven't opened any of them. Why would I? I know what they say. Excuses.

...Okay, I'll look at one. Just to see how fake the excuse is.

Where had Eshaan gone, according to his mother?
He'd gone to the cricket nets with the Class 10 boys.
Why does Chinmay refuse to open Eshaan's messages?
He is hurt and has already decided Eshaan is a fake, so he believes he knows what the messages say. The label saves him from having to think about Eshaan's side.
What small choice at the end could change things, and why?
Deciding to look at one message. Even if it's out of suspicion, reading it gives Eshaan a chance to explain and brings back some curiosity.
How might Didi see Chinmay's anger, having known both boys?
Didi probably understands the hurt but also remembers Eshaan helping with maths and sitting with Chinmay after the grandfather's death. Didi may want to nudge Chinmay to hear the other side.

The terrace of Ira's building in Pune was strung with fairy lights, and everyone had phones out when Ira held up her hand and said, "We're engaged!" Aadhya screamed with the rest and hugged her hard. Then she went to refill the lemonade and stood by the water tank for a minute, breathing. Ira was her oldest friend. Ira was happy. And Aadhya felt, very suddenly, like the only one on the terrace still at the starting line. Later, when the others had left, Ira found her washing glasses. "You went quiet." Aadhya put down the glass. "I'm really happy for you. And a small, silly part of me feels left behind. I didn't want to hide it and be weird with you." Ira laughed and hugged her. "You're not behind. You're my maid of honour. Now dry these."

Where was the engagement announced?
On the terrace of Ira's building in Pune, under fairy lights.
Why did Aadhya stand by the water tank for a minute?
She needed to steady herself, suddenly feeling like the only one still at the starting line, even while happy for Ira.
What did Aadhya choose to do when Ira said "You went quiet", and why did it help?
She admitted both the happiness and the left-behind feeling, so she didn't have to act weird and the friendship stayed honest.
How might Ira have felt hearing Aadhya's confession?
Ira seems relieved and warm, laughing, hugging her, and reassuring her by naming her maid of honour.

At the Pongal fair in the village, bullocks with painted horns stood by the temple tank, and Charu wanted to see all of them. Her Appa, Chinmay, sat on the steps with the sugarcane. 'Go with your cousins. I'll be right here.' Charu ran off, then stopped at the first bullock, turned round, found Appa's white shirt on the steps, and waved. He waved back. She went further, to the balloon man, then ran all the way back just to touch his knee. 'You're here.' 'I'm here.' Off she went again, braver each time.

Where did Chinmay sit?
On the steps with the sugarcane.
Why did Charu run back just to touch Appa's knee?
Charu wanted a quick moment of safety; touching him made her feel secure enough to go further.
What did Chinmay's 'I'll be right here' do for Charu?
It gave her a fixed, safe spot to return to, which made exploring the fair possible.
What is it like for Chinmay watching Charu go further each time?
Chinmay probably feels proud and content, seeing his daughter grow braver while knowing she can always come back.
It rains a lot in July, but today is not raining. Fix this.

It rains a lot in July, but today it is not raining.
Why: English weather verbs need "it" as the subject, and "today" cannot play that role.

In Lisbon, Clara had an essay due Monday. On Saturday morning she opened her laptop, read the question, and closed it again. "I'll do it after lunch."
The relief was instant. She texted Omar and they went to the beach. The sun was warm, the waves loud, and she forgot the essay completely.
On the tram home, it came back. A low hum of guilt under everything. She pretended not to notice.
Sunday morning, she opened the laptop again. The hum got louder. She closed it. Instant relief again.
"You okay?" Omar texted.
"Totally," she wrote. Then she stared at the ceiling, uneasy.

When was Clara's essay due?
On Monday.
What was Clara feeling on the tram home?
She felt a low hum of guilt under the good day, which she tried not to notice.
What went wrong on Sunday, and what could help?
Closing the laptop brought relief again and rewarded avoiding; writing just one paragraph before stopping could break the pattern.
What might Omar sense from Clara's "Totally"?
Omar may not suspect anything, or he might sense she is uneasy from the short reply.

At 11 p.m. the power went out. Pradeep's physics assignment was due at eight the next morning, and he was only on question three of ten. His phone battery was at twelve percent.
Then a message from his classmate Sarika in the group: photos of her finished answers. "For anyone stuck 🙂"
Pradeep hesitated. His father had said if his marks dropped again, no more cricket academy. Everyone in the group was probably copying anyway. Just this once.
He copied all seven by torchlight, changing a few words. He felt a small knot in his stomach, but mostly relief. He slept at midnight.
He got nine out of ten.
Two weeks later, the unit test had the same kind of questions. Pradeep stared at the paper. He recognised the questions but not the steps. He had written them, but never done them.
He scored eleven out of thirty. Sarika scored twenty-seven.

What was Pradeep's phone battery at?
His phone battery was at twelve percent.
What was Pradeep feeling as he copied by torchlight?
Pradeep felt a small knot of guilt in his stomach, but mostly relief at escaping the deadline.
What went wrong, and what could Pradeep have done instead?
Copying got the marks but not the skill, so the test showed the gap; he could have done fewer questions honestly or asked the teacher for more time.
How might Sarika feel if she learned her answers were copied?
Sarika might feel uneasy, since Sarika meant to help people who were stuck, not to have her work copied whole.
