In the office canteen, Dilnaz pushes her lunch box away. 'Six months married, and I haven't had one cup of morning tea in peace,' she tells Vaibhav from accounts. 'Up at five for the family breakfast, home by six for dinner. My mother-in-law says the last bahu gave up her job, so why can't I cut my hours?'
'Do you want to?'
'No. I miss my mother's kitchen, my own routine, everything. But I love this work.'
Her phone buzzes. A message from her husband, Zaid: 'Talked to Ammi. From Monday I cook dinner three nights, so you don't have to rush. And she wants to hear what you think, on Sunday.'
Dilnaz reads it twice and lets out a long breath.

By what time does Dilnaz have to be home for dinner?
By six.
What is Dilnaz feeling as she pushes her lunch box away?
She feels worn out and homesick, missing her mother's kitchen and her own routine, and worried about being pushed to cut her work hours.
What in Zaid's message could help Dilnaz settle in, and why?
He is taking on three dinners and his mother wants to hear Dilnaz's view on Sunday, which shares the work fairly and gives her a voice.
How might Dilnaz's mother-in-law see things differently after listening on Sunday?
She may realise the job matters deeply to Dilnaz and that what the last bahu did need not be the rule, which could ease the tension.

Mahima, you're talking to that chatbot again at midnight? Come, sit with your Sumit Chacha a minute. When I was twelve, we moved to Nagpur, and I didn't know a single boy in my new school. Every night I typed to a chat program on Papa's computer. It never got bored and never said "not now". It was comforting, I won't lie. But one evening my mother found me crying at the screen, because it had answered "I understand" to everything, even when I wrote that I missed my old friends. She sat down and asked what was wrong, and I told her. That weekend she took me to the colony's table-tennis club. I made one friend there, Irfan. One real friend changed everything. So talk to the bot if you like, but tell me how you are really feeling, okay?

Which city did young Sumit's family move to?
Nagpur.
Why did young Sumit type to the chat program every night?
He felt lonely at the new school, and the program was comforting because it never got bored.
What was the turning point in Chacha's story?
Telling his mother how he felt, which led her to take him to the table-tennis club, where he made a real friend.
How might Sumit's mother have felt when she found him crying at the screen?
She was probably worried and sad to see him so lonely, so she sat down and listened.

At 3 am the nurses' break room at the city hospital was quiet except for the humming fridge. Dilnaz stirred her tea for far too long.
'My navjote was the proudest day of my parents' lives,' she said. 'Now I read about Zarathustra and the fire temple and I don't know if I believe any of it. Or if I just love my grandmother.'
Zeenat's prayer mat was folded in her locker; she had prayed Fajr at the end of night shifts for years. She could have said, try what works for me. She didn't.
'What are you reading?' she asked instead.
Dilnaz showed her. They talked it through, Zeenat asking questions, not giving answers, until a monitor alarm down the ward called them back.
'Thanks for not trying to fix me,' Dilnaz said, rinsing her cup.
'You're not broken,' Zeenat said. 'You're thinking.'

What does Zeenat keep folded in her locker?
Zeenat keeps her prayer mat folded in her locker.
What doubt is Dilnaz feeling when she mentions her grandmother?
Dilnaz is unsure whether she truly believes or whether her attachment is mostly love for her grandmother.
What does Zeenat do that makes Dilnaz feel accompanied?
She asks about the reading and poses questions without offering her own path as the answer, so Dilnaz can think aloud safely.
How does Dilnaz experience Zeenat's listening?
Dilnaz feels grateful and understood, thanking Zeenat for not trying to fix her.

Under a dim streetlight after the power cut, the officer raised a torch. "Stop. Where are you going at this hour?" Jaya's heart pounded and the tuition bag felt heavy. The legs wanted to run; Jaya kept them still and took both hands out of the pockets, open and visible. "Good evening, sir. I'm Jaya, coming home from tuition. My house is two lanes ahead." "Bag?" Jaya opened it: notebooks. "May I call my mother? And am I free to go after?" Officer Gautam nodded. "Call. Then I'll walk you to the corner, the lane is dark." Jaya's phone was at five percent, just enough for Mamma's voice, shaky but steady.

Where was Jaya coming home from?
Jaya was coming home from tuition.
What was Jaya feeling when stopped, and what did Jaya do about the urge to run?
Jaya felt scared, with a pounding heart, and kept the legs still and hands visible instead of running.
What helped keep this stop calm?
A polite greeting, giving a name, visible hands, asking if free to go and calling Mamma.
How might Officer Gautam see a teenager on a dark lane at night?
As someone to check briefly and keep safe; offering to walk Jaya to the corner because the lane is dark shows concern.

Mohit: made the pasta?
Afreen: yes! sending a photo

Mohit: sana used to make it with fresh basil. hers was amazing

Read this:

For weeks my whole routine was: sleep till noon, scroll, lie there, repeat. I told myself it was just a phase and that if I waited long enough I'd wake up feeling normal. Some days I skipped meals because getting up felt like too much work.

The strange part is that the phone kept my hands busy while my mind went quieter and quieter. The bed got heavier, the curtains stayed closed, and messages piled up. Nobody noticed for about a month because I answered with a thumbs-up and said I was busy.

When Vasudha came over and found me still in yesterday's clothes at four in the afternoon, she sat on the floor and asked me one question: 'What's been going on?' That was the first time I said it out loud. Jatin

What time was it when Vasudha found Jatin in yesterday's clothes?
It was four in the afternoon.
What might Jatin have been feeling while telling everyone 'I'm busy' from bed?
Jatin was probably low and withdrawn, wanting the mood to lift by itself and not wanting to worry anyone.
What could Jatin have tried in the first week instead of waiting, and why?
Jatin could have told someone or asked a counsellor for help, because sleep and scrolling did nothing to change the low mood and only delayed support.
How might Vasudha have felt when she saw Jatin that afternoon?
Vasudha was probably worried and gentle, choosing to sit on the floor and ask an open question instead of lecturing.

metadata.subtype: Approach: wait for it to pass through sleeping and scrolling [Pitfall]

Read this:

Divyansh texts his friend Mohit during a lunch break.

Divyansh: He made me redo the whole sheet at 9pm again. Called me useless in front of the client.
Mohit: bro just quit
Divyansh: Can't. Papa's medicines and my sister's fees run on my salary. It's not weakness, it's just the maths right now.
Mohit: True. Sorry. So what do you do?
Divyansh: Stay, but not swallow it whole. I keep a note on my phone with dates. I eat lunch away from my desk and switch off at eight even if he pings. Two applications every Sunday.
Mohit: That's an actual plan.
Divyansh: I keep hearing "everyone gets shouted at, it's normal". It's not normal, Mohit. It's just where I am for now.
Mohit: Agreed. This Sunday I'll help with your CV.

How many applications does Divyansh send every Sunday?
Divyansh sends two applications every Sunday.
How does Divyansh feel about staying in the job?
Divyansh feels stuck but clear-eyed: quitting is not possible because Papa's medicines and the sister's fees run on the salary, and Divyansh refuses to think of the shouting as normal.
How is Divyansh protecting his dignity and health while staying?
He keeps dated notes, eats lunch away from his desk, switches off at eight and sends two applications every Sunday, so he is planning a way out.
How does Mohit's view change during the chat?
Mohit first says to just quit, then accepts the money constraint, calls it an actual plan and offers to help with the CV. 🤍

Read this:

Beside the canal in Amsterdam, Noa pointed at the black water. "I bet you will not jump in." Gabriel looked at the cold water and the slippery stone edge. No way. But he did not want to lose the game either. "Jumping is boring," he said. "Let us see who lasts longest in a plank, right here on the pavement. Loser carries the winner's bag." Noa grinned. Four of them dropped to their elbows on the warm stones while their teacher, walking behind, raised a thumb. Gabriel's arms shook at forty seconds; Noa collapsed at fifty, laughing so hard that a woman with a pram smiled as she passed. The canal stayed quiet and nobody was wet.

What did Gabriel suggest instead of jumping?
He suggested a contest to see who could hold a plank longest on the pavement.
What was Gabriel feeling as he looked at the water?
Wary, since he thought "no way" but did not want to lose the game either.
What other safe challenge could the group try?
A race along the pavement or a balancing contest on flat ground, because it keeps the competition without the danger.
How might Noa feel when the contest replaced the jump?
Amused and glad to be included, since Noa grinned and collapsed laughing.

Read this:

“Devika, it's so hot. Come under the fan,” Mumma called. It was mid-May, the cooler humming.
“I'm drawing.”
“Who is it for? For Nani?”
“It's for nobody.”
“Nobody?” Sharmila laughed. “Then why so many colours?”
“Because.” Devika pressed hard with the orange. “It's a mango tree. Now it has a swing. Now a parrot.”
Later: “Mumma, the parrot has a baby.”
Later still: “Now it's raining on the mango tree.”
Almost an hour later, Devika sat back. “Finished.”
“Can I put it on the fridge? 😊”
Devika shrugged and ran off to the cooler. The drawing stayed on the floor.

What did Devika draw first?
She drew a mango tree, and then added a swing and a parrot.
What does Devika's shrug about the fridge suggest?
It suggests she felt happy and finished already; she enjoyed drawing for itself and didn't care about showing it.
How could Sharmila support this kind of play?
By letting Devika draw as long as she wants and not turning it into a gift or display each time.
How does Sharmila seem to see the drawing compared with Devika?
Sharmila thinks of an audience, like Nani or the fridge, while Devika is interested only in the fun of making it.

Read this:

I was at Faiz's place that evening to finish our geography chart, so I saw most of it, though I can't say what either of them was really feeling. After the shouting at dinner, Faiz had shut himself in his room, and I was sitting on his floor with the chart paper. About an hour later there was a knock. Wasim Uncle stood in the doorway, not coming in. He said, "I was scared and I said it badly. Can we talk about what you want and what worries me?" Faiz didn't answer at first. Wasim Uncle just waited. Then Faiz said, "The concert's on Saturday. Everyone's going." Wasim Uncle nodded, asked who was driving and where it was, and didn't say no. I rolled up the chart and said I'd finish it at home. When I left, they were both sitting on the bed. I'm Yash, just the friend who happened to be there.

Why was Yash at Faiz's place that evening?
To finish their geography chart.
How did Yash seem to feel on the floor when the knock came?
Yash seems awkward and a little uneasy at being caught in a family moment, and tactful enough to leave so they could talk.
Why did Wasim Uncle's knock work as a turning point?
He admitted his fear and his harsh words first, then asked to hear what Faiz wanted, which invited talk instead of another fight.
What might Faiz have felt when Wasim Uncle apologised at the door?
Faiz may have felt surprised and wary at first, hence the silence, then relieved enough to explain about the concert.

Read this:

Amandeep stepped onto the balcony of his Pune flat at eleven, lit a cigarette and felt his shoulders drop for the first time since the audit call. The traffic below hummed. For a few minutes the knot in his chest loosened. By one in the morning it was back, tighter, and he went out for another. Then another. Next morning his flatmate Rajni counted the stubs in the saucer and raised an eyebrow. "Rough week?" she asked. Amandeep looked at the saucer too. Four months ago it had been one on Fridays. Now the calm lasted less and the jitters came sooner. That evening, when the worry rose again, he left the packet in a drawer, walked two rounds of the colony with Rajni and told her about the audit. He also booked a chat with the company counsellor for Monday.

Where did Amandeep go to smoke at eleven?
He stepped onto the balcony of his Pune flat.
What did Amandeep feel when he looked at the saucer of stubs?
He felt uneasy, even a little alarmed, because he could see the calm was lasting less while the jitters came sooner than four months ago.
What turning point in the evening helped Amandeep, and why?
Leaving the packet in a drawer, walking with Rajni and booking the counsellor gave him other supports for the worry, before the habit grew stronger.
How might Rajni feel seeing the stubs pile up?
Rajni probably felt concerned but did not want to lecture, so she asked a gentle question and later joined him on the walk.

Read this:

Nanny's note, Sunday.

Sudha's parents started arguing loudly in the kitchen. Sudha, two, froze, covered her ears and began crying.

I picked her up. Lokesh saw her and lowered his voice. "Not in front of her," he said, and they went out to the balcony to talk.

Afterwards Lokesh knelt by Sudha. "Papa and Mama were loud. You're safe." She clung to him, then calmed.

Where did Sudha's parents go to talk?
They went out to the balcony.
Why did Sudha cover her ears and cry?
Sudha felt frightened by the shouting, sensing danger she couldn't understand.
What did Lokesh do right once he saw Sudha?
He lowered his voice, moved the argument away and reassured Sudha afterwards.
How might the nanny feel during the argument?
The nanny likely feels concerned for Sudha and focused on comforting her.

Read this:

Mahima refreshed the trading screen behind the counter of her uncle's hardware shop. Last week a tip had turned a small stake into three thousand. The thrill had hummed in her fingers all day, so the next stake was bigger. Then came a loss. Then a bigger stake "to get it back".

Sharmila, a friend from school who had come in for a packet of screws, noticed the phone tucked under the counter. "You've been on that since I arrived."

"It's just a small thing."

"Bigger bets after every win, and after every loss too?"

Mahima opened her mouth, then closed it. That was exactly what she had been doing.

That evening she wrote a limit in her notebook and moved the rest of her money back to her savings account, keeping some aside for emergencies. "Boring," she told Sharmila the next day. "But I can sleep."

How much had the small stake turned into last week?
The small stake had turned into three thousand.
How did Mahima feel when Sharmila described the pattern, and what shows it?
Mahima seemed caught out and uneasy: she opened her mouth, then closed it, because that was exactly what she had been doing.
What could Mahima do to avoid repeating the pattern?
Keep the written limit, leave the rest in the savings account with some aside for emergencies, and talk to a qualified adviser if the urge returns.
How does Sharmila see Mahima's trading?
Sharmila notices the phone tucked under the counter and the pattern of ever-bigger bets, and raises it plainly but without a lecture.

Read this:

Nazia, you asked about my garden. I'm Madhav. For three years, I hand-built a watering system on our terrace: bamboo pipes, clay pots, a timer I soldered myself.
I loved it. But half the plants died every summer because the timer failed.
Last month I finally asked myself: if I were starting fresh today, would I build this, or buy a simple drip kit? Honestly? I'd buy the kit.
It was hard. I felt like I was throwing away three years. But I kept the bamboo pipes for the jasmine by the door, where they work fine, and I kept my soldered timer in a drawer.
This summer, nothing died. And I'm still proud of the bamboo.

What did Madhav build on the terrace?
Madhav hand-built a watering system on the terrace.
What did Madhav feel when deciding to buy the drip kit?
Madhav felt torn and sad, as if throwing away three years, but clear about the choice.
How did Madhav honour the effort while choosing the better option?
Madhav kept the bamboo pipes for the jasmine and saved the timer, while using the drip kit for the rest.
How might Nazia see Madhav's decision?
Nazia might see it as wise and a little brave, since Madhav chose what works without dismissing the work.

Read this:

Hafsa,
I've been thinking about Saturday, and I want to say sorry properly, not in a text.
When you came to dinner, you were quiet and kept checking your phone. I thought you were bored with me, and I got sulky and made that comment about "better things to do". I didn't ask what was wrong.
Your sister's call later made it clear: your grandmother was in hospital, and you were waiting for news. You came anyway, because you'd promised.
I read your mood as being about me. Next time I see you go quiet like that, I'll ask, "Is something going on?" before I decide what it means.
How is your grandmother today? If you want, I can come with you to the hospital on Sunday, or I can just bring food and stay out of the way.
Shankar

Why was Hafsa checking the phone at dinner?
Hafsa's grandmother was in hospital, and Hafsa was waiting for news.
How did Shankar feel during the dinner, and how does Shankar see that now?
Shankar felt hurt and sulky, thinking Hafsa was bored, and now feels sorry for misreading Hafsa.
What will Shankar do differently next time, and why does it help?
Shankar will ask "Is something going on?" before deciding what a quiet mood means, because it stops Shankar making Hafsa's feelings about Shankar.
How might Hafsa feel reading this letter?
Hafsa would likely feel understood and cared for, and relieved that Shankar sees what was really happening.

Read this:

On the bus home in Stockholm, Ingrid was telling Rafael about her future again. "I'm going to be a surgeon. Heart surgery, like in that documentary. I'll work in a big hospital, maybe travel to places that need doctors." Rafael nodded. "Cool. So what are you doing for it this month?" Ingrid opened her mouth. "Well... I mean, I'll study." "Study what, though? You said you hate chemistry." "I'll get to it." She looked out of the window. Her biology test was in two weeks. She hadn't opened the chapter. The dream felt so bright and so far away that there was nothing to do about it today.

What kind of surgeon does Ingrid want to be?
A heart surgeon, like in that documentary.
Why did Ingrid feel there was nothing to do about her dream today?
Ingrid felt excited about the dream but lost about how to start, since it was so bright and far away that it pointed to no action now.
What nearer step could Ingrid set for this month?
She could study the biology chapter a little each day before the test in two weeks, and ask a teacher for help with chemistry.
Why might Rafael ask about this month rather than the dream?
Rafael seems to sense the dream has no path yet, and gently asks the question that could turn it into a first step.

Read this:

Mangoes were costly that week, so Maa bought just one and kept it on the shelf for Tanvir, who was home with a cough. While Maa was at the tap, Bidisha, six, took a bite. Then another. Soon only half was left. She looked at the sticky seed, and her stomach felt tight. When Tanvir called for his mango, Bidisha went and stood beside Maa. "I ate half of Tanvir's," she said, eyes wet. "I knew it was his." She pushed her own biscuit across to her brother.

Why did Maa buy only one mango?
Mangoes were costly that week.
What does Bidisha's tight stomach suggest?
She knew she had done something wrong by eating her brother's mango and felt sorry about it.
How could Maa respond in a way that helps Bidisha learn?
Thank her for telling the truth, say clearly that eating it was not okay, and let her make it up to Tanvir, as she has started to.
What might Tanvir think when Bidisha pushes her biscuit across?
He may still be disappointed, but he can see she is sorry and trying to make it up to him. 🙏

Read this:

Daycare note, Friday. During today's fire alarm test, Avni screamed and clung to me. When another staff member tried to take her so I could help the others, she arched away, screaming harder. I kept her, held her close and took her into the quiet room until she calmed. For the next test we will warn her first, hold her before it starts and cover her ears. Maria, daycare teacher

What happened today at daycare?
A fire alarm test.
What was Avni feeling when she arched away from the other staff member?
She was frightened and overwhelmed, and needed the person she was already clinging to.
What is the plan for the next alarm test?
To warn her first, hold her before it starts and cover her ears.
How might Avni's parents feel reading the note?
They might feel worried about her fright but reassured by the calm care and the plan.

Read this:

Pradeep's phone had rung four times since breakfast: the same 'wealth manager' from a firm he'd never heard of, each time with a new product that 'closes Friday'. By lunch he couldn't think.
In the noisy hostel mess, Bidisha pushed a paper napkin at him. 'Stop deciding each one. Decide once.'
So he wrote a policy on the napkin, half shouting over the clatter of steel plates. 'One: ₹1,000 a month, on the 5th, no more for now. Two: only regulated products, the plain kind that hold lots of companies. Three: if anyone promises a fixed high return, I say no without discussing it.'
'And the calls?'
'Rule four: I never buy anything on a phone call.'
The fifth call came during dessert. Pradeep listened for ten seconds, heard 'guaranteed twenty percent', said, 'Not for me, thank you,' and hung up. He felt oddly light. The napkin went into his wallet.

How much did Pradeep decide to put in each month?
₹1,000 a month, on the 5th.
How did Pradeep feel after hanging up on the fifth call?
Oddly light and relieved, because the rules made the decision before the pressure could.
What else could Pradeep add to the napkin policy?
When to review the amount, and a trusted adult or registered adviser to ask before changing any rule.
How does the situation look to Bidisha?
Bidisha sees Pradeep worn out by the calls and offers a simple fix: decide once instead of every time.

Read this:

'Harish is crying, Joseph. His truck broke.'
Joseph looked at his own red truck, then toddled over and pushed it into Harish's hands. He patted Harish's head. 'There. There.'
'That's kind, kanna,' said Amma. 'Can you bring me the spoon?'
Joseph fetched it, beaming.
Later Amma saw him watching Harish zoom the red truck, his thumb in his mouth.
'Joseph, did you want to keep your truck?'
Joseph's chin wobbled. 'Mine. Also.'
'Then after lunch it comes back to you.'

What did Joseph give Harish?
His red truck.
What does Joseph's thumb in his mouth, watching Harish, suggest?
He may be feeling a little sad and missing his truck, a want he didn't say out loud.
Why was Amma's question a good idea?
It let Joseph say he wanted his truck too, so his kindness didn't hide his own wish, and a turn after lunch made it fair.
How might Harish feel when Joseph pats his head?
Harish probably feels comforted, getting a truck and a pat just when his own toy broke.

Read this:

The school's anonymous confession page was all anyone talked about in the hostel. Late one night, Amandeep, sixteen, sat with three friends in the common room as someone posted about Deepika from class eleven: that she'd cried during the debate finals. The comments piled up, hundreds of them. "Drama queen." "Fake tears." Amandeep had never spoken to Deepika. Without a name on his account, it felt like a game. He typed "cry baby" and laughed with the others. But next morning, in the dining hall, Deepika sat alone, eyes swollen, not eating. Amandeep couldn't swallow his paratha. The warden announced that the page had been reported and that the school counsellor was meeting everyone involved that day. Amandeep felt caught. He knew what he'd written, even if no one else did.

What did Amandeep type?
He typed "cry baby".
Why did Amandeep's comment feel like a game at the time?
Without a name on his account and with everyone commenting, Amandeep felt hidden, detached and amused, so the cruelty felt less his own.
What could Amandeep do to take responsibility?
Amandeep could go to the counsellor himself, admit what he wrote and apologise to Deepika, instead of hiding behind the anonymous page.
How did Deepika experience the pile-on?
Deepika felt crushed and isolated, sitting alone with swollen eyes after hundreds of cruel comments.

Read this:

Dear Ganga,
I need to tell someone who won't judge me. You know the card app I started playing in April, just for fun? I've lost about thirty thousand rupees. It started small. Then I had a bad week, and I kept thinking, after this many losses a win is due; the app can't keep beating me. So I played more, and bigger, to catch the win when it came. It never came the way I thought.
Last night I sat on the hostel stairs until 3 a.m. and realised the cards don't know I've been losing. Each hand is new.
This morning I told Didi everything. She's coming on Saturday, and we have an appointment with the college counsellor on Monday. I've deleted the app.
Can you call me tonight? I don't want to be alone with this.
Nandini

How much has Nandini lost?
About thirty thousand rupees.
Why did Nandini keep playing bigger after losing?
Nandini felt sure a win was due after so many losses and was desperate to catch it, so bigger bets felt like the way back.
What steps has Nandini taken, and why are they wise?
Telling Didi, booking the college counsellor, deleting the app and asking Ganga to call, so the problem is shared with people who can help.
How might Ganga feel reading this letter?
Ganga would probably feel worried but glad Nandini reached out, and want to call that night.
I caught cold after getting wet in the rain. Do I need an article?

I caught a cold after getting wet in the rain.
Why: "Catch a cold" is the usual modern phrase, where "a cold" is a countable illness. "Caught cold" is older and less common.

Read this:

Chetan, listen, it's me, Saurabh, and you'll laugh. Yesterday's match against B section. Last over, eight to win, everyone shouting from the boundary. I hit it to cover and just ran. Didn't look, didn't call, just ran, because everyone was screaming "RUN!" Run out by a mile. Lost the match. I was so angry at myself I kicked my own kit bag. Papa just said, "That's my boy, fast feet, no brain." But here's the strange part. Last night at home I sat with the maths problem set, the probability one, and took forty minutes on one question. Drew a table, checked each case, got it right. Calm as anything. Same brain! When the whole ground is yelling, my head goes fast and hot. Alone at the desk, it goes slow and careful. So next match, before each ball, I'm going to take one breath and look at the fielder. Just one breath.

How many runs did Saurabh's team need in the last over?
Eight to win.
Why did Saurabh run without looking?
Everyone was shouting "RUN!" and the moment was tense, so excitement and the crowd pushed him into a snap decision.
What plan did Saurabh make for the next match, and why might it help?
Taking one breath and looking at the fielder before each ball, which gives his slower thinking a moment to join in.
How might Chetan see the way Saurabh tells this story?
Chetan might find it funny but also be impressed that Saurabh noticed the difference between his hot and calm moments.

Read this:

Tuesday. In the team meeting Disha joked about Mehak's typo in the client deck: "Well, at least the client now knows we can't spell their name." Everyone laughed, Mehak too, though her smile was tight and she closed her laptop.
Thursday. Disha noticed Mehak had stopped chatting at lunch. She said, "I made that joke about your typo and I think it landed badly. I'm sorry. Did it?" Mehak took a moment. "A bit. I was already worried about it."
The following Wednesday. In the meeting Disha joked about her own late-night snacks, and Mehak laughed properly. Later Mehak said, "Thanks for asking."

What did Disha joke about in the team meeting?
Mehak's typo in the client deck.
What was Mehak feeling when she laughed with a tight smile?
Probably embarrassed and worried about her typo, though laughing along may also have been an effort to fit in.
What did Disha do that repaired things?
She noticed the change, apologised and asked directly, then moved to jokes about herself.
How might Disha have felt on noticing Mehak had stopped chatting at lunch?
Disha probably felt uneasy and a little guilty, sensing the typo joke had landed badly, which is why she apologised and asked.

Turn this dialogue into reported speech. "She" is Aditi.

"I do not know," Kishore admitted.
"Neither do I, it seems." She flipped her notes back. "I skipped collisions. Give me twenty minutes, and then let's try again."

Kishore admitted that he did not know. Aditi said that it seemed she did not know either. She flipped back through her notes and said that she had skipped collisions. She asked for twenty minutes, and then they would try again.

Read this:

"Mummy! Pallavi is being MEAN! She's so angry at me!" "Pallavi, are you angry?" "No, I'm sad. Uday took my crayons." "I'm just holding them!" "Uday, whose crayons are in your hand?" "...Hers. But she's angry." "Your face looks very cross, beta. Your fists are tight. Mine get tight when I'm angry too." Uday looked down at his fists. Then, very slowly, he held out two crayons. "Only the red and blue." Pallavi sniffed. "Thank you." Uday stamped off to the sofa, still frowning.

What did Uday hold out to Pallavi?
Only the red and blue crayons.
Why did Uday keep saying Pallavi was the angry one?
He had grabbed the crayons and felt angry himself, but owning that felt too bad, so he pushed the angry feeling onto her.
What did Mummy do that helped Uday notice his own feeling?
She pointed out his cross face and tight fists and said her own fists get tight when she's angry, without shaming him.
How might Pallavi feel being called mean and angry when she felt sad?
Pallavi might feel confused and hurt, since her crayons were taken and then she was blamed for being angry.

At the crowded fair on Sunday, Hemant, two, screamed and arched away from the loudspeakers. Raghav snapped, "Stop it, everyone is looking!" and Hemant screamed harder. On Wednesday Raghav picked him up at the same noise, stepped into a quiet lane, and held him until he stilled. On the next Saturday Raghav stayed near the fair's edge, away from the speakers, and Hemant watched the crowd with his head against his father's shoulder.

What did Raghav do on Wednesday when Hemant got upset?
He picked him up, stepped into a quiet lane and held him until he stilled.
What might Hemant have been feeling on Sunday, and what else could have made him scream harder?
He was probably frightened by the loud noise. He may also have been more upset by his father's sharp voice.
What did Raghav learn that helped?
He read the trigger, the loudspeakers, and planned a quieter spot instead of scolding.
How might Raghav have felt on Sunday?
He may have felt embarrassed and stressed by the crowd looking, which is why he snapped. 🙂

Read this:

Vinita had two versions of herself, and until Saturday they had never met. At tuition she was the girl who nearly made the state swimming team, which was true of one trial, once. At school she was the one who wrote songs and might start a band. Then Mridul from tuition turned up at Pallavi's birthday, in the same small flat, with the power out and everyone crammed around candles. "So, champion, when's the next meet?" he said loudly. Pallavi frowned. "Swimming? You said you hate chlorine." Vinita's cheeks burned in the candlelight. Both stories had felt true when she told them. She took a breath. "I tried swimming once, seriously. I hated the chlorine. And the songs are only in my notebook so far." Mridul grinned. "Honestly, both sound cooler than my hobbies." The lights came back on.

Whose birthday party was it?
It was Pallavi's birthday.
How did Vinita feel when her two stories collided?
She felt embarrassed and exposed, her cheeks burning, because both versions had felt true when she told them.
What helped Vinita get through the moment?
She told the plain version of both stories, one real trial and songs still in a notebook, instead of adding another exaggeration 🙂
How did Mridul react to the honest version?
He took it lightly and warmly, saying both sounded cooler than his own hobbies.

Read this:

Before Sachin's birthday party in Delhi, Tenzin sat on his bed and made a short list on his phone. He had heard some of the older cousins would bring vapes, and that Sachin's cousin Rocky drove everyone home, usually too fast. Tenzin didn't want to decide those things with music blaring and people watching. So: not trying anything, even once. Not riding with Rocky. Home in Papa's car at eleven, already arranged. Reading it back, he felt calmer. At the party a vape went round the balcony, and someone held it out to him. "Nah, I'm good," Tenzin said, and went back inside for cake. At eleven, Rocky jingled his keys. "Who's coming?" Tenzin shook his head. His father's car was already waiting downstairs.

How was Tenzin getting home?
In Papa's car at eleven, already arranged.
How did Tenzin feel after reading his list back?
He felt calmer, knowing the hard choices were already made.
Why decide limits before the party?
With music and people watching it is hard to think clearly; a rule decided earlier lets Tenzin refuse quickly without debate.
How might Sachin see Tenzin's choices at the party?
Sachin may barely notice, or may respect that Tenzin quietly said no without spoiling the celebration.

metadata.subtype: Approach: deciding values and limits in advance [Thinking]

messages.content: Why should you read a story twice if you did not understand it at first?
The second reading often shows what you missed. Because you now know how it ends, so the earlier clues make sense and the details fall into place.

Read this:

Saturday, 10 pm.

Dad moved out today. His bags were by the door at nine and the car left before lunch. Mum kept saying "we're all fine" in a bright voice. I said I was fine too. I wasn't. I went to the bathroom, turned on the tap and cried until my head ached.

Still set my alarm. Still did homework. It helps to have things that stay the same.

Told Vandana at lunch. She didn't say anything smart, just sat next to me on the steps and let me cry a bit more. She's going to come over tomorrow.

I keep thinking of our old Sundays. I miss a family that turns out not to have been there. It's my loss too.

Payal

What time were Dad's bags by the door?
His bags were by the door at nine.
What was Payal feeling when saying "fine" and then going to the bathroom to cry?
Payal was grieving and sad, and said "fine" to match Mum's bright voice.
What did Payal do that helps with coping?
Payal cried instead of holding it in, kept the alarm and homework routine, and told Vandana about it.
What might Vandana have been thinking as she sat on the steps without saying anything?
Perhaps that there were no right words and that staying close mattered more than advice, so she simply sat with Payal and let the crying happen. 🤍

"But I did mind you, Pip," he returned with tender simplicity. "When I offered to your sister to keep company, and to be asked in church at such times as she was willing and ready to come to the forge, I said to her, 'And bring the poor little child. God bless the poor little child,' I said to your sister, 'there's room for him at the forge!'"

Answer from the text. What did Joe say when he offered to keep company with Pip's sister?
Joe says he asked her to bring the poor little child, asked God to bless the child, and said there was room at the forge for the child.

In Moga, everyone in Vinita's college group knew she read the business pages and had won the commerce olympiad in Class 12. So when Gurpreet and four others pooled their Diwali money, they came to her house with a steel box. 'You understand markets. Invest it for us. Just double it by next Diwali,' Gurpreet said, laughing, but the others were serious. Vinita felt flattered, and then heavy, as if the box weighed a hundred kilos. She pictured losing it, and five friendships with it. She pushed the box back gently. 'I read about markets. That's not the same as knowing. I can't take your money or promise anything back.' Gurpreet looked disappointed. 'You're the only one who knows this stuff.' 'Then let's all go to the bank's free investor session on Saturday. We can learn it together, instead of me guessing with your money.' Three of them came.

Where did Gurpreet and the others bring the money?
They brought it to Vinita's house in a steel box.
What did Vinita feel when asked to invest the money?
Vinita felt flattered and then burdened, as if the box weighed a hundred kilos.
What made Vinita's reply wise?
She was honest about her limits, refused to take their money or promise returns, and suggested learning together at the bank's session.
How does Gurpreet see Vinita's refusal?
Gurpreet is disappointed, seeing Vinita as the only one who knows this stuff.

Thursday night, hostel

Ammi is in hospital for tests. Indu Apa called at lunch and said not to panic, but her voice was shaky. I sat through the whole statistics lecture and heard nothing.
I keep thinking: I'm here, eating canteen rajma, and Apa is sleeping on a hospital chair. What kind of daughter does that make me?
At nine I called Apa again and just said it. She laughed tiredly and said, "You're not a bad daughter, Sabina. You're a far one. Help me from there."
So we split things. I'll call Ammi every evening so she's not bored, and I'll handle the hospital's online appointment system. Apa will do the visits. I've booked a bus home for Saturday week.
Still scared. But less useless.

What will Sabina handle for the hospital?
Sabina will handle the hospital's online appointment system.
How was Sabina feeling during the statistics lecture?
She felt so anxious about Ammi that she heard nothing, and guilty for being away while Apa slept on a hospital chair.
Which choice helped Sabina most, and why?
Telling Apa honestly how she felt, which led to splitting tasks, so Sabina could help from a distance.
How does Indu Apa see Sabina's distance?
Apa sees Sabina as far away, not bad, and welcomes her help from where she is.

Friday: Bhupen couldn't stop grinning about the college fest concert. His cousin Aditi had got passes for them both.
Saturday night: The band was halfway through the second song when someone near the gate shouted, "Fire!" Nobody saw smoke. But the crowd surged, and Bhupen's heart slammed. He pushed too, elbowing a smaller boy, dragging Aditi by the wrist, not thinking at all. Near the fence a volunteer with a torch yelled, "It's the smoke machine! Walk slowly!" The crowd slowed. Bhupen's legs shook.
Sunday: At breakfast he told Aditi, "I shoved a kid. I've never shoved anyone." She nodded. "Everyone was pushing. It got into you." He decided that next time he'd find the exits before the music started.

What did the volunteer with a torch shout?
It's the smoke machine! Walk slowly!
What was Bhupen feeling at breakfast on Sunday?
He felt ashamed and shaken, surprised that the crowd's fear had made him shove a smaller boy.
What did Bhupen decide for next time, and why is it sensible?
To find the exits before the music starts, so he has a calm plan ready if panic spreads.
How does Aditi make sense of what Bhupen did?
She sees that everyone was pushing and the fear "got into" him, so she doesn't judge him harshly.

Thirty minutes, Rehana. That's how long the group discussion round lasted, and for the first ten I didn't open my mouth. Twelve of us around a table for a campus placement. I had one good point about rural banking, and I kept thinking, Jyoti, what if your English slips? What if I say something wrong? They'll talk about it in the hostel corridor for a month.
Then a boy across the table said "less people" instead of "fewer people", and you know what? Nobody blinked. I only noticed because I was hunting for mistakes.
So I spoke. My voice shook on the first sentence. I think I made one small slip.
That evening I asked my roommate, who was in the same group, what she remembered about me. She said, "You made the rural banking point. It was good." That's all.

How many people sat around the table in the group discussion?
Twelve of us sat around the table.
What was Jyoti afraid of during the first ten minutes?
Jyoti feared a small English slip would be talked about in the hostel corridor for a month, so staying silent felt safer.
What turning point pushed Jyoti to finally speak?
Seeing a boy's "less people" slip go completely unnoticed showed Jyoti that small mistakes don't hold the room's attention. 👍
Why might the roommate remember the rural banking point but not the slip?
The roommate was following the discussion and thinking about her own turn, so a useful idea stood out while a tiny slip slid past.

I'm Vikas. On Monday, Sir told Class 5 we couldn't use the big playground at break any more. Everyone groaned. Siddharth stood up. I thought he'd shout, like he does at cricket. Instead he said, “Sir, that feels unfair. Class 6 still uses it. Can you tell us why?” Sir didn't get angry. “Fair question. They're digging for the new water tank near the swings, and your break is when the trucks come in. Class 6 has break after the trucks leave.” Siddharth thought. “Then can we have the small ground instead?” “Yes. That I can do.” The big playground stayed a no. I don't know what Siddharth felt, but he sat down calm.

What was being dug near the swings?
They were digging for the new water tank near the swings.
What was Siddharth likely feeling when he stood up?
Siddharth was likely frustrated and felt the rule was unfair, since Class 6 still used the playground.
How did Siddharth object in a way that worked?
He said calmly that it felt unfair, asked for the reason, then suggested an alternative, the small ground.
How did Sir respond to being questioned?
Sir called it a fair question, explained the safety reason about the trucks and agreed to the small ground while keeping the no.

The community hall smelled of incense and warm rice. Disha sat between her cousin Mehak and a row of relatives, her feet not reaching the floor. Everyone had come for the prayers after Nana's death. An older cousin began to sing, and one by one the others joined in, low and slow. Disha didn't know all the words but she hummed along. Her throat felt tight, but she wasn't alone in it. Afterwards, plates of khichdi and sweet rice were passed down the row, and Mehak put an extra spoon of sweet rice on hers without a word. Disha leaned her head on Mehak's arm. Around them, people were crying and smiling at the same time.

What food was passed down the row after the prayers?
Plates of khichdi and sweet rice.
What did Disha feel while humming along with the songs?
A tight throat of sadness, but also comfort at belonging; she wasn't alone in it.
How could the rituals help a family carry sorrow together, according to this scene?
The shared songs, the food and being seated together let each person grieve in company, whatever they believe.
What might Mehak be trying to say by adding an extra spoon of sweet rice?
That she cares for Disha and wants to comfort her without needing words. 🙂

The day-care in Hyderabad was full of paper lanterns for Eid. Madhuri, five, didn't look at them. She sat on the mat in the corner holding her mother's hairclip, the one with the blue flower, which she had taken from the dressing table that morning. Every few minutes she looked at the door. Noor, her friend, brought her a lantern to colour. Madhuri took the crayon but didn't colour. She was very quiet. The teacher sat down and said, 'That's a pretty clip.' 'Ammi's,' Madhuri whispered. 'Ammi will come after lunch,' the teacher said. Madhuri held the clip tighter and put her head on the teacher's shoulder.

What did Madhuri hold from home?
Her mother's hairclip with the blue flower.
What was Madhuri feeling as she kept looking at the door?
She held Ammi's hairclip, kept looking at the door, and was very quiet, which suggests a quiet ache of longing.
What did the teacher do that helped?
The teacher noticed the clip, spoke gently about it, told Madhuri when Ammi would come and let her rest on a shoulder.
How might Noor feel when Madhuri doesn't colour the lantern?
Noor may feel puzzled or a little sad, wanting to cheer up a quiet friend.

In Dr Joseph's waiting room, Swati's father sat with his arms folded, eyes on the door. "I told you, I'm fine," Siddharth muttered. "If anyone from our building sees me here, they'll say the old man has gone soft in the head." For three months he hadn't gone on his morning walk and had barely touched dinner. Swati had tried once already, and he'd said only weak people talk to psychologists. So today she had put it differently. "Papa, Dr Joseph has looked after you since your knee operation. We're here because you're not sleeping. Sleep is health, same as your knee." He grunted. When his name was called, Swati stood too, then sat back down. "Do you want me in there, or would you like to talk to her alone?" Siddharth hesitated. "Alone," he said, and straightened his collar before going in.

What hadn't Siddharth done for three months?
Gone on his morning walk.
What was Siddharth worried about in the waiting room?
That someone from the building would see him and say he had gone soft in the head.
Which choice by Swati protected her father's dignity?
She asked whether he wanted her in the room or to talk to Dr Joseph alone, and let him decide.
What might Siddharth's straightening his collar suggest about how he felt going in?
It suggests he wanted to walk in with self-respect, feeling that the choice was his own.

By the third night of her sister Jyoti's wedding in Bhilwara, Uma's feet were blistered and her smile felt glued on. One aunty had already said her lehenga was 'too simple for the bride's sister'. Another counted the sweets on the thali and sniffed. Uma had run between the caterer, the mehendi and Dadi's medicines since dawn. Then, during the pheras, she stood close enough to see Jyoti's hands shaking in Rakesh's, and heard Jyoti laugh nervously at the fourth round. Uma's eyes filled. Her big sister, who had shared her bed for twenty years, was stepping into a new life. The aunties could say what they liked. Uma stopped watching them and watched Jyoti.

Where was Jyoti's wedding?
In Bhilwara.
What was Uma feeling during the pheras?
Uma felt moved and a little sad, eyes filling as she saw her sister step into a new life, forgetting the aunties' comments.
What helped Uma get through the exhausting wedding?
Shifting her attention from the relatives' judgements to the real meaning of the ceremony, her sister's new stage of life.
How might Jyoti have felt during the pheras?
Jyoti seemed nervous and emotional, her hands shaking and her laugh uneasy as she began a new life.

In English: "Where have you been all these days?" Or, more simply, "Where have you been for so long?"

"No, Shreya Didi. That's the whole point. I'm deciding what it's allowed to do."
"Allowed?"

"It can check my maths steps after I finish. Not before."

Why the Non-Cooperation Movement was called off.

Shankar feels confident and a little proud, having worked out a rule first and then found it fits the school's policy.

Shreya starts off suspicious that the AI is writing the project, but ends up approving and suggesting a sticky note to keep the rule in view.

First Sunday. Karthik went to his first residents' association meeting because the lift had been broken for three weeks. Two retired men did all the talking; everyone else stared at their phones. When Yamini from 3B tried to speak about the lift, the treasurer said, "Next agenda," and she sat down.
Second Sunday. Karthik came early, with Yamini and three others from the upper floors. He had printed the association's own by-laws. "Sir, clause 6 says any member can add an agenda item in writing. Here is ours: the lift, with quotes from two repair firms." The room went quiet. The treasurer frowned, then read the paper.
Fourth Sunday. The lift was working. At the meeting, Karthik noticed three people who had never spoken before raise their hands. The chairman now kept a list of speakers on the whiteboard.

Which clause did Karthik point to?
Clause 6, which says any member can add an agenda item in writing.
What might Karthik have felt at the first meeting when Yamini was cut off?
Karthik probably felt frustrated and uneasy at how two men dominated and a neighbour was silenced.
Which of Karthik's steps changed how the meetings worked?
Showing up with neighbours, bringing the written by-laws, and adding a clear agenda item with repair quotes.
How might Yamini have felt at the second meeting?
Yamini probably felt supported and less alone, since her lift concern was finally heard with others backing her.
My dog barks at every visitor and it's embarrassing.
Barking at visitors is natural for many dogs, because they guard the home. It can be improved with patient training.
How do I begin?
Teach a calm command like 'sit' or 'quiet', and reward the dog with a treat when it follows. Practise when no visitors are there, then with a family member acting as a visitor.
How long will it take?
It differs from dog to dog. Some learn in a few weeks, others in months. Short daily practice works better than long sessions.
Should I shout at the dog?
No. Shouting can make the dog more excited or fearful. Keep your voice calm and your praise warm when it behaves.
Is a trainer worth it?
A trainer can help if progress is slow or the barking looks like fear or anger. Ask a local vet clinic or animal shelter for trainers they trust.
Does "turn down" have more than one meaning?

Yes. "Turn down" can mean to lower the sound or heat. It can also mean to say no to an offer or request.
Examples: Please turn down the music; the baby is sleeping. Hana turned down the job because it was too far away.

You asked how the new school is going. Honestly? It's over. On Monday I tried to sit with the group from the basketball team at lunch, and one of them said, 'Seat's taken,' and they all laughed. One of them said, 'Seat's taken,' and they all laughed.

I was halfway through my 300-piece jungle puzzle on the floor when Mummy called me to help clean the fans. I'm Yamini.
All through the cleaning, I kept thinking about the tiger's missing ear. Shankar asked me to pass the duster twice and I didn't hear him. I finished the curtains, then the shelves, and I don't even remember doing them.
The moment Mummy said, "Done!" I ran back to the puzzle. I found the tiger's ear in five minutes.
Funny thing: I've finished lots of puzzles and can't remember any of them. But this one I couldn't stop thinking about, just because it wasn't done.

How many pieces was Yamini's puzzle?
It was a 300-piece jungle puzzle.
Why didn't Yamini hear Shankar ask for the duster?
Yamini felt restless and distracted, still thinking about the unfinished puzzle.
What could help Yamini focus on cleaning next time?
Yamini could stop the puzzle at a clear point, or note the next piece to find, so it doesn't keep nagging.
How might Shankar feel when Yamini doesn't hear?

Pooja had been avoiding her tax-filing paperwork for three weeks. Every evening in her Mumbai flat she'd look at the folder, feel a hot wave of guilt, call herself useless, and turn on the TV.
Her friend Kavitha, visiting, watched this happen twice. The second time, she said, “What if, instead of shouting at yourself, you just said, ‘Okay, I delayed. That's human.’ And then did five minutes?”
Pooja laughed bitterly. “Five minutes won't finish it.”
“It's not supposed to. It's supposed to start.”
That evening, Pooja said the sentence out loud, feeling silly. Then she set a timer for five minutes and opened the folder. She found the first form. Filled in her name, address, PAN.
The timer rang. She kept going for another half hour. The guilt was still there, but quieter.

How long had Pooja been avoiding the paperwork?
She had been avoiding it for three weeks.
How did Pooja feel each evening before Kavitha's suggestion?
She felt a hot wave of guilt and called herself useless, which pushed her to avoid the folder.
Why did the kind sentence and five-minute timer work?
Forgiving the delay eased the guilt that fed avoidance, and five minutes made starting small enough to do.
How does Kavitha see Pooja's delay?
Kavitha sees it as normal and human, and seems patient and caring rather than judging.

Vaibhav had always told the group he lived 'near the mall'. In truth, his family's one-room home was behind it, above his father's ironing stall, where Papa pressed clothes for the whole lane from seven in the morning. On Sunday, Siddharth turned up unannounced to return a charger. Vaibhav saw him from the stall and wanted the ground to swallow him. His stomach twisted; he almost pretended not to know Papa. 'Uncle, this is the fastest ironing I've ever seen,' Siddharth said, watching Papa fold a shirt in three sharp moves. Papa laughed and pressed Siddharth's crumpled collar for free. Upstairs, Siddharth ate two parathas and asked if Vaibhav could teach him to fold like that. Later, alone, Vaibhav thought about the kids at school who had taught him to feel small. Papa's hands had paid for his school, his books, even that charger.

What does Vaibhav's father do?
He runs an ironing stall, pressing clothes for the whole lane from seven in the morning.
What was Vaibhav feeling when he saw Siddharth from the stall?
He felt deeply ashamed and panicked, his stomach twisting, wanting the ground to swallow him.
What could Vaibhav do differently next time friends visit?
Give his real address and introduce Papa with pride, trusting that friends like Siddharth care about him, not the house.
How does Siddharth see Vaibhav's home and Papa's work?
He sees skill and warmth, admiring Papa's fast ironing and enjoying the parathas 😊
Write a goodnight for a small child in one sentence with the word "moon", ending on the word "dreams".
Goodnight, little one, the moon is watching over your dreams.

Kunal, five, made a sock puppet rabbit talk on the sofa in the flat. "Rabbit is sad because his friend went away." Samir Uncle, at the other end of the sofa, sat lower. "Rabbit, what happened with your friend?" "He didn't share the swing. Rabbit stood alone." "That sounds lonely. What does Rabbit want?" "A friend who says, come play." Samir just nodded, and Kunal's rabbit hopped onto his lap.

Why did Kunal say Rabbit was sad?
Because his friend went away.
What might Kunal be feeling as he talks through the rabbit?
Perhaps lonely or left out, but we cannot be sure the story is about him. The puppet may simply be a safe way to say it.
How did Samir handle the story wisely?
He asked the rabbit questions and did not press Kunal to say it was about him.
How might Samir feel as he listens to Rabbit's story?
Samir seems caring and calm, sitting lower, asking what happened and saying it sounds lonely.

Worried about the whispering in your class, Uma? Let your old Elizabeth Aunty tell you about my Class 4, long ago. A story went round that little Sophia's father was in prison. It wasn't true, and she stopped eating her lunch. I didn't shout, and I didn't say her name. I asked the class, "Has anyone ever said something untrue about you? How did it feel?" Hands went up, one by one. Then I said, "Words can hurt like a push. If you hear a story about someone, bring it to me." At lunch I told Sophia quietly, "You can talk to me or to Mrs Rao any time." She came that same afternoon. The next week a boy stood up and said calmly, "That story is false." Nobody laughed at him.

What story went round about Sophia?
A story went round that Sophia's father was in prison.
How was Sophia feeling when she stopped eating her lunch?
She was probably hurt and ashamed by the false story, too upset to eat.
What choice did Elizabeth make with the class, and why did it help?
She talked about how words hurt without naming Sophia, so nobody was shamed, and gave the children and Sophia a trusted adult to go to.
What might the boy have felt when he stood up and said, 'That story is false'?
He may have felt nervous but brave, and then steadier when nobody laughed at him for saying the truth calmly.

Dear Sumit,
I owe you an apology for the science exhibition.
When our model collapsed an hour before judging, you were trying to fix it and I just sat there saying "It's only an exhibition, bro, chill." You thought I didn't care. I did. That's the problem.
I had spent three weeks on the wiring. When it fell, I felt so stupid that pretending not to care was easier than admitting I was gutted. So I acted bored and left you to do everything.
I'm sorry. You deserved a partner, not a shrug.
Can we fix it together this weekend and enter the district round? I'll bring the soldering iron and actual effort this time.
Jatin

How many weeks had Jatin spent on the wiring?
Three weeks.
What was Jatin really feeling when the model collapsed?
Jatin felt gutted and stupid, and hid it behind acting bored.
How did the letter help, and what else could Jatin do?
It admitted the truth and apologised; Jatin can follow through by showing up this weekend with the soldering iron.
What was it like for Sumit to see Jatin shrug before judging?
Sumit likely felt alone and frustrated, fixing the model while thinking the partner didn't care.

Preschool note, Holi week. Hansa, class teacher.
On Tuesday a water balloon flew over the wall and burst on our window. Jeevan was nearest. I was flustered and asked him, "Was it a big boy in a red cap?" He nodded slowly. By lunchtime he was telling everyone about "the red-cap boy". Today, describing it to his mother, he added a feather to the cap.
Our guard, who saw the whole thing, says it was two girls from the lane, no caps at all. My question put the cap there.
From now on I will ask children only "What did you see?" and write down their first words.

What burst on the window?
A water balloon.
How does Jeevan seem to feel about the red-cap boy now?
He seems sure and excited about the memory, not knowing the cap came from the teacher's question.
What will Hansa do differently, and why?
Ask only "What did you see?" and note the first words, so questions don't plant details.
What might Jeevan's mother think on hearing about the feather?
She may believe the vivid detail, not knowing the teacher's question had seeded it.
Why do old photographs fade when they are left in the sunlight?
Strong light bleaches the colours in photographs. Because the energy in sunlight slowly damages the dyes that make the picture, the colours become paler year after year.

Childminder's note, Thursday. Divyansh spent a long time with our old cat today, patting her very gently and kissing the top of her head. At pick-up, I opened my arms for a goodbye hug, and he turned away and ran to his Papa. I just waved instead. He waved back from Papa's shoulder. He's very loving, and he's learning he can choose. What did Divyansh do with the cat?
He patted her very gently and kissed the top of her head.
What might Divyansh have been feeling when he turned away from the hug?
He probably wanted his Papa at that moment and felt ready to go, not unfriendly; his wave back shows he still felt warm toward Eshaan.
What did Eshaan's choice to wave instead teach Divyansh?
That he can say no to a hug and still stay friends.
How might Divyansh's Papa feel reading this note?
He would likely feel pleased that Divyansh is affectionate and that his choice was respected.
Write a railway announcement in exactly two sentences that uses the word "platform".
The express to Chennai will arrive shortly at platform four. Please stand behind the yellow line.

Supervisor's note, legal firm.
Payal, a first-year associate, came to me today. A senior, Sabina, had asked her to backdate a document for a client. Payal said, "I'm scared to lose this job. But I think this is wrong."
She's right. I told her backdating documents can be fraud and she should never do it, whoever asks.
I also told her she did the right thing by coming to me and not just refusing silently. I spoke to Sabina and to the partners the same day.
Payal looked relieved but shaky. I told her the firm would protect her. I'll check in with her next week. — Mr Varghese

What did Sabina ask Payal to do?
Backdate a document for a client.
What was Payal feeling when she came to the supervisor?
Payal felt scared of losing her job but sure the request was wrong.
What did Mr Varghese do that supported Payal?
He confirmed it was wrong, praised her for coming to him, spoke to Sabina and the partners that day, and promised protection.
How might Sabina feel when the supervisor speaks to her?
Sabina likely feels embarrassed and defensive, realising the request has been taken seriously.

The interview I think about most was for the museum internship in Kolkata, last spring. I'm Devika, and I used to answer everything instantly, as if silence meant I was stupid. Sabina, my senior who'd done the internship before, told me: "Take a second. They want to see you think." When the panel asked what I would change about their children's gallery, I felt the urge to blurt something. Instead I paused, looked at the table, then answered. My answer was calmer than anything I'd have blurted. But then something strange happened. After I finished, the head curator said nothing for a long time. I thought I'd failed. Later Sabina explained that the head curator always leaves a long silence so people can add more if they wish; to the curator it is respect, not pressure. I hadn't known silence could mean that.

Where was the museum internship?
In Kolkata.
What was Devika feeling during the head curator's long silence?
Devika felt anxious and sure of having failed, reading the silence as pressure, though it was meant as respect.
What small step helped Devika give a better answer?
Pausing briefly to think before answering, as Sabina advised, instead of blurting.
How did the head curator see the long silence?
As a respectful space for the candidate to add more if they wished, not as pressure.

Bidisha, you say your sister and you can't agree who keeps Nani's old sewing machine. Sit. I'm Nazia, and when I was twenty-five my brother and I fought over our late father's shop. He wanted to sell, I wanted to keep it going. We stopped speaking for a week. Then I said, "What if we keep it open for six months, and if it doesn't pay its own rent, I agree to sell? And if we do sell, you pick the buyer." He thought, then said, "Six months." He hadn't lost and neither had I. In the end the shop stayed open a year. Even after it closed, we were never strangers.

How long did Nazia propose keeping the shop open?
Six months.
What did Nazia want when making the offer?
Nazia wanted to keep the shop going but also to keep the brother's respect; giving him the choice of buyer shows Nazia thought of his dignity. 🙂
What could Bidisha propose to the sister?
A trial period, like one of them keeping the machine for six months and then swapping, with each naming what they are giving up.
How might Nazia's brother have felt about the offer?
He may have felt heard and not beaten, since he agreed to "Six months" and also got the choice of buyer.

Put this account briefly: three sentences.

People always ask me on this show what saved the bakery. Honestly? My friend Sunaina. I'm Nandini, and two years ago I was sure everyone loved my cakes. My family said so, my cousins said so. Orders were slow, but I told myself it was the location. So one night I called Sunaina, who had worked in a restaurant kitchen for years, and said, "Please tell me what I'm not seeing. Don't be nice." She was quiet for a bit, then said, "Your cakes are lovely. But your prices change every week, and you reply to customers after two days. People think you're not serious." That stung for a whole evening. But she was right. I fixed the price list and started answering messages the same day. Orders doubled by Diwali.

Nandini says a friend, Sunaina, saved the bakery. Sunaina, who worked in a restaurant kitchen, said the cakes were lovely but prices changed every week and replies took two days. Nandini fixed both, and orders doubled by Diwali.
Meaning of 'third wheel'? My friends call me that when I go out with them and their girlfriend.
A "third wheel" is a person who is with a couple and feels a little extra or left out. Example: "I didn't want to be the third wheel, so I stayed home." Your friends probably say it as a joke.

In Keerthana's Chennai school, some teachers joked that girls from the hostel "don't have the head for physics". Keerthana, fifteen, lived in the hostel.
In class practice, she solved every circuit problem. Her lab partner Manoj copied her method.
But on the unit test, she felt the teacher's eyes on her. Her heart raced. She doubted her first answer, crossed it out and wrote a wrong one. She rushed the last section.
Her marks were low. The teacher nodded as if expecting it.
Manoj looked at her paper and frowned. "You crossed out the right answer. You taught me this."
Keerthana's throat tightened. "I know. I just couldn't stop thinking they were waiting for me to fail."

What did Manoj copy from Keerthana?
He copied her method for circuit problems.
Why did Keerthana cross out the right answer?
She felt anxious and watched, doubting herself because she believed the teacher expected her to fail.
How could the school reduce this kind of pressure on hostel girls?
Stop the jokes about ability, frame tests as a way to grow, and look at practice work, not just test marks.
How does Manoj see Keerthana's test result?
Manoj is puzzled and concerned, knowing she taught him the method she crossed out.

"If you eat enough carrots, you can see in the dark," Saurabh announced at the colony park. "Everyone knows." He had heard it from Anu on the swings, from two boys in his school van, and from a cousin at a wedding. It had come round so many times that it sat in his head next to "seven days in a week". Chetan, who was eleven, frowned. "Who told you first?" "Everyone." "Which book?" Saurabh opened his mouth and shut it again. That evening he ate four carrots, switched off his room light and stood very still. He could not see his cupboard. Then he sat on the bed, thinking about all the voices that had said it, and how none of them had ever tried.

How many carrots did Saurabh eat that evening?
Four carrots.
What was Saurabh thinking about as he sat on the bed?
All the voices that had repeated the carrot claim and how none of them had tried it, so he was beginning to doubt a "fact" that had felt certain 🤔
What turning point led Saurabh to test the carrot fact?
Chetan asking "Who told you first?" and "Which book?" Saurabh could not name a source, which pushed him to try it himself.
How might Chetan see Saurabh's announcement at the park?
Chetan seems doubtful and wants to know where the idea came from, rather than believing it just because Saurabh says everyone knows.

Manjula: how did the meeting with your co-founder go?
Devika: we're closing the app 😔
Manjula: oh no. after 18 months??
Devika: yeah. I asked myself, if I'd never started, would I start this today with what we know now? answer was no
Manjula: that's brave. are you ok?
Devika: sad. I cried in the auto home. but not ashamed
Devika: we learned so much. user interviews, fundraising, what not to build
Manjula: and the money?
Devika: gone either way. staying won't bring it back, it'd just burn more
Manjula: proud of you, sis 🤍 dinner friday? my treat
Devika: yes please

How long had Devika worked on the app?
Devika had worked on the app for 18 months.
How does Devika feel about closing the app?
Devika feels sad and cried on the way home, but is not ashamed, because the decision was made honestly from where things stand now.
What reasoning helped Devika decide, and why is it sound?
Devika asked whether the app was worth starting today with what the team knows now, and saw that the money is gone either way; staying would only burn more.
What does Manjula's dinner invitation show about how Manjula sees the decision?
It shows Manjula sees the decision as brave and wants to support a friend through a loss, not treat it as a failure.

Check my English: "The flowers smells sweet."
Is my brother awake now?
I don't understand "fulfill". Can you help?
What does "cut corners" mean?
Why do shops hold sales before a festival?

1. Corrected: The flowers smell sweet. Why: "flowers" is plural, so the verb has no "-s".
2. I can't check that, since I can't see your home. Go and look, or call out his name softly.
3. Fulfill is a verb that means to carry out a promise or to achieve a wish.
4. It means to do a job quickly and cheaply by skipping important steps. For example: do not cut corners when you build the model.
5. They give discounts. Because many people are about to shop, and a lower price helps a shop win more customers.

Leila's phone buzzed during dinner, and the class group chat was full of laughing faces under a photo of her mid-sneeze, mouth wide open. Her cheeks burned. She typed "not funny!!" and deleted it, then typed something meaner and deleted that too. Her thumbs shook. Instead she took a screenshot and put the phone face down. Her older sister Elif saw her pushing peas around the plate. "What happened?" Elif asked. Leila showed her. Elif did not laugh. "Thank you for showing me. Tomorrow we take this to your teacher, and we keep the screenshot." Leila breathed out slowly. It still hurt, but it was no longer only hers to carry.

What did Leila do with the photo instead of replying?
She took a screenshot and put the phone face down.
Why did Leila type messages and then delete them?
She was hurt and angry and part of her wanted to snap back, but she seemed to sense that an angry reply would not help.
What would you advise Leila to do with the screenshot?
She should keep it safe and show it to her teacher with Elif's help, rather than answering the group in anger.
How might Elif feel on seeing the photo?
Elif was probably upset for her sister but stayed calm, since she did not laugh, thanked Leila for showing her and planned to go to the teacher.

'Asif, why aren't you eating your sheer khurma? It's Eid!'
'I don't want it, Tanvir Bhai.'
'You love it.'
'I feel funny.'
'Funny how? Sick?'
'No. Just... funny.' Asif rubbed his chest. 'Here. It's heavy.'
'Since when?'
'Since Abbu said we're moving to Pune.'
Tanvir sat down next to him. 'Heavy in the chest. Maybe that's sad? Or scared?'
Asif shrugged. 'I don't know. Both? I don't know what it's called.'
'That's okay. It's a big thing. You don't need the perfect word.'
'Can it be heavy-sad?'
'Heavy-sad is a good word,' Tanvir said.
Asif took a small spoon of sheer khurma.

Where is Asif's family moving?
To Pune.
What was Asif feeling that he found hard to name?
Asif felt sad and scared about moving, feeling it as a heavy weight in the chest.
How did Tanvir Bhai help Asif?
He asked where it was felt, offered possible words and let Asif make up 'heavy-sad' without pressure.
How might Tanvir feel hearing Asif describe the heaviness?
Tanvir probably felt tender and protective towards his little brother.

In the village near Karnal, Nilesh, eight, found a box of matches on the kitchen shelf. He took it behind the cowshed, where the hay was stacked, and struck one to see the flame. He struck another and dropped it on a few loose straws. They caught at once. His older brother Ujjwal, fifteen, came round the corner, saw the smoke and stamped out the straw, then poured a bucket of water over it. Nilesh stood frozen. "I only wanted to see," he whispered. Ujjwal took the matches and called their father. That evening, Papa put the matchbox on a high shelf and made a rule: no fire without a grown-up, ever.

Where was the hay stacked?
Behind the cowshed.
What was Nilesh feeling when he whispered "I only wanted to see"?
He felt frightened and shocked, not having imagined that the straw would catch so quickly.
What protective steps did the family take?
Ujjwal put out the fire and called their father, who put the matches out of reach and set a clear rule: no fire without a grown-up.
How might Ujjwal have felt when he saw the smoke?
Ujjwal was probably alarmed and scared for his brother, acting fast to put out the fire.

"Omkar, why do you hate Chandrika now?"
"Because of how it ended. She shouted at me in the canteen in front of everyone."
"You were friends for three years."
"Yes, and that last fight ruined everything."
"What about the time she sat with you in the hospital when your dad had surgery?"
"...That was nice."
"And when she helped you with your whole second-year project?"
"Fine. That too."
"And the road trip to Lonavala?"
"The best weekend of my life."
"So three years of that, and one bad week at the end?"
"It felt like the real her."
"Or it felt big because it was last."
"...Maybe. I still think about the canteen fight every day."
"Think about the hospital for a day. See what changes."

Where did Chandrika shout at Omkar?
In the canteen in front of everyone.
Why does Omkar say he hates Chandrika now?
Omkar feels hurt and angry about how it ended, and the canteen fight at the end overshadows three years of friendship.
What does the friend suggest Omkar try, and why?
Thinking about the hospital visit for a day, so the good memories get as much weight as the angry ending.
How might Chandrika remember the friendship?
Chandrika might also remember the fight most sharply, even though she stayed with Omkar in hospital and helped with Omkar's project.

At the government school in Satna, every day at lunch, three older boys took Abhinav's tiffin and ate his parathas. They laughed while he stood there.
Farida, eleven, saw it for the third day. The others watched and giggled. Farida didn't.
“That's bullying,” she whispered to her friend.
She walked straight to the headmaster's room. “Sir, three boys take Abhinav's food every day.”
The headmaster came to the ground that same lunch. He spoke to the boys and sent a note to their parents. He asked Abhinav to eat near the staffroom that week and thanked Farida quietly.
Abhinav sat next to Farida the next day.

What did the older boys take from Abhinav?
His tiffin, and they ate his parathas.
How did Farida feel watching the boys laugh at Abhinav?
She felt upset and uncomfortable, refusing to giggle along.
Why was going to the headmaster the right step?
It got an adult with authority to stop the bullying the same day.
How might Abhinav feel the next day, sitting next to Farida?
He probably feels safer and grateful that someone stood up for him.

You asked me to tell the group about last term, so here goes. I'm Asif. There's a girl in our class, Arohi, who is really quiet. For months, me and two friends made remarks about her. Her old bag. Her hair oil smell. "Arohi, did you bathe in coconut?" Every day. When anyone said it was mean, I said, "It's banter, yaar. Everyone jokes like that." I really believed it. Then one day, Arohi told our class teacher. Sir called the three of us in during the last period, the same day. He didn't shout. He showed us a note Arohi had written: "I don't want to come to school any more." I remember my face going cold. Banter is when everyone's laughing. Arohi never laughed. I had just never looked at her face long enough to notice. We apologised to her that week. I still feel bad about it.

What did Arohi's note say?
"I don't want to come to school any more."
Why did Asif keep calling the remarks banter?
The word made the teasing feel normal and harmless, so Asif didn't have to feel guilty or see how Arohi was hurting.
Which of the class teacher's choices helped most, and why?
He acted the same day, stayed calm, and showed the three students Arohi's own words so they could see the real effect.
What was it like for Arohi during those months?
Arohi felt hurt and humiliated every day, enough to not want to come to school at all.

In Leeds, the school bus came at eight, and every weekday Emeka's stomach ached by half past seven. A boy from Year 7 kept taking his hat and shoving him against the window. Emeka told no one. He felt stupid for being scared.
On Saturday at football, coach Anders noticed him sitting out. "You look miles away, Emeka."
Emeka stared at his boots, then said it all.
Anders sat beside him. "Being scared makes sense. It's your body telling you something's wrong." He helped Emeka write down what had happened and when. Then he phoned Emeka's mum from the clubhouse, and she said she'd speak to the head teacher first thing Monday.

What time did the school bus come?
At eight.
Why had Emeka told no one about the Year 7 boy?
He felt ashamed and stupid for being scared, so he hid the fear.
What did Anders do well when Emeka spoke up?
He listened, told Emeka the fear made sense, helped him write down what happened, and phoned Emeka's mum that same afternoon.
How might Emeka's mum feel when Anders calls?
She may feel worried and protective, and relieved to know, since she plans to go to the head teacher straight away.
Two sentences on the Moon, please. The first must start with "The" and the second with "It".
The Moon travels around the Earth. It shines because it reflects sunlight.
What does "set off" mean in a travel plan?

"Set off" means to start a journey. It can also mean to cause something to start, such as an alarm.
Examples: We set off for Ooty at five in the morning. The smoke from the toast set off the alarm.

Hi Ayesha,

Ammi says you're struggling to start homework in Class 9, so here's something I've been doing since the summer. Don't laugh.

I made a playlist of my favourite songs, the good ones, and I only play them while doing homework. Not on the bus, not while gaming. So when it's homework time there's actually something I want. It made starting so much easier 😊. Diagrams, maps, copying notes, all fine.

But I found out the hard way it doesn't work for everything. Last week I did physics numericals with the songs on and got half of them wrong, silly mistakes, because I was humming instead of thinking. Now I do the playlist for the easy stuff and total quiet for problems.

Try it and tell me what you'd put on yours.

Your cousin, Jeevan

Where does Jeevan refuse to play the homework playlist?
Not on the bus and not while gaming.
How did Jeevan feel after getting half the physics numericals wrong?
Jeevan sounds embarrassed and a bit annoyed at the silly mistakes, realising the humming had pulled attention away from thinking.
What would you advise Ayesha if Ayesha copies Jeevan's idea?
Keep a few favourite songs only for homework to help start, but switch to silence for anything that needs careful thinking, like sums or reading.
How might Ayesha feel getting this letter from a cousin?
Ayesha might feel relieved that someone older also struggles to start, and curious to make a playlist too.
