Rain had soaked Nagpur since morning, and the sole of Hrithik's left shoe had started to flap. New shoes would have to wait until his father's pay came at the end of the month.
On the walk to tuition, every squelch felt like an announcement. Hrithik was sure the girls at the bus stop were laughing at his feet. Nobody in the history of Class 9 had ever been this embarrassed, he decided.
At tuition he tucked both feet under the bench. Pankaj, sitting beside him, leaned over. "Yours too?" He lifted his own foot: a strip of tape wound round the toe. Across the room, the new boy from Wardha had plastic bags inside his sandals against the wet.
Hrithik looked at the three pairs of feet and, for the first time that day, laughed.

What did Pankaj have round the toe of his shoe?
A strip of tape.
Why was Hrithik sure the girls at the bus stop were laughing at his feet?
Ashamed of the flapping sole, Hrithik felt as if every eye was on him, so any laughter nearby seemed to be about his shoe 😰
What turning point eased Hrithik's embarrassment?
Seeing Pankaj's taped shoe and the plastic bags in the new boy's sandals showed him he wasn't the only one.
Why might Pankaj have chosen to show his own taped shoe?
Pankaj may have noticed Hrithik hiding his feet and wanted him to know it happens to others too, easing the shame without a speech.

In their village above Gangtok, Pema, ten, sat on the steps with the phone pressed to her ear. Mola, her grandmother in town, had been talking for half an hour. Pema had told her about school, the new goat, and the rain. Now her tea was cold and her homework was waiting. But every time Mola paused, Pema said "Mm" and Mola started a new story. Her brother Ojas watched from the doorway. When Mola paused again, Ojas whispered, "Say: 'Okay Mola, I have to do homework now. I'll call on Sunday. Love you!'" Pema hesitated, then said it. Mola laughed. "Of course, go study! Sunday, then." Pema hung up, surprised. "She didn't mind at all!" Ojas grinned. "She just needed a signal."

How long had Mola been talking?
Half an hour.
How did Pema feel as the call went on?
Pema felt stuck and a bit restless, with cold tea and homework waiting, unsure how to end the call.
What made Ojas's suggested closing work?
It gave a clear signal, a reason, a plan to call again and a warm 'Love you', so Mola didn't feel cut off.
How did Mola feel when Pema ended the call?
Mola didn't mind at all, laughing and agreeing to talk on Sunday.

At the drinking tap today, Tarun noticed a Class 7 boy shouting at a younger boy, fists clenched, face red. Tarun didn't join in or argue. He walked to the group of children near the bench and then came straight to me.
"Sir, that boy looks like he'll hit someone," he said quickly.
I went at once. The older boy stopped shouting when I arrived. I sent the younger boy to class with a friend and spoke to the older boy in my room.
Later I called Tarun and told him he did the right thing: moving away, staying with others, and telling an adult.
I will inform both families this evening.
- Ujjwal Sir

Where did Tarun go before telling the teacher?
To the group of children near the bench.
What might Tarun have been feeling when he said the boy looked like he'd hit someone?
Tarun probably felt anxious and worried for the younger boy, sensing danger from the shouting and clenched fists.
What steps did Ujjwal Sir take after Tarun told him?
He went at once, stopped the older boy, sent the younger boy with a friend, spoke to the older boy, praised Tarun, and planned to inform both families that evening.
How might the younger boy have felt when the teacher arrived?
He probably felt relieved and safer, knowing an adult had stepped in.

Four months into her job at the digital agency, Kavitha found a spreadsheet on her desk from her manager: fifty five-star reviews to post for a new restaurant client, each from a "different customer." "Use the spare accounts," he said, and left for a meeting. Kavitha stared at the screen. Her salary covered her younger brother's college fees; she could not afford to lose this job. She walked to the pantry, where Maria from the content team was making tea. "If I say no, am I finished here?" Maria listened, then said, "I refused something like this last year. They moved me to another account. I wasn't fired." Kavitha went back, wrote a short message to her manager offering to plan a real review drive with customer feedback cards instead, and hit send before she could delete it. Her hands were cold.

How many reviews did the manager want posted?
He wanted fifty five-star reviews posted.
What was Kavitha feeling as she sent the message?
She felt scared and torn, because the job paid her brother's college fees, yet she chose honesty; her cold hands show the fear.
Why was Kavitha's reply a wise way to refuse?
She declined the fake reviews but offered an honest alternative, a real review drive, which keeps the client's goal without deceiving anyone.
How might Maria see Kavitha's question in the pantry?
Maria recognises the dilemma from her own experience and wants to reassure Kavitha that refusing may not cost the job.

PE department note to Class 5 teachers
For three weeks Chaitanya has been kept in during PE to finish unfinished classwork. I've noticed that on those days he is more restless, not less. He fidgets in the corridor, argues with classmates and, according to his mother, sleeps badly. On Thursday, by mistake, he came out and played football for the full period. Afterwards Vikas Sir from Class 5B told me Chaitanya finished his English worksheet quietly and even helped tidy up. I'd like to request that PE not be used as a punishment for any child. Running and play help children settle; taking them away seems to make things worse. Happy to discuss other consequences.
Mr Joseph, PE teacher

How long has Chaitanya been kept in during PE?
For three weeks.
What might Chaitanya be feeling on days he misses PE?
He seems restless and cranky, fidgeting and arguing with classmates.
What did Mr Joseph suggest instead of keeping children in?
That PE should not be used as punishment, and that other consequences be discussed.
How did Vikas Sir see Chaitanya after the football period?
Vikas Sir saw a calmer boy who finished his worksheet quietly and helped tidy up.

On Deepika's fourth day at the auto-parts firm in Chennai, visitors from the partner company in Osaka arrived for a plant tour. Deepika froze at her desk. Bow? Shake hands? Fold her hands? She watched Lavanya, the plant supervisor, who had worked with the Osaka team for years. Lavanya stood up as they entered and gave a small bow from the waist. Then the senior visitor, Mr Takeda, pressed his palms together and said "Vanakkam" with a grin, and she laughed and returned the namaste. Deepika copied the small bow, then the namaste, and it felt right. Later, in the canteen, she asked, "How deep should the bow be?" Lavanya tilted her head. "Depends on who and where. With him, a small one is fine; he's relaxed. With his boss next month, I'll go lower. I watch what they do first, then follow." Deepika wrote it in her notebook: watch, then follow.

Where were the visitors from?
The partner company in Osaka.
What was Deepika feeling as the visitors arrived?
Deepika felt unsure and nervous, not knowing whether to bow, shake hands or fold her hands, so she watched Lavanya for a lead.
What approach did Lavanya use to avoid giving offence?
She watched what the visitors did first and followed, adjusting the depth of her bow to the person and the relationship.
How might Mr Takeda have felt when Lavanya returned his namaste?
He likely felt pleased and welcomed that his attempt at a local greeting was met warmly.

Gabriel had found the flat in Lisbon online: bright, near the university, cheap. The landlord, who said he was working in Switzerland, sent photos, a scanned passport and a rental contract. Gabriel sent a deposit of four hundred euros.
Two days later the landlord wrote: "Keys are with the agency. Send one more month's rent today, or I give the flat to another student and the deposit is lost."
Gabriel sat in the university café, typing and deleting. Four hundred euros was his whole summer job.
Ingrid, from his Portuguese class, looked at the screen. "Have you seen the flat? In person?"
"No."
She was quiet. Then: "I think the four hundred is gone. Please don't send more."
He felt sick. But he took screenshots, called his bank on the number from his card, and they walked together to the police station on the corner to report it. That night he called his mother and told her everything.

How much deposit did Gabriel send?
Four hundred euros.
What was Gabriel feeling as he typed and deleted in the café?
He felt torn and panicked, desperate not to lose his summer job money but sensing something was wrong.
Why is stopping at the first loss the right choice?
Sending more rent would only grow the loss; screenshots, the bank, the police report and telling his mother give the best chance to limit harm.
What might Ingrid have felt saying the four hundred is gone?
Ingrid likely felt sorry for Gabriel and uneasy delivering hard news, but sure it would spare him more pain.

In the lobby of the government office where he worked, Naveen, twenty-six, got the call from home: his mother had collapsed in the kitchen, and his younger brother Tanvir was alone with her. Naveen felt his chest tighten. He wanted to rush home, call the family doctor, think about the hospital bills and tell his aunts, all at once. He stopped himself. "Tanvir, listen. Hang up and call 108 now. Then call me back." Tanvir did. Naveen then called the neighbour to go and sit with Tanvir. Only then did he take an auto home. By the time he reached, the ambulance was there. He called his aunts from the hospital corridor.

Who was alone with Naveen's mother?
His younger brother Tanvir was alone with her.
What was Naveen feeling when he got the call?
He felt his chest tighten with panic, wanting to do everything at once.
Which order of steps did Naveen follow, and why was it right?
He had Tanvir call 108 first, sent a neighbour to help, then went home and informed relatives later, so emergency help came first.
How might Tanvir feel alone with his mother before the ambulance came?
Tanvir was likely very frightened, but steadier with clear instructions from Naveen and a neighbour arriving.

Kavitha,
I've started this letter three times. The first two were angry.
When you said at the bus stop that I only made the state swimming team because Appa pays for the club pool and the coach, I wanted to shout. I've been in that pool at 5 am since I was nine. My shoulders ache every winter. I felt like you'd rubbed all that out in one sentence.
But then I remembered you practising in the river near your grandmother's village in the holidays, because there's no pool near you, and still reaching district level.
So here's what I think now. I did work hard. And I had a pool, a coach and someone to drive me at 5 am. Both are true. One doesn't erase the other, but I shouldn't pretend the second isn't there.
Can we talk tomorrow?
Shalini

At what time has Shalini been in the pool since age nine?
At 5 am.
Why did Shalini's first two letters come out angry?
Kavitha's remark made Shalini feel that years of 5 am practice had been rubbed out in one sentence.
What changed Shalini's mind, and what did Shalini choose to do?
Remembering Kavitha practising in the river helped Shalini see both truths, and Shalini chose to admit the advantage and ask to talk.
How might Kavitha feel reading "I had a pool, a coach and someone to drive me"?
Kavitha would likely feel heard, since the point was never that Shalini was lazy, only that the start was different.

Bessie's presence, compared with the thoughts over which I had been brooding, seemed cheerful; even though, as usual, she was somewhat cross. The fact is, after my conflict with and victory over Mrs. Reed, I was not disposed to care much for the nursemaid's transitory anger; and I was disposed to bask in her youthful lightness of heart. I just put my two arms round her and said, "Come, Bessie! don't scold."

Why does the narrator not mind Bessie's anger?

After the clash with Mrs. Reed and the victory over her, the narrator does not care much about the nursemaid's passing anger and wants to enjoy her youthful light-heartedness. Both arms go round Bessie with the words, "Come, Bessie! don't scold."

By Rail.--There is no one in charge of the box. It would have to take its chance of being delayed; and delay would be fatal, with enemies on the track. True, he might escape at night; but what would he be, if left in a strange place with no refuge that he could fly to? This is not what he intends; and he does not mean to risk it.

Keeping to the passage, why does the writer rule out sending the box by rail?

No one would be in charge of the box, so it would take its chance of being delayed, and delay would be fatal with enemies on the track. Even if the one being sent escaped at night, that one would be left in a strange place with no refuge to fly to.

Wednesday
At the bike stand after school, Thomas from Class 8 was waiting by my cycle. He was glaring, his fists were tight, and when I said "Excuse me," he shouted that I had told on his friend. His face was right near mine. My legs went like jelly. I didn't argue. I backed away and walked fast to where the Class 5 group was waiting with Mr Kurian at the gate. I told Mr Kurian everything. He stayed with me, said I had done exactly the right thing, and walked me back for my cycle. Then he phoned Mummy, and I saw him go straight into the head teacher's office. Mummy gave me an extra long hug tonight. I'm still a bit shaky.
Trisha

Where was Thomas waiting?
By Trisha's cycle at the bike stand.
What was Trisha feeling when Thomas shouted?
Trisha felt frightened, with legs like jelly, and still feels a bit shaky at night.
Which steps kept Trisha safe?
Reading the glare, tight fists and shouting as danger, moving away to a group with an adult, and telling Mr Kurian, who acted the same day.
What would change if Trisha had argued back?
The shouting could have grown into something more dangerous, with no adult close by to step in.

metadata.subtype: Hostile and furious in bullying situations [Interpreting]

messages.content: Our neighbours are very kind peoples. What is wrong?

Our neighbours are very kind people.
Why: "People" is already the plural of "person", so it takes no -s in this sense.

In Helsinki, the university business course split into project teams, and Ulla's group had to choose a leader. Mikko spoke first, fluent and confident, with slides already in his head. "I've got this." Ulla voted for him at once. He looked like a leader. Sami, who rarely spoke, had quietly finished every reading and sent the group a clear task list the night before. Ulla hadn't even opened it. Over three weeks, Mikko kept giving great speeches in meetings but missed deadlines. Sami kept doing the work, fixing the spreadsheets at midnight. At the final presentation, Mikko froze on a question about numbers. Sami answered it calmly. Walking out, Ulla felt a bit ashamed. She had picked the voice, not the work.

Who sent the group a clear task list the night before?
Sami.
Why did Ulla vote for Mikko so quickly?
Mikko's fluent, confident style matched her picture of a leader, so it felt like competence, and later she felt a bit ashamed of that choice.
What could Ulla look at next time the group picks a leader?
She could look at who actually does the work, like Sami's task list and finished readings, before being swayed by confident talk.
How might Sami have felt when the group chose Mikko?
Sami may have felt overlooked but carried on doing the work quietly.

"Varun, dinner. You've been in your room since four."
"Coming, Papa. I'm studying."
Nitin came into his son's room and looked at the desk. The maths book was open at the first page of the chapter. Beside it lay a sheet covered in writing.
"What's this?"
"Things that could go wrong in the exam." Varun didn't look up. "If the paper's long. If I get the calculus questions. If my pen stops. If I get sick. If I don't get into the science stream..."
"That's a long list."
"I need to be prepared."
"How many sums have you done?"
Varun was quiet. "None yet."
Nitin sat on the bed. "Worrying feels like work, beta. But the list isn't doing the sums. Let's pick the first three questions of the chapter. After dinner, together."

How many sums had Varun done?
None yet.
Why does Varun say "I need to be prepared" about his list?
Varun is anxious about the exam, and listing every possible problem feels responsible, as if imagining disasters is the same as getting ready for them.
What choice does Nitin suggest, and why might it help?
Doing the first three questions together after dinner, which turns the worry into a small, concrete action.
How might Nitin feel seeing the long list and no sums?
Nitin is likely concerned but calm, recognising that his son is anxious rather than lazy, and choosing to help rather than scold.

At the tea stall by the bus stop in their village, Shankar showed his cousin Lokesh a video on his phone. 'Look. They're saying the dam money was stolen by outsiders. It makes my blood boil.'
Lokesh, who taught at the block school, didn't argue about the dam. He asked, 'Who made it? Why does the music get louder there? Why does it end with "share before they delete it"?'
Shankar watched it again. It was true: the music swelled, the words came in red, the ending told him to share, not to check.
That weekend Lokesh showed him how the app picks what to show: the more you react, the more it sends. Shankar muted four angry channels. He followed the district newspaper and a farmers' radio show that interviewed people on different sides.
Next time a red-lettered video came up, he felt the heat rise and stopped. Built to make me angry, he thought. He scrolled past.

What did the video say about the dam money?
It said the dam money was stolen by outsiders.
What was Shankar thinking when he stopped at the next red-lettered video?
He recognised that the video was built to make him angry, and chose not to react.
Which steps helped Shankar break the anger loop?
Learning how feeds reward reactions, muting angry channels, following sources with more than one side, and pausing before reacting.
How might Lokesh feel seeing his cousin scroll past such videos now?
Lokesh may feel relieved and proud, having helped by asking questions rather than lecturing.

In the girls' batch at the district sports complex, Zeenat was the last one who couldn't float. On Tuesday she tried again and sank. Her coach, Jasleen ma'am, got into the water beside her. "Zeenat, your body is like a fist. Floating needs an open hand." Zeenat realised her jaw was clenched too. She took a long, slow breath, let her arms spread and her head go back until the water covered her ears. It felt strange, like lying on a wobbly bed. She felt her legs rise. The coach's hand was under her back, then it wasn't. "You're doing it yourself," said Jasleen ma'am. Zeenat didn't answer. She was too busy breathing slowly.

Where did Zeenat attend the swimming batch?
At the district sports complex.
How did Zeenat feel being the last one who couldn't float?
She probably felt embarrassed and tense, which may have made her body even stiffer.
What other approach could help Zeenat keep relaxed in the water?
She could practise slow breathing on the pool steps first, so she arrives at the float already calm.
How does floating on her own look to Jasleen ma'am?
Jasleen ma'am is pleased and encouraging, quietly telling Zeenat she is doing it herself.

In the school library, Gautam stared at the list: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The exam was tomorrow. He tried saying them again and again. The teacher, Vidya, looked up from her desk. "What would help you?" Gautam frowned, then his eyes lit up. "The first letters! M, V, E, M, J, S, U, N. Let me make a sentence. My Very Elegant Monkey Jumps Skipping Under Nets." He laughed. "A monkey with a skipping rope! Now I can see it." He wrote it in the corner of his notebook and repeated it once, then closed his eyes and recited the planets in order without a mistake.

What silly sentence did Gautam make?
Gautam made the sentence 'My Very Elegant Monkey Jumps Skipping Under Nets.'
How did Gautam feel when he made the sentence, and what did he think it would do?
Gautam felt amused and excited; he laughed at the monkey with a skipping rope and thought the funny picture would help him see and recall the planets in order.
What alternative approach could Gautam use for the planets, and why?
Gautam could draw the planets in a row or say them in rhythm as a chant. A picture or a rhythm gives another route to the order.
How might Vidya see Gautam's idea?
Vidya asked a simple question and let Gautam find the answer, so Vidya probably feels pleased to see the boy solve the problem alone.

metadata.subtype: Approach: making a funny sentence from the first letters [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Mehak, you asked for the school podcast what I learned about hugs. Okay, this is embarrassing, but here goes.
I used to hug everyone. Friends, cousins, whoever. I thought it showed I cared. Then one day, my friend Rhea stiffened when I hugged her after a match. She said, 'Please ask first. I'm not really a hugger.'
I felt awful. I thought she was angry. But she just wanted to decide for herself.
Now I ask, 'Hug?' Most people say yes. Some say, 'High-five instead.' And that's okay. No sulking, no 'Why not?'
It's her body, her choice. Same for everyone. I, Anirban, am a reformed hugger."

What did Rhea say after Anirban hugged her?
"Please ask first. I'm not really a hugger."
What was Anirban feeling when Rhea stiffened?
Anirban felt awful and worried that Rhea was angry.
What did Anirban change after that?
Anirban now asks before hugging and accepts a no without sulking or pressuring.
How might Rhea see Anirban's new habit?
Rhea would likely feel respected and more comfortable, since her choice is now asked for.

Read this:

Rafael had missed Yara's father's funeral in Valencia because of a client presentation he told himself he couldn't move. He had sent flowers. For three months Yara barely looked at him.

One evening in their Madrid kitchen, she said, "I've decided to forgive you. I'm not over it. But I forgive you."

Rafael's eyes stung. Gratitude flooded him, and with it a sense of being completely undeserving. "Thank you. I don't think I've earned it."

"You haven't. That's why it's forgiveness."

He wanted to hug her, to make it all normal again. He held back. "I won't rush you."

Over the next months he kept every family date in a shared calendar. He drove her to Valencia every month to visit her mother, and sat with them, and listened to the stories about her father. He never said "I said sorry already". Yara noticed.

Why did Rafael miss the funeral?
Rafael missed it because of a client presentation.
What was Rafael feeling when Yara said she forgave him?
Rafael felt deeply grateful and moved, and also undeserving.
How did Rafael show he understood the harm?
Rafael didn't rush Yara, kept family dates, drove her to visit her mother every month and listened, instead of demanding quick forgiveness.
How does Yara see her own forgiveness?
Yara sees it as a gift she chooses, not something Rafael earned, while she is still healing.

Read this:

I'm Tenzin. I shared a hostel room with Zubin in final year, and I saw him get serious about placements.
One night he sat with his laptop for three hours, scrolling back through his old posts, mouth moving as he read. Every few minutes he'd groan and hit delete: a party photo with someone passed out, a joke about a girl from his batch, a fight in the comments with a stranger.
Then he made a proper profile: clear photo, summary of his projects, links to his code. He asked me to pretend to be a recruiter and search his name. I found only one old thing, a comment on a cricket forum, harmless.
I can't say if he felt ashamed or just careful. But when he got his offer, he said, "The first thing they did was look me up." He wasn't smiling when he said it.

What did Zubin link on his new profile?
Links to his code.
What does Zubin groaning at old posts suggest about how he felt?
It suggests Zubin felt embarrassed and uncomfortable, seeing how the posts might look to strangers.
What would you add to Zubin's clean-up for other students?
Think about how posts affect the people in them too, like the passed-out friend, and pause before posting in future.
How might the girl in the old joke have felt if she had seen it?
She would likely have felt hurt and disrespected, which makes deleting it about more than placements.

Teacher's note, Uma, Class 4. This morning Rafiq came to me with a card he'd made himself. Yesterday his cycle chain broke on the way to school, and the bus driver, Mani Anna, stopped, put the cycle in the back and brought him in, even though Rafiq doesn't ride that bus. The card said, "Thank you for stopping. You didn't have to." Rafiq asked if he could give it himself. At dismissal he held it out with both hands. I have asked the class to think of one person who helped them on purpose this week.

What happened to Rafiq's cycle?
Its chain broke on the way to school.
What does "You didn't have to" in Rafiq's card show he understood?
He understood that Mani Anna chose to help him out of kindness, not because it was his job.
Why is Uma's class activity useful?
It helps other children notice kindness done on purpose and feel thankful for it.
How might Mani Anna feel receiving the card?
Touched and appreciated, since a driver's small kindnesses often go unthanked. 🙏

Friday

Worst day ever.

Everyone was looking at me and giggling. At lunch Meenu told me: they're saying I copied my science project from the internet.

I did NOT. My Nani helped me cut the pictures, that's all, and I wrote everything myself. But I did look at one website for the volcano picture. So it's half true and half a lie and I don't even know how to explain it.

I felt hot and small. I wanted to hide under the bench, then to shout at all of them.

After school I told Omkar bhaiya, and he took me straight to Mummy. Mummy listened to everything and said, "You are not in trouble. We'll show Ma'am your notebook tomorrow, and I'm calling her tonight."

She did. I feel a tiny bit better.

— Ritu

Who helped Ritu cut the pictures for the project?
Her Nani.
Why is Ritu so confused as well as upset?
The rumour is half true, because Ritu did look at one website for a picture, so she feels ashamed and angry but doesn't know how to explain it.
How did Omkar bhaiya and Mummy respond, and why did it help?
Omkar took Ritu straight to Mummy, who listened, said Ritu was not in trouble, and called the teacher that night, so Ritu wasn't alone.
How might Meenu have felt telling Ritu at lunch?
She may have felt awkward but wanted to warn Ritu about what people were saying.

Rafael came home from school in Seville and threw his maths test on the kitchen table. Four out of ten. "Señora Ortiz hates me," he said. "She was in a bad mood, so she marked hard." His older brother Javier, sixteen, picked up the paper. "Did you practise the fractions she gave you?" "What's the point? Last time I got six and I didn't practise either. It's luck." "Lucía got ten." "Because she sits at the front. Teachers like the front." Javier turned the page over. Every wrong answer was a fraction sum from the practice sheet, still folded in Rafael's bag, blank. Rafael didn't look. He was already switching on the TV, sure that next week would depend on Señora Ortiz's mood too.

What mark did Rafael get on the maths test?
Four out of ten.
Why does blaming Señora Ortiz's mood feel right to Rafael?
It spares him the idea that practice matters; if marks are luck or mood, a low score isn't his fault and skipping the sheet costs nothing.
What could Javier try to help Rafael see the link between preparation and marks?
Sit with him to do the blank practice sheet, point out that the wrong answers were exactly those sums, and compare next week's result.
What might Javier be thinking as he turns the page over?
Javier probably sees the pattern clearly, wrong answers matching the blank sheet, and may feel frustrated that his younger brother won't look.

messages.content: My friend said she is "under the weather". What does that mean?

"Under the weather" means feeling a little unwell or tired, not seriously ill.
Example: Nikhil felt under the weather, so he stayed home and rested.

In their Kolkata school, Anirban liked Irawati. He liked how she laughed loudly in drama class. When she walked by his desk, his hands got sweaty.
His friend Rohit said, "Just keep following her after school. She'll notice you."
Anirban shook his head. "No. That's creepy."
He knew she might not like him back, and that was okay. So he just said hi like normal, helped when she dropped her books, and didn't make it a big deal.
One day, Irawati asked him to help paint the drama club backdrop. He said yes, as a friend. It felt nice, just being friendly.

What did Rohit suggest Anirban do?
Keep following Irawati after school so she'd notice him.
How did Anirban feel when Irawati walked by his desk?
He felt nervous and excited, with sweaty hands.
Why did Anirban refuse Rohit's suggestion?
He knew following her would be creepy and disrespectful, and she had every right not to like him back.
How might Irawati feel about Anirban's behaviour?
Irawati likely feels comfortable around him, since she asks him to help paint the backdrop.

Read this:

Mohit: saw your comment on the bridge report. you're changing the load assumptions??
Lalit: yeah. the new soil survey came in. the clay behaves nothing like what we learnt
Mohit: but we've used that method for years. it's in every textbook
Lalit: I know. I defended it in the review meeting last month 😅
Lalit: then I spent the weekend with the new data. it just doesn't hold here
Mohit: so you're saying we were wrong
Lalit: I'm saying the ground changed and we have to change with it
Lalit: I still trust the maths. I just can't trust my old starting point
Mohit: the senior engineer won't like this
Lalit: I'll show him the numbers. if I'm wrong, he'll tell me
Mohit: ok. send me the file, I'll check your working
Lalit: thanks. two pairs of eyes 👍

What new information made Lalit change the load assumptions?
The new soil survey.
How does Lalit seem to feel about having defended the old method last month?
Lalit seems a bit embarrassed, but more committed to getting it right than to protecting an earlier position.
Which of Lalit's steps shows rigour, and why?
Spending the weekend testing the new data and inviting Mohit to check the working, because it grounds the change in evidence, not opinion.
How might the senior engineer see Lalit's change?
He may resist at first, since the method is long trusted, but clear numbers could persuade him.

The monsoon clouds had been black all morning, and the village fair was supposed to start at four. Sumit sat at the door in his new shirt. “It will stop. It will be the biggest fair ever!” Zeenat Phuppo looked at the sky. “We all hope it stops. But we don't know yet.” Thunder rolled. Sumit's eyes went wide. “No way. Really raining more?” Phuppo sat beside him. “If it rains, we'll go tomorrow. If it stops, we'll run.” At half past three, the rain stopped.

What time was the fair supposed to start?
At four.
What was Sumit feeling when thunder rolled and his eyes went wide?
He felt disbelief and worry that the rain might spoil his hope of going to the fair.
Which choice by Zeenat Phuppo worked, and why?
She said everyone hoped it would stop but they didn't know, and gave a plan for both cases, which helped Sumit handle not knowing.
What would change if Phuppo had promised the rain would stop?
If it hadn't stopped, Sumit would have felt let down and confused about what was promised.

The day attendant didn't come, the monsoon had knocked out the lift, and Himani had a client call at eleven. Her father, whose memory had been slipping for two years, kept asking where her mother was; she had died three years ago. Each time Himani answered gently, 'She's not here, Papa. I'm here.' At 10:50 she called her sister Pallavi in Bhopal. 'I can't do this call and watch him.' Pallavi, who usually sent money rather than time, said, 'Put me on video with him. I'll talk to him for an hour.' Papa loved it. Himani took the call from the balcony, hair unwashed, voice steady. Afterwards she sat on the floor and cried a little, mostly from tiredness. That evening the sisters made a plan: Pallavi would take two video hours a week and visit every month, and they would look for a backup attendant.

What time was Himani's client call?
At eleven.
How did Himani feel after the call, and why?
She sat on the floor and cried a little, mostly from exhaustion after juggling work and her father's care alone.
What did the sisters change so that care is shared more fairly?
Pallavi will give two video hours a week and visit every month, and they will look for a backup attendant.
How might Pallavi's role have felt different after that day?
She moved from sending money to giving time, which may have made her feel closer to her father and sister.

Suraj's job offer was delayed by three months, and the first instalment of the education loan was due in five weeks. Sitting in the flat in Bengaluru with the loan papers, Suraj felt the old urge to wait and hope. Instead, the next morning, Suraj went to the bank branch before any payment was missed and asked for Disha, the officer who handled the account. "My start date has been pushed back. I don't want to default. What are my options?" Disha listened, checked the file, and explained that the tenure could be discussed and a new schedule drawn up in writing. Suraj brought the papers home and saw that the situation had turned from a dread into a task with a date.

How many weeks until the first instalment was due?
The first instalment was due in five weeks.
What did Suraj feel before deciding to go to the bank?
Suraj felt the urge to wait and hope, which suggests worry and a wish to avoid the problem.
What could Suraj do while waiting for the job, and why?
Suraj could set aside whatever small income arrives to be ready for the first payment, because preparing shows good faith.
How might Disha see a customer who comes before missing a payment?
Disha probably sees someone who takes the loan seriously, and finds it easier to work out options together.

Exam month: Rashmi, twenty-one, studied fourteen hours a day, snapped at everyone and stopped answering her friend Pradeep's calls. Two weeks in: Pradeep turned up at her hostel with a cheap karaoke speaker. "One song. Then I leave." She sang, badly, an old film song, and laughed for the first time in days. After exams: they started Friday karaoke nights with friends, off-key and loud. Rashmi noticed she slept better and studied more clearly on Saturdays. "I thought fun was a reward for after," she told Pradeep. "Turns out it's part of the fuel."

What did Pradeep bring to Rashmi's hostel?
A cheap karaoke speaker.
What was Rashmi feeling when she laughed for the first time in days?
She felt a burst of relief and lightness after weeks of stress.
What did Pradeep's visit do well?
It offered a small, time-limited break that reminded Rashmi how to play.
How might Pradeep feel about the Friday karaoke nights?
Happy and glad his friend found a way back to fun.

Payal waited outside the school counsellor's room, reading Kunal's last message again: "Did I do something?" Two weeks ago they'd spent every free period together, planning the science fair. Then, the night he said, "You're my closest friend," she blocked him. She didn't know why, only that her chest had gone tight and she'd wanted to run. It had happened before, with a girl in class eight. Inside, Mrs Rao listened without interrupting. "Wanting people near and then needing to escape is exhausting," she said. "We can work on this together, weekly. With your parents' okay, I'd also like you to meet our visiting psychologist." Payal nodded, then unblocked Kunal and typed, "Not you. Me. I'll explain soon."

What did Kunal's last message say?
It said, "Did I do something?"
What did Payal feel the night Kunal called her his closest friend?
Her chest went tight and she wanted to run, a fear that came just as the friendship got close.
What turning point happened in the counsellor's room?
Mrs Rao offered weekly sessions and a visiting psychologist, Payal agreed, and then unblocked Kunal to tell him it wasn't his fault.
How might Kunal have felt after being suddenly blocked?
He was likely confused and hurt, wondering what he had done wrong.

Leela, you want to know about our team's first-Friday plant? I'm Gargi, I lead a small support team at an insurance office, and I used to hate how new people were just thrown in. So now, on a new person's first Friday, the whole team buys a small potted plant, and everyone writes one tip on a card: where the good stapler is, which manager hates emojis in emails, how to escape the long meetings. We sit around the plant and explain each card. Last month a new joiner, Ibrahim, told us he'd been scared we'd test him with trick questions. By the end he was laughing and writing his own card for the next person. The plant's on his desk now. Honestly, that's the whole culture.

What does the team buy on a new person's first Friday?
A small potted plant.
How did Ibrahim feel before the first-Friday plant?
He was scared the team would test him with trick questions.
Why do the tip cards work so well?
They make the unwritten habits clear, like where the stapler is or which manager hates emojis, so the newcomer feels included, not tested.
What might it mean for Ibrahim to write his own card for the next person?
It shows he now feels part of the team and wants to pass the welcome on.
Cathedrals come up in my history book about Europe. What makes a church a cathedral?

A cathedral is the main church of a district, where a bishop has his seat. That, not size, is what makes it a cathedral, though many are large and old. It is a noun, and in the plural it is Cathedrals.
Example: The great cathedrals of Europe often took over a hundred years to build.
Dukaan mein bolna hai "Mujhe ye wali nahi, doosri wali chahiye."
Say: "I don't want this one. I would like the other one, please."

The monsoon forecast was on the radio when Kavitha pulled down half the shutter of her stationery shop in T. Nagar and sat on the stool with a notebook. Siddharth, her assistant, watched her write TWO WEEKS UNDER WATER? across the top.
'What goes first?' she said, half to Siddharth. 'Stock on the bottom shelves: notebooks, chart paper. All ruined in an hour. So the heavy stock goes up to the top racks now, and the bottom two stay empty till October.'
She tapped the pen. 'Bills. If the ledger gets wet, I don't know who owes me what.' She would photograph each day's bills every evening and upload them.
'And if customers can't come in?'
'Then school orders by phone. You deliver on the scooter when roads open. I'll tell the regular schools this week.'

What did Kavitha write across the top of the notebook?
TWO WEEKS UNDER WATER?
What seems to worry Kavitha most about the ledger?
She is anxious that a wet ledger would leave her not knowing who owes her what, which could hurt the shop more than lost stock.
What other approach could strengthen Kavitha's plan?
She could write a short list of who does what on the day of a flood warning, such as shifting stock and calling schools, so the plan runs fast.
How might Siddharth see the plan?
Siddharth gets a clear role, delivering phone orders when roads open, which may feel reassuring rather than chaotic.

Read this:

When I was eight, my big sister Ishita didi was studying for her board exams. I kept going into her room. "Didi, why is the sky blue? Didi, what's the biggest animal? Didi, how do planes stay up?" I didn't care about the answers. I just wanted her to look at me.
She kept saying, "Manjula, I'm studying." Then I'd ask another one.
One evening she put her pen down. She said, "You're asking a lot of questions. Do you just miss me?" I nodded. I felt a bit silly.
She said, "Okay. Every evening at seven, I'll take a ten-minute break, and we'll play something. Deal?" I said deal.
After that, I stopped interrupting. I waited for seven o'clock. We played carrom mostly.

What time did Ishita didi take her break?
At seven, every evening.
What was Manjula feeling while asking so many questions?
Manjula felt lonely and missed Ishita didi, wanting attention more than answers.
What did Ishita didi do that helped?
She noticed the need for connection behind the questions and offered a daily ten-minute break to play together.
How did Ishita didi feel before she put her pen down?
She was probably frustrated and distracted, trying to study with constant interruptions.

Kamal had managed the dairy cooperative in Anand for a year when the grumbling started. At Diwali the milk-collection staff had got a bonus for the record monsoon season; the plant workers had not. Everyone was paid fairly by the book, but Kamal noticed the plant workers eating separately and the jokes turning sharp. Shankar, who had run the chilling plant for twenty years, stopped saying good morning. Kamal didn't wait for things to boil over. He called a meeting under the neem tree and put the bonus criteria on a chart: litres collected, new farmers signed. 'You're right that it only rewarded one kind of work,' he said. 'That's my mistake.' He proposed a new rule for next year, with a plant target too, and asked Shankar to help set it. Shankar folded his arms, then nodded slowly.

Where did Kamal call the meeting?
Under the neem tree.
What did Kamal feel when Shankar stopped saying good morning?
Kamal felt uneasy and concerned, sensing resentment building even though pay was fair.
Why did putting the criteria on a chart help?
It made the reasons transparent, admitted the gap honestly and invited the plant workers to shape the next rule.
Why might Shankar have stopped saying good morning?
Shankar likely felt left behind and unappreciated after twenty years, when only the collection staff got a bonus.
Which one is cheapest, this bag or that one? Correct my question.

Which one is cheaper, this bag or that one?
Why: When you compare only two things, use the comparative form ("cheaper"). The superlative ("cheapest") is for three or more.

Last year my photo page looked perfect: the debate trophy, the beach trip, the new haircut. I spent twenty minutes on every caption. People left hearts under everything, and I, Yamini, still ate lunch pretending to text so nobody would notice I had nobody to talk to. I was scared that if anyone saw how often I doubted myself, they'd leave. Then in March, Vaibhav from my bus stop asked why a girl with such a perfect page never looked happy in person. I almost said, "I'm fine." Instead I said, "I don't know who I am when I'm not performing." He didn't laugh. He said he felt the same about his gym videos. We talk at the bus stop most mornings now. It's only one person. It's more than all those hearts.

What did Vaibhav ask Yamini in March?
He asked why a girl with such a perfect page never looked happy in person.
Why did Yamini pretend to text at lunch?
She was afraid people would notice she had nobody to talk to, and worried that showing her doubts would make them leave.
What was the turning point for Yamini, and why did it matter?
Choosing to say "I don't know who I am when I'm not performing" instead of "I'm fine." One honest answer let a real friendship begin.
What might Vaibhav have gained from Yamini's honest reply?
It gave him room to admit he felt the same about his gym videos, so he didn't have to feel alone either.
It is a long time that I saw you. How can I say this more naturally?

It has been a long time since I saw you.
Why: The usual pattern is "It has been a long time since" plus the past simple. The "that" pattern is heard in Indian English but is not standard.

Monday, a cold winter morning: Jasleen shuffles around the flat in Papa's big slippers, flap, flap. "I'm going to the hospital," she says, in his deep voice.
Wednesday: She lines up her dolls and listens to their tummies with a toy stethoscope. "Breathe in. Good girl. Drink warm water," she says, exactly like Papa.
Saturday: Her little cousin Kalyani wants a turn. Jasleen hands her the stethoscope and puts Papa's reading glasses on her own nose. "Now I'm the big doctor," she says, standing very tall. Papa, watching from the door, grins and hands her his old white coat.

What did Jasleen listen to the dolls' tummies with?
A toy stethoscope.
How does Jasleen feel wearing Papa's glasses?
Proud, big and grown-up, standing very tall like the doctor Papa she admires.
How does Papa respond, and why does it help?
He grins and gives her his old white coat, encouraging her play instead of teasing, so she feels big and safe.
How might Kalyani feel getting the stethoscope?
Excited and included, getting to join the game.

In Lagos, Christmas Eve had Emeka bouncing off the walls. Mum's jollof rice was bubbling, his new shirt with gold buttons hung on the door, and cousins were arriving from Enugu. He couldn't stop grinning. Then, through the window, he saw the girl from the flat opposite, Yuki, sitting alone on her steps. Her family had moved from Osaka a month ago, and she had told him her parents would be working at the port over Christmas. Emeka stopped bouncing. He went to the kitchen. 'Mum, can Yuki come for rice? She's by herself.' Mum wiped her hands. 'Go and ask her. And take her a plate of chin chin now.' Yuki's face, when he held out the plate, made his Christmas even brighter.

Where had Yuki's family moved from?
Osaka.
How was Emeka feeling on Christmas Eve before he saw Yuki?
Bubbling with excitement; he was bouncing off the walls and couldn't stop grinning 🎉
How did Emeka share his joy?
He noticed Yuki alone, asked Mum if she could come for rice, and took her a plate of chin chin.
How might Yuki have felt when Emeka held out the plate?
Surprised and warmed, and less alone while her parents worked.

Session note, couple's session two. Vidya did most of the talking again. When she described last week's argument about Jagdish's late nights at the lab, he looked at the floor and said, "It's not a big deal." I watched her hands clench and her voice rise; she leaned forward, repeating herself. He leaned further back. I paused them and asked Vidya to say, slowly, one sentence about what she needed. She said, "When you go quiet, I feel alone. I need ten minutes of talk each night, even if it's short." Jagdish looked up for the first time. I noted her relief. Next step: both will try the ten minutes this week, and I will see Jagdish alone once to hear his side.

What did Jagdish say about the argument?
"It's not a big deal."
What was Vidya feeling as she repeated herself?
She felt alone and dismissed, with clenched hands and a rising voice.
Why did the one slow sentence work better than repeating herself?
A calm, specific request was easier for Jagdish to hear than pressure, so he looked up instead of leaning back.
How might Jagdish experience Vidya leaning forward and repeating herself?
He may feel pressured and retreat further, which is why he leaned back.

The chemistry paper was at nine the next morning, the corridor throbbed with someone's speaker, and Jasleen was waving a highlighter. "Sleep is a luxury tonight," she said. "We study till dawn."
Indu closed her notes at half past nine. She had already eaten a proper dinner and walked once round the hostel garden, listening to frogs. "If I can't answer it now, two more hours won't fix it," she said, and set her alarm.
Jasleen scoffed, but by midnight she was rereading the same page. In the hall Indu's mind was clear; she recalled the reaction steps in order and even had time to check. Jasleen yawned through the last question.

When was the chemistry paper?
At nine the next morning.
What does Indu feel about closing her notes while Jasleen keeps studying?
Indu seems calm and confident. She says two more hours won't fix what she cannot answer now, and she sets her alarm.
What choice did Indu make that helped in the exam hall?
She ate a proper dinner, took a walk and stopped studying at half past nine, so her mind was clear and she recalled the steps in order.
How might Jasleen feel as midnight passes and she rereads the same page?
Probably anxious and tired, since she is stuck on the same page and yawns through the last question.

Indu, come, let me tell you about the launch that taught me to sort my worries. I'm Minakshi, and I was a new manager then. We ran a pre-mortem, and the board filled with thirty-odd ideas: printers, pigeons on the roof, a vendor's mood. Next morning I looked at it and my stomach dropped; it was a wall of worry and I couldn't act on any of it. So I sat with a pen and marked each idea twice: how likely, and how costly. Only three scored high on both: the payment gateway going down, our one trained person falling ill, and stock arriving late. For those I planned backups. The rest I decided to live with. A pigeon did cause a hiccup, and we laughed. The gateway did stumble, and the backup carried us.

Which three risks did Minakshi keep?
Minakshi kept the payment gateway going down, the one trained person falling ill, and stock arriving late.
What did Minakshi feel on looking at the board the next morning?
Minakshi felt overwhelmed, as Minakshi's stomach dropped at a wall of worry that could not be acted on.
Which choice turned the list from a wall of worry into a plan, and why?
Marking each idea for how likely and how costly it was, and keeping only those high on both, gave backups for the few risks that mattered.
How might the team have felt when the gateway stumbled and the backup carried them?
They were probably relieved and reassured that the plan had worked, after having already laughed at the pigeon hiccup.

The next day commenced as before, getting up and dressing by rushlight; but this morning we were obliged to dispense with the ceremony of washing; the water in the pitchers was frozen. A change had taken place in the weather the preceding evening, and a keen north-east wind, whistling through the crevices of our bedroom windows all night long, had made us shiver in our beds, and turned the contents of the ewers to ice.

Why do the writer and the others skip washing that morning?

The weather turned in the evening and a keen north-east wind whistled through the window cracks all night. The water in the pitchers froze to ice, so they dressed by the dim light of a rush candle without washing.

Rain was coming down hard on the flyover road when a scooter skidded and slid across the tarmac. Binita, walking home with her classmate Omkar, felt her stomach drop. Her phone showed nine percent battery.

Safety first, she told herself, the way the first-aid instructor had put it. Are cars still coming? She pulled Omkar behind the barrier. "Hold your torch up and wave it at the traffic." Then: call for help. She dialled 112 with wet fingers. Don't move the rider unless there's danger. There was no fire, so she crouched beside the rider and kept still. Say only what you know. "A scooter has fallen near the bus stop on the flyover. One person on the ground, awake, talking. I don't know more than that."

The phone dropped to eight percent as the siren sounded.

What was the battery percentage on Binita's phone?
Her phone showed nine percent battery.
What is Binita feeling as she stands over the rider in the rain?
Binita is nervous and frightened, and she steadies herself by repeating the checklist from the first-aid class.
What could Binita do if she couldn't remember the checklist, and why?
She could ask the emergency operator what to do next and stick to what she can see, because the operator is trained to guide callers.
How might the situation look to Omkar?
Omkar probably feels unsure but relieved to be given a clear job with the torch, because Binita's calm steps give the moment some structure.

Briefly, what does Nelly discover?

One day, as she inspected this drawer, I observed that the playthings and trinkets which recently formed its contents were transmuted into bits of folded paper. My curiosity and suspicions were roused; I determined to take a peep at her mysterious treasures; so, at night, as soon as she and my master were safe upstairs, I searched, and readily found among my house keys one that would fit the lock. Having opened, I emptied the whole contents into my apron, and took them with me to examine at leisure in my own chamber. Though I could not but suspect, I was still surprised to discover that they were a mass of correspondence—daily almost, it must have been—from Linton Heathcliff: answers to documents forwarded by her. The earlier dated were embarrassed and short; gradually, however, they expanded into copious love-letters, foolish, as the age of the writer rendered natural, yet with touches here and there which I thought were borrowed from a more experienced source. Some of them struck me as singularly odd compounds of ardour and flatness; commencing in strong feeling, and concluding in the affected, wordy style that a schoolboy might use to a fancied, incorporeal sweetheart. Whether they satisfied Cathy I don't know; but they appeared very worthless trash to me. After turning over as many as I thought proper, I tied them in a handkerchief and set them aside, relocking the vacant drawer.

Nelly notices that Cathy's private drawer now holds folded papers instead of toys. She opens it at night and finds almost daily love letters from Linton, which she thinks are silly and worthless, and she takes them away.

Subject: Yesterday's thread

Hi Disha,

I wanted to write to you directly instead of replying in the team group.

Yesterday, when the vendor sent the wrong samples, you wrote in the group, "Wow, amazing quality control as always 👏". I understand; it was the third mistake this month and you had to redo your whole report. I'd have been annoyed too.

But our group has twelve people, including two from the vendor's side. A line like that can be screenshotted and read as an insult to their whole company, not as a tired joke from a busy day.

For the group, I've posted just the facts: wrong samples, new ones due Friday. For the frustration, let's talk. I'm free at four today for a quick call, and I'd like to hear what else has been piling up.

You're doing good work. I just want the chat to protect it.

Siddharth

How many people are in the team group?
The group has twelve people, including two from the vendor's side.
Why did Siddharth choose to email Disha rather than reply in the group?
Siddharth was concerned that a public reply would embarrass Disha, and wanted to respect Disha's frustration while keeping the matter private.
What is the strength of Siddharth's approach?
It separates the facts, posted clearly in the group, from the feelings, discussed on a private call, and it names the risk of screenshots without scolding.
How might Disha feel reading the email?
Disha might feel a little embarrassed but also understood and valued, since Siddharth admits to feeling the same annoyance and praises Disha's work.

In the Lisbon flat, Noa tiptoed up to the pram where her baby cousin was sleeping.
“Ba-by,” she breathed, so softly it was almost air, her eyes wide.
“Yes, sleeping baby,” whispered her father, Rafael.
That afternoon, a neighbour knocked with a cake. Noa slipped behind Rafael's legs and breathed, “Hi,” barely audible, face half hidden.
“She's a bit shy,” Rafael said. “Give her time."

What did the neighbour bring?
The neighbour knocked with a cake.
What was Noa feeling when she breathed "Ba-by" by the pram?
She seemed full of wonder and was being careful and quiet around the sleeping baby, which is why her voice was hushed.
How did Rafael read Noa's breathy voice correctly both times?
He looked at the context: by the pram it was gentle politeness and awe, and behind his legs with a hidden face it was shyness.
How might the neighbour feel about Noa's whispered "Hi"?
The neighbour would probably understand she was shy and feel pleased she said hello at all.

When I turned twenty-three, I thought I'd feel like a man. I didn't. I'm Shankar, and that year I still let my mother fix my doctor's visits, forgot my friend Santosh's wedding sangeet, and owed him money I'd borrowed for a laptop. So I tried an experiment: one adult thing a week, no speeches. Week one, I made my own appointment for the knee that had hurt for months. Week three, I set up a small monthly transfer to pay Santosh back and told him the date it would finish. Week six, I kept a promise to help at his father's shop every Sunday in December, even the rainy ones. Nothing magical happened. But last month Santosh asked me to carry the naming papers for his newborn at the temple. That's when I felt it, a little.

What had Shankar borrowed money from Santosh for?
A laptop.
How did Shankar feel when Santosh asked about the naming papers?
Shankar felt quietly proud and trusted, finally a little like an adult.
Why did 'one adult thing a week' work better than waiting to feel grown up?
Small, steady acts like appointments, repayments and kept promises built trust bit by bit, so the feeling came gradually.
How might Santosh's trust in Shankar have changed over the year?
Santosh likely went from being let down over the sangeet and the money to relying on him for something important.

Farhan: haven't seen you in forever. birthday dinner friday? everyone's coming
Rashmi: I can't. and honestly I don't know if I should hang out with the old group anymore
Farhan: what? why?
Rashmi: our coach says people who don't understand the Movement drain your energy
Rashmi: you guys just talk about exams and movies. it's so small
Farhan: we've been friends since 6th standard
Rashmi: that's what they said you'd say. people use the past to pull you back
Farhan: who is "they"?
Rashmi: the group. they actually care about the world. my parents don't get it either, they're just scared
Farhan: are you ok? you sound really different
Rashmi: see, this is what I mean. any doubt and you think something's wrong with me
Farhan: I'm not attacking you. I just miss you. the dinner offer stays open
Rashmi: ...maybe

Since when have Farhan and Rashmi been friends?
Since 6th standard.
What does Rashmi's line 'that's what they said you'd say' reveal about Rashmi's thinking?
Rashmi feels defensive and suspicious, reading an old friend's care as the outsiders' pull the group warned about.
Which of Farhan's choices helps most, and why?
Staying calm, saying 'I just miss you' and keeping the dinner offer open, because it keeps a door out without a fight.
How might Farhan feel reading Rashmi's replies?
Farhan feels hurt and worried, suddenly treated as an enemy by a friend of many years.

Give me the instructions in this speech as three bullet points.

"There is but one thing to do. It must be done at once. You must put this piece of paper which you have shown us into the brass box which you have described. You must also put in a note to say that all the other papers were burned by your uncle, and that this is the only one which remains. You must assert that in such words as will carry conviction with them. Having done this, you must at once put the box out upon the sundial, as directed. Do you understand?"

- Put the paper into the brass box.
- Add a note saying that the other papers were burned by the uncle and that this one is the only one left.
- Then put the box out on the sundial straight away, as directed.

The power had gone out across the hall, the generator was coughing, and the first guests were due in forty minutes. Tanvir paced beside the empty buffet tables. "The caterer said six-thirty. I was standing right next to you when he said it." Arohi remembered seven-thirty just as clearly, but she didn't argue. "I remember it differently," she said. "Let's check before we shout at anyone." Her phone was on four percent. She scrolled fast through the booking chat by torchlight. There it was: "Food will reach by 7:15." Neither of them had it right. "Huh," Tanvir said. "I'd have sworn." "Me too," Arohi said, already calling the caterer to confirm the van was on its way. Tanvir went off to find extra candles.

What time did the booking chat say the food would reach?
What might Arohi have been feeling when Tanvir insisted on six-thirty?
She was likely tense, with the power cut and guests coming, and sure of seven-thirty herself, yet calm enough to hold her memory lightly and check.
What would you advise someone in Tanvir's place next time?
Pull up the written booking first, especially under pressure, instead of relying on "I was standing right next to you".
What is it like for Tanvir when Arohi says "I remember it differently" instead of "you're wrong"?
Tanvir is not pushed into self-defence, so admitting "I'd have sworn" is easy and Tanvir can move straight on to helping with candles.

In their village house, Disha was exhausted after the harvest. Each night she closed the door on Kalyani, two, and went to the fields at dawn.

Kalyani's grandmother noticed. "She used to call for you. Now she just lies there, silent."

Disha went in. Kalyani's eyes were open, blank. Disha lay down beside her, humming. Kalyani grabbed her finger and cried hard, then slept.

After that, Disha stayed until she slept.

What did Disha do after going into the room?
Disha lay down beside Kalyani, humming.
What was Kalyani feeling when she lay silent with blank eyes?
Kalyani felt alone and had given up, not calm, after being left crying night after night.
What changed that helped Kalyani?
Disha began staying with her, humming until she slept, showing that someone would come.
How does Kalyani's grandmother see the silence?
The grandmother sees it as a worrying sign, not good behaviour, because Kalyani used to call out.

“Naveen, shall we do the rhyme?”
“Yes, Dadu!”
Arnab-dadu started. “Aay re aay, tiye…”
“Nayey chore Ganga dhiye!” Naveen shouted.
“Good! Next line?”
Naveen scrunched his face. “I forgot.”
“Clap it,” Dadu said, and clapped the beat.
Naveen clapped along, then his eyes lit up. “Dhaan kete jaay!”
Dadu laughed and hugged him. “Now you know it better than your father did at six.”

What did Dadu do when Naveen forgot the line?
He clapped the beat and told Naveen to clap it.
How did Naveen feel when he remembered the line?
He felt excited and proud, his eyes lighting up.
Why did clapping the beat help Naveen remember?
The rhythm helped him recall the words, since rhymes are learned with their beat.
How does Arnab-dadu feel teaching Naveen the rhyme?
He feels joyful and proud, laughing and hugging his grandson 🤗

During chemistry, Dorje checked his phone under the desk again: 212 likes yesterday, 148 now. His stomach dropped. Madhuri leaned over from the next bench. “You look like you failed a test.”
“Likes are down. I need something bolder.” He had already posted the neon-dyed hair photo, then a pouting close-up he didn't even like, and each time the number jumped, he felt light for an hour. Then it dipped, and he felt heavy again. All day his mood moved with a counter he couldn't control. At lunch he opened the app twelve times. Madhuri said quietly, “You were happier when you posted the picture of your dog.” Dorje shrugged, but he put the phone face down for the rest of the lesson.

How many likes did Dorje's post have yesterday, and how many now?
It had 212 likes yesterday and 148 now.
How is Dorje feeling as the likes drop?
Dorje feels anxious and heavy, since his stomach dropped and his mood moves with the counter.
What could Dorje try instead of chasing bolder pictures?
Dorje could post what he enjoys, like the picture of his dog, and check less often, since his mood should not depend on numbers he cannot control.
How might Madhuri see Dorje's chasing of likes?
Madhuri seems concerned but gentle, since Madhuri remembers when Dorje looked happier and says so quietly.

"I think that this should do," said he, glancing into the glass above the fireplace. "I only wish that you could come with me, Watson, but I fear that it won't do. I may be on the trail in this matter, or I may be following a will-o'-the-wisp, but I shall soon know which it is. I hope that I may be back in a few hours." He cut a slice of beef from the joint upon the sideboard, sandwiched it between two rounds of bread, and thrusting this rude meal into his pocket he started off upon his expedition.

Please summarize this in one line.
A man checks his looks, says he wishes Watson could come, and hurries off with a beef sandwich to follow a possible trail.

Losar was two days away, the Delhi winter fog thick outside the PG window, and Pema's train ticket home to Kalimpong was still waitlisted. Her part-time café wage covered food, not fares. She stared at her phone, thumb over Amala's name. Twenty-one, choosing her own courses, cooking her own dal, and still about to ask for ticket money. Her roommate Rajni, packing for Lohri at her own home, glanced up. "Just call." "It feels like admitting I'm a kid." "My dad still pays my phone bill," Rajni said. "I also fixed the landlord's leaking pipe myself last week. Nobody's fully one thing at our age." Pema laughed, a small surprised laugh, and pressed call. The fog didn't lift. But something in her chest did.

Why was Pema's train ticket a problem?
It was still waitlisted, and her café wage covered food, not fares.
Why did calling Amala feel hard for Pema?
Pema felt embarrassed and caught in between, independent in so many ways yet still needing help, as if asking meant admitting she was a kid.
What helped Pema, and why?
Rajni sharing her own mix of leaning on family and doing things alone made the in-between feeling seem normal 🙂, so Pema could make the call without shame.
How does Rajni see their stage of life?
Rajni sees it as normal to be part dependent and part grown up, like a dad paying the phone bill while fixing the pipe herself.

In the courtyard of their village house near Mangalore, Chandrika, five, sat on the step with her new school shoes and their long, floppy laces.
Her grandfather Francis bent down. "Come, I'll tie them."
Chandrika pushed his hand away. "No! I do it myself!"
She made one loop. It fell apart. She tried again, tongue sticking out, while the bus horn sounded down the lane.
"Wait, Grandpa!"
The second loop held. A wobbly bow.
She stamped her foot to show him. "I did it!"
Francis laughed and clapped, and they ran for the bus together.

What was Chandrika trying to tie?
The laces of her new school shoes.
What was Chandrika feeling when she stamped her foot and said "I did it!"?
She felt proud and pleased, having tied the laces by herself.
How could Francis support Chandrika's wish to do things herself on busy mornings?
He could give her a little extra time to try, and step in only if she asks, so she can keep building her independence.
How might Francis feel about being pushed away?
He might feel a little amused and proud, seeing her so determined to do it herself.

Baljeet, you think I was always this talkative? At nine, in our Thrissur house, I didn't say a word at the dinner table. My grandfather sat at the head, and children spoke only when spoken to. I'd look down at my rice even when I thought my uncle was completely wrong about the cricket. But out in the paddy fields with my cousins, I was the boss of every game, making rules, arguing, shouting. My mother noticed. One evening she whispered, "You have a lot to say, don't you?" I, Gopika, nodded. She said, "Say one thing tomorrow. Respectfully." So I told my grandfather, softly, that I liked his old stories. He smiled, for the first time I could remember.

Where was young Gopika the boss of every game?
Out in the paddy fields with the cousins.
How did young Gopika feel at the dinner table?
Gopika felt full of opinions but held them back out of respect for the elders.
What was the turning point in the story?
The mother's suggestion to say one thing respectfully, which led Gopika to speak to the grandfather.
How did the grandfather react when Gopika spoke?
He smiled, for the first time Gopika could remember.

Note from Neelam, Madhav's mother, to his badminton coach.
Madhav came home from the district trials on Saturday and went straight to bed. He hasn't come out much since. He won't talk about the trials. When I ask what he wants to eat, it's only the moong dal khichdi I made when he was little, with ghee, in his old blue plate. He's fifteen, but he has his childhood blanket back on his bed. What does Madhav want to eat?
Only moong dal khichdi with ghee, in his old blue plate.
Why has Madhav brought his childhood blanket back?
He feels hurt and disappointed after the trials, and childhood comforts help him feel soothed and safe.
What makes Neelam's approach a good one?
She gives warmth and time without pushing, and asks the coach for a kind message so Madhav feels supported from both sides.
How might the coach respond after reading the note?
The coach might feel sympathetic and send a warm message, understanding why Madhav has missed practice.

Thursday, 11:50 pm
Kashish's father died three weeks ago. The first week I was on the phone with her every night till 2. She cried and cried and I cried too. I couldn't sleep after. I kept seeing her face at the funeral.
Second week I was so tired I fell asleep in chemistry. Mum asked if I was ill.
This week she called four times. I didn't pick up twice. I told her my phone was on silent. It wasn't.
I feel horrible. She's my best friend. But every time her name comes up on the screen my chest goes tight and I just want to hide.
I don't know how to help her without drowning.
Maybe I'll tell Mum tomorrow. She'll know what to do.
– Sangeeta

How long ago did Kashish's father die?
Three weeks ago.
Why does Sangeeta not pick up Kashish's calls?
Sangeeta feels exhausted and overwhelmed by Kashish's grief, and guilty for hiding.
What would be a wise next step for Sangeeta?
Sangeeta could talk to Mum as planned and get help to support Kashish in a way that doesn't drain Sangeeta, like shorter calls and involving other adults.
How might Kashish feel when Sangeeta doesn't pick up?
She might feel hurt and lonely, missing her best friend just when she needs her most.

In the school sports office, Kunal told Rashmi ma'am his secret. "On days I wear my red socks, our kho-kho team wins. Every time." She checked the chart on the wall. Their team had won four matches. "Which days did you wear the red socks?" "All four!" "And which teams did we play on those days?" Kunal looked at the chart. The names were the smaller schools. "And the day we lost?" "I... wore blue socks. Against St. Mary's." "Who are the district champions?" "St. Mary's." Rashmi ma'am smiled. "So the socks and the wins came together. But what else came with the wins?" Kunal thought. "Easy teams?" "So what really made us win?" He grinned slowly. "Maybe not the socks."

Which team did they lose to?
St. Mary's.
What was Kunal feeling when he told Rashmi ma'am his secret?
He felt excited and proud, sure his red socks made the team win because they always came together.
How did Rashmi ma'am help Kunal find the real reason?
She asked which teams they played on red-sock days, so he saw that easy opponents came with the wins too.
How might Rashmi ma'am see Kunal's belief?
She seems amused and kind, using it to teach him to look for other reasons behind a pattern.

Playgroup note, summer.

At our mango picnic, Shalini, twenty months, tasted a slice of raw green mango. Her whole face crumpled. She stuck out her tongue, spat it out, and wiped her mouth with both hands, saying "Ew!"

We didn't force it. I gave her ripe mango instead, which she ate happily. I've told her parents she can try raw mango again another day, maybe with a little salt. — Vaibhav

What did Shalini taste at the mango picnic?
She tasted a slice of raw green mango.
How did Shalini feel about the raw mango?
Shalini was disgusted by the sour taste, crumpling her face and spitting it out.
How did Vaibhav handle Shalini's reaction well?
He did not force her, offered ripe mango instead, and suggested trying again later.
How might Shalini's parents feel reading the note?
They would probably be amused and reassured that the teacher handled it gently.
