On the first day after the summer holidays in Chennai, the new girl, Yamini, walked into Class 5B laughing, taller than everyone, her plait swinging. By lunch Lavanya had decided three things: Yamini must be the cleverest, she would never lie, and she should be Lavanya's partner for Friday's quiz. When Miss asked who would keep the class-trip slips, Lavanya's hand shot up. "Yamini should! She's so nice." On Friday the quizmaster asked for the capital of Australia. "Sydney," Yamini said, smiling brightly. Lavanya wrote it down without a second thought. It was wrong. Lavanya stared at the red mark. Nobody had ever told her Yamini was good at geography. She had just felt sure.

Which city did Yamini give as the capital of Australia?
Sydney.
Why did Lavanya feel so sure about Yamini on the first day?
Yamini's height, laughter and friendliness made Lavanya feel admiring and certain she must also be clever and honest, though nobody had told her so.
What could Lavanya try before choosing a quiz partner next time?
She could think about what she actually knows of a person's skills, like how they did in past quizzes, instead of how nice they seem.
How might Yamini feel about being chosen for everything on her first day?
Yamini might feel pleased and welcomed, but also under pressure to live up to things nobody had checked.
Rewrite this as the start of a speech for the school assembly: Hey guys, today I wanna talk about being kind.
Good morning, everyone. Today I would like to talk to you about being kind.

Read this:

You asked why I did it, Binita Ma'am. I'm Naveen, and honestly? I didn't want to be the boring one. It was after tuition. The others dared me to ride my cycle down the flyover ramp with no hands, and Deepak said, "Naveen won't, he's too boring." In that moment, being called boring felt worse than anything the ramp could do. I knew it was stupid. My stomach knew it. I did it anyway. Halfway down, the front wheel hit a crack. I broke my wrist and scraped my whole arm. The others ran. None of them came to the hospital. My mother did, crying, and she still had to go to work the next day. Six weeks of plaster during exams, and all for three seconds of not being boring.

What did the others dare Naveen to do?
Ride his cycle down the flyover ramp with no hands.
What was Naveen feeling when Deepak called him boring?
He felt anxious and stung, as if being seen as boring was worse than the danger, even though his stomach told him it was stupid.
What else could Naveen have done in that moment?
Laughed it off and cycled home the normal way, or offered a race on flat ground, since a joke about being boring fades but a crash does not.
What was that day like for Naveen's mother?
She was frightened and upset, crying at the hospital, and still had to go to work the next day.

metadata.subtype: Approach: going along to avoid being excluded [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

The art exhibition was supposed to be on the school lawn, but the rain came down so hard that all of Class 5 had to squeeze into the music room with their paintings. Aadhya held hers above her head and frowned at Tejas across the room.
"His painting is messy," she whispered to Ira. Last month she had seen Tejas copy answers from the boy beside him in the spelling test. Since then his jokes seemed silly and his handwriting looked lazy.
Ira tilted her head. "It's a kingfisher. Look at the blue."
When the bell rang, the rain was still pouring. Tejas held out his big umbrella. "We can share to the bus."
Aadhya almost said no. Then she looked at her own soaked shoes and stepped under it, still frowning, as if he might be playing a trick.

Why did Class 5 have to squeeze into the music room?
The rain came down so hard that the exhibition could not be on the school lawn.
Why did Tejas's painting and jokes seem bad to Aadhya?
Since she saw him copy in the spelling test, she felt he was a bad person all round, so even his painting and jokes looked messy and silly to her.
What small step could help Aadhya see Tejas more fairly?
She could look at the kingfisher the way Ira did, noticing the blue, and judge the painting on its own instead of through the copying.
How might Ira see the painting differently from Aadhya?
Ira did not carry the memory of the spelling test in the same way, so Ira simply saw a kingfisher with lovely blue, not a messy picture.

Read this:

On Saturday mornings, Vijay now takes the 9:15 bus to a learning centre in Shivajinagar instead of sleeping till noon.

It started after he told Dolma, the centre's coordinator, that he'd always wanted to teach but was stuck doing audits. She didn't tell him to quit. She said, "Take the Class 6 maths group for two months. See how you feel."

The first Saturday was chaos. Twelve kids, one broken marker, and a boy who asked why fractions existed at all. Vijay went home tired and oddly light.

By the fifth week he'd made fraction cards from cereal boxes. Dolma watched from the door. "They listen to you," she said. "But you're still slow with the quiet ones."

Vijay wrote that down too. At his audit desk on Monday he hummed, and a colleague asked what had happened.

What did Vijay make by the fifth week?
He made fraction cards from cereal boxes.
What was Vijay feeling after the first chaotic Saturday?
He felt tired but oddly light, a sign that the teaching gave him energy and satisfaction even when it was hard.
Why is Dolma's suggestion a good small experiment?
Two months with one group gives Vijay real feedback on teaching, including his weak spot with quiet students, without leaving his audit job.
How might Dolma see Vijay's progress?
Dolma seems pleased that the children listen to him and honest about where he needs to grow, treating him as a real learner-teacher.
What is an archway? The guidebook says to enter through the old one.

An archway is a passage or entrance with a curved top. It is a noun.
Example: We walked through the old stone archway into the courtyard of the fort.
"Mere dada ji roz subah park mein tahalte hain." Translate.
It is: "My grandfather walks in the park every morning." In English, "grandfather" is the usual word, and "grandpa" is casual.
Aur dadi ke liye?
Use "grandmother" for the polite form and "grandma" for the casual one.
Aur nana-nani?
They are also "grandfather" and "grandmother". English does not separate the mother's side from the father's side.

Read this:

At the village fair in Nandgaon, the sugarcane juice man had a long queue, and Abhinav, five, could see the green juice pouring into glasses. He hopped from foot to foot. "Now, Kiran maushi! Now!" He tugged at her sari and whined. Kiran maushi turned him around. "Let's count the bullock carts. First to ten wins." Abhinav counted loudly: "Six, seven, a white one!" He argued about whether a tractor counted. He didn't notice the queue moving at all. When the glass was pushed into his hands, he looked surprised. "Already?"

What did Kiran maushi suggest counting?
She suggested counting the bullock carts, first to ten wins.
Why was Abhinav hopping and whining in the queue?
Abhinav felt impatient and eager, watching the juice pour right in front of him, which made the wait feel endless.
What made the wait easier, and how could this help at other times?
Turning him away from the juice and playing a counting game; the same trick can help whenever he has to wait for something he can see.
How might Kiran maushi have felt when Abhinav said 'Already?'
She was probably amused and relieved that the game had worked so well.

Read this:

Joseph, you're struggling with your wife and your mother in the kitchen? Let me, Vinita, your grandmother, tell you what I learned as a new bride in Kottayam.
My mother-in-law cooked everything. Every meal, every day. If I tried to make even the fish curry, she would take the spoon from my hand. At first I thought she didn't trust me.
Then one evening I saw her sitting alone after dinner, when everyone had praised the fish. Her face was so happy. And I understood: it wasn't about me. After her husband died, the kitchen was where she still mattered.
So I stopped trying to take it over. I asked her to teach me her fish curry. Then I asked her to plan the Sunday lunches, while I did the weekday cooking.
She became my best friend in that house, Joseph. Look for what the demand is protecting.

Where was Vinita a new bride?
In Kottayam.
What did Vinita realise about her mother-in-law's feelings after seeing her sit alone after dinner?
Vinita realised the mother-in-law felt happy and valued when cooking; after being widowed, the kitchen was where she still felt needed.
What was the turning point in Vinita's story, and what choice followed?
The turning point was seeing the mother-in-law's happy face after dinner; Vinita chose to ask to learn her recipes and let her plan Sunday lunches instead of resisting.
How might the mother-in-law have felt when asked to teach the fish curry?
She likely felt respected and needed, which is why she later became like a best friend.

messages.content: What is embroidery, and do I need a machine for it?

Embroidery is decorative sewing, making patterns on cloth with a needle and coloured thread. It is a noun. You can do it by hand or by machine.
Example: Her grandmother's embroidery on the scarf shows tiny red birds.

Read this:

Three dates in, Tejas knew. Ishita was kind and funny, and he didn't feel anything more than that. Her message had been sitting on his phone since Tuesday: "Movie this weekend? 🙂"
He had opened it four times on the metro between Andheri and Ghatkopar and closed it each time. It would be so easy not to reply. People did it all the time. She'd get the hint.
Then he remembered last year, when someone he liked had vanished on him, and he'd spent a week wondering what he had done wrong.
He got off at his station, sat on a bench and typed: "Hi Ishita, I've really enjoyed our evenings, and I want to be honest: I don't think this will be more than friendship for me. Sorry to say it by text, but I didn't want to leave you guessing. Have a good weekend."
He read it three times and sent it. It felt awful for about ten minutes. Then lighter.
Her reply came an hour later: "Thanks for telling me. Honestly, I appreciate it."

How many dates had Tejas and Ishita been on?
Three.
Why was Tejas tempted not to reply?
He felt awkward and uncomfortable about a hard conversation, and silence seemed easy.
Why was Tejas's message kinder than vanishing?
It was short and honest, so Ishita wasn't left guessing about what she had done wrong.
How did Ishita take the message?
She appreciated the honesty and thanked him.

Read this:

Damini had joined the meditation-and-study group in Pune for the free Sunday sessions, and stayed for the feeling of belonging. Sahil, the senior member who first invited her, now texted daily: reminders, praise, 'the family is proud of you.' This weekend was the retreat. It was also Nani's eightieth birthday. 'Real growth means loosening old ties,' Sahil said when she mentioned it, handing her the retreat form. 'Your family keeps you small.' That night Damini sat on a bus-stop bench and ran a test in her head. Could she question the leaders? She had seen how cold they went on the last person who did. Could she skip one retreat without being frozen out? She texted Sahil: 'I'm going to Nani's birthday. I'll miss the retreat.' An hour later: 'Disappointed. Think about where your loyalty is.' Damini called her mother.

What did Sahil hand Damini when she mentioned Nani's birthday?
Sahil handed her the retreat form.
What was Damini feeling on the bus-stop bench?
Damini felt uneasy and torn, still drawn to the group's warmth but worried by the pressure to drop her family.
What small test helped Damini see the group clearly?
Choosing Nani's birthday over one retreat and watching the reaction, which showed that disagreeing or stepping back was not really allowed.
How does Sahil see Damini's family?
Sahil casts them as a rival loyalty that 'keeps her small', so a birthday visit becomes disloyalty in his eyes.

metadata.subtype: Cult or group × Love and belonging with control [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Yogesh: late again, eat without me
Swati: ok
(Swati stared at her husband's word 'again'. Then she opened her chat with her sister.)
Swati: he's late AGAIN
Swati: third time this week. anniversary dinner last month, Ma's birthday, now this
Nandita: did he say why?
Swati: does he ever? it's always work. I'm always the thing that can wait 😔
Nandita: maybe something came up?
Swati: something always comes up
Nandita: want me to come over?
Swati: no. I'm fine. I'll eat alone. like always
(She put the phone face down. The actual message had said nothing about her at all. It didn't matter. She had already written the rest of the story herself.)

What three occasions does Swati list to her sister?
Anniversary dinner last month, Ma's birthday, and now this.
Why does Swati read 'late again' as proof she doesn't matter?
She links it to other late nights, so old grievances turn a neutral message into a pattern in which she is always the thing that can wait.
What question from Nandita could help Swati most, and why?
'Did he say why?', because it points out that Swati doesn't actually know the reason, and asking Yogesh could replace the story with facts.
What might Yogesh have meant when he typed 'late again'?
He may simply have been apologising for another late night in a rush; the chat never shows his reason, only Swati's reading.

Read this:

You want to know what happened after they found out? I'm Yamini, and I'll tell you exactly.
My mother took my phone, my laptop, and my allowance. No friends. No weekend outings. For two months.
I'd always been the good girl. And did I learn my lesson? Sort of. I learned how to hide better. I used Rajni's phone at school. I told my mother I was at the library and met my friends in the park behind it instead. I became really good at deleting chats.
Nobody at home ever asked why I lied in the first place. They just punished. So I figured, if honesty gets you punished and lying gets you punished too, why not just be better at lying?
I'm not saying it was right. I'm saying that's what happened.

Whose phone did Yamini use at school?
Rajni's phone.
What was Yamini feeling during the months of punishment?
She felt resentful and unheard, deciding that honesty wasn't worth it because nobody asked why she lied.
What turning point was missed at this stage?
Her mother could have asked why Yamini lied and set clearer, fairer terms, rather than heavy punishment that taught hiding.
What might Yamini's mother have been experiencing during those months?
She likely felt betrayed and worried, and may have thought the strict rules were working without knowing Yamini was hiding more.

Read this:

On Mahima's first day at the Pune software firm, her team lead, Vikas, noticed something at lunch. She had a notebook with eleven pages of scribbles, a laptop with twenty tabs open, and she hadn't touched her food.
"Everyone's been sending you links, haven't they?" he asked.
She nodded, a little desperately. "The code rules, the testing rules, the release calendar, the old project, the new project... I don't know what matters."
Vikas remembered his own first week, nodding through everything and understanding nothing.
That afternoon he closed her tabs. "This week, only the login module. Here's one bug I fixed last month, with my notes. Here's a checklist for testing. Fix one small bug by Friday. Everything else can wait."
On Thursday Mahima fixed her first bug and walked him through it. On Monday he added the next piece.

How many pages of scribbles were in Mahima's notebook?
Mahima's notebook had eleven pages of scribbles.
What did Vikas feel as he noticed Mahima at lunch?
Vikas felt concern and sympathy, remembering his own first week of nodding through everything and understanding nothing.
How did Vikas break down the information?
One module for the week, a past bug with notes as an example, a testing checklist, and one small bug to fix by Friday.
How did Mahima feel before Vikas stepped in?
Mahima felt overwhelmed and desperate, with twenty tabs open and no idea what mattered.

Read this:

In their Toronto apartment, dinner had become a one-word show. "How was school, Xin?" "Fine." "Swimming?" "Fine." Then the phone came out, and Xin's eyes stayed on it until the plates were cleared. Ivan, who had married Xin's mother two years before, felt the old urge to say "You're being rude," and swallowed it. He didn't know if Xin was tired, sad, private or just bored with him. So he tried something slower. Every evening he knocked once, said, "Making hot chocolate, want one?" and left it at that. Most nights the answer was "No." On the ninth night it was "Okay." On the twelfth, Xin sat on the kitchen stool while the milk heated and said, without looking up, "Morning practice is at five now. And everyone in Vancouver has stopped replying." Ivan nodded, stirred, and didn't lecture. "That's a lot at once," he said. Xin took the mug. "Yeah."

What time is morning practice now?
Morning practice is at five now.
What might Xin have been feeling behind the one-word answers?
Xin was likely exhausted from the early practice and lonely, hurt that old friends in Vancouver had stopped replying; from outside it could have looked like boredom or rudeness.
Why did the hot chocolate routine work better than calling Xin rude?
It offered a low-pressure chance to connect every evening without accusation, so after twelve nights Xin was ready to say what was going on.
What was dinner like for Ivan during those weeks?
Ivan felt shut out and tempted to scold, unsure whether the silence was about him, but chose patience instead.
Before the results, we were "on pins and needles". Were we hurt?

No. To be on pins and needles means to feel nervous and excited while waiting for something.
Example: We were on pins and needles until the results appeared on the board.

Read this:

I'm Chetan, and last winter I spent most evenings in my room with the door closed. Mum thought I was studying. My friend Yogesh thought I was busy. I told everyone I liked being alone.
Some nights that was true. I'd draw, listen to music, and feel full, like I was filling up a tank.
Other nights, I'd sit on the bed and watch the group chat, everyone laughing about some plan I wasn't in, and something in my chest ached. I'd want to text Yogesh and then not. The door was the same door. What was behind it wasn't.
Honestly, I didn't always know which kind of night it was until it was over.
One of the aching nights, Yogesh texted: "cycling tomorrow?" I nearly said "busy". I said "yes". We rode for an hour and I laughed more than I had in weeks.
Now I ask myself: am I recharging, or am I hiding?

Who texted Chetan about cycling?
Yogesh texted: "cycling tomorrow?"
What was Chetan feeling on the aching nights?
Chetan felt lonely and left out, watching the group chat laugh about plans that left Chetan out, and aching to reach out.
What question could help Chetan, or anyone, on a closed-door night?
Asking "Am I recharging, or am I hiding?" helps tell whether time alone is filling them up or cutting them off.
How might Yogesh have seen Chetan's closed door?
Yogesh thought Chetan was just busy, not knowing that some nights Chetan was lonely and hoping for a message.
"Kal match mein hum haar gaye" kaise kahte hain?
It is: "We lost the match yesterday." Remember: you win a match, and you lose a match.
Aur "hum jeet gaye"?
It is: "We won." You can add the match: "We won the match."

Read this:

The day after Nana's funeral Nazia went to school and felt nothing at all, like a coat hung on a hook. Then in maths, the smell of cardamom tea from a classmate's flask made her cry so hard the teacher let her step into the corridor. That evening she sat with the family for prayers, and let her aunt's arm stay round her shoulders.

What she could not shake was the last phone call: she had hung up on Nana after a quarrel about screen time. The thought looped every night. She finally wrote him a letter. "Nana, I am sorry for my tone. I meant to tell you your stories were my favourite thing." Some nights she was furious, and once she said it aloud in the prayer room, "Why him?" Her mother did not shush her. She only said, "Say it. It's allowed."

At school Anand and Darshan talked about cricket scores and nobody mentioned Nana. It stung, until Nazia told Anand at lunch, "Please don't act like it didn't happen. Just ask how I am, or sit with me." Anand went red. "I didn't know what to say." Next day he sat beside her with two rotis, and Darshan brought a small card.

What smell made Nazia cry in maths class?
The smell of cardamom tea from a classmate's flask made her cry.
How did Nazia's guilt about the last phone call and her anger in the prayer room differ, and how did each get voiced?

The guilt was about hanging up on Nana after a quarrel, and she voiced it in a letter of apology. The anger was aimed at whoever let Nana die, and she said it aloud in the prayer room while her mother let her.
What was Nazia feeling when Anand and Darshan talked about cricket and said nothing about Nana?
She felt hurt and alone, because it stung to have her loss ignored.
How could a friend like Anand support Nazia in the days after the funeral?
He could ask how she is, sit with her at lunch and bring something small, as he did, instead of staying silent.

Read this:

Monday, 4 p.m.: Mehak had been solving chemistry papers since seven in the morning, choosing which chapter next, which answers to recheck, which doubts to leave for later. When her cousin Sonali messaged, "Want to split the bio notes? 🙂", Mehak typed "k" and went back to staring at the page. At the corner shop she grabbed two packets of chips and a cold drink without looking at anything else.
Wednesday, 3 p.m.: After lunch and her fifth past paper, she felt the same pull toward the shop. This time she didn't decide anything. She opened the note she had written at breakfast: "After study: banana, water, one walk round the block."
Friday, noon: Mehak met Sonali before the long afternoon session, while her head still felt clear. They planned the bio notes properly, and her reply that evening was a full message with a list.

What did Mehak buy at the corner shop on Monday?
She grabbed two packets of chips and a cold drink without looking at anything else.
Why did replying "k" to Sonali feel reasonable to Mehak on Monday?
After nine hours of choosing chapters, answers and doubts, even a small reply felt like one more decision, so the shortest one seemed like all she could manage.
Which choice on Wednesday turned things around for Mehak, and why did it work?
She followed the note she had written at breakfast instead of deciding in a tired moment, so the snack was already chosen while her mind was fresh.
How might Sonali have felt reading that "k" on Monday compared with Friday's reply?
On Monday Sonali may have wondered whether Mehak was annoyed or didn't want to work together; Friday's full message with a list would show that Mehak did care about the plan.

Read this:

"Why do you sit with Anirban now?" asked Gargi's cousin after the school football match.
"He's on my team. He's the goalkeeper," Gargi said.
"But Dadi says his family eats different food, they have different gods. She says be careful."
Gargi shrugged. "He shares his luchi and aloo at lunch. It's nice. And his mum makes the same sweets as ours at Durga Puja."
"Really?"
"And he's scared of spiders, like me." Gargi laughed. "We have the same stupid jokes too."
"So he's not different?"
Gargi thought. "A bit. But mostly not. I was a little scared before. Now he's just Anirban."

What position does Anirban play on the team?
He's the goalkeeper.
How did Gargi's feelings about Anirban change?
Gargi was a little scared before, from what the family said, but now feels comfortable and friendly with Anirban.
What helped Gargi see past the differences she'd been told about?
Playing on the same team, sharing lunch and discovering common things like sweets, jokes and fear of spiders.
How might Gargi's cousin see Anirban now?
The cousin is surprised and curious, maybe starting to question what Dadi said.

Read this:

Bhaiya, you asked why I was so weird on Saturday. Okay. I'm Nilesh, I'm fifteen, and I'm a bit dramatic. Here's what happened.

I sent Tarun a message at four: "coming for cricket?" Blue ticks. No reply. Five o'clock, nothing. By six I'd worked it out. He's angry because I dropped his catch on Thursday. He's told Imran. Imran's told the whole group. They've made a new chat without me. On Monday nobody will sit with me at lunch.

Each step felt like a fact. I even started deciding where I'd sit alone.

At nine, Tarun called. "Sorry yaar, I read it on the bus and then we went to my nani's village, zero network." That's it. He hadn't even remembered the catch.

What gets me is how sure I was. I didn't know anything. I just had one blue tick and a lot of fear.

When did Tarun call Nilesh?
At nine, Tarun called.
Why did each step feel like a fact to Nilesh, even though it wasn't?
Nilesh was scared, and fear filled the silence with the worst explanations, linking them into a chain that seemed logical. The dropped catch gave the story something real to hang on.
What could Nilesh try next time a friend goes quiet?
Notice the chain as it starts and list other simple reasons for no reply, like travel or no network. Waiting a bit, or sending one light message, is better than planning where to sit alone.
How might Tarun have felt if Nilesh had skipped cricket and ignored him on Monday?
Tarun would probably have been confused and hurt, since he hadn't even remembered the catch. Nilesh's fear could have created the very distance Nilesh was afraid of.

Read this:

Dear Zainab Apa,
Eid in Leeds was not like home, but it wasn't sad either, so don't worry.
I woke early and made sheer khurma the way Ammi does, burning the vermicelli only a little. We video-called at noon, you remember, everyone shouting at once and Abbu's face too close to the camera. I cried after, just for a minute, missing the sound of the whole mohalla on Eid morning.
Then I took the leftovers to the common room in my building. Wanjiru from Kenya, Tom from Wales and the Polish girls upstairs came. None of them had tasted sheer khurma. Tom had three bowls.
I'm keeping Hyderabad in my kitchen, Apa, and making a little home here too. Both fit.
Your Rehana

What did Rehana make on Eid morning?
Sheer khurma, the way Ammi does.
Why did Rehana cry for a minute after the call?
Rehana was missing the sounds and togetherness of Eid morning at home, even though the call itself was joyful.
What did Rehana choose to do after crying, and how did it help?
Rehana took the leftovers to the common room and shared them with new friends, letting the longing turn into connection in Leeds.
How might Zainab Apa feel reading this letter?
Zainab Apa would likely feel relieved that Rehana isn't lonely, and proud that Ammi's recipe is making a home abroad.

metadata.subtype: Carrying home while building a new one [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

"So people think I'm restless. And fine, I am, a bit. My name's Vidya, I'm sixteen, and there's always a pen cap in my mouth. I tap my foot through every class. To study I need loud music, really loud, or my brain won't sit still. My best friend Nilesh is the opposite. At the school fest he wore ear defenders and ate only the plain parathas he brought from home. Some people laughed. But he knows himself. That's what we worked out together. We both have bodies that react strongly, just in different directions. So I carry a chewy bracelet instead of wrecking pens, and I ask to sit at the back so my tapping doesn't bother anyone. Nilesh plans his quiet corner before every event. It's not weird. It's a plan."

What did Nilesh bring from home to the school fest?
Plain parathas, and he wore ear defenders.
How does Vidya seem to feel about being called restless?
Vidya accepts it without shame and seems proud that Vidya and Nilesh understand themselves well enough to plan.
What choices does Vidya make to manage the need for movement?
Vidya carries a chewy bracelet instead of chewing pens and sits at the back so the tapping doesn't bother anyone.
How might the people who laughed at Nilesh see him if they heard Vidya?
They might see him as someone who knows what his body needs and plans for it, not as someone strange.

Read this:

I'm Bhavna. My brother Kunal is eight, and on Sunday he planned the whole colony kids' afternoon without asking anyone.
He stood on the bench by the swings and announced: "First cricket, because everyone loves cricket. Then chocolate ice cream from the cart, because that's everyone's favourite. Then we watch the robot film at our house."
Ishita said she wanted to skip. Two boys wanted hide-and-seek. Someone asked for mango, not chocolate. Nobody had seen the robot film, and one girl said robots scared her.
Kunal went red. He kept saying, "But it's the best," louder each time. Then he climbed down and walked home alone.
I'm not sure if he was angry or just embarrassed. At dinner he asked me, quietly, what my favourite ice cream was. I said butterscotch. He looked really surprised.

What did Kunal say they would do first?
First cricket, because everyone loves cricket.
How did Kunal feel when the other kids wanted different things, and what shows it?
Kunal felt upset and embarrassed, going red and saying "But it's the best" louder each time before walking home alone.
What small step by Kunal at dinner could help him next time?
Asking Bhavna about her favourite ice cream was a good start; asking friends what they like before planning would stop him from being caught out.
How might the other colony kids have felt when Kunal announced his plan?
They may have felt ignored, since nobody was asked, and some, like the girl scared of robots, may have felt uneasy saying no.

Read this:

Sudha, come here. I'll tell you why your Uma Nani still checks the garden before walking barefoot. When I was nine, I was picking guavas behind our house when I saw a snake curled under the tree, as thick as my wrist. I wanted to be brave. My brother would have poked it with a stick. But I thought, "I don't know this snake. If I'm wrong, I can't undo it. This is a grown-up problem." So I backed away, very slowly, and ran for my father. He came with a long bamboo pole and sent everyone inside. Then he called the old man from the next village who knew snakes. It was a cobra. I've never forgotten how right it felt to call for help.

How old was Uma when she saw the snake?
She was nine.
What was young Uma feeling as she backed away?
She was frightened but clear-headed, knowing she didn't understand this snake and that it was a grown-up problem.
What was the turning point in the story, and why was it right?
Choosing to back away and call her father instead of being brave alone, because a mistake with a snake couldn't be undone.
How might Uma's father have felt when she came running?
He was probably alarmed but proud she had come straight to him instead of trying it herself.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asks an adult when the problem is unsafe or too big [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Every day after school, when Imran walked past the village well, Madhav and his friends were waiting. “Here comes the crow,” they'd say, flapping their arms, and they blocked the path so he had to go the long way through the thorns. Yesterday Madhav said, “Tomorrow we'll throw you in the well.” Imran's hands shook all night. Today he didn't argue or pick up a stone, though he wanted to. He walked home the long way, past Salim Chacha's tea shop, where grown-ups always sat. At home he told his Dada everything, even the well. Dada put down his newspaper. “You did nothing wrong.” That evening, Dada walked to the headmaster's house, and then to Madhav's father.

What did Madhav's group say when Imran walked past the well?
“Here comes the crow,” flapping their arms.
What was Imran feeling after the threat about the well?
Imran was frightened, his hands shaking all night after being threatened.
Which of Imran's choices kept him safe?
He didn't retaliate, walked home past the tea shop where adults sat, and told his Dada everything, including the threat.
How did Dada respond to Imran?
Dada told him he did nothing wrong and that same evening went to the headmaster's house and to Madhav's father.

Read this:

When I moved to Delhi for college, I shared a one-room flat in Laxmi Nagar with my older brother Tushar. I'm Sunaina, and I'll admit it: with Tushar around, I never once worried about rent day or the water bill. He kept a notebook for it, dated and ruled. But he also had opinions about how I folded my dupatta, where my shoes went, why my books were on the bed. For months I said nothing and just seethed. Then one night I threw my shoes at the rack and said something awful. We didn't speak for two days. What finally worked was boring. I made two lists and showed him. Keep doing: the rent notebook. Just your preference: my dupatta. He read it twice and laughed. 'Fine. Your dupatta, your problem.'

Where did Sunaina and Tushar share a flat?
In a one-room flat in Laxmi Nagar, Delhi.
What was Sunaina feeling during the months of saying nothing?
Sunaina felt resentful, silently seething at the constant comments, until it burst out over the shoes.
Why did the two lists work better than the outburst?
They named plainly what was a real need, the rent notebook, and what was only preference, without attacking Tushar.
How might Tushar have felt reading the lists?
He seemed relieved and amused, laughing, perhaps glad that his careful notebook was valued.

Read this:

"Charu, you cancelled again? That's three times this month."
"Sorry. Bad day."
"You could've said more than two words. I'd booked the tickets."
"I said sorry, Sid."
"It feels like you don't care anymore."
"That's not it."
"Then what is it?"
"My back. It's been bad since the accident, and some days two hours in a cinema seat is too much. By evening I've got nothing left, not even words."
"Why didn't you tell me it was that bad?"
"Because I'm tired of being the sick friend. People get annoyed."
"I was annoyed. I thought it was about me."
"It's never about you. I just run out of battery."
"Okay. Next time, a film at my place on the laptop? You can lie on the floor if you want."
"I'd like that," Charu said, and for the first time that week, Siddharth heard a smile.

What had Siddharth booked?
The tickets.
What was Siddharth feeling when Charu cancelled?
Siddharth felt hurt and annoyed, thinking Charu didn't care anymore.
What did Siddharth do that kept the friendship kind?
Siddharth asked what was really going on, listened, and suggested a plan that fits the pain, like a film on the laptop at home.
Why has Charu been so curt?
Charu is drained by constant back pain and tired of being the sick friend, so by evening there is no energy left for words.

messages.content:
Read this:

Thomas had started with "I'm only saying this because I care" and was now eight minutes into a talk about sleep, screens and his own board exams in 1998. Jomon sat on the edge of the sofa in their Thrissur flat, jaw clamped, staring at the ceiling fan. Every sentence landed as another rule. When Thomas paused for breath, Jomon muttered, "Can I go now, Pappa?" and went. Thomas stood in the hallway, stung. Mariamma, folding clothes, shrugged. "You gave him a sermon. He asked you for nothing." The next evening Jomon was frowning at a chemistry worksheet. Thomas leaned on the doorframe and this time said only, "Do you want a tip, or should I just bring tea?" Jomon glanced up. "Tea. And... maybe one tip. About the mole thing." Thomas kept it to two sentences. Jomon actually wrote them down.

How long had Thomas been talking when Jomon asked to go?
Thomas was eight minutes into the talk.
What was Jomon feeling during the eight-minute talk?
Jomon felt lectured and controlled, clamping his jaw and staring at the fan. Underneath there may also have been tiredness or a little guilt about screens, not only annoyance.
What changed in how Thomas offered advice the next evening?
Thomas kept it brief, asked what help Jomon wanted, a tip or tea, and stopped at two sentences, so the advice was invited instead of imposed.
What was it like for Thomas when Jomon walked out?
Thomas felt stung, since he meant the talk as care; Mariamma's comment helped him see it had sounded like a sermon.
'Main paise bacha raha hoon nayi cycle ke liye' English mein?
Say: "I'm saving up for a new bicycle." "Save up for" means keeping money aside to buy something later.

Last summer in Seville, cousin Ulla had won hide-and-seek by squeezing into Grandma's big wardrobe. This year Pablo remembered. When his friend Mateo began counting, Pablo ran straight to the wardrobe, pulled the door almost shut and crouched among the coats. Mateo, who hadn't been there last summer, searched the kitchen and the garden. Ulla walked past and winked. Pablo stayed hidden until Mateo gave up.

Where did Pablo crouch?
He crouched among the coats in the wardrobe.
What was Pablo feeling as he stayed hidden?
He was probably excited and pleased that Ulla's trick was working for him.
What else could Pablo try when playing with Ulla?
He would need a new spot, because Ulla knows the wardrobe trick and would look there first.
How does the wardrobe trick look to Ulla?
Ulla recognises her own trick and is amused, winking because she knows Mateo won't guess.

In the computer lab at the engineering college in Warangal, Ganga ma'am was explaining loops on the big screen. Farhan had three windows open: the code editor, the class chat and a live cricket score. He typed along with her, replied to a joke in the chat, checked the score, came back. "I'm keeping up with everything," he told the boy next to him. At the end, Ganga ma'am set a ten-minute exercise: write a loop to print a times table. Farhan stared at his editor. His code had half of her example and three typos. He couldn't remember why the loop stopped. The boy next to him, who had only the editor open, was already done. Farhan closed the cricket window, then the chat, and started again from the first line.

What exercise did Ganga ma'am set at the end?
Write a loop to print a times table.
What does Farhan closing the cricket window and the chat suggest?
It suggests he realised the switching had cost him, and felt frustrated enough to try again with his full attention.
What turning point does the exercise give Farhan, and what could he do from now on?
Being stuck while his neighbour finished showed the cost of switching; he could keep only the editor open in lectures and check chat and scores afterwards.
How might Ganga ma'am see Farhan during the lecture?
She may have seen a student typing busily and assumed he was keeping up, without knowing how much of her example he was missing.

Wednesday
Physio again. Good news: the ankle bends further. I've been telling myself "it's healing, it's healing" every morning, and honestly it makes the exercises easier. Varun keeps saying, "Just think positive, Pema, pain is mostly in the mind." Some of it, maybe. But the swelling in the evening is still there, and that's not my mind. So today I didn't just smile and say fine. I told the physio about the swelling and that I'd been worried it was something more. I asked her what's normal and what isn't. She took it seriously, pressed around the bone and said she'll ask the doctor to look again. I left feeling hopeful AND looked after. Both. Varun can think positive for himself.
Pema

What was still there in the evenings?
The swelling was still there.
How did Pema feel leaving the physio, and why?
Pema felt hopeful and looked after, because the positive thoughts made the exercises easier and the physio took the swelling seriously instead of brushing it off. 🙂
What turning point did Pema choose at today's session?
Instead of smiling and saying "fine", Pema told the physio about the swelling and the worry and asked what's normal, so hope didn't replace proper care.
Why might Varun say "pain is mostly in the mind"?
Varun probably means to encourage, having seen that attitude can help, but can't see the evening swelling, so may not notice where hope ends and a real symptom begins.

Since his father left for work in the city, eight-year-old Manoj had grown very quiet. At the village well, at the shop, at night, he asked Jaya the same thing: "Will Papa come back? What if he doesn't?" At first she said, "Of course he will, don't ask again." He asked twice as often. Then one evening, while shelling peas on the step, she asked softly, "What makes you think he won't?" Manoj's lip wobbled. "Raju's father went and never came." Jaya put the peas down. She didn't laugh or scold. She called his father on the phone that night, and his teacher the next day. Together they made a calendar on the kitchen wall with call days ticked in red and the day Papa comes home circled. Each morning Manoj ticked one box himself.

What did Jaya and Manoj make on the kitchen wall?
A calendar with call days ticked in red and the day Papa comes home circled.
Why was Manoj so worried his father wouldn't come back?
Raju's father went to work away and never came back, so Manoj feared the same.
Which change in Jaya's approach helped?
She stopped brushing off his question and asked gently what made him think so, then made a plan with his father and teacher.
What might it be like for Manoj to tick a box on the calendar himself each morning?
It likely makes him feel calmer and more in control, because he can see the calls and the day Papa comes home getting closer.
Write me a haiku on a monkey sitting on a roof.

A monkey sits still
Watching the street from the roof
Then it takes my fruit

Monday. Farhan asked Manoj why he'd agreed to host his whole office team on Saturday without checking. Manoj sat on the sofa, arms crossed, eyes on the floor. Farhan asked again, louder. Nothing. "Say something!" he shouted, and Manoj walked into the bedroom and shut the door. Farhan slept badly, feeling locked out.
Wednesday. Over dinner Manoj said, "When you get loud, my head fills up. I can't find a single word. It's not that I don't care."
Farhan put down his spoon. "It looks like you've left the room even when you're sitting there."
"I know. I have to be able to tell you when I'm flooding."
The next Sunday, the Saturday plan came up again and voices rose. Manoj uncrossed his arms. "I'm flooding. Back in thirty minutes?"
Farhan breathed out. "Okay. Thirty."
At half past, Manoj came back with a list.

What did Manoj do on Monday when Farhan shouted?
Manoj walked into the bedroom and shut the door.
What was Farhan feeling on Monday night?
Farhan felt shut out and hurt, locked out of the conversation and then the room, which is why he slept badly.
What small step helped them next time?
Manoj named what was happening with the words "I'm flooding" and asked for thirty minutes, and Farhan agreed, so the silence became a break with a return.
How does Manoj experience the arguments?
Manoj feels overwhelmed when voices rise, his head fills up and he cannot find words, so his silence is not coldness but overload.

Read this:

Monday: By 7.40 Arohi had said 'Tushar, brush your teeth' five times. He was building a paper plane. She shouted, he cried, and they both left the flat angry. On the bus to work she stared out of the window, aching with love and frustration.
Thursday evening: She and Tushar drew a morning chart together: a toothbrush, a shirt, a bag, a shoe. 'You tick, I don't shout,' she said. She also called her sister and just talked for half an hour.
The next Monday: Tushar stood at the chart in his vest, ticking boxes. 'Look, Mumma, three already!' 'You're working hard,' Arohi said, and meant it. They left on time. He even had his plane.

What was Tushar building instead of brushing his teeth?
A paper plane.
What was Arohi feeling on the bus to work on Monday?
She was aching with love and frustration after a morning of shouting and tears.
What choices on Thursday made the next Monday calmer?
Drawing a picture chart with Tushar so he could tick steps without her shouting, and calling her sister for support.
How might Tushar feel ticking boxes on the chart?
He may feel proud and in charge of his own morning, especially when Arohi says he's working hard.

It happened slowly. First the cricket group stopped saving me a place on the bus. Then, when I walked up to them at break, they'd go quiet, look at each other, and burst out laughing at something I wasn't part of.
I kept trying for a month. I laughed along to jokes I didn't get. That was the worst part, pretending.
Then one Tuesday I just turned round and walked away. My face was burning, but I didn't beg.
That evening at dinner I told Papa everything. He put down his roti and said, "Vaibhav, I'm glad you told me. Groups like that often need someone outside to feel inside. It's not about you." He came to school the next week to talk to my class teacher too.
I joined the chess club after that. A boy called Siddharth taught me an opening. We've been friends since.

How long did Vaibhav keep trying with the cricket group?
For a month.
How did Vaibhav feel during the month of trying to fit back in?
Vaibhav felt hurt and humiliated, and pretending to laugh at jokes Vaibhav didn't understand felt worst of all.
Which choices helped Vaibhav move on?
Walking away without begging, telling Papa the same day, and joining the chess club where Vaibhav found a new friend.
How does Papa see the cricket group's behaviour?
Papa sees it as the group's own insecurity, needing an outsider to feel close, rather than anything wrong with Vaibhav.
Where does my classmate Ritu live?
I don't know, because I can't see a private person's address and shouldn't share one. If you need it for an invitation, ask Ritu directly.

Kamal, your new game has no end, so everyone just runs till they fight. Let your Kalyani Paati tell you something. When I was ten, in our street in Thanjavur, we made up games every evening, and they always fell apart. One day I said, 'Wait. How does anyone win?' Nobody knew. So we decided that first: five flags, made from old saree bits, hidden at each end. First team to bring home all five wins. Only then did we make the other rules: you carry one flag at a time, and you can be caught only on the other side. That game lasted all summer, and we even taught it to my cousins from Madurai.

What were the flags made from?
Old saree bits.
How might young Kalyani have felt when the games kept falling apart?
She was likely frustrated and puzzled, which led her to ask how anyone wins.
What was the key choice in the story, and why did it help?
Deciding the goal first, five flags, so every other rule could be built to serve that end.
How did the other children in the street experience the new game?
They got a game with a clear finish that lasted all summer, good enough to teach to the cousins from Madurai.

metadata.subtype: Approach: deciding the goal and how someone wins first [Thinking]

I share an office with Zeenat, who handles incident reports at the warehouse, and yesterday I watched her work. A forklift had clipped a shelf, and Thomas, the loader, came in shaking. Zeenat didn't ask, "Was the driver speeding?" She asked, "What did you see, from the start?" and typed while he talked, stopping only to check times. When Thomas said, "I'm sure he was going to hit me," she said, "That fear sounds real. Let's write what you saw and what you felt, separately." Within the hour she had saved his account, dated and signed, before canteen gossip could reshape it. I can't know what she was thinking, but she seemed calm and careful the whole time.

What did Zeenat ask Thomas first?
"What did you see, from the start?"
How was Thomas feeling when he came in?
Thomas was frightened and shaken, sure the driver was going to hit him.
Which of Zeenat's choices protected the account?
She avoided a leading question about speeding, recorded his words within the hour before gossip could reshape them, and kept what he saw separate from what he felt.
How might the forklift driver be affected by Zeenat's approach?
The driver gets a fair record based on what was seen, rather than a story shaped by fear or canteen talk.

I tried this board game for the first time yesterday, and I loved it.
Why: "For the first time" is a fixed phrase that needs "the".

Imran sat on the steps of the engineering college in Bengaluru with two forms. One for staying in mechanical. One for switching to architecture, the subject he'd drawn in the margins of every notebook.
His mother had said, "Mechanical is safe." His drawing teacher, Ganga ma'am from school, had said, "You come alive when you sketch."
He had spent a month on it: sitting in architecture studio classes, talking to seniors, looking at the fees and the extra year. He was scared. Architecture meant starting again, alone.
He called Ganga ma'am. "What if I regret it?"
"Then you'll learn from it. But what will you regret more?"
Imran signed the architecture form and sat very still, heart pounding.

What had Imran drawn in the margins of every notebook?
Architecture, the subject he had drawn in every notebook.
How did Imran feel after signing the architecture form?
He felt scared but determined, sitting still with his heart pounding.
What did Imran do well before deciding?
He spent a month testing the choice by sitting in studio classes, talking to seniors and checking fees and time.
How might Imran's mother feel about his choice?
She may feel worried about safety, but could come to accept it if she sees how much it means to him.

I took what Joe gave me, and found it to be the crumpled play-bill of a small metropolitan theatre, announcing the first appearance, in that very week, of "the celebrated Provincial Amateur of Roscian renown, whose unique performance in the highest tragic walk of our National Bard has lately occasioned so great a sensation in local dramatic circles."

What does Joe hand over, and what does it announce?

A crumpled play-bill of a small theatre. It announces the first appearance that very week of a celebrated provincial amateur, praised for a unique performance in the highest tragic walk of the national bard.

Zubin, you call your mentor before choosing a shirt. Sit down. Your Nirmala aunty was worse.

At twenty-four I joined a publishing house, and Mrs. Anand took me under her wing. She was so wise that I stopped thinking. Which manuscript to read first? I asked her. Whether to take a day off? I asked her. Once I even asked which pen to buy.

One day she was away in Delhi, and a writer called wanting an answer on his contract by evening. I sat there frozen, sweating, terrified of choosing wrong.

When Mrs. Anand came back, I expected praise for waiting. Instead she said, very gently, "Nirmala, I don't want to be your brain. I want to be your sounding board."

That was the turning point. From then on I made small decisions myself and brought her only the big ones, with my own view first. "Here's what I think. What am I missing?" She smiled every time.

Where was Mrs. Anand when the writer called?
She was away in Delhi.
How did young Nirmala feel when she had to answer the writer alone?
She felt frozen and terrified, sweating with fear of choosing wrong.
What was the turning point in Nirmala's story?
Mrs. Anand told her she wanted to be a sounding board, not her brain, so Nirmala began making small decisions herself and bringing her own view first.
How did Mrs. Anand seem to feel about Nirmala's dependence?
Mrs. Anand seemed gently concerned, wanting Nirmala to trust her own judgment rather than rely on her for everything.

"Sanjaya continued, 'Hearing these words of Radheya, king Duryodhana then, accompanied by his brothers, O monarch, proceeded towards Drona's car. The noise there was deafening, of Pandava warriors returned to the fight on their cars drawn by excellent steeds of diverse hue, all actuated by the desire of slaying Drona alone.'"

Answer from the text. Where does Duryodhana go after hearing Radheya's words, and what is the scene there?
Duryodhana goes with his brothers toward Drona's car. The noise there is deafening from Pandava warriors returned to the fight on cars drawn by excellent horses, all wanting to kill Drona alone.

On Holi morning, the colony courtyard in Jaipur was wet and pink. Arohi, twenty-two months, toddled after the bigger children, her white frock streaked green. Her foot slid on a puddle. She swayed, flung both arms out wide, bent her knees, and stayed up. Her mother, Anjali, one step behind, let out a breath and didn't pick her up. Arohi looked back at her, surprised at herself, then carried on, arms still out like wings.

What was the courtyard like on Holi morning?
Wet and pink.
What did Arohi's look back at her mother suggest?
Arohi seemed surprised and a little proud that she hadn't fallen.
How did Anjali support Arohi's balance on the slippery courtyard?
She stayed one step behind, close enough to help, but let Arohi catch herself instead of picking her up.
What was it like for Anjali when Arohi slid?
Anjali felt a moment of fear, then relief, choosing to trust Arohi's steadiness.
What time did I wake up today?
I can't tell, as I have no way of seeing your day. If you note it down each morning, you can look back.

Divyansh, thanks for having me on. People ask about the job I didn't get, so here it is.
Final round, three people on the panel. Technical questions went well. Then one of them looked at my CV and said, "Aparna... and your surname is? What community is that?" Another asked, "Your family is vegetarian?" None of it had anything to do with the role.
I remember my face going hot and my mind going blank. I answered. I didn't get the job.
Afterwards I did three things. I wrote down every question and the time. I spoke to my college placement cell, and two other students said the same panel had asked them the same things. And we went together to a legal-aid clinic to understand what we could do.
The company changed its panel guidelines after our complaint. I still didn't get that job. But Aparna made some noise, and that counts.

What did one panel member ask about Aparna's family?
Another asked, "Your family is vegetarian?"
What was Aparna feeling during those questions?
Aparna felt humiliated and shocked, with a mind gone blank at questions that had nothing to do with the role.
What did Aparna do afterwards that was wise?
Aparna wrote down every question, found other students who had been asked the same things, and went with them to a legal-aid clinic.
How might the two other students have felt when Aparna spoke up?
They were probably relieved that someone named the problem, and less alone in their own experience.

"Harsha, you think you talk fast when you're nervous? Let your Urmila Mausi tell you something.
When I was sixteen, I was chosen to read the news on All-School Radio. I was so scared that I read the whole page in two minutes. My teacher told me afterward that nobody understood a word.
I cried in the washroom. Then she came and found me. She said, 'Breathe out before you start. Then pause at every full stop, like you're stepping on stones in a river.'
Next week I tried it. Pause, breathe, next sentence. I didn't just sound calmer. I actually felt calmer, and I could hear my own voice for the first time.
So tomorrow, before your presentation, remember: stepping stones."

What was Urmila chosen to read?
The news on All-School Radio.
What was young Urmila feeling when she cried in the washroom?
She felt embarrassed and disappointed after rushing the news because of nerves.
What choice inside the story helped Urmila?
Her teacher chose to come find her and teach her to breathe out and pause at full stops, which helped her feel and sound calmer.
How might the teacher have felt when Urmila read calmly the next week?
The teacher probably felt proud and pleased that the advice worked.
Why does a bell go on ringing for a while after it has been struck?

The metal keeps shaking for a while after the blow. Because the blow sets the whole metal body vibrating and the vibration only dies down slowly, the shaking air carries the sound to our ears for some time.

At the community centre playgroup, Sabina had cried and shouted for ten minutes because her painted kite had to stay until it dried. Now she was quiet, hiccupping. Abbu, who had come to fetch her, sat on the low bench. Sabina edged closer, peeking at him, then climbed into his lap and hid her face in his shirt. "I said you're a bad Abbu," she whispered. "Am I still your Sabina?" Abbu held her close. "Always. Even when you're angry." Sabina's shoulders dropped. Jahnavi Ma'am, packing away paints, smiled. "The kite will be dry tomorrow, Sabina."

Why did Sabina's painted kite have to stay at the playgroup?
It had to stay until it dried.
How did Sabina feel as she hid her face in Abbu's shirt?
She felt ashamed of calling him a bad Abbu and relieved to be held, needing to know she was still loved.
Why was Abbu's answer the right one at this stage?
By saying 'Always. Even when you're angry', he showed her that her anger had not broken their bond.
How might Jahnavi Ma'am feel watching them?
Jahnavi Ma'am seems warm and pleased to see Sabina comforted, and adds a reassuring word about the kite.

Monday, the week of Navroz. Ira said the fire temple was "weird" because she wasn't allowed inside. Zubin went quiet and didn't share his chips at break.
Wednesday. Ira asked him why he was sulking. Zubin said, "It's not weird. It's just ours." He explained that the fire has been kept burning for years and years, and only Parsis go in. Ira said, "That's not fair to me." Zubin shrugged: "Your family's puja room isn't for everyone either."
Ira thought about that all afternoon.
Saturday. Zubin's mother invited her for Navroz lunch. Ira sat outside the temple gate while they prayed, then ate sali boti and falooda at their table. "Thanks for waiting," Zubin said. She said, "It's your place. I get it now."

What did Ira eat at Zubin's Navroz lunch?
Ira ate sali boti and falooda.
Why did Zubin go quiet and not share his chips on Monday?
Zubin felt hurt and offended that Ira called his fire temple weird.
Which comparison helped Ira understand, and why?
Zubin compared the temple to her family's puja room, which let her see the rule from her own experience.
How might Zubin's mother see Ira waiting at the gate?
His mother might feel respected and warm towards Ira, seeing she honoured their custom instead of complaining.

It was the last day of the summer holidays and the last bus to the village left in fifteen minutes. Pema had just enough money for one thing from the market stall: a skipping rope or a jigsaw puzzle of a tiger. Her sister Vandana tapped her watch. "Quick, Pema!" Pema grabbed the rope. On the bus, Vandana said, "The tiger puzzle was nice." Pema said, "Puzzles are boring. You just sit. Skipping is way better. I'm glad I didn't get the stupid puzzle." She said "stupid puzzle" three more times before they reached home. That evening their neighbour's son was doing the same tiger puzzle on his veranda. Pema skipped loudly beside him, counting out loud. "Two hundred! See? Much better than a puzzle." But she kept glancing at the half-finished tiger.

What were the two things Pema could choose between?
A skipping rope or a jigsaw puzzle of a tiger.
Why did Pema keep calling it the "stupid puzzle"?
Pema felt uneasy about the rushed choice, and running down the puzzle made her feel sure she chose right.
What could Vandana say to help Pema relax about the choice?
Vandana could say both were nice and that choosing one doesn't make the other bad, maybe offering to borrow a puzzle sometime.
How might the neighbour's son see Pema skipping loudly beside him?
He might be puzzled or amused, not knowing she was trying to prove her choice was better.

messages.content:
Can you fix my sentence? She is senior than me by two years.
One more thing: why do we put a bandage over a small cut?

1. Say it this way: She is senior to me by two years. Why: "senior" and "junior" take "to", not "than".
2. It keeps the cut clean and covered. Because a cover keeps dirt and germs out and stops the cut from being bumped.
