"You're limping," Uday said, as Vinita came in from her run.
"It's nothing. My knee's been clicking."
"Since when?"
"Since last week." She sat down carefully. "Day forty-two of my streak. I'm not breaking it."
"Vinita, you winced on the stairs."
"Everyone's knees hurt when they run."
The next morning she ran again. Uday heard her come back slower than usual and put ice on it without saying anything.
Four days later she couldn't bend her leg at all. At the physiotherapist's that evening, she came out with a brace and a printout.
"Well?" Uday asked.
"No running for at least six weeks. Exercises only." She threw the brace on the sofa. "Forty-six days. And now zero."
"If you'd rested last week?"
She didn't answer. She just stared at the printout.

What did Vinita bring home from the physiotherapist?
She came out with a brace and a printout.
What was Vinita feeling when she refused to break her streak?
She felt stubbornly determined and proud of forty-two days, which made her brush off the pain.
What approach would have protected both Vinita's knee and her habit?
Resting and getting the knee checked when it first clicked would have cost a few days, not six weeks.
How does Uday feel watching this happen?
Uday seems worried from the start, noticing the limp and the wince, and quietly helps with ice even though she won't listen.

metadata.subtype: Approach: push through pain to keep the streak [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: Kunal posted an angry thread about the city's new water tariff: 'Another way to loot the middle class.' Samir, his friend from college, replied under it: 'Did you read why they're raising it?' Kunal hadn't. Saturday: He went with Samir to the municipal public hearing at the town hall. An official explained that old pipes were leaking almost a third of the water, the extra charge would fund repairs, and low-income households would get a free basic amount. A woman from a colony near the river said her area got water once in three days. Kunal realised the trade-offs were real: more cost for some, better supply for others. He asked how the repair money would be tracked. Three weeks later: He and Samir had joined the ward water committee and were helping residents file leak complaints online. His next post was a how-to guide.

What was the extra water charge meant to fund?
Repairs to old pipes that were leaking almost a third of the water.
How did Kunal's feelings about the tariff change at the public hearing?
His anger gave way to understanding that the tariff involved real trade-offs, more cost for some and better supply for others, not just a scheme to loot people.
How did Kunal move from anger to constructive participation?
He listened to the reasons, asked how the repair money would be tracked, then joined the ward committee and helped residents file complaints.
How might the woman from the colony near the river see the tariff?
As a possible way to finally get regular water, since her area got supply only once in three days.
Is "my cousin and I" okay as the subject? My cousin and I walked to the lake after breakfast.

This is already correct.
Why: "I" is the subject pronoun, and putting the other person first is the usual polite order.
What is the avaroha of Raga Madhmad Sarang?
The avaroha of Raga Madhmad Sarang is: S' N P M R S.
She asked me to not to go. Please correct.
The correct sentence is: "She asked me not to go." Why: after "asked me", "not to" comes before the verb and "to" is not repeated.
To "to not go" bolna galat hai?
It is understood, and some people use it, but "not to go" is the usual and safer form.
Our teacher Mrs. Kapoor is at home with flu. Write a get-well card message from the class (Class 4A), about 45 words, with no medical advice.

Dear Mrs. Kapoor,
We hope you are feeling better soon. We miss you very much in class. Please rest well, and do not worry about us. We will work hard while you are away. Take care and come back soon!
Your students, Class 4A

Read this:

Sat. 11:15 pm. Heard a scream from the street below the flat. Maria and I froze mid-chat. My first thought was a horror film someone was streaming. Then it came again, higher, and a voice shouting "Leave me alone!" My legs wanted to run downstairs. Maria held my arm and said, "Do not go alone." We called the emergency number and told them the address and what we heard. Then we watched from the window. Two neighbours came out and a police vehicle arrived. It was a quarrel that got out of hand. Nobody was badly hurt. I am still shaky, but I am glad we called.
- Simran

What did Simran and Maria do after the second scream?
They called the emergency number and gave the address and what they heard.
What did Simran feel when the scream came again, and how do you know?
Simran felt alarmed and wanted to run downstairs, and the first guess of a film gave way to worry once the words "Leave me alone!" were heard.
Which choice was wise, and why?
Calling the emergency number instead of going down alone was wise, because trained people could reach the street safely.
How might Maria have felt when Simran wanted to run down?
Maria was probably worried about Simran's safety, which is why Maria held the arm and said not to go alone.

Read this:

Dear Ira,
You start at the flood relief camp next week, so here's what I wish someone had told me last year.
I went in thinking I was there to save people. I photographed children holding the biscuits we handed out and posted them with long captions about "giving back". A woman at the camp, Shanthi, quietly asked me to delete the one with her son. She said, "He is not your story." I have never felt so ashamed.
After that I changed. I asked the camp coordinator what was actually needed, not what I wanted to do. Mostly it was dull: sorting donated clothes by size, writing names in the medicine register, filling water cans. Nobody saw it. It helped more than any photo.
So: ask first, listen longer, do the boring jobs, and never post a face without permission.
Proud of you for going.
Sunaina Didi

What did Shanthi ask Sunaina to delete?
The photo with her son.
What was Sunaina feeling when Shanthi said 'He is not your story'?
Sunaina felt deeply ashamed, realising the posts had used people's hardship for her own image.
What changed in how Sunaina volunteered afterwards?
She asked the coordinator what was needed and did unglamorous jobs like sorting clothes and filling water cans, without posting faces.
How might Shanthi have felt seeing her son's photo online?
Shanthi probably felt exposed and hurt that her son's hardship had become someone else's display.

Read this:

Sumit had spent the whole morning at the Kolkata zoo with his uncle Abhinav: elephants, a roaring tiger, candyfloss and a big crowd. Back in the flat, Abhinav said, "Shall we go to the park now?" Sumit threw himself on the rug and howled. Abhinav sat down instead. Sumit crawled over with his old cloth elephant, climbed into his lap and sucked his thumb. Soon he was murmuring, "Big tiger. Roar," his eyes half closed.

What did Sumit bring when he crawled over?
His old cloth elephant.
Why did Sumit howl when Abhinav suggested the park?
He was tired and overloaded after the busy zoo morning, and one more outing felt like too much.
What did Abhinav get right after the howl?
He dropped the plan and sat down, letting Sumit rest with a familiar toy and closeness.
How might Abhinav have felt when Sumit murmured about the tiger?
He probably felt tender and relieved, seeing Sumit calm and still turning the day over.

metadata.subtype: Toddler recharging after a big day [Actor]

messages.content: Sentence: 'First you boil the milk and then you put the sugar in it.' Ok for recipe?
It is correct, but recipes usually use short commands: "Boil the milk. Add the sugar and stir." Leave out "you" and start each step with a verb.
I'd like to start sketching but my drawings look childish.
Everyone starts there. Sketching is a skill that improves through regular practice, and early drawings often look rough.
What should I practise first?
Begin with simple shapes like circles, boxes and cylinders, and try to draw everyday objects as a mix of those shapes. Look closely and draw what you see, not what you expect.
How often should I practise?
Short sessions on most days work better than one long one a week. Even ten minutes helps. Keep your old sketches so you can see your progress.

Read this:

I'm Sunaina, and I teach in the classroom next to Nazia's. On Tuesday the power went out in the middle of her Class 8 science lesson, which she had built entirely around a projector video. I was watching through the glass door. For a second she just stood there. Then she pulled the curtains wide, handed out rulers, and turned the whole thing into an experiment with shadows on the wall. Twenty minutes later the principal walked in and announced the unit test was moved up to Friday. Nazia nodded, wrote 'Friday' on the board, and changed the homework on the spot to revision. She didn't complain once. I would have. I don't know whether she felt panicked inside, but her voice stayed the same the whole time.

What was Nazia's lesson built around?
A projector video.
What might Nazia's brief pause when the power went out suggest?
It may show a moment of surprise or worry before she adjusted, though Sunaina can't know what she felt inside.
How could other teachers build this kind of flexibility?
Keep a simple backup activity for each lesson and practise adjusting plans calmly when something changes.
How might the Class 8 students have experienced the change?
They probably enjoyed the unexpected shadow experiment, and their teacher's calm made the test news easier to take. 🙂

He took it. "You give it up very gleefully," said he; "I don't quite understand your light-heartedness, because I cannot tell what employment you propose to yourself as a substitute for the one you are relinquishing. What aim, what purpose, what ambition in life have you now?"

Using nothing beyond this text, what puzzles him about the speaker's light-heartedness?
He cannot tell what employment the speaker plans in place of the one being given up, and he asks what aim, purpose or ambition lies ahead.

Here is a short passage from Great Expectations. What is the narrator sure of after seeing the housekeeper?

Only twice more did the housekeeper reappear, and then her stay in the room was very short, and Mr. Jaggers was sharp with her. But her hands were Estella's hands, and her eyes were Estella's eyes, and if she had reappeared a hundred times I could have been neither more sure nor less sure that my conviction was the truth.
He is sure that her hands and eyes are Estella's hands and eyes. He feels so certain that seeing her many more times would not change his mind.

Read this:

Anand: did you tell them?
Pradeep: tell who what
Anand: the whole football group knows i write poems. someone sent me a heart and "roses are red" in the team group
Anand: only you knew. i showed you on the terrace
Pradeep: …
Pradeep: i didn't mean for it to spread
Pradeep: sameer was asking about you and i just said it. everyone laughed and i felt like i was finally in their circle
Pradeep: it was stupid
Anand: i trusted you with that
Anand: i'm not going to practice tomorrow
Pradeep: please come. i'll tell them it's my fault and to lay off
Anand: that doesn't undo it
Pradeep: i know
Pradeep: i'm really sorry. i'll say it in person too
Anand: whatever
Pradeep: i'll wait at the gate at 6

What secret had Anand shown Pradeep on the terrace?
Anand writes poems.
Why did Pradeep tell the group about the poems?
Pradeep wanted to feel included and felt a thrill of being in their circle when everyone laughed, which Pradeep now sees as stupid.
What is Pradeep trying to do to repair the damage?
Pradeep apologises, offers to tell the group it's Pradeep's fault, and plans to say sorry in person at the gate.
How does Anand feel after the secret spreads?
Anand feels betrayed and exposed, so much that Anand doesn't want to go to practice.

Read this:

Dear Rukmini,
I need to tell you something before you hear it from anyone else, and I need you to read to the end.
For three months I've been the person you message at one in the morning, and two, and three. I wanted to be. I thought if I answered every time, you'd be okay, and nobody else had to know how bad it's been. I didn't tell anyone, not once.
But I'm falling apart. I barely sleep. I failed two unit tests. And you're not better; you're still where you were in June, and you still haven't talked to anyone who actually knows how to help. That's partly on me, because I let myself be enough when I'm not.
So tonight I told my mother everything. She called your mother straight away, and they are talking now, while I write this. Tomorrow the counsellor will see you.
I'm still your friend. I'm just not your only one any more.
Jatin

How long has Jatin been answering Rukmini's late-night messages?
For three months.
How is Jatin feeling as he writes the letter?
Jatin is exhausted and guilty, falling apart from lack of sleep and feeling responsible that Rukmini hasn't got real help.
What should Jatin have done back in June?
Told a parent or the counsellor early, so Rukmini got professional help while Jatin stayed a friend rather than the only support.
How might Rukmini feel reading this letter?
Rukmini may feel hurt or betrayed at first, but also cared for, and less alone once adults are involved.

metadata.subtype: Approach: trying to fix everything alone [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

School counsellor note. Dolma, Class 11. Self-referred, first session.
Dolma said she decided about two weeks ago that she wants to end things with Anirban, her boyfriend of five months. She hasn't told him. "He's not a bad person. I just don't feel it any more."
She listed reasons to wait: his birthday is next week; their friends are all in one group and "everyone will take sides"; she's scared he'll cry at school. Meanwhile, she said, he has been planning a surprise for their six-month mark. She twisted her sleeve while saying this and looked close to tears.
We talked about how delaying can feel kind but may add hurt, since Anirban is still hoping and planning. We discussed choosing a private time, face to face, and short, honest words. She wants to tell him after his birthday but before the six-month date. Will check in next week.

How long has Dolma been with Anirban?
Anirban has been her boyfriend of five months.
Why has Dolma delayed telling Anirban?
Dolma is afraid of hurting him, of friends taking sides and of him crying at school, so waiting feels kinder.
What turning point did the counsellor help Dolma see?
That the delay is adding hurt while Anirban plans a surprise; a private, face-to-face talk with short, honest words soon would be kinder.
How might Anirban feel if he learns Dolma decided weeks earlier?
Anirban might feel foolish and more hurt, realising he was planning a surprise for a relationship that had already ended in Dolma's mind.

Read this:

Dear Tarun,

I'm writing because I find it easier to say this without watching your face. You told me about the affair three weeks ago. Since then I've been angry every morning and hopeful every night, and I don't know which one is telling the truth. You say you want to rebuild, and part of me wants that too.

So here is what I need. Full honesty, including the answers I don't like. Time, without being asked how I'm doing every day. And your patience if I go cold.

I also want you to know that I might decide our marriage can't be saved. If I do, it won't mean I didn't love you or that I gave up too easily.

I'll give you my answer when I have one.

Nilesh

How long ago did Tarun tell Nilesh about the affair?
Three weeks ago.
What two feelings does Nilesh describe, and how does Nilesh feel about them?
Anger every morning and hope every night. Nilesh does not know which one is telling the truth.
What conditions does Nilesh set, and why are they reasonable?
Full honesty, time without daily check-ins, and patience with coldness. They give Nilesh a way to judge whether trust can grow again without rushing.
How might Tarun react on reading that Nilesh may decide the marriage cannot be saved?
Tarun may feel afraid or sad, but the letter also says that choice would not mean Nilesh didn't love Tarun, which may make it easier to hear.

Read this:

Navratri, day one. Indu told herself she must win the colony drawing contest like last year. She stayed up late colouring. Her little sister Sabina asked her to come and dance garba. "No. I must practise. I should be the best."
Day four. The results were out. Indu came third. She went home and hid in the cupboard. She was not supposed to cry. Crying was for babies. But she did. Then she felt worse for crying.
Day nine. Sabina came and sat with her while she was drawing again. "Why are you always sad when you're not first?" Indu said, "Because I should be." "Says who?" Indu thought. "I don't know." Sabina pulled her to the garba circle. Indu danced, messily. She didn't win anything. She laughed anyway, and for the first time that festival, she didn't feel bad.

What place did Indu get in the colony drawing contest?
Indu came third.
Why did Indu feel worse after crying in the cupboard?
Indu felt ashamed, because her rule said she should never cry, so breaking it added guilt to the sadness.
What helped Indu ease up by day nine?
Sabina asked who made the rule, and pulled her into garba, where she could enjoy something without needing to be first.
How might Sabina have felt when Indu refused to dance on day one?
Sabina may have felt disappointed and puzzled that her sister chose practice over fun.

Read this:

Last year I thought a good selfie needed twenty tries and three filters. My friend Tanuja and I had a private group where we posted only our funniest edits: Tanuja's face on a potato, my face on a sad monsoon crow. Those memes were the best part of my day, and we never shared the ordinary photos. Then Tanuja stayed at my place after a cousin's wedding and scrolled through my page. "You look like you're always at a party," she said. I laughed, but I looked at my grid afterwards and it did show a sparkling girl I didn't quite know. I still post memes. I just leave a few plain photos in too. - Nikita

What did Nikita and Tanuja post in their private group?
They posted only their funniest edits, such as Tanuja's face on a potato and Nikita's face on a sad monsoon crow.
What did Nikita feel when she looked at her own grid after Tanuja's remark?
She felt a little unsettled, since the grid showed a sparkling girl she didn't quite know, though she also laughed, so she may have taken the remark partly as a compliment.
What small change did Nikita make, and why might it help?
She added a few plain photos among the memes, which keeps the humour while showing more of her ordinary life.
How might Tanuja have meant her comment?
It could be admiration, or a gentle observation that the page shows only parties. Tanuja's own edits were chosen too, so she may be noticing something familiar. 🙂

Read this:

On library day at the primary school in Melbourne, everyone in Jin's class had to choose a chapter book. Oskar grabbed one about dragons with three hundred pages. Jin picked it up after him, read the first line twice, and put it back. 'I'm too stupid for chapter books,' he told the librarian, and chose a picture book about trucks he'd read before. Back at his desk, during quiet reading, he turned the pages without really looking. When Ms Tran asked him to try the first page of the dragon book with her, he shook his head. 'I'm just slow. I'm always going to be slow.' Ms Tran didn't argue. She put a bookmark in the dragon book at page two and left it on his desk.

What book did Jin choose instead of a chapter book?
He chose a picture book about trucks he'd read before.
Why did Jin choose the truck book he had already read?
He felt discouraged and embarrassed after reading the first line twice, and calling himself stupid made avoiding the hard book feel safe.
What was clever about Ms Tran's bookmark?
It made the task tiny and specific, just one page, which treats reading as a skill to practise rather than a verdict on Jin.
What would change if Jin saw 'slow' as a skill to practise?
He might try a page a day of the dragon book, and in time reading would get easier instead of becoming a reason to stop.

Read this:

Ganga: new city, 3 months, still know nobody outside work 😔
Disha: remember what we said? pick one thing and keep showing up
Ganga: I went to that Saturday book club twice. felt awkward
Disha: twice is a start. go a third time
Ganga: also that senior in my team, Leela, offered coffee. I said I was busy
Disha: were you?
Ganga: no. I was scared I'd be boring
Disha: say yes next time. ask her how she got where she is
Ganga: ok but what if I'm needy
Disha: people like being asked. and you're good at listening
Ganga: fine. book club Saturday, coffee with Leela next week
Disha: and call me after. I want updates 🙂

How long has Ganga been in the new city?
3 months in the new city.
Why did Ganga turn down Leela's offer of coffee?
Ganga was scared of being boring and seeming needy, so the chance was avoided.
What small steps does Ganga plan to build connections?
Going back to the book club on Saturday and having coffee with Leela next week.
How does Disha see Ganga's worries?
Disha thinks they're exaggerated and believes people like being asked, especially by someone who listens well.

Read this:

'I deleted the whole club website, sir. The backup too. Three years of stuff.' Akash stared at the floor of the computer lab.
Nilesh sir leaned back in his chair. 'Want to hear something?'
'Not really.'
'When I was sixteen, I wiped my father's shop accounts. Two years of them. I thought I was cleaning up his computer.'
Akash looked up. 'Seriously?'
'He didn't speak to me for a week. We rebuilt it from paper receipts over the whole summer.'
'And you still became a programmer?'
'I became a programmer who makes backups of backups. That mistake taught me more than any class.' He smiled. 'Yours is smaller, by the way. The hosting company keeps copies for thirty days.'
Akash let out a breath he'd been holding since lunch. 'So there's hope.'
'There's always hope. Now pull up a chair. And next time you mess up, find someone who'll tell you theirs.'

What did Nilesh sir wipe when he was sixteen?
His father's shop accounts, two years of them.
What was Akash feeling when Nilesh sir told his story?
He felt surprised and then hopeful, letting out a breath he'd held since lunch 🙂
What could Akash take from this conversation for the future?
Make backups of backups, and look for people who will share their own honest mistakes.
Why might Nilesh sir have chosen to share his own story?
He likely saw Akash's shame and knew that hearing a worse mistake from a mentor could bring hope.

Read this:

Winter sports day, Friday

Came last in the 100 metres. LAST. Kashish came first, again. Everyone crowded round her.

I stood by the water cooler and felt like the slowest person in the world. Why is she good at everything? Running, maths, drawing. I'm not good at anything.

Then Kashish came over. "You ran really straight. I always wobble." I don't know if she was just being nice.

Mumma says I'm good at looking after the class plants. That's not a sport. But still.

Alka

Who came first in the 100 metres?
Kashish came first.
How did Alka feel after coming last?
Alka felt inferior and defeated, like the slowest person in the world.
How could Mumma help Alka with this feeling?
Mumma could keep noticing Alka's real strengths and remind her that everyone is good at different things.
How might Kashish feel coming over to Alka?
Kashish may have felt kind and wanted to encourage Alka.

Read this:

The ink stain on the new sofa cover in their Kolkata flat was shaped like a fish. 'Minakshi did it,' Sharmila said at once when Ma saw it. 'She was holding my pen.'
Minakshi, who was five, cried and said she hadn't.
Sharmila told the story again at dinner, and to Dida on the phone next morning: Minakshi grabbing the pen, the blue drop falling. By the weekend she was sure. She could almost feel Minakshi's sticky hand on hers.
On Sunday, Baba scrolled through photos from Friday evening. There was Sharmila on the sofa, pen in her mouth, homework on her knees, and through the doorway, Minakshi asleep on the mat.
Sharmila stared at the photo. Her cheeks went hot. 'But I remember...' she started, and couldn't finish.

What shape was the ink stain on the sofa cover?
It was shaped like a fish.
Why does Sharmila feel so sure by the weekend that Minakshi did it?
Sharmila grew confident because she had retold the story at dinner and to Dida until details like the sticky hand felt like a real memory.
What choice does the photo give Sharmila, and what would be the brave one?
Sharmila can keep insisting or admit the story was wrong; owning the stain and saying sorry to Minakshi would be the brave choice.
What has the week been like for Minakshi?
Minakshi, only five, was blamed for something she didn't do and kept saying so; she probably felt confused and unfairly treated. 😢

Read this:

I watched my cousin Zubin bargain with his mother about phone time last Sunday, and I was surprised because he stayed calm. Last month he used to argue until doors banged. This time he said, "Amma, can we try an hour of phone after homework for two weeks? If I keep my marks up and you see me put it away at nine, we can talk about more." His mother looked at him a long moment. "Two weeks," she said. "Show me." He did not sulk or promise the moon. I can't tell what he felt, maybe nervous, maybe just tired of fighting. Later he told me it felt good to be trusted a little. Ritu.

What did Zubin ask his mother for?
He asked to try an hour of phone after homework for two weeks.
What might Zubin have been feeling as he made his proposal?
He may have felt nervous and hopeful, and perhaps tired of arguing. Ritu admits not being certain, since he stayed calm on the outside.
What made Zubin's approach more likely to succeed?
He offered trust-building steps and a trial period, instead of arguing or demanding.
How might Zubin's mother have felt hearing it?
She may have felt reassured that he was thinking about responsibility, while still wanting to see it work. 🙂
The teacher corrected all our homework and gave us a feedback. Anything wrong?

The teacher corrected all our homework and gave us feedback.
Why: "Feedback" is uncountable, so it takes no "a".
The number of students in our club are increasing. Is the verb right?

The number of students in our club is increasing.
Why: "The number of" is singular, so it takes "is". "A number of" would take a plural verb.

Read this:

I am Tanvi, and last week in our building compound I watched Idris, five, put on a snarl, hunch his shoulders and stalk towards a smaller child, growling, "I'm a tiger!" He was giggling, and his body was loose and bouncy. The smaller child squealed and ran, laughing. But her mother watched closely for a moment. I think it was play, though I could not know how the small child felt.

What did Idris say he was?
He said he was a tiger.
What does Idris's giggling and bouncy body suggest, and what else could the snarl mean?
It suggests the snarl was posed and playful, not real anger. It could also have tipped into real frustration if the chase stopped being fun.
What could an adult do when a play scare might go too far?
They can keep an eye on the smaller child and step in with a light word if the laughing stops. 🙂
How might the smaller child experience the game?
She seems to enjoy the chase, since she squealed and laughed, but her feelings could change quickly.

Read this:

The Rath Yatra crowds were thick outside when Sachin spread the Class 11 form on the dining table. It had to be submitted by ten tomorrow.
He ticked Humanities.
His mother, Rukmini, saw it from the kitchen door. "Science. We agreed. And no more of that theatre group. They're the reason your marks slipped."
"You agreed," Sachin said. His voice shook, but he kept going. "I love history. And those are my friends, Maa. I chose them."
"At your age you don't know what's good for you."
"Then when do I start knowing?"
The drums of the procession rolled past the window. Neither of them moved. Sachin kept his hand flat on the form, as if someone might take it.

By what time did the form have to be submitted?
By ten tomorrow.
What does Sachin keeping a hand flat on the form suggest about his feelings?
He feels nervous but determined, afraid the choice will be taken from him, because choosing his stream and friends feels like part of who he is.
What could Sachin try so the talk becomes less of a clash?
Explain calmly why history matters to him and what the theatre friends give him, and ask to talk it through with a teacher or counsellor before ten tomorrow.
Why might Rukmini react so strongly?
Rukmini likely feels worried about his future, blames the theatre group for the slipping marks, and sees science as the safe route.

messages.content: How many copies did the first edition of that old poetry book print?
I'm not sure, and a made-up figure would not help you. A library catalogue or the publisher's records may list print runs.
Can you write an email, about 75 words, to my colleague Gaurav handing over my work before a week of leave. The reports are due on Tuesday and the client calls are on Wednesday. I'm Mansi.

Subject: Work Handover for My Leave

Dear Gaurav,
I will be on leave for a week, and I would be grateful if you could take care of a few things for me. The reports are due on Tuesday, and the client calls are on Wednesday. I have saved all the files and notes where you can easily find them. Please call me if something is unclear. Thank you so much for your help.
Best wishes,
Mansi

Read this:

Usha had been proud of her 78 per cent all week. She had even bought her mum a sweet from her own savings to celebrate. At lunch on Monday her phone lit up with Sahil's story: "91%!! 🎉", and a dozen friends replied with fireworks.
She looked at the number for a long time. Then at the report card in her bag, which hadn't changed by a single digit. "It's just marks," she told herself, but her lunch tasted like paper.
That night she opened the app again and scrolled past three more numbers. By the time she shut it, 78 felt like a failure she had invented herself.

What mark did Usha get?
Usha got 78 per cent.
What was Usha feeling as her lunch tasted like paper?
Usha felt deflated and inadequate, though her own mark was exactly what it was that morning.
What could Usha do to bring back her earlier contentment?
Usha could take a break from the app and remember what she worked on for the 78. She could also talk to her mum about it.
How might Sahil have felt posting the mark?
Sahil was probably proud and excited, since a dozen friends were cheering. Sahil may not have thought about how others would feel seeing it.

As I sat in my usual nook, and looked at him with the light of the girandoles on the mantelpiece beaming full over him—for he occupied an arm-chair drawn close to the fire, and kept shrinking still nearer, as if he were cold, I compared him with Mr. Rochester. I think (with deference be it spoken) the contrast could not be much greater between a sleek gander and a fierce falcon: between a meek sheep and the rough-coated keen-eyed dog, its guardian.

How does the narrator compare this man with Mr. Rochester?
She thinks they are total opposites: this man is like a sleek goose or a meek sheep, while Mr. Rochester is like a fierce falcon or a keen guard dog.

Read this:

"Hansa Ba, the laddoos are missing from the puja plate."
"Vidya, look at me."
Vidya looked at the floor. "Maybe the cat? Or Chotu from next door? The window was open. Or maybe—"
"Vidya."
"...I ate two. They were for Ganpati, I know. But they smelled so good, and I was so hungry after school, and I thought one wouldn't matter, and then—"
"Enough, beta." Hansa Ba's voice was calm. "You told the truth. That was brave."
"Will Ganpati be angry?"
"Ganpati won't be angry. But the plate is empty. What can you do?"
Vidya thought. "Help you make more? I can roll them."
"Good. Wash your hands."
They rolled laddoos together, and Vidya put the roundest two on the plate.

How many laddoos did Vidya eat?
Two.
What was Vidya feeling while blaming the cat and Chotu?
Vidya felt guilty and scared of getting in trouble, which is why the answers kept changing and pouring out.
How did Hansa Ba keep the response fair and proportionate?
She praised the truth, calmed the worry about Ganpati, and gave a simple way to repair it by making more laddoos together.
How might Hansa Ba have felt when Vidya kept giving excuses?
She probably felt patient and a little amused, waiting calmly for the truth.

In the NGO's cramped office above a pharmacy, Meenal pinned her plan for the children's reading festival on the wall. Siddharth read it and raised an eyebrow. "You've got a whole column called 'If this fails'." "I expect it to go brilliantly," Meenal said. "That's why I'll work nights on it. But the school hall is booked for a backup date, a tenth of the budget is kept for surprises, and the storyteller has a stand-in." Three weeks later, the main sponsor cut its money by half, two days before the event. Pradeep, the director, came in looking grim. Meenal had already opened her 'If this fails' column. The surprise money covered the printing, and the book stall moved into the free school hall. "Annoying," she said, crossing out a line. "But it's the plan that took the hit. Not me."

What was the column on Meenal's plan called?
The column was called 'If this fails'.
How can you tell Meenal is still hopeful about the festival?
She says she expects it to go brilliantly and will work nights on it, so the backup column is preparation, not doubt.
What could other planners borrow from Meenal's approach?
Keep a backup date or venue, set aside part of the budget for surprises, and decide the fallback before trouble starts.
How might Pradeep feel when he sees Meenal already handling it?
Pradeep came in grim, so Pradeep would likely feel relief and more trust in Meenal's planning.

Dear Tenzin,
I’ve been meaning to write since Sunday’s listening party. When I moved into the hostel in a new city, I ate dinner alone for a month. Then I found our fan group online and you, Mira and Joel wrote to me.
Someone drew my favourite character. Someone else shared a playlist when I had a bad week. On Sundays we listen together and talk about anything. When a group from another band mocked us, you said, “Let them be. We’re here for the songs.”
It’s the first place here that felt like mine. Thank you for that. ❤️
Sabina

How long did Sabina eat dinner alone after moving to the hostel?
Sabina ate dinner alone for a month after moving into the hostel.
What was Sabina feeling before finding the fan group?
Sabina was lonely in a new city, which is why the group felt like the first place that was Sabina's own.
What did Tenzin's reply to the mocking group show about how the fan group works?
Tenzin answered the mockery calmly and said they were there for the songs. It shows connection here does not depend on hating anyone.
What might Joel or Mira have felt on hearing Sabina's message?
They may have felt glad and a little proud that the group made a lonely person feel welcome. The letter thanks Tenzin mainly, so their feelings are a guess.

The rain hadn't stopped for three hours, and Naveen was already late for his first job interview in Pune when his old car stalled at the traffic light. He slapped the steering wheel. 'Not today, Laddoo! Why do you always do this to me?' His friend Suraj, in the passenger seat, raised an eyebrow. 'Laddoo?' 'She's moody. She hates rain.' Naveen tried the key again, whispering, 'Please, please, just this once.' The engine coughed and started. 'See? She listens when I'm polite.' Suraj laughed but said, 'Or the engine was wet and it dried a bit.' Naveen grinned. 'Maybe. But it feels better thinking she's grumpy than thinking it's random.' They made it with four minutes to spare. That evening Naveen booked a service.

What did Naveen call his car?
Laddoo.
What was Naveen feeling when he slapped the steering wheel?
Naveen felt frustrated and anxious about being late for the interview.
What sensible step did Naveen take after the interview?
He booked a service, dealing with the real cause instead of only coaxing the car.
How does Suraj see Naveen's explanation of the car's behaviour?
Suraj finds it funny and offers a practical reason, a wet engine, instead of a mood.

Read this:

Okay, I'll say it, since this podcast is about online stuff. I'm Kamal, I'm fifteen, and last month I was part of a pile-on.
A boy from another school, Wasim, posted a dance video. His foot slipped at the end. Someone reposted it with a laughing caption, and it blew up. Two thousand comments. Everyone was writing stuff like "bro fell harder than my marks." I thought it was funny. I added one: "bro dances like a folding chair." It got forty likes. I felt clever the whole evening. With two thousand people, one more comment didn't feel like anything.
A week later, a friend of a friend said Wasim had stopped coming to school. That's when it hit me. He'd read every single one. Including mine.
I deleted it that night and told my class teacher, who said she'd contact his school's counsellor the next morning. I still don't know if that's enough.

How many comments did the reposted video get?
Two thousand comments.
How did Kamal feel after posting the comment, and then a week later?
Kamal felt clever and pleased with the forty likes, then guilty and shaken on hearing Wasim had stopped coming to school.
What could Kamal do besides deleting the comment?
Kamal could send Wasim a short private apology and stay out of future pile-ons, remembering the target reads every word.
What might it have been like for Wasim to read the comments?
Wasim was probably humiliated and hurt, with two thousand strangers mocking one slip, so staying home felt safer.
What is one teaching note for Raga Asavari?
Descent shows komal Ga, Dha, Ni.

Class teacher's note, Class 3B, drama week
Divyansh has a short speaking part in our class play. For two weeks he has found reasons to miss rehearsal: a headache, a lost script, a trip to the washroom. Today I found him in the corridor, pale, and he said, "Ma'am, what if they laugh at me?" He had not practised at home either. I think the less he rehearses, the more frightened he gets, and the more frightened he gets, the less he rehearses. I sat with him for five minutes and we read his three lines together, quietly. Tomorrow I will let him rehearse alone with me first, then with two friends, then with the class. I have also called his mother.
- Usha

How many lines does Divyansh have?
He has three lines.
What was Divyansh feeling when he asked, "What if they laugh at me?"
He was frightened of being laughed at, and pale with worry.
What does Usha's plan get right, and what else could help?
It builds up the audience slowly, alone, then two friends, then the class; practising at home with his mother could add more calm repetitions.
How does Divyansh's avoidance look to his classmates at rehearsal?
His classmates probably notice he keeps missing and may be confused or even annoyed, without knowing he is scared.

Read this:

At the primary health centre in Barsana, Devika worked at the reception desk. That afternoon the doctor handed her a note for Lalit, who was waiting for his mother's test results. The doctor had written: "Sugar high. Must see me tomorrow, 9 a.m." Devika didn't want to scare him. "Your mother's results are... a little unusual," she said gently. "Nothing to worry about too much." Lalit smiled with relief and got up to leave. "So we can skip coming back?" Devika's stomach dropped. Her softness had blurred the one thing that mattered. "Wait, Lalit. I said that badly. The doctor needs to see your mother tomorrow at nine. Her sugar is high. It's important not to miss it." Lalit sat down again, serious now. "Okay. Nine. I'll bring her." Devika wrote the time on a slip for him, clearly, in big numbers.

What time does the doctor want to see Lalit's mother?
Tomorrow at 9 a.m.
What was Devika feeling when Lalit asked if they could skip coming back?
Her stomach dropped; she felt alarmed and guilty that her gentle wording had blurred the important message.
What went wrong, and how did Devika fix it?
Her soft wording made the result sound unimportant; she corrected herself with a clear message about the time and why it mattered, and wrote it down.
How did Lalit understand the first message?
He took it as good news and felt relieved, thinking they could skip coming back.

Read this:

Teacher's note, Class 5 maths. Rehana Siddiqui.
In the first fractions lesson, Pooja (ten) pushed her notebook away and wrote “I can't do fractions” across the top.
I didn't erase it. I wrote one word after it in green: “yet.”
For two weeks, she did five practice sums every day with me at lunch. She got most wrong at first. She groaned. She kept going.
Today she solved a sum on the board, explaining her steps to the class. Afterwards she crossed out “can't” in her notebook herself and wrote “can, slowly.”
Next step: I'll pair her with Ritvik, who is where she was two weeks ago.

What did Pooja write across the top of her notebook?
She wrote “I can't do fractions.”
How did Pooja feel when she crossed out “can't” herself?
She felt proud and confident, realising her ability had grown.
Why is pairing Pooja with Ritvik a good next step?
It lets her share her “not yet” experience and strengthens her own understanding.
How might Ritvik feel working with Pooja?
He may feel encouraged, seeing someone who struggled like him and improved.
Tell me about bees in one sentence with the words "flowers" and "honey".
Bees visit flowers to collect nectar, which they turn into honey.

“Before you press share, tell me one thing,” Vidya Masi said. “Why are you posting it?”
Mahima looked at her sketch of the monsoon terrace. “I want people to see it.”
“Which people?”
“Not everyone.” She frowned. “Amma, Nani, my friends from class. Not strangers who say weird things about my drawings.”
“So who should be able to see it?”
“Only people I know. Which means a private account, not a public one.” She flipped the settings on her phone, laughing as she switched on approval for followers. “And I only post art. No location, no school uniform, no midnight selfies.”
“Sounds like a plan.”
“It's my plan. I made it.”

Who does Mahima want to see her art?
Mahima wants Amma, Nani and her friends from class to see it.
What does Mahima's reply, It's my plan, I made it, suggest she feels?
Mahima feels proud and independent, since she worked out the purpose and the rules herself.
What could Mahima do if a stranger asks to follow?
She could decline or ignore the request and keep the account private, since her purpose is to share with people she knows.
How might Nani see Mahima's private account?
Nani may feel happy and included, since she is one of the chosen viewers and can enjoy the art safely.

I don't know, because cut-offs differ by college and year. The college's own notice or office will have the exact figure.

Day 1, Monday: “I'll start when I feel like it,” Vaibhav told his sister Trisha, and lay on the sofa with a comic. The evening drifted by. He drew a little, ate a banana, watched the ceiling fan and went to sleep with the spelling list untouched.

Day 3, Wednesday: Same sentence, same sofa. The feeling did not come.

Day 5, Friday, nine o'clock at night: The test was next morning. Vaibhav grumbled, opened the notebook only because there was nothing else left to try, and copied out the first five words. By the tenth word, he had forgotten he wasn't in the mood.

What did Vaibhav tell his sister Trisha?
Vaibhav told Trisha, “I'll start when I feel like it.”
Why did Vaibhav open the notebook on Friday night?
Vaibhav felt cornered and a bit grumpy, because the test was the next morning and waiting had not brought the feeling.
What could Vaibhav try on Monday instead of waiting?
Open the notebook and copy out just the first five words, and let the mood catch up after he has started.
How might Trisha feel watching Vaibhav wait for the mood?
Trisha probably feels a mix of patience and worry, having heard the same sentence twice without the spelling list moving.

On Adeyemi Street in Lagos, the boys played football every evening in the gap between the parked cars. Emeka was the best dribbler, and he made the rules. 'Nobody from Harbour Road,' he said when Daniel from the next street came to watch. 'They're like wild animals over there. They kick your legs and steal the ball.' The other boys nodded. Daniel sat on the kerb for three evenings, watching. On the fourth, the ball flew over a wall into a compound. Daniel climbed up, dropped over, threw it back, and walked home without a word. Emeka's mother had seen it all from the balcony. At dinner she asked, 'Which wild animal gave you the ball back?' Emeka ate his rice and didn't answer. The next evening, he told Daniel he could play in goal.

Where did the boys play football?
They played in the gap between the parked cars on Adeyemi Street.
Why did Emeka call the Harbour Road boys wild animals?
The label let him see them as a group to keep out rather than as boys like him, so he felt no guilt or sympathy while excluding Daniel.
What helped Emeka change his mind?
Seeing Daniel return the ball, and his mother's question, made him face one real, kind person instead of a label.
What were those three evenings like for Daniel?
Daniel sat on the kerb watching, left out and probably lonely, yet he still helped when the ball was lost.
Why is the sky red at sunset?
At sunset, sunlight passes through more air to reach your eyes. The air scatters blue light away, so what's left is mostly red and orange.
So the colours were always in the sunlight?
Yes, sunlight contains all colours mixed together. At midday, the blue scatters across the sky and makes it blue. At sunset the long path leaves the warm colours.

1) If one person in a group project does no work, what can the others do?
2) How many chapters are left in the book I'm reading?

1. Talk to that person kindly and share the tasks clearly. Because people often help when they know what is expected.
2. I don't know which book you mean or how far you are. Look at the contents page.

The clinic waiting room was full. Zubin, five, zoomed his little red car along the bench. Beside them, a boy named Arnab was crying and pointing at the car. "Zubin, beta, give it to him for a bit," Papa said. "He's poorly." Zubin looked at Papa, then at the car. Papa nodded again. Zubin held it out without looking. Arnab stopped crying at once. Zubin climbed into Papa's lap, pressed his face against Papa's shirt, and stayed there, very quiet, peeking at his car every few seconds.

Where were Zubin and Papa waiting?
In the clinic waiting room.
What does Zubin peeking at his car every few seconds suggest?
It suggests Zubin still missed his car and felt a little sad, even though he had handed it over.
How could Papa support Zubin after this?
Papa could hug him and say, 'That was hard, and it helped Arnab,' and make sure the car comes back before they leave.
How might Arnab's family see Zubin's action?
They were probably relieved and grateful that the crying stopped in a crowded waiting room.

I've watched football with Saurabh at the same café in Kolkata every Saturday for four years. He is the loudest supporter of our club in the room: scarf, drum, the lot. But I've seen what he does after a loss. Last month we lost on a penalty our own striker had clearly dived for. Our table erupted about the referee. Saurabh sat quietly, then said, "He dived. We'd be furious if their man did that." Nobody liked hearing it. Across the room Uday, a rival fan, was being heckled by our lot. Saurabh walked over, shook his hand and bought him a lime soda. "Good game. You deserved it." Then he came back, picked up the drum, and started the song for next week.

Where does the narrator watch football with Saurabh?
At the same café in Kolkata, every Saturday.
What does Saurabh's quiet moment after the loss suggest he was feeling?
He was disappointed but honest, uncomfortable letting loyalty hide that his own team's striker dived.
How did Saurabh show loyalty and honesty together?
He admitted the dive, treated Uday with respect, then still picked up the drum to back his club for next week.
How might Uday have felt when Saurabh came over?
After being heckled, Uday probably felt relieved and respected to get a handshake and a lime soda from a rival fan.
Write four words, separated by commas, that describe a quiet morning.
calm, soft, gentle, bright
There are cobwebs in the corner of my room. What does cobweb mean?

A cobweb is the thin sticky web of a spider, especially an old one covered with dust. It is a noun.
Example: Maya took a long broom and cleared the cobwebs from the corners of her room.
Our flight has a three-hour layover in a big airport. How should we spend it?
Check your next gate early, then relax. A three-hour gap leaves time to eat and rest. Whether you can leave the airport in that time is another matter.
Can we leave to look around?
That depends on your tickets, visa rules and the length of the queues, and I cannot check those. Ask the airline or the airport's information desk before deciding, and keep a margin for the return.

At dinner in their Melbourne flat, Tuan, two, sat on his father Daniel's lap. The family passed rice and fish round the table. No phones, no TV.

Daniel put a little rice on Tuan's spoon. Tuan copied Grandma, bringing the spoon to his mouth with a big grin.

When Grandma laughed, Tuan laughed too and offered her some rice.

What did the family pass round the table?
They passed rice and fish.
What does Tuan's big grin suggest about how he feels?
It suggests Tuan felt happy and loved, enjoying the shared meal on his father's lap.
Why is the screen-free family meal good for Tuan?
It lets him copy loved faces and feel he belongs, which regular shared meals build.
How does Grandma experience the meal with Tuan?
Grandma enjoys it, laughing when Tuan copies her and offers her rice.

On the way to school in Seville, Mateo, five, crouched beside a snail on the pavement.

"Someone will step on it," he told Diego, his older brother.

He picked it up gently by the shell and carried it to the damp flowerbed. "There. That's your home."

At home that evening, he poured his leftover water into the tomato plant on the balcony. "It's thirsty too," he said.

Diego rolled his eyes but carried the watering can the next morning.

Where did Mateo carry the snail?
He carried it to the damp flowerbed.
What was Mateo worried about when he saw the snail?
He was worried someone would step on it and hurt it.
What small habit could help Mateo keep caring for plants?
He could be given the job of watering the tomato plant each day.
How does Diego seem to feel about his brother's kindness?
He acts unimpressed by rolling his eyes, but carrying the watering can shows Mateo is influencing him.

Their Johannesburg calendar now had a new line in green: Wednesday, 8 pm, walk to the park, phones at home. Lucia had written it; Thabo had drawn a small tree beside it. The first Wednesday felt a bit forced. By the third, they were laughing about his mother's long voice notes all the way round the pond. The other rule got tested on Friday. Thabo came in grey-faced after a double shift. The old Thabo would have gone silent and let her wonder. Instead he said, "I'm spent. Give me an hour, then I'm yours." Lucia nodded. She didn't chase him down the corridor. She knew exactly when he'd be back, and he knew he wasn't letting her down by resting. At nine, he came to find her.

What was written in green on the calendar?
Wednesday, 8 pm, walk to the park, phones at home.
Why could Lucia let Thabo rest without chasing him?
She felt secure because she knew exactly when he would be back, so his rest no longer felt like being shut out.
Which two agreements make this work?
A regular, unhurried Wednesday walk without phones, and a clear line Thabo can use to ask for an hour before coming back.
How does Thabo experience resting after the double shift now?
He can rest without guilt, knowing he isn't letting Lucia down, because he has said when he will return.

On the last day of Class 9 at the high school in Bishnupur, Anirban tore up his maths result on the way home. Forty-one out of a hundred. "This was the worst year of my life," he told Sunaina as they cycled past the paddy fields. Sunaina braked. "Worst? You won the district science fair in August. You got picked for the football team. You finally beat Ranjan at chess." "That was ages ago." "It was this year." Anirban kept pedalling, jaw tight. The final exam was the last thing, and it sat on top of everything else like a stone. That evening, though, he found the science fair certificate on the wall and stood in front of it a long time. "Okay. Not the worst year," he told his mother at dinner. "Just the worst ending."

What did Anirban score in maths?
Anirban scored forty-one out of a hundred.
Why did Anirban call Class 9 the worst year of his life?
Anirban felt angry and ashamed about the maths result, and because it came at the very end, it weighed on top of all the good months.
What helped Anirban change his view, and what could help him next?
Seeing the science fair certificate on the wall; next he could talk to his maths teacher about the result as one problem to work on.
How does Sunaina see Anirban's year?
Sunaina sees a year full of wins, the science fair, football and chess, with one bad result at the end.

He landed me on the pavement. As John took his horse, and he followed me into the hall, he told me to make haste and put something dry on, and then return to him in the library; and he stopped me, as I made for the staircase, to extort a promise that I would not be long: nor was I long; in five minutes I rejoined him. I found him at supper.

What does he ask of the narrator when they arrive?
To change quickly into something dry and come back to him in the library. He makes her promise not to be long.

Last winter I became the pass supervisor at the restaurant, the person who calls every order to the kitchen. The first week, I wrote everything on tickets and still mixed up table six and table nine twice. Arohi, the head chef, didn't shout. She said, 'Disha, stop reading. Picture the room.' So I started holding the dining room in my head like a map: who's on mains, who's waiting for dessert, which table has the child who can't have dairy, which order the grill is behind on. By March I could change the whole sequence on the fly when a party of twelve walked in without a booking. Looking back, it wasn't that my memory got bigger. I learned to hang things on a picture instead of a list.

How many times did Disha mix up tables six and nine in the first week?
Twice.
How did Disha probably feel on mixing up the tables?
Likely flustered and embarrassed, since Disha was new in the role and still making mistakes.
What advice from Arohi could help someone in a similar role?
Picture the space and attach details to it, rather than trying to hold a long list.
How might Arohi have seen Disha's progress by March?
As proof that her patient advice worked, with Disha now handling surprises smoothly.

Thursday night
Farhan got suspended for a week for bunking the maths exam. On Tuesday he'd asked me to tell Ma'am he was sick, and I said no. So it's my fault. If I'd covered for him he wouldn't be in trouble, and his Ammi wouldn't have cried at the school gate. I couldn't eat dinner.
Told Amma at bedtime. I thought she'd say, "Yes, you should have helped." Instead she put her phone down and hugged me. She said, "Ganga, you didn't choose to skip the exam. Farhan did. Saying no to lying was right." She said I can still be a good friend: message him, share my notes.
I still feel heavy. But lighter than at dinner.
Sending him the notes tomorrow.

Why was Farhan suspended?
Farhan got suspended for a week for bunking the maths exam.
Why does Ganga feel it's all Ganga's fault?
Because Ganga refused to cover for Farhan, that 'no' seems to have caused the suspension and his Ammi's tears; taking on that much control turns into guilt.
What was the turning point, and what did Ganga decide after it?
Amma saying that Farhan chose to skip and that refusing to lie was right; Ganga decided to stay a good friend by sending the notes instead of carrying the blame.
How might Farhan feel when Ganga's notes arrive?
Farhan might feel relieved that his friend isn't angry or distant, and supported while catching up on a week of missed classes.

Thursday, 1 am, finally quiet. The site went slow tonight, so I wrote my guess on a sticky note first: the pool of database connections has run dry. If that's true, raising the pool size a little should ease things. Changed only that. Waited ten minutes and watched the graph: waiting requests dropped, but errors stayed. So the guess was partly right, not the whole story. I didn't touch the timeout or the cache at the same time, even though Keerthana pinged, 'just try everything?' Next idea: a slow query hogging connections. One change again, a limit on that query, and the errors stopped. Notes are in the incident doc so the morning shift can see the order I tried things. Tired, pleased. — Kalyani

What did Kalyani write on the sticky note?
Kalyani wrote a guess that the pool of database connections has run dry.
How does Kalyani feel at the end of the night?
Kalyani feels tired but pleased, having found the fix by changing one thing at a time. 🙂
What could Kalyani do if a single change showed no result at all?
Kalyani could ask a second engineer to compare the graphs from before and after, since fresh eyes may spot a pattern the first guess missed.
How might Keerthana see the one-change-at-a-time method?
Keerthana may find it slower than trying everything, but would likely value it later, since the notes show which change helped.

Coach's note for Rafiq's parents, after sports day practice.
Rafiq and Hemant raced three times. Rafiq wanted to win so much that he started before I said "go", twice. The second time he looked back at Hemant and laughed, but his eyes were worried. Hemant said, "Not fair!" I called both back. I told Rafiq, "You can be proud if you try your best, whatever happens." On the third try he waited for "go". Hemant won by a step. Rafiq stamped once, then ran over and gave Hemant a high five.

How many times did Rafiq start before "go"?
He started before "go" twice.
Why might Rafiq's eyes look worried while he laughed?
He wanted to win badly, but part of him felt uneasy and guilty about breaking the rule.
What did the coach say that could help Rafiq next time?
The coach said he can be proud if he tries his best whatever happens, which moves the focus from winning to effort.
How might Hemant feel after the high five?
Hemant may feel happy about winning fairly and respected by Rafiq.

Karthik called at seven. "Where are you? The farewell's started."
"I'm not coming," Asif said.
"What? You helped plan the whole thing!"
"Did you see my haircut? The barber ruined it. There's literally a gap on one side."
"So?"
"So everyone will stare. There'll be photos. It'll be in everyone's phone forever."
"Asif, nobody's looking at your head. Half the class is freaking out about their own outfits. Hema's crying because her dupatta ripped."
"That's different."
"How?"
"It's… mine."
Karthik laughed, not unkindly. "Wear a cap. Or don't. Honestly, if you don't come, people will notice that more than any haircut."
Asif touched the side of his head, then looked at his kurta hanging on the door. "Give me twenty minutes."
When he arrived, three people said hi. Not one mentioned his hair.

What was wrong with Asif's haircut, according to Asif?
There's literally a gap on one side.
How did Asif feel about his haircut, and why?
Asif felt self-conscious and anxious, sure that everyone would stare at the gap and that it would be in everyone's phone forever.
What did Karthik say that turned Asif's decision around?
Karthik pointed out that the others were busy worrying about their own outfits, and that people would notice Asif missing more than any haircut.
How might Karthik see Asif's worry?
Karthik finds it a little funny but cares, knowing Asif helped plan the farewell and wants him there.
Why does fourth have a u but forty does not?

"Fourth" and "fourteen" keep the u, but "forty" does not. English spelling is irregular here, so just learn it: f-o-u-r-t-h, f-o-r-t-y.
Example: He finished fourth in the race, and he is forty years old.

I'm Siddharth, and I shared a flat with Anjali in our final year. I noticed her doing something odd: every morning she stood outside the college gate counting students buying breakfast. She told me the only canteen opened at nine, but first classes started at eight. "People are hungry," she said. She started with twenty packets of poha, made in our kitchen, sold at the gate for a small price. She sold out in fifteen minutes. The next week she made forty. She kept a notebook: cost of rice, oil, onions, packets, and what she earned. Some days she made barely anything. She adjusted the price. I didn't know if she'd keep going, but by the end of term she was earning enough to pay her own phone bill.

How did Anjali start her poha business?

She noticed students had no breakfast because the canteen opened at nine and classes started at eight. She made twenty packets at home, sold them at the gate in fifteen minutes, made forty the next week and kept a notebook of costs and earnings.

The whole class was shouting about the kite festival on the temple ground, and Karthik was loudest. “Mine will go higher than the water tank!” Pallavi Teacher stood at the front and pressed both palms slowly downwards, twice. Karthik stopped. Is she cross? He checked her face. She was smiling, eyebrows relaxed, and her voice when it came was soft: “Lower, lower. I want to hear about the kites, not the whole village.” The class giggled and dropped to a murmur. Karthik raised his hand and said, in a normal voice, “Teacher, mine has a tail made from my Paati's old sari.” “Then it will fly beautifully,” she said.

What is Karthik's kite tail made from?
Karthik's kite tail is made from his Paati's old sari.
What was Karthik feeling when Pallavi Teacher pressed her palms down?
He felt a flash of worry that she was cross, until her smile and soft voice showed otherwise.
Why did Pallavi Teacher's gesture work without upsetting anyone?
The palms-down meant lower your voice, and pairing it with a smile, relaxed eyebrows and a soft joke made it kind, not dismissive.
What would change if Pallavi had made the same gesture with a frown and a sharp voice?
The class might have felt scolded and gone silent, and Karthik might not have shared his kite story.

It was the third time that week Sonali, the floor manager, had yelled at Nikita in the small meeting room of the Noida office. Today it was about a report Nikita hadn't even been assigned. Sonali slammed her palm on the table. "Are you stupid?" Nikita's hands were shaking. She kept her voice low and steady. "I can see you're upset. I'm not able to talk when I'm being shouted at. Can we continue later, with Anand from HR?" Sonali shouted louder. "Sit down!" Nikita stood up. "I'm going to step out now." She left the room, walked straight to the HR desk and told Anand what had happened, including the other two times. Anand listened, wrote it down, and said, "Thank you for telling me today. I'll speak to Sonali's manager this afternoon, and you won't be in a meeting alone with her until we've sorted this."

What did Sonali slam on the table?
Her palm.
What was Nikita feeling during the meeting?
She was frightened, her hands shaking, but determined to stay calm and not accept being shouted at.
Why was leaving and going to HR the right step?
Sonali kept shouting after Nikita asked to continue later, and it was the third time that week, so getting support from HR was safer than staying.
How did Anand respond when Nikita reported the shouting?
Anand listened, wrote it down, thanked Nikita, promised to speak to Sonali's manager that afternoon, and made sure Nikita wouldn't be alone with her.

Note from Siddharth, IT support lead, Friday.
Jomon came to my desk at lunch with his phone and a question: "Can you look at this with me before I do anything?"
For three weeks he had been chatting with "Anjali", who said she was a nurse abroad. Today she asked for gift cards to cover a stuck visa fee. Before coming to me, Jomon had already done three things: asked for a live video call (she said the hospital blocks cameras), run her photo through a reverse image search (it matched a model's page), and refused to send any money or photos.
He asked if he was being paranoid. I told him no, these were exactly the right checks, and a real person would not get angry at them. "Anjali" did.
Next steps: helped him report the profile to the app and file a complaint on the cybercrime portal. Suggested he share his three checks at Monday's team meeting.

What did Anjali say she was?
She said she was a nurse abroad.
What was Jomon worried about when he came to the desk?
He worried he was being paranoid and wanted a second opinion before doing anything.
How did Siddharth support Jomon?
Siddharth confirmed the checks were right, helped report the profile to the app and file a cybercrime complaint, and suggested Jomon share the checks with the team.
What would change if Jomon had skipped the checks?
He might have bought the gift cards and lost money, and the anger at his request for a call would not have stood out as a warning.
Write an Eid greeting entirely in lowercase, shorter than ten words.
eid mubarak to you and your loved ones

I'm Ira, and looking back on my year in the robotics club, what I notice most is how ordinary Pema ma'am kept everything. Every message went to the team group, with our parents in it. When I needed help with my code, we sat in the library with the door open, and she mentioned it to Amma at pickup. When I tried to give her a gift after the regional round, she smiled and said a card signed by the whole team was plenty. So in March, when a grown man from an online coding contest messaged me privately, offered me a prize and wrote, "Keep this just between us," something felt wrong at once. I showed Amma that night. She stayed beside me, listened calmly, and said I'd done nothing wrong. Before bed we reported it to the contest organisers and told Pema ma'am.

Where did Ira and Pema ma'am sit when Ira needed help with code?
They sat in the library with the door open.
Why did the stranger's message feel wrong to Ira at once?
Ira had learned from Pema ma'am that safe mentors keep things open, so a private offer with "Keep this just between us" felt like a warning sign.
What makes Amma's response a wise one?
She stayed with Ira, listened calmly, said it wasn't Ira's fault, and acted that same night by reporting it and telling a trusted adult.
How might Pema ma'am feel on hearing what happened in March?
She would likely be concerned but relieved that Ira spoke up, and glad the club's open habits helped Ira spot something unsafe.

Sam asked, "Can I borrow your pen?"

Maria: remember my new year thing?
Jahnavi: "get fit" 💪
Maria: lol yes. update: I'm not fit
Jahnavi: what happened
Maria: nothing happened. that's the problem
Maria: January I did yoga twice and ran once. then work got busy and I kept thinking I'll do it when I feel like it
Jahnavi: and you never felt like it
Maria: correct 😩
Jahnavi: did you ever decide when?
Maria: no?? I just thought wanting it enough would do it
Jahnavi: I did the same with reading last year. nothing till I said: 9 pm, bed, 10 pages
Maria: that sounds so boring
Jahnavi: boring is why it worked lol
Maria: ok. yoga. Tuesday and Saturday. after work, before dinner
Jahnavi: ping me Tuesday
Maria: you're going to nag me aren't you
Jahnavi: 100% 🙂

How many times did Maria do yoga in January?
Maria did yoga twice in January.
How does Maria feel about the "get fit" resolution now?
Maria feels a bit embarrassed and frustrated, joking "I'm not fit" because wanting it enough never turned into action.
What does Jahnavi suggest, and why is it better than "get fit"?
Jahnavi suggests a set time and place, like 9 pm in bed for reading, so Maria picks Tuesday and Saturday yoga after work, which does not rely on mood.
How might Jahnavi feel about nagging Maria on Tuesday?
Jahnavi seems cheerful and caring, happy to help because the same trick worked for Jahnavi's reading.

My name is Bhupen. On the evening train home there is a woman from my building, Jyoti, whom I like talking to. Last Tuesday she was sitting by the window with her earphones in, forehead resting against the glass, bag on the lap like a shield. I had a joke ready about the lift being broken again. I looked at her posture, the way she turned her whole body away from the aisle, and I kept the joke to myself. I read my book instead. At our stop she took out the earphones, saw me and said, "Sorry, long day." I said, "No problem. The lift's broken again, by the way." She laughed properly.

Where did Bhupen see Jyoti last Tuesday?
On the evening train home, sitting by the window.
What was Bhupen thinking when looking at Jyoti's posture?
That Jyoti might want to be left alone right now, since the body was turned away and the earphones were in.
What did Bhupen choose to do with the joke, and what happened?
Bhupen held it back and read a book, then shared it at the stop when Jyoti removed the earphones, and Jyoti laughed.
What might Jyoti have been feeling on the train?
Tired after a long day and in need of quiet. Jyoti said sorry for the long day, which suggests the silence was not about Bhupen.

Vaisampayana continued,--"That foremost of the Bharatas--king Yudhishthira the just--then, thus addressed by his uncle, having gone through every ceremony of politeness, set out with his brothers for Khandavaprastha. And accompanied by Draupadi and ascending their cars which were all of the hue of the clouds, with cheerful hearts they all set out for that best of cities called Indraprastha."

Where do Yudhishthira and his brothers set out for, and with whom?
They set out for Khandavaprastha, and on to the city called Indraprastha, with Draupadi. They ride in cars the colour of clouds and travel with cheerful hearts.

Monday. Damini watched Ms Varghese hand back the spelling test. “Kabir got six right, up from two,” the teacher said. “That is real work.” Kabir sat up straight.
Wednesday. A boy copied the way Lalremsiami counted on fingers under the desk, and a few children giggled. The teacher put down her chalk. “In this room nobody laughs at how somebody works things out. Show us, Lalremsiami, and we'll watch.” Lalremsiami counted again, openly this time, and got the sum right. The giggling boy went red and looked at his desk.
Friday. Another child got a sum wrong. Damini heard the girl next to her whisper, “Good try, look, you're nearly there.” The teacher, at the board, did not turn around, but she smiled.

On which day did the teacher stop the giggling?
On Wednesday the teacher stopped the giggling after a boy copied how Lalremsiami counted on fingers.
How might Lalremsiami have felt when the teacher said, “Show us, Lalremsiami, and we'll watch”?
Lalremsiami probably felt protected but still exposed, since Lalremsiami counted again in front of everyone after being mocked, and the room then watched.
What small choice by the teacher on Wednesday did the most to change the room?
Stopping the mockery straight away, and then asking Lalremsiami to show the method, so that the child who was laughed at was heard and not shamed further.
What might Damini have noticed about how the teacher's habits spread by Friday?
Damini noticed that a girl now whispered, “Good try,” to the child beside her after a wrong sum, the same effort-praising tone the teacher used, which shows children copy what the teacher does.

I want to email my professor Dr Menon to thank her for writing my recommendation letter and to say I will tell her the result. say her advice helped me, and add a subject line. Subject line please, 40 words. From Yash.

Subject: Thank you for the recommendation letter

Dear Dr Menon,
Thank you for writing my recommendation letter. Your advice helped me a great deal, and I am very grateful for your support. I will tell you the result as soon as I hear it.
Yash
Simpler words, please: The train's arrival has been postponed by approximately an hour.
The train will come about an hour late.

People ask me why I still fast every Navratri, even in a hostel where the mess serves egg curry four nights a week. I'm Saurabh, from Varanasi, and honestly, it's my mother's kitchen I'm keeping, not just a rule. Nine days, fruit and sabudana, a small clay lamp on my desk each evening. My roommate thought I was crazy the first year. Then Rukmini from the next wing asked if she could join the evening aarti, just to see. Now four of us sit around that lamp. I'm not blind; I argue with some old customs too. I don't accept the stuff about who can enter which kitchen. But when I light that lamp, I feel as if my grandmother's hand is on my head. That's not something I want to debate away.

What does Saurabh place on the desk each evening during Navratri?
A small clay lamp.
What does Saurabh feel when lighting the lamp?
Saurabh feels comforted and connected to family, as if a grandmother's hand were resting there.
How does Saurabh hold tradition and new ideas together?
By keeping the practices that give meaning and belonging, while openly rejecting customs like rules about who can enter which kitchen.
How might Rukmini experience joining the evening aarti?
Rukmini may enjoy the calm and the sense of belonging, finding a small warm ritual shared across hostel wings.

The land records office in Nashik opened at ten, and Siddharth was first in the queue with a folder and a list. His father, his uncle and his aunt had barely spoken in a year over the ancestral house in the old town, and a family meeting was set for Sunday. Everyone was very sure of things. Nobody had checked.
At the counter, the clerk, Zeenat, helped him request certified copies of the property card and the mutation entries. While he waited on the plastic chairs, he wrote in his notebook: Baba says Dada put it in all three names. Kaka says only his own name. Atya says it was never divided at all. Beside each he left a blank.
When the copies came, he filled the blanks carefully. Kaka was partly right. Baba was not. Siddharth's stomach sank a little. Still, Sunday would be about the paper now, not about who shouted loudest.

What did Siddharth request at the counter?
Certified copies of the property card and the mutation entries.
How did Siddharth feel when he found that Baba was not right?
His stomach sank; he felt uneasy about facing his father with it, though relieved the meeting would now rest on the papers.
What could Siddharth do before Sunday to use the copies well?
He could ask a qualified person to explain the entries, then share the same copies with everyone so all start from the same facts.
How might Baba feel on Sunday when the papers are shown?
Baba may feel embarrassed or defensive at being shown wrong, so Siddharth may need to present the papers gently.

Two years after his mother died, after four winters of her illness, Ivan began volunteering at the hospice on the edge of Bergen every Thursday evening. He read newspapers aloud to Mr Olsen, helped families find the coffee machine, and sat with people who didn't want to be alone at night. He was good at it. The nurses said he had a calm that couldn't be taught.

Ingrid, the volunteer coordinator, noticed something else. Ivan never took the chair by the window, the one like the chair in his mother's ward. And after Mr Olsen died, Ivan came in the next Thursday as if nothing had happened.

"You're allowed to miss your own mother here too," Ingrid said quietly, handing him coffee. Ivan held the cup a long time. "I thought this was how I was doing that."
"It's part of it," she said. "Not all of it."

What did Ivan read aloud to Mr Olsen?
Ivan read newspapers aloud to Mr Olsen.
Why might hospice work feel meaningful to Ivan?
Ivan's grief for his mother found a purpose in comforting others, which made the loss feel less helpless, even while the sadness itself stayed unspoken.
What was wise in Ingrid's words?
Ingrid honoured Ivan's caring work but reminded him that his grief needed its own space too, not only the work.
How might Ingrid see Ivan's calm?
Ingrid values it but is gently concerned, noticing the avoided chair and how he carried on after Mr Olsen's death.

Tuesday night. Third week of living with my flatmate Parveen, and I finally worked out the eyebrows. Whenever she tells a story at dinner, her brows go up so high they nearly touch her hair, then crash down when she gets to the serious bit. For two weeks I thought she was always shocked or angry with me. Tonight I asked, "Are you cross?" She burst out laughing. "No! That's just how I talk. My whole family does it." She said she'd noticed my face stays very still and had wondered if I was bored. We agreed to stop guessing. Funny how one flat face and one lively one can each feel like a complaint. - Imran

Which week of living with the flatmate is it for Imran?
It is Imran's third week of living with the flatmate Parveen.
What did Imran think Parveen's eyebrows meant at first?
Imran thought she was always shocked or angry with Imran, until asking her.
What could Imran and Parveen do to avoid misreading each other?
They could keep checking with a quick question and remember each other's usual level of expression instead of guessing.
How did Parveen see Imran's still face?
She wondered if Imran was bored, so Imran's still face gave her the same kind of wrong reading that Imran had made of her.
My parents want me to learn classical music, but I prefer rock.
Both are worth learning, and classical training can actually help with rock. It builds strong basics like rhythm, scales and ear training. Have you told your parents how you feel?
Not really. I don't want to upset them.

You could suggest a middle path. For example, keep classical lessons for a set time each week while you also practise rock on your own. Showing them you're serious about music in both forms may help them listen.
