messages.content:
Read this:

After Ritu's dance audition, I used to ask, "Did it go well?" She'd say, "Yeah, I think so," and that was it. I thought she just didn't want to talk.
Then my cousin, who's a counsellor, told me I was asking questions that only needed a yes. So after Ritu's next audition, I tried something different. "What was it like, being up there?"
She sat down on my bed. "My legs were shaking. But when the music started, I forgot everyone. Except one judge who kept yawning. That made me so angry I danced harder." She laughed. "I think it was my best ever."
She talked for almost an hour. I'd never heard any of that before.
I'm Rehana. I still catch myself asking yes-or-no questions. But now I notice.

What did one judge keep doing during Ritu's audition?
The judge kept yawning.
How did Ritu feel during the audition?
Her legs were shaking with nerves at first, then she felt angry at the yawning judge and danced harder, feeling it was her best ever.
What small change did Rehana make, and why did it help?
Rehana asked 'What was it like?' instead of 'Did it go well?', which invited Ritu to tell a real story.
What would change if Rehana kept asking yes-or-no questions?
Ritu would probably keep answering 'yeah, I think so', and Rehana would miss the real stories.

Read this:

Sunday
Went bag shopping with Ritu. At the first store, she picked up a designer handbag, eighteen thousand, gasped and put it down like it was hot. Then the salesman showed her a "simple one" for four thousand five hundred. "After that, this is nothing!" she said. Ritu, who was complaining on Friday that she can't pay her phone bill. I wanted to say something but didn't know how without sounding like her mother. So I said, "Let's see the stalls outside first, then decide." Outside, bags were five hundred. She looked at the photo of the four-thousand-five-hundred bag on her phone, then at the stall, and said, "Oh. It's actually expensive, isn't it?" She bought a seven-hundred one. Felt like a good friend today.
Kalyani

How much was the designer handbag?
Eighteen thousand.
Why did Kalyani hesitate to say something in the store?
Kalyani didn't know how to raise it without sounding like Ritu's mother, and worried about seeming preachy.
What choice did Kalyani make, and why did it help?
Suggesting they see the stalls outside first; five-hundred-rupee bags gave Ritu a new comparison, so she saw the price clearly herself. 👍
How might the four-thousand-five-hundred bag have looked to Ritu if she had seen the stalls first?
She would probably have seen it as expensive from the start, especially with the phone bill on her mind, instead of "nothing" beside the designer bag.

metadata.subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Come on, Swati. Everyone kisses in the park. Everyone."
"Rishabh, I said I'm not ready."
"You're being so childish. My friends' girlfriends don't make such a fuss."
"Then maybe you should go out with them."
"That's not what I mean. I just thought you liked me."
"I do like you. And I'm still saying no."
He kicked a stone. "Whatever." He walked off towards the gate.
That evening, Swati sat on Vandana's balcony, hugging her knees.
"Maybe I should've just done it. So he doesn't leave."
Vandana shook her head. "Swati. You said no. That's a full sentence."
"He said everyone does it."
"Everyone doesn't. And even if they did, so what? Someone who actually respects you would say 'okay' and mean it."
Swati was quiet for a long time. "He didn't say okay."
"No," Vandana said gently. "He didn't."

Where did Rishabh want to kiss Swati?
In the park.
How did Swati feel after Rishabh walked off?
She felt hurt and anxious, even wondering if she should have given in so he wouldn't leave.
What was wise about Vandana's response?
Vandana reminded Swati that no is enough and that a respectful person would accept it, instead of pushing her to give in.
How does Rishabh react to Swati's no?
He seems frustrated and sulky, calling her childish and walking off, which shows he did not respect her answer.

Read this:

Kamal, you keep looking at Dinesh sir's cabin as if it might bite. Let me tell you something from when I was about your age. My first manager, Mrs Lobo, stopped greeting me in the mornings. Just stopped. For a whole week I built the case in my head: she'd seen my typo in the tender, she'd heard me joke in the lift, she was going to move me to records. I had whole conversations with her in the shower, both sides. I was very good at her lines. On the Friday I was so tired of it that I knocked on her door and asked, 'Have I done something wrong?' She looked up. 'Arohi, no! I've got new glasses and can't see anyone past three feet.' Two minutes. A week of my life. So go and knock.

What reason did Mrs Lobo give for not greeting Arohi?
Mrs Lobo had new glasses and couldn't see anyone past three feet.
Why did the imagined conversations feel so convincing to Arohi?
Arohi was anxious all week, and with real details to hang the fears on, the typo and the lift joke, the imagined lines began to feel like things actually said.
What was the turning point in Arohi's story, and what does it suggest for Kamal?
The turning point was knocking and asking 'Have I done something wrong?'; it suggests Kamal can end the guessing about Dinesh sir with one direct question.
How might Kamal feel after hearing that a week of worry ended in two minutes?
Kamal may feel braver and a little amused, seeing that a senior colleague once lived inside a made-up story and got out simply by asking.

Read this:

Chinmay, you're fighting with your cousin over what Nani said at the wedding? Let your Arohi masi tell you something. When I was twenty-four, my mother fell very ill, and one evening she held my hand and said, I was sure, "Arohi, the sewing machine is yours." I remember her voice, the fan turning, the smell of the hospital. After she passed, my sister Meenu remembered Amma saying the machine should stay in the house for whoever sewed. We both cried, both certain. I nearly said, "I was there, I heard it." Instead I went through Amma's old notebook, where she wrote everything down. On the last page: 'Machine to whoever keeps sewing.' I still treasure that evening, Chinmay. But I didn't use it as proof. Meenu sews. The machine is with her.

What did Amma's notebook say on the last page?
'Machine to whoever keeps sewing.'
What did young Arohi feel about that evening at the hospital, and what did she choose?
Arohi felt certain and full of love for the memory of Amma's voice, but chose to check the notebook instead of using it as proof.
What was the turning point in Masi's story, and why does it matter for Chinmay?
Reading the notebook's last page; it shows Chinmay that a treasured memory can be respected without being used to win an argument.
How might Meenu have felt when the machine came to her?
Meenu probably felt relieved and grateful, and perhaps moved that Arohi checked instead of insisting.

Read this:

Monday. Sumit brought his favourite football card to school. Vaibhav wanted it. "I'll give you three cards." Sumit said, "Ten." Vaibhav laughed and walked away.

Wednesday. Sumit asked other children. Nobody offered more than three. "You're all cheating," he said, angry. He put the card back in his bag.

Saturday. At the stationery shop, Sumit saw a packet of cards. Inside was the same football card. Sumit bought two packets and got the card twice. He stared at them. Then he went to Vaibhav's house. "You can have one for three cards," he said. Vaibhav grinned. "What changed?" Sumit shrugged, a little embarrassed. "Now I have two."

How many cards did Vaibhav first offer?
Three cards.
Why did Sumit think the others were cheating?
Because the card was his, he felt it was worth much more, so fair offers felt unfair and made him angry.
What helped Sumit see the card's real value?
Finding the same card in a shop packet showed it was common, so three cards suddenly seemed fair.
How does Vaibhav seem to feel when Sumit comes back?
Vaibhav seems amused and pleased, noticing Sumit's change of mind.

Read this:

At the peer-support room in the Hyderabad college, Uday drew a diagram on the whiteboard. "So: anxious attachment, that's me, meets avoidant attachment, that's her. Classic pursue-withdraw cycle. She pulled back, I pushed harder, she pulled back more. It was predictable." Gurleen, the volunteer, listened. It was a good diagram. Everything he said made sense. "That's a really clear explanation," she said. "How did it feel when it ended?" Uday uncapped the marker again. "Well, the research says breakups activate the same brain areas as physical pain, so..." "Uday. Not the research. You." He stopped. The marker hovered. His jaw worked. "Bad," he said at last, very quietly. Then he put the marker down and sat, and for a while neither of them said anything.

What did Uday draw on the whiteboard?
A diagram of anxious attachment meeting avoidant attachment.
Why did Uday reach for the research again when Gurleen asked how it felt?
The analysis was real, but it also kept the hurt at a distance; talking about his feelings directly felt too painful.
What did Gurleen do well?
She respected his explanation, then gently but firmly asked about him, not the research, which helped him name the feeling.
What might Gurleen feel sitting in the silence with Uday?
Gurleen might feel caring and patient, sensing that the quiet "bad" was the first real step.

metadata.subtype: Analysing a breakup like a case study [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The Mumbai local was packed shoulder to shoulder, but Divyansh always found a corner by the door and opened his German workbook. Thirty minutes, Andheri to Churchgate, every working day.
His colleague Sarika started German the same month. She spent whole weekends on it, eight hours at a time, then got busy and skipped three weeks. She'd come back and have to start the chapter again.
For six months Divyansh felt he knew nothing. He couldn't follow a film. He nearly stopped twice. The train was noisy, and some days he only managed a page.
In month eleven, their company's Berlin office posted a role that needed basic German. The interview was a fifteen-minute conversation. Divyansh understood every question. He answered slowly, with mistakes, but he answered.
Sarika had given up in month four. "How?" she asked him.
"Train," he said. "Every day. Even the boring ones." He got the role.

Which stations did Divyansh study between?
Andheri to Churchgate.
How did Divyansh feel during the first six months?
Divyansh felt discouraged, sure he knew nothing and nearly stopping twice.
Why did Divyansh's approach work better than Sarika's?
Thirty minutes every day added up steadily, while Sarika's long weekend bursts were followed by gaps that made her restart.
How does Sarika feel when she hears Divyansh got the role?
Sarika seems surprised and curious, perhaps a little regretful that she gave up in month four.
Write it in a warmer way for a thank-you card: Thanks for the gift. It was useful.
Thank you so much for your thoughtful gift. It has been really useful, and it made me smile.

Read this:

Sunday night

Gautam brought up moving in again at dinner. He's so excited. He's already chosen which room would be the study.

And I just... went quiet. Again. Third time this month.

I love him. That part isn't the question. But when I picture it, my own flat gone, my Sunday mornings alone with the newspaper and nobody to talk to, something in my chest tightens. Like a door I can't open again.

I told myself I'd sort it out in my head first. But it's been weeks and I'm hiding it by being "tired" every time he brings it up. That's not fair to him.

Tomorrow I'm going to say it: "I want this, and I'm scared of it. Both." Better he hears it now than after we've signed a lease.

— Minakshi

What has Gautam already chosen for the new home?
Which room would be the study.
What does the tightening in Minakshi's chest reveal?
It reveals fear of losing her freedom and her own space, even though she loves Gautam.
Why is Minakshi's plan for tomorrow a kind choice?
Saying early that she wants this and is scared of it lets Gautam understand, instead of being confused by her being "tired".
How might Gautam feel when Minakshi tells him?
He may feel surprised and a little hurt at first, but also relieved to understand why she has gone quiet.

metadata.subtype: Stage 4: Fear of loss of freedom [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

College counsellor's note, Tuesday.
Irfan, second year, came in about exam stress, but most of our talk was about Simran. They were close friends until two months ago. When Irfan's father was in hospital, Simran didn't visit or call, though she'd promised. Irfan was hurt. He never told her. Instead he started skipping their study group, leaving the canteen when she arrived and replying to her messages with single words. He said, "I thought it would just fade." It hasn't; he's more upset now, and Simran has asked others what's wrong. He looks tired. What I did next: I asked what he would want Simran to know. He said, "That I needed her." We practised how he might say it, gently. He'll decide this week whether to talk to her.

Where was Irfan's father when Simran didn't visit?
In hospital.
Why did Irfan start leaving the canteen when Simran arrived?
He felt hurt and let down, and avoiding her brought short-term relief from the painful conversation.
How did the counsellor help Irfan move toward repair?
The counsellor asked what he wanted Simran to know and practised gentle wording, making the hard talk feel possible.
How might Simran feel asking others what's wrong?
Simran seems confused and worried, sensing the distance without knowing its cause.

metadata.subtype: Dodging a hard talk with a friend [Actor]

messages.content: What does a cricket ground feel like just before the match begins? Describe it in 50 words.

The ground is hushed before the first ball. The grass is freshly cut and shining, and the white lines are sharp. Players stretch and chat quietly while the umpires check the stumps. In the stands, the crowd waits with a deep, happy buzz. Everyone knows that the game is about to begin.

Read this:

Saturday. Nikita's class won the inter-school quiz, and the team went for pizza afterwards. Nikita had missed the practice sessions, so nobody had told her. She saw the photos that night on her phone: everyone laughing, one empty seat at the end.
Monday. In the corridor, groups were replaying the day. “You should've seen Kabir's face!” Nikita walked past with her bag held close. Vinita glanced at her but got pulled into the laughter.
Thursday. Vinita found Nikita at the library window. “I saw the photos,” she said. “I should have called. Want to come for tea after school? Just us.” Nikita nodded, not quite smiling.

What did Nikita see on her phone on Saturday night?
Nikita saw photos of everyone laughing, with one empty seat at the end.
What might Nikita have been feeling as she walked past the groups in the corridor on Monday?
Nikita probably felt left out and alone, since everyone else was celebrating and the bag held close suggests she was guarding herself.
What did Vinita do on Thursday that helped?
Vinita named it, said she should have called and offered tea, just the two of them, which left Nikita room to say yes at her own pace.
How might Vinita have been feeling on Monday when Vinita glanced at Nikita but got pulled into the laughter?
Vinita may have felt torn and a little guilty, noticing Nikita but carried along by the group's joy.

Read this:

The power cut came just as Binita was putting Kishore to bed. In the dark, he said, "Mumma, the dog next door said he'll eat my shoes. And he barked, and I ran, and my shoe... no, first the gate was open..."

Binita lay down beside him. She didn't ask, "Did it bite you?" She said, "Tell me what happened."

"The gate was open. The dog barked really loud. I ran and my shoe fell off."

"How did you feel?"

"Scared." A pause. "Dogs can't talk, right?"

"No, but barks can sound like words. Were you hurt?"

"No. Just scared."

What was open when the dog came out?
The gate.
What was Kishore feeling as he told the story in the dark?
He was most likely still scared from the dog's loud barking, which is why he mixed pretend, a talking dog, with what really happened. Asking "Dogs can't talk, right?" suggests he was also unsure.
How did Binita listen without leading Kishore?
She lay beside him and asked open questions like "Tell me what happened" and "How did you feel?" instead of suggesting a bite with "Did it bite you?", then checked calmly if he was hurt.
What would change if Binita had asked, "Did it bite you?" straight away?
Kishore might have become more frightened, or given an answer that fit her question instead of telling what really happened.

metadata.subtype: Telling stories about feelings and events [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

Reena didi,
You asked why I've been so short on the phone. I'm sorry. I think something's off with me.
I've had headaches nearly every day for a month. My stomach is a mess. On Sunday evenings I start to feel sick just thinking about the week. Last Sunday I shouted at my flatmate because he left a cup in the sink. That's not me.
I keep telling myself I'm just soft, that real engineers push through. But writing this down, it doesn't look like softness. It looks like my body is trying to tell me the eighty-hour weeks aren't working.
I've booked a doctor for Thursday. Will you call me after?
Lalit

When has Lalit booked the doctor?
For Thursday.
What does Lalit realise while writing the letter?
Lalit feels uneasy and a little scared, realising the symptoms are the body warning about the schedule, not softness.
Why is booking the doctor a wise step at this stage?
It treats the headaches and stomach trouble seriously and may give Lalit support to change the schedule.
How might Reena feel reading this?
Reena would likely feel worried and relieved that Lalit is reaching out and seeing a doctor.

metadata.subtype: Stage 5: Body and mood sound the alarm [Actor]

messages.content: We want to invite our cousins to a Raksha Bandhan lunch at our house. Write a warm invitation in about 55 words. Mention that all the sisters will tie rakhis before lunch.

Dear cousins,
Raksha Bandhan is almost here, and we would love to celebrate with you. Please join us for lunch at our house. All the sisters will tie rakhis before we eat, so come a little early. We will have plenty of food and plenty of laughter. It would not feel complete without you!
With love

Read this:

At the engineering office in Frankfurt, the induction started at nine. Saurabh, an intern from Jaipur, walked in at half past nine, smiling and apologising about the tram. Vasudha, the HR coordinator, was already handing badges to the others. "We began at nine," Vasudha said evenly. "Here, arriving on time means being there before the start." Saurabh's smile faded. Back home, half an hour late for a family gathering hardly counted. "I didn't know," Saurabh said. "Could you tell me what I missed, and how to let you know if something delays me?" Vasudha handed over the printout and wrote a phone number at the top. "Call before, not after." Next morning Saurabh was in the lobby at ten to nine.

What time did the induction start?
The induction started at nine.
What was Saurabh feeling when the smile faded?
Embarrassed and uneasy, realising that being late had been taken seriously.
What small steps could Saurabh take to avoid offence?
Arrive before the start and call ahead if something delays the journey.
How does Vasudha see arriving on time?
As being there before the start, which respects everyone's schedule.

Read this:

The board exams were ten days away, and there was a family wedding all weekend. Vidya didn't worry. "I'll revise the whole chemistry syllabus on Monday and Tuesday," she told her cousin Tarun during the haldi. "It's only fourteen chapters."

"You said that before the mocks," Tarun said. "And you only did half."

"That was different. I was tired."

On Monday, Vidya sat at her desk at nine. By lunch she'd finished one chapter. Organic chemistry took forever. By Tuesday night, she'd done five.

She sat back, shocked. "How did it take this long?"

Tarun, dropping off wedding sweets, looked at her notebook. "You planned for the best case again."

Vidya groaned. She'd imagined every chapter going smoothly, forgetting how the mocks had actually gone. She made a new plan: two chapters a day, for seven days, with one spare.

How many chemistry chapters did Vidya plan to revise on Monday and Tuesday?
It's only fourteen chapters.
How did Vidya feel on Tuesday night?
Vidya felt shocked and frustrated, having done only five chapters instead of fourteen.
What did Vidya change in the new plan, and why is it wiser?
Vidya planned two chapters a day with one spare day, based on how long things really took instead of the best case.
How might Tarun feel seeing Vidya's notebook?
Tarun might feel sympathetic but not surprised, having seen the same thing before the mocks.
Is it right: 'I am very much excited for trip'?
Better: "I'm really excited about the trip." Use "really" or "very" with "excited", not "very much". Say "excited about", and add "the" before "trip".

Read this:

Looking back, the numbers were never as frightening as the secret. For a year I paid my credit card minimum and two EMIs and told my family my salary was "tight but fine". At dinner I laughed in the right places and felt like a stranger.

One Sunday I finally wrote every due on paper: the card, the phone EMI, the two-wheeler EMI, with the interest beside each. The card's interest was the highest, so that became the first target.

Then I told my sister Ira. She was quiet for a second and said, "Show me the list." She didn't lecture. She sat with me while I called the card company.

The debt didn't vanish, but the loneliness did.

Aadhya

What did Aadhya tell the family about the salary?
Aadhya told them it was "tight but fine".
Why did Aadhya feel like a stranger at dinner?
Hiding the EMIs and card dues made Aadhya feel cut off, laughing in the right places while carrying a secret.
Which steps made the debt more manageable for Aadhya?
Writing every due on paper with its interest, going after the highest-interest card first, and telling one trusted person.
What does Ira's reaction suggest about how Ira saw the news?
Ira went quiet for a second, asked to see the list and did not lecture, which suggests Ira cared more about helping than blaming.

Read this:

Hemant, you're stuck between science and humanities. Let me tell you about my choice.
I was fifteen. Everyone said, "Chaitanya, you're bright, take science." I did. I got decent marks, but I hated every lab. I was always reading history books under the desk.
In Class 11, a teacher saw my notebook full of history notes and asked, "Why aren't you doing what you love?" I said my father wanted science. She said, "Talk to him. Show him what you do."
I did. It was a hard conversation. He was worried. But he said, "Try one year." I switched.
Now I teach history at a college, and I love it. Your Chaitanya chacha says: look at what you do when no one tells you to.

What did young Chaitanya read under the desk?
History books.
What was young Chaitanya feeling in science class?
Chaitanya felt bored and unhappy, hating every lab.
What choice inside the story made the difference for young Chaitanya?
He chose to talk honestly with his father and show him his real interest, instead of silently staying in science.
How might Chaitanya's father have felt during that hard conversation?
His father was worried about his son's future but willing to trust him for a year.

Read this:

Nkechi worked as a project coordinator at a small charity in Manchester. Her manager Bilal asked when the volunteer handbook would be ready. Her gut said a week. She had felt that same confidence before. So she opened her tracker and looked at the last three documents: nine, eleven and twelve working days. "Twelve working days," she said. "The average is ten, and I've added two for interruptions, like the phones." Bilal laughed. "You used to say a week." "I used to be late," she said. On day eleven, after a surprise office move, she sent the handbook. Bilal forwarded it with a note: "On time, as promised."

What was Nkechi's gut estimate for the handbook?
Her gut said a week.
How can you tell Nkechi felt wary of her confident gut feeling?
She had felt that confidence before and been late, so she checked her tracker instead of trusting it.
What could other staff learn from Nkechi's estimate?
They could look at how long similar documents actually took and add slack for interruptions, rather than guessing from how the day feels.
How does Bilal see Nkechi's new way of estimating?
Bilal is amused at first but appreciative, forwarding the handbook with a note saying it came on time as promised.

metadata.subtype: Using past durations and a buffer [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Week one. Karthik lay awake till three, running through it: what if he failed chemistry, what if the headache meant something serious, what if his friends were laughing at him in the group chat. At breakfast, when his sister Ganga asked for the salt, he snapped at her. Week four. It hadn't stopped. He'd dropped cricket practice because his mind wouldn't sit still long enough to bat. Ganga found him at midnight on the balcony, jaw tight. "It's every night, isn't it?" He nodded. Week five. Ganga walked with him to the school counsellor's room. "I'll wait outside," she said. Inside, Karthik said it out loud for the first time: "I can't stop the what-ifs." The counsellor listened, then said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's work on this together."

What did Karthik drop because his mind wouldn't sit still?
Cricket practice.
What was Karthik worried about at night in week one?
He worried he would fail chemistry, that his headache meant something serious, and that his friends were laughing at him.
What turning point came in week five?
With Ganga's support, Karthik went to the school counsellor and said the worries out loud for the first time.
How might Ganga have felt when Karthik snapped at her?
She may have felt hurt at first, but later saw it was part of how tense and sleepless he was.

Read this:

In the school staffroom, Imran spread a chart across two desks. The annual sports day was on 10 December. Darshan, the new PE teacher, had planned to "start preparing in November". Imran shook his head. "Let's walk backwards. On the ninth, the field must be marked. For that, the lime powder must arrive by the fifth. For the lime, we need the principal's signature on the purchase form by late November." Darshan wrote fast. "Parents' permission slips? Those take ten days to come back." "Then they go out by the fifteenth." When they reached today's date, 28 October, Darshan laughed nervously. "So we start tomorrow." "We start today," said Imran.

When was the annual sports day?
The annual sports day was on 10 December.
What does Darshan's nervous laugh suggest?
It suggests Darshan felt anxious and caught out, realising the plan to start in November was already too late.
What did Imran's method reveal that Darshan's plan missed?
Working backwards revealed dependencies on the principal's signature, the lime supplier and parents returning slips, which pushed the real start to today.
How might the principal see the purchase form arriving on time?
The principal would probably feel relieved and see the PE department as organised, rather than being rushed at the last minute.

Read this:

Sunday
Two offers, and I've gone round in circles for three days. Tonight I did what Minakshi suggested: a proper table.
Five things: learning, pay, commute, team, stability. First I gave each a weight out of 5 based on what I actually care about now, not what sounds impressive. Learning 5. Team 4. Commute 3. Pay 3. Stability 2, because I live with my parents and can take some risk.
Then I scored both offers out of 10.
Big firm: learning 6, team 6, commute 5, pay 8, stability 9.
Small product company: learning 8, team 7, commute 6, pay 6, stability 5.
Multiplied and added. Big firm: 111. Small company: 114.
So the small company edges ahead. Only just. But what surprised me was the feeling when I saw it: relief. I think I wanted it to win all along.
Indu

What weight did Indu give learning?
Learning got a weight of 5.
How did Indu feel on seeing the totals?
Indu felt relief, a sign of already wanting the small company to win.
What else could Indu do, since the scores are so close?
Indu could talk to someone working at each company or ask each about training, since a small change in one score could flip the result.
How might Minakshi see the table?
Minakshi, who suggested it, may be pleased it ended the circles, and might point out that Indu's relief is useful information too.

Read this:

At the bus stop, the bus to the fair was full and left without them. Dilnaz, five, dropped her shoulders and pushed out her lip. "But I wanted the balloons." Her aunt Maria crouched beside her in the rain. "You're disappointed. Me too. We'll have to wait for the next bus." Dilnaz kicked a pebble and sulked for a moment. Then she leaned on Maria's arm. "Can we watch for it?"

What did Dilnaz want at the fair?
The balloons.
What was Dilnaz feeling at the bus stop?
Disappointment, shown by her dropped shoulders, pushed-out lip and kicked pebble.
What did Maria do that helped?
She named the disappointment, shared it and let Dilnaz feel it without rushing her.
How might Maria feel about the missed bus?
Sorry too, since she said "Me too" and stayed beside Dilnaz in the rain.

Read this:

Javier had one job that week at the design studio in Lisbon: finish the client presentation by Thursday at nine. On Monday, Aiko from the events team messaged him. "Can you make posters for the office quiz night? 🙂" He liked Aiko and loved quiz night. He opened a blank poster file, then closed it. The slides were half done. He wrote back: "I'd love to, but my Thursday deadline has to come first. Could I help next month?" He stared at the screen, feeling like a bad teammate. Aiko replied, "Totally fair!" Javier blocked Tuesday and Wednesday mornings for slides and delivered on time.

What was Javier's one job that week?
He had to finish the client presentation by Thursday at nine.
How did Javier feel after sending his reply?
He felt guilty, like a bad teammate, even though he had politely explained his deadline.
What step helped Javier protect the main goal after saying no?
He blocked Tuesday and Wednesday mornings for the slides, so the saved time went straight to the important work.
What is it like for Aiko to receive Javier's no?
She seems fine with it and replies "Totally fair!", since he explained why and offered to help next month.

messages.content: What is one teaching note for Raga Ahir Bhairav?
Komal Re and komal Ni with Bhairav mood.

Read this:

Teacher's note, project week. I asked Afreen whether she had used an AI helper for her project on rainwater. She looked at her shoes and said, "No—" and stopped. After a moment she said, "I did. I asked it how rain forms, but the drawing and the paragraph about our tank at home are mine." I thanked her for telling me and asked to see her rough notes. Her hands stayed tight on the folder until I said I cared more about what she understood than about whether she had used help. We agreed she will add one line to the project saying what the assistant helped with. Next step: sit with her on Thursday and look at how to check what a helper tells her. — Ms Jagdish

What did Afreen say she made herself?
She said the drawing and the paragraph about our tank at home were hers.
What might Afreen have been feeling when she began with "No" and stopped?
She seems torn between the temptation to deny it and unease about hiding it; her downward look and tight hands suggest nervousness, though that is not certain.
How did Ms Jagdish's reply make honesty easier for Afreen?
She thanked Afreen, said she cared more about understanding than about whether help was used, and agreed a line crediting the assistant. 👍
How might Ms Jagdish see Afreen's first "No"?
As a moment of hesitation rather than a fixed lie, since Afreen corrected herself and gave a chance for guidance.
Give me a pre-journey check for a long train trip: three dash bullets, each under six words.

- Your ticket and ID
- Phone charger
- Water for the trip

Wednesday.
Another day of forty tiny decisions at the agency. Which font. Which client first. Which draft. By 7 I couldn't choose between two dals at the shop, so I ordered pizza and watched two episodes of something I didn't even like. The yoga mat stayed rolled up. Again.
Disha texted: “Yoga?” I sent a sleepy emoji and felt guilty.
Honestly I don't know if it's “decision fatigue” or if I just find evening yoga boring, or if my priorities have shifted and I don't want to admit it.
But I know what might work: yoga at 7 a.m., with Disha, before emails. And I'll plan three dinners on Sunday so the 7 p.m. me doesn't have to decide anything.
Trying tomorrow. Alarm set.
— Sharmila

How many tiny decisions does Sharmila mention making at the agency?
Sharmila mentions forty tiny decisions.
How does Sharmila feel after ordering pizza and skipping yoga?
Sharmila feels guilty and flat, unsure whether the cause is fatigue, boredom or shifting priorities.
What is Sharmila's plan, and why is it sensible?
Morning yoga with Disha and planning dinners on Sunday; it puts the hard thing earlier and removes evening choices.
How might Disha feel about a 7 a.m. yoga partner?
Disha might feel pleased and supportive, glad to help Sharmila keep going.

Read this:

So, Disha, you asked how the call with my mother went. Honestly? Hard.
I told her I'd accepted the job in Bangalore. There was silence. Then she said, "Go. What do I matter? I raised you alone, and now I'll grow old alone." Then she hung up.
I sat there with this huge weight. For an hour I was ready to call back and say I'd stay.
Then I did the thing my counsellor taught me. I asked, "Did I actually wrong her?" I'm Chetan, I'm twenty-four, I found a good job, and I'll be a two-hour flight away. That's not a wrong. Her loneliness is real. My leaving isn't a crime.
So I called back. I said, "Ma, I love you. I'm still going. I'll call every Sunday, and I'll fly home for Diwali." She cried. I stayed calm. I didn't argue about who sacrificed what.
It still hurts. But I'm going.

When did Chetan promise to call his mother?
Every Sunday.
How did Chetan feel after his mother hung up?
Chetan felt a huge weight of guilt, almost ready to call back and stay.
What helped Chetan separate real guilt from pressure?
Asking whether any wrong had actually been done, then keeping the decision while offering care: Sunday calls and coming home for Diwali.
How might Chetan's mother be feeling?
Chetan's mother is probably lonely and scared of growing old alone, which is real, even if her words put pressure on Chetan.

Read this:

Jomon, you asked why old Sahil Sir still teaches at the night school after office. At sixteen I was at a good school in Pune, and there was a boy, Gopal, whose fees were paid by a trust. The others called him "charity case" and hid his books. One day I said, loudly, "His marks are better than yours." That cost me a few friends. Gopal told me the kids in his basti had no one to help with homework. So every Saturday I went there with two friends and a blackboard propped on bricks. Twelve children came the first week. By the monsoon, forty. My father thought I was wasting study time, until Gopal's sister topped her class. That blackboard is still in my office.

How many children came the first week?
Twelve children came the first week.
How did young Sahil feel after speaking up for Gopal and losing friends?
He probably felt lonely for a while, but also sure and determined that it was the right thing.
What choice turned Sahil's defence of Gopal into a lasting mission?
Listening when Gopal described the basti children's need, then going every Saturday with a blackboard, turned one stand into ongoing service.
How did Sahil's father see the Saturday classes at first?
His father thought they were wasting study time, until Gopal's sister topped her class.
Using no more than ten words, tell me what a compass does.
A compass shows you which direction is north.

Read this:

In the lift of their Kolkata building, Nilesh squeezed his father's hand. "Baba, a ghost lives here. It makes the lights blink." Kishore didn't laugh. He crouched down. "Tell me about the ghost." "It's tall. It blinks when it's hungry for children." "That sounds scary. Can I tell you what I know?" Nilesh nodded. "There's an old bulb up there. When it's tired, it blinks. Mr Das is changing it tomorrow." "So no ghost?" "Just a sleepy bulb. Shall we wave to it?" Nilesh waved, still holding tight.

Who is changing the bulb tomorrow?
Mr Das is changing it.
Why did Kishore ask about the ghost instead of laughing?
He cared about Nilesh's fear and wanted to understand how scared his son really was before gently explaining.
What makes Kishore's way of explaining a good one for a young child?
He asked permission, gave a simple true reason with a friendly picture of a sleepy bulb, and didn't mock or add new dangers.
How might Nilesh feel waving at the bulb?
Nilesh might feel braver and a bit relieved, though still holding his father's hand tightly.
Reword without the word "nice": It was a nice day, so we had a nice walk by the nice river.
It was a sunny day, so we had a pleasant walk by the peaceful river.

Read this:

"Bhupen, can you come here a minute?"
"Yes, Damini-ma'am?"
"I found this storybook behind the encyclopedias. The last three pages are torn. The card says you borrowed it last."
Bhupen's hands went cold. "I... it was an accident. I tore it pulling it out of my bag."
"And then?"
"I didn't know what to do. I thought you'd fine me or stop me borrowing. So I put it behind the big books."
"How long ago?"
"Two weeks. I've been scared every library period since."
"Two weeks of being scared, for three pages." She sighed, not unkindly. "If you'd told me that day, we'd have taped it together."
"Will you stop me borrowing?"
"No. But you'll help me tape it now. And next time, you come straight to me."

Where did Damini-ma'am find the book?
Behind the encyclopedias.
How has Bhupen felt for the last two weeks?
Scared every library period, afraid of being fined or banned.
What should Bhupen do next time something gets damaged?
Go straight to the librarian that day, when it can simply be taped.
How does Damini-ma'am see the hiding?
With a kind sigh, pointing out that two weeks of fear was a lot for three torn pages.

Read this:

At the biotech lab on the third floor, Avni watched Amandeep open the freezer and go pale. The samples for their project, six weeks of work, had thawed. Amandeep had left the door ajar the night before. "It's not my fault," Amandeep said immediately. "This freezer is ancient. Someone should have fixed the seal." Avni nodded, but she'd seen the door open at seven. For the next two days Amandeep snapped at everyone, skipped the team lunch, and kept muttering about the seal. Avni wasn't sure what to say. On Thursday, while they were restarting the cultures, Amandeep stopped pipetting. "I left it open. I checked my phone and walked off." Avni just said, "Okay. Thanks for saying it." Amandeep let out a long breath. The rest of the afternoon, the snapping stopped.

How many weeks of work had thawed in the freezer?
Six weeks of work.
What was Avni feeling when Amandeep blamed the freezer?
Avni felt uneasy and unsure what to say, since she had seen the door open at seven.
Why did Avni's simple reply help?
She didn't scold or lecture; she thanked Amandeep for owning it, which let the guilt finally ease.
How was Amandeep affected by admitting the mistake?
Amandeep let out a long breath and stopped snapping, which suggests the unresolved guilt had been weighing heavily.
If two paths lead to the same village and one is blocked by a fallen tree, which should you take?
Take the clear path. Because both go to the same place, so the open path gets you there without delay or the risk of climbing over a tree.

Note from Chandrika, nursery teacher. In the play corner Amandeep, two, sat a doll in a small chair and offered her a spoon, saying "Eat, baby." Then he wagged his finger and said gruffly, "No, no, bed!" and laid her down. He then made a puppet ask "Mummy?" in a wobbly voice. I read this as play, trying out roles he sees at home, and did not treat it as a report of anything. I sat close and asked the doll if she was sleepy.

What did Amandeep offer to the doll?
He offered her a spoon and said "Eat, baby."
What does Amandeep's gruff voice with the doll suggest, and what else could it mean?
It suggests he is trying out the caregiver's voice and role from what he sees around him. It could also be just a funny voice he enjoys.
What could Chandrika do to support this kind of play?
Chandrika can join gently, follow his lead and keep it as practice, without questioning him as if it were real. 🙂
How might the doll play feel to Amandeep?
It probably feels safe and powerful, because he can try out being the one who cares and decides.

The long rains had come to Addis Ababa, and the power went out most evenings. Abebe's neighbour Rosa, who looked after him while his parents worked late, expected bedtime to be a battle in the dark.
But at eight, when the church bell down the road rang, Abebe got up from the floor without a word. He found the torch on the shelf, brushed his teeth at the basin by its light and climbed into bed.
"Story, Rosa," he said. "The one about the monkey and the market."
Rosa told it, rain drumming on the tin roof. Halfway through, Abebe's breathing slowed.
She sat there a while, surprised. No arguing, no "five more minutes." The bell, the brush, the story, then sleep, one step pulling the next, even with no lights at all.

What did Abebe use to see while brushing his teeth?
He used the torch from the shelf.
How did Rosa feel as Abebe fell asleep?
Rosa felt surprised and quietly pleased, because she had expected a battle and instead the routine ran smoothly.
Why did bedtime go so smoothly even without electricity?
Abebe's steps happen in the same order at the same time each night, starting with the eight o'clock bell, so each step follows the last without needing lights or reminders.
What would change if Abebe's bedtime happened at different times each night?
Without a steady cue like the bell and the same order, the steps might not follow automatically, and bedtime could turn into arguing.

Sunday. Rukmini spread her 600 rupees on the bed in three piles. “Half for the guitar fund,” she told her brother Sumit, dropping 300 into the tin. “A third for me. That's 200. The rest for Amma's birthday and the temple box.” “Seems fair,” Sumit said. “Can I get a share?” “Only from the gift pile.”
Friday, two weeks on. At the school fair Rukmini bought a bracelet for 60 rupees and felt no guilt at all; that pile was hers to spend.
A month later, on a Sunday, she opened the tin. It held 300 rupees, and the gift envelope's 100 bought a scarf for Amma and rice for the temple kitchen. Nothing felt taken away.

How much did Rukmini put into the tin on the first Sunday?
Rukmini dropped 300 rupees into the tin.
How did Rukmini feel about buying the bracelet at the fair?
She felt comfortable and free of guilt, since that pile was hers to spend.
What could Rukmini do if her allowance goes up or down?
She could keep the same shares, half, a third and the rest, and recalculate the amounts, since the plan stays fair as the numbers change.
How might Sumit see the plan?
Sumit sees it as fair and asks for a share of the gift pile, so he seems interested and perhaps hopes for a present.

messages.content: What is a pinafore? The old photo shows a girl in one.

A pinafore is a sleeveless dress worn over a blouse or sweater, or an apron-like covering that protects clothes. It is a noun.
Example: Her mother made her a blue pinafore for school.
Write a sentence of exactly nine words about a sleeping baby.
The baby sleeps quietly while the fan hums softly.

At two, Jomon ran laps round the living room after lunch, shrieking with laughter, throwing cushions and refusing every suggestion. His mother Sonali glanced at the clock. It was long past his nap. Then he tripped, burst into tears and rubbed his eyes. She lifted him, dimmed the lights and said, "You are so tired, aren't you?" He was asleep in ten minutes.

At nine, Jomon slumped at his desk with his chin on his arm, yawning through the first period and snapping at a friend. His teacher did not send him out. They asked quietly after class, "You seem worn out. How is bedtime going, and how is the noise at home?" Jomon said the new baby next door cried half the night.

At twenty-five, Jomon made three small errors in a report and stopped laughing at meetings. His colleague Joseph found him alone at the kitchenette one afternoon. "You've seemed drained lately. Anything I can take off your plate?" Jomon let out a shaky breath.

What did Sonali do after Jomon tripped and burst into tears?
She lifted him, dimmed the lights and told him he was so tired.
What do the three scenes show about how adults and colleagues can read tiredness in Jomon?

At two a wild burst is a sign that a nap is overdue, at nine slumping and a short temper lead a teacher to ask about bedtime, and at twenty-five small mistakes lead Joseph to check in kindly, so each observer looks past the behaviour to the tiredness.
How was Jomon probably feeling as he slumped at his desk at nine?
Jomon was worn out and irritable, low on sleep because of the crying baby next door, which shortened his temper.
What could a colleague do besides criticising the errors?
A colleague can check in privately, as Joseph did, and ask what could be taken off the plate, since kindness helps more than gossip.

The scholarship form had sat on Nandini's desk in the Pune paying-guest room for eleven days. Maria picked it up. "Deadline's Friday. Why haven't you filled it?" "Because I wasted all of last year," Nandini said. "Skipped classes, slept till noon, failed two papers. People like me don't get to ask for things." Maria sat down on the bed. "You were nineteen and your dad had just moved away for work. What did you know then about handling that?" "Nothing," Nandini said slowly. "I didn't even know how to ask anyone for help." "So that girl did what she knew. You know more now." Nandini stared at the form for a long moment. Then she uncapped a pen and started on page one, hearing the old voice that said she hadn't earned it, and writing anyway.

How long had the scholarship form sat on Nandini's desk?
It had sat there for eleven days.
Why hadn't Nandini filled in the form?
She felt ashamed of wasting last year and believed she didn't deserve to ask for anything, so she kept punishing herself.
Which question from Maria helped, and why?
Asking what Nandini knew back then about handling it helped her see that her past self did what it could, so she could forgive it and act now.
How might Maria see the old version of Nandini?
Maria sees a nineteen-year-old struggling after a big change at home, not someone who should lose chances forever.

Read this:

Tomas had a plan, written in green pen on a card: invite both parents to the same football match and sit them together. The stadium in Valencia was loud and sunny. His mum arrived first, then his dad, and they sat with one empty seat between them, polite as strangers. Tomas watched them instead of the game. On the tram home, his older brother Mateo said, "You can't fix it, you know. It's not your job." Tomas stared out the window. "I know," he said at last, "but I hoped." Mateo put an arm around him. The next Saturday Tomas went to a match with his dad and just enjoyed the goals.

What did Tomas write his plan on?
He wrote it in green pen on a card.
What did Tomas hope would happen when he invited both parents to the match?
He was hoping they would sit together and get back together, which is why he watched them instead of the game.
What might help Tomas as he slowly accepts things?
He can enjoy time with each parent separately, as he did with his dad at the next match, and talk with Mateo about his hope.
How might Mateo see Tomas's plan?
Mateo sees that fixing it is not Tomas's job and says so gently, then comforts him with an arm around him, so he seems kind rather than harsh.

Read this:

Toddler music class note, Saturday. From Ojas, class leader.
When Zeenat's Nani came through the door at the end of class, Zeenat spread her arms wide and flapped them up and down, running in a wobbly line, shrieking.
One parent pulled her son back, worried Zeenat might hit him.
I don't think so. Her face was all smile; it was joy, lots of energy with nowhere to go.
Next time I'll make a clear space by the door for pickups.

Who came through the door at the end of class?
Zeenat's Nani came through the door.
What was Zeenat feeling when she flapped her arms and shrieked?
She was feeling excited and happy to see her Nani; her smiling face shows joy, not anger.
What is Ojas's plan, and why does it help?
Ojas plans a clear space by the door at pickup, so excited children can move freely without bumping others.
How did the other parent read Zeenat's flapping arms?
The parent was worried Zeenat might hit her son and read the movement as a possible threat.

Read this:

So you want to know when Pune started feeling like home? Honestly, it was a Tuesday in my second month here. My name's Kunal, by the way, and back then I was a mess. I'd called home, heard the pressure cooker whistle in our kitchen in Nagpur, and after hanging up I just sat on my bed staring at the wall. My flatmate Hemant knocked, didn't ask anything, and put a steel glass of ginger chai on my desk. Then he sat on the floor and complained about his lab partner, loudly, for about an hour. I laughed twice. He did the same thing the next Tuesday, and the one after. I never asked him to. I think that's the point: he just kept turning up, so I stopped feeling like a guest in my own life.

What did Hemant put on Kunal's desk?
A steel glass of ginger chai.
What was Kunal feeling after hanging up the call home?
Kunal felt homesick and low, sitting on the bed staring at the wall after hearing the pressure cooker whistle back home.
What makes Hemant's way of helping work so well?
It asks nothing of Kunal: Hemant brings chai, fills the silence and comes back each week, so the care feels steady rather than a one-time rescue.
How might Hemant see those Tuesday evenings?
Hemant may see them as ordinary time with a flatmate rather than a big favour, which is partly why Kunal found them easy to accept.

Read this:

Jahnavi, since this podcast is about asking for help, here's why I waited so long. I'm Farida, and I kept a list of excuses. First: people would call me weak. In our class, anyone who cried was a joke for weeks. Second: my parents already work double shifts, and I thought a counsellor would cost money we didn't have. Third, the big one: it wasn't bad enough. Other people had real problems. So I waited. In Class 10 I stopped sleeping properly, then stopped reading, which I used to love, then stopped answering my friends. By the time I told our sports teacher, I'd missed a whole term. She listened, took me to the school counsellor that same afternoon, and it turned out the service was free. If I could talk to the Class 10 me, I'd say: the day you start making excuses is the day to ask.

Whom did Farida finally tell?
Farida's sports teacher.
Why did Farida believe it "wasn't bad enough"?
Farida felt unsure her struggle counted, since other people had real problems, so asking for help seemed unjustified.
What did waiting cost Farida, and what choice would Farida make now?
Farida missed a whole term; now Farida would ask for help as soon as the excuses start.
How might the sports teacher have seen Farida's decision to speak up?
The teacher would likely see it as brave and act quickly, taking Farida to the counsellor that same afternoon.

"Why are you still awake?" Anirban whispered from the top bunk.
Vinita didn't answer for a while. "Do you ever think we're too late for everything?"
"Too late for what?"
"For good jobs. For clean air. For anything to be normal. Everyone keeps saying study hard and you'll be fine. I don't believe them."
"That's a lot for midnight, didi."
"I know." She pulled the blanket up. "It's just there. All the time. Like background noise."
Anirban climbed down and sat on the edge of her bunk. "I don't know the answers. But you're not the only one. Half my class says the same."
"Really?"
"Really. Tell Maa tomorrow? She keeps asking why you're so quiet."
Vinita nodded in the dark. "Tomorrow."

What does Vinita say the feeling is like?
Like background noise, there all the time.
How is Vinita feeling as she talks in the dark?
She feels anxious and hopeless about the future, not believing that studying hard will make things fine.
What small step does Anirban suggest, and why might it help?
He suggests telling Maa tomorrow, since sharing the worry with a trusted adult can ease it and bring support.
How might Anirban feel hearing his older sister say this at midnight?
He may feel worried and a bit out of his depth, but caring enough to climb down and sit beside her.

Hafsa, nine, heard the substitute teacher say, "Everyone will read one paragraph aloud before the bell." Only ten minutes left. Her stomach dropped. The words on page forty were long and slippery; "was" kept looking like "saw." When her turn was three children away, she pushed her book into her bag and whispered, "I forgot it." At break she told her friend, "I'm stupid, that's why." Kunal Sir, the class teacher, had seen the book slide into the bag. He called Hafsa over at lunch. "You explained the water cycle better than anyone yesterday. Reading is hard work for you, not thinking." He phoned her Ammi that evening, and the next week Hafsa started reading sessions with the school's special teacher.

What word kept looking like "saw" to Hafsa?
The word "was" kept looking like "saw."
How was Hafsa feeling as her turn to read came closer?
She felt frightened and ashamed, so she hid her book and said she forgot it rather than read in front of everyone.
What did Kunal Sir do that protected Hafsa's confidence?
He told her she thinks well and only reading is hard, then called her Ammi the same evening so she could start extra reading help.
If you were Hafsa's friend at break, how might you see her comment?
You might feel sad and surprised to hear her call herself stupid, because she seems clever to you.

In a Seoul flat, Paulo, two, was told by Soo-ah it was time to leave the blocks and get dressed for the park. "No!" He hurled a block, whined and flopped on the floor. Soo-ah waited a breath, then sat near him. "You wanted to keep building. It's hard to stop." She took his hand firmly. "Blocks stay here, we come back later." He sniffed, then let her help him with his shoes.

Why was Paulo told to leave the blocks?
He had to get dressed to go to the park.
What does Paulo's throwing and flopping suggest, and what else might be behind it?
It suggests frustration because his play was stopped. He might also have been tired or hungry, which makes stopping harder.
What could Soo-ah do to help him next time?
Soo-ah can give a warning before stopping and promise when he can play again, then stay calm as she did. 😊
How might Soo-ah feel when Paulo throws a block?
Soo-ah might feel a flash of stress, but the calm reply shows Soo-ah understands it as a big feeling.

Read this:

Trainer's note, monsoon membership review: Indu.
Indu signed up in June with a plan I liked: she would watch her favourite crime series only on the gym treadmill. For two weeks it worked beautifully. She came four evenings a week, headphones on, walking faster during chase scenes.
Then the rains started. She messaged that she would "just watch one episode at home because of the rain, and come tomorrow". Tomorrow became three episodes on the sofa. By July she had finished the season and come in twice.
Today she laughed about it, a bit embarrassed. "The series was supposed to be my reward for the gym. It became my reward for staying home."
We agreed: the series stays on the gym tablet only, and on rainy days she uses the indoor bikes here. Anirban at the front desk will keep her headphones as a joke reminder.

Where was Indu supposed to watch her crime series?
Only on the gym treadmill.
How does Indu feel about what happened?
Indu is a bit embarrassed but can laugh about it, seeing clearly that the reward escaped from the gym.
What makes the new agreement stronger?
The series now lives only on the gym tablet and rainy days have an indoor option, so the treat is truly reserved for the workout and can't become an excuse.
What would change if the series had stayed gym-only from the start?
The rain alone probably wouldn't have stopped her; with the episodes waiting only on the treadmill, the pull to come in would have stayed.

Read this:

Subject: Papa's week on one page

Darshan,

I have put everything in one place so we can stop guessing. Papa has physio on Tuesdays and Fridays, and a heart check-up every second month with blood tests beforehand. Evenings are fine: you finish by five and I am home by six. Weekends are fine too. Costs are covered for now from his pension and what we each put in. What we cannot fill is weekday mornings. He needs help getting up, washed and to his tablets, and neither of us can be there before ten because of our offices. So the problem is not everything. It is the hours from seven to ten. Can we talk on Sunday about who or what could cover them? 🙂

Your sister,
Ankita

Which hours are the real gap in Papa's week?
Weekday mornings, the hours from seven to ten.
What does Ankita's phrase "so we can stop guessing" suggest about how Ankita feels?
It suggests Ankita feels worried and wants clarity, using facts on one page to replace vague worry.
What other approach could they use to fill the morning gap?
They could arrange a paid helper for those hours or ask one of their offices about flexible timing, because the page shows the gap is narrow and specific.
How might Darshan see the email?
Darshan may feel relieved to see the problem set out clearly without blame, and perhaps a little anxious about changing work hours.

metadata.subtype: Approach: mapping needs, resources and who can help [Thinking]

Read this:

I'm Nilesh, and I'm writing this down so I remember how close I came.

Ramesh, my junior, sent the client the wrong pricing file. Last year's rates. The client's procurement head called me directly: "Nilesh sir, are you trying to cheat us?" Two years of trust, gone in one phone call.

I was shaking with anger. I walked towards Ramesh's desk ready to say it in front of the whole floor. Halfway there I turned into the stairwell instead and stood there till my breathing slowed.

First, the client. I called back, apologised, sent the correct file within the hour, and offered a call with our director. They calmed down.

Then, at five, I asked Ramesh into a room. Facts only. "The file was last year's. It cost us the client's trust. Here's what we'll do: a two-person check before any pricing goes out." He was pale. "Sir, I'm so sorry."

He learned the check. Nobody learned to fear me.

What did Ramesh send the client?
He sent the wrong pricing file, with last year's rates.
What was Nilesh feeling as he walked toward Ramesh's desk?
Nilesh was shaking with anger, ready to confront Ramesh in front of the whole floor.
Why did Nilesh fix the client problem before talking to Ramesh?
Cooling down and fixing the problem first protected the client, and it let him give calm, private, factual feedback with a plan rather than humiliating Ramesh.
How might Ramesh have felt in the private meeting?
Ramesh was pale and deeply sorry, likely ashamed but relieved not to be shamed in public.

Read this:

So, Sonali, you asked why I've been posting about plastic straws all week. I'm Thomas, and it started with one click. There was this pledge online: "I care about clean beaches." Of course I do. Click.
Next day, an email: "Thank you! Will you share the pledge with five friends?" I did; it felt rude not to. Then: "You're a Beach Guardian! Will you post daily for a week?" I didn't really want to, but saying no felt like saying I didn't care after all.
Today they asked me to raise money from my relatives. And I felt the pull again, like, I'm the Beach Guardian, right? I haven't answered yet. Honestly, part of me still feels I have to.

What did the first pledge say?
I care about clean beaches.
Why did saying no feel hard for Thomas?
Thomas felt guilty and pressured, as if refusing would mean not caring after all.
What could Thomas ask before answering the latest request?
Whether raising money from relatives would be a yes if it were the first thing asked, and whether it is wanted at all.
How might Thomas's relatives feel if asked for money?
They might feel awkward or pressured, especially if the request comes from a group Thomas barely knows.

metadata.subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

When our team won the inter-school debate last year, I felt like I could fly. The judges announced it and I actually jumped out of my chair. We hugged, screamed, took a hundred photos.
That part was fine. The part I regret came later. In the big group chat with both schools, I posted, "Imagine losing to US 😂 Shalini's team needs a new topic."
Within a minute, Shalini left the group.
I didn't think about how it would feel to be her, reading that after preparing for weeks. I only thought about how good I felt.
Next day I messaged her privately: "That was a nasty message. You argued really well on the second point. I'm sorry." She replied, "Thanks. It stung."
Now when I win, I celebrate with my team, and I say one kind true thing to the other side.
- Rashmi

What did Shalini do within a minute of the message?
Shalini left the group.
What was Rashmi feeling when the win was announced?
Rashmi felt triumphant and elated, as if able to fly, jumping up and celebrating.
What does Rashmi do now after a win?
Rashmi celebrates with the team and says one kind, true thing to the other side, instead of gloating.
How did Shalini feel reading the gloating message?
Shalini felt hurt and stung after weeks of preparation, which is why she left the group.

Every evening at six-thirty, Pooja left her Pune office and went straight to her parents' flat. Cooking, medicines, her father's dressing, her mother's blood-pressure reading, dishes. Home by eleven.
"You should get help," her colleague Kalyani said one day.
"They're my parents. It's my job."
Her brother lived in Bengaluru and sent money. Pooja never asked for more. Asking felt like failing.
By the third month, she was falling asleep on the bus. At work she sent a client the wrong invoice and missed a deadline. Her manager called her in.
One evening, her mother asked for her tea to be less sweet. Pooja snapped, "Can't you just drink it?" Her mother went quiet. Her father looked away.
On the bus home, Pooja stared at her reflection in the window. She had been trying so hard to be a good daughter, and she had just made her mother feel like a burden.

What time did Pooja leave her office each evening?
At six-thirty.
How did Pooja feel on the bus home after snapping at her mother?
Pooja felt guilty and exhausted, ashamed that her effort to be a good daughter had made her mother feel like a burden.
What else could Pooja have done instead of managing everything alone?
She could have asked her brother to share tasks or pay for some daytime help, and looked at a schedule that included rest for herself.
How is Pooja's mother affected by Pooja doing everything alone?
Her mother goes quiet and likely feels hurt and like a burden when Pooja, worn out, snaps at her over tea.

In the kasba near Satara, a forwarded message said the new fertiliser at the cooperative was poisoning the soil. By evening, farmers were cancelling orders. Vaibhav, home from college, read it three times. It had no name, no date, only capital letters. His uncle, Jagdish kaka, said, 'Everyone's sharing it, it must be true.' Vaibhav wasn't sure either way, and that bothered him. He checked the agriculture university's page, called his soil science lecturer and read a farmers' forum where people argued both sides. The lecturer said the fertiliser was fine if used as labelled; one forum member pointed out the message was from last year, about a different product. Vaibhav explained this at the chai stall. Some farmers believed him, some didn't. Jagdish kaka grumbled, but reordered.

What did the forwarded message claim?
That the new fertiliser at the cooperative was poisoning the soil.
What was Vaibhav feeling after reading the message?
Vaibhav felt uneasy and unsure, not knowing either way, and that uncertainty troubled him.
What steps did Vaibhav take that others could copy?
Checking the agriculture university's page, asking a lecturer and reading a forum with both sides before sharing a view.
How might Jagdish kaka feel about being corrected by his nephew?
Probably a bit embarrassed and grumpy, but willing to reorder once the facts were clear.

“Gurpreet, this is Imran Sir, your new maths tutor.” “Hello, Gurpreet.” Gurpreet gave a small smile, lips closed, and slid half behind her mother's chair. “Say hello properly, beta. Give a nice big smile.” The smile flickered and went. Imran pulled his chair back a little. “No rush. I was the same at your age. Shall I just start, and you tell me when I'm wrong?” He wrote 7 + 8 = 16 on the page. Gurpreet leaned forward. “That's fifteen.” “Is it? Oh no.” This time her smile had a gap in it, a missing front tooth showing.

What sum did Imran write on the page?
Imran wrote 7 + 8 = 16 on the page.
Why did Gurpreet's smile flicker and go when her mother asked for a big one?
She likely felt shy and more self-conscious when pushed, since a forced smile can feel like being watched.
What did Imran try instead of pushing?
He gave her space, said he had been shy too, and made a small mistake for her to fix, letting her join in her own way.
How might Gurpreet's mother feel seeing the gap-toothed smile?
She might feel relieved and see that time and a gentle start work better than asking for a big smile.

Dear Ishita,
You asked me at your wedding why my husband Nikhil looked so tired, and I got angry and walked away. I owe you the truth.
I check his phone every night. I keep his salary in my account "for savings." I choose what he wears to office. I've told him your husband is a bad influence, so he doesn't come to your place anymore.
I always told myself this was love. I worried about him. But when I'm honest, it was fear. Fear that if I didn't hold everything, he'd drift away and I'd have nothing.
At your wedding I saw him standing alone by the wall, checking his phone to see if I needed him. I saw how small his life has become around my rules.
I've made an appointment with a counsellor for myself on Friday. I want to learn to love him without owning him.
Please don't tell anyone yet.
Bhavna

What does Bhavna do with Nikhil's salary?
Bhavna keeps his salary in a personal account "for savings."
What was Bhavna afraid of, underneath the control?
Bhavna says it was fear: without holding everything, Nikhil might drift away and Bhavna would have nothing.
What step is Bhavna taking?
Bhavna has made an appointment with a counsellor on Friday to learn to love without controlling.
How has Nikhil's life been affected by Bhavna's rules?
Nikhil's life has become small and tired, standing alone and checking his phone in case Bhavna needed him.

Planner's note — Ojas and Mitali, wedding on 12 February

I'm recording this because I want to use it with future couples.
When the family priest fixed 12 February as the date, most couples I know would panic. Ojas and Mitali sat in my office and started from the end.
"If the wedding is on the twelfth," Ojas said aloud, "the halls will be the hardest thing. Everyone wants February." So hall first, booked by the end of October.
Mitali went on: "Invitations need printing, and relatives abroad need six weeks' notice. So cards by mid-December." Tailoring came next: fittings need two tries, so cloth bought in November. Travel for Ojas's brother Pranav's family from Pune: tickets in December before the fares rise.
They wrote a month-by-month list on my whiteboard and photographed it.
What I did next: I called the hall that afternoon and held the date for them.

By when did Ojas and Mitali plan to book the hall?
By the end of October.
How did Ojas and Mitali seem to feel while working backward in the planner's office?
They seemed calm and focused rather than panicked, thinking aloud step by step from the fixed date.
What else could Ojas and Mitali do with their month-by-month list?
They could divide the items between them and check in weekly, so nothing on the list is missed.
How might Pranav see the plan for the family's travel?
Pranav's family would likely feel reassured and included, since tickets are planned early rather than rushed at the end.

metadata.subtype: Approach: working backward from the auspicious date [Thinking]

In their small flat in Lyon, Nadia had spent the whole evening sighing loudly while Layla packed for a week-long field trip. 'Go, enjoy,' Nadia said, not looking up. 'I'll be fine alone. Like always.' Layla stopped folding a sweater. 'Do you want me to cancel?' The word yes sat on Nadia's tongue, and she recognised what she was doing: the sulk had been meant to make Layla feel guilty enough to stay. Under it was something plainer. She was scared that a week apart would show Layla she didn't need her. Nadia put her mug down. 'No. I was guilt-tripping you. I'm sorry. Could you call me Wednesday night? That's all I actually want.' Layla smiled. 'Wednesday. I'd like that.' Nadia got up and helped her find the charger.

How long was Layla's field trip?
It was a week-long field trip.
What was Nadia afraid of underneath the sulking?
Nadia was scared and insecure, afraid that a week apart would show Layla she was not needed.
What small step changed the evening?
Naming the guilt-trip and asking directly for a Wednesday call, which gave Layla a clear, fair request instead of pressure.
What would change for Layla if Nadia had kept sulking?
Layla might have cancelled out of guilt and begun to resent Nadia, feeling controlled rather than loved.

Jaya, you think your Masi was always the sensible one? Sit, I'll tell you. I was sixteen, at my friend Pooja's birthday on a rooftop in Pune. Her cousins brought beer and a packet of cigarettes, and soon the whole circle was holding a can. Someone pushed one at me: 'Madhuri, don't be boring.' My stomach dropped. I laughed and said, 'Boring is my speciality, yaar. I'll be the one who remembers your party,' and grabbed a cola instead. A few laughed, one rolled her eyes. When the cigarettes came round, I said I had to call home and went downstairs to wait for my father's scooter. Pooja phoned me the next day to say sorry about her cousins. That's how I learned who my real friends were, Jaya. Pooja is still one of them, and she still teases me about that cola.

What did Madhuri take instead of the beer?
Madhuri grabbed a cola instead.
What was Madhuri feeling when the can was pushed at her?
Madhuri felt a jolt of nervous pressure, since the stomach dropped, but stayed steady enough to joke a way out.
Which choice at the party helped Madhuri most, and why?
The light joke, followed by the exit of waiting downstairs, let Madhuri refuse without a fight and get home safely.
How did Pooja see what happened at her party?
Pooja seemed sorry about her cousins pushing drinks, because she phoned the next day to apologise and stayed a real friend.

On Monday, the slide deck for the client update thanked Zainab and nobody else, though Bhupen had built half the numbers behind it. He sat through the presentation with his notebook shut. Afterwards Zainab shrugged, "Oh, that was an oversight, I'll add your name next time," and went to refill her water bottle.

Bhupen said nothing to her. By Wednesday he had told a colleague all about it over tea. His emails to Zainab shrank to a single line, and the shared tracker he usually updated stayed a day stale. Zainab read the clipped tone as coldness and began replying in kind.

The following week the lunch table split. Someone said Zainab was grabbing credit; someone else said Bhupen was sulking. A team chat group filled with pointed questions like "who is right here?" Jagdish, the manager, walked into a silent stand-up and felt the room tighten. He asked a few people what was going on and got three different stories. None of them mentioned a slide.

Whose name did the slide deck thank on Monday?
It thanked Zainab and nobody else.
How did the unspoken slight at the start lead to the tension Jagdish noticed later?

Bhupen's hurt over the missing credit stayed unspoken and turned into short emails and a stale tracker. Zainab read that as coldness, and then colleagues took sides, so Jagdish saw the tension but never heard the slide as the cause.
What was Bhupen feeling as he sat through the presentation with his notebook shut?
He felt overlooked and hurt but kept it inside, which the closed notebook and his silence suggest.
What could Jagdish try in order to find the real cause of the tension?
Jagdish could speak to Bhupen and Zainab privately and ask each what happened and how it affected them, instead of relying on lunch-table stories.
There are 7 rows of desks with 6 desks in each row, and 5 desks are empty. If each desk seats one student, how many students are present?
There are 37 students present. Because 7 times 6 is 42 desks, and 42 minus the 5 empty ones is 37.

Friday, late.
Deleted everything today. All four accounts. Photos, messages, the lot. After the posts about me and the DMs from people I don't know, I just wanted it gone. For about an hour I felt light, like the noise had been switched off.
Then Gautam came to the room. He said the college committee needs the threatening DMs to act, and asked if I'd saved them. I hadn't. They're gone with the accounts.
I haven't been to class since Tuesday. I kept thinking someone there would say something. Now I'm scared of the classroom and I have no proof of why.
At nine Mumma called because Gautam had told her. She's taking the early bus tomorrow and made me promise to keep the phone on tonight. She stayed on the line until I'd eaten.
Payal

How many accounts did Payal delete?
Payal deleted all four accounts.
What did Payal feel right after deleting everything, and how did that change?
Payal felt light and relieved for about an hour, but that turned into fear of the classroom once the lost evidence became clear.
What would you change first in how Payal escaped the pile-on?
I would save screenshots of the threats before deleting anything, so the college committee can act while Payal gets space.
How might Gautam feel after telling Payal's mother?
Gautam may feel worried and a bit uneasy about going over Payal's head, but relieved that an adult is now involved.

Team lead's note, analytics team

Almost everyone in Tenzin's joining batch has applied for MBA programmes this year. It's become the thing to do: the lunch table talks of little else.

Tenzin came to me last week, unsure. She had the forms half filled. I asked her a simple question: "Why do you want it?"

She thought, then said, "Honestly, because everyone else is." Then she asked herself, out loud, "If nobody knew what I chose, would I still apply?"

She was quiet for a while. Then she said, "No. I'd do a data science certification. That's what I'm actually excited about."

She didn't mock her friends' choice. She said the MBA is right for some of them. She just decided, deliberately, that it wasn't right for her this year.

She submitted her certification application yesterday. She seemed calm, even happy.

Vinita

What had almost everyone in Tenzin's batch applied for?
MBA programmes.
How did Tenzin seem to feel after deciding?
Tenzin seemed calm and even happy, having chosen deliberately rather than following the crowd.
What two questions helped Tenzin decide, and why do they work?
Asking why she wanted it and what she'd choose if nobody knew separated her real wish from the pull of the group.
How might Tenzin's friends see her decision?
Her friends might be surprised at first, but since she didn't mock their choice, they're likely to respect it.
Text my mother that I reached school safely. Keep it under ten words.
Reached school safely, Mummy. Will call at lunch.

Van Helsing said solemnly, "You are always right; but this is life and death. All chambers are alike to the doctor; and even were they not they are all as one to me to-night. Friend John, when I turn the handle, if the door does not open, do you put your shoulder down and shove; and you too, my friends. Now!"

Answer from the text. What instructions does Van Helsing give about the door?

Van Helsing tells friend John that if the door does not open when the handle is turned, John should put a shoulder down and shove, and so should the others. Van Helsing adds that this is life and death.

Jagdish, you asked how I improved the portfolio, and the honest answer is: I watched. I'm Sachin, and for two weeks I checked which projects people actually opened, since the site kept a simple count. Twelve visits went to the chess timer that had a live link. Two went to the report analyser. The recruiter emails I got mentioned the timer every time. So I moved it to the very first spot on the page, above everything else. And I noticed the pattern, so I spent a weekend putting one more project online with a link that works. Now two of my projects can be tried by anyone. The count of visits tripled, and one recruiter wrote, "I clicked the link and it worked."

How many visits went to the chess timer?
Twelve visits went to the chess timer.
What did Sachin feel when noticing which project people opened?
Sachin felt curious and motivated, seeing a clear pattern that pointed to what to do next.
What alternative approach could Sachin add to learn more, and why?
Sachin could ask two recruiters what they looked at first, because visit counts show clicks but not the reasons behind them.
How might a recruiter see the live link?
A recruiter can try the project at once and see it work, which builds trust faster than reading a description.
