“Yogesh, who spilled water on the floor?”
Yogesh shrugged, eyes on the puddle.
“Hmm, a shrug. Do you not know, or do you not want to say?” Varun asked.
Another shrug, smaller.
“If it was you, that's okay. Water dries. I just need to know so no one slips.”
Yogesh rubbed his foot on the tiles. “…The glass was too full.”
“Ah. Thank you for telling me. Let's get the mop.”
Yogesh ran for it, looking relieved. “Can I do the mopping?”

Why did Yogesh say the water spilled?
He said the glass was too full.
What was Yogesh feeling when he gave a smaller shrug?
He was probably nervous about being blamed and used the shrug to avoid answering. Once he told the truth he looked relieved.
How did Varun's gentle prompts help?
He named the two possible meanings of the shrug and said the spill was okay, which made it safe for Yogesh to answer.
What would change if Varun had shouted about the spill?
Yogesh would probably keep shrugging or deny it, and Varun would not learn what happened.

Damini had forty minutes to catch the last bus back to her flat in Amman, and Zainab's mother was not letting her leave.

"One more piece of knafeh!"

"No, thank you, I'm full."

The plate came anyway. Damini ate it. Then came the coffee. She drank one tiny cup; it was refilled at once. A second; refilled again. She glanced at the clock, panicking.

Zainab leaned over, laughing. "Shake the cup side to side when you're done. Otherwise my mother thinks you're just being polite."

Damini tilted the cup gently from side to side. Zainab's mother smiled, took it, and finally let her stand.

On the bus, Damini laughed to herself. At home in Nagpur she did exactly this to guests, insisting till they gave in. She had never once wondered how it felt from the other side.

How long did Damini have to catch the last bus?
Damini had forty minutes.
What was Damini feeling as her coffee cup kept being refilled?
Damini felt panicked and a little embarrassed, full, watching the clock, and unsure how to refuse politely.
What local rule helped Damini, and why?
Shaking the cup side to side signals you're finished; knowing it let her decline without offending her host.
How might Zainab's mother see Damini's first 'No, thank you'?
She took it as polite modesty, not a real no, so she kept offering the way her custom expects.

Bhavna, you asked why I believe some secrets can't be kept. Last year, in the working women's hostel in Pune, my roommate Ritu told me something at midnight. She'd been hurting herself, and she'd been thinking she'd be better off not here. Then she said, "Promise you won't tell anyone." I didn't promise. I sat on her bed, held her hand and said, "Thank you for telling me. You're not a burden. And I care too much to keep this to myself tonight." She cried. I stayed right beside her and called the warden, Mrs. Gomes, from my phone. She came up in five minutes, sat with us, and called the crisis helpline with Ritu on speaker. By morning Ritu had an appointment with a counsellor, and her sister was on the way from Nashik. Ritu was angry with me for a week. Then she said thank you. So, from me, Trisha: listen without judging. But when someone's at risk, you get help that same night.

Where was the working women's hostel?
In Pune.
What might Ritu have been feeling when she asked Trisha to promise not to tell?
Ritu was likely frightened and ashamed, afraid of being judged or exposed, even as she reached out.
Why was Trisha right not to keep the secret that night?
Ritu was at risk, so Trisha stayed with her, reassured her, and called the warden, who got the crisis helpline on the line that same night.
How did Mrs. Gomes respond when Trisha called?
She came up within five minutes, sat with them, and called the crisis helpline with Ritu on speaker.
What grade did the boy at the next desk get in maths?
I don't know, because grades are private. Only he can choose to tell you.
Was the boxing match in the city stopped early tonight?
I wouldn't know, because I can't see tonight's fights. A sports news page will carry the report.

For five days Santiago avoided the university cafeteria in Córdoba, because Abebe would be there. Abebe had lost his scholarship the week before, and since then he'd gone grey and quiet, sleeping through classes. Santiago kept typing messages and deleting them. Everything sounded like a greeting card, or like a lecture. What if he said the wrong thing and Abebe shut down completely?

On Friday he saw Abebe alone on the library steps, and his feet carried him over before his fear could stop him.

"Hey. I'm sorry I disappeared. I didn't know what to say. I'm here. I care. Can we go and get some help together?"

Abebe looked at him for a long moment. "The counselling office closes at five."

It was four-fifteen. They walked there together, not talking much, and Santiago waited in the corridor until Abebe came out.

What time did the counselling office close?
It closed at five.
Why did Santiago avoid the cafeteria for five days?
Santiago was scared of saying the wrong thing and making Abebe shut down, so helplessness made him stay away.
Which words worked, and why?
Simple words worked: "I'm here. I care. Can we go and get some help together?" They were honest and led straight to real help.
How might Abebe have felt during the days Santiago stayed away?
Abebe may have felt even more alone and forgotten, adding to the hurt of losing his scholarship.

"Ganga, can I tell you something weird?"
"Mm-hm." Her thumb kept scrolling.
"My Abbu might be moving to Muscat for work. For two years."
Ganga's thumb stopped. She put the phone face down on the bench.
"Wait. When did you find out?"
"Last night. I heard them talking. They don't know I know."
"How are you feeling about it? Honestly."
Rafiq opened his mouth to say "fine", and instead said, "Scared. He's the one who picks me up from cricket. Everything."
"That's a lot to carry since last night." She didn't offer a fix. She just waited.
He let out a long breath. "Yeah. Thanks for putting your phone down."
"It can wait. Tell me the rest."

Where might Rafiq's Abbu move for work?
He might move to Muscat, for two years.
How did Rafiq feel when Ganga put her phone face down?
He felt noticed and relieved, safe enough to admit he was scared instead of saying fine.
What did Ganga do that helped most?
She put her phone away, asked how he honestly felt, and then waited instead of offering a fix.
What would change if Ganga had kept scrolling?
Rafiq would probably have said "fine" and kept the fear to himself, feeling he didn't matter much to her.

It was a joke I posted at nineteen, about how my cousin's wedding band played the same song eleven times. Three years later someone cropped out the context and it spread as if I had mocked the whole community. By Saturday night I had four hundred messages. Some called me names I won't repeat. One said they knew my college.

I'm Sonali, and I'll admit the first night I didn't sleep. I kept refreshing, my stomach tight, typing angry replies and deleting them.

On Sunday Ayesha came over with chai. She helped me mute the words, screenshot the threat, and report it to the platform and the college grievance cell before lunch. My hands stopped shaking around evening. I haven't replied to anyone. That was the hardest and best choice.

How many messages had Sonali received by Saturday night?
Sonali had four hundred messages by Saturday night.
How did Sonali feel on the first night, and what shows it?
Sonali felt sick with fear and exposed; not sleeping, a tight stomach and typing then deleting angry replies show the panic.
Which steps helped Sonali on Sunday, and why?
Muting the words, saving the threat as a screenshot, and reporting it to the platform and grievance cell protected Sonali without feeding the mob.
How does Ayesha likely see Sonali's situation?
Ayesha sees Sonali being attacked by strangers and needing practical help and company, not a lecture about an old joke.

"Amandeep, you want to start the gym tomorrow, I know. Let me, your Uma Bua, tell you something first.
When I was your age, twenty, I decided to start badminton seriously. Five mornings a week, hard games. But my mother, your Dadi, had a heart problem, and so did her brother. My friends said, 'You're young, you'll be fine.' A fitness app said the same.
I wasn't sure. So before the first hard game, I went to our family doctor and told her everything. She checked me, sent me for a test, and said to start with lighter games and build up, and to stop and see her if I ever felt pain or dizziness.
The test was fine. I played for fifteen years. But I played knowing, not guessing. That's all I'm asking, beta. One visit before the first heavy lift."

What sport did Uma Bua decide to take up at twenty?
She decided to start badminton seriously.
How did the young Uma feel when her friends said she'd be fine?
She felt unsure and uneasy, because of her mother's and uncle's heart problems, so she didn't just trust them.
What was the key choice in Uma Bua's story, and why did it matter?
Going to the family doctor before the first hard game was the key choice, because it meant starting with advice based on her own history.
How might Uma's mother have felt about her daughter's visit to the doctor?
Her mother, who had a heart problem herself, would likely feel relieved and reassured that her daughter checked first.

In the school corridor, Anjali tugged Vijay Sir's sleeve. "Is the zoo trip today?"
"Tomorrow."
"Is tomorrow now?"

What was drawn on the calendar for tomorrow?
A lion.

Anjali felt impatient and a bit disappointed that the zoo trip wasn't today.
How did Vijay Sir help Anjali understand when the trip was?
He used the calendar to show yesterday, today and tomorrow, and put it in terms of one sleep.

Describe a rainy market street in about 50 words, as if for a travel magazine.

The rain came suddenly, and the market turned into a river of colour. Umbrellas of red and blue bobbed above the crowd. Vendors pulled plastic sheets over mounds of oranges and spices. The smell of hot tea and wet earth floated through the lane, while puddles shook with every passing cart.

Dear Ujjwal Mama,

I'm writing because I don't know how to say this on the phone. Since the separation, Mummy sleeps very late and often forgets things. Last Tuesday there was no dinner, and I had cereal. She forgot to sign my exam form, and the last date is Friday. I'm not blaming her. I think she's sad and tired, and it isn't because of me.

Could you help me with the exam form on Wednesday? And could I have dinner at your house two evenings a week for now? I'll get myself there after school.

I'd also like someone to ask how I'm doing. Sometimes I feel forgotten.

Thank you,
Parveen

Mama's reply, that same evening: "Thank you for telling me. None of this is your fault. I'm coming over tomorrow, and we'll do the form together."

Which day is the last date for the exam form?
The last date is Friday.
What is Parveen feeling about Mummy's forgetfulness?
Parveen feels hurt and sometimes forgotten, yet does not blame Mummy and thinks she is sad and tired.
What is Parveen doing that could help meet Parveen's needs?
Parveen is asking clearly for help with the form, regular dinners and someone to check in, and is turning to a relative.
How might Ujjwal Mama feel reading the letter?
Probably worried and touched that Parveen trusted him, and eager to help Parveen and check on his sister as well; he replies that same evening.

Dear Dadi and Dada,
I'm leaving this letter with the card I've stuck next to your landline, so you know why it's there.
Last month your neighbour lost money to a caller who said he was from the bank. It scared me. So Divyansh and I wrote three rules in Hindi, in big letters:
1. OTP kabhi kisi ko mat batana. (Never tell anyone an OTP.)
2. Shak ho to phone rakho, aur ghar par phone karo. (If in doubt, hang up and ring someone in the family.)
3. Inaam ke liye paisa kabhi mat do. (Never pay money for a prize.)
Below the rules, Divyansh wrote Papa's number and mine.
When I come on Sunday, let's practise once. I'll pretend to be a caller, and you say rule 2 and hang up on me. You're allowed to enjoy that part.
With love,
Francis

Whose numbers did Divyansh write below the rules?
Papa's number and Francis's.
How did the neighbour's loss make Francis feel?
It scared Francis, and that worry turned into a practical plan to protect Dadi and Dada.
Why would a practice call on Sunday help beyond the written card?
Saying rule 2 aloud and hanging up once makes it easier to do under real pressure, not just to read it.
How might Dadi and Dada feel finding the card and the letter?
They may feel cared for and a little amused, and more confident knowing exactly what to do when a strange call comes.

metadata.subtype: Approach: teaching the plan to grandparents [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Creche note, first day after the Christmas break. Joseph (2) arrived without his blue teddy; his mother said it was left at his grandmother's in Kottayam. He cried at the door, then sat by the window, saying "Teddy gone" softly. I didn't try to cheer him up fast. I sat with him and said, "You miss Teddy." After a while he let me read him the bear book. I've asked his mother to send a photo of Teddy tomorrow. — Shankar

Where was Joseph's teddy left?
At his grandmother's in Kottayam.
What was Joseph feeling as he sat by the window?
Joseph felt sad and lonely without his teddy.
What did Shankar do that helped Joseph?
He sat with him, named the feeling instead of rushing to cheer him up, then offered the bear book, and asked for a photo of Teddy.
How might Joseph's mother feel reading the note?
She would likely feel sympathetic and grateful that Joseph was comforted, and happy to send the photo.
The branches of my neighbour's tree are blocking the light into my window. Write a friendly request, about 55 words, asking him to trim them.

Dear Neighbour,
I hope you are well. I wanted to mention that the branches of your tree have grown across my window and are blocking much of the light. Would you be willing to trim them when you have a moment? I would be very grateful. Please let me know if I can help in any way.
Warm regards

Read this:

Chaitanya, the harmonium teacher at the village school, watched Preeti's hands fly through a film song at the Friday class. The runs were bright but smudged, and he knew why: she had stopped doing her scales weeks ago. "Come, play sa re ga ma with me first," he said. She sighed. "That is boring, sir." He smiled. "The fast run in your song is only this scale wearing a costume. If the plain scale is muddy, the costume will be muddy too." They played it slowly together, twice. Preeti heard the smudge on the fourth note and stopped by herself. "Again," she said quietly.

Who was watching Preeti play at the Friday class?
Chaitanya, the harmonium teacher at the village school, was watching Preeti.
What might Chaitanya be worried about as he listens to the smudged runs?
He is worried that the gaps left by skipped scales will show later and hold Preeti back, though he handles it gently instead of scolding.
What could Chaitanya try if Preeti still finds scales boring?
He could connect each scale to a bar of her favourite song so she can hear how the basic notes make the fun part clean.
What is it like for Preeti when Chaitanya asks her to play the plain scale?
Preeti finds it dull at first and sighs, but once she hears the smudge herself she wants to try again, which shows the request moved from a chore to something she cares about.

Read this:

I'm Dolma, one of five on Trisha's team at the design studio. We're all around twenty-five, and until April we were just colleagues who ate lunch together.
When Trisha became lead, she brought in her old boss's system. Stand-up every morning for forty minutes, each of us reporting every task. A tracking sheet updated by the hour. Messages at nine at night asking why a column was still yellow.
Her old boss had run a team of twenty senior designers. We were five people who used to share chips.
Within three weeks, lunch got quiet. In stand-ups people said "on track" and nothing else. Nobody mentioned problems any more, because every problem became a question in front of everyone. Farhan started eating at his desk.
By May, Trisha looked puzzled and tired. I heard her say to herself, "It worked so well for Meera ma'am." I don't know if she saw why it didn't work for us.

How long were the morning stand-ups under Trisha?
They were forty minutes every morning.
What might Trisha have been feeling by May?
She seemed puzzled and tired, confused that her old boss's method wasn't working for her team.
What approach would have fit this team better?
Short, informal check-ins and asking the team what support they wanted would suit five peers better than strict tracking built for twenty seniors.
How does the new style look to Dolma and the team?
Dolma sees the team feeling watched and going quiet, with lunch turning silent and people hiding problems.

metadata.subtype: Approach: copying the previous lead's style without fit [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Shalini, and the first time I really noticed silence at work was watching Tanvir in a call with our printing vendor.
He'd proposed a two-week deadline for the brochures. The vendor said, "Two weeks is difficult." Then Tanvir just... waited. Friendly, calm, pen down. I counted: eight seconds. It felt like a year.
Then the vendor said, "Actually, the problem is paper stock. If you can accept matte instead of gloss, two weeks is fine."
I'd never have learnt that if Tanvir had rushed in.
But I've also seen the opposite. Our old manager used silence like a weapon: he'd go quiet and stare until a nervous junior agreed to anything. That silence wasn't room. It was pressure.
Now I try to wait like Tanvir. It's still uncomfortable. But it works.

How many seconds did Shalini count during Tanvir's silence?
Shalini counted eight seconds.
What was Shalini feeling while counting the silence?
Shalini felt uncomfortable and tense, as though the eight seconds lasted a year.
What could someone learn from the two kinds of silence Shalini saw?
Wait calmly and kindly to give others room to share, but never use silence to stare someone down into agreeing.
How might the vendor have experienced Tanvir's silence?
The vendor probably felt it as room to think, not pressure, and so felt comfortable enough to explain the paper stock problem.

Read this:

When I was in Class 5, I thought history was just dates. Then my friend Akash's grandfather took us to the old church near our village in Goa.
He showed us a stone with carved ships. "This is where the fishermen prayed before the big storm of 1890," he said. "They all went out together, and they all came back, because they tied their boats to each other."
Akash and I stared at the ships. That night I kept thinking about the tied boats.
Our teacher later read us a Panchatantra story about doves caught in a net who flew away together. The same idea.
I'm Francis. I still think of that stone when I work in a group.

What was carved on the stone?
Ships.
What was Francis feeling that night, thinking about the tied boats?
Francis felt fascinated and moved by how the fishermen survived together.
What could Francis do to learn more local stories?
Francis could ask other elders in the village about old events and visit other places like the church.
How might Akash's grandfather feel sharing this story?
He likely feels proud and happy to pass the village's history to the children.
My phone keeps hanging, so I will restart it. Is "hanging" right?

My phone keeps freezing, so I will restart it.
Why: "Hanging" for a stuck screen is common in Indian English, but "freezing" is understood everywhere.
What are mushrooms? Are they plants?

Mushrooms are not plants but a kind of fungus. The part we see and eat is the fruiting body that rises above the ground. Mushrooms is the plural form of this noun.
Example: We bought mushrooms from the shop and cooked them with onions.

Read this:

In the counsellor Binita's room, Raghav drew arrows on a whiteboard. Tuesday: the picture was sent to one friend. Thursday: it appeared in the group. He pulled out a screenshot, showing which account posted it first, then went quiet. “The first post came from the friend's own phone,” he said slowly. Binita ma'am only asked, “What does that tell you?” Raghav thought aloud. “Not that my friend did it. The phone has no lock, and it stays in the bag at gym time. Someone else could have copied it.” He wrote three lines: tell the friend gently, tell the school with the timeline, and from now on keep private things off any phone that is not locked. Raghav put down the marker. It didn't erase the hurt, but it gave the mess a shape.

Where did the first post come from, in the end?
From the friend's own phone.
What did Raghav feel when he saw the source of the first post?
Shocked and torn: he went quiet, hurt but still wanting to be fair to the friend.
What else could Raghav do with this finding, and why?
Tell the friend gently so they can lock their phone, since the friend may not know how the picture got out.
How might the friend feel when told?
The friend may feel guilty and scared, and needs to hear that nobody thinks they did it on purpose.

metadata.subtype: Approach: root-cause thinking about how the image got out [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

At nine, Hemant lost at carrom three afternoons running. He did not sulk. "If I practise my bank shot, I'll win," he said, and he set the board up in the hall again. By Friday he won a round. At fifteen, his grandmother's death left the house quiet. His mother Rashmi told him at the funeral, "It was her time. Nothing you did could change it." He felt his shoulders loosen. He still rose at five for the mock exam, saying to himself, "Destiny decides much, but I have to study." At twenty, Hemant's group project failed in front of the panel. He stayed up thinking of everything he should have done, including the slides that his teammate Ankita had promised and never made. "All of this is on me," he said. Ankita only shrugged. "The panel was unfair, and the deadline was silly." Neither mentioned that she had not started her part. Hemant wrote two lists later: what he had done, and what belonged to others and to the schedule. The lists were uneven, and he slept better.

How many afternoons in a row did Hemant lose at carrom?
He lost at carrom three afternoons running.
How does Hemant's belief about what he can influence show up at nine, fifteen and twenty?

At nine he believed practice would change his carrom results, at fifteen he held destiny and effort together after his grandmother's death, and at twenty he blamed himself for everything while Ankita blamed the panel and the deadline. Only his later lists split what was his from what belonged to others.
What was Hemant feeling when he said all of it was on him?
He felt guilty and heavy, taking on the blame for the whole failed project, including things Ankita had promised.
How might Ankita move toward a more balanced view of the failed project?
She could list what she did and did not do, alongside what was out of her hands, and admit she had not started her part.

Read this:

The school fair had begun, and Yusuf had just enough pocket money for one thing. His geometry box had broken that week, and the maths test was on Monday. But the slime stall was glowing green and purple, and his friends were already squishing it. His sister Preeti tugged his sleeve. "What do you need?" Yusuf sighed. "The geometry box." "And what do you want?" "Slime." He stood between the stalls for a long moment. Then he bought the geometry box. Preeti let him hold her slime for five minutes.

Why did Yusuf need a new geometry box?
His geometry box had broken that week, and the maths test was on Monday.
What does Yusuf standing between the stalls for a long moment suggest?
It suggests he felt torn between what he needed and what he wanted.
How did Preeti help Yusuf decide?
She asked him to separate what he needed from what he wanted.
How might Preeti see Yusuf's choice at the fair?
She probably sees that giving up the slime was hard for him, which may be why she let him hold hers for five minutes.

Read this:

In Ghoti village, Class 5 had to make a leaf book: twenty different leaves, pressed and labelled. It was due on Monday. "It'll take me ten minutes," Vijay told his sister Tanuja on Friday. "The leaves are right there, on the trees." Tanuja reminded him of the seed chart he'd rushed last term. "That was different," Vijay said. On Sunday afternoon he went out to collect. Some leaves were too high. The tamarind leaves were too small to label. The neem ones curled up in the heat. By sunset he had eleven. He went to bed with the book half empty, his stomach in a knot. Tanuja slipped a torch under his pillow in case he wanted to try the mango tree at dawn.

How many leaves did Vijay have by sunset on Sunday?
By sunset he had eleven.
What was Vijay feeling when he went to bed on Sunday?
He felt anxious, his stomach in a knot, because the leaf book was only half done after he'd expected ten minutes.
What would you advise Vijay for his next project?
Remember how long the seed chart really took and start on the day the project is given, not the day before it is due.
How does Tanuja see Vijay's plan?
Tanuja remembers his rushed seed chart, so she seems doubtful but kind, helping with a torch for dawn.
Is it a "letterbox" or a "mailbox" at the gate?

It depends on the variety. British English says "letterbox" for the slot in a door or a box for letters, and American English usually says "mailbox".
Examples: The postman put the card through the letterbox. Please check the mailbox for the parcel.

Read this:

Saturday: On the road above Pema's village, Vinita Aunty's roadside stall had baskets of oranges, a price board and a wooden box. No one minded it. Pema chose six oranges, dropped in her coins and ran to catch her friends.
Sunday: Counting her leftover coins for a pen, Pema froze. Six oranges were thirty rupees. She had put in only twenty. Nobody had seen. Nobody would know. But the box had trusted her, and her face went hot every time she thought of it.
Monday: After school she walked up the road with a ten-rupee note. Vinita Aunty was there, stacking baskets. Pema pushed the note into the box and explained. Vinita Aunty laughed and patted her cheek. "Some weeks the box is short. This week it's exactly right, because of you." She gave Pema one extra orange.

How much had Pema put in the box on Saturday?
Twenty rupees.
Why did Pema's face go hot on Sunday?
She felt guilty, knowing the box had trusted her and she had underpaid.
How did Pema set things right?
She walked back on Monday and paid the missing ten rupees, explaining to Vinita Aunty.
How does Vinita Aunty see Pema's return?
She is touched and grateful, since the box is sometimes short, so she gives Pema an extra orange.

Read this:

"Shoes on the rack, please, Shreya, so nobody trips," said her mother Nazia, standing in the doorway of the flat.
"Yes," said Shreya, five, and nodded. She carried her shoes over, then stopped. "Toes to the wall?"
"Whichever way you like."
"Okay!" She set them down, patted them once, and ran off to wash her hands.

What reason did Nazia give for putting the shoes on the rack?
So nobody trips.
How might Shreya be feeling when she asks about the toes?
She seems eager to get it right and happy to go along with the rule, since she asks how to place them and then pats them. She could also have been stalling a little.
Why might giving a reason help Shreya more than just saying "Do it"?
It helps her see the rule as fair and safe, so she follows it because it makes sense.
How might Nazia feel watching Shreya pat her shoes into place?
Probably quietly pleased that the reason worked. She may also be relieved not to have had to repeat herself.

Read this:

Dear Gargi Masi,
At Sunday lunch I told everyone about the night the roof leaked at Nani's house and we all slept in the kitchen by a lantern. I can see it: the drip into the steel bucket, your blue shawl over my feet, the smell of kerosene.
Then Mummy and you both said it never happened. Nani's house has a concrete roof, and I only stayed there in summer. I was hurt, honestly. It felt as if you were taking away something that was mine.
I've been thinking since. Maybe I built it from your stories about your own childhood there. It still feels so real that letting go of it is strange.
Could you tell me the lantern story again, properly? I want to know whose memory it is.
Love, Harsha

What did Mummy and Gargi Masi say about the leaking roof?
They said it never happened, since Nani's house has a concrete roof and Harsha only stayed there in summer.
Why did Harsha feel hurt when told the leak never happened?
The memory was so vivid, with the drip, the blue shawl and the kerosene smell, that losing it felt like having something taken away.
What step does Harsha take towards understanding the memory?
Harsha asks Gargi Masi to tell the lantern story again, properly, to find out whose memory it really is.
How might Gargi Masi feel reading this letter?
She might be touched that her childhood stories stayed so strongly with Harsha, and a little sorry the correction at lunch hurt. 🤍

Read this:

You're sulking just like your Bua Madhuri used to, you know. Sit, I'll tell you. The mango summer she turned fifteen, your Dadi made a rule: no going to the lake without me, Ramesh, her big brother.
Madhuri didn't argue. Oh, no. She said, "Fine." Then she took forty minutes to put on her chappals. She walked three steps behind me the whole way. Every question got "Hmm" or "No." She peeled mangoes so slowly the juice dried on her fingers.
Your Dadi said she was obeying. I knew she was furious.
One evening I finally said, "Madhuri, just tell me you hate the rule." She glared, then burst out, "I'm not a baby!" And that was the first real conversation we'd had all summer.

How long did Madhuri take to put on her chappals?
Forty minutes.
What was Madhuri feeling behind her "Fine"?
She was furious 😠 and resentful about the rule, but showed it through slow, silent compliance instead of saying it.
What turning point changed things in the story?
Ramesh inviting her to say it straight, "just tell me you hate the rule", let her anger out in words and started a real conversation.
How did Dadi see Madhuri that summer?
Dadi saw only the obedience, reading the slow compliance as Madhuri following the rule rather than the anger underneath.

Read this:

"Sarita, sit with your Irfan Chacha a minute. When I was ten, my best friend was Nasreen, the girl next door. Then a new girl, Lalita, came to our school. Nasreen started playing hopscotch with her. I said, 'Fine, go and play with her,' like I didn't care.
But I cared. I counted every day she chose Lalita, like marks on a wall. After a month, I was so full of it that I hid Lalita's slate before a test. She cried. Nasreen looked at me as if she didn't know me.
If I'd just said once, calmly, 'I feel left out,' none of that would have happened."

What did young Irfan hide before a test?
He hid Lalita's slate.
What was young Irfan really feeling when he said "Fine, go and play with her"?
He felt hurt and left out but hid it, pretending not to care while counting every time Nasreen chose Lalita.
What turning point in the story could Irfan have handled differently?
At the start, he could have said calmly and once that he felt left out, instead of saying "fine" and silently keeping score.
How did Nasreen see Irfan after the slate was hidden?
Nasreen looked at him as if she didn't know him, shocked that her friend could be cruel.
Write a message, about 35 words, thanking my colleague Meena for covering my shift yesterday. I'm Rohan.

Hi Meena,
Thank you so much for covering my shift yesterday. It really helped me, and I am truly grateful. Please tell me when you need a favour, and I will gladly return it.
Rohan

Read this:

I'm Kamal. For two days our group had not agreed on a single plan for the model bridge. Ramesh wanted matchsticks, Tara wanted cardboard, and I wanted to stop the shouting. On Thursday I said, "We're stuck. Let's ask Miss, our teacher." We all trooped to the staff room. She listened, asked each of us for one reason, and then said, "Cardboard base, matchstick rails. And one person speaks at a time." She wrote it on a sticky note. We walked back and started measuring. Ramesh was quiet, but he handed me the ruler. That was the first time in two days that nobody argued.

What did the teacher say the bridge would be made from?
The bridge would have a cardboard base and matchstick rails.
What did Kamal want when suggesting to go to the teacher?
Kamal wanted the shouting to stop and the group to get unstuck.
What alternative approach could the group have used earlier, and why?
They could have listed each idea and voted, or combined the two materials themselves. A quick decision earlier would have saved the two days of arguing.
How might Ramesh have felt about the teacher's plan?
Ramesh was quiet but handed over the ruler, so the plan probably felt acceptable, even if Ramesh had hoped for matchsticks alone.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asking the teacher to settle a stuck point [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Usha, you asked why I got passed over for team lead. I'll tell you, since you're dealing with your own parents now. I'm Kiran, and last year I was the king of last-minute leave.
My mother has heart trouble, and my father's memory is going. We had no plan at all. Every time something happened, I'd get a call and just run: grab my bag in the middle of a meeting, half-finished work left on my desk.
It happened maybe ten times. Each time felt like the right thing. It was my mother!
But my manager said, at my review, "I never know if you'll be here tomorrow." The lead role went to someone else.
And the worst part is, one day I was stuck in traffic on the highway when my father wandered out, and there was nobody else to call. My neighbour found him two hours later.
So please, Usha. Make a plan before you need it.

What did Kiran's manager say at the review?
"I never know if you'll be here tomorrow."
How does Kiran feel looking back on that year?
Kiran feels regretful and shaken, especially about the day the father wandered out and there was nobody else to call.
What else could Kiran have done instead of running out at each crisis?
Kiran could have made an emergency plan with backup contacts, a neighbour with a key and regular help, and told the manager about it in advance.
How might Kiran's manager have seen the repeated last-minute leave?
The manager likely felt unable to rely on Kiran for important work, which is why the lead role went to someone else.

metadata.subtype: Approach: reacting to each crisis as it comes [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Irfan Bhai,

You asked why I sounded low on the phone. It's silly. Ammi and Abbu are fine, the shop is doing okay, and we got the roof fixed before the rains. But my friends' families all seem a step ahead. Rehan's dad bought a car, and Adil's family is moving to a bigger flat. When I'm with them I feel like we're struggling, and I come home angry at nothing. Then last week I helped Abbu with the month's accounts. We owe no one. We ate out on Eid. Our roof doesn't leak. If I compare us to five years ago, when we lived in one room, I should be grateful. I suppose it depends on who I'm looking at. Anyway, how is college? Write back.

Abhinav

What did the family get fixed before the rains?
The roof.
How does Abhinav feel when with friends, and why?
Abhinav feels the family is struggling and comes home angry, because the friends' families seem a step ahead.
What was the turning point in Abhinav's view?
Helping Abbu with the month's accounts and remembering living in one room five years ago, which showed the family is actually doing well.
How might Abbu feel if he heard Abhinav say 'we're struggling'?
Abbu might feel hurt or puzzled, since the shop is doing okay and the family owes no one.

Read this:

Coach's note, university badminton squad, Friday.
Vidya and Jatin (mixed doubles) disagreed on Monday about who covers the back court. Since then Vidya has not spoken to Jatin at all: no eye contact, turning away at drinks breaks, answering his questions only through me. Jatin has apologised twice, each time more anxiously; on Wednesday he offered to switch to the front court "if that fixes it". Vidya looked satisfied, but stayed silent.
After practice today I asked Vidya to stay back and asked what the silence was doing for her. She took a long time, then said, "When I stop talking, he comes round. When I argue, I lose." She seemed surprised to hear herself say it.
We agreed she will tell Jatin what she actually wants on court, in words, by Monday. I will sit in if both want. I will check in with Jatin separately too.

What did Jatin offer on Wednesday?
He offered to switch to the front court if that fixes it.
What did Vidya's answer reveal about her silence?
Vidya seemed to feel powerless in arguments and in control when silent; she looked surprised, even uneasy, hearing herself say it.
How did the coach respond, and why does it help?
The coach asked Vidya privately what the silence was doing, then agreed a plan for her to state her wishes in words by Monday, with an offer to sit in and a separate check on Jatin.
What is it like for Jatin under the silence?
Jatin seems anxious and keeps apologising, even offering to change position, just to make the silence end.

Read this:

Jomon, you told your manager about the fake overtime claims and now nobody eats with you? Sit. Your Madhuri aunty knows this feeling. In 1998, as a young nurse in Thrissur, I reported that a senior was taking medicines home from the ward store. The inquiry was quiet, and she was transferred. But the ward never forgave me. Tea-break conversations stopped when I walked in. Someone left a note in my locker: 'Snake.' My review called me 'difficult'. I nearly resigned. Then one ward aide, Thankamma chechi, started sitting next to me at lunch every single day, saying nothing special, just sitting. It was enough. One person, Jomon. Find your Thankamma. And be one for someone else.

What was written on the note in young Madhuri's locker?
'Snake.'
How did young Madhuri feel in the months after reporting?
Isolated and hurt, close to resigning as conversations stopped when she walked in.
What choice in the story made the isolation bearable?
Thankamma chechi choosing to sit beside her at lunch every day, one quiet ally.
What might Thankamma chechi have risked by sitting with Madhuri?
Being gossiped about or isolated too, which makes her quiet support brave.

How can I remember my homework?
And one more: what is the largest number anyone has ever counted aloud?
Next, I keep seeing "nuisance" in my reading. Meaning?

1. Write it in a diary as soon as the teacher says it. Check the diary before you leave school.
2. I don't know; nobody keeps a record of that. Maybe you could try a counting game with friends.
3. As a noun, "nuisance" means a person or thing that keeps annoying you.

Read this:

Monday: Behind the school water tank, Francis, ten, whispered to Jahnavi that he still couldn't swim. "Best friends keep everything," she said, hooking her little finger into his.
Thursday: On the pool trip, Jahnavi giggled to two girls, "Francis needs armbands!" The whole bench turned. Francis stared at the wet tiles, throat tight, and didn't talk to anyone on the bus. That night he told his mother he never wanted a best friend again. She sat on his bed, listened to all of it, and said being hurt meant he had really trusted someone.
The next Tuesday: Jahnavi pushed a folded note onto his desk: "Sorry. I wanted them to laugh with me." Francis read it twice, then slid it into his pencil box, not ready to smile yet.

What secret did Francis whisper to Jahnavi?
Francis whispered that he still couldn't swim.
What was Francis feeling on the bus after the pool trip?
He felt humiliated and betrayed, so hurt that he later said he never wanted a best friend again.
How did Francis's mother support him, and why did it help?
She listened to all of it and told him the hurt showed he had really trusted someone, which helped him see trust as worth something, not foolish.
Why might Jahnavi have told the secret, according to her note?
Jahnavi wrote that she wanted the other girls to laugh with her, so she seems to have traded Francis's trust for a moment of belonging.

You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret; and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine? Sometimes, seized with sudden agony, he could not continue his tale; at others, his voice broken, yet piercing, uttered with difficulty the words so replete with anguish. His fine and lovely eyes were now lighted up with indignation, now subdued to downcast sorrow and quenched in infinite wretchedness. Sometimes he commanded his countenance and tones and related the most horrible incidents with a tranquil voice, suppressing every mark of agitation; then, like a volcano bursting forth, his face would suddenly change to an expression of the wildest rage as he shrieked out imprecations on his persecutor.

Tell me in two sentences what this says.
The writer asks Margaret if this strange tale does not freeze the blood with horror. The man telling it is sometimes too pained to go on, and his face swings from sorrow to calm to wild rage.

Read this:

Preeti, sit down. You're off on this trekking trip, and your Vijay Mama has a confession. When I was twenty, in Indore, my friend Ashok announced he was taking a year off to travel the Himalayas by bus. I was furious. I told everyone he was a loafer, that his father's hard-earned money was being wasted, that travellers were just people running from responsibility. I went on about it for months, far more than anyone needed. Finally your Nani asked me, "Vijay, why do you keep talking about Ashok's trip?" I had no answer. That night I took out the map I'd hidden inside my accounts textbook, with routes marked in pencil. I had been planning that same trip for years and was too scared to go. The anger was about me, beta, not Ashok. So go, and send me photos.

Where had Vijay hidden his map?
Inside his accounts textbook, with routes marked in pencil.
Why did Vijay's anger at Ashok last for months?
Ashok was doing the very trip Vijay secretly longed for and feared; condemning it kept his own wish buried.
What turning point helped Vijay see the truth?
Nani's simple question about why he kept talking about Ashok's trip, which sent him back to the hidden map.
How might Ashok have felt hearing he was called a loafer?
Probably hurt and confused, since his friend's anger was much bigger than a travel plan deserved.

metadata.subtype: Fierce scorn for a secret temptation [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

For months Francis had carried the year he left college and told his parents it was a transfer. He wanted Yogesh to know, and he was afraid Yogesh would see him differently. So he began small, on a walk. "I wasn't very good at the job I had at twenty. I quit before they could fire me." Yogesh only nodded and said, "That sounds like a hard time." Nothing changed in his face, and Francis felt his shoulders drop a little.

Three weeks later, on the balcony, he took a breath. "There's something else. I never transferred. I dropped out, and I've been ashamed of it since." His voice shook on the last word.

Yogesh felt honoured and completely unsure what to say. His mind offered him solutions, a phone call to the college, a plan, and he set them all aside. He put a hand on the railing next to Francis's and said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm glad you did." He did not ask why. He did not fix it.

Next week Gurpreet asked casually over tea, "What's up with Francis lately? He seems lighter." Yogesh smiled and stirred his cup. "He's doing better. That's all I'll say."

He told them it was a transfer.

Dear Biji,

I was so sorry. I understand now: every roti was your way of saying welcome. In my family in Mangalore, love comes as endless questions; in yours, it comes hot off the tawa.

So let me say it in words: your makki roti was the best thing I've eaten this year. I stopped at three only because I was full. Next time I'll come hungry, have one more, and then ask you to teach me.

With love,
Chandrika

Avni could spread the search wider and ask more people for tutoring leads, because a second income source keeps pressure off.

The friend may feel a twinge of regret and envy, since Avni had space to be choosy.

messages.content:
Read this:

Jomon came home from the city for a weekend to help his father Manoj update the pension form at the bank in the small town. Manoj held the pen like a proud teacher, and Jomon wanted to grab it and finish the lines himself. Instead he said, "You read out the field, Appa, and I'll point." They went slowly: name as on the passbook, account number, mobile number. When Manoj mixed up two lines, Jomon did not snatch the form. He asked, "Which one is your birth date?" and Manoj tapped it himself. At the counter the clerk asked a question, and Manoj answered before Jomon could open his mouth. On the bus home Manoj said, "Next time I'll fill the whole thing and you just check it."

Which form did Jomon help his father fill in at the bank?
Jomon helped his father Manoj update the pension form.
What did Jomon want to do at first, and what does his holding back show about his feelings?
Jomon felt impatient and wanted to grab the pen, but held back out of respect for his father's dignity.
What did Jomon do instead of taking over when his father mixed up two lines?
He asked "Which one is your birth date?" so that Manoj could tap it himself.
How does Manoj likely feel about being asked to read out the fields himself?
Respected and proud, since he keeps the pen, taps the answers himself, and says he will fill the whole form next time.
I'm going to live alone for the first time next month. I'm excited but nervous.
That's a big step. Both feelings are normal. What are you most worried about?
Cooking, and feeling lonely at night.
For cooking, start with five easy dishes you can make well, like dal, rice, eggs and a simple vegetable. For the evenings, keep a routine, like a phone call to family or a walk.
What about safety?
Keep your door locked, share your address with a trusted family member and know your neighbours. Save emergency numbers in your phone.
I'm making a list of what to bring.
Add a first-aid kit, a torch, a few basic utensils and a small lock for important papers. You'll be set.
Thanks. I feel calmer now.
Good. Take it one step at a time, and call home when you need to.

Read this:

Sunday night.
Had the talk with Deepak today, about him taking over my room in the flat when I move out. I'd been dreading it all week. Ten minutes before, standing in the stairwell, my shoulders were up round my ears and my breath was stuck in my throat. So I did the thing from the yoga class: dropped my shoulders, pressed both feet into the floor, and breathed out slowly, longer than the in-breath, five times. It didn't make the talk easy. Deepak still got prickly about the deposit and I still stumbled once. But I didn't raise my voice, and I could actually think about what he was saying instead of just defending myself. We'll finish it next weekend. Writing this down so I remember it works.
Anirban

Where was Anirban standing ten minutes before the talk?
In the stairwell.
How was Anirban feeling before the talk, and what body signs showed it?
Anirban was dreading it and tense, with shoulders up round the ears and breath stuck in the throat.
What did the grounding routine change, and what did it not change?
It kept Anirban calm enough to think and not shout, but it didn't make the talk easy or settle the deposit question.
How might Deepak have experienced the conversation?
Deepak was prickly about the deposit, but probably found it easier to talk because Anirban stayed calm and listened.

metadata.subtype: Using the body to steady the mind [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday. Neelam's parents were away for the night. Nikita Masi played a lullaby on a small speaker. Neelam kept fussing, twisting in the cot.
Tuesday. Nikita picked her up, held her close, swayed slowly and sang the same lullaby herself, off-key and soft. Neelam's head grew heavy on her shoulder.
Thursday. Nikita forgot the words, so she hummed a made-up tune at the same slow pace. Neelam was asleep within minutes.

What did Nikita do when she forgot the words on Thursday?
She hummed a made-up tune at the same slow pace.
Why did Neelam settle on Tuesday but not on Monday?
On Tuesday she felt safe and comforted in Nikita's arms, with her warm voice and slow swaying; the lullaby from the speaker alone didn't give her that closeness.
What could Nikita keep doing on nights when Neelam is unsettled?
Hold her close and sing or hum slowly in her own voice, since the closeness and rhythm matter more than the right tune or words.
How might Nikita feel when a made-up tune works just as well?
Nikita would likely feel relieved and more confident about caring for Neelam while her parents are away.

Read this:

Saturday: Outside the metro station, a drunk man started shouting at Raghav for bumping into him. Chaitanya stepped between them, chest out, fists half closed. "Back off!" The man shoved Chaitanya, and a crowd gathered. Only a passing guard pulling them apart stopped a real fight.
Sunday: Chaitanya's hands still shook over breakfast. "I wanted to protect you," Chaitanya told Raghav, "and I nearly got us both hurt." Raghav nodded. "Next time just pull me away. We walk. We call someone."
Three weeks later, Friday: At the crowded Durga Puja pandal, a man was pushing and yelling in the queue, right beside a little girl who had lost hold of her mother's hand. This time Chaitanya didn't square up, but crouched, spoke softly to the girl, and with Raghav guided her away from the pushing to the volunteers' desk. Raghav told the police constable there about the man. The girl's mother came running within minutes.

Who stopped the fight outside the metro station?
A passing guard pulled them apart.
How did Chaitanya feel the morning after the metro incident?
Chaitanya felt shaken and regretful, hands still trembling, realising the urge to protect Raghav had nearly got them both hurt.
What did Chaitanya do differently at the pandal, and why was it wiser?
Instead of squaring up, Chaitanya moved the girl away from the pushing to the volunteers while Raghav told the police constable, protecting her without escalating.
How might Raghav have felt standing behind Chaitanya outside the metro?
Raghav was probably frightened, grateful for the loyalty but worried it was making the danger bigger, which is why Raghav later asked to simply walk away.
Bank ki line mein agar koi beech mein ghus jaye toh kya bolun?
Say: "Excuse me, the line starts there. Could you please join the end of it?"

Read this:

When Miss Kulkarni gave the new girl, Lalremsiami, the narrator's part in the Class 4 play, Damini, who had been narrator last year, clapped the loudest.
After that, Damini was everywhere Lalremsiami went. She walked her to the water cooler. She lent her the new twenty-four colour pencils she never let anyone touch. "You're SO good at reading aloud! You're the best in the whole class!" she said, three times before lunch.
Lalremsiami smiled, a little puzzled. "Thanks... you don't have to wait for me."
"I WANT to!" Damini said, too loudly.
At home in their Pune flat that evening, Damini coloured a picture of the play stage. She pressed so hard on the crayon that it snapped, and she threw both halves in the bin. When Mummy asked about school, Damini said, "I have a new best friend," and didn't look up.

What did Damini lend Lalremsiami?
The new twenty-four colour pencils she never let anyone touch.
Why might being extra sweet to Lalremsiami feel right to Damini?
Damini seems hurt about losing the narrator's part, but being jealous feels wrong, so loud kindness hides it even from herself; the snapped crayon hints at what is underneath.
What small step could Mummy take when Damini doesn't look up?
Mummy could sit with Damini and ask about the play, perhaps saying it's okay to feel sad about not being narrator, so the hidden feeling can be named.
What is it like for Lalremsiami to be followed everywhere and praised so much?
Lalremsiami seems puzzled and a little crowded, grateful yet unsure why Damini won't let her walk alone, which makes settling in feel strange.

messages.content:
Read this:

In the college newspaper's office, Vidya pinned the week's page stats to the board: her dry piece on hostel food had 80 reads; the angry one, “Mess committee doesn't care,” had 2,000. The team clapped. “More of that,” said the sub-editor, grinning. Vidya's next headline was sharper still. Mridul, who edited the sports page, read it over lunch and raised an eyebrow but said nothing. At the meeting, Vidya's opening line drew laughter, then more applause. Afterwards, by the photocopier, Mridul murmured, “Is that what you actually think?” Vidya opened her mouth, then closed it. “I think it gets read.”

How many reads did the angry piece get?
The angry piece had 2,000 reads.
Why did Vidya write a sharper headline after the team clapped?
Vidya felt encouraged and proud after the applause and the reads, so the harsher tone felt like what the audience wanted.
What could Vidya do after Mridul asks, “Is that what you actually think?”
Vidya could reread the sharp pieces and ask which claims Vidya truly believes, and try a headline that is clear without performing anger.
What might Mridul have been feeling when Mridul raised an eyebrow but said nothing at lunch?
Mridul may have been uneasy about the change and unsure whether to say so in front of others, and chose a private moment by the photocopier.

Read this:

It was the last day of the Diwali holidays, and Hafsa and I were flipping a one-rupee coin on the terrace to decide who got the last laddoo. Heads for her, tails for me. Heads. Heads again. Heads, heads, heads. Five heads in a row! "Now it has to be tails," I said. "The coin knows it owes me." I made her flip once more, then again, sure each time that tails was coming. Heads. Tails. Heads. "Best of twenty?" I begged. Hafsa laughed so hard she dropped the coin. "Vishal, the coin doesn't remember anything!" I still think that coin was cheating. But we split the laddoo in half.

How many heads came in a row?
Five heads in a row.
Why was Vishal so sure tails had to come next?
After five heads it felt fair and certain that the coin owed a tails, so Vishal felt hopeful and impatient, as if chance kept score.
What could help Vishal understand the coin?
Flipping it many times and writing down each result would show that every flip starts fresh, whatever came before.
How does Hafsa see Vishal's idea?
Hafsa finds it very funny, because to her the coin doesn't remember anything 😄

It was Rashmi's first trip without family, a college fest in Pune with her friends. Before she left, her boyfriend Chaitanya walked her to the bus stand.
"Send a photo of the stage when you can. Only if you want," he said.
"You're not going to call every hour?"
Chaitanya laughed. "Why would I? You're with your friends. Have fun."
On the bus, her friend Nikhita was on the phone with her own boyfriend, arguing: "No, I told you who's here. Why do you need names?"
Rashmi listened, then looked at Chaitanya's message: "Hope the bus has good music." She smiled. It felt like air.

Where was the college fest?
In Pune.
What was Rashmi feeling when she said "It felt like air"?
Rashmi felt relieved and free, trusted to enjoy her trip.
What makes Chaitanya's behaviour healthy?
He trusts Rashmi, lets her choose when to message, and doesn't demand check-ins.
How might Nikhita feel during the call?
Nikhita seems stressed and frustrated, having to explain who she's with.

I'm Minakshi, and in Class 11 I did an experiment on myself. My friend Pallavi said I was always on my phone, and I laughed. "I just check it." So she made me note every time I picked it up during a Sunday of studying. I lost count at forty. Worse, one "quick look" at a video at two o'clock ended at three. I didn't remember choosing to keep watching; the next video just started. I felt sick, honestly, and a bit cheated. After that I switched off autoplay and kept the phone in my bag during study hours. It didn't make me perfect. It made stopping possible.

At what count did Minakshi lose track?
Minakshi lost count at forty.
How did Minakshi feel after seeing the numbers?
Minakshi felt sick and a bit cheated, realising the videos had carried on without any choice.
What changes did Minakshi make, and why do they help?
Switching off autoplay and keeping the phone in a bag during study added stopping points, so willpower didn't have to do all the work.
How might Pallavi feel about the experiment's result?
Pallavi might feel a little vindicated but mostly glad her friend saw the pattern and changed something.

Rain drummed on the tin roof, so all twenty children were stuck inside the playschool, and there was only one red toy car. Kishore and Jasleen both had a hand on it. "Mine!" "I had it first!" Jasleen let go and ran to Miss Rekha. Miss Rekha came over and knelt down. "Kishore, tell me." He said he'd found it in the box. "Jasleen?" She said she had only put it down to fix her shoe. Miss Rekha nodded at both. "So what can we do?" After a moment, Kishore pushed the car to the middle of the mat. They drove it together, one pushing, one catching.

Why were all the children stuck inside?
Rain drummed on the tin roof, so they were stuck inside the playschool.
Why did Jasleen let go and run to Miss Rekha?
She felt frustrated and unfairly treated, since she had only put the car down to fix her shoe, and she trusted the teacher to sort it out.
What else could Kishore and Jasleen try before running to a teacher next time?
They could agree to take turns or push it together from the start, which is where they ended up anyway.
What is it like for Miss Rekha to settle quarrels on a rainy day?
With twenty children indoors and one red car, Miss Rekha has to listen patiently to both sides, which takes time but keeps things calm.

Monday: Pallavi, fifteen, sat on the bus stop bench. The bus was late. Her hand pulled out the phone before she'd even noticed she was bored. Thirty seconds of short videos, then another thirty.
Wednesday: Her cousin Indu, visiting, pointed it out. “You picked up your phone four times while we were talking.” Pallavi hadn't noticed once. That night she felt embarrassed, lying in bed.
Saturday: Pallavi tried an experiment. At the bus stop, she kept the phone in her bag and a small sketchbook in her pocket. The boredom came, like an itch. Her hand twitched toward the bag. Instead she drew the auto-rickshaw across the road, badly.
It wasn't as exciting as the videos. But she noticed the bus arriving.

What did Pallavi draw at the bus stop on Saturday?
She drew the auto-rickshaw across the road.
How did Pallavi feel on Wednesday night after Indu's comment?
She felt embarrassed, realising she had picked up the phone four times without noticing.
What did Pallavi's experiment change about the loop?
She kept the same cue of boredom but put the phone away and had a sketchbook ready, swapping the action.
How might Indu have felt pointing out the phone habit?
Indu may have felt a little awkward but honest, wanting a cousin to notice.

Vera had seen both flats twice. The first was near the tram line, with a small kitchen and good light. The second had a big kitchen and a five-minute longer walk to the station. She wrote a list for each, and every time she read them the balance tipped the other way.
On the second Sunday she sent both listings to her friend Lucia and typed, "You know how I live. You pick."
Lucia answered within the hour. "The second. You cook at eleven at night and you hate noise, and the trams would wake you every morning."
Vera read it twice, felt the loop stop, and emailed the second agent that same evening.

What was the difference between the two flats?
The first was near the tram line with a small kitchen and good light, and the second had a big kitchen and a longer walk to the station.
What does Vera feel when she reads Lucia's answer?
Vera feels relief as the loop stops, showing the choice was tiring her more than either flat.
What could Vera do if she disagreed with Lucia's choice?
Vera could notice her own reaction, since a sinking feeling at the answer would be a sign that she prefers the other flat.
How does the choice look to Lucia?
Lucia knows Vera's habits, cooking late and hating noise, so Lucia can decide from real knowledge of how Vera lives.

Dear Pema Ma'am,
Before I submit my essay on climate and farming, I wanted to tell you how I used an AI tool. I asked it for five angles I could take, and I picked the one on water use. I also asked it to point out grammar mistakes, and I fixed them myself. All the sentences and arguments are mine, and I have attached my rough notes so you can see how the essay grew. I wasn't sure if this is within the rules for the assignment, so I would like to ask you directly. If any of it is not allowed, I'm happy to change it before you mark it. P.S. I would rather ask now than have you wonder later.
Yours sincerely,
Parveen

What did Parveen ask the AI tool to do?
Parveen asked it for five angles and to point out grammar mistakes.
Why did Parveen write to Pema Ma'am before submitting?
Parveen was unsure whether it is within the rules, and feels honest but a little nervous, wanting to keep the teacher's trust.
What could Parveen do if Pema Ma'am says part of it is not allowed?
Parveen could redo that part without the tool and ask what help is acceptable, as the email offers.
How might Pema Ma'am see the email?
Pema Ma'am is likely to appreciate the openness, since it is easier to guide a student who says how the tool was used.

messages.content: The recipe asks for "mince", but the American site says "ground beef". Is mince a different thing?

They are close. "Mince" is British for meat that has been chopped very small, and "ground beef" is the American term for minced beef.
Examples: We made a pie with mince and peas. We made a burger with ground beef.

Read this:

Trisha, you asked why I always make chai with cardamom and a pinch of pepper. It's Dadi's way. She died five years ago, when I was twenty.
The first year was awful. I couldn't make chai at all without crying. I stopped going into the kitchen. My mother finally took me to a grief counsellor, and slowly, slowly, things moved.
Now? I make it her way every morning. Sometimes I talk to her while the water boils. "Too much pepper, Dadi?" It makes me smile more than cry now.
She also taught me to never let a guest leave hungry. So, Trisha, you're not leaving until you've had a second cup. That's Ayesha's rule, inherited from Dadi.

What does Ayesha add to her chai?
Cardamom and a pinch of pepper.
How does Ayesha feel when she talks to Dadi while the water boils?
Ayesha feels warm and fond, smiling more than crying, though the loss is still there.
What helped Ayesha through the first year?
Seeing a grief counsellor when the kitchen felt impossible, which helped the pain move.
What might Trisha experience being told she can't leave without a second cup?
Trisha may feel touched and welcomed, receiving Dadi's value through Ayesha.
On the road sign, what is a junction?

A junction is a place where two or more roads, tracks or lines meet. It is a noun.
Example: Turn left at the junction near the petrol pump.

Read this:

For three months Zainab had told her Khala and cousins in Lucknow that she worked at a call centre. In truth she delivered groceries on her scooter across Gomti Nagar, in a helmet that hid her face when she passed their street. The money paid for her typing course. But the lie had a cost: she had stopped going to the course on Saturdays in case a cousin saw her near the institute. On Friday her friend Anand, who rode for the same company, asked why she had missed class twice. 'In case someone sees me in the uniform,' she said. Anand shrugged. 'Your Khala sells pickles from home. Is that low?' Zainab laughed despite herself. That night at dinner she told Khala everything: the scooter, the money, the typing course, the plan to apply for office jobs by December. Khala was quiet, then said, 'Next time you're in our lane, stop for tea.' On Saturday Zainab went to class.

What had Zainab told her Khala she did?
Zainab had said she worked at a call centre.
What was Zainab afraid of when she skipped the Saturday class?
Zainab was afraid and ashamed that a cousin might see her in the delivery uniform.
Which choice worked, and why?
Telling Khala the truth and the December plan, because it ended the lie and let her return to the course that was the point of the work.
How does Anand see Zainab's worry about status?
Anand sees nothing low in honest work and gently points out that Zainab's Khala also works from home.

'Papa, I wanted you to hear it from me first,' Usha said into the phone, while Farida sat beside her on the hostel bed, holding her hand. 'I've accepted the Pune job. I start on the first.'
A pause. 'You didn't ask us.'
'I know. I didn't want to ask permission this time, Papa. I wanted to tell you properly, because you matter to me. I thought about Mummy's health, the distance, everything. Pune is three hours by train. I'll come home every second weekend.'
'And if we had said no?'
'I would still listen to why. But this one's my decision.' Her voice shook a little.
Another pause. Then: 'Your mother will want to pack you pickles.'
Usha laughed, eyes wet. 'Tell her the big jar.'
Farida squeezed her hand and mouthed, 'Well done.'

How far is Pune by train?
Three hours by train.
What does Usha's shaking voice suggest?
It suggests Usha felt nervous and afraid of hurting Papa, even while standing firm on the decision.
What made Usha's way of telling Papa respectful?
She told him first and warmly, explained what she had weighed and promised regular visits, neither asking permission nor defying him.
How might Papa be feeling during the pauses?
Papa is probably surprised and a little hurt at not being asked, but his line about the pickles shows he is accepting it with love.

Two days before the panchayat vote in Rampur, a voice note went round the village: if Shreya's panel won, the water tanker would stop coming to the lower mohalla. Hafsa's mother heard it at the handpump and came home pale.

"Ammi, who sent it?" Hafsa asked.

"Everyone has it."

Hafsa listened twice. The voice was a stranger's. No name, no date. She thought: who gains if the lower mohalla is scared?

In the evening she walked to the panchayat office and asked the clerk. The tanker was paid for by the district, not by any panel. She also found Shreya at a tea stall and asked her straight. Shreya laughed tiredly. "I've heard it too. It's not true. Come to the meeting tomorrow."

Hafsa went to the meeting and to the other panel's meeting as well. Then she told her mother, and the women at the handpump, what she'd found.

Who pays for the water tanker, according to the clerk?
The district, not any panel.
How did Hafsa's mother feel after hearing the voice note?
She felt frightened, coming home pale with worry about losing water.
What steps did Hafsa take to check the rumour?
She asked who sent it, noticed there was no name or date, asked who would gain, checked with the panchayat clerk, asked Shreya directly and attended both panels' meetings.
How does Shreya see the rumour about her panel?
Shreya seems tired and frustrated by it, since it is false and meant to scare people away from her.

Observation note, Class 4B, Friday
During lunch I saw Farhan break his samosa in half and slide one piece to Naveen without a word. Naveen ate it and, a little later, offered his orange segments back. Small, but both kept glancing at each other to see how it landed.
At the end of the day, Farhan whispered to Naveen, "I still can't ride a cycle. Don't tell." Then he looked around quickly. Naveen nodded, very serious.
In the line, another boy started teasing about who comes to school by bicycle. Naveen just said, "Who cares about cycles?" and changed the topic to cricket. Farhan's shoulders dropped.
The secret is a harmless one, so I left it with them. I've put both boys in the same reading group and will keep an eye on how this new friendship holds.

What did Farhan slide to Naveen at lunch?
Farhan slid one piece of his samosa to Naveen.
What do Farhan's dropping shoulders suggest?
They suggest Farhan felt relieved, because Naveen kept the secret safe instead of laughing. 🙂
How could the teacher support this growing trust?
The teacher can give the boys chances to be together, like the same reading group, and quietly watch how it goes without prying into their secret.
What might Naveen be feeling when Farhan whispers 'Don't tell'?
Naveen may feel trusted and a little important, and he takes it seriously, which is why he nodded and later steered the talk away.

A winter afternoon: Usha Dadi hides her face behind her shawl and pops out. Shalini, eight months, watches solemnly.

Three days later: the shawl comes down, Dadi says "Boo!", and Shalini gives a small gasp, then a laugh.

Lohri evening, by the bonfire: Dadi only lifts the shawl a little, and Shalini is already kicking her legs and squealing, waiting for "Boo!"

What did Dadi hide her face behind?
She hid her face behind her shawl.
How was Shalini feeling on Lohri evening?
Shalini was delighted and excited, kicking and squealing before Dadi even said "Boo!"
How did Dadi help Shalini's joy grow?
She kept repeating the same playful game over days, so Shalini learned to expect the fun.
What might Dadi feel hearing Shalini laugh for the first time?
Dadi would likely feel happy and touched, since Shalini's laugh rewarded her play.

Before: The week Lokesh started preschool, he began crawling to the table and asking for his milk in a bottle again. On Monday Thomas laughed. "You're too big for that!" Lokesh cried until dinner went cold.
During: By Wednesday Thomas tried something else. When Lokesh crawled in, Thomas scooped him up, gave him an extra-long cuddle and said, "Big day, huh?" The milk still came in his usual steel cup, and bath and story still happened at eight. Thomas didn't mention babies once.
After: The next Monday, Lokesh walked to the table, drank from the cup and told his father all about the class tortoise. At bedtime he asked for one extra cuddle, and Thomas gave him two.

What did Lokesh ask to drink his milk from?
A bottle.
What was Thomas feeling when he changed his approach on Wednesday?
After Monday's tears, Thomas seems regretful and tender, wanting to comfort Lokesh rather than tease him.
Which choice worked, and why?
Extra cuddles without mocking, while keeping the steel cup and the eight o'clock routine, reassured Lokesh so he moved forward within a week 🙂.
What was it like for Lokesh when Thomas laughed on Monday?
He felt hurt and embarrassed, which is why he cried until dinner went cold.

At the Saturday dance class in the community hall, Guru Maa stopped the music. "Lakshmi, left foot! We have done this step fifty times. Are you even listening?" Everyone froze. Lakshmi's face crumpled, and she stood very still in the middle of the floor. In the back row, Bidisha's whole body went hot. She looked down at her own ankle bells, as if she had missed the step. Her throat tightened. She couldn't look at Lakshmi, and she couldn't look away either. When the music started again, Bidisha danced badly, stiff and out of time. After class, she found Lakshmi tying her shoes and sat down next to her. "That was horrible," Bidisha whispered. "I felt it too."

Where was the Saturday dance class?
In the community hall.
What was Bidisha feeling when she looked down at her own ankle bells?
Bidisha felt Lakshmi's embarrassment as if it were her own, with her body going hot and her throat tightening.
What did Bidisha choose to say after class, and why might it help?
Bidisha sat beside Lakshmi and said she felt it too, which tells Lakshmi she isn't alone in the embarrassment.
How might Guru Maa see Bidisha dancing badly after the scolding?
Guru Maa might think Bidisha wasn't concentrating, not realising the scolding had shaken Bidisha too.

Selin pasted a summary of a research paper into her notes, and it read beautifully: one clear claim, a percentage, and two citations. Before using it in her seminar talk, she made a small list. One: find the paper. Two: read the abstract and the results table. Three: look for the percentage. Four: search for each citation.

From her flat in Istanbul, she opened the original on her laptop. The percentage was close but not the same, and the paper said "in a small sample," which the summary had dropped. One of the citations did not exist at all.

She corrected the number, added the caveat, and sent her friend Sofia a quick message: "Glad I checked. Never trusting a tidy summary again."

How many citations did the summary give, and how many turned out not to exist?
The summary gave two citations, and one of them did not exist at all.
What was Selin feeling when she saw the citation did not exist?
Selin was surprised and relieved, since the check had caught an error before it reached her talk.
What could Selin do next time she wants a quick overview, and why?
Selin could use the summary only as a map and read the original paper's abstract and results herself, because a tidy summary can be wrong while still sounding sure.
How might Sofia see Selin's message?
Sofia may feel the lesson is useful for Sofia's own work and admire the care Selin took before speaking to the seminar.

messages.content: My brother needs to "cool off" after the argument. Does he need a fan?

No. Here "cool off" means to become calmer after being angry. It can also mean to become less hot.
Examples: Go for a walk and cool off before you reply. We sat under a tree to cool off.

Home-to-daycare diary, from Karthik's father, Pradeep
On Sunday we visited Thatha. When Thatha said, 'Karthik, shoes off inside,' Karthik stopped and pulled at his sandals right away, though at home he fights us about it. He sat close to Thatha all evening and kept patting his knee. At dinner, when I said 'enough sweets,' he pouted but put the laddu down. We were pleasantly surprised.

Whom did the family visit on Sunday?
They visited Thatha.
What might Karthik have felt towards Thatha, based on his behaviour?
He seems to feel both respect and warmth for Thatha, since he obeyed him quickly and stayed close, patting his knee.
What could the daycare teacher take from this note?
She could see that Karthik listens well to calm, trusted adults, and use short, friendly instructions with him.
Why might Thatha's words work better than the parents' at home?
Karthik may see Thatha as a special elder and be eager to please him, while at home he is testing limits with his parents.

On the steps outside the Chennai coaching centre, Indu leaned in. "Guess who writes Arvind's name in the back of her rough book? Meena." Kavitha shrieked; Divya covered her mouth. For five whole minutes Indu was the centre of the circle, adding details: the little hearts, the way Meena went red in chemistry. It felt warm, being the one who knew things.
Then Meena herself walked past with her bag. The circle went silent, then burst into giggles. Meena looked at them, puzzled, and walked faster.
On the bus home, Indu scrolled through her phone. Kavitha had already sent "Meena + Arvind" to someone else. Indu stared at it. If they could pass on Meena's rough book this fast, what would they do with her own diary, the one Kavitha had flipped through last week?

Whose name did Meena write in the back of her rough book?
Arvind's name.
What was Indu feeling on the bus home?
Indu felt a nervous unease, worried the group might one day spread her own secrets just as fast.
What could Indu do next time the group wants juicy news?
Change the subject or keep other people's private things private, even if it means not being the centre of the circle.
What was it like for Meena walking past the giggling circle?
Meena felt puzzled and uncomfortable, sensing she was being laughed at without knowing why.

Chandrika came off the tiny stage at the Indiranagar café after her first open-mic set, gripping the bottle of water with both hands.
"Tell me," she said. "Was it terrible?"
Shreya had watched every minute. The opening joke had fallen flat, and Chandrika had spoken too fast in the middle. But the story about her grandmother haggling at the vegetable market had made the whole room laugh, including a grumpy man by the window.
Shreya didn't say "It was amazing." Chandrika would never believe her again.
"The grandmother story was real," Shreya said. "You had the whole room there. Even the man by the window."
Chandrika's shoulders came down. "And the start?"
"Start with the grandmother next time."
Chandrika grinned and pulled out her notebook right there on the pavement, crossing out the first page.

What story made the whole room laugh?
The story about her grandmother haggling at the vegetable market.
How was Chandrika feeling when she came off the stage?
She felt nervous and exposed, gripping the water bottle and asking if it was terrible.
What would you advise someone who wants to support a friend after a shaky performance?
Name one true strength warmly, like Shreya did, and answer honest questions simply, without a lecture or a fake "amazing."
Why might Shreya have avoided saying "It was amazing"?
Shreya knew Chandrika would stop believing Shreya's praise, so a true compliment kept Shreya's words worth trusting.
