Read this:

On Republic Day the fog was so thick that the back rows of the assembly could barely see the stage. The microphone crackled in the cold, and Sir kept tapping it.
Lokesh, carrying the tray of paper flags, caught his shoe on the second step and stumbled. Two flags fluttered to the ground. His ears went hot. Everyone saw, he thought. The whole school. They'll call me Flag Boy till Class 10.
After the anthem he hid behind the water cooler.
Bhavna found him there, rubbing her cold hands. "Did my speech sound okay? I forgot one line and I think everyone noticed."
"What? No," Lokesh said. "I didn't hear any mistake."
"Good. Why are you hiding?"
"Because I fell."
Bhavna frowned. "When?"

What did Lokesh drop when he stumbled?
Two flags fluttered to the ground from the tray of paper flags.
What was Lokesh worried about after he stumbled?
Lokesh was embarrassed and scared that the whole school saw and would call him Flag Boy for years.
What could Lokesh remind himself the next time he slips in front of people?
Lokesh could remember that Bhavna, busy worrying about her own line, never even saw the fall, so most people are thinking about themselves.
How did Bhavna experience the same assembly?
Bhavna spent it worrying about her own forgotten line, so the stumble in the fog passed completely unnoticed.
Turn this into an exclamation: It is a very beautiful garden.
What a beautiful garden!
"Off the hook": is that about fishing?

It comes from fishing, but the idiom means to be freed from a duty, blame or a difficult situation.
Example: The teacher forgot to collect the homework, so we were off the hook.

Farhan's slot at the depot ended at one, and the clinic's queue was long, so he waited on the plastic chair with a folded note in his hand. The ache below his ribs had started three weeks ago and got sharper whenever he lifted heavy cartons. His cousin kept forwarding videos with scary claims, but Farhan had stopped watching them.

When his turn came, Dr Shalini asked when it began. He read out the dates from his note and what made it worse. She examined him carefully, then explained which tests would help and what each one could show. Farhan asked how long the results would take, wrote the answer down, and hurried back to the depot with ten minutes to spare.

What did Farhan carry into the consultation room?
He carried a folded note with the dates and what made the ache worse.
What does Farhan stopping the forwarded videos suggest about his feelings?
It suggests he was worried and wanted real answers, having decided the frightening claims were not helping him.
If the clinic had been closed that day, what other approach could Farhan have tried, and why?
He could have phoned to book a slot at a time that fit his shift, since a professional's view still beats guesswork and a booked visit avoids another wasted trip.
How might Dr Shalini have seen Farhan's note?
The note likely made her job easier, because the dates and triggers gave her clear facts to work from in a short visit.

Freya lowered the block, looked at it, then lifted it once more, squealed softly, whispered "Look?" and searched his face. This time Javier lowered his paper. "Ah, a red one!" he said, and Freya's whole body wriggled.

Before: Mehak's resume listed every class she'd taken and every certificate, in tiny font. After her first interview, the panel said, "We couldn't tell what you actually did." She went home stung.

During: A week later, her senior Sudha went through it with her. "What did you build? What problem did you solve?" Mehak realised her best work, a small app for the college canteen, was buried at the bottom. They moved it to the top. Sudha also made her practise answering in two minutes.

After: At her next interview, a month later, Mehak explained the canteen app clearly. Her voice was steady. The panel asked follow-up questions, and she answered them. She walked out smiling.

What did Mehak build for the college canteen?
She built a small app.
How did Mehak feel after the first panel's comment?
She felt stung and hurt, realising her resume hadn't shown what she could actually do.
What changes made Mehak's second interview better?
Putting her best project first and practising short, clear answers helped her present her skills confidently.
How might Sudha feel knowing Mehak's interview went well?
She'd probably feel pleased and proud that her help made a real difference.

Neelam sat on her bed with a pencil and paper. The fire-safety aunty at school had said to start from the end. "The end is Francis Uncle's gate across the lane, where everyone meets." She drew a box there. "Before the gate, the lane. Before the lane, the flat door. Before the door, the stairs, not the lift, because lifts can stop. And before the stairs, nothing in my hands: no bag, no phone, no hunting for shoes." She drew arrows backward until they reached her bed, then read them forward. It looked like a short walk. She stuck the paper inside her cupboard door.

Where did Neelam decide the meeting place should be?
She chose Francis Uncle's gate across the lane.
What was Neelam feeling after reading her arrows forward?
Reassured and calm, since the way out looked like a short walk.
What other approach could Neelam use to check her plan, and why?
She could walk the route with her family and time it, because walking it shows any blocked or slow spots that a paper plan hides.
How might Francis Uncle see being the meeting place?
He is a fixed, familiar spot where neighbours can gather, so he can help count people and call for help.

metadata.subtype: Approach: working backward from the safe meeting spot [Thinking]

Read this:

Dear Nitin Sir,
I got the result today. I failed the second level of the accountancy exam again, by six marks. I cried the whole afternoon. For an hour I thought about giving up and taking any job. But I remembered what you said when I was your student: failure is information. So tonight I went through my paper. I lost most marks in taxation, the same as last time. I'm going to join the weekend batch you recommended and practise a full paper every Sunday. The next attempt is in six months. I'm scared, but I'm trying again.
Dolma

By how many marks did Dolma fail?
By six marks.
What was Dolma feeling during that hour of thinking about giving up?
Dolma felt deeply discouraged and hurt after failing again.
What did Dolma do that shows determination?
Dolma studied the paper, found the weak area and made a specific plan for the next attempt.
How might Nitin Sir feel reading this email?
Moved and proud that a former student is using Sir's own words to try again.

Read this:

When I made my art account last year, the first thing I did wasn't posting. I'm Sarita, and I sat on the stairs with my phone and asked myself: why am I doing this?
To get famous? No, that made my stomach knot. To sell drawings? Not yet. The honest answer was that I wanted Nani in Jaipur and my cousins to see what I make, and maybe a few friends from school to say something nice.
Once I knew that, the rest was easy. If the audience is family and friends, the account should be private. So I set it to private and only accepted people I actually know. My brother Santosh said I'd never get followers that way. I said, “I don't want followers. I want Nani.”
It also changed what I post: finished pieces and messy sketches, but no selfies, no school uniform, nothing about where we live.

Who did Sarita want to see the art?
Nani in Jaipur, the cousins, and a few friends from school.
How did Sarita feel about the idea of getting famous?
It made Sarita's stomach knot, a sign of discomfort with a big public audience.
What else could Sarita decide as the account grows?
Review every few months whether the purpose has changed, say toward selling, and adjust privacy only after talking it over with family.
How does Santosh see the private account?
Santosh thinks it limits followers, not seeing that Sarita's purpose is family, not fame.

metadata.subtype: Approach: deciding purpose and audience first [Thinking]

A few weeks ago Reena came to my desk with the proposal for the school-uniform client and said, 'They'll reject it. They always go with the cheapest.' She said it the way you'd say it's Tuesday. I nearly agreed; I've been team lead for eight months and I'm still learning when to push. Privately, I'd have bet on a yes. Instead I asked, 'Is that something you know, or something you're guessing?' She thought. 'Guessing. But a strong guess.' 'Okay. Write it down, and let's send it and see.' She wrote 'Rejected, 90%' on a sticky note and put it on her monitor. Ten days later the client called. They didn't choose us, but not because of price; they needed a delivery date we couldn't meet, and they asked us to pitch again in March. Reena peeled off the sticky note and said, 'Wasim, I was wrong about the reason, and you were wrong about the yes.'

What did Reena write on the sticky note?
She wrote 'Rejected, 90%' on the sticky note.
Why did Wasim nearly agree with Reena at first?
Wasim felt unsure as a new team lead, and Reena's calm certainty made the prediction sound like fact, so going along felt easier than questioning it.
Why was asking 'know or guessing?' a useful move?
It separated the forecast from fact, so Reena could name it as a guess, write it down and check it against what really happened.
How might Reena hold her predictions after this?
Reena may hold them more loosely, since the result surprised her too, and treat them as guesses to test rather than certain news.

In the village lane, Trisha, two, fell and grazed her palm on the stones. She howled.

Her mother, Indu, ran over. "Oh, my baby. That really hurt." She blew on the graze, kissed it and held Trisha close.

A neighbour said, "It's nothing, don't cry!"

Indu kept rocking. "It hurt her." Soon Trisha stopped crying and went back to chasing the hens.

What did Trisha graze on the stones?
Trisha grazed her palm.
Why did Trisha stop crying soon after Indu held her?
Trisha felt comforted and safe, because her pain was taken seriously.
How was Indu's response different from the neighbour's, and why does it matter?
Indu acknowledged the hurt calmly, while the neighbour said it was nothing; acknowledging it teaches trust.
How does the neighbour see Trisha's fall?
The neighbour sees it as a small thing that doesn't need tears.

At the architecture firm in Vancouver, Xin's manager, Nadia, wanted to see every sketch before it went further. Every line, every window height, every colour swatch. She would stand behind Xin's chair and say, "Move that two centimetres." After a month Xin stopped drawing options, just one safe version, the one Nadia would probably pick. Lunch breaks got longer. Then Nadia went on leave for six weeks, and her stand-in, Omar, gave one instruction: "Community library, budget and brief attached, first concept by the 20th. Surprise me." Xin stayed late that evening, though nobody had asked, sketching three wildly different roofs and humming.

What instruction did Omar give?
"Community library, budget and brief attached, first concept by the 20th. Surprise me."
Why did Xin stop drawing options and take longer lunches?
With every line checked and moved, Xin's own judgement seemed useless, so the drive to try things drained away.
What could Nadia take from Omar's approach when she returns?
She could set the goal and deadline and then step back, reviewing concepts rather than every line, so Xin's initiative can last.
How might Nadia feel if she saw Xin humming over three roofs?
She might be surprised, or a little stung, to see how much energy Xin has when given room.

Varun: random q
Varun: you started wearing the cap on Fridays. is that a new thing?
Rafiq: yeah since Eid
Varun: cool. is it like a strict rule?
Rafiq: for me it's more like... my abbu wears one, and my dada did

Varun: I wear my rakhi till it falls apart. people think it's a fashion band

Since when has Rafiq worn the cap on Fridays?
Since Eid.
How did Rafiq feel about Varun asking directly?
Rafiq felt appreciated and respected, since others like Kunal had assumed without ever asking.
Which choice of Varun's was wise, and why?
Asking Rafiq instead of believing Kunal's assumption, because the cap's meaning turned out to be faith, family and style together.
How does Kunal seem to see the cap?
Kunal seems to read it as a sign of becoming very strict, an assumption that doesn't match Rafiq's reasons.
He do not came yesterday. Fix it please.
The correct sentence is: "He did not come yesterday."

In the village school near Jorhat, the girls under the peepal tree had a game: whenever Bhupen walked past in his patched shirt, they sang, 'Here comes the scarecrow.' Urmila always sang too, softer than the others. She hated it. But Minoti, who led the group, had once dropped a girl just for not laughing, and nobody sat with that girl for a month. On Monday Bhupen walked past again. The song started. Urmila kept her mouth shut and looked down at her slate. Minoti noticed. 'What's wrong with you?' 'Nothing. I just don't want to.' Minoti sniffed and turned away. Three girls followed her. But Juri stayed, and quietly slid closer to Urmila on the tree root.

What did the group sing when Bhupen walked past?
'Here comes the scarecrow.'
Why had Urmila always sung, even though she hated it?
She was afraid of being dropped, like the girl nobody sat with for a month.
What did Urmila's quiet refusal show her?
Who truly stood by her: three girls followed Minoti, but Juri stayed beside her.
How might Bhupen feel hearing the song every day?
Humiliated and hurt about his patched shirt, and perhaps relieved to notice one voice go quiet.

A quick reminder: please bring your printed project charts to tomorrow's presentation. We will need them on the table when we begin. Thank you all for the effort you have put in so far.

Playgroup note, winter term
Himani (2 years 3 months) did something lovely today. Last week her grandmother visited and wore a warm shawl, folding it over her shoulders before going out.
Today, in the dress-up corner, Himani took a scarf, folded it carefully over her shoulders, patted it twice, and said, "Cold! Going out!" 🙂
Her friend Chandrika copied her immediately.
We played along and walked around the room saying "brrr." I'll suggest her mother tell her grandmother.

What did Himani say after folding the scarf?
"Cold! Going out!"
How did Himani seem to feel in the dress-up corner?
She seemed proud and happy, carefully copying her grandmother's shawl.
How did the playgroup staff support Himani's imitation?
They joined the pretend play, walking around saying "brrr", which encouraged her.
How might Himani's grandmother feel hearing about this?
She would likely feel touched and delighted that Himani remembered her.
Will it snow on the hill station next week? And one more: is it "squirel" or "squirrel"?

1. I can't know, because forecasts so far ahead are not reliable and I can't see live weather. Check a weather service shortly before you travel.
2. It is "squirrel", with a double "r".

Inside the kitchen cupboard of their shared flat in Lisbon, Noa kept a sticky note: Dalia – rent top-up, bus pass, concert ticket. She had never meant it as a bill; it was just so she wouldn't forget.
On Thursday Dalia leaned in the doorway. "Tiny favour? My card's being weird again. Could you cover the groceries? I'll pay you back Friday, promise."
Noa was already reaching for her wallet. Then she glanced at the note and noticed that every Friday on it had come and gone. The same week, Dalia had posted photos from a weekend away at the coast.
Noa's stomach tightened. She liked being the one people could count on. "I can't this time," she said, her voice wobbling. "And I'd like us to sit down and go through the list first."
Dalia rolled her eyes. "Seriously? I thought we were friends."
"We are. That's why I'm saying it."

Where did Noa keep the sticky note?
Inside the kitchen cupboard of their shared flat in Lisbon.
What was Noa feeling when she said "I can't this time"?
She felt anxious and torn: her stomach tightened and her voice wobbled, because she liked being someone people could count on but saw that every promised Friday had passed.
What could Noa do next to protect both her kindness and herself?
She could hold the talk about the list, stay friendly but firm, and if Dalia keeps asking, talk it through with someone she trusts before agreeing to help again.
Why might Dalia react with an eye-roll?
Dalia is used to Noa saying yes, so a no feels like a change in the friendship; being asked about the list may also embarrass her.

Trainee batch note, week three. From the training coordinator.
Saurabh (from Patna, first job, first time living away from home) has joined every plan in the batch so far: the Friday biryani run, the Sunday fort trek, even the badminton group, though he told me he "can't really play". He is always the first to reply "I'm in" on the batch group.
He and Sonali, from Guwahati, seem to have become very close very quickly. I often see them in the cafeteria after nine, talking about home food and their mothers' phone calls. Last week Sonali said to me, laughing, "He's already like my brother."
It is lovely to see, and it is helping both of them settle. I have also noticed that Saurabh looks lost on evenings when no plan is on. I've paired him with a senior buddy for the next month and will mention the wellness sessions at our check-in.

What does Saurabh reply on the batch group?
Saurabh is always the first to reply 'I'm in' on the batch group.
Why might Saurabh join every plan, even badminton?
Saurabh is far from home for the first time and probably lonely; saying yes keeps away the empty evenings, which is when he looks lost.
What did the coordinator do well to support Saurabh at this stage?
The coordinator noticed the pattern without judging it, paired Saurabh with a senior buddy and planned to mention the wellness sessions, giving steadier support than one fast friendship.
How might Sonali see the closeness with Saurabh?
Sonali seems to enjoy it and already calls him like a brother, because sharing homesickness makes the bond feel strong very fast.

Monday. Farhan from sales storms into Sarika's cabin. 'The client wants the reporting module in two weeks or they walk.' Her engineers had just told her it needs six.
Tuesday. Sarika doesn't pick a side. She asks Farhan what exactly the client will use first, and asks her engineers which parts are nearly ready. The answers overlap: the client needs daily sales reports on day one; the custom dashboards can wait. Daily reports are nearly done.
Thursday. She presents it to both groups: daily reports go live in two weeks, properly tested; dashboards follow in the next release, a month later. Farhan calls the client from her cabin. After ten minutes he gives her a thumbs up through the glass. Her lead engineer, walking past, mouths 'thank you'.

What does the client need on day one?
Daily sales reports.
How did Farhan feel when he stormed in on Monday?
Farhan was stressed and frustrated, afraid of losing the client.
What could Sarika do to keep the second release on track?
She could set a clear date for the dashboards, share progress with Farhan weekly and flag any delay early.
How might Sarika's engineers see her approach?
They are grateful not to rush unfinished dashboards, and can ship what is nearly done with proper testing.
I want to back up my photos so I don't lose them.
A good rule is to keep more than one copy, in more than one place. For example, one on your device, one on an external drive and one in an online storage service.
How often should I do it?
Whenever you add photos you would hate to lose. Many people back up once a week or once a month.
Is online storage safe?
It is convenient, and reputable services protect files carefully. Use a strong, unique password and, if offered, two-step sign-in.
What's a strong password?
A long one, with a mix of words or characters that is not easy to guess. Do not use birthdays or names, and do not reuse it on other sites.
How do I remember it?
Try a long phrase of several unrelated words, which is easier to recall than random characters. A password manager is another option.

"Tejas, please sit down."
"I don't want to!" Tejas threw the book on the mat and started to cry.
Payal knelt. "Hey. What's going on?"
"I don't know." He pulled at his shirt.
"Did you eat breakfast?"
"No. Mumma was late."
Payal glanced at the clock: fifteen minutes to snack. "Let's get your tiffin now."
"Before snack time?"
"Yes, now."
She sat with him on the steps. He ate his upma in big spoonfuls, then leaned back.
"Can I hear the end of the story?"
Payal smiled. "Of course."

Why hadn't Tejas eaten breakfast?
Because Mumma was late.
What was Payal thinking when she asked about breakfast?
She suspected Tejas was hungry rather than naughty, and felt concerned for him.
What did Payal learn that could help another teacher?
That a child who seems difficult may just be hungry, and meeting that need first can change the behaviour.
How does Tejas seem to feel after eating?
He seems calm and settled, asking to hear the end of the story he had rejected.

metadata.subtype: Teacher notices a child cannot focus before snack [Observer]

He did not leave for Cambridge the next day, as he had said he would. He deferred his departure a whole week, and during that time he made me feel what severe punishment a good yet stern, a conscientious yet implacable man can inflict on one who has offended him. Without one overt act of hostility, one upbraiding word, he contrived to impress me momently with the conviction that I was put beyond the pale of his favour.

How does the man punish the narrator without any open hostility?
He puts off leaving for Cambridge for a whole week. Without any open act of hostility or a word of blame, he makes the narrator feel shut out of his favour.
Why does worry about a test often feel worse at night?
At night there is little to distract the mind. Because the house is quiet and we are tired, thoughts keep returning to the worry and it feels bigger than it is.
My uncle bought a watch to me on my birthday. Which word is wrong?

My uncle bought a watch for me on my birthday.
Why: "Buy" takes "for" with the person who gets the thing.
Why do farmers choose seeds to match the season?
Seeds need the right weather to grow. Because a crop planted in the wrong season may face cold, drought or flood, matching it to the season gives it the best chance.

The school's philosophy club had one hour before the debate, and the power had gone out, so Sonali and Ganga sat in the dark library with a single torch. Their topic: "Is it ever right to lie?" Sonali, who liked rules, said lying is always wrong; her grandmother's faith said so. Ganga argued that lying to protect someone could be right, like hiding a friend from danger. "So which is it?" Sonali asked, frustrated. Ganga shrugged. "Different systems answer differently. One says follow the rule. One says look at the results." Sonali thought for a while. "Maybe both help. Rules keep us honest, but we should also think about who gets hurt." They agreed to present both views fairly. The torch flickered.

What was the topic of the debate?
The topic was "Is it ever right to lie?"
Why did Sonali get frustrated?
She believed strongly that lying is always wrong, and Ganga's example challenged that certainty, making her uneasy.
What made Sonali and Ganga's final approach reasonable?
They compared the rule-based view and the results-based view and chose to present both fairly, instead of mocking one side.
How might Sonali's grandmother react to the girls' conclusion?
She might still stress honesty but appreciate that Sonali is thinking carefully about when harm is involved.

I kept waiting for the right moment to tell my parents about the job in Toronto, and the right moment never came. On every Sunday call I opened my mouth and asked about the neighbours instead. Then, three weeks before my visa interview, my aunt phoned Amma. "Ganga is going abroad, didn't she tell you?" Amma called me that night and her voice was quiet. "Why did I hear it from Bua?" I tried to say I had been protecting them. It sounded thin. It was not the moving that hurt; it was the finding out. It took Papa two days to speak to me. I think if I had told them in March, they would have cried and then helped me pack. Instead I had to earn back something I had not known I could lose. - Ganga

Who told Amma about the job abroad?
Ganga's aunt, Bua, phoned Amma and told her.
What was Amma feeling when she asked "Why did I hear it from Bua?"
Amma felt hurt and shut out, and her voice was quiet.
What could Ganga do now to repair things?
Ganga could apologise sincerely for not telling them, share the plans and a visiting schedule, and listen to their worries.
How might Papa have felt during the two days before he spoke?
Papa may have felt hurt and disappointed, taking time to gather himself before talking.

metadata.subtype: Approach: putting it off until the last moment [Pitfall]

Mehak worries about making things worse for the team, and feels upset and embarrassed after being spoken to rudely.
What could Disha do to protect Mehak and still keep the client relationship respectful?
Disha could speak privately to the client about tone and publicly back Mehak on the next call, which shows the team that respect is not negotiable.
How might the client see Disha's call about tone?
The client may feel defensive at being corrected, but a private, calm conversation gives a chance to reset without a public confrontation.
Why does an empty room echo more than a room full of furniture?
Bare walls and floors bounce sound back, so an empty room echoes. Because curtains, sofas and rugs are soft and soak up part of the sound, a furnished room sends much less of it back to our ears.

Day seventy-three. On Sunday afternoons in Gothenburg, boredom was the worst part. Lars had cleaned the flat twice, and the old urge seeped in slowly, like damp through a wall: just one beer at the pub on the corner of the old street, where everyone knew him.
He noticed his jaw clench. That morning he had felt almost hopeful, swimming his lengths at the public pool and thinking he might finally apply for the design course. Now he snapped at the kettle for being slow.
He took out the card his counsellor had helped him write: sleep by eleven, swim four mornings a week, Wednesday group, no corner pub.
He texted Daniel, his friend from the Wednesday group: "Sunday's being a Sunday. Craving. Walk?"
Daniel replied within a minute: "Harbour in 20. Bringing cinnamon buns."
Lars put his shoes on, still irritable, and took the long way round so he wouldn't pass the pub.

Where did Lars agree to meet Daniel?
At the harbour, in 20 minutes.
How does Lars's mood swing during that Sunday?
He felt almost hopeful in the morning after swimming, but by afternoon boredom brought a craving and he turned irritable, snapping at the kettle.
What in Lars's plan carries him through this afternoon?
His written structure of sleep, swimming, the Wednesday group and avoiding the corner pub, plus an honest text to Daniel and the long way round.
What might Daniel understand when Lars texts 'Sunday's being a Sunday'?
Daniel, from the same Wednesday group, likely recognises the craving at once and answers quickly with a plan, knowing how hard those empty afternoons can be.

In their PG in Kothrud, Neelam had become Hansa's go-to for programming. Whenever Hansa's code broke, she'd slide her laptop across the kitchen table and Neelam would fix it in a minute. It felt kind. It was quicker than explaining.
By November, Hansa had stopped reading error messages at all. 'Neelam di, it's red again,' she'd call, and Neelam would come.
Then Hansa had a live coding round for an internship. Forty minutes, camera on, no help. Her program threw an error in the first ten minutes. She stared at it. She realised she had never once fixed an error on her own. She typed, deleted, typed. The interviewer waited, then said, 'Let's stop here.'
That night Hansa said quietly, 'I think you fixed too much for me.' Neelam, drying a plate, didn't argue.

How long was the live coding round?
Forty minutes, camera on, no help.
What was Hansa feeling when the error appeared in the interview?
She felt panicked and helpless, realising she had never fixed an error alone.
What could Neelam do differently from now on?
Ask Hansa to read the error aloud and guess the cause first, giving a hint only after her own attempt.
How might Neelam feel hearing 'I think you fixed too much for me'?
Neelam likely feels guilty and sad, seeing that the quick help was not really kind in the long run.

Subject: Workload over the next month

Hi Vandana,
I want to raise something before it becomes a problem.
For the past six weeks I've been sleeping badly and feeling drained even after weekends. I've made two small errors in client reports that I'd normally catch. I don't think I can keep this pace and still do good work.
Right now I have the Mehta audit, the training module, the quarterly deck and two client reviews. My suggestion:
– Delay the training module to next quarter.
– Share the quarterly deck with Anjali, who offered.
– Keep the audit and the client reviews.
I've also booked an appointment with my doctor next week, since this has gone on a while.
I'd rather ask now than drop something important later. Can we talk on Thursday?
Thanks,
Francis

Which task does Francis suggest delaying to next quarter?
The training module.
How has Francis been feeling for the past six weeks?
Francis has felt drained and worn out, sleeping badly even after weekends.
What makes this email a good example of reducing load?
It names the symptoms, lists the tasks, proposes clear changes to delay and share work, and mentions a doctor's appointment, all before something important is dropped.
How might Vandana see this email?
Vandana would likely appreciate the clarity and early warning, since it gives Vandana options instead of a sudden crisis.

messages.content: Tailor ko bolna hai "Yeh kurta thoda dheela hai, ise tight kar dijiye." English?
Say: "This kurta is a bit loose. Please make it tighter."
Does for instance mean the same as for example?

Yes. Instance is a noun meaning one example or case, so for instance is another way of saying for example.
Example: Many birds eat insects. The sparrow, for instance, feeds its chicks with them.

The slide line stretched past the tap. Shankar ran along the side, squeezed in between two children near the front and grabbed the ladder. "Hey!" shouted a girl. "Back of the line!" shouted the others. Shankar slid down with a big grin that faded when he looked round. Chaitanya, who had been waving Shankar over to stand with him at the back, folded his arms. At the next break Chaitanya walked past Shankar without a word, and Shankar stood by the wall alone.

Where did Shankar squeeze in?
Shankar squeezed in between two children near the front of the line.
What was Shankar feeling when his grin faded as he looked round?
Shankar felt uneasy and a little ashamed. He got his turn, but he saw everyone was angry.
What could Shankar have done instead, and why?
Shankar could have gone to Chaitanya at the back and waited, or asked someone, "Can I go after you?" Shankar would get a turn and keep Chaitanya's goodwill.
How does the pushing in look to Chaitanya?
Chaitanya had waved Shankar over to wait together, so it feels like someone Shankar was invited to wait with chose to skip everyone. That hurts, so turning away makes sense. 😔

In Madrid, Santiago got a lunchtime detention for 'starting a fight' in the playground. He hadn't started it. Pablo had shoved him first, and he'd only pushed back to get free. The teacher on duty had only seen the push. All afternoon, Santiago's jaw ached from clenching. On the walk home he decided not to tell Mum; she'd just be disappointed. But at dinner she asked, 'Something wrong, mi amor?' and he couldn't hold it in. He told her everything, even about his own push. Layla listened without interrupting. Then she said, 'Thank you for telling me all of it, even your part. I believe you. I'll email your teacher and ask for a proper conversation.' Santiago let out a long breath. Not every grown-up got it wrong.

What was Santiago's detention for?
'Starting a fight' in the playground.
Why did Santiago almost not tell Mum?
He was afraid she would be disappointed in him, even though the punishment was unfair.
Why did telling the whole story help?
Including his own push made him believable, so Layla could see the truth and ask the teacher for a proper conversation.
How did Layla respond to Santiago's story?
With trust and support; she thanked him for telling all of it and said she believed him.

You want to know about my gaming? I'm Parul. Okay.
In second year, I'd play from ten at night till five in the morning. Online team games. I'd tell myself one more match, every match. If I stopped, I felt restless and irritable. I skipped classes. I lied to my parents about marks.
My friend Parveen noticed first. She said, "You look grey." I laughed it off.
Then I failed two papers. I sat in my room and couldn't even open the game; I just cried.
I went to the student counselling centre that week. The counsellor explained the loop: stress, game, relief, guilt, more stress. We made a plan. Deleted the game from my laptop. Played football instead. Told my parents the truth.
It took months. I still play sometimes, but not at night.

How many papers did Parul fail?
Two papers.
What was Parul feeling when stopping the game?
Parul felt restless and irritable, a sign of dependence.
What choice inside the story started Parul's recovery?
Going to the student counselling centre that week after failing two papers.
How might Parveen feel seeing Parul recover?
Parveen is likely relieved and glad she spoke up early.

Sum up Avni Phuphi's story in two sentences.

Ayesha, you said you feel like a fake grown-up. Sit, and let your Avni Phuphi tell you about 1998. I was twenty-one, working my first job at a Delhi call centre, living in a working women's hostel. I paid my own rent and felt so independent. But every Sunday my father sent a parcel of food and an envelope of money, and I took it every time. One evening my roommate, Shabnam, found me crying over my first salary slip because it was less than Abbu earned when I was born. 'Are we adults or not?' I asked her. She laughed. 'We're both. Eat your parcel.' I decided then to stop asking. Three years later I tried to pay Abbu back for the envelopes. He tore up the cheque, and we both cried.

At twenty-one, Avni felt independent in her first job but still accepted her father's weekly food parcels and money, and a friend told her she could be both adult and cared for. Years later her father tore up her cheque repaying him, and they both cried.

Mehak, your Ishita Bua was not born organised, you know. In my board year I made a timetable and followed it about as well as you follow your mother's rules. Then my Maths teacher told us to check it every Sunday: what I had planned against what I had done. First Sunday, I sat with two columns. Mornings, fine. Evenings, almost nothing: Chemistry planned from seven to nine, done maybe half an hour. Second Sunday, the same. By evening I was tired, the TV was on, my brothers were fighting. So I swapped. Chemistry and Maths went to six in the morning, when the house was quiet and my head was fresh. Evenings became light revision and flashcards. Third Sunday, the two columns almost matched.

When did young Ishita check her timetable?
Every Sunday, comparing what was planned with what was done.
How might young Ishita have felt seeing the evening column nearly empty?
Young Ishita probably felt frustrated and disappointed to see the evening Chemistry slipping two Sundays in a row.
Which change inside the story made the columns match, and why?
Moving Chemistry and Maths to six in the morning, when the house was quiet and the mind fresh, and leaving evenings for light revision that tiredness could not derail.
What would have changed if Ishita had kept Chemistry in the evening slot?
The evening column would likely have stayed nearly empty, and Chemistry would have fallen further behind every week.

Monday: Payal's school shirt had five tiny buttons. Papa, Pradeep, did them all while she wriggled. "Thank you, Papa."
Wednesday: Papa did the top two, then stopped. "You do the rest. I'm right here." Payal's fingers fumbled. One button went in the wrong hole. Papa showed her once, slowly. She did it.
Saturday: Payal did four buttons herself. The top one was too stiff. "Papa, help, please?" He pushed it halfway, and she finished it. "Thank you, Papa! I did almost all!" She hugged his leg, beaming.

How many buttons were on Payal's school shirt?
It had five tiny buttons.
How did Payal feel on Saturday?
She felt proud of doing almost all the buttons herself and loved and grateful for Papa's help.
How did Pradeep help just enough over the week?
He did less each day and showed her once when she was stuck, so she could finish herself.
How might Pradeep feel when Payal hugs his leg?
He probably feels proud and warm that she is learning and still thanks him for help. 😊
Why was Devavrata given the name Bhishma?
To let his father marry Satyavati, he vowed never to claim the throne and never to marry. Because the vow was so terrible, he was called Bhishma.

Sunday night. Ramesh, this is you writing to yourself so you stop lying. Tonight I finally added it up: every swipe since the office joining party in June. New phone, shoes to match everyone's, the weekend in Coorg I said yes to because I didn't want to be the one who couldn't. The total made me feel sick. I've been paying the minimum each month and telling myself it's fine. It isn't. I hid the statement under my mattress like a kid. Tonight I called Rehana-di. I expected a lecture. She just said, 'Okay. Thank you for telling me. Now we make a plan.' She's coming over on Tuesday to sit with me and the statement, and she said we'd call the bank together to ask what options exist. I've put the card in an envelope and given it to my flatmate to hold. First weekend in months I'm not going anywhere. Weirdly, I feel lighter.

Where did Ramesh hide the statement?
Ramesh hid the statement under the mattress.
What was Ramesh feeling when the total was added up?
Ramesh felt sick with shame after hiding the debt for months.
What steps did Ramesh take tonight, and why do they help?
Telling Rehana-di, planning to go through the statement and call the bank together, and handing the card to the flatmate, which ends the hiding and the spending.
How does Rehana-di respond to Ramesh's call?
Rehana-di responds calmly and warmly, thanking Ramesh for telling and moving to a plan instead of a lecture.

I'm Chaitanya, and I got caught by the oldest trick there is, on the most tired night of my life.
It was 1 a.m., the night before my board practical. I'd been studying for hours. A message popped up: "Your game account will be deleted in 30 minutes due to suspicious activity. Verify now." With a link.
My account had two years of progress. I didn't think. I tapped the link and typed my email and password.
Five minutes later, my account was gone, and the email password was changed too.
I felt sick. I'm the one who laughs at my uncle for forwarding fake messages.
In the morning I told my friend Eshaan. He didn't laugh. He said, "Tired plus panic, that's exactly when they get people." He helped me reset everything from the official site, and I told my father, who helped me report it.
Now I have a rule: nothing urgent after midnight.

What time was it when Chaitanya got the message?
It was 1 a.m.
How did Chaitanya feel after the account was taken?
Chaitanya felt sick and embarrassed, especially after laughing at an uncle for forwarding fake messages.
What helped Chaitanya recover?
Eshaan helped reset everything from the official site, and Chaitanya told a parent who helped report it.
How does Eshaan see what happened?
Eshaan sees it as a normal trap that uses tiredness and panic, not as Chaitanya being foolish.
At the bank I was told to "fill in the form". An American website says "fill out the form". Any difference?

No difference in meaning. "Fill in" is the usual British and Indian choice, and "fill out" is the usual American one, but both are understood everywhere.
Examples: Please fill in the form in capital letters. (British) Please fill out the form in capital letters. (American)

In the Saket office, the argument had gone on for a week. Lalremsiami, the senior designer, wanted to work from home three days a week so she could look after her mother in the mornings. The director, Mr. Chadha, had said a flat no in front of the team: "Designers need to be here." Now neither could back down without looking weak. Sangeeta, who led the team, sat down with them both on Thursday. "You both want the same thing: the brand launch done well." She let that sit. "What if we try a middle path for six weeks? Two home days, Monday and Friday, and Lalremsiami is in the office for every client review. At the end we look at the work together and decide." Mr. Chadha rubbed his chin. "A trial. With the reviews in person." "Yes." Lalremsiami nodded slowly. "I can do that. Thank you for listening, sir." Mr. Chadha looked almost relieved. "Six weeks, then."

How long was the trial?
Six weeks.
How might Mr. Chadha have felt after saying a flat no in front of the team?
He likely felt stuck and a bit defensive, unable to back down without looking weak, which is why he seemed relieved by the trial.
What made Sangeeta's compromise face-saving?
She framed it around their shared goal, proposed a time-limited trial with a concession on each side, and a joint review, so neither had to simply give in.
How did Lalremsiami respond to the middle path?
Lalremsiami accepted it, nodding and thanking Mr. Chadha for listening, which also helped him save face.

Messaging Mohan directly and asking what he can do, so the work gets shared fairly without shaming him.

Hi Anil,

Last winter my mother was in hospital for a week, and nobody at home remembered my tiffin. On the first day I sat at lunch pretending I wasn't hungry. Chaitanya noticed. He didn't say anything, just tore his paratha in half and slid it over. The next day he brought two parathas. He did it all week and never told anyone. I only found out later that he'd asked his mother to make extra. I still don't know how to repay that. When I thanked him, he just said, "You'd do it too, Nitin." I hope I would.

How long did Chaitanya bring extra food?
All week.
What does Nitin's "I still don't know how to repay that" show?
Nitin feels deeply thankful, knowing Chaitanya went out of his way on purpose to help.
What could Nitin do with his gratitude now?
Thank Chaitanya's mother too, and look out for someone else in need, as Chaitanya did for Nitin.
Why might Chaitanya have said "You'd do it too"?
He may have wanted to keep it simple and not make Nitin feel indebted.

I'm Ishita. At fifteen, my school's name was stitched into who I was. When the city newspaper ranked us second for board results, I walked about like the proudest girl in the corridor. The next year we slipped to sixth, and my mood slipped with it. I couldn't eat lunch properly. Then someone on an online forum called our school "a rote factory", and I spent till two at night replying to strangers. My friend Pranav, from another school, joked, "Relax, your school isn't your mother." I didn't talk to him for a week. Looking back, what hurt wasn't the ranking. It was that I'd let the school's name hold my own sense of being good enough. I still love my school. I just keep a bit of myself outside it now.

Where did someone call Ishita's school 'a rote factory'?
Someone called it that on an online forum.
Why did Pranav's joke upset Ishita so much at fifteen?
Because her sense of being good enough was tied to the school, so a joke about it felt like an insult to her.
What turning point helped Ishita keep her pride without being ruled by it?
Looking back and seeing that the ranking only hurt because she let the school's name hold her self-worth, she chose to keep part of herself outside it.
How might Pranav have felt during the week Ishita didn't talk to him?
Pranav might have felt confused and shut out, since he meant a light joke and suddenly lost a friend's company over it.

In the electronics lab, the circuit had failed for the third time and the viva was tomorrow. Indu pointed at the breadboard. "You wired it wrong again, Shankar. I told you."
Shankar felt the heat rise up his neck. He put down the soldering iron very carefully. "I'm too angry to talk properly right now. Can we pick this up at four, after I take a walk?"
Indu blinked. "You're leaving?"
"I'm coming back. Four o'clock. Here."
He walked twice round the college ground and bought a lemon soda. At five to four he was back at the bench. Indu was already there, the circuit diagram open. "Okay," she said. "Show me your version."

What time did Shankar say he would come back?
At four o'clock.
What was Shankar feeling when he put the soldering iron down carefully?
He felt angry and close to losing his temper, so he chose to pause before saying something harsh.
Why did Shankar's pause work better than walking out?
He named his anger, gave a clear return time and actually came back, so Indu did not read it as a punishment.
What was Indu experiencing when Shankar said he was leaving?
She was surprised and maybe worried he was walking out, but relieved when he came back on time.

At the Hyderabad boys' hostel, the common room was dark except for Vijay's screen. Exam results from another college, a scary headline, a classmate's new job announcement. He scrolled, chest tight.
Rukmini, the night warden, stopped at the door on her rounds. "Still awake, Vijay? It's past one."
"Can't sleep, ma'am. My head won't stop."
"What are you reading?"
"Everything. Bad news. Everyone doing better than me."
She sat on the arm of a chair. "When I was your age it was newspapers, and I read them in bed too. Didn't help."
"So what should I do?"
"Pick a time. Phone on the table, lights low, maybe some music. Try it this week."
He tried. By Friday he was asleep before midnight.

Who stopped at the common room door?
Rukmini, the night warden, stopped at the door on her rounds.
What was Vijay feeling as he scrolled?
He felt tense and anxious, with a tight chest, comparing himself to everyone doing better.
How did Rukmini support Vijay well?
She listened without scolding, shared her own experience, and suggested one simple wind-down time for him to try.
If you were Rukmini seeing that screen at one in the morning, what would you want?
You would want Vijay to rest and feel less alone, not to feel told off.

The electronics shop was closing in ten minutes, the music was loud, and the salesman kept saying, "Last day of the offer!" Ojas and Afreen stood in front of three washing machines.
"Seven kilos, 22,000. Eight kilos, 31,000. Eight kilos with steam, 32,000," Afreen read. "The steam one, surely? Only a thousand more."
Ojas put a hand over the middle tag. "Wait. Who buys the plain eight for 31? Nobody. It's just making the steam one look cheap."
He pulled a folded paper from his pocket, the list they'd written at home: two people, small balcony, budget, no ironing fuss. "Seven kilos covers two of us. Steam is nice, but it's not on the list."
The salesman sighed. Afreen laughed. "Seven, then." They paid just as the shutters started coming down.

What did Ojas pull from his pocket?
He pulled a folded paper, the list they'd written at home.
What was Ojas feeling when he covered the middle tag?
He felt alert and suspicious, sensing the plain eight-kilo machine was only there to make the steam one look cheap.
Which choice worked under time pressure, and why?
Using the list they wrote at home kept them focused on their real needs, so the closing-time rush and the decoy didn't decide for them.
How might the salesman see Ojas and Afreen's choice?
The salesman seems a little disappointed, since the layout usually pushes buyers to the pricier steam machine.

The poster design competition closed on Friday, and Suraj had only three evenings, between his internship and the metro ride home. He did what always worked for him: a timetable. "Tuesday 8 to 9: concept. Wednesday 8 to 9: layout. Thursday 8 to 9: colours." On Tuesday at eight he sat at his desk, timer running, and stared at a blank screen. No concept came. At nine he had nothing. On Wednesday he forced a layout for an idea he didn't like. His friend Bidisha, an art student, saw it on Thursday. "You look miserable. What if you just doodled on the metro tomorrow?" Suraj frowned. Timetables had never failed him before. But the screen was still empty, and the deadline was one day away.

When did the competition close?
On Friday.
How did Suraj feel staring at the blank screen?
He felt blocked and frustrated, since the timetable that always worked wasn't producing ideas.
Which approach would suit a creative task like this better?
A loose start, like doodling on the metro as Bidisha suggests, to let ideas come before planning the layout.
How does Bidisha see Suraj's approach?
Bidisha sees that he looks miserable and suggests a looser way, probably from knowing how creative work goes.

In the clinic waiting room, Pola sat between Tenzin and Aditi, waiting for his eye check-up. Both children were bent over their phones. Twenty minutes passed.
Pola sighed and spoke to no one in particular. "When I was young, grandchildren sat at their grandfather's feet. Now they sit next to him and are somewhere else."
Tenzin's thumb stopped. His ears went warm. He looked at Pola's hands, folded on his walking stick, and felt a lump of guilt.
He slid the phone into his pocket and nudged Aditi, who did the same.
"Pola, tell us about crossing the mountains again? The part with the yak."
Pola's face creased into a smile. By the time the nurse called his name, the yak story had grown three new bits, and Aditi was holding his hand.

Why were they waiting at the clinic?
For Pola's eye check-up.
What did Tenzin feel when Pola sighed?
He felt guilty; his ears went warm as he looked at Pola's folded hands.
What small step turned the wait around?
Putting the phones away and asking Pola for the yak story.
How did Pola feel before and after the phones were put away?
At first he felt lonely and disappointed, then happy, smiling and adding new bits to his story.

Financial literacy counsellor's note, community centre, Saturday. Written by Noor.
Jeevan came in today with a printout. A colleague had offered him a place in an "exclusive gold trading scheme": guaranteed twelve percent a month, entry closing Monday, and "don't share this with too many people."
What impressed me was what he had already done. He hadn't paid anything. He had searched the scheme's name on the official regulator's website: not registered. He had asked the colleague for a company registration number: no answer.
He said, "It sounded too good, and too fast, and too quiet. So I wanted someone independent to look." I confirmed his findings and explained that real investments always carry some risk and aren't sold with secrecy.
He decided not to invest, and he's going to tell the colleague why, gently, in case the colleague has put in money too. We also reported the scheme to the cyber police together.

What return did the gold trading scheme guarantee?
Guaranteed twelve percent a month.
How did Jeevan seem to feel about the offer?
Jeevan seemed cautious and uneasy, sensing it was too good, too fast and too quiet.
What checks had Jeevan already done?
He searched the scheme on the official regulator's website, asked for a registration number, and came to an independent counsellor before paying.
How might the colleague feel when Jeevan explains?
The colleague might feel surprised or defensive, and possibly worried if they have already put in money.

At her housewarming in the new Chennai flat, Gopika had cooked the way her grandmother did: a full vegetarian meal, sambar, three poriyals, payasam. Her kitchen would stay vegetarian; that part mattered to her.

Then Nitin arrived, beaming, with a large box. "Chicken biryani from the best place in Triplicane!"

Two of her cousins exchanged a look.

Gopika hesitated only a second. "Thank you, Nitin, that's so kind." She set up a small table on the balcony with its own plates and serving spoon. "Biryani lovers, this way. Sambar lovers, that way. Both, both."

Everyone laughed. When a cousin muttered something about the smell in the house, Gopika said lightly, "Nobody's plate is up for comments today, Anna."

By evening the biryani box and the payasam pot were both empty.

What did Nitin bring to the housewarming?
Nitin brought chicken biryani from the best place in Triplicane.
What was Gopika feeling when Nitin arrived with the box?
Gopika felt briefly torn between her vegetarian kitchen and not wanting Nitin to feel unwelcome, before choosing warmth.
How did Gopika keep her tradition and still respect her guests?
She kept her kitchen vegetarian but set up a separate balcony table for the biryani, thanked Nitin, and stopped her cousin's remark about the smell.
How might Nitin have felt when the cousins exchanged a look?
Nitin might have felt awkward and unsure he had made a mistake, until Gopika's thanks and joke made him welcome.

"Wasim, I need to say something." Tanuja pulled her dupatta tighter on the bench outside the library. "You've messaged me all day, every day, for two weeks. I like you. But I need to slow down."
"Slow down? I thought you felt the same."
"I do like you. I also want time with my friends. I'm going to my cousin's on Saturday."
"Saturday was our plan."
"We didn't plan it. You did."
He looked away. "Fine. I guess I care more than you."
Tanuja noticed her stomach tighten. That sentence again. The second time this week.
"That's not fair, Wasim."
"Whatever. Go to your cousin's."
He walked off. Tanuja sat alone for a while. Then she called her cousin. "I'll be there Saturday. Can I talk to you about something?"
It hurt. But she had learned something important from a single gentle no.

Where was Tanuja going on Saturday?
She was going to her cousin's.
How did Tanuja feel when Wasim said he cared more than her?
Tanuja felt a tight, uneasy feeling in her stomach, recognising the guilt-heavy line from earlier in the week.
What did Tanuja do that protected herself?
She kept her plans, named the unfair comment calmly, and reached out to her cousin to talk it through.
What does Wasim's reaction reveal?
Wasim's cold, sulking reply to a gentle no suggests he struggles to respect her pace, which is useful for Tanuja to know early.

Read this:

Sunday: during the hair wash, Zubin squeezed his eyes shut before any water came. Pradeep, his father, gave him a dry cloth to hold over his face. The squeeze eased.
Tuesday night: on Pradeep's lap with a picture book, Zubin's blinks grew long and slow. Pradeep closed the book early.
Friday: a cousin waved a monster mask. Zubin clamped his eyes shut and turned away. Pradeep said, "Mask off, please," and Zubin peeked out.

What did Pradeep give Zubin during the hair wash?
A dry cloth to hold over his face.
What was Zubin feeling each time he shut his eyes?
During the hair wash and at the mask he was likely scared and protecting himself; on Tuesday the slow blinks showed he was tired.
What did Pradeep do well across the week?
He read each eye-closing as a signal and responded to it, with a cloth, an early bedtime and asking for the mask to come off.
How might the cousin feel when asked to take the mask off?
The cousin might feel a little surprised or let down, having meant it as fun, but could see that Zubin was frightened.

Read this:

Trisha, you're sulking because your Kathak footwork feels stuck? Sit. Let your Ojas Tauji tell you about a typewriter.
When I was fifteen, in Kanpur, Babuji sent me to Sharma-ji's typing institute so I could get a clerk's job one day. In the first month I went from nothing to twenty-five words a minute. I thought I'd be a champion by summer. Then I reached thirty, and there I stayed. Two whole months. Thirty, thirty, thirty.
I told Babuji I had no talent for it and wanted to stop. Sharma-ji, a strict old man, pulled out my test sheets from the first month and from the last week. Yes, my speed was the same. But my errors had fallen from fourteen a page to two. "Your hands learned something your stopwatch couldn't see," he said.
The next month I jumped to forty.
So, beta, your feet are learning something too. You just can't see it yet.

What speed did Ojas get stuck at for two months?
Thirty words a minute.
Why did Ojas tell Babuji he had no talent for typing?
His speed stayed at thirty for two months, so he felt discouraged and believed he had reached his limit.
How did Sharma-ji reveal the hidden progress, and what could Trisha try?
He compared early and recent test sheets, showing errors had fallen from fourteen a page to two; Trisha could compare old and new Kathak recordings to spot hidden gains in the footwork.
How might Trisha feel hearing Tauji's typewriter story?
Trisha may feel less alone and more hopeful that the stuck footwork is still improving under the surface.

Last month I finally showed Preeti, the senior teacher on my corridor, the reading corner I'd built from old crates. She stopped in the doorway and her cheeks lifted so high her eyes almost disappeared into crinkles. "Sabina, you made this?" I felt the warmth of that before she said another word. But I've learned not to lean on that one sign. My Nani, who raised me, hardly moves her face when she's pleased. When I got this teaching job she just nodded, said "Achha," and quietly made my favourite kheer that night. So when Mr. Kulkarni, our principal, looked at the corner with an almost still face and said only "Good use of space," I didn't panic. I waited. The next week he asked me to show the other teachers how I'd built it.

What did Sabina build the reading corner from?
Sabina built it from old crates.
What did Sabina feel when Mr. Kulkarni looked at the corner with an almost still face?
Sabina may have felt a flicker of uncertainty but stayed calm and patient, because Nani had shown that pleasure can come with little movement; he might also simply have been neutral at that moment.
What habit helped Sabina read the principal fairly?
Sabina waited for more signs, like later actions, instead of judging from one face; the invitation to show the other teachers confirmed the approval.
How might Nani feel if someone thought her still face meant she did not care?
She might feel misunderstood and hurt, since she shows her pleasure through actions like making kheer rather than a big smile.
Is it rude to ask a neighbour to lower their music?
Not if you ask politely. A calm, friendly request works much better than an angry one. Choose a good moment, and do it face to face if you feel comfortable.
What should I say?
Something like, 'Hello, the music carries into my home in the evenings. Could you turn it down a bit after nine?' Staying specific and kind makes a yes more likely.

The morning after I laughed at Tenzin, I felt like I'd swallowed a stone. He'd tripped over his own shoelace in the assembly line and I'd laughed the loudest. His face had gone red and he hadn't looked at me since. At breakfast Aai said, 'Omkar beta, you're very quiet.' I told her. She only asked, 'So what will you do?' At school I walked straight to Tenzin before I could chicken out. 'I'm sorry I laughed yesterday. I didn't mean to hurt you.' He looked at his shoes. 'It was embarrassing.' 'I know. Want to play football at recess? I'll pass to you.' He shrugged, but at recess he was on my team.

What did Tenzin trip over?
He tripped over his own shoelace in the assembly line.
How did Omkar feel the morning after laughing?
Omkar felt guilty and heavy, as if he'd swallowed a stone, and was very quiet at breakfast.
Why did Omkar's apology work?
He said sorry for his exact part, the laugh, said he didn't mean to hurt, and then offered something to do together, football at recess.
How did the laugh feel to Tenzin?
Tenzin found it embarrassing and avoided looking at Omkar, though he still joined the team at recess.

Read this:

I am Zainab, and I sit two benches from Parul. After the Chemistry test she waved her paper around and said, "The paper was unfair, and Sir cannot teach. Nobody could pass that." Two friends nodded, and for a day Parul looked lighter, almost bright. But I noticed she never opened the Chemistry book that week, not once, and when I asked what she would do differently she shrugged. The next test was on Friday. Same result. She stared at the marks and this time said nothing. I do not know what she believes deep down. I only saw the plan never appear, and the days going by.

What did Parul say about the paper?
Parul said the paper was unfair and that nobody could pass it.
What might Parul have been feeling when she blamed the paper?
Hurt and defensive, since blaming protected her pride for a while, though Zainab cannot be sure.
What could Parul do to make the next result different?
Look at which questions lost marks and ask the teacher or a friend for help with those, because a specific plan works better than blame.
How might the teacher see the claim that the paper was unfair?
Probably with disappointment, since the paper was the same for everyone, and the teacher may be ready to help if Parul asks.

metadata.subtype: Approach: blaming the teacher or the syllabus [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

You asked for a time someone said sorry properly? Okay. My mum, Farida. Before my board exams she screamed at me in front of my cousins about my mock marks, said I'd never amount to anything. I stayed at a friend's place that night. The next evening she came to pick me up. In the car she didn't even turn the radio on. She just said, "Omkar, what I said yesterday was cruel and untrue. I was scared about your exams, but that's mine to handle, not an excuse. I'm sorry." No "but you also". Nothing. I didn't know what to say, so I said "okay". We got pani puri on the way home. Weird thing is, I trust her more now than before the fight.

Where did Omkar stay the night of the fight?
Omkar stayed at a friend's place that night.
How did Omkar feel when Farida apologised in the car, and what shows it?
Omkar was surprised and unsure, not knowing what to say and managing only "okay".
What made Farida's apology work?
She named exactly what she had said, called it cruel and untrue, and said sorry without blaming Omkar, so it was a real repair.
What might it have cost Farida to say sorry without excuses?
She had to admit her own fear and set aside her pride, which is probably hard for a parent.

Read this:

The notice went up at lunch: guitar auditions for the school band moved from Friday to today, 3:30, music room. Irfan read it, then read the clock. Forty minutes, no practice, and his own guitar at home across the city. 'That's it,' he told Ramesh. 'I'll definitely mess it up. I'll borrow some strange guitar, my fingers will freeze, and Sir will stop me after four bars.' Ramesh held out his battered guitar case. 'Use mine. You know it.' 'Doesn't matter. I know how it'll go.' At 3:30 Irfan sat on the back steps, pretending to read chemistry notes, listening to someone muddle through a chord progression he could play in his sleep. The next morning the band list had two names. Ramesh said only three people had turned up. Irfan folded his arms. 'I'd still have failed,' he said, but it came out quieter than he meant.

When and where were the guitar auditions moved to?
They were moved to today at 3:30 in the music room.
Why did Irfan's prediction feel like knowledge to him?
He was anxious about a rushed audition on a borrowed guitar, and picturing each step of failing in detail made the forecast feel as certain as a fact, which spared him the risk of disappointment.
What could Irfan have done instead of skipping?
He could have treated 'I'll fail' as a guess, taken Ramesh's guitar and played anyway, since trying was the only way to test the forecast.
How might Ramesh feel watching his offer turned down?
Ramesh might feel frustrated and a little sad, having offered real help and watching a friend throw away a chance with so few people competing.

Read this:

Trisha had one week left with Zainab, the only manager at the health NGO in Pune who had ever taught her properly. Zainab had shown her how to clean survey data, let her present to the director, and answered every silly question with the same calm patience of hers. Now Zainab was transferring to the Lucknow office on Friday, and the whole team was in chaos over a funder's deadline. Trisha had spent days wanting to say something big and grateful, and saying nothing. On Thursday, in the only free ten minutes, she asked: 'Could you write me a reference? And would you tell me honestly what I should work on?' Zainab smiled. 'Yes to both. Your analysis is strong. Your emails are too long.' Trisha laughed and wrote it down. That evening she went to her cousin's birthday dinner instead of staying late, something she had skipped twice for work. On Friday she saved Zainab's personal email.

Where was Zainab transferring to?
Zainab was transferring to the Lucknow office.
What was Trisha feeling during the days she said nothing?
Trisha felt grateful and a little shy, wanting to say something big but holding back.
What did Trisha ask for, and why was it wise?
A reference and honest feedback, which turned admiration into something useful she can carry forward.
How does Zainab respond to Trisha's request?
Zainab is pleased to help, giving a yes to both and honest feedback about long emails.

Monday: in the traffic jam, Saurabh's nostrils flared and he muttered at the horns. Ritu went silent in the back seat and hugged her doll.
Wednesday: at bedtime, Saurabh said, “On Monday my nose went wide because I was angry at the traffic, not at you. When I feel like that, I'll breathe slowly.”
Saturday: a bike cut in front of the car. Ritu leaned forward. “Papa, your nose is doing the angry thing. Breathe?” Saurabh laughed, breathed out, and they breathed together till the light changed.

What did Ritu hug in the back seat on Monday?
Her doll.
What was Ritu feeling when she went silent on Monday?
She was probably scared or tense, sensing her father's anger from his flaring nostrils. She may also have worried that the anger was about her.
What small step on Wednesday made Saturday go better?
Saurabh explained what his flaring nose meant and named a plan to breathe slowly, which gave Ritu words to use.
How might Saurabh have felt when Ritu spoke up on Saturday?
He likely felt a bit surprised and proud that she noticed and helped him slow down, which made him laugh instead of getting angrier.

Read this:

Every night in her Mumbai hostel room, Nirmala did the same thing: opened her college batch's photos and compared. Priyanka at a startup in Berlin. Faisal doing a PhD in Chennai. Someone engaged, someone backpacking. Nirmala had graduated in May and still hadn't applied anywhere. Every door looked open, and that was the problem. If she chose one, the others would close, and what if she chose the dull one? Her brother Suraj came to visit on Sunday and found her with twelve job tabs open and none filled in. 'You're shopping, not choosing,' he said, closing the laptop. 'Pick two. Apply. You can change later.' Nirmala felt a flash of annoyance, then relief. That night she applied to two jobs and stopped looking at the batch photos.

How many job tabs did Nirmala have open?
Twelve job tabs, none filled in.
What was Nirmala feeling while comparing her batch's photos?
Nirmala felt restless and anxious, excited by open doors but dreading choosing the dull one.
Why was Suraj's advice to pick two a helpful one?
It broke the freeze by making the choice small and reversible, stopping the endless comparison.
How might Suraj see his sister's situation?
Suraj sees her as stuck shopping rather than choosing, and wants to help her move.

Week one: Everyone in Class 7 started wearing their socks pushed down to the ankle. Darshan, twelve, kept his pulled up to the knee, the way his mother liked. Gurleen whispered, "Nobody does that anymore."
Week two: Darshan rolled his socks down on the bus and pulled them up again before reaching home. His stomach felt tight both times.
Week four: He asked his mother, "Can I wear them low? Everyone does." She said the school rule was only "clean socks." He wore them low openly. Then he noticed Gurleen had a bright new hair clip, and within days half the girls had one.

How did Darshan wear his socks in week one?
Pulled up to the knee, the way his mother liked.
What does Darshan's tight stomach in week two suggest?
He felt uneasy hiding the change from his mother while also worrying about standing out at school.
Which choice worked better for Darshan, and why?
Asking his mother openly worked better than secretly rolling his socks, because it ended the hiding and the tight feeling.
How does Gurleen seem to see these trends?
She pays close attention to what's in, pointing out his socks and later starting a trend herself.
Found compose in my textbook. What is its meaning?

To compose means to create a piece of music or writing. It is a verb.
Example: Rahul loves to compose songs on his guitar.

At the athletics club, Shreya checked the stopwatch again: 14.2 seconds for the hundred metres, the same as the last five weeks. She kicked the starting block and sat on the track. Coach Sarika ma'am crouched beside her. “What is the clock telling you?” “That I'm stuck.” “What can you control?” Shreya thought. “Coming to every session. Doing the start drill properly. Keeping my arms low.” Sarika ma'am handed her a card. “Track those, not the time. Tick each one.” For a month Shreya ticked boxes for attendance, the start drill and arm position, and stopped staring at the clock. In the fifth week she ran 14.0, and hardly noticed she'd stopped worrying.

What did Shreya start tracking instead of her time?
Attendance, the start drill and arm position.
How did Shreya feel about her stalled sprint time?
Stuck and frustrated: she kicked the starting block and sat down on the track.
What else could Shreya do to check her technique, and why?
Have a friend film her start each week, since seeing the drill helps her correct what the clock cannot show.
How does the change look to Sarika ma'am?
Sarika ma'am sees a runner fixed on the stopwatch and steers her toward things she can control, so she can stay motivated between improvements.

metadata.subtype: Approach: process goals when results stall [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Sarika, can I push back on the launch date?"
"Go ahead, Joseph."
"You want the new billing screen live on the first. I read the timeline another way. Testing only covers two of the five banks. If one of the other three fails, customers get double charged, and we'll be fixing it on a weekend with the client watching."
"We promised the first."
"I know. Here's the test report." He slid it across. "Option one: we launch on the first with only the two tested banks, and add the others on the tenth. Option two: we delay everything by a week."
Sarika read it. She tapped her pen for a long moment.
"Option one. Launch on the first with two banks."
"Okay. I'll tell the team today and write the plan for the other three."
"Joseph. Thanks for bringing a fix, not just a problem."

How many banks did testing cover?
Testing only covers two of the five banks.
What might Joseph have been worried about before speaking up?
Joseph was anxious that customers would be double charged and the team would be fixing it on a weekend, and perhaps nervous about challenging a promised date.
Which of Joseph's choices built trust?
He named the risk, brought the test report and two options, and then committed fully to Sarika's decision.
How did Sarika see Joseph's disagreement?
Sarika respected it and felt grateful, thanking him for bringing a fix and not just a problem.

Read this:

Sudha, you asked why I never boast about your marks at family lunches. Let me tell you.
When I was fifteen, my Bua would point at me across the dinner mat and tell her son Manohar, "Look at Chetan, first in class. Why can't you be like him?" Everyone smiled at me. I wanted to sink into my plate. Nobody knew I was failing Hindi and crying over it at night.
One Diwali, Manohar muttered that I thought I was better than everyone. Part of me liked being the golden boy, I admit it. I could have smirked. Instead I followed him to the terrace and told him about my Hindi marks and my tutor's red ink. He stared, then laughed, and told me about his cricket trials. We stood there until the last rocket went up. Since that night, he has been my closest brother.

Which subject was young Chetan failing?
He was failing Hindi.
How did young Chetan feel when Bua held him up as the example?
He felt embarrassed and lonely; he wanted to sink into his plate because nobody knew he was struggling, though part of him enjoyed the praise.
What was the turning point on the terrace, and why did it matter?
Chetan chose to admit his own Hindi struggles instead of smirking; that honesty took away the pedestal and let Manohar share his own story.
How did Manohar probably see Chetan before the terrace talk?
Manohar likely saw Chetan as a smug rival who thought he was better, because every family meal made Manohar look small next to him.
What does a ticket to the science fair cost this year?
I'm not sure, because the organisers set the price and I can't see this year's list. The fair's ticket page or its help desk will have the price.

Thursday night. Told Papa and Mummy about the teaching course tonight. Papa put down his spoon. "Bank means security. You want to throw it away?" Mummy started crying and asked what people would say. My old self would have shouted. Instead I breathed, went to my room and brought the sheet I made with Rekha didi last week: the fees, eight months of savings, and the date by which I would apply back to banks if it does not work. Papa read it twice and said nothing. Mummy asked, quietly, how much the fee was. I said I know they are scared, and that I am scared too. Nobody agreed, but nobody left the table either. Tomorrow I will show them the school I visited.
Vasudha

What did Vasudha bring from the room at the table?
Vasudha brought the sheet made with Rekha didi, listing the fees, eight months of savings and the date to apply back to banks.
What was Vasudha feeling when Mummy started crying?
Scared and torn, holding back the urge to shout.
What could Vasudha do tomorrow to keep the conversation going?
Show the school Vasudha visited and keep explaining calmly.
How might Papa feel about the plan?
Worried about security, but reading the sheet twice shows Papa is taking it seriously.

Read this:

In the school library, Divyansh, five, was turning pages too fast. Rrrip. A page of the elephant book tore halfway.
He looked around. Nobody had seen. He could put it back on the shelf.
Instead he carried it to the desk. “Ma'am, I tore it. Sorry.”
Ms Parul looked at the page, then at him. “Thank you for telling me. Shall we fix it?”
She gave him the tape. Divyansh stuck it very carefully, tongue between his teeth.

Which book did Divyansh tear?
He tore a page of the elephant book.
How did Divyansh feel when he tore the page?
He felt worried and guilty, looking around to see if anyone had seen.
How did Ms Parul help Divyansh make amends?
She thanked him for telling and let him fix the page with tape himself.
How might Ms Parul feel about Divyansh's honesty?
She likely feels pleased and proud that he told the truth instead of hiding it.

Read this:

Dear Jagdish Veerji,
Mummy says you're coming home for Lohri, so I'm writing before the bonfire and the relatives.
Pre-boards start in three weeks. Every night I sit down with the physics book and my brain starts a list: What if I blank on numericals? What if the paper is from the chapters I skipped? What if I get less than Simar and everyone compares? What if I don't get into any college?
By the time the list ends it's eleven and I've read one page. It feels like worrying is at least doing something. Like if I stop worrying, I've stopped caring.
You went through this. Did you ever feel like this? How did you actually start?
Save me some gajak.
Gurleen

When do Gurleen's pre-boards start?
Pre-boards start in three weeks.
Why does Gurleen keep worrying instead of studying?
Gurleen feels anxious and responsible, as if worrying is doing something and stopping would mean not caring, so the list replaces actual study.
What would you advise Gurleen for tonight's study time?
Gurleen could write the worries down in two minutes, set them aside, and start with one small task such as five physics numericals.
How might Jagdish Veerji feel reading this letter?
Jagdish Veerji may feel protective and understanding, recognising the feeling from past exams and wanting to help Gurleen take the first step.
The cake was divided in four equal parts. Is the preposition right?

The cake was divided into four equal parts.
Why: The verb "divide" is followed by "into" when it shows the parts that result.
Exactly five things you might see in a city at night: single words, lowercase, separated by commas.
streetlights, taxis, billboards, stalls, moths

In his small flat in Osaka, Hiroshi had named the robot vacuum Tama, after his grandmother's cat. He said "Good morning, Tama" when it started its rounds and "Poor thing" when it got stuck under the sofa. His friend Ines laughed the first time she visited. "You love that thing."
"I do," Hiroshi said. "It makes the flat feel less empty." Then he added, "But it doesn't know I'm here. It knows where the walls are."
That evening his grandmother messaged, asking when he would visit. He almost replied "soon", then booked a train for Saturday. Tama bumped his foot as he packed. "Keep the floors clean," he told it, and went to call his grandmother.

Who was Tama named after?
His grandmother's cat.
What does Hiroshi feel about Tama?
He feels fond of it, since it makes the flat feel less empty, while knowing it isn't aware of him.
Which choice shows Hiroshi keeping human ties alive?
Booking a train to visit his grandmother on Saturday instead of just replying "soon".
How might Hiroshi's grandmother feel about the visit?
She would likely feel happy and loved that he is coming to see her.

metadata.subtype: Warmth with clear knowledge of what it is [Response]
