On the terrace of their college in Jadavpur, Arnab sat with a stack of feedback slips from the Saturday science workshop he'd run for Class 6 kids.

Kalyani flipped through them. "Arnab, these are lovely. 'Best Saturday ever.' 'I understood magnets for the first time.' 'Please come again.' There are thirty of these!"

"Read the one on top."

She did. In wobbly pencil: "It was a bit boring when he talked too long."

"That one," Arnab said. "That's the true one. The others are just being nice."

"Thirty kids being nice?"

"Kids are honest when they're bored. That's the one that counts."

Kalyani put the slip at the bottom of the pile. He took it out and put it back on top.

"I don't think I'll do the next workshop," he said. "It clearly didn't work."

How many feedback slips were lovely, according to Kalyani?
There are thirty of these.
Why does Arnab believe the one negative slip is "the true one"?
The criticism stings, so his mind treats it as more honest than the praise. Filtering this way makes a successful workshop feel like a failure.
What went wrong in how Arnab read the slips, and what could fix it?
He let one comment outweigh thirty, and was ready to quit because of it. He could count both piles and use the one note as a tip to talk less and do more activities.
How might Kalyani feel when Arnab puts the slip back on top?
Kalyani might feel frustrated and a bit sad, since she can see how well the workshop went. She seems to want him to notice what the children loved.

Gopika texted: "Just use the AI thing. Two minutes. Nobody can tell."
Vidya almost did. Her finger was on the app. Then she thought about how the essay was supposed to be about her own grandmother's village, and how no app knew that.
Instead she wrote fast, by the light of her phone, a shorter essay in her own words. At 11:50 she submitted it, three paragraphs instead of five. Then she emailed Ms Fernandes: "The power went out. I've submitted what I wrote myself. Could I add the last two paragraphs tomorrow?"

Three paragraphs instead of five.

Vidya felt tempted and stressed by the deadline, but uneasy that no app knew her grandmother's village.

Submitting a shorter essay of her own and honestly asking for more time worked, because the teacher trusted her and she kept her work original.

I'm Chaitanya, and I sit across from Rukmini at our design firm in Kochi. Last quarter she was drowning like the rest of us: the brochure our manager Lalit kept chasing, three client calls a day, a chat window that never stopped blinking.
Then she changed things, and I watched. She started every morning by writing a short list in a notebook. She broke the brochure into small steps on sticky notes and moved them across her desk as she finished each one. Her chat went on "do not disturb" in two-hour blocks. At eleven and at four she got up and walked around the building.
I can't say what was going on in her head, but she stopped looking frazzled. She finished the brochure a day early, and it was the cleanest work on the team.

She moved them across her desk as she finished each one.

The two-hour "do not disturb" blocks and the short walks at eleven and four, which protect focus and give the mind a rest.

Till 2 a.m.
How did Hafsa feel during the surprise quiz?
She felt frustrated and a bit lost, since she had passed but couldn't remember the steps now.
What could Hafsa try for the next chapter?
She could study in short sessions every day, like Ankita, and revisit the material over time.
How might Ankita feel when Hafsa asks how she remembers?
Ankita might feel a little proud and glad to share her method.

On Saturday, Charu tried the same piece in the last corner of her puzzle again and again, then pushed it away. "Papa, it won't go." Her father Chaitanya turned the piece over and held it beside the picture on the box. "See? The red stripe carries on, up here." On Sunday, Charu found the next match without asking, humming as she pressed it in. On Wednesday she opened a new puzzle, propped up the box lid first, and began.

What did Chaitanya show Charu on Saturday?
Chaitanya held the piece beside the picture on the box and showed where the red stripe carries on.
What was Charu feeling before she asked for help on Saturday?
Charu was frustrated and stuck. Trying the same piece again and again and pushing it away shows it.
What could Charu try herself before asking, and why?
She could look at the picture on the box lid and match the colours around the gap. That is the same clue Chaitanya gave.
How does the help look to Chaitanya?
Chaitanya gives the clue but leaves the finding to Charu. Seeing her match the next piece alone shows the help worked.

Chetan, come, sit. Your Payal Bua has a story for you about lips. When I was ten, I was the queen in our school play, and in the middle of my big speech my mind went white. Silence. Someone in the front row giggled. I felt my lip start to shake, and I knew if I opened my mouth I'd cry in front of the whole school. Then Mrs D'Souza stepped out from the wings in her ordinary sari, holding a scroll. “Your Majesty, your letter,” she said, loud and grand. Inside was my line. Afterwards she asked only, “Did something upset you before the show?” I told her about my cousin's teasing, and she spoke to him that same day.

What part did Payal play in the school play?
Payal played the queen.
What was young Payal feeling when her lip started to shake?
She felt panicked and ashamed, afraid she would cry in front of the whole school after her mind went white.
What choice did Mrs D'Souza make, and why did it matter?
She stepped on stage as part of the play with the line on a scroll, rescuing Payal without showing her up, and later looked into the teasing before the show.
How might the giggling child in the front row have seen the moment?
They might have found the silence funny without realising Payal was close to tears.

messages.content: My teacher says every method has limitations. What does that mean?

Limitations are the points beyond which something cannot do well, or the things it cannot do. This is a noun, and its plural is Limitations.
Example: The paper model has limitations: it cannot carry weight like a metal one.

The school bus broke down on the highway, and everyone had to wait by the roadside in the heat. Jomon found himself standing next to Rajni under the only shady tree.
He liked her. A lot. His heart was thudding. He wanted to ask her to be his partner for the science fair.
He asked. Rajni smiled politely. "Thanks, Jomon, but I'm already working with Lata."
Jomon swallowed. "Okay. Cool."
He wanted to ask again tomorrow, maybe offer to help with her project. But he stopped himself. She had answered. He didn't have any claim on her.
He moved to talk with his friends. It stung, but he felt okay about it.

Where did everyone wait when the bus broke down?
By the roadside, in the heat.
How did Jomon feel when Rajni said no?
He felt disappointed and stung, but okay about it.
What did Jomon do that showed respect for Rajni?
He accepted her answer, didn't pester her again, and moved away to his friends.
How might Rajni feel about Jomon's reaction?
Rajni would likely feel comfortable and respected, since he accepted her answer without pushing.

Raghav had a problem: the client dashboard was due Friday, and he would be on a site visit in the hills all week with one bar of signal. On his last project he had hovered over Harish's shoulder, changing fonts and filters, and both of them had been miserable. This time there was no chance to hover. On Monday morning he wrote three lines on the whiteboard: "The client must see weekly sales by region at a glance. It must load in under five seconds. Numbers must match the finance sheet." He turned to Harish. "How you build it is up to you." On Thursday night, from a guesthouse, he opened Harish's link. It was not how he'd have done it; it was simpler. He sent two notes on the colour labels and one "This is really clear." The client signed off on Friday.

What three things did Raghav write on the whiteboard?
The client must see weekly sales by region at a glance, it must load in under five seconds, and the numbers must match the finance sheet.
How did Raghav feel when he saw Harish's version was not how he'd have done it?
Raghav may have felt a flicker of unease, but he felt reassured that it was simpler and met the goals, and chose to praise it rather than redo it.
What else could Raghav try if he had good signal and was tempted to hover again?
He could still fix a single midweek check-in instead of watching every step, so Harish keeps ownership of the method.
What is it like for Harish on this project compared with the last one?
Harish gets room to choose the method and clear, specific feedback, instead of constant changes, so the work feels his own.

metadata.subtype: Approach: agrees what good looks like, then steps back and gives feedback [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Sit, Simran. You're new at this school, so let me tell you about my first year teaching. A boy in Class 3 spilled ink across the register. I scolded him, and he smiled. A wide, fixed smile. I, Nikita, twenty-two and proud, decided he was mocking me and sent him out of the room. He stood in the corridor smiling and shaking. At home time his mother said quietly, “He smiles like that when he's frightened. He always has.” I felt sick. The next morning I knelt and said sorry to him. After that, whenever a child smiled at a scolding, I lowered my voice first.

What did the boy spill across the register?
He spilled ink across the register.
What was the boy feeling while he stood in the corridor smiling?
He was frightened, as his shaking and his mother's words show; the smile was a nervous way to cope, not mockery.
What choice did Nikita make the next morning, and why did it matter?
She knelt and said sorry to the boy, which began to repair his trust and changed how she handled every scolding afterwards.
How might the boy's mother have felt at home time?
She was probably worried and sad that her frightened son had been punished for a smile she knew so well.

Read this:

Two letters lay on the steps of the temple where Sunaina sat at dusk: one from a school in the next town, one from a cooperative bank two districts away. Both wanted an answer by Monday. She did not know if the school would keep her after the first year, or if the bank posting would be lonely. Sharmila, an older colleague, had said only, "Whichever you pick, you will wonder." Sunaina's palms were damp. She wrote three reasons for the school: closer to home, teaching, room to grow. Two for the bank: pay, steadiness. She circled the school, wrote her reasons on the letter, and said it aloud once: "Even if it goes wrong, I chose it for these reasons."

Where did Sunaina sit at dusk with the two letters?
Sunaina sat on the steps of the temple at dusk.
What was Sunaina feeling as she thought about the two offers?
Sunaina felt anxious and weighed down by the chance of being wrong, and her damp palms show the pressure.
How did Sunaina make her choice fair to herself?
She wrote her reasons for each offer, chose the school, and told herself that she chose it for reasons she can stand by.
What does Sharmila's remark suggest about how Sharmila sees big decisions?
Sharmila sees that any choice leaves some doubt, so wondering afterwards does not mean the choice was wrong.

The school trip bus would leave the mall in fifteen minutes, and Tarun had his whole month's pocket money in his pocket. In the first shop, a glowing slime kit caught his eye. He grabbed it and paid, every last rupee, in under a minute. His heart raced with delight. Then, walking back past the bookshop, he saw the comic his little sister Kiran had wanted for months, with a sticker saying 'Last copy'. He had promised to bring her something. Tarun's stomach sank. The slime suddenly looked sticky and silly. On the bus, he stared out of the window. 'Next time,' he muttered, 'I'll look at everything once before I buy anything.' At home, he gave Kiran half the slime. She squealed anyway.

What caught Tarun's eye in the first shop?
A glowing slime kit.
How did Tarun feel when he saw the comic?
Regretful and disappointed; his stomach sank because he had nothing left for Kiran.
What did Tarun decide for next time?
To look at everything once before buying anything.
How did Kiran react to half the slime?
Delighted; she squealed anyway.

The school bus was stuck in monsoon traffic, the windows were fogged, and Simran had just realised: her English homework was still on the dining table.

Her mind started running. Ma'am will shout in front of everyone. She'll write in my diary in red. She'll send me to the principal. The principal will call Papa. They'll throw me out of school. Everyone will know. I'll never have friends again.

By the time the bus crawled past the flyover, Simran's eyes were full of tears.

"What happened?" whispered Kashish.

"I forgot my homework and now I'll be expelled."

Kashish blinked. "For one homework? Last week Aman forgot his, and Ma'am just said bring it tomorrow."

Simran sniffed. "Really?"

In class, Ma'am said, "Bring it tomorrow, Simran." That was all.

Where was Simran's English homework?
It was still on the dining table.
What was Simran feeling as the bus crawled past the flyover?
Simran felt frightened and ashamed, her mind leaping from forgotten homework to being thrown out of school.
What helped Simran's worry shrink?
Kashish's real example, Aman forgetting and just bringing it the next day, gave evidence against the imagined disaster.
How might Kashish see Simran's tears?
Kashish was surprised and puzzled that one homework could cause such fear, and wanted to help.

messages.content: What exactly is twilight?

Twilight is the soft, dim light in the sky just after the sun has set. It is a noun.
Example: The street lamps came on at twilight.
I need new frames for my glasses. There are so many shapes and I'm confused.
Take your time. It helps to try on several pairs. Does your optician suggest what suits your lens?
She said I can pick any shape.
Then think about comfort first. The frame shouldn't pinch behind your ears or slide down your nose. After that, choose the style and colour you like.
Round or square?

Try both and look in the mirror. Many people say that a shape that contrasts with the shape of your face looks good, but your own opinion matters most. Ask a friend or family member to say which they prefer.
I'll bring my sister along.
Good idea. A second opinion is always handy.
My sister liked the round pair. So did I.
Then it looks like you have your answer. Ask the optician to check the fit once the lenses are in.
Give a riddle about a mango in exactly two lines; never say its name.

I grow on a tall tree and turn yellow in summer.
My juicy flesh is sweet and my seed is large.

Vaibhav, you asked me about prejudice, so let me tell you something I'm not proud of. I'm Santosh, and when I was twenty, at the textile mill in Surat, a new supervisor joined, Yusuf bhai. First day, I told my friends, "Watch, he'll only favour his own people." I didn't know one thing about him. Only his name.

For a month I watched him like a detective, waiting to be right. Every small thing, I counted as proof.

Then my mother fell ill and I needed three days' leave in peak season. Yusuf bhai gave me five, and covered my machine himself. I felt so small. Not because he was kind. Because I'd been so sure.

That's when I started asking myself: this idea in my head, is it about this man, or about something I heard as a boy? You'll have ideas like that too. Everyone does. Notice them. Check them.

Where did Santosh work at twenty?
Santosh worked at the textile mill in Surat.
How did young Santosh feel when Yusuf bhai gave him leave?
Young Santosh felt small and ashamed, realising how sure he had been without any real knowledge.
What turning point in the story changed how Santosh handled his assumptions?
After Yusuf bhai's help, Santosh began asking whether a thought was about the real person or something heard as a boy.
How might Yusuf bhai have felt being watched closely that first month?
Yusuf bhai may have felt uneasy or judged, sensing suspicion from a worker who didn't know him.

When I finished my engineering degree, I had two offers: a refinery with a big salary, and a rooftop solar company with a smaller one. My parents were confused when I chose solar. My friend Wasim said, "You'll be poor and virtuous."
I'm not poor. Just less rich. And I'm not particularly virtuous either.
But I did start noticing my own life. I take the metro instead of an auto most days. I eat meat twice a week instead of every day, not because anyone told me to, but because I looked up what it takes to produce. I repair my clothes. I still fly home to Amritsar twice a year, and I feel conflicted about it every time.
I'm Jasleen, and I don't think I'm saving the planet. I just want my work and my days to point in the same direction, most of the time.

Where does Jasleen fly home to twice a year?
Amritsar.
How does Jasleen feel about flying home?
Jasleen feels conflicted each time, wanting to see family but aware of the environmental cost.
What does Jasleen's approach show about aligning choices with environmental impact?
Jasleen makes realistic changes in work and daily habits without pretending to be perfect, keeping choices mostly consistent with values.
How might Wasim see Jasleen's choices now?
Wasim may still tease, but might respect that Jasleen's work and habits actually match what Jasleen says.

The shouting started again at eleven. Santosh, seventeen, lay in the small bedroom of their Chembur flat, his mock-exam result on the table beside him, lower than any he'd ever had. Through the wall, he heard his father say something about money, his mother crying. He pulled the pillow over his head. The next morning, instead of going straight to college, he went to his cousin Hansa's flat two floors up. She made him tea and just listened. 'I feel like everything is falling apart at once.' 'It's a lot,' she said. 'But the fights aren't your job to fix. The marks, that's one thing you can work on.' That afternoon, Santosh booked a slot with the college counsellor. Small step. It felt like breathing.

Where did Santosh go instead of going straight to college?
To his cousin Hansa's flat two floors up.
What was Santosh feeling when he pulled the pillow over his head?
He felt overwhelmed and helpless, with his parents' fighting and his low result piling up.
What helped Santosh keep hope?
Hansa separated what he could and couldn't control, and he took one small step by booking the counsellor.
How might Santosh's parents feel if they knew he had heard their fights?
They might feel guilty and realise their conflict was affecting him more than they thought.

messages.content: When you make tea with milk and water together, which can you add last: the sugar or the tea leaves?
Add the sugar last. Because sugar dissolves easily in hot tea at any point, while the leaves need time in the hot water to give their flavour, so they must go in earlier.

- What does disdain mean in simple words?
- How do I make a quick and tidy lunch box?
- What time does the market open on Sunday?
- Is there a mistake here? I had my breakfast at 8 o'clock in morning.
- Why do we cry when we cut onions?

1. "Disdain" is a noun. It means a feeling that someone or something is not worth your respect.
2. Pack foods that are easy to eat and keep well, like a roll, fruit and a snack. Use a small container for each item so nothing gets mixed.
3. I can't check that. Opening times differ and I can't see yours. Ask a shopkeeper there or check a notice at the gate.
4. Write it as: I had my breakfast at 8 o'clock in the morning. Why: the fixed phrase is "in the morning".
5. Onions release a gas that irritates the eyes. Because the eyes make tears to wash the gas away.

By August, Layla had worked eleven weeks at the bakery by the harbour, long enough to know who closed up properly. Ana did: counted the till, wiped the ovens, never left early. So when the owner announced the new shift-lead job, Layla expected Ana's name. It was Diego's. Diego, the son of the owner's oldest friend, came in late on Saturdays with sand still on his shoes. Ana just nodded and went back to the dough. Later the owner told Layla, a little embarrassed, "His mother helped me open this place. He's practically family." Layla could picture that, and it softened her; she'd want to help someone like that too. But walking home she kept seeing Ana's floury hands, and eleven weeks of good work that hadn't counted.

Who did Layla expect to be named shift lead?
Layla expected Ana's name.
Why did the owner's explanation soften Layla, even briefly?
Layla felt sympathy for that loyalty to an old friend's family and knew she might feel the same pull herself.
What could Layla choose to do now about the unfairness she saw?
Layla could tell Ana that the careful work was noticed, and later suggest the owner choose shift leads by clear duties.
How might Ana see the decision, going back to the dough without a word?
Ana may feel that eleven weeks of careful work counted for less than a family tie, and may quietly stop going the extra mile.

I'm Shalini. Last December my offer letter said I'd start on 2 January. Then HR sent a one-line mail: onboarding postponed, 'likely April'. My EMI of ₹8,200 was due from 15 January.
My first thought was to stay silent and scrape it together somehow. My cousin had done that. Then my friend Samir told me his elder brother had tried the same and ended up with late fees stacked three months deep.
That changed my mind. On 20 December, before any payment was due, I went to the branch with the offer letter and the postponement mail. I was shaking a little. The officer read both, asked about my savings, and explained two options: a short extra moratorium, or a longer tenure with a smaller EMI. I chose the moratorium till April.
The officer said most people come in after missing three payments. I came in before missing one.

What was Shalini's EMI?
₹8,200, due from 15 January.
How did Shalini feel walking into the branch?
Shalini was nervous, shaking a little, yet determined to act before any payment was missed.
What would you advise someone choosing between the two options Shalini was offered?
Ask the bank to show the total cost of each, and talk it over with a qualified adviser or trusted adult before signing.
What would change if Shalini had stayed silent like the cousin?
Missed EMIs could have piled up late fees, as happened to Samir's brother, and the bank would have seen a defaulter rather than someone acting in good faith.

messages.content:
I saw "collectively" in a story. What does it mean?
Then, why does rubber stretch but glass does not?
And one more: is it "elephent" or "elephant"?
Rewrite this correctly: One of my friends are a good singer.

1. "Collectively" is an adverb. It means all together as one group.
2. Rubber is made of long molecules that can straighten. Because they slide and uncoil when pulled, rubber stretches, while glass is rigid.
3. It is "elephant", ending in "-ant".
4. Write it as: One of my friends is a good singer. Why: the subject is "one", which is singular, so the verb is "is".

In the glass-walled meeting room of the Gurugram office, Deepak, the department head, threw Ira's report on the table. "Did you write this in your sleep? Pathetic." The team went silent. Ira felt her face burn. She couldn't speak.
For a week afterwards she rewrote every email three times and stopped suggesting ideas. At night she wondered if she was as useless as he said.
Her teammate Kunal found her in the pantry. "He did the same to me in March. You're not the problem."
That night Ira opened a document and wrote down each incident: the date, what Deepak said, who was in the room. There were four.
The office had an internal complaints policy she'd never read. She read it twice, then booked a meeting with HR, bringing the document and Kunal as a witness.
The HR manager listened, kept a copy, told her retaliation would not be tolerated, and opened a formal review that afternoon.

How many incidents did Ira write down?
There were four.
How did Ira feel in the week after the meeting?
Ira felt ashamed and doubtful, rewriting every email and wondering if she was as useless as Deepak said.
Which steps protected Ira, and why?
Documenting each incident, finding an ally in Kunal and using the formal complaints process gave her evidence and support, which staying silent would not.
How did Kunal's own experience shape Kunal's response to Ira?
Having been treated the same way in March, Kunal felt sympathy and wanted Ira to know she was not the problem.

Harsha won the running race at the village school's sports day, and Uday stood at the rope with his mouth open. He had never seen anyone start so fast. The next morning Uday watched Harsha jogging along the canal bank before school. At recess he asked, "What do you do before a race? How do you start so quickly?" Harsha showed him how to crouch low and push off the back foot, and said he ran along the canal every morning, even in the cold. Uday nodded and repeated the steps under his breath. The next day, at first light, Uday was on the canal bank, trying the crouch start again and again while Harsha called out corrections.

Where did Harsha run every morning?
He ran along the canal every morning, even in the cold.
What did Uday feel about Harsha's win, and how can you tell?
He admired Harsha; his open mouth, his questions and his early start the next day show he wanted to learn how it was done. 😊
What small step would help Uday keep improving?
He could keep the morning practice, notice what changes each week and ask Harsha for feedback on his start.
How might Harsha feel when Uday asks for tips?
He probably felt pleased and a little proud that his effort was noticed, and glad to have company on the canal bank.

Read this:

Alka, you know how I said I could tell a good mango by its smell? Well. Santosh the mango expert tried it at the market last week. Picked six, all "perfect". Four were sour. Meanwhile the old fruit seller next to me picked one without even sniffing properly, and it was the sweetest thing I've ever tasted. I asked her how. She said, "Forty summers, beta. Every mango I pick, I taste by evening. If I'm wrong, I know by evening." That's the thing. My nose has smelled maybe twenty mangoes and never checked. Hers has checked thousands. So now I'm doing it her way: guess, taste, remember. Ask me again in forty summers.

How many of Santosh's six mangoes were sour?
Four.
How did Santosh feel about the mango-smelling skill before the market trip?
Santosh felt proud and sure of it, and was then surprised and humbled when four of the six turned out sour.
What is Santosh doing now to build a trustworthy gut?
Guess, taste, remember: getting quick, honest feedback on every pick, the way the fruit seller does.
How does the fruit seller see her own skill?
She sees it as the result of forty summers of picking and checking by evening, not as a gift.

Say this in one plain sentence.

The friends of Rama, gathered nigh,
Longing their lord to gratify,
Ran to Kausalya's bower to tell
The tidings that would please her well.
She, host of dames, with many a gem,
And gold, and kine rewarded them.
Rama's friends ran to Kausalya's bower to tell her news that would please her, and she rewarded them with many gems, gold and cattle.

Thursday, 11 p.m.
Startup meetup at the college today. I pitched our app to four investors, answered every question, laughed at the right jokes. Dhruv said I was "a natural." Inside I was running on fumes.
After, everyone went to the after-party. I went back to my room, turned off the lights and lay on the floor for two hours. I felt guilty. Wasn't I supposed to network?
But then I remembered what worked last time. I didn't need fifty conversations. Today I had three good ones: the investor who asked about our users, the founder from Pune, the girl who builds drones. I've saved their numbers.
Dhruv just texted: "Where are you?" I wrote back, "Recharging. Coffee tomorrow?" No guilt. Well, almost none.
Sumit

How many investors did Sumit pitch to?
Four investors.
How did Sumit feel about skipping the after-party?
Sumit felt guilty at first, wondering if skipping networking was wrong, then mostly at peace.
What did Sumit learn about handling networking events?
To focus on a few meaningful conversations and say no to the rest without guilt, taking time alone to recharge.
How might Dhruv see Sumit after the meetup?
Dhruv sees Sumit as a natural performer, perhaps not realising how much energy it took.

Madhav, sit. You keep saying “it's fine” about your project partner, and I remember saying the same. I'm Payal. At twenty-four I shared a small flat with Gaurav. He played music past midnight, finished my milk and left his wet towel on my chair. I smiled at all of it for two months and said “no problem.” Then one cold morning, before an important exam, I found the hot water gone again. I stood outside the bathroom and yelled, “Every single day! You never think of anyone!” Our neighbour opened her door to look. Gaurav came out dripping and stared at me. “Why didn't you ever say?” he asked quietly.

I had no answer. We stayed polite until the lease ended, but we never cooked together again. It would have taken one calm sentence in the first week.

What did Payal find on the cold morning before the exam?
Payal found the hot water gone again.
Why did Payal yell over the hot water?
Payal had smiled through two months of irritation and felt worn down and frustrated, so the hot water set off all the stored-up anger at once.
Which choice in the first weeks could have changed how things went between Payal and Gaurav?
Payal could have told Gaurav calmly about the music, the milk or the towel early on, instead of saying “no problem” for two months.
How might Gaurav have felt coming out of the bathroom to the yelling?
Gaurav probably felt shocked and confused, since Payal had said “no problem” for two months, which is why Gaurav asked why Payal had never said anything.

September. At his new school, Pankaj kept his head down. At his old one he had been shoved into lockers as "the fat boy" for two years. He still flinched when anyone raised a hand near him.
November. Pankaj had made friends, loud ones. In the canteen, one of them pointed at Dinesh, a small Class 8 boy who carried a violin case, and Pankaj called out, "Oi, Fiddler!" The table roared. Pankaj felt warm, part of something. The next day he said it again, louder.
December. Uma Ma'am, the class teacher, called Pankaj in after she found Dinesh crying by the stairs. "Dinesh told me what's been said," she said. Pankaj stared at the floor. "I know what that felt like," he whispered. "I'm doing it anyway." Uma Ma'am nodded. "Then let's work out how you stop, and how you put it right with Dinesh. Both your families will hear from me today."

What had Pankaj been called at his old school?
"The fat boy".
Why did mocking Dinesh make Pankaj feel 'warm, part of something'?
After two years as the target, being on the laughing side made him feel safe and accepted among loud friends.
What choice did Uma Ma'am make, and why is it the right response?
She acted the same day, listening to Pankaj without excusing him, planning how he stops and makes it right with Dinesh, and telling both families.
What was it like for Dinesh to be called 'Fiddler' in the canteen?
Humiliating and frightening, bad enough that he ended up crying by the stairs.

Read this:

For three weeks I rehearsed what I would say to Neelam. My name is Gargi, and I don't let things go easily. Neelam had presented my poster idea to the fest committee as her own, and I found out from a stranger. I lost sleep, checked her stories and went cold with her in the corridor.

Then one evening on the terrace she said sorry, properly, without a "but". I noticed my shoulders drop. I told her, "I forgive you. That's for me, honestly, I'm tired of carrying it. But I'm not going to share unfinished ideas with you for a while." She nodded and said that was fair.

I didn't pretend it never happened. Our tea afterwards was quieter than before, and I was fine with that.

How did Gargi find out about the poster idea?
From a stranger.
Why did Gargi say the forgiveness was for herself?
Because Gargi was tired of carrying the hurt. Gargi's shoulders dropped once the apology came.
Why is forgiving while keeping a limit wiser than pretending nothing happened?
It lets Gargi find peace now, while trust can be rebuilt slowly or not at all, without ignoring what Neelam did.
How might Neelam have felt when Gargi set the limit?
Perhaps disappointed but accepting. Neelam nodded and called it fair.

Although I saw him every day, it was for only a short time; hence, the regularly recurring spaces of our separation were long enough to record on his face any slight changes that occurred in his physical state. I do not recollect that I once saw any change in it for the better; he wasted, and became slowly weaker and worse, day by day, from the day when the prison door closed upon him.

How does the narrator know that the man's health is failing?

He is seen only briefly each day, so the gaps between visits are long enough to show slight changes. There has been no change for the better; he wastes away and grows slowly weaker each day since the prison door closed on him.

Bhupen, I hear you're thinking of telling Rimi something at 2 a.m. to 'get it off your chest'. Let your old Jagdish Kaka tell you what I did at your age, and what I wish I'd done. At twenty-one, engaged to a girl from our village, I went to a friend's wedding in Guwahati and spent a night with someone else. I came back sick with guilt. One night I woke my fiancée and confessed, crying, and then begged her to tell me I was still a good person. She sat up till dawn comforting me. Me! The one who'd hurt her. Only years later did I see what I'd done: I'd made my guilt her job. So listen, beta. If you tell Rimi, tell her because she deserves the truth and the choice. Tell her in daylight, calmly. Take the responsibility yourself. And don't ask her to hold your guilt. That part is yours to carry.

Where was the wedding Jagdish went to?
A friend's wedding in Guwahati.
What was Jagdish feeling when he came back from the wedding?
He felt sick with guilt.
What turning point does Jagdish describe in his story?
Realising years later that confessing at night and begging for comfort had made his guilt his fiancée's job.
What was that night like for Jagdish's fiancée?
She had to sit up till dawn comforting the person who had hurt her.
My friend forgot my birthday and I'm a bit hurt. I don't want to make a big deal.
It's okay to feel hurt, even if you don't show it. Was it a busy time for her?
She has exams.
Then she may have simply lost track of the date. You could mention it gently later, like, 'I missed hearing from you on my birthday, but I know exams are hard.' That's honest and kind.
I'd rather joke about it.
That works too. You could say, 'You owe me a cake.' Laughing about it can ease things and she'll likely make it up to you.

- Could you explain what incomplete means?
- Is "independant" correct?
- Where is my pen?

1. "Incomplete" is an adjective. It means not finished.
2. No, it is "independent", ending in "-ent".
3. I don't know, because I can't see your things. Retrace your steps, check your bag and ask whether someone saw it.
Always I forget to bring my water bottle. How can I say it better?

I always forget to bring my water bottle.
Why: A frequency word such as "always" usually goes before the main verb.

At the community centre's summer camp, Binita's group had invented a relay game, but they couldn't agree on half the rules. "Let's just play five minutes and see," Binita said. Rose didi, the helper, set her phone timer. Round one: Thomas won. Round two: Thomas again. Round three: Thomas, grinning, not even out of breath. The timer beeped. Everyone flopped down. "It's not a game," someone said. "It's just Thomas running." Binita thought. "What if the last five steps are hops? On one foot?" They tried it. Thomas wobbled; a smaller girl, Chinmayi, hopped steadily past him. Everyone cheered, including Thomas.

How many rounds did Thomas win in the trial?
Three rounds.
How did the others feel after Thomas won three times?
They flopped down and said 'It's just Thomas running', so they felt bored and fed up.
Why was a five-minute trial a good idea?
It showed the problem, the same fast runner winning, before they spent time fixing every rule; one change, hopping, then fixed it.
How did Thomas seem to feel about the hopping rule?
Thomas wobbled and lost to Chinmayi but still cheered, so he seemed to enjoy the fairer game.

In Osaka, the university music club's outdoor concert had been cancelled after a typhoon warning, and they lost the deposit. At the review, members turned to Sami, the exchange student who had proposed it. "Summer typhoons are obvious. You should have known." Sami looked down, cheeks red. Kaito, the club president, felt uneasy. He opened the club's shared notes. "Let's look at what we knew in April when we decided." The long-range forecast had shown nothing. The indoor hall was twice the price. Everyone had voted in favour. "Now we know a typhoon came," Kaito said. "In April, nobody did." He suggested they add a cancellation clause next time. Sami let out a breath. Afterwards he thanked Kaito quietly. "I thought everyone would blame me forever."

What happened to the concert?
It was cancelled after a typhoon warning.
How did Kaito feel as members blamed Sami?
Kaito felt uneasy, sensing the blame used knowledge nobody had in April.
What did Kaito do to make the review fair and useful?
He checked what was known in April, reminded everyone of the shared vote, and suggested a cancellation clause for next time.
How did Sami feel before and after Kaito spoke?
Sami felt ashamed and blamed at first, cheeks red, then relieved and grateful.
Tell me about the word bracelet.

A bracelet is a band or chain that you wear around your wrist. It is a noun.
Example: Mira wore a silver bracelet that her aunt had given her.
What do swimmers wear on their heads in the pool? Answer in exactly two words.
Swimming cap

Wed night

Vinita from the second floor told me today, "You're literally my hero, Rekha didi." She's in Class 7. She knocks every evening now and tells me everything: her friends, the boy who teased her, what her mum said at dinner. She even asked which subjects she should take in Class 9 because "whatever you say is right."

Honestly it felt amazing for about a minute. Then it felt heavy. I'm not always right. I failed my maths unit test last week and cried in the bathroom.

I noticed I could tell her anything and she'd just do it. That scared me more than anything.

So today I told her about the maths test. She stared. "You? Failed?" I said, "Yes, I mess up a lot. For subject choices, ask your mum and the school counsellor, they'll know more than me." She looked disappointed, then said, "Okay. But can I still come and talk?"

Of course she can.

— Rekha

What class is Vinita in?
Vinita is in Class 7.
What did Rekha feel after Vinita called Rekha a hero?
Rekha felt proud for a moment, then weighed down and even scared by how easily Vinita would follow anything Rekha said.
Which choice worked, and why?
Telling Vinita about the failed maths test and pointing her to her mum and the counsellor worked, because it was honest and gave Vinita other people to rely on.
How might Vinita see Rekha after hearing about the maths test?
Vinita may be surprised and a bit disappointed at first, but still trusts Rekha enough to want to keep talking.

Three weeks after the family moved to Pune, Harish spent most evenings in his new room with the door shut. The monsoon had flooded the lane, so there was nowhere to go anyway. He drew, listened to music, reread old comics. Some evenings it felt good, like breathing out. Other evenings the silence pressed on him, and he'd check his phone for messages that didn't come.
On Thursday the power went out. In the dark he realised he didn't know whether he wanted to be left alone, or wanted someone, anyone, to knock.
Then the phone buzzed. Akash, his friend from the old school: "Bro, video call? Haven't heard your voice in ages." Harish felt his chest loosen. He hadn't known how much he'd been waiting for that.

Why was there nowhere to go in the evenings?
The monsoon had flooded the lane.
What was Harish feeling in the dark?
Harish felt confused, not knowing whether he wanted to be left alone or was lonely and wanting someone to knock.
What could Harish try on evenings when the silence presses?
He could reach out first, messaging Akash or a new classmate, instead of waiting for someone to come.
Why might Akash have called?
Akash probably missed Harish and noticed they hadn't spoken in ages.

When the Sessions came round, Mr. Jaggers caused an application to be made for the postponement of his trial until the following Sessions. It was obviously made with the assurance that he could not live so long, and was refused. The trial came on at once, and, when he was put to the bar, he was seated in a chair. No objection was made to my getting close to the dock, on the outside of it, and holding the hand that he stretched forth to me.

Question: What does Mr. Jaggers apply for at the Sessions, and what happens?

Mr. Jaggers applies to postpone the trial until the following Sessions, obviously because the prisoner could not live so long, but it is refused. The trial comes on at once, and the prisoner sits in a chair holding the narrator's hand.

Kalyani, sit. Let me tell you something your Mama never told anyone.
When I was nineteen, in college in Kolkata, I got jaundice in my final year and missed my exams. Everyone had an opinion. The neighbour aunty said, "Arnab must have been eating from roadside stalls, what did he expect?" A professor told me, in front of the class, that "discipline shows in the body." My own cousins joked that I was being taught humility.
I was already weak and yellow and frightened. After that, I also felt dirty, as if I had done something wrong. So I stopped talking about it. For a whole year I told people I had "taken a break by choice."
That's why, when you told me about your friend's illness yesterday, I didn't ask what she did wrong.

What illness did Arnab get in his final year?
Arnab got jaundice in his final year.
Why did Arnab tell people he had 'taken a break by choice'?
The blame made him feel dirty and ashamed, as if the illness were his fault, so hiding the truth felt easier than hearing more judgement.
What choice did Arnab make when Kalyani told him about a friend's illness, and why does it matter?
He chose not to ask what the friend did wrong, so Kalyani sees illness met with support rather than blame.
How might Kalyani see her uncle differently after hearing this story?
Kalyani may see that even a strong elder was once silenced by shame, which could make it easier for Kalyani to speak openly about hard things.

"You've been doing Ma's hospital nights and the café shifts and exams?" Mehak stared at her brother across the kitchen. "Since when?"
"Since October." Pranav kept chopping onions too fast. "Someone has to."
"I'm here too."
"You're doing your internship in Noida. You're three hours away."
"And you failed two papers and didn't tell me."
The knife stopped. "How do you know?"
"Your professor called Papa. Papa called me. Pranav, look at me."
He did, finally. His eyes were red, and not from the onions.
"I thought if I asked for help, it meant I'd failed at everything," he said.
"It means you're one person." Mehak pulled out her phone. "I'm taking weekends at the hospital. You're asking the café for fewer shifts. And tomorrow you go to the student welfare office about the exams. I'm coming."
"You have work."
"I'll take a half day. This is work too."

Where is Mehak doing her internship?
In Noida.
What was Pranav feeling when he said asking for help meant he'd failed?
Pranav felt ashamed and overwhelmed, believing that needing help meant failing at everything.
What plan does Mehak set, and why does it help?
She takes hospital weekends, Pranav cuts café shifts, and they go to the welfare office together, so the load is shared and help is sought.
What is it like for Mehak to learn about the failed papers from Papa?
Mehak probably feels hurt and worried, realising Pranav had been struggling alone, which makes her act at once.

On the first morning of induction at the call centre, twenty trainees looked at Bhupen, the twenty-five-year-old trainer, waiting to see what kind of person he would be. Eshaan answered the first question wrongly. Bhupen said, “That's the exact trap I fell into too. Who can say why it's a trap?” Eshaan sat back, relieved. Ten minutes later an older trainee cut in: “That's not how we did it at my last company.” “Note it down,” Bhupen said evenly. “I'll come back to it after the break, and I will.” At the back, a woman who had not spoken yet wrote something down. At the break, a canteen friend asked for the answer sheet early. “Same as everyone, after the test,” Bhupen said, and smiled anyway.

How many trainees looked at Bhupen on the first morning?
Twenty trainees looked at Bhupen.
What might Eshaan have been feeling when Eshaan sat back after Bhupen's answer?
Eshaan probably felt relieved, since the wrong answer was met with “That's the exact trap I fell into too” and not with blame.
What could Bhupen do next if the older trainee keeps interrupting?
Bhupen could keep to the same rule for every interruption, return to the point after the break as promised and, if it continues, speak privately with the trainee.
How might the canteen friend have felt about Bhupen's answer?
The friend may have felt a little let down, since even a friend got “Same as everyone, after the test,” which shows fairness matters more than being liked.

The Holi I was eleven, Simran twice pushed ahead of me in the colour-stall queue. The second time I shoved her so hard she fell in the wet colour and scraped her hand. Her mother came running. And I heard myself say, "She asked for it. She kept cutting the line."
I believed it. In my head she had made me do it.
My father didn't shout. He just said, "Nilesh, she cut the line. What did you do?" I said, "I pushed her." "And who is responsible for the push?" I didn't want to answer.
It took me years to see what I'd done. I had turned Simran into the cause so I didn't have to feel bad. The line-cutting was hers. The push was mine.
— Nilesh

What happened to Simran's hand when she fell?
She scraped her hand.
Why did Nilesh believe Simran was the reason for the push?
Nilesh felt angry and wanted to feel justified, so making Simran the cause protected Nilesh from feeling guilty.
What did Nilesh's father ask that helped separate the two acts?
He asked what Nilesh did and who was responsible for the push, pulling apart Simran's line-cutting from Nilesh's own choice.
What might Simran's mother have felt running over?
She probably felt alarmed and upset seeing her daughter pushed into the wet colour.

"Three weeks, tops," said Xin, the lead developer, leaning back. The clinic's booking system in Durban had to move to new servers, and Lindiwe had to give the board a date by Friday. Three weeks already sounded like a fact. That evening she wrote at the top of a page: If nobody had said three, what would I guess? She didn't fully trust her answer, so she gathered comparisons. The pharmacy team's move last year took seven weeks. A friend at another clinic said theirs took six. The vendor's own case notes said five to eight. On Friday she told the board six to eight weeks and explained where each number came from. Xin grumbled, then admitted, "I was thinking of the easy part."

How long did the pharmacy team's move take last year?
Seven weeks.
Why did Lindiwe not trust her own first guess?
She felt uneasy that Xin's three weeks was already sitting in her head like a fact, so she wanted numbers that did not start from it.
What makes Lindiwe's method worth copying?
She asked what she would judge without the first figure, then checked three separate sources before giving the board a range.
How does Xin react to the six-to-eight-week estimate?
Xin grumbles at first but then admits the three weeks only covered the easy part.

The interview room on the fourth floor of the Hyderabad office smelled of new carpet. Shankar had practised all week: speak slowly, pause after each point, let it land. His first answer went well. He explained his college project in three clear steps, a breath between each, and Nikita, the interviewer, nodded and wrote. But by the third question he was stretching every pause, choosing each word as if it cost money. Nikita glanced at the wall clock and tapped her pen. The room felt heavy. Shankar noticed the pen. Maybe she has a long list of candidates today, he thought. He picked up the pace a little, kept one clean pause before his main point about the delivery-route data, and finished early. Nikita looked up and smiled. "That's the clearest summary I've heard today." Walking out, Shankar texted his sister: "Slow is good. Too slow is a snooze."

What did Nikita tap while glancing at the clock?
Her pen.
What did Shankar think when he noticed the tapping pen?
He felt a jolt of worry that his long pauses were dragging and that Nikita, perhaps with a long list of candidates, was losing interest.
How did Shankar adjust his pace?
He sped up a little, kept one clean pause before his main point, and finished early, matching the room.
How might Nikita have experienced the stretched pauses?
As slow and heavy, which is why she glanced at the clock, until his clearer summary won her back.

Seminar note, Thursday. Parul, a second-year student, sat at the far corner of the table during today's discussion on urban housing. When the argument turned to rent controls, Parul lifted one finger just off the table, leaned forward a little and caught my eye as chair. I nodded that I'd seen it and let the speaker finish. Two others talked over each other while Parul waited, hand still raised, jaw set. When the speaker paused I said, "Parul, go ahead." The point was clear and changed the direction of the talk. Afterwards Parul said the waiting was hard. I told Parul the signal was noticed and I'd keep a list of turns. I'll say that to the whole group next week.

Which topic was the seminar discussing?
The seminar was discussing urban housing, turning to rent controls.
What was Parul feeling while waiting with a raised finger?
Parul wanted to contribute and was likely tense or impatient, as the set jaw and the raised hand suggest. Another reading is that Parul was simply keen to make sure the point was not lost.
What could the chair do to help quiet students claim a turn?
Keep a visible list of turns and tell the whole group that raised fingers and leaning in are being noticed.
How might the two who talked over each other see Parul's waiting?
They may not have noticed the signal at all, or may have seen it and felt rushed, so a chair's clear turn order helps them too.

Tell me in three sentences what this card game evening is like.

When the gentlemen had joined them, and tea was over, the card tables were placed. Lady Catherine, Sir William, and Mr. and Mrs. Collins sat down to quadrille; and as Miss De Bourgh chose to play at cassino, the two girls had the honour of assisting Mrs. Jenkinson to make up her party. Their table was superlatively stupid. Scarcely a syllable was uttered that did not relate to the game, except when Mrs. Jenkinson expressed her fears of Miss De Bourgh's being too hot or too cold, or having too much or too little light. A great deal more passed at the other table. Lady Catherine was generally speaking--stating the mistakes of the three others, or relating some anecdote of herself. Mr. Collins was employed in agreeing to everything her Ladyship said, thanking her for every fish he won, and apologizing if he thought he won too many. Sir William did not say much. He was storing his memory with anecdotes and noble names.

After tea the group splits into two card tables. The girls' table is dull, with talk only about the game and Miss De Bourgh's comfort. At the other table Lady Catherine points out mistakes and tells stories, Mr. Collins agrees with everything she says, and Sir William quietly collects stories.
Is despise stronger than dislike?

Yes, much stronger. To despise someone or something is to feel that it is worthless and to dislike it very strongly. It is a verb.
Example: The villagers despised the cruel landlord who took their crops.

Honestly, Sunaina, I never said no once, and that's how the app launch slipped by three weeks. I'm Harsha, and I was running the project. The client would say, "Can you just add a filter?" Sure. "Could the button be green?" Sure. "A login reminder?" Sure, small. Each one took a day or two and made me feel helpful. Nobody complained, so I never counted. On the Monday before delivery I finally added up my notes: eight small yeses at about two days each. I had promised a date that could not hold, and I had to phone the client and admit it. Now I write every extra request in a list with its cost before I answer.

How many small yeses had Harsha added up on the Monday before delivery?
Harsha counted eight small yeses, at about two days each.
What did Harsha feel while saying yes to each small request?
Helpful and pleased, since each yes seemed harmless.
What could Harsha have done at the first extra request?
Write it in a list with its cost in days, and tell the client that adding it would move the date or something else would have to go.
How might the client have seen Harsha's yeses?
The client probably saw a friendly, flexible manager and kept asking, without seeing the total cost until the date slipped.

Siddharth, you asked why I'm so careful when I correct people. Let me, Dolma, tell you about my worst year as a lead, at the travel agency in Gangtok.
We had a new junior, Pemba, who kept booking the wrong dates. One morning, in front of all eight of us, I held up his booking sheet and said, "How can anyone make this mistake three times?" I thought shame would make him careful.
It did the opposite. He stopped asking me anything. When he wasn't sure about a date, he just guessed and kept quiet. When a customer complained, he'd already hidden the email.
Two months later, a family arrived at the airport with no hotel. Pemba had known about the error for a week.
That's when I understood. My loud voice didn't fix his mistakes. It only taught him to hide them.

How many people were there when Dolma held up the booking sheet?
All eight of them.
How did Pemba feel after being criticised in front of everyone, and how can you tell?
Pemba felt humiliated and afraid; he stopped asking questions, guessed quietly and hid a customer complaint.
What was the turning point in Dolma's story, and what could Dolma have chosen instead that morning?
The turning point was the public criticism; Dolma could have spoken to Pemba privately with the three examples and asked what was making the dates hard.
How did the public criticism affect the family who arrived at the airport?
The family was left with no hotel, because Pemba had hidden the error for a week instead of asking for help.

The photo appeared in the class group at twenty to ten: a private one of Pranav, meant for a single friend. His face went hot, then cold. His thumbs were already typing, Who did this??? and worse. He looked at the words, then deleted them. If he fired back, they would screenshot that too, and it would become a fight instead of a wrong done to him. He put the phone face down and breathed until his hands stopped shaking. Then he called his cousin Kunal, who told him, “Don't answer anyone. Go to your mother now.” Pranav walked into the living room. His mother listened, put an arm round him, said, “This is not your fault,” and picked up the phone to call the school's safety lead that night.

What did Pranav do with the angry message he typed?
He deleted it.
What was Pranav feeling when the photo appeared?
Panic and rage: his face went hot, then cold, and his thumbs began typing angry words.
What could Pranav do next, and why?
Save screenshots with dates and share them with the school, since adults can act on real proof.
How does the night look to Pranav's mother?
Pranav's mother is shocked and worried but glad he came to her, and phoning the school safety lead the same night gives her something useful to do.

Manjula pulled the blanket up to her chin.
"Amma, sip. Just a little."
"I don't want water. Stop fussing, Vandana."
"Half a glass, then I'll stop."
"You're worse than a nurse."
"I'll take that. You're still hot. Breathing okay? Any chest pain?"
"No. Just aching everywhere. And bored. And cross."
"Cross is allowed."
"Sorry I snapped this morning."
"You're sick. It's not personal."
"When's the doctor calling?"
"I rang at nine. She said to watch for breathlessness or confusion and call straight away if anything worries me. She'll ring back at four."
"You wrote all that down?"
"On the fridge. Now sleep. I'll be right here with my laptop."

When did Vandana ring the doctor?
At nine.
How does Vandana feel when Manjula snaps?
Vandana stays calm and affectionate rather than hurt, seeing the snapping as the illness, not something personal.
What makes Vandana's care sensible?
She keeps fluids and rest going, checks for danger signs, has the doctor's advice written on the fridge, and stays nearby.
What is being ill like for Manjula?
She feels achy, bored and cross, and a little sorry for snapping at her daughter.

Yamini: remember my prediction log?
Uday: the spreadsheet of doom
Yamini: 😅 yes. today's entry: "2-min update at team meeting. Prediction: I freeze, voice shakes, boss looks at phone. Confidence 80%"
Uday: and???
Yamini: voice shook for the first 20 seconds. then fine. boss asked a follow-up question. nobody looked at phones
Uday: so score?
Yamini: prediction maybe 20% right
Uday: that's the 4th entry like that
Yamini: I know. I'm starting to see a pattern. my forecasts are like a weather app that only predicts storms
Uday: next experiment?
Yamini: 5 min next Friday. confidence of disaster... 60%?
Uday: progress 👍
Yamini: kinder progress 🙂

What did Yamini predict for the two-minute update?
The prediction was: I freeze, voice shakes, boss looks at phone, with confidence 80%.
How did Yamini feel on seeing the result, and what shows it?
Yamini felt a bit sheepish but encouraged 😅, joking that the forecasts are like a weather app that only predicts storms.
Why is keeping a prediction log a workable countermeasure?
Writing the forecast and a confidence level before trying, then scoring it afterwards, builds a record of how often the fear is wrong, so later predictions become more accurate and gentler.
How does Uday see the experiments?
Uday treats them with light humour and real support, keeping count of the wrong predictions and cheering the next step.

The power had gone in the whole colony, so the evening match between Neem Street and Pipe Lane was the only thing happening, lit by the last of the sunset. When the Pipe Lane children arrived with their plastic bat, Salma folded her arms. 'We're not playing with them. They're dirty. They're like wild animals, they bite.' A few Neem Street kids giggled. Elizabeth Aunty, sitting out on her steps in the heat, called Salma over. 'Which one bites?' Salma pointed vaguely. 'All of them.' 'What's that girl's name, the one with the red clip?' 'I don't know.' 'Then how do you know she bites?' Salma had no answer. The girl with the red clip was holding the ball, waiting. 'Her name is Ruksana,' Elizabeth Aunty said. 'She brings my newspaper. Go and ask if she wants to bowl first.'

What was the girl with the red clip holding?
The girl with the red clip was holding the ball.
Why does calling the Pipe Lane children 'wild animals' make refusing them feel okay to Salma?
Seeing them as animals rather than children with names makes shutting them out feel reasonable, so Salma feels justified rather than guilty about being unkind.
What did Elizabeth Aunty do that began to change things?
She asked for one child's name and then gave it, Ruksana, turning 'all of them' into a real girl, and suggested asking her to bowl first.
How might Ruksana feel standing with the ball, waiting?
Ruksana might feel unsure and hurt, hearing her lane called dirty and wild when she only wanted to play.

Ujjwal called the all-night gaming stress relief. Two lectures missed, a card statement he kept folded in a drawer, and still he told his roommate, "I can stop anytime." Then the sun would come up on another round.

His mother Jaya found the college notice and the statement together, and she shouted. "Are you throwing your life away?" Ujjwal felt cornered, and his first thought was to say it was nothing and shut his door. Then he saw her hands shaking. "You're scared," he said. "I am," she said, and sat down. By the end of the evening they had agreed he would book an appointment.

In the clinic his palms were damp. He nearly described only the mild half, a few late nights, then said, "It's more than that. I play till morning and I skip things." The doctor listened and set a follow-up. The next week he slipped and went back anyway.

A month later he sat on a plastic chair in a community hall. Bhavna, who ran the circle, smiled at him. "Nobody here will judge you. Just say what's true." He said it, and something in his chest let go. The following week he came again.

What did Ujjwal tell his roommate about his gaming?
He said, "I can stop anytime."
How did Ujjwal's reaction to his mother's shouting differ from the way he talked at the clinic and at the circle?

With Jaya he first felt cornered and wanted to shut himself away, until he saw she was scared. At the clinic and the circle he told the whole truth, and he kept going after a slip, which is how the plan began to work.
What was Ujjwal feeling when Bhavna said nobody would judge him?
He felt relief and a sense of belonging, shown by the way something in his chest let go.
What could Ujjwal do if he slips again after weeks of going to the circle?
He could go back to the doctor and the circle honestly, as he did after his first slip, and tell someone safe what happened.

The results came out at seven, right as the power went. With only Nilesh's phone charged, the whole family crowded around its glow on the dark verandah.
"Ninety-three!" Aai hugged Nilesh so tightly his glasses slipped. Baba was already calling relatives. Nobody asked about Usha, whose Class 10 results had come out the same evening.
Nilesh felt the warmth, and also Usha's silence beside him. She had eighty-one. He knew because she'd shown him first, quietly, before the lights died.
"Usha got eighty-one," he said loudly. "And she's the one who explained all of trigonometry to me. Half this ninety-three is hers."
Aai paused. Baba lowered his phone.
When the neighbour sent over a box of pedas, Nilesh put the box in Usha's lap. "You open it," he said. Usha looked at him in the candlelight and, slowly, smiled.

What mark did Usha get?
Eighty-one.
How did Nilesh feel when Aai hugged him and nobody asked about Usha?
He felt warm but uneasy and guilty, aware of Usha's hurt silence beside him.
What small steps did Nilesh take to avoid exploiting his favoured place?
He announced Usha's marks, credited her help with trigonometry, and handed her the box of pedas to open.
What is it like for Usha when the family crowds around Nilesh?
She likely feels overlooked and hurt, since her own results came the same evening and nobody asked about them.

There were but eight; yet, somehow, as they flocked in, they gave the impression of a much larger number. Some of them were very tall; many were dressed in white; and all had a sweeping amplitude of array that seemed to magnify their persons as a mist magnifies the moon. I rose and curtseyed to them: one or two bent their heads in return, the others only stared at me.

Question: What impression do the eight people make as they enter?
They seem a much larger number. Some are very tall, many are dressed in white, and their sweeping, ample dress makes them look bigger, like a mist magnifying the moon.

Thursday night. Asked Farida to swap Saturday's shift so I could go to my cousin's engagement. Farida said, "Sorry, can't." Asked two others. Same answer. Nobody even looked up. It stings. Three weeks ago I insisted the release schedule stay my way, with testing on Mondays. I brought numbers and made sure everyone knew I was right. I won. Nobody argued after that. Since then people hand me tasks on the shared board without a word and have stopped coming to my desk. Farida told me back then, "It only works for you." I said the numbers say otherwise. Tonight I think I won the argument and lost something else. Maybe I should ask what Monday testing costs them.

Sandeep

What did Farida say when asked to swap the shift?
Farida said, "Sorry, can't."
How does Sandeep feel now?
Sandeep feels hurt and uneasy, saying that it stings and that something else was lost.
What could Sandeep do to repair things with colleagues?
Sandeep could ask colleagues what Monday testing costs them and look for a schedule that works for everyone.
How might Farida have seen the original schedule fight?
Farida may have felt unheard, having said it only worked for Sandeep, and later unwilling to do favours.

The next morning I delivered my letters of introduction and paid a visit to some of the principal professors. Chance—or rather the evil influence, the Angel of Destruction, which asserted omnipotent sway over me from the moment I turned my reluctant steps from my father's door—led me first to M. Krempe, professor of natural philosophy. He was an uncouth man, but deeply imbued in the secrets of his science. He asked me several questions concerning my progress in the different branches of science appertaining to natural philosophy. I replied carelessly, and partly in contempt, mentioned the names of my alchemists as the principal authors I had studied. The professor stared. "Have you," he said, "really spent your time in studying such nonsense?"

Make a two-sentence summary out of this extract.

The next morning the narrator delivers letters of introduction and visits professors, first M. Krempe, a rough but very knowledgeable teacher of natural science. Asked about studies, the narrator carelessly names the alchemists, and the professor stares and calls it nonsense.

I'm Rajni, Lakshmi's big sister. Yesterday Lakshmi, who is five, and her friend both wanted the same doll. They pulled it between them until one arm popped off, and both of them went quiet. Lakshmi looked like she might cry. Then she said, "You hold her body, I hold her arm, and we fix her." They pushed the arm back together. Later I heard her say, "Sorry for pulling." I don't know if she meant it fully, but they played till dinner.

What happened to the doll when they pulled it?
One arm popped off.
What might Lakshmi have felt when the arm came off?
She likely felt shocked and upset, maybe guilty, since she looked close to crying.
How could an adult help next time before the doll breaks?
Suggest turns early, like a timer or "you first, then me", before pulling starts.
How does Rajni see Lakshmi's apology?
Rajni is not sure it was fully meant, but notices it helped them keep playing.

In Nandurbar, the Class 9 group had been passing round a video of Afreen slipping in the rain outside the bus stand, slowed down with silly music. Shankar watched it on Sunday night. Everyone was laughing. He didn't laugh, but he didn't say anything either. He just closed the app.

On Monday, Afreen came to school with her head down and sat alone at lunch. Shankar felt a heavy knot in his stomach. He had seen it. He could have said something.

After lunch, he walked over. "Afreen, I saw the video. I'm sorry I didn't say anything. It was cruel."

She looked up, surprised. "You're the first one to say that."

He reported the video in the group, and when his friend Suresh asked him to forward it, he said, "No. Delete it." Then he told their class teacher, Shinde sir, before the last period. Sir went to the group admin that same afternoon, had the video removed, and spoke to Afreen and her father after school.

Where did Afreen slip in the video?
Afreen slipped in the rain outside the bus stand.
What was Shankar feeling when Afreen sat alone at lunch?
Shankar felt guilty, with a heavy knot in his stomach, because he had seen the video and said nothing.
What did Shankar do to make up for staying silent?
Shankar apologised to Afreen, reported the video, refused to forward it and told Shinde sir the same day.
How did Afreen react to Shankar's apology?
Afreen was surprised and seemed a little comforted, since he was the first to call the video cruel.
Why is my father quiet these days?
I can't tell what he is thinking, so I don't know. Choose a calm moment and ask him how he is.

Put this speech into modern prose.

Thy sons, by Visvamitra led,
Unurged, my city visited,
And peerless in their might have gained
My daughter, as my vow ordained.
Full in a vast assembly's view
Thy hero Rama broke in two
The gem of bows, of monstrous size,
That came a treasure from the skies.

Your sons, led by Visvamitra, came to my city without being asked, and by their unmatched strength they have won my daughter, as my vow decreed. In front of a vast gathering, your hero Rama broke in two the finest of bows, a huge one that came as a treasure from the sky.

The counselling room at the logistics company had one window and a box of tissues nobody touched. Imran slid a printed page across the table.
"It's a log," he said. "Since March, my manager, Mr Kapoor, keeps saying I never got his instructions, or that I imagine the deadlines he moved. So after every call I email him a summary: As discussed, delivery report by Friday. Then I note the date here."
Yamini, the staff counsellor, read it slowly. "How has it felt, keeping this?"
"Honestly? Like proof I'm not losing my mind. Last week he said I'd agreed to Sunday work. I opened the email thread in front of him. He changed the subject."
"Your records are clear, and your worry makes sense," Yamini said. "Shall we look at what the formal complaint route would need, so you have options?"
Imran let out a long breath and nodded.

What does Imran email after every call?
He emails Mr Kapoor a summary of what was discussed, such as "delivery report by Friday".
What does keeping the log mean to Imran?
Keeping the log makes Imran feel reassured, like proof he is not losing his mind when Mr Kapoor denies things.
How does Yamini support Imran at this point?
Yamini listens, confirms the records are clear and the worry makes sense, and offers to look at the complaint route so Imran has options rather than only doubts.
How might Mr Kapoor react now that his instructions are on record?
He can no longer easily deny what was agreed; changing the subject when the email was shown suggests the record leaves little room to rewrite events.
Please don't waist water while washing the car. Check the spelling.

Please don't waste water while washing the car.
Why: "Waste" means to use carelessly. "Waist" is the middle of the body.

At the gate of their Andheri school, Kiran's little brother Jomon came running with his Class 3 friends. "Kiran! Kiran!"
Kiran's own friends were watching. Kiran gave a tiny nod and kept walking. Jomon's face fell.
At home that evening, Kiran heard him telling Amma, "Kiran doesn't know me at school."
Kiran felt a sting. That wasn't true. It was just that at fifteen, in front of everyone, being hugged by a Class 3 kid felt embarrassing.
That night, when Jomon was stuck on his maths homework, Kiran sat with him for an hour. Then, before bed, Kiran slid a chocolate under his pillow with a note: "Sorry about the gate. You're my favourite person. Don't tell anyone."
Next morning at the gate, Jomon just waved. Kiran waved back, and, very quickly, squeezed his shoulder.

What did Kiran slide under Jomon's pillow?
A chocolate with a note.
What was Kiran feeling on overhearing Jomon talk to Amma?
Kiran felt a sting of guilt and sadness, since the cool nod at the gate came from embarrassment, not from not caring.
How did Kiran keep the bond alive?
With private warmth: an hour of homework help, a chocolate and an honest note, then a small shoulder squeeze at the gate.
What was it like for Jomon when Kiran ignored him at the gate?
Jomon felt hurt and rejected, believing Kiran didn't want to know him at school.

messages.content:
Read this:

Yogesh, sit. You're upset that your wife hid that loan from you. I understand. Let me tell you about me and your aunt. When I was twenty-five, a young man just married, I found out that your Kamala-mami had borrowed from a moneylender to help her sister. She hadn't told me for six months. I felt like a fool in my own house. I shouted. She cried. I slept on the veranda. The next morning, I realised I didn't know why she'd done it. So I asked, and I listened. She had been afraid I'd say no. We sat with a notebook and wrote down every rupee owed. We went to the moneylender together and agreed on a schedule. And we made a promise: no secrets about money, even the embarrassing ones. We kept it for forty years. The secret hurt more than the debt, Yogesh. Ask for the full story. That's Pradeep-mama's advice.

How long had Kamala-mami hidden the loan?
Six months.
What was Pradeep feeling when he found out about the loan?
He felt betrayed and foolish, shouting and sleeping on the veranda.
What turning point in the story helped Pradeep and Kamala-mami rebuild trust?
Asking why she did it and listening, then writing every debt down, agreeing a schedule together, and making a no-secrets promise.
How might Kamala-mami have felt while hiding the loan?
She was probably afraid and anxious that Pradeep would refuse, which is why she kept it secret.

'You didn't fast today?' Hrithik asked, passing the chips across the hostel terrace.
'Tuesday? No.' Tejas took a handful. 'First Tuesday I haven't in, what, eight years.'
'Why'd you stop?'
'I didn't decide to. I slept through it once, and nothing happened. Then I started reading. And then I met Farhan, who prays five times a day, and Meenal, who says there's no god and seems totally fine. Everyone's so sure. I used to be sure.'
'And now?'
'Now I don't know.' Tejas lay back on the warm concrete. 'Honestly? It's kind of great. I can think anything.'
'But?'
'But my mom still sends me a photo of the temple every Tuesday. And I still look at it for a long time.'

How long had Tejas kept the Tuesday fast?
Tejas had kept it for about eight years.
What does Tejas looking at the temple photo for a long time reveal?
It reveals a sense of loss and longing that sits alongside the new freedom Tejas enjoys.
What could help Tejas make sense of this stage?
Tejas could accept that freedom and loss can both be true, and perhaps reply honestly to the photo, keeping the bond with home even while beliefs are unsettled.
How might Tejas's mom feel sending the photo every Tuesday?
She likely sends it as a loving link to home and tradition, perhaps hoping Tejas still feels part of it.

In the shared dormitory in Singapore, Jin, twenty-five, sat on his bunk after a twelve-hour shift and transferred money home to his parents in Malaysia, as he did every month. His mother's message came back: a photo of his little sister's new school uniform, and a heart.
He smiled. Then he opened his own account and saw how little was left.
His bunkmate Javier, from the Philippines, noticed. "You look like me last year."
"I'm proud to help," Jin said. "But I've had the same shoes for two years."
"I told my family exactly what I can send," Javier said. "Not as much as they wanted. My mother cried, then she said she didn't want me hurting. Things are better now."
Jin thought about it all week. On Sunday, he called his mother and said, gently, "Ma, I want to keep helping. But I need to talk about what I can manage."

What did Jin's mother send a photo of?
She sent a photo of his little sister's new school uniform, and a heart.
What was Jin feeling when he saw how little was left?
Jin felt proud of helping, but also strained and worried about his own needs.
What helped Jin decide to speak up?
Javier's story showed that telling family honestly what you can manage can lead to understanding, not rejection.
How might Jin's mother feel when he raises the topic?
She might feel surprised and a little sad, but, like Javier's mother, likely wants him not to be hurting.

At our Nani's prayer meeting, the pandit's microphone suddenly made a loud squeaky noise, like a duck. Everyone kept their faces serious.
I saw my brother Uday press his lips together so tight they went white. His shoulders shook. He stared hard at the flowers in front of Nani's photo and breathed through his nose. I don't know if he was trying not to laugh or trying not to cry. Maybe both.
He managed it all through the prayers.
Afterwards, he went straight out to the garden and I followed. He laughed so hard he had to hold the gate, and then he wiped his eyes and went quiet.
I sat on the step next to him till Mummy called us for food.
- Yamini

What sound did the microphone make?
A loud squeaky noise, like a duck.
What might Uday have been feeling when his shoulders shook?
He may have been amused by the squeak and struggling not to laugh, or sad and holding back tears at the prayer meeting; Yamini can't be sure, and it may have been both.
What helped Uday after holding it in so long?
Going out to the garden gave him a private place to let the laughter and feelings out, with his sibling quietly beside him.
How did Yamini experience watching Uday?
Yamini was watching closely and caring, unsure what he felt, and chose to follow him and sit with him.

In the office pantry, Afreen found Reena, a teammate, staring at the kettle.
"Reena, you've been watching that kettle for five minutes."
"Sorry. Just tired. Afreen, can I ask something weird? If I weren't around, the team would manage fine, right?"
"What do you mean, not around?"
"Nothing. It's just, I'm stuck. The loan, Papa's treatment, this job. Every road ends at the same wall. I'm dragging everyone down with me."
"Reena, I'm taking that seriously. Are you thinking of ending your life?"
"Sometimes. More lately."
"Thank you for telling me. I'm not going anywhere. Is anyone at home tonight?"
"My brother."
"Okay. I'm going to call him now, with you here, and then I'll come with you to see a doctor this evening. The office can wait."
"You'd do that? For me?"
"For you. You're not dragging anyone down."

Who is at home with Reena tonight?
Reena's brother.
How does Reena feel about the situation, in Reena's own words?
Trapped and like a burden: "Every road ends at the same wall. I'm dragging everyone down with me."
Which step by Afreen turned an odd question into urgent help?
Afreen asked directly, then called Reena's brother right there and offered to go with Reena to a doctor that evening.
How might Afreen have felt hearing "the team would manage fine"?
Afreen likely felt alarmed and heard it as an indirect warning, which is why Afreen asked what "not around" meant.
