After my thread ceremony I thought I'd feel different. Mostly I felt itchy. In the changing room before PE a boy asked if it was some fashion thing. Kalyani, who sits behind me in Bengali class, said, "My uncle wears one to pray, my cousin wears one because his mother insists, and I know a boy who just likes it." She looked at me. "Which are you?" I realised I had no clean answer. Ma wants me to keep it on. Dadu says it has to do with learning, and I like feeling close to him. Some days I tuck it under my shirt, some days I don't. I'm still working it out. - Arnab

Where did the boy ask Arnab about the thread?
He asked in the changing room before PE.
What did Arnab feel when Kalyani asked which he was?
He felt uncertain, since he had no clean answer; his reasons seem to mix his mother's wish, closeness to Dadu and his own feeling.
How could Arnab reply when someone asks what his thread means?
He could share what he knows or say he is still working it out, without needing a tidy answer.
What does Kalyani's list of people show?
It shows that the same thread can be prayer, family insistence or personal taste, so nobody should assume what it means for someone else.

In Istanbul, Selin, twenty-five, had been waiting eight months for the municipality to approve the ramp outside her grandmother's building. Her grandmother used a wheelchair and hadn't left the flat since winter.
Every call ended with, "It's in process."
Her friend Sofia, a journalist, said, "File a formal information request. Ask exactly where the application is, who has it, and what the legal time limit is."
Selin wrote it that night, calmly and clearly, and submitted it online. She printed a copy and kept the reference number.
Three weeks later, a reply came: the application had been sitting with one department, past its legal deadline. Two days after that, an engineer called. "We'll start next Monday."
When the ramp was finished, her grandmother rolled out into the sunlight for the first time in months and held Selin's hand.

How long had Selin been waiting for the ramp approval?
She had been waiting eight months.
How might Selin have felt hearing "It's in process" every time?
Selin probably felt frustrated and helpless, while her grandmother was stuck in the flat.
What made Selin's approach work?
She filed a calm, clear formal information request, kept a copy and reference number, and the reply exposed the delay, which made the system move.
How might Selin's grandmother feel rolling into the sunlight?
Her grandmother would likely feel joyful and grateful after months stuck indoors.

The school counsellor's room smelled of the jasmine the gardener had left on the windowsill. Urmila sat on the plastic chair, sleeves pulled over her hands.

"He broke up with me on Monday," she said. "Sachin. He was nice about it. That's what makes it worse."

"How have you been since?"

"I check his page every hour. I haven't eaten lunch. My chest feels empty, like there's a hole in it."

The counsellor listened, then asked, "Who have you told?"

"My friend Hina. Not my mother."

"Would you be willing to tell your mother tonight? Not the details. Just that you're sad."

Urmila nodded slowly.

"And the checking?"

"I wrote a mean post yesterday. I didn't send it."

"Good. That pain is real, Urmila. And it does ease. Let's meet again on Friday."

When did Sachin break up with Urmila?
On Monday.
What does Urmila mean when she says her chest feels empty?
She feels hollow and rejected, grieving the relationship even though Sachin was kind about it.
How does the counsellor support Urmila?
The counsellor listens, encourages her to tell her mother that evening, affirms not posting the mean message, reminds her the pain eases, and sets a follow-up for Friday.
How does the counsellor seem to view Urmila's unsent post?
The counsellor sees it as a real strength, saying "Good", because not posting protects Urmila from regret while the pain eases.

In the corridor of their school in Madrid, Santiago slammed his locker. "Señora Ruiz is the worst teacher this school has ever had. She makes us act out every scene. It's embarrassing." He looked round, waiting for nods.
Kofi shifted his bag. "I actually like her class. It's the only one where I talk."
"You're joking."
"No. And Lucía said drama is her favourite subject."
Santiago felt heat rise up his neck. He had been so sure everyone groaned the way he did. "Great, so you're all on her side."
"It's not sides," Kofi said. "You just hate acting. That's fine."
Santiago walked to maths alone, going over it. He'd said "everyone" as if it were obvious. Maybe it had only been obvious to him.

What does Señora Ruiz make the class do?
Act out every scene.
What does the heat rising up Santiago's neck suggest?
He feels embarrassed and a bit defensive, because he had been sure everyone felt the way he did.
What went wrong, and what could Santiago try next time?
He presented his dislike as everyone's view; next time he could say he finds her class embarrassing and ask how others find it.
What is Señora Ruiz's class like for Kofi?
It's the only class where Kofi talks, so it matters to him, which is why he gently disagrees.
Write two sentences about a village well. The first must be a question.
Who first dug the old well at the edge of the village? Families have drawn water from it for generations.

"Ma, don't cook that rice," Rafiq said from the kitchen door. "They're making fake rice out of plastic now. You can bounce it like a ball."
His mother, Vinita, kept stirring. "Who told you?"
"Everyone knows it."
"Everyone who?"
Rafiq thought. "I've heard it loads of times."
"Heard it, or read it?"
He pulled out his phone and scrolled. "Here. The colony group. And here, the cricket group. And here, from Nanu." Three forwards of the same video.
"So one video, three times," Vinita said. "Did anyone test it? Or say where it came from?"
Rafiq read them again. "No." He rubbed his neck. "It just felt true because I kept seeing it."
"Then let's roll a ball of this rice after dinner and see if it bounces."

Where had Rafiq seen the fake rice claim?
In the colony group, the cricket group and a forward from Nanu, the same video three times.
Why did Rafiq say, "Everyone knows it"?
He had seen the claim so often that it felt like common knowledge, and he had forgotten it all came from one forwarded video.
Which question from Vinita changed Rafiq's thinking?
"Heard it, or read it?" made him check his phone, where he found one video forwarded three times with no source or test.
How might Vinita feel when Rafiq says it only felt true because he kept seeing it?
She may feel relieved that he noticed it himself, which is why she turns it into a playful rice test instead of a lecture. 😊
Write instructions for feeding a goldfish in no more than three numbered steps.

1. Sprinkle a small pinch of fish flakes on the water.
2. Watch the fish eat for about two minutes.
3. Scoop out any food still floating.

You want to hear about the flood? I'm Akash, and I was fifteen. I've told this story at every family function since.

I always say I was at the market with my friend Salma when the water came in, and we climbed onto a bus shelter roof. I can see the brown water, the floating slippers, Salma's pink dupatta.

Last month I met Salma after years. I told the story, and she looked at me strangely. "Akash, I was at home that day. You came to my house after, soaked. You told me about the bus shelter."

I felt dizzy. I still see her there. But maybe I just pictured her so many times, telling it, that she moved into the memory. I was sure. I'm less sure now.

What does Akash remember climbing onto?
A bus shelter roof.
How did Akash feel when Salma said she was at home?
Akash felt dizzy and shaken, because the memory of her there was so clear and certain.
What could Akash do next time he tells the flood story?
He could tell it honestly as his memory, while admitting some details may have shifted over the years.
How might Salma feel hearing that she's been in Akash's story all these years?
Salma might feel surprised and a little touched that he remembered her so strongly, even wrongly.
Concern means what, exactly?

Concern is a feeling of worry about something, or of care for someone. It is a noun; as a verb it means to worry or to be about.
Example: The teacher showed concern when Ana looked sad.

Dear diary, Lakshmi here.

I have decided I am going to be exactly like Veer Shetty, the kabaddi raider on TV. I cut my fringe short like his. I practise his crouch in the corridor. And I say, "Come on then!" before every raid, like he does, with my chin up.

Today in PE, I did the crouch and the chin and I actually got two points! I felt like Veer. Like nothing could stop me.

But then when I was out, I kicked the mat like he did in the final. Coach said, "Lakshmi, we don't kick the mat here." Madhuri, my sister, said it looked silly.

I don't think it looked silly. He's the best.

Okay, maybe the mat part was a bit much. But the crouch stays.

How many points did Lakshmi get in PE?
Two points.
How did Lakshmi feel doing the crouch and chin like Veer Shetty?
Lakshmi felt powerful and proud, as if some of the hero's strength came from copying him.
What could Lakshmi keep from Veer Shetty, and what could she drop?
Lakshmi could keep the crouch and the confidence, which help her play, and drop the mat-kicking, which is swagger that doesn't fit the team.
How might Madhuri see Lakshmi's new style?
Madhuri finds parts of it silly, though Madhuri may also notice how proud and excited Lakshmi is.

Vikas saw Tanvir coming out of the stationery shop near the Sector 15 market and waved hard. Tanvir looked straight through him and walked on, fast, head down. Vikas felt his cheeks burn. They had sat together all year. That evening he told his cousin, "Tanvir's become so full of himself since he made the football team. Didn't even say hi." He left Tanvir out of the group chat plan for Sunday's movie. On Monday Tanvir wasn't in school. On Tuesday he came in quiet and pale, and at lunch he said, "Sorry about Saturday. I'd just got a call that my Nani had collapsed. I was running to the auto stand." Vikas stared at his lunchbox. He had built a whole story about Tanvir from one walk past.

Where did Vikas see Tanvir on Saturday?
Coming out of the stationery shop near the Sector 15 market.
What was Vikas feeling when Tanvir walked past without a word?
Vikas felt embarrassed and snubbed, his cheeks burning, and quickly decided Tanvir had become full of himself.
What could Vikas do before judging a friend who seems rude?
He could ask the friend if everything is all right, or wait to hear more, before deciding it is about their character.
What was Saturday like for Tanvir?
Tanvir had just heard his Nani had collapsed and was rushing to the auto stand, too frightened to notice anyone waving.

Lavanya, you leave for Dubai next month, so let me tell you how I survived my first year there.
I was twenty-four, at a construction office. The first Onam, I sat alone in my room and ate bread and jam. I called home and heard everyone laughing around the sadya, and I hung up and stared at the wall.
After that I made two rules. First, every Sunday I called your grandmother. Every Onam I cooked at least three dishes, badly. Second, I said yes to anything my colleagues asked. Cricket with the Pakistani engineers on Fridays. Karaoke with the Filipino accountants. Biryani at Salim's.
By the next Onam, I had eleven people around a sadya on newspaper on my floor. I cried again, but differently.
I'm Darshan, and I'm telling you: carry home, but don't hide inside it.

What did Darshan eat on that first Onam?
Bread and jam.
What was Darshan feeling while staring at the wall after hanging up?
Darshan felt lonely and homesick after hearing everyone laughing around the sadya.
What was the turning point in Darshan's story, and why did it work?
Making two rules, keeping home rituals and saying yes to colleagues, was the turning point, because it kept home alive while building new friendships.
How might Darshan's colleagues have seen that Onam sadya?
They probably felt welcomed and happy to share a meal that clearly meant a lot to Darshan.

At the girls' hostel meeting, Deepika stood up before the warden had finished the notices. "Why do phones get collected at eight? We're not kids. It's a stupid rule and nobody has ever explained it." A few girls clapped. Someone at the back whispered, "She's done now." Irawati Ma'am put the register down. "Fair question. The rule is there so study hour stays quiet. What does eight o'clock cost you?" Deepika's chin was still up, but her voice dropped. "My father drives the night bus. He can only call at nine, on his break." The room went quiet. Irawati Ma'am wrote something in the margin. "Then that's the real request, and it's reasonable. Anyone with a family call after eight, give me the time. You'll get your phone for fifteen minutes, in the office." Deepika sat down, arms still folded, but nodding.

When can Deepika's father call?
He can only call at nine, on his break.
What was Deepika feeling when she called the rule stupid?
Deepika was frustrated and probably worried about missing her father's calls. The raised chin also suggests wanting to be treated as grown-up, not only anger at the rule.
How did Irawati Ma'am turn the challenge into something useful?
She called it a fair question, gave the reason for the rule, then asked what it cost Deepika, which uncovered the real request and led to a fair fix.
Why might the girls who clapped see the challenge differently from the warden?
The girls who clapped likely saw a bold stand against a rule, while the warden listened for the need underneath and found a request she could meet.

Dear diary, I'm Sonali. Last night I had a nightmare where I was lost in a huge market and nobody could hear me. I woke up with my heart pounding and my pyjamas all sweaty. I called Amma, and she came in and sat beside me on the bed without saying anything at first. Then she said in her calm voice, "You are safe. I am here. It was only a dream." She rubbed my back slowly and my heart slowed down too. This morning I told my brother Saurabh. He said he once dreamed about a giant crab in the bathtub. We laughed. Telling it out loud made it smaller.

What did Sonali dream about?
Sonali dreamed of being lost in a huge market where nobody could hear.
What made Sonali's heart slow down?
Amma's calm presence: Amma sat beside Sonali, said Sonali was safe and rubbed Sonali's back slowly.
What can Sonali do the next time Sonali wakes frightened?
Sonali can call Amma or tell someone what happened, since sharing the fear made it smaller.
How might Saurabh have felt when Sonali told him about the nightmare?
Understanding, since he shared his own dream about a giant crab, which made them both laugh.

In the college hostel in Jaipur, Madhuri, nineteen, saw Harsha's father and two uncles arrive at the visitors' room on Saturday morning. Harsha, her roommate, went pale.
Through the half-open door, Madhuri heard one uncle: "Photos of you with that boy are all over the family group. You've destroyed our honour. Pack your bag. You're coming home, and you're done with college." Harsha was crying. "Papa, please."
Madhuri felt her heart race. She knew Harsha had been frightened for weeks, hiding her phone.
She didn't go in. She ran to the warden's office. "They're forcing her to leave. They're threatening her."
The warden came at once, stood beside Harsha, and said calmly, "She's an adult and a student here. She will not be taken against her will." Then she called the college's women's cell and the police helpline. Madhuri sat with Harsha until the officer arrived.

Where did Harsha's father and uncles arrive?
They arrived at the visitors' room.
What was Madhuri feeling when she heard the uncle's words?
Madhuri felt afraid for Harsha, her heart racing, knowing her roommate had been frightened for weeks.
What made Madhuri's and the warden's response protective?
Madhuri went straight for help rather than confronting the family alone, and the warden stood beside Harsha, refused to let her be taken and called the women's cell and police.
How might Harsha feel with Madhuri beside her until the officer arrived?
Harsha would likely feel less alone and a little safer, knowing someone had believed her and acted.
My grandmother keeps telling the same stories again and again.
That can feel repetitive, but those stories often matter a lot to her. People tend to return to memories that are important to them. Listening patiently can mean a great deal to her.
Is there a way to make it more interesting for me?

You could ask questions she hasn't answered before, like "What did you wear that day?" or "What happened next?" You might hear new details. You could also record her telling them, so the family keeps them for years.

'Pema, put out a plate for your Dadu. He'll be home at eight.'
Pema glanced at her mother across the kitchen. Dadu had died four years ago. Her mother mouthed, 'Don't argue.'
'Okay, Urmila Dadi. Were you thinking about Dadu today?'
'He always comes home hungry. I made his favourite dal.'
'You miss cooking for him.'
Urmila's eyes filled. 'He liked it with extra ghee.'
'Tell me about when you first cooked for him.'
Urmila smiled. 'I burnt the rotis. He ate every one.' She laughed.
Pema set out a plate, then sat beside her. 'Let's eat together now, Dadi. I'm hungry too.'
Urmila picked up her spoon. The question of eight o'clock didn't come again that evening.

When did Urmila say Dadu would be home?
At eight.
What was Urmila feeling as she talked about Dadu?
She was longing for him and missing cooking for him, with her eyes filling.
What did Pema do instead of correcting Dadi?
She asked about Dadu, named the feeling of missing him and gently moved them into eating together.
How might Pema's mother have felt watching this?
She was probably relieved and proud that Pema avoided an upsetting argument.

'Nice post,' Dhruv said, sliding his phone across the canteen table. 'Five hundred likes for a sunset.'
'Five hundred and twelve,' Anirban said, grinning.
'You looked so happy in the pic.'
'I was.'
'You were panicking about the physics test five minutes before. I was there.'
Anirban's grin stayed, but he started folding his napkin into smaller and smaller squares. 'So?'
'So I don't know which you is real sometimes.'
'That's the point, na. Nobody wants the real one.'
'I might.'
Anirban stopped folding. 'I'm not sure about anything right now. Marks, college, what I'm even good at.' He looked up fast. 'Don't make it a thing.'
'Not a thing,' Dhruv said. 'Eat your samosa. Then tell me more.'

How many likes did the sunset post get?
Five hundred and twelve.
What does Anirban's napkin-folding suggest?
It suggests Anirban felt uneasy and exposed when Dhruv pointed out the gap between the post and reality.
What did Dhruv do well in responding?
He noticed gently, said he might want the real Anirban, and kept it low-key, so Anirban felt safe enough to share more.
What is it like for Dhruv to see the gap between the post and the real Anirban?
Dhruv feels unsure which Anirban is real and wants to be let in, not just shown the happy picture.

He flicked the horse with his whip, and we dashed away through the endless succession of sombre and deserted streets, which widened gradually, until we were flying across a broad balustraded bridge, with the murky river flowing sluggishly beneath us. Beyond lay another dull wilderness of bricks and mortar, its silence broken only by the heavy, regular footfall of the policeman, or the songs and shouts of some belated party of revellers. A dull wrack was drifting slowly across the sky, and a star or two twinkled dimly here and there through the rifts of the clouds. Holmes drove in silence, with his head sunk upon his breast, and the air of a man who is lost in thought, while I sat beside him, curious to learn what this new quest might be which seemed to tax his powers so sorely, and yet afraid to break in upon the current of his thoughts. We had driven several miles, and were beginning to get to the fringe of the belt of suburban villas, when he shook himself, shrugged his shoulders, and lit up his pipe with the air of a man who has satisfied himself that he is acting for the best.

In two sentences, what happens on this drive?

Holmes drives Watson through dark, empty London streets and across a bridge, lost in silent thought. Watson is curious but does not interrupt, until Holmes finally shrugs, lights his pipe and seems to settle his mind.

Class note, third-year sociology, Tuesday. Urmila Rao.
We covered the classic obedience studies today: the switches, the actor's cries, the researcher's calm phrases. Most students reacted as usual, shocked at 'those people'. Darshan did not. He sat very still, then put his hand up: 'Ma'am, none of them sounded like villains. They kept asking "Is he all right?" and then carried on.' A few laughed. He didn't. Later he added, 'My uncle works in a shop. The owner tells him to short-weigh customers, and he does it, and he's the kindest person I know.' He looked angry, more with himself than anyone.
What I did next: I stayed back with him for ten minutes, then set the class a short writing task for Thursday: describe one small order you followed that you now doubt. I'll read them privately.

What did the participants keep asking, according to Darshan?
They kept asking "Is he all right?" and then carried on.
What does Darshan's stillness and anger suggest he was feeling?
Darshan seemed shaken and angry, more with himself than anyone, realising that kind people like his uncle can obey harmful orders.
What did Urmila choose to do with the moment, and why was it a good choice?
Urmila stayed back with Darshan and set a private writing task about one small order students now doubt, turning his insight into reflection for everyone.
Why might the students who laughed see the study differently from Darshan?
They still saw 'those people' as strangers unlike themselves, while Darshan had connected it to someone kind he loves.

On the mud veranda, Ishita pulled her knees to her chin while the village women cooed over the new baby. "Now you'll love him more," she mumbled to Baba. Arnab put down the fish basket and sat beside her. "You are still my big and little one. There's room for both of you, just like two birds in one nest." He put her hand on the baby's head. "He'll need you to show him the pond." Ishita sat up straighter. "I'll show him where the frogs are." She hummed to the baby all afternoon.

What did Arnab put down before sitting beside Ishita?
Arnab put down the fish basket.
How did Ishita feel when she mumbled to Baba?
She felt jealous and afraid that Baba would now love the baby more than her.
What helped Ishita's jealousy soften?
Baba told her there was room for both children and gave her a special role, showing the baby the pond.
How might Arnab see Ishita's humming to the baby?
He may feel glad and proud that she now feels secure and is starting to act like a caring big sister.

Subject: Following up on today

Hi Sonali,
Thanks for coming to talk to me after the stand-up. I could hear how frustrated you are, and I want to take it seriously.
I've noticed that over the last few weeks, colleagues have swung quickly between "amazing" and "impossible" for you. Last month Mohan was "the only one who pulls his weight"; today he "sabotaged" the launch. I'm not saying your feelings aren't real. I just can't be fair to anyone, you included, without specifics.
Could you jot down exactly what happened on Tuesday: what was said, what was missed, and when? I'll ask Mohan for his account too, and then the three of us can sort out the handover.
You're a strong analyst, and I want this to work for everyone.
Vandana

What did Sonali say about Mohan last month?
That he was "the only one who pulls his weight".
What was Vandana feeling while writing the email?
Vandana felt concerned and careful: sympathetic to Sonali's frustration but uneasy about the swings between "amazing" and "impossible".
Why is asking for specifics a wise step?
Details of what was said and missed let Vandana judge fairly, hear Mohan too, and move from heroes and villains to fixing the handover 👍.
How might Sonali feel reading the email?
Sonali might feel heard and a little challenged, perhaps defensive at the pattern being named but reassured by the praise and the fair process.

At the temple fair in their village, Ira let go of her mother's hand and ran to the toy stall. She pointed at a small wooden cricket bat.
"That one!"
The stall-keeper laughed. "For a girl? Take this doll, sister, it's prettier."
Usha saw Ira's face fall. Her own father had once laughed when she climbed trees. She took a breath and paid for the bat.
"Show me how you hit," Usha said.
Ira swung hard, nearly toppling over, and grinned.

What did Ira point at?
Ira pointed at a small wooden cricket bat.
What might Usha have been feeling when she saw Ira's face fall?
Usha likely felt protective and a pang of old hurt, remembering her own father laughing when she climbed trees.
What did Usha do that helped Ira?
She stayed calm, paid for the bat, and asked Ira to show how she hits, so Ira learned her interest was fine.
How might Ira have felt if Usha had agreed with the stall-keeper?
Ira might have felt ashamed and learned that wanting a bat was wrong for a girl.

Omkar was twenty-six and the youngest head chef the hotel kitchen had ever had. Every Friday after the dinner rush, he pulled up an upturned crate and asked the same question: "What did I get wrong this week?" The first month, nobody answered. Then Jagdish, the oldest cook, said, "The new 6 am prep shift. You didn't ask who takes the first bus." Three of the dishwashers came from villages an hour away. Omkar went quiet, then moved prep to seven. When a food critic praised the new mango kulfi, Omkar pointed at the pastry section. "Ask Lata. It's her recipe." Some nights he rang an old friend from catering college who never let him win an argument. "Still humble, chef?" "Trying," Omkar said.

What time did Omkar move the prep shift to?
Seven.
Why did Omkar go quiet after Jagdish spoke?
He felt surprised and a little ashamed to realise his 6 am shift had cost the dishwashers who took the first bus, and he wanted to fix it.
Which of Omkar's habits guard against self-importance?
Asking every Friday what he got wrong, crediting Lata for the kulfi, and keeping a friend who argues with him all keep him curious about others.
How might Jagdish feel after the prep shift moved?
Jagdish would likely feel respected and trusted, seeing that honest feedback to the young chef actually changed things.

Hi team,

Before we launch the new delivery route next Monday, I'd like us to try something. In the shared sheet, please add:
1. What you expect to happen.
2. How confident you are (as a percentage).
3. Your main reason.

I'll add mine too: "Deliveries 15% faster. 65% sure. Based on the pilot in Andheri."

Why? Last quarter, when the Pune route failed, we spent a whole meeting blaming Yash for a choice that looked sensible at the time. That wasn't fair, and we learned nothing. If we write our thinking down now, in a month we can compare what we knew with what happened, and see whether it was the plan, the information, or plain bad luck.

No blame, just learning.

Thanks,
Manoj

What does Manoj expect from the new delivery route?
Deliveries 15% faster.
What does Manoj seem to feel about the Pune route review?
Manoj seems regretful that Yash was unfairly blamed and determined to avoid that happening again.
How will the shared sheet help the team later?
It records what they knew and expected before launch, so they can later separate a poor plan from missing information or bad luck.
How might Yash feel reading this email?
Yash might feel relieved and recognised, since the email admits the earlier blame was unfair.
Why did my cousin Zara stop calling me?
I'm not sure, because I can't see her reasons or her life. A kind message asking how she is might open the conversation.

In the review meeting Pradeep took the client account from Urmila and gave it to a newer favourite. Urmila said, "That doesn't match the numbers." Pradeep smiled thinly. "If you keep pushing, your renewal might get looked at again." A couple of people looked at their laptops. Urmila's cheeks burned, and she said nothing more in the room.

Leela watched from the corner and knew it was unfair. Her stomach hurt. She needed her job, the rent was due, and speaking up could put her next. She thought about it honestly for a night: what could go wrong, what silence would cost. She found Urmila at the pantry and said, "I saw what happened. Can I help?"

Urmila had already started noting dates and the exact words in a notebook. "I'm taking it to HR, and to Ms. Iyer, the senior director." She felt shaky, but she wasn't going to accept it as normal. Leela took a breath and wrote a calm email that stuck to what she had witnessed, and sent it to HR too.

Two days later Ms. Iyer asked both of them to come to her office. Leela's hands were cold, and she went anyway.

Who was the senior director Urmila planned to approach?
Ms. Iyer.
How did Urmila's and Leela's views of the meeting differ, and what did each do afterwards?

Urmila was the one threatened, so she kept dated notes and took it to HR and a senior director. Leela was afraid for her own job but weighed the risk, offered help and sent a calm written account of what she had seen.
What was Leela feeling in the corner of the review meeting?
She felt afraid and uneasy, since she knew it was unfair but needed her job.
What could Urmila do if Pradeep keeps threatening her after the HR meeting?
She could keep her records up to date, ask the senior director for support, and look at her options.
Is it bad to imitate a friend?

Not always. To imitate is to copy the way someone acts, speaks or looks. It is a verb. It is fine as practice or fun, but copying someone's work and calling it yours is not fine.
Example: The parrot can imitate the sound of the doorbell.

Two-year-old Aditi stood beside her grandmother at the small shrine in the hallway. When the bell rang, Aditi rang her toy bell too, pressed her palms together and bent her head, wobbling. "Clever girl," her grandmother whispered. Aditi giggled and did it again. At fifteen, she went with her classmate Zubin's family to a gurdwara for a festival. She had watched people at the door: shoes on the rack, a scarf over the hair. Aditi copied them, then quietly asked Zubin's aunt, "Where should I stand?" The aunt smiled and pointed to the line. Nobody spoke above a murmur. Nine years later, Aditi's colleague Sahil lost his grandfather. At the house she saw white clothes, no cooking smells, and Sahil's aunts sitting quietly on the floor. She had not brought flowers, since she was not sure the family used them. She sat where they showed her and said softly to Sahil, "I am so sorry. Tell me what helps." He nodded and held her hand for a moment.

Where did Aditi stand with her grandmother when she was two?
She stood beside her grandmother at the small shrine in the hallway.
How did Aditi's way of showing respect change between age two and age twenty-four?

At two she copied her grandmother's bell and folded hands because she was imitating the family. At fifteen she watched others and asked before acting, and at twenty-four she followed Sahil's family's lead at the funeral house.
What was Sahil probably feeling when he held Aditi's hand?
He felt grief and was comforted that she came and asked what would help, so his nod and held hand show gratitude.
What could Aditi do if she was unsure about a custom at another family's ceremony?
She could watch what others do and quietly ask a family member, as she did at the gurdwara, and follow their lead.

When Suraj became supervisor of the village milk-collection centre, he moved the morning pickup from six to eight without asking anyone. It would save one tanker trip, he told the cooperative, and they praised him for it.
Raghav, who had run the chilling unit for twelve years, had said once, quietly, "In May, two hours matters." Suraj had waved it off.
On the third hot morning the tanker was late, and eight hundred litres turned sour in the cans. Farmers crowded the gate, shouting. The cooperative chairman arrived on his scooter.
"The staff didn't switch on the chiller in time," Suraj said at once.
Raghav stood holding the logbook, the chiller times written in his neat hand. He didn't argue. He just held it out.
Suraj looked at the numbers, then at the farmers. The back of his neck went cold. For the first time since the promotion, he didn't know what to say.

How many litres turned sour?
Eight hundred litres.
What was Suraj feeling when Raghav held out the logbook?
He felt shaken and exposed, the back of his neck cold, as his blame on the staff fell apart.
What turning point does Suraj face in front of the chairman?
He could admit the pickup change was his decision, apologise to the farmers and Raghav, and bring back the six o'clock pickup in summer.
What is it like for Raghav at the gate?
Raghav likely feels wronged but calm, letting the logbook speak rather than fighting a new boss in public.

Damini, sixteen, sat on the balcony in Andheri after losing the inter-school debate. Her older sister Neelam brought her tea. "What happened in there?" Damini stared at the traffic. "I was fine until their speaker made that point about school uniforms. Then I just... started talking fast and saying things I didn't plan." "Why?" Damini thought. "I think when I get nervous, I jump to conclusions. I assumed she was attacking me, not the argument." Neelam nodded. "So what would you do differently?" "Write down their point first, then answer. Slow down." Damini blew on her tea. "It's weird, noticing how my own head works." "Weird good or weird bad?" "Weird useful," she said.

What did Neelam bring Damini?
Tea.
What was Damini feeling as she stared at the traffic?
She felt disappointed and frustrated after losing the debate.
What did Damini decide to do differently next time?
Write down the other speaker's point first, then answer, and slow down.
How might Neelam see her sister's reflection?
Neelam seems supportive and pleased that Damini is thinking clearly about what went wrong.

There was one umbrella and a monsoon downpour, and Ganga and her brother Ojas fought over it all the way down the stairs. "I have a test!" "I'm younger!" She won, and Ojas walked to the bus stop getting soaked, sulking. At the school gate, two Class 8 boys pointed at his dripping hair. "Look, a wet rat!" Ojas's lip trembled. Ganga turned back at once, held the umbrella over him and faced them. "He's my brother. Go find your own joke." They wandered off. Ojas glared at her. "You still took the umbrella." "And you still owe me a chocolate from last week," she said, and shared the umbrella the rest of the way in.

What did the Class 8 boys call Ojas?
They called Ojas "a wet rat."
What was Ganga feeling when she turned back at the school gate?
Ganga felt protective and angry at the older boys, even though she had just fought Ojas over the umbrella.
What does Ganga's choice at the gate show about sibling conflict?
Ganga could fight Ojas over the umbrella yet defend him instantly outside, showing that conflict at home doesn't cancel loyalty.
How does Ojas see his sister standing up to the older boys?
Ojas probably feels protected and less humiliated, even while still grumbling about the umbrella.

Week one. Chaitanya was made lead of a five-person team building a new booking system. He looked at the list and thought, the search engine and the pricing logic are the hardest. If someone else gets them wrong, I'll look bad. So he took both. Gurleen, who had built pricing logic at her last job, got the login page.
Week four. Chaitanya was at the office past midnight most days. The others finished their small tasks early and waited for his reviews. Gurleen offered twice to help with pricing. "I've got it," he said.
Week eight. Launch week. Search worked; pricing didn't. Gurleen's login page had been finished for a month. The manager postponed the launch by three weeks. In the meeting, Chaitanya stared at the table.
Afterwards Gurleen said gently, "You don't have to carry it all." He nodded, too tired to answer.

How long was the launch postponed?
The launch was postponed by three weeks.
Why did Chaitanya keep both hard modules, and how was he feeling?
He was afraid of looking bad if someone else got them wrong, so he held on to them out of fear and ended up exhausted.
What would you change first in Chaitanya's plan?
I would give the pricing logic to Gurleen, who had built it before, and review her work, so the hardest parts move in parallel.
How might Gurleen feel during those eight weeks?
Gurleen likely felt underused and a bit frustrated, finishing early and having her offers to help turned down.

Noor, you asked why my portfolio has a shop sheet in it instead of another clone, so listen, I'm Abhinav. I was about to build my fifth tutorial app when I walked past Sharma Stores, the family shop near my hostel. The owner keeps stock in a notebook and runs out of things without noticing. I offered to build something. He said, "As long as it's simple." That word, simple, shaped everything. He does not use a laptop, only a phone. So I built a small sheet with three columns and a colour that turns red when stock is low. I sat there while he tried it and he got confused by one button, which I changed the same day. Now I have a story to tell an interviewer, and a real person who uses it.

Where did Abhinav notice the stock problem?
Abhinav noticed it at Sharma Stores, the family shop near the hostel.
What did Abhinav feel when the shop owner got confused by a button?
Abhinav felt alert and responsive, changing the button the same day because a real person's confusion counted.
What alternative approach could Abhinav add, and why?
Abhinav could count how many stock-outs happen before and after the sheet, because a small number would turn the story into evidence for interviewers.
How might the shop owner see Abhinav's sheet?
The owner asked for something simple, used the sheet on a phone and got confused once, so the owner sees a helpful student who listens.

The bus stop was a long walk from Jasleen's room above the seed shop, and the scooter search had dragged on for a month. Every evening brought another listing, another friend of a friend with a bike to sell.
On Friday night, tired of it, Jasleen took a notebook and wrote: three scooters, decide by Sunday. Saturday morning meant visits to two of them, and the third was one that Karthik at the corner garage had already looked over. For each, Jasleen wrote the price, the sound of the engine and the distance to the shop.
On Sunday evening Jasleen tapped the notebook, picked the one with the quieter engine, and paid a small advance. On Monday, Jasleen rode to work.

Where does Jasleen live?
Jasleen lives in a room above the seed shop.
Why did Jasleen feel ready to stop searching on Friday night?
Jasleen was tired of the month-long search and wanted an end to it, which is why the notebook limit of three scooters and a Sunday deadline was written.
What other approach could Jasleen have used to choose among the three scooters?
Jasleen could have asked Karthik at the corner garage to rank them, since a mechanic's judgement can settle a close call.
How might Karthik see Jasleen's plan?
Karthik had already looked over one scooter, so may see the plan as a clear task that makes helping easier than an open-ended search.

metadata.subtype: Approach: sets a deadline and a limit on how many options to consider [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: Jagdish, six, watches Lokesh, four, trip over his loose laces again. "I'll teach you," Jagdish says, just like Papa did with him.
Wednesday: On the front step, Jagdish kneels. "Make bunny ears. Cross them. Pull!" Lokesh's loops flop. Jagdish shows him again, slower.
Saturday: Lokesh ties a lopsided bow by himself and yells. Jagdish runs to Mummy. "I taught him! It was me!" He stands very tall.

What does Jagdish tell Lokesh to make first?
He tells him to "Make bunny ears."
What is Jagdish feeling when he runs to Mummy on Saturday?
Jagdish feels proud and excited, standing very tall because he was the one who taught Lokesh.
Which choice helped Lokesh learn, and why?
Jagdish showed him again slower when the loops flopped, giving Lokesh patient practice instead of taking over.
What would change if Papa hadn't taught Jagdish first?
Jagdish might not have had a model of teaching to copy, so he might not have offered to help Lokesh in the same way.

Read this:

Nkechi and Ulla kicked a football around the park until the streetlamps came on. “Spelling later,” Nkechi said, waving the list of fifteen words in her pocket. At home there was rain on the windows and rice on the table, and by the time her plate was clean her eyes were heavy. She wrote out five words with her head on her hand and went to bed. On Friday the test came back with six words wrong, and Nkechi stared at the red marks. On Thursday of the next week she sat at the kitchen table before shoes and park, and finished the spellings first. The park felt better after that.

How many words were on Nkechi's spelling list?
There were fifteen words on Nkechi's spelling list.
Why did Nkechi stare at the red marks on Friday?
Nkechi was probably disappointed and surprised: she had been sure there would be time for spelling later, and the six wrong words showed otherwise.
What did Nkechi change the following week, and what was the result?
Nkechi did the spellings at the kitchen table before going out, and the park felt better afterwards because the work was already done.
What would Ulla have seen if Nkechi had stayed at the park again?
Ulla would probably have had someone to play football with again but Nkechi might have arrived at the next test tired and unprepared, so the same bad evening could repeat.
Why do students sometimes feel nervous when a teacher says the test will be a surprise?
Not knowing what to expect makes them uneasy. Because they cannot prepare for something they cannot predict, the surprise feels like a threat.

Read this:

Two months after his brother's death, Pranav was back at the bank branch, first in every morning, last to leave. "I'm fine, really," he told anyone who asked, already turning back to his screen. At the team lunch he laughed in the right places and ate nothing. When the printer jammed, he slammed the tray so hard the whole row looked up, then muttered sorry. Pooja, at the next desk, noticed the photo he had turned face down by his keyboard. That evening, as they locked the cabinets, she asked, "Can I ask about Rohan? What was he like?" Pranav went very still. For a second she feared she had made it worse. Then he laughed, a real laugh. "He was terrible at cricket and never admitted it." He talked for twenty minutes. At the door he said, "Everyone avoids his name. I didn't know how much I needed someone to say it."

What was Rohan terrible at?
He was terrible at cricket.
What does Pranav slamming the printer tray suggest?
It suggests anger and pain held under "I'm fine", spilling out over something small.
What could colleagues learn from Pooja's question?
Asking about the person by name, like "What was Rohan like?", can open a door that "Are you okay?" does not, as long as the listener then lets them talk.
What was it like for Pooja when Pranav went very still?
Pooja feared she had made things worse, then felt relieved when he laughed and began to talk about Rohan.

Chetan, nineteen, moved into a PG in Pune for his engineering course. In week two, the building's water supply started coming only from six to eight in the morning. He hadn't planned for that. By Friday, his bucket of dirty clothes was full, his steel plate had dried dal stuck to it, and he had no clean socks. His neighbour Disha, from the room across, saw him scrubbing a plate at midnight with a bottle of drinking water. "You have to do a little every morning while the water runs," she said. "Otherwise it all waits for you." Chetan groaned. The next morning, at six, he washed two shirts and his plate. It took twelve minutes.

When did the water supply come in week two?
Only from six to eight in the morning.
How did Chetan feel scrubbing a plate at midnight?
He felt frustrated and surprised at how quickly everything had piled up.
What small habit did Chetan start, and why does it help?
Washing a little every morning while the water runs, which prevents a big weekly mess.
How does Disha see Chetan's midnight scrubbing?
Disha sees it as the result of not doing small tasks daily, and offers practical advice.

Read this:

The wedding band was so loud in the Ludhiana marriage hall that Himani had to lean close to her father's ear. Every cousin had asked her the same question since dinner: "So, you're a senior associate now?" Papa had told them all, months ago, that it was certain.
It wasn't. The letter came on Monday. Somebody else.
"Papa, can we step outside?"
In the car park, away from the dhol, her face burned. "I didn't get the promotion. I'm sorry you told everyone. I should have told you on Monday."
Papa rubbed his forehead. Her brother Pranav, who had followed them out, said quickly, "It's one year, Himani. You'll get it."
Papa nodded slowly. "I was showing off. That's my embarrassment, not yours. What happened?"
She told him: a stronger candidate, a review in March. He squeezed her shoulder, and they went back in to dance.

Where did Himani tell her father about the promotion?
In the car park outside the Ludhiana marriage hall, away from the dhol.
Why did Himani's face burn in the car park?
She felt ashamed and embarrassed for letting her father down after he had told all the relatives the promotion was certain.
How did Himani handle her father's pride in front of the family?
She stepped outside and told him plainly what had happened, including the stronger candidate and the March review.
How might Papa see the situation after hearing the truth?
Papa feels embarrassed at his own boasting, but he recognises it as his feeling, not Himani's failure, and supports her.

Monday. Darshan got the call: interview on Thursday, junior analyst. "They'll grill me on statistics and I'll blank," he told Kishore over dinner. Kishore offered to run practice questions with him. "Pointless. Either I know it or I don't." He watched a cricket match instead.
Thursday. In the waiting room his palms were wet. When the panel asked about regression, he heard himself say, "Sorry, I'm not good at this part," before he'd even tried. He stumbled through the case study he had never looked at, avoiding their eyes.
Saturday. The rejection email came. "See?" he told Kishore, almost relieved. "Knew it." Kishore didn't argue. He only asked, "How many practice questions did you do?" Darshan opened his mouth, then shut it.

What did Darshan do instead of practice questions?
He watched a cricket match.
Why did Darshan feel almost relieved on Saturday?
The rejection matched his prediction, so it felt like proof he had been right rather than something he had helped cause.
Where was the real turning point, and what could Darshan have chosen then?
On Monday, when Kishore offered practice questions; saying yes, even for an hour on regression, might have changed Thursday.
Why might Kishore ask a question instead of arguing?
Kishore likely saw that the fear had shaped the preparation, and a question lets Darshan notice it himself instead of feeling lectured.

metadata.subtype: Predicting failure and drifting into it [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Friday night

Didn't sign up for the inter-school fest in Mumbai. Zeenat is going. Everyone is going. I told Ma I had a stomach ache.

The truth: I can't stop watching those videos. Trains packed with people hanging out the doors. A car flipping on the expressway. A bus in the rain. My feed is full of them, maybe twenty a day. Every time I open my phone there's another one.

So in my head, travelling to Mumbai = accident.

Zeenat laughed at me. She said, "Kamal, my Chacha has taken that train every day for eleven years. Nothing happened." I said he was lucky.

But now writing this I'm thinking. Twenty videos a day. From the whole country. Maybe from the whole world. And my feed keeps showing them because I keep watching them.

Maybe the trains aren't more dangerous. Maybe my phone just is.

How many accident videos a day does Kamal say the feed shows?
Maybe twenty a day.
Why does Kamal feel that travelling to Mumbai means an accident?
Kamal feels anxious because the feed keeps showing crash videos, so the danger seems everywhere even though the clips come from the whole country.
What could Kamal try to get a truer picture of the risk?
Kamal could stop watching the clips for a while and ask an adult or look up how many people travel that route safely every day.
How might Zeenat see Kamal's decision to skip the fest?
Zeenat probably finds it surprising and a bit sad, since her Chacha has taken that train for eleven years without trouble.
A two-line rhyme, please, that reminds a child to wash their hands before eating.

Before you eat your rice and dal,
Wash your hands with soap, that's all!
Why do players change ends in some games between halves?
Conditions can favour a team. Because the wind, the sun or the slope of the ground may help a team, switching ends makes the game fair.

Read this:

When I, Trisha, got my first big raise last year, I didn't notice my spending grow. It just did. A flat with a balcony because "I deserved it". A new phone because my old one looked embarrassing in meetings. Weekend brunches at the café where everyone from work went. Six months later my salary was forty percent higher and my savings were exactly where they had been. My friend Parul, who earns less than me, had quietly saved for a trip to Ladakh. I asked how. She said, "I only upgrade when something is broken or making me miserable. Not when someone at work has a nicer one." That stayed with me. I went through my spending and marked each item: need, want, or image. The image column was long. I kept the balcony flat, because I truly love it. I stopped the brunches I only went to so I'd be seen.

How much higher was Trisha's salary after six months?
Forty percent higher.
What was Trisha feeling on comparing savings with Parul?
Trisha felt surprised and a little embarrassed that a friend earning less had saved more.
How did sorting spending into need, want and image help?
It separated real value, like the balcony, from spending for appearances, like brunches to be seen, so Trisha could cut the right things.
How might Parul feel about Trisha asking?
Parul probably felt pleased to share, and quietly glad her simple habit helped a friend.

Read this:

In the Powai colony, the boys with cycles rode round the park every evening. Saurabh had watched for months from his balcony. When he finally got a second-hand cycle, he rode slowly near the gate. Francis, the oldest, circled back. "You're the one on the fourth floor, right? Come." By the third round they were calling him "Speedy," because he'd almost crashed into a bench. Saurabh laughed louder than anyone. At home he couldn't stop talking about it. "They gave me a name, Mummy. A real one." He went to bed smiling.

What did the boys start calling Saurabh?
"Speedy."
How did Saurabh feel about getting a nickname?
He felt thrilled and accepted, as though he was truly part of the group.
What could Saurabh's mother say to support him?
She could share his happiness and ask about the new friends, while encouraging him to keep his other friendships too.
How might Francis see the new boy?
Francis likely sees Saurabh as a friendly addition and enjoys welcoming him.

Read this:

At the birthday party in Leeds, two-year-old Chidi raced laps around the sofa, shrieking with laughter and rubbing his eyes. "He's full of beans!" someone said. Clara, his aunt, watched him trip over a balloon and burst into loud sobs. She scooped him up. "Not beans," she murmured. "You're done in." His eyes were red. She carried him to the quiet bedroom, drew the curtains and lay beside him. He was asleep before the second song.

What did Chidi trip over?
A balloon.
What did Clara think was really going on while Chidi raced and shrieked?
She thought he was overtired rather than just excited; the eye-rubbing and sudden sobs told her he needed sleep.
What small step helped Chidi settle?
Clara took him to a quiet bedroom, drew the curtains and lay beside him, giving his tired body a calm place to sleep.
What was the party like for Chidi by the time he tripped?
It was probably too much for him; he was so worn out that a small fall tipped his loud laughter straight into tears.

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Sarika, Payal's older sister. I was in the kitchen when it happened. Mummy had found Payal's phone in her schoolbag during exams, even though she'd promised to leave it at home. Mummy took it.
Payal went red. She shouted, "You never trust me! Never!" and slammed her door so hard the calendar fell off the wall.
Then silence. For two hours, nothing. No music, no footsteps. I didn't know if she was crying or sleeping or planning revenge.
Mummy wanted to go in. I said, "Maybe wait."
At dinner time Payal came out. Her face was calm, a bit puffy. She sat down and said, "I'm sorry I shouted. I was so angry I couldn't think. I did break the promise. Can we talk about the phone rule?"
Mummy nodded. They talked. Nobody raised their voice.
I think the two hours were Payal's way of cooling down.

What fell off the wall when Payal slammed the door?
The calendar fell off the wall.
What was Payal feeling when she slammed the door?
Payal was furious, feeling mistrusted, and too angry to think clearly.
Which choice helped the evening end well?
Payal stepping away for two hours, and Mummy waiting instead of following her in, let the fury fade so they could talk calmly.
How might Mummy have felt during the two hours of silence?
Mummy was probably worried and unsettled, wanting to go in, but trusted that giving space might help.

Read this:

Pranav, when you answered me just now in that tight voice, you sounded exactly like your father at ten. Let your Lakshmi Paati tell you. His best friend had moved away to Delhi that morning. When I asked him to set the table, he said, “I. Will. Do it. Later,” every word squeezed. My mother-in-law said, “Such cheek!” But I saw his chin wobbling. I didn't argue. I poured him a glass of water, sat beside him and breathed slowly, loud enough for him to copy. After a few breaths his voice came back, soft and wet: “I miss Ravi.” We sat there a long while. The table got set later.

Where had the best friend moved to?
His best friend had moved away to Delhi.
What was the boy feeling as he squeezed out each word?
He was sad and holding back tears about his best friend leaving, and the strain was his effort to cope.
What choice did Lakshmi make, and why did it help?
She didn't argue but gave him water and breathed slowly beside him, which loosened his voice so he could say he missed Ravi.
How did the boy's grandmother read his voice?
She heard it as cheek, missing the wobbling chin that showed he was close to tears.

Read this:

Diary, 11 p.m.

I GOT THE INTERNSHIP. Madhuri from Room 14, summer analyst, actual stipend. I screamed in the corridor.

Then, in one afternoon, I said yes to:
- running the cultural fest decoration team (they asked, I was glowing, why not?)
- tutoring Bhupen's cousin for board maths, three evenings a week
- the Himachal trek in May, even though the internship starts in May
- rewriting the club newsletter by Sunday

It all felt easy. Like I had extra hours hidden somewhere. Bhupen asked, "Are you sure about the trek dates?" and I laughed and said I'd manage.

Now I'm looking at the calendar and May has two of me in it. Also mid-sems are next week, which I forgot existed.

Tomorrow, when I'm less buzzy, I'll go through this list again. Some of these yeses need to become "actually, sorry."

What was the first thing Madhuri said yes to after the internship news?
Running the cultural fest decoration team.
Why did all those yeses feel easy to Madhuri at the time?
Madhuri was thrilled and glowing about the internship, and that happy mood made every task seem light and every clash look manageable.
What could Madhuri do tomorrow to fix the overload?
Madhuri could check each yes against the calendar and the mid-sems, keep the ones that fit, and politely withdraw from the clashing ones soon.
How might Bhupen see Madhuri's quick yes to the trek?
Bhupen seems doubtful and a little concerned, since Bhupen noticed the date clash and got only a laugh in return.

Read this:

Four analysts at different firms each noticed something wrong at work. Minakshi saw figures that looked padded in a client's report. Before accusing anyone, she re-checked the calculations and the sources and wrote down what she knew and what she only suspected. Wasim spoke in broad strokes to a mentor at another firm. He wanted to test his judgement and hear how others had handled such moments, and he left out any confidential details. Alka feared for her salary, which was tied to a loan, and told herself it was not her business. She said nothing. Later the problem grew, and her silence began to weigh on her. Divya raised it with her manager, who brushed it aside. She then wrote a message to the compliance department, following the official process, and did not discuss it with colleagues or post about it.

What did Wasim leave out when he talked to his mentor?
He left out any confidential details.
How does Alka's reaction to the problem differ from Divya's, and what followed?

Alka stayed silent to protect her salary, and the problem grew while her silence weighed on her. Divya sent a written note to compliance after her manager dismissed it, following the official process.
What was Alka feeling as the problem grew?
She felt uneasy and guilty, because her silence weighed on her conscience.
What could Alka do now?

She could check the facts once more, perhaps talk to a trusted mentor without sharing confidential details, and then use the company's official route to report it. Waiting longer would let the problem grow.
Why does the sea have tides?
Mostly because of the moon's gravity. It pulls on the ocean, creating a bulge of water on the side facing the moon, and another on the opposite side.
Why twice a day?
The Earth rotates through those two bulges roughly once a day, so most coasts see two high tides and two low tides daily.
Does the sun matter?
Yes, it also pulls on the oceans, but less than the moon. When the sun and moon line up, at new and full moon, the tides are especially high.
Do lakes have tides?
They do in a tiny way, but the effect is too small to notice. Tides are visible mainly in the oceans.

Help me read this: change it into prose that is easy today.

He ceased. The wondrous arrow flew,
And Jamadagni's offspring knew
Those glorious worlds to him were barred,
Once gained by penance long and hard.
Then straight the airy quarters cleared,
And the mid regions bright appeared,
While Gods and saints unnumbered praised
Rama, the mighty bow who raised.
And Jamadagni's son, o'erawed.
Extolled his name with highest laud,
With reverent steps around him strode,
Then hastened on his airy road.
Far from the sight of all he fled,
And rested on Mahendra's head.

He stopped speaking, and the wondrous arrow flew. Jamadagni's son realised that the glorious worlds he had won by long and hard penance were now closed to him. Then the airy quarters were cleared at once, and the middle regions looked bright, while countless Gods and saints praised Rama, who had lifted the mighty bow. Jamadagni's son, overawed, praised his name highly, walked around him with respect and hurried on his way through the air. He fled far from everyone's sight and rested on the top of Mahendra.

Read this:

In the small town, the ration office was always crowded with elderly people who couldn't read the forms. Chetan, seventeen, started going there on Saturdays with a pen and a folding stool, filling forms for anyone who asked. His classmate Tenzin, whose family came from a Tibetan settlement nearby, joined him. One Saturday a man in the queue told Tenzin, "Outsiders shouldn't be helping here." Chetan put down his pen. "He was born two streets away, uncle. Same as me." The man grumbled but let Tenzin fill his form. Afterwards Tenzin said, "You didn't have to." Chetan shrugged. "Yes, I did."

What did Chetan bring to the ration office?
A pen and a folding stool.
What was Chetan feeling when he put down his pen?
He felt protective and indignant at the unfair remark about Tenzin.
What made Chetan's response effective?
He corrected the man calmly with a fact, without insulting him, and kept helping.
How might Tenzin feel after Chetan stood up for him?
Grateful and supported, though perhaps still hurt by the remark.

Read this:

At the school store a notebook costs forty rupees. On the way home I saw the same notebook in the lane shop for thirty. "Ten rupees less," I said aloud, and Harish Uncle grinned. "Tell your friends too, beti." I did the sum: two notebooks here save twenty rupees, which is almost a whole pencil set. The walk is only three minutes longer. I told my friend Parveen, and now we go together. Nobody told me to do it. I just noticed the price and decided a little walking was worth it. - Divya

How much cheaper was the notebook at the lane shop?
It was ten rupees cheaper, thirty instead of forty.
What was Divya thinking when Divya noticed the lower price?
Divya was pleased with the discovery and thought a little extra walking was worth the saving.
What else could Divya check, and why?
Divya could compare pencils and other items, and check the notebooks are the same quality, so the saving is real.
How does Harish Uncle see Divya's discovery?
Harish Uncle grins and encourages Divya to tell friends, since a careful shopper brings more customers.

messages.content:
Read this:

With Republic Day a week away, Class UKG practised the flag poem every morning. Gurleen stood in the second row, lips moving a moment behind everyone.
On Tuesday, Nirmala Ma'am gave each line an action: arms up for "sky", hands on heart for "home". Gurleen did the actions and her voice got louder.
On the day itself, the microphone squealed and everyone stopped. Gurleen kept going, arms up, hand on heart. The others caught up.
Afterwards she said, "My hands remembered."

What action did Nirmala Ma'am give for "sky"?
Arms up.
What was Gurleen feeling when she kept going after the microphone squealed?
Gurleen seemed confident and calm because the actions helped her remember the words.
Why did adding actions help Gurleen?
The movements gave each line a cue, so Gurleen could recall it even when the sound stopped.
How might Nirmala Ma'am see what happened on Republic Day?
Nirmala Ma'am would likely be pleased that her actions helped, and that Gurleen could lead the others back in 🎉.
Describe the waiting room of a clinic in three short sentences, each under ten words.
The chairs are arranged in neat rows. A fan hums softly overhead. Patients wait quietly for their turn.

Read this:

In the small meeting room of the city library, Charu opened the folder she had kept since January before Joseph's yearly review.
Joseph came in tense. The last month had been rough: he had mixed up two event dates, and a school group had turned up to a locked hall. He expected that to be the whole review.
"Let's go month by month," Charu said. She had a page for each. February: he set up the children's reading corner. April: he cleared the late-return backlog. July: three thank-you letters from readers. September: he helped train the new assistant. November: the date mix-up.
"I'd forgotten half of this," Joseph said.
"So had I, until I read my notes this morning," Charu admitted. "That's why I keep them."
They spent five minutes on November: what went wrong and what would help. The rest of the hour was about the other months.

What happened in November?
Joseph mixed up two event dates, and a school group turned up to a locked hall.
Why does Charu admit she had forgotten half of it too?
Charu feels honest and a little humble, knowing her own memory favours the latest month, which is why she trusts the notes.
How does Charu's folder make the review fairer?
A page for each month means the whole year counts, so one bad November doesn't outweigh the reading corner or July's letters.
What is the review like for Joseph?
Joseph goes from tense to relieved, seeing his whole year counted and not just the mix-up.

Read this:

Friday: Arnab's short film wins the college prize. He is buzzing. At the party, his friend Noor asks if he'll co-host the fest, edit her documentary and join a road trip to the beach, driving there and back the same night. "Yes, yes, yes!" he laughs. Everything feels easy.
Tuesday: The co-hosting rehearsal clashes with the documentary edit. He hasn't slept properly in three days. The road trip is Thursday, and he realises he would be driving eight hours overnight, exhausted.
Thursday: Arnab texts Noor: "Sorry, I said yes while I was floating. I can do the edit, not the co-hosting, and not the night drive. Driving that tired isn't safe." Noor replies with a thumbs-up. He sleeps for ten hours.

How long would the overnight drive have been?
Eight hours.
How did Arnab feel when he said yes three times at the party?
He felt buzzing and elated after the prize, so everything felt easy and risks like a tired night drive did not register.
What did Arnab do right on Thursday?
He reassessed calmly, kept one commitment, and cancelled the co-hosting and the unsafe night drive, explaining honestly.
How might Noor see Arnab's change of plan?
She accepts it easily with a thumbs-up, probably glad he was honest rather than letting her down at the last minute.

Read this:

On a cold winter evening in the village, Chandrika roasted sweet potatoes in the embers of the chulha.
Deepika, two, pointed and shouted, "Now! Now!"
"Hot, baby. Soon," Chandrika said.
Deepika threw herself on the floor and wailed. Soon meant nothing.
Chandrika picked her up, blew on a small piece until it was cool, and held it out. Deepika stopped mid-sob and grabbed it with both hands.

What was Chandrika roasting?
Chandrika was roasting sweet potatoes in the embers of the chulha.
Why did Deepika throw herself on the floor?
Deepika felt frustrated and upset, because 'soon' meant nothing to her and she wanted the sweet potato now.
What did Chandrika do that helped?
Chandrika picked Deepika up and cooled a small piece, giving a little right away instead of only promising.
What was the evening like for Chandrika?
Chandrika was busy cooking and stayed patient, keeping Deepika safe from the hot food while she wailed.
Why do potters keep their hands wet while shaping clay on a wheel?
Water keeps the clay slippery. Because wet clay lets the hands slide over the spinning surface instead of grabbing and tearing it, the potter can pull the shape up smoothly.

Read this:

In the community centre hall, rows of clay lamps glowed along the walls, and a rangoli of orange and pink flowers covered the floor. Amandeep spun in her new green kurta so the sleeves swished. Her friend Jatin pointed at the lights. "Look, so many!" An elder told the story of a prince who came home, and everyone sang together. Amandeep sang too, loudly and slightly off tune. When the laddoos came round, she took two, and the sweet crumbs stuck to her fingers. She felt part of something big and happy.

What colours were the flowers in the rangoli?
The rangoli was made of orange and pink flowers.
What was Amandeep feeling at the celebration?
Amandeep was happy and felt she belonged. Spinning in her new kurta and singing loudly show her joy.
What do festivals like this teach a child about belonging?
They show a child she belongs to a family and community that share stories, songs and food. Taking part with others, rather than watching, helps her feel it.
How might Jatin feel about the lights and songs?
Jatin seems excited, since he pointed and said "Look, so many!" Jatin may enjoy sharing the festival with a friend.
How is implore different from ask?

To implore is to beg someone strongly and in a serious way. It is a verb and is much stronger than ask.
Example: The boy implored his mother to let him keep the stray kitten.
I forgot my homework. Write a short apology to my teacher in exactly two sentences, including the word "tomorrow".
I am sorry, Ma'am, I left my homework notebook at home today. I will bring it to you first thing tomorrow.

Read this:

Tuesday practice: Siddharth, a second-year from a small town in Bihar, argued the motion better than anyone in the debate club. Jeevan, the club mentor, wrote 'excellent rebuttal' twice in his notebook.
Saturday, inter-college round: someone from the rival team whispered, loud enough, 'Watch the Bihari boy mix up his tenses.' Siddharth stood up, opened his mouth, and his English came out stiff and slow. He lost his thread twice. Jeevan watched him grip the edge of the podium. This wasn't the boy from Tuesday.
The next Monday: Jeevan went back through his notebook and saw the pattern: brilliant in practice, frozen in three high-stakes rounds, each time before an audience from bigger colleges. He didn't write 'weak speaker'. He asked Siddharth for coffee and said, 'Your practice is the real you. Let's work on the room, not the English.'

What did Jeevan write in his notebook on Tuesday?
'Excellent rebuttal', twice.
What did Jeevan feel watching Siddharth grip the podium?
Jeevan felt concerned and puzzled, sensing this wasn't the confident speaker he had seen on Tuesday.
Why is working on 'the room, not the English' a wise approach?
The problem is the pressure of the label in high-stakes rounds, not his skill, so practising under audience conditions targets the real cause.
How might Siddharth feel hearing 'Your practice is the real you'?
Siddharth would likely feel relieved and believed in, less ashamed of the frozen round.

"Six hours," Bhavna said, dropping into the chair beside Darshan's desk. "The nightly sales report took six hours again. Finance wants it by seven, and it finished at seven-forty."
"Did anyone look at why?"
"Everyone says it's always been slow. Big data, old server."
Darshan pulled up the job. "It's low stakes to look. Let's not guess. Where does the data start?"
"The shop database."
"And where does it end?"
"One summary table."
He drew boxes on a sheet of paper and traced each step between them. Pull from the shop database. Copy to a staging table. Copy the staging table again into a second staging table. Then summarise.
"Why is there a second copy?" he asked.
Bhavna squinted. "I... don't know. Nobody uses it."
He removed the extra copy in a test run. The report finished in two hours and ten minutes.

How long did the test run take after the extra copy was removed?
The report finished in two hours and ten minutes.
How might Bhavna have felt when she couldn't explain the second copy?
Bhavna was probably surprised and a bit embarrassed, since everyone had just accepted the report as slow.
What else could Darshan check now that the report is faster?
He could ask Finance whether they need every column in the summary, since trimming the output might speed it up further.
How might the Finance team be affected by the change?
They would get the report well before seven, so they no longer have to wait or chase it each morning.

messages.content:
In under 50 words, what happens in this?

Counsellor's note, Thursday. I am Madhuri, the counsellor at the community centre. Vandana lost her brother last month. During the group session, one member reached to hold her shoulder as she began to cry. Vandana went rigid and leaned away, hands in her lap. The member, Sunil, withdrew his hand at once and said, "Sorry. Would you like water instead?" Vandana nodded and drank. A few minutes later she said, "A hug from a friend of mine would be fine, but not from someone I hardly know." I noted that Sunil's quick retreat helped. I will remind the group that asking first respects each person's choice, and I will check on Vandana next week.

Vandana, grieving her brother, stiffens when a group member reaches to hold her shoulder. Sunil withdraws and offers water, and she explains that she would accept a hug only from a close friend. The counsellor will remind the group to ask first.

Read this:

I'm Ishita, and last winter I learned something about being angry. Papa and Dada kept fighting about selling the old house in the village. They shouted so loud the neighbours' dog barked. I hated it. My whole body felt hot and fizzy, and once I nearly threw my water bottle at the wall.
Instead I took my football down to the back wall of our building. Left foot, right foot, bang, bang, bang. I counted: fifty, a hundred. When I kicked hard, the ball came back hard, so I had to be quick and careful.
After a while the fizz went out of my arms and legs. I came back up tired and sweaty, and I could tell Mumma how I felt.
Now I can do two hundred passes without missing. Coach picked me for the under-eleven team.

Where did Ishita take the football?
Down to the back wall of the building.
How did Ishita feel during Papa and Dada's fights, and how can you tell?
Angry and upset; Ishita's whole body felt hot and fizzy, and once there was an urge to throw the water bottle at the wall.
Which choice turned Ishita's anger into something useful?
Taking the football to the wall instead of throwing the bottle; the kicking used up the fizz safely and built a real skill.
How might Mumma see Ishita coming back tired and ready to talk?
Mumma probably feels relieved that Ishita found a safe way through the anger, and glad they can talk about the fighting calmly.

Read this:

Dear Reena Bua,
You asked why I sounded so quiet on the phone on Sunday. I'll tell you now.
Last Wednesday in social science, Mr Bhalla made me stand up and said, "Look at him. Head full of cricket, nothing else. Some people are born average." Everyone stared. I felt my face burn. I wanted to run out.
I didn't cry in class. At home I wrote down exactly what he said, the date and the time, like you taught me to do when something feels wrong.
I showed Papa that night. He said it was about Mr Bhalla's behaviour, not about me. On Thursday Papa and I met the coordinator. She read my notes and said, "This should never have happened. I'll speak to him today and check on you next week."
I still feel ashamed sometimes, Bua. But I'm starting to believe it wasn't about me.
Your nephew,
Divyansh

What did Mr Bhalla say about Divyansh's head?
That it was full of cricket, nothing else.
How did Divyansh feel when Mr Bhalla singled him out?
He felt deep shame and humiliation, face burning, wanting to run out.
Which steps did Divyansh take, and why are they wise?
He kept a written record, told Papa that night and went to the coordinator, so the problem was reported with facts.
How does the coordinator respond to Divyansh's notes?
She takes it seriously, says it should never have happened, promises to speak to Mr Bhalla that day and to check in with Divyansh.
What sounds do a cow, a dog and a duck make? Answer in that order, lowercase, comma-separated.
moo, bark, quack
Note for the delivery person: please leave the parcel with the neighbour in flat 6 if I'm not home. Keep it under 35 words, from Mr Khan.

Dear delivery person,
If I am not at home, please leave my parcel with the neighbour in Flat 6. Thank you very much for your help.
Mr Khan
Boss aur dost ko promotion ki badhai alag-alag kaise dun?
To your boss: "Congratulations on your promotion, sir." To a friend: "Congrats on the promotion!"

'Papa, my stomach is hurting.'
'Come here, Nitin. Where?'
'Here. It's twisting.'
'Too much birthday cake at Chiku's?'
'Only two pieces. And the chips.'
'Hm.' Varun felt his forehead. 'No fever. Lie on the sofa. I have something special.'
'Medicine?'
'Better. The lemon drop from my secret tin. Every time I had a tummy ache, my mother gave me one.'
'Does it work?'
'Suck it slowly and see. I'll rub your back.'
'...It's sour.'
'Good sour or bad sour?'
'Good sour.'
A few minutes went by. The TV murmured.
'Papa?'
'Hm?'
'It's getting smaller. The twist.'
'Told you. Special tin.'
'Can I have another one tomorrow?'
'Only if your stomach asks nicely. And if it keeps hurting or worries you, we'll show the doctor.'

Where did the lemon drop come from?
It came from Papa's secret tin.
How did Nitin feel after sucking the lemon drop with Papa rubbing his back?
He felt comforted and the twist felt smaller, helped by the special sweet and his father's calm care.
What did Varun do well, and what safety point did he keep?
Varun checked for fever, stayed close and offered a harmless sweet with reassurance, and still said they'd show the doctor if it keeps hurting or worries Nitin.
Why might Varun's mother's old habit matter to Varun now?
Remembering how the lemon drop comforted him as a child helps Varun pass on the same feeling of care to Nitin.

Oskar dashed at the sofa and scrambled up the tall armrest, feet kicking, grinning. Halfway up a foot slid on the smooth cloth and Oskar dropped backward. Oma Clara, standing close, caught Oskar under the arms. The grin vanished, then a wail came. Clara sat down with Oskar on her lap, waited for the crying to ease, and patted the low seat cushion. "This way?"

Who caught Oskar when the foot slid?
Oma Clara caught Oskar under the arms.
What was Oskar feeling at the start of the climb?
Oskar was excited and eager, shown by the dash, the kicking feet and the grin.
What could Oskar try instead of the tall armrest, and why?
Oskar could use the low seat cushion with a knee up first, because it is closer to the floor and safer than a slippery armrest.
How does Oma Clara see Oskar's dash at the armrest?
Clara sees a risk; she stays close enough to catch Oskar and afterwards shows the safer seat without scolding.

Jasleen: WHO

How old is Gurnoor?
He's 11.
What was Jasleen feeling when she saw the edited photo of Gurnoor?
Jasleen felt angry and fiercely protective of her younger brother, wanting to act right away.
What would you advise Jasleen after this chat?
Show the same loyalty at home by being kinder to Gurnoor, like helping with his model project instead of calling him lazy.

Gurnoor seems to admire her deeply, thinking she is the coolest person alive, even though she bosses him at home.
