Thursday, 11:40 pm
Can't sleep, so writing it down.
This morning I found my own mistake in the clinic drawings. The staircase landing was 20 cm short, and the client had already signed. The contractor would have quietly adjusted it on site, and nobody would ever have traced it back to me.
I sat with it through lunch. My stomach was in knots.
At four I walked into Asif's cabin and said it plainly: my error, here is the fix, I'll redo the sheets tonight.
Asif read the page twice and said, "Thank you for catching it before the pour."
Redid four sheets. Missed a friend's birthday dinner.
Still, driving home I felt lighter than I have in weeks.
Then at nine a message from Asif: "Can you check the Thane site alone next week?"
— Jaya

What mistake did Jaya find in the clinic drawings?
The staircase landing was 20 cm short, and the client had already signed.
How was Jaya feeling while deciding whether to speak up, and what shows it?
Jaya felt anxious and torn; Jaya sat with it through lunch with a stomach in knots.
Which choice was the turning point for Jaya, and why did it matter?
Walking into Asif's cabin at four and naming the error along with a fix; it came before the pour, so the landing could still be corrected.
How might Asif see Jaya after that conversation?
Asif now seems to trust Jaya's work without checking it, which is why Asif asks Jaya to check the Thane site alone.

Help me out here:
What does "a taste of your own medicine" mean?
Why do we put a helmet on when riding a bike?

1. It means the same unkind treatment that you gave to others. For example: he was teased, and it was a taste of his own medicine.
2. A helmet spreads out the force of a fall. Because its hard shell and soft lining absorb the knock before it reaches the head.

I'm Rafiq, and I sit behind Samir in Class 5. On Monday the new boy, Kenji, smirked when Samir read his poem aloud. Samir's neck went red. At break he told me, “Did you see? He thinks my poem's rubbish.” I didn't know. I'd seen Kenji smirk at the fan and the blackboard too. Samir didn't shout, though. He watched Kenji for two days. On Wednesday he asked him straight out, at the tap. I couldn't hear the answer, but Samir came back shrugging. “He says he smiles like that when he's lost.” Now they share a bench.

In which class does Rafiq sit behind Samir?
Rafiq sits behind Samir in Class 5.
What was Samir feeling when his neck went red?
He felt embarrassed and hurt, believing Kenji thought his poem was rubbish.
Which of Samir's choices worked, and why?
Watching for two days and then asking Kenji directly worked, because it showed the smirk came from feeling lost, not from mockery.
How does Rafiq read Kenji's smirk?
Rafiq isn't sure, having seen Kenji smirk at the fan and the blackboard too, so the look seemed less aimed at Samir.

messages.content:
Read this:

Saturday

Did a stupid test with Vidya today. I've bought the same instant coffee for four years, the one from the TV ads with the mountain. I told her it's obviously better than the plain shop-brand jar she buys. She said, 'Prove it.' She made two cups without telling me which was which. I tasted both, three times, very seriously. Picked cup B as 'mine'. It was hers. The cheap one. I didn't believe her, so we did it again. I picked wrong again. Vidya didn't gloat much. Walking home, I kept thinking: I never actually compared. I just saw the mountain ad a thousand times and the jar felt like a friend. That's not the same as it tasting better. I'm still buying mine this month. But I'm less sure why.

Chinmay

For how long has Chinmay bought the same instant coffee?
Four years.
How did Chinmay feel after picking wrong twice?
Chinmay felt surprised and a little embarrassed, and less sure of the reason for liking the advertised coffee.
What does the blind test show, and what could Chinmay do next?
It shows the preference came from the familiar advert, not taste; Chinmay could choose by trying options side by side rather than by habit.
How might Vidya have felt during the test?
Vidya was probably amused and quietly pleased that the blind test proved the point, though she didn't gloat much.

messages.content: Name four school subjects. Write them on one line separated by a vertical bar.
Maths | Science | History | Art

Read this:

In the staff room of the government school in Nashik, Hansa sat with the transfer letter: a two-year posting as head teacher of a village school, or staying in the city with her friends and her Saturday dance class.
"Stay," said Ayesha, sipping tea. "You'll hate the bus."
Hansa didn't answer. On the back of the letter she wrote one question: Which choice will I respect in ten years? Under it: Village school. Under that, smaller: I will miss dance. That's allowed.
She showed Ayesha. "Some regret either way. I'd rather regret the bus than the chance."
The next Monday she signed the acceptance, gave up her dance-class place, and spent her lunch break reading about the village school's library, planning her first week, not looking back at the other road.

How long was the village posting?
The posting was two years as head teacher of a village school.
What did Hansa feel when she wrote 'I will miss dance. That's allowed'?
Hansa felt a pang of sadness but accepted it, understanding that some regret comes with any choice.
What question did Hansa use, and why is it a good check?
Which choice will I respect in ten years? It looks past today's comfort to what really matters, and once it was answered, Hansa committed fully.
How might Ayesha feel about Hansa leaving?
Ayesha may feel sad to lose a friend at school, though she can see Hansa's reasons.

Read this:

I'm Nikita, Gautam's neighbour on the third floor. We've walked to tuition together since Class 6, so I noticed when Gautam went quiet after Sneha said no to him at the Holi party. He didn't rant, didn't block her, didn't say one bad thing about her to anyone.
Instead, every evening I heard his old keyboard through the wall: the same few notes, over and over, and his voice trying words, stopping, trying again. His notebook, which used to be all physics, filled up with short lines crossed out and rewritten.
Three weeks later he played the song at our building's Sunday music evening. It was about a coloured handprint fading from a sleeve. He didn't look at anyone while he sang. Afterwards two aunties hugged him, and a boy from the fifth floor asked for the words.
I don't know if it hurt less. But he looked lighter.

What was Gautam's song about?
A coloured handprint fading from a sleeve.
What might Gautam have been feeling as he tried the words over and over?
He was likely hurt by Sneha's no, and shaping it into a song gave the pain somewhere to go instead of turning it on her.
Which choice after the Holi party worked well for Gautam?
Not ranting or blocking Sneha but writing and rewriting the song, then sharing it, which gave the hurt a form others could see.
Why might the boy from the fifth floor ask for the words?
The song may have matched something the boy felt too, showing how Gautam's private hurt became something others could hold on to.

Three months into my first internship, someone added me to a group chat called Monday Survivors. It was six interns and one topic: our team lead, Pallavi. Screenshots of her emails with jokes on top. A nickname for her voice. Someone planned to “forget” to invite her to a lunch.
I laughed at the first two jokes. I'm not proud of that. Then I read one of her emails properly, the one they were mocking, and it was just a polite note asking us to reply before Friday.
That night I left the group. No speech, no announcement. The next morning I replied to her email on time and said good morning when she walked past, the way I always had.
A couple of interns went cold on me. It stung. But when Pallavi asked me to present our work to the client, I didn't wonder whether I'd earned it. — Mridul

What was the group chat called?
The group chat was called Monday Survivors.
How did Mridul feel about laughing at the first two jokes?
Mridul felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed afterwards, admitting to not being proud of it 😔
Was leaving the group quietly a wise choice? Why?
Yes; it stepped away from the gossip without starting a fight, and Mridul kept being courteous and on time with Pallavi.
What would change for Pallavi if the lunch plan and jokes went on unchecked?
She could be quietly shut out of her own team's plans, which would make her work harder and more isolating.

At the tuition centre in Chembur, Francis and Ankita were paired for a ten-minute history talk on the salt march. They agreed to rehearse on Tuesday and Thursday. On Tuesday Ankita messaged, "Can't come, cousin's engagement. You're so good at speaking, you'll manage." Francis felt a small relief. If Ankita wasn't bothering, why should he? On Thursday he skipped too, telling himself Ankita would read up at home. On Saturday they stood before the class with one printed page each. Francis forgot the dates. Ankita lost her place twice. The talk lasted four minutes. Afterwards, on the stairs, Ankita said, "I thought you'd carry it." Francis said, "I thought you would." They both laughed, but not happily.

How long did their talk last?
Four minutes.
Why did Francis feel a small relief at Ankita's message?
He took it as permission to skip too, thinking that if Ankita wasn't bothering, he needn't either.
Where did things go wrong, and what could Francis have done at that point?
At Thursday's rehearsal; Francis could have messaged Ankita to fix a new time instead of assuming she would read up at home.
What is it like for Ankita on the stairs when Francis says 'I thought you would'?
Ankita realises they both counted on the other, and feels embarrassed and let down by both of them.

Monday: Samir lost at carrom and walked straight out of the room. Bhupen Chacha followed him down the corridor. "Come back! Say good game! Don't be a bad loser!" Samir ran into the bedroom and slammed the door.

Thursday: Samir lost again and turned away. This time Chacha stayed put. "The board's here when you're ready." A few minutes later, Samir crept back and sat down.

The next Sunday: Samir lost, frowned hard at the board, and stayed. "Again," he said.

What game did Samir lose?
Carrom.
What was Samir probably feeling when he walked out after losing?
He was most likely upset and embarrassed about losing. On Monday, being followed with demands seemed to make him feel more cornered, so he slammed the door.
What went wrong on Monday, and what fixed it later?
Following Samir with demands pushed him further away; a calm invitation on Thursday gave him space and he came back on his own.
How does Bhupen Chacha's approach change between Monday and Thursday?
On Monday he chases Samir and lectures him, but on Thursday he stays put and leaves the door open for him to return.

Read this:

Friday, 9 June
Result came at 11. I cleared the bank PO exam. Rank 212. Papa cried on the phone, Mummy distributed sweets to the whole lane. Gopika sent fifteen party poppers. 🎉
So why am I sitting here at midnight feeling nothing?
Two years of coaching. Two years of skipping cousins' weddings and the photography club. Papa's dream since I was in Class 8: "a secure bank job, like Sharma uncle's daughter." I said it so often I thought it was mine.
Today I opened my old camera bag, the one I haven't touched since first year. The lens was dusty. I cleaned it for an hour and felt more doing that than I did when the result came.
I don't know what to do with that.
Sangeeta

What rank did Sangeeta get in the bank PO exam?
Rank 212.
Why might Sangeeta feel nothing at midnight after clearing the exam?
Sangeeta may feel empty because the goal was Papa's dream, repeated so often it seemed like Sangeeta's own, so reaching it didn't touch what Sangeeta actually values.
What turning point does the dusty camera offer Sangeeta?
Cleaning the lens stirred more feeling than the result; Sangeeta could make time for photography again and think honestly about next steps before deciding anything big.
How might Papa feel if he read this diary entry?
Papa, who cried with joy, might be confused and hurt, but could also begin to see that the dream he chose wasn't the one his child held.

In Class 9 I decided I needed to be on the quiz team, and Lokesh Sir picked the team. So I started telling him things. "Sir, your explanations are so much better than last year's." "Sir, that tie really suits you." "Sir, everyone says you're the best." I stayed behind to carry his books.
I wasn't actually thinking about his teaching. I was thinking about the list on the notice board.
One day he said, kindly, "Ayesha, thank you. The selection is a written test, though." My face went hot. He had seen through it, and he wasn't even angry.
Looking back, what embarrasses me isn't that I wanted the team. It's that I never once looked at him as a person, only as a door I wanted open.

How did Lokesh Sir say the team would be selected?
He said the selection is a written test.
How did Ayesha feel when Lokesh Sir mentioned the written test?
Ayesha felt embarrassed, face going hot, realising Lokesh Sir had seen that the praise was aimed at the team place, not at him.
What could Ayesha have done instead to try for the quiz team?
Ayesha could have prepared for the written test and asked Lokesh Sir honestly how to get ready.
How might Lokesh Sir have seen Ayesha's compliments?
He seemed to see they were aimed at the selection, but he responded kindly rather than angrily.

Keep this to three sentences by cutting detail.

In Class 9, Nazia always answered so softly that Nandini Ma'am had to ask her to repeat. Some classmates rolled their eyes. Ma'am wrote in her notebook: "Nazia seems disinterested."
One day, Ma'am found Nazia alone in the library. She asked quietly, "Is everything okay? You seem so quiet in class."
Nazia looked at her book. "Last year, when I answered wrong, the whole class laughed. Now I'm scared to speak loudly."
Nandini Ma'am's face softened. "I'm sorry that happened. You're not disinterested at all, are you?"
"No, Ma'am. I like science."
"Then let's start small. Would you tell me your answers here, just us, first?"
Nazia nodded, and her voice came out a little clearer.

In Class 9, Nazia answered so softly that Nandini Ma'am had to ask her to repeat, some classmates rolled their eyes, and Ma'am noted that she seemed disinterested. When Ma'am found her alone in the library and asked if everything was okay, Nazia said that last year the whole class laughed when she answered wrong, so she was now scared to speak loudly. Ma'am said she was sorry that happened and suggested starting small by hearing Nazia's answers in the library first, and Nazia nodded and spoke a little clearer.

Monday: Suraj, nearly two, stands at the bottom of the park slide's ladder and slaps the first rung. Damini, his mother, lifts him onto it; he freezes and reaches back for her. Thursday: he puts one knee up, then a foot, and climbs two rungs before looking round at her. She stays close but keeps her hands down. The next Sunday: he climbs all four rungs alone, sits at the top, and shouts "Again!" before sliding into her lap.

How many rungs did Suraj climb on Thursday?
He climbed two rungs.
What was Suraj feeling when he reached back for Damini on Monday?
He seemed unsure or a little scared on the ladder, so he wanted her to hold him.
Which choice by Damini helped Suraj most, and why?
Staying close with her hands down on Thursday let him try the climb himself while still feeling safe.
What would change if Damini had kept lifting Suraj up every time?
He would get fewer chances to use his own arms and legs, so the solo climb might have come later.

You want to know how I help Sachin? Honestly, it's Zubin who learned from Sachin, not the other way round. When his condition flared up in our first year as flatmates, I went into rescue mode. Cooked for him without asking, told everyone he was 'so brave', cancelled our trip without checking. He was furious. He said, 'I'm not a project, Zubin.' That stung. So I changed. Now I ask, 'What would help today?' Sometimes it's soup. Sometimes it's just leaving him alone. When he can't manage the stairs to the terrace, we move movie night to his room without a speech. And I don't call him inspirational. He hates that. He's just my friend who's sometimes exhausted. The big thing? Showing up when I say I will. That matters more than any grand gesture.

What did Sachin say when Zubin went into rescue mode?
'I'm not a project, Zubin.'
How did Zubin feel when Sachin said that?
Zubin felt stung, realising the rescuing had hurt instead of helped.
What changed in how Zubin supports Sachin?
Zubin asks what would help, adapts plans quietly, avoids calling Sachin inspirational and shows up reliably.
How might Sachin have felt when Zubin called him brave to everyone?
Sachin probably felt embarrassed and turned into a story, not treated as an ordinary friend.

messages.content:
Rewrite this in fewer than 60 words.

In the kindergarten circle in Margao, Maria Teacher held up a paper flower and a paper candle. 'First we smell the flower, slow and long. Then we blow out the candle, soft and slow.' The children sniffed and blew, laughing. They did it every morning before prayers. On Thursday, Nitin tripped in the playground and grazed his hand. He screamed, then sat crying hard. Maria Teacher crouched. 'Nitin, can you find your flower?' Nitin sniffed, shakily. 'Now the candle.' He blew. Three times. His crying slowed enough for her to wash the graze.

In Margao, Maria Teacher's kindergarten children sniffed a paper flower and blew out a paper candle every morning. When Nitin grazed his hand and cried hard, she asked him to find his flower, then the candle. He sniffed and blew three times, and his crying slowed enough for her to wash the graze.

How does Bhishma arrange the army for battle?

Vaisampayana continued, "These words spoken by the high-souled Bhishma were acceptable to them, and the king of the Kauravas acted accordingly without delay. And having sent away the king and then the kine, Bhishma began to array the soldiers in order of battle. And addressing the preceptor, he said, 'O preceptor, stand thou in the centre, and let Aswatthaman stand on the left, and let the wise Kripa, son of Saradwata, defend the right wing, and let Karna of the Suta caste, clad in mail, stand in the van. I will stand in the rear of the whole army, protecting it from that point.'"

Bhishma places the teacher in the centre, Aswatthaman on the left, Kripa to defend the right wing, and Karna, wearing armour, at the front. Bhishma himself will stand at the rear, protecting the whole army.
The word for the belly button is "naval", right?

No. The belly button is spelled "navel". "Naval" is an adjective that means connected with a navy.
Examples: Ships of the naval force sailed past. The baby's navel healed quickly.
Why do pebbles on a beach look smooth and round?
The waves keep rolling the stones against each other. Because their rough edges wear away when they rub together year after year, the pebbles become smooth.

Read this:

Reena was the youngest in their house in Jaipur, and her older brothers, Sonu and Yogi, had a secret club in the storeroom. A sign on the door said NO GIRLS, NO BABIES.

"I'm not a baby!" Reena shouted through the door.

"You're seven!" Sonu shouted back.

She sat outside, arms folded. When they came out, she asked, "Can I carry the torch next time?"

"Maybe," said Yogi, which meant no.

At dinner she complained to Papa. "They never let me in! It's not fair!"

Papa said, "Boys, let her in sometimes."

"Fine," Sonu sighed. "She can sit in the corner."

Reena didn't want to sit in the corner. She wanted to be the one holding the torch.

What did the sign on the storeroom door say?
NO GIRLS, NO BABIES.
What did Reena mean by wanting to hold the torch?
She wanted to be taken seriously and given a real role, not just tolerated in the corner; she felt left out and bossed.
How could Papa help more than "let her in sometimes"?
He could suggest the brothers give Reena a real job in the club, like holding the torch, so she feels valued.
How might Sonu and Yogi see their club?
They probably see it as their own special space and Reena as too young, not noticing how excluded she feels.

metadata.subtype: Stage 4: The middle child's or younger one's view [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Siami, you asked how I kept at the gym all these years. When I was twenty-four and new at the post office in Aizawl, I tried three times and quit three times. Each time I paid by the month, and each time the first bad weather stopped me. So I sat down and thought: what will stop your Lokesh Uncle from quitting? I knew myself. I hate losing money more than I hate cold mornings. So I paid for three whole months, all at once, and told my friends. On the wet, grey mornings, I lay in bed and thought, "That money is already gone. If you stay here, you're throwing it away." And up I got. After three months, I didn't need the trick.

How old was Lokesh when he started at the post office?
Lokesh was twenty-four and new at the post office in Aizawl.
What did young Lokesh feel on the wet, grey mornings?
Young Lokesh felt reluctant and tempted to stay in bed, but the thought of wasting the money pushed him up.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
Paying for three months at once, because he knew he hated losing money more than cold mornings, so quitting now had a cost.
How might young Lokesh's friends have seen his plan?
They probably found it funny, but knowing they'd heard about it may have added to his wish not to quit.

metadata.subtype: Approach: pays or books something in advance to create a cost for quitting [Thinking]

messages.content: Thank someone for a book they gave me, in two sentences; the second must start with "I".
Thank you for the lovely book you sent me. I have already started reading the first chapter.

Read this:

Dear Salma,
You once told me a lead's real job is to be a good plumber: find what's blocked and clear it. I didn't get it when you said it. I think I do now.
When I took over the team in January, I spent the first month in meetings making decisions. The team got quieter. So I changed. Every Monday I now ask everyone one question: what's in your way this week? Last week it was a broken test server, a vendor who wasn't replying, and Ramesh's leave that kept getting stuck in approval. I spent my week on those three things. Nothing glamorous.
When the director praised our release, I named the four people who built it. I still eat lunch with the old gang on Thursdays; they tease me more than ever.
Ramesh runs the stand-ups now, and he's better at it than I was.
Thank you for the plumbing lesson.
Shankar

What question does Shankar ask every Monday?
What's in your way this week?
How does Shankar seem to feel about the role now?
Shankar seems settled and content, finding meaning in clearing blockages rather than in making every decision.
Which of Shankar's habits builds the most lasting authority, and why?
Clearing the team's blockers and naming the four builders to the director, because it earns trust through service, not position.
How might Ramesh see Shankar's leadership?
Ramesh likely feels supported and trusted, since Shankar fixed the stuck leave and handed over the stand-ups.

Read this:

Samir, you asked me straight, so I'll answer straight. It's Lakshmi. Yes, I'm still with Hemant. Six months after I found out about the affair.

People think staying means I'm weak. My own sister said so. Others think I should forgive and move on because he's sorry. Neither of them lives in my body.

Some days I look at him and I remember why I married him. Other days I want to throw his phone into the lake. Both feelings are real. Hope and anger, all tangled up.

What's helped is conditions. I told him: you answer every question, however many times I ask. You don't rush me. We go to counselling every Thursday. He's kept all of it so far.

And I've told him plainly that I might still leave. That door is open. If I walk through it someday, it won't be weakness either. It'll just be my decision.

On which day do Lakshmi and Hemant go to counselling?
They go every Thursday.
What is Lakshmi feeling about staying with Hemant?
Lakshmi feels hope and anger tangled together, sometimes remembering why they married and sometimes furious.
How is Lakshmi making rebuilding possible without giving up her choice?
Lakshmi has set conditions, honest answers, no rushing and weekly counselling, while keeping the freedom to leave.
How might Lakshmi's sister see her choice to stay?
Lakshmi's sister sees it as weakness, not understanding what Lakshmi is actually feeling and deciding.

Read this:

The puppet crow came out of the bag, and Asif shot up off the mat in the building clubhouse. "Me first! Me first!" His hand waved so high he wobbled.

Mrs D'Souza smiled. "The crow is going round the circle, starting with Eshaan. Everyone gets a turn."

Asif sat back down on his hands and bounced. He counted the children between him and Eshaan: one, two, three, four. Eshaan made the crow say caw. Then the next child. Asif's knees jiggled. When the crow finally landed in his lap, he hugged it first.

Who got the puppet crow first?
Eshaan.
What do Asif's bouncing and jiggling knees suggest while he waited?
He was eager and excited to hold the crow, and probably a bit impatient with the wait.
What helped Asif manage the wait?
The clear rule that the crow goes round the circle so everyone gets a turn; counting the children let him see when his turn was coming.
How might Eshaan feel if Asif had grabbed the crow instead of waiting?
Eshaan would likely feel upset and pushed aside, because it was Eshaan's turn first.

Read this:

The layoff list had come out on Monday, and by Wednesday Gautam's floor at the Gurugram office was half empty. Vikas, his desk-mate for three years, was on the list. Gautam wasn't.
He felt guilty every time he walked past Vikas's cleared desk. He had written a long sad post online about "losing family at work", and it got two hundred likes. Vikas had not liked it.
That night, with the building's lift broken and his phone at ten per cent, Gautam climbed nine floors and sat on the stairs with his laptop. He opened a message to Vikas instead of another post. "I'm sorry. I don't know what to say, but I know what I can do." He wrote a recommendation on Vikas's work profile, emailed two managers he knew at other firms with Vikas's resume, and deleted the post.
Vikas replied at midnight: "Thanks, bro. That actually helps."

How many likes did Gautam's post get?
Two hundred likes.
What was Gautam feeling as he walked past Vikas's cleared desk?
He felt guilty and uncomfortable for keeping the job while Vikas, a desk-mate of three years, lost one.
What went wrong at first, and what did Gautam do instead?
His sad post performed grief without helping; instead he wrote Vikas a recommendation, sent Vikas's resume to two managers, and deleted the post.
How might Vikas have seen Gautam's post compared with his message?
Vikas likely found the post empty or even hurtful, but felt genuinely helped and grateful for the direct message and referrals.

Read this:

I'm Chinmay, and I work the grill next to Thomas at a restaurant kitchen in Kochi. Last month Chef announced that Ruth would be the new sous-chef. Ruth joined after Thomas. The kitchen went quiet in that way kitchens never do. Thomas put his tongs down and said, not loudly, "Honestly? I'm jealous. Give me a minute." Then he walked out to the back step. When he came back, he went straight to Ruth, shook her hand and said, "You earned that. How did you prepare for the tasting?" She told him about practising the sauces every night for weeks. The next morning I saw him asking Chef what he'd need to work on to be considered next time. I don't know what went through his head on that back step. But he's been coming in an hour early since.

Where does Chinmay work alongside Thomas?
At the grill of a restaurant kitchen in Kochi.
What does Thomas's saying "I'm jealous. Give me a minute" suggest about him?
It suggests he noticed his envy and chose to name it honestly instead of letting it come out as a dig at Ruth.
Why was Thomas's question to Chef the next morning a turning point?
It turned his envy into a clear goal, finding out what he needed to improve to be considered next time.
How might Ruth feel when Thomas shakes her hand and asks about her preparation?
Ruth might feel relieved and respected, especially after the tense silence, since a senior colleague is backing her.

Rain kept the boys indoors, and toys lay everywhere in Abebe's room. Abebe's aunt said they could have a story once the floor was clear. Emeka groaned and lay flat on the rug. Abebe thought, then held up one finger. "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story." "Deal," said Emeka, sitting up. Abebe rolled the cars into a crate and counted them aloud. Emeka stacked the books on the low shelf. When they finished, they flopped down and opened the book about the tortoise.

What did Abebe offer Emeka?
Abebe said, "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story."
How did Emeka feel about clearing up at the start, and how can you tell?
Emeka felt reluctant. Emeka groaned and lay flat on the rug.
What other approach could work if Emeka had refused the deal, and why?
Abebe could turn the clearing into a race or a shop game. Play can make a chore feel lighter.
How does the plan look to Emeka?
Emeka gets a clear, fair share of the work and a story to look forward to. That is why sitting up and saying "Deal" makes sense.

Friday, 9 pm. I wrote three opening lines for Vikas on the back of my rough copy. One was a pun. One was about the physics test. One was so clever I crossed it out because it didn't even sound like me. All I could think was, what if he thinks I'm trying too hard? I kept picturing Vikas walking away. Then at the corridor stall today I just said, "Hey, I really liked your poster." Nothing else. Vikas smiled and said, "Thanks, I worked on it all week." That was it. I walked home surprised how ordinary it felt. Maybe simple was always enough.
Lalit

What did Lalit say to Vikas at the corridor stall?
"Hey, I really liked your poster."
What was Lalit worried about while writing the opening lines?
That trying too hard would look bad, and picturing Vikas walking away, a fear of being judged.
What did Lalit decide at the stall, and why did it work?
Lalit dropped the clever lines and said one honest thing about the poster, which was easy to answer.
What might Vikas be feeling when hearing about the poster?
Pleased that the work was noticed. Vikas smiled and said it had taken all week.

Read this:

In the village of Ambegaon, Deepika's cousin Sunaina turned nine, and the whole family gathered under the mango tree. There were swings, lagori and fried snacks all afternoon. The best moment was when Sunaina's grandfather brought out a big cake from the town bakery, and everyone cheered so loudly the goats ran off. Then, just before sunset, Deepika's bicycle chain snapped on the way home, and she had to walk the last mile in the dark, crying. The next day her teacher asked about the weekend. "It was horrible," Deepika said. Her mother laughed. "Horrible? You played lagori for two hours!" Deepika thought. She had forgotten lagori completely. She remembered the cake, and the dark road. "Only the end was horrible," she admitted.

What made the goats run off?
Everyone cheered so loudly when the cake came out.
Why did Deepika tell her teacher the weekend was horrible?
She felt upset and frightened walking home in the dark, and that sad ending coloured her memory of the whole afternoon.
What could Deepika try next time a day ends badly?
She could think through the whole day, like the lagori and swings, before deciding how it was.
How does Deepika's mother see the day?
Her mother sees it as a happy day, laughing because Deepika played lagori for two hours.

metadata.subtype: Remembering the best or worst bit and the end [Actor]

messages.content: A rainbow needs both sun and rain. Why?
Sunlight needs raindrops to split it. Because each drop bends and bounces the light inside, and that separates it into its colours. Without drops or without sun, there is nothing to split.

Give me the short version of this paragraph, under 55 words.

It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils. With an anxiety that almost amounted to agony, I collected the instruments of life around me, that I might infuse a spark of being into the lifeless thing that lay at my feet. It was already one in the morning; the rain pattered dismally against the panes, and my candle was nearly burnt out, when, by the glimmer of the half-extinguished light, I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs.
On a dreary November night, the narrator prepares to bring a lifeless thing to life. At one in the morning the creature's dull yellow eye opens, and it breathes hard and twitches.

Read this:

"Lokesh, you've been eating at your desk all week."
"Busy."
"Since my promotion was announced?"
Lokesh kept typing. "Congratulations, Harish. Really. You deserved it."
"You helped me get it. That client migration last year, you stayed back with me three nights. I said that to the director, you know."
Lokesh's hands paused. "You did?"
"I did. And I'm not going to pretend I don't want the job. I do. But I miss our lunches."
"It's weird, man. We applied for the same thing."
"I know. Take your time. I'm not going anywhere."
"You're my boss now, technically."
"Technically. But I'm still the one who can't order at the dosa place without you."
Lokesh almost smiled. "Friday. Not before."
"Friday."

How many nights did Lokesh stay back with Harish during the client migration?
Three nights.
What might Lokesh be feeling when he says "It's weird, man"?
He probably feels envious and sad, having applied for the same job, and awkward now that Harish is his boss.
What did Harish do that helped the friendship?
He credited Lokesh's help to the director, did not apologise for wanting the job, said he missed their lunches, and gave Lokesh time.
If you were Harish, what would you want from Lokesh?
Harish wants the friendship back and understands that Lokesh needs space for a loss, so he patiently accepts "Friday. Not before."

During the Sankranti break, the fields around Kondapur were stubble and kite string. Raghav spent the whole morning under the old water pump behind the temple, and by noon it was running again. Anjali, who studied at the same town college, watched him wipe grease off his hands. "You look happier now than in two years of accounts class," she said. "I'm leaving B.Com after this semester. I've got a seat in the ITI electrical course." Raghav laughed too loudly. "And throw away two years? Amma sold her gold earrings for my first fee." "Those years are spent either way." He looked at the humming pump, then down the road to the bus stand where the college bus would leave on Monday. "If I leave now, it means everything was a waste," he said, and walked home to find his ledger notebooks.

What did Raghav repair during the Sankranti break?
He repaired the old water pump behind the temple.
Why does leaving B.Com feel so hard for Raghav?
He feels guilty and scared that leaving would make the two years, and Amma's gold earrings, feel wasted, so staying seems like the loyal choice.
What question could help Raghav decide more fairly?
He could ask which course he would choose if he were starting today, knowing how much he enjoys repair work, and talk it through with Amma and a college counsellor.
How does Anjali see Raghav's choice?
Anjali sees that he is happiest working on the pump and believes the spent years should not decide his future, just as they did not decide hers.

Thursday. I broke Amma's blue vase with the football. Amma came running and I said, "Meenu did it." Meenu, my little sister, is five. She cried and said no, and I said she had been standing right there. Amma gave her a long scolding and no dessert. Meenu looked at me with her wet face and I could not look back. Then Amma asked why Meenu was lying, and I said a third thing that was not true, that Meenu had touched it before. Three lies in one evening. My stomach feels sick. Every time I think it is over, I need one more story to hold it up. I keep thinking I should tell Amma. Kishore

How old is Meenu?
Meenu, my little sister, is five.
What is Kishore feeling as Meenu is scolded?
Guilty and sick, since Kishore watched Meenu take the blame and could not look back.
What could Kishore do to fix this?
Tell Amma the truth and say sorry to Meenu, because the lie keeps needing more lies and Meenu is paying for it.
How does the evening feel to Meenu?
Unfair and upsetting, since Meenu cried, was scolded and lost dessert for something Meenu did not do.

metadata.subtype: Approach: blaming a sibling or the dog [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Summarise this as three bullet points.

"Aunt Isabella had not you and me to nurse her," I replied. "She wasn't as happy as Master: she hadn't as much to live for. All you need do, is to wait well on your father, and cheer him by letting him see you cheerful; and avoid giving him anxiety on any subject: mind that, Cathy! I'll not disguise but you might kill him if you were wild and reckless, and cherished a foolish, fanciful affection for the son of a person who would be glad to have him in his grave; and allowed him to discover that you fretted over the separation he has judged it expedient to make."

- The speaker says Cathy's father is happier than Aunt Isabella was, because he has Cathy and the speaker to care for him.
- Cathy should look after the father, stay cheerful and give him nothing to worry about.
- Wild behaviour, or a foolish attachment to the son of a man who wants the father dead, could kill the father.

The hospital's pharmacy staff had a social group called "Pharma Family", and it ran all day: birthday photos, lunch plans, a long thread about whose tiffin smelled best. Swati, who had just started night duty and was studying for her licensing exam, found it buzzing through her sleep.
At the staff canteen she stopped Trisha, who managed the group. "Trisha, can I tell you something before I do it? I'm going to leave Pharma Family for a while. Nothing wrong with anyone. I just need to sleep in the day and study."
Trisha laughed. "Thank God you told me. When Sudhir left last month, the whole group thought he was angry with us."
"That's why I'm telling you. And I'll post a short goodbye."
Her message went up that evening: "Stepping back for exams and nights. Please keep my birthday cake slice safe. 🙂"
Hearts and laughing replies followed.

What was the social group called?
The group was called "Pharma Family".
Why did Swati want to tell Trisha first?
Swati was worried that leaving silently would seem like anger, as it had when Sudhir left, and she cared about her colleagues' feelings.
What could others learn from how Swati left?
Tell the admin in person, give a simple reason like sleep and study, and post a short, light goodbye.
How did Trisha feel when Swati explained?
Trisha felt relieved and grateful, since Sudhir's silent exit had left the whole group thinking he was angry.

Read this:

Monday, winter holidays. Jatin opened a new 1000-piece jigsaw of a boring grey bridge. He found it dull after ten minutes. But he'd spent his whole birthday money on it.

Wednesday. Jatin had done the edges. His back hurt. Imran came to call him for cricket. "Two more hours," Jatin said. "I've already done so much."

Saturday. Jatin was still hunched over the grey bridge. Imran came again. "Are you even having fun?"

"No. But if I stop now, all those hours are wasted."

"They're gone anyway," Imran said. "Are the next hours going to be fun?"

Jatin looked at the grey pieces, then out of the window at the sunny street. He slowly put the lid on the box and went to get his bat.

What was the jigsaw a picture of?
A boring grey bridge.
Why did Jatin keep doing the jigsaw even though it was dull?
Jatin felt that stopping would waste the birthday money and hours already spent, so continuing felt necessary even though he was bored.
What question from Imran helped Jatin decide, and why?
Imran asked whether the next hours would be fun, which turned Jatin's thinking toward what comes next rather than what was already spent.
How might Imran have felt when Jatin kept saying no to cricket?
Imran probably felt disappointed and a bit puzzled, missing his friend during the holidays.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Class 5, Wednesday.

Harsha loves science. He always says it's easy and the most useful subject. Today during Hindi, he said, "Hindi is so hard and useless. Why do we even learn it?"

His classmate Yamini said, "But you wrote the best story last month."

Harsha frowned. "That was luck."

I think Harsha's feelings about the subjects colour how he judges them. When he likes something, it feels easy and important. When he doesn't, it feels hard and pointless, even when he does well.

Next week I'll try a science-themed Hindi reading for him and see if it helps.

What did Yamini say Harsha wrote last month?
The best story.
Why did Harsha say his good story was just luck?
He dislikes Hindi and feels frustrated by it, so he feels it must be hard and pointless, and success in it doesn't fit his feeling.
What does the teacher plan to try, and why might it help?
A science-themed Hindi reading, which links the subject he dislikes to something he enjoys.
How might Yamini feel when Harsha calls Hindi useless?
Yamini might feel surprised or slightly offended, especially if Yamini enjoys Hindi.
A friend has a small cut at school. What do I do?
Take her to the teacher or the nurse. Because the cut needs to be cleaned and covered by someone who knows how, so it does not get infected.

Read this:

Jomon, you're counting the chocolates again, I can see your lips moving. Come here, mone. When your Seema aunty was nine, I was worse. I kept a tally on the kitchen wall with charcoal: who pumped water, who fed the hens, who helped whom with sums. One day my father cut a jackfruit and gave me the biggest share because I had swept the yard. I shouted, "No! Thomas pumped water twice, he gets more!" Everyone laughed, and my father said, "Seema, just eat." I wouldn't touch it until Thomas had the bigger piece. I was right about fairness, mind you. But I was so busy counting that I never enjoyed a single bite. Share them, mone, and don't keep a wall.

Where did young Seema keep her tally?
On the kitchen wall, with charcoal.
Why wouldn't young Seema touch her jackfruit?
She felt the split was unfair because Thomas had pumped water twice, and she couldn't enjoy extra she felt she hadn't earned.
What is Seema aunty hoping Jomon will choose with the chocolates?
She hopes Jomon will share them freely rather than counting every piece, keeping fairness without letting the tally spoil the fun.
How might Thomas have felt when young Seema shouted that he should get more?
Thomas may have been surprised and a bit embarrassed by the fuss, but perhaps pleased that his work was noticed.

Read this:

At the end of our marketing project, our professor did something sneaky. She asked each of the four of us, privately, to write what percentage of the work we had done. I wrote 45%, and honestly I thought I was being modest. I had stayed up all night for the final deck. Then she read out the numbers. Zeenat, 40%. Kiran, 50%. Tushar, 55%. Me, 45%. That's 190% of one project. Zeenat laughed first. "Samir, you remember the deck. I remember the survey I ran for two weeks." She was right; I'd barely noticed the survey. Each of us had seen our own late nights up close and everyone else's from far away. On the next project, we kept a shared log of who did what, with dates.

What percentage did Samir write?
Why did Samir think 45% was modest?
Samir felt proud of staying up all night for the final deck, and that night felt so big that 45% seemed a modest share.
What did the team do on the next project, and why does it help?
They kept a shared, dated log of who did what, so credit rests on a record rather than on each person's memory.
How did Zeenat see the 190% total?
Zeenat found it funny and pointed out that each of them remembered their own work, like her two-week survey, more than anyone else's.

The rain had trapped everyone under the bus shelter, and the bus was late. Hansa, five, had discovered the concrete step at the edge. She stood on it, bent her knees, and jumped down with both feet. Splash! "I did it! Rukmini Masi, look!" She climbed back up. Jump. "Again!" Up. Jump. "Again!" Her frock was soaked at the hem. Masi held the umbrella over the step and counted each jump out loud. By the time the bus came, Hansa had jumped nineteen times, and she climbed on grinning, still bending her knees.

How many times had Hansa jumped by the time the bus came?
Hansa had jumped nineteen times.
Why did Hansa keep shouting 'Again!'?
Each jump made her feel able and proud, and that good feeling made her want to do it over and over 😊.
What did Rukmini Masi choose to do in the rain, and why did it help?
She held the umbrella over the step and counted each jump, making Hansa's new skill feel seen and safe to practise.
What might the other people at the shelter think, watching Hansa?
They might smile at the small girl's delight, which makes the late bus and the rain a little easier to bear.

At the Toronto daycare, Dalia pushed both hands through the blue paint and dragged them across the paper, round and round, then squashed a lump of clay between her fingers and laughed.
At pickup her father held up the paper. “What is it, sweetheart? A fish? A car?”
Dalia just patted the paint.
“She loved making it,” said Aiko, her teacher. “Look at all these big circles. She worked on it a long time.”
Her father grinned. “Big circles. Wow."

What colour paint did Dalia use?
She used blue paint.
What was Dalia feeling as she dragged her hands through the paint?
She was happy and absorbed, enjoying the feel of the paint and clay rather than trying to draw something.
Why was Aiko's comment more helpful than asking what it is?
Aiko praised Dalia's effort and described the marks, since at this age the joy is in making marks, not picturing something.
What might Dalia's father have felt when she didn't answer his question?
He might have felt a little puzzled, until Aiko explained, and then pleased to join in admiring the circles.

Home in Kumbakonam for the holidays, Lakshmi, a second-year psychology student, watched her cousin Disha drop onto the veranda after a long day at the tailoring shop. 'Don't ask me to study for my typing test,' Disha said. 'My willpower is finished. I read it on my phone: it's like petrol, it runs out.' Lakshmi smiled. Two weeks ago her professor had spent a whole lecture on exactly that idea. 'It was a famous theory,' she said. 'But when big teams repeated those experiments with thousands of people, most couldn't find the effect.' Disha frowned. 'So I'm not tired?' 'You're definitely tired. That part's real. It's just that nobody's sure it's a tank. Some studies even suggest that believing it runs out makes people give up sooner.' Disha thought about it. 'So what do I do?' 'Maybe rest first, then try fifteen minutes. See what happens.'

What did Disha say willpower is like?
She said it's like petrol and runs out.
How does Lakshmi feel about the petrol idea, given what she has learned?
Lakshmi feels doubtful about it but careful, respecting Disha's real tiredness while being unsure the tank explanation is right.
What balanced suggestion does Lakshmi make?
Rest first, then try fifteen minutes and see what happens, since tiredness is real but the mechanism is uncertain.
How might Disha feel hearing 'You're definitely tired'?
Disha would likely feel understood and relieved, not accused of being lazy.

metadata.subtype: Skeptic of the fuel tank idea [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the ITI in Jhunjhunu, the lathe workshop roared all morning, and Sumit caught maybe half of what Urmila madam said. He had worn a hearing aid in one ear since childhood, but in that noise it helped little. For two weeks he copied his neighbour's work and nodded along, stomach tight, afraid of being called slow. Then he misread a measurement and ruined a part. That night, at his uncle's tea stall, he practised the sentence under his breath. The next morning he waited until the others left. 'Madam, I have hearing loss. In the workshop I miss instructions. Could I stand near you, and could you write the measurements on the board?' She looked surprised, then nodded. 'Why didn't you say earlier?' From that week the measurements went up on the board in big chalk. Two other boys used them too.

What did Sumit ask Urmila madam for?
To stand near her and to have the measurements written on the board.
Why did Sumit copy his neighbour and nod along for two weeks?
He was anxious about being seen as slow, so he hid that he could not hear the instructions.
What helped Sumit ask effectively?
Practising the sentence, choosing a private moment, naming his need plainly and suggesting simple, specific adjustments.
How did the change affect the other trainees?
Two other boys used the board measurements too, showing that an adjustment for one person can help others.

Read this:

It had been three weeks since the breakup, and Shalini, Jahnavi's roommate in the girls' hostel, had heard her crying most nights. Tonight it was over a dropped plate in the mess. Jahnavi stood at the sink, tears running, hands shaking. "It's a plate," she laughed, crying harder. Shalini guided her back to the room and sat with her. "You're allowed to cry. But it's every night now. How are you sleeping?" "Badly. And I can't focus in class." Shalini listened for a long time. Then she said, "The college counsellor has evening hours till eight. It's seven now. Shall I walk with you?" Jahnavi hesitated. "What if they think I'm being dramatic?" "They won't. And I'll wait outside." Jahnavi washed her face. They walked there together, and Shalini sat on the bench outside until the door opened again.

How long had it been since the breakup?
Three weeks.
What was Jahnavi worried about before seeing the counsellor?
She was anxious that the counsellor would think she was being dramatic; underneath, she was exhausted and sad from weeks of crying.
What did Shalini do that made the next step easier?
She said crying was allowed, listened, noticed the pattern, and offered to walk Jahnavi to the counsellor that same evening and wait outside.
What would change if Shalini had only said "It's just a plate"?
Jahnavi might have felt dismissed and kept crying alone each night without reaching the counsellor.

Last Diwali, when we went to see Nani and Nana in Nagpur, Mummy let me, Seema, be the list-maker. A week before, I sat at the dining table with a pad and broke the trip into jobs: tickets, clothes for four days, food for the twelve-hour train, a present for Nana, and someone to water our plants. Every evening Mummy and I went down the list together. Some jobs took one minute; my little sister Indu packed her own socks. Some took three evenings, like finding Nana's favourite tea. On the day we left, the only thing not ticked was "relax". On the train, while other families ran to buy food at stations, we opened our steel tiffins and ate slowly. I felt very grown-up.

How long was the train journey?
Twelve hours.

Seema felt proud and grown-up, eating calmly while other families rushed for food.

Starting from an old checklist of past trips would save time, but breaking this trip into its own jobs fitted what this visit needed.
What was it like for Indu to be part of the plan?
Indu got a small job of her own, packing her own socks, so she was included too.

They were already forty minutes late for Kiran's sister's engagement when the car scraped the side of a parked auto-rickshaw in a narrow Madurai lane. The driver wasn't around. 'Nobody saw,' Kiran said, hands tight on the wheel. 'Let's go. Please, Karthik, Amma will be furious if we're later.' Karthik looked at the dented door, at the driver's name painted on the back, at a child's school bag on the seat. That man would lose days of fares getting it fixed. But Kiran was his oldest friend, and Kiran's mother had fed him through every exam. His phone buzzed: 'Where are you both??' Karthik took a breath. 'Give me five minutes. We leave a number, or I wait here alone and you go.' Kiran stared, then sighed, pulled out a receipt and wrote a phone number to tuck under the wiper.

What was on the auto-rickshaw's seat?
A child's school bag.
What was Karthik feeling as he looked at the dented door?
Karthik felt torn: sympathy for the driver who would lose fares, and loyalty and gratitude towards Kiran and Kiran's mother.

He paused and offered a concrete plan instead of choosing in a panic, so the driver was treated fairly without abandoning Kiran.

I'm Tenzin, Binita's roommate, and I watched her decide how to vote in the student council election. Two weeks before, she had a list on her desk: hostel water, library hours, the women's safety committee. She'd even read both manifestos. Then, three days before polling, the whole corridor started wearing Rakesh's yellow badges. Posters on every door. In the mess, people just said, "Everyone's voting Rakesh." Binita came back one evening with a yellow badge. When I asked what his plan for the library was, she said, "Honestly, no idea. But half the campus can't be wrong." Her list was still on the desk, and his name wasn't on it. I don't know exactly why she changed. Maybe she just didn't want to be on the losing side.

They were yellow.

It suggests she was treating the number of supporters as proof, even though she didn't know his plan for the library.

She could check Rakesh's plans against her own list about water, library hours and safety, then vote for whoever matches it best.

Naveen asked why Farhan keeps drumming fingers on the table.

Dear Diary, Tuesday.
Something happened near the bus stop today that I keep thinking about. An old man on a scooter skidded and fell. People gathered, maybe twenty of us. Everyone was looking. I thought, someone has surely called the ambulance already. I didn't move.
Then Sharmila didi, who works at the pharmacy, came out and pointed straight at me. "You. Call 108. Tell them outside the Shiv Mandir bus stop." My hands shook but I did it. She sent two other boys to stop the traffic. The ambulance came.
Afterwards I realised: nobody had called. Everyone thought someone else had. That could have been Dadaji.
Omkar

Where did the old man fall?
Near the bus stop, outside the Shiv Mandir bus stop.
What was Omkar thinking before Sharmila didi pointed?
Omkar assumed someone had surely called the ambulance already, and felt unsure and hesitant, so did nothing.
What broke the crowd's inaction?
Sharmila didi pointing at one person to call 108 and sending others to stop the traffic.
How might the old man have been affected if no one had been named?
He might have lain there much longer, since everyone assumed someone else had called.

"Why are you leaving the college alumni group?" Sunaina asked, peering at Gurleen's phone.

"Because it sends two hundred messages a day and I read none of them."

"But what if you miss something?"

"Then someone will tell me. That's what you're for."

Sunaina laughed. "Rude. What else?"

"Notifications off for everything except calls, and messages from you, Mumma and my manager. News only in the morning, one site. And the shopping apps are going."

"The shopping apps? You love the sales."

"That's the problem. I don't need anything. They just tell me I do."

Sunaina was quiet for a moment. "I feel anxious just hearing this."

"I did too, last week. I thought I'd feel cut off." Gurleen put the phone face down on the table. "Mostly I feel like I have my evenings back."

"Can you show me how to do the notification thing?"

"Only if you promise not to send me two hundred messages."

Which notifications did Gurleen keep on?
Gurleen kept notifications for calls and for messages from Sunaina, Mumma and the manager.
How did Sunaina feel hearing about Gurleen's changes?
Sunaina felt anxious, worried about missing things, even just hearing the plan.
Why did Gurleen delete the shopping apps, and what could a friend learn from that?
Gurleen realised the apps created a feeling of needing things, so a friend could ask whether an app serves a real need or creates one.
What is it like for Sunaina to watch Gurleen make these choices?
Sunaina is first surprised and anxious, then curious enough to ask for help setting up her own notifications.

“Pankaj, phone again,” Pema Auntie said, holding out the receiver.
“Coming.” He wiped his eyes with the back of his hand, took the phone and said in a steady voice, “Yes, Dada passed this morning. The prayers are at four tomorrow. Yes, please come.” He wrote the caller's name and the time on the pad by the phone.
“You're managing so well,” his aunt murmured.
“It helps,” he said quietly. “If I stop, I just think about him.” He filled another jug of water for the guests and paused at the window. “I still feel it. I just need something to hold.”
Pema Auntie pushed a tray of cups toward him. “Then hold this. And when you need to sit, sit. Nobody's counting.”
Pankaj sat, took the youngest cousin onto his lap, and let himself cry.

What did Pankaj write on the pad by the phone?
Pankaj wrote the caller's name and the time.
Why does Pankaj say It helps?
Pankaj is sad, and tasks steady him, since if he stops he just thinks about Dada.
What could Pankaj do when the tasks run out?
Pankaj could sit with the family, share memories or talk to someone he trusts, since tasks give structure but do not replace grief.
How might Pema Auntie see Pankaj's work?
Pema Auntie seems grateful and caring, since she praises him and tells him to sit whenever he needs to.

messages.content: My shoes squeak loudly on the classroom floor. Everyone turns to look.
That can be embarrassing, but it's only a noise. Often the sole is damp or smooth.
Is there a way to stop it?
Dry the soles well, and rub them lightly on a rough mat. A little baby powder inside the shoe sometimes helps. If it continues, a shoe shop can look at it.

Monday: under the stairs at school, Ujjwal, Keerthana and Manav invented the Tiger Club. The handshake was two slaps, a fist bump and a growl. Rule one: nobody tells the password. Ujjwal felt ten feet tall. Thursday: a new boy, Arif, asked to join. Keerthana said, 'Tiger Club is only three.' Arif walked off, and Ujjwal felt a strange mix of pride and guilt. The next Monday: Ujjwal saw Arif eating alone again. At the stairs, Ujjwal said, 'What if we had a joining test? Like, he has to growl.' Manav rolled his eyes but agreed. Arif growled so loudly that a teacher looked round. The Tiger Club was four.

What was the Tiger Club handshake?
Two slaps, a fist bump and a growl.
How did Ujjwal feel when Arif walked off on Thursday?
A strange mix of pride in the club and guilt at shutting Arif out.
What did Ujjwal do to let Arif in, and why did it work?
Suggested a joining test, a growl, so Arif could belong without the club losing its special ritual.
What was it like for Arif to be turned away and then let in?
He likely felt rejected and lonely at first, then happy and accepted, growling loud enough for a teacher to look round.

Thursday night
Noticed Binita again today. Third week she's eaten lunch on the steps by the library, earphones in, nothing playing (the wire wasn't even plugged in). She used to be all over our class group chat, and now when someone makes a plan, she's never tagged. I don't think anyone's being mean on purpose. People just forgot her, which is kind of worse.
So today I took my tiffin to the steps and sat two steps above, like I just wanted the shade. Asked her if she'd done the geography map. She had. Then I said, "Want to be in our group for the model? We need someone who can draw." She said, "Okay," very fast.
Didn't make a big deal. Nobody noticed. Good.
Tenzin

Where has Binita been eating lunch for three weeks?
On the steps by the library, earphones in, with nothing playing.
Why does Tenzin think people forgetting Binita is "kind of worse"?
Tenzin feels that meanness at least gets noticed, while quiet forgetting makes Binita invisible and nobody even sees the need to fix it.
Why did Tenzin sit two steps above and ask about the geography map first?
Tenzin chose a casual opening so it didn't look like a rescue, which let Binita say yes without feeling singled out.
How might the invitation feel from Binita's side?
After weeks of not being tagged, being asked because "we need someone who can draw" may feel like being wanted rather than pitied.
My manager wrote "Send it ASAP". How is "ASAP" read, and is it rude?

It stands for "as soon as possible" and is read letter by letter, or sometimes as "ay-sap". It is common in work messages but can sound pushy, so a polite request such as "Could you send it as soon as possible, please?" is gentler.
Example: Could you please send the report as soon as possible?

The bus dropped Zeenat at the edge of Kheri village just after sunset, her nurse's bag still on her shoulder. Gurleen, her friend from the hospital hostel, had come along for the weekend.
Abba was waiting by the gate. Before tea was poured, he mentioned the tractor repair, and then Phuppo's daughter's wedding in Kartik. Zeenat felt her chest tighten. She already sent money every month. She had not bought new shoes in a year.
Later, on the charpai, Gurleen whispered, "Tell him. He'd want to know."
In the morning Zeenat sat beside Abba with a notebook. She showed what she earned, what she sent, and the small amount she keeps for emergencies. "Abba, I can help with the tractor. For the wedding I can give this much, no more." Abba rubbed his jaw for a long time. Then he said, "I didn't know you kept so little for yourself, beti."

Whose wedding did Abba mention?
Abba mentioned Phuppo's daughter's wedding in Kartik.
What was Zeenat feeling when Abba mentioned the two expenses?
Zeenat felt tense and quietly resentful; her chest tightened because she already sent money and had not bought shoes in a year.
How did Gurleen help, and what did Zeenat do well next?
Gurleen nudged her to speak, and Zeenat then showed Abba her real numbers and offered a clear, limited amount instead of refusing or silently agreeing.
How does Abba see his daughter after the talk?
Abba seems surprised and moved, realising for the first time how little Zeenat kept for herself.

Outside the photocopy shop, Binita caught up with Rekha. "You snapped at the photocopy uncle just now. That's not you."
"I'm fine."
"You've said 'I'm fine' for five weeks. You look exhausted. You answer everything in two words."
Rekha was silent for a long moment. "Papa's been in and out of hospital since August. I do the nights with him, then come to college. I can't remember the last time I slept properly."
"Five weeks of that. No wonder."
"I thought if I just pushed through the semester..."
"What if you didn't do it all alone? Could your brother take two nights a week?"
"He's offered. I kept saying no."
"Say yes. And the college counsellor has evening slots. Would you go if I walked you there tomorrow after lab?"

Rekha laughed for the first time in days. "Bossy."
"Caring. Same thing."

Since when has Rekha's Papa been in and out of hospital?
Since August.
What was Rekha feeling behind the short answers and snapping?
Exhaustion and strain from five weeks of nights caring for Papa on top of college, feelings Rekha had been hiding behind "I'm fine".

Accepting the brother's offer of two nights a week, visiting the college counsellor together, and a nap in the reading room right away.

As not like Rekha at all: tired-faced, curt and snapping, which worried Binita enough to name the pattern.

why does a phone battery last less time in a very cold place? What does "the apple of my eye" mean? Spot the error: Always she is smiling. What is today's gold rate in my city? I don't understand "benefactor". Can you help?

1. Cold makes a battery deliver its energy less well. Because the chemical reactions inside it slow down in the cold.
2. It means a person that you love and cherish above all. For example: the little girl is the apple of her grandfather's eye.
3. Corrected: She is always smiling. Why: a frequency adverb like "always" usually goes after the subject and a form of "be".
4. I'm not sure. Prices change every day and I can't see them. Ask a local jeweller or check the official market rates.
5. "Benefactor" is a noun. It means a person who gives money or help to a person or a cause.

Day 1, Sunday evening: Tarun's third mock score was 96, down from 128. He sat with his uncle Ramesh in the courtyard and pulled out a notebook. "First, sleep," he said. "I slept around one all week. Before, it was eleven." Then topics. Physics had dropped the most, mostly mechanics.

Day 15, the next Sunday but one: Fourth mock: 118. Physics up by fourteen marks. Tarun showed Ramesh the chart. "Not back to 128 yet. But climbing." Ramesh nodded. "Then you keep the problem sets, and bring cricket back next week?"

96, down from 128.

He could keep watching his mock scores and sleep, to make sure adding cricket back does not undo the recovery.

The hostel had to be empty by six, the rain was coming sideways, and Karthik's books were still in cardboard boxes going soft at the corners. Yogesh had come to help him move to his uncle's flat after he'd dropped out of the semester.

When Yogesh taped a box wrong, Karthik exploded. "You always do this! You think you're so helpful. You just like feeling better than me."

The words hit like a slap. Yogesh wanted to throw the tape down and leave him to it. Instead he took a breath, said, "Okay," and carried the box to the autorickshaw.

They finished at 5:50. In the auto Karthik stared out at the rain.

Two weeks later, over tea, Yogesh said quietly, "That day really hurt." Karthik looked down. "I know. I was angry at everything. Not you. Sorry."

By what time did the hostel have to be empty?
The hostel had to be empty by six.
What was Yogesh feeling when Karthik exploded, and what did he want to do?
Yogesh felt hurt, as if slapped, and wanted to throw the tape down and leave.
Which choice worked, and why?
Staying steady that day and raising the hurt two weeks later when calm worked, because Karthik could hear it and apologise.
How might Karthik have seen that moving day?
Karthik was likely overwhelmed and ashamed about dropping out, so his anger at everything spilled onto the friend helping him.

Monday. Afreen had forgotten her ruler. Zubin, eight, held his up. "You can use it if I get your eraser for the whole day." Afreen agreed. Zubin looked pleased. A fair deal.
Wednesday. Zubin's water bottle leaked all over his bag in the hot sun at PE. Afreen held out hers without a word. Zubin drank, then said seriously, "Okay. Now I owe you one water." He wrote it on his hand in pen: A: 1 water.
Friday. On sports day, Afreen's shoelace came undone right before her race. Zubin knelt and tied it fast. Then he rubbed the ink off his hand. "There. Now we're even."

What did Zubin write on his hand?
A: 1 water.
Why did Zubin feel glad when the count was back to zero?
He sees helping as a fair trade, so owing Afreen made him uneasy and being even felt right to him.
What could a teacher or friend help Zubin notice about Afreen's water on Wednesday?
They could point out that Afreen shared without asking for anything, helping him see kindness can be given freely, not only traded.
How might Afreen see Zubin's 'Now we're even'?
Afreen seems amused rather than hurt, perhaps finding his careful counting funny, since she helped him without keeping score.

Pallavi, a girl from Eshaan's class, was pressed against the window and mouthed, "Is she asleep?" Eshaan wanted to shout for the driver, but what if she was only tired and everyone laughed at him? Why was Eshaan on the bus in a hurry?
Eshaan was late for the maths exam.

What might it have been like for the woman on the floor while nobody moved?
The woman may have felt frightened or helpless, or may not have been aware at all; the bus stayed silent until an older man knelt beside her.

Correct this sentence: I didn't saw him yesterday.

The demo for the hospital client was at ten, and at eight the office internet went down. Chinmay, who had built the appointment app's first version, could have taken over and patched it himself; he knew the code best. Instead he turned to Vandana, the junior he had been coaching for six months. 'You rewrote the booking module. You know it better than me now. What do we need?' She blinked, then rattled off a plan: run it locally, use her phone hotspot, skip the payments screen. It worked. In the meeting, when the client praised the booking flow, Chinmay said, 'That's Vandana's design. She'll walk you through it.' Afterwards his manager said, 'You could have presented it yourself.' Chinmay shrugged. 'She's going to be better than me. I'd like to have helped with that.'

The office internet.

It suggests Chinmay felt calm and content, proud of Vandana rather than anxious about being outgrown.

She knew the booking module best, so letting her lead solved the problem and gave her the chance to show her skill.
