The Christmas market in Madrid was packed. Lucia buckled Santiago into the stroller so he wouldn't get lost.

Santiago did not want the stroller. He stiffened his legs, pushed against the straps and yelled, "No! No!" His hat fell off.

Lucia crouched down. "You want to walk. It's too crowded." She gave him a small drum from the stall to hold.

He banged it, still sniffling, and let her push.

What did Lucia give Santiago to hold?
She gave him a small drum from the stall.
What was Santiago feeling when he pushed against the straps?
Santiago was angry and frustrated at being strapped in when he wanted to walk.
What did Lucia do that helped Santiago calm down?
She named what he wanted, explained simply, and gave him something to do with his hands.
How might the crowd around them see Santiago's yelling?
Some people might feel annoyed, but many would see it as an ordinary toddler moment.

Read this:

There were eleven people in the Dadar flat and not one closed door that belonged to Tejas. When Thomas called about the band audition, Tejas tried the balcony: Aaji was drying papads. The bedroom: two cousins doing homework. The bathroom: his uncle, shaving.

He ended up on the stairwell, whispering. "Can you hear me? Yeah, I want to try out, but—"

"Tejas! Who is it?" his mother called through the grille.

"Nobody!"

He hung up, stomped back in, and when his little cousin asked what a band was, he snapped, "Can't anyone mind their own business in this house?" He slammed the bathroom door behind him the moment his uncle came out.

Inside, he sat on the upturned bucket, ashamed and relieved at once.

Where did Tejas end up taking the call?
Tejas ended up on the stairwell, whispering.
What did Tejas feel sitting on the bucket after slamming the door?
He felt ashamed of snapping at his little cousin and relieved to finally have a closed door to himself.
What could Tejas try instead of sulking or slamming doors?
Calmly ask his mother for a regular half hour alone in one room for calls, explaining it is about space, not secrets.
How might his mother see the 'Nobody!' and the slammed door?
She might feel shut out or worried about what he is hiding, not realising he just wants one private call.

Read this:

Monday: Manoj Chacha was drying dishes when Kashish shouted "I hate you!" at her papa over a toffee. Her papa, just back from a double shift, shouted louder: "Then no toffee all week!" Kashish howled. Manoj put the plate down slowly and said nothing.
Thursday: Same kitchen, same toffee tin. "I hate you!" This time Manoj saw his brother's fists close, then open. His brother turned to the window and took a long breath before turning back.
Saturday: Kashish yelled again. Her papa sat on the floor first, breathed, then said quietly, "Still no." Manoj noticed the kitchen stayed calm.

On which day did Kashish's papa shout louder than her?
On Monday, just back from a double shift.
What was Manoj feeling on Monday when he put the plate down slowly?
He seemed uneasy and worried by the shouting, choosing to stay quiet rather than make it worse.
What small step helped Kashish's papa change between Monday and Saturday?
He began to notice his fists and take a breath, even sitting down, before answering her.
What is it like for Kashish's papa when she yells after his long shift?
He is exhausted and hurt by her words, and at first matches her volume before learning to pause.

Read this:

The drought had lasted all June in the village near Bijapur. Pankaj, restless, climbed onto the flat roof and did the silly rain dance his friend Vikas had made up: three stamps, a spin, and a shout. That evening dark clouds rolled in, and it poured. Pankaj ran down, soaked and shouting, "I did it! My dance brought the rain!" The next day he danced again, twice as long. The sky stayed blue. "You didn't dance properly," Vikas said. Pankaj frowned. His grandfather called him over. "The radio said rain was coming on Monday," he said. "You danced on Monday too." Pankaj sat down beside him, thinking. "So it would have come anyway?" "The clouds don't watch you dance, beta."

What did Pankaj's rain dance involve?
Three stamps, a spin, and a shout.
What was Pankaj feeling when the rain came that evening?
He felt thrilled and proud, sure his dance had brought the rain because it came right after.
How did Pankaj's grandfather help him see it differently?
He pointed out that the radio had already forecast rain for Monday, so the rain would have come without the dance.
How does Vikas explain the second day's clear sky?
Vikas says Pankaj didn't dance properly, still believing the dance can cause rain.

metadata.subtype: After this, therefore because of this [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Pranav. It still surprises me that the thing I built in a weekend hackathon is now how our ward books its community hall.
The prototype was ugly: a form, a calendar, a text message confirmation. It won third prize. I nearly forgot it.
Then Noor, the ward's junior engineer, called. The hall register was a mess of double bookings and fights, she said. Could my thing handle it?
It couldn't, not yet. Over four months, we sat in her tiny office after hours. She told me how real people booked: by phone, through the corporator's office, sometimes on paper. So I added a paper form that the clerk could type in, reminders for elderly users, and a fair way to handle clashes.
Last week a bride's mother called to thank the clerk. There hasn't been a double booking since March.

What did Noor say the hall register was?
She said it was a mess of double bookings and fights.
How does Pranav feel about the hackathon project now?
Pranav feels surprised and proud that a nearly forgotten weekend project became something the ward depends on.
What was the most important change Pranav made, and why?
Adding a paper form for the clerk and reminders for elderly users, because it fit how real people actually booked.
How does Noor's view help turn the idea into something real?
Noor knows how people really book the hall, so she helps shape the prototype into a system that works for everyone.

Read this:

Imran had been dating Anirban's cousin for a year, but the one who never said how he felt was Anirban, his closest friend since school. When Imran lost his job, Anirban came over every evening with food, fixed his broken fan, and sat with him. But he never said 'I'm sorry' or 'That's hard'. Imran started to feel it as coldness. One night in the Kolkata flat, he said, 'Do you even care? You never say anything.' Anirban set down the screwdriver. 'I'm here every day.' 'You don't say what you feel.' Anirban frowned. 'I don't know how to say it. My family never did. I feel it. It just doesn't come out as words.' Imran looked at the fixed fan, the food, the screwdriver. Maybe he'd been listening for the wrong language.

What did Anirban fix in Imran's flat?
The broken fan.
What was Imran feeling before he spoke up?
Imran felt hurt and shut out, taking Anirban's lack of words as coldness.
What could Imran do now to understand Anirban better?
Imran could notice Anirban's actions as care, and gently help him find words without demanding them.
How might Anirban feel when accused of not caring?
Anirban probably felt hurt and confused, since he had shown up every day.

Read this:

In the Class 4 room at the government school in Moradabad, Varun Sir wrote a sum on the board. "Seventeen laddoos, five children, share equally. How many each? How many left?"
Zeenat stared at it. The numbers kept sliding around in her head.
So she drew five smiling faces in her rough notebook, and seventeen small dots below. She gave one dot to each face, drawing a line from dot to face. Another round. A third.
She counted. Each face had three dots. Two dots at the bottom had no lines.
She put up her hand. "Three each, Sir. Two left over."
Varun Sir looked at her page. "Can you show everyone how you did it?"
Zeenat blushed, but she carried her notebook to the front.

How many faces did Zeenat draw?
She drew five faces in a row.
How did Zeenat feel when Varun Sir asked her to show everyone?
She felt shy and a bit embarrassed, since she blushed, but also proud enough to carry her notebook to the front.
What else could Zeenat try with bigger numbers, where drawing every dot takes too long?
She could draw groups, like bundles of five, or use the drawing only to check a division she has worked out.
How might the other children in the class be affected when Zeenat shows her drawing?
Children who also find numbers slide around in their heads may find the picture method easier to follow.

metadata.subtype: Approach: draws a picture of the problem to think through it [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

"So? How's day one, madam architect?" Reena asked.
"Reena, I'm hiding in the stairwell."
"What? Why?"
"Everyone is so confident. In the morning meeting they kept saying FAR and setbacks and model coordination, and I just nodded like a dashboard doll."
"You studied five years of this!"
"Not like this. A girl who joined last year was arguing with the partner. Arguing! I can't even find the printer."
"But you're happy you got it?"
"Of course! When they gave me my ID card I wanted to take a selfie with it." Himani laughed, then went quiet. "I keep thinking they'll realise they picked the wrong person."
"Himani, they interviewed you three times."
"Maybe they were tired the third time."
"Go back in. Ask someone where the printer is. That's your only task today."
"...Okay. The printer. I can do the printer."

Where is Himani hiding?
In the stairwell.
What does Himani mean by 'they picked the wrong person'?
She feels anxious that her selection was a mistake, even while she is excited and proud to have the job.
Why is Reena's suggestion about the printer a good one?
It turns a huge worry into one small, doable task, getting Himani back to her desk and talking to colleagues.
What is it like for Reena on this call?
Reena is amused but supportive, trying to calm Himani's panic with reminders and one tiny task.

Read this:

Supervisor's note, Tuesday, packing floor. Friction between Ganga and Jeevan over the loading bay has been building for a week, and the rest of the shift has started taking sides. Tonight Ganga asked me to sit in while she spoke to him. She was calm and specific: 'When the pallets are left in bay two, I lose twenty minutes moving them, and I feel my work is invisible.' Then she asked, 'What's stopping you from clearing it?' Jeevan said the forklift is booked until ten, so he has nowhere to put them. Neither of us knew that. Ganga suggested bay four for the overflow, and Jeevan agreed as long as someone signs the log. Salim from the other crew offered to check the log at shift change. I will put the bay-four rule on the board tomorrow and review it with all three next Tuesday.

Why couldn't Jeevan clear bay two?
The forklift is booked until ten, so he had nowhere to put the pallets.
What was Ganga feeling about the pallets left in bay two?
She felt frustrated and unseen, saying she lost twenty minutes moving them and felt her work was invisible.
What did Ganga do that turned a week of friction into a fix?
She named the specific problem and its effect on her, then asked what stopped Jeevan, which uncovered the forklift issue and led to the bay-four plan.
How might the rest of the shift, who had been taking sides, be affected by tonight's talk?
They see the conflict settled with a shared rule, so they no longer need to pick a side, and Salim even becomes part of the solution.

metadata.subtype: Resolving conflict with facts and feelings [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

The glass vase lay in pieces in the Nagpur drawing room. Tauji stood over Chetan, ten, his voice filling the flat. "Careless boy! Running inside like a goat!" Chetan had not run. His cousin Imran had knocked it with a cricket bat and gone upstairs. Chetan's throat burned. He looked at the floor and said nothing. Talking back to Tauji was not done, not ever. Mummy made him say sorry. He did, quietly.
That night, when his little sister took his pencil, Chetan shouted at her until she cried. He kicked his school bag across the room. Mummy came in. "What's wrong with you today?" He turned to the wall. Upstairs, he could hear Imran laughing at a cartoon. Chetan lay awake a long time, hot and hard inside, thinking about Tauji's finger pointing at him.

Who actually knocked the vase?
His cousin Imran, with a cricket bat.
Why did Chetan shout at his little sister that night?
He was holding in hurt and resentment from the unfair scolding, and it burst out at someone smaller.
What could Mummy do to help Chetan now?
She could sit with him calmly, ask what really happened with the vase, and let him tell it without calling it talking back.
How might his little sister have experienced Chetan's shouting?
She was probably frightened and confused, not knowing that his anger was really about Tauji.

Read this:

You asked how I got calmer in quizzes, Naveen? My speech used to race. In the quiz round I'd say the whole answer in one breath, like a train with no brakes, and then blank at the end. I'm Farhan, and my nerves were so loud I couldn't hear myself. You told me, "You sound like a train." I laughed, but it helped. So I practised: breathe out first, then speak, then stop at every full stop. Just stop. It felt slow, almost silly. But halfway through the next quiz my hands weren't shaking. The steadier pace made me feel calmer, not just sound it.

What did Naveen say Farhan sounded like?
Naveen said Farhan sounded like a train.
What was Farhan feeling when the speech raced in quizzes?
Farhan was nervous, and the nerves were so loud that Farhan couldn't hear the words. Racing speech was part of that anxiety.
What could Farhan do before answering a quiz question?
Breathe out first, then speak, and stop at every full stop. A steadier pace helps Farhan feel calmer as well as sound calmer.
How might Naveen's train comment have felt to Farhan?
Farhan laughed, so it landed lightly, and it helped Farhan see how the speech sounded. It was said as a friend.

Read this:

The college auditorium had been decorated with the old batch photo blown up huge on the stage, and Kishore stood under it holding a paper cup of juice. Five years since graduation. Around him, the talk moved fast. Hansa had just come back from a master's in Berlin. Two friends had a startup with an office. Someone showed wedding photos, someone else a new car key. "And you, Kishore? Still at the bank branch?" Hansa asked, kindly enough. "Yes," he said, and heard how small it sounded. A month ago he'd been proud of his promotion to assistant manager. Now it felt like standing still while everyone else ran. He laughed at the right moments and clapped for the slideshow, but his chest felt tight. On the drive home, he didn't turn the radio on.

Where had Hansa just come back from?
Hansa had just come back from a master's in Berlin.
How did Kishore feel when he answered Hansa's question?
Kishore felt small and suddenly behind, with a tight chest, although he had been proud of his promotion a month ago.
What could help Kishore after this reunion?
He could remind himself what he valued about his own path and talk honestly with a friend, remembering that a reunion shows others' highlights, not their whole lives.
How might Hansa have meant the question about the bank branch?
Hansa probably meant it kindly, as simple catching up, without realising how it landed after all the talk of degrees and startups.

Read this:

It was wedding season in the small town, and at every function the band played the same new film song. The first time Tenzin heard it, at his cousin's mehendi, he wrinkled his nose. "It sounds like a cat." His cousin Bidisha laughed. By the third wedding, he found himself humming it on the way home. By the fifth, he knew all the words. At the last function in February, when the band started it, he jumped up to dance before anyone else. Bidisha raised her eyebrows. "The cat song?" "It's the best song," he said. He wasn't sure when he'd started loving it. He'd just heard it so many times that it felt like his.

Where did Tenzin first hear the song?
At his cousin's mehendi.
How did Tenzin's feelings about the song change?
He went from disliking it to loving it, feeling happy and excited enough to dance first.
What does this show Tenzin about why he likes some things?
That sometimes liking grows from hearing something many times, not only from how good it is.
How does Bidisha see Tenzin's change of heart?
Bidisha is amused, teasing him about "the cat song" when he jumps up to dance.

Read this:

Sunday night. My daughter Irawati came home with a new phrase, "that's so mid", and a new circle from art class, Meher and Ishaan and a girl everyone calls Sunny. They hummed a song I have never heard. At lunch I laughed and said, "Mid? Like middle?" Her fork stopped. She took her plate to her room. I felt stupid. Tonight I knocked and asked her to teach me three of the new words. She rolled her eyes, but she taught me, and then told me Meher does funny voices and Ishaan draws maps of imaginary towns. Note to self: ask, do not mock. She is still the same girl. — Sangeeta

Which phrase did Irawati bring home?
Irawati brought home the phrase "that's so mid".
What was Sangeeta feeling after Irawati took her plate to her room?
Sangeeta felt stupid and regretful about having laughed; the knock on the door that night shows a wish to repair it.
What did Sangeeta do that opened the conversation, and why did it work?
Sangeeta knocked and asked Irawati to teach three new words, which shows interest instead of ridicule and lets Irawati be the expert.
What might it have been like for Irawati when Sangeeta laughed at "mid" in front of everyone at lunch?
Irawati probably felt embarrassed and dismissed, which fits stopping the fork and leaving the table; a new identity is easily hurt by mockery.

metadata.subtype: Sudden shifts in taste and friends [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

At five, Sarika spilled the milk jug, and Mridul's voice shot up, face hard, arms flung wide. "Look what you've done! Every day!" Sarika froze with wet eyes and later asked in a small voice, "Do you still love me?" Mridul crouched down and softened. "I love you. The milk spilled. Let's wipe it up together." Sarika sniffed and took the cloth.

At nine, Sarika forgot the homework, and Kalyani, the class teacher, said in front of everyone, "This is the third time." Sarika stared at the floor with knotted hands and said nothing at all. Kalyani's first thought was that Sarika did not care. After class, though, Kalyani crouched by the desk. "About the homework. What got in the way? Let's make a plan." Sarika's shoulders came down. "The bus was late and my bag stayed at Nani's," Sarika said, and the two wrote a reminder on a card.

What did Sarika ask Mridul after the milk was spilled?
Sarika asked, "Do you still love me?"
How did Mridul at five and Kalyani at nine first react to Sarika, and what helped each time?
Mridul shouted and Kalyani spoke up in front of everyone, leaving Sarika frozen or silent; each then got through with a calm talk about the milk or the homework and a plan, not about Sarika's worth.
What was Sarika feeling when asking, "Do you still love me?"
Sarika was frightened and unsure, afraid the anger meant losing Mridul's love.
How could Kalyani handle a forgotten-homework moment better next time?
Kalyani could speak privately from the start, name the behaviour, ask what got in the way and agree on a fix without a public remark.

Read this:

Snow had closed the playground, so Class R stayed in for circle time in Leeds. Mrs Clarke passed round the talking stone. "Only the one holding it speaks." Hiroshi held it carefully and told everyone about his snowman. Abebe called out, "Mine was bigger!" and rolled onto his back, kicking. "Abebe, it's Hiroshi's turn." Abebe kicked harder. Mrs Clarke moved beside him and said quietly, "The stone comes to you next." Abebe sat up, arms folded, and waited, staring at the stone.

What did Mrs Clarke pass round at circle time?
The talking stone.
What does Abebe kicking harder after being reminded suggest?
It suggests he felt frustrated and impatient about waiting for his turn to share.
What did Mrs Clarke do that helped Abebe settle?
She moved close, spoke quietly, and told him he would have the stone next.
How might Hiroshi have felt when Abebe called out during his turn?
Hiroshi may have felt interrupted, perhaps a little hurt that his snowman story was cut off.

On the bench outside the tea shop in the small town, after Class 10 tuition, Anand held up his phone. “Everyone's using AI for the essays. Half of 10-B. So it's fine.”
Ishita frowned. “Sir said the assignment has to be your own.”
“Sir doesn't know how many do it. If everybody does, that's basically the rule.” He liked that sentence and repeated it in his head all the way home. He pasted the prompt, submitted the answer and felt good. Then Ishita's essay, stumbling and honest, got 7 marks and his got 9 for no effort of his own, and he felt a small, unpleasant pinch. He shrugged it off. Later, when the teacher asked him to write two lines on the topic in class, he found he couldn't.

What did Anand say about the rest of the class?
Anand said everyone is using AI for the essays, half of 10-B.
What might Anand's small pinch mean?
Anand may feel uneasy and a little guilty, sensing it is not fair that his effortless answer beat Ishita's honest one.
What could Anand do differently?
Anand could follow the school's rule, use AI only to explain ideas and write the essay himself, since a crowd's habit does not change fairness or his own learning.
How might Ishita feel about the marks?
Ishita may feel frustrated or unfairly treated, since Ishita's honest work earned fewer marks than an answer with no effort.

metadata.subtype: Approach: reasoning that everyone does it [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Note on the fridge, for Abbu to read when he gets home
I watched something nice today. Tanvir's final exams start Monday, and at lunch he said to Zoha, "You can take my computer hour for the next two weeks. I have to study anyway." Zoha looked shocked, then asked, "And after?" Tanvir said, "After, you give me back a few days. It'll balance." They sat together at the chart and changed two weeks of names in pencil. I didn't have to say a word. I've put a star on the chart and promised both of them a family film night when exams finish, so the trade feels like a win for both. Please praise them at dinner.
- Ammi (Vidya)

When do Tanvir's final exams start?
They start on Monday.
How did Zoha feel when Tanvir offered his computer hour?
Zoha looked shocked at first and then asked about afterwards, which suggests surprise and a careful kind of pleasure.
What else could help keep the trade fair after exams?
They could mark on the chart exactly which days Zoha gives back, so no one has to remember the deal.
How does the trade look to Ammi?
Ammi is pleased and proud, noting that she did not have to say a word, and adds a reward for both.

metadata.subtype: Approach: changing the plan when exams come [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Swati's ear had been aching for a week when Simran Masi came to stay at their flat in Lucknow. 'Warm mustard oil with garlic at night,' Masi said, patting her cheek. 'It's nothing, beta. We never went to doctors for such small things.'
It felt good to hear. Masi's voice was so sure, and the clinic meant taking leave from her new office job. So every night Masi warmed the oil, and Swati said the ache felt a little better, because she wanted it to.
By the third week she could barely hear on that side, and chewing brought a sharp pain. On Monday she finally went to an ENT clinic. The doctor examined her ear, asked about the oil, and said she should have come sooner; treatment would now take longer.
At home Masi was quiet. 'I thought I was helping,' she said.
'You were being kind,' Swati said. 'I just needed kind and a doctor.'

What remedy did Simran Masi suggest?
Warm mustard oil with garlic at night.
Why did Swati go along with the oil for so long?
Masi's certainty felt comforting and Swati wanted it to be nothing, so she felt reassured instead of checking.
What could Swati have done while still respecting Masi?
Thanked Masi and booked a clinic visit anyway once the ache kept going; kindness and a check-up can go together.
How does Simran Masi feel when the truth comes out?
Quiet and regretful, having meant only to help, and perhaps hurt that her reassurance delayed care.

metadata.subtype: Approach: rely on a home remedy from a relative instead of a check-up [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

“Five minutes, Mummy, just five minutes!” Kishore called, crayon already moving over the paper. The school bus came at 7:40, and it was 7:25. His mother Swati kept an eye on the clock while she packed the tiffin. The sun took three minutes. Then the mountains needed a river, and the river needed a boat with a flag, and the flag needed all the colours. At 7:38 the bus honked. Kishore looked up, astonished. “Already?” he said, and meant it. He grabbed the drawing, still wet in the corners, stuffed his shoes on the wrong feet and ran down the stairs with the picture smudging against his shirt.

What time did the school bus come?
The school bus came at 7:40.
Why was Kishore astonished when the bus honked?
Kishore sincerely believed only five minutes had passed and felt surprised and a little shocked that the time had run out so soon.
What could Kishore and Swati try tomorrow so the drawing does not collide with the bus?
Set a timer for the drawing, or start earlier, and decide which part gets finished before the bus.
How might Swati feel watching the clock while packing the tiffin?
Swati is likely anxious about the bus and patient with Kishore at once, since the promise of “five minutes” was sincere but unreliable.

Read this:

Sunday night.
Told the band today that I'm leaving after the Diwali gig.
I've been thinking about it for months. I love them, but with my new job I miss half the practices, and I hate being the one who's always late with new songs. It's not fair to them.
I almost just stopped replying to the group, the way Karan did last year. We never really forgave him.
Instead I asked Trisha to meet me for coffee first, since she started the band. I said it straight: I'm leaving, it's my schedule, not anyone's fault. I'll play the Diwali gig, all four songs, and I'll help teach my parts to whoever replaces me.
She was quiet, then said, "Honestly, I guessed. Thank you for telling me properly."
Then I told the rest at practice. Nobody was angry. Rohit asked if I'd come to the gig after that as audience. I said yes.
I'm Himani, and this is the first time I've left something without feeling like I ran away.

After which gig is the narrator leaving the band?
After the Diwali gig.
How does Himani feel about the way this ending went?
Himani feels relieved and at peace, for once not feeling like running away.
What did Himani do that made this a clean exit?
Himani told Trisha first and in person, gave an honest reason without blame, committed to the Diwali gig and offered to teach the parts.
How did Trisha react to the news?
Trisha was quiet but grateful, saying she had guessed and thanking Himani for telling her properly.

Read this:

"Papa, why can everyone run and I can't?" Parveen asked, as her father, Tushar, lifted her into the car after the park.
"Your legs work differently from theirs. That's why you have your wheelchair. It helps you get around."
"But they were playing tag."
"You were sad you couldn't catch them?"
Parveen nodded. "A bit."
"That makes sense. But guess what I saw? I saw a girl catch the ball every time Rohit threw it. Even the tricky ones."
Parveen smiled. "I caught them all."
"You did. Tomorrow, a catching game?"
"And I'll win."
"Maybe!"

What did Parveen catch every time?
She caught the ball every time Rohit threw it.
How did Parveen feel when the others played tag?
She felt a bit sad and left out because she couldn't catch them.
What did Tushar do that protected Parveen's self-worth?
He gave a simple honest answer, named her sad feeling and then reminded her of her catching skill.
How might Tushar feel hearing Parveen's question?
He may feel a pang of sadness for her but wants to answer calmly and truthfully so she feels proud, not less.

Read this:

"Look at this!" Omkar held the phone out across the canteen table. "The constable told me to move my bike and I said, 'Do what you want.' Look at the views!"
Hemant watched the clip twice. Part of Hemant wanted those views too.
"You should try it next time we get stopped," Omkar said. "Just act bold."
"Weren't you scared? Your voice went up at the end."
"A bit."
"That's what I'm thinking about," Hemant said. "Staying calm would've taken more nerve. If it goes wrong, nobody in the comments walks into the station with you."
Omkar shrugged and pulled the phone back. "Maybe." But the phone stayed face down for the rest of lunch.

What did Omkar say to the constable, according to the story?
Omkar said, "Do what you want."
What does Hemant feel while watching the clip, and how can you tell?
Hemant feels a pull to copy; the passage says part of Hemant wanted those views too, yet Hemant asks about the fear in Omkar's voice.
What could Hemant say next time a friend pushes to film a stand-off?
That staying calm and safe matters more than views, and that the comments will not help if things go wrong.
How might Omkar feel about Hemant's comment?
A little defensive but also thoughtful; admitting "A bit" and leaving the phone face down suggest the words landed.

Read this:

Dear Devika didi,

Something happened at the education fair today and I need your advice before Papa gets home.

A man at a stall said his college gives a "hundred per cent guaranteed job" after the hotel management course. He showed photos of students in suits. Then he said there are only three seats left at the special rate and I must pay a deposit today, or I'll lose it. He kept pushing a form at me and saying, "Decide now, beta, your future is waiting."

I almost called Papa to send the money. My heart was racing. But something felt off. Why would a real college need an answer in ten minutes?

I took the brochure and said I'd come back. He looked annoyed.

Can you check if this college is real and recognised? You did your course in Pune, you'd know. I'll also ask the career counsellor at school tomorrow. I'm not paying anything until we all look at it together.

Love,
Aditi

How many seats did the man say were left at the special rate?
He said there were only three seats left at the special rate.
What was Aditi feeling when the man pushed the form?
Aditi felt pressured and nervous, with a racing heart, and almost called Papa to send money.
Which choice worked, and why?
Taking the brochure, leaving, and asking Devika didi, Papa and the school counsellor to check worked, because it slowed things down and brought in trusted people.
How might Devika didi feel reading this letter?

On the eighth, at the Andheri station ticket counter, his card was declined. His sister Lavanya, a year older, was with him. She paid for both tickets without a word.
On the train she said, 'I'm not lecturing. But what if you park the stipend in my account for a while, and for every buy over a thousand, you wait two days?'
Tushar stared at the tracks flashing by. 'Deal. Can I still have biryani?'

At the Andheri station ticket counter.

Monday. At school in Bhopal, an older boy offered Wasim a sheet of shiny dinosaur stickers. "Fifty rupees." Wasim gasped. Fifty was a lot. He only had twenty in his pocket.

Wednesday. Wasim asked his sister Sunaina for money. "He'll give it for thirty now! I bargained!" He was so proud. Twenty whole rupees less! Sunaina frowned. "Thirty for one sheet of stickers?" "It was fifty!" Wasim said. She gave him ten, still frowning.

Saturday. At the stationery shop near the market, Wasim saw the same dinosaur stickers on a hook. The price tag said ten rupees. He stared. He counted on his fingers. He had paid thirty. He felt his face go hot. "But he said fifty," he whispered to Sunaina. She put an arm around him. "That's why he said fifty first."

How much did the stickers cost at the stationery shop?
Ten rupees.
Why did Wasim feel proud paying thirty rupees?
The first price of fifty stuck in his mind, so thirty felt like a big win, even though it was still too high.
What could Wasim do next time someone names a price?
He could check the price in a shop first, or ask Sunaina, before deciding if a deal is fair.
How does Sunaina seem to feel when Wasim sees the ten-rupee tag?
Sunaina seems sympathetic and gentle, putting an arm around him instead of saying 'I told you so'.

Explain what happens in these Ramayana verses in plain English, as a short summary.

Then spoke the hermit pious-souled:
"Rama, dear son, the bow behold."
Then Rama at his word unclosed
The chest wherein its might reposed,
Thus crying, as he viewed it: "Lo!
I lay mine hand upon the bow:
May happy luck my hope attend
Its heavenly strength to lift or bend."
"Good luck be thine," the hermit cried:
"Assay the task!" the king replied.
Then Raghu's son, as if in sport,
Before the thousands of the court,
The weapon by the middle raised
That all the crowd in wonder gazed.
With steady arm the string he drew
Till burst the mighty bow in two.
As snapped the bow, an awful clang,
Loud as the shriek of tempests, rang.
The earth, affrighted, shook amain
As when a hill is rent in twain.
Then, senseless at the fearful sound,
The people fell upon the ground:
None save the king, the princely pair,
And the great saint, the shock could bear.

Rama opens the chest and lifts the great bow that no one else could manage. When he draws the string, the bow snaps in two with a terrible crash, the earth shakes, and nearly everyone falls down. Only the king, the two princes and the sage stay standing.
Why do some songs get stuck in my head?
Catchy tunes have simple, repeated patterns that the brain remembers easily. Repetition and a rhythm you can predict make a song easy to replay in your mind.
How do I get rid of one?
There is no sure method, but many people find that listening to the whole song, or humming a different tune, helps. Keeping your mind busy with a task also helps it fade.

That night Camila couldn't sleep. She asked herself: am I proud because we built something good, or because I need to be the best one? The next morning she found Hana by the lockers. By the lockers.

She apologised, credited Hana's work and accepted Hana's correction about the code without collapsing.

I'm Yusuf, and my twin sister Yamini spent the whole of last summer interviewing people. That's how it looked to me, anyway.

It started with our cousin Farah, who's a chartered accountant. Yamini sat with her at Eid lunch with a small notebook, asking about "a normal day". Then she went to see the architect who designed our building's new wing. Then she knocked on the door of Mrs. Joseph, our neighbour, a nurse at the district hospital.

Every time she came home, she'd write in two colours. I peeked once. Green: "likes solving puzzles for clients". Red: "boring: filing returns", "stressful: night shifts", "architect says clients change their minds endlessly".

I don't know what she decided inside her head. But by the end of summer, she'd crossed out one career and circled another twice.

What did Yamini write in red?
"boring: filing returns", "stressful: night shifts" and "architect says clients change their minds endlessly".
What might Yamini have been feeling as she wrote in two colours?
She seemed curious and determined, wanting an honest picture of each job, not just the good parts.
What else could Yamini ask in her next interview?
She could ask what training each person needed and what they wish they had known at her age, to plan her next steps.
How did Yamini's summer look to Yusuf?
To Yusuf it looked like a string of interviews and colour-coded notes, though Yusuf does not know what Yamini decided inside.

"You've been sitting on these steps for an hour." Chaitanya looked up. Pradeep, from the room next door in the hostel block, stood there holding two paper cups of canteen chai. "How did you know?" "Saw you from the window. Here." Chaitanya took the cup. "My grandmother called. Everyone's at home for the festival. I'm just... here." "Yeah." Pradeep sat down one step below. "Want to talk?" "Not really." "Okay." They drank. A crow hopped near. "Same time tomorrow?" Pradeep asked. Chaitanya looked at him. "You'd come again?" "Every day of the festival, if you want." Chaitanya felt something in his chest unknot. "Yeah. I'd like that."

What was Pradeep holding when he came to the steps?
Two paper cups of canteen chai.
What does Chaitanya feel when his chest unknots?
He feels relief and safety, sensing that someone cares about him while he is away from home during the festival.
What choice made Pradeep's kindness work so well?
Pradeep brought chai without being asked and accepted 'not really' without pushing, then offered to come every day, which made the care feel dependable.
How might Chaitanya's grandmother feel if she knew about Pradeep?
She would likely feel relieved and comforted that someone was looking out for her grandson while the family celebrated without him.

The storm had been blowing for two days when Pista the cat slipped out through the torn window net. Samir, nine, pressed his nose to the glass. "She'll be back tomorrow. Cats always come back." His older sister Mehak bit her lip. The lanes were flooded to the ankle. "Maybe. We could also make posters, just in case." "We don't need posters. She'll come." Next morning Samir ran to the door with the milk saucer. The step was wet and empty. He waited there through breakfast and lunch while the milk went cold. At four he came inside and cried so hard he hiccupped. "You said maybe," he whispered. "I did," Mehak said, sitting down beside him. "Now let's make the posters. Together." He nodded and fetched the crayons.

How did Pista get out of the house?
She slipped out through the torn window net.
How did Samir feel when he found the step empty?
He felt crushed and heartbroken after being so sure; he waited all day and then cried until he hiccupped.
How did Mehak make room for both hope and reality?
She said "maybe" instead of promising, suggested posters just in case, and sat with Samir when his certainty broke.
What was it like for Mehak when Samir said posters weren't needed?
She was probably worried, knowing the flooded lanes made it uncertain, but she did not want to crush his hope.

Sunday. Taught Manoj chess again today. Three weeks ago I had to point out every hanging piece: "Your bishop! Your knight! Check your queen!" Today I kept quiet on purpose. He spotted two threats before I could open my mouth, and he only looked at me once, like he was checking I was still there. I sat on my hands. Honestly it's hard. I want to help, and part of me likes being the one who knows. But Nani did the opposite with me and carrom: she called every shot for me till I was twelve, and I still freeze when nobody's guiding me. And once I left Manoj alone with a puzzle way too hard, and he cried and didn't play for days. So: fewer hints, but I stay at the table. - Dhruv

Two threats.

Six months into the job, I started a document called "Facts". It was Varun's idea. He had heard me say, for the third time, "I have no idea why they hired me," and said, "Pallavi, write down what you've actually done. Not how you feel. What happened." So I did. Shipped the onboarding flow, two days early. Client email: "clearest demo we've had." Fixed the invoice bug nobody else could find. Asked for the analytics project and got it. Last Thursday, after a rough review, the old thought came roaring back: you're a fraud, they'll find out. Instead of arguing with the feeling, I opened the document and read it slowly, like evidence in a court case. The feeling didn't vanish. But the thought looked weaker next to eleven facts. I added a twelfth that night.

What did Pallavi call the document?
"Facts".
How did Pallavi feel after reading the document last Thursday?
The anxious feeling didn't vanish, but Pallavi felt steadier, with the fraud thought looking weaker next to eleven facts.

It tests the thought against facts a doubting mind can accept, instead of fighting a feeling with another feeling.

I still waste time. Less now. And I've stopped laughing at planners.

Esther sat cross-legged on the sofa in Accra while her flatmate Ada made tea. "Say it aloud," Ada said. "What is the worst that happens if you report the false expense claims?"

"They freeze me out," Esther said slowly. "My manager gives me a bad review. Lunch alone. Someone whispers that I am not a team player."

"Then what?"

"Then I keep copies of my own appraisals and targets, in my own folder. I save the HR contact's number. And I keep three months of salary untouched, just in case." She wrote the list down.

"Do you still want to report it?"

Esther exhaled. "Yes. But now I know what to do if it goes badly."

What did Esther plan to keep in her own folder?
Copies of her own appraisals and targets.

Thursday.
Irfan presented the budget today, and halfway through I realised I wasn't listening either. I was answering a supplier on my laptop. When he asked me a question, I had to say, "Sorry, say that again?" He repeated it politely, but I saw his jaw tighten.
I looked around. Everyone else was typing too. We'd been in the room for fifty minutes and hadn't decided anything.
That's on me. I'm the team lead. I set the tone.
So tomorrow I'm sending a short note: from next week, our meetings are 25 minutes, laptops shut, phones in bags, one person takes notes on paper. If something isn't worth 25 minutes of full attention, it can be an email.
And I'll apologise to Irfan first thing. He deserved better.

In my new class, a few girls laughed. "Leela, you're like a traffic policeman!" I started keeping my hands in my lap. My stories came out flat.

A traffic policeman.

Kunal, you ask how I managed when my mother fell ill. I was twenty-five, newly married, and just promoted.

Amma had a stroke that winter. I wanted to do everything myself: leave early, sleep at the hospital, cancel work. In two weeks I was snapping at your aunt Mala and falling asleep in meetings.

My sister Rekha stopped me. "You're not the only child," she said. So we sat down with paper: I took doctor visits and bills, Rekha took mornings, our younger brother took Sundays. Mala said she would do Amma's hair every evening, because Amma always liked it neat.

The part I'm proudest of? Amma couldn't use her right hand well, but she still chose her own saris each day, even if it took twenty minutes. We waited. It was her life.

That's what your old Chetan Mama learned: share the load, and let the person stay themselves.

What did Mala offer to do every evening?
Mala offered to do Amma's hair every evening.
How did young Chetan feel in the first two weeks of Amma's illness?
Chetan felt overwhelmed and exhausted, snapping at Mala and falling asleep in meetings from trying to do everything alone.
What turning point in the story changed how young Chetan handled the care?
When Rekha said he wasn't the only child, they split tasks on paper among the siblings and Mala.
How might Amma have felt being allowed to choose her own saris?
Amma likely felt respected and still herself, keeping dignity and choice despite her illness.

The engagement guests were due at six, and it was already half past four. Parul, twenty-four, sat on her bed in a new saree she hadn't chosen while her mother pinned flowers in her hair. "Everything is settled, beta. The boy's family is good. You only have to nod." Parul had met him once, for twenty minutes, with six relatives in the room. She didn't know if he wanted children, where they'd live, or whether she could keep her job. Her throat felt shut.
Chandrika masi came in with the tea tray, saw Parul's face and asked her mother to check the kitchen. She shut the door. "Tell me honestly. Do you want this?" Parul whispered, "I don't know him." Masi nodded. "Then you need time. And if the answer is no, no one in this house will punish you. I'll make sure." She went out and told Parul's parents the ceremony would wait.

What time were the engagement guests due?
At six.
How did Parul feel being told she only had to nod?
She felt trapped and frightened, her throat shut, because she barely knew the man and nothing had been asked of her.
What did Chandrika masi do that made real consent possible?
She asked Parul privately, promised she would not be punished for saying no, and got the family to wait so Parul could have time and information.
How might Parul's mother have felt when the ceremony was delayed?

His pen stopped. "The caterer needs a deposit this week. I thought I had a month." He picked up the phone.

She will need to decide on colours sooner than expected, but she can trust that the wedding tasks will be ready on time.

Anirban: Wait, don't start! Listen. Rule one, the ball can't touch the drain. Rule two, you may only hop on the left leg. Rule three, if the ball hits the wall twice...
Yamini: How many rules are there?
Anirban: Twenty. I wrote them all. Rule four...
Tanmay: I forgot rule two already.
Yamini: Me too. My legs are getting stiff standing here.
Anirban: But you need to know them!
Tanmay: I'm going to play kho-kho with the others.
Yamini: Sorry, Anirban, it's too much.
Anirban stood in the colony courtyard holding two pages of rules, and the ball rolled quietly away.

How many rules did Anirban write?
Anirban wrote twenty rules.
What was Anirban probably feeling as the others walked away?
Anirban was likely hurt and frustrated, standing alone with the pages after all the effort of writing so many rules.
What alternative approach could Anirban use, and why might it work?
Anirban could start with three simple rules, play a round, and add rules only when a problem shows up. Friends can remember a few rules, and playing keeps them interested.
How do Yamini and Tanmay see the rule list?
Yamini and Tanmay find it too long to remember and tiring to stand through, so to them the list stopped the fun instead of protecting it.

metadata.subtype: Approach: making many complicated rules before playing [Pitfall]

messages.content: Soften this complaint a little: Your dog is always noisy and it's annoying.
I'm sorry to say it, but your dog is always noisy and it bothers me.

Read this:

For the first year I chased. Whenever my wife, Payal, went silent in a fight, I followed her from room to room: "What's wrong? Talk to me!" louder each time. She'd go to the balcony, then put her headphones on, then leave for a walk. I'm Rafiq, and I felt invisible in my own flat. One night a friend asked, "Does chasing ever work?" It never had. So I tried something else. When she went quiet about my mother's visit, I said once, calmly, "I need us to decide by Sunday. Can we talk after dinner?" Then I made tea. She came into the kitchen at nine. I also told her I won't keep having fights with a closed door. That limit is mine to keep.

Where did Payal go first when Rafiq followed her?
To the balcony.
How did Rafiq feel during the year of chasing?
Rafiq felt invisible and shut out, and grew louder as Payal withdrew further.
What changed, and why did it work better?
Rafiq made one calm, direct request with a time and then gave space, which let Payal come back on her own.
What might it be like for Payal when Rafiq follows her from room to room?
Payal likely feels cornered, so she retreats further to the balcony, headphones and walks.

Monday. Sunaina's phone buzzed: the popular group had tagged her in a photo. Twelve likes in ten minutes. She stared at it, smiling.

Thursday. At lunch Sharmila waved from their old table by the window. Sunaina looked at the group's table, then at her plate. “Tomorrow,” she mouthed, and sat with the others. Someone said, “Isn't that your friend with the weird lunchbox?” Sunaina laughed.

The following Tuesday Sunaina saw Sharmila sitting alone, folding a paper bag into smaller and smaller squares. Something twisted inside her. She turned her phone face-down and kept looking at the group's table anyway.

How many likes did the tagged photo get in ten minutes?
The tagged photo got twelve likes in ten minutes.
What did Sunaina feel on the following Tuesday, seeing Sharmila alone?
Sunaina felt a private twist of guilt and ache, though staying with the popular group still felt important.
What choice did Sunaina make on Thursday at lunch?
Sunaina mouthed “Tomorrow” to Sharmila and sat with the popular group instead.
What might Sharmila be feeling while folding the paper bag into smaller squares?
Sharmila probably feels hurt and lonely, trying to look busy while wondering why Sunaina stopped coming.
Does the toy store open at nine or ten on weekdays?
I don't know the store's hours. Call them or look at the sign on the door.
Say the opposite of "ancient" in a sentence of exactly six words.
The opposite of ancient is modern.

In the school hostel common room, Yash sat with his phone during free period, answering a quiz about which element he was.
"Fire," he announced. "Listen. 'You're driven, but you have a soft side few people see. You'd do anything for the people you love.'" He grinned. "That's scary accurate."
Charu, his classmate, leaned over. "Mine said Water. 'Calm outside, strong feelings inside, loyal to close friends.' Also scary accurate."
"No, fire is different. Fire is more me."
He posted the result in the batch group with three flame emojis and a line: "Now you all know." For the rest of the evening he kept opening the group to see who had reacted.

Which element did Yash's quiz say he was?
The quiz said he was Fire.
What does Yash keep opening the group suggest about how he feels?
It suggests he feels eager and a little anxious for others to accept the result as proof of who he is.
How could Yash check whether the quiz really knows him?
He could compare his result's words with Charu's and notice how both describe hidden feelings and loyalty in general terms.
What might Charu think when Yash insists fire is different?
Charu might feel amused or slightly frustrated, since the Water result said nearly the same things about Charu.

At a Saturday workshop in a community centre in Indore, Tanvir, a software tester, was handed a sheet titled 'What keeps pulling you?' Vinita, the facilitator, asked everyone to list problems they kept reading about or raising without being asked. Tanvir wrote quickly: village school dropouts, water quality in the old city, and, after a pause, lonely elderly neighbours. Vinita's second question was, 'Which of these fit what you can actually do?' Tanvir crossed out the third, since it needed skills Tanvir didn't have, and circled the first. 'I can build simple tools, and I keep thinking about the school in my grandfather's village.' Vinita asked one more thing: 'Whose voices haven't you heard yet?' Tanvir wrote it as the first line under the circle: talk to the teachers.

What was the title of the sheet Tanvir was handed?
The sheet was titled 'What keeps pulling you?'
How did Tanvir feel about the third problem, and why was it crossed out?
Tanvir cared about it, but felt unequipped, since it needed skills Tanvir didn't have.
What other approach could Tanvir use to test the first choice?
Tanvir could volunteer for a month with a local group working on school dropouts, since real contact shows whether the interest lasts.
How might Vinita see Tanvir's choice?
Vinita probably sees a sensible one, joining a real concern to real skills, with a first step of listening to teachers.

Madhuri's diary, Sunday
Everyone in our group cut their hair the same way this week, short and layered. Keerthana said, "You'll look so good, just do it." I almost did. I sat in the salon chair and then said, "Just a trim." I like my long hair. I like my plait. At school tomorrow Keerthana will probably say I'm not part of the look. My stomach hurts a bit thinking about it. But I kept thinking: if I change something I love just to match, what's next? I'm fourteen. I want to figure out what I like before everyone decides for me.

What haircut did the group get?
Short and layered.
How is Madhuri feeling about going to school tomorrow?
Madhuri feels nervous and a little anxious about Keerthana's reaction.
What would you advise Madhuri if Keerthana teases about the plait?
Stay calm, say plainly that Madhuri likes the plait, and remember a good friend will accept that.
How might Keerthana see Madhuri's choice?
Keerthana might feel disappointed that Madhuri didn't match the group, or quietly respect the choice.
Reusing things: one sentence in which no word is longer than seven letters.
We can reuse jars and sort paper from plastic.

(1) Is "suvenir" right?
(2) How can I make a garden at home with little space?
(3) What does "keep your chin up" mean?
(4) My teacher used the word "jubilee". What is it?

1. No, it is "souvenir", with "ou" after the "s".
2. Use pots on a balcony or windowsill, and choose plants like mint, tulsi or chillies. Water them regularly and keep them where they get sunlight.
3. It means to stay cheerful when things are hard. For example: keep your chin up, the next test will go better.
4. "Jubilee" is a noun. It means a special anniversary that people celebrate.

Read this:

The power had gone out, so Mummy, Jaya, was cooking by the light of a lantern. The big pot of dal bubbled on the stove. Nitin crept closer. "Can I touch the pot? It's making funny sounds." "No. Hot pots burn. That's a firm no." Nitin pouted and reached a finger out anyway. Jaya gently moved his hand back. "I won't let you touch it. But you can be my helper." She gave him a small bowl of cold water and a spoon. "Stir the pretend dal." Then she let him hold the lantern while she served. He held it very high.

Why was Jaya cooking by lantern light?
The power had gone out.
How was Nitin feeling as he crept closer to the pot?
He felt curious and excited by the funny bubbling sounds, and didn't understand the danger.
What did Jaya do that is a wise way to handle curiosity?
She set a firm limit about the hot pot and gave him safe ways to help and explore, like pretend stirring and holding the lantern.
How might Jaya feel when Nitin reaches out anyway?
She may feel a quick flash of worry, but she stays calm and moves his hand back gently.
What does St. John Rivers ask Jane to do?
He asks her to marry him and go with him to India as a missionary's wife. Jane refuses to marry him because he does not love her.

Read this:

Rajni pulled up a chair beside Jatin's desk and lowered her voice. "Jatin, you're new, so let me tell you something from my first job. I was twenty-three, a junior at a construction firm. On site, workers signed an attendance register. One month my supervisor asked me to add names of people who hadn't come, so the contractor could claim extra wages. 'Everyone does it,' he said. My hand actually shook holding the pen. I thought of my father, who'd worked on sites for thirty years and never cheated anyone. I told the supervisor I couldn't. He made my life hard for a while: late shifts, cold looks. But the next year, when an audit caught the others, the managing director called me in and promoted me. I'm not saying honesty always gets rewarded, beta. But it lets you sleep."

What did Rajni's supervisor ask her to add to the register?
Names of people who hadn't come to work.
What was Rajni thinking about as her hand shook holding the pen?
She was thinking of her father's honesty and felt torn between pressure from her supervisor and her own values.
What would Rajni advise Jatin to do if he faces a similar request?
Refuse to falsify records, even if it brings short-term trouble, because honesty protects his integrity.
How might Jatin see this story as a new employee?
He may feel warned about pressures he might face and reassured that a senior values honesty over office tricks.

"Swati, look! Snow!" Vishal said, crouching by the window of the Shimla cottage.
Swati, twenty months, turned toward his voice. He pointed outside. She followed his finger and gasped.
"Snow," he said again.
"No!" she said, which was her word for most things.
She pressed her hand to the cold glass and turned to him, eyes huge.
"Cold!" he laughed.
She pointed at a bird hopping on the white ground, then looked at him.
"Bird, yes!"

Where were Swati and Vishal?
At the window of the Shimla cottage.
How did Swati feel when she saw the snow?
She felt amazed and excited, gasping with huge eyes.
What is Vishal doing that supports Swati's learning?
He points, names what they see together, and answers when she points, sharing her focus.
What is it like for Vishal to share Swati's first snow?
He feels delighted and warm, laughing and naming things with her.

(1) My teacher used the word "veranda". What is it?
(2) What is a good way to learn a poem by heart?
(3) how can I keep my books from getting torn
(4) Why is a library kept quiet?

1. As a noun, "veranda" means a roofed platform along the outside wall of a house.
2. Read it aloud a few times, one line at a time. Then say it without looking and check the lines you missed.
3. Cover them with plastic or paper and pack them carefully. Do not stuff the bag too full.
4. A library is kept quiet. Because people there are reading and thinking, and noise breaks their attention.

Put this in plainer words.

Evening light came through the courtyard of the house in Sangli. Indu stretched for the tin rattle on the wooden rack, missed, stretched, missed. Then she sat down hard on the floor and whimpered. Parveen aunty, sorting rice by the step, watched. Indu looked around, found Amma at the stove, crawled over and pointed up at the rack. Amma wiped her hands, lifted the rattle down, and Indu shook it happily.

Evening light came into the courtyard of the house in Sangli. Indu reached for the tin rattle on the wooden rack, missed, reached, missed. Then she sat down hard on the floor and whimpered. Parveen aunty was sorting rice by the step and watched. Indu looked around, found Amma at the stove, crawled over and pointed up at the rack. Amma wiped her hands and lifted the rattle down, and Indu shook it happily.

Community lead's note, parents-of-toddlers forum, Monday. Yogesh has moderated our forum for six months and looks exhausted. This week a member, Kashish, posted a product link in a thread about sleep. Yogesh removed it under Rule 4, no selling. Kashish accused Yogesh of bias, because a similar post had stayed up last month, when a different moderator was on duty. Twenty members joined in, half defending Kashish, half defending Yogesh. Yogesh messaged me at midnight: 'Whatever I do, someone's angry.' We agreed on three things: pin Rule 4 with examples, apply it the same way to the older post, and write a short public note explaining the decision. We also set moderator shifts, so Yogesh isn't online after ten. Kashish replied to the note: 'Fair enough.'

Which rule did Yogesh use to remove Kashish's post?
Rule 4, no selling.
How was Yogesh feeling at midnight?
Yogesh felt exhausted and stretched, frustrated that whatever the decision, someone was angry.
What changes protect both Yogesh and the members?
Pinning Rule 4 with examples, applying it equally to the older post, explaining the decision publicly, and setting shifts so Yogesh isn't online after ten.
How might Kashish see the removal at first?
Kashish saw it as bias because a similar post had stayed up earlier, and felt singled out until the rule was applied equally.

The school Diwali mela was packed, and Yamini's class had ten minutes to sell the last diyas before closing. As she counted coins, Anand called across the stall, "Yamini, is it true you're repeating Class 5?"
Heads turned. Yamini's cheeks burned. It was true. She had been ill for months last year and missed too much.
For a second she wanted to lie. Then she looked straight at him. "Yes, that happened. I was ill. It's private, so let's not talk about it here."
Anand shrugged. "Oh. Okay." A girl beside him nudged him to be quiet.
Yamini went back to counting coins. Her face was still warm, but the whispers had nowhere to go.

How long did the class have to sell the last diyas?
Ten minutes before closing.
How did Yamini feel when Anand asked in front of everyone?
She felt ashamed and exposed, her cheeks burning, and was tempted to lie.
Why did owning it calmly work for Yamini?
By saying it happened, that it was private and asking to stop, she left the rumour with nothing more to feed on.
How might Anand feel after Yamini's answer?
Anand seems a little awkward and drops it, since there's no drama to chase.

Creche note, Monday. When her mother left this morning, Hafsa watched the door close. Her lower lip turned down and began to tremble, and her eyes filled. I picked her up before the crying started, held her close and sang the washing song softly. She cried for a little while into my shoulder, then went quiet and watched the others. By snack time she was playing. Baljeet, creche teacher

What did the teacher sing to Hafsa?
The washing song, softly.
What did Hafsa's trembling lip show she was feeling?
It showed sadness at her mother leaving, perhaps with some worry; the filling eyes and later crying confirm she was upset.
Which of Baljeet's choices worked, and why?
Picking Hafsa up early and singing softly worked, because closeness and a gentle voice helped her calm down enough to watch and then play.
How might Hafsa's mother feel reading this note?
She would likely feel relieved and reassured that Hafsa was comforted quickly and was playing by snack time. 🙏

On Tuesday, Rekha came home from work and Charu, two, raised both arms until she was lifted, then rested her head under Rekha's chin. On Thursday an uncle visited and asked for a kiss; Charu shook her head and hid her face. "High five?" said Rekha. Charu slapped his palm and giggled. On Sunday Charu climbed onto Rekha's lap with a picture book and cuddled in, turning the pages herself.

What did Charu do on Tuesday when Rekha came home?
She raised both arms until Rekha lifted her, then rested her head under Rekha's chin.
What might Charu's shaking her head at the uncle suggest, and what else could explain it?
It suggests she did not want a kiss from him, though she was happy to join in when the choice was a high five. She might also have been tired or shy after the day.
What did Rekha model by offering a high five?
Rekha showed Charu her no would be heard, and gave the uncle another way to say hello. 🙂
How might the uncle feel about the high five?
He may feel relieved to have another way to connect, and understand that Charu is simply not ready for kisses.

Read this:

Dear Yusuf,

It's been three weeks since Abbu. I'm writing because every time we talk, we end up hurting each other.

When you went back to the shop two days after the funeral, I thought you didn't care. I said so, and I'm sorry. Last night Ammi told me you sit in his chair at the counter after closing, in the dark. I didn't know.

Maybe you think I'm dramatic. I cry at the dhaba where he used to take us, at the smell of his attar, at nothing. I think we're both grieving; we just do it differently.

So, a question, not an accusation: how are you managing, really?

And a memory, because I keep thinking of it: Abbu teaching us to count change with his old brass coins, you always cheating.

The papers about the shop can wait. Let's not decide anything until the first wave of this has passed.

Your sister,
Hafsa

How long after the funeral did Yusuf go back to the shop?
He went back to the shop two days after the funeral.
What did Hafsa feel when she learned Yusuf sits in Abbu's chair after closing?
Hafsa felt sorry and softened, realising his quiet was his way of grieving and that she had misjudged him.
What makes Hafsa's letter a good step between the siblings?
She apologises, asks how he is coping, shares a memory, and delays the shop papers until the first wave of grief has passed.
How might Yusuf have felt when Hafsa said he didn't care?
Yusuf probably felt hurt and misunderstood, since he was grieving privately in the dark shop.

At the government school in Indore, the weekly spelling test came back on Friday. Gautam, nine, had six out of twenty. He shoved the paper into his desk. "Nikita Ma'am gives me the hardest words," he told his bench-mate. "She reads fast when it's my row." Nikita Ma'am, walking past, heard. She crouched beside him. "Gautam, which words did you practise this week?" He shrugged. "None. It doesn't matter. Some weeks I'm lucky, some weeks not." "Last month you practised with your sister and got fourteen, remember?" Gautam frowned. "That was a good day." He picked at the edge of the desk. It had not occurred to him that the good day and the practice might be the same thing.

What did Gautam score on the spelling test?
Six out of twenty.
Why does Gautam call the fourteen 'a good day'?
Gautam feels discouraged and sure results come from luck or Ma'am's speed, so even his best score seems like chance rather than something his practice caused.
What could Nikita Ma'am do next to help Gautam link practice and marks?
Start a simple weekly chart of words practised and marks, so Gautam can see the practice and the fourteen side by side.
How might Nikita Ma'am feel hearing that she reads fast for his row?
She may feel a little stung but more concerned, seeing that Gautam believes his marks depend on her rather than on his preparation.

In the lunchroom of the school on Maple Street, Amara slid a folded note along the table: "Don't sit with Gabriel. Pass it on." It moved from hand to hand. When Gabriel came with his tray, the chairs next to Amara's group were suddenly saved. He stood there, then sat at the end near the bins. Amara laughed a little too loudly at something Chloe said. It felt good, everyone following her note. Safer, too. Last week Chloe had whispered with Lily all through art, and Amara had spent the whole lesson wondering if she'd be next. Now nobody would leave her out; she was the one deciding. Anyway, Gabriel had copied her maths answers once, she told herself. He probably deserved it. She didn't look at the bins end again.

What did Amara's note say?
"Don't sit with Gabriel. Pass it on."
What was Amara afraid of before she started the note?
After Chloe whispered with Lily all through art, Amara worried about being the next one left out.
What could Amara do the next time she feels that fear, instead of passing a note?
She could tell a friend or a teacher she felt left out in art, dealing with her own worry instead of pushing it onto Gabriel.
What is lunch like for Gabriel, sitting near the bins?
He probably feels humiliated and confused, not knowing why the chairs were suddenly saved.

Why should we switch off the lights when we leave a room?
And what is the difference between "few" and "a few"?
Then, what is the plural of "tomato", "tomatos" or "tomatoes"?
I keep seeing "unavoidable" in my reading. Meaning?

1. It stops us wasting power and money. Because a light uses electricity all the time it is on, even when nobody is there.
2. "A few" means some, which is a small but useful number. "Few" means almost none, so it sounds negative.
3. It is "tomatoes". Many nouns ending in "o" take "-es".
4. Unavoidable is an adjective that means impossible to avoid.

Monday: Gopika walked Santosh through the new invoicing system in ten fast minutes: codes, approval steps, the vendor portal. Santosh nodded at every step, though he'd lost the thread by the second screen. Asking felt like admitting he wasn't smart enough.
Wednesday: He processed thirty invoices with the wrong approval code. Accounts bounced all thirty back, and Gopika spent her lunch hour helping him undo them. She wasn't angry, just tired. "Why didn't you say you were stuck?"
The following Monday: Gopika started explaining the quarterly report template. This time, after the first screen, Santosh raised a hand. "Can I say where I am? I'm clear on pulling the data. I'm not clear on which column the regional totals go in. What I need is one example filled in." Gopika smiled and opened last quarter's file. "That's the most useful question I've had all week."

How many invoices did Santosh process with the wrong code?
Thirty invoices.
Why did Santosh keep nodding on Monday?
Santosh felt embarrassed and afraid that asking would show he wasn't smart enough, so he faked understanding.
What did Santosh do differently the following Monday, and why did it help?
He said what was clear, what wasn't, and exactly what he needed, one example, so Gopika could help precisely before any mistakes.
How did Gopika experience Wednesday's mistake?
Gopika felt tired rather than angry, losing her lunch hour to undo the invoices and wishing Santosh had said he was stuck.

metadata.subtype: Confusion and lack of knowledge at work [Expressing]

messages.content: Did the local football club sign a new player this month?
I don't know, because I can't see this month's club news. The club's official page or notice board would announce signings.

I'm Keerthana, Jahnavi's roommate in Hyderabad. Last month I noticed Jahnavi making phone calls and taking notes.
She was booking a preventive health check-up. Her mother had diabetes, and a doctor had told her to keep an eye on it. She compared two clinics, asked which tests her insurance covered, and chose one nearer the metro.
On the day, she went early, came back and filed the reports in a blue folder with her old records.
When I asked why, she said, "I want to understand my health before something goes wrong."
I don't know if she was worried or just organised. But I booked mine the next week.

Where did Jahnavi file the reports?
In a blue folder with her old records.
What might Jahnavi have been feeling while booking the check-up?
Jahnavi may have felt a little worried because of her mother's diabetes, but mainly calm and responsible.
What steps did Jahnavi take that others could copy?
She compared clinics, checked insurance coverage and kept her reports organised.
How does Keerthana see Jahnavi's check-up?
Keerthana isn't sure of Jahnavi's feelings, but finds the example useful enough to book her own.

Friday, hostel room, 11 pm
Okay. Writing this down so I can't pretend tomorrow. The mess office has sent me three notices about unpaid dues since August. I didn't open the last two. I saw the first one was bigger than I thought and just shoved the others in my drawer under my socks. Out of sight = fine, right?
Not fine. Today the mess manager stopped me at the counter in front of everyone and said there's now a late fee on top. My face burned.
Jasleen found me sulking and made me open the drawer. We read all three together on her bed. It's bad but not impossible. I'm calling Papa tomorrow morning and asking to pay it off in two parts.
Next time a notice comes, I open it the same day. With chai, maybe. 😅
Alka

Where did Alka hide the mess notices?
Alka shoved them in the drawer under the socks.
What did Alka want to avoid feeling by not opening the notices?
Alka hoped that keeping them out of sight would keep the worry away; not opening them felt easier than seeing a bigger number.
What small step has Alka planned?
Calling Papa tomorrow morning to ask about paying in two parts, and opening any new notice the same day it arrives.
How does Jasleen help, and what might Jasleen be feeling?
Jasleen makes Alka open the drawer and reads the notices together, probably feeling caring but firm, not wanting a friend to keep sinking deeper.

Ten minutes before the maths exam, Chinmay was in the school sick room again, curled on the bed, holding his stomach. The counsellor, Joseph, came in and pulled up a stool. "Is this the same feeling as before the science test?" Chinmay nodded. "And the thing at assembly?" Chinmay winced. Three weeks ago he had tripped on the stage steps, and he still went red thinking of it. Joseph handed him a card with faces drawn on it. "Point to the loudest one. Scared? Embarrassed?" Chinmay pointed to both. "Okay. One small step: sit the first section only, then come and tell me how it went. And if these stomach aches keep coming, we'll talk to your parents about the doctor." Chinmay stood up slowly. He finished the whole paper.

What did Chinmay trip on three weeks ago?
He tripped on the stage steps.
Why did Chinmay wince when the assembly was mentioned?
He was still embarrassed, replaying the trip weeks later.
What small step did Joseph suggest, and how did it turn out?
Joseph suggested sitting only the first section and reporting back; Chinmay finished the whole paper.
How might Chinmay's classmates see his visits to the sick room?
They may not realise how strongly he feels things, and could think he is just avoiding exams.

The conference slot was in forty minutes, the college projector kept flickering, and Payal was still fixing slides when Dr Aparna Iyer swept into the seminar room. For a year Payal had called her "the only real scientist in this department" and kept a photo of her lecture notes on her phone.

Aparna glanced at the screen. "Your graph is misleading. Fix the axis or don't show it." Then she left to find a working cable.

Payal's face burned. By the time Aparna came back, Payal had decided: she was cold, she'd always been cold, she only mentored students who flattered her. Payal messaged a friend: "Worst guide ever. Can't believe I worshipped her."

She fixed the axis anyway, fingers shaking, because it was, annoyingly, misleading. The talk went well. Aparna nodded once from the back row. Payal refused to look.

How long was it until the conference slot?
The conference slot was in forty minutes.
Why did Payal suddenly decide Aparna was "always cold"?
Payal felt stung and embarrassed under time pressure, and because Aparna had been idolised, one sharp comment flipped her into a villain.
What could Payal try after the talk?
Payal could admit the comment was harsh but useful, since fixing the axis helped, and ask Aparna for feedback at a calmer moment.
How might Aparna see Payal's refusal to look at her?
Aparna may be puzzled, having meant the comment as a quick fix under time pressure and then nodding approval.

Naveen had been in bed with flu for three days in their Chennai flat, and his thoughts felt as if they were wading through syrup. When Karthik called about the group project, Naveen listened to his idea of changing the topic and exploded. "Fine, do whatever you want. I don't care about the stupid project!" He hung up and threw the phone onto the blanket. Ten minutes later he was staring at the ceiling, ashamed and worried: what if the others dropped him? What if he failed the term? His mother brought him rasam and found him close to tears. "You're sick, kanna. Everything looks worse right now. Don't settle anything today." The next evening, feeling a little better, he called Karthik back. "Sorry about yesterday. Your topic's actually good. Can we talk properly when I'm back?"

How long had Naveen been in bed with flu?
Three days.
How did Naveen feel staring at the ceiling after hanging up?
He felt ashamed and anxious, worried the group would drop him and he would fail the term.
What made the second call go better?
Waiting until he felt better meant he could think clearly, apologise, and see that Karthik's topic was good.
How might Karthik have felt when Naveen hung up?
Karthik was probably hurt and confused, having only suggested an idea.
