Read this:

Under the guava tree behind the village school near Mathura, Nandini and Yusuf, both five, shared one guava: bite and pass, bite and pass.

On the way home Nandini stopped at the roadside shrine where Dadi lit a lamp each evening. She held the half-eaten guava up to the stone Hanuman. "For you!"

"Nahi, beti," Dadi said, gently catching her wrist. "For God, only what nobody has bitten. That one is jootha."

Nandini looked at the guava, then at Yusuf, puzzled. "But it's still good."

"Good for you two. For God, we give fresh." Dadi took a whole guava from her bag, and Nandini placed it very carefully.

What did Nandini hold up to the stone Hanuman?
She held up the half-eaten guava.
Why was Nandini puzzled when Dadi called the guava jootha?
Nandini felt confused, because to her a shared, bitten guava was still good; she follows the rule without yet understanding it.
How did Dadi handle the moment gently?
She caught Nandini's wrist softly, explained simply that offerings are fresh, and gave her a whole guava to place herself.
How might Yusuf see the moment at the shrine?
Yusuf may feel curious or puzzled too, since sharing the guava had been perfectly normal for them both.

Read this:

Omar ran the bike-repair workshop's small team in Kraków, and review week had come round again. Ivan was the obvious star: fastest mechanic, customers asked for him by name, and he made everyone laugh during the long winter shifts. Last year Omar had given him top marks everywhere without really thinking.
This year Omar printed the form with four separate lines: repair quality, speed, teamwork, paperwork. For each, he asked two colleagues for one real example, good or bad.
The examples surprised him. Repair quality and speed were outstanding. Teamwork was mixed: Ivan helped newcomers but sometimes took the best jobs for himself. Paperwork was weak; three warranty claims had been sent back for missing details.
When they met, Ivan was taken aback. "Paperwork? I thought I was your best guy."
"You are, at repairs," Omar said. "The rest I've scored on what people saw. Here are their examples."

How many warranty claims had been sent back for missing details?
Three warranty claims had been sent back for missing details.
Why was Ivan taken aback by his review, and what does it show about his expectations?
Ivan felt surprised and a little hurt, because being the obvious star with top marks last year made him expect a high rating on everything, including paperwork.
What did Omar change in the process this year, and how did that help?
He split the form into four lines and asked two colleagues for a real example for each, so outstanding repairs did not automatically lift teamwork and paperwork.
How might the newer colleagues see the fairer review process?
They may feel reassured that ratings rest on what people actually saw, not on who is funniest or fastest, which makes their own reviews feel fairer too.
My budgie sleeps with his head tucked in his feathers. Is something wrong?
That's normal. Many birds sleep with their head turned back and tucked under a wing. It keeps them warm and comfortable.
Okay. I was worried.
It's kind of you to notice. If he seems sleepy all day, puffed up or stops eating, ask a vet who treats birds. Otherwise, sleeping like this is part of his routine.

Read this:

Thursday

Dear Diary,
A new boy called Lokesh joined our class today. He walks with crutches. At break everyone stared, and Manav said loudly, "What's wrong with your legs?" Lokesh went red and looked at his shoes.
Mrs. Fernandes heard. She said, "Manav, if you're curious, you can ask Lokesh kindly if he'd like to tell you. And nothing is wrong with him. His body just works in its own way." Then she started a game of pass-the-ball in a circle so everyone could play.
Lokesh was really good at it. I didn't talk to him today, and I feel a bit bad about that. Tomorrow I'm saving him a seat at lunch.

Afreen

What game did Mrs. Fernandes start?
She started a game of pass-the-ball in a circle so everyone could play.
How does Afreen feel about not talking to Lokesh?
Afreen feels a bit guilty about it and plans to make up for it by saving him a seat at lunch.
How did Mrs. Fernandes turn the moment around?
She showed Manav a kind way to be curious, said difference is not something wrong, and chose a game that included Lokesh.
What was it like for Lokesh when Manav asked about his legs?
It was embarrassing for him, which is why he went red and looked at his shoes.
We ordered a birthday cake for my daughter and it arrived stale. Write a polite complaint to the bakery, about 45 words, and ask for a replacement or refund.

Dear Sir or Madam,
We ordered a cake from your bakery for my daughter's birthday. It arrived stale, and we were very disappointed. I request you to either replace the cake or give us a refund. Thank you for your attention.
Yours faithfully

Read this:

The rains were late in their village near Akola, and Tejas stayed in the fields long after dark. His wife Jaya, heavy with their first child, noticed he barely ate and answered in grunts. At the chai stall he laughed with the others when they teased him about becoming a father, then walked home silent. One night on the charpai, Jaya said, "You've disappeared. Where have you gone?" For a while Tejas said nothing. Then it came out: the crop loan, whether the cotton would fail, whether he could be a better father than his own, how he would miss evenings with his friends. "I didn't want to burden you." Jaya took his hand. "I'm scared too. Tell me. Don't vanish." They decided to ask his brother for help at harvest, and Tejas promised to come to the next check-up at the health centre.

Where did Tejas and Jaya talk that night?
On the charpai.
Why did Tejas keep his worries to himself?
He felt pressured and afraid about money and fatherhood, and did not want to burden Jaya, so he tried to seem strong.
What choice helped, and why?
Tejas sharing his worries with Jaya; it let them plan together, with his brother's help at harvest and his promise to come to the check-up, instead of him withdrawing.
How was Jaya affected by Tejas going quiet?
She felt him slipping away and worried, which is why she asked where he had gone.
Agenda items should be short, so trim this: Discussion about the problems with the printer in the office.
Problems with the office printer

Read this:

Thursday night

Long day. At the market stall this morning I kept thinking about what the design adviser told me last week: "Switch all your pottery to matte glaze, it sells better." A week ago I would have just done it. Today I actually rang and asked why. Answer: in the city galleries, buyers want a modern look. Fair. But my buyers are tourists and local families who pick up mugs to use every day. So after lunch I called Payal, who has made pottery near the lake for years. She said matte shows tea stains faster, and her customers complain. Interesting! So here's my plan: matte for the decorative bowls, glossy for everyday mugs. I'll put six of each on the stall on Sunday and see what goes. Feeling clearer than I have all month. Manjula, you're learning.

Who did Manjula call after lunch?
Payal, who has made pottery near the lake for years.
How is Manjula feeling at the end of the entry?
Manjula feels clearer and more confident than all month, even a little proud: "Manjula, you're learning."
Which other approach could Manjula use to test the plan?
Ask a few regular buyers directly which finish they prefer, alongside the Sunday test with six of each.
How might Payal see being asked for her view?
Payal probably felt respected that her years of experience with local customers were valued.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asks for the reasoning and checks it against a second source [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Wasim was the only hearing person at Tanvir's birthday dinner in a Pune café. Tanvir's Deaf friends signed fast across the table, laughing, and Wasim tried to join in by waving his hands and pulling faces, the way he might play charades. Tanvir's sister Farah watched him, amused but tired. Then Wasim noticed something. When Farah told a story about two friends, she set one to her left and one to her right in the air, and later just pointed back to those spots instead of repeating them. Her face changed with every line. It was like watching someone keep a map as they spoke. Wasim put his hands down. He typed on his phone and turned it to Tanvir: "I've been acting things out. That's not how it works, is it? Can you show me how to say happy birthday properly?" Tanvir grinned and taught him.

Where was Tanvir's birthday dinner?
In a Pune café.
Why did Wasim put his hands down during Farah's story?
He seemed to feel embarrassed and newly respectful once he saw she was using space and her face like a grammar; he may also have been simply fascinated.
What small step helped Wasim connect with Tanvir?
He admitted he had been acting things out and asked Tanvir to show him how to sign happy birthday properly.
How might Farah see Wasim's charades-style waving?
She watched it amused but tired, which suggests she has seen hearing people treat signing as loose gestures many times.

Read this:

At five, Nilesh clung to Mummy Nandini's leg outside the wedding hall and would not say hello to the aunties. "Say namaste, beta," someone urged. He tightened his grip. Mummy crouched down. "We'll stand by the pillar until you feel ready." Nilesh stayed there with his cheek against her side, and by the time the music started he was peeking around the pillar at the dancers.
At fifteen, Nilesh held a folded paper of practised sentences in his pocket. He had rehearsed the answer to a question about the poem for two hours, and when the teacher asked it, he lowered his eyes and said he did not know. He skipped the school trip and the science club party. His friend Zeenat noticed and asked, "Do you want to come and sit with us at the canteen?" Nilesh nodded but did not come. That evening Mummy sat with him and said gently, "This looks like a big worry, and I think someone who helps with this could make it lighter. Shall we talk to the school counsellor together?"

How long had Nilesh practised his answer about the poem?
He had rehearsed the answer for two hours.
How is Nilesh's behaviour at the wedding hall like, and unlike, his behaviour in class at fifteen?

At the wedding hall Nilesh clung to Mummy Nandini's leg and stood by the pillar until he was ready. At fifteen he rehearsed sentences for hours, lowered his eyes and skipped the school trip and the science club party, so the fear of embarrassment shrank his life and Mummy suggested the school counsellor.
What was Nilesh feeling when he lowered his eyes and said he did not know the answer?
He felt afraid of embarrassment, so even though he had practised the answer, he could not risk saying it.
How could Zeenat keep supporting Nilesh?
Zeenat could keep inviting him without pressure, sit with him where it is quiet, and let him join at his own pace.
The committee "watered down" the rule. What does "water down" mean?

To water something down means to make it weaker, either by adding water or by changing it so that it has less force.
Example: The committee watered down the rule so that more students could take part.

Read this:

You asked about my internship? Okay. I'm Nilesh, and the one moment I'm proud of was a question.
Our demo for the client crashed. In the meeting afterwards, the whole team piled on Nitin, the youngest. “Nitin pushed the code.” “Nitin didn't test it.” The manager nodded along. It was almost a relief in the room, like we'd found the answer.
I remembered we'd all agreed to skip testing to meet the deadline. All of us. The manager too.
So I asked, quietly, “If it's all Nitin, what are we not talking about?”
Silence. Then someone said, “The deadline.” And someone else, “We skipped testing together.”
Nitin looked up for the first time. The meeting became about fixing the process, not him.

What did the team agree to skip?
They'd all agreed to skip testing to meet the deadline.
What was Nilesh feeling before asking the question?
Nilesh felt uneasy, sensing the room's relief at blaming Nitin was hiding a shared mistake.
Why did Nilesh's question shift the meeting?
It named the pattern quietly and let others admit the shared cause, so the focus moved from Nitin to the process.
How might Nitin have felt when he looked up?
Nitin likely felt relieved and less alone after being piled on as the youngest.

metadata.subtype: Asking who really benefits from blame [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

It was 1 am, three days before the board exams, and Farida should have been asleep. Instead she was scrolling the school's anonymous confessions page, where someone had posted an unflattering photo of Sachin tripping at sports day. Two hundred comments already. Everyone was piling on. Farida's thumb hovered. Sachin had once corrected her in front of the class, and she had never forgiven him. She typed something mean about his walk and hit send. No name, just a cartoon avatar. For a second it felt like nothing, one more voice. Then she read it back, and it looked like something a stranger had written. But it was hers. She deleted it at 1:04 and lay awake. In the morning she messaged Sachin under her real name: 'I said something cruel on the page last night. I'm sorry. I've reported the post.'

How many comments did the post already have?
Two hundred comments.
How did Farida feel when she read her comment back?
Farida felt uneasy and ashamed, realising the cruel words were hers even behind a cartoon avatar.
What did Farida do that helped undo some of the harm?
She deleted the comment, apologised to Sachin under her real name and reported the post.
How might Sachin feel reading two hundred comments?
Sachin would likely feel overwhelmed and humiliated, mocked by many faceless people at once.

metadata.subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Joseph. In our family, every son goes to the seminary after Class 12. My grandfather went, my uncle went. So when the parish priest asked me last year, I said yes straight away. It felt settled. I didn't have to think.
My friend Shalini asked me once, "Do you actually want to be a priest?"
I said, "Of course." It came out automatically.
But lately I sit in church and feel nothing much. Not bad. Just flat. I watch Shalini argue about books she loves, and I don't know what I love.
I haven't said anything to anyone. My certainty came from never questioning it. Now I'm not sure it's mine.

Where does every son in Joseph's family go after Class 12?
Every son goes to the seminary.
How does Joseph feel sitting in church lately?
He feels flat and empty, not bad, but unsure whether his certainty is truly his own.
What could Joseph do to explore without dishonouring his family?
Talk quietly with a trusted adult, perhaps the priest or a counsellor, about his doubts, and try other interests before committing.
How does Shalini seem to see Joseph's choice?
Shalini seems curious and a little doubtful, asking whether he actually wants it.

metadata.subtype: Foreclosure under family or community pressure [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The café was packed, the project was due at nine the next morning, and Pradeep and Deepika had four slides left. Deepika's vocal tic, a short "hup," came every few seconds, louder when she was stressed. A man at the next table turned and glared. Pradeep didn't look at him or at Deepika's mouth. He kept pointing at the laptop. "This graph needs a title. What about 'Water use by ward'?" Deepika nodded. "Hup. Yes. Good." They finished at eleven. Walking out, she said, "That guy was staring." Pradeep said, "I noticed. Does it bother you when people do that?" "Sometimes. Thanks for just carrying on." "Always," he said.

What title did Pradeep suggest for the graph?
He suggested 'Water use by ward.'
How did Deepika feel about Pradeep carrying on with the work?
She felt grateful and accepted, thanking him for just carrying on despite the man's stare.
What did Pradeep do that made Deepika feel accepted?
He ignored the tic, kept working on the slides and only talked about it when Deepika raised the staring, asking how it felt for her.
How might Pradeep feel when Deepika thanks him?
He likely feels glad and a little moved, answering "Always" to show he will keep treating her the same way.

Read this:

Dear Lavanya,

You'll laugh, but I finally understood what Miss Kurian meant about buffers.

Our Science Day assembly was supposed to open with a talk by a scientist from the university. At 9:00 she messaged: bus broke down, reaching by 9:45. I had 300 students on the ground and nothing planned for forty-five minutes.

My brain froze for about ten seconds. Then I grabbed the quiz team and asked them to start early. After the quiz I moved the model display forward and let kids walk around it. By the time the scientist arrived, people were still excited.

At our review, Aman said we should always keep fifteen spare minutes and one filler item ready. He's right. I'd been so proud of a tight timetable that I forgot tight means fragile.

Write soon,
Trisha

How many students were on the ground?
There were 300 students on the ground.
How did Trisha feel in the first moments after the message?
Trisha felt panicked and frozen for about ten seconds before recovering enough to act.
What lesson does Trisha take from the review, and why does it matter?
Trisha learns to keep fifteen spare minutes and a filler ready, because a timetable with no slack breaks as soon as one person is late.
How might the waiting students have seen the morning?
They probably saw a lively morning with a quiz and models, not a delay, so they stayed interested until the scientist came.

metadata.subtype: Approach: adapting when things go wrong on the day [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Jasleen, you asked why I get so serious when your friends joke about vaping. When I was sixteen, it was cigarettes behind the bus depot. First only on Saturdays with the boys. Then Saturdays and Wednesdays. Then most days. If anyone asked, I had my answers ready. 'I can stop whenever I want.' 'Look at Bittu, he smokes twice as much as me.' I said it so often I believed it. Once I tried to stop for a week, just to prove it, and lasted two days. I told myself two days proved I could. That is how clever the mind gets when it doesn't want to look. It was my Nani who finally asked me, calmly, 'What does it do for you, beta?' I had no quick answer. That question sent me to the school counsellor. So yes, your Abhinav mama knows those lines by heart."

Where did young Abhinav smoke?
Behind the bus depot.
Why did young Abhinav keep comparing himself with Bittu?
He was uneasy about his own pattern, and the comparison let him feel safe instead of looking at it.
What turning point came inside the story?
Nani calmly asked what smoking did for him, which left him without a quick answer and sent him to the school counsellor.
How might Nani have felt when asking that question?
Nani was probably worried but chose calm curiosity over anger, hoping he would answer honestly.

Read this:

"Shankar, the deadline was Friday. Where's the report?" Jyoti asked, in front of the whole team.
"Waiting on your figures, Jyoti. Like always."
"Like always? I sent them Wednesday!"
"Incomplete. Again."
"You could have said that on Wednesday instead of saving it for today."
"And you could have checked your own work."
The team lead cleared her throat. "Let's take this offline."
"Fine," Jyoti said. She stood and walked out, cheeks hot.
"Fine," said Shankar, to the closed door. He sat back down and opened the report file, still half empty. The team lead looked at the ceiling. Nobody else moved.

When did Jyoti say she sent the figures?
On Wednesday.
What was Jyoti feeling as she walked out?
She felt embarrassed and angry, her cheeks hot, sure Shankar had disrespected her in front of the team.
What turning point does "Let's take this offline" offer?
A private conversation, perhaps with the team lead, where both can look at the timeline instead of trading blame.
What might Shankar be experiencing as he says "Fine" to the closed door?
He is probably angry and defensive too, feeling blamed publicly and just as sure she broke the respect.

Read this:

In the district town of Sagar, Mohit managed the software rollout for a mid-sized hospital. On Thursday he learned that go-live would be three weeks late. The lab machines' data wasn't matching the new system, and fixing the connection would take time.
He had to tell the hospital administrator, Dr Ritu, on Monday. His first impulse was to call right away and just say "delay". He stopped himself. She'll ask why. She'll ask when. She'll ask what it means for patients.
So he spent Friday preparing. The cause, in one sentence: the lab machines send results in an older format. The new date: 14 August. And two ideas to soften the blow: keep the old lab system running in parallel until then, and move the outpatient module live on the original date, since it didn't depend on lab data.
On Monday, Dr Ritu listened, frowned, then said, "Thank you for coming with a plan." They chose both options.

What was the new go-live date?
The new date was 14 August.
What was Mohit thinking when he stopped himself from calling right away?
He was anxious and thinking ahead, knowing Dr Ritu would ask why, when and what it meant for patients.
What else could Mohit prepare for such a meeting?
He could prepare a short written note of the cause, date and options to leave with Dr Ritu, so the hospital staff can plan too.
How does Dr Ritu see the way the news was delivered?
Dr Ritu is unhappy about the delay but appreciates that Mohit came with a plan, not just bad news.

metadata.subtype: Approach: preparing facts, cause and options first [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Amara wrote it on the back of her maths notebook during study hall, words for her friend Selin. Start small: "Lately you seem really down, and I'm worried about you. Can I sit with you?" She whispered it to the bus window, then again to the mirror at home. What if Selin gets angry? Then: "Okay, no pressure. I'm still here." What if Selin goes silent and stares at the floor? Then wait, don't fill the quiet, and say, "We don't have to talk right now." What if nothing works? Then tell Mrs Okafor, the school nurse, tomorrow. She read the list twice, folded it into her pocket and found Selin by the lockers, heart thudding, hoping the words would come out the way they sounded at home.

Where did Amara write her plan?
Amara wrote it on the back of her maths notebook during study hall.
What was Amara feeling as she went to find Selin?
Amara was nervous: her heart was thudding and she hoped the words would come out the way they sounded at home.
What other step could Amara add if Selin shuts down, and why?
She could do as her list says, leave the quiet and say they don't have to talk now, then tell Mrs Okafor, because a trusted adult can offer help she cannot.
How might Selin experience being approached by the lockers?
Selin might feel surprised, exposed or relieved that someone noticed, and calm words like no pressure leave room to answer.

Read this:

Under the peepal tree near the bus stand, the village children played marbles every evening after the last bus left. Whenever there was an argument about whose marble touched the line, everyone turned to Mohit. He had once given a win to Hafsa's side even though it made his own team lose, and since then they trusted his eyes.
A new boy from the brick kiln, Salim, won three games in a row, but twice his marble seemed to jump forward in the dust. Nobody accused him. They just stopped calling his name.
On Friday Mohit noticed Salim sitting alone and walked over. "Play on my side," he said. "But slow shots, where everyone can see."

Where did the village children play marbles?
Under the peepal tree near the bus stand.
What might Mohit have felt seeing Salim sitting alone?
Mohit probably felt sorry for Salim and wanted to give a fair second chance, knowing being left out stings.
Why is Mohit's offer of "slow shots, where everyone can see" a wise one?
It lets Salim rebuild trust in the open, so others can watch him play fair and start calling his name again.
How do the other children see Mohit?
As fair and trustworthy, because he once gave a win to Hafsa's side even when his own team lost.

metadata.subtype: Being known as fair or a cheat [Actor]

messages.content:
- What does the word "plunder" mean?
- What is a good way to water indoor plants?
- Why do cats' eyes shine in torchlight?
- Help me correct this: Please borrow me your ruler.
- Can you tell the difference between "say" and "tell"?

1. As a verb, "plunder" means to steal goods by force, especially in a war.
2. Water them when the top of the soil feels dry, and pour slowly so the water soaks in. Make sure the extra water can drain away.
3. Their eyes reflect the torch light back. Because cats have a mirror-like layer at the back of the eye, so light that enters bounces out again.
4. Correct form: Please lend me your ruler. Why: "lend" means to give, and "borrow" means to take.
5. "Tell" needs a person right after it, as in "tell me the story". "Say" can follow without a person, as in "say hello".
Mausi ko phone par poochna hai "Aap kab aayengi?" English?
Ask: "When will you come?"

What happens in this? Use three sentences.

Shalini joined Class 6 at the government school in Hazaribagh in July, after her father's transfer. For the first three days she said very little. She sat where the teacher put her and watched. "The girls near the window share tiffin," she noted to herself. "The loud group plays kho-kho, and they only pick fast runners. That girl with the plait reads alone under the peepal tree, but she laughs when anyone passes." On the fourth day she noticed the reader was Hemant's sister, and that Hemant helped everyone with maths. "Maybe start with the tree," Shalini thought. At lunch she walked over with her own book and sat down on the root beside the girl.

Shalini is new in her class and spends three days quietly watching how the other children behave. She notices a girl reading alone under a tree, who laughs when people pass. On the fourth day she takes her own book and sits next to her.

Read this:

Wednesday
At lunch Jatin was ranting because a parcel had gone missing. 'These delivery boys are all thieves. Animals on bikes. Can't trust any of them.' A couple of people nodded. I felt the old urge to just eat my rice and stay out of it. Instead I asked, 'What about Irfan? The one who comes every afternoon?' Jatin stopped. 'Irfan's okay.' 'He carried Mrs Joshi's water cans up four floors last month when the lift was broken. He's doing a correspondence degree; I've seen him reading on the stairs.' Jatin shrugged. 'Fine, Irfan's decent.' 'And the others you've never spoken to?' He didn't answer. After lunch he went down to ask Irfan about the parcel. It turned out to be sitting in reception with the wrong floor number on it.
Small thing. But I'm glad I didn't just eat my rice.
Ayesha

Where was the missing parcel?
It was sitting in reception with the wrong floor number on it.
What did Ayesha feel before speaking up?
Ayesha felt the uncomfortable urge to stay quiet and avoid conflict, but was also uneasy hearing a whole group called animals.
Why did asking about Irfan work?
Naming one real person with a real story made the contemptuous label hard to keep, and it led Jatin to check the facts.
How might Irfan feel if he heard 'animals on bikes'?
Irfan would likely feel hurt and insulted, having carried water cans up four floors for the office.

Read this:

Day one: Hansa clicked a link about an unpaid electricity bill and entered her card details. Within minutes, eighteen thousand rupees was gone. She sat frozen on her bed in her Guwahati flat, face burning. How could she be so foolish? She told no one.
Day two: She almost didn't mention it. But at lunch, her colleague Jatin talked about his aunt who got scammed and recovered part of it by reporting fast. Hansa's stomach dropped. She excused herself, went to the stairwell, and called her bank's official helpline to block the card and dispute the payment. Then she filed a complaint on the national cybercrime portal, with the screenshot of the message and the transaction ID.
Three weeks later: The bank called: part of the money had been frozen and would be returned. Hansa told Jatin, then posted a short warning in her building's residents' group with a picture of the fake message. Four neighbours said they'd received the same one.

How much money was taken from Hansa's account?
Eighteen thousand rupees.
What was Hansa feeling on the first day?
She felt foolish and ashamed, her face burning, and told no one.
What did Hansa do once she stopped hiding the loss?
She called the bank's official helpline to block the card, filed a cybercrime complaint with the screenshot and transaction ID, and warned her neighbours.
How might Jatin feel when Hansa tells him what happened?
Jatin may feel glad his story helped, and sympathetic rather than judgmental about the scam.
The shopkeeper said, "Put your bag on the counter." What does counter mean there?

Here a counter is a long flat surface in a shop, bank or kitchen where goods are sold or work is done. It is a noun. It is not the same as the verb that means to answer or go against something.
Example: She waited at the counter while the baker wrapped the bread.

Read this:

The inspector's car was already turning into the clinic lane, and the power had been off since noon. Sangeeta Ma'am pushed the vaccine fridge log at Lakshmi. 'Three days are blank. Just fill in the usual reading with last week's dates. Quickly.'
Lakshmi's heart hammered. She was eleven days into the job.
'Ma'am, I can't write readings I didn't take,' she said. 'If the fridge was off, the inspector needs to know, for the vaccines' sake.'
'We'll look careless.'
'We can write today's reading now and add a note that the entries were missed and why. And I'll set a phone reminder so it doesn't happen again.'
Sangeeta Ma'am stared at her, then at the car door slamming outside. 'Fine. Write the note. Fast.'
Lakshmi wrote it in her neatest hand, fingers barely shaking.

How many days of the log were blank?
Three days were blank.
What was Lakshmi feeling as she refused?
Her heart hammered because she was new and nervous about refusing a senior, but she was clear she couldn't write readings she hadn't taken.
What made Lakshmi's refusal work under pressure?
She gave one simple reason and offered an honest alternative, today's reading plus a note and a reminder, so her senior had a quick way forward without backdating.
What might Sangeeta Ma'am be feeling as the inspector's car door slams?
She is likely anxious about looking careless and irritated at first, but accepts the note because it is honest, quick and she has little time.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Damini, February
Hemant (10) used to bring his toy car to show everyone. This term he's stopped. He now wears three friendship bands like the other boys and asked his mother for the same pencil box everyone has. When I asked about the car, he said, "Nobody brings toys in Class 5." I told him it was fine either way. He's happier in the group, which is good, but he looked sad when I mentioned the car. I'll set up a hobby show so children can share what they like without worry.

How many friendship bands does Hemant wear?
Three friendship bands.
What does Hemant looking sad about the car suggest?
He may miss sharing the toy he loved, and feel a pang about giving it up to fit in.
Why is Damini's hobby show a good idea?
It gives children a safe, approved chance to share what they like without breaking the class's unspoken rules.
How might Hemant's mother see his request for the same pencil box?
She might feel both understanding and a little worried about how much he wants to fit in.
How do I make a paper boat? Answer in two sentences. The second sentence must start with "Finally".
Fold a square sheet of paper into a small hat and then pull its sides apart. Finally, press the base flat and set your boat on the water.
How do I politely say no to an extra task?
Thank the person for thinking of you, explain briefly what you are already handling, and ask what should take priority. Saying no clearly and kindly is usually respected.
What if I can't say no because of the boss?
Then you can ask which of your current tasks should wait. That shows the time limit without refusing and lets the boss decide what matters most.

Read this:

Eshaan, since you ask what your Masi Ira was like at sixteen: scared. There was a boy in the next row, Vikram, who lent me his ruler in class nine, and I decided that was a sign. For months I rehearsed in the bathroom mirror. "Would you like to..." Every version had a hole in it. I wrote the sentence down and tore it up. Some days I got as far as his desk and asked about homework instead. Then one winter afternoon I saw Vikram walking to the library with Nalini, the two of them sharing one umbrella and laughing. I stood there holding my perfect sentence like a bag of stones. Vikram never knew. I can't say the answer would have been yes. But by never asking, I made sure of the no.

What did Vikram lend Ira in class nine?
Vikram lent Ira a ruler.
What was Ira feeling when Ira saw Vikram walking with Nalini?
Ira felt crushed and full of regret, holding the perfect sentence 'like a bag of stones'.
What could the young Ira have done instead of rehearsing for months, and why?
Ira could have asked once, quietly and simply, accepting yes or no, because a real answer even a no is better than months of waiting.
How might Vikram have seen Ira during those months?
Vikram probably saw a classmate who sometimes asked about homework and had no idea of the feelings behind it, so there was never a question to answer.

metadata.subtype: Approach: never acting due to fear of rejection [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Tuition teacher's note. Ayesha has been putting aside her pocket money for six weeks to buy a toy castle. Today at the shop window she stopped and stood for a long time. "Will I still play with it in a month?" she said quietly. She looked at the picture of the castle stuck on her notebook cover. After some thought she told me, "I think a book series and an art set will last longer." She crossed out the castle and wrote two new lines. I did not push her either way. She seemed calm about it, and took her time. Kalyani, tuition teacher.

How long had Ayesha been saving?
Ayesha had been saving for six weeks.
How did Ayesha feel as she stood at the shop window and changed her plan?
Ayesha felt unsure whether she would still want the castle in a month, then calm about switching; the note says she seemed calm and took her time.
What alternative approach could Ayesha use to test the want, and why?
Ayesha could wait another week and see if she still wants it, or ask a friend how long they played with theirs. Time shows whether a want lasts.
How does Kalyani see Ayesha's choice?
Kalyani watched and chose not to push, so Kalyani sees a child making a calm, thoughtful choice without a grown-up steering it.

metadata.subtype: Approach: changing her mind after thinking again about the want [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the practice match at the district football academy, Nilesh and a defender clashed heads going for the ball. Nilesh sat down hard and didn't get up. Play went on around him. Varun, his teammate, stopped dead, turned towards the coach's bench and made a big T with both hands. “Time out! Nilesh is hurt!” The coach blew the whistle at once and jogged over. Nilesh was holding his forehead, dazed. The coach knelt, checked his eyes, asked him a few questions, then sent him to the medical room with the assistant. Afterwards the coach found Varun. “Good call. That's exactly what the T is for.”

Where did the coach send Nilesh?
The coach sent Nilesh to the medical room with the assistant.
What was Varun feeling when he stopped dead?
Varun was worried and alarmed that Nilesh was hurt and that nobody had noticed.
Why was Varun's time-out an honest use of the signal?
It paused the game to get help for a real injury, which is exactly what the T is meant for.
What might Nilesh have felt sitting dazed while play went on?
Nilesh may have felt confused and alone until Varun's signal brought the coach over.

metadata.subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the crowded family flat in Berlin, two-year-old Zeynep tripped on the balcony step and wailed. Her cousin Felix, nine, was nearest. He scooped her up and bounced her the way he'd seen Babaanne do. Zeynep hiccupped, grabbed his ear and went quiet. When her aunt came out of the kitchen, Zeynep leaned into her arms too, then pointed back at Felix, smiling through wet lashes.

Who was nearest when Zeynep fell?
Her cousin Felix, nine, was nearest.
How can you tell Zeynep felt safe with Felix?
She hiccupped, grabbed his ear and went quiet in his arms, then smiled back at him through wet lashes, calm and comforted.
How could the adults support Zeynep's many bonds?
Let whoever is closest comfort her, as Felix did, and keep the same soothing habits across the family so every face feels familiar.
What is it like for Felix when Zeynep calms in his arms?
Felix probably feels proud and trusted, because copying Babaanne's bounce actually worked.

Read this:

Tarun, you asked why I don't just quit mridangam and play drums in a band like normal people. Fair question. In class nine they called me 'uncle' for a whole term. Someone drew a little mridangam with a walking stick on my notebook. I laughed along, but I went home and didn't practise for two weeks. Then my teacher played a korvai, this pattern that lands exactly on the beat after all these twists, and I felt my whole chest go light. I thought, this is mine. Nobody gave it to me as a costume. So now I practise every evening. The jokes still come sometimes. I'm Nilesh, the uncle, and I'm fine with it.

What did classmates call Nilesh in class nine?
They called Nilesh 'uncle' for a whole term.
What does Nilesh's chest going light suggest about Nilesh's feelings?
It suggests Nilesh felt a deep joy and connection with the rhythm, a sense that the music truly belonged to Nilesh.
What was the turning point for Nilesh?
Hearing the teacher play a korvai reminded Nilesh the music was truly theirs, so Nilesh chose to practise every evening again rather than quit to avoid jokes.
If you were Tarun listening to this, what might you understand now?
Tarun might understand that Nilesh isn't being stubborn; the music means more to Nilesh than fitting in, so the jokes matter less.

Read this:

It was late at the temple fair. Jeevan had missed his afternoon nap. He whined, rubbed his eyes and clung to Pranav's leg. When Pranav said no to a plastic whistle, Jeevan threw himself on the ground, screaming.
"Spoilt boy," muttered a relative.
"He's not spoilt, he's worn out," said Pranav, lifting him. By the time they reached the road home, Jeevan was asleep on his shoulder.

What had Jeevan missed?
His afternoon nap.
What was Jeevan feeling when he threw himself on the ground?
He was overtired and frustrated, not simply spoilt.
Which of Pranav's choices worked, and why?
Reading the meltdown as tiredness and carrying him home worked, because sleep was what he needed.
How does the relative see Jeevan's meltdown?
The relative sees it as spoilt behaviour, not tiredness.

Read this:

At the community centre in Chennai, Jatin sat through the residents' meeting with five-year-old Karthik beside him. After ten minutes Karthik tugged his sleeve.
"Appa, there's nothing to do."
"We'll go soon."
"I'm BORED." He climbed onto Jatin's lap and hung on his neck.
Jatin didn't hand him his phone. He whispered, "I don't know what to do either. What could you do with that paper cup?"
Karthik frowned at the cup. Then he started turning it into a hat. Then a telescope.
By the end of the meeting, he was spying on the committee members through it.

What did Karthik turn the paper cup into?
He started turning it into a hat, then a telescope.
Why did Karthik cling to Jatin's neck?
Karthik felt bored and restless, and didn't yet know how to find something to do on his own.
What did Jatin do that helped Karthik get past his boredom?
Instead of giving his phone, Jatin asked what Karthik could do with the paper cup, nudging him to invent his own activity.
What might Jatin have been feeling during the meeting?
Jatin was likely a little stressed about keeping Karthik quiet, then relieved and amused to see him playing with the cup.

Read this:

Monday: Walking back from class, Yamini told Ramesh she wasn't ready to stay over at his flat. He went quiet, kicked a pebble, then said, 'Okay. Thanks for telling me straight instead of making an excuse.' Thursday: On the sofa watching a film while his flatmates were out, he paused before sliding closer. 'This fine?' She nodded, then added that kissing was fine but she wanted to stop there for now. He said, 'Then that's where we stop.' Later they talked, a bit awkwardly, about how any bigger step would come with a real conversation first and proper protection, and how a clinic visit together would not be embarrassing. The next Sunday: Yamini told her roommate she felt safer with Ramesh than with anyone before. 'He asks. And he listens when I answer.'

What did Ramesh ask on Thursday before moving closer?
He paused and asked, 'This fine?'
How can you tell Ramesh felt disappointed on Monday but still chose respect?
He went quiet and kicked a pebble, which hints at disappointment, yet he thanked her for being honest instead of pushing.
What made their talk about bigger steps a responsible one?
They agreed any bigger step needs a real conversation first and proper protection, and that seeing a clinic together is nothing to be ashamed of, so both stay informed and safe.
What would change for Yamini if Ramesh had argued on Monday?
She might have felt pressured and less safe saying no later; his respect is what built the trust she describes on Sunday.

Read this:

The school van honked twice outside. Ira, four, was still fighting the top button of her uniform, her fingers slipping. "Other children do this in one minute," Zeenat snapped, grabbing the button herself. Ira's arms dropped. She stared at the floor. "I'm a bad Ira. Bad, bad." She didn't pick up her bag. Zeenat stopped. The van honked again. She knelt anyway. "You're not bad. Buttons are hard. Amma was cross because of the van, not you." Ira let out a long breath and reached for her bag.

What was Ira trying to do when the van honked?
She was trying to fasten the top button of her uniform.
Why did Ira say "I'm a bad Ira"?
After her mother compared her to other children, she seemed ashamed, as if failing at the button meant she herself was bad.
What went right after Zeenat stopped?
She knelt, separated the button from Ira's worth and owned her own crossness, which let Ira breathe and move again.
What would change on a morning without the van honking?
Zeenat might have had time to wait or help calmly, and Ira might never have heard the comparison.
When do I write "anyone" and when "any one"?

Write "anyone" when you mean any person. Write "any one" as two words when you mean a single one from a group.
Examples: Is anyone at home? You may choose any one of these books.

Read this:

The Tunga river was high and brown after three days of rain. Behind the temple in their village, four boys stood on the old stone steps.
"Jeevan, jump from the third step. We all did it last year."
The water was moving fast, carrying branches. Jeevan's stomach dropped. "No. Not today."
"Scared?"
"Appa's rule. No river in monsoon. He'll skin me." It was true, and it helped to say it.
"Come on, just once!"
His cousin Alka, sitting on the wall with her slippers off, said loudly, "He said no. Let's go play cricket in Gowda's field before it rains again."
Jeevan grabbed the bat from her. "First innings is mine."
Two of the boys followed straight away. The others grumbled but came too. That evening Jeevan told Appa anyway, and Appa went to have a word with the temple priest about chaining the steps in monsoon.

How many days had it rained?
It had rained for three days.
What was Jeevan feeling when he looked at the river?
Jeevan felt frightened, his stomach dropping at the fast brown water, and also under pressure from the boys.
Which moves helped Jeevan resist the pressure?
He said a clear no, blamed Appa's rule, and with Alka's help suggested cricket instead, and later told Appa, who took a protective step.
How might Alka have seen the boys' pressure on Jeevan?
Alka seemed to see it as unfair and unsafe, which is why she backed up his no and offered another plan.

Read this:

Emil, twenty, had come to the university in Copenhagen from a vocational college, where he had spent two years fixing ship engines. In the first week of linear algebra a classmate joked, "Mechanics take this course twice, right?" Emil laughed, then felt his neck go hot every time a quiz came round.
Before Friday's quiz he walked to the harbour and made himself remember: the engine he had rebuilt after the certified man gave up; why he wanted this degree, to design quieter ferries. A quiz measures what I've practised, he told himself. Not who I am.
In class Dr Priscila Santos handed out the sheets. "This is a map, not a grade. It shows us both what to work on next." Afterwards she sat beside him and went through his two mistakes as if they were interesting.
Emil folded the sheet into his pocket. For once it felt like information.

What had Emil spent two years fixing at the vocational college?
Ship engines.
Why did Emil walk to the harbour before Friday's quiz?
He wanted to calm the hot-necked fear by reminding himself of his past success and why he wanted the degree.
What did Dr Santos do that reduced the threat for Emil?
She framed the quiz as a map for growth, not a grade, and treated his mistakes as interesting rather than as proof of anything.
What would change for Emil if the quiz were framed as a verdict on ability?
His neck would likely go hot again, and the fear of confirming the classmate's joke could crowd out his real skill.
Write a message for our society's group, around 60 words, asking for volunteers to help organise the children's drawing competition on 15 August.

Hello everyone,
We are holding a drawing competition for children on 15 August at 10 am in the clubhouse. We need about six volunteers to help with registration, handing out paper and colours, and keeping the little ones happy. It will take only two hours. If you can help, please reply to this message by Sunday.
Thank you!
Sunita, Cultural Committee

Read this:

Sarika had three weeks to send four drawings for the district art scholarship. Her older cousin had won it once, and everyone at home said, "Your turn now." Sarika kept her sketchbook shut. "The light's bad in the evenings," she told Irawati, which was true: the power in their lane went off most nights. But she didn't draw on bright Sunday afternoons either. She sorted her pencils, watched videos of other artists and said she was waiting to feel inspired. With four days left, the power cuts got worse, and she drew by the torch on Irawati's phone, hurrying, smudging the charcoal. She sent the drawings at midnight. "At least if they reject it," she said, "it's because I rushed, not because I can't draw." Irawati didn't answer.

How did Sarika light her drawings in the last four days?
She drew by the torch on Irawati's phone.
What does Sarika's final remark reveal about why she waited?
She was afraid her best effort might not be good enough; rushing gave her something else to blame, which felt safer than risking a real verdict on her skill.
How could Sarika have handled the power cuts and the fear?
Using the bright Sunday afternoons for rough sketches, even imperfect ones, so the scary first step happened early and the power cuts mattered less.
Why might Irawati stay silent after Sarika's remark?
Irawati may see that the excuse hides fear and not know how to say so kindly at midnight, or may simply be worn out after lending the phone torch for days.

Read this:

Dear Manjula Chechi,
You asked why I didn't forward the message about child-kidnappers in white vans to our family group, when you sent it with three warnings.
Honestly, my first feeling was fear. Anu walks to school. My hand went straight to the forward button.
Then I stopped and asked myself a few things. Who wrote it? There was no name, no place, no date. What did it want me to feel? Scared, and angry at strangers. Who gains if a hundred people panic? Not the children.
I called the local police station's helpline number from their official page. The constable said they had no such reports and that this message had come up in other towns too.
So I didn't send it on. It felt oddly brave, just not pressing a button.
Please do call me before sending the next one. I would rather talk than panic together.
With love,
Yogesh

Whom did Yogesh call to check the message?
Yogesh called the local police station's helpline number from their official page.
What was Yogesh feeling when the message first arrived?
Yogesh felt fear for Anu, who walks to school, and Yogesh's hand went straight to the forward button.
Which questions helped Yogesh pause before forwarding?
Yogesh asked who wrote it, what it was trying to make people feel, and who gains if a hundred people panic, then checked with an official source.
How might Manjula Chechi feel reading this letter?
Manjula Chechi might feel a little embarrassed, but the warm tone and the invitation to call first make the letter feel caring rather than scolding.
Who built the Red Fort in Delhi?
Emperor Shah Jahan ordered it built in the seventeenth century, when he moved his capital to Delhi. The work finished in 1648.
Why is it called red?
Most of its massive walls are made of red sandstone. That stone gives the fort its colour and its name.

Read this:

In the São Paulo flat, Noa and Priscila were playing with a toy guitar, taking turns strumming. When Priscila held it a little too long, Noa snatched it, ran to the sofa and shoved it behind a cushion. She sat on the cushion, arms folded. Priscila burst into tears. "I don't want to play anymore!" She went to find her mother, and the game was over.

Where did Noa hide the guitar?
Behind a cushion on the sofa.
What was Priscila feeling when she burst into tears?
She was hurt and upset that Noa snatched the guitar.
What would you change first in Noa's approach?
Ask for a turn or use a timer, because grabbing kept the toy but ended the game.
How does the snatch look to Priscila?
It feels unfair and mean, so she stops playing.

Read this:

School log, Thursday.
Mr Shankar came today to see the lab he gave us last June. Twelve computers, new tables, a banner with his company's name. The room has been locked since Diwali. Power comes for about four hours a day here, mostly after school, and there is no inverter. None of our teachers has used these machines before, so nobody felt confident to take a class in there.
I unlocked it for him. Dust covers on every screen. A few Class 6 children pressed their faces to the window glass as we stood inside.
He was quiet for a long time, then asked why nobody had told him. I said we did not want to seem ungrateful.
Next step: I have asked him to meet our four teachers on Saturday and hear what they actually need before anything else is bought.
— Parveen, Head Teacher

How long has the lab been locked?
The room has been locked since Diwali.
What might Shankar have been feeling when he stood quietly in the dusty lab?
He was likely shocked and disappointed, seeing that his gift had been unused for months while children could only look in through the window.
What approach could Shankar have tried before buying the computers?
He could have asked the teachers first about power and training, and planned a backup supply and teacher sessions along with the machines.
How do the Class 6 children at the window experience the unused lab?
For them the lab is something to look at but never use, which may feel like a promise that was not kept.

Read this:

Monday: Mohit tried to ride his new bicycle without stabilisers, fell twice, then kicked it and walked away. “I'll never ride it.” Neelam, his mother, said, “You tried hard.”
Wednesday: Neelam broke it into steps. “Today, just sit and push with your feet.” Mohit scooted along. “Now lift your feet for one second.” He did.
Saturday: Mohit pushed off, lifted his feet and pedalled five pushes before wobbling to a stop. “Mummy! I rode it!” Neelam cheered from the gate.

How many pushes did Mohit pedal on Saturday?
Five pushes.
What was Mohit feeling on Monday when he kicked the bicycle?
He was frustrated and discouraged after falling twice, ready to give up.
What changed on Wednesday that helped?
Neelam broke riding into small steps, first pushing with his feet, then lifting them for a second.
How might Neelam feel on Saturday at the gate?
She likely feels proud and delighted that Mohit kept going.

Read this:

Friday, 9 p.m. (Preeti's diary)
Got ₹3,600 from the Class 8 tuition today. Before I could even think about the jacket in the Sarojini lane, I did what Vandana Masi told me to try in April: ₹1,200 straight into the steel box marked 'fees + emergencies', the rest in my wallet.
Four months of this now. The box has ₹3,700, even after paying my exam form fee last month without asking Papa. That felt good in a quiet way.
The first weeks were annoying. I'd look at the box and think of momos. Now I don't open it unless it's real.
Today Isha from class borrowed my notes and said she was broke again, three days after her payment came in. I didn't lecture her. I just remembered being exactly that.
Jacket next month, maybe. From the other two-thirds.

How much went into the steel box today?
₹1,200 straight into the steel box.
How does Preeti feel about the box now compared with the first weeks?
At first it felt annoying and tempting, but now there is a quiet pride and calm in having money ready for real needs.
What else could help Preeti keep the box working when the jacket tempts again?
Deciding in advance what counts as 'real' for opening it, and talking to Vandana Masi if a big need comes up.
How might Vandana Masi see the last four months?
Vandana Masi would likely be pleased that the April idea became a habit, one that paid the exam form fee without anyone asking Papa.

metadata.subtype: Approach: saving a fixed share as a buffer [Action]

messages.content:
Rewrite for a child, using simpler words:

Heavy rain flooded the lower streets, and the municipality advised residents to avoid unnecessary travel.
A lot of rain filled the low streets with water. The city office told people to stay home unless they had to go out.

Read this:

Monday: An email landed in Zubin's inbox at 9:02, apparently from the managing director: "Urgent and confidential. I need you to buy vouchers for a client today. Reply only to this address." Zubin felt a jolt. Then he noticed the sender's address was one letter off. He forwarded it to IT without replying.
Wednesday: Sonali, at the next desk, got the same kind of email and was halfway to the shop. Zubin caught her at the lift. "Did you check the address? Call the MD's office first." She did. The MD's assistant had never heard of it.
The following Monday: A real message came from the MD's assistant: "The MD needs the budget file within the hour, sorry for the rush." Zubin's first thought was "scam again". But the address was right, and it asked for nothing strange. He rang the assistant anyway, took thirty seconds to confirm, and sent the file. Suspicion, he decided, was a tool for checking, not for refusing everything.

What did the fake email ask Zubin to buy?
Vouchers for a client.
What was Zubin feeling when the first email arrived?
Zubin felt a jolt of urgency and alarm, then suspicion once the address turned out to be one letter off.
How did Zubin help Sonali?
He caught her at the lift and told her to check the address and call the MD's office first, which showed the email was fake.
What might Sonali have felt when she learned the email was fake?
Sonali probably felt shaken and relieved, having nearly bought vouchers for a scammer.
Why do many shoppers carry a cloth bag to the market?

A cloth bag can be used again and again. Because plastic bags are often thrown away after a short use and then pile up as rubbish, a cloth bag keeps waste low and is also strong enough for heavy things.

Read this:

At the after-school club in the Bengaluru community centre, Aparna, eight, had shared her crayon box every day for a month. When Ankita forgot her colours, Aparna gave her the whole box.
On Thursday Aparna forgot her snack. She asked Ankita for one of her biscuits. Ankita said, "No, I'm hungry," and turned away.
Aparna's lip shook. She marched to the club leader. "I gave her crayons for a MONTH. She won't give me one biscuit. That's not fair. I'm never sharing again."
The club leader crouched down. "You feel cheated."
"Yes!"
"That makes sense. Shall we talk to Ankita together?"
Aparna nodded, still angry, still hungry. The club leader gave her an apple from the office first.

How long had Aparna shared her crayon box?
She had shared it every day for a month.
How did Aparna feel when Ankita refused a biscuit?
She felt cheated, hurt and angry, believing her month of sharing should be paid back.
Which of the club leader's responses helped Aparna most?
Named her feeling, offered to talk with Ankita together, and gave her an apple first so she wasn't hungry.
What would change if Ankita knew Aparna had forgotten her snack?
Ankita might have shared the biscuit, since she may simply not have thought about Aparna being hungry.

metadata.subtype: Feels cheated when kindness is not returned [Receiver]

messages.content: My friend says "I live in Delhi itself". What is "itself" doing there?

In Indian English "itself" is added for emphasis, meaning "right here" or "in that very place". In standard English you can drop it or use "right in".
Example: I live right in Delhi, so the school is close.
In our family, who "calls the shots"? My dad says it is Grandma.

To call the shots means to make the important decisions and be in charge. It is informal.
Example: In our house, Grandma calls the shots about festival plans.

Read this:

In the school corridor after PT, three boys were imitating Pooja's stammer, loudly. "P-p-pooja, p-p-please!" Pooja stood by the lockers, face red, trying to open her bag. Nirmala, fifteen, saw it from the stairs. She didn't march over to shout. She just walked up to Pooja and said, "Come, we'll be late for maths. I'll carry your bottle." Pooja looked at her, then nodded. They walked off together. The boys' laughter trailed off; nobody was watching them anymore. In class, Nirmala slid her chair closer to Pooja. At the end of the day she went to the class teacher and told her what she'd seen. The teacher said, "Thank you. I'll speak to the boys and to Pooja today." Pooja caught Nirmala's eye at the gate and smiled a little.

What were the boys imitating?
They were imitating Pooja's stammer, loudly.
What was Nirmala feeling when she saw the boys from the stairs?
Nirmala felt uncomfortable and protective, wanting to help Pooja quietly rather than cause a scene.
What small steps did Nirmala take, and why do they matter?
She walked Pooja away, sat near her in class, and told the teacher that day, which showed solidarity and brought in adult help.
How might Pooja have felt walking away with Nirmala?
Pooja probably felt relieved and less alone, which is why she smiled at the gate.

Read this:

Tuesday
Diary, I found fifty rupees in the school yard today, stuck in the grass by the water tap. I didn't know what to do. Is it mine now? I thought about it all the way home. At dinner I asked Papa. He said, "Beta, someone at school probably lost it. Give it to your class teacher tomorrow, in case they come looking." That made sense. Tomorrow I'll give it to Sharmila ma'am first thing. I folded it into my pencil box so it won't get lost again. I feel lighter already, like I'm not carrying a secret.
- Aadhya

Where was the fifty rupees stuck?
In the grass by the water tap.
How did Aadhya feel after talking to Papa?
Aadhya felt lighter and relieved, as if no longer carrying a secret.
What else could Aadhya do if Sharmila ma'am is absent tomorrow?
Aadhya could give it to the school office, so it is still handed to a responsible adult.
How might the person who lost the money feel?
The person who lost it would feel worried now and very relieved if it turns up with the teacher.

Read this:

On Monday Yash saw his name on the hostel notice board with a fail in engineering drawing. He gave himself three days: skipped the library, played cricket in the corridor, slept. Gargi, the hostel warden, noticed and said only, "Tea in my office when you want." On Thursday Yash went. On her whiteboard he wrote two columns: what I controlled (starting late, no practice sheets) and what I didn't (the paper was longer than usual). Then Gargi asked for one small action. Yash chose one practice sheet that evening. He did it. The next week it was two sheets, and then a note to the department about the supplementary date.

Which two columns did Yash write on the whiteboard?
Yash wrote what he controlled and what he did not control.
What was Yash feeling during the first three days?
Low and disappointed, needing rest and distance from studying.
What small next step did Yash choose?
Yash chose one practice sheet that evening.
How might Gargi's "Tea in my office when you want" have felt to Yash?
Supportive and without pressure, leaving room to come when ready. 🙂

metadata.subtype: Rest, reframe, then a small next step [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Irawati, you're stuck on those fractions and asking me to just do them. Let me tell you about two teachers I had.
At ten, my tutor did every one of my sums. My homework was perfect. But in the exam I sat there like a stone. I felt so small, like everyone else knew a secret I'd never been told.
The next year, a new teacher gave us algebra and left the room. I looked at the page for an hour and gave up.
Then my aunt, Kusum Masi, started sitting next to me in the evenings. She never did a sum. She'd just say, "What do you know? What's the first step?" and wait.
I'm Sonali, your Nani. That's how I learned maths. Now, show me what you've tried.

Who sat next to Sonali in the evenings?
Kusum Masi, her aunt.
What was Sonali feeling in the exam after her tutor did her sums?
She felt small and stuck, as if everyone else knew a secret she'd never been told.
What was the turning point in Sonali's story, and why did it work?
Kusum Masi sitting beside her and asking about the first step was the turning point, because the task stayed hard but a guide was near.
How might the teacher who left the room have seen the class?
The teacher might have thought the students should manage alone, not realising they were being left to give up.

messages.content: It feels awkward to meet a friend straight after a quarrel. Why?
Neither friend knows what to say. Because neither of you is sure what the other is thinking or whether the friendship is still fine, it is hard to know how to begin.

Saturday: At his friend Suraj's house, Amandeep found an old board game with no rule sheet: wooden pegs, a board of holes and coloured tiles. Suraj shrugged. "Nobody knows how it works."

Sunday: Amandeep came back. "Let's just try moves and see what happens. If it's wrong, who cares? It's only a game." He moved a peg two holes. Nothing. He jumped it over a tile. Suraj gasped. "Maybe that captures it!"

The next Saturday: The boys had invented a full set of rules through trying. Jumping captured tiles, and corners were safe. They'd played eleven rounds. "I think we made it better than the real one," Amandeep said, grinning.

How many rounds had the boys played by the next Saturday?
Eleven rounds.
Why was Amandeep happy to just try moves?
He felt relaxed and curious, because mistakes cost nothing and playing was the fun part.
When would trial and error not be the best approach?
When mistakes are costly or unsafe, like with electricity or money, asking an adult or reading instructions is better.
How does Suraj see the game by the end?
Suraj seems excited and proud, having helped invent rules for a game nobody understood.

Every evening after the kiln cooled, Kalyani stayed back in her uncle's pottery shed at the edge of the kasba and threw the same water pot, again and again. Thin walls, even rim. She crushed most of them back into clay.
Mridul, who had joined the shed the same year, was already selling his own designs at the Tuesday market and talking about opening a shop on the highway.
'You'll be making pots for your uncle till you're old,' he said, washing up. 'Don't you want anything?'
Kalyani pressed her thumb into the spinning clay. 'I want this rim to be the same thickness all the way round.'
He laughed. She didn't mind. Last week the old potter from the next village had picked up one of her pots, tapped it, listened to the ring and nodded once.

What pot did Kalyani throw again and again?
The same water pot, with thin walls and an even rim.
What does Kalyani crushing most pots back into clay show about what she wants?
It shows she wants true skill more than quick sales, holding herself to a standard others can't see.
What moment showed Kalyani that her private practice was paying off?
The old potter tapping her pot, listening to its ring and nodding once was quiet recognition from someone who knows the craft.
How does Mridul read Kalyani's quiet evenings in the shed?
Mridul reads them as a lack of ambition, since for him drive means selling designs and opening a shop.

At Lola's apartment in Quezon City, Paulo crouched beside his daughter. "Fatima, mano po to Lola." He lifted Lola's hand and helped Fatima press it to her own forehead. Fatima, two, blinked, then grabbed the hand and did it again by herself, bonking Lola's knuckles against her nose. Lola laughed. "God bless you, anak!" and kissed both her cheeks. Fatima held out her hand for another turn.

What did Lola say after the mano?
Lola said, "God bless you, anak!"
What does Fatima's holding out her hand for another turn suggest?
Fatima feels happy and loved; the greeting has become a game that brings laughter and kisses.
How could Paulo help Fatima keep liking this greeting?
Keep it playful and gentle, and let her lead when she wants another turn.
How might Lola feel about the nose bonk?
Lola finds it funny and sweet, and the blessing and kisses show her affection.
Make a notice announcing that the community hall will be used for a free stitching class for women on Tuesdays and Thursdays at 11 am. About 55 words. Sign it Women's Welfare Group.

FREE STITCHING CLASS

A free stitching class for women will be held in the community hall every Tuesday and Thursday at 11 am. Come and learn a useful skill in a friendly group. All women are welcome, so bring a friend along. We look forward to seeing you there, and we hope you will enjoy every class.

Women's Welfare Group
Our flight leaves early in the morning and I'm worried I'll oversleep.
Set two alarms at different times, and put one phone across the room so you have to get up. Pack your bag and keep your documents by the door the night before.
What if both alarms fail?
Ask a family member to wake you as a backup, and sleep a little earlier than usual. A calm last evening makes the morning smoother.

Day one: Vandana, twenty-two and newly made team lead at a Kochi billing office, watched intern Madhuri proudly demo a script she had written to sort invoices. It took forty seconds per file.
Day four: Vandana showed her the office's standard reporting tool, which did the same job in two seconds and handled rupee symbols correctly. Madhuri nodded, then quietly kept using her script. "I've already fixed so many bugs in it," she said, eyes on her screen.
Day nine: A client complained about a mis-sorted invoice. It came from the script. Madhuri looked stricken. Vandana pulled up a chair beside her. "Your script taught you a lot. Let's keep a copy, and use the tool for clients." Madhuri let out a long breath and opened the tool.

How long did Madhuri's script take per file?
Forty seconds per file.
Why did Madhuri keep using her script after seeing the faster tool?
She felt tied to it because she had already fixed so many bugs in it, and all that effort made it feel worth more than the job it did.
Which choice on day nine helped Madhuri let go of the script?
Vandana sat beside her, said the script taught her a lot and suggested keeping a copy while using the tool for clients. That honoured the effort without keeping the flawed tool.
How is the client affected by Madhuri's attachment to the script?
The client got a mis-sorted invoice, so the attachment stopped being a private matter and caused a real problem for someone outside the team.

Dear Gurleen,
We said we'd review roles after three months, so here's my honest review, in writing, because I'd probably ramble in person.
I'm not good at sales calls. You've seen it. On the hospital call last Thursday I spent ten minutes on our database design, and the purchase manager checked her phone twice. Of the nine demos I led this quarter, one turned into a sale. The two you stepped into both did.
Meanwhile you've been fixing bugs at midnight, which is my strength, not yours.
So I'm proposing we swap. You lead every customer conversation from 1 July. I own delivery and product quality, and I'll join calls only when there's a hard technical question. Let's try it for a quarter and review again.
I'm a bit embarrassed writing this. But I'd rather be embarrassed than keep losing customers.
Shalini

How many of the nine demos Shalini led turned into a sale?
One.
How does Shalini feel about writing the letter?
Shalini feels a bit embarrassed but determined, preferring that to losing more customers.
What makes Shalini's proposal likely to work?
It plays to each founder's strengths, sets a clear start date and includes a review after a quarter.
How might Gurleen feel reading the proposal?
Gurleen may feel relieved to stop the midnight bug fixing and pleased that Gurleen's sales skill is recognised.

messages.content: The teacher explained us the lesson. Please fix.
The correct sentence is: "The teacher explained the lesson to us." Why: "explain" needs "to" before the person.

Jomon, you asked why I don't like groups with one boss. Let me tell you. This is your Rashmi aunty, and this is from Class 9.
Our group had a leader, Sheela. Every Monday, she decided who was “in”. If she liked your bag, you were in. If you talked to the wrong girl, you were out, and nobody would sit with you till she said so.
I watched it happen to my friend Mini. For a whole week, Sheela ignored her, and so did everyone. Even me. I was scared I'd be next.
We all behaved perfectly for Sheela. We laughed at her jokes. We gave her our best pens. We were so busy watching her face, we forgot to be friends with each other.
I never stood up to her. That's what I remember most.

Who decided who was "in" every Monday?
Sheela did.
How did young Rashmi feel when Mini was frozen out?
She felt scared and anxious that she'd be next, so she ignored Mini too.
At what point in the story could young Rashmi have made a different choice?
During Mini's week of being ignored, she could have kept sitting with Mini, even if it risked Sheela's favour.
How might Mini have felt that week?
She probably felt hurt and alone, with even her friend Rashmi ignoring her.

It was 1 a.m. in Seoul, and Soo-ah was still watching short videos. She'd opened the app "for five minutes" after dinner.
Every video ended and the next one started by itself. Dance clips, then a cat, then a makeup video, then more dance clips. She kept thinking, "Just one more."
The next morning, her friend Clara showed her the app's settings. "See? It learns what you watch longest and shows more of that. And autoplay is on by default. It's designed so you don't stop."
Soo-ah felt strange, like she'd been tricked. That night she turned off autoplay and set a timer. When the video ended, the screen just stopped.
She sat in the quiet for a second, then put the phone on her desk and went to sleep.

What time was it when Soo-ah was still watching videos?
1 a.m.
What was Soo-ah feeling when she learnt how the app works?
Soo-ah felt uneasy and a bit tricked, realising the app was designed to keep her watching.
What changes did Soo-ah make, and why do they help?
She turned off autoplay and set a timer, which removed the automatic next video and gave her a natural stopping point.
How does Clara see the app?
Clara sees it as designed to keep users hooked, not neutral, which is why she shows Soo-ah the settings.

“Top of the class again!” Papa said, tapping Leela's report card. “Our Leela never lets us down.” The guests clapped. Her younger sister Rehana kept stirring her dal. “Papa, can Rehana have a sweet too?” Leela asked. “Of course, but Rehana knows she has to study more.” Later, on the stairs, Leela held out her laddu. “Half is yours.” Rehana shrugged. “Papa only says your name.” Leela's stomach twisted. “What if I get less next time? Will he stop?” “Maybe,” Rehana said. Leela looked at the card in her hand as if it had grown heavier.

What did Rehana keep doing while the guests clapped?
Rehana kept stirring her dal.
What is Leela worried about when she asks, “What if I get less next time?”
Leela is worried that Papa's praise depends on her marks and could disappear, and she feels uneasy that her sister is hurt.
What could Papa do differently at the next report card?
Papa could praise effort from both sisters and avoid comparing them, so Leela feels less pressure and Rehana is not left out.
How does Rehana see the praise given to Leela?
Rehana feels overlooked. She says, “Papa only says your name,” and shrugs it off as if she has learned not to expect more.

I sit two benches behind Harshita at lunch, so I saw it. She carried her tiffin to the table by the window where a group of girls from our class sat, and one of them said, "There is no space here," though there were two empty seats. She stood there a moment, then went and sat on the steps outside. I could not tell how she felt; her face was very still. The next day I told her I liked her drawing of the train, and she sat with me. She joined the art club after that. Later, I saw her talking to the class teacher quietly, so maybe she mentioned it. I am Tejas, from Class 6.

Where did Harshita sit after she was turned away from the table?
She sat on the steps outside.
What might Harshita have been feeling on the steps, and why can Tejas not be sure?
She may have felt hurt, but her face was very still, so Tejas cannot tell for certain whether it was hurt or just holding it in.
What small step did Tejas take that helped?
Tejas complimented Harshita's drawing of the train and made room for her, giving her one kind classmate to be near. Joining a club also gave her a place.
What is it like for Tejas to watch this from two benches behind?
Tejas sees the empty seats and the refusal clearly but cannot read Harshita's still face, so Tejas is left unsure, and that uncertainty turns into a kind word the next day.

Monday: Pooja put her socks on before her shorts and got muddled. Late again.
Wednesday: Madhav, her brother, drew pictures on a chart: vest, then shirt, shorts, socks and shoes. He stuck it on the wardrobe door. Pooja followed it slowly.
Friday: Pooja dressed alone, ticking each picture in order, and was waiting at the door before Madhav.

What did Madhav stick on the wardrobe door?
A chart with pictures.
What was Pooja feeling on Friday at the door?
She was proud and happy to be ready before Madhav.
What else could be added to the chart?
A picture for combing hair or packing her bag, so the whole morning is covered.
How does the change look to Madhav?
Madhav probably feels proud his chart helped her.

Saturday
Usha Mami and everyone came for lunch today. The whole time it was Vikram this and Vikram that. My brother Vikram got 98 in maths. Vikram is going to be a doctor. Nani even gave him a hundred rupees. When Usha Mami asked about me, Amma said, "Manjula is good at drawing," and everyone said, "Oh, nice," and went back to Vikram. I went and sat on the stairs. I love Vikram, he helps me with fractions, but today I kind of hated him too. Maybe they love him more because he's clever. I got 71 in maths. Nobody gave me anything. I'm ten and I think I'm the less good one in this house.
Manjula

How much did Vikram get in maths?
Vikram got 98 in maths.
Why did Manjula go and sit on the stairs?
Manjula felt hurt and jealous, left out while everyone praised Vikram, and began to fear being the less loved one.
What could Amma do to ease this comparison?
Amma could notice Manjula on the stairs, spend time looking at Manjula's drawings, and praise each child's own efforts instead of letting marks decide.
How might Vikram feel if he read this diary?
Vikram might feel sad and surprised, since he helps with fractions and probably never wanted to be a rival.

The results of the city hackathon came out on Saturday morning in Hyderabad. Madhuri's team had won first prize.
In the hostel mess, Aadhya from the next room was already on her third story about her own internship: the famous manager, the big project, the praise.
Madhuri waited until she finished. "Congrats on the internship. What's the project actually about?"
Aadhya blinked, then started explaining properly, and it turned out to be interesting.
Later someone asked Madhuri, "Didn't your team win something?"
"Yes, first prize. We built a tool for tracking water tanker deliveries. My teammate Farzana did the hardest part." Then she went back to her dal.
That evening Aadhya knocked on her door. "You didn't even post about it?"
Madhuri shrugged. "I told my parents. The tool works. That's the part I care about."

What did Madhuri's team build?
A tool for tracking water tanker deliveries.
What does Madhuri's shrug about not posting suggest?
It suggests Madhuri feels quietly proud and secure, needing no applause because the working tool is what matters.
Which of Madhuri's habits show quiet confidence?
Asking Aadhya about her project, sharing the win simply when asked, crediting Farzana, and not needing to post about it.
How might Aadhya see Madhuri after that day?
Aadhya seems puzzled and curious, knocking to ask about not posting, perhaps noticing a different way to carry success.
