Monday: His mother, Lakshmi, announced that Akash's phone would stay in the kitchen after ten. "You're controlling my whole life!" he shouted, and banged his cupboard shut.
Wednesday: Late at night Akash noticed Amma sitting up with his exam timetable, rubbing her eyes. He remembered she had caught him scrolling at 2 a.m. twice last week. He knocked on her door. "I get that you're worried about my sleep. But I need the phone for the group study call till ten-thirty on weeknights."
Saturday: They sat down and agreed: phone in the kitchen by ten-thirty on school nights, eleven on weekends, and a review after exams if his marks held up. Akash still grumbled, but he put the phone on the kitchen shelf himself.

When did Amma first want Akash's phone in the kitchen?
Amma wanted it in the kitchen after ten.
What was Akash feeling on Monday when he banged the cupboard?
Akash felt controlled and angry, as if Amma was running his whole life.
Which step turned the argument into an agreement?
Akash named Amma's worry about his sleep and proposed specific conditions, like ten-thirty on school nights and a review after exams.
How does Lakshmi see Akash knocking on her door on Wednesday?
Lakshmi likely feels relieved that he understood her worry and is talking instead of shouting.

Karthik: everyone at work is booking the new rooftop place for Friday. 4.8 stars, 3 week waiting list
Karthik: my whole team says it's the best food in the city
Vidya: have any of them eaten there?
Karthik: ...one guy's cousin

Vidya: pretty much. if you want the view, go. if you want to talk to your team, the Kerala place near your office is much better
Karthik: ok, Kerala place it is. I'll tell them why

A three-week waiting list.
What was Karthik feeling on admitting only 'one guy's cousin' had eaten there?
Karthik felt doubtful and a little amused, realising the team's excitement came from videos, not experience.
Which question helped Karthik most, and why?
Vidya asking whether anyone had eaten there, because it separated real information from people copying each other.
How might Karthik's team react to the change of plan?
Some teammates may be disappointed, but they may also appreciate a place where they can actually talk.

The lane was still pink with Holi colour when Dadi held up two notes. "Remember Monday, Abhinav? I asked: ten rupees on Saturday, or twenty on Sunday. You said twenty, no question."
"That was different," Abhinav said, eyes on the ten-rupee note.
"How is it different?"
"Then both days were far away. Now it's Saturday! And the ice-cream cart is outside right now, Dadi."
Sharmila, his elder sister, laughed from the sofa. "He'll be sulking tomorrow when I show him my twenty."
"I won't!" Abhinav snatched the ten. "Tomorrow is ages."
"It's one day," Sharmila said.
"One day is ages," he called, already out of the door, the cart's bell ringing down the lane.

What did Abhinav choose on Monday?
Abhinav said twenty, no question.
Why does the ten-rupee note feel better to Abhinav now?
The note and the ice-cream cart are right here, so he feels excited and impatient, and tomorrow suddenly feels like ages.
What could Dadi try next time to help Abhinav wait?
She could keep the Sunday reward where he can see it and plan the ice-cream trip together for Sunday, so the later choice feels just as real.
How does Sharmila see Abhinav's choice?
She finds it funny and expects him to regret it tomorrow when she shows him her twenty.

The offer letter from the Singapore office gave Zubin forty-eight hours to sign. He read it in the hospital canteen, where his mother was recovering from a knee replacement upstairs.

When he told her, she turned to the wall. "Your father left me alone for work. Now you. A son stays." The nurse came in to take her pressure and Zubin went out to the corridor, heart pounding. He loved her. He also wanted this job more than anything in years.

He spent the night making calls. His cousin Freny could move into the spare room. A day attendant could come from eight to six. He called the office and asked if the start could move by two months.

In the morning he sat by her bed. "Mamma, I'm going, but not yet, and not leaving you alone. I'll be here until you can walk to the market. Then I'll call daily and come every three months."

She didn't answer. But she held his hand.

How long did the offer letter give Zubin to sign?
It gave him forty-eight hours.
How did Zubin feel when his mother turned to the wall?
Zubin felt torn and anxious, his heart pounding, loving her but wanting the job badly.
How did Zubin try to honour both his mother's needs and his own life?
He arranged a cousin and a day attendant, asked to delay his start, and told his mother honestly what he could and could not do.
What might Zubin's mother be feeling when she holds his hand?
She may feel afraid of being alone and hurt, yet reassured by his plan and his honesty.

Dear Tanvir,
Maasi said you just started posting, so big-sister-cousin advice, whether you want it or not.
Last month I applied for the student editor post at college. In the interview, the teacher said, 'We had a look at your public profile.' My stomach dropped. At thirteen, I'd left a nasty comment under a classmate's dance video. I'd forgotten it. They hadn't. I explained, apologised, said I'd changed. I still got the post, but I felt about six inches tall.
So, three things. Before you post, ask: would I be fine with a teacher, a future boss or Nani seeing this? Screenshots last forever, even after you delete. And be the kind of person online you are at dinner.
Love,
Sudha didi

What had Sudha done at thirteen that came up in her interview?
She had left a nasty comment under a classmate's dance video.
How did Sudha feel when the teacher mentioned her public profile?
Her stomach dropped and she felt ashamed, about six inches tall, even though she had changed.
Which of Sudha's tips would help Tanvir most before posting?
Asking whether Tanvir would be fine with a teacher, future boss or Nani seeing it, since posts and screenshots can last.
How might the classmate from the dance video feel if they knew about that comment years later?
They might still remember the hurt, showing that online comments can affect people long after they're written.

The floodlights at the district ground had failed, the monsoon had turned the outfield to mud, and Suraj was still running shuttles at nine at night in the one pool of light from the pavilion.

Coach Hemant watched from under the tin roof. Since Suraj had been dropped from the state squad after a shouting match with a selector, he'd been first in and last out every day. He bowled until his fingers split. He skipped the team dinner twice.

It was better than the shouting. Hemant knew that. But he also saw how Suraj's jaw stayed clenched even after a good spell.

He walked out into the drizzle. "Enough for tonight."
"One more set."
"No. This fire is useful, Suraj. But tomorrow is rest. And on Friday, before nets, you and I sit and talk about the selector. Properly."
Suraj stared at the mud, then nodded.

Where was Suraj running shuttles?
Suraj was running shuttles in the one pool of light from the pavilion.
What was Coach Hemant feeling as he watched Suraj train?
Coach Hemant felt relieved the anger had gone into training instead of shouting, but uneasy about the clenched jaw and the missed dinners.
What caution did the coach give, and why does it matter?
The coach called the fire useful but ordered rest and a real talk about the selector, because training alone can't settle what is underneath.
What is it like for Suraj to be told "Enough for tonight"?
Suraj probably feels frustrated at first, wanting one more set, but also seen, since the coach names the selector without scolding.

Ten minutes before the maths exam, Asif's calculator was missing. He turned to Jomon, who sat next to him. "Did you take it?"
Jomon held both hands out, palms open. "I swear, I didn't touch it."
Asif wanted to believe him. The open palms looked honest. But open palms can be faked too.
He didn't argue. He checked his bag again, then ran to the science lab where he'd had the last class. The calculator was on the bench.
He came back panting. "Sorry. Found it in the lab."
Jomon laughed. "Told you."
Asif sat down. The palms had been true this time, but checking was what proved it.

Where did Asif find his calculator?
On the bench in the science lab.
What was Asif thinking when Jomon showed open palms?
Asif felt torn: he wanted to believe the palms meant honesty, but was unsure since palms alone aren't proof.
What did Asif do that was fair?
He didn't accuse Jomon further and checked the facts himself, which proved Jomon was telling the truth.
How might Jomon have felt when Asif asked if he took it?
Jomon was probably a bit hurt at first but relieved when the calculator was found.

Hi Pankaj bhaiya,

Something happened with Papa that I keep thinking about.

Last week he told me he had handed in my school trip form at the office. Two days later I was hunting for a charger in the car and found the envelope under the passenger seat, still sealed.

I held it up. For a second Papa started, "The office must have sent it back—" and then he stopped. He sat down on the front steps and said, "No. I forgot it, and I told you I'd done it because I felt silly. That was a lie. I'm sorry."

The next morning he took an hour off work and came to the school office with me to sort it out. The clerk said it was fine, just late.

Honestly, I was ready to be angry at him for days. Instead I felt oddly proud of him. I think I'll remember that envelope longer than the trip.

Pradeep

Where did Pradeep find the trip form envelope?
Pradeep found the envelope under the passenger seat in the car, still sealed.
What did Pradeep feel after Papa admitted the lie?
Pradeep had been ready to be angry for days, but instead felt oddly proud of Papa for saying it plainly.
Which choice worked for Papa, and why?
Stopping the excuse halfway, saying simply that he forgot and lied, apologising, and then fixing it at the school the next morning; it showed honesty instead of defending the lie.
What might it have been like for Papa when the sealed envelope came out?
Papa probably felt exposed and embarrassed, which is why he began an excuse before stopping to tell the truth.

Okay, Parul, is this recording? Good. My strange memory is from the terrace, two winters ago. A group of us were lighting sparklers, and a spark landed on Neel's sleeve. Everyone tells it the same way: he yelled, jumped into a bucket of water, and the bucket tipped over.
I told that story for a year. I could see the bucket rolling. Then Neel himself told me, "There was no bucket. I just shook my arm and it went out." And I thought, no, I remember the bucket! But when I checked, I'd gone downstairs for matches right then.
The bucket came from Joel's version. It moved into my head and sat there like mine.
Now I say, "I heard that..." if I didn't see it. I'm Vasudha, by the way.

Where had Vasudha gone at the moment the spark fell?
Vasudha had gone downstairs for matches right then.
Why did Vasudha feel sure about the rolling bucket?
Vasudha had told the story for a year and could see the bucket, even though it came from Joel's version; repeating it made the detail feel owned.
What habit did Vasudha adopt, and why does it help?
Vasudha says "I heard that..." when not an eyewitness, which keeps borrowed details apart from real memories.
How might Neel feel hearing the bucket story told for a year?
Neel might be amused or a little annoyed, since the story made his moment more dramatic than it was and nobody asked him.

At the temple fair in their village near Madurai, Ramesh spent his whole ten rupees on a big, bright green sweet from a cart. One bite, and his face twisted. It tasted like soap and far too much sugar. His sister Aparna laughed. "Give it to the crows." "No! It cost ten rupees!" Ramesh took another bite, then another, chewing slowly with his eyes shut. His Ammamma, Rukmini, watched from the bangle stall. "Kanna, are you enjoying it?" she asked. "No," he said, taking another bite. "But I paid." By the time he finished, his stomach felt heavy, and he had no appetite for the hot bajji his Ammamma bought for everyone.

How much did the green sweet cost?
The sweet cost ten rupees.
Why did Ramesh keep eating a sweet he disliked?
Spending ten rupees made giving it away feel like losing the money, so he kept eating even though it tasted bad and made him feel heavy.
What could Ammamma say to help Ramesh with this kind of choice?
She could gently point out that the ten rupees are gone either way and eating more only adds a bad feeling, so next time he can stop and save room for something he likes.
How might Aparna see her brother's choice?
Aparna finds it funny and a little silly, since to her the obvious answer was to give the sweet to the crows.

"Open-air quiz on the terrace, four o'clock, in May," said Mehak. "Done?" "Done!" said Ritesh at once. "Sounds great," said Pia. "Fine with me," said Karan. Hansa, holding the pen, looked at the sun burning on the window. It will be very hot at four, she thought. "Hansa? Minutes?" "Yes. Open-air, four o'clock, May." She wrote it down. "Perfect," said Mehak. "Meeting over." Ritesh grabbed his bag. In the corridor Hansa whispered to Pia, "Do you think the terrace will be too hot?" "I was thinking the same," said Pia, "but nobody said."

What time and month did Mehak propose for the quiz?
Mehak proposed a quiz on the terrace at four o'clock in May.
Why did Hansa write down the plan without mentioning the heat?
Hansa did not want to spoil the mood or be the only doubter, so the worry stayed inside; the whisper in the corridor shows the doubt was real.
What could the committee do differently at the moment Mehak says "Done?"
Someone could ask "Does anyone see a problem?" or set a short pause, so doubts like the heat can be raised before the plan is fixed.

Thursday. Aditi's class talk on the water cycle was on Monday. In bed, she pictured it: walking to the front, thirty faces looking up. Her stomach flipped.
Friday. At the bathroom mirror she practised her first line. "Every raindrop you've seen was once part of the sea." Slow, fast, smiling. Her brother Madhav banged on the door. "Are you talking to yourself?"
"Practising!"
Saturday. She did the whole talk into the mirror. After "evaporation," her mind went blank. Again. Blank at the same place.
She drew a tiny cloud on the back of her hand. Cloud meant condensation. She practised three more times, glancing at it.
Monday. In front of the class, she looked at her hand once, and kept going.

What did Aditi draw on the back of her hand?
She drew a tiny cloud on the back of her hand.
How did Aditi feel when she first pictured giving the talk?
She felt nervous, with her stomach flipping as she imagined thirty faces looking up.

On the school trip to the museum in Lagos, Emeka walked past the glass cases with his hands clasped behind his back. Wei, next to him, noticed and nudged him. “Why are your hands hidden? Did you take something?” Emeka rolled his eyes. “No. If I don't put them behind me, I'll touch things. Mum says I always do.” Wei laughed. The guide, who had overheard, smiled and said, “That's a good trick. The glass is there to protect the old pots.” Emeka kept his hands behind him and stared at the pots.

Where was the school trip?
The school trip was to the museum in Lagos.
How might Emeka have felt when Wei asked if he had taken something?
Probably a bit annoyed, since he rolled his eyes before explaining that he clasps his hands so he won't touch things.
What did Wei do that helped, and what could he do next time?
He asked Emeka directly and laughed, which cleared it up. Next time he could ask more gently before suggesting anything about taking things.
How might the guide see Emeka's clasped hands?
As a sensible way to avoid touching the old pots, and as respect for the exhibits.

Nirmala's first client report went out on time, and the client emailed, "Clear and thorough, thank you." She read it once and filed it away. They were being polite. The data had been easy. When the team praised her, she said the assignment was simple and that Manjula had done half the checking. But a typo on page four stayed in her mind for a week.

In Monday meetings she watched Mohit speak in whole confident paragraphs, and her own doubts, hidden underneath, felt louder by contrast. She stayed silent and jotted notes. The silence made her smaller; nobody asked for her view, and that felt like proof that she had none.

In week ten she got stuck on how the cost sheet linked to the quarterly summary, and finally messaged Manjula. "Sorry, silly question: how does the sheet feed into the summary?" Manjula replied within a minute. "Not silly. It's tucked away. I'll show you at three." No sigh, no raised eyebrow. Nirmala stared at the screen. The humiliation she had rehearsed for weeks had not come.

What did the client say about the first report?
The client said it was clear and thorough.
How did Nirmala's discounting of praise and her silence in meetings feed each other, and what did the question to Manjula change?

She filed praise as politeness or an easy assignment while keeping every typo in mind, and compared her hidden doubts with Mohit's confidence and stayed silent, which made her smaller and seemed to prove she had no view. Asking Manjula and getting a kind reply showed that the feared humiliation might not arrive.
How did Nirmala feel when she watched Mohit speak?
She felt doubtful and small, as her hidden doubts felt louder next to his confidence.
What could Nirmala do next after Manjula's reply?
She could ask another basic question, share one idea in a meeting, and keep a note of the praise she receives.

In the daycare above the chemist's shop in Lajpat Nagar, nap time was nearly over. Jatin, eighteen months, sat on his mat sucking his thumb, sleepy and calm. Then Ramesh, on the next mat, woke with a start and screamed. Jatin's thumb popped out. He stared at Ramesh, chin trembling, and burst into tears, arms out for the caregiver. Soon three mats were crying. The caregiver scooped up Ramesh first, rocking and humming. As Ramesh quietened, Jatin's sobs slowed too, and he crawled closer to pat Ramesh's foot.

Where was the daycare?
Above the chemist's shop in Lajpat Nagar.
Why did Jatin burst into tears when he had been sleepy and calm?
Jatin seemed to catch Ramesh's sudden upset; seeing and hearing Ramesh scream made Jatin upset too.
The caregiver comforted Ramesh first. Why was that a good choice?
Calming the child who started it helped stop the crying from spreading, and Jatin settled as Ramesh quietened.
How might Ramesh feel when Jatin pats Ramesh's foot?
Ramesh, just woken and frightened, might feel a little comforted by a friendly touch from the next mat.

Thursday, 11 p.m. Minakshi knew about the reshuffle before HR did. Again. She stands at the pantry with her coffee and people drift over like she's a small radio. Today three people went silent when I walked past, then started again. I heard “Vikas is moving to another city” before anyone told me my own team was changing. My stomach knotted.

Weird thing: Minakshi isn't unkind. When Kabir asked her something, she said, “I'm not sure that's true.” I think she likes being the person who knows. I might like it too. I just don't want to be the one waiting for crumbs.

Note to self: ask the manager directly tomorrow.
— Rehana

What did Rehana hear before anyone said the team was changing?
Rehana heard that Vikas is moving to another city before anyone told Rehana about the team changing.
Why does Rehana feel a knot in the stomach?
Rehana feels shut out and anxious, hearing news about the own team from the pantry before official word.
What does Rehana decide to do the next day?
Rehana decides to ask the manager directly.

Three days later: she puts a shoebox on the table, drapes a dupatta on it, and says, "This is the mandap." She sits her doll inside.

Last day of the festival: she waves a stick with a marigold on top. "This is my aarti," she sings, walking round the shoebox.

She sat her doll inside the shoebox mandap.

Damini was happy and absorbed in her pretend festival, singing as she walked around.

In the Monday meeting at a Melbourne design studio, Diego sat at the far end with a closed notebook while everyone else argued about the timeline. Layla noticed the silence again: eyes down, chair pushed back. She wondered if it was fear of her.

After the meeting she caught Diego by the coffee machine. "I'd like your view on the client mock-ups. Not in the meeting, just between us." Diego hesitated, then said the navigation would confuse older users. It was a good point. "Thank you. That's exactly what I needed," Layla said.

The next week she said in the meeting, "Diego raised a concern about the navigation. Let's look at it." Diego's shoulders eased. Layla had seen what happens on a team where nobody speaks: the problems arrive all at once.

Where did Layla catch Diego after the meeting?
Layla caught Diego by the coffee machine.
What do Diego's closed notebook and pushed-back chair suggest to Layla?
Layla suspects Diego may be afraid of speaking up, maybe out of fear of her, though these are only cues and not proof.
What did Layla do to help Diego speak?
Layla asked for Diego's view privately, thanked Diego for the point, and credited the concern in the next meeting.
How might Diego have felt when Layla credited the concern in the meeting?
Diego's shoulders eased, suggesting relief at finding it safe to disagree.

Sunday, two weeks before the exams. Suraj flipped through his biology textbook in twenty minutes. "I know all this," he told his sister Seema. "Easy syllabus." Every page looked familiar; he'd highlighted most of it in class.

Wednesday, one week later. Seema offered to quiz him. "What are the stages of mitosis?" Suraj frowned. "Pro... something. I know it when I see it." He laughed it off and went to play cricket. He didn't revise.

Monday, exam day. The paper asked him to draw and label the stages of mitosis. Suraj stared at the blank space. He could picture the page in the textbook, even the yellow highlighter. But the words wouldn't come.

He left three questions half done. At home he told Seema, "I really thought I knew it."

"You recognised it," she said. "That's not the same as remembering it."

How long did Suraj spend flipping through the biology textbook?
Twenty minutes.
Why did Suraj feel so sure he knew the syllabus?
Suraj felt confident because every page looked familiar from highlighting, so recognising it felt like knowing it.
What could Suraj do differently before the next exam?
Suraj could test himself by closing the book and writing or saying answers, like Seema's quiz, instead of just rereading.
How might Seema have felt when Suraj went to play cricket instead of revising?
Seema was probably a bit worried and frustrated, since her quiz had already shown gaps he ignored.

She tried ten, and got all of them wrong.

What could Amandeep try so she experiences getting better?
Start with one fraction so simple she gets it right, then praise the specific step, building small wins.
How might Amandeep feel seeing ten neat, careful crosses?
He likely feels sad and protective, seeing that she really tried and is giving up anyway.

I need to buy a new notebook before school starts.
Why: "Buy" means to pay for something; "by" is a preposition.

Note from Sudha, nursery teacher.
Today Divyansh asked questions all morning. "Why is the ant small? Why does it walk in a line?" At first Divyansh accepted any answer, nodding at whatever I said. So I tried a change. When Divyansh asked why the ants walk in a line, I said, "What do you think?" Divyansh watched them for a long time and said, "Maybe they're holding hands with their feet." The summer months passed while I was thus engaged, heart and soul, in one pursuit. And the same feelings which made me neglect the scenes around me caused me also to forget those friends who were so many miles absent, and whom I had not seen for so long a time. Divyansh typed it into his class group before he could chicken out: "I'm finishing the web design tutorial in 30 days. You can check." Twelve thumbs came back, and one "sure bro 😏". That stung. The night before the district meet, Preeti lay on her bed with her eyes closed. She walked herself through the day. Arrive early. Warm-up: light jog, drills, two short strides. At the line, feet in the blocks, wait for the gun. Then the first ten steps, low and quick, and the long push to the final stretch. Then the part she'd rarely rehearsed: what if she stumbled? She'd shorten the next stride, keep her eyes on the finish line, and not look at the others. Last, the breathing Bhupen Sir had taught her: in for four, out for six, three times. Her hands unclenched. She opened her eyes. It was only practice in her head, but her chest felt quieter.

What would Preeti do if she stumbled?
Shorten the next stride, keep her eyes on the finish line and not look at the others.
How was Preeti feeling before the race, and how can you tell?
Nervous but steadying: her hands unclenched and her chest felt quieter after the mental walk-through.
What else could Preeti do to make the rehearsal stronger, and why?
Walk the real track before the meet, since seeing the actual surface and lines makes the mental picture more accurate.
How does the plan look to Bhupen Sir?
Bhupen Sir sees his athlete using the breathing he taught, so he may feel proud and reassured that she is calm before the meet.

Squeeze this passage into two sentences.

When Lady Catherine and her daughter had played as long as they chose, the tables were broken up, the carriage was offered to Mrs. Collins, gratefully accepted, and immediately ordered. The party then gathered round the fire to hear Lady Catherine determine what weather they were to have on the morrow. From these instructions they were summoned by the arrival of the coach; and with many speeches of thankfulness on Mr. Collins's side, and as many bows on Sir William's, they departed. As soon as they had driven from the door, Elizabeth was called on by her cousin to give her opinion of all that she had seen at Rosings, which, for Charlotte's sake, she made more favourable than it really was. But her commendation, though costing her some trouble, could by no means satisfy Mr. Collins, and he was very soon obliged to take her Ladyship's praise into his own hands.

When the card games end, Lady Catherine lends her carriage and announces the next day's weather, and the guests leave with thanks and bows. In the carriage Elizabeth praises Rosings more than she means for Charlotte's sake, but it does not satisfy Mr. Collins, who soon praises Lady Catherine himself.
I'm scared to ask my professor a question because I think it's silly.
Most professors enjoy questions, and no honest question is silly. Chances are that others in the class wonder the same thing.
What if he thinks I wasn't listening?
Try asking it in a way that shows you've thought about it: 'I understood this part, but I'm not clear about that part.' That shows effort.

"Maria's by herself again," Indu whispered to her friend. "Third day." "She left our group chat, na?" "Did she leave, or did someone remove her?" "Don't know." Indu watched Maria turn the pages of a book she clearly wasn't reading. At the next free period, Indu walked over. "Maria, we're one short for the quiz team. Want to be our science person?" "Me?" "You got full marks in that physics test." Maria hesitated. "Won't the others mind?" "It's my team," Indu said, shrugging. "Practice is after lunch. Just come." Maria nodded, a small smile. After lunch, she came. By the end, she was arguing about Newton with everyone, and nobody remembered she'd been alone.

What did Indu ask Maria to be?
Their science person on the quiz team.
What does Maria's question "Won't the others mind?" suggest about how she feels?
It suggests she feels unsure and unwanted, worried she will be rejected again.
How could Indu keep Maria included after the quiz?
She could keep inviting her to practices and add her back to the group chat without making a fuss.
How does Indu see Maria's situation?
Indu sees that Maria has been alone for days and uses a simple task, the quiz team, to include her without drawing attention.

Coordinator's note, Thursday. Farah writing about Zubin and Vishal, the two founders in our programme.
Over three weeks it became clear they disagreed on a basic point: whether to sell customer contact lists to outside firms. Vishal wanted to, and Zubin would not. Neither would move.
I did not push either way. I sat in on their meetings and reminded them to list what each had done and what was left. What could the founders do if they later disagree about the handover?

Ojas, you asked why I keep that crooked clay figure on my desk. Let your Zubin mama tell you. When I was twenty, my father died suddenly, a week before my exams. I didn't cry. I couldn't talk to anyone. My sister thought I didn't care. At the art college studio, I took a lump of clay and pressed and twisted it for three nights, not planning anything. It became a man bent over, hands pressed to his chest. My teacher, Mrs Irani, looked at it and said, "It's very strong. It looks like pride." I nearly laughed. For me it was all the grief I couldn't say. But she wasn't wrong either. My father was a proud man. Later my sister saw it and cried, and then I cried, finally, with her. That lump said what my mouth couldn't. And each of us saw our own father in it.

How many nights did young Zubin work on the clay?
Three nights.
What was young Zubin feeling while shaping the clay?
He was grieving deeply, unable to cry or talk, and the clay let that grief out.
What turning point came from the sculpture?
His sister saw it and cried, and then Zubin finally cried with her, sharing the grief he couldn't speak.
How did Mrs Irani read the sculpture?
She saw it as strong and full of pride, a reading different from Zubin's intent but still true to his father.

What does "jump the gun" mean?
Then, why do we close the door when the air conditioner is on? Next, fix this: "The train arrived at 8 in the morning yesterday, was it late?"
Also, any idea what "inquisitive" means?
And one more: when will the next big sale begin at the market?

1. It means to start something too soon. For example: he jumped the gun and sent the message before the plan was final.
2. It keeps the cool air inside. Because an open door lets warm air in.
3. Better: The train arrived at 8 in the morning yesterday. Was it late? Why: Two separate sentences should be divided by a full stop, not joined by a comma.
4. As an adjective, "inquisitive" means curious and fond of asking questions.
5. I don't know; I can't see the shops' plans. Look for notices at the market or ask a shopkeeper.
