In the April heat of their village near Bundi, Sarita's rose, growing in a clay pot on the flat roof, suddenly looked scorched. Every afternoon the leaves at the top turned crisp and papery. Sudha-kaki, drying chillies next door, called across, "The roof is a tawa at three o'clock." Sarita crouched by the pot and touched the soil. Dry as dust, though she had watered it that morning. She watched the shadows: after lunch, the neem tree's shade crept over one corner of the courtyard. So she carried the pot down and set it where the shade fell, with light in the morning. Then she tucked a layer of dry straw round the stem. A week later, the new leaves stayed soft and green.

What did Sudha-kaki compare the roof to?
A tawa at three o'clock.
What was Sarita thinking as she watched the shadows?
She felt concerned and determined, looking for a spot with morning light but afternoon shade.
What else could Sarita try if the courtyard gets hot too?
Water in the evening as well, and ask Sudha-kaki which corner stays coolest.
How might Sudha-kaki see Sarita's fix?
Sudha-kaki gave the hint, so she would likely be pleased to see the rose recover.

metadata.subtype: Approach: moving the pots after the leaves burn [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Aman's not coming again?" Nandini asked, as Hemant put the second badminton racket back on the shelf.
"Third time this month. Said he'd be here at five."
"Are you going to fight with him about it?"
"I did, in September. He said sorry. Then he did it again." Hemant sat on the sofa. "I don't think he's doing it to hurt me. He's just... somewhere else now."
"That sounds sad."
"It is a bit." He shrugged. "But I'm not going to keep waiting by the door. I'll still say hi, still wish him on his birthday. I'm just not planning my Saturdays around him."
"So who are you playing with?"
"Joseph from tuition asked last week. I said maybe. I'm going to say yes."
Nandini handed him the racket back. "Go on, then."

How many times this month has Aman not come?
This is the third time this month.
How does Hemant seem to feel about Aman?
He seems sad and a little resigned, but not angry, believing Aman isn't trying to hurt him.
Why is Hemant's plan healthier than fighting again?
He already tried talking and the promises kept breaking, so staying polite while making time for new friends like Joseph protects him without blame.
How does Nandini respond to Hemant's decision?
Nandini is sympathetic, calling it sad, and then encourages him by handing back the racket.

metadata.subtype: Approach: accepting that the friendship is changing [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Observation note - Chandrika Menon, Class 11 Chemistry, international school
Chetan joined this term from Pune. On Monday I asked him if his lab report was finished and he gave a quick head wobble with a small smile. I read it as yes and moved on.
On Wednesday the report still wasn't in. I nearly marked it late, but I remembered the wobble and wondered if I had read it wrongly.
I asked him after class, "When you did this," and I copied the wobble, "did you mean yes, or something else?" He laughed. "Ma'am, it meant 'I heard you, I'm on it.' Half done."
Since then I ask a second question when I'm not sure: "Is that a yes, or not yet?" He answers straight away. Two other students have started doing the same with each other.

When did Chandrika first ask Chetan about his lab report?
Chandrika asked him on Monday if his lab report was finished.
What was Chetan feeling and meaning when he wobbled, and how could it have been read another way?
He meant "I heard you, I'm on it," with the report half done, and he seemed calm and at ease about it. Chandrika had read the same wobble as a plain yes.
What small step did Chandrika add to avoid the mix-up?
She now asks a clarifying question such as "Is that a yes, or not yet?" whenever a wobble or nod leaves her unsure.
What would change if Chandrika had marked the report late without asking?
Chetan would likely have felt unfairly judged, since in his mind he had never promised it was finished, and the misunderstanding would have stayed hidden.

Read this:

Day 4. Tejas woke at noon, the whole to-do list staring at him like a wall. That evening he told himself: if I can't do everything, I shouldn't try to do anything. Then he changed the thought. Just three things tomorrow. Up by eight. A real meal. Ten minutes outside.

Day 9. His roommate Tanuja saw him drinking tea on the balcony at eight-thirty and said nothing, only slid a plate of poha toward him. He whispered to himself, that's two.

Day 16. The list still had only three lines. But he also added a call with his mother, then a short walk to the tea stall. He noted that the small list didn't feel like giving up. It felt like holding on until his energy returned.

What three tasks did Tejas set for himself?
Up by eight, a real meal and ten minutes outside.
What does Tejas's thought on Day 16 about the small list suggest about his feelings?
Tejas feels a quiet steadiness and self-acceptance, seeing the short list as holding on rather than failing.
What could Tejas do on a day when even three tasks feel too much, and why?
Tejas could keep just one, such as a drink of water on the balcony, because a smaller step still keeps the habit and avoids the all-or-nothing trap.
How might Tanuja see Tejas's change over those days?
Tanuja may notice him surfacing slowly, with the plate of poha and the silence being a low-pressure way to show support.

metadata.subtype: Approach: cut all plans down to a minimum routine [Thinking]

messages.content: What is the aroha of Raga Bageshri?
The aroha of Raga Bageshri is: S g M D n S'.
Science fair mein judge ko dikhana hai ki mera model paani ko saaf karta hai. Kaise bolun?
Say: "This model cleans water." Use the simple present tense to say what a thing does.
A Mother's Day line, please, under ten words, ending with the word "you".
Thank you for everything, Amma. I love you.

Sum this up in one sentence.

Anxiety on Jane's behalf was another prevailing concern; and Mr. Darcy's explanation, by restoring Bingley to all her former good opinion, heightened the sense of what Jane had lost. His affection was proved to have been sincere, and his conduct cleared of all blame, unless any could attach to the implicitness of his confidence in his friend. How grievous then was the thought that, of a situation so desirable in every respect, so replete with advantage, so promising for happiness, Jane had been deprived, by the folly and indecorum of her own family!
Darcy's explanation shows Bingley truly cared, so it hurts to think Jane lost such a chance through her family's foolish behaviour.

Read this:

"Tushar, your turn to read."
"No, didi. I'm stupid at reading."
"Who said that?"
"Me. I'm the slowest in summer reading club."
Nirmala didi put the book down on the mat. "Slow and stupid aren't the same."
"They are for me."
"Okay. What happens when you read?"
"The long words get stuck."
"All of them?"
"...The ones with 'tion'."
"Like station?"
"Station. Yes."
"So you can read station."
"Only because you said it first."
"Then let's make a list of 'tion' words. You read them. I won't say them first."
"And if I get them wrong?"
"Then we'll know exactly what to practise. Not that you're stupid."
Tushar pulled the paper toward him. "Na... tion. Nation." He looked up. "That wasn't that bad."

Which long words get stuck for Tushar?
The ones with 'tion'.
Why did Tushar say he was stupid at reading?
Tushar felt ashamed of being the slowest in reading club, so one label seemed to explain everything.
How did Nirmala didi help Tushar move from a label to a skill?
She asked exactly which words got stuck, then made a list of 'tion' words for Tushar to practise without her saying them first.
What might Nirmala didi feel when Tushar read "Nation"?
She would likely feel pleased and encouraged that he tried and saw the problem was smaller than he thought.
I have many works to finish before the weekend. What is wrong?

I have a lot of work to finish before the weekend.
Why: "Work" meaning tasks is uncountable, so it has no plural and cannot follow "many".

Read this:

Day 1. At recess Francis mimicked Ankita's stammer and the boys roared. He felt ten feet tall, until Ankita's eyes went shiny and he noticed his own laugh sounded thin.

Day 3. At home his father shouted about the electricity bill, then about Francis's marks, then about nothing. Francis stayed in his room, smaller than he had felt all day. The next morning he shoved a Class 8 boy's books off a bench and everybody laughed again. The strong feeling lasted about a minute.

Day 10. His class teacher asked him to stay back. "You seem angry lately. Is something happening?" Francis stared at his shoes and said, "Home isn't good." The teacher walked him to the counsellor. He didn't feel strong, but he felt less alone.

What did Francis mimic at recess on Day 1?
He mimicked Ankita's stammer.
What might Francis be covering with the bullying, and what shows it?
Hurt at home. After his father's shouting he feels smaller than all day and shoves a boy's books the next morning, while the feeling of strength lasts only about a minute.
What helped Francis on Day 10?
His teacher asked kindly, Francis said home was not good, and the teacher took him to the counsellor.
How might Ankita have felt when Francis mimicked her?
Humiliated and hurt. Her eyes went shiny while the boys roared.

Read this:

My name is Yash, and you asked why I always explain the household bills to children. Let me tell you about Elizabeth, who lived in our building when she was nine. One night she sat on the stairs and heard her parents arguing in low voices about school fees. The next morning she told her mother she did not need new shoes and would skip the class trip. Her mother stared, then sat down beside her. That evening her father told her plainly: "Fees are tight this year. We are worried, we are managing, and it is not your job to fix it." Elizabeth cried, then ate two rotis. After that she stopped asking for less. She asked for extra chutney instead.

Where did Elizabeth sit when she heard her parents arguing?
She sat on the stairs.
What was Elizabeth feeling when she told her mother she did not need new shoes?
She was worried and anxious about the fees she overheard, and tried to help by asking for less.
What choice by Elizabeth's father changed the situation?
He told her plainly that fees were tight, that they were worried but managing, and that it was not her job to fix it, which calmed her more than silence would.
What might Elizabeth's mother have felt when her daughter offered to skip the trip?
She was probably surprised and sad, since she stared and then sat down beside her daughter.

Read this:

Friday
Got 17 out of 20 in the Hindi test. I hid it in the back of my geography book. Papa only smiles when it's 20. When I got 20 in maths, he took me for ice cream and hugged me and told Dadi on the phone. When I got 16 last month he didn't say anything at dinner, just looked at the paper and put it down. Nikita didi says he's just busy. But I think he likes me more when I get full marks. Tomorrow he'll ask about the Hindi test. I'll say it's not back yet. My stomach feels funny writing this. I wish he'd hug me even when it's 17.
Gautam

Where did Gautam hide the Hindi test?
In the back of the geography book.
Why does Gautam's stomach feel funny writing this?
Gautam worries that Papa's love depends on full marks, and feels guilty about planning to hide the test.
What could help Gautam and Papa most?
Gautam telling Nikita didi or Papa how it feels, and Papa showing warmth for effort and for Gautam, not only for 20 out of 20.
How might Papa feel if he read this diary?
Papa would probably be shocked and sad to learn that his silence felt like love being taken away, when he may only have been busy.

Read this:

Francis and Seema had been dating for a year in Bengaluru. Seema often asked, "Why don't you ever talk about your family? Your worries?"
Francis would shrug. "Nothing to tell." He kept his weekends for his cycling group and his evenings for himself. He liked Seema a lot. But getting close felt risky, like handing someone a map to hurt him.
One evening Seema said quietly, "I feel like I'm dating a locked door."
That night Francis lay awake. He realised he'd kept everyone at arm's length since his parents' divorce. Safe, but lonely.
The next evening he called her. "Can I tell you about my father?" His voice shook. Seema listened for an hour.
He didn't stop cycling. But he started letting her in.

What did Francis keep his weekends for?
He kept his weekends for his cycling group.
What was Francis feeling when he lay awake that night?
He felt lonely and uneasy, realising he'd kept everyone at arm's length since his parents' divorce to stay safe.
How did Francis begin to find a balance between closeness and self?
He kept his cycling but began sharing his inner life with Seema, starting with the call about his father.
How did Seema feel before Francis opened up?
Seema felt shut out and lonely, as if dating a locked door.
Write a 60-word description of my dog, a lazy old Labrador called Bruno, for my class blog.

Bruno is our eleven-year-old Labrador, and he is the laziest member of the family. He spends most of the day stretched across the cool floor near the front door, so everyone has to step over him. His golden fur has turned white around his nose. He only runs when he hears the fridge door open. We love him completely.
Write a story of about 100 words about a girl, her mango tree and a squirrel who keeps taking the fruit. The ending must be that she learns to share.

Nisha watched her mango tree all summer. When the first fruit turned yellow, a squirrel snatched it and ran. The next day, it took another. Nisha was cross and made a scarecrow, but the squirrel simply sat on its hat. One evening she found the squirrel sitting on a branch, nibbling happily, with its tiny face covered in juice. Nisha laughed. The tree had plenty of fruit. From then on, she picked what she needed and left a few on the lowest branch for her small friend.

Read this:

So, Sarika, you asked why I didn't ask for help sooner. I'm Rashmi, Class 11, and honestly, I had a whole list of reasons.
One: people at school say only weak people go to the counsellor. Two: I thought it would cost money, and home was already tight. Three: I was scared of what Papa would say. "What will people think?" is his favourite line. Four, the big one: I kept telling myself it wasn't bad enough. Other people had real problems.
So I waited. For almost a year. I stopped sleeping, stopped drawing, cried in the washroom most days.
Then I finally knocked on the counsellor's door. Turns out it's free at our school. She helped me talk to Papa, and he actually listened.
If you're waiting until it's bad enough, don't. Going early wasn't weak. It was the bravest thing I've done.

How long did Rashmi wait before asking for help?
Almost a year.
What was Rashmi feeling while putting off asking for help?
Rashmi felt afraid of looking weak and of Papa's reaction, anxious about cost, and unsure the problem was bad enough.
What would you advise someone with the same list of reasons?
Ask early, since services like the school counsellor may be free and can even help with family talks; waiting only lets things get worse.
How might Papa have felt when the counsellor helped Rashmi talk to him?
He might have been surprised and worried at first, then caring, since he actually listened.
I don't know wear I kept my specs. Spelling please.

I don't know where I kept my specs.
Why: "Where" asks about a place. "Wear" means to have clothes on your body.

Read this:

Class 9 life-skills note. Yogesh, maths teacher.
This month the class tracked their own pocket money for three weeks, then we discussed patterns. I asked them not to share amounts, only what they noticed.
Aadhya's notebook was the most honest. She'd written every item: bus, a pen, snacks. When she added it up, snacks from the school gate were more than everything else together. She was surprised and a little embarrassed. "They're so small each time," she said.
She decided on her own to carry fruit twice a week and to keep a simple table: what came in, what went out, what was left. She also asked whether she should keep her money in the family's bank account. I told her that's a question for her parents, and a bank official if they want.
I'll ask the class to reflect again at the end of term.

What was Aadhya surprised to find she spent most on?
Snacks from the school gate were more than everything else together.
How did Aadhya feel when she added up her snacks?
Aadhya felt surprised and a little embarrassed, since each purchase had seemed so small.
What did Yogesh handle wisely when Aadhya asked about a bank account?
He pointed her to her parents and a bank official instead of giving personal money advice himself.
How might Aadhya's classmates see her findings?
They might feel curious to check their own small spends, since hers surprised her so much.

Read this:

"Aditi, why are you checking the window again?"
"I just want to be sure it's locked, Lakshmi."
"You checked it five minutes ago. You never did that before."
"I don't know. Since Amma got so worried about my exams, I keep checking things."
"Oh. I thought it was just me."
"What do you mean?"
"I've started checking my bag three times before college. Every morning."
"Since when?"
"Since you started staying up checking your answer sheets. And Amma checking the gas every hour."
"So the whole house is checking."
"Pretty much."
Aditi laughed, then sighed. "Maybe we should tell Amma."
"Tonight. At dinner. All of us."
"And maybe one check each. Then done."
"Deal."

How many times does Lakshmi check her bag before college?
Three times.
How does Lakshmi seem to feel on realising the bag-checking started with Aditi's worry?
Lakshmi seems surprised and a little relieved, realising the worry spread through the house and isn't just hers.
What plan do Aditi and Lakshmi make, and why might it help?
They decide to talk to Amma at dinner and agree to one check each, which brings honest talk and clear limits to reduce the tension.
How might Amma feel when Aditi and Lakshmi raise it at dinner?
Amma might feel surprised and a bit guilty, but also relieved to talk openly about the worry.

Read this:

Hansa stood in the hostel corridor at the one spot where the network held. Her Dadi, Kalyani, had moved from the old house to a cousin's flat in another city and was quietly missing the courtyard. The texts Hansa sent were shown in a font too small for Dadi's eyes.
The warden walked by and Hansa lowered her voice, then pressed record. "Dadi, main Hansa. Aaj mess mein tumhari jaisi kadhi bani, par tumhari wali better hai. Sunday ko aati hoon video call par. Khana kha lena, theek?"
That night the warden's phone rang and it was Dadi's cousin: "She keeps replaying it. She says she can hear the corridor behind you."

Why did Dadi Kalyani miss the old house?
Dadi Kalyani missed the courtyard after moving from the old house to a cousin's flat in another city.
What was Hansa feeling as she lowered her voice in the corridor and recorded?
Hansa felt affectionate and a little homesick herself. Comparing the mess kadhi with Dadi's, and promising a Sunday call, shows how much Hansa cared.
What made a voice note the better choice than another text for Dadi?
The font in Hansa's texts was too small for Dadi's eyes, so hearing was easier than reading. The voice note carried warmth, and Dadi kept replaying it.
What might Dadi Kalyani have felt on hearing the corridor behind Hansa's voice?
Dadi Kalyani probably felt closer to Hansa and less lonely, since even the hostel background made Hansa feel near. Replaying the note suggests it soothed the missing.

Read this:

The panchayat office in the small town held its monthly meeting under the neem tree because the hall roof was leaking. Preeti, the data operator, is deaf and uses Indian Sign Language, and the district office had arranged an interpreter by video for the day. When the connection dropped, Vijay, the clerk beside her, didn't talk over her or write across her desk. He turned to face her so she could see his lips and hands, and signed the two signs he had learnt: "wait" and "again." Preeti smiled and pointed at the phone. She wrote a note: "Try the hotspot." Vijay laughed, held up his own phone, and the interpreter's face came back. Later he asked Preeti how he could learn more signs, and she showed him three.

Where was the monthly meeting held, and why?
Under the neem tree, because the hall roof was leaking.
What did Vijay intend by turning to face Preeti and signing "wait" and "again"?
He wanted to include her and show respect, not talk over her, and he used the few signs he knew.
What could the office do so Preeti has equal access at every meeting?
It can arrange a backup way to connect, such as a hotspot, book interpretation ahead, and let colleagues keep learning signs.
How might Preeti have felt when the connection dropped?
Possibly worried about losing the meeting, but her smile and note suggest she trusted Vijay and had a fix in mind.

metadata.subtype: Sign language in workplaces and public life [Expressing]

messages.content:
Do the maths from this passage: how many men are in one Gulma?

Between the two sides, the total number was eighteen Akshauhinis. Of this, the Pandava force consisted of seven Akshauhinis, while the Kaurava force consisted of ten Akshauhinis and one more. Five times fifty men constitute a Patti. Three Pattis make a Senamukha or Gulma. Three Gulmas make a Gana. In Duryodhana's army, there were thousands and hundred of such Ganas consisting of warriors capable of smiting (the foe) and longing for battle.
750 men. A Patti is five times fifty, which is 250, and a Gulma is three Pattis, so 3 x 250 = 750.

Read this:

Deepak, you've answered emails through our whole conversation. Let old Avni tell you what I learned at twenty-four, when I started as a translator at the publishing house in Kolkata. I had a phone that rang all day, a pile of manuscripts, and a boss who expected replies within minutes. I was translating and taking calls and checking proofs all at once, and I was always behind. One day my mentor, Mr Ganguly, locked my phone in his drawer from ten to twelve. I was furious. In those two hours I translated eleven pages, more than in the whole previous week. After that I kept those hours sacred: one manuscript, door closed. I returned calls after lunch, all together, then walked to the tea stall. I've translated forty books since. Close the email, Deepak.

How many pages did young Avni translate in the two locked hours?
Eleven pages.
How did young Avni feel when Mr Ganguly locked the phone away, and afterwards?
Avni felt furious at first, then amazed and relieved at doing more in two hours than in the whole previous week.
What was the turning point in Avni's story, and what routine followed?
Mr Ganguly locking the phone away; afterwards Avni kept two sacred hours for one manuscript, returned calls together after lunch, then walked to the tea stall.
Why might Mr Ganguly have locked the phone in his drawer?
Mr Ganguly probably saw Avni constantly switching and falling behind, and wanted to show what focus could do.
Why do so many people carry umbrellas when the morning sky is dark grey?
They expect rain later in the day. Because thick, dark clouds often mean rain is coming, and an umbrella keeps them dry if it starts.
What does a postman do? Answer in a sentence of exactly ten words.
A postman delivers letters and parcels to homes every day.

Read this:

In the small town near Nagpur, Nilesh's family always celebrated Buddha Purnima at the vihara at the end of their lane, and this year Nilesh had asked Tarun to come.

Tarun brought a box of pedhas from the station sweet shop and wore his best white shirt. At the vihara he took off his shoes, sat cross-legged on the mat beside Nilesh's father, and stayed silent through the chanting, watching the lamps float in the brass bowl.

Afterwards, Nilesh's aunt served kheer to everyone in the lane, whatever their faith. The old man from the flour mill clapped Tarun on the back. "You came for our festival? Good boy."

Walking home, Nilesh said, "You didn't have to sit through all that."

"I wanted to see what matters to you," Tarun said. "Now come for Ganpati. Aai's making modaks."

What did Tarun bring?
Tarun brought a box of pedhas from the station sweet shop.
What does Tarun's 'I wanted to see what matters to you' show about his feelings?
It shows warmth and respect for Nilesh; he cared about his friend's festival without needing to share the belief.
Which of Tarun's actions showed respect for the customs?
Taking off his shoes, sitting quietly through the chanting, and bringing sweets, then inviting Nilesh back for Ganpati.
How might Nilesh's family see Tarun's visit?
They likely feel honoured and more trusting, like the old man who clapped him on the back.

Read this:

Hiroshi had a red T-shirt with a small tiger on it. In Osaka, his football team had won the last three Saturdays, and each time, Hiroshi had worn the tiger shirt. "It's the shirt," he told Daniel, the goalkeeper. "When I wear it, we win." Daniel shrugged. "Maybe." On the fourth Saturday, the shirt was in the wash. Hiroshi was sure they would lose. He played nervously, looking at his plain blue shirt. They won anyway, 2–0. He didn't understand. The next Saturday he wore the tiger shirt, and they lost 1–3. Coach sat everyone down. "We won three because the other teams were weak. We lost today because this team is strong." Hiroshi looked at his tiger. "So it's not the shirt?" "It's the other team," Coach said.

What was on Hiroshi's red T-shirt?
A small tiger.
Why was Hiroshi nervous on the fourth Saturday?
He felt anxious because his tiger shirt was in the wash, and he believed the shirt caused the team's wins.
What did Coach help Hiroshi see, and what could he look at next time?
That wins and losses came from how strong the other teams were; next time he can look for other reasons behind a pattern.
How does Daniel seem to see the shirt?
Daniel seems unconvinced, just shrugging and saying "Maybe".

Read this:

Monday. Shankar, fourteen, got nineteen out of twenty in the algebra test. Lokesh Sir handed it back with raised eyebrows. "Nineteen? From you? Hm." Shankar's grin faded. Thursday. Lokesh Sir asked the class a hard question. Shankar knew the answer, but his hand stayed flat on the desk. What if he got it wrong and Sir thought, 'Yes, that's more like him'? He let someone else answer. The following Monday, Shankar hadn't done the homework. When his friend asked why, he shrugged. "Sir thinks I'm a back-bencher anyway. Why try and look stupid?" He drew in the margin of his notebook the whole period.

What did Shankar get in the algebra test?
Nineteen out of twenty.
What was Shankar worried about when his hand stayed flat on the desk?
He worried that a wrong answer would confirm what Lokesh Sir seemed to think of him.
What could Lokesh Sir have said on Monday instead, and what difference would it make?
He could have praised the nineteen plainly and asked how Shankar prepared, which would build belief instead of doubt.
How might Lokesh Sir see Shankar by the following Monday, and why is that unfair?
Sir might see an unmotivated back-bencher, not realising his own surprised remark helped push Shankar to stop trying.
Simran's savings of ₹2,000 grow by 5 percent in a year. How much does she gain?
She gains ₹100. Because 5 percent means 5 out of every 100, and there are 20 hundreds in 2,000, so 20 times 5 is 100.

Make this more formal, as if for a meeting report.

She closed her own laptop. "New rule. Laptops closed. We finish in twenty minutes, not two hours."

There were groans. But the meeting was sharp and quick, and Rafiq caught a bug in the plan that everyone had missed for weeks.

The team lead closed her laptop and introduced a new rule: all laptops were to stay closed, and the meeting would end in twenty minutes rather than two hours. Although some team members objected, the meeting was focused and efficient, and Rafiq identified a bug in the plan that had gone unnoticed for several weeks.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Thursday. Simran, second-year, came in to think aloud, not in crisis. Her girlfriend, Chandrika, has started an internship in another city and asked for fewer calls while she settles. Simran said that on the first night she felt panicky and typed three long messages, then deleted them and sent one: "Miss you. Call when you can. I'm okay." She described their fight last week: she said she needed a fixed Sunday call, and they both apologised the next day. She laughed at how ordinary it sounded. What I noticed: she can hold missing Chandrika and trusting her at the same time. Next step: we agreed she would book again only if she wanted to.

What message did Simran finally send on the first night?
"Miss you. Call when you can. I'm okay."
What was Simran feeling on the first night, and how did she handle it?
She felt panicky and typed three long messages, but deleted them and sent one calm line, showing she could trust Chandrika despite the fear.
How did Simran handle last week's fight?
She said clearly that she needed a fixed Sunday call, and both apologised the next day.
How might Chandrika experience Simran's short message?
Chandrika probably feels free to settle in without guilt, knowing Simran misses her but is okay.
Please revert back to me by evening. Is that the right phrase?

Please reply to me by evening.
Why: "Revert back" is common in Indian workplace English, but "revert" already includes the idea of "back" and in wider English it usually means returning to an earlier state. "Reply" or "get back to me" is clearer for all readers.

(1) I saw "defiance" in a story. What does it mean?
(2) What does "scale down" mean?
(3) Please improve this sentence: Their house is bigger than our.

1. "Defiance" is a noun. It means open refusal to obey.
2. It means to make something smaller in size or amount. For example: the school scaled down the annual day because of rain.
3. Fixed: Their house is bigger than ours. Why: when no noun follows, we use "ours", the possessive pronoun.

As we glided nearer, the stranger showed French colours from his peak; and by the eddying cloud of vulture sea-fowl that circled, and hovered, and swooped around him, it was plain that the whale alongside must be what the fishermen call a blasted whale, that is, a whale that has died unmolested on the sea, and so floated an unappropriated corpse. It may well be conceived, what an unsavory odor such a mass must exhale; worse than an Assyrian city in the plague, when the living are incompetent to bury the departed.

What is a 'blasted whale', according to this passage?
A whale that died naturally at sea and was left floating, with no one claiming it. Its rotting body gives off a terrible smell.

Read this:

Okay, you want to know about me and my dad? I'm Reena, fifteen, and lately we fight about everything: my phone, my friends, why I need the door shut. Papa, Uday Sharma, famous for his 8 pm curfew, thinks my friends are a bad influence because they wear ripped jeans. I argue back hard. Last week I told him I trust Ishani more than him, which was mean. And honestly, I don't tell him half of what happens. But here's the weird part. After every fight I go to the kitchen at night for water I don't need, just to walk past his room and hear him snoring. If he's snoring, we're okay. I don't want a different family. I want to be a different me, and I need them there while I figure it out.

What time is Papa's curfew?
His 8 pm curfew.
What does Reena's night walk past Papa's room show?
It shows Reena feels anxious after fights and needs to know home is still safe, even while pushing away.
What could help Reena and Uday argue less about the curfew?
Talking calmly about a slightly later time with clear check-ins, so Reena gets some freedom and Uday feels reassured.
How might Uday have felt when Reena said she trusts Ishani more?
Uday was probably hurt and worried, feeling pushed aside by his daughter.

Read this:

I'm Ojas, Harish's classmate. On Friday the district band results went up on the music-room door. Neel, who'd spent a month telling everyone he was a "sure thing" on drums, wasn't on the list. Harish was standing next to me. I saw it: a quick grin, a squeezed fist, like he'd scored a goal. Harish lost the drum spot to Neel last year, and Neel never let him forget it. But then Neel came round the corner, read the list, and just walked off with his hands in his pockets. Harish's grin went. He stared at the floor for a while. On the bus he was quiet, and I saw him type something to Neel. I don't know what it said, or whether he felt guilty or just awkward. But he didn't join the jokes at the back of the bus.

Where did the district band results go up?
On the music-room door.
What does Harish's grin fading and his stare at the floor suggest?
After a flash of pleasure at his rival's failure, he seemed uneasy, perhaps guilty, once he saw Neel walk off hurt.
What choice did Harish make on the bus, and why does it stand out?
He stayed out of the jokes at the back and typed something to Neel, choosing not to pile onto Neel's fall.
How might Neel have felt reading the list?
Neel had called himself a "sure thing", so missing out in front of everyone probably felt crushing and embarrassing; he walked off with his hands in his pockets.

metadata.subtype: Rival's failure feels good and bad [Actor]

messages.content: Is it "travelled" with two l's or "traveled" with one?

Both are accepted. British and Indian English usually double the l, as in "travelled", and American English usually uses one, as in "traveled".
Examples: We travelled to Goa by train. We traveled to Goa by train.
How is "water under the bridge" used after a quarrel?

It means that something unpleasant happened in the past and is no longer important, so there is no need to be upset about it.
Example: Forget the old argument, Vimal; it is water under the bridge.
Put this into reported speech: Neha said, "I am going to the library because I need a book on volcanoes."
Neha said that she was going to the library because she needed a book on volcanoes.
My British aunt said she will go to the "surgery". Is she having an operation?

Not necessarily. In British English "surgery" can also mean the place where a doctor or dentist sees patients. American English says "doctor's office".
Examples: The surgery opens at nine. The doctor's office opens at nine.

Read this:

Break-time note, Class 3. Chandrika, class teacher.
This week the class is mad about the elephant card game. I watched who gets asked to play. Gargi is first choice every day. On Monday she lost her best card in a bet and handed it over straight away, though she looked close to tears.
A boy from the other row has twice peeked at others' cards and swapped them when he thought nobody saw. By Thursday, when he walked up, the circle "accidentally" got too small. Nobody said why. He sat on the steps alone.
Tomorrow I will talk with him privately about fair play and how to win friends back, and read the class a story about keeping your word.

What did Gargi lose on Monday?
Her best card, in a bet.
What was Gargi feeling as she handed over her best card?
She was sad and close to tears, but determined to keep her word.
How could the teacher help the boy who was left out?
Talk privately about fair play and show that keeping promises over time can win back a place in the game.
What is it like for the boy when the circle gets too small?
He likely feels rejected and confused, sitting alone because his tricks have quietly cost him friends.

metadata.subtype: Being known as fair or a cheat [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

So the school podcast asked me to talk about doubt, and here goes. Around fifteen, namaz stopped feeling like anything. I stood, bowed, repeated the words and felt nothing, and I was scared that meant something was wrong with me. I told my friend Jomon first, after cricket practice. He didn't panic. He said, "You're allowed to wonder." It took me two more months to tell Abbu. I picked a Sunday, when he was calm. I said, "Abbu, I'm not sure I believe the way you do. I still love you, and I'll come for Eid and sit with the family." He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "I need time. But you're my son." I haven't stopped being kind to him, and he hasn't stopped saving me the first plate of biryani. It's slow, but it's ours. Rafiq

When did Rafiq tell Abbu about the doubts?
Rafiq chose a Sunday, when Abbu was calm.
What was Rafiq afraid of when namaz stopped feeling like anything?
Rafiq was scared that something was wrong, and afraid of hurting Abbu by saying it.
Which choice by Rafiq helped the family adjust?
Rafiq picked a calm Sunday and spoke respectfully, saying he still loves Abbu and will come for Eid and sit with the family.
How might Abbu have felt hearing this?
Probably hurt and unsettled, since he was quiet for a long time and asked for time. Yet he also said, "you're my son," which shows love.

Read this:

I'm Sarita. Last spring my college friend Kartik became a shift supervisor at the call centre where I also work. Kartik is the person who remembers everyone's birthday and cries at weddings. So it took me a while to believe what I saw: him standing behind Himani, a new trainee, reading her call transcript aloud to the floor and saying, 'This is what not to do.' She kept her eyes on her keyboard. I was angry. My first thought was to post about it in our friends' chat. Instead I thought about the floor: the live scoreboard, the managers upstairs listening in, the way everyone there talks faster and colder. It wasn't an excuse, but it explained something. Over chai I said, 'Kartik, that's not how you are at home. I think this place is getting into you.' He was defensive for a minute, then asked, 'What would you have done?'

What did Kartik read aloud to the floor?
Himani's call transcript, saying, 'This is what not to do.'
What did Sarita feel at first, and what changed Sarita's mind?
Sarita was angry and wanted to post in the friends' chat, but thinking about the scoreboard and managers listening in helped Sarita see how the place was shaping Kartik.
Which choice did Sarita make instead of posting, and what did it open up?
Sarita talked to Kartik over chai, naming the change and the place, which moved Kartik from defensive to asking what Sarita would have done.
What was the moment like for Himani?
Himani, a new trainee, was humiliated in front of the whole floor and could only keep her eyes on her keyboard 😔

metadata.subtype: Seeing the role, not the person [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Preeti, Hafsa's big sister. The lift in our building jerked and stopped for a second between floors. Hafsa, in Ammi's arms, went stiff, then started whimpering and clung to Ammi's neck. I said, "Ignore her, she'll stop." Ammi didn't. She held her tight, whispered, "I've got you, I've got you," and swayed. By the time the doors opened, Hafsa had stopped. Maybe I was wrong about ignoring.

Where did the lift stop?
Between floors, for a second.
What was Hafsa likely feeling when she whimpered and clung?
She was frightened by the jerk of the lift and wanted comfort and closeness from Ammi.
Why did Ammi's approach work better than ignoring?
Holding and soothing Hafsa helped her calm down quickly, while ignoring would have left her scared on her own.
How does Preeti see things by the end?
Preeti starts to think ignoring was the wrong idea after seeing Ammi's soothing work.
Write a story, about 100 words, about a village lantern festival where a small boy's lantern keeps going out, but a girl helps him. It should end with both lanterns floating up together.

At the village lantern festival, everyone carried a glowing lantern to the river. Little Ashok held his own, but a breeze blew it out again and again. He felt sad as the other lanterns floated away. A girl standing nearby saw him and came over. "Let me help," she said. She cupped her hands around his lantern and lit it again with her own. Together they walked to the water and set both lanterns on the river. They floated up in the warm night, side by side, and Ashok smiled.

Read this:

Seema, you're upset your favourite singer said those ugly things? Your Thomas appachan had a hero too. In 1972, in Kochi, it was Joseph Ittiyavira, the best striker in our district. I copied his hairstyle, his celebrations, even the way he tied his laces. Then the newspaper said he'd taken money to lose a match. I was sixteen. I cried, then shouted that it was lies. My father sat with me and said, 'He can be a great player and have done a wrong thing. You don't have to pick one.' It took me months. I stopped defending him. But I kept practising his left-foot shot, because that was mine now, not his. I'm still good with my left foot.

What was Joseph Ittiyavira accused of?
Taking money to lose a match.
How did sixteen-year-old Thomas feel when he read the newspaper?
Heartbroken and angry, crying and then insisting it was lies.
What choice in the story helped young Thomas move forward?
His father's words that a great player can do a wrong thing, which let Thomas stop defending the striker while keeping the left-foot shot as his own.
What might Thomas's father have been hoping when he sat with him?
To help his son grieve the hero without losing his love of football or his sense of right and wrong.

Read this:

I was taking notes at the planning meeting when Chetan read out his list of speakers for the conference. Six names. I knew at least four; they were his batchmates. Bhavna listened, nodded, and then did something I'd never seen a chair do. She asked everyone to write the selection criteria on the whiteboard first: expertise, fresh ideas, a mix of regions, a new voice. Then she put Chetan's six beside the criteria. Two fitted well. Four were friends of friends. She didn't say that. She just asked, "Who's missing?" Someone mentioned a researcher from Guwahati. Someone else, a woman who ran a rural lab. Bhavna added them. Then she said, "Let's check: would we pick these same people if none of us knew them?" Chetan went red, but he nodded. The final list kept two of his names.

How many speakers were on Chetan's list?
Six names.
How might Chetan have felt when he went red?
Chetan probably felt embarrassed, seeing that most of his picks were friends rather than the best fits for the criteria.
What made Bhavna's approach fair?
She set clear criteria first, asked who was missing, and checked whether they'd choose the same people as strangers.
Why did Bhavna ask "Who's missing?" instead of criticising Chetan's list?
She seemed calm and fair-minded, wanting to widen the list without shaming Chetan in front of everyone.
My friend said "I got 85 percentage in the exam". Is that correct?

Standard English says "I got 85 percent" for a score. "Percentage" means a share of a whole, as in "A large percentage of the class passed."
Examples: I got 85 percent in the exam. A large percentage of the class passed.

Read this:

Varun: ok weird theory. the dog next door barks right before every power cut
Nitin: every one?
Varun: last 3. I'm telling you it knows
Nitin: how often does it bark when the power doesn't go?
Varun: …a lot actually
Nitin: then log it for two weeks. every bark, every cut
Varun: fine. scientist mode 🤓

Two weeks later
Varun: results. 41 barking fits. 4 power cuts. 3 after barking
Nitin: so it barks all day and sometimes the power goes
Varun: yeah. if it were chance it'd look exactly like this 😅
Varun: honestly I was getting jumpy at night listening for it
Nitin: glad you checked. if it keeps you up, talk to someone ok
Varun: I will. sleeping fine now tbh

How many power cuts happened in the two weeks?
Four power cuts, three of them after barking.
What does Varun's admission about getting jumpy at night suggest?
It suggests the theory had started to unsettle Varun, and checking it brought relief.
What did Nitin's suggestion to log every bark do well?
It tested the pattern on new data, including all the barks without power cuts, which showed it looked just like chance.
How might Nitin feel reading that Varun was jumpy at night?
Nitin seems caring and a bit concerned, which is why the offer to talk to someone comes in.

metadata.subtype: Testing the pattern before believing it [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Zeenat, and my little brother Zayan is five. Every night he checks under the bed with a torch, then says, "Go away, go away, zoom zoom," three times, to keep the monsters out. Only then will he let Ammi switch off the light.
Last week his tooth fell out, and he put it under his pillow with a drawing for the tooth fairy. In the morning there was a coin. He told everyone at breakfast the fairy had sparkly shoes.
I don't know how much he believes. But when he forgets the zoom words, he can't sleep. Now our cousin Dilnaz, who's four, says them too.

What does Zayan say three times at bedtime?
"Go away, go away, zoom zoom."
Why can't Zayan sleep when he forgets the zoom words?
The words feel like real protection to him, so without them the monsters seem able to come in and he feels unsafe.
How could Ammi help if Zayan forgets the words one night?
Say them with him calmly, check under the bed together with the torch, and stay a little while until he settles.
What might Dilnaz get from copying the zoom words?
Dilnaz probably feels braver too, since the older cousin's special words seem to work.
My coach tells us to "keep our cool" when the score is close. What does it mean?

To keep your cool means to stay calm in a difficult or stressful moment. It is informal.
Example: Keep your cool, Zara; the bus will come soon.

Read this:

Nitin came home from tuition, dropped his bag in the doorway of the Pune flat and announced, "My life is literally over. I wore the wrong shoes to the farewell and everyone will remember it forever." Sudha, his mother, was chopping onions and felt the old urge to say, "Nobody cares about your shoes." Then she remembered crying over a bad haircut at his age. Instead she said, "That sounds awful to walk in with." Nitin sat down and talked for twenty minutes. A week later, over tea, Sudha asked what his friend Arvind had worn. Nitin paused. "Actually, Arvind's trousers were torn. No one said anything." He looked at her, half embarrassed, half amused. Sudha only smiled and passed the biscuits.

What did Nitin say had gone wrong at the farewell?
He said he wore the wrong shoes to the farewell.
What was Sudha feeling when she held back "Nobody cares about your shoes"?
She felt tempted and a little impatient, but remembering her own teenage upset made her sympathetic, so she chose to listen instead.
Which choice worked, and why?
Listening first and asking about Arvind a week later worked, because Nitin felt taken seriously and then noticed by himself that others have awkward moments too.
How does Nitin see the shoe problem once Sudha has listened?
At first it feels huge and permanent to him; a week later he sees that Arvind's torn trousers went unnoticed and feels half embarrassed about his worry.

Read this:

The university sports complex was nearly empty at six, just the thud of a basketball from the far court. Keerthana had asked Baljeet to meet her on the bleachers, not over text. For weeks she'd been drafting ways to fade out: slower replies, 'busy with exams', letting it die quietly. But she knew how that would feel from his side. When he sat down, smiling, her stomach twisted. 'Baljeet, I need to be honest. I've thought about this a lot. I want to end our relationship.' His smile fell. 'Did I do something?' 'No. You didn't do anything wrong. I just don't feel the way I did, and I don't think that's coming back. I didn't want to lie or disappear.' He was quiet. 'Can we try?' 'I don't want to give you false hope. I'm sorry.' She stayed while he sat with it. Walking home, she felt guilt and, under it, a clear, quiet relief.

Where did Keerthana meet Baljeet?
On the bleachers of the university sports complex.
What did Keerthana feel walking home?
Guilt, and underneath it, a clear, quiet relief.
What did Keerthana do instead of fading out?
She told Baljeet face to face, honestly, without blaming him or giving false hope, and stayed while he took it in.
How does Baljeet react?
His smile falls and he asks if he did something and whether they can try.

- Meaning of loathsome, please.
- Help me correct this: He is fond to sweets.
- Why do we get sleepy after a big meal?
- Who won the match last night?

1. "Loathsome" is an adjective. It means causing hate or disgust.
2. Better: He is fond of sweets. Why: "fond" goes with "of".
3. The body sends effort to digesting a heavy meal. Because digesting takes a lot of energy, we can feel slow and sleepy.
4. I don't know; I can't see live or recent scores. Check a sports news site or ask a friend who watched.

Write this as a short note from Mrs D'Souza to Kamal's parents.

Monday: At recess, Sunaina's group was playing house. "You can't play, Kamal. It's only for us." Kamal's lip wobbled. He kicked their play kitchen over and ran off.
Wednesday: The same words again. This time Kamal went to Mrs D'Souza, eyes wet. She knelt. "Tell me with words." "I feel sad. They said no." She nodded. "That hurts. Let's find someone else to play with." She walked him to the sandpit, where two children were digging a river.
Friday: Kamal ran straight to the sandpit and shouted, "I'll dig the bridge!"

Note for Kamal's parents

On Monday at recess, Sunaina's group was playing house and told Kamal, "You can't play, Kamal. It's only for us." His lip wobbled. He kicked their play kitchen over and ran off.
On Wednesday they said the same words again. This time Kamal came to me with wet eyes. I knelt and said, "Tell me with words." He said, "I feel sad. They said no." I nodded and said, "That hurts. Let's find someone else to play with." I walked him to the sandpit, where two children were digging a river.
On Friday Kamal ran straight to the sandpit and shouted, "I'll dig the bridge!"
Can you help me thank the neighbour who watered my plants while I was away for two weeks? About 40 words.

Dear Mrs. Khan,
Thank you so much for watering my plants while I was away. They look healthier than when I left! I've brought you some tea from Darjeeling as a small thank-you. I owe you a favour anytime.
Warmly,
Sneha

Read this:

In the courtyard behind the house, five-year-old Tushar crowned the calf king of the whole village with a marigold garland. "Why is the well water so cold? Why do crows hop? Why does the calf have no top teeth?" His sister Vidya, drawing water, laughed and answered what she could. When she suggested hopscotch again, like yesterday, Tushar groaned. "Same-same is boring." At lunch he stirred jaggery into his curd rice and called it royal food. Vidya almost said, "Don't be silly," and then stopped. "What does the king eat for sweet?" she asked. Tushar's eyes lit up.

What did Tushar stir into his curd rice?
He stirred jaggery into his curd rice.
Why did Tushar groan at the idea of hopscotch?
He felt bored at repeating yesterday's game and wanted something new, as "Same-same is boring" shows.
What choice did Vidya make at lunch, and how did it help Tushar?
She stopped herself from calling him silly and asked what the king eats for sweet, which let his make-believe keep growing.
What might it be like for Vidya to have a brother who asks so many why questions?
It can be a lot while she is busy drawing water, but she laughs, answers what she can and seems to enjoy joining his game.

Read this:

In the Hyderabad office, during Tuesday's review, Yusuf had presented the customer analysis as "my findings." Swati had done most of it. She'd said nothing, but he saw her face. On Wednesday morning, before the team huddle, he asked her for five minutes in the small meeting room. "Swati, yesterday I took credit for your analysis. That was wrong, and I'm sorry. No excuse." Swati looked surprised. "Okay." "What would help?" She thought about it. "Say it to the team. And put names on slides from now on." At the huddle, Yusuf said, "Correction from yesterday: the customer analysis was Swati's work. It was excellent." That afternoon he added a line to the team template: "Prepared by:". Two weeks later, Swati invited him to co-lead her next project.

What line did Yusuf add to the team template?
"Prepared by:"
Why did Yusuf ask Swati what would help rather than deciding himself?
He felt guilty and wanted the repair to meet Swati's needs, not just ease his own discomfort.
What made Yusuf's apology something Swati could actually feel?
He named the specific wrong, corrected it publicly, and changed the template so it wouldn't happen again.
How might Swati feel when invited to co-lead with Yusuf?
Swati seems to feel she can trust him again, since the repair was real and lasting.

Read this:

Subject: I need to tell someone

Mehak,
You know me. In college I returned extra change to canteen uncle. So believe me when I say I don't recognise myself this week.
Our investors want the quarter to show growth, or the next round won't happen and twelve people lose their jobs. Nobody checks exactly when a contract is counted as revenue. I noticed that in January.
On Friday I counted a deal that isn't signed yet. The client said "very likely". I told myself it's only timing, investors can easily afford a small surprise, and every founder I know stretches a bit.
The report went out Saturday. Nobody said anything.
And I felt relief, Mehak. That's what I can't stop thinking about. Relief, not guilt.
I've always thought people who did this were a different kind of person. I think I was wrong.
Can we talk tonight?
Ayesha

When did the report go out?
The report went out on Saturday.
Why does Ayesha find the relief more disturbing than guilt would be?
The relief shows how natural the wrong step felt, which frightens Ayesha, who always seemed the honest one who returned extra change.
What wise step is Ayesha taking by writing to Mehak?
Ayesha is telling a trusted person quickly and asking to talk that night, which could lead to correcting the report before it grows.
How might the twelve employees see the choice if they knew about it?
They might feel grateful Ayesha was trying to protect their jobs, yet uneasy that their company's future now rests on a report that isn't true.

Read this:

"Ganga beta, you think your Nanaji was always a quiet man? He was. Let me tell you about our first year.
I, Mehak, your Nani, was married at twenty. I came to his house from a big, loud family where everyone shouted their feelings. Your Nanaji came home from the mill, ate, and said, 'Good food.' That was all.
I cried for months. I thought, this man does not love me. When my father died, he did not say sorry. He just sat outside my door all night.
One day I asked him straight, 'Do you feel anything for me?' He went red and said, 'I don't know how to say such things.' Then he showed me the savings book. He had opened it in my name.
After that I learned to read him, and he learned a few words. Very few."

What did Nanaji do the night Mehak's father died?
He sat outside her door all night.
How did young Mehak feel in the first months of marriage?
She felt shut out and unloved, crying for months because her husband never spoke his feelings.
What turning point in the story changed how Mehak saw her husband?
Asking him directly; his red face, his admission that he didn't know how to say such things, and the savings book showed his care came without words.
How might Nanaji have felt when Mehak asked if he felt anything for her?
He was probably embarrassed and awkward, going red, because he cared but found feeling-words very hard.

Read this:

So on the school radio show they asked, what changed how you see things this year? For me it was Afreen. She topped the maths test, and I asked if she wanted to revise at my place, and she said she had to catch the six-ten bus, because there's no later one. I had always thought everyone had a fan, a desk and a quiet corner. Afreen does her homework on a shared table with her little brothers. That day I realised that my marks come partly from my things. I don't think that's something to feel guilty about. It just means I should say thank you at home, and make sure Afreen gets the same practice papers I get. We share them now, and she explains the tricky ones better than my tutor does. Shankar

What bus did Afreen have to catch?
Afreen had to catch the six-ten bus, because there is no later one.
What did Shankar realise that day, and how does Shankar feel about it?
Shankar realised that the marks come partly from having a fan, a desk and a quiet corner. Shankar feels thankful and more aware, not guilty.
Which choice did Shankar make after realising this?
Shankar decided to say thank you at home and to share the same practice papers with Afreen, so both have equal practice.
How might Afreen see the sharing of practice papers?
Afreen probably sees it as fair and friendly, since she also explains the tricky ones and helps in return, so it is exchange and not charity.

Read this:

Teacher's note, Christmas term.

Sarita and Meenu have been best friends all year. For the Christmas carol duet, Meenu chose Tina as her partner instead of Sarita.

Sarita went very quiet. At break she snapped at Tina and told Meenu, "Fine, go sing with her." Later she cried in the corridor. She said, "Meenu will like Tina more now."

I sat with her and said it's normal to feel scared of losing a friend. I suggested she tell Meenu how she felt. She did at lunch. Meenu said the duet was only because Tina's voice matched hers.

— Hansa

Who did Meenu choose for the duet?
Meenu chose Tina as her partner.
What was Sarita feeling when she snapped at Tina?
Sarita was jealous and afraid of losing Meenu's friendship to Tina.
How did Hansa help Sarita with her jealousy?
Hansa sat with her, said the fear was normal, and suggested talking honestly to Meenu.
How might Tina have felt when Sarita snapped at her?
Tina may have felt hurt or confused, since she only sang with Meenu for the duet.

Read this:

The release was due at nine the next morning, and at seven in the evening the payment screen still froze on older phones. Ira noticed it first. Two months ago she would have rolled her chair over to Anirban's desk and said, "Look at this, it's weird." Now Anirban sat in the glass cabin by the window, and the last two times she had raised something in the stand-up he had cut her off with "Let's take that offline" and never come back to it. She opened a message to him, wrote "Small thing on payments," and stopped. The office lights clicked to night mode. Beside her, Farhan was quietly patching around the same bug without telling anyone. "Should we flag it?" Ira whispered. Farhan shrugged. "He'll say we're slowing things down." They both kept typing, and the message stayed unsent.

What was due at nine the next morning?
The release was due at nine the next morning.
Why does Ira stop before sending the message to Anirban?
She feels hurt and unsure of her place, because the last two times she raised something he cut her off and never came back to it.
What turning point is available here, and who could take it?
Ira could still send the message, framed as a risk to the release; Anirban could make it safe by asking the team directly what is worrying them before a launch.
What is Anirban likely missing from inside the glass cabin?
He probably thinks the team is fine because it is quiet, while a real bug is being hidden from him and fixed in secret.

Read this:

The subject form was due at nine the next morning, and Sachin still had two boxes half-ticked: Maths with Computer Science, which his friends were taking, or Biology. The power was out, so he sat on the balcony with a torch and his sister Vinita's old notebook. What do I actually want at the end? he asked himself. A doctor. Like the one who sat with Dadi every day last winter. So, backward: to study medicine, I need to clear NEET. NEET asks Physics, Chemistry and Biology. Those come from Class 11 and 12. So Biology isn't one choice among many. It's the only road there. Vinita came out with a candle. "Still deciding?" "Not deciding any more," he said, and ticked Biology. "The goal decided."

Where did Sachin sit to think during the power cut?
On the balcony with a torch.
How does Sachin seem to feel once he ticks Biology?
He seems settled and relieved, no longer torn between the two boxes.
What else could Sachin check before handing in the form?
Ask a teacher whether he can keep Maths as an extra subject, so the plan has some flexibility if the goal changes.
How might Vinita see her brother's quick decision?
Vinita may be surprised by his certainty after a long evening of doubt, and glad the choice comes from a clear goal.

metadata.subtype: Approach: working backward from a career goal [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Sunday
Our first "money Sunday". Kunal made chai, I opened the shared sheet, and we went through the month line by line, his side and mine. He had to explain a cricket bat he'd bought for his nephew and actually blushed. That helped more than he knows. It wasn't just me on trial.
Then my cousin Deepika texted asking if I could lend her something for her course fees. Old me would have sent it and deleted the message. Instead I showed Kunal, and we used the rule we agreed with the counsellor: any family help beyond small things, we talk first and decide together, even when the answer is yes. The answer was yes.
Kunal joked that his wife now keeps better records than his office. We've said we'll keep this Sunday habit for six months and then see if we still need it. It feels less like a cage than I feared. More like a handrail.
Trisha

What did Kunal have to explain on the shared sheet?
Kunal had to explain a cricket bat he'd bought for his nephew.

Arohi had twenty minutes before the next shift at the helpline office in Hyderabad, and the canteen was shut. Her last caller, Lakshmi, an elderly woman whose house had been damaged by the rains, had cried through the whole call. Arohi could still hear her.
She stood by the window and did the thing her supervisor had taught her: she named it. "That grief is Lakshmi's. My job was to hear it, not to keep it." Her shoulders loosened a little.
She drank water, walked the corridor twice and did not open the news on her phone.
Before logging back in, she wrote a note to follow up on the repair grant for Lakshmi's house with the team. It was small, but it was something she could actually do.

She worked at the helpline office in Hyderabad.

She felt weighed down by the caller's grief, still hearing her crying, but she named it as Lakshmi's feeling, and her shoulders loosened with some relief.

Naming whose feeling it is, taking a short real break away from heavy content, and turning the care into a small action like a follow-up note.

She might feel that someone truly heard her and that her call led to real help, not just sympathy.

Every afternoon that summer, Indu picked up her two younger brothers from school in Hyderabad, gave them lunch, helped with homework and kept them out of trouble until her parents got home at eight.
When her father, Lalit, asked, "All okay, beta?" she said, "Yes, fine." Every day.
But Lalit started noticing things. She had stopped humming in the kitchen. Her own books lay unopened on the table. One night she fell asleep sitting up.
On Sunday he made two cups of tea and sat beside her on the balcony. "Indu, you've gone quiet. I'm not angry. What's hard right now?"
She held the cup for a long moment. "Everything. I have no time for my own studies. I'm tired all the time. I didn't want to say, because you're both working so hard."
Lalit nodded slowly. "Thank you for saying it. Let's change the plan together."

What time did Indu's parents get home?
Her parents got home at eight.
What was Indu feeling underneath her daily "Yes, fine"?
Indu felt overwhelmed and exhausted, but afraid of adding to her parents' burden since they were working so hard.
What small step did Lalit take that helped?
He noticed her withdrawal, sat with her over tea, said he wasn't angry, and asked what was hard, which let her state her needs plainly.
How might Indu's younger brothers see those afternoons?
They probably saw only their big sister managing everything and had no idea how tired and stretched she felt.

Kavitha, you asked for your podcast about small habits at work. Here's mine. I'm Lalremsiami, twenty-six, a nurse on a busy surgical ward in Chennai. There's never time to stop and chat. So when I pass a colleague across the ward, I flash my eyebrows up and smile: quick, silent, friendly. Most of the team knows it now. But a new ward boy, Selvam, joined last month, and for two weeks I flashed my eyebrows at him every morning. He never reacted. I started to wonder if he disliked me. Then one day he said, very politely, "Sister, are you angry with me? You make a face every morning." I laughed so hard. He'd thought my eyebrows were a frown! I told him it was my hello. Now I say, "Good morning, Selvam," out loud as well. He says it back and flashes his own eyebrows, badly. It's our joke now.

Where does Lalremsiami work?
On a busy surgical ward in Chennai.
What was Selvam feeling about the morning eyebrow flash?
He was worried and confused, wondering if Lalremsiami was angry with him.
What did Lalremsiami change, and why did it help?
Adding a spoken "Good morning, Selvam" made the greeting clear instead of relying on the easy-to-miss eyebrow flash.
What would change if Lalremsiami had never added the spoken greeting?
Selvam might have kept thinking she was angry with him every morning, and they would never have shared the joke.

Week one. Keerthana had just taken over the warehouse move from a colleague who had left a list of nineteen risks. Abhinav, her deputy, sighed. "We'll never plan for all of these."
"We won't," she said. She marked each one for how likely and how costly. Three stood out: trucks not available on moving day, the new racks arriving late, and staff overtime running out. Each got a trigger. If trucks aren't confirmed ten days before, book a second company. If racks aren't shipped by the 5th, rent temporary shelving. If overtime passes forty hours, bring in the weekend temp team.
Week three. The racks were shipped on time. Keerthana crossed that line out in front of Abhinav.
Week five. At the last review, only the overtime rule was left. It triggered once, the temps came in, and the move finished on the planned Saturday.

When did the move finish?
The move finished on the planned Saturday.
How did Abhinav feel on seeing the list of nineteen risks?
Abhinav felt overwhelmed and discouraged, sighing that they would never plan for all of them.
Why was crossing out the rack line after it shipped a good step?
It kept the list short and focused on what could still go wrong, so attention didn't go to risks that had already passed.
How might the staff in the warehouse experience the overtime rule?
They get help from the weekend temp team once overtime passes forty hours, so they aren't pushed too far.

messages.content: I'm moving to a new city for college and I'm nervous.
Feeling nervous is natural. Moving means new people, places and routines. A little planning makes it easier. Is there anything in particular worrying you?
Mostly finding my way around.
Look at a map of the area before you go, and note the route to college, shops and the nearest hospital. Walk the route once in daylight to get familiar.
What if I get lost?
Keep your phone charged and a note of your address. You can ask shopkeepers or other students for directions. Most people are happy to help.
How do I make friends?
Join a club, talk to people in your class and say yes to simple invitations. Friendships often start with small, ordinary conversations.
What if I feel homesick?
It is common and usually eases over weeks. Calling home helps, but also keep busy with new routines. If it feels too heavy, a college counsellor can help.

In a Copenhagen playground, two-year-old Yosef slipped off the low slide. He opened his mouth, gulped air, and for a long moment made no sound at all. Then came hiccupping sobs. Yosef slipped off the low slide.

The hospital canteen closed at nine, and Amandeep had forty minutes, a cold samosa and a paper napkin. His mother's treatment had moved to three days a week, his final-year exam was in eleven days, and his phone kept buzzing with the group project.
His cousin Rukmini sat across. "You look like you're trying to do everything."
"I am." He smoothed the napkin and wrote everything: Mum's appointments, the exam, the group project, two assignments, cooking, electricity bill, cousin's wedding function, gym.
"Okay," he muttered. "What breaks if I miss it? Mum's appointments. The exam. Those two first." He drew a box around them. "Assignments I can ask to delay. Cooking, Masi offered. Bill takes five minutes. Wedding and gym..." He crossed both out.
"You're saying no to the wedding?"

His exam was in eleven days.

“Nine hours left,” Elizabeth said, tapping her laptop. “I work best under pressure.” Nazia, her roommate, glanced at the clock and at the empty document. At 2 pm the campus internet crashed. Elizabeth ran to the library, found every table taken, and typed on the staircase with the laptop on her knees. At 4:20 she attached the file, but the charts were missing, and the conclusion ended mid-sentence. She submitted at 4:58 anyway, and lay on her bed, exhausted, with a headache. “It'll be fine,” she said. But she had not slept the night before, and she knew the essay was not what she had meant it to be. Nazia handed her some water and said nothing.

The campus internet crashed at 2 pm.

Elizabeth was exhausted and uneasy, trying to reassure herself, while knowing the essay was not what she had meant.

The internet crash and a crowded library left no slack, and the essay went in with missing charts and an unfinished conclusion, showing the habit has costs.

Nazia is probably sympathetic and a little worried, having seen the pattern, but chooses kindness over saying “I told you so”.

Friday night
Declined the bank offer today. The famous one, with the logo everyone knows. I sat in the canteen for twenty minutes before I pressed send.
Then I emailed the wildlife trust and said yes. Field researcher. Tents, leeches, camera traps in the Western Ghats. A tiny fraction of the pay.
Damini called. "Are you okay?" I said I didn't know. My stomach was in knots. Papa's face when I told him. The cousins' comments.
But after we hung up, I sat on the terrace and felt something I haven't felt since the forest trip in second year. Quiet. Like I'd stopped wearing someone else's shoes.
Scared and calm at the same time. Didn't know that was possible.
– Gautam

In the Western Ghats.

School counsellor's note, Class 9. Shreya (14) came to see me on Tuesday, near tears. Since getting braces last month, she says the whole class stares at her mouth and thinks she looks "disgusting." She has stopped answering questions aloud and eats lunch in the library. When I asked what, exactly, people had said, she paused. "Nothing. But I can tell." She described catching two girls looking her way and "knowing" they were judging. I noticed she called herself ugly three times in ten minutes. I didn't argue with her feeling. I asked her to write down, for one week, every comment anyone actually made about her braces. We'll look at it together next Tuesday. I have also asked her class teacher, Ms Manjula, to invite her to read aloud gently, without singling her out. — Mrs Dsouza

Three times.

The cyclist kept weaving through traffic. I only know weaving as making cloth.

You want me to be honest on this podcast? Okay. I'm Maria, I'm twenty-two, and last spring I became someone I didn't recognise.
Thomas had gone quiet. Normal quiet at first, then more. And his quiet felt like proof, like he'd already decided to leave me.
So I got louder. Paragraphs at midnight. Crying on video calls. "You don't care, you never did." Once I showed up at his flat at eleven because he hadn't answered for three hours.
And every time I pushed, he went further away. Fewer words. Longer gaps.
In my head he was the one who started it by shutting down. In his, I was. We were both completely sure.

At eleven, after he hadn't answered for three hours.

At the yoga centre in Rishikesh where Pooja had volunteered every summer since she was eighteen, the teacher preached simple living: one meal a day, no possessions. Shalini met Chinmay at a café in Koramangala for the first time in a year. He had spread the rumour at their office that she'd been fired for cheating, when in fact she'd resigned. Last month he had messaged her a long apology, admitting he'd been jealous. Today he said it again, face to face, looking at the table. Shalini listened. She had already decided, walking there, that she forgave him; carrying the anger had worn her out. But forgiving him didn't mean telling him things again the way she used to. "I accept your apology," she said. "I'm happy to meet for coffee now and then. I'm not ready to talk about work or my personal life with you yet." Chinmay nodded slowly. "That's fair." Teacher's note, October
Francis, second-year history, has not submitted a single draft this term, only final essays. His work is excellent. But on Monday, after getting 17 out of 20, he stayed behind and cried. He said, "I should have got full marks. I'm not good at this."
I am worried he connects his worth to every mark.
I have made three changes. I now praise effort and specific progress in his feedback. I showed the class a draft of my own with my editor's comments. And for the next essay, drafts are required and marked only for trying.
Today he submitted a rough draft. It had a question mark in the margin. Small step.
Chetan

What mark did Francis get on Monday?
17 out of 20.
What is Chetan worried about?
Chetan feels worried that Francis ties his worth to every mark.
Which changes did Chetan make, and why might they help?
Praising effort, showing a personal draft with an editor's comments, and requiring drafts marked only for trying, which make mistakes feel safe.
What might Francis be feeling as he hands in a rough draft?
Francis is probably nervous, but slightly braver, trying something that isn't perfect.
How do I tell a simile from a metaphor?
A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as', such as 'her smile was like sunshine'. A metaphor says one thing is another, such as 'her smile was sunshine'.
What about 'He ran as fast as a cheetah'?
That is a simile, because it uses 'as ... as' to compare. 'He was a cheetah on the track' would be the metaphor version.

Anand had three days to find a flat near his new office in Bengaluru before the company's guest house kicked him out. Rain had flooded half the roads. He'd seen four places already.

The fifth was a one-bedroom in Koramangala. The owner, Joseph, a retired bank manager, said at the door: "Twenty-eight thousand a month."

Anand's stomach dropped. He was tired and wet. "Twenty-four?" he said.

Joseph shook his head. "Twenty-six. Final. Many people want it."

Anand agreed and felt he'd done well: two thousand off!

That night, in the guest house, his colleague showed him a rental site. Similar flats two lanes away: eighteen to twenty. Anand checked twice.

He'd negotiated down from twenty-eight. He had never once asked what the flat was actually worth.

How much did Joseph first say the flat cost?
Twenty-eight thousand a month.
Why did Anand feel he had done well at twenty-six?
Anand felt relieved and pleased because twenty-six seemed like a win against the first figure of twenty-eight, and he was tired and rushed.
What could Anand do before the next viewing?
Anand could check what similar flats nearby usually cost, ideally with a colleague or someone who knows the area, before hearing any quote.
How might the colleague have felt showing Anand the rental site?
The colleague may have felt a bit sorry for Anand, seeing he had agreed quickly under pressure.

Monday. Papa called Vandana at 5:10, 5:40 and 6:15. "When are you coming? The house is too quiet." Since Mummy died, he wanted her there every evening. Vandana cancelled her pottery class for the fourth week and sat with him through the news, loving him and feeling the walls press in.

Thursday. On the bus she called her sister in Pune. "Reena, I need you to do something specific. Video-call Papa every evening at seven. Every single one." Reena hesitated. "I didn't know he was calling you so much." "He is. And I'm not managing." Reena agreed, and said she'd come for two weekends a month.

Three weeks later. On Tuesday evening Vandana's hands were grey with clay. At seven, Papa was laughing at something Reena said on the tablet, and Sharma uncle from next door had come for carrom. Vandana still visited four evenings a week, but now she wanted to.

How many times did Papa call Vandana on Monday evening?
He called her three times, at 5:10, 5:40 and 6:15.
How did Vandana feel sitting with Papa on Monday?
Vandana felt loving but trapped, as though the walls were pressing in.
Which of Vandana's choices made the biggest difference?
Asking Reena for a specific task, a daily video call and two weekends a month, shared the load instead of hoping for vague help.
How might Reena feel after learning how often Papa called Vandana?
Reena might feel guilty and surprised, which is why she agreed to regular calls and visits.
