"Parveen, what do you want for dinner tonight?" Sangeeta khala asked, opening the fridge.
"Anything is fine."
"Rajma or egg curry?"
"Anything."
"You've lived with me four months now. You always say anything."

"Then let's start small. Rajma or egg curry. Just pick one."
Parveen was quiet for a long moment. "Egg curry," she whispered.

How long has Parveen lived with Sangeeta khala?
She has lived with her for four months.

She feels resigned and unsure her wishes count, because at the old house what she wanted never mattered, and that belief has stayed even in a new home.
Which choice by Sangeeta khala worked, and why?
She made the choice very small, rajma or egg curry, so Parveen could safely say what she wanted and see that it counts.

messages.content: Can associates be friends or are they only co-workers?

They can be either, but usually associates are people you work or spend time with, often through a job. It is a noun here, the plural of associate.
Example: The manager introduced her associates at the meeting.

She told me that she had lost her ring.

In Class 10, I told the class teacher that Nilesh and his friends were planning to jump from the school's first-floor roof into the sandpit, for a video. I'd heard them planning it at lunch.
Part of me was scared someone would get hurt. But part of me, honestly, was still angry at Nilesh for a fight we'd had.
The teacher didn't ask why I was telling. She said, "Thank you. This matters." That same afternoon she spoke to the boys and called their parents, and the roof door was locked.
Nilesh called me a snitch for weeks. I felt bad. But later I realised, whatever my mixed reasons, someone could have broken their neck.
- Saurabh

Where were Nilesh and his friends planning to jump into?
The sandpit.
What was Saurabh feeling when reporting Nilesh?
Saurabh felt scared that someone would get hurt, and also some leftover anger about an old fight.
What did the teacher do that was right?
She thanked Saurabh, listened without assuming motives, and acted that same afternoon on the safety concern.
How did Nilesh see Saurabh's report?
Nilesh called Saurabh a snitch, seeing it as betrayal rather than protection.
What is the use of a doormat outside the front door?
It keeps dirt out of the house. Because people wipe their shoes on it, and the mud and dust stay on the mat instead of on the floor inside.

Ritu, you asked for the college radio what it's like being hostel secretary. I'm Zainab, and I'll be honest.
I stood because I wanted a say. The mess food was awful, the Wi-Fi died every night, and nobody listened to us. I wanted to be the person who could fix things. And yes, I liked the idea of people respecting me.
First month, it was great. I got the Wi-Fi fixed. People thanked me in the corridor. I felt tall.
Then I started deciding things alone. The movie night date. The rules for guests. I stopped calling committee meetings because they were slow.
One day Meenal, on my committee, said, "You're acting like the warden." That stung. She was right.
Now I have a rule: no decision without the committee. It's slower. But it's ours, not mine.

What did Zainab get fixed in the first month?
The Wi-Fi.
What was Zainab feeling when Meenal said "You're acting like the warden"?
Zainab felt stung and ashamed, realising the wish to fix things had turned into control.
What rule did Zainab make, and why is it wise?
No decision without the committee, because it keeps influence serving the group instead of becoming control.
How might the committee members have felt when meetings stopped?
They probably felt ignored and frustrated, left out of decisions they were elected to share.
I have two sister-in-laws in Pune. Is the plural right?

I have two sisters-in-law in Pune.
Why: In compound nouns like this one, the main noun takes the plural: "sisters-in-law".

The monsoon had flooded the underpass, so Sunaina reached the construction firm's office forty minutes late, soaked to the knees, on the one morning it mattered most. Three weeks ago she had written to the project head that the scaffolding inspections on the Kharghar site were being signed without anyone climbing up. Work there had stopped the same day while the scaffolds were re-checked. The concern was fixed, but she wasn't forgiven. Now her name was missing from the site list on the notice board. Her desk had been moved beside the photocopier. At the tea counter, the conversation stopped when she walked up. Nazia, who used to share her lunch every day, suddenly remembered a call and left. On the group chat, someone had forwarded a line from the project head: "Some people care more about complaints than delivery." Sunaina read it standing up, dripping, her throat tight.

Where had Sunaina's desk been moved?
Her desk had been moved beside the photocopier.
What was Sunaina feeling as she read the forwarded line?
Sunaina felt hurt and humiliated, her throat tight, seeing her honest report turned into an attack on her reputation.
What turning point could Sunaina reach for now?
Sunaina could write down each change since her report, with dates, and quietly reach out to anyone she still trusts, inside or outside the firm, for support and proper advice.
Why might Nazia have left the tea counter so suddenly?
Nazia may be afraid of being seen with Sunaina and blamed too, and possibly guilty about avoiding a friend.

Looking back, the scariest thing is how normal it felt. I'm Joseph, and in Class 9 I found a preacher's channel that seemed to explain why I felt so alone. He said most people, even families, were "blind." Only his followers could see.

Then came the private group. Every night he posted things like, "If your family mocks your faith, they are not your real family." He asked for "seed offerings." He said, "What we share here stays here."

I sent him my birthday money. I stopped eating dinner with my parents because he said they would pull me down. I felt guilty all the time, guilty at home, guilty in the group.

My elder sister Jaya noticed I'd stopped laughing. She found me crying on the stairs and asked, very gently, what was going on. I showed her the group.

She sat with me, then took me straight to our mother. Amma read it all that evening, held my hand and said, "None of this is your fault." We reported the group together that night.

What did the preacher call the money he asked for?
He called them "seed offerings."
What was Joseph feeling during the months in the group?
Joseph felt lonely and constantly guilty, both at home and in the group.
What warning signs of manipulation are in the preacher's messages?
He asked for money, demanded secrecy, and told Joseph the family at home was not a real family, which isolates and controls someone.
How did Jaya help Joseph, and why did that matter?
Jaya noticed Joseph had stopped laughing, asked gently and took Joseph to their mother that evening, so a trusted adult could step in the same day.

"Sachin, what's in the box?"
"Just some sweets for your mother, Mohit. From the shop near my hostel."
"You didn't have to."
"My Nani would kill me if I came empty-handed."
Mohit's mother opened the door. "Arre, Sachin! Come, come."

After lunch, Sachin stood up and began stacking plates.

She laughed and let him. In the kitchen he dried the dishes while she washed.
At four, Mohit's father yawned for the third time.

At the gate, Mohit said, "My mother's going to compare every friend to you now."

What did Sachin bring for Mohit's mother?
Sweets from the shop near Sachin's hostel.
How might Sachin have felt when Mohit's father yawned for the third time?
Sachin probably felt thoughtful and a little concerned, sensing the hosts were tired and it was time to leave.
What made Sachin a good guest?
He brought a small gift, helped in the kitchen, thanked his hosts warmly and left before they were too tired.
How does Mohit's mother see Sachin?
She sees him as a warm, well-mannered guest, so much that Mohit thinks she will compare every friend to him.

In their Chennai flat, Tanuja was feeding the new baby when Tushar, two, climbed onto the sofa and whined, "Carry me!"

"I'm feeding your sister now," Tanuja said. Tushar pushed the baby's foot.

Tanuja took a breath. "Tushar, after this, you and Amma will have our special time. Can you bring me her little socks?"

Tushar ran to fetch them, proud. Later, just the two of them blew bubbles on the balcony.

What did Tanuja ask Tushar to bring?
Tanuja asked Tushar to bring the baby's little socks.
Why did Tushar whine "Carry me!" and push the baby's foot?
Tushar felt jealous and left out, wanting to know there was still room for him.
How could a parent handle this kind of jealousy, as Tanuja did?
She promised and kept a special time for Tushar and let him help in a small way, instead of scolding.
How might the baby be affected if Tushar's jealousy were only scolded?
The baby might face more pushing, because Tushar's need for attention would remain unmet.

I think that through the cloudiness of his insanity he saw some antagonism in me, for he at once fell back on the last refuge of such as he--a dogged silence. After a short time I saw that for the present it was useless to speak to him. He was sulky, and so I came away.

Why does the doctor give up talking to his patient?
The patient seems to sense hostility and falls into stubborn, sulky silence. Seeing it is useless to go on, the doctor leaves.

"Deepak, it's ten. Dinner."
"In a minute, Amma."
"You've been in your room since five. How much did you study?"
"I... made a list."
"Of chapters?"
"Of things that could go wrong. The paper could be hard. The invigilator could be strict. I could forget formulas. What if my calculator stops?"
Ganga sat on his bed. "That's a long list."
"I have to think about it. If I don't, it'll happen."

What did Deepak say he made a list of?
Things that could go wrong.
Why does Deepak feel he has to think about everything that could go wrong?
He feels anxious and believes worrying protects him, as if thinking about disasters will stop them.
How does Ganga help Deepak move from worry to action?
She points out that worrying isn't preparing and suggests one chapter tonight, making the task small and clear.
How might Ganga feel seeing Deepak's list?
Ganga seems concerned but calm, wanting to help her son without adding pressure.

In Guadalajara, Clara still set the table for Sunday lunch at her abuela Rosa's house, still lit a candle for her grandfather on his day, still volunteered at the Saturday food bank the parish ran. She no longer went to Mass.
It had taken her three years of reading, arguing and long walks to say it plainly: she didn't believe in God. Saying it hadn't made her feel lost, as she had feared. It had made her feel honest.
'And yet you still come to the food bank,' Rosa said, passing the rice.
'I still believe people shouldn't go hungry,' Clara said. 'That part didn't go anywhere.'
Rosa looked at her for a long moment, then nodded. 'Your grandfather would have liked that answer.'

Where does Clara still volunteer on Saturdays?
At the Saturday food bank the parish ran.
How did Clara feel after saying she didn't believe in God?
She felt honest rather than lost, which surprised her because she had feared the opposite.
What shows Clara's values stayed intact after she stopped believing?
She keeps volunteering because people shouldn't go hungry, still lights the candle for her grandfather and still comes to Sunday lunch.
What might Rosa be thinking during her long look at Clara?
Rosa may be weighing sadness that Clara left the faith against respect for her kindness, and she settles on acceptance.

Kashish beti, you think you're the first wife to eat dinner alone? Sit with your Yamini Dadi a minute. When I was twenty-four, your Dada worked nights at the steel plant. For months I kept his plate covered and ate with only the radio for company. On Diwali he slept through the lamps, and I sulked for two days. He came home grey with tiredness and said sorry so often it stopped meaning anything. Then one morning, instead of sulking, I sat him down with his tea. On the back of the calendar we wrote a promise: Sunday lunch together, no matter what. I hung a thick curtain and told the children, 'Papa's sleeping, play in the courtyard.' And he told me honestly when he was too tired to talk. That is how we stayed friends.

What promise did Yamini and Dada write on the back of the calendar?
Sunday lunch together, no matter what.
How did young Yamini feel when Dada slept through Diwali?
She felt neglected and hurt, and she sulked for two days.
What was the turning point in those night-shift years?
The morning Yamini sat Dada down over tea instead of sulking, and they planned shared time, a quiet house for his sleep and honest talk.
How did Dada seem to feel about missing family life?
He seemed guilty and worn out, coming home grey with tiredness and apologising so often that the word lost its meaning.

Read this:

Dear Usha,
You asked why I refused the extra contract last week. I'll be honest because you're my deputy and you'll face this too.
The client wanted us to certify a building's safety faster than our checks allow. They offered double the fee. My boss said, "Just sign, everyone does."
I said no. Then I went home and couldn't eat. I was scared of losing the client and maybe my job.
But I kept thinking of the families who'll live there. If I cut corners here, where do I stop? At home? With my team?
The client left. My boss was angry. Then two days later, the head office praised the decision.
Be consistent, Usha. It's harder in the moment, easier after.
Karthik

What did the client want certified faster?
A building's safety.
How did Karthik feel after saying no?
Karthik felt scared and uneasy, unable to eat and worried about the job.
What makes Karthik's leadership an example for Usha?
Karthik refused to cut corners despite pressure and explained the reasons to a deputy, showing consistency.
How might the boss feel after head office praised the decision?
The boss may feel embarrassed and a little humbled.
The womens hostel is next to the library. Where does the apostrophe go?

The women's hostel is next to the library.
Why: "Women" is an irregular plural that does not end in -s, so the possessive is "'s".
I can't get my volleyball serve over the net. It keeps hitting the bottom.
That's a common problem for beginners. Tell me how you hit the ball.
I throw it up and hit it with my fist.
Try to toss the ball a little higher and hit it with the heel of your open palm or the base of your fist, with your arm swinging up, not straight. Follow through toward the net.
Should I stand closer to the net?
Yes, move a few steps closer until you can serve reliably, then slowly step back. Success builds confidence.
I'll try that at practice tomorrow.
Good. Hit twenty serves from the shorter distance, and stop when your arm feels tired.

Read this:

The four girls in Room 12 of the working women's hostel had a problem: the bathroom. Payal cleaned it every Sunday; the others forgot. By the third week, she was furious. She left a sticky note: "I'm not your maid." Madhuri, the youngest, took it personally and cried. That evening the warden suggested they sit together. Payal took a breath and said, "I'm sorry about the note. I'm tired of doing it alone." Madhuri said she hadn't known it was a problem because nobody said anything. They made a rota on the fridge, split the cost of cleaning supplies, and agreed to raise things at a weekly ten-minute check-in. It wasn't perfect, but Payal stopped seething on Sundays.

What did Payal write on the sticky note?
She wrote, "I'm not your maid."
Why did Madhuri cry after reading the note?
She took it personally and felt accused, especially since nobody had told her there was a problem.
What made the roommates' final solution fair?
They talked openly, split chores with a rota, shared supply costs and set up weekly check-ins to raise issues early.
How might the warden see the girls' solution?
She might be pleased they resolved it themselves with a clear system instead of letting the conflict grow.

Read this:

The salesman in the Pune showroom knew his job. First he brought out a suede jacket, 14,500, and let Dhruv try it on in front of the long mirror. Dhruv whistled at the tag and handed it back. Then, almost carelessly, the salesman laid a linen shirt on the counter: 3,200. 'Arre, that's reasonable, yaar,' Dhruv said to Hemant. Hemant said nothing. He was watching the order in which things had come out. At Dhruv's flat an hour later, his mother turned the bag over. 'Thirty-two hundred? For one shirt?' Dhruv opened his mouth to say it was cheap and stopped. Standing in his own kitchen, next to the vegetable basket and the electricity bill, it didn't look cheap at all. Hemant caught his eye and shrugged. 'It only looked small next to the jacket.'

What was the first item the salesman brought out?
A suede jacket priced at 14,500.
What was Hemant thinking as he stayed quiet at the counter?
Hemant was curious and a little uneasy, noticing that the shirt only seemed reasonable because the costly jacket came first.
How could Hemant have helped at the counter instead of waiting?
Hemant could have gently asked Dhruv whether 3,200 would feel reasonable if he had seen the shirt first, so he could decide on the shirt alone.
How does Dhruv's mother see the shirt?
She sees only a shirt for thirty-two hundred, with no jacket beside it, so to her it looks expensive.

metadata.subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Fatima worked the customer complaints line at a furniture company in Warsaw. After a hard call, her hand went to her phone, and she'd scroll until her supervisor coughed. She had tried locking the phone in her drawer. Then she just sat staring at the drawer, tense and irritable. Marek, who sat opposite, mentioned that he stood at the window after bad calls. So Fatima tried it: call ends, headset off, walk to the window, three slow breaths, look at the trams. Back. On a sticky note, she kept a tally: window or phone. On the first Friday, it was four windows and seven phones. By the third Friday, eleven windows and two phones. "Still need a break," she told Marek. "Just a different one." He nodded. The trams below kept moving, and Fatima's shoulders felt a little looser.

How many windows and phones did Fatima tally on the third Friday?
Eleven windows and two phones.
Why did locking the phone away leave Fatima tense and irritable?
The hard calls still left her needing relief, and with nothing to replace scrolling, she felt stuck and frustrated staring at the drawer.
Which choice worked for Fatima, and why?
Keeping the same cue but swapping in the window and breathing worked, because it still gave her the break she needed, and the tally showed her progress.
How does Marek influence Fatima's change?
Marek shares his own window habit casually, giving Fatima an idea without pushing her, and later quietly supports her with a nod.
I forgot my homework at home and the teacher is strict. I'm scared.
That is a tough start to the day. The best step is to tell the teacher honestly before class begins, so you are not caught out later.
What do I say exactly?
Something simple: 'I am sorry, I forgot my homework at home. May I bring it tomorrow?' Say it calmly and look at the teacher while speaking.
What if they punish me anyway?
That may happen, and it would be hard. Honesty usually earns more respect than hiding the problem, though. Accept what the teacher says politely, and bring the work the next day.
How do I stop forgetting things?
Pack your bag the night before and check it against your timetable. Keep homework in the same pocket every day. Within a week, it becomes a habit.
The principal dismissed the class early. Does dismiss mean sack someone?

Dismiss has more than one meaning. It can mean to tell people they may leave, as a teacher does. It can also mean to remove someone from a job, or to refuse to consider an idea. It is a verb.
Example: The teacher dismissed the class when the bell rang.

Read this:

Hi Kashish,
I've been thinking about Saturday's meeting, and I want to argue for something before we start building. Please read to the end before replying!
Our list has twelve features. Your login page design looks great, honestly. But if we build all twelve, the notes site will be ready after the exams it's meant for. So I asked myself: what is the least we can put online that still helps someone on Monday? My answer is one page with subject headings (Physics, Chemistry, Maths, Biology) and the PDFs people have already shared with us listed under each. No accounts, no ratings, no comments.
Then we watch. If people use it and ask for logins, your design goes in next. If nobody opens it, we've lost a week, not a term.
Can we talk about this at lunch tomorrow?
Tushar

How many features are on the team's list?
Twelve features.
What might Tushar be worried about while writing this email?
Tushar is worried the site will be ready only after the exams, and seems a little anxious about disappointing Kashish by setting the login design aside.
What would make Tushar's case stronger at lunch?
A rough sketch of the single page and a couple of classmates' requests for notes, so the idea is concrete and tied to real need.
How might Kashish feel reading that the login page is set aside?
Kashish may feel a pang of disappointment, but also reassured, since the email praises the design and promises it comes next if people ask.

metadata.subtype: Approach: defining a minimum viable version first [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Rekha, you asked on the podcast what Class 10 was like for me. Okay. I'm Sonali, and it was bad.
My parents are both doctors. Everyone assumed I'd be one too. Every test, I'd check the rank list before I checked my own answers. Rank 5 felt like failing because rank 1 existed.
One day I got a 12 out of 20 in chemistry and I couldn't stop crying in the school washroom. My friend found me and walked me to our class teacher, who called my mother right away. My mother left the hospital and came. She held my hands in the car and said, "I never needed you to be first. I needed you to be okay." I didn't know that. I'd never asked.
After that we talked properly. I still care about marks. But now I ask what I learned, not where I stand.

What mark did Sonali get in chemistry that day?
Sonali got 12 out of 20 in chemistry.
Why did rank 5 feel like failing to Sonali?
Sonali felt anxious and inadequate because Sonali was measured against rank 1 and against the parents' expected path.
What turned things around for Sonali, and what could others learn?
A friend and teacher bringing in Sonali's mother, and then an honest talk, showed Sonali the expectations were partly assumptions; others can ask their parents directly.
How might Sonali's mother have felt in the car?
Sonali's mother was probably shocked and sad that Sonali had carried so much pressure, and deeply relieved to be told.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, student wellbeing centre, Tuesday

Sunaina, a second-year engineering student, came in without an appointment. She had heard this morning that her father fell at home in Nashik and is in hospital for tests. She kept saying, "I should be there. My brother is doing everything." She was tearful and had not slept.
I listened first. When she was calmer, we made a short list together: a daily call with her father in the evening, a call with her brother tonight to split tasks she can do from here, like speaking to the doctor on the phone and keeping track of reports, and a train home over the long weekend.
I also helped her email her tutor about a short extension. She left looking tired but steadier. I'll check in on Friday.

Leela

Where did Sunaina's father fall?
He fell at home in Nashik.
What was Sunaina feeling when she said she should be there?
She felt guilty and helpless for being far away while her brother did everything.
How did Leela's plan ease the strain for Sunaina?
It gave her regular calls, a fair share of tasks she could do from college, and a visit home, so she could help instead of only worrying.
What might Sunaina's brother gain from tonight's call?
He could get real help with calls to the doctor and tracking reports, so he carries less alone.

Read this:

The evening bus was packed and steamy with rain, and Sabina was wedged against a pole with her bag clutched to her chest. Someone behind her pressed closer each time the bus braked, and when she shifted away, he followed. His hand brushed her back again. Her heart was pounding, and under the fear she felt a hot spike of anger. "Stop. Move away," she said loudly, turning to face him. Nobody spoke, but a few heads turned. She pushed through to the front, where Bhupen the conductor was collecting tickets. "That man behind me won't stop," she said. Bhupen looked back, rang the bell and called out, "This man gets off at the next stop." The next morning Sabina wrote down the bus number and gave it to the campus women's committee. She was still shaking, but she knew it was not her fault.

Who did Sabina tell at the front of the bus?
She told Bhupen, the conductor.
What was Sabina feeling when she told the man to stop?
She felt fear with a hot spike of anger. Her heart was pounding, but she still said it loudly.
Which of Sabina's steps are worth repeating?
She said a firm no, moved towards staff, and reported it the next morning with the bus number. She can also tell a friend or warden. 🤍
How might Bhupen the conductor have seen the moment?
Bhupen seems to have taken her seriously, since Bhupen looked back at the man and announced that he must get off. A rider speaking up lets the conductor protect the other passengers too.

Read this:

The temple fair had a big screen, and the whole village sat on durries to watch the film. Sonali leaned against her cousin Sahil. When the demon with red eyes came roaring out of the smoke, Sonali squeezed her eyes shut and pushed her face into Sahil's arm. Sahil didn't laugh. He held out his hand. “Squeeze if you want. Tell me when to look, I'll tell you when it's gone.” Sonali gripped his fingers. A minute later he whispered, “Gone,” and she peeped out.

Where did the village watch the film?
At the temple fair, sitting on durries in front of a big screen.
What does Sonali squeezing her eyes shut suggest she was feeling?
She was frightened by the roaring demon and was shutting her eyes to handle the fear. She might also have been startled by the sudden noise more than the picture itself.
What did Sahil do that helped?
He did not laugh, offered his hand to squeeze, and told her when the scary part was over, so she could cope and come back when ready.
What would change if Sahil had teased her for closing her eyes?
Sonali might feel ashamed and try to keep watching, which could make her more scared, or she might want to leave the fair.

metadata.subtype: Eyes shut against a scary scene [Regulating]

messages.content: My manager told that the report was ready.

My manager said that the report was ready.
Why: "Say" can be used without naming the listener. "Tell" needs a person right after it, as in "told me that".

Read this:

Chetan waited for Anand outside the school gate in Andheri, hands in his pockets, looking nothing like the boy who had spent all of Class 9 calling him "skeleton" and hiding his shoes.
"I'm sorry," Chetan said. "For all of it. The counsellor made me think about it. It was cruel."
Anand felt three things at once. Relief, that it might finally be over. Doubt, because Chetan had been nice for a day before. And a hot flash of anger: a whole year, and now just "sorry"?
He took a breath. "Okay. I accept the apology." He paused. "But I'm not ready to be friends. I don't want you sitting with us yet."
Chetan nodded slowly. "Fair."
On the bus home, Anand's hands were still shaking. He told his sister, "I forgave him. I think. But I'm not forgetting." She squeezed his arm. "That's allowed. Forgiving isn't the same as trusting."

What did Chetan call Anand in Class 9?
"Skeleton."
What did Anand feel when Chetan apologised?
Anand felt mixed feelings: relief that it might be over, doubt because Chetan had been nice before, and anger that a whole year was answered with just sorry.
What was wise about how Anand responded?
He accepted the apology but kept a clear boundary, not rushing into friendship and giving trust time.
How might Chetan see Anand's answer?
Chetan seems to accept it as fair, perhaps disappointed but understanding that trust has to be earned back.

Give four short bullet points for this paragraph.

"Kunal, you asked how I, Chinmay, survived my first lead role. Honestly, the first week I just stared at the word 'billing' on the whiteboard. It felt like a mountain. Then I asked myself: what is this actually made of? And I broke it into five pieces. Customer accounts. Invoice creation. Tax rules. Payment connection. Monthly reports. Next, I didn't guess the time. I got the four of us in a room and we estimated each piece together. People argued. The tax rules went from 'a week' to 'three weeks' once Meenal explained the state variations. Then I asked, which piece could sink us? The payment connection, because it depends on another company's system. So we started that on day one, even before the easier bits. Each piece got one owner's name beside it. The mountain became five hills. Still work, but you can see the top of each one."

- Chinmay stared at "billing" on the whiteboard in the first week as lead.
- Chinmay broke it into five pieces, from customer accounts to monthly reports.
- The team estimated each piece, and tax rules grew from one week to three.
- They started the risky payment connection first and gave each piece one owner.

Read this:

The band was so loud at the wedding that nobody heard Jyoti cry. She had pinched her finger in a folding chair and sat under the table, sobbing. Hemant, crawling after a balloon, found her. He looked at her finger, then at her face. He wrapped both arms round her, awkward and tight, then pushed his half-eaten laddoo into her good hand. When that didn't help, he ran out and tugged his Masi's sari until she bent down. Masi scooped Jyoti up and said to him, “You saw she was hurting and you brought help. That was caring, Hemant.”

Where did Hemant find Jyoti?
Hemant found her under the table, sobbing.
What was Hemant feeling when he looked at her finger and then her face?
He likely felt worried and sorry for her, which shows in his tight hug and the laddoo; he may also have felt a bit helpless when neither worked.
Which of Hemant's choices helped most, and why?
Fetching his Masi helped most, because in the loud hall an adult could look after the pinched finger when a hug and a sweet could not.
What would change if the band had been quiet?
An adult might have heard Jyoti straight away, and Hemant would not have had to find her and bring help himself.

Read this:

Monday. Gurleen heard in the lift that Vikas's big promotion had been cancelled. Vikas, who had told the whole floor about his new cabin. A flash of pleasure shot through her, bright and mean.
She noticed it. "Huh," she thought. "That was glee."
Tuesday. The office group was buzzing. Someone sent a joke about "the cabin that never was". Gurleen's thumb hovered over a laughing reply. She put the phone down instead. That night she wrote in her notebook: "Why did I enjoy that?" The answer came slowly. She'd been in the same job three years. She wanted something that was hers.
Next Monday. She sent Vikas a short message: "Sorry about the promotion. That's rough." Then she booked a meeting with her manager about her own next step.

What joke did someone send in the office group?
A joke about "the cabin that never was".
What was Gurleen feeling when she heard about Vikas's promotion?
She felt a bright flash of glee, then noticed it and became curious about why she enjoyed it.
Which of Gurleen's choices worked, and why?
Not sending the laughing reply, writing about what the glee pointed to, and booking a meeting about her own career turned an envious flash into kindness and action.
How might Vikas feel receiving Gurleen's message?
He might feel surprised and comforted that someone reached out kindly instead of joking about his loss.

metadata.subtype: Noticing the pleasure without acting on it [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

“Nandini, you're running now?”
“Trying, Ujjwal. Day twelve.”
“You? You said running was torture.”
“It is. That's why I cheat.”
“Cheat how?”
“Two things. One: every night I put my shoes right next to the bed, with socks inside them. So in the morning I step into them before my brain can argue.”
“And two?”
“Ten minutes. That's all I ask myself. If I want to stop at ten, I stop.”
“Do you stop?”
“Some days. Most days I do fifteen or twenty, because I'm already out.”
“Ten sounds too easy.”
“It's supposed to be easy. Last year I tried an hour a day and quit in a week.”
Ujjwal thought about it. “Can I join you? Tomorrow?”
“Shoes by the bed tonight,” Nandini said. “Socks inside.”

What day of running is Nandini on?
Nandini is on day twelve.
How does Nandini feel about running, and what keeps the habit going?
Nandini still finds it hard, calling it torture, but feels determined because the setup makes starting easy.
Why do Nandini's two “cheats” help the habit survive?
Shoes and socks by the bed lower friction, and the ten-minute target makes starting tiny, unlike last year's hour a day.
How does Ujjwal react to Nandini's method?
Ujjwal is surprised, then curious enough to ask to join Nandini the next day.

Read this:

I'm Kavitha, and in the drama society's winter play I played a mother whose son goes missing at a railway station. In the last scene I had to collapse on the platform bench and wail his name. Every night the hall went silent. On opening night my friend Lalremsiami came backstage with red eyes and hugged me. "Are you okay? That looked so real. Was it about your own family?" I laughed, a little guiltily. Honestly, during that scene I was counting. Three steps to the bench, drop on the fourth beat of the music, breathe from the stomach so the wail carries, and don't kneel on the loose nail at the edge of the stage. Inside I was focused, and a bit worried about that nail. The grief was on my face and in my voice because we'd rehearsed for six weeks, not because I was living it. Lalremsiami looked almost cheated. "So you're a very good liar." "No," I said. "A very good actor. Different thing."

Where does the son go missing in the play?
At a railway station.
What was Kavitha actually feeling during the wailing scene?
Kavitha felt focused, counting beats and steps, and a little worried about the loose nail, rather than grieving.
What should an audience keep in mind after a performance like this?
That visible emotion can be crafted through rehearsal, so the display is not proof of what the actor feels.
How did Lalremsiami feel on learning Kavitha had been counting beats?
Almost cheated, having been so moved by grief that looked completely real.

metadata.subtype: Acting a role versus feeling it [Mismatch]

messages.content:
Read this:

The night train to Nagpur had no signal and a flickering reading light, and Santosh had only until the Jhansi stop, where he could post it, to finish the letter. Jahnavi's mother had died on Tuesday. He had sent a two-line text then. It felt too small.
He wrote slowly on a notepad balanced on his knee. He remembered her mother's lemon pickle, the way she packed extra for him in hostel days, how she called him "the thin one." He crossed out a line about a better place; he didn't know what Jahnavi believed. He crossed out "I know how you feel"; he didn't.
He knew Jahnavi might keep this, might read it again in a year. So every line had to be something he would still mean then.
At Jhansi he dropped it into the postbox on the platform: two pages, one memory, and "I'm here whenever you want to talk."

What did Jahnavi's mother call Santosh?
She called him "the thin one."
Why did Santosh feel the text he had sent was not enough?
Santosh felt sad and uneasy that two lines were too small for such a loss, and wanted to give Jahnavi something more lasting.
Which choices made the letter comforting rather than hollow?
Sharing a specific memory of her mother, crossing out lines he couldn't honestly stand behind, and offering to talk whenever she wanted.
What might the letter mean to Jahnavi later?
She might keep it and reread it in a year, finding her mother remembered in someone else's words, along with a standing offer of support.

metadata.subtype: Letters and poetry for meaning and memory [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the town fair in Beawar, the giant wheel had been full of shrieks all evening, the happy kind that rise and fall with each turn. Wasim and Kashish were buying roasted chana when one scream didn't fall. It went on, high and thin, from the top car, and the wheel had stopped. Kashish grabbed Wasim's sleeve. "That's not fun screaming." Wasim squinted. A boy was half standing in the swaying car, and a woman was pulling at him. Wasim's feet were already moving toward the wheel's frame; he had climbed trees all his childhood. Kashish held on. "No. Police booth. Now." They ran the thirty steps to the tent with the loudspeaker, and Wasim told the constable exactly where. The constable radioed the operator, the announcer told everyone to stay seated, and two fair staff with a harness went up the service ladder. The boy was down in ten minutes, crying but unhurt.

What were Wasim and Kashish buying?
Roasted chana.
What did Kashish feel when this scream didn't fall, and why?
Kashish felt a jolt of alarm because the scream didn't rise and fall like the fun shrieks; it went on, high and thin, and the wheel had stopped.
Why was going to the police booth wiser than climbing the frame?
The constable could get the operator to act, the announcer to keep everyone seated and trained staff to climb with a harness, while climbing alone could have put another person in danger.
What might the woman in the top car have been feeling?
She was likely terrified, struggling to keep the boy seated in a swaying car, and relieved when help came up the ladder.

Link these two sentences into one.

The first bow was lopsided. The second one held all the way to the park.
The first bow was lopsided, but the second one held all the way to the park.

Read this:

Zainab, remember me grumbling about our daily nine o'clock meeting? Here's what I did. Everyone hated it, but nobody questioned it because it had always been there. So I asked myself: if we were starting the team from scratch, would I choose a daily meeting? No. Maybe twice a week, plus a shared notes page. But I was scared. What if people stopped talking? What if the manager thought I was lazy? So I didn't overhaul anything. I asked for a two-week test, Tuesday and Friday meetings only, and told everyone that if things slipped, we'd go back. Things didn't slip. The notes page actually got used. And Pema, the girl who hates change, now gets thanked in the corridor. Weird feeling, honestly.

Which days did the two-week test keep meetings on?
Tuesday and Friday.
What was Pema scared of before asking for the test?
Pema was scared that people would stop talking or that the manager would think she was lazy.
Why was a two-week test with a way back a wise way to question the default?
It let the team check whether the feared problems really appeared, with a promise to go back if things slipped.
How do Pema's colleagues seem to feel about the change?
They seem grateful, thanking Pema in the corridor, since nobody liked the daily meeting.

Read this:

Monday, 3 June. Anand slammed the German textbook shut in the hostel common room. Four months of classes, and he still froze whenever the teacher asked anything out loud. "I'm done. I'm dropping it," he told Joseph.
Joseph didn't argue. "Before you drop it: is it the goal you don't want, or the way you're learning?"
Friday, 7 June. Anand sat with a notebook and made three columns. Goal: the master's in Aachen, still yes. Method: grammar drills alone every night, no speaking; that was the problem. Phase: exam week, sleeping badly. He decided to join a weekend speaking circle, drop half the drills, and take one week off after exams. On the last page he wrote, "Review: 15 July. If I still hate it, I stop."
Monday, 15 July. Anand ordered coffee in German at the speaking circle and got the right cup. He opened the notebook, read the review line, and wrote: "Continue."

What review date did Anand set?
15 July.
How was Anand feeling on 3 June?
Anand felt frustrated and defeated, still freezing whenever asked to speak after four months, and wanted to drop German.
What did Joseph's question help Anand do?
It helped Anand separate the goal from the method and the phase, so he changed how he learned and set a review date instead of quitting on a bad day.
What would change if Joseph had simply agreed that Anand should drop it?
Anand might have given up the master's plan because of a poor method and a hard exam week, not because the goal was wrong.

Read this:

In the back room of the farmhouse, Afreen held up her school tie. "This is my cape," she announced, and swung it round her neck. "Superheroes put on their power in order. Cape first!" Her sister Vasudha, plaiting her hair at the mirror, snorted. "Then?" "Power shirt." Afreen pushed her arms through. "Power skirt. Power shoes." "And the cape?" "Tucked under the collar. Superheroes hide their capes at school." She knotted the tie, struck a pose and was dressed before the school bus honked.

What did Afreen call her tie?
Afreen called her tie her cape.
What was Afreen feeling as she knotted the tie and struck a pose?
Afreen felt proud and excited, like a superhero. Posing after the tie shows she was enjoying it.
What could help on a day when the superhero game does not work, and why?
A picture chart on the wall, with a tick for each piece of clothing, could do the job. The order is the same and the child needs no game.
How does the game look to Vasudha?
Vasudha snorts at first, but she plays along with a question. She sees her sister get dressed without a fight.

Read this:

Jaya, you're so angry at your guide, so let me tell you about Professor Rao. At nineteen, people called me Harsha the front-bencher. I was doing chemistry in Mysuru, and I thought Rao was a god. I copied his handwriting. I sat in the front row. I told my whole family, "Rao sir is the greatest teacher in India."

Then, in second year, I gave him my project. He read two pages and said, in front of the whole lab, "This is careless. You can do better." That was all.

And overnight he was nothing to me. "Rao is arrogant. Rao is outdated. Rao never cared." I moved to the back row and told everyone.

It was my lab partner Nalini who said, "He was harsh. He's also the one who stayed till ten to help you in first year. Both." It took me a month to see she was right. I went back and asked him what careless meant. He showed me.

What did Professor Rao say about Harsha's project?
Professor Rao said, "This is careless. You can do better."
Why did young Harsha turn so bitter after one comment?
Young Harsha felt hurt and humiliated in front of the lab, and after putting Rao on such a high pedestal, one harsh remark made him seem worthless.
What turning point in the story brought Harsha back to Rao?
Nalini's reminder that Rao was harsh and also the one who stayed late to help, both true, led Harsha to ask what "careless" meant.
How might Professor Rao have seen Harsha's move to the back row?
Rao may have been puzzled or a little hurt, perhaps not realising how deeply one comment had landed.
I know primary as meaning main, but what does it mean in primary school?

In primary school, primary is an adjective meaning of the first stage of education, for the youngest children. The usual meaning is first in importance, or main.
Example: My brother is in a primary class and is learning to write in cursive.

Read this:

Olga and Marek had been divorced for a year, and in their small city outside Kraków, every handover of their daughter Ada ended in a quarrel on the pavement. This Sunday it was about a missing mitten.

"You never pack properly," Olga snapped.

"And you never let me finish a sentence," Marek shot back.

Ada, five, stood between them in her pink coat, looking at the ground. Then she said, very quietly, "Can I go inside?"

Olga felt as if someone had slapped her. She saw it suddenly from Ada's height: two giants shouting over her head, every week.

She took a breath. "Marek, I'm sorry. Let's not do this here. We'll write to each other about her things, not argue at the door."

He blinked, then nodded. "Okay. Good."

They kept it up. Handovers became two minutes: a hug, a bag, "Bye, see you Wednesday." Ada began to skip up the steps.

What was the quarrel about this Sunday?
It was about a missing mitten.
How did Olga feel when Ada asked to go inside?
Olga felt stung and ashamed, as if slapped, seeing the quarrels from Ada's point of view.
What changed about Olga and Marek's handovers?
They agreed to discuss Ada's needs in writing instead of arguing at the door, keeping handovers short, calm and focused on her.
How was Ada affected by her parents' quarrels?
Ada felt caught in the middle and unhappy, looking at the ground, and later skipped up the steps once the fights stopped.

Read this:

The cooperative society office in the small town closed at four, but Yamini stayed. The payment list for the sugarcane farmers had different amounts from the ones she had entered on Monday, and nobody had told her why.
She wrote down the date, the page number and what she had seen, and initialled the note. She kept a copy of her own entries. Then she read the society’s grievance rules pinned to the wall.
Next morning Simran, at the next desk, said, “I saw it too. I’ll come with you.” They carried the note together to the district cooperative officer, and asked for it to be looked into.

How did Yamini record what she saw?
Yamini wrote down the date, the page number and what she had seen, and initialled the note.
Why might Yamini have stayed after four o'clock?
Yamini was troubled by the different amounts on the payment list and wanted to understand and record what she had seen. Staying late also shows she was being careful.
What made Yamini's steps safe and lawful?
She kept her own entries, wrote factual notes, read the grievance rules and took the note to an officer whose job was to look into it. She did not take or alter anything else.
How might Simran have felt about joining Yamini?
Simran may have felt nervous but glad to share the load, since Simran had seen the same thing. Saying I'll come with you shows support.

Read this:

The milk cooperative's monthly meeting in the village hall moved fast. The loud voices argued about the truck's fuel bill while Seema, the youngest member, held her idea in her lap: collect milk from the far hamlet on one fixed weekday, so the truck did not run half empty. Twice she raised her hand and twice someone talked over her. Her face went warm, and she looked at the floor. Then the chair, Rashmi, tapped the table. "Wait. Seema, you've been trying to say something. Please go ahead." Seema spoke in a small voice, and the room quietened. The secretary wrote it down, and the trial began the following week.

What was Seema's idea?
Seema's idea was to collect milk from the far hamlet on one fixed weekday so the truck did not run half empty.
What was Seema feeling when her face went warm and she looked at the floor?
Embarrassed and discouraged, since she had been talked over twice.
What did the chair do that made a difference?
Rashmi tapped the table to stop the noise and invited Seema by name to speak.
Why might the members who talked over Seema not have noticed anything wrong?
They were absorbed in the fuel bill argument and probably did not see that Seema had raised a hand.

Read this:

Tuesday. After the relay race was lost by a hair, Pranav said loudly, "It's Vidya's leg. She's slow." Vidya's face fell. Pranav felt relieved for a moment, as if the loss now belonged to someone else.

Thursday. Replaying the race in his head, he counted his own dropped baton at the first exchange and another teammate's late start. His neck went warm. Blaming Vidya had been easy, but it wasn't the whole truth.

Friday. At practice he said, "I shouldn't have said that. Our handovers were messy, mine too. Want to practise them together?" Vidya nodded slowly and picked up the baton.

What did Pranav say about Vidya after the relay?
He said, "It's Vidya's leg. She's slow."
What did Pranav feel right after blaming Vidya, and what did he feel later?
Relief at first, as if the loss belonged to someone else; later his neck went warm as he saw his own mistakes.
What could the team do to improve for the next race?
Practise baton handovers together, since the exchanges were messy for several runners, not only Vidya.
How might Vidya feel when Pranav offers to practise handovers?
She may still feel hurt, but her slow nod and picking up the baton suggest she is willing to trust him a little.
Was there an earthquake somewhere in the world today?
I don't know if there was an earthquake today, as I can't see live reports. A national seismology website lists recent tremors with their places.
If you heat ice, it melted. Is the second verb right?

If you heat ice, it melts.
Why: A general fact uses the present simple in both parts of the sentence.

Read this:

The result page loaded slowly on the library computer at her Kolkata college, and there it was: Kashish had failed Statistics, the only red among six subjects. She logged out and sat very still. The voice in her head was her own but sounded like a stranger: You always do this. You're lazy. You'll never finish. On the tram home she opened a note on her phone to list everything wrong with herself. Her friend Uma called instead. "I saw your face in the library. Speak." Kashish recited the list. Uma listened, then said, "Now say it the way you'd say it to me if I'd failed." Kashish was quiet a long moment. "I'd say you missed four weeks when Nani was in hospital, and you still passed five. Book the supplementary exam and ask Ma'am for the missed notes." Uma said, "Right. Now say that to yourself."

How many subjects did Kashish have?
Six subjects.
What was Kashish feeling when she logged out and sat very still?
Kashish felt shocked and ashamed, with a harsh inner voice calling her lazy.
What did Uma's question help Kashish do?
It let Kashish speak to herself as she would to a friend, naming the real cause, Nani's hospital stay, and practical steps like the supplementary exam and notes.
How might Uma have felt seeing Kashish's face in the library?
Uma was probably worried and wanted to help straight away, which is why the call came instead of waiting.

Read this:

"How did you get the kite?" Gurpreet asked.
"With this." Her brother Arjun held up a long stick. "Hook it, then pull."
Later, Gurpreet's teddy was on top of the cupboard.
"Rehana, hold this?" She handed her friend the dustpan and grabbed the broom.
"What are you doing?"
"Arjun's trick." Gurpreet poked the teddy with the handle. It fell. "Got it!"

What did Gurpreet grab?
The broom.
What was Gurpreet feeling when she said "Got it!"?
She was pleased and proud that Arjun's trick worked for her.
What else could Gurpreet try if the broom didn't reach?
Ask a grown-up or Arjun to help.
How does the trick look to Rehana?
Rehana is curious at first, then likely impressed.

Read this:

"Vikas, why aren't you eating?"

"Not hungry, Noor didi."

"You said that yesterday. And you had a stomach ache on Monday."

"It's just my stomach."

"Only on school days?"

"...Yes."

"Vikas. Is someone bothering you?"

"No."

"You can tell me."

"If I tell, you'll tell Ammi, and Ammi will go to school, and then Sameer will know I told."

"So it's Sameer."

"...He takes my tiffin. Every day. He says I'm a baby who needs his mummy's food."

"That's not your fault."

"Maybe it is. Maybe I am a baby."

"You're not. Listen. We'll tell Ammi together, tonight, and we'll ask her to talk to your teacher quietly. You won't be alone."

What does Sameer take from Vikas every day?
His tiffin.
Why is Vikas afraid of telling Ammi?
He fears Ammi will go to school and Sameer will know he told, which could make things worse; he also feels ashamed, wondering if he is a baby.
How does Noor didi respond, and why is it helpful?
She notices the pattern, tells Vikas it isn't his fault, and plans to tell Ammi together that night, so he isn't alone.
What might Noor didi be feeling as she hears about Sameer?
She is probably worried and protective of her younger brother, wanting to make him feel safe.

metadata.subtype: Stage 3: The target's confusion and shame [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Pema, you want to know how to give a client bad news? Let me tell you about a time I did it well enough. I'm Reena. I was a young woman of twenty-six, so nervous my tea went cold. The migration had failed and the go-live would slip. I named the cause plainly, once. I said sorry once, not five times. Then I put a page on the screen: week one, week two, week three, each with a name beside it, and a promise of a short update every Tuesday and Friday. The client's operations head stopped asking how this could have happened and started asking about week two. They could judge the recovery, not just the problem. That was the whole trick, if you can call it one.

On which days did Reena promise updates?
Reena promised a short update every Tuesday and Friday.
How was Reena feeling before giving the news?
Reena was so nervous that the tea went cold.
Which choice in the story helped the client stay engaged, and why?
Putting up a page with weeks and named owners helped, because the client could judge the recovery instead of only dwelling on the problem.
How did the client's operations head see the plan?
The operations head probably felt steadier, since the plan gave something concrete to ask about and shifted the questions from blame to week two.

metadata.subtype: Approach: pairing the news with a recovery plan [Action]

Read this:

"Parul, I give up. Six months for a simple address change on my voter ID. Six!"
"You look exhausted, Bidisha."
"I am. They lose the file, they ask for the same paper, they don't answer the phone. What's the point of any of it?"
"I felt like that about my ration card last year."
"And?"
"And then I realised the people who give up are exactly who the system forgets. So I learned the online tracking system and filed an appeal."
Bidisha rubbed her eyes. "I don't have the energy to become an expert."
"You don't have to be. Sit with me on Saturday. I'll show you the portal. And there's a residents' group that's pushing the office to publish file timelines. They need people who've actually had bad experiences."
"You think it'll change anything?"
"Slowly. But complaining in our kitchen changes nothing."
Bidisha laughed tiredly. "Saturday, then. Bring snacks."

How long had Bidisha waited for the address change on the voter ID?
Six months.
What was Bidisha feeling when she said "What's the point of any of it?"
She felt exhausted and disillusioned, ready to give up on the system.
What did Parul suggest instead of cynicism?
Learning the online tracking system together, filing an appeal if needed, and joining a residents' group pushing for published file timelines.
How might Parul see Bidisha's frustration?
Parul recognises it from the ration-card struggle last year and wants to help Bidisha turn tiredness into engagement.

Read this:

Alka had run the tiny momo counter in a Guwahati market for three months, and she made the chutney the way she loved it: fiery, with bhut jolokia. "Everyone likes it hot," Bhupen said, stirring the pot. "You and me both."
But Alka had noticed some plates coming back half-full. On Saturday she stuck a small card on the counter: "Too spicy? Not spicy enough? Tell me!" She also asked the college students, the office workers and an old couple who came every Sunday, not just the regulars who were her friends.
The old couple said the chutney made them cough. Two students wanted a milder sauce for dipping.
"Huh," Alka said, surprised, then pleased. "We've been cooking for the two of us."
The next week there were two bowls on the counter, one red, one pale green.

What did Alka's card on the counter say?
"Too spicy? Not spicy enough? Tell me!"
Why was Alka surprised, then pleased, by the answers?
She'd assumed most people liked the chutney as hot as she did, and the answers showed her something she could fix to serve more people. 😊
Why was it smart of Alka to ask the old couple and the students, not only her friends?
Her friends share her taste, so only people unlike her could show who the chutney was putting off.
How does the change affect the old couple who come every Sunday?
They now have a milder option and can enjoy their momos without coughing, and may feel their visits matter.

Read this:

Dear Seema,
I need to tell someone this. Every evening I post a photo and then check the likes like a pulse. Yesterday my sketch got nine, and I felt as though I had done something wrong. Then I saw that my classmates' posts had hundreds, and I spent the whole night refreshing. My chest felt tight and I couldn't focus on chemistry.
This morning I noticed the loop: post, check, feel low, post again. So I muted three accounts that always make me feel less, and I'll only share a drawing if I still like it, not because I need a number. Can I send you my next one instead? I miss our summer evenings drawing in the courtyard 🙂
Your Leela

How many likes did Leela's sketch get yesterday?
Leela's sketch got nine likes.
Why did nine likes make Leela feel so low?
The few likes felt like a verdict on Leela's worth, bringing a low, anxious feeling and a whole night of refreshing.
What could Leela try if the urge to check likes returns?
Leela could remember the loop of posting, checking and feeling low, keep the accounts muted, and post only drawings Leela still likes, for personal reasons.
How might Seema feel on receiving this letter?
Seema may feel trusted and a little worried, and glad to be asked for the next drawing, since Leela is reaching out to a person rather than to the likes.

Joseph here. Tenzin, who sits opposite me, keeps a small notebook by her keyboard, and for two weeks I watched her write down start and end times for everything. I asked once. "My boxes are wrong," she said, "but I need the numbers first." On the second Friday she opened her schedule and changed it. The weekly report block went from one hour to ninety minutes, because her notes showed it never took less. After every meeting she put a fifteen-minute gap labelled "notes and messages", since she had been rushing into the next task with half-written follow-ups. Her week looked calmer after that, though I cannot say what she felt, only that she stopped skipping lunch. She told me the first week with the new boxes ended with everything sent on time.

What did Tenzin change the report block to?
The weekly report block went from one hour to ninety minutes.
What did Tenzin want from writing down the times?
Tenzin wanted the real numbers before changing anything, expecting the notes to show how the boxes should change.
What else could Tenzin do if meetings still overrun the gap?
Tenzin could keep tracking for another week and lengthen the gap, or ask for shorter meetings, using the notes as evidence.
Why does Joseph say only what Tenzin did and not how Tenzin felt?
Joseph only watched from the opposite desk and cannot know Tenzin's feelings for sure; the notebook, the schedule and the lunches are what could be seen.

metadata.subtype: Approach: adjusts box lengths from tracked actuals and adds gaps [Revision]

Read this:

Bhavna's phone was full of them: the girl from Nagpur who left school at fifteen and now had two million followers, the boy who failed Class 12 and built a sneaker brand. Every video ended the same way: "School is a waste. Just start." One evening in their Andheri flat Bhavna told her elder sister Sarika she wanted to drop out after Class 10 and make videos full time. "Look how easy it is. They all made it." Sarika put down her laptop. "How many people do you think tried the same thing?" Bhavna shrugged. "I don't know. These people did it." "The ones who didn't make it don't make videos about it," Sarika said. "You're only seeing the winners. Where are the thousands who quit and are stuck?" Bhavna opened her mouth, then scrolled her feed again, slower this time.

What did every video on Bhavna's phone end with?
School is a waste. Just start.
Why did dropping out seem so easy to Bhavna?
She felt excited and inspired because every video she saw showed someone who had made it, so success seemed normal and certain.
What question could Bhavna ask whenever she sees a success story?
How many people tried the same thing and didn't make it, since the ones who failed rarely post videos.
How does Sarika see the videos Bhavna shows her?
Sarika sees them as a small, visible slice of winners, hiding the many who quit and are stuck.

Read this:

Dear Amma,
Leela Aunty from next door will have told you where I'm staying. I'm safe. The working women's hostel near my office is clean, and the warden is kind.
I didn't leave because I stopped loving you. I left because when I said no to the match, Papa broke the TV and said he would lock me in until I agreed. After that night I called a women's helpline, and they helped me find this place.
Here is what I can promise. I'll call you every Tuesday and Friday. I'll meet you at the temple on Sundays, if you want. I'll come home for the festival once Papa agrees, with someone else present, that there will be no threats.
What I won't do is let anyone else decide who I marry. That part is mine.
I miss your rasam. I miss you.
Your Shreya

Where is Shreya staying now?
Shreya is staying at the working women's hostel near the office.
What does Shreya most want Amma to understand?
Shreya wants Amma to know the love and missing are real, and that leaving was because of Papa's threats, not to cut Amma off.
Which choice kept Shreya safe after that night?
Calling a women's helpline, which helped find the hostel, gave Shreya safe housing and outside support before setting any terms with the family.
What might Amma feel reading about the Tuesday and Friday calls?
She may feel relief that Shreya hasn't cut contact, mixed with sadness and worry about what happened at home.

Outside the colony kirana shop, Aditi pointed at the jar of orange toffees. "One, Dadi?"
Vasudha Dadi shook her head. "We came for milk only."
Aditi's face crumpled and she cried, loud and wet. Between sobs she looked up to check. Dadi was counting coins.
"I'll sleep early! I'll brush my teeth two times!"
Dadi smiled but shook her head again. "Still no, chinni."
Aditi stamped and shouted, "You never give me anything!" Then she stopped to see what would happen.
Dadi picked up the milk packet and held out her hand. After a long moment, Aditi took it.

What did Vasudha Dadi say they came to the shop for?
Milk only.
Why did Aditi stop shouting to see what would happen?
She was testing, curious and hopeful that the shouting might finally change Dadi's answer, and uncertain when it did not.
Which of Dadi's choices worked at this stage, and why?
She kept the same calm no through crying, promises and shouting, so Aditi saw that none of them moved the limit.
What is it like for Vasudha Dadi to hold the line outside a busy shop?
She may feel tender towards Aditi and a bit tired, yet steady, since she smiles while still saying no.

In their village near Margao, Maria used to play football on the church ground every evening for an hour and a half. With the Class Ten boards seven weeks away, her mother wanted her to stop completely.
Maria thought it through on the walk home. If I stop, I'll sit at the desk longer, but I already stare at the same page after dinner. If I play the full ninety minutes, I lose too much time. So what's in between?
She proposed it at dinner: twenty minutes, fixed, six to six-twenty, just passing drills with her cousin Sumit, then straight home to study. “It's not football against marks. It's so my head works.”
Her mother agreed to try it for two weeks.
By the end of the first week, Maria was finishing her evening maths set before nine, something she hadn't managed all month. Sumit complained that twenty minutes was too short. She didn't budge.

What slot did Maria propose?
Twenty minutes, six to six-twenty, passing drills with Sumit.
How did Maria feel about stopping football completely?
Maria was worried it wouldn't help, since sitting longer already meant staring at the same page, and felt determined to find something in between.
What else could Maria try if twenty minutes gets hard to fit in near exams?
Keep the same slot but make it a brisk walk or skipping, so the habit of a head-clearing break continues.
How might Maria's mother see the two-week trial?
She may start doubtful, but seeing the maths set finished before nine would likely reassure her.

metadata.subtype: Approach: planning around exams and study load [Thinking]

messages.content: Does heroism need a big act, like saving a life?

No. Heroism is great courage and goodness in difficult moments, and it can be small too. It is a noun.
Example: The firefighter was praised for his heroism in the flood.

In the second-year chemistry lab, Asif had quietly moved to the bench by the window with his new project group. For weeks Rekha had eaten lunch alone in the lab corridor, telling herself she didn't care.
On Thursday, rinsing burettes side by side, she almost said, "I guess I'm not interesting enough for you now." She could already hear how it would land.
Instead she turned off the tap. "Asif, can I ask something, just once? We used to talk every day, and now we barely do. Did I upset you?"
He looked surprised, then awkward. "No, not at all. The project's eating my time, and... honestly, I've been needing a different crowd for a bit. It's not about you."
It stung. Rekha nodded slowly. "Okay. Thanks for being straight. I'll stop wondering."
At lunch she sat with the two girls from the next bench for the first time. It was quieter than she wanted, but it was a start.

Where had Asif moved in the lab?
To the bench by the window with his new project group.
How did Rekha feel when Asif said he needed a different crowd?
Stung and hurt, but she accepted it calmly and was relieved to stop wondering.
What went well in how Rekha handled it, and what did she do next?
She dropped the guilt-trip line and asked once, directly; afterwards she sat with the two girls from the next bench instead of eating alone.
How might Asif have felt when Rekha asked directly?
Surprised and awkward, but likely relieved to be asked kindly rather than blamed.

October. Elizabeth gets 31 in the Physics unit test. At lunch she tells Jahnavi, "Mr Menon can't teach. And that paper was unfair, half of it wasn't even in the notes." Jahnavi, who got 58, says nothing. By the time the bell rings, Elizabeth feels better.
November. Jahnavi asks if she wants to go through the wrong answers together. "What's the point? He'll just set something weird again." Elizabeth spends the weekend on her English project instead.
December. The second unit test comes back: 33. Elizabeth stares at it. The pre-boards are six weeks away, and she has no list, no plan, nothing to show for two months except a story about Mr Menon. She crumples the paper, then smooths it out again.

What did Elizabeth get in the second unit test?
She got 33.
How does Elizabeth seem to feel when she stares at the second result?
She seems shaken and worried, realising the blame gave her no plan and the pre-boards are close.
What else could Elizabeth have done in November?
Accept Jahnavi's offer and go through the wrong answers, since finding her own gaps would give her a plan whatever the teacher is like.
How might Jahnavi see Elizabeth's complaints about Mr Menon?
Jahnavi, who scored 58 with the same teacher, may quietly doubt the blame, yet still offers help.

metadata.subtype: Approach: blaming the teacher or the syllabus [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Briefly, what does this passage say about kings and gifts?

In the case of kings observant of their duties, that gift is most meritorious. Sovereignty is always painful. It is incapable of being borne by persons of uncleansed souls. In the generality of cases, kings fail to attain to auspicious ends. By always making, however, gifts of earth, they succeed in cleansing themselves (of all their sins). Thou hast, O prince of Kuru's race, discoursed to me on many duties. Thou hast discoursed to me on the gifts of kine made by king Nriga in days of old. The Rishi Nachiketa, in ancient times, had discoursed on the merits of this act. The Vedas and the Upanishads also have laid down that in all sacrifices,--in fact, in all kinds of religious acts,--the Dakshina should be earth or kine or gold.
Ruling is hard, and kings often fail to reach a good end, but giving land as a gift can cleanse them. The speaker adds that the Vedas say the fee in every sacrifice should be land, cows or gold.

Read this:

I'm Avni, and last year I was house captain for the school camp. On the second night, a Class 3 boy, Ujjwal, sat outside his tent crying because he missed home. The other captains were busy with the campfire. I sat with him, told him about my first camp when I also cried, and walked him to the teacher on duty so he could phone his mother. Then I stayed until he fell asleep. Being captain wasn't about the badge. It was about noticing who needed help first.

Why was Ujjwal crying outside his tent?
He missed home.
What does Avni staying until Ujjwal fell asleep suggest?
Avni felt responsible for him and caring, wanting him to feel safe.
What did Avni get right in helping Ujjwal?
Avni comforted him, shared a similar story and took him to the teacher on duty to call home.
How might Ujjwal remember Avni?
As a kind older student who made a scary night feel safe.

Read this:

“Maria Aunty, can I tie the ribbon?” It was Christmas Eve, and Aunty's flat was full of gifts and paper.
“Try, Parveen. Make two bunny ears.”
“Bunny ears… cross… through…” A pause. “Aunty! It's a bow!”
“It is! A perfect bow.”
“Can I do another one?”
“Of course.”
“And another?”
“There are twelve gifts, sweetheart.”
“I'll do all twelve!”
Twelve bows later, some lopsided, Parveen held up the last one. “I can do bows now. Forever.”
“Forever,” Maria Aunty agreed, smiling.

How many gifts were there to tie ribbons on?
There were twelve gifts.
How did Parveen feel when the first bow worked?
She felt excited and proud, shouting “Aunty! It's a bow!” and asking to do more.
What did Maria Aunty do that encouraged Parveen?
She gave a simple tip, praised the first bow and let Parveen try all twelve, even the lopsided ones.
How might Maria Aunty feel hearing “I can do bows now. Forever”?
She probably feels warm and amused, glad to see Parveen so proud.

Read this:

Monday: Gargi, fifteen, read the forwarded message three times. "Scientists predict a strong earthquake in our city this Thursday, 3:12 pm." There was a map with red circles, the name of a professor, even a reference number. "Look how exact it is," she told Neelam. "Nobody makes up 3:12."
Thursday: At three, Gargi was sitting in the school ground with her bag packed and her shoes on. Neelam sat beside her. "How many times has an earthquake ever been warned to the minute?" Neelam asked. Gargi didn't answer. At 3:12 a crow landed on the goalpost. Nothing else happened.
Saturday: Gargi searched for the professor's name. She found the same message, word for word, sent around three other cities in past years. "It sounded so real," she said.

What exact time did the forwarded message give for the earthquake?
3:12 pm on Thursday.
Why did the message feel so trustworthy to Gargi?
The map, the professor's name, the reference number and the exact minute all felt like proof, so the vivid detail pushed aside how rarely such a warning ever comes true.
What turning point changed Gargi's view, and what could she do earlier next time?
Finding the same message sent around other cities in past years; next time she could first ask how often such events really happen and check where the message came from before packing her bag.
What was Thursday afternoon like for Neelam, sitting beside Gargi?
Neelam seemed calm and a bit doubtful, choosing to stay with Gargi and ask a gentle question instead of mocking her fear.
Why do we blink so often?
Each blink spreads tears over the eye. Because a blink also wipes away dust, the surface stays wet and clean.

Read this:

Arohi,
Not a lecture, I promise. Just a letter, because you keep leaving the chat before I can say anything.
I've noticed you haven't come to stats class since the results. You skip the canteen when I'm there, and when Megha mentioned the supplementary exam, you changed the subject so fast it was almost funny. You're the person who normally drags all of us to the library. I miss that version of you, and I get it. Failing stats stings, and avoiding it probably feels like the only way to not feel stupid.
Here's my offer. Tomorrow at 10, I'll be at the second-floor table of the library with the chapter 1 notes. We'll look at just the first ten pages together. No talk about marks, no advice. If you don't come, that's okay too. I'll be there Thursday as well.
Your friend,
Bhupen

Where will Bhupen be tomorrow at 10?
At the second-floor table of the library, with the chapter 1 notes.
How does Bhupen feel about Arohi's retreat, going by the letter?
Bhupen feels worried and misses the lively Arohi, but also understands that avoiding stats is a way to not feel stupid.
Why is Bhupen's offer likely to help more than advice?
It gives company and a small concrete step, ten pages together, without making Arohi feel judged.
What might Arohi feel when reading the letter?
Arohi might feel ashamed at first but also relieved that someone noticed kindly and made the first step small.

Read this:

I'm Ishita, Hrithik's older sister. On Sunday Mummy made one big paratha and said Hrithik and I had to share it with Papa and her. Hrithik, who's nine, cut it in half, then stopped. "No, four people," he said, and cut each half again. "So each is one quarter." Then he picked up a piece and said, "If I give you my quarter, you get two quarters, that's half!" I don't know what went on in his head, but last month he got mixed up with fractions. Today he looked so sure.

How many people shared the paratha?
Four people: Hrithik, Ishita, Papa and Mummy.
What might Hrithik have felt when he worked out that two quarters make a half?
He likely felt confident and pleased to finally understand fractions.
How could Ishita support Hrithik's new understanding?
Ishita could make more everyday fraction puzzles with food or paper for him to solve.
How does Ishita see her brother's change?
Ishita sees he has improved since last month, though she can't be sure what he was thinking.
We discussed about the plan yesterday. Any mistake?
Yes. Say: "We discussed the plan yesterday." The verb "discuss" takes its object directly, so "about" is not needed.

I'm Thomas. I live on the floor above Nikita's family. On Saturday, on the stairs, Nikita stopped and pointed down at the landing. "Ca! Ca!" A white cat was curled there. Her mother said, "Cat! A white cat." Nikita said, "Ca," again, very pleased, then pointed at my shoes. "Shoo!" Her mother laughed. "Yes, shoes!" I don't know how many words she knows. She seemed to want us all to look.

What was curled on the landing?
A white cat.
What might Nikita be feeling as she pointed and named things?
She seemed pleased and excited to share what she noticed, wanting everyone to look.
What did Nikita's mother do that helps Nikita's vocabulary?
She named back what Nikita pointed at, "Cat! A white cat" and "shoes", adding words.
How does Thomas experience the moment?
Thomas seems amused and charmed at being included when she points at the shoes.

Madhav had been in the counsellor's room three times this term, always saying he was "just tired." Ms Anjali, the school counsellor, had noticed his marks dropping and then, strangely, his homework becoming neat and early.
On Wednesday he finally said it. "My parents fought about my maths tuition fees. Two months later, Papa moved out. So."
Ms Anjali did not rush to disagree. "That's a heavy thing to carry alone. Would you let me invite both of them in, so you can hear it from them?"
On Friday afternoon, Madhav's mother and father sat side by side on the small sofa, stiff but present.
"Beta, this is between your mother and me," his father said. "It started years before your tuition."
"You did not cause this," his mother said. "We both love you. That doesn't change."
Madhav stared at the carpet, then nodded. His shoulders dropped for the first time in weeks.

What did Madhav's parents fight about, according to him?
His maths tuition fees.
What had Madhav been feeling that made him say he was 'just tired'?
He felt guilty, secretly believing the fight over his tuition fees had caused his father to move out.
How did Ms Anjali support Madhav wisely?
She listened without rushing to argue, named how heavy the feeling was, and brought both parents in so he could hear the truth from them.
How might Madhav's parents see this meeting?
They probably feel awkward and sad sitting together, but they come because they want their son to know clearly that the split is not his fault.

In the courtyard of their village home, Binita oiled little Anirban's hair.
"Tell me the rule," she said.
"My body is mine," Anirban said. "Nobody touches where my chaddi is."
"Good. And if someone says, 'Don't tell your Ma'?"
"I tell Ma. Fast fast."
"And if you're scared to tell?"
"You won't be angry."
"Never." Binita kissed his oily forehead. "Some secrets are fun, like hiding Baba's birthday sweets. But nobody should ask you to hide things from me."
Anirban grinned. "Baba's sweets are in the steel box."
"Shh! That one is a surprise."

Where were Binita and Anirban sitting?
In the courtyard of their village home.
How does Anirban feel when saying the rules?
Anirban feels relaxed and confident, grinning and joking, because the rules are familiar and gentle.
How did Binita teach body safety without fear?
She used simple repeated rules, explained that she would never be angry, and showed the difference between a fun surprise and a secret.
How might Binita feel as she teaches the rule?
Binita feels loving and protective, wanting Anirban to know he can always tell her.
What is 52,891 times 7,463?
I'm not sure of the product, as a multiplication this long needs a tool. A calculator will do it.
The quiz says: identify the bird in the picture. What am I being asked to do?

To identify something is to recognize it and say what it is or who it is. It is a verb.
Example: Can you identify the bird from its song?
