Mentor's note, Thursday
Aditi came to our check-in upset about Payal, who had sent a client the wrong invoice on Monday. "I can't trust her with the Kolkata account," Aditi said. Then she stopped herself. "Actually, since Monday I've been looking at everything Payal does through that one invoice." I asked what would help. Aditi pulled up Payal's last six months: eleven clean invoices, a client email praising her, and a week when Payal covered two people's work without complaint. She also checked the context: Monday's error came from a template someone else had changed. Aditi decided to keep Payal on the account and fix the template. I suggested she tell Payal both parts, the error and the record. She did, that same afternoon, and came back looking lighter.

What mistake did Payal make on Monday?
Payal sent a client the wrong invoice.
What did Aditi realise about her own view of Payal?
Aditi felt uneasy on noticing that she had been seeing everything Payal did through that one invoice, and that her frustration was colouring her judgement.
Which steps helped Aditi decide fairly?
Looking at Payal's full six-month record and checking the context of the error, which turned out to be a changed template, before deciding about the account.
How might Payal feel after hearing both parts from Aditi?
Payal is likely relieved and respected, since the mistake was named but her good record was seen too.

'Oye, four-eyes, can you even see the ball?' Zainab called across the playground.
A few girls laughed. Payal pushed her glasses up and didn't answer.
Later, at the tap, Payal said quietly, 'Can you stop calling me that?'
'Calling you what? Four-eyes? It's a joke, yaar.'
'You say it every day.'
'Because it's funny. Everyone jokes. You're too sensitive.'
'It's not funny to me.'
'It's just a joke. Relax.'
'You wouldn't say it if Miss Kaur was there.'
Zainab opened her mouth, then shut it. 'That's different.'
'How?'
'It just is. Fine. Whatever.'
Payal walked back to class alone. Miss Kaur, on corridor duty, had heard enough. Before the bell she called Zainab over, and then sat down with Payal.

What did Zainab call Payal?
Zainab called Payal four-eyes.
Why does Zainab keep insisting it's just a joke?
She feels defensive and a bit uncomfortable, and calling it a joke makes the teasing seem harmless, so Payal becomes the problem for being 'too sensitive'.
What could Zainab do after this conversation?
She could stop using the nickname, apologise to Payal, and notice that she wouldn't say it in front of Miss Kaur.
How does the daily joke feel to Payal?
It hurts; she stops answering, asks quietly for it to stop, and walks back to class alone.

In their Hyderabad flat, Reena had left the iron cooling on the ironing board. Ramesh toddled over and reached for it.
"No! Hot!" Reena gasped, sharp and loud.
Ramesh froze, hand in the air, then pulled it back. His lip wobbled.
Reena moved the iron to the top shelf, then picked him up. "Hot. Ouch. Mumma keeps you safe." Ramesh held on and sniffed.

Where did Reena move the iron?
To the top shelf.
What was Ramesh feeling when his lip wobbled?
He was startled and frightened by the sharp "No! Hot!", reading it as danger; he may also have felt he was in trouble.
Which of Reena's choices worked, and why?
Using short words and then moving the iron out of reach worked, because it kept him physically safe and then comforted him.
How might Reena have felt when Ramesh reached for the iron?
She was likely alarmed and scared he'd be burned, which is why she gasped so sharply.

At the dining table in their Nagpur flat, Ojas pressed his lips together and shook his head at the spinach on his spoon.
"Just one bite," said Harish.
"No." It came out through closed teeth.
"Okay. Spinach on the plate or in the roti roll?"
Ojas thought. "Roll."
"Then you fold it."
Ojas folded it carefully, lips still tight, then bit down and chewed. "Tastes okay," he said, sounding surprised.

What did Ojas choose to have his spinach in?
He chose to have it in the roti roll.
What did Ojas want when he pressed his lips together?
He seems to have wanted a say in what he ate, because he accepted the spinach once he could choose how it came and fold it himself. It might also have been dislike of the look of it.
What could Harish try the next time Ojas refuses food?
He could offer two acceptable choices again and let Ojas take part in preparing his food.
How might Harish feel when Ojas bites the roll and says it tastes okay?
Harish may feel relieved and pleased that offering a choice worked, since Ojas ate the spinach without a fight.

Last spring I posted "WORST DAY OF MY LIFE!!!!!" with three broken-heart emojis. What actually happened: I dropped my ice cream on the way home. That's it.
I didn't even feel that bad. But I'd noticed that dramatic posts got way more comments. People asked "what happened??" and I liked that.
Then Gopika messaged me privately: "Hey. Just checking you're okay? You don't have to say what it is."
I felt awful. She was actually worried. I'd been performing for followers and a real friend thought something terrible had happened.
I wrote back, "Oh no, it was ice cream. I'm fine. Sorry for scaring you."
She sent a laughing face and said, "Good. But if it's ever real, tell me."
Now I try to make my posts match my actual mood. Mostly. Sometimes the ice cream really does deserve capitals.
- Pema

What actually happened on Pema's "worst day"?
Pema dropped an ice cream on the way home.
What was Pema feeling after reading Gopika's message?
Pema felt guilty and embarrassed, realising the performance for followers had genuinely worried a real friend.
What did Gopika do well when she saw the post?
Gopika checked privately and gently, without demanding details, and offered support if it was ever real.
How did the post look to Gopika compared with Pema's real mood?
To Gopika it looked like real distress, while Pema was only mildly annoyed and exaggerating for attention.

In the college library, Mehak stood at the window with her phone on video, while Mahima sat in a hostel room across the city. "Give me your dates." "Internals start on the ninth, finals on the twenty-second." Mehak typed both into a shared calendar in blue. "Mine are red. The fifth to the eighteenth." They looked at the screen: a solid block of colour. "So fewer calls those weeks. Two short ones?" "Two short ones, and no guilt." Mehak added a green star after the twenty-second: "Long call, no books." Mahima smiled at it. A student at the next table looked up, and Mehak lowered her voice, still smiling. That night neither wondered what a quiet day meant.

What colour did Mehak use for Mahima's exam dates?
Mehak used blue for Mahima's exam dates.
What is Mahima feeling when she sees the green star?
Mahima feels happy and reassured, smiling at the planned long call after the exams.
What alternative approach could the couple add if one of them still worries during exam weeks, and why?
They could agree on one short check-in message, because a small agreed signal covers the gap when full calls are paused.
How might the student at the next table see Mehak on the phone?
The student looks up at the voice in the library, so the student sees a person quietly having a personal call and not a distraction from work.
What is the sum of all whole numbers from 1 to 5,000?
I'm not sure of the total, as a long sum is easy to get wrong. Multiply the last number by one more than itself, then halve it, and check on a calculator.

Dear Sarika,
You asked how the 'chore money' plan is going. Badly, and it's my fault.
Remember I started paying Meenu two rupees for every job? Now she won't fold a towel without asking, 'How much?' Yesterday Paati dropped a whole box of rice, and Meenu stood there and asked if picking it up counted.
That one stung. So I'm trying something different. No money for everyday jobs. Instead I tell her exactly what I noticed: 'You matched every sock; that saved me ten minutes.' 'You helped Paati, and she smiled.' Pocket money stays, but it isn't tied to jobs.
Day three: she laid the table tonight without being asked and said, 'I did it because Paati was tired.'
I almost cried into the dal.
Love,
Lavanya

How much did Lavanya pay Meenu for each job?
Two rupees for every job.
Why did Meenu's question about the rice sting Lavanya?
It showed Lavanya that the payments had turned even helping Paati with a mess into a deal; Lavanya felt the plan had pushed out Meenu's own wish to help.
What change did Lavanya choose, and why does it seem to work?
Stopping payment for everyday jobs and naming exactly what Meenu did and why it mattered; Meenu has started helping for reasons of her own, like Paati being tired. 🙂
How might Paati have felt when Meenu asked if picking up the rice counted?
Paati might have felt a little hurt or amused at being treated as a paid job, and much warmer later when Meenu laid the table because Paati was tired.

In the small town of Sirsi, everyone knew when a family bought something new. When the Hegde family next door got a car, Deepak's mother mentioned it twice at dinner. When Sabina's colleague at the school went to Kerala for a holiday, the staff room talked about it for a week.
So Deepak and Sabina bought a scooter on instalments, then a big fridge, then took a trip to Goa on the credit card. They never sat down to see if their two salaries, his at the cooperative bank and hers at the school, could carry it all.
By the monsoon, the card bills were arriving faster than the salaries. They paid one card with another.
The quarrels started small, about who had wanted the fridge. Then they happened almost every night. Their little son started going quiet whenever the phone rang.
One evening Sabina sat on the step with the bills and simply cried.

Where did Sabina's colleague go for a holiday?
To Kerala.
What was Sabina feeling when she sat on the step with the bills?
She felt overwhelmed and hopeless, crying because the spending had turned into debt and nightly quarrels.
What would you change first in Deepak and Sabina's approach?
Sit down together with both salaries and decide what they can actually afford, and speak to someone qualified at the bank about the card debt.
How is the couple's little son affected?
Their son has become anxious, going quiet whenever the phone rings because of the tension at home.
This year I'm going pandal hopping for Durga Puja with three friends. It's my first time in such a big crowd.
That sounds exciting. The lights, the music and the food stalls make it a special time. Plan a meeting spot in case someone gets separated from the group.
Like where?
Pick something easy to find, like a particular stall or a gate near the first pandal. Make sure everyone knows its name, and save each other's phone numbers on paper too, in case a battery dies.
Good idea. What should we wear? We'll walk a lot.
Choose light cotton clothes and comfortable footwear you can walk in for hours. Sandals with a strap are better than slippers that slide off.
Perfect. Any food I should try?
Ask the locals. Many pandals have favourite snacks. Try small portions so you can taste more things, and carry a little water.

You keep saying "fine" about your in-laws, Trisha, and your face says something else. So let your Vinita maasi tell you what "fine" cost me.

When I married, your uncle's family lived two floors down. My mother-in-law came up every evening, opened my pots, and said, "Kamla's daughter-in-law makes softer rotis." I said nothing. For eleven years, nothing. But I stopped laughing when she laughed. I found reasons to be busy when they came. Your uncle thought I simply disliked his family.

One night he asked why I had gone so cold. I nearly shouted, but I didn't blame his mother. I told him, "I feel inspected in my own kitchen." He was shocked. Together we asked that visits be on Sundays. It helped. But eleven years of silence had already put ice between us that took long to melt. Don't wait eleven years.

What did Vinita's mother-in-law compare her with?
She compared her with Kamla's daughter-in-law, who made softer rotis.
How did young Vinita feel during those silent years?
She felt resentful and inspected in her own kitchen, and it came out as coldness rather than words.
What was the turning point in Vinita's story?
When her husband asked why she had gone cold, she described her own feeling without blaming his mother, and they agreed on Sunday visits together.
How did Vinita's husband see her coldness before she spoke?
He simply thought she disliked his family, because her silence gave him no other explanation.

"Anjali, the interview is tomorrow. Have you prepared?"
"What's the point, Leela? I'll mess it up like last time."
"Last time you prepared for one day."
"Because I knew I'd fail."
"So you didn't prepare. And then you failed."
"Exactly. Proof."
"No, that's a loop."
"What do you mean?"
"You think you'll fail, so you don't prepare, so you're nervous, so you fail. Then you think, see, I was right."
"...That sounds bad when you say it."
"Let's do one mock tonight. Just thirty minutes."
"Fine. But I'll still be nervous."
"Nervous and prepared is better than nervous and not."

How long did Anjali prepare for last time?
Anjali prepared for one day.
What is Anjali feeling about the interview?
Anjali feels hopeless and anxious, sure of messing it up again.
What does Leela suggest, and why might it break the loop?
One thirty-minute mock tonight; preparing even while nervous can change the result, so the fear doesn't come true.
How does Leela see Anjali's belief that failing is proof?
Leela sees it as a loop, where the fear causes less preparation and nerves, which then produce the failure.

Monsoon week one: Pradeep gives Sarika, five, a sticker each night she brushes her teeth. She brushes fast, then asks, "Where's my sticker?"

Week three: she asks, "If I brush, what do I get?" Pradeep says, "Clean teeth." Sarika frowns and doesn't move.

Week five: Pradeep says, "No brushing, no story." Sarika runs to the sink at once.

What did Pradeep give Sarika in week one?
He gave her a sticker each night she brushed.
Why did Sarika frown in week three?
Sarika felt disappointed and unconvinced, because clean teeth didn't seem like a real reward.
How could Pradeep help Sarika move beyond rewards?
He could talk simply about why brushing matters while keeping the routine, so she learns the reason too.
How might Pradeep feel when Sarika asks what she will get?
Pradeep might feel amused but a little frustrated that she only brushes for a reward.

You asked how I became the person who eats anything, Gautam. Honestly, I'm Urmila, and I used to be the fussiest eater in my family. Last year I noticed something: every food I 'loved' was something I'd had since I was five. Every song on my playlist was from school. Even my friends were all from the same colony. It made me wonder if I liked things, or just knew them. So I made a rule: three fair tries before I decide. The first time I ate Naga pork with bamboo shoot, I hated the sourness. The second time, less. The third time I asked for more. The same with a Portuguese singer my colleague played, and with a quiet guy at work I'd written off. He's now one of my closest friends. Some things I still don't like after three tries, and that's fine too.

How many tries does Urmila give before deciding?
Three fair tries.
What did Urmila feel on noticing that every 'loved' food was from childhood?
Urmila felt curious and a little unsettled, wondering whether liking was real or only familiarity.
What makes Urmila's rule useful for others?
It gives new foods, music or people a fair chance to become familiar before judging, while still allowing a real dislike after three tries.
How might the quiet colleague see Urmila's change?
He may feel glad and valued that Urmila gave him another chance and got to know him.

"Neelam, it's almost midnight. Still on the essay?"
"Papa, it's due at eight. I've written one paragraph."
"Show me."
"It's bad. Manoj said he'll send me his from last year. Same topic."
Manoj Uncle's son had topped the class. Papa sat down. "And then?"
"And then I change some words."
"Would your teacher know?"
"Maybe not." She paused. "Maybe yes. She reads everything twice."
"And would you know?"
Neelam rolled her eyes. "Papa, don't do the philosophy thing."
"Fine. What's your one paragraph about?"
"How rivers shaped old towns." She looked at it again. "Actually, I had one more idea about the ghats."
"Write that. I'll make tea."
She groaned, but she deleted Manoj's message without opening it.

What was Neelam's essay about?
It was about how rivers shaped old towns.
Why did Neelam roll her eyes at "And would you know?"
She was tired and a bit defensive, but the question also pricked her, because she knew copying would feel dishonest to her.
What worked about Papa's way of handling the temptation?
He asked questions instead of lecturing, then turned her attention back to her own ideas and offered tea, so she chose not to copy.
What would change if Neelam had used Manoj's essay?
She might have finished faster but risked being caught, and she would have missed writing her own idea about the ghats.

From my bed in our hostel room, I watched Kunal and Sabina tape three printed job ads to the cupboard door. All three were for junior backend developers. Sabina read aloud while Kunal made tally marks on a sheet. "Databases. Tally. APIs. Tally. Cloud basics. Tally. Testing. Tally." After twenty minutes the sheet showed four skills that came up in every ad and a long tail that came up once. Kunal tapped the sheet. "Databases, I'm fine. Testing, I've never done. APIs, one small project. Cloud, nothing." Sabina said, "So testing and cloud first. You have five months." He wrote two lines in his planner, and under them, "Ignore the once-only ones." I couldn't tell if he was worried or relieved. He went to bed early, which he never does.

How many skills came up in every ad?
Four skills came up in every ad.
How might Kunal have felt reading his gaps aloud?
Kunal may have felt worried about the missing testing and cloud skills and relieved to have a clear list, though the roommate couldn't tell which.
What else could Kunal do with the five months?
Kunal could build one small project that uses testing and a cloud setup together, so both gaps are practised in something he can show.
How does the roommate see the evening?
The roommate notices the method and Kunal going to bed early, reading it as a sign the plan affected him, without knowing the exact feeling.

Three months after the breakup, Jana noticed she was still not sleeping through the night, and her seminar notes had gone blank for weeks. For two months a heaviness had followed her from class to the library and back. Her flatmate Jamal said one evening, "It's been long. Maybe someone could help?" Jana had been telling herself to wait. This time she opened the university's website, found the counselling page and picked a time for Thursday. The counsellor in a small warm room did not hurry her. "It's good you came," they said. "Tell me what the last two months have been like." She talked for forty minutes. Walking out, she felt lighter, like someone had shared the weight.

On which day did Jana book the counselling visit?
Jana booked the visit for Thursday.
What is Jana feeling as she leaves the counsellor's room?
Jana feels lighter and supported, as though someone has shared the weight.
What alternative approach could Jana add, and why?
Jana could keep a few regular habits, such as meals and a short walk, because support from a counsellor works best alongside small steady routines.
How might Jamal see Jana's decision?
Jamal saw the long low stretch and gently suggested help, so Jamal is probably relieved that Jana acted instead of waiting.

"Jomon, where's the star?" Harish asked, sitting by the paper lantern on the balcony. It was Christmas week in Kochi.

Jomon, fifteen months, looked straight up and pointed at the lantern.

"And where's Appa's nose?"

Jomon reached out and grabbed it.

Wednesday night, staff room diary.
Avni, Class 11, stays after every physics class to redo problems. Her working is careful and neat, but the final numbers keep going wrong: 36 becomes 63, a minus sign vanishes. Today a boy said, "She just doesn't try," and she went red. It isn't true. I've watched her try harder than anyone.
When she brought me her notebook, the students were still calling me "Ujjwal Sir" through the doorway, and I kept my voice low. I said, "Your method is right. Let's look at the numbers together." I will not ask her to solve at the board in front of everyone again. Tomorrow I'll speak to her parents about screening for a number difficulty, and I'll mark her method separately.

What happens to 36 in Avni's working?
36 becomes 63.
How did Ujjwal Sir feel when the boy said Avni doesn't try?
He felt protective and frustrated, knowing he had watched her try harder than anyone.
Which of Ujjwal Sir's plans treats this as a learning difference rather than laziness?
Suggesting screening for a number difficulty to her parents, marking her method separately and not putting her on the spot at the board.
How might Avni have felt when the boy made his comment?
Avni probably felt humiliated and hurt, going red because her real effort was being called laziness.

Lakshmi planted tomatoes in March. She watered them every evening. By May they had small green fruits. She picked the first red one in June. It tasted sweet.
Lakshmi planted tomatoes in March and watered them every evening. By May they had small green fruits. She picked the first red one in June, and it tasted sweet.

Sunday night
Realised something bad today. I've done every chemistry numerical this month with the AI open. Mole concept, all of it. Preeti asked me to explain one and I couldn't even start without typing it in.
So I closed the tab. Took question 14 from the exercise, similar to the ones I'd "done", and tried it cold with a timer. Twenty minutes. I got stuck converting grams to moles, which, apparently, I never actually learned. I just watched it happen.
New rule, written on the inside cover:
1) Try every question alone for at least 15 minutes.
2) If stuck, ask the AI for a HINT, not the solution.
3) Redo it the next day without any help.
Did three more that way. Two done alone, one needed a hint. Slow. But it's mine now.
Sumit

Which question did Sumit try cold?
Question 14 from the exercise.
What did Sumit feel on failing to explain the problem to Preeti?
Sumit felt uneasy and a little alarmed, realising the tool had been doing the thinking all month.
What else could Sumit add to the new rule?

In the college chemistry lab, Aditi, a final-year student helping the juniors, showed Kalyani around on her first day. At the gas cylinder in the corner, Aditi said, "This one's a bit temperamental. Just be gentle with it." Kalyani nodded, smiling. An hour later, Aditi smelled gas. Kalyani was standing at the cylinder, twisting the valve hard. Aditi rushed over, shut it, opened the windows and called the lab assistant. Nobody was hurt. Afterwards her hands were shaking. She sat Kalyani down. "That was my fault. 'Temperamental' was the wrong word. What I meant: the valve leaks if you force it. Never open it without Ramesh sir checking the seal first. If you smell gas, leave and tell him." Kalyani nodded, pale. "I thought 'temperamental' meant slow." Aditi wrote the rule on a card and taped it to the cylinder that same afternoon.

In the chemistry lab, Aditi told Kalyani that the gas cylinder was "a bit temperamental" and to be gentle with it. An hour later, Aditi smelled gas and found Kalyani twisting the valve hard, so she shut it, opened the windows and called the lab assistant, and nobody was hurt. Aditi admitted the word was her mistake and explained the rule: the valve leaks if forced, so never open it without Ramesh sir checking the seal, and if you smell gas, leave and tell him. Kalyani, pale, said she had thought "temperamental" meant slow, and that afternoon Aditi taped a card with the rule to the cylinder.

Thursday: during the thunderstorm, he clung to her leg and wouldn't let go until she picked him up.

"Third quarter running," Darshan said, pulling a chair over. "What happened with the hospital account?"

Darshan left the log on the shared drive.

Looking would sting her pride, so blaming the boss and the market feels safer and protects her from feeling ashamed about her own part.

She could open the call log once and mark which delays were hers, perhaps with Darshan, and change one habit such as sending follow-ups the same day.

Darshan probably feels awkward and a bit shut out, having raised it gently and still got a hard close of the laptop, yet cared enough to leave the log.

A scarf.

The last train into Porto arrived at midnight, and Tariq had promised to pick Rosa up. She stood under the station awning for forty minutes, rain dripping off the edge, calling a phone that went to voicemail.
In the taxi home the old voice started: He doesn't care. He never did. She caught it. That wasn't true either. In March, Tariq had sat with her in the emergency room for six hours when she broke her wrist. He'd learned to make her grandmother's soup.
Rosa said it to herself slowly, like a sum: Tariq is caring. Tariq was careless tonight. Both are real.
In the morning he appeared at her door, grey-faced. "I fell asleep on the sofa. I'm so sorry."
"I was really upset," Rosa said. "I still am, a bit. And I know you care. Can you set an alarm next time?"
He nodded, and they made coffee.

How long did Rosa wait under the station awning?
Forty minutes.
Why did "He doesn't care. He never did" feel true to Rosa in the taxi?
She was cold, tired and hurt after waiting in the rain, and in that disappointment one careless night seemed to wipe out everything good.
What choice in the taxi kept the disappointment from exploding?
Rosa remembered the emergency room and the soup and held both facts, caring and careless, so she could say she was upset and ask for an alarm without calling the friendship a lie.
What might it be like for Tariq to hear "And I know you care"?
Tariq, grey-faced and ashamed, would probably feel relieved that the mistake was named honestly without being treated as proof that he didn't care.

On the terrace of their building in Hyderabad, Afreen was in charge of riddles. "Karthik, a bat and a ball, together, weigh one hundred and ten grams. The bat weighs a hundred grams more than the ball. How much does the ball weigh?" "Ten grams!" said Karthik instantly. Afreen shook her head. "Then the bat would be one-ten and the total would be one-twenty." Karthik groaned. "It sounded so easy." "That's why it's a trick," Afreen said. She gave him another: "If it takes five minutes for five kites to fly up, how long for a hundred kites?" Karthik's mouth opened, then closed. He tapped the railing, counting. "Five minutes," he said slowly. "Each kite takes five minutes, on its own." Afreen clapped. Karthik clapped for himself too.

I still remember that feeling, like the whole world was just the marble.

After weeks of standing at the edge, she was invited in by Gurleen, the group's leader, with a big smile, and Nazia felt relief mixed with wariness; she kept sitting with her art club friends too. Zainab, you asked on the student podcast how I cut down my night scrolling. I'm Dolma, and here's the honest answer: I stopped asking how to stop, and asked why I was doing it.
One night I wrote down what I felt right before I picked up the phone. Three nights running, it was the same two things. First, lonely. We'd moved to Delhi in June and I didn't really have anyone yet. Second, homework dread. The maths I hadn't started sat on the desk like a rock, and scrolling meant I didn't have to look at it.
So the phone was doing two jobs, badly. I gave those jobs to better things. For lonely: I call my old friend in Gangtok at nine, ten minutes, voice only. For dread: I open the maths and set a ten-minute timer. Just ten. Usually I keep going.
I still scroll sometimes. Just not till two.

When does Dolma call the old friend in Gangtok?
At nine, for ten minutes, voice only.
What two feelings did Dolma find before picking up the phone?
Dolma felt lonely after the move to Delhi, and full of dread about the maths homework.
What else could Dolma do about the loneliness in Delhi?
Join one club or activity at the new school, so there are people nearby to talk to as well as the old friend.
How might the old friend in Gangtok feel about the nine o'clock calls?
The friend probably enjoys staying close and feels valued, perhaps without knowing the calls replaced scrolling.

Read this:

You want the honest version, Harsh? Pour the tea.
I'm Ira. When I was made team lead on the city survey project last year, I was twenty-six and had two camps: the old field staff from the city, and new recruits from the districts, who spoke with different accents. The city lot joked about the accents. The district lot called the city lot lazy. I didn't give a speech about unity; they had heard plenty.
Instead I rebuilt the teams. Every survey pair had one old hand and one new, the same targets, the same pay, and they took turns as pair leader. The ward had to be finished in six weeks or the funding went.
The first time someone mocked an accent at the morning meeting, I stopped the meeting. "Not in this team. Next point." I did it every time, for anyone.
By week four the pairs were covering each other's sick days. Nobody lectured anyone. The work did it.

How long did the team have to finish the ward?
Six weeks, or the funding went.
Why did Ira decide not to give a speech about unity?
Ira felt the staff had heard plenty of speeches and that words alone would not change their attitudes.
Which of Ira's choices made the mixed pairs work?
Pairing old and new with equal targets, pay and turns as leader, and stopping every accent joke at once, for anyone.
How might a new district recruit feel when Ira stops the meeting over a joke?
The recruit may feel protected and taken seriously, which makes it easier to trust the old hand in the pair.

Read this:

In their student flat in Paris, Leila, nineteen, pulled her laundry out of the machine: every white shirt was now pale pink. A red sock lay at the bottom like evidence. Her flatmate Nour laughed so hard she had to sit down. "Welcome to adult life." Leila groaned. That evening Nour showed her how to sort colours, check labels and pick the right setting. On Sunday, Leila made her first proper lentil soup, cleaned the stove afterwards without being asked, and wrote a weekly chore chart for the fridge. The pink shirts stayed pink. She wore them anyway.

What turned Leila's white shirts pink?
A red sock.
How did Leila feel when she saw the pink shirts?
She felt frustrated and a bit embarrassed at her laundry mistake.
What did Leila do well after the mistake?
She learned from Nour, cooked and cleaned on her own, and set up a chore chart.
How might Nour see Leila's progress?
Amused at first, then pleased to see her flatmate learning to run the home.

Read this:

At the Kuala Lumpur kindergarten the Lunar New Year lanterns were up, and Cikgu Fatima put one pineapple tart in front of Mei. "If you can wait till I come back from the office, you get two."
Mei stared at the tart. She licked her lips. Then she sat on her hands, turned her whole chair to face the window, and sang the lantern song, loud, swinging her feet. She counted the red lanterns. One, two, three, four...
When Cikgu Fatima came back, the tart was still there. Mei's face lit up. "Two!"

What did Cikgu Fatima put in front of Mei?
One pineapple tart.
How was Mei feeling while she stared at the tart?
Mei wanted it badly and felt tempted, since she licked her lips, and then happy and proud when she earned two. 😊
Which of Mei's tricks worked, and why?
Sitting on her hands, turning to the window, singing and counting lanterns; keeping her mind busy elsewhere helped more than just trying hard not to eat it.
What would change if Mei had to keep staring at the tart?
The wait would likely feel much harder and she might have eaten it; looking away made waiting bearable.
Describe a cat sleeping on a window ledge, about 50 words.

The cat lies curled on the window ledge, a soft grey ball in a patch of sunshine. Her chest rises and falls slowly. Her tail wraps around her paws, and one ear twitches at a sound outside. She is warm and completely at peace. The whole afternoon seems to slow down just to let her sleep.

Please write a short summary of this study session.

After school in Kinhai village, Pallavi stayed back to help Uday with the Class 9 science practical. She had topped the district quiz, and acids and bases felt like her own language.
"Simple," she said, dipping the paper strip. "pH below seven is acidic, so more H-plus ions; above seven, more OH-minus. Neutralisation gives salt and water. Done."
Uday stared at the strip. "Ions?"
"H-plus. Hydrogen ions. I just said."
"And why does the colour change?"
"Indicator!" Pallavi tapped the bottle, a little sharply. The bell for the last bus rang. "Honestly, Uday, it's the easiest chapter."
Uday packed his bag without a word. On the bus, Pallavi watched the fields go by and wondered why he never seemed to get anything.

Pallavi tries to help Uday with a science practical, but she explains it too fast and gets impatient with his questions. Uday leaves silent, and Pallavi wonders why he never understands, without seeing her own part in it.

Read this:

Friday: After dance practice, Rohit, a senior, grabbed Binita's phone and found the clip of her tripping on stage. "You don't mind if I post this, right?" Binita's mouth opened, but nothing came out. Her legs wouldn't move. He laughed, said, "Silence means yes," and posted it.
Saturday: Binita told Devika, voice shaking. "I didn't say no. I just stood there." Devika held her hand. "Freezing isn't saying yes. Your body got scared. Let's tell your mum now." They went straight to Binita's home, and her mother listened to all of it, said, "This is not your fault," and emailed the school counsellor and the dance teacher that afternoon.
Monday: The counsellor met Binita first thing, and the clip was taken down by lunch. Rohit was spoken to. In the corridor, Binita still felt her legs go stiff, but now she knew what it meant.

What was on the clip Rohit posted?
Binita tripping on stage.
What was Binita feeling when her legs wouldn't move?
Binita was frightened and overwhelmed, frozen so that speaking was impossible; it was not agreement.
Which steps put things right?
Telling Devika, then telling Binita's mother the same day, who said it wasn't Binita's fault and emailed the counsellor and dance teacher; the clip was down by Monday lunch.
How did Devika see Binita's silence?
Devika saw it as a fear response, not a yes, and said so before helping Binita tell an adult.

"Ah, you are my favourite pupil still. It is worth to teach you. Now that you are willing to understand, you have taken the first step to understand. You think then that those so small holes in the children's throats were made by the same that made the hole in Miss Lucy?"

Answer from the excerpt alone: what does the speaker say about the pupil, and what question is asked?

The pupil is still a favourite and worth teaching, having taken the first step by being willing to understand. The speaker asks whether the small holes in the children's throats were made by the same one that made the hole in Miss Lucy.

Read this:

Tuesday, 11:20 pm.
The shop closes on Friday. I signed the last paper today and put the key in an envelope. Gautam came by with samosas and said, "Everything happens for a reason." I nearly threw the tea at him. He meant well. He looked so awkward that I let it go, but I wrote "no" on my palm with a pen afterwards.
It's not that I think there's no lesson. It's that I don't want it yet. It still feels like a hole in the floor.
Tonight, though, I opened the notebook and wrote three things I'd never do again with suppliers. It didn't fix anything. It just sat there on the page, small and true. Maybe that's how it starts. Not tonight though.
— Disha

What was closing on Friday?
The shop was closing on Friday.
What was Disha feeling when Gautam said everything happens for a reason?
Disha was angry and hurt, nearly throwing the tea, though Disha saw that Gautam meant well and looked awkward.
What small step did Disha take that night that was her own?
Disha wrote three things never to do again with suppliers. It was a small, true note in Disha's own words, not a consolation someone handed her.
How might Gautam have felt after saying everything happens for a reason?
Gautam probably felt awkward and unsure how to help. He came with samosas because he cared, and his face showed he did not know what else to say.
Tell me what a compass does in two sentences. The first must begin with "A compass".
A compass shows which direction is north. Its needle is a small magnet that lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.

Read this:

This is something I've been thinking about. At twenty-five I had a finance job, a fiancée my family chose, and a secret. Every weekend I volunteered with a theatre group, and I felt more like myself there than anywhere. I told nobody at home. My friend Manoj said, 'You're living two lives, Akash. Which one's yours?' I got angry with him. But he wasn't wrong. So I started small. I told my fiancée first. She laughed and said she already knew, she'd seen photos. Then I told my parents. My father thought it was a waste of time. I didn't quit my job. I just stopped hiding. Now I'm one man, not two. It's messier, but it's mine.

Where did Akash volunteer every weekend?
He volunteered with a theatre group.
Why did Akash get angry with Manoj?
Manoj's comment touched something true that Akash wasn't ready to face, so it stung.
What small step helped Akash stop living two lives?
He told people one at a time, starting with his fiancée, instead of hiding his theatre work.
How did Akash's fiancée react differently from his father?
She laughed and already knew, while his father saw the theatre as a waste of time.
Compose an email for my son Arjun's teacher, Ms. Alvarez, asking for a meeting about his reading. Say that I am free after 5 pm on weekdays. About 70 words. My name is Peter Dsouza.

Subject: Request for a short meeting

Dear Ms. Alvarez,
I am Peter Dsouza, Arjun's father. I would like to talk to you about his reading and how I can support him at home. Could we meet for a few minutes soon? I am free after 5 pm on any weekday. Please suggest a time that suits you. Thank you for all your help.
Kind regards,
Peter Dsouza

Read this:

The generator at the printing press had failed at four, and Rafiq had until nine to get two thousand exam booklets bound for the district office. Under the one working tube light, he puffed out a long breath, cheeks ballooning, then clenched his jaw so hard the muscles in his cheeks jumped.
Sabina, feeding covers into the stapler, glanced up. "That's the third time you've done the balloon face."
"What face?"
She puffed her own cheeks to show him. He laughed despite himself, then noticed how tight his face felt, like a fist.
"Five minutes," Sabina said. "Go stand outside. I'll keep stapling."
He stood by the gate in the drizzle, let his jaw hang loose and breathed slowly. When he came back, he spotted the missing box of covers he had walked past twice.

How many exam booklets did Rafiq need to get bound?
Rafiq had to get two thousand exam booklets bound for the district office.
What did Rafiq's puffed cheeks and clenched jaw suggest?
They suggested Rafiq was tense and stressed about the nine o'clock deadline; they might also have shown plain tiredness after the power failed.
What small step helped Rafiq get back on track?
A five-minute break outside, letting his jaw loosen and breathing slowly, cleared his head enough to spot the missing box of covers.
How did Sabina see the balloon face?
Sabina read it as a sign he was strained, so she mirrored it back lightly and kept stapling so he could step out.

Read this:

In the village near Ludhiana, Gurpreet's grandfather was arguing with a tractor driver over the muddy lane. Six-year-old Gurpreet watched from the doorway and saw his grandfather's nostrils flare as his jaw set. He went quiet, and tugged his mother Nirmala's dupatta. "Dada is very angry," he whispered. Nirmala knelt and said, "Yes, he's upset about the lane. Let's take some slow breaths with him. In through the nose, out through the mouth." Grandfather's shoulders lowered a little as he heard them.

What was Gurpreet's grandfather arguing about?
He was arguing with a tractor driver over the muddy lane.
What did Gurpreet notice, and what did he seem to be feeling as a result?
He noticed his grandfather's nostrils flaring and sensed that he was angry, and he went quiet and tugged his mother's dupatta, which suggests he felt tense or uneasy. He might have wanted comfort.
How could Nirmala help Gurpreet handle the moment?
She can name the feeling calmly and model slow breathing, as she did, so Gurpreet learns that anger can be slowed down.
How might Grandfather feel when he hears the family breathing slowly?
He may feel a little embarrassed or calmer, since his shoulders lowered a little.

Read this:

In Copenhagen, Emil's group had to build a bridge from paper straws. Emil was the leader. He had a plan, but it kept collapsing.
Sofia, who hardly spoke, tapped the table. "What if we make triangles? They're stronger."
Emil hesitated. It wasn't his idea. Then he said, "Let's try it."
The triangle bridge held twenty coins.
When the teacher asked who had the winning idea, Emil could have said "our team." Instead he said, "Sofia thought of the triangles."
Sofia turned pink, but she smiled. Emil felt a small tug of envy, then something better.

How many coins did the triangle bridge hold?
Twenty coins.
What was Emil feeling when he hesitated?
Emil felt a bit reluctant and envious because the idea wasn't his.
Which choice by Emil made him a good leader?
He tried Sofia's idea and gave her the credit clearly, instead of taking it for the team or himself.
How might Sofia feel when Emil names her?
Sofia feels shy but proud and valued, knowing her quiet idea was recognised.

messages.content: She is one of the my closest friends from college. Fix the extra word.

She is one of my closest friends from college.
Why: A possessive such as "my" already points to the noun, so "the" is not added.
What is the meaning of posterity?

Posterity means all the people who will live in the future. It is a noun.
Example: The town saved the old letters for posterity.

Thursday night

The climate march is on Saturday and I really want to go. But I didn't want to just turn up like last time, when that street thing got scary and I had no plan.

So today I did the boring stuff. I checked the city police website: the march has permission, the route is from the park to the town hall. The organisers are a students' environment group that my science teacher knows. Their notice says peaceful, no masks, no damage.

At dinner I told Amma and Appa the route and the timings. Appa said he'd come if I wanted. Alka's aunt is going too, so we'll be a group of five.

I've packed water, charged the power bank, and saved Amma's number as the first speed dial. We agreed: if it turns angry or the crowd gets too tight, we walk out by the library road, no arguing.

I'm Harsha, and for once I feel excited instead of nervous.

What route will the march take?
From the park to the town hall.
How does Harsha feel about going to this march?
Harsha feels excited rather than nervous, thanks to the careful planning.
What else could Harsha add to the plan?
Harsha could agree on a meeting point in case the group gets separated, since phones can fail in crowds.
How might Amma and Appa see Harsha's preparation?
They probably feel reassured and trusted, since Harsha shared the route and timings and Appa could choose to come along.

messages.content: Grow or grow up: can plants grow up?

No, plants just grow. "Grow" means to get bigger, and it is used for people, plants and animals. "Grow up" is only for people, and means to become an adult.
Examples: These tomatoes grow fast in the sun. Kwame grew up in a village near the hills.
Everybody in Class A has a bicycle, and Naman has a bicycle. Is Naman in Class A?
We cannot be sure. Because the rule says that each pupil in Class A has a bicycle but does not say that only those pupils have bicycles, Naman may belong to another class.

Relocation coordinator's note — Irfan, transfer from Jaipur to the Hyderabad office. Written by Noor.

Most transferees ask me for a list of "good areas" and sign the first lease a broker shows them. Irfan asked for three days' leave instead.
He arrived on a Thursday and did something simple: he travelled to our office from three different areas at peak hour. Gachibowli, Kondapur and Miyapur. He timed each trip on both mornings, eight-thirty and nine. He walked around each area in the evening, looked at the markets, checked where the nearest clinic was.
On Saturday he messaged me: "Kondapur looks fine online, but the morning traffic is forty-five minutes. Miyapur has the metro; it's thirty-five, reliable."
He signed a lease in Miyapur the following week.
What I did next: I've added a line to our relocation guide suggesting a peak-hour visit before signing.

How long did the Kondapur morning trip take?
Forty-five minutes.
How might Irfan have felt after timing the commutes himself?
He likely felt more confident and reassured, trusting his own experience rather than online guesses.
What else could Irfan check before signing the lease?
He could ask colleagues who moved earlier about broker fees and landlord issues in Miyapur.
How does Irfan's approach look to the relocation coordinator?
The coordinator sees it as a model, adding a peak-hour visit to the relocation guide for others.

Read this:

At the drama society meeting in a Jayanagar classroom, the same three voices had been running the discussion about the annual play for forty minutes. Rashmi noticed Chinmay in the corner, nodding, saying nothing, though he had directed two plays in school. When the loudest member paused to check her phone, Rashmi said, "Chinmay, you've directed before. What would you do with the second act?" Chinmay hesitated. "I'd cut the long speech and show it instead. Maybe with shadows." There was a pause. Then the others leaned forward. "Shadows how?" For the next fifteen minutes, Chinmay talked, sketching on the board. The play changed. After the meeting he walked out beside Rashmi. "I didn't know how to get in," he said. "It felt like there was no space." "There was," Rashmi said. "Someone just had to make it."

How many plays had Chinmay directed in school?
Two plays.
What was Chinmay feeling before Rashmi asked him?
He felt shut out and unsure how to join, since it seemed there was no space for him to speak.
What did Rashmi do that made the meeting fairer?
She used a pause to ask Chinmay a specific question based on his experience, opening a turn for him.
How did the others respond once Chinmay spoke?
They leaned forward, asked questions, and let him sketch his idea, which changed the play.

Read this:

Tuesday. Nazia found out her flat's lease wasn't being renewed; she had three weeks to move. She called Vishal, talking so fast he could barely follow. He listened, then said, "Okay. Come over Thursday. We'll make a list."
Thursday. At his table, Nazia started spiralling again: deposit, packing, work. Vishal just kept writing, slowly, one line at a time, asking, "And next?" His calm voice made hers slow down. By the end there were twelve lines, and she was breathing normally.
The following Saturday. Nazia signed a new lease. She texted Vishal a photo of the keys: "I don't know how you do that. I walk into your kitchen in pieces and walk out in one."

How many lines were on the list by the end?
Twelve lines.
How did Nazia feel on Tuesday?
Nazia felt panicked, talking so fast Vishal could barely follow.
What did Vishal do that helped Nazia's panic ease?
He listened, gave one simple next step, then kept writing a line at a time, asking "And next?" in a calm voice.
How might Vishal feel receiving the photo of the keys?
Vishal would probably feel happy and quietly proud to have helped.
A British recipe site says "washing-up liquid", but an American blog says "dish soap". Same?

Yes. Both mean the liquid soap used to clean plates and pans. "Washing-up liquid" is British, and "dish soap" is American. In India, you may also hear "dishwash liquid".
Examples: We ran out of washing-up liquid. (British) We ran out of dish soap. (American)

Read this:

Nandini, you're worried your new team doesn't trust you. Let your Jatin chacha tell you about the dye works in Surat. Six of us supervisors, and every morning we blamed the night shift for every bad batch. The owner hung a banner about unity. Nothing changed. Then one morning I said, 'The maroon batch was my mistake. I set the wrong temperature.' The room went quiet. Old Hameed looked at me as if I had lost my mind. But the next week Hameed admitted he had skipped a check himself. Slowly we started saying 'my mistake' before anyone pointed a finger. When the big export order went out clean, the owner thanked me, and I told him the night shift deserved it. Small things, beta. Nobody remembers that banner.

What did the owner hang up that changed nothing?
A banner about unity.
How did Hameed probably feel when Jatin first owned up to the maroon batch?
Hameed seemed startled and doubtful, looking at Jatin as if he had lost his mind, because blaming the night shift was the usual habit.
Which choice in the story turned the team around, and why did it work?
Jatin admitting the maroon batch mistake first; it showed that owning an error was safe, so Hameed and the others began to do the same.
What might the night shift have felt when Jatin gave them credit for the clean order?
After being blamed every morning, they likely felt surprised and respected, finally seen for their work.
We want to start a Sunday cricket match in our neighbourhood.
Find a safe open space, and ask whoever looks after it for permission. Then invite people through notices or the residents' group.
How do we make teams fair?
Let two captains take turns choosing players, or mix ages and skills so both sides are balanced. Rotate captains every week.
What if someone argues about a decision?
Agree on simple rules before the first game, such as who umpires and what counts as out. When a dispute comes up, the umpire's decision stands.
Any safety points?
Check the ground for stones and holes, use a soft ball for younger players and keep windows and cars away from the playing area.
How do we keep it going?
Pick a fixed day and time so people can plan, and keep matches short enough for everyone to bat and bowl.

Mehak's first period had started on Sunday, and by Wednesday she knew all the new rules: don't enter the puja room, don't touch the pickle jar, sit apart at dinner. Her Nani said it was so she could rest. It felt like being dirty.

At school she hadn't told anyone, not even Arohi. In the biology lab, when the teacher said, "Today, menstruation," two boys sniggered, and Mehak went red to her ears.

Mrs Pinto stopped the class. "This is a normal body process that half of you will have and all of you should understand. Nothing about it is dirty or funny." Then she explained it plainly, with diagrams, and said anyone could come to her with questions.

At lunch Mehak told Arohi. Arohi squeezed her hand. "Mine started in June. Same kind of rules at my house. Let's go and ask Mrs Pinto together."

What rules had Mehak learned by Wednesday?
Don't enter the puja room, don't touch the pickle jar, sit apart at dinner.
How did Mehak feel about the new rules at home?
Mehak felt ashamed and set apart; though Nani said it was for rest, it felt like being dirty.
How did Mrs Pinto replace stigma with facts?
She stopped the sniggering, said plainly it is a normal body process, explained it with diagrams, and invited questions.
What was it like for Arohi when Mehak told her?
Arohi felt close and supportive, sharing that hers started in June and offering to go to Mrs Pinto together.

messages.content: Why does a firecracker make such a sudden loud bang?
The bang comes from a quick burst of gas. Because the burning powder makes a lot of hot gas in a flash and the gas shoves the air outward sharply, we hear a loud crack.

Dear Diary, Tuesday.
I finally went to Kalyani ma'am about my thesis stats. Last time I asked her anything, I just said "I'm confused about regression" and she spent twenty minutes asking what I meant. I felt awful for wasting her time.
This time I prepared. I wrote: "I ran the regression. Results are here. I don't know whether to include the age variable, because it changes the other results. I've read chapter 6. I need help deciding, not the whole method explained."
She read it, nodded, and answered in eight minutes. Then she said, "I wish all my students asked like this." I almost floated home. 😊
Sunaina

What had Sunaina already read before asking?
Sunaina had read chapter 6.
How did Sunaina feel after Kalyani ma'am's comment?
Sunaina felt proud and delighted, almost floating home.
What did Sunaina include that made the request work?
What had been done, the exact question about the age variable, and the kind of help needed, which let ma'am answer in eight minutes.
How does Kalyani ma'am see this way of asking?
She appreciates it, wishing all her students asked so clearly, since it respects her time.

How long has Arnab been sleeping badly?
5 weeks, every night since Diwali.
What is Arnab feeling during the day?
Arnab feels heavy and low all day, as if nothing is worth doing, and a little embarrassed that seeing a doctor might seem dramatic.
Why is Afreen right that this is no longer a try-harder problem?
The poor sleep has lasted weeks despite good habits and now comes with low mood, so a doctor should help plan the next step while the routine continues.
What might Afreen be feeling while sending these messages?
Afreen seems worried and caring, offering to come along and staying reachable until Arnab books.
