Read this:

Two days before Holi, Jeevan, five, stood at the window of their Jaipur flat. "Is it Holi today?"
His father Vishal pointed to the calendar. "Yesterday we bought colours. Today we fill water balloons. Tomorrow is Holika fire. Then Holi."
Jeevan frowned. "Too long!"
"Let's cross off today."
Jeevan drew a big X. Then he filled balloons, carefully, counting.
"One more sleep and one more day," he told himself.

What did they buy yesterday?
Colours.
How did Jeevan feel about waiting for Holi?
He felt impatient, saying it was too long.
How did Vishal help Jeevan understand the days?
He used the calendar and let Jeevan cross off today.
How might Vishal feel hearing Jeevan count the days?
Vishal likely feels pleased that Jeevan understands.

Read this:

At 5:52 on a Friday, eight minutes before the office emptied, Rashmi's phone lit up: a message from a number with her director's photo. "In a meeting, can't talk. Urgent: buy four gift cards for a client and send me the codes in 10 minutes. Keep this between us."
Her heart jumped. The director was travelling; it was possible. But "keep this between us" and the ticking clock made her skin prickle.
She didn't reply to the number. She called the director's saved office line; no answer. She walked to Hrithik's desk. "Does this look real to you?"
Hrithik read it and frowned. "Different number. And she's never asked anyone for gift cards." Together they forwarded it to the IT security desk, which replied within minutes: a known scam going round.
Ten minutes later Hrithik's own message came: "Can you check my slide numbers before I send?" Rashmi laughed. "That one I'll trust."

At what time did the message arrive?
At 5:52 on a Friday, eight minutes before the office emptied.
Why did Rashmi's skin prickle when she read the message?
Rashmi felt suspicious and uneasy because of the secrecy request and the ten-minute pressure, even though the director really was travelling.
What steps did Rashmi take to check the message?
She didn't reply to the number, tried the director's saved office line, asked Hrithik, and forwarded it to the IT security desk.
What would change if Rashmi treated every message as a scam, even Hrithik's?
She would waste time and strain teamwork; healthy doubt suits surprising, secret, urgent requests, not every ordinary one.

Read this:

I'm Hemant, and I sit next to Gurpreet in Class 6. He never checks the timetable; every book he owns goes into the bag, every day. By the second period he was leaning forward like an old man, and on the stairs he held the railing. Then the teacher asked for the English notebook. He dug past the atlas, the drawing file and a spare geometry box, pulling out crumpled sheets before he found it. The whole class waited, and he went red. At lunch he rubbed his shoulder, and when the strap slipped I saw the red marks.

What did Gurpreet dig past before he found the English notebook?
He dug past the atlas, the drawing file and a spare geometry box.
How might Gurpreet have felt while the whole class waited?
Embarrassed; he went red while everyone watched him search. 😔
What other approach could Gurpreet try, and why would it work better?
He could read the timetable and pack only tomorrow's books, since a light bag is easier to carry and a neat bag is easier to search. A short checklist at the door would also help.
How does Hemant see Gurpreet's habit?
Hemant sees a plan that costs Gurpreet comfort and time, and seems concerned rather than mocking, since he notices the strap marks and how the class waited.

metadata.subtype: Approach: throwing everything in the bag just in case [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: A message from Hafsa in the project chat: "THE BUILD FAILED AGAIN!!!" Pema, who had pushed the last update, felt her face go hot. She typed back, "It's not my code, before you start." Hafsa didn't reply for an hour.
Tuesday: Over lunch, Hafsa said quietly, "I wasn't blaming you yesterday. I type in caps when I'm stressed. Or excited. My whole family does." Pema winced. "I read it as shouting at me. Sorry for snapping."
The following Wednesday: "PEMA. THE CLIENT DEMO. CALL ME." Pema's stomach lurched out of habit. This time she didn't type anything. She just rang. Hafsa picked up, breathless. "They want to extend the contract! I had to tell someone!" Pema laughed, relieved. "Next time add a smiley so my heart survives." "No promises."

What did Hafsa's Monday message say?
"THE BUILD FAILED AGAIN!!!"
What was Pema feeling when she read Monday's message?
Pema felt defensive and a bit hurt, reading the caps as shouting and blame for her code; it was really Hafsa's stress.
What did Pema do differently the following Wednesday, and why did it help?
Instead of typing a reply to a guessed tone, Pema called straight away, which revealed excitement and avoided another quarrel.
How had Hafsa experienced Pema's 'before you start' reply?
Hafsa likely felt hurt and misread, since she wasn't blaming anyone, which may explain the hour of silence.

metadata.subtype: Loud reactions online and voice notes [Mismatch]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the chemistry lab, Dilnaz was rinsing a pipette when a boy at the next bench said to Maria, "Go back to where you came from." A few others snorted.
Dilnaz froze. Her heart thumped, and while she searched for words the moment passed. Maria packed her bag in silence. Mr. Fernandes was at the far end of the room, writing on the board.
In the corridor Dilnaz caught up with her. "I should have said something. That wasn't okay. Are you alright?"
"I wasn't sure anyone had heard," Maria said.
"I heard. Do you want to sit together at lunch? And if you decide to tell Mr. Fernandes, I'll say what I heard."
Maria let out a slow breath. "Maybe. Lunch first."

Where did the remark happen?
It happened in the chemistry lab, at the bench next to Dilnaz's.
Why did Dilnaz freeze instead of speaking up?
She was caught off guard: her heart thumped and she was still searching for words when the moment passed.
What could Dilnaz do if she hears a remark like that again?
She could say plainly 'that isn't okay' right away, and keep checking on Maria afterwards, as she did in the corridor.
How might Maria have felt when nobody spoke in the lab?
Maria may have felt alone and unsure anyone had heard, which is why she said so, and why Dilnaz's check-in mattered to her.

Read this:

You want to know why I stopped giving Farida rides? Fair question, since I drive half the office. I'm Deepak, and honestly, I like helping. Last month I drove Sunil to the hospital for his mother, helped Joan move her boxes, covered two shifts for the new guy. Didn't expect anything back. Farida was different. Every day she'd wait by my car. Never once asked if I minded. Once she made me detour to her cousin's place, forty minutes. When my car broke down, she found another lift before I'd finished calling the mechanic. So last Monday I told her, calmly, "I'm not going to do the daily rides anymore." She was annoyed. I still help people. I just watch where it goes.

How long was the detour to Farida's cousin's place?
Forty minutes.
How did Deepak feel about telling Farida no?
Deepak felt calm and settled about it, having noticed that Farida only took, even though Deepak generally enjoys helping others.
What does Deepak's approach show about being generous and setting limits?
Deepak keeps helping freely, but when someone habitually takes, Deepak says clearly and calmly that it will stop.
How might Farida see Deepak's decision?
Farida was annoyed and may feel Deepak suddenly turned cold, not having noticed that she never gave anything back.

Read this:

Tuition teacher's note, Class 4, Saturday.
For three weeks, Vaibhav has told me, “I will do better in maths, Ma'am. I promise.” Each week, no homework was done. He is sincere, but the promise has nothing in it he can start.
Today his grandfather, Mr Jagdish Rao, came to collect him and mentioned they have tea at 5 every evening.
So we tried something small. I wrote on a card: “After 5 o'clock tea: 5 problems from page 42. Tick when done.” Vaibhav read it aloud and said, “Only five? That's easy.”
His grandfather agreed to sit with him and check the ticks. I asked Vaibhav to bring the card next Saturday.
What I will do next: check the card with him, praise each tick, and if all seven days are done, move him to page 43.

What was written on the card?
“After 5 o'clock tea: 5 problems from page 42. Tick when done.”
How did Vaibhav feel when he read the card aloud?
He felt relieved and confident, saying “Only five? That's easy,” instead of feeling stuck with a big promise.
Why is the card more useful than Vaibhav's promise?
It gives a specific small goal with a set time, which is easier to start and to check than a vague wish.
How might Mr Jagdish Rao feel about helping with the ticks?
He might feel pleased and involved, glad to have a simple way to support his grandson.

Read this:

In the small town of Dhrangadhra, Samir had been paying "release charges" for three months on an insurance policy that a caller said had matured. Each time, the officer promised the cheque for next week.
This week there were new cracks. The "head office" letter spelled the company's name wrong. The officer's number changed twice. When Samir asked for the branch address, the man laughed and said, "Trust me, Samir bhai."
At night Samir lay awake beside his wife, Neelam, doing sums in his head. Part of him knew. Part of him kept hoping the cheque would arrive and he'd never have to explain the savings missing from the tin they had been filling for her brother's wedding gift.
When Neelam asked why he had stopped eating, he said, "The shop is slow." He couldn't bear her face, or her father's, if they learned he'd been fooled.

What did the head office letter get wrong?
It spelled the company's name wrong.
Why is Samir afraid to tell Neelam?
He feels ashamed and afraid of losing face with Neelam and her father, so he clings to hope instead.
What could help Samir break the denial?
Checking the insurer's official number himself, telling Neelam the truth, and reporting to the bank and cyber-crime helpline.
What might Neelam be noticing in Samir?
Neelam notices his sleeplessness and lost appetite and feels worried, sensing it is more than a slow shop.

Read this:

In the Class 6 writing lesson, students swapped paragraphs to review. Lokesh got Jahnavi's, and Jahnavi got his.
Lokesh's said: "Our school should have a longer lunch break. It would be nice. Everyone wants it."
Jahnavi wrote in the margin: "Why would it be nice? Who is everyone?"
Lokesh read it and felt his face heat up. Then he looked at Jahnavi's paragraph. It had a topic sentence, three reasons, and an ending.
He rewrote his: "First, many of us don't finish eating. Second, we'd have time to play and then focus better. Third…"
He handed it back to her with a small nod.

What did Jahnavi write in the margin?
"Why would it be nice? Who is everyone?"
What was Lokesh feeling when his face heated up?
Lokesh felt embarrassed that his paragraph had no real reasons.
How could the teacher use this kind of peer review again?
The teacher could keep having students ask each other "why?" questions so they learn to add reasons.
How might Jahnavi feel when Lokesh hands back the rewritten paragraph?
Jahnavi probably feels respected, seeing that her comments helped him improve.

Read this:

I'm Bhavna, from the ground floor. This morning a street dog chased Damini at the gate, barking. It didn't touch her, but she ran screaming to her mother and buried her face in her dupatta. Her mother didn't say, “Don't be silly.” She picked her up, sat on the step, and said, “You were scared. The dog ran at you.” Damini sobbed, “It was so loud.” Her mother rocked her. I don't know how long it took, but by the time I came back from the shop, Damini was waving at the dog from her lap.

What did Damini bury her face in?
Her mother's dupatta.
What was Damini feeling when she ran screaming to her mother?
She was frightened by the barking dog, even though it didn't touch her.
What did Damini's mother do that helps later self-soothing?
She held her and named the feeling, “You were scared,” instead of calling it silly.
How did Bhavna see the change in Damini?
When Bhavna came back from the shop, Damini was already calm enough to wave at the dog from her mother's lap.

metadata.subtype: Accepting comfort from a trusted adult [Regulating]

messages.content:
Read this:

Snow was piling against the window of the Toronto flat when Tariq came back from his shift. "Oh, you're home," Amira said. "Thought you might stay out with your new favourite coworker." She laughed, but it came out thin. Tariq frowned and put the groceries down. Later she took her plate to the bedroom and shut the door, waiting to see if he would knock. He did, after twenty minutes, looking tired. While he showered, his phone lit up on the bed. Her hand hovered. She picked it up, read nothing but a delivery message, and felt no better at all. When he came out, he saw the phone in a different spot. He said nothing, and the silence sat between them all evening.

Where did Tariq's phone light up?
His phone lit up on the bed while he showered.
Why did Amira shut the bedroom door with her plate?
She wanted to test whether Tariq would come after her, hoping it would prove he still cared.
What turning point is available for Amira now?
Instead of more tests, she could tell Tariq plainly that she has been feeling insecure, because the checks are not calming her and are starting to hurt him.
How is Tariq likely experiencing these tests?
He seems worn out and uneasy; the joke, the closed door and the moved phone may make him feel watched and distrusted. 😔

Read this:

The robotics lab at the Pune school closed at six, but Vidya was there until the guard came to switch off the lights. Her team's robot kept turning left when it should go straight. Mr Mridul, the teacher in charge, found her crouched over the motor again. "You've been here every evening this week." "It's so close, Sir." Her hands were greasy, and there was a pencil behind her ear. "When it works, it'll be the best feeling." He sat down. "Show me what you've tried." She explained six changes, one after another, eyes lit up. He pointed at one wire. She tightened it. The robot rolled straight across the floor. Vidya jumped up so fast she knocked over a chair.

What time did the robotics lab close?
At six.
What was Vidya feeling when the robot finally rolled straight?
She felt thrilled and elated, jumping up so fast she knocked over a chair.
What did Mr Mridul do that helped?
He asked her to explain what she'd tried before pointing to the loose wire.
How might Mr Mridul see Vidya staying late every evening?
He seems impressed by her dedication, and perhaps a little concerned she's working too long.
Message a friend to say you will be late. Keep it under twenty words and end with the word "soon".
Sorry, my bus is stuck in traffic, but I will reach the cafe soon.

Read this:

To: Jaya, Customer Support
Subject: Help after data leak

Dear Jaya,

I'm writing because I did the wrong thing. On 4 February your company sent an email saying some customer details had leaked. It looked like junk, so I deleted it without reading past the first line.

Six weeks later I began getting calls from people who knew my name and the address I gave you, saying they were from my delivery service. I lost a whole afternoon and gave one of them a code before I realised something was off.

Could you tell me what exactly was in the leak, and whether anything can still be done? I know I waited too long.

Mohit

Reply: "We're sorry. We will help, though the delay does make tracing harder."

On what date did the company send the notice?
4 February.
What was Mohit feeling when writing that the wrong thing was done?
Mohit felt regret and worry, blaming the delay in reading the notice and realising too late that the calls were a trick.
What could Mohit do now besides asking the company, and why?
Mohit could tell the bank and keep a record of the calls, because reporting quickly and keeping details helps others trace what happened.
How might Jaya see Mohit's email?
Jaya may see a customer who is embarrassed but honest, and would want to help while knowing the six-week gap limits what can be traced.

metadata.subtype: Approach: ignore the notice as spam [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Hi everyone, I'm Kashish from Class 11, and the radio club asked me to talk about how I stopped dreading homework. So. I have this one playlist, soft covers of old ghazals, that I love more than almost anything. Last year I made a rule: I only get to hear it when my books are open. My brother Sachin thought I was mad. "Just listen to it whenever, na?" But it changed things. At seven, when I'd normally stall, I think about those songs and I sit down. Starting stopped hurting. The one thing I learned the hard way was essays. I tried writing my English essay with the playlist on and everything came out rhythmic and meaningless. For essays and new chapters, I need silence. The songs are for practice sums.

What playlist does Kashish save for homework?
Soft covers of old ghazals.
Why does thinking about the songs help Kashish sit down at seven?
The songs are something Kashish loves and only gets with the books open, so the wish to hear them outweighs the urge to stall.
Which choice about essays shows good judgement?
Keeping essays and new chapters silent after noticing the music made the writing rhythmic but meaningless, and saving the playlist for practice sums.
Why might Sachin have found the rule strange at first?
To Sachin a favourite playlist is something to enjoy any time, so rationing it seems pointless until the change in Kashish's homework shows its purpose.

Read this:

At the community centre after tailoring class, Vasudha waited until the room emptied and then sat beside her Mausi, who ran the class. "Mausi, I've asked Papa and Mummy three times for a rehearsal evening until nine-thirty. They say seven. It always ends in raised voices." Mausi put down her tape measure. "Let me hear it from both of you. Saturday, at home." On Saturday Mausi listened to Omkar first. "The auto stand is dark after eight," said Papa, "and she'd ride alone." Vasudha said, "The recital is in three weeks and I'll miss every practice." Mausi looked from one to the other. "What if rehearsal ends by eight-thirty and Omkar picks her up at the door?" Papa breathed out slowly. "That I can do."

How many times had Vasudha asked for the rehearsal evening?
Vasudha had asked three times.
How does Vasudha feel about the talks at home?
Vasudha feels frustrated and stuck, because every request ends in raised voices.
What else could Vasudha try if Mausi could not help, and why?
Vasudha could ask the rehearsal teacher to speak with the parents or write a plan with a pick-up time, because parents may hear a trusted adult more easily.
How does Omkar see the request?
Omkar's worry is the dark auto stand and Vasudha riding alone, not distrust, so a pick-up at the door meets the concern and he can agree.

metadata.subtype: Approach: involving a trusted relative as mediator [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Why is there always dal? I hate dal!" Gopika pushed her plate so hard it slid. Sangeeta looked at her daughter's red eyes. "You were online at two again. I saw the light under your door." "So? I finished the essay." "And signed up for three competitions at midnight, you told me." Gopika's voice cracked. "I don't even know why I did that. Now I have to withdraw from two." She put her head on the table. Sangeeta sat beside her. "Tired brains say yes to everything and hate the dal. Phone charges in the hall tonight. Lights out by eleven, breakfast together at seven, for one week. Then we see." Gopika sniffed. "Fine. One week."

Where will the phone charge tonight?
The phone charges in the hall tonight.
Why did Gopika's voice crack when she talked about the competitions?
She regretted signing up at midnight and felt confused and embarrassed that she did it, and she now has to withdraw from two.
What choice at the table could change how Gopika's week goes?
Agreeing to one week of phone outside, lights out by eleven and breakfast together gives her rest and regular meals, so her mood and decisions can settle.
How does Sangeeta see Gopika's outburst about the dal?
Sangeeta sees it as tiredness talking, not rudeness, which is why she sits beside her and plans sleep rather than arguing about food.

metadata.subtype: Sleep loss changes mood and choices [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The hospital ward hummed and beeped. Kashish stood at the foot of Nanu's bed, staring at the tubes running from his arm to a big humming machine. Her hands were cold. 'Mummy, is the machine hurting him?' she whispered. Her mother, Jahnavi, squeezed her shoulder. 'Let's ask.' When the doctor came round, Mummy said, 'Doctor, can you explain it simply for Kashish?' The doctor crouched down. 'Nanu's kidneys are tired. This machine cleans his blood for them. It doesn't hurt, but it makes him sleepy.' Kashish nodded slowly. 'Will he get better?' 'We're working on it. Some days will be good, some not so good.' Kashish breathed out. She pulled a chair close and held Nanu's free hand.

What does the machine do, according to the doctor?
It cleans Nanu's blood for his tired kidneys.
What did Kashish's cold hands suggest she was feeling?
She was frightened by the tubes and the machine and worried it was hurting Nanu.
What helped Kashish cope in the ward?
Asking Mummy, who got the doctor to explain simply, and then sitting close and holding Nanu's hand.
How might Nanu feel with Kashish holding his hand?
Comforted and less alone during a tiring treatment.

Read this:

"Watch, Noor. I can wink." Jasleen shut both eyes.
"That's two eyes," said Noor.
"It's my wink!"
"Winking is one eye. Like this." Noor shut one eye slowly and grinned.
"Why do people wink?"
"When it's a joke only you two know."
Jasleen thought. "Like when Rajni hides the biscuit tin?"
"Exactly. She winks and you don't tell."
Jasleen tried again, one cheek scrunching, and squealed, "Was that one?"
"Nearly!"

How does Noor say a wink differs from shutting two eyes?
She says winking is one eye, and shows it by shutting one eye slowly.
What does Jasleen seem to understand about winking after Noor explains?
She thinks a wink is a joke or secret shared between two people, and her example of the biscuit tin shows she has linked it to something real. Her squeal suggests she is excited to try.
What small step would help Jasleen get closer to a real wink?
She could practise in a mirror with one hand gently covering the other eye, and keep it playful rather than serious.
What might Noor be thinking as she teaches her?
She may enjoy feeling like the expert and share the joke, and her "Nearly!" shows she wants Jasleen to keep trying.
My parents don't allow me to stay out late. Is this right?

Your sentence is correct.
Why: "Allow" is followed by an object and "to" plus the base verb, so "allow me to stay" is correct.

Read this:

I'm Suraj, and I've made peace with being the uncool friend. Last month Wasim and I went to a crowded music night in an old hall. Before sitting down, I did my usual thing and found the two exits, one beside the stage and one behind the snack counter. Wasim laughed. Halfway through, the lights flickered and a burning smell drifted in. A staff member took the mic: "As a precaution, please make your way outside." Plenty of people stayed put, filming the stage. I didn't wait to see smoke. I tapped Wasim, said "Let's go," and walked to the counter exit. He followed, grumbling. It turned out to be a burnt fuse in the kitchen. We missed three songs, and Wasim teased me all the way home. My face went warm, sure. But a warm face is a small price. I'd rather be early and wrong than late and right.

What had caused the burning smell?
A burnt fuse in the kitchen.
How did Suraj feel while Wasim teased on the way home?
A little embarrassed, with a warm face, but at peace with it, seeing it as a small price to pay.
What habit made Suraj's quick exit possible?
Finding the two exits before sitting down, so when the staff member asked people to go outside, Suraj knew exactly where to walk.
How might Wasim see the evening, having followed Suraj out?
Wasim missed three songs and enjoyed the teasing, but was also outside early and safe in case it had been serious.

Read this:

In Room 214 of the engineering hostel, the notes started in the second week. The first was taped to the shared kettle: "Thank you, sir, for cleaning the kettle. Oh wait." Then one on Kamal's cupboard: "Congratulations on remembering your tiffin exists 👏" Deepak wrote them in neat capitals and never mentioned them aloud. Kamal read each one in silence. They felt like being judged in a court where he wasn't allowed to speak. He started leaving the room early and coming back after lights-out. He wrote a reply twice and tore both up. On Friday, during the power cut, both of them were stuck in the dark room. Kamal switched on his torch and said, "The notes. What do you actually want me to change?" After a pause, Deepak said, "The tiffin smells by Wednesday. And I feel like a nag if I say it." Kamal laughed a little. "Say it. I'd rather hear it than read it."

What was the first note taped to?
The first note was taped to the shared kettle.
How did the notes make Kamal feel?
Kamal felt hurt and judged, like being in a court where he wasn't allowed to speak, so he avoided the room.
What could hostel roommates try so notes don't pile up?
They could agree on a short weekly talk about room problems, so each says what bothers them directly instead of writing it.
What was it like for Deepak to keep writing notes instead of speaking?
Deepak was bothered by the tiffin smell but worried about seeming a nag, so writing notes felt safer to him than saying it.

Read this:

Irfan, you say the ward meeting is a waste of time. Let your Urmila Aunty tell you about the first one I went to, at twenty-four, in Bhopal. Our lane flooded every monsoon. I went in angry, ready to shout at the corporator. An old engineer at the back stopped me. He showed me the budget sheet on the notice board: that year the ward had money for either a new drain or a park, not both. The park had been promised to the colony next door, where children had nowhere to play. Suddenly it wasn't villains and victims. It was a trade-off. So I didn't shout. I collected photos of the flooding from twenty households, presented them at the next meeting, and asked whether the drain could come first with the park in next year's plan. The colony agreed, for a written promise. It took eighteen months, but the lane hasn't flooded since. Come with me on Sunday, Irfan.

What choice did the ward budget force that year?
Either a new drain or a park, not both.
What was young Urmila feeling when she went to the first meeting?
Urmila felt angry, ready to shout at the corporator about the flooding.
What was the turning point, and why did it work?
Seeing the budget trade-off, she gathered photos from twenty households and proposed an order with a written promise, which the other colony could accept.
How might the colony next door have seen Urmila's proposal?
They probably worried about losing the promised park, but the written promise for the next year made it fair enough to agree.

Read this:

Chaitanya's end-of-term exam was three weeks away, so instead of one long night of reading, he and his study partner Uma made a plan: forty minutes a day, a different chapter each time. Every session began with a blank page. Chaitanya wrote down everything he could remember about the last chapter, then checked. "It's so much slower than rereading," he said, wincing at the gaps. Uma shrugged. "That's the gap we're fixing." Three days later they revisited the same chapter just as it had gone hazy, and the answers came back with a tug of effort. He passed with room to spare. Four years on, Chaitanya was working at a logistics firm. His new colleague Naveen watched him open a notebook before a client call. "Forgot the export steps again?" Naveen asked. Chaitanya nodded without embarrassment. "I only use them twice a year. I keep the steps here, and every few weeks I run through the important ones from memory." He tapped the notebook. "The rest can fade. My head has to make room for something." Naveen grinned and pulled out his own list.

How long was Chaitanya and Uma's daily study session?
Their session was forty minutes a day, with a different chapter each time.
How did Chaitanya's way of dealing with forgetting change between his exam term and his working years?

As a student he went back to the chapter just as it had gone hazy and wrote down what he could remember; at work he keeps the steps in a notebook and runs through the important ones from memory every few weeks, letting the rest fade.
What was Chaitanya feeling when he opened his notebook in front of Naveen?
He felt at ease, not ashamed; he nodded without embarrassment and explained his system.
What small step would help Naveen after seeing Chaitanya's notebook?
He could write his own list of rarely used steps and set a regular time to run through the important ones from memory. 🙂

Read this:

Study hour at the girls' hostel of Shanti Vidyalaya was silent except for fans. Mehak stared at the notice: Model Exhibition, Friday.
Last year she had stayed up Thursday night and her volcano had cracked on the table. This time she took a pencil and turned her diary to the week.
Friday: carry the water filter model to the hall. Thursday: chart must be done. Tuesday: pour muddy water through and time it. Sunday: get sand, gravel and a bottle from the canteen and the sports store.
She wrote each day on a sticky note and stuck them in a line on the edge of her desk.
Vikas Sir, doing his rounds, stopped and read them. "Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday. Good gaps between them." He tapped Tuesday. "Give yourself Wednesday too, in case the water stays muddy."

What did Mehak's volcano do last year?
Her volcano cracked on the table after she stayed up Thursday night.
How might Mehak have been feeling when she read the Friday notice?
She was probably anxious, remembering the cracked volcano, and determined not to repeat the rush.
Which change suggested by Vikas Sir would make the plan stronger, and why?
Keeping Wednesday free as a spare day helps, because if the filter test fails on Tuesday she can still fix it before Thursday.
How might Vikas Sir see Mehak's sticky notes?
He sees a careful plan with good gaps and wants to help her protect it from surprises, which is why he suggests a spare day.

metadata.subtype: Approach: counts back from a fixed date to set small deadlines [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Vishal,

Remember I told you I'd fix my cracked phone screen myself with that repair video? Update: I didn't.

I ordered the screen, the tiny screwdrivers and the suction cup. I watched the video five times. It all looked so easy. But when I heated the edge and pried it open, a thin cable tore. Now the new screen works, but the camera doesn't. I spent an hour staring at it, feeling like an idiot.

Last month I fixed the wobbly table from a video and felt like a genius. I think I forgot that phones are not tables.

Next time, the repair shop.

Lokesh

What stopped working after the repair?
The camera doesn't work.
How did Lokesh feel after the cable tore?
Lokesh felt like an idiot, dismayed after an hour of staring at the phone.
What lesson does Lokesh take away about video repairs?
That some jobs, like a wobbly table, are fine to try, while delicate ones, like a phone, need a professional repair shop.
How might Vishal react to this letter?
Vishal might feel sympathetic and a little amused, and glad Lokesh plans to use the repair shop next time.

Read this:

I'm Trisha, and my brother Francis is five. Today at Grandma's he looked at the sweet jar, then at the kitchen door where Mum was on the phone, then back at Grandma. "Mum said I can have two," he told her, very seriously.
Mum hadn't said anything. I was right there. But the funny thing was his face: he was watching Grandma really carefully, like checking whether she could tell.
Grandma smiled. "Let's ask Mum together." Francis's ears went pink. "Maybe she said one," he mumbled.

What did Francis tell Grandma?
Francis told her, "Mum said I can have two."
How was Francis feeling as he watched Grandma so carefully?
Francis was nervous about being caught, watching Grandma closely to check whether she could tell that Mum hadn't said anything.
What did Grandma do that worked well?
She calmly suggested asking Mum together, which checked the claim without scolding him.
How does Trisha see her brother's fib?
Trisha finds it funny and notices him testing Grandma, seeing it as something he is figuring out rather than being bad.

Read this:

Monday. Chetan's notebook held a list of twenty-two tasks for the week at the bank branch. By Tuesday night he had crossed off six small ones and none of the big ones. He felt heavy.
Wednesday. Zeenat, his team lead, showed him her card: three outcomes, nothing else. That evening Chetan tore out a fresh page and wrote: close the loan file audit, train the new cashier, send the quarterly report. He checked it before sleeping and moved one step forward on each.
Next Monday. Chetan wrote three new lines. By Friday all three had ticks, and the long list felt less like guilt.

How many tasks were on Chetan's first list?
Chetan's notebook held a list of twenty-two tasks for the week.
What was Chetan feeling on Tuesday night?
He felt heavy and discouraged because he had only crossed off small tasks and none of the big ones.
Which change worked for Chetan, and why?
Writing only three outcomes and checking them each evening kept his attention on what mattered, so all three were done the next week.
How might Zeenat see Chetan's progress?
Zeenat would likely feel pleased that sharing her simple card helped her team member finish the important work.
Why does a guitar string make a higher note when it is tightened?
Its vibrations get faster. Because tightening speeds up the string's shaking, and faster vibrations are heard as a higher pitch.

So, I'm Tushar, and last term I finally learnt how to hand work over properly. Our civil engineering group had traffic counts from four junctions, typed by four different people. Total mess. Indu offered to clean it. Earlier I'd have said "just sort it", then lain awake wondering what she was doing. This time I sat with her for ten minutes. I showed her exactly what I needed: times in 24-hour format, one junction per tab, and vehicle types spelt the same way every time, "two-wheeler", never "bike" or "scooty". Then I said, "Don't spend more than an hour before you show me. Send me Junction B by Wednesday lunch." She sent it Wednesday at noon, and there was one problem: she'd merged buses and vans. We fixed it in five minutes, not five days.

Which junction did Indu send first, and when?
Junction B, on Wednesday at noon.
How did Tushar feel about handing over work in the past?
Tushar felt anxious and out of control, lying awake wondering what the other person was doing after just saying "just sort it".
What would you change first if the group had missed the Wednesday check?
Set a new short check straight away on one small piece, so a mistake like merging buses and vans is still caught early.
What is it like for Indu to get such clear instructions?
Indu can work confidently without guessing, and the early check means her one mistake was cheap to fix rather than embarrassing at the end.

I'm Urmila, and I've worked next to Sahil at the publishing house for three years. When I joined, he was the one with ideas in every meeting: a podcast, a new cover style, school visits. Our old editor ignored all of them, or took one and gave it to someone else. By last year Sahil had gone silent. In meetings he'd say, "Whatever you think." Someone called him lazy behind his back. I didn't think so. I'd seen him fix our catalogue at midnight without being asked. When our new editor asked for volunteers to choose the autumn list, I said, "Sahil should pick two titles. He's got the best eye here." He looked startled. Then, slowly, he opened his notebook.

What did Sahil fix at midnight?
The catalogue.
What was Urmila thinking when someone called Sahil lazy?
Urmila felt protective and unconvinced, believing his silence came from being ignored, not laziness.
Which of Urmila's choices helped Sahil, and why?
Suggesting he pick two titles gave him a small, real choice, which can restore his sense of agency.
What is it like for Sahil when Urmila names him?
Sahil is startled, then cautiously hopeful, opening his notebook after years of being ignored.

Pranav, twenty-four, was on a client call with Singapore when a message from his mother flashed on his phone: Dadi had been taken to hospital. The call had ten minutes left, and he was presenting. His eyes filled. He blinked rapidly, squeezed them shut for a second, and looked up at the ceiling, trying to steady his voice. "As you can see on slide six..." His voice cracked. His colleague Tushar, sitting next to him, noticed the wet eyes and the phone. He leaned into the microphone. "Sorry, a quick technical pause. I'll take slide six." He muted Pranav's line and nodded at the door. Pranav stepped out, called his mother, and learned Dadi was stable. He breathed slowly in the corridor, washed his face, and came back for the last three minutes. After the call, Tushar said, "Go to the hospital. I'll send the summary."

How long did the client call have left when Pranav saw the message?
Ten minutes.
What was Pranav feeling when he saw his mother's message?
He was frightened and upset, his eyes filling as he tried to hold back tears and keep his voice steady.
What did Tushar do that helped Pranav?
He covered the slide, muted Pranav's line and signalled him to step out, giving him a short break.
How did Tushar notice Pranav was struggling?
He saw Pranav's wet eyes and the phone message, and heard his voice crack.

Store supervisor's note, Friday. Written by Manjula, inventory team.
Aadhya, our summer intern, has been checking deliveries this month. Today a vendor's representative spent ten minutes praising her. "You're the sharpest person here. Your seniors are lucky. Honestly, you're wasted in a stockroom." Aadhya was smiling, clearly pleased.
Then he said, "The count's fine, na? We're in a rush." And she signed without opening the last four boxes. When I asked about it afterward, she said, "It felt rude to question him after he was so nice."
I didn't scold her. I told her that's exactly how flattery works: once someone makes you feel special, disagreeing feels like bad manners. We opened the four boxes together. Two were short.
She was upset. I said it happens to everyone, even me. From Monday, every delivery gets counted, however friendly the driver is.

How many of the last four boxes were short?
Two were short.
How did Aadhya feel when the representative praised her?
Aadhya felt pleased and special, which made her less careful and uncomfortable about questioning him.
What did the supervisor put in place from Monday?
Every delivery gets counted, however friendly the driver is, so the check doesn't depend on how someone makes you feel.
How might the vendor's representative have seen the praise?
He likely used it as a tool to hurry Aadhya past the count, knowing praise makes disagreement feel rude.

Ira lives across the landing, so I saw most of it. In the first week of June she came home with football boots. The next week it was a second-hand guitar, and by the third week Parveen Aunty had signed her up for a coding class on Saturdays. Monday football, Wednesday guitar, Saturday coding. I heard the guitar through the wall for maybe ten minutes on Thursdays, the same three chords. At the end of the month she sat on the stairs with her boots untied. "I can't do any of them," she told me. "My passing is bad, my fingers hurt and my code never runs." I don't know if she was more tired or more sad. Parveen Aunty came out and sat beside her for a long time.

Which day was Ira's coding class?
It was on Saturdays.
What did Ira seem to feel sitting on the stairs?
She seemed discouraged and tired, sure she could not do any of the three, though the narrator couldn't tell which feeling was stronger.
What would you suggest Ira change first?
Pick one hobby to focus on for a couple of months, so there is time to get past the hard early stage and actually improve.
How might Parveen Aunty see the month?
She may feel concerned and partly responsible for signing Ira up, and sitting beside her suggests she wants to help her choose what to keep.

messages.content:
Sum up what Walton did to prepare for his voyage.

Six years have passed since I resolved on my present undertaking. I can, even now, remember the hour from which I dedicated myself to this great enterprise. I commenced by inuring my body to hardship. I accompanied the whale-fishers on several expeditions to the North Sea; I voluntarily endured cold, famine, thirst, and want of sleep; I often worked harder than the common sailors during the day and devoted my nights to the study of mathematics, the theory of medicine, and those branches of physical science from which a naval adventurer might derive the greatest practical advantage. Twice I actually hired myself as an under-mate in a Greenland whaler, and acquitted myself to admiration. I must own I felt a little proud when my captain offered me the second dignity in the vessel and entreated me to remain with the greatest earnestness, so valuable did he consider my services.

For six years Walton trained for his journey. He sailed with whalers, put up with cold, hunger and little sleep, and studied science and mathematics at night. He worked so well that a captain asked him to stay on as second-in-command.

At the summer camp run by the community centre, each cabin had to choose teammates for the treasure hunt. The girls from Cabin 3 agreed, in whispers, that nobody would pick Vasudha, because she was 'weird' and talked too much about insects. Zeenat didn't think she was weird. But when the counsellor asked who wanted Vasudha, Zeenat kept her hand down like everyone else. Vasudha was put with the counsellors' team. Later, at the water tank, the counsellor, Mrs Rego, asked Zeenat why nobody had picked her. 'Everyone decided,' Zeenat said. 'I didn't say anything mean. Nobody picked her.' Mrs Rego nodded. 'When everybody does it, each person thinks it was nobody. But it was nine hands staying down. One of them was yours.' Zeenat looked at her wet hands.

Which team was Vasudha put with?
Vasudha was put with the counsellors' team.
Why did Zeenat keep her hand down even though she didn't think Vasudha was weird?
She felt nervous about going against the group, and when everyone did the same, her own part seemed not to count.
What could Zeenat do at the next activity?
She could pick Vasudha or sit with her even if nobody else does, since one person breaking the pattern matters.
How might Vasudha feel being put with the counsellors' team?
Vasudha might feel lonely and embarrassed, noticing that no one her age chose her.

"Sunaina Ma'am, can I ask something about the project marks?"
"Of course, Eshaan."
"I'm not trying to get anyone in trouble. But could you see who did which parts?"
"Go on."
"I made the model. Ravi did the labels. Ankit and Gopal didn't bring anything."
"Are you upset about the marks?"
"A bit. I just think it should be fair."
"You're not asking for all the credit?"
"No. Ravi did a lot too."
"Thank you, Eshaan. I'll ask each of you to fill in a short form about your part."
Eshaan nodded. His hands had stopped shaking.

What did Eshaan make for the project?
The model.
How did Eshaan feel as he spoke to Sunaina Ma'am?
He felt nervous, his hands shaking, and a bit upset about the marks.
What made Eshaan's request fair rather than blaming?
He stated the facts calmly and made sure Ravi got credit too, instead of wanting it all for himself.
How might Sunaina Ma'am see Eshaan's request?
Sunaina Ma'am sees it as a fair question and decides to ask everyone to fill in a form.
I'm lost in a new town. Write a polite question asking a stranger the way to the railway station, under 15 words.
Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the railway station?
Round 7,486.2954 to the nearest hundredth after multiplying it by 3.6.
I'm not sure of the exact digits, as there are two steps. Multiply first on a calculator, then round to two decimal places.
I just started swimming backstroke, and water keeps going up my nose.
That's very common. Are you keeping your head still?
I don't think so. I keep lifting it.
Keep your head resting back in the water with your eyes looking up, and breathe out through your nose gently as you move. That stops water from entering.

"Oof, it's raining cats and dogs out there," said Hafsa Miss, shaking her umbrella in the classroom doorway.

Vishal's head snapped up. He climbed onto the bench and pressed his nose to the window, scanning the puddles. "Where? I can't see any puppies."

A few children giggled. Hafsa Miss came and looked out with him. "You're right, there aren't any. It's a funny saying. It just means it is raining very, very hard."

Vishal frowned at the rain. "Then why didn't you say that?"

"Good point," she laughed.

What was Vishal looking for in the puddles?
Puppies; he said, "I can't see any puppies."
What does Vishal's frown and "Then why didn't you say that?" suggest?
He feels puzzled and a little annoyed that the words didn't mean what they said, and perhaps embarrassed by the giggles.
How can adults make sure a young child like Vishal understands them?
Use plain, direct words such as "it is raining very hard", and explain a saying straight away when one slips out.
How might Hafsa Miss feel when Vishal asks why she didn't just say that?
She finds it funny and fair, as her laugh shows, and it reminds her to speak plainly with little ones.

"Everyone's already been to Ritika's flat when her parents are out," Ayesha said, tugging Kavitha's sleeve at the school gate. "Come after lunch. Bunk maths."
"I don't want to."
"Why not? It's just an hour."
"Because I'm not ready for that. And I don't want to lie to my mother."
"Everyone does it. You're being a child."
Kavitha's voice shook a little but held. "Maybe everyone does. I'm still not going. No is enough, isn't it?"
Ayesha kicked a pebble. "Fine. I thought you liked me."
"I do. That's why I'm telling you the truth."
Ayesha was quiet for a while. "Okay. Sorry. Want to walk to the chai stall instead?"
"Yes," Kavitha said, feeling her shoulders drop. "Let's do that."

Whose flat did Ayesha say everyone had already been to?
Ayesha said everyone had already been to Ritika's flat.
How can you tell Kavitha is nervous but firm?
Her voice shook a little but held, and she says no again despite being called a child. She also does not want to lie to her mother.
What does this scene suggest a person can do under this kind of pressure?
Kavitha shows that saying no is enough and that she does not need to give in to keep Ayesha. Someone who respects her can accept it.
How does Ayesha seem to feel when Kavitha refuses?
Hurt and a little sulky at first, kicking a pebble and saying, "I thought you liked me," and then willing to apologise and suggest something else.

Monday. Dolma lined up chairs for a bus. Her mother Farida said, "Let's make it a train with a whistle!" Dolma's face fell and she wandered off to her blocks.
Wednesday. Farida sat on the floor and asked, "What can I be?" "A passenger with a big bag," Dolma said, and told her where to sit.
Saturday. Dolma announced, "Today the bus goes to Nani's, and you are sleepy." Farida yawned and nodded, and Dolma beamed from the driver's seat.

Where does the bus go on Saturday?
It goes to Nani's.
What was Dolma feeling when her face fell on Monday?
She felt disappointed and overruled, because her mother turned her bus into a train.
What turning point helped Farida and Dolma enjoy the game?
On Wednesday Farida asked what she could be instead of directing, and took the small role Dolma gave her.
What might Farida notice about Dolma from Wednesday to Saturday?
She may notice Dolma growing confident and pleased, giving orders and inventing the story herself.

Dear Damini,
About yesterday's shouting match over the debate schedule: I owe you a proper reply, not another angry text.
Last night I tried something. First I wrote the whole thing down as if it had happened to my cousin Shafiq. Reading it, I'd have told Shafiq, "You both want the event to work. You just want different things first."
Then I tried writing it from your chair. You'd booked the auditorium for Friday because the Wednesday slot clashes with the practical exams your whole batch has. I'd pushed for Wednesday because the visiting judges can only come then. Neither of us said our reason out loud; we just called each other stubborn.
Can we meet at the canteen at four and look at both problems together?
Tanvir

Why had Damini booked the auditorium for Friday?
Because the Wednesday slot clashes with the practical exams Damini's whole batch has.
What did Tanvir realise by writing it as Shafiq's story?
Tanvir saw that both of them wanted the event to work and just wanted different things first, which cooled the anger.
Why is meeting at the canteen to look at both problems a good plan?
It moves the talk from 'you're stubborn' to the real limits, the exams and the judges, which they can solve together.
How might Damini feel reading that the exam clash was understood?
Damini may feel respected and more willing to meet, since the letter names Damini's reason instead of calling Damini stubborn.
What is difference between 'dinner' and 'supper'? In book they write supper.

Both are evening meals. "Dinner" is the common word today. "Supper" is often a lighter or later evening meal, and it appears more in older books and in some parts of Britain. In daily speech, "dinner" is the safe choice.

'Three nights this week past ten,' said Zeenat, dropping onto the sofa in the break room. 'So much for our seven o'clock rule.'
'The release wasn't optional,' said Tanuja. 'If we'd left at seven, it wouldn't have shipped.'
'So the rule is useless?'
'No. It's just too stiff. What if crunch weeks are allowed, but only when a release truly needs it, and the day after is lighter? No meetings, leave on time.'
'And the rest of the month stays seven o'clock?'
'Yes. The rule stays. It just bends for the real peaks.'
'I can live with that,' Zeenat said. They wrote it on the whiteboard: Crunch allowed. Lighter day after. Otherwise seven.
'Better than pretending we'll never work late,' said Tanuja.

What did Zeenat and Tanuja write on the whiteboard?
They wrote: Crunch allowed. Lighter day after. Otherwise seven.
What was Zeenat feeling when dropping onto the sofa?
Zeenat felt tired and frustrated, and doubted whether the seven o'clock rule meant anything.

Every week might get labelled a crunch week, so they could agree what counts as a real release peak and review the rule each month.
How might the rest of the team feel about the new rule?
They may feel relieved that limits still exist but bend for real peaks, and that a lighter day follows.

Usha had shared her pharmacology notes with Farida all semester: neat diagrams, colour-coded, sent every Sunday night. Farida always said "thank you so much" and never sent anything back, not even the lecture Usha missed when she had fever.
The rank list went up on the notice board in the Delhi college corridor. Farida was fourth. Usha was ninth.
Usha stood there feeling stupid. Her own diagrams had pushed someone past her.
That night, when Kavya from her hostel floor asked for the biochemistry notes, Usha typed "sorry, don't have them" and put her phone down. Kavya, who had always helped her with practicals, replied, "Oh, okay."

Where did Farida come on the rank list?
Farida was fourth.
What was Usha feeling as she stood in front of the rank list?
She felt foolish and angry, seeing that the notes she shared freely had helped Farida rank above her.
What could Usha do instead of refusing everyone?
She could share with people like Kavya who help her back, and set limits with people who only take.
How might Kavya feel reading "sorry, don't have them"?
Kavya may feel confused and a little hurt, since she always helped Usha with practicals and is now paying for Farida's behaviour.

Sunday night in São Paulo, Gabriel's phone buzzed on the kitchen table.
Aiko: send me a photo of your maths page pls
Aiko: real friends help each other 🙏
Gabriel stopped eating his rice. His stomach twisted. Aiko had been his friend since first grade.
Aiko: guess I know who my friends are then
He typed, deleted, typed again.
Gabriel: I'm your friend. That's why no photo. Call me in 5 min? I'll show you how I did question 3, then you do the rest
Three dots appeared and disappeared for a long time.
Aiko: fine. but explain slow 😅
Gabriel smiled and put his plate in the sink. His mum raised an eyebrow. 'Homework help,' he said. 'The real kind.'

Which question did Gabriel offer to explain?
Question 3.
What does Gabriel's twisting stomach suggest?
He felt uneasy and guilty at Aiko's message, since they had been friends since first grade.
How did Gabriel answer the guilt-trip?
He said he was still Aiko's friend, refused the photo, and offered a call to show how to solve it 👍
What might Aiko be feeling while the three dots appear and disappear?
Probably embarrassed and unsure, then relieved enough to accept the call and ask Gabriel to explain slowly.

'Saurabh, she's up again. Third time.'
'I heard. I have a meeting at nine.'

Taking turns with the nights, earplugs in the other room, and asking Binita's mother to take Mishti one afternoon so they can nap.

Every time Rukmini spoke in the marketing meeting, Aparna looked at the ceiling. In the pantry she turned her back. Nobody at the firm could say why. Rukmini spent a week bringing her tea, offering to share notes, laughing a bit too hard at Aparna's jokes. Nothing changed. On Friday evening, walking to the metro, she asked herself just once: had she ever taken credit that was Aparna's, or spoken sharply? She went through the months slowly and found nothing. It stung. But she made herself stop. Monday she said a normal good morning, and when Aparna did not answer, she simply went to her desk. She did not complain to anyone or hint at anything. Her lunch with two other colleagues was easier than it had been in weeks.

What did Aparna do whenever Rukmini spoke in the meeting?
Aparna looked at the ceiling.
Why did Rukmini keep offering tea and notes for a week?
She wanted Aparna's approval and hoped kindness would end the dislike. It hurt when nothing changed.
What could Rukmini do if Aparna's coldness continues?
She can keep being polite and professional, keep her good relationships with others, and speak to a supervisor only if it starts affecting her work.
How might Aparna see Rukmini's changed behaviour on Monday?
Aparna may notice that Rukmini has stopped trying so hard and simply says good morning. The passage does not say what Aparna thinks or why she dislikes her.

I joined the design team the same month as Arnab, so I watched how things went for him. He's Deaf and signs, and on day one he asked for an interpreter for meetings and captions on video calls. For the first two weeks, people kept talking to the interpreter instead of to him. "Tell him the deadline is Friday," our manager said, looking at her. Arnab's jaw tightened each time.
Tanvir changed things, quietly. He started sitting where Arnab could see his face, and he learned a few signs from a video course: good morning, thanks, coffee. His signing was clumsy. Arnab laughed at it, but he clearly liked that someone tried.
One day the manager said to the interpreter, "Can he handle the client pitch?" Tanvir answered before anyone: "Ask Arnab." She turned, a bit red, and asked him directly. He said yes, and led the pitch the following week.

What did Arnab ask for on day one?
He asked for an interpreter for meetings and captions on video calls.
What did Arnab's tightening jaw suggest when people spoke to the interpreter?
It suggested Arnab felt frustrated and sidelined at being talked about instead of to; it might also have been general tension in a new job.
What small things did Tanvir do that helped?
He sat where Arnab could see his face, learned a few signs, and redirected the manager's question to Arnab himself.
How might the manager have felt when Tanvir said "Ask Arnab"?
She seemed embarrassed, going a bit red, as she saw she had assumed instead of asking Arnab directly.

Darshan, come, eat this sewaiyan while I tell you why I make it every Eid, though our family never kept Eid.
I was nine. We lived in a chawl in Byculla, eleven families sharing one long balcony. On Eid morning, Rashida Aunty from the corner room sent over a bowl of sewaiyan. My mother said, "Take something back. Don't return a bowl empty."
So I carried our Diwali ladoos, the last six, to their door. Rashida Aunty hugged me, and her son pulled me in to eat with them on the floor. I remember thinking our balcony was one big house.
Years later, a man at my office said something ugly about "those people." I didn't believe him for a second. I'd eaten from their plates.
That's why, Darshan. Your Damini Nani remembers.

How many families shared the long balcony?
Eleven families shared one long balcony.
How did young Damini feel eating on the floor with Rashida Aunty's family?
She felt happy, welcomed and part of something bigger, like the whole balcony was one big house.
What was the turning point inside Damini's story?
When she carried the ladoos back and was pulled in to eat, the friendship became so real that later prejudice at her office meant nothing to her.
How might Rashida Aunty have felt when Damini brought the ladoos?
Rashida Aunty was likely touched and happy, which is why she hugged Damini.

I'm Joseph, and I used to send voice notes like podcasts. Seven minutes, starting with the weather, ending with the point. Then Tanvir, who works nights at a call centre, told me he'd been listening to them on the bus with the volume down, catching one word in three.
So I changed how I do it. Now I start with the point. "Tanvir, Joseph here. Main thing: Sunday cricket is moved to eight. That's it. Thirty seconds." If there's more, I ask first: "Got two minutes for a longer one, or should I type?"
Last week I needed his advice on a job offer, which was going to be long. I texted, "Voice note or call later? Whatever suits you." He wrote, "Call at six, I'm free then."
At six he said, "Thanks for asking first. I actually had time to think."
It felt good to be the friend who makes things easier.

What time did Tanvir suggest for the call?
Tanvir wrote, "Call at six, I'm free then."
What was Joseph feeling after Tanvir said thanks?
Joseph felt pleased and proud of being the friend who makes things easier.
What habit could others take from Joseph?
Start a voice note with the main point, keep it short, and ask whether the other person has time or prefers text before sending a long one.
How does Tanvir experience Joseph's new voice notes?
Tanvir feels respected and less rushed, since he can catch the point quickly after night shifts and choose a time to think about longer matters.

In the office canteen in Bengaluru, Aditi scrolled through screenshots for Joseph: green numbers, big percentages, a trading group with thousands of members. "Forty percent in a month, Joseph. Guaranteed. The mentor picks everything."
Joseph was nearly twenty-five, still sharing a flat, watching everyone around him buy cars. His stomach did a nervous flip. What if everyone got rich and he didn't?
He joined the group that night and deposited ₹10,000 through the app. In a week, it showed ₹13,500. He withdrew ₹2,000, and it actually arrived in his bank. He felt a rush of relief. It was real.
The next message from the mentor came on Friday: "Special VIP round. Minimum ₹2 lakh. Only 24 hours. Don't miss this."
Joseph looked at his savings account. Two lakh was almost everything he had. His finger hovered over the transfer button. Something about "only 24 hours" made his chest tight.

How much did Joseph withdraw that actually arrived in his bank?
He withdrew ₹2,000, and it actually arrived in his bank.
What was Joseph feeling when Aditi showed him the screenshots?
Joseph felt nervous and afraid of missing out, worried everyone else would get rich except him.
What should Joseph do before transferring any more money?
Pause, not rush for the 24-hour deadline, check whether the scheme is registered with the official regulator, and talk to someone independent.
How might Aditi see the trading group?
Aditi seems to trust it fully, perhaps because she has also seen early gains, without noticing the warning signs.

Last month, with three coaching tests a week, I kept opening old photos from when I was five: me in a yellow frock on our Hyderabad terrace, eating mango, laughing at nothing. I'd think, that girl had no worries at all. I missed her so much it hurt. Then, clearing my cupboard, I found my kindergarten drawing book. On one page, in wobbly letters, I had written "I am skared of thunder" beside a black cloud. Another page showed me alone at the gate, waiting for the school van, a tear drawn on my face. I sat on the floor for a long time. I told Aditi the next day. She said, "Maybe you miss being looked after, not being little." That felt right. I'm Zainab, and I still keep the mango photo on my wall, next to the thunder page.

What had Zainab written beside the black cloud in the drawing book?
"I am skared of thunder."
Why did Zainab miss her five-year-old self so much during that month?
The pressure of three coaching tests a week made the easy-looking photos feel like a lost comfort, so she saw only the laughter, not the fears.
What did Zainab choose to do with the photo and the drawing, and why does it help?
She kept the mango photo next to the thunder page, holding both the happy and the scared memories together.
How did Aditi's view change the way Zainab saw her longing?
Aditi suggested Zainab missed being looked after, not being little, which gave the feeling a clearer and kinder name.

It was Friday evening, the science chart on the water cycle was due Monday, and Elizabeth's little brother was banging a spoon on a pot in the next room. She unrolled the big sheet and stared at it. So much white. She sharpened three pencils, wandered to the balcony, came back and sat down with her chin on her arms. Her mother Sarita looked in. “Don't do the whole chart. Draw just one cloud, at the top left,” she said. Elizabeth drew a cloud. Then she added rain under it because that was easy. By bedtime she had three boxes drawn, and the white sheet no longer looked so large.

What did Sarita ask Elizabeth to draw?
Sarita asked Elizabeth to draw just one cloud, at the top left.
Why did Elizabeth sharpen pencils and wander to the balcony?
Elizabeth felt overwhelmed by the size of the blank chart and was avoiding it, since she could not see where to begin.
What worked in Sarita's suggestion?
Naming one small first piece gave Elizabeth something to start on, and then the next piece felt possible.
How might Sarita feel watching her daughter stare at the paper?
Sarita probably feels concerned and patient, wanting to help without doing the chart for Elizabeth.

The care home in Nashik was two staff short all week, and Pradeep, the young shift supervisor, had no one spare to call in. On Friday he noticed Irawati, usually the one who sang to the residents, feeding Mrs Joshi without a word, her jaw tight.
Later he found her in the store room, eyes wet, folding the same towel over and over. "Sorry, sir. It's nothing. Two of my ladies died this month."
Pradeep sat on an upturned crate. "It's not nothing. You've been doing the work of two."
He could not give her the week off with no cover. So he took her difficult evening rounds himself, swapped her to the day shift, and arranged a call with the home's counsellor for Monday. "Talk to me every day this week," he said.

How many staff short was the care home that week?
The care home was two staff short all week.
What did Pradeep feel when he found Irawati in the store room?
He felt concerned and caring; he did not dismiss her tears as nothing, because he could see how worn down she was.
How did Pradeep support Irawati even without spare staff?
He took her difficult evening rounds himself, moved her to day shift, arranged a counsellor call and asked her to talk to him daily.
What is it like for Irawati when two of her residents die in a month?
She is grieving and exhausted, losing her usual warmth and struggling to keep going.

Since Pranav got sick, the Lajpat Nagar flat had turned into a hospital ward. Every phone call was about his temperature; every visitor brought him oranges and comics. Rashmi, ten, felt like furniture. On Sunday, when Nani asked her to be quiet because Pranav was sleeping, Rashmi kicked the door and shouted, "Pranav, Pranav, always Pranav!" Then she ran to the balcony and cried. Papa found her there. He didn't lecture. "I've been so busy with your brother that I forgot to ask about your dance exam. Come on. You and I are going to the market for that glitter pen set, and you can tell me everything." Rashmi wiped her face. At the market she talked for an hour. That night she took Pranav one of her own comics.

What did Rashmi shout?
"Pranav, Pranav, always Pranav!"
What was Rashmi feeling before she kicked the door?
She felt invisible and resentful, like furniture, while all the attention went to Pranav.
Why did Papa's market trip help?
It gave Rashmi one-on-one time and real interest in her dance exam, showing she was still seen.
How might Nani see Rashmi's outburst?
Nani may see a rude child disturbing a sick brother, without noticing how left out Rashmi feels.

Tuesday: On day forty of his probation at a transport company in Nashik, Dhruv's supervisor told him to sign the load sheet for a truck he hadn't weighed. 'It's the same as always. Sign it, or I'll tell head office you're slow.' Dhruv's family had moved into a new rented flat on his salary. He went home and didn't sleep.
Thursday: He told his cousin Sabina, who worked in HR at a bank. She didn't tell him what to do. She asked, 'What does your offer letter say about safety rules? Is there a grievance email?' They found both. 'Now weigh it honestly. What really happens if you refuse? What happens if that truck is overloaded and you signed?'
Friday: Dhruv went to the weighbridge before the supervisor arrived, weighed the truck, and wrote the true figure. It was over the limit. He showed his supervisor calmly and saved the grievance email address in his phone. The truck left lighter. The supervisor didn't speak to him all day.

On which day of his probation was Dhruv asked to sign?
Dhruv was asked on day forty of his probation.
What was Dhruv feeling on Tuesday night?
Dhruv felt afraid and sleepless, worried that refusing would cost his probation and the family's rent.
What steps did Dhruv take before refusing?
He checked the safety rules and grievance email with Sabina, weighed the consequences honestly, then weighed the truck and recorded the true figure.
How does Sabina help Dhruv think it through?
Sabina asks questions instead of deciding for him, helping him see both the risk of refusing and the risk of signing.

Gopika: Okay, imagine the cyclone knocks out the towers and the power. Two days, no phone. What do we do?
Irawati: Charge everything tonight?
Gopika: A power bank helps, but say it dies too. Then what?
Irawati: Then... I only know my brother's number by heart, and that's because it never changed.
Gopika: So we write numbers on paper. Warden, both our families, the ward office, the clinic. Tape the list inside the cupboard door.
Irawati: The caretaker has a small radio. I'll ask if we can borrow it.
Gopika: Good. And we download an offline map of the way to the school shelter tonight.
Irawati: Who calls whom?
Gopika: Whoever finds signal first calls your brother in Nagpur, and he tells everyone else. One person outside the city.
Irawati: Fine, I'll warn him now. Nothing fancy, just what the phones can't do.

Where will the paper list of numbers be kept?
The list will be taped inside the cupboard door.
What does Irawati's remark about knowing only one number by heart suggest about how Irawati feels?
It suggests Irawati feels a little uneasy and exposed, since the phone holds nearly all the contacts.
What else could Gopika and Irawati agree on, and why?
They could agree a fixed meeting point in case the hostel is unsafe, because without phones they cannot message each other to find one another.
How might Irawati's brother in Nagpur see his part in the plan?
He would probably feel responsible and a little anxious, since he is the one outside contact who passes messages to everyone.

messages.content: We're going to visit a hill station soon. Any tips for the journey?
Winding roads can make some people feel unwell, so a seat near the front, fresh air and a light meal beforehand can help. Carry a jacket, since it gets cold up there.
Do I need to book places to stay in advance?
During busy seasons and holidays, yes. Rooms fill up quickly, and prices can rise. Check the cancellation rules when you book.
What about the weather?
Hill weather can change fast, with sudden rain or fog. Look at the forecast before you go, and keep an umbrella or raincoat handy.
Anything I should avoid doing?
Do not litter, and stay on marked paths. Leaving the place as clean as you found it keeps it beautiful for others.
I every day walk to school. Is the order okay?

I walk to school every day.
Why: The verb comes right after the subject, and a time phrase such as "every day" usually goes at the end.
I want to do an appointment with the dentist. Is "do" right?

I want to make an appointment with the dentist.
Why: "Make an appointment" is the fixed phrase.

I remember the exact evening Jatin and I became real friends, not just classmates who shared notes.

We were sitting on the steps outside the library after an exam that went badly for both of us. I said, half joking, that if I failed again my mother would stop introducing me as her daughter the doctor.

Jatin didn't laugh. He said, "My brother dropped out last year. My parents still don't say his name at dinner."

We sat with that for a while. Then I told him the thing I hadn't told anyone, about the boy from school who left without a word, and how I still check his page some nights.

Jatin didn't judge. He just nodded and said, "That sounds lonely."

I watched him closely as I said it, I admit. I was checking whether he'd make it a joke. He didn't.

— Avni

Where were Avni and Jatin sitting that evening?
On the steps outside the library after an exam.
Why was Avni watching Jatin so closely while sharing?
Avni was nervous and vulnerable, checking whether Jatin would turn the disclosure into a joke or respond with care.
What did Jatin do that helped the friendship grow?
He shared something painful about his own family and then answered Avni's secret without judging, simply saying it sounded lonely.
How might Jatin have felt telling Avni about his brother?
He may have felt anxious and sad, since his parents don't even say his brother's name, but also trusting that Avni would care.

Coach's note, Saturday sports hour, Lokesh Sir
Pema did well on the balance beam today, arms out, eyes on the far end. In 'traffic lights' she stopped when a slower child was in front of her instead of pushing through. When the group was making a circle, she asked her neighbour, 'Can I hold your hand?' and waited for a nod. I pointed this out to the group. 👍

What did Pema do when a slower child was in front of her?
She stopped instead of pushing through.
What does Pema waiting for a nod suggest about her thinking?
It suggests she understood that her neighbour's hand and body belong to them, so she wanted permission first.
How could Lokesh Sir help the other children learn from Pema?
He could make asking before touching part of every circle game, praising children when they do it.
How might the neighbour feel being asked before their hand is held?
They would likely feel respected and comfortable, since they got a choice.
The ball rolled off the table and fell in the floor. Fix the preposition.

The ball rolled off the table and fell on the floor.
Why: Use "on" for a surface such as a floor or a table. "In" is for something inside a space.

During the Friday spelling test, Vandana saw it: Lalremsiami had a tiny paper in her sleeve and kept glancing at it. They had shared a bench and secrets since Class 2.
After the bell, Vandana sat on the library steps, twisting her plait. If she told, Siami might never talk to her again. If she didn't, it felt like lying too.
Mrs Lyngdoh, the librarian, sat beside her. 'You look like you're carrying something heavy.'
Vandana told her, without the name.
'That's a hard spot,' Mrs Lyngdoh said. 'Caring about your friend is good. Caring about fairness is good. What feels right to try first?'
Vandana thought. 'Maybe I talk to her first. And tell her she should tell Ma'am herself.'
'That's one way. Tell me how it goes.'

Where did Lalremsiami hide the paper?
In her sleeve; she kept glancing at it.
What was Vandana worried about while sitting on the library steps?
She worried Lalremsiami might never talk to her again if she told, but staying quiet felt like lying too.
What choice did Vandana reach after talking with Mrs Lyngdoh?
She decided to speak to Lalremsiami first and suggest she tell the teacher herself, a step Vandana found without being shamed or pushed.
How might Lalremsiami feel if Vandana comes to her before going to the teacher?
She might feel scared or defensive at first, but also cared for, because her friend came to her directly.

In the panchayat hall, Minakshi stood before thirty farmers to explain a new way of storing onions. The night before, she had practised aloud on the roof, twice, until the main message fit in one sentence: "Air gaps keep onions from rotting." Her slides, on a borrowed projector, had one picture each and hardly any words. After ten minutes she asked for questions. Sharmila, a farmer at the front, asked what would happen if the rains came early. Minakshi paused. "I don't know that yet. I'll find out from the district office and tell you at the next meeting." Sharmila nodded. At the next meeting Minakshi came with the answer.

How many times did Minakshi practise aloud on the roof?
Minakshi practised aloud on the roof twice.
What does Minakshi's pause and honest reply suggest about how she felt?
She felt steady and confident enough to admit not knowing, which preparation makes possible.
What did Minakshi do afterwards to keep her promise?
She asked the district office and brought the answer to the next meeting.
How might Sharmila have seen Minakshi's honest answer?
As trustworthy, since Sharmila nodded and Minakshi later came back with the answer.

Warden's note, Girls' Hostel Block C, 14 March

There was tension in the common kitchen this week. A first-year complained that Maria's beef fry was in the same fridge as her vegetarian tiffin and called it "disgusting". Maria cried.

Hafsa, a second-year who is fasting for Ramzan, came to me the same evening with a plan: separate labelled shelves by diet, lids on everything, and one rule written at the top: "Respect every restriction. Nobody's food is dirty."

She said, "I don't eat pork, and I'd hate it touching my food. But I'd hate even more being called disgusting."

What I did next: I put up her notice, sat the three of them down together, and asked the first-year to apologise for the word, not the preference. She did. On Friday, Maria waited until sunset to eat so she could break the fast with Hafsa.

What rule was written at the top of Hafsa's plan?
Respect every restriction. Nobody's food is dirty.
What does Hafsa's comment about being called disgusting suggest she feels?
Hafsa feels protective and a bit indignant; she understands food limits but finds calling someone's food disgusting far more hurtful.
Why was the warden's response fair to everyone?
It kept each person's restriction with labelled shelves and lids, while asking for an apology for the insulting word, not the preference.
What was it like for Maria when Hafsa stepped in?
Maria, who had cried, likely felt supported, and showed it by waiting until sunset to eat with Hafsa.

Omkar's first project as lead was a hospital booking app for a Bengaluru clinic chain. From week two, the payment connection kept failing in testing. He told nobody.
Every Monday his manager, Madhav, asked, "Any blockers?" and every Monday Omkar said, "All good." He stayed late trying fixes alone. He thought asking for help would make everyone wonder why they'd promoted him.
His status dashboard stayed green for five weeks. Madhav was relaxed. The client was told the launch was on track.
Then, a week before release, the full test ran with real bank sandboxes. Payments failed forty percent of the time. Madhav called an emergency meeting. "Why am I finding this out now?"
Omkar looked at his laptop. "I thought I could fix it."
Madhav had to call the client that afternoon and move the launch. Walking out, he said, "I could have got you help in week two."

How often did payments fail in the full test?
Payments failed forty percent of the time.
Why did Omkar hide the problem, and what was he afraid of?
He was afraid everyone would wonder why they had promoted him, so he felt pressure to look capable and fix it alone.
What should Omkar have done when the payment connection first failed?
He should have told Madhav in week two, since the manager could have brought in help before the problem grew.
How does the situation look to Madhav?
Madhav feels blindsided and frustrated, having to move the launch with the client when he could have helped weeks earlier.
