Bhavna, you asked how Rhea and I stopped having those big money fights. Honestly, it's thirty minutes and a pot of tea.
In our first year, we'd only talk about money when something went wrong. I'd see a big charge and get upset, or she'd find out I'd paid for my brother's trip without telling her. Every conversation felt like an ambush.
So we made a rule. The first Sunday of every month, after breakfast, we sit at the table with the expenses from the month. Thirty minutes, no longer. What we spent, anything coming up, anything worrying either of us.
Last month Rhea said she was thinking about a new laptop. Because it came up at the meeting, we planned for it together. No surprise charge, no fight.
It sounds boring, I know. I'm Siddharth, and I never thought I'd say this, but boring is great.

When do Siddharth and Rhea hold their money meeting?
The first Sunday of every month, after breakfast.
How did Siddharth feel about money conversations in the first year?
Siddharth felt ambushed and upset, since money only came up when something had already gone wrong.
What else could Siddharth and Rhea add to their monthly meeting?
They could keep a short shared list of upcoming big purchases, so each meeting starts with what's ahead as well as what was spent.
How does the monthly meeting look from Rhea's side?
Rhea can raise plans like the new laptop calmly and plan together, rather than worrying about a fight later.

The group project on the village pond was due Monday, and Wasim was tired of waiting. Sachin kept going off to the fields; the others hadn't even collected leaves. On Saturday night, by the light of the kerosene lamp, Wasim did everything himself: the map of the pond, the list of birds, the drawing of the lotus, the neat heading. He went to bed after the roosters had started. On Monday the chart was the best in the class. But Wasim was yawning in the prayer line, and Sachin, looking at the chart, said, 'So we're not needed.' Masterji asked the group to explain the birds list. Only Wasim could. Masterji looked at the others for a long moment.

What was the group project about?
The village pond.
How might Wasim have felt yawning in the prayer line?
He was exhausted from working till the roosters started, and probably still resentful that the others hadn't helped.
What would have been a better way for Wasim to handle the delays?
Split the jobs and give each person a day to finish, or ask Masterji for help; doing everything alone cost him sleep and cut out the group.
How does Sachin feel when he sees the chart?
Sachin says 'So we're not needed', which suggests he felt left out and a little hurt.

messages.content: Please make me a favour and lock the gate. Correct it please.

Please do me a favour and lock the gate.
Why: The fixed phrase is "do someone a favour", not "make".

The community garden behind the flats in Accra had one hose and a lot of thirsty tomatoes. People watered whenever they felt like it, some for an hour, and by March the tank was often empty by noon. Kofi, twenty-four, who grew okra in plot 6, wrote a proposal on a whiteboard at the gate: morning slots by plot number, fifteen minutes each, a shared logbook on a nail, and anyone who ran over twice would skip a day. Dalia, from plot 2, frowned. "You'll be the first to break it." "Then write my name in the book," Kofi said. For a week he watered at six, fifteen minutes on the dot, and signed each time. Neighbours started checking the book, and then signing it too. The tank lasted until evening.

How long was each watering slot?
Fifteen minutes each.
What does Dalia's frown and remark suggest Dalia thought?
Dalia doubted Kofi, suspecting the person proposing rules would not keep them.
How did Kofi answer that doubt, and why did it work?
He asked for his name to go in the book and then watered on the dot and signed every time, so neighbours saw the rule was fair and kept.
How might the tomato growers feel when the tank lasts until evening?
They are likely relieved and more trusting, since their plants now get water and the logbook shows everyone sharing fairly.

metadata.subtype: Setting rules everyone can live with [Response]

Every Wednesday evening Vinita took the metro to a small bookshop café in Bengaluru where a mixed group met to discuss big questions: a Jain accountant, a Catholic nurse, a student of Sufi music, and Vaibhav, an engineer who didn't believe in anything and said so cheerfully.
She had started going after her grandmother's death left her with more questions than the prayers could answer. She took notes. She read Kabir on the metro and argued with his couplets in the margins. She kept a list titled Things I actually believe after this week, which changed often.
Tonight Vaibhav asked her, "Why not just decide? It would be easier."
Vinita laughed. "Easier, yes. But I want something I've tested, not something I've grabbed."
On the metro home she reread the list. Two items had been crossed out this week. One had been added: Kindness is not optional. She underlined it twice.

What is Vinita's list titled?
Things I actually believe after this week.
What does Vinita feel when she laughs at Vaibhav's question?
She feels settled and determined, content to live with uncertainty while testing her beliefs.
Why is Vinita's approach a serious form of seeking?
She reads, talks with believers and sceptics, and revises her list against experience instead of grabbing a quick answer.
How might Vaibhav see Vinita's seeking?
Vaibhav seems curious and friendly, a little puzzled by her patience but respectful of it.
My sibling and I share a room and we keep clashing about space.
Shared rooms often cause friction. A calm talk about what bothers each of you is a good start.
We just argue when we try.
Try picking a time when you are both calm, and take turns speaking without interruption. Say what you need, such as quiet during study time.
What kind of rules could help?
Agree on things like a tidy-up time, quiet hours, and a space that is each person's own. Writing them down makes them easier to remember.
What if it still doesn't work?
Ask another family member to help you both talk it through. A neutral person can suggest a fair plan.

Thursday night
Ramesh called at nine. There's a concert at the city ground on Saturday and his parents said no. His plan: he tells them he's studying at my place, and if Aunty phones, I say yes, he's here.
I said "haan, obviously" before I'd even thought. That's what friends do. Ramesh covered for me at school twice. If I back out, the whole group will know by Monday, and I'll be the one who ditched.
But Aunty feeds me every time I go over. She calls me "the sensible one". And Mummy thinks Ramesh's family trusts both of us. I keep hearing Aunty's voice on the phone, and me lying into it.
I don't want to be a bad friend. I don't want to be a bad son either. Why does being good to one side mean letting down the other?
Can't sleep. Will talk to Ramesh at the bus stop.
Jatin

What does Aunty call Jatin?
She calls him the sensible one.
Why did Jatin agree to Ramesh's plan so quickly?
He wanted to be seen as a loyal friend, since Ramesh had covered for him twice, and he feared being called the one who ditched.
What choice is Jatin facing at the bus stop, and what might help him make it?
Whether to back out of the cover story; he could tell Ramesh honestly that he won't lie to Aunty but still stands by him as a friend.
If Aunty found out about the plan, how might she feel about Jatin?
She might feel let down by the boy she trusted as the sensible one, which is exactly the disappointment Jatin dreads. 😔
Tell me what exchange is.

To exchange means to give something and receive something else in return. It is a verb; it can also be a noun.
Example: The friends exchanged gifts at the party.

Read this:

Incubator mentor's note: Sumit and Sunaina, quarterly review

This is the eighth quarter I've reviewed their tutoring app. Active users are down for the fifth quarter in a row. The two schools that piloted it have left. When I asked Sumit what would make things turn around, he talked for ten minutes about how much they had built, the two years, the savings they had both put in, the features "almost ready". He did not describe a single customer who wanted it now. Sunaina was quiet; afterwards she told me she has wanted to stop since last year but Sumit "can't let it go". I have suggested they meet me next week with one question answered honestly: knowing what they know now, would they start this today?

How many quarters in a row have active users dropped?
Down for the fifth quarter in a row.
What does Sunaina's quietness suggest about how she feels?
She seems weary and conflicted, wanting to stop but hesitant to push against Sumit.
How could the mentor's question help Sumit?
It asks him to judge the future, not the past, so the two years and savings stop being the reason to continue.
How is Sunaina affected by Sumit's refusal to stop?
Sunaina keeps putting time into a product she has doubted for a year, which likely leaves her frustrated and stuck.

The all-staff call at the Lagos logistics firm lasted twelve minutes. The new director spoke about "rightsizing for agility" and "streamlining the delivery team". Slides with arrows. Everyone nodded. Chidi unmuted. "Sorry, can I ask something simple? What does rightsizing mean here? How many people lose their jobs, which teams, and when?" There was a long pause. The director said, "Around thirty roles in delivery. Notices go out next Friday." The chat filled with messages. Zanele, who led the delivery drivers, sent Chidi a private note: "Thank you. Nobody told us." After the call Chidi and Zanele drafted a list of questions for HR: notice periods, support for the thirty, whether any could move to other teams. "Rightsizing sounded like something happening to a spreadsheet," Chidi said. "It's happening to Emeka and Joy and twenty-eight others."

How many roles in delivery were affected?
Around thirty roles in delivery.
Why did Chidi push for plain words during the call?
Chidi felt uneasy that "rightsizing" hid real people losing jobs, and wanted everyone to see what was actually happening.
What did Chidi and Zanele do after the call that was useful?
They drafted a list of questions for HR about notice periods, support and moving to other teams.
How might Zanele feel after Chidi's question?
Zanele felt grateful and relieved, since the delivery team had been told nothing until Chidi asked.

The wedding band in the next building had started, drums thumping through the window, and Zaid's subtraction homework was due in the morning. Ammi was at work till nine. "Asif, help him," she had said on the phone. Asif, twelve, looked at the first sum: 52 minus 27. "Easy. Seven from two, can't, so borrow, twelve minus seven is five, four minus two is two. Twenty-five." Zaid's pencil hung in the air. "Borrow from where?" "From the five! Obviously!" The drums got louder. Zaid's eyes filled. Asif slammed the book shut. Then he remembered his own teacher bundling matchsticks into tens with a rubber band. He grabbed the matchbox from the kitchen. "Okay. Five bundles of ten, and two loose ones. You need seven loose. What do we do?" Zaid stared, then slowly untied a bundle.

What was the first subtraction sum?
The first sum was 52 minus 27.
Why did Asif slam the book shut?
Asif felt frustrated and pressured by the drums and the deadline, and borrowing seemed so obvious that Zaid's confusion felt like not trying.
What made Asif's second try work better?
Using bundles of matchsticks showed where the ten comes from, one step at a time, and let Zaid work it out instead of hearing the answer fast.
What was it like for Zaid when Asif rattled off the steps?
Zaid felt lost and upset, with no idea where 'borrow' came from, his eyes filling as the drums got louder.

Hi Chetan,
I wanted to write properly instead of just messaging.
I think I've been unfair to you this month. When you replied slowly, I assumed you didn't care about the project. Then I found out your time zone meant my messages arrived at midnight for you, and you'd been answering first thing every morning.
So I'd like to try something: I'll send all my questions by 4 p.m. my time, in one clear message, and I'll mark what's urgent. You reply when you start your day. If something is truly blocking, I'll call.
Also, can we do a fifteen-minute video call on Fridays? Just to talk, not only tasks. I'd like to actually know you.
Thanks for your patience.
Nirmala

By what time will Nirmala send all questions?
By 4 p.m. Nirmala's time.
What was Nirmala feeling about the way Chetan had been treated?
Nirmala felt guilty and a bit embarrassed for assuming Chetan didn't care.
What changes does Nirmala suggest to work better asynchronously?
Sending questions by a set time in one clear message, marking urgent items, calling only if blocking, and a weekly social video call.
How might Chetan feel reading this email?
Chetan likely feels understood and relieved that the time-zone issue is recognised.

Kamal, you think your Nani doesn't understand games? Let me tell you about your Suresh mama. When he was fifteen, a video game parlour opened near our market. Ten coins a game. He began going after school, then instead of tuition. He'd come home at night saying he'd been at a friend's. His eyes were red, he slept in class. One day his teacher came to our house. I wasn't angry first; I was frightened. He cried and said, 'Amma, I can't stop, I keep thinking about the next level.' We made a plan together: the parlour only on Sundays, and I'd walk him to tuition. He hated it for a month. Then he got better at studies, and cricket. You see the tiredness in your own eyes, beta?

What did Suresh start skipping to go to the parlour?
He began going to the parlour instead of tuition.
What did Suresh feel when he told his mother he couldn't stop?
He felt out of control and upset, crying because he kept thinking about the next level.
What worked in the plan Suresh and his mother made?
It set a clear limit together, only Sundays, and added support by walking him to tuition.
How might Kamal feel hearing that Suresh mama struggled in the same way?
Kamal might feel less judged and more willing to look honestly at their own tiredness and gaming.

In the Mumbai flat, Maria, ten months, lay on the mat while her uncle Imran rolled a red ball slowly across the floor. Her eyes followed it all the way to the sofa. When it rolled underneath, she stared at the other side, waiting. The ball came out. She kicked her legs and squealed. Imran rolled it again. This time Maria looked at the other side before it even disappeared.

What colour was the ball Imran rolled?
The ball was red.
What does Maria kicking and squealing suggest about how she felt?
It suggests she was excited and happy when the ball came out where she expected.
How can Imran keep building Maria's tracking skills?
He can keep rolling toys slowly behind objects so she can practise predicting where they'll come out.
How might Imran feel watching Maria look ahead the second time?
He might feel delighted and amazed that she had already learned where the ball would reappear.

When Emil's grandmother died, the flat in Copenhagen filled with relatives he barely knew. His father cried at the kitchen table, which Emil had never seen before, and Emil hid behind the door. Aunt Lise found him there. She didn't send him to his room. 'Your farmor died last night. We're all very sad. It's okay to see Papa cry.' Then she asked if he wanted to help. Emil folded napkins for the memorial coffee and put a drawing of farmor's cat into the box going to the church. At school, his friend Bao gave him half of his lunch without saying anything. At the memorial, when everyone sang, Emil held his father's hand and sang the words he knew.

What did Emil put into the box going to the church?
A drawing of farmor's cat.
Why might Emil have hidden behind the door?
He was probably frightened and confused, never having seen his father cry before.
What did Aunt Lise get right in how she helped Emil?
She told him the truth simply, said it was okay to see Papa cry, and gave him small tasks so he could take part.
How might Emil's father feel when Emil holds his hand at the memorial?
He likely feels comforted and less alone in his grief, sharing the moment with his son.

metadata.subtype: Sharing a loss in class or family [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

For most of last year I was tired in a way sleep didn't touch. I went to bed early, drank water all day and was still thirsty, still dragging myself through the office. I told myself I was lazy and needed more discipline. I tried cold showers, a new planner, no screens at night. Nothing changed. My sister Shreya noticed me refilling my bottle again and again at her birthday lunch. "Sumit, this isn't willpower," she said. "Please see a doctor." I nearly laughed it off. But I went. The doctor listened, asked a lot of questions and ran some tests. It turned out there was a physical reason, and a plan to manage it. I'm less tired now. I wish I'd stopped guessing sooner.

What did Shreya notice at her birthday lunch?
Sumit refilling the bottle again and again.
How did Sumit feel about the tiredness before seeing the doctor?
Sumit felt frustrated and ashamed, blaming it on laziness and a lack of discipline.
What was the wise choice, and why?
Seeing a doctor instead of trying more tricks, because tiredness and thirst that rest and water do not fix can have a physical cause.
How does Shreya see what is happening?
She sees that it is not about willpower and is worried enough to ask Sumit plainly to see a doctor.

Read this:

It was 11 p.m., the night before the chemistry exam, and Sabina's phone was at nine percent. Then she saw the group chat: Nandini had posted a photo from the party Sabina wasn't invited to. Her face went hot. She typed fast: "Wow, thanks for inviting me, fake friends. Hope you had fun." Her thumb hovered over send. The screen dimmed. She called Nandini instead, but Nandini didn't answer. Sabina put the phone down, breathing hard. She reread her message. In the morning, would she still mean it? She deleted it and wrote in her notebook instead: "Ask N tomorrow, calmly." She plugged in her phone and opened the chemistry book, though her hands were still trembling.

What percentage was Sabina's phone at?
Nine percent.
What was Sabina feeling when she typed the message?
She felt hurt and angry, left out of the party.
What helped Sabina avoid sending the angry message?
Pausing, rereading it and asking herself if she'd still mean it in the morning, then writing a calmer plan.
How might Nandini feel if she had received the angry message?
She may have felt hurt and defensive, making it harder to sort things out.

Week one: Rehana's Spanish notebook sat on her desk, untouched since the flu. She walked past it every morning.
Week two: The notebook had slid under a pile of lecture notes. When Jahnavi asked at lunch, "How's the Spanish going? You were so into it," Rehana said, "Oh, busy with exams," and changed the subject fast.
Week three: Rehana saw the corner of the notebook poking out and felt her face go hot. Opening it would mean seeing the last date, forty days ago, and admitting she'd quit. So she didn't. She pushed the notes back over it and went to bed, heavy and restless.

What had slid under a pile of lecture notes?
Rehana's Spanish notebook.
What was Rehana feeling in week three when she saw the notebook?
She felt ashamed and heavy, her face hot, dreading the reminder that she had quit.
What small step could break the avoidance at this stage?
Opening the notebook for just five minutes without looking back at the gap, treating it as a fresh start.
What might Jahnavi be thinking when Rehana changes the subject?
Jahnavi may sense something is off and feel curious or concerned, but not want to push.

In Hosur, Ira and Vaibhav both worked at the same electronics unit and rode home together on his bike. On the way there was a tea stall, then a bakery, then the phone recharge shop. A chai here, egg puffs there, and most nights a small online order of phone covers or hair clips. "It's only thirty rupees," Ira would say, and each time she was right.
On the 24th the landlord's rent reminder came, and their joint account didn't have enough. They sat on the steps of their rented room, scrolling through the bank app.
"Where did it go?" Vaibhav asked. "We didn't buy anything big."
Ira scrolled and scrolled through tiny entries. "We didn't buy anything big," she repeated slowly. Neither of them could say what the month had been spent on.

What would Ira say about each small purchase?
"It's only thirty rupees."
How did Ira feel as she repeated "We didn't buy anything big"?
She was confused and uneasy, starting to see that the many tiny entries had added up.
What could the couple try next month?
They could note every small purchase for a few weeks so they can see where the money goes before deciding what to change.
What would have changed if they had counted the chai and puffs from the start?
They would have seen the small daily costs adding up well before the 24th, instead of being caught short on rent.

Fog hung over the colony park in Ludhiana so thickly that the swings looked grey. Hemant and Gurpreet crouched beside a circle scratched in the cold dirt, fingers stiff inside their woollen gloves. Hemant's first shot knocked one of Gurpreet's marbles out of the ring. He pocketed it with a small "yes" and moved on. Two turns later Gurpreet hit Hemant's blue-swirl marble clean out of the circle. Hemant's face crumpled. He sat back on his heels and wailed, loud enough that a man walking his dog turned around. "It's just one," said Gurpreet. "You won one of mine." "It's not the same!" Hemant sobbed, staring at his empty palm while the fog swallowed the far end of the park.

What happened on Hemant's first shot?
Hemant's first shot knocked one of Gurpreet's marbles out of the ring.
Why does losing the blue-swirl marble upset Hemant so much more than winning one pleased him?
The blue-swirl marble was already his, so losing it feels like something taken away; he feels hurt and cheated, while the won marble only felt like a small extra.
How could an adult help Hemant calm down?
They could let him be sad for a moment, then point out that he won one and lost one, so he has the same number of marbles as when he started.
How does Gurpreet see Hemant's crying?
Gurpreet is puzzled, because to Gurpreet the game is even: Hemant won one marble and lost one.

"Have you seen Mridul's post?" Eshaan asked. "The song is so sad."
"He's doing that dance thing everyone's doing," said his sister.
"But he added a caption. 'Can't shake this one.'"
"That might mean he's stuck on the tune. Or that he's feeling low. I can't tell."
"Should I say something?"
"Just a quick message. Nothing dramatic."
Eshaan wrote to Mridul: 'Love the song. Everything okay with you or is it just the dance craze?'
Mridul answered within minutes: 'Ha, dance craze, and also I failed a quiz and the song fits. But I'm fine. Thanks for checking.'
Eshaan sent back a hug. "Good," said his sister. "That was the right size of check-in."

What did Mridul's caption say?
His caption said, 'Can't shake this one.'
What might Mridul's post have meant, according to Eshaan's sister?
It might mean he is stuck on the tune or that he is feeling low, and she cannot tell. Mridul later says it was the dance craze and a failed quiz.
What made Eshaan's check-in the right size?
It was short, private and friendly, and asked whether it was something serious or just a trend without assuming anything.
How might Mridul have felt when Eshaan checked in?
He probably felt noticed and cared for, since he answered quickly and thanked him.

Read this:

"Anirban, how are you already done with the budget sheet?"

"Started at nine. Stopped at ten-thirty."

"I started at nine too," Nitin said. "But the team chat, the emails, two calls..."

"I turned all that off. Put a note on my status: back at ten-thirty."

"And if something's urgent?"

"They can call. Nobody did."

"Then what?"

"Then I replied to everything in one go. Took fifteen minutes. Then I got coffee and walked around the block."

"You walked? In the middle of the day?"

"That's why I'm not fried by three."

Nitin looked at his own screen, twelve tabs open, and closed eleven.

What did Anirban put on his status?
Back at ten-thirty.
How does Anirban seem to feel about his way of working?
He seems relaxed and confident, not fried by three, because fewer switches make work easier.
What could Nitin try, based on Anirban's routine?
He could block time for one task, turn off chat and email, answer messages in one batch, and take a short walk.
How does Nitin react after hearing Anirban's method?
Nitin seems curious and a bit envious, and closes eleven tabs to try it.

At the village school playground, Sunaina hooked her little finger round Disha's. “Pinky promise you'll save me a swing.” Disha looked puzzled and crossed two fingers instead. “In our lane we do this.” “Crossed fingers are for luck!” said Sunaina. “Not in my lane,” Disha giggled. “Crossed means promise.” They tried each other's signs, laughing. In the end they did both, pinkies hooked and fingers crossed, and ran to the swings, which Disha had saved.

What does crossed fingers mean in Disha's lane?
Promise.
What were the girls feeling as they tried each other's signs?
They felt amused and playful, enjoying the mix-up. At first Sunaina was a little puzzled that Disha used a different sign.
What does this scene show about how to handle different signs?
Trying each other's signs and laughing about it works better than insisting only one meaning is right.
How might a child from a third lane see their double promise?
They might find it confusing or funny, and have their own sign to add, since these signs vary by group.

The hostel mess committee met after dinner, the tables still sticky with dal. Francis read the complaint letter aloud: the new cook's food was bland and should be reported to the warden. "Everyone agrees?" Twenty heads nodded. Simran raised a hand. "The cook told me the vegetable budget was cut last month. Maybe we should ask about the budget, not blame him." The room turned to look at her. Someone muttered, "Always has to be different." Francis's pen tapped the table. "We'll put it to a vote." Simran was the only hand against. Back in her room, she stared at the ceiling. Maybe she was naive. Maybe the food really was just bad. But she also thought of the cook's tired face. She didn't sleep well.

How many heads nodded when Francis asked if everyone agreed?
Twenty heads nodded.
Why might Simran have trouble sleeping after the meeting?
She feels uneasy and doubtful, wondering if she was naive, while still feeling protective of the tired cook she thinks is being blamed unfairly.
How could Simran raise the budget question another way?
She could ask the warden directly what changed in the mess budget, or suggest the letter include that question alongside the complaint.
What is it like for the cook when the committee blames only him?
The cook may feel unfairly judged for something outside his control, and may not know one student tried to explain his side.

Kashish, thanks for having me on the college podcast. I'm Sabina, third-year, and you asked how I picked up that web framework in two weeks when I'm usually the slowest learner in our batch.
Honestly, I cheated a little. Before I opened a single tutorial, I sat with a blank page and asked: what pain was this thing invented to fix? The answer was that plain pages get messy when many parts change at once. Fine. Then I asked what its pieces are. Components, which are small reusable blocks. State, which is whatever changes. Props, which a parent hands to a child. I drew three boxes and arrows between them on a sheet above my desk.
After that, every tutorial just slotted into a box. When a video talked about 'lifting state up', I thought, oh, that's an arrow moving. Without the sheet I'd have been memorising steps I didn't understand.

What three pieces did Sabina draw as boxes on the sheet?
Components, state and props, with arrows between them.
How did Sabina feel about being the slowest learner, and how did the sheet change that?
Sabina felt a bit insecure about it, and the sheet made the tutorials feel manageable, because each new idea had a box to go into.
What else could Sabina try if a new idea still would not fit on the sheet?
Build a tiny practice page that uses only that idea, because seeing it work shows whether the boxes and arrows match what the tool really does.
How might Kashish, as the podcast host, see Sabina's 'cheating'?
Kashish may see that it is not cheating at all but a faster way to learn, since the sheet gave every later tutorial a place to fit.

School library note, Class 4, end of term.
Before the reading challenge, Divyansh was the child I had to chase out at the bell. He once spent three weeks on a thick book about volcanoes and told me every chapter. Since we started giving a star sticker for each book finished, with a prize at twenty stars, he has read twenty-two books in six weeks. Almost all are the thin picture books from the lower shelf, which he finishes in ten minutes at the counter. When I asked about the volcano series, he said, 'Those take too long. I'd only get one star.' He no longer tells me what the books are about. He asks how many stars he has. Next step: I'll end the star chart after this month, set up a 'tell me one thing you found' corner instead, and talk to his class teacher.
Afreen

How many books has Divyansh read in six weeks?
He has read twenty-two books in six weeks.
Why does Divyansh now choose the thin picture books?
He has become eager for stars and the prize, so the thick books he used to love feel like a waste of time, and his interest in what's inside has faded.
What change does the librarian plan, and why?
Ending the star chart and starting a 'tell me one thing you found' corner, to bring the focus back to the joy of reading rather than counting.
What might Afreen feel noticing he only asks about stars?
Afreen likely feels disappointed and a little worried, missing the reader who used to tell every chapter about volcanoes.

Raghav, you think you're the first teenager in this family to doubt the fasts? Your Kalyani paati was worse. At fifteen I refused to fast on Ekadashi. I said, 'If God is love, why does love need hunger?' My mother cried, and my grandmother didn't speak to me for two days. I felt awful. I loved them, and I also couldn't pretend. Then my grandmother called me to the kitchen and said, 'Don't fast, then. But sit with me while I cook for the evening, and ask me your questions.' So every Ekadashi I sat there, asking and arguing, while she explained what her mother had told her. I still don't fast. But I know every story, and now I tell them to you.

On which day did young Kalyani refuse to fast?
On Ekadashi.
How did young Kalyani feel when the grandmother stopped speaking for two days?
She felt awful and torn, loving her family but unable to pretend to believe.
What choice in the story helped both sides?
The grandmother inviting Kalyani to sit and ask questions while she cooked, so Kalyani could stay close without pretending.
How might the grandmother have felt when young Kalyani refused?
She was likely hurt and worried at first, then chose to keep her granddaughter close through questions and stories.

I'm Farhan, and I'll admit my first try was a disaster. I found Afreen, my fifteen-year-old, on her phone at one in the morning and simply took it away for a week. She stopped talking to me. She borrowed her friend's old phone instead. My own phone, of course, stayed on my pillow.
After a week of cold dinners, I sat down with her and said, "I got that wrong." I explained what I'd read about light and sleep, and asked what she thought was fair. She suggested a basket by the front door. She added, "Yours too, Abbu."
Now we both drop our phones there at ten. Some nights she grumbles. But she's less tired, and honestly, so am I.

What did Afreen suggest?
She suggested a basket by the front door, for his phone too.
How did Farhan feel about his first attempt, looking back?
He feels regretful and a bit embarrassed, calling it a disaster and admitting to her that he got it wrong.
What was the turning point that made the rule work?
Farhan admitted his mistake, explained the reason and let Afreen help make a rule that he follows too.
What was the week of punishment like for Afreen?
She probably felt angry and treated unfairly, so she stopped talking to him and found another phone.

The rain began before dawn on Eid, and by six the lane outside Rehana's house in Lucknow was ankle-deep. Abbu's train from Kanpur was running three hours late, and Ammi was worried he'd miss the namaz. Rehana didn't think about whether to pray; she simply tied her dupatta, helped her little sister with hers, and stirred the sheer khurma while Ammi wrapped the gifts. When the call to prayer sounded, faint through the rain, something in her chest settled, the way it did every year. Eshaan from next door arrived dripping, as he had every Eid since they were five, for his bowl. "Same taste as last year," he said, which from him was high praise. At ten, Abbu walked in soaked, laughing, and the whole family hugged him at once. Rehana felt, as always, that everything was exactly where it belonged.

How late was Abbu's train from Kanpur running?
Abbu's train from Kanpur was running three hours late.
How does Rehana feel when the call to prayer sounds?
Rehana feels calm and settled, a warm, familiar comfort that comes every year without any question.
What might help Rehana later, if questions ever come?
Knowing that her family's warmth and her own belonging are real could help her talk openly with Ammi or Abbu rather than feel alone with new questions.
How does Eshaan experience Eid at Rehana's house?
For Eshaan it is a happy yearly tradition, coming for his bowl of sheer khurma, and he feels part of the neighbourhood's celebration too.

Monday. In the tuition centre, Swati forwarded another meme about the new batch from the mill colony: a herd of buffaloes with "Mill colony toppers". Her friends laughed. The mill colony kids sat at the back, heads down.
Wednesday. The tutor paired everyone for a maths project. Swati got Ganga, from the mill colony. Swati rolled her eyes. But Ganga knew a shortcut for percentages that saved them twenty minutes. At the break, Ganga said her mother worked double shifts at the mill so Ganga could come to tuition.
Friday. Another buffalo meme appeared in the group. Swati's thumb hovered over the laugh button. She thought of Ganga's shortcut, and her mother's double shifts. Instead she typed, "Can we stop these? Ganga's in my project and she's brilliant." The chat went quiet. Nobody sent another one that day.

What did the meme call the mill colony students?
It showed a herd of buffaloes with "Mill colony toppers".
Why did the buffalo memes feel funny to Swati on Monday?
Swati saw the mill colony students only as a group, not as faces, so the cruelty felt harmless and empathy never came.
What did Swati do on Friday, and why was it a good choice?
She asked the group to stop and named Ganga as brilliant, giving the group a real person to think about.
How might Ganga have felt seeing Swati's message?
Ganga may have felt surprised and respected, seen as a person rather than a joke.

metadata.subtype: Mocking a group as not real people [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Pradeep had seen it coming for weeks. His friend Sahil had decided to leave their college band to focus on his exams, but he hadn't told the others. "I don't want to upset them before the fest," Sahil said. Every rehearsal, Pradeep watched Sahil nod through plans for songs he knew he wouldn't play. The drummer, Ruchi, booked two extra gigs, counting on him. Pradeep urged Sahil twice. Sahil said, "Next week." Two days before the fest, Sahil finally told them. Ruchi went white. "You knew for a month? We've promised the organisers!" The band scrambled, found a stand-in, and played badly. Afterwards Sahil sat with Pradeep on the hostel steps. "I thought waiting was the nice thing." Pradeep shook his head. "If you'd told them in week one, they'd have been sad, but they'd have had time."

How many extra gigs had Ruchi booked?
Two extra gigs.
What was Pradeep feeling as he watched Sahil nod through the plans?
Pradeep felt uneasy and worried, knowing Sahil wouldn't play the songs and that the delay would make it worse.
What small step could Sahil have taken in week one?
He could have told the band plainly and kindly that he was leaving, giving them time to find someone.
How did Ruchi feel when Sahil finally told them?
Ruchi was shocked and angry, going white because they had made promises to the organisers.

I was on the other bed pretending to do my maths when Didi called Ritu. I'm not sure what Damini was feeling; her hand kept smoothing the bedsheet flat. She didn't text it, which I thought she would. She said, "Ritu, I need to tell you something properly. I don't feel the same any more, and I don't want to mislead you."
There was a long quiet on the other end. Didi didn't say "maybe later" or "it's not you, it's me", or anything about Ritu being clingy, which she had grumbled to me about before. She just said, "You were good to me. I'm sorry this hurts." Then she listened.
After the call she sat with her face in her hands. I brought her a glass of water. She said, "That was the hardest ten minutes of my life," and I believed her.

What was the narrator pretending to do during the call?
The narrator was on the other bed pretending to do maths.
What might the narrator have been feeling while watching Damini make the call?
The narrator seems tense and protective, noticing her hand smoothing the sheet, and caring enough to bring water afterwards.
Which parts of Damini's call made the ending clear and kind?
She called instead of texting, said plainly that she didn't feel the same, left out excuses, blame and 'maybe later', and then listened.
What is Ritu likely experiencing on the other end of the call?
Ritu is probably hurt and stunned, hence the long quiet, but is spared false hope and insults, which may make healing easier later.
Why does a crying baby often calm down when it is picked up and held?
A held baby feels safer. Because being close to a caring person's warmth and heartbeat tells the baby it is not alone, and being picked up shows that its cry was heard, the baby relaxes.
Who is Helen Burns in Jane Eyre?
Helen is Jane's first real friend at school. She is patient and forgiving, and she dies of consumption with Jane lying beside her.

Tomas started his second year in Valencia with a rule he made for himself: bed by midnight, library from nine to twelve, no exceptions for five weeks. His roommate Mateo bet him a paella that he wouldn't last a fortnight. Tomas made a spreadsheet and filled in every day: hours slept, hours studied, and one line on how he felt. The first week was rough. By week three the numbers settled, and his notes started making sense. In week five his statistics quiz came back with the best mark he'd ever had. He scrolled through the spreadsheet slowly, row after row of small green cells. "I built this," he told Mateo. Mateo paid for the paella.

What did Mateo bet Tomas?
A paella, that he wouldn't last a fortnight.
How did Tomas feel scrolling through the spreadsheet after the quiz?
Proud and a bit amazed; the rows of green cells showed him that his steady choices had built the best mark he'd ever had.
What choice kept Tomas going through the rough first week?
Recording every day, including how he felt, so he could watch the numbers settle instead of judging the plan too early.
How might Mateo feel paying for the paella?
Mateo lost the bet but may be happy to, having watched a roommate prove Mateo wrong through five weeks of effort.

Teacher's note: Class 9 chemistry, practical lab, 12 August. Written by Nikita Sharma.
Today I let students pick lab partners for the titration practical. Gautam, usually thoughtful, avoided Birsa, the tall boy who joined on the sports quota. I heard Gautam tell his friend, "He's a footballer, he won't know titration." He chose the student with the neatest notebook instead. During the practical, Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times. Birsa and his partner got a clean result on the first try, and Birsa explained the colour change to the next table. Gautam watched with his mouth half open. After class he came to my desk and said, "Ma'am, I thought he'd be bad at this. I was wrong." We talked about how he had decided before seeing any evidence. Next week I'll rotate partners at random, and I've asked Gautam to work with Birsa.

What happened to Gautam's pair during the practical?
Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times.
Why did it seem sensible to Gautam that Birsa wouldn't know titration?
Gautam felt confident because Birsa was tall and joined on the sports quota, which fit his idea of a footballer, not a chemist. The match to a type felt like enough reason.
What did Nikita decide to do next, and why might it help?
She will rotate partners at random and has asked Gautam to work with Birsa, so Gautam can learn about Birsa from real work instead of assumptions.
What might it be like for Birsa to be overlooked as a lab partner?
Birsa may be used to people assuming sports is all he is good at, and explaining the colour change to the next table may have felt like a quiet way of proving otherwise.

When Bhavna and I set up our team's "no work after 7" rule in January, I was proud of it. Then came release week in March. Four nights in a row we were on calls till midnight fixing a payment bug. By Friday I felt like a fraud for breaking our own rule, and Bhavna was snapping at everyone. "Jasleen, this rule is making us miserable," Bhavna said.
The next Monday we sat down with the rule on a sticky note and looked at it properly. The problem wasn't the late nights; releases happen. The problem was pretending they wouldn't. So we rewrote it: in a release week, late nights are allowed, but the day after the release everyone starts at noon and there are no meetings.
We tried it in May. It wasn't perfect, but nobody felt guilty, and the noon start actually happened.

How many nights in a row were they on calls during release week?
Four nights in a row, till midnight, fixing a payment bug.
What does "I felt like a fraud" tell you about Jasleen's feelings?
Jasleen felt guilty and ashamed for breaking a rule the pair had made, even though the late nights were needed.
What would you change first if the noon start kept getting skipped?
Jasleen and Bhavna could block the noon start in everyone's calendar ahead of time and ask the manager to protect it.
How might the rest of the team see the rewritten rule?
The team will likely find it more believable, since it admits releases happen and still promises them a rest afterwards.

In São Paulo, Priscila had worked beside Xin on the same project for a year. Xin was usually chatty, sent jokes in the team chat, brought pastries on Fridays.
This week, Xin's replies were one word. "Ok." "Done." The camera stayed off in meetings. On Thursday, Xin snapped at a junior over a small error, then apologised too many times.
Priscila noticed. She didn't mention it in the group chat, and she didn't assume it was about her. She sent a private message: "Hey, you seem a bit off this week. No need to explain. Want to grab coffee, or should I just take the Friday report so you have one less thing?"
An hour later Xin wrote: "Coffee. Thanks for noticing." Over coffee, Xin said a family member was unwell back in Shanghai.
Priscila took the Friday report.

What did Xin's replies become this week?
One word, like "Ok" and "Done".
What does Xin apologising too many times suggest?
It suggests Xin felt stressed and on edge, and guilty about snapping.
What did Priscila do well in responding to Xin's mood?
Priscila reached out privately, didn't pry or take it personally, and offered practical help as well as company.
How might the junior have felt after Xin snapped?
The junior was probably hurt and confused, since Xin was usually friendly.

Read this:

At the wedding in Sehore, Saurabh's aunts sat in a row on plastic chairs, and Indu could feel their eyes follow her to the food counter.

"The nurse," one said, not quietly. "Night duty, strange men in wards. What family allows that?"

Indu's plate shook slightly. She had held a dying farmer's hand at three that morning. Here she felt about two inches tall.

She breathed, walked over, and touched the eldest aunt's feet. "Namaste, Bua. The pedas are very good, have you tried?" Bua sniffed and did not answer.

Saurabh had heard. He sat down beside his uncle. "Chachaji, Indu saved Pappu's life when he had dengue. She is my wife and I am proud of her." His uncle looked at his shoes.

On the bus home Indu said, "They may never like me." Saurabh took her hand. "Then they'll just have to keep watching you be yourself."

Where was the wedding held?
The wedding was in Sehore.
What did Indu feel when she heard the aunts' comment?
Indu felt hurt and small, about two inches tall, though she had done important work that very morning.
How did Indu keep her dignity without fighting?
She stayed courteous, greeting the eldest aunt warmly, and let Saurabh speak up to his family instead of arguing herself.
How might Saurabh's uncle have felt when Saurabh spoke up?
He was likely embarrassed and caught out, looking at his shoes as he realised Indu had saved Pappu's life.
On which day did the first rain reach my village this monsoon?
That day wasn't recorded anywhere I know of, so I can't tell. A village elder or the local weather office may have kept a note.
The fort was built on the sixteenth century by a local chief. Which word is wrong?

The fort was built in the sixteenth century by a local chief.
Why: Use "in" with centuries, years and months.

Read this:

Aparna here. Harsha, who sits opposite me at the design studio, told me over lunch what he had done. "I paid for three months at the gym, all at once," he said. "I know myself. If I pay month to month, I'll skip and tell myself I'll pay next time. But money already gone will make me feel silly for not going." He said it like a rule he had checked. The first week I saw his gym bag under the desk every morning. On day nine it stayed on the chair and he left at six sharp. I don't know if he enjoys it or just doesn't want to waste the money. When I asked, he shrugged and said, "Either is fine with me."

How many months did Harsha pay for?
Harsha paid for three months, all at once.
What did Harsha expect from paying everything at once?
Harsha expected that money already gone would make him feel silly for skipping, so he would go.
What could Harsha do if he still skips despite having paid?
Harsha could add a workout partner or fixed times in his calendar, since the payment alone may not be enough.
Why can Aparna not say whether Harsha enjoys the gym?
Aparna only sees the bag and Harsha leaving at six, and Harsha said either reason was fine.

metadata.subtype: Approach: pays or books something in advance to create a cost for quitting [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Yash,
Since you start college next month, I want to tell you something I'm not proud of. At our fest in March, I was a volunteer with the red security T-shirt and a walkie-talkie. We were told to keep first-years out of the backstage area. By the second day I was shouting at them, checking their bags when there was no need, making one girl cry because she had come to find her friend. I told myself they were careless kids who needed control. The strange thing is, I felt powerful and right the whole time. It was only on the last night, when I took the T-shirt off, that I thought: would I ever talk to anyone like that in normal clothes? No. If they give you a role like that, remember: the T-shirt isn't you.
Love,
Aparna Didi

What was Aparna told to keep first-years out of?
The backstage area.
How did Aparna feel while shouting at the first-years?
Aparna felt powerful and smug, sure of being in the right and believing they were careless kids who needed control.
What advice does Aparna give Yash?
To remember, if given a role like that, that the T-shirt isn't him, and to treat people as he would in normal clothes.
How might the girl who came to find her friend have felt?
She likely felt frightened and humiliated, made to cry for doing nothing wrong.

Read this:

At the athletics club in Stockholm, Coach Anders was known for two things: winning medals and never being questioned. On the hottest day of the summer he told the group, "No water breaks today. Thirsty runners get tough." Nkechi, fifteen, felt her mouth go dry just hearing it. In biology last month they had learned that the body needs water when it sweats. But Anders had coached national runners. Who was she to argue? After the third lap her head started to pound. She stopped by the fence, face hot with embarrassment, and said, "Coach, I'm sorry, but my biology teacher said we need water in heat. Can I drink?" A few runners stared. Anders frowned, then waved a hand. "Fine. Everyone, two minutes." Nkechi drank, cheeks still burning, and her head began to clear.

What did Coach Anders say about water?
No water breaks today; thirsty runners get tough.
Why did Nkechi's cheeks burn when she spoke up?
She felt embarrassed and nervous questioning a famous coach, even though she trusted what she had learned in biology.
What made Nkechi's question respectful and effective?
She apologised, gave her reason from biology and asked a simple question, so it didn't sound like an attack.
How might the other runners feel after the water break?
They were probably relieved and grateful, since they got water too because Nkechi spoke up.

Read this:

Noa had been sitting on the stairs for twenty minutes with the two halves of the broken blue bowl in her lap. Her friend Hiroshi, waiting by the door with his football, whispered, "Just tell your mum. Mine was cross for one evening, then it was over." Noa stood up and carried the pieces to the kitchen, where her mum was chopping onions. "Mum, I dropped your bowl. I'm so sorry. I was going to hide it." Her mum put the knife down. "Oh, Noa. Thank you for telling me. Are you hurt?" "No." "Then it's only a bowl. We'll see if glue works." Noa's shoulders dropped for the first time all afternoon, and she leaned against her mum.

What did Noa carry into the kitchen?
She carried the two halves of the broken blue bowl.
What was Noa feeling as her talk with Mum ended?
Relief. Her shoulders dropped for the first time all afternoon and she leaned against her mum.
What could Noa do next to help mend things?
She could help try the glue on the bowl, and next time tell her mum sooner instead of waiting on the stairs. 🙂
What did Noa's mum seem to care about more than the bowl?
She asked first whether Noa was hurt, so Noa's safety and honesty mattered to her more than the bowl.

Read this:

Supervisor's note, water project, Latur, 4 November.

After Friday's review, Jagdish told me the rainwater tank pilot was "a total failure" and asked to be taken off it. He was pale and had clearly not slept.

I asked him to rate the pilot from one to ten instead of pass or fail. He said two. Then I asked him to list, in two columns, what worked and what didn't. Worked: eleven of fifteen tanks built on time; the village committee now meets weekly; the women's group keeps the logbook. Didn't: four tanks leak at the joints, and the pipe order came late.

By the end he said, "Maybe six." We agreed he stays on the project, with one job this month: find out why the joints leak.

I'll check in with him on Wednesday.

Nirmala

How many tanks were built on time?
Eleven of fifteen tanks were built on time.
Why did Jagdish ask to be taken off the project?
Jagdish felt ashamed and discouraged after the review, and saw the whole pilot as a total failure.
What did Nirmala's two columns make possible?
They showed real successes beside fixable problems, moving the rating from two to six and giving Jagdish one clear job: find out why the joints leak.
How might the village committee see the pilot?
The committee likely sees real progress, since they now meet weekly and have working tanks, even with four leaking.

Read this:

At bedtime Pallavi stroked Vinita's hair.
"Park," Vinita said sleepily.
"You wanted to stay at the park. That was hard."
"Hard," Vinita said. "Cry."
"Yes, you cried. You were sad."
"Sad." Vinita touched her own cheek.
"We had to leave. And I still love you. We can go again tomorrow."
"Tomorrow swing?"
"Tomorrow swing."
Vinita smiled and closed her eyes.

What did Vinita ask for tomorrow?
She asked for the swing tomorrow.
How did Vinita feel when she touched her own cheek and said 'Sad'?
She seemed calm and comforted, starting to link the word sad with how she felt at the park.
Which parts of Pallavi's bedtime talk help Vinita most?
She names the feeling in simple words, keeps the limit, says she still loves Vinita, and promises they can go again tomorrow.
What would change if Pallavi had said 'You were naughty at the park'?
Vinita would learn shame instead of a word for her feeling, and the bond might feel less safe.

metadata.subtype: Stage 6: Repair and naming the feeling [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Subject: My workload, and a request
Hi Disha,
I'd like to be straight with you before this becomes a bigger problem.
Since the Chennai account moved to our team, I've been covering two clients plus the vendor audits. I've worked until 1 am most nights, skipped dinner more often than not, and last Friday I blanked on the client call. That isn't like me, and I don't want it to become normal.
I'd like to propose:
1. Handing the vendor audits to Rohit, who has asked for audit experience.
2. Keeping my calendar clear after 8 pm, except for real emergencies.
3. A check-in with you in two weeks to see how it's going.
I care about this work, which is exactly why I'm raising it now.
Thanks for hearing me out,
Anand

Reply, forty minutes later: "Thank you for flagging this early, Anand. Yes to all three. Let's also look at whether the Chennai account needs one more person. Disha"

Who does Anand suggest should take the vendor audits?
Rohit, who has asked for audit experience.
Why does Anand write 'I care about this work, which is exactly why I'm raising it now'?
Anand wants the email read as commitment rather than complaint, and seems worried it might look like weakness.
What in Anand's email makes it easy for a manager to act on?
It is honest about the late nights, skipped dinners and the blank on the call, and offers three concrete proposals with a check-in date.
How does Disha respond, and what does that suggest about Disha as a manager?
Disha replies within forty minutes, thanks Anand for flagging it early and agrees to all three, which suggests a manager who adjusts rather than blames.

Read this:

On Holi in the village near Mathura, Alka and Kamal, both five, had only one pichkari between them.

Kamal grabbed it. Alka pulled. Kamal pushed her, and she fell in the coloured mud.

Alka cried. Kamal stared, then knelt. "Sorry. You can have it first."

Alka sniffed. "Then you next."

They took turns squirting the goats' water trough until both were pink.

How many pichkaris did Alka and Kamal have?
They had only one pichkari between them.
How did Kamal feel after pushing Alka?
Kamal seemed shocked and sorry, kneeling to apologise.
What helped Alka and Kamal make up?
Kamal apologised and let Alka go first, and Alka offered him the next turn.
How might Alka feel when Kamal said sorry?
Alka probably felt better and ready to play again.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Thursday

Hafsa came to me after the last bell, very upset. Her close friend Meenu has been skipping school for the past week and spending the day at the bus stand with older boys. Hafsa kept saying, "It's my fault, sir. I should have stopped her. I knew on Monday." She has not been sleeping well, she said, and she missed her own maths test to look for Meenu.

I told Hafsa that telling me was exactly the right thing, and that Meenu's choices are Meenu's, not hers. She cried, and said she still felt responsible. I did not argue; I sat with her until she was calmer.

Next steps: I informed Meenu's class teacher and the school counsellor today, and they are calling Meenu's parents this evening. I've asked Hafsa to meet the counsellor tomorrow too.

— Sahil

What did Hafsa miss to look for Meenu?
Her own maths test.
Why does Hafsa believe Meenu's skipping is her fault?
Hafsa feels guilty and responsible because she knew on Monday, so she thinks she should have been able to stop Meenu, as if she controls her friend's choices.
What did Sahil do well in handling Hafsa's worry?
Sahil listened, told Hafsa it was right to share and that Meenu's choices aren't hers, informed the counsellor and Meenu's class teacher the same day, and set up support for Hafsa.
How might Meenu's parents feel when the school calls them?
They may feel worried and shocked, but glad the school found out quickly so they can help Meenu.

Read this:

Class note, February. Teacher: Ishita.
Today Pema (five) told the class about Losar, her family's new year. She brought khapse, twisty fried biscuits her Ama had made.
She showed us how her family says “Tashi Delek” with hands together. “That's how we say happy new year at home,” she said, standing very straight.
The other children tried saying it. Pema corrected them, giggling.
Next step: I've invited Pema's Ama to tell a folk story next week.

What did Pema bring for the class?
She brought khapse, twisty fried biscuits her Ama had made.
How did Pema seem to feel sharing her tradition?
She seemed proud and confident, standing very straight.
Why is inviting Pema's Ama a good next step?
It brings Pema's family tradition into the classroom and helps all children learn about it.
How might the other children feel learning to say “Tashi Delek”?
They probably feel curious and enjoy learning something new from their classmate.

Read this:

First week of monsoon term: Jahnavi, five, shouts answers, won't sit in the circle, and throws her crayons when told to wait. Jagdish Sir stays calm.

Third week: she sits in the circle but calls out once. Jagdish Sir says, "Hand up, please," and she slowly raises it.

Sixth week: she raises her hand, waits for her turn, and gives her answer. She smiles.

What did Jahnavi throw in the first week?
She threw her crayons.
How did Jahnavi feel in the sixth week when she gave her answer?
Jahnavi felt proud and happy, smiling after waiting her turn.
How did Jagdish Sir help Jahnavi learn classroom habits?
He stayed calm, gave clear reminders, and let her practise week after week.
How might the other children feel as Jahnavi learns to wait?
They might feel calmer and get more turns themselves.

Read this:

In the computer lab of a college in Valencia, Pablo stared at a red error on the screen and turned to the mentor, Mateo. "It doesn't work. Can you fix it?" Mateo pulled up a chair but kept both hands off the keyboard. "What have you tried so far?" Pablo listed two changes. "And what does the message say?" Pablo read it aloud, slowly, and frowned. "It says the variable isn't defined." "Where do you define it?" A pause. Pablo scrolled up, found the line, and laughed. The variable was set after it was used. Mateo only nodded. Later, when Pablo got stuck on a harder loop, Mateo offered a single hint, and the rest came from Pablo.

What did the error message say?
The error message said the variable isn't defined.
What did Pablo feel when finding the line that caused the error?
Pablo laughed, with a mix of relief and amusement at having found the mistake alone.
What could Mateo do if Pablo gets stuck again with no ideas to try?
Mateo could suggest one small thing to test, since a hint after an attempt is better than the full answer. 🙂
How might Mateo see Pablo finding the line alone?
Mateo is likely pleased, since keeping both hands off the keyboard let Pablo find the mistake, which is why Mateo only nodded.
Why do trains have a loud horn?
The horn warns people. Because a heavy train needs a long distance to stop, so people on the track must hear it early and get out of the way.
She played an important roll in the street play. Is "roll" right?

She played an important role in the street play.
Why: A "role" is the part a person plays; "roll" is something that turns or a kind of bread.
What does sparkles mean? The song says the river sparkles.

To sparkle is to shine with many small, bright flashes of light. It is a verb, the form used with he, she or it. As a noun it means a small bright flash.
Example: In the morning sun the river sparkles like a thousand small lamps.

Read this:

In their flat in London, Hana, two, cried in three ways that afternoon. First a thin, whining cry as she rubbed her eyes, which her mother Nkechi knew meant sleepy. Then a sharp, loud scream when the tower fell, with clenched fists. Later a wobbly, trembling cry when the vacuum cleaner started. Nkechi answered each differently: a cot and lullaby, a hug and a new tower, and switching off the vacuum. Hana's cries all stopped in time. Nkechi said, “She's telling me, not tricking me.”

How many different cries did Hana have that afternoon?
Three: a thin whining cry, a sharp scream and a wobbly trembling cry.
What did each of Hana's cries mean, in Nkechi's reading?

The whining cry meant sleepiness, the scream meant frustration at the fallen tower, and the trembling one meant fear of the vacuum. Nkechi could have been wrong about one, but she checked each in context.
What could Nkechi do if she is unsure what a cry means?
She could look at what happened just before, check the basics such as hunger and tiredness, and comfort first.
How might Hana feel when her cries are answered?
She may feel safe and learn to trust that someone hears her, so she cries less over time.

metadata.subtype: Crying as a signal of need [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

Counselling note, Thursday, 5 p.m. Aadhya, 25, came in holding a printout: the college portal showing her brother Arnab had not attended a single MBA class since March. He had told her every week that classes were "fine, tiring". When she asked last month, he lied again, then twice more. Today she swung between anger ("He looked me in the eye") and self-doubt ("How did I not see it? Am I stupid?"), then cried quietly about "the brother I thought I had". I told her that people who trust are not stupid; they are trusting. We worked on two boundaries she can keep: she will stop covering for Arnab with their parents, and she will not discuss his fees until he tells them himself. She wrote both in her own words. She plans to talk it through with her cousin Riddhi, whom she trusts, before speaking to Arnab on Sunday. Follow-up booked for next Thursday.

Since when had Arnab not attended a single MBA class?
Since March.
What was Aadhya feeling when she asked "Am I stupid?"
Aadhya felt self-doubt and shame, wondering how she had missed the lies, alongside anger at being deceived.
What steps did the counsellor help Aadhya take?
Naming two boundaries in her own words, no covering and no talk of fees until he tells their parents, and talking to Riddhi, a cousin she trusts, before facing Arnab.
What would change if Aadhya kept covering for Arnab with their parents?
The lies would stay easy for Arnab and the weight would stay on Aadhya, so trust would keep wearing down with nothing changing.

Read this:

Two-year-old Mahima went rigid in the shop, fists clenched, when the sweets were taken away. Then she folded to the floor like a doll. Her father Irfan crouched beside her and waited. She crawled onto his shoulder, rubbing her eyes. "You're tired, aren't you," he said, and carried her home. At five, she was scolded at school for pushing in the queue, and after school she tucked her chin down and curled into the corner of the sofa, knees up, hugging a cushion. Irfan did not ask twenty questions. He sat at the other end of the sofa with the newspaper and left one hand resting on the cushion. After a while Mahima shuffled closer. At twenty, Mahima sat in her first written exam of the semester, shoulders hunched to her ears, breath held while she read the paper. Her friend Zubin, two rows behind, saw her pen not moving. She felt her toes clenched inside her shoes. She let out a long breath, pressed her feet flat on the floor, dropped her shoulders and began to write.

Where did Mahima curl up after she was scolded at school?
She curled into the corner of the sofa.
How does Mahima's body show her state at two, five and twenty?

At two her body went rigid and then limp because she was angry and tired, at five she curled inward after being scolded, and at twenty she hunched and held her breath under exam stress. Each time the body showed the feeling before words did.
What was Mahima probably feeling when she curled into the sofa corner at five?
She felt sad and ashamed after the scolding, and wanted to hide, which is why she tucked her chin down and hugged the cushion.
How did Irfan's response suit Mahima's needs at two and at five?
At two he waited and carried her home because she was tired, and at five he sat nearby without questions so she could come closer when ready.

Read this:

Monday. In the school corridor, Ramesh's friend Jatin went pale when he saw the notice board with the results. Ramesh laughed and said, "Scared?" Jatin's lips were tight and he said nothing.

Wednesday. During assembly in the hot sun, Jatin's face went white again, he swayed and his hands felt cold. Ramesh held his arm and said, "Sit down." A teacher brought water and asked him to rest.

Friday. Jatin's mother took him to the doctor. He was fine, just skipping breakfast. He told Ramesh, "Monday was fear, Wednesday was the sun and no food." Ramesh nodded. "Now I know to ask."

What did Ramesh do when Jatin swayed at assembly?
He held Jatin's arm and told him to sit down.
What could Jatin's pale face on Monday and Wednesday have meant, and how did they turn out?
Monday's paleness came from fear about the results, while Wednesday's came from the hot sun and no breakfast. The same look had two different causes.
What should someone do when a friend goes pale and dizzy?
Help them sit down, get water and call an adult, as Ramesh and the teacher did.
How might Ramesh have felt when he said "Scared?" and later saw Jatin sway?
He may have felt guilty for joking and worried when Jatin swayed. His "Now I know to ask" suggests he learned to check first.

Read this:

In the conference room of the software firm in Gurugram, Chinmay watched his colleague Dhruv negotiate with a new client. The client said, "We were thinking of paying thirty lakhs for the project." Dhruv had planned to ask for fifty. But now Dhruv started at thirty-eight. The client came up to thirty-five. They shook hands. Chinmay noticed something that bothered him: the whole talk had stayed close to thirty, the first number said. Afterwards, in the corridor, Dhruv said, "Not bad, right? Five above their offer." Chinmay didn't want to spoil his mood, but he felt uneasy. That weekend, he pulled out the rates from their last ten projects and wrote down a range. The next month, before his own client meeting, he said the range first, calmly, and explained where it came from.

What did the client say they were thinking of paying?
Thirty lakhs for the project.
Why did Chinmay feel uneasy in the corridor?
Chinmay noticed the whole talk stayed near the client's first number, even though Dhruv had planned fifty, and felt uneasy that Dhruv didn't see it.
What did Chinmay do to avoid the same trap?
He researched rates from past projects, wrote down a range, and stated it first in his own meeting with the reasons behind it.
How does Dhruv seem to see the deal?
Dhruv seems pleased, thinking five above the client's offer was a good result, not noticing the first figure pulled it down.

Read this:

The power went out, so the classroom was dim and noisy. Yash and Salma both wanted the one torch to play shadows.

Yash's lip trembled. He thought he'd be in trouble for shouting.

The teacher crouched between them. "I heard you both. Yash, then Salma. I'll count to fifty for each turn."

Yash made a shadow bird, feeling calmer. When she said "fifty", he passed the torch. "You're not in trouble," the teacher told him. "You asked me for help."

What did Yash make with the torch?
Yash made a shadow bird.
What was Yash worried about when his lip trembled?
Yash was worried and anxious that he'd be in trouble for shouting.
How did the teacher help the children feel safe?
The teacher listened to both, set counted turns, and told Yash he wasn't in trouble for asking for help.
How might Salma feel waiting for her turn?
Salma probably feels patient because she knows her turn will come after fifty.
How many bees live in the hive in our garden?
I don't know how many bees live in the hive, as I can't see it. A local beekeeper could help you estimate safely, from a distance.

Read this:

Saturday night.

Saw Vidya at Chinki's wedding today. First time in six years.

In college, she spread that rumour about me and the professor. Totally false, but it followed me for two years. I hated her for it. I used to rehearse what I'd say if I ever saw her again.

Today she came up to me at the buffet. Older, tired. She said, "Lalit, I was jealous and stupid back then. I'm sorry." Just that.

I felt the old anger rise. Then I noticed I didn't want to carry it anymore. I'd been holding it longer than the rumour lasted.

I said, "Thank you for saying it." We talked about work for five minutes. Not friends. But the stone in my stomach is gone.

Where did Lalit see Vidya?
At Chinki's wedding.
How did Lalit's feelings shift when Vidya apologised?
The old anger rose at first, but Lalit then felt ready to let it go and lighter, realising it had been held longer than the rumour lasted.
What was wise about Lalit's reply to Vidya's apology?
He accepted it simply without forcing a friendship, letting go of resentment while keeping healthy boundaries.
How might Vidya have felt after apologising?
She probably felt nervous but relieved that Lalit heard her and responded with grace.

Read this:

Bidisha watched the video twice on the bus home. The finfluencer, smiling beside a beach, promised freedom in six months for anyone who followed the method. Bidisha had just seven thousand rupees left from her first salary savings. The number felt small, but the promise felt big, and her chest was fizzing.

She was about to tap "join the course" when Lakshmi, her flatmate, glanced at the screen.

"How does the finfluencer earn?"

"Um. Investing."

"Check."

Bidisha scrolled: course fees, referral codes at the bottom, a tiny line saying "not a registered adviser".

"And if it goes wrong?" Lakshmi asked.

Bidisha stared. The video hadn't answered that. She closed the tab, a little deflated, still liking the ambition. "I'll ask a registered adviser first."

What did Bidisha find at the bottom of the page?
Bidisha found referral codes and a tiny line saying "not a registered adviser".
What was Bidisha feeling before Lakshmi asked the questions?
Bidisha felt inspired and excited, her chest fizzing, and was about to tap "join the course" on the strength of the promise.
What could Bidisha do next before putting any money in?
Ask a registered adviser, and find out how the finfluencer earns and what happens if the method goes wrong.
How does Lakshmi see the finfluencer's video?
Lakshmi treats it as something to be checked, asking how the finfluencer earns and what happens if it goes wrong.

Read this:

At the village library under the peepal tree, Santosh Sir asked the children what the story's ending meant. Asif put up his hand, then said, “Hmm… uh… um.” Two older boys sniggered. “He doesn't know.” Santosh Sir held up one finger to them and turned back to Asif, waiting. The breeze rattled the leaves. A cow lowed somewhere. Asif's eyes were moving, as if reading something inside his head. “Um… the crow didn't really want the cheese,” he said slowly. “It wanted the fox to see it was clever.” Santosh Sir's eyebrows went up. “Nobody's ever said that. Tell me more.”

Where was the village library?
The village library was under the peepal tree.
What was Asif feeling while he hummed and paused?
Asif was thinking hard and a bit unsure, working out a new idea, not showing that he didn't know.
How did Santosh Sir make space for Asif's answer?
He silenced the sniggering boys with a finger and waited, which let Asif finish a thoughtful new idea.
How did the older boys read Asif's thinking sounds?
They took the umms as a sign he didn't know the answer.

metadata.subtype: Hmm, uh and um as thinking sounds [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

In their Toronto apartment, Jin washed his hands after touching the door handle, after touching his backpack, after touching the washing, until the skin on his knuckles was red and cracked. Before bed he checked the stove knobs, one by one, then again, then again. "Jin, enough! You're wasting water!" his father Tomas shouted one night. Jin burst into tears. "If I don't, we'll get sick, or there'll be a fire. I have to." Tomas stopped. He had never heard the fear under it before. He sat down on the bathroom floor beside his son. "I'm sorry I shouted. This isn't your fault." The next week they saw a child psychologist together. She explained that scolding makes the urge stronger, and began showing them how to face the fear, step by step.

What did Jin check before bed?
The stove knobs, one by one, again and again.
What was Jin afraid would happen if he didn't wash and check?
He was afraid they would get sick or there would be a fire.
What changed when Tomas heard Jin's fear?
Tomas stopped scolding, apologised, said it wasn't Jin's fault and took him to a child psychologist.
How did Tomas see the washing at first, and how did that change?
He first saw it as wasting water, but then understood it came from a real, frightening urge.

metadata.subtype: Rituals to keep bad things away [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Class note, Sunflower group, Tuesday. Written by Hansa Ma'am. Santosh, five, spent twenty minutes on the thirty-piece farm puzzle today. When I came near he said, "Don't tell me! I know it." He didn't, yet: the cow's head was upside down. I asked only, "Which corner has the blue sky?" He looked, tried the top corner, and the cow sat right. Then he pushed me gently away. "Now go, Ma'am." I went. He finished it alone and showed everyone. I will keep my clues this small with him; the win clearly matters to him.

How many pieces did the farm puzzle have?
Thirty pieces.
What was Santosh wanting when he said 'Now go, Ma'am'?
He wanted to finish on his own and own the win, now that the small clue had got him unstuck.
What does Hansa Ma'am plan for next time, and why is it wise?
She plans to keep her clues this small, because a nudge lets Santosh stay in charge while still getting unstuck.
How might it have felt for Santosh if Hansa Ma'am had simply fixed the cow's head?
He might have felt his puzzle was taken over and lost the pride of showing everyone something he finished himself.

metadata.subtype: Wanting a hint, not the answer [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Jagdish and I run the tea stall by the school gate. Every afternoon little Preeti comes for a biscuit with her grandmother. Today she tugged her sleeve and whined, "Biscuit, biscuit!" Her grandmother waited and said, "How do we ask?" Preeti sighed and sagged. Then, "Biscuit please, Dadi." And to me, "Thank you." I gave her a wide smile. She might have been hungry, or just tired from school. I can't tell.

Where does Jagdish run his stall?
By the school gate.
Why might Preeti have whined before asking politely?
Perhaps she was frustrated, hungry or tired after school. Jagdish himself says he cannot tell.
What did Preeti's grandmother do to coach the polite form?
She waited and asked, "How do we ask?" instead of handing over the biscuit to the whining.
How might Jagdish feel when Preeti says thank you?
Pleased and warm, shown by his wide smile. It is a small moment of being appreciated.

"Hemant, you didn't ask about the transfer?"
"No point, bhaiya."
Omkar put down the newspaper. "You were so sure in March."
"I asked in March. And May. And July. Each time: 'We'll look into it.' Nobody looked into anything." Hemant shrugged. "So I stopped."
"You could go above your manager."
"Why? Same answer."
"You've been saying 'why' to everything lately. Even the trek."
"I just don't feel like anything, bhaiya. Everything's grey."
Omkar was quiet. "How long has it been grey?"
"Since spring, maybe."
"That's a long time. Will you talk to someone about it? A counsellor, a doctor, someone trained. I'll come with you to book it."
Hemant looked at him for a long moment. "Tomorrow?"
"Tomorrow."

In which months did Hemant ask about the transfer?
In March, May and July.
Why does Hemant say "No point" about asking again?
Hemant feels hopeless: each request got "We'll look into it" and nothing happened, so he believes asking changes nothing, and the greyness has spread to everything.
What choice by Omkar helps, and why?
Asking how long it has been grey, then suggesting a trained counsellor or doctor and offering to go along, because a low mood lasting months needs more than a pep talk.
How might Omkar feel hearing that Hemant doesn't even want the trek?
Omkar is likely worried, since losing interest in things Hemant used to enjoy shows the problem is bigger than one transfer.

messages.content: My relatives say "cousin brother". Is that correct English?
"Cousin" already covers boys and girls, so "cousin brother" sounds odd to others. In standard English, just say "my cousin".

Binita had just become secretary of the school's eco club. On Monday she posted in the club group: "Meeting at 5. Be on time. Bring your notebooks."
Within minutes, Himani messaged her privately. "Um, are you angry with everyone?"
Binita was confused. "No? Why?"
"It sounds like a teacher telling us off. Short sentences. Full stops. Some of the juniors think they're in trouble."
Binita read it again. In her head it had sounded efficient. On the screen, with no smile, it looked stern.
She added a second message: "Hi all! Just to be clear, nobody's in trouble 🙂 Excited for our first meeting. See you at 5, and bring notebooks for ideas."
Three juniors sent hearts within a minute.
At the meeting, a Class 8 boy said, "I thought you were going to scold us."
"Me too, apparently," Binita laughed.

What time was the eco club meeting?
The meeting was at 5.
What was Binita feeling when Himani asked if she was angry?
Binita felt confused and surprised, since in her head the message had sounded efficient, not stern.
What did Binita do that worked?
She added a friendly clarifying message with a smile emoji, making clear nobody was in trouble.
How did the juniors first read Binita's message?
They read the short sentences and full stops as a stern telling-off and thought they were in trouble.
