On Diwali morning in their Kolkata lane, Binita and Rajni, both five, were given one rangoli to colour together. Both reached for the centre flower at once. "Mine!" Binita knocked Rajni's bowl of red powder over. Rajni burst into tears. Binita stared at the red mess and at her friend's face, then said quietly, "Sorry. I didn't mean to spill." Rajni sniffed. "You do the petals. I do the middle?" "Then I do the middle next Diwali?" "Okay." They shook red-powdered hands on it.

On Diwali morning in their Kolkata lane, Binita and Rajni, both five, reached for the centre flower of their shared rangoli at once, and Binita knocked over Rajni's bowl of red powder. Rajni burst into tears, and Binita said sorry and that she had not meant to spill. They agreed that Rajni would do the middle and Binita the petals, with Binita doing the middle next Diwali, and shook hands on it.
What are the entry charges at the zoo for children?
I don't know the current charges, because ticket rates change. The zoo's official website or gate will list them.

Smoke curled from the clay chulha in the corner of the village kitchen. Yogesh toddled straight towards it, hand out.
“NO! Hot!” Kalyani's voice rang out sharp.
Yogesh froze and stared at her, lip trembling.
She was already there, scooping him up and stepping back. “Hot. Ouch,” she said, touching his hand. Then she dragged the wooden plank across the corner so he couldn't reach it.
Yogesh stared at the fire, then buried his face in her neck.

What did Kalyani drag across the corner?
She dragged the wooden plank across the corner.
What was Yogesh feeling when he froze at Kalyani's sharp "NO!"?
He was startled and a little frightened, reading the sharp voice as a sign of danger, which stopped him.
Which choices kept Yogesh safe, and why?
A short, sharp warning, lifting him away at once and putting the plank across the corner; simple words and physical safety matter more than a long explanation at his age.
How might Kalyani feel after the moment passes?
She probably feels shaken and relieved that she stopped him in time.

At five, Deepika stood half behind her father Francis at a cousin's birthday party, whispering "fine" when asked how she was. She watched the other children build a tower for a long while before she crept over and placed one block on top.

At fifteen, she stopped putting her hand up in class, skipped the annual day and spent hours at night rehearsing how to ask for a library book. The dread of a wrong word made everything smaller. The school counsellor, Yusuf, noticed she had missed three events and asked her in for tea. He listened first, and they agreed on one tiny step: answering a single question in class each week.

At twenty, Deepika sits quietly at fresher gatherings, then spends her evenings with two close friends over noodles and long conversations. She is asked sometimes whether she wants to be louder. She shrugs and says, "I like how it is." Nothing about it troubles her.

What did Deepika whisper when asked how she was at the party at five?
She whispered "fine" while standing half behind her father Francis.
How does Deepika's quietness at five, fifteen and twenty differ in how it affects her life?

At five she needed time to warm up; at fifteen the fear of embarrassment shrank her life through skipped events and silence, and Yusuf's support was needed; at twenty her quietness is simply how she is and she is content with a few close friends.
What might Deepika be feeling as she rehearses asking for a library book?
Deepika is afraid of a wrong word and of being judged, so she practises for hours to avoid embarrassment.
What did Yusuf do that helped Deepika?
Yusuf noticed the missed events, invited her for tea, listened first and agreed one tiny step, answering a single question in class each week.
List three safe things to do in a thunderstorm, numbered, each four words or fewer.

1. Stay indoors.
2. Keep away from windows.
3. Switch off the television.

Nikita's diary, Tuesday
Today I finally got fractions! Gurleen and I had one roti to share at lunch, and Ma'am had just taught halves and quarters. I tore it into two: halves. Then Gurleen said, "What if Palak wants some?" So we tore each half again: four quarters. Gurleen ate one, I ate one, Palak ate one, and one was left. That's three quarters gone, one quarter left! Dadi laughed when I told her I ate my maths.

Into how many pieces did they tear the roti in the end?
Four quarters.
How was Nikita feeling about fractions by the end of the day?
Nikita felt excited and proud to finally understand them.
What would you advise Nikita to try next with fractions?
Try splitting other things at home, like a chapati or a fruit, into halves, quarters or thirds and counting what's left.
How might Gurleen see the roti lesson?
Gurleen probably found it fun and helpful, especially since the question about Palak led to quarters.

In the site cabin, the foreman laughed. “Keerthana, you’ll want to sit near the door in case the dust bothers you.”
“It doesn’t,” said Keerthana. She was the only woman engineer on the team of nine, and she had checked the drawings three times before the meeting. Her jaw was tight.
Samir, the project manager, put down his coffee. “Let’s start with the report. Keerthana wrote it.”
Afterwards Keerthana said, “I’m not here to speak for all women.”
“Noted,” said Samir. “I’ll rotate the site walks and put names on every report. Tell me if anything slips.”
Keerthana nodded but said nothing.

How many people are on the team in the site cabin?
The team has nine people.
What was Keerthana feeling when she said she was not there to speak for all women?
Keerthana was probably tired and a little resentful at being treated as a representative rather than an engineer. Checking the drawings three times and her tight jaw show the pressure she felt.
What did Samir do to make treatment fairer?
Samir began the meeting with Keerthana's report, promised to rotate the site walks and to put names on every report. He also asked to be told if anything slipped.
How might the foreman have seen the remark?
The foreman probably thought the remark was polite or funny and may not have noticed how it sounded. The passage shows only the laugh.

In the hospital's quality-improvement meeting, Kavitha presented a new idea for shortening the wait at the pharmacy counter: colour-coded tokens for refill patients. The medical superintendent nodded. "Excellent thinking, Kavitha."
Zainab sat very still. She had suggested exactly that in the pantry two weeks earlier, with a sketch on a napkin.
Her first urge was to speak up right there: "That was mine!" She pictured the room turning, Kavitha's face burning. She didn't.
After the meeting she found the email she'd sent Kavitha the next morning, sketch attached, subject line "pharmacy token idea". Then she asked Kavitha for a word in the empty meeting room.
"Kavitha, the token idea is the one I sent you on the 4th. I'd like us to tell the superintendent it came from both of us, and I'd like to be on the pilot."
Kavitha went pink. "I... forgot where it came from. You're right. I'll email him today."
From then on, Zainab put every idea in writing, copied to their supervisor.

What idea did Kavitha present?
Colour-coded tokens for refill patients at the pharmacy counter.
What was Zainab feeling in the meeting?
Angry and betrayed; she wanted to shout "That was mine!" but held back.
How did Zainab raise the issue calmly?
She found her dated email with the sketch, spoke privately to Kavitha, asked for shared credit and a place on the pilot, and afterwards put ideas in writing copied to the supervisor.
How did Kavitha respond when Zainab spoke to her?
Embarrassed; she went pink, admitted Zainab was right, and agreed to email the superintendent.

Use two sentences to tell me what this passage means.

The king once more said, 'Bring Gandhari hither without delay, and all the Bharata ladies. Bring hither Kunti also, as well as all the other ladies with her.' Having said these words unto Vidura, conversant with every duty, Dhritarashtra of righteous soul, deprived of his senses by sorrow, ascended on his car. Then Gandhari, afflicted with grief on account of the death of her sons, accompanied by Kunti and the other ladies of the royal household, came at the command of her lord to that spot where the latter was waiting for her.
The king orders Vidura to bring Gandhari, Kunti and the other royal ladies, and then rides out in his chariot. Gandhari, grieving for her sons, comes with Kunti and the others to where he waits.

Read this:

Arohi and I share a desk in the college library, so I've watched her study all term. She does something odd. She reads a page of her accountancy notes, closes the file and writes down everything she can remember on a blank sheet. Then she checks and circles what she missed.
She doesn't study one subject all day, either. She does a little of each and comes back to old chapters every few days, just when I'd expect her to be forgetting them.
Once I asked if it was fun. She laughed. "It's horrible. It feels like I'm failing every time."
But in the mid-terms she got the top mark in our section, and she didn't look tired.
I'm Hansa. I tried it for one week. It's horrible. I'm keeping it.

What does Arohi do after reading a page of accountancy notes?
She closes the file and writes down everything she can remember on a blank sheet, then circles what she missed.
Why does Arohi keep using a method that feels "horrible"?
It feels like failing every time, but she seems to trust that the struggle is what makes the material stick, and her results back that up.
What small part of Arohi's routine could Hansa start with?
Writing everything remembered on a blank sheet after reading a page, then checking it, is an easy first step.
How does Hansa's view change after trying the method?
Hansa agrees it feels horrible but decides to keep it, which suggests one week of trying was convincing enough. 😅

In the UKG classroom, Rukmini stood up to read the picture card. "Ell-y-fant," she said.
Laughter rippled across the room. Her cheeks burned and she wanted to shrink into her shoes.
Aparna, the teacher, raised a hand. "Everyone here is still learning words, even me. Let us say it together: el-e-phant." The class repeated it.
One boy near the front was still giggling. Rukmini took a breath. "That is unkind, Rohit."
Rohit stopped and studied his desk. Rukmini said the word again, slowly, and got it right.

What word did Rukmini mispronounce?
She said "ell-y-fant" for elephant.
How did Rukmini feel when the class laughed?
She felt small and embarrassed: her cheeks burned and she wanted to shrink into her shoes.
What could Rukmini do when someone keeps laughing?
She can say calmly that it is unkind, as she did with Rohit, and keep trying the word.
How might Aparna see the laughter in the class?
Aparna seems to see it as part of learning together and steps in gently, saying even the teacher is still learning, so no one is singled out.

Day one: Miss Varghese gave gold stars to the children who could say the whole poem. Thomas forgot the second line. He was the only one without a star. At home he told Amma, "I'm the stupid one," and wouldn't eat.
Day four: He hid his notebook when his friend Ojas asked to see it.
Day nine: Amma had practised the poem with him as a silly song. In class he said it all. Ojas clapped. Thomas smiled a small smile, but that night he asked, "Am I still stupid?" Amma hugged him. "You never were."

What did the teacher give to children who could say the whole poem?
She gave them gold stars.
What does Thomas calling himself "the stupid one" show?
He seems to feel bad about who he is, not just about one forgotten line, because he was the only one without a star.
What helped Thomas, and what more could the teacher do?
Practising in a playful way helped; the teacher could praise effort and avoid public prizes that leave one child out.
How might Ojas see what happened on day nine?
He seemed glad for his friend and clapped, probably without knowing how bad Thomas had felt before.

Monday: Raghav came back from his night shift at the call centre to find the sink full: Hemant's dal pot, three mugs, a frying pan with egg stuck to it. He washed his own plate around them and said nothing.
Wednesday: Same pile, taller. Raghav had also covered the electricity bill again, and Hemant still hadn't transferred his half.
Thursday: The pot was growing something. Hemant was on the sofa, headphones on, laughing at a video. Raghav stood at the sink and said, loud enough, "Wow. Maybe the dishes will wash themselves if we believe hard enough." His voice had an edge he didn't recognise. It wasn't really the pot. It was feeling like the only adult in the flat, like nobody saw what he did.

What had Raghav covered again by Wednesday?
He had covered the electricity bill again.
What is Raghav really feeling behind the sarcastic remark?
He feels unseen and resentful, like the only adult in the flat, covering the bill and the dishes while nobody notices what he does.
What turning point is available to Raghav at this first spark?
He could name the real issue calmly, such as "I'm feeling taken for granted with the dishes and the bill, can we set up a system?", instead of sarcasm.
How might Hemant hear the remark from the sofa?
Hemant may hear only mockery out of nowhere, not knowing about the bill or the build-up, and feel attacked rather than asked.

Read this:

School counsellor's note, Tuesday

Today I met Vinita and her daughter Madhuri, after Madhuri lied about a weekend trip.
Vinita started by saying, "I'm hurt by the lie. And I also want to understand why you felt you couldn't ask me."
Madhuri was silent for a long time. Then she said, "Because I thought you'd say no, and then be angry for days."
Vinita looked shocked. "I didn't know you were afraid of me."
"Not afraid. Just… scared of the no."
They both went quiet. I asked each of them to say one thing they had just learned. Vinita said, "That my no's feel so final." Madhuri said, "That Mummy was hurt, not just angry."
We'll meet again next week.

What did Madhuri lie about?
A weekend trip.
What was Madhuri feeling when she explained why she lied?
She was scared of her mother's no and of the anger that followed.
What made this conversation work?
Vinita named her hurt but also asked why Madhuri couldn't ask, which let Madhuri admit her fear, and the counsellor helped both say what they had learned.
What was Vinita experiencing when she heard Madhuri's reason?
She was shocked, realising that her no's felt so final to her daughter.

I'm Bhupen, and my cousin Kishore was doing a big puzzle on our floor. The edges were done, but the middle wouldn't come together. He tried a few pieces, sighed, then tipped every piece back into the box. "It's broken," he said. I don't know if he really thought so, but he put the box away and didn't open it again.

What did Kishore say?
"It's broken."
What was Bhupen thinking as Kishore put the box away?
Bhupen was unsure and a bit disappointed, not knowing if Kishore really thought it was broken.
What else could Kishore have tried?
Taking a break, or sorting the middle pieces by colour, so the puzzle feels less hard.
How might the unfinished puzzle feel to Kishore?
It probably felt frustrating, and blaming the puzzle was easier than keeping going.
Who is an ambassador?

An ambassador is an official sent by one country to live in another country and represent it there. It is a noun. It can also mean someone who represents a group or idea.
Example: The students acted as young ambassadors for their school at the science fair.

Sun beat down on the mango orchard. Harsha came back from the pump with a full bucket and cheeks as red as ripe fruit. A girl from the next farm waved at him. An uncle on the cot laughed. “Look, Harsha's gone red! Is it for your friend?” Harsha dropped the bucket and hid behind his Nana, Tanvir. Tanvir laid a wet towel on his head. “So many trips in this heat,” he told the uncle. Then, quietly, to Harsha: “Red from the sun, or from being looked at?” Harsha peeked out. “From the sun. And a little from him.”

Where did Harsha hide?
Harsha hid behind his Nana, Tanvir.
Why did Harsha hide after the uncle laughed?
He felt embarrassed at being teased about his red cheeks; his answer shows the heat mattered too, so both the sun and shame played a part.
What small step did Tanvir take to calm things down?
Tanvir cooled him with a wet towel, told the uncle about the heat and quietly asked Harsha which cause it was.
How might the uncle see his joke after Tanvir's words?
He might realise the red face could be from heat and work, and that his joke made the boy hide.

At ten, Jomon told everyone that his favourite batter was the best in the world. He remembered every century. When the batter scored a duck, Jomon said the umpire had been blind. When the team lost, he said the pitch was bad. At twenty, Jomon had already decided to skip campus placements and start a small workshop. He read three articles about founders who had dropped everything and asked two seniors who had done the same. His cousin Rajni said, "Did you ask anyone who regretted it?" He shrugged. "I've done my research." At twenty-five, he worked beside a new colleague, Yamini. In her first week she missed a bracket in a report. Jomon thought, I knew it. When she spotted a serious mistake in his figures, he noted it only as luck. When she mislaid a folder, he told his manager, "This is typical." By month's end he had three examples for his list and none of the good ones. Nobody had asked Yamini a single question about her method.

What did Jomon say when his favourite batter scored a duck?
He said the umpire had been blind.
What do Jomon's habits at ten, twenty and twenty-five have in common?

He collected only what agreed with what he already believed: the centuries of his batter, the articles and seniors backing his choice to skip placements, and Yamini's small slips. He explained away or ignored everything that pointed the other way, such as the duck, the regretful people and the serious mistake she spotted.
What was Jomon thinking when he said he had done his research?
He felt sure and a little defensive, believing three articles and two seniors counted as thorough, although he had only gathered agreement.
What could Jomon try before he gives his manager a list about Yamini?
He could keep a note of her good work as well, and ask her about her approach so his first impression does not decide everything.

In their terraced house in Birmingham, a clap of thunder shook the windows, and Siddiq, five, ran out of his room.
“Baba! I'm scared!”
Jamal opened his arms. Siddiq pressed his face into his father's chest.
“Let's breathe together,” Jamal said. “Smell the flower… blow the candle.”
They did it three times. Siddiq's shoulders came down.
Another rumble. Siddiq flinched but didn't run. “Smell the flower,” he whispered to himself.

What did Jamal say to do when breathing?
Smell the flower, blow the candle.
How was Siddiq feeling when he heard the thunder?
He felt scared and ran to his father.
What helped Siddiq calm down?
A hug from his father and breathing together three times.
How might Jamal feel when Siddiq whispers the breathing words himself?
He probably feels relieved and proud that Siddiq is learning to calm himself.
I have to go to bank today to deposit this cheque. Is an article missing?

I have to go to the bank today to deposit this cheque.
Why: A particular, known bank needs "the" before it.
Describe a school playground during the break, 35 words: swings creaking, children running, a teacher's whistle, a vendor selling ice candy.

The playground is busy during the break. The swings creak, and children run in every direction. A teacher blows a whistle, and a vendor at the gate sells ice candy to the children, who gather around him.

Up to this time I had remained standing, not to disguise that I wished him gone. But I was softened by the softened aspect of the man, and felt a touch of reproach. "I hope," said I, hurriedly putting something into a glass for myself, and drawing a chair to the table, "that you will not think I spoke harshly to you just now. I had no intention of doing it, and I am sorry for it if I did. I wish you well and happy!"

Can you tell me what the narrator say to the man, and what does the narrator do first?

First the narrator pours something into a glass and pulls a chair up to the table. Then they say they hope the man does not think they spoke harshly, are sorry if they did, and wish him well and happy.

Tuesday, after the film: Jatin stopped walking outside the metro station. "Something happened to me at my old job. I've never told anyone." Amandeep's stomach dropped, but she kept her voice low. "I believe you. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to." They sat on the steps until his hands stopped shaking.

Saturday: Amandeep texted, "No need to reply. I'm around." He answered that evening with a single "thanks". She did not ask for details.

Two weeks later: Jatin asked whether she knew any counsellors. Amandeep found two clinic numbers and sent them with a question: "Want me to come with you, or would you rather go alone?" "Alone first," he said. She told nobody, not even her sister.

What did Amandeep text on Saturday?
She texted, "No need to reply. I'm around."
What was Amandeep feeling and wanting when Jatin told her?
Her stomach dropped, so she was shaken, but she wanted Jatin to feel believed and unpressured, which is why she kept her voice low and said he need not tell her more.
Which choice by Amandeep helped Jatin most, and why?
Sending the clinic numbers and asking whether he wanted company or to go alone helped, because it let him keep control of his own pace.
What might it have been like for Jatin when Amandeep asked no questions?
He probably felt safer and less exposed, which fits with him replying with a thanks that evening and later asking about counsellors. 🤍

In the home corner of their Kolkata preschool, Arnab set a wooden block on the toy shelf and put a paper flower in front of it. He rang the little tin bell three times, folded his hands and swayed, murmuring, "Ma, Ma, Ma." Darshan watched. "What are you doing?" "Puja. Like Thakuma does for Ma Kali every evening." "Why?" Arnab thought hard. "I don't know. It's for Ma. Everyone goes quiet and the lamp smells nice." Darshan folded his hands too. Miss Priya smiled and let them finish before calling them for snack.

How many times did Arnab ring the tin bell?
Arnab rang it three times.
What does Arnab's answer "I don't know. It's for Ma" suggest?
It suggests Arnab feels awe and belonging in Thakuma's evening puja, even though he doesn't yet understand its meaning.
How did Miss Priya handle the pretend puja respectfully?
She smiled and let them finish before snack, without mocking or questioning the family's faith.
How might Darshan see Arnab's puja?
Darshan seems curious and drawn in, folding his hands too to share the moment.

Why does Pierre speak mostly to the battalion commander?

The officers were about to take leave, but Prince Andrew, apparently reluctant to be left alone with his friend, asked them to stay and have tea. Seats were brought in and so was the tea. The officers gazed with surprise at Pierre's huge stout figure and listened to his talk of Moscow and the position of our army, round which he had ridden. Prince Andrew remained silent, and his expression was so forbidding that Pierre addressed his remarks chiefly to the good-natured battalion commander.
Prince Andrew sits silent with a forbidding look, so Pierre addresses his remarks chiefly to the good-natured battalion commander instead.

Write a fable, about 100 words, for children, about a crow who is too proud to ask for help.

A proud crow named Kalu built his nest at the very top of a tall tree. When a strong wind began to shake the branches, his nest started to slip. The sparrows below called, "Let us help you tie it with grass!" But Kalu puffed up his feathers. "I need nobody's help," he said. That night the storm grew worse, and the nest fell to the ground. Shivering and wet, Kalu had to ask the sparrows for shelter. They made room for him without a word. The next morning, he helped them build a stronger nest. Moral: there is no shame in asking for help.

Kiran, you feel trapped because your parents spent so much on your hotel management course? Listen. When I was twenty-four, in Kochi, my parents had sold a piece of land to send me, their only daughter, for nursing training in Ireland. I finished, came back, and hated hospital work. But every time I thought of quitting, I saw my father signing the land papers. How could I throw that away? For two years I worked nights, miserable. Then one Sunday I sat with my parents and said the truth. "I'm grateful. And I'm unhappy. I want to teach nursing, not do night shifts." My mother cried. My father was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "We didn't sell the land for you to be unhappy." I started teaching the next year. So talk to them, Kiran. Kindly, honestly. That's what Elizabeth learned.

What did Elizabeth's parents sell to send her for training?
A piece of land.
How did young Elizabeth feel during the two years of night shifts?
Elizabeth felt miserable and trapped, unable to quit because of what her parents had given up.
What choice in the story released Elizabeth from the pressure?
She chose to talk to her parents kindly and honestly, thanking them and sharing her unhappiness, which let them release her.
How did Elizabeth's father respond to the conversation?
Her father was quiet, then said they hadn't sold the land for her to be unhappy, showing love over pride.
