Friday night

Uma apologised today. A real one, not a "sorry if". She said, "I told your parents about the concert, and it got you in trouble. I'm sorry."
I felt something unclench. But I wasn't ready to hug and go for chaat.
So I said, "Thanks for saying that. I need a little time." My voice shook a bit.
Uma said, "Okay, that's fair." And then she went back to her side of the lab and didn't look sad at me or send twenty messages.
That's what's making me want to forgive her, honestly. She's letting me take my time. Maybe next week. — Parveen

What did Uma tell Parveen's parents about?
About the concert.
What was Parveen feeling after Uma's apology?
Parveen felt some relief, something unclenching, but still hurt and not ready to forgive fully.
Why does Uma's response help Parveen move towards forgiving her?
Uma accepted the need for time without pushing, sulking or sending lots of messages.
What might Uma be experiencing as she goes back to her side of the lab?
She is likely anxious but respectful, tolerating the wait because she knows Parveen needs time.
Is venerable a polite way of saying old?

Yes. Venerable describes an old person or thing that is respected because of age and wisdom or history. It is an adjective.
Example: The venerable old teacher was greeted warmly by his former pupils.
My little brother always "acts up" when we go shopping. Does that mean he is acting in a play?

No. "Act up" means to behave badly, especially for a child, or, for a machine, to work badly.
Examples: The children acted up during the long bus ride. My old laptop is acting up again.

Read this:

"Trisha, you asked why I don't laugh when your cousins make fun of people. Let your Harsha Mausi tell you.
When I was fifteen, my friends in Jaipur used to mimic a new girl's accent. She came from a village and said some words differently. Everyone laughed, and I laughed too. Loudly. But inside I felt sick. I wanted them to like me.
One day the girl heard. She looked at me, only at me, like she expected better. That night I couldn't sleep.
The next time they started, I said, very calmly, 'That's not funny.' They stared. A few stopped talking to me. But two others quietly agreed.
Those two are still my friends. The loud ones, I don't even remember their names."

What did Harsha's friends mimic?
A new girl's accent.
What was young Harsha feeling while laughing along?
She felt sick and uneasy inside, laughing only because she wanted to fit in.
What choice inside the story was healthier for Harsha?
Saying calmly "That's not funny" set a boundary and led her to safer, kinder friends.
How might the new girl have felt when Harsha laughed?
The new girl probably felt hurt and let down, especially by Harsha, from whom she expected better.

metadata.subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]

messages.content:
Read this:

Sunday, Lohri night: When the last ball of the final is hit for four, Baljeet is on the roof with his cousin Binita, the bonfire crackling below and a radio on the parapet. He screams so loudly that the neighbour's dog barks.
Wednesday: At school, Baljeet tells the story in perfect detail: the red shawl Binita wore, the smell of peanuts, the exact moment the commentator shouted. "I'll remember it forever," he says.
Next Saturday: Binita visits and laughs. "We weren't on the roof, silly. It was too cold. We watched on Chacha's TV in the drawing room." Baljeet shakes his head hard. He can see the stars. He can feel the wind. "I was THERE," he says. "I know."

Where does Binita say they watched the final?
On Chacha's TV in the drawing room.
Why does Baljeet shake his head so hard?
He feels sure and a bit indignant, because he can still see the stars and feel the wind; the thrill of the win makes the picture feel perfectly true.
How could Binita talk to Baljeet about it without a fight?
She could say "I remember it differently" and suggest asking Chacha or looking for a photo, rather than calling him silly.
How might Binita feel when Baljeet insists?
Binita might feel amused, then a little frustrated, because she remembers the cold drawing room just as clearly.
Write one sentence that has the words "first", "second" and "third" in that order.
First we washed the rice, second we boiled it, and third we added salt.

Read this:

When his mother, Indu, left for the office, Sumit didn't cry. He sat on the mat of the Andheri flat stacking cups and did not look up. Later he slipped on the balcony step and grazed his knee. His lip trembled, but he turned away from the nanny's open arms and crawled behind the sofa. When Indu came home, he glanced at her once, then went on lining up his cars, cheeks still blotchy.

Where did Sumit crawl after grazing his knee?
Behind the sofa.
What do Sumit's trembling lip and blotchy cheeks suggest?
That he was hurt and upset inside, even though he looked calm and did not seek comfort.
How could Indu gently help Sumit over time?
Stay close and offer comfort calmly and often, without forcing it, so he learns that showing need brings care.
What is it like for the nanny when Sumit turns away from her arms?
The nanny may feel rejected or worried, unsure how to comfort a child who hides his hurt.

metadata.subtype: Toddler who does not seek comfort [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

You asked me, 'Binita, when did you first notice?' Honestly, it was small things. My brother Divyansh used to call me every Sunday from his college hostel. Then it was every other Sunday. Then he'd say, 'Can't talk, I'm at the centre.'
When he came home at Holi, he used words I didn't know. 'Awake ones.' 'Noise people.' He called his old school friends noise people. He'd stopped replying to them.
I asked about his exams. He said he'd dropped two papers because 'the real learning is at the centre now'. When Papa asked a question about the fees, Divyansh said, very calmly, 'Only the guide's word is true. Questions are a test of loyalty. People who ask too many get asked to sit out of the circle.'
Then he told me, gently, that maybe I should give him some space. That family can be a distraction.
That's when I got scared. That's why I'm talking to you.

What did Divyansh call his old school friends?
He called his old school friends noise people.
What was Binita feeling when Divyansh said family can be a distraction?
Binita was frightened, seeing Divyansh being pulled away from the people who love him.
Which warning signs did Binita spot that a counsellor would recognise?
Only one source of truth, questions punished by being made to sit out, dropping studies and old friends, and pressure to distance from family.
How might Papa have felt when his question about fees was treated as a loyalty test?
Papa may have felt shut out and alarmed, realising ordinary questions were no longer allowed.

Read this:

Dear Disha didi,
You said I could write to you about anything, so here goes.
Last week some girls in my building started a trend from a video site: sitting on the edge of the terrace wall for a photo, legs over the side. Sunita said it gets loads of likes and "don't tell anyone, parents freak out." Everyone in our group did it except me. I kept saying maybe tomorrow.
I felt like a coward. But the "don't tell anyone" part kept bothering me.
Yesterday I told Amma. She didn't shout. She went straight to the building secretary that evening, the terrace door was locked by night, and she phoned the other parents too. Sunita is angry with me, but Amma says that anger is safer than a fall.
Was I wrong? Tell me honestly.
Love,
Rukmini

What did Sunita say about the terrace photo trend?
Sunita said it gets loads of likes and "don't tell anyone, parents freak out."
What was Rukmini feeling about refusing the trend?
Rukmini felt like a coward for not joining, and uneasy about the "don't tell anyone" part. Now Sunita's anger leaves Rukmini torn, still asking if it was wrong.
What would you advise Rukmini about her choice?
Telling Amma was the right step, because a trend that is dangerous and kept secret is exactly when to go to a trusted adult, even if a friend is upset for a while.
How might Sunita see Rukmini's choice right now?
Sunita probably feels betrayed and embarrassed, but she may later see that the locked door protected her and the others from a real fall.
What am I wearing right now?
I can't tell what you're wearing, because you haven't described it. Tell me, and I can help you decide if it suits the occasion.
"Usne mujhe bataya ki wo kal nahi aayega." English?
It is: "He told me that he would not come tomorrow." In reported speech, "will" often changes to "would". Say "she" if you mean a woman.
Describe a small town library in the afternoon, about 80 words.

In the afternoon, the town library is quiet and cool. Sunlight falls through the tall windows onto long wooden tables. An old man reads the newspaper, and a girl with plaits sits cross-legged on the floor, lost in a picture book. The librarian stamps cards with a soft thump. The ceiling fan creaks as it turns. There is a smell of old paper and polish. Nobody speaks above a whisper, yet the whole room feels full of stories.

Read this:

Yosef had already priced a flat in Rotterdam when Noa put her fork down.

"The lab in Bergen wrote back," she said. "They want me in September."

His stomach dropped. His own plan had a place for her in it, and that place was Rotterdam. He breathed out slowly. "Tell me about the lab first. What would you actually do there?"

She talked for ten minutes about kelp surveys and a supervisor she admired, and he listened without doing sums in his head. Then he pulled over a napkin. "Two people, two offers. What are our options?"

They wrote them down: he goes, she goes, or a year of visits between the two cities. Nothing was decided. Afterwards he washed the dishes, since she had cooked.

Where had Yosef already priced a flat?
He had already priced a flat in Rotterdam.
How did Yosef feel when Noa mentioned the lab, and why?
He felt thrown and anxious, his stomach dropping, because his own plan had a place for her in Rotterdam and he realised he had expected her to adjust.
What could Yosef do next so the decision stays shared?
Keep asking what each of them wants, compare the options honestly, and agree who adjusts when, so it is not always Noa who moves.
How might Noa have felt if Yosef had answered that Rotterdam was better anyway?
She might have felt her ambitions counted for less and that she was being asked to follow, not to choose.

Read this:

Farida was the captain of the girls' kabaddi team and the loudest voice in 9B. So on parent-teacher day, when she walked into the classroom behind her father, Darshan barely recognised her. She stood with her hands folded, eyes on the floor. Mrs Pillai praised her leadership, and Abbu said, "Leadership? At home she hardly speaks." Farida gave a tiny smile and said nothing. Darshan, waiting with his own mother by the door, whispered, "Is that the same Farida?" Later, in the corridor, he asked her. She shrugged. "At home, I keep quiet and there are no fights. At school, I can be loud. Easy." But she looked at the kabaddi trophy in the display case for a long time. "Abbu has never seen me play," she said, very quietly. "He doesn't even know I'm captain."

What team is Farida captain of?
Farida is the captain of the girls' kabaddi team.
How does Farida seem to feel about keeping the two worlds apart?
She feels it is easier and safer because it avoids fights, but staring at the trophy shows she is also sad that Abbu does not know this side of her.
How could Mrs Pillai support Farida after this meeting?
Mrs Pillai could gently invite Farida's father to a match, or ask Farida privately if she would like him to see her play.
What might Abbu feel if he learned Farida is the team captain?
He might be surprised and perhaps proud, and also puzzled or hurt that she never told him.

metadata.subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]

messages.content: There were so many butterflies in our garden today. Why are they here now?
Butterflies come out when the weather is warm and flowers are in bloom, because flowers give them nectar to drink.
They seem to like the yellow flowers.
Many butterflies are attracted to bright colours, and yellow and orange are popular. If you plant more flowers like these, more butterflies will visit.

Read this:

Dear Elizabeth,
I went to the group on Thursday, the one I told you about. I sat by the door with my coat on for twenty minutes. Then a man in a green cap said, "Nobody here will judge you, we've all said worse." I cried a little and nobody rushed to fix me. Someone just passed tissues. I said out loud that I'd been drinking every night since March, and the room stayed warm. I walked home lighter than I've felt in months. I'm going back next week and I'll keep telling the truth there. But a part of me worries I could start needing their clapping more than my own steadiness, so I'll keep calling you too. Maybe one day I'll be the one passing tissues.
Love,
Salma

How long did Salma sit by the door before someone spoke?
Salma sat by the door with a coat on for twenty minutes.
What is Salma worried about, even while feeling relieved?
That the group's clapping could become more important than Salma's own steadiness, which is why Salma plans to keep calling Elizabeth too.
What plans in the letter make this a healthy path?
Going back next week, telling the truth there, staying in touch with Elizabeth, and maybe one day helping others as someone passing tissues.
How might the man in the green cap have seen Salma's first visit?
He probably recognised the nervousness from his own start, since he said everyone there has said worse, and wanted Salma to feel safe.
How much did my colleague pay for her new flat?
I don't know, and that is her private business. If she wants to share it, she will.
How can I say no politely with "I'm afraid"?

"I'm afraid" is a polite way to introduce bad news or a refusal. You are not scared; it softens what follows.
Example: I'm afraid I cannot come to the meeting on Friday.

Reduce this brief extract to three sentences.

On the birth of a second son, my junior by seven years, my parents gave up entirely their wandering life and fixed themselves in their native country. We possessed a house in Geneva, and a campagne on Belrive, the eastern shore of the lake, at the distance of rather more than a league from the city. We resided principally in the latter, and the lives of my parents were passed in considerable seclusion. It was my temper to avoid a crowd and to attach myself fervently to a few. I was indifferent, therefore, to my school-fellows in general; but I united myself in the bonds of the closest friendship to one among them. Henry Clerval was the son of a merchant of Geneva. He was a boy of singular talent and fancy. He loved enterprise, hardship, and even danger for its own sake. He was deeply read in books of chivalry and romance. He composed heroic songs and began to write many a tale of enchantment and knightly adventure. He tried to make us act plays and to enter into masquerades, in which the characters were drawn from the heroes of Roncesvalles, of the Round Table of King Arthur, and the chivalrous train who shed their blood to redeem the holy sepulchre from the hands of the infidels.

After the narrator's brother is born seven years later, the parents settle in their home country and live quietly, mostly at Belrive. The narrator avoids crowds and forms a close friendship with schoolfellow Henry Clerval, a Geneva merchant's son. Henry is talented, loves adventure and danger, reads tales of knights, and writes songs and stories.

Read this:

Samir and I have been together six years. We have a rhythm. I make the coffee, he does the dishes. Sunday is biryani and a film. We finish each other's grocery lists.

I love it. It's safe.

But last month, at a friend's wedding, someone asked Samir what he was reading these days, and he talked for ten minutes about a book on the history of trains. I'd never heard him mention it. I didn't know he liked trains.

On the drive home I asked him, "When did you start that book?"

"Two months ago," he said. "You were busy with your exams."

It wasn't a fight. We laughed about it. But I kept thinking: what else have I stopped asking about? When did the comfort turn into not knowing?

I've started asking him one real question every evening. It feels awkward. It also feels necessary.

— Chetan

What book was Samir talking about at the wedding?
A book on the history of trains.
How did Chetan feel on the drive home?
Chetan felt surprised and a little unsettled, realising the comfortable routine had let Chetan stop asking about Samir's inner life.
What did Chetan decide to do, and why is it wise?
Chetan started asking Samir one real question every evening, so small changes don't go unspoken inside the comfort.
How might Samir feel when Chetan starts asking real questions?
He may feel pleased and seen, perhaps a little surprised by the sudden interest.
The program has a musical interlude. What is an interlude?

An interlude is a short break between two parts of something, such as a play, or a short piece of music filling that break. It is a noun.
Example: A song was played in the interlude between the two acts of the play.

Read this:

Placement cell note, written by Vandana, coordinator. Bidisha came in on Tuesday with three printouts, one for each of the last three years of a logistics firm's hiring. She read them aloud: every year began with an aptitude test, then a coding round, then an HR chat. "Aptitude I can manage, my mocks are fine," she said. "HR I can talk through. But their coding questions are all trees and graphs, and I have barely touched graphs." She drew three boxes on my whiteboard and wrote her current level under each. The widest gap sat under coding, so she declared that stage comes first. I only asked how many weeks she had left. She counted, then wrote her own schedule. I have asked her to bring her first graph solutions on Friday.

Which stage did Bidisha say had the widest gap?
The coding round, because its questions are all trees and graphs and she has barely touched graphs.
What might Bidisha be feeling as she writes her level under each box?
She seems steady but a little concerned: she is confident about aptitude and HR, and she admits her graph practice is thin.
What alternative approach could Bidisha add alongside this comparison, and why?
She could run a mock interview with a friend, because comparing stages finds the gap but does not show how she sounds under live questions.
How does Vandana see Bidisha's plan?
Vandana sees a student who found her own gap, which is why Vandana only asks how many weeks are left and then asks for graph solutions on Friday.

metadata.subtype: Approach: means-end analysis from company pattern to gap [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Thursday, midnight

I put salt in my tea this morning. Salt. Amandeep laughed so hard she had to sit down.

Then in the stats test I skipped a whole question without noticing. At the library desk where I work part-time, I stamped the wrong return date on five books. And I forgot to call home.

It's the internship applications, the test, the library hours, and the fight with my roommate. My brain feels like a phone with forty apps open.

I'm not stupid. I know that. I'm just full.

Tomorrow: write everything on one list, pick three things, and tell the library supervisor I need one lighter shift this week. — Indu

What did Indu put in the tea?
Salt.
How does Indu feel at midnight on Thursday?
Indu feels overwhelmed and foggy, like a phone with forty apps open, but also knows the problem isn't stupidity.
Is Indu's plan for tomorrow a good one? Why?
Yes, writing one list, choosing three things and asking for a lighter shift frees up some mental space.
What might Amandeep have been thinking when she laughed at the salty tea?
Amandeep probably found it funny at first, though she might also notice Indu seems unusually scattered.

Read this:

It was the morning of Eid, and the house was a rush of cooking and guests about to arrive. Farida, five, was carrying Payal Aunty's special blue cup to the table when it slipped. Crack. It broke into three pieces.
Nobody had seen. Farida looked at the pieces, then at the kitchen door. Her tummy felt tight.
She picked up the biggest piece and walked into the kitchen. "Payal Aunty," she whispered, "I broke your cup. It fell."
Payal Aunty wiped her hands and knelt down. "Thank you for telling me, Farida. That was brave. Are your fingers okay?" Then they swept up the pieces together. "Cups break. Telling the truth is what matters."

What colour was the cup?
Blue.
How was Farida feeling before she walked into the kitchen?
Farida was scared, her tummy tight, afraid of being scolded.
What did Payal Aunty do that made honesty feel safe?
She thanked Farida, called it brave, checked her fingers and swept up together with her, saying telling the truth is what matters.
What would change if Payal Aunty had shouted?
Farida might learn that telling the truth is costly and hide the next broken thing.

Read this:

I'm Tarun, Vinita's uncle. Last Sunday she fell off the sofa at our house and howled. I tried talking fast and waving toys; it made things worse. Then her mother lifted her, rocked side to side, and sang the same short lullaby slowly, again and again. Her mother's hand made small circles on Vinita's back. Within a minute Vinita's crying slowed. She tucked her head under her mother's chin. I don't know exactly what changed inside her, but I noticed the slow rhythm did what my toys couldn't.

What did Tarun try first when Vinita cried?
He tried talking fast and waving toys, which made things worse.
Why might Vinita have tucked her head under her mother's chin?
She seemed to feel safe and comforted, looking for closeness as her body calmed, though Tarun cannot be sure what she felt.
What could Tarun try next time Vinita is upset?
He could hold her close, slow down, and use a calm voice and steady rocking instead of fast talk and toys.
How might Vinita's mother feel when she calms her daughter?
She would likely feel steady and connected, glad that her touch and song can settle Vinita.

Read this:

The first monsoon rain hit the colony. Pema, two, ran straight into the puddles by the gate, laughing and stamping.
Her neighbour Jomon, the same age, stood in the doorway and howled. His socks were wet. He tugged at them and would not move.
Jomon's father took the socks off and dried his feet. Jomon calmed, then watched Pema from the step.
"Same rain," Pema's mother said, smiling. "Two very different children."

Where did Pema run when the rain started?
Straight into the puddles by the gate.
What was Jomon feeling when he tugged at his wet socks?
Jomon felt upset and uncomfortable; the wet socks bothered him far more than the rain bothered Pema.
What did Jomon's father get right?
Jomon's father dealt with the wet socks that were bothering him, instead of telling him to be like Pema.
How does Pema's mother see the two children?
Pema's mother sees that each child reacts in their own way to the same rain, and doesn't judge either of them.

Read this:

Anand was the agriculture extension officer for six villages around Sirsi, and for months his monthly reports were late. He blamed himself: lazy, careless, bad with paper.
In April he noticed something. By two in the afternoon, after the field visits in the heat, he could barely read a form. At dawn, with the crows and the cool air, his head was sharp.
So he changed the day. Reports from five-thirty to seven, before anyone else woke. Every night he packed his field bag, filled the water bottles and wrote the next day's village list on a chit. Evenings were for easy things: dinner, the radio, a phone call home.
His brother Uday, who used to tease him, found him one morning writing by the window. "You? At this hour?"
"Me," Anand said. "Report's done. Go back to sleep."

When does Anand now write his reports?
He writes them from five-thirty to seven in the morning, before anyone else wakes.
How did Anand feel about himself before he changed his day?
He felt ashamed and frustrated, blaming himself as lazy, careless and bad with paper.
What steps helped Anand, and why are they wise?
He moved the reports to the cool, sharp dawn hours and packed his bag and wrote the village list each night, so hard work fits his best time and evenings need few decisions.
How might Uday see Anand now?
Uday, who used to tease him, is likely surprised and a bit impressed to find Anand finished with his report so early.

Read this:

"Ammi, the birthday dinner at Kabeer's goes on till ten-thirty. Can I stay?"
"Asif, no. Home by eight."
"Everyone's staying!"
"I said eight."
Asif went to his room and sat on the bed. Why eight? It's not the dinner she minds. He went back out. "Ammi, what's the worry, exactly?"
She put down the dishcloth. "That last bus. Empty roads. You alone."
"So it's the travel, not the party."
"It's the travel."
"What if my cousin Ayesha picks me up? She finishes work at ten near there."
Ammi looked at him for a long moment. "If Ayesha says yes, and you're at the gate when she comes."
"I'll call her now."
Ayesha texted back in a minute: "Fine, 10:30 sharp."

What time did Ammi first say Asif should be home?
Home by eight.
What was Ammi really worried about?
Ammi was anxious about the travel: the last bus, empty roads and Asif alone, not the party itself.
Which approach worked for Asif, and why?
Asking what the worry was, then solving that worry with a safe pickup; arguing "everyone's staying" had gotten him nowhere.
If you were Ayesha, what would you want from Asif?
You'd want him to be at the gate at 10:30 sharp, so the favour stays easy and trust grows.

metadata.subtype: Approach: separates a demand from the interest behind it [Thinking]

messages.content: We all "chipped in" for the farewell gift. Is that correct English?

Yes, it is correct and informal. "Chip in" means to give a share of money or help so that a group can do something together. It can also mean to add a comment in a conversation.
Examples: Ten of us chipped in for the gift. Elena chipped in with a useful idea.

(1) Why do we keep milk in the fridge?
(2) Could you explain the difference between "each other" and "one another"?
(3) Fix my grammar: My mother cooks very good.
(4) How would you explain "withstand" to a child?
(5) Is it "mischievious" or "mischievous"?

1. Cold keeps it from going sour quickly. Because the low temperature slows the growth of the germs that spoil milk.
2. They mean the same. Many writers use "each other" for two people and "one another" for more.
3. Write it as: My mother cooks very well. Why: use the adverb "well" to describe the verb "cooks".
4. "Withstand" is a verb. It means to survive or resist something strong.
5. It is "mischievous", with only three syllables.

Read this:

Last March, during my Class 10 exams, I did something my friends thought was crazy. Every evening at seven I shut my books and went for a walk with my brother Yash around the lake near our house. We didn't talk about exams. We counted ducks, argued about cricket, bought roasted corn. At nine I ate dinner with everyone, and at ten-thirty I was asleep.
My friends were studying till two. On the phone they sounded shaky and snappish. Sometimes I felt guilty, as if I wasn't trying hard enough.
But in the science paper, when a question on circuits came up that I'd revised only once, the answer was just there. I think my brain had done the filing while I slept. I'm Usha, and I still walk to that lake before anything important.

Where did Usha and Yash walk each evening?
Around the lake near their house.
How did Usha sometimes feel about the evening routine?
Usha sometimes felt guilty, as if not trying hard enough, while friends studied till two.
Why did Usha's routine help in the science paper?
Regular sleep, walks and meals kept Usha rested, so an answer revised only once came back easily.
What might the evening walks have meant for Yash?
For Yash they were probably a relaxed time with a sibling, counting ducks and arguing about cricket, away from exam talk.

Read this:

At Westlake High in Los Angeles, Soo-ah was the one who led debate practice, slammed the table when she made a point, and made Camila laugh until she snorted. At home, she answered her grandmother with "Ne, Halmeoni" and nothing else. She ate quietly, washed her bowl, and went to her room. She never invited anyone over. When Camila asked why, Soo-ah said, "My place is boring," and changed the subject. It worked. There were no questions from her grandmother about loud friends, and no questions from friends about her strict home. Then one Saturday Camila turned up unexpectedly with a borrowed book. Soo-ah opened the door, bowed slightly, and whispered, "Hi." Camila stared. "Who are you and what did you do with Soo-ah?" Later, Soo-ah lay on her bed thinking that nobody, not even her grandmother, knew both of her.

What did Soo-ah say when Camila asked why she never invited anyone over?
She said, "My place is boring," and changed the subject.
Why did keeping home and school apart feel sensible to Soo-ah?
It spared her tense questions from both sides, so she felt safer, though later she felt lonely that nobody knew both of her.
What small step could Soo-ah try to let the two worlds meet?
She could tell one trusted person, like Camila, a little about home, or let her grandmother hear one story about debate.
What was it like for Camila to see Soo-ah at her front door?
Camila was surprised and confused, since the quiet girl at the door didn't match the loud friend she knew.

metadata.subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Thursday night.
Aditi stopped me after the review today and said, very carefully, that the new approval process I set up is confusing people. That three vendors have complained. That it takes four days now instead of two.
Honestly. She has been like this since I got the role. She applied for it too, everyone knows that. Of course she thinks my process is bad.
And the vendors? They'll adjust. People always complain about change. The ones who can't see why we need it just aren't thinking big enough.
Riyaz said something similar last week. I told him it was a teething problem. He didn't bring it up again, which proves my point.
I'm not going to change a process just because a few people are unhappy. That's what weak leads do.
Still, four days. I'll check the numbers. Maybe next month.
— Zainab

How long does approval take now, according to Aditi?
It takes four days now instead of two.
Why does Zainab decide Aditi's feedback comes from jealousy?
Zainab feels threatened by the criticism and finds it easier to blame Aditi's motives than to admit the new process might be wrong.
What went wrong in how Zainab handled the feedback, and what could fix it?
Zainab treated every challenge as an attack and stopped learning; checking the four-day figure this week and asking Riyaz and the vendors for details would help.
What is it like for Riyaz after his concern was called a teething problem?
Riyaz may feel brushed off and decide it's pointless to raise problems with Zainab again.

Read this:

Note from the reception class, Pooja. Sarita opened a hospital in the book corner today. She made stethoscopes from wool and handed out roles: "You are the nurse, you are the patient." When Imran laughed during an injection she stopped everything. "Doctors don't laugh, it scares the patient." The children reset without adult help.
Later she spoke softly to a soft-toy patient: "It won't hurt much. I'm here." I stayed nearby and did not direct. Tomorrow I will bring some old bandage rolls for the corner.

What did Sarita make the stethoscopes from?
She made them from wool.
What does Sarita seem to feel about the hospital game being spoiled?
She takes the game seriously and wants it to feel real. She is protective of the pretend patient, so she stops the game when someone laughs.
What did Pooja choose to do while the hospital game went on?
Pooja stayed nearby without directing, then planned to bring some old bandage rolls to extend the play.
How might Imran feel when Sarita stops the game?
Imran may feel a little told off or embarrassed, but the children reset the game themselves, so the story carries on.
The teacher told good morning and we all stood up. Is 'told' right?

The teacher said good morning and we all stood up.
Why: Greetings go with "say". "Tell" needs a person right after it, as in "told us".
Courier wale se poochna hai "Parcel kab tak pahunchega?" English?
Ask: "When will the parcel arrive?"
Aur "Kya aap use kal laa sakte hain?" kaise bolun?
Say: "Can you bring it tomorrow?"

Read this:

Coach Chetan blew his whistle. "Neelam! That's the third pass you've dropped."
"I'm trying, Sir!"
"You're dragging your feet. Where's the fire from last week?"
"I don't know. My head hurts and everyone's annoying me."
"Everyone?"
"Everyone. Priya won't stop talking."
"Hm. When did you last drink water?"
"At lunch? Maybe."
"It's four o'clock and baking out here. Sit in the shade. Drink half this bottle, slowly."
"I'm fine."
"You're thirsty. Drink."
Five minutes later:
"Sir, my head's better. Sorry for snapping."
"Not your fault. New rule, whole team: water break every fifteen minutes."

What time is it when Chetan asks about water?
Four o'clock.
What made Chetan suspect thirst rather than laziness?
He was puzzled and concerned that Neelam, usually full of fire, was dragging her feet and complaining of a headache, so he asked about water.
Why is Chetan's new rule wiser than pushing Neelam harder?
Regular water breaks prevent the slump for the whole team, while pushing would only make a thirsty player slower and sharper.
What was practice like for Neelam before the break?
She had a headache and felt everyone was annoying, dropping passes even though she was trying.

metadata.subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

March: Avni, twenty-four, was offered a team-lead post with a raise at her Surat firm. But it meant sixty-hour weeks, and she was halfway through her chartered accountancy exams. Her friends said, "Take it! Money now." Her mentor, Vidya, asked, "Where do you want to be in five years?"
April: Avni turned down the post and kept her regular role. She studied every evening and all Sundays, skipping weddings and weekend trips. Some nights she cried from tiredness and questioned the decision.
The next January: Avni passed her final exams. Within a month, she was offered a senior role better than the one she'd turned down. She called Vidya, laughing and crying. "It was worth it."

What exams was Avni halfway through?
Her chartered accountancy exams.
How did Avni feel on some nights while studying?
She felt exhausted and doubtful, sometimes crying from tiredness.
What choice did Avni make, and what helped her make it?
She turned down the team-lead post to finish her exams, after Vidya's question about where she wanted to be in five years.
How might Vidya feel when Avni called?
She would likely feel proud and happy for Avni.
I usually have my dinner at the 8 o'clock. Is "the" correct?

I usually have my dinner at 8 o'clock.
Why: A clock time takes no "the" in front of it.
"Wo hamesha der se aata hai." Translate.
It is: "He always comes late." You can also say: "He is always late." Say "she" if you mean a woman.

Read this:

"Bidisha, you're in HR now, na?" Lakshmi Mashi put a sweet in her mouth. "Just put Pintu's CV on top. No interview drama. He's your own cousin."
Bidisha put her tea down. "Mashi, I can forward it. But I can't skip the interview for him."
"Why not? Who will know?"
"I will." Bidisha's cheeks went hot. "There are two hundred people who applied. Some of them have nobody inside. If I push Pintu ahead, I'm cheating them."
"So strangers matter more than family?"
"No!" Bidisha looked at Ma for help. "I love Pintu. I'll help him prepare. I'll do mock interviews with him all weekend. I just won't jump the line."
Ma said quietly, "Didi, she's right. If Pintu gets it fairly, nobody can ever say anything."
Lakshmi Mashi was silent, then sniffed. "Mock interviews, then. Saturday. And feed him properly, he forgets to eat when he's nervous."

What did Bidisha offer to do with Pintu all weekend?
Mock interviews.
What was Bidisha feeling when her cheeks went hot?
She felt uncomfortable and torn, not wanting to hurt her aunt or cousin, but sure that skipping the interview would be unfair to the other applicants.
What choice did Bidisha make, and why was it thoughtful rather than careless?
She refused to skip the process but offered real help preparing Pintu, keeping fairness to strangers while still showing loyalty to family.
How might Lakshmi Mashi see Bidisha's refusal at first, and how does it shift?
At first she sees it as choosing strangers over family, but Ma's words and the offer of help soften her into accepting the mock interviews.

metadata.subtype: Universal principle against loyalty to own circle [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the playgroup, Aditi's mother Vinita crouched and said, "Mama goes to buy milk, and I come back after snack." She waved from the door and did not sneak away. Aditi wailed for a moment, then picked up a wooden duck and returned to the sand tray. When a new volunteer sat down, Aditi edged behind Vinita's knee and stared, and only took a block once Vinita chatted easily and laughed with the volunteer. Nearby, Tejas's mother arrived late, and Tejas hit her arm and turned his back. She knelt and said, "You got very upset when Mama left the room. I'm back now." Tejas wept, then climbed into her lap. In the corner sat Zayn, who no longer cried when his caregiver left. He played silently with a spoon, flat and still, and grown-ups often remarked what a good boy he was. The playgroup leader noticed, sat beside him, spoke softly and offered a lap. That same afternoon the leader shared what they had seen with the centre's child welfare worker, so that someone could gently check in with Zayn's family.

What did Aditi pick up after her brief wail?
Aditi picked up a wooden duck.
How did Aditi's goodbye differ from Zayn's silence, and what did each show about what the children had learned?

Aditi's mother said a clear goodbye, waved from the door and came back after snack, so Aditi wailed for a moment and returned to the sand tray; Zayn no longer cried when his caregiver left and played silently, flat and still, which looks like being good but suggests his crying had brought no comfort.
What was Tejas feeling when he hit his mother's arm and turned his back?
He felt upset and angry, the fear of being left turned into fury.
How could Tejas's mother respond so that he does not learn to hide his needs?
She could keep welcoming him calmly and naming the feeling, as she did, rather than punishing the anger.

Read this:

Dear Naveen Sir,
You used to say college would be 'freedom with a hidden bill.' I get it now. In my first semester I had classes only in the mornings and nothing after two. No bells, no one checking. I slept through afternoons, watched series, and told myself I'd study 'in the evening.' The evening kept moving. I nearly failed the statistics mid-term. After that I sat down and made my day into a timetable I set for myself: library from three to five, a walk at six, calls home at nine. I even put in a 'lazy hour', so I'd stop feeling guilty about resting. It isn't perfect, but I passed the finals with a B. I wanted you to know your line stayed with me.
Regards,
Sharmila

What grade did Sharmila get in the finals?
A B.
Why did Sharmila add a 'lazy hour' to the timetable?
Sharmila wanted to rest without feeling guilty, making it easier to stick to the rest of the plan.
What would you advise a new college student based on Sharmila's letter?
Build your own timetable early, with fixed study blocks and planned rest, before a bad test forces it.
How might Naveen Sir feel reading this?
Touched and pleased that his warning stayed with Sharmila and helped. 🙂

Read this:

The mobile shop on the main road of Hoshiarpur had forty phones in the glass case, and Divyansh had been inside for two hours. The shopkeeper had brought out eleven, one by one. Camera, battery, storage, colour.
"This one," Divyansh said finally. Then, "No, wait, show the blue one again."
Jasleen, waiting outside on her scooter, came in. "You said you only need a good battery and a camera for your project photos."
"Yes, but this one has more storage, and that one is thinner."
He bought the thinner one. On the way home, riding pillion, he kept looking at it. "I think the other camera was better," he said. "Should I go back?"
Jasleen sighed. "You chose from eleven. Any of them would have been fine. Let this one be good."

How many phones did the shopkeeper bring out?
The shopkeeper brought out eleven phones.
Why did Divyansh want to go back after buying?
Divyansh felt unsure and dissatisfied, because with eleven options he kept wondering whether another camera was better.
What could Divyansh do to feel happier with a choice like this?
Divyansh could stick to the two things that mattered, battery and camera, compare a few phones and then let the choice be good.
How does Jasleen feel after two hours?
Jasleen is patient but tired and a bit exasperated, trying to help Divyansh accept a good choice.

Read this:

Monday: "Why is the sky blue? Why? But why? Why?" By the tenth why, Kalyani was chopping onions with a headache. "Because I said so!" Rafiq went quiet and wandered off to his room.

Wednesday: "Why do cats have whiskers?"

"To feel their way in the dark," Kalyani said. "Why do you think?"

Rafiq thought hard. "So they don't bump their heads?"

"Good idea."

The following Monday: "Why does bread go hard?" Kalyani smiled. "What do you think?" Rafiq's answer took five minutes, and she kept chopping happily.

What was Kalyani chopping on Monday?
Onions.
What was Rafiq feeling when he went quiet and wandered off on Monday?
He was probably hurt and disappointed that his questions were shut down; his whys came from curiosity. He may also have been wanting his mother's attention.
Which approach worked better, and why?
Giving a short honest answer and then asking "Why do you think?" worked, because it fed his curiosity and let Kalyani rest while he did the thinking.
How does the change affect Kalyani?
Instead of feeling exhausted by the questions, she can smile and keep chopping while Rafiq thinks aloud.

Read this:

"Darshan, this drawing of the old fort is amazing."
"It's nothing, Disha. Anyone can do it."
"Anyone? I can't draw a straight line."
"It was luck. The pencil just went right."
"For three hours? I watched you shade those stones."
"The stones are easy."
"Ma'am put it on the notice board."
"She puts everyone's up."
"She put three up. Out of forty."
"She probably felt sorry for me."
"Why would she feel sorry for you?"
"Because I'm bad at maths."
"What does maths have to do with the fort?"
Darshan shrugged. "I don't know. Nothing's ever really good. There's always a reason."
Disha looked at the drawing again. "Well, I think it's good. And I'm not saying it out of pity."
Darshan picked at the corner of his sketchbook. He didn't say thank you. But he didn't say luck again either.

How many drawings did Ma'am put on the notice board?
She put three up, out of forty.
Why does Darshan keep saying the drawing was luck?
Darshan feels uncomfortable with praise and sees himself as not good enough, so he explains away every compliment to keep that view.
What did Disha do that challenged Darshan's excuses?
She answered each excuse with facts, the three hours of shading and three out of forty, and said she wasn't praising out of pity.
How might Disha feel when Darshan waves away her compliment?
Disha might feel a little frustrated and puzzled, since she means it sincerely.

Read this:

Noor, you keep teasing me about ordering the same paneer roll every Friday, so let me explain properly. I'm Kashish, I've eaten at the same stall outside college for two years, and I know exactly what I like. It's not that I'm scared of new things. It's that when I know the ground, I can go deep. Same with my lab routine: same bench, same order of steps, same notebook layout. That's why my notes are the ones everyone photocopies before exams. What got me was last month, when the trip plan changed four times in one week. Goa, then Lonavala, then nowhere, then Goa again. I felt sick every time the group chat buzzed. You all thought I was being difficult. I just needed one plan to hold on to. Give me a fixed plan and I'll be the one who remembers the tickets.

What does Kashish order every Friday?
The same paneer roll.
How did Kashish feel when the trip plan kept changing?
Kashish felt anxious, even sick, every time the group chat buzzed, because there was no single plan to hold on to.
How could the friends plan the next trip so Kashish can enjoy it?
Fix the plan early, change it only if they must, and maybe let Kashish handle the tickets, since Kashish is the reliable one once a plan is set.
How might Noor see the Friday paneer roll after this explanation?
Noor might stop seeing it as boring and see it as Kashish's steady style, the same one that makes Kashish's notes worth photocopying.
Why do we put a lid on a pot when we want water to boil sooner?
The lid keeps the heat in. Because it stops warm steam from escaping, so the water gains heat faster than it loses it.

Read this:

At the nursing college hostel in Bhubaneswar, the warden, Nirmala Ma'am, found Damini's bed empty at study hour. She was at the gate when Damini came back at eleven, holding a half-eaten ice cream and a friend's hand, both of them laughing.
"Where were you?"
"Sorry, Ma'am. A friend's birthday at the ice cream place. It was so much fun." Damini's smile faded a little. "I know I missed revision for the pharmacology test."
"Was it worth it?"
Damini thought honestly. "The evening, yes. The guilt, no. I've been feeling it since the ice cream."
Nirmala Ma'am nodded. "Then study hour tomorrow is yours to make up. Goodnight."
Damini went up the stairs slowly, still smiling, still a little uneasy.

What was Damini holding when she came back?
She was holding a half-eaten ice cream and a friend's hand.
How does Damini feel about the evening, according to her own words?
She enjoyed the evening but has felt guilty since the ice cream, torn between the fun and the revision she missed.
How did Nirmala Ma'am handle Damini's late return?
She asked honestly and gave Damini a chance to make up study hour the next day, rather than punishing harshly.
How might Nirmala Ma'am see Damini's honesty?
Nirmala Ma'am likely appreciates it, seeing that Damini understands the pull between fun and duty.

metadata.subtype: Pleasure versus duty in the hostel [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Last spring I got into a six-month design residency in Lisbon. My first reaction was panic: I'll lose my job, I'll come back with nothing.
Tanvir made me sit down with a notebook. Three questions. What's the worst that can happen? That I come back and need to look for work for a few months. Could I survive that? Yes; I've done it before. What's the likely gain? A portfolio I couldn't build here, and people I'd never meet otherwise.
Then the back-up plan. I asked my manager about unpaid leave. She said no, but offered to write me a strong reference. I reached out to two former clients who said they'd send freelance work.
So I went. The residency was hard and wonderful. When I came back, it took me seven weeks to find a new role. Scary weeks, but survivable ones, exactly as I'd planned.
Eshaan

How long was the design residency?
Six months.
How did Eshaan feel on first getting into the residency?
Eshaan felt panic, afraid of losing the job and coming back with nothing.
How did Eshaan turn the choice into a calculated risk?
By asking about the worst outcome, whether it was survivable and the likely gain, then setting up a back-up with a reference and freelance clients.
How might Tanvir have felt watching Eshaan panic at first?
Tanvir was probably concerned but steady, helping Eshaan think it through with three questions instead of deciding for Eshaan.
My office people say "He is out of station." My foreign client did not understand.
"Out of station" is common in India, but other English speakers may not know it. Say: "He is out of town." That is clear everywhere.

Read this:

"Mummy, I have to tell you something about my mark sheet."
"What is it, Sangeeta?"
Sangeeta's palms were sweating. She had thought of stuffing the paper into her school bag and saying it had not come. "I got low marks in maths. I was scared to show you."
"Let me see." Gopika read it slowly. "Thank you for telling me at once."
"I made a plan. I will do a page of sums every day and ask Sir to explain fractions again."
"That is a good plan. Shall I sit with you sometimes?"
Sangeeta let out her breath.

What did Sangeeta think of doing with the paper before she told her mother?
She thought of stuffing it into her school bag and saying it had not come.
Why was Sangeeta scared to show the mark sheet?
She feared her mother would be disappointed in her, and that fear made her palms sweat.
What worked in the way Sangeeta shared her result?
She told her mother right away and came with a plan, which kept the fear from growing as it would have if she hid the paper.
How might Gopika have felt while reading the mark sheet?
Gopika probably felt concerned but chose to stay calm and thank her daughter, and to offer help instead of blame.

Read this:

At the hospital billing office, Ayesha found the error on a Monday: a patient had been charged twice for the same scan. The money had already been collected.
She took it to her senior, Vikas. He looked at it and sighed. "If we refund now, the month's report shows a mistake from our desk. Just adjust it quietly in next month's bill. Nobody will notice."
Ayesha felt her face grow hot. Vikas had trained her. He had covered for her when she was new. And he was the one who would write her appraisal in June.
She went back to her desk and stared at the screen for an hour.
Then she walked back to Vikas's desk. "I can't hide it. The patient paid twice. I'll write the refund note today and say it was a system double-entry, which it was. I'll take the question from finance if they ask."
Vikas didn't speak to her for two weeks. The refund went through on Wednesday. Her hands shook when she signed it.

What had the patient been charged twice for?
The same scan.
What was Ayesha feeling during the hour at her desk?
Ayesha felt caught between loyalty to Vikas, fear for her appraisal and her own conscience about the patient's money.
Which choice did Ayesha make, and what did it cost her?
Ayesha refused to hide the error and wrote the refund note, which cost her two weeks of cold silence from Vikas.
How might the patient feel when the refund arrives?
The patient would likely feel relieved and more trusting of the hospital, having been treated fairly.

Read this:

Himani, you keep saying I'm lucky I got into the Delhi college. Okay, let me be honest. Yes, I was lucky. My school had a proper library and a teacher who stayed after class for us. My parents could pay for entrance coaching; lots of families can't. And the economics paper that year was easy. All luck. But I also woke up at five for eight months and did every past paper twice. Both things happened. I try to remember both, because if I only remember the luck, I feel like a fraud, and if I only remember the work, I start judging people who didn't get in. So this semester I just work on what I can: attendance, notes, sleep. The rest I let go. I'm Sarita, by the way, not a genius.

What did Sarita do for eight months?
Sarita woke up at five and did every past paper twice.
Why does Sarita try to remember both luck and effort?
Remembering only luck makes Sarita feel like a fraud, and only effort leads to judging others; holding both keeps the pride honest and the view of others kind.
What does Sarita focus on this semester, and why is that wise?
Attendance, notes and sleep, the parts within reach; acting on those while letting go of the rest avoids both blame and helplessness.
How might Himani hear Sarita's answer to 'you're lucky'?
Himani might feel taken seriously rather than brushed off, since Sarita agrees about the luck while also sharing the hidden work.

metadata.subtype: Balanced view of luck and effort [Response]

messages.content:
Hi, I have three quick questions.
Can you help with these? I saw the word "intricate" in a book. What is it? If a neighbour's door is open and nobody answers, what is a careful step? Correct this sentence: My phone is more cheaper than yours.

1. Intricate means having many small parts that are closely connected. It is an adjective.
2. Call out from outside and wait for a reply. Because walking in without being asked is not polite and may not be safe.
3. It should be: My phone is cheaper than yours. Why: "Cheaper" is already a comparative, so "more" is not needed.

Read this:

Note, KG-B, Tuesday.
Clean-up time was loud. Zubin and two others kept building. When our helper, Mrs Rao, snapped "Stop NOW," Mahima dropped her blocks at once and stood stiffly by the shelf, first to finish. Mrs Rao praised her, but Mahima did not smile. She kept glancing at Mrs Rao and twisting her pinafore.
Later she whispered to me, "Is Rao ma'am angry?" I sat beside her and said nobody was cross with her. I will suggest a calm clap-song signal for clean-up, and mention it to her parents at pickup.

Who snapped "Stop NOW" at clean-up time?
Mrs Rao, the helper, snapped "Stop NOW."
What does Mahima's twisting of her pinafore suggest?
It suggests Mahima felt anxious and scared of disapproval, not proud, even though she looked like the best-behaved child.
Why is a calm clap-song signal a better idea for clean-up?
It gets the children moving without fear, so tidying comes from the routine rather than from worry about an angry voice.
How might Mrs Rao see Mahima's quick tidying?
Mrs Rao probably sees it as good discipline and feels pleased, without noticing the worry behind it.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, 9B, Thursday

Arnab has been running the animal shelter donation drive almost single-handedly since October. He is at the collection table every break, on the phone with the shelter after school, and I have seen him doing the spreadsheets in maths class. His homework has been missing for two weeks.

Today his friend Tenzin came to me quietly. "Arnab hasn't eaten lunch all week. He says every rupee matters and he can't stop." I asked Arnab to stay back.

He looked exhausted. When I asked about rest, he said, "If I rest, dogs go hungry. I feel guilty even sitting here."

I told him the shelter needs people who will still be helping next year, not someone who collapses in November. We made a rota together: Tenzin and four others each take a break shift. Arnab keeps the spreadsheets, but only on Wednesdays.

He agreed, reluctantly. At lunch I saw him eating, with Tenzin at the table.

How long has Arnab's homework been missing?
His homework has been missing for two weeks.
What was Arnab feeling when asked about rest?
Arnab felt guilty and anxious, as if resting would mean dogs going hungry.
How did the class teacher help Arnab keep the cause going without burning out?
The teacher made a rota with Tenzin and four others and limited the spreadsheets to Wednesdays, so Arnab could rest and still help.
How does Tenzin see what Arnab is doing?
Tenzin is worried about Arnab not eating, which is why Tenzin quietly told the teacher.

Read this:

“Suraj Bhaiya, I'm going to be better at maths this year.”
“Great. How?”
“Just… better. I'll work harder.”
Two weeks later.
“Santosh, how's the ‘better at maths’?”
“Bad. I got 9 in the class test.”
“Did you practise?”
“I meant to. Every day I say ‘today I'll do maths’, and then it's night.”
“Okay. Try this. After tea, five problems. Only five. From the exercise at the back.”
“Only five?”
“Five. Then tick them off on this paper.”
A week later, Santosh ran in waving the paper. “Look! Seven days, seven ticks! Thirty-five problems!”
“And?”
“And I understood the multiplying thing. The one with the zeroes.”
Suraj grinned. “See? ‘Better’ is hard to start. ‘Five after tea’ is easy.”

How many problems did Santosh do in a week?
He did thirty-five problems, five a day for seven days.
How did Santosh feel when he ran in waving the paper?
He felt excited and proud, because he could see seven ticks and had finally understood the multiplying with zeroes.
Why did “five problems after tea” work when “better at maths” didn't?
A specific small goal was easy to start and easy to check, unlike a vague wish.
How might Suraj Bhaiya feel seeing the seven ticks?
Suraj Bhaiya likely feels pleased and proud that his simple idea helped his little brother.
My brother do his homework after dinner.
My brother does his homework after dinner. Why: "Brother" is third person singular, so "do" becomes "does".

Read this:

I'm Vijay. On prize day last year, the chief guest held out her hand for a handshake, and I was so excited I bumped it with my fist instead. She blinked, then laughed and bumped back. My friend Gargi nearly fell off her chair. Afterwards she explained, like a teacher: “High-five is for winning something with your mates. Fist bump is for saying hi to friends. Handshake is for being polite to grown-ups you don't know.” I made her practise all three with me behind the stage. Now I think about who's in front of me before my hand moves. The chief guest didn't mind, though.

What did the chief guest hold out on prize day?
The chief guest held out her hand for a handshake.
What was Vijay feeling when the fist bump happened?
Vijay was so excited that the fist bump came out by mistake, and afterwards felt a bit embarrassed and amused.
What did Gargi teach Vijay, and why is it useful?
She explained when to use a high-five, a fist bump and a handshake, so Vijay can choose the right greeting for each person.
How did the chief guest react to the fist bump?
She blinked in surprise, then laughed and bumped back, taking it as warmth rather than rudeness.

Read this:

I help in the reception class at a Leicester school, and during the Diwali term I noticed something about Tanvir, who is five. Every morning just before snack he'd roll on the carpet, cry about nothing and push other children. Mrs Patel, the teacher, would move him to the quiet corner. After snack he was gentle and chatty. I can't know what was going on inside him. But one day I saw him eyeing the fruit bowl before he got cross. I told Mrs Patel. She started offering him a snack when he arrived, and the rolling stopped.

Jahnavi

Where did Jahnavi notice Tanvir eyeing something?
At the fruit bowl, before he got cross.
What might Jahnavi have felt watching Tanvir before snack?
Jahnavi probably felt concerned and curious, sensing there was more to his crossness than naughtiness.
Why was Mrs Patel's change a good one?
Offering Tanvir a snack on arrival met his hunger, which stopped the behaviour better than the quiet corner did.
How might Tanvir feel after the change?
Tanvir would likely feel calmer and happier, no longer struggling through a hungry morning.

metadata.subtype: Teacher notices a child cannot focus before snack [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the small school at Bylakuppe, Aparna stood up to read her Kannada poem. Halfway through, from the back row, came a loud hrrm-hrrm. She stumbled. A moment later: a snort. Aparna's cheeks burned. She finished fast and sat down, glaring back at Tenzin. At break she marched up to him. "You think my Kannada is funny?" Tenzin looked baffled, then sneezed. "What? No! I've had a cold for days. My nose is completely blocked." He pulled out a crumpled handkerchief as proof. "The snort was me trying to breathe. Sorry it came in the middle of your poem." Aparna's shoulders dropped. "I thought you were laughing at me." "Your poem was good. The part about the monsoon." She almost smiled. "Okay. Maybe carry two handkerchiefs."

What had Tenzin had for days?
A cold, with a completely blocked nose.
What was Aparna feeling when her cheeks burned?
Aparna felt embarrassed and angry, thinking Tenzin was mocking her Kannada.
What would have been a calmer way to find out what the sounds meant?
Asking Tenzin calmly before glaring or accusing; once she asked, it turned out to be a cold, not mockery.
How did Tenzin experience Aparna's accusation?
Tenzin was baffled and apologetic, since the snort was only him trying to breathe through a cold.

Read this:

"You quit? Why would you quit? What were you thinking? What about the loan? Did you even talk to anyone?"
"Tarun, stop. You sound like a lawyer."
"I'm just asking!"
"You're firing at me. I can't think." Ayesha turned toward the window.
Tarun stopped. Breathed. Sat down beside her. "Sorry. I got scared. Can I try again?"
"...Okay."
"What happened at work that made you want to leave?"
Ayesha was quiet. Then: "My manager's been shouting at me for months. On Friday he threw a file at the wall near my head. I couldn't go back."
Tarun's face changed. "Oh, Ayesha. I didn't know."
"You didn't ask like that before."
"I'm asking now. What do you need?"
"Just help me tell Ammi. And maybe look at job listings with me."

What did Ayesha's manager throw at the wall?
A file, near Ayesha's head.
What was Ayesha feeling when Tarun fired his first questions?
Ayesha felt attacked and overwhelmed, unable to think, and turned away toward the window.
What did Tarun change that led to a better answer?
Tarun apologised, slowed down and asked one open, caring question: what happened at work that led to leaving.
How did Tarun feel once he heard the real reason?
Tarun felt shocked and sorry, realising how little was known about what Ayesha had been going through.
Tell me the final word of chapter seven in that novel on my shelf.
Your copy of the novel is not here with me, so I can't tell. Open the book to the chapter and read the final line.

Read this:

At the Lucknow school canteen, Avni's friends were laughing about Rehana's new haircut. "She looks like a boy now." "Maybe her mum cut it with kitchen scissors."
Avni looked across the canteen. Rehana was sitting alone, touching the back of her head.
Avni remembered when her own hair had been cut too short, and how she'd worn a cap for a week.
"What if it were you they were talking about?" she said. "How would you feel?"
Her friends shifted uncomfortably.
"Anyway, is anyone going to the science fair?" Avni asked. The conversation moved on. Later, she told Rehana, "Your hair looks nice."

What were Avni's friends laughing about?
Rehana's new haircut.
What did Avni feel when she saw Rehana touching her hair?
She felt empathy, remembering her own too-short haircut and wearing a cap for a week.
How did Avni stop the gossip?
She asked her friends how they would feel if it were them, then changed the subject to the science fair.
How might Rehana feel when Avni compliments her hair?
Rehana would likely feel comforted and less self-conscious.

Read this:

Jaya, you want to know why I got so quiet that summer? Let me just say it.

I'm Shankar. My parents run a tea stall at the bus stand, and that year my uncle, who helped them, moved to Dubai. So when my school selected me for the state-level science camp, I knew what the answer would be before I asked. So I didn't ask. I threw the selection letter in my drawer and told my teacher I couldn't go.

My parents never knew. I worked the stall all May, pouring tea and counting coins, telling myself I was being a good son.

But inside, something went sour. I stopped studying science. I got annoyed at small things, like Amma asking me to fetch milk. Last month Amma found the letter while cleaning. She sat down on my bed and asked, "Why didn't you tell us?" I didn't have an answer that made sense.

Where did Shankar put the selection letter?
In his drawer.
How did Shankar feel inside during that summer?
Shankar felt quietly bitter and resentful, which showed in losing interest in science and getting annoyed at small things.
What might have happened if Shankar had shown the letter?
The family might have found a way, like help from a neighbour or a shorter stay, and at least would have known what was being given up.
How might Amma have felt finding the letter?
Amma likely felt hurt and sad, realising her son had given up a chance without letting the family even consider it.

Read this:

"Urmila, you okay? You've been staring at your phone for ten minutes."
"Fine, Saurabh. Nikhil just cancelled dinner again."
"Third time this month?"
"He's busy. And he says my cooking's not worth rushing home for anyway." She laughed.
Saurabh didn't laugh. "He says that?"
"Oh, he's joking. That's just how he talks."
"Last week he called you useless in front of your sister. You told me."
"He was stressed." She shrugged. "Everyone's partner is a bit like that."
Saurabh paused. He could argue. He'd tried with a friend before, and it had ended the friendship.
"Can I say one thing, and then I'll drop it?"
"...Okay."
"It doesn't sound like joking to me. It sounds hurtful. And if you ever want to talk, my door's open. No lectures."
Urmila looked down. "Noted," she said. Then, softer: "Thanks."

How many times did Nikhil cancel dinner this month?
Three times this month.
Why did Saurabh decide not to argue with Urmila?
Saurabh felt concerned for her but wary, remembering that arguing with a friend before had ended the friendship, so he chose to speak once and stay open.
What small step did Saurabh take that keeps him useful to Urmila?
He asked permission, named the hurt once, promised to drop it, and offered an open door without lectures.
What might Urmila be feeling when she says "Thanks" more softly?
Urmila may feel touched and a little exposed, as if part of her agrees that the comments hurt.
Dukaan par bolna hai "Ye mera size nahi hai, thoda bada chahiye." English?
Say: "This is not my size. I need a slightly bigger one."

Read this:

Monday. Over dinner, Ankita told Tanuja her team manager had shouted at her again in front of everyone, and made her stay till ten to redo a report. Tanuja's first words were, "Why do you let him do that?" Ankita put down her fork and didn't finish her food.
Wednesday. Tanuja kept thinking about her question. Why do you let him. As if Ankita were the one choosing. She wrote it differently in her head: who shouted? He did. Who decided she must stay till ten? He did. Who had the power in that room? Not Ankita.
Saturday. Tanuja sat with Ankita on the balcony. "I asked the wrong question on Monday. I'm sorry. He chose to shout. He chose to keep you late. What do you want to do?" Ankita let out a long breath. "I want to write it all down and take it to HR." "Then let's write it now." They started a list, with dates.

Until what time did the manager make Ankita stay?
He made her stay till ten to redo a report.
How did Ankita react to "Why do you let him do that?"
Ankita felt hurt and blamed, putting down her fork and not finishing her food.
What question did Tanuja learn to ask instead, and why is it better?
Who acted and who had the power, because it puts responsibility back on the manager who shouted and kept Ankita late.
What was the week like for Tanuja after asking the wrong question?
Tanuja felt uneasy and regretful for days, until she found a better question and could support Ankita properly.

Read this:

Zubin, you're fifteen now, so listen to something from your Manjula aunty's school days.
The new maths teacher, Mr D'Souza, was very shy. My whole gang decided to hide the duster and chalk before his class. Leela said, “Everybody's doing it, Manju. If you back out, you're not one of us.”
I felt sick all morning. Not about the chalk, you know, but about being alone at lunch.
When the bell went, I stood at the door and couldn't make myself go in first. Then I watched him search the table, go pink, and apologise to us, of all things. That's when I went to the cupboard and handed him the chalk. Leela didn't speak to me for a week. Mr D'Souza thanked me every day for a month.

What did the gang decide to hide before class?
They decided to hide the duster and chalk.
What was young Manjula most afraid of that morning?
She was afraid of being alone at lunch; she felt sick about losing her gang, not about the prank itself.
What turning point in the story changed Manjula's choice?
Watching Mr D'Souza go pink and apologise made her see the real cost, so she handed him the chalk despite Leela's threat.
How might Mr D'Souza have experienced that class?
He was likely embarrassed and flustered, then grateful, which is why he thanked Manjula every day for a month.

Study hour at the girls' hostel ran from six to half past eight. Himani spread out her homework and chose the nicest bits first: a poster of the solar system, then copying a poem in her best writing. The glitter pens came out. Urmila, at the next desk, was already scratching away at fractions. By eight the poster was beautiful and the poem neat, but eight sums still waited. Himani's eyes kept closing. She rushed through them, guessing at two. Next day the teacher returned the notebook with three red crosses and a note: 'Careless. Were you tired?' Himani stared at the crosses, cheeks hot.

What were the first two things Himani did during study hour?
A poster of the solar system, then copying a poem in her best writing.
What was Himani feeling when she stared at the red crosses?
Her hot cheeks suggest she felt embarrassed and disappointed, since the mistakes came from rushing while sleepy.
What would you change first in Himani's plan?
Do the fractions at six while fresh, and keep the poster and poem for the end when she's tired; the fun parts need less thinking.
How might Urmila see Himani's evening?
Urmila did the fractions first, so Urmila might admire the poster but wonder why the hard sums were left so late.

From her balcony in their Bengaluru apartment, Mehak had watched pigeons for a week. Why did their heads bob when they walked? None of her textbooks said. She tried walking with her head bobbing and felt silly. She asked her uncle, Vijay, who shrugged. 'Ask the internet.' Instead, Mehak filmed a pigeon on his phone, slowed it down and noticed the head stayed still for a moment, then jerked forward. 'It's like they're taking photos!' she said. She made a small chart of her findings and pinned it above her desk, though no teacher would ever see it.

Whose phone did Mehak use to film the pigeon?
She used her uncle Vijay's phone.
Why did Mehak keep investigating even though no teacher would see her chart?
She was driven by her own curiosity and enjoyed finding the answer for its own sake.
What could Vijay do to encourage Mehak's inquiry next time?
He could ask her what she thinks is happening and help her test it, rather than just shrugging.
How might a science teacher react if Mehak showed her chart?
The teacher would likely be delighted and might invite Mehak to share it with the class. 🙂

After school on Tuesday, Rania and Emil sat at the kitchen table in Emil's flat in Copenhagen with their geography books open at volcanoes. "Five questions each," Rania said. "Then swap." They wrote in silence. Rania's questions were all about types of volcanoes. Emil's were all about why they erupt: the plates and the magma. They swapped and answered. Rania got stuck on Emil's question about plates sliding under each other. Emil explained it with two slices of bread pushed together on the table. Then Emil couldn't name a shield volcano, and Rania showed him the picture of the wide, flat one.

What did Emil use to explain plates sliding under each other?
Two slices of bread pushed together on the table.
How might Rania have felt when the bread made the plates clear?
She probably felt relieved and pleased that a gap she was stuck on suddenly made sense 😊
What could make their next session even better?
Swap topics, so each writes questions on the part they know less; mixing their questions is what showed the gaps.
What was the session like for Emil?
Emil got to teach with the bread and learn about shield volcanoes from Rania, so he gained as both teacher and learner.

I'm Keerthana, Zainab's roommate. When her mother fell ill in August, Zainab said it would be a few weeks. By October it clearly wasn't. She was taking the night bus home every Friday and coming back on Monday grey-faced, and she'd missed two quizzes.
One evening she came back from the academic adviser's office with a stapled sheet. She sat on her bed and read it out to me. "Drop two of my five courses this term. Take them next year. Keep the three I can manage from home on weekends." At the bottom there was a line: "Return to full load: January, review with adviser in December."
She didn't cry, which surprised me. She looked almost lighter, though I can't say what she felt. That week she went home on Thursday instead of Friday and came back with her notes actually finished.

How many courses did Zainab drop that term?
She dropped two of her five courses.
What might Zainab have been feeling in October before seeing the adviser?
She was likely exhausted and worried, coming back grey-faced every Monday after missing two quizzes.
What else could Zainab have done if even three courses became too much?
She could have asked the adviser about a full term break with a plan to return, since adapting the goal is better than failing several courses.
How does the change look to Keerthana?
Keerthana is surprised Zainab didn't cry and sees her looking lighter and finishing her notes, though Keerthana can't know her feelings for sure.

The summer our electricity got cut for two weeks, I did my Class 10 revision under the streetlight outside our building. I'm Himani, and that's the summer I got angry in a useful way. I was also angry in a useless way, for a while. I'd watch Papa come home tired from the loading dock and think, why couldn't you have done better? Then I'd feel disgusted with myself for thinking it. My friend Farhan, whose family runs the tea stall on our corner, sat with me under the light one night and said, 'You know your papa carries sacks all day so you can sit here with books, right?' That stayed with me. I stopped blaming Papa, and I stopped blaming myself for our small flat. I kept the anger, but I pointed it at the syllabus. I topped the district. Papa framed the certificate above the gas stove.

Where did Himani revise when the electricity was cut?
Under the streetlight outside the building.
What was Himani feeling when watching Papa come home tired?
Himani felt resentful, then guilty and disgusted at having such a thought about Papa.
How did Himani use the anger in a helpful way?
By pointing it at the syllabus instead of at Papa or at being poor, which led to topping the district.
How does Farhan see Papa's work?
Farhan sees it as a sacrifice made so Himani can study, and wants Himani to see it that way too.

At the inter-school relay in Chennai, Uma dropped the baton on the last exchange, and her team finished fourth instead of first. Walking back past the stands, she felt it burn: the gasp from the crowd, Mahima's face as she waited with her hand out for a baton that never came. On the bus, the old voice started: you always choke. Uma caught it. She thought of what she had said to Mahima last month after Mahima's false start: 'One bad exchange doesn't make you a bad runner. Let's drill it.' So she said it to herself, quietly. Then she turned round in her seat. 'Mahima, that was on me. I'm sorry. Can we practise exchanges every morning this week?' Mahima blinked, then grinned. 'Seven o'clock?' For five mornings they passed the baton until it felt like a handshake. At the zonal meet, the exchange was clean.

Where did Uma's team finish in the relay?
Fourth instead of first.
What was Uma feeling walking back past the stands?
She felt the burn of shame and disappointment, replaying the gasp and Mahima's face.
How did Uma treat herself in a way that led to improvement?
She talked to herself as she had to Mahima, owned the mistake, and set up daily exchange practice.
How does Mahima respond to Uma's apology?
She seems surprised, then happy to practise, suggesting she values the apology and the plan.

Suraj, you asked why I disappeared for a month. I'm Disha, twenty-two, and when my father had his surgery in March, everything fell on me at once. The hospital forms, the electricity bill, my little brother's school fees, my own job. I'd sit at the table with a pile of papers and just stare. I couldn't start anything. One night I cried in the bathroom for an hour. The next morning, my manager noticed and asked if I was okay. I told her. She gave me two days off, and my aunt came to stay. We made a list together and split it. It's still a lot, but I'm moving again.

Who noticed Disha was struggling at work?
Her manager.
What was Disha feeling while staring at the pile of papers?
Disha felt overwhelmed and paralysed, flooded by the sudden weight of responsibilities.
What turned things around for Disha?
Telling the manager, accepting help from an aunt and splitting the tasks into a list.
How might Suraj feel hearing why Disha disappeared?
Concerned and sorry, and glad Disha finally shared it.

On Monday Yamini wore the new blue kurta her mother had ironed twice and took the 8:12 fast local to Lower Parel, grinning at her reflection in the train window. A real job. A salary slip with her name on it.
By eleven the grin had gone stiff. Her team at the bank spoke a different language: KYC exceptions, T+1, recon breaks. Leela, at the next desk, cleared a queue of forty cases while explaining a process on the phone and eating an apple. Yamini opened the training manual and read the same page three times.
At lunch she hid in the washroom and texted a friend: "Everyone here is so smart. I think HR picked the wrong CV." Then she added, "But the view from the 14th floor is unreal 😍"
She went back to her desk, opened a blank page in her notebook and titled it: Words I don't know yet.

What title did Yamini give the page in her notebook?
Words I don't know yet.
What does Yamini's text to her friend reveal about her mixed feelings?
She feels anxious that HR picked the wrong CV, yet excited and proud about the job and the view.
What could help Yamini in her first weeks?
Keep her list of unknown words and ask Leela to explain a few each day, instead of hiding in the washroom.
How might Leela see the new colleague at the next desk?
Leela is probably busy and doesn't realise how intimidating that speed looks, and might happily help if asked 🙂
