Two hours into the power cut Leela had sighed thirty times, and Deepak had kicked the sofa twice. Rain drummed on the window, so going out was no use. "This is the worst evening," Deepak said. Then the torch beam slid across the wall and Leela's fingers moved without thinking. A rabbit. "Deepak, look." He frowned, then made a dog with his hand, and the dog chased the rabbit. A crocodile joined, then a giant bird, and they invented a story about a rabbit crossing a river with mangoes for a sleeping king. Amma looked in from the kitchen and stayed, holding her tea, to watch the crocodile. When the lights returned, both groaned. "Switch it off," said Deepak. "We are not finished."

What animal did Leela make first with her hands in the torch beam?
Leela made a rabbit first.
What was Deepak feeling at the start of the evening?
Bored and cross, as shown when he kicked the sofa and called it the worst evening.
What other approach could the siblings try if the power cut lasted even longer?
They could play a guessing game or sing, because those also need no electricity and keep them busy together. 😊
How might Amma see the siblings' game after such a restless start?
With relief and warmth, since she stayed in the doorway with her tea to watch instead of leaving.

"Jaya, when I was about your age, I planted two bean seeds. One in the sun, one in the dark cupboard. I was sure the dark one would grow faster, because I thought seeds like to hide. I watered both every day. After a week, both sprouted! But the cupboard one was tall, thin and yellow, and the sunny one was short, strong and green. I was so surprised. That's when I learned to guess, then test, then look properly." Manoj pointed at her science book. "What's your guess about the ice cubes?"

Where did Manoj plant the two bean seeds?
One in the sun and one in the dark cupboard.
How did Manoj feel about the dark-seed guess before and after the test?
Manoj felt sure the dark seed would grow faster, thinking seeds like to hide, and was then surprised when the sunny one grew short, strong and green.
What could Jaya learn from Manoj's story for her ice experiment?
She could make a guess, test it and then look carefully at what actually happens.
How might Jaya feel hearing that Manoj's guess was partly wrong?
She might feel it's okay to guess wrong, since that's part of learning.

Monday: The principal announced that Arjav from 10C had died in a road accident over the weekend. The hall went silent. Lalit didn't cry. He felt nothing at all, like cotton wool in his chest. He and Arjav had played on the same football team.
Wednesday: The school held a candlelight vigil in the courtyard. Parul, beside him, was sobbing. Others laid marigolds by Arjav's photo. Lalit held his candle and watched the flame, still numb. He felt terrible for not crying. Was something wrong with him?
Friday: Lalit went to the counsellor, Mrs Bose. "Everyone was crying. I just stood there."
She said gently, "People grieve differently. Some cry. Some feel numb, especially at first. Neither means you cared less."
Lalit let out a long breath. On Saturday, alone at the football ground, he cried for the first time.

What did others lay by Arjav's photo?
Marigolds.
What was Lalit feeling during the vigil?
Lalit felt numb and then guilty for not crying, worried something was wrong with him.
How did Mrs Bose help Lalit?
She explained that people grieve differently and that numbness doesn't mean caring less, which eased his guilt.
How might Parul have experienced the vigil differently?
Parul seemed to feel her grief openly and strongly, sobbing, while Lalit's grief came later and alone.

Thursday, Darjeeling

Ama-la had a good morning. She remembered the neighbour's name and asked for her tea with extra salt, the old way. I logged into work at nine from the kitchen table so I could hear her if she called.

Afternoon was harder. She thought I was my mother and kept asking when Papa was coming home. I had a client call. I muted myself twice to answer her gently. By six my shoulders were up by my ears.

Video call with Indu in Dubai tonight. I finally said it: "I can't do all of this alone and keep my job." She went quiet, then said, "What can I take from here?"

We decided: Indu manages her medicine orders and the doctor's appointments online. She'll also pay for a helper three mornings a week, and I'll handle the rest of the bills. Saying it out loud was the hardest part.

Tenzin

What did Ama-la ask for with her tea?
She asked for her tea with extra salt, the old way.
How was Tenzin feeling by six in the evening?
Tenzin felt tense and stretched thin, with shoulders up by the ears after juggling work and gently answering Ama-la.
What made the call with Indu useful?
Tenzin named the problem honestly, and they split concrete tasks, so the care no longer rested on one person.
How might Indu feel about hearing Tenzin's words from far away?
Indu might feel guilty for being far away, but also relieved to be asked for real tasks she can do from Dubai.

Every Sunday, Jaya borrowed her mother's phone at the tea stall by the village bus stand and sent Pema a long voice note about the new school in Palampur, the apple orchard and the goat that chewed her dupatta. At first Pema sent long ones back from Gangtok. Then short ones. Then just a heart. This week, nothing. Jaya sat on the stone wall, feeling hollow. Had Pema forgotten her? Her mother sat down beside her. 'Pema has a new class too, new homework, new friends. It's no one's fault.' Jaya thought about that. Then she recorded a short, cheerful note: 'Miss you. Summer holidays, I'm coming to Gangtok. Save me a momo.' She meant it, and it didn't hurt quite so much.

Where did Jaya send her voice notes from?
The tea stall by the village bus stand.
How did Jaya feel on the stone wall this week?
Hollow and hurt, worried that Pema had forgotten her.
What wise step did Jaya take after talking with her mother?
She sent a short, cheerful note and planned a visit in the summer holidays, instead of blaming Pema.
How might Pema's life explain the shorter replies?
Pema has a new class, homework and friends too, so replying less may not mean she cares less.

Mohit, you're sixteen and your friends are full of rumours, I can see it. Let me tell you one small thing from when I was seventeen, before nursing college. There was a boy in my tuition, Anil. We liked each other. One evening, on the way home, he stopped and asked, 'Can I hold your hand?' Just like that, asked. I hesitated, and he said, 'Okay, not today then,' and walked on talking about cricket. I admired him so much for that. Asking, and meaning it when the answer isn't yes. Now I work in a clinic, and I see young people hurt by myths about protection and infections that they picked up from friends. So, respect a no, and bring your questions to me or a doctor, not to rumours.

What did Anil say when the narrator hesitated?
'Okay, not today then,' and he walked on talking about cricket.
Why did the narrator admire Anil so much?
He asked before touching them and accepted their hesitation without sulking or pushing.
What does the narrator want Mohit to do with questions about sexual health?
Bring them to the narrator or a doctor, rather than trusting rumours from friends.
How might Anil's response have felt different if he had just grabbed the narrator's hand?
The narrator would likely have felt uncomfortable and disrespected instead of safe and admiring.

“Jagdish, where's the summary?” Sabina asked. “It was due yesterday.”

“Uh... almost done.”

“You said that on Monday.”

“I was busy.”

Nita looked up from her laptop. “We waited for it before starting the slides. Now we have two hours.”

“I could have told you it was late,” said Jagdish.

“Yes,” said Sabina quietly. “That's the part that hurts more. I'd have started the summary myself if I'd known.”

“Okay. Sorry.”

“Next time just say, ‘I'm stuck.’ I can plan around stuck. I can't plan around silence.”

Jagdish nodded. Nita closed her laptop. “I'll believe you next time,” she said, “if you tell me early.”

What was due yesterday?
The summary was due yesterday.
What did Sabina mean by saying, “That's the part that hurts more”?
Sabina was hurt more by Jagdish's silence than by the delay, since hearing nothing made it impossible to plan or to trust future promises.
What did Sabina ask Jagdish to do next time?
Sabina asked Jagdish to say “I'm stuck” early, since Sabina can plan around stuck but not around silence.
How might Nita feel about having waited for the summary before starting the slides?
Nita probably feels frustrated and worried about time, having lost some trust in the timing.

I'm Trisha, Tejas's big sister. Last Sunday he was making clay animals. I rolled one ball into a long snake. "Now yours has less," I teased. Tejas, who's seven, looked at it, then said, "No. You just made it long." "Look, mine's bigger!" "It's the same clay, Didi. Roll it back." I did. It was the same ball. He crossed his arms and grinned. Last year he'd have cried that I had more. I can't know how he worked it out, but he was very sure.

What did Trisha roll the clay ball into?
A long snake.
What does Tejas crossing his arms and grinning suggest?
He felt confident and pleased that he was right about the clay.
How could Trisha keep building on Tejas's understanding?
Try other changes with him, like flattening or breaking the clay, and ask if the amount changes.
How does Trisha see Tejas's change since last year?
She notices he used to cry about having less but now understands the clay stays the same.

Deepika noticed her parents lowering their voices whenever she came in. One evening she asked her mother gently, "Has something changed?" Her mother sighed and told her that Papa's income had dropped since the factory cut hours. The vague worry became a clear problem with limits, and Deepika felt steadier for knowing.

Next morning she asked Parul Ma'am, the class teacher, what help existed with fees. Parul Ma'am told her about a scholarship form. Deepika gathered certificates with her parents over the weekend and handed in the application days before the last date.

Omkar, in the next row, had heard similar things at home and said nothing. He joked with friends, smiled, and told his mother school was fine. His marks slipped and he stopped sleeping well. His parents, unaware of his load, could not reassure him or share it.

To help with costs, Deepika began tutoring younger children. A month later she was falling asleep over her own notes. She and her parents cut the tutoring to two evenings and looked for another source of aid, agreeing that her studies came first.

Why had Papa's income dropped?
The factory cut hours.
How did Deepika's way of handling the worry differ from Omkar's, and what happened?
Deepika asked questions, applied for help, and later rebalanced her tutoring with her parents, while Omkar hid his worry and his marks slipped without his parents knowing.
What was Omkar feeling behind the jokes?
Worry and strain, hidden behind smiles.
What could Omkar do?
Omkar could tell his parents or a teacher what he is worried about so they can help him share it.
What does a postman do? One sentence, ten words at most.
A postman delivers letters and parcels to homes.

At the playground in Madrid, Tomas pushed Mateo off the little slide, and Mateo landed on his bottom and cried. Tomas's grandmother hurried over. "Tomas!" Tomas's cheeks went red. "He was too slow! He started it!" He crossed his arms and looked at the ground. His grandmother took a breath and knelt down. "You wanted your turn. That's hard. And now Mateo is hurt." She didn't raise her voice. Tomas's arms slowly came down. He peeked at Mateo.

What did Tomas say about Mateo?
He said, "He was too slow! He started it!"
Why did Tomas say "He started it"?
His red cheeks and crossed arms suggest he felt bad and was pushing that uncomfortable feeling away, not lying on purpose.
What did the grandmother do that helped the feeling pass?
She stayed calm, named his wish for a turn, and gently pointed out that Mateo was hurt, without shaming him.
How might Mateo feel hearing "He started it"?
Mateo may feel even more upset and blamed, since he is the one who got pushed and hurt.
Ananya is taller than Kavya, and Kavya is taller than Meena. Who is the shortest?
Meena is the shortest. Because Kavya is taller than Meena, and Ananya is taller than Kavya, so both of them are taller than Meena.

Read this:

When the results came, I'd failed the corporate law paper. I sat in the college library and let myself feel it. I was disappointed. Properly disappointed; I'd wanted a first class. I didn't tell myself it didn't matter. It did. After a while, I asked a different question: what does this tell me about how I prepared? I went back through my notes. I had read the cases, but never practised writing answers under time. My friend Lalit had done three mock papers. I had done none. That wasn't about my brain. It was about my method. So I signed up for the re-exam and asked Lalit if we could do timed papers together on Saturdays. I still felt the sting. But I also felt I had somewhere to go. I'm Tanuja, and failing that paper taught me more than passing some others.

How many mock papers had Lalit done?
Three mock papers.
How did Tanuja feel after failing, and what did Tanuja do with that feeling?
Tanuja felt properly disappointed and let that be real, then turned it into a question about how the preparation went.
What did Tanuja's reframe open up?
Seeing the problem as method, not brain, led to the re-exam sign-up and Saturday timed papers with Lalit.
How might Lalit feel being asked to study together?
Lalit might feel pleased and trusted, happy to help a friend who is taking the setback seriously.
The post office is in front the bank, near the bus stop.

The post office is in front of the bank, near the bus stop.
Why: "In front of" is a fixed phrase, and the word "of" cannot be dropped.

Thursday
Study group again. Every time I started explaining the circuit problem, Rafiq cut in: "Yeah, yeah, basically it's—" and then explained MY method, badly. Twice. Then the others thanked him.
By the third time I just stopped. I sat there doodling, feeling invisible, wondering if my accent makes people stop listening. Or if it's because I'm the only girl in the group.
Walking back, I was so angry I almost cried.
But then I remembered what Ammi says: "Your voice has a right to be in the room."
So tomorrow I'm going to try it. When he cuts in, I'll say, calmly, "Rafiq, can I finish? I'm nearly there." I practised it three times in the mirror. It sounds less rude than I thought.
Zainab, you're not invisible. Just interrupted.
Friday update: I said it. He actually stopped. The others listened.

What was Zainab explaining when Rafiq cut in?
Zainab was explaining the circuit problem.
What was Zainab feeling after being cut off three times?
Zainab felt invisible and angry, close to tears, and doubted whether her accent or being the only girl made people stop listening.
What made Zainab's plan work?
She practised a calm, short line, "Rafiq, can I finish? I'm nearly there," which claimed her turn without attacking him.
How might Rafiq have felt when Zainab asked to finish?
Rafiq might have felt a little surprised and embarrassed, realising he had been cutting her off.

Dear Madhav Bhaiya,
I know Amma told you I turned down the Dubai offer. I know you're angry. I want you to hear it from me.
When Revathi and I got married, we sat on the terrace with two cups of chai and a sheet of paper. We wrote what we wanted our lives to add up to. Mine was this: children in the tea estate clinics getting care before it's too late. Hers was teaching nurses there.
Every choice since has come from that sheet. We rent near the clinic, not in the city. Revathi's night course. The Dubai job would have been easy money and nothing on that sheet.
It isn't always easy. Some months are tight. Last week I missed Appa's birthday for an outbreak call and felt awful.
But I'm not drifting. For the first time, my work, my marriage and my days point the same way.
Your stubborn brother,
Naveen

Where did Naveen and Revathi sit to write what they wanted their lives to add up to?
They sat on the terrace with two cups of chai and a sheet of paper.
What was Naveen feeling when he missed Appa's birthday?
Naveen felt awful and guilty, torn between family and the work he had chosen.
How could Naveen and Madhav talk about this without a bigger rift?
Naveen could invite Madhav to visit the clinic and see the work, and Madhav could share what worries him, so they discuss real concerns rather than just the job offer.
Why might Madhav Bhaiya react differently to the Dubai offer than Naveen did?
Madhav may see the offer as security and a chance his brother threw away, and may worry about the tight months, while Naveen measures it against the sheet of shared purpose.

Read this:

Vishal, you say your supervisor keeps changing your roster and you want to vent in the group chat. Let me tell you what I did at your age. I'm Rajni. I worked in a garment unit and hated one supervisor's habit of skipping the guard on the cutting machine. I grumbled in the canteen for weeks, and nothing changed except that people started avoiding me. Then I stopped, wrote down the dates when the guard was left off, three of them, and took it to the safety officer with a suggestion: a checklist before each shift. The officer looked into it, and the guard stayed on. It wasn't quick, and the supervisor didn't speak to me for a month. Grumbling felt good for a minute. The paper changed something.

How many dates did Rajni write down?
Three.
What was Rajni feeling during the weeks of grumbling in the canteen?
Rajni was frustrated and resentful about the guard being skipped, and the grumbling gave brief relief but no change.
What could Vishal do about the roster instead of venting in the group chat?
Vishal could note the dates of the changes, suggest a fix and take it to the manager or the proper channel.
How might the supervisor have felt after Rajni's report?
The supervisor did not speak to Rajni for a month, which suggests they were unhappy or embarrassed, though the story does not say.
My hair are very long. What is wrong?
The correct sentence is: "My hair is very long." Why: "hair" is a singular uncountable noun in English, so it takes "is".
A song has been stuck in my head all day and it's driving me mad.
Ha, that's called an earworm. Do you know the whole song, or only one line?
Just the chorus, over and over.
Try listening to the full song once, since your brain often wants to hear the ending. Then listen to something different, or chew gum, or talk to someone.
Why does it get stuck?
Repetitive, catchy tunes tend to play on a loop in the mind, and not finishing the tune can keep the loop going. Finishing it or switching activities usually breaks it.
I'll finish the song then. Hopefully it leaves.
If it doesn't, try humming something different. Your brain may take the hint.
It left for ten minutes and then a different song arrived.
You have a full playlist in your head. Keep busy with something that needs thinking, like a puzzle, and the tunes tend to fade.

Emeka and his friend Oskar were walking home from school in Leeds when a van slowed down beside them. The driver leaned over. "Boys, I've lost my kitten. Can one of you check under the seats for me? I'm too big." Oskar started to step forward. Emeka grabbed his sleeve. "Wait," he said quietly. "Why would a grown-up ask us? There's a lollipop lady right there." Emeka said loudly, "Ask the crossing lady," and they walked quickly to her. They told her what had happened. She noted the van's colour and number, walked them to the corner shop, phoned the school office, and called both their parents. That evening Oskar's mum came round to thank Emeka.

Who did the boys walk to?
The crossing lady, the lollipop lady.
What was Emeka thinking when he grabbed Oskar's sleeve?
He felt uneasy and suspicious, thinking it was odd for a grown-up to ask children for help.
What else should Emeka and Oskar remember next time?
Never go near or into a stranger's vehicle, and always tell a trusted adult straight away, as they did.
How does the afternoon look to Oskar's mum?
Oskar's mum is shaken but grateful, and comes round that evening to thank Emeka.

(1) how much is the entry fee at the science fair
(2) how do I stay focused during a long lesson
(3) Why do we need a break after studying for a long time?
(4) What's the meaning of the word wardrobe?
(5) My sentence is "He gave me a good news about the exam." Can you fix it?

1. I don't know, because fees differ and I can't see the poster. Check the fair's website or call the organisers.
2. Sit upright, take short notes and ask yourself questions as the teacher speaks. If your mind wanders, bring it back to the next point.
3. A break lets the brain rest. Because the brain gets tired after long study, and rest helps it focus again.
4. "Wardrobe" is a noun. It means a tall cupboard for clothes, or all the clothes that a person has.
5. Corrected: He gave me some good news about the exam. Why: "news" is uncountable, so it does not take "a".

Wednesday, 11:40 p.m.
Another late night at the design studio. Third week in a row. Ever since I sent the client the wrong version of the brochure and they printed 500 copies, I've been trying to fix it by working harder than anyone. I redid three other projects nobody asked me to redo. Arnab offered to take the Kumar account off my plate, and I nearly bit his head off. "I'll manage."
Tonight on the bus I did the maths: about sixty extra hours. The brochure mistake took maybe ten minutes. I'm paying for a ten-minute mistake with sixty hours, and nobody even asked me to.
What I haven't done is sit with my boss and say plainly, "I made this error, and here's how I'll prevent it." That would take fifteen minutes. Tomorrow. Fifteen minutes. Then home by seven.
Gopika

How many extra hours has Gopika worked?
About sixty extra hours.
Why did Gopika nearly bite Arnab's head off when he offered help?
Guilt made Gopika feel the fixing had to be done alone, and the offer may have felt like a reminder of the mistake.
What choice does Gopika plan for tomorrow, and why is it better than more late nights?
A fifteen-minute talk with the boss owning the error and a prevention plan, which settles it far more cheaply than sixty hours of penance. 🙂
How might Arnab feel after having the offer snapped at?
A bit hurt and worried, since he was trying to help a tired colleague who wouldn't let anyone in.

Read this:

I'm Dolma, and I'm telling this on your podcast, Anand, because last year I thought my life was over. A message came from an unknown account: a picture with my face, my hostel room behind me, but a body that wasn't mine. "Pay by Friday or this goes to your family and your college group." I was shaking so hard I dropped the phone. My first thought was, it's my fault for posting my photos. It wasn't. Someone took ordinary pictures and faked the rest. My roommate Pema made me do three things that same night. We saved everything: screenshots, the account name, the payment details they sent. We reported the account to the platform. And we went to the cyber police station together, where the officer said they see this every week and that I must not pay. Then I called my elder sister. Telling her was the hardest part. She just said, "I'm with you."

What did the message demand?
Payment by Friday, or the picture would go to Dolma's family and college group.
What did Dolma first believe about whose fault it was?
Dolma felt terrified and ashamed, first thinking it was Dolma's own fault for posting photos.
What steps did Dolma and Pema take that night?
They saved all the evidence, reported the account to the platform and went to the cyber police station without paying; then Dolma called an elder sister.
How did Dolma's sister respond, and why did it matter?
The sister simply said “I'm with you”, meeting the hardest moment with support instead of blame.

messages.content:
In two sentences, what is the main idea of this extract?

Mrs. Bennet was perfectly satisfied; and quitted the house under the delightful persuasion that, allowing for the necessary preparations of settlements, new carriages, and wedding clothes, she should undoubtedly see her daughter settled at Netherfield in the course of three or four months. Of having another daughter married to Mr. Collins she thought with equal certainty, and with considerable, though not equal, pleasure. Elizabeth was the least dear to her of all her children; and though the man and the match were quite good enough for her, the worth of each was eclipsed by Mr. Bingley and Netherfield.

Mrs. Bennet leaves satisfied that one daughter will soon be settled at Netherfield and expects another to marry Mr. Collins, which pleases her somewhat less. Elizabeth is her least dear child, and she thinks Mr. Collins is good enough for her but not as good as Mr. Bingley and Netherfield.

"Wasim, you look the way I looked in my first month in Delhi," said Tenzin uncle, stirring his butter tea. "I was twenty-four, just out of Dharamshala, in a government office. At lunch, everyone talked about cricket players I'd never heard of, and a boss they called 'the Colonel', and some wedding where somebody fell in a pond. I understood the words. Not the jokes. I ate my momos in silence for three weeks.
Then one day an older clerk, Mr. Bhatia, said, 'Tenzin, the Colonel is our section head. He was never in the army, he just shouts like one.' Everyone laughed, and he winked at me. Then he asked, 'What do people eat for lunch in Dharamshala?'
Small thing. But after that, I belonged. So if you see a new person at your office lunch, you be the Mr. Bhatia."

Who did the office call 'the Colonel'?
The section head, who was never in the army but shouted like one.
How did young Tenzin feel during his first three weeks at lunch?
He felt lonely and excluded, understanding the words but not the jokes, eating in silence.
What was the turning point in Tenzin uncle's story?
Mr. Bhatia explaining the Colonel joke and asking about Dharamshala food, which made Tenzin feel he belonged.
How might Mr. Bhatia have seen that lunch?
He may have seen it as a small, easy kindness, perhaps remembering what it felt like to be new.

At the after-school club, Bidisha's lunchbox wouldn't fit in her bag. Her big brother Thomas squashed it in for her. "There. You owe me your biscuit." Bidisha looked at her biscuit. It was her favourite. She felt unsure. Did she have to give it? The club teacher, Mrs D'Souza, overheard. "Thomas, big brothers can help just because. No charge." Thomas grinned sheepishly. "Okay, okay. Free service." Bidisha said, "Thank you, Thomas." She kept the biscuit. But at pick-up, when Thomas dropped his water bottle, she ran and got it for him.

What did Thomas say Bidisha owed him?
He said she owed him her biscuit.
How did Bidisha feel looking at her biscuit?
She felt unsure and uneasy, not sure whether she had to give away her favourite biscuit for the help.
What did Mrs D'Souza say, and why was it wise?
She told Thomas that big brothers can help just because, which keeps help about love instead of bargaining.
How might Thomas feel when Bidisha picks up his water bottle?
He may feel pleased and a little surprised that his sister helps back without being asked.

Dear Diary,

Today Omkar and I had the biggest fight of Class 5. He said I copied his drawing for the competition. I didn't. I said he was a liar and he said I was one. We were both shouting and I was nearly crying.

Rawat Ma'am came. She didn't say who was right. She just said, "Dolma, go and fill your bottle. Omkar, walk to the gate and back." I was angry she didn't take my side.

When I came back I felt less hot. Ma'am sat with me first and asked what happened and how I felt. I said I felt blamed for nothing. Then she talked to Omkar alone.

I still don't like what he said. But my stomach doesn't hurt anymore.

Dolma

What did Omkar say Dolma copied?
Omkar said Dolma copied his drawing for the competition.
What was Dolma feeling when Rawat Ma'am didn't take her side?
Dolma felt angry and let down, wanting the teacher to say who was right.
Why did Rawat Ma'am's approach work?
She separated them and let each cool down first, then listened to each one's story and feelings, so they could talk calmly.
How might Omkar have felt walking to the gate and back?
Omkar was probably still angry at first but calmer by the end, ready to tell his side when Ma'am talked to him alone.
At Eid, we wear new clothes and visit to our relatives. Which word is extra?

At Eid, we wear new clothes and visit our relatives.
Why: "Visit" takes its object directly, so no "to" is needed.

The class group in Valencia lit up at ten at night. Someone had posted Lucia's old dance video with cruel captions, and within minutes thirty people were adding comments about her weight and her voice.
Rafael watched from his bed. His thumb hovered, but he typed nothing. If he defended her, they'd turn on him next. He felt sick and cowardly at the same time.
After twenty minutes, he closed the group. Then he opened a private chat with Lucia. "I saw what they're doing. It's cruel and it's not okay. I'm sorry I didn't say anything there."
She replied a minute later: "Thanks. I thought everyone agreed with them."
Rafael went downstairs to the kitchen, where his mother was still working. He showed her the screenshots. She read them, frowning, and said, "You did the right thing to show me." She emailed his form tutor that night, and Rafael added a short note of his own.

What had someone posted in the class group?
Lucia's old dance video with cruel captions.
How did Rafael feel as he watched the comments?
He felt sick, scared of being targeted next, and guilty for staying silent.
Which steps helped more than staying quiet?
Sending Lucia a supportive private message and showing the screenshots to his mother, who reported it to the form tutor that night.
How does Lucia seem to feel before Rafael's message?
Lucia felt isolated and hurt, believing that everyone agreed with the cruel comments.

Whats the name of the book you're reading
Can you fix the punctuation?

What's the name of the book you're reading?
Why: The contraction of "what is" needs an apostrophe, and a direct question ends with a question mark.

The client report was due at five, it was 4:20, and Gargi, three days into her first job, was stuck on the pivot table.
Pradeep rolled his chair over. His fingers itched for the keyboard; he could fix it in two minutes. He folded his hands instead.
"What have you tried so far?"
"I dragged region into rows, sales into values... and it shows the same total everywhere."
"Good. Check one thing: what's in the filter box?"
Gargi looked. Her face cleared. "Oh. Last month is still selected." She fixed it, then rebuilt the chart herself, slowly, tongue between her teeth.
At 4:52 she hit send. Pradeep's own work was now twenty minutes behind. He didn't mind. Next month she would be doing this without him.

How many days had Gargi been in her first job?
Three days.
What was Pradeep feeling as his fingers itched for the keyboard?
He felt impatient and tempted to take over, knowing he could fix it in two minutes, but chose to hold back.
Which of Pradeep's coaching moves would you copy?
Asking what she had already tried, giving one hint about the filter box, and letting her finish the chart herself, even under a deadline.
How might Gargi feel after hitting send at 4:52?
Gargi would likely feel relieved and more confident, having fixed it and rebuilt the chart herself.

Friday.
Did my usual bit in class today. When the maths results came back, I held mine up and said, "Another masterpiece from the family failure!" Everyone laughed. Even Anirban laughed, and he never laughs. It felt good for about ten seconds. Then at lunch, someone at the next table said, "Ask the family failure, she won't mind." And I did mind. I minded a lot. I think I've been teaching them the joke. If I keep calling myself stupid, why wouldn't they? Tomorrow I'm going to try just taking my paper and saying nothing. That's going to be harder than any joke.
Payal

What did Payal call herself in class?
"The family failure."
How did Payal feel when someone used the nickname at lunch?
Hurt; Payal minded a lot, even though the joke had felt good for about ten seconds in class.
What is Payal planning, and why?
To take the paper and say nothing tomorrow, because the self-mockery was teaching others to mock her.
How might Anirban have seen Payal's joke?
As genuinely funny, since he rarely laughs, without realising it hurts her underneath.

I'm Harish, and for thirty years I was "the one who isn't Alka". Alka topped the class. Alka got the scholarship. At every wedding, some aunt would ask me what I was doing now, in a voice that already knew.

So when Appa died and the house in Mysuru had to be divided, I was ready for battle. I had lists. I had old grudges. I rehearsed what I'd say about who paid for Appa's hospital stays.

Then Alka arrived at the house with a box of old photos. There was one of the two of us on the scooter, me on the front, her arms around me so I wouldn't fall.

I put my lists away. At dinner I said, "I've felt compared with you my whole life, and I don't want this house to be one more contest. Can we just say fairly what each of us wants?" Alka's eyes filled. "I felt compared too," she said.

What did Alka bring to the house?
She brought a box of old photos.
How did Harish feel as he prepared for the house discussion?
Harish felt bitter and ready for battle, carrying decades of hurt from being compared with Alka.
What changed the way Harish handled the house?
Remembering the bond in the photo led Harish to put away the score-keeping and ask to talk fairly and openly.
How might Alka have experienced the years of comparison?
Alka seems to have felt the pressure too, as her tears and reply show she was also hurt by being compared.
We drove South along the coast and reached Goa in the evening. Is "South" right?

We drove south along the coast and reached Goa in the evening.
Why: Compass directions are lowercase unless they are part of a name, such as "South India".

Dear Vandana,

I have to tell you something I have been carrying since the debate. When you smiled that lopsided smile at me during my speech, I decided you were laughing at me. I lost my place and spoke faster, and I did not talk to you afterwards. I was so cross with you all week. Then Priya told me you do that when you are nervous for someone. Is that true? I want to believe it, because I know you, and you are not mean. I should have asked you straight away instead of guessing. Can we talk on Saturday? I will bring the samosas.

Your friend,
Payal

What did Payal offer to bring on Saturday?
Payal offered to bring the samosas.
Why did Payal spend the week feeling cross with Vandana?
Payal read the lopsided smile as mockery during the speech, which was upsetting. Now Payal suspects it may have been Vandana's nervous habit, though Payal is not sure.
What would you advise Payal to do the next time a smile is unclear?
Ask Vandana straight away, since the smile could be warm or mocking, and their friendship gives a good reason to check.
How might Vandana feel on reading the letter?
Vandana may feel surprised and sad that a nervous smile hurt a friend, and glad Payal wrote and wants to talk.

Counsellor's note, Kashish, career guidance centre, Tuesday:
Avni, 25, came in half laughing. Over the weekend her friends had booked an 'aura reading' at a café. The reader told her, 'You are a creative soul held back by the people around you.' Avni said she enjoyed it and felt a little flattered. Then, she said, she asked the reader whether 'a practical soul held back by her own doubts' would fit too. The reader agreed it might. She also asked for one thing she could check, like when her promotion letter would come. The answer was 'when the energy shifts'. Avni told me the reading was a nice mirror for thinking about whether she wants more creative work. But she said she won't resign from her accounts job because of it. We made a plan to look at design courses she can try on weekends first.

What did the reader tell Avni at the café?
The reader told her, 'You are a creative soul held back by the people around you.'
How did Avni feel about the reading, based on the note?
She enjoyed it and felt a little flattered, but she was also clear-headed enough to test it rather than believe it.
Which question helped Avni most, and how does it link to her job decision?
Asking whether the opposite line would fit too showed the reading was vague, so she used it for reflection and planned weekend courses instead of resigning.
How might Avni's friends see her questions to the reader?
Her friends might find her questions funny or a bit of a spoilsport at first, but they may also see she could enjoy it without being led by it.
Give me one sentence about a painter that uses exactly three adjectives.
The painter wore a bright, old, blue apron.
The boy which was crying near the gate is my neighbour.

The boy who was crying near the gate is my neighbour.
Why: We use "who" for people and "which" for things.

You asked how I became a better team lead? I'm Kiran, and it started with a bad Monday.
I came into the standup angry about a server crash. I talked fast, sighed a lot, cut people off. By the end, Ganga, our newest developer, looked like she might cry. The whole room felt heavy for the rest of the day.
That night I realised my mood had become everyone's mood.
So now, before every meeting, I stand outside for one minute and take slow breaths. I say things like, "Yes, this is stressful. Here's what we'll do first." The team's energy has changed. We still have crashes. We just don't panic together any more.

What was Kiran angry about on Monday?
Kiran was angry about a server crash.
What was Kiran feeling on realising the mood had spread?
Kiran felt guilty and uneasy, seeing that the anger had become everyone's mood.
What steps help Kiran set a calmer tone?
Taking slow breaths before meetings and naming stress honestly while giving a clear first step.
How did Ganga seem to feel after that Monday standup?
Ganga seemed hurt and anxious, looking like she might cry.

Dear Diary, Thursday
Stuck on my architecture model all evening. The roof wouldn't sit flat on the walls, no matter how many times I trimmed it. I was nearly crying with frustration.
Minakshi dragged me out to buy chai. I said I didn't have time. She said, "Ten minutes."
Walking back, I wasn't even thinking about the model, and suddenly I saw it in my head: the back wall was two millimetres taller than the front. I'd been trimming the roof when the wall was the problem!
Fixed it in five minutes.
Note to self: when I'm stuck, walk. It's not quitting.
Sangeeta

By how much was the back wall taller than the front?
Two millimetres.
How was Sangeeta feeling before the chai walk?
Sangeeta was nearly crying with frustration after an evening of trimming the roof.
What did the walk give Sangeeta that the evening of work did not?
A fresh view: away from the model, Sangeeta saw that the wall, not the roof, was the problem.
How might Minakshi feel when the model is fixed in five minutes?
Minakshi might feel pleased and a little smug that the ten-minute chai break worked.

In the school staff room during Diwali week, Principal Rashmi proposed moving the Saturday half-day to a Wednesday afternoon off. Same hours overall. The teachers bristled. "We'll lose our Saturdays!" Uday, a young maths teacher, watched the room. When the principal had said "You'll gain a free Wednesday afternoon," nobody smiled. But when she said "Saturday half-days end," everyone frowned. He raised his hand. "Ma'am, can I suggest how we present it? Your total hours off stay the same. You'll have Wednesday afternoons free for family or errands. And yes, Saturday mornings will be working." A few teachers nodded slowly. One said, "Put that way, Wednesday is actually more useful for the bank." Uday felt quietly pleased. He hadn't hidden the loss. He'd just put the whole picture in order.

What did the principal propose to replace the Saturday half-day with?
A Wednesday afternoon off.
What was Uday feeling as he suggested a new framing?
Uday felt quietly confident, and later pleased, having noticed that the loss was upsetting people more than the gain was cheering them.
What made Uday's framing both helpful and honest?
It led with what was protected, explained the gain, and clearly said Saturday mornings would be working, so nothing was hidden.
How did the teachers react to the new framing?
A few nodded, and one said Wednesday was actually more useful, showing they felt less threatened.

"Uday! Can you like my page? New skincare business," Lavanya said over coffee.
"Sure." He tapped it.
"And come to my demo evening on Friday? Just an hour."
"Okay, I can do Friday."
On Friday, after the demo, Lavanya handed him a form. "Starter kit! You'd be amazing at selling this. Only eight thousand to join."
Uday looked at the form. He'd said yes twice already. Saying no now felt awkward.
"Lavanya, give me a second." He thought: if she'd messaged me cold asking for eight thousand to join a selling scheme, would I say yes? No. Not even close.
"I'm really happy for you. But I'm not joining. I'll still share your page."
Lavanya's smile slipped, then came back. "Fair. Thanks for coming."

How much did Lavanya say the starter kit cost to join?
Only eight thousand to join.
What was Uday feeling when he looked at the form?
Uday felt awkward and pressured, because after saying yes twice, saying no now seemed hard.
Which question helped Uday decide, and why?
Asking whether he'd say yes if she had first asked for eight thousand to join made the real answer clear, so he could decline the current step.

Gurleen visited Uday in London.

messages.content: How do I use "e.g." and "i.e." in a school report?

"E.g." means "for example" and introduces some examples. "I.e." means "that is" and restates something more exactly. In American style a comma usually follows each.
Examples: Bring sports equipment (e.g., a bat or a ball). The test is on the last day of term (i.e., Friday).

Hrithik, before you start at that big office, let me tell you about my first job. I was twenty-one, at a call centre in Gurgaon. Our manager ordered the team leaders to put a paper crown marked SLOWEST on the lowest scorer each evening and make them read their numbers aloud. The first week it was me. The team leader, Bunty, a nice boy who shared his lunch with me, put the crown on my head and read my number like a price tag. I felt like a thing on a shelf, not Simran. Afterwards he said, 'Sorry yaar, orders. I have no choice.' The next day I went to HR with two colleagues and a written complaint. HR stopped the crown that week. Bunty avoided me for a month. I didn't hate him. But I never believed that 'no choice' again.

What was written on the paper crown?
SLOWEST.
How did Simran feel wearing the crown?
Simran felt dehumanised and humiliated, like a thing on a shelf with a price tag.
Simran went to HR the next day with two colleagues and a written complaint. Why was that a turning point?
It turned private humiliation into a record that forced HR to act, ending the crown for everyone.
How might Bunty have felt putting the crown on Simran?
Bunty probably felt guilty and uncomfortable, hiding behind 'orders' to avoid owning the choice.
My book mentions mincemeat pies. Is mincemeat made of meat?

Today, mostly not. Mincemeat is a sweet mixture of dried fruit, spices and sugar, used in pies. In the past it did include chopped meat. It is an uncountable noun.
Example: At Christmas the baker filled small pies with mincemeat.

On Bohag Bihu, Ritu, nineteen, sat in her Pune hostel room watching her cousins' videos from Jorhat: the dhol, the mekhela sadors, her aunt making pitha on the fire. Her chest ached. She hadn't known a festival could hurt from far away. Her roommate Anjali found her with swollen eyes. "Is everything okay?" Ritu shook her head. "It's Bihu. Everyone's home except me."
Anjali sat down. "What do you eat on Bihu?" "Pitha. Rice cakes, with jaggery and sesame." "Do we have rice flour?" They didn't, but the shop downstairs did. At midnight the two of them burnt the first batch on Anjali's hot plate and laughed until they cried. Ritu video-called her Ma, holding up a wonky pitha. Ma laughed too. The next day, Anjali found an Assamese students' group meeting on Sunday. Ritu still missed home. But she went.

What did Ritu and Anjali make on the hot plate?
Pitha, rice cakes with jaggery and sesame.
How was Ritu feeling while watching her cousins' videos?
She felt a sharp ache of homesickness, missing her family at Bihu.
Which small steps eased Ritu's homesickness?
Cooking pitha with Anjali, video-calling Ma and going to the Assamese students' group, which eased the ache without pretending it was small.
How might Ritu's Ma have felt seeing the wonky pitha on the call?
Ma probably felt amused and moved, glad her daughter was celebrating even far from home.

"Noor, you asked how to find a good therapist. Let me tell you what I learnt the hard way. When I was twenty-four, I went first to a man who promised to cure my sadness in one week with herbs. Nothing changed, and I lost months. Then my sister found a licensed psychiatrist at the district hospital. After a month I stopped going; I felt better and thought I was done. Two months later I was worse. I went back and stayed the full course. And once, on a very bad night, I didn't wait for my appointment. I went to the hospital emergency. That's how I learnt: check the licence, give it time, find someone who fits, and in a crisis, go straight for help." Naveen smiled.

To cure his sadness in one week with herbs.
How did young Naveen feel after stopping treatment early?
Naveen felt relieved and better at first, then low and discouraged two months later, which led to going back.
What turning points in Naveen's story show wise choices?
Switching to a licensed psychiatrist, returning to finish treatment and going to the emergency in a crisis instead of waiting.
How might Naveen's sister have felt finding a licensed psychiatrist?

Noor knew Uday's profile by heart. She checked it before school, at lunch and again before bed, studying every photo, sure that a boy who quoted old poems had to be perfect. She hung on his words in maths class and secretly played his kind of music, though it gave her a headache. One Friday she asked him to the school fair. Uday went red. "I'm sorry, no. I like you as a friend." Noor's face burned, and she hid in a corner of the library through break, feeling shattered and silly.

Her friend Usha found her there and sat on the floor beside her, saying nothing at first. Later she said, "That was a no to the fair. It was not a no to you as a person." Noor cried. Over the next weeks she noticed things: Uday forgetting her name once, crumbs on his desk, a snappy answer to a teacher. He was an ordinary boy. She put her own playlist back on.

Usha, though, had gone quiet. Her boyfriend wanted her location on all day, asked her to skip her cousin's birthday, and sulked until she apologised for things she had not done. Noor saw it and said gently, "That is not how caring looks." Usha admitted she felt watched and guilty. The next morning she went to the school counsellor, who listened and made a plan with her before the week was out.

Where did Noor ask Uday to go?
Noor asked Uday to the school fair.
What separates Noor's crush on Uday from the way Usha's boyfriend acted?

Noor's feelings idealised Uday and hurt mostly herself, and she recovered as she noticed he was an ordinary boy. The boyfriend's tracking, isolating and sulking-until-sorry controlled Usha and left her feeling watched and guilty.
What was Noor feeling right after Uday said no?
She felt shattered and embarrassed. Her face burned and she hid in a corner of the library through break.
How could Usha's friends support her now?
They could stay with her, keep saying that being tracked and made to apologise is not caring, and go with her to the counsellor.

"Share. He's younger."

Wasim, ten, walked home through Tolichowki with his ears still hot. In maths, Ma'am had held up his notebook. "Is this handwriting or an ant walking in ink?" The whole row had laughed, even Farid, his best friend.
At the flat door he kicked his school bag so hard it skidded under the sofa. He slammed the bedroom door. When his older brother Suraj knocked to ask about evening cricket, Wasim yelled, "Go away! Nobody asked you!"
He sat on the bed, fists tight. Suraj hadn't laughed. Suraj hadn't done anything. But Ma'am was far away and too big to shout at, and at home yelling didn't cost anything.
Later, Ammi sat beside him. "Something happened at school?" Wasim stared at the floor, and then the whole story came out.

What did Ma'am say when she held up Wasim's notebook?
She said, "Is this handwriting or an ant walking in ink?"
Why did yelling at Suraj feel okay to Wasim in that moment?
Wasim was burning with embarrassment from class, but Ma'am was too big to shout at; home felt safe, so the anger came out there even though Suraj had done nothing.
What turning point let the real story come out?
Ammi sitting beside Wasim and asking about school rather than scolding the slammed door; that pointed straight at where the feeling came from.
How might Suraj see the evening, left outside a slammed door?
Suraj only wanted to ask about cricket, so the shout would feel hurtful and puzzling, as if Suraj had done something wrong without knowing what.

messages.content: Our science fair is on Friday and I'm making a model volcano. Everyone else seems to have fancier projects.
A volcano is a classic that people enjoy, especially when it erupts. What matters most is that you can explain how it works.
I'm using baking soda and vinegar for the eruption.
That works well. The two mix and make gas bubbles, which push the foam out. Put the model on a tray so the mess stays in one place.
What if it doesn't erupt during the judging?
Test it once at home first and keep spare baking soda and vinegar in a small bag. Even if it fails, you can calmly show how it should work and repeat it.
Okay. And what should I tell the judges?
Say what you built, what makes the eruption happen and what you learned. Keep it to a few sentences and speak slowly.
I'll practise with my dad tonight.
Good plan. Ask him to interrupt with a question, so you get used to answering.

Saturday night.
Sangeeta asked me today if I'd join her in the six-month weekend course on sign language at the community centre. "Just say yes! It'll be fun!" And I wanted to. But I've quit two things this year already, the gym and the guitar class, and each time I felt terrible.
So I asked her what it would actually take. Every Saturday, 9 to 1. A small fee. Homework practice with a partner twice a week. Sangeeta would be my partner.
I looked at my calendar. Saturdays are fine. Weekdays, I work till 8. Twice a week practice is not realistic, but once, on Sunday mornings, is.
I told her exactly that. She laughed and said, "Once a week, fine, but you're not allowed to quit." I said I'm not promising what I can't do, but I can promise that.
We signed up. Six months. Let's see.
— Payal

Every Saturday, 9 to 1.
How did Payal feel about joining the course at first?
Payal felt eager to say yes, but also wary and a bit ashamed about quitting the gym and the guitar class earlier this year.

Payal asked exactly what it would take, checked the calendar, and agreed only to the practice that was realistic.

"You're not getting a phone until your marks come up," Dilnaz said from the kitchen. Zeenat's jaw locked. She had a dozen replies ready, each sharper than the last. She walked to the bathroom, shut the door and ran the tap. In the mirror she saw her clenched jaw. She unclenched it, stretched it wide like a yawn, and breathed out slowly, three times. When she came out, Dilnaz was standing by the door with two cups of tea. "I shouldn't have said it like that. Sit with me?" Zeenat took one. "Can I tell you why I want it?" "Yes," said Dilnaz. She walked to the bathroom, shut the door and ran the tap.

Step away for a moment, stretch the jaw and breathe slowly, then return to talk. Adults can also offer tea and a chance to talk without pressure.

When the highway crew put up tin sheds outside Pimpalgaon, Akash's uncle locked the tractor shed twice. "Outsiders," he said. "Keep the goats in." But Akash, home after his farming diploma, needed the water pump fixed, and the only mechanic within ten kilometres was Harsha from the camp. Harsha fixed it in an hour and waved away the chai money, saying his father had grown ragi back in Karnataka until the rains failed. They started meeting at the tea stall after work. Harsha taught Akash to read the wind before spraying; Akash helped him fill in a form for his daughter's school. At dinner, Akash began telling the stories: Harsha's daughter topping her class, Harsha pulling a boy out of the canal. His uncle only grunted at first. Then one Sunday he packed a tiffin of bhakri and walked it over to the camp himself.

What did Harsha teach Akash?
Harsha taught Akash to read the wind before spraying.
What does Akash's habit of telling the stories at dinner suggest about how he feels?
He is fond of his new friend and hopeful his family will see Harsha as a person, so he keeps telling the stories even when his uncle only grunts.
Which of Akash's choices did most to soften his uncle, and why?
Sharing real stories at dinner, because details like the daughter topping her class and the canal rescue replaced the word "outsiders" with a real neighbour.
How has Akash's uncle's view changed by the end?
He moves from locking the shed and calling the crew outsiders to carrying bhakri to the camp himself, a sign his suspicion has eased.

He emptied his glass, got up, and stood at the side of the fire, with his heavy brown hand on the mantel-shelf. He put a foot up to the bars, to dry and warm it, and the wet boot began to steam; but, he neither looked at it, nor at the fire, but steadily looked at me. It was only now that I began to tremble.

What does the man do by the fire, and what does the narrator feel?
He empties his glass, stands by the fire with his hand on the mantel-shelf, and props a wet boot on the bars so it steams. He looks only at the narrator, who begins to tremble.
My little sister saved over my homework file by mistake.
That's upsetting. Does your computer keep older versions or a recycle bin?

Right-click the file and look for an option to see earlier versions, or check any copy you may have emailed or saved on a pen drive. Ask an adult to help if you're unsure.

Good news. Copy it back to the computer and finish the rest. From now on, keep a backup of your work in another place.

Alka, you're saying you never do your laundry until you have nothing to wear. Let me, your Raghav Dadu, tell you about my hostel days in Allahabad, 1972.
I loved cricket commentary on the radio. Test matches, five days long. I'd sit by the transistor from morning to evening.
And my clothes? A mountain in the corner. My room-mate threatened to move out.
So I made a rule. The transistor stays in the washing area. If I want cricket, I have to be scrubbing my shirts or ironing.
It sounds foolish, but it worked. Every wicket, I'd be washing a collar. By the end of the series, my clothes were cleaner than they'd been all year.
I didn't start loving laundry, mind you. I just loved cricket enough to put up with it.

He kept it in the washing area.
Why did young Raghav start washing his clothes?
He wanted to hear the cricket commentary so much that pairing it with laundry made the dull job bearable.
At what point in the story did Raghav's habit change?
When he made the rule that the transistor stays in the washing area, so cricket came only with scrubbing or ironing.
How might Raghav's room-mate have felt when the mountain of clothes disappeared?
The room-mate was probably relieved and amused, no longer needing to threaten to move out.

Exams began in three weeks, so Noor had a single Sunday and two evenings to spare. On the kitchen table he wrote his skills: fixing phones, drawing, teaching basic maths. His sister Vandana, home from college, read over his shoulder. “Now ask which ones are allowed for someone your age, and safe,” she said. Noor crossed out the phone stall in the market: it wanted full days and ran till nine at night. Drawing wedding-card sketches at home on Sundays stayed. Maths lessons for the neighbour's child after school, in daylight, in their own building, stayed too. “Show it to Mum before you say yes to anybody,” Vandana added. Noor sighed at the crossed-out line; he had liked the phones best. Then he copied the two remaining lines onto a clean page.

Fixing phones, drawing and teaching basic maths.

Disappointed but sensible: he liked the phones best, yet accepted that full days and late hours did not suit school or his age.

Note from Kalyani Bhattacharya, garden committee, Lake View Housing Society.
Arnab (25), from B-wing, has the best balcony garden in the building. He has named every plant. The chilli is Mishti, the mint is Pagla, and he tells me Mishti "sulks" when he travels. He talks to them while watering, and he laughs about it.
Last month, when I asked if he was lonely up there, he said, "I love them, but I know they're plants. Mishti won't text me if I'm having a bad week." Then he asked about our Sunday gardening group. He has come every week since, brings cuttings, and stays for tea with the older members.

I still think about my first year as a warehouse supervisor in Nashik. I was twenty-five, a young man with twelve people under me. When the morning shift got new jackets and hot lunch because they handled the refrigerated section, the evening shift turned cold on me. Deepak, the evening loader, a hard worker, stopped joking. He said once, not quite to me, "Some people are more valuable, I guess." Their pay was the same as the morning shift's, and fair. I knew that. But I hadn't explained why the jackets and lunches went to one group. So I called both shifts together, showed them the cold-room rules, and said evening staff could rotate into the cold room if they wanted. Deepak was the first to sign up. I'm Tejas. That was when I learnt that fair isn't enough; it has to look fair too.

How many people did Tejas supervise?
Tejas had twelve people under him.
What was Tejas thinking when Deepak stopped joking?
Tejas felt uneasy and responsible, realising the evening shift felt undervalued because nothing had been explained.
Which change worked, and why?
Explaining the cold-room rules and letting evening staff rotate in made the perks' criteria clear and open, easing the resentment.
How might Deepak have felt when he signed up first?
Deepak probably felt included and respected again, seeing that the perks weren't about some people being more valuable.

Gabriel brought apricots.

Today Samir tied a knot in his scarf for the first time. He'd been trying all week. When it held, he gasped and held it up. "Look! Look!" Then he untied it and tied it again. And again. Seven times. Each time he looked at me and grinned. At going-home time he showed his mother. "I can do knots!"

Yamini, you and your husband are thinking about children? Let me, Zubin, your old grandfather, tell you how your grandmother and I did it, back in Bombay in 1975.
Back then, people just assumed. Get married, have a baby, the wife stays home. But your grandmother was a teacher and loved it.
So one evening on the Marine Drive wall, she said, "Zubin, let's not assume. Let's decide." We talked for three evenings. When? After she finished her B.Ed., two years later. Who would take time off? She would take her leave, and I'd come home by six every day, no excuses. Money? I stopped smoking and put that money aside. What scared us? Her: losing her work. Me: not earning enough.
Your father came along in 1977. Your grandmother went back to teaching after a year.
We didn't assume, Yamini. We planned together. That's why it worked.

What year was Yamini's father born?

She was afraid of losing her work, and Zubin was afraid of not earning enough.

How might Zubin's wife have felt about the plan they made?
She likely felt respected and relieved, since her teaching career was part of the plan rather than assumed away.

In the computer lab of their Johannesburg school, Lindiwe was helping Valentina with loops for the coding assignment. Lindiwe had been coding since she was eleven. "It's simple," she said, typing fast. "You initialise the iterator, set the condition, increment, and the body executes until the condition's false. Then you break out. See?" Valentina stared at the screen. "What's an iterator?" "The counter variable." "What's a variable?" Lindiwe laughed, not kindly. "Seriously? It's week six." Valentina's face went red. She closed her notebook. "Never mind. I'll figure it out." Lindiwe shrugged and went back to her own work, thinking Valentina just wasn't trying. Later, the teacher explained loops to the class using a skipping rope: "Jump ten times, count each jump, stop at ten." Valentina's hand went up first with the right answer.

A skipping rope.

Lindiwe felt impatient and a little superior, because coding felt so obvious to her that she couldn't imagine not knowing what a variable is.

Explaining with a simple, everyday example and plain words instead of jargon, starting from what the listener already knows.

Monday: At Dadar station, Vijay saw a man following a young woman, Dolma, too closely, muttering at her. She walked faster. Hundreds of people pushed past. Nobody looked twice. Vijay thought, if it were bad, someone would do something. He caught his train.
Wednesday: He saw her again on the same platform, alone, glancing over her shoulder. The same man was near the stairs. Vijay's chest tightened. He walked over and stood beside her. “Everything okay? Want me to walk you to the ladies' coach?”
Dolma let out a long breath. “Yes. Please.” The man turned away. Vijay pointed him out to the railway police constable at the gate, who went after him.
Friday: Vijay kept thinking about Monday, and how the crowd's calm had fooled him.

They were at Dadar station.
What was Vijay feeling on Wednesday when he saw the man again?
His chest tightened; he felt anxious and alarmed, and this time he trusted his own concern over the crowd.

He stood beside Dolma, offered to walk her to the ladies' coach, and pointed the man out to the railway police.

Gautam felt small and attacked, like a child being marked, and avoided Sandeep by cooking at odd hours.

Asking Sandeep over poha what he wanted changed, because it moved them from sarcasm to the real problem, the dirty cooker, which they fixed with a simple rule.

The notes would likely have become a silent battle, and the cooker problem would have stayed unspoken.

I was on the bench at the park when Nandini, about two, toddled toward the road gate. Her father shouted, "No! Stop!" in a sharp voice. Nandini froze mid-step and looked back at him, lip trembling. He reached her in a few strides and picked her up. Then he crouched and said just "Road. Cars. Stay with me," as she watched his face. What did Nandini's father say when she headed toward the gate?
He shouted, "No! Stop!" in a sharp voice.

Pick the child up to keep her safe, then use a few short words and stay close, rather than a long lecture. 🤍
How might Nandini's father feel in that moment?

Family diary, written by Meena.

Sunday, 5 pm. Varun sat with my father Shankar on the veranda for almost an hour. I watched from the kitchen door. Instead of arguing about the new tax rules, Varun asked, "Nana, what made you feel so strongly about this?" My father spoke of the years he ran a cooperative shop, when prices jumped and the shelves emptied. Varun did not interrupt once; he only nodded and asked one more question.

At the end, Varun said calmly, "I see why it worries you. I think differently about one part, and here's why." My father raised an eyebrow, then laughed and said, "Well, at least you listened." I brought them tea and did not say a word.

Where did Varun and Shankar talk?
On the veranda, for almost an hour.
What does Shankar's laugh at the end suggest he felt?
Shankar likely felt heard and a little disarmed, as Varun's calm way of asking softened any defensiveness.
What could Varun try in a later conversation to keep the talk open, and why?
Varun could keep asking about Shankar's experiences and share a second view in the same calm tone, because curiosity keeps the door open even when opinions differ.
How might Meena feel watching from the kitchen door?
Meena may feel relieved and quietly proud, since the talk that might have been feared turned warm and was left uninterrupted.

I need to tell you something I'm ashamed of.
You know the jokes we always make about the Eastside school kids? "Eastside donkeys", the memes, the braying sounds when their bus passes. I've been sending them for a year. I thought it was harmless because they're not real to us. Just "them".

On the way home I looked at our group chat and saw the donkey memes, and I felt sick. Rukhsar is one of the "donkeys".

Vasudha

She knew every capital in Africa.

Because the Eastside kids were just "them" without faces, so the cruelty didn't register and there was no guilt.

To stop sending the memes too, because knowing even one Eastside student makes the jokes feel cruel.

For three weeks I'd kept a little log on my phone: date, what I did, who I sent it to. The budget tracker, the vendor call notes, the supplier map. All of it had turned up in Saurabh's updates to the director with only his name.
This morning I asked him for five minutes in the small meeting room. My palms were sweaty. I'd practised one sentence in the shower: "I want to talk about how my work is being credited." I said it, then showed him the log. No "you always", no "you stole".
He was quiet. Then he said he hadn't realised how it looked. I said, "From today, can we both sign the updates?" He agreed.
If it happens again, I'll take the log to Ma'am. But tonight I feel lighter than I have all month.
Vijay

What did Vijay record in the phone log?
Date, what Vijay did, and who it was sent to.
How did Vijay feel before and after the talk?
Vijay was nervous beforehand, with sweaty palms, and felt lighter afterwards than in the whole month.
What made Vijay's talk calm and effective?
Vijay practised one clear sentence, showed the dated log, avoided accusations like 'you stole', and asked for a concrete change: both signing the updates.
What would change if Vijay had accused Saurabh in front of the director?
Saurabh would likely have turned defensive, and the talk could have become a fight about tone rather than the facts in the log.

Sunday, 11 p.m.

Wrote down everything I said yes to this quarter. Nineteen things. Nineteen! Newsletter, intern buddy, two lunch-and-learns, the office move spreadsheet...
Then I put the team lead criteria next to it. The ones that count: moving the team's onboarding target, and owning a project end to end. Which of my nineteen touch those? Two. The onboarding redesign and the partner portal.
So here's the thinking. If I spread thin, I finish nothing well. If I pick those two and do them properly, I'll have real results to show.
Tomorrow I'm telling Naveen I'll hand back the newsletter and the lunch-and-learns. Politely. "I'd love to, but I'm focusing on onboarding this quarter." Practised it twice already.
Scary. Also a relief.
— Vasudha

How many things had Vasudha said yes to this quarter?
Nineteen things.
How does Vasudha feel about saying no to Naveen?
Vasudha feels scared about turning down requests but also relieved, because focusing on two projects makes the goal feel reachable.
What else could Vasudha do to check the choice of the two projects?
Vasudha could ask Naveen whether the onboarding redesign and partner portal are the results the criteria reward, so the focus is confirmed before declining the rest.
How might Naveen see Vasudha handing back the newsletter?
Naveen may be a little disappointed to lose the help, but a polite, clear reason about onboarding makes the choice easy to respect.

messages.content: Our window has a squeaky latch that wakes me up every time the wind blows.
A tiny drop of oil on the hinge or latch usually fixes that. Do you have cooking oil or any light oil?
We have coconut oil.
That's fine in a pinch. Put a drop on a cotton bud, rub it on the latch and move the latch back and forth to spread it. Wipe off any extra so it doesn't drip.
What if the squeak is from the frame?
Then ask a family member to look at it with you. A small bit of cloth wedged in the gap can stop the rattle in the meantime.
The oil worked. Now the door hinge creaks too.
Same trick. One drop of oil on the hinge pin, then open and close the door a few times. Wipe off any extra.
I'm becoming the oil person of the house.
Ha, it's a useful title. Keep the bottle in one place so people know who to ask.

Read this:

I'm Francis, Ishita's older brother. Today I played with Ishita, eleven months, in the living room. I hid her rattle under a blanket while she watched. She stared at the blanket, then reached out and pulled it off. There was the rattle! She shook it and laughed. I hid it again under a pillow. She crawled straight to the pillow and lifted it. She knows it's still there.

Where did Francis hide the rattle the second time?
He hid it under a pillow.
What does Ishita's laughing after finding the rattle suggest?
It suggests she was pleased and excited to find it where she expected.
How could Francis make the game a bit harder for Ishita?
He could hide the rattle under one of two covers so she has to remember which one.
How does Francis see Ishita's new skill?
He notices that she knows the rattle still exists even when it's hidden.

Chaitanya won first prize in the district quiz and came back to the village school with a steel trophy. The headmaster made him stand on the verandah while everyone clapped.
But on the walk home past the fields, Lavanya and three other children kept calling, "Oh, the big quiz king! Too good for us now?" One of them pretended to bow.
The next week, when the half-yearly results came, Chaitanya folded his report card small and put it inside his math book. When someone asked his marks, he said, "Just average." He stopped raising his hand in class.
At home he put the trophy behind the grain tin, where nobody would see it.

Where did Chaitanya put the trophy at home?
He put the trophy behind the grain tin.
Why did Chaitanya start saying his marks were "just average"?
He felt embarrassed and hurt by the teasing, and wanted to fit in again instead of standing out.
What could the headmaster or his parents do to help Chaitanya?
They could praise his effort privately, notice the teasing and talk to the class about cheering each other's success.
How might Lavanya see the teasing?
Lavanya might think it is just fun, not realising it made Chaitanya hide his success and stop raising his hand.

The school-bus tracking project was due to the client in two days, and the office generator had failed again, so Rajat held the team meeting by the window in the afternoon heat. "Any concerns about the launch?" he asked. Deepika and Farida looked at their notebooks. Silence. It was always silence. Rajat was about to say, "Great, let's go," when he remembered a line from his last job: if nobody disagrees, you haven't heard the truth yet. He was the founder; of course they didn't want to be the one who slowed him down. So he tried again. "I'll go first. My worry is the rural routes. Now each of you, one worry, and I'll thank you for it." Farida hesitated, then said the tracking failed in the hills during testing. Deepika added that two schools hadn't sent route lists. Rajat wrote both down. "Thank you. That's the most useful thing anyone's said all week."

What did Farida say failed in the hills during testing?
The tracking failed in the hills during testing.
Why did Rajat decide the silence wasn't agreement?
He remembered that if nobody disagrees you haven't heard the truth yet, and realised that as founder his staff didn't want to slow him down.
Why did going first with his own worry help?
Naming his own worry first made it safer for others to share theirs, and promising thanks lowered the risk of speaking.
What might it be like for Deepika to report the missing route lists?
Deepika might feel nervous about delaying the launch, then relieved when Rajat calls it the most useful thing all week. 🙏

Hrithik: you went quiet in the group after that joke
Disha: yeah. been thinking about something
Disha: at the party last month someone kept asking me to go outside with him. I said no like four times and just stood there feeling awkward
Hrithik: that sounds horrible
Disha: I talked it through with Mom that night. she helped me make a rule for myself
Disha: IF someone pushes after I say no ONCE, THEN I leave the conversation and tell an adult. no second explaining
Hrithik: why so strict
Disha: because under pressure my brain goes blank. if the answer is already decided I don't have to negotiate
Hrithik: makes sense. who's the adult
Disha: Mom at home, Ms. Rao at school, or whoever is hosting
Hrithik: can I use the same rule
Disha: obviously. it works for anyone

Who are the adults Disha would tell?
Mom at home, Ms. Rao at school, or whoever is hosting.
Why does Disha want the answer decided in advance?
Disha felt awkward and stuck at the party because the mind goes blank under pressure, so a ready rule feels safer than negotiating.
What could make Disha's rule easier to use at a party?
Agreeing with a friend like Hrithik to leave together, and knowing who the host is, would make the leaving part quick.
How does Hrithik see the rule?
Hrithik first finds it strict, then sees the sense in it and wants to use it too.
