messages.content:
Read this:

Thursday night
Dear diary, I'm writing this with a scraped elbow, so the handwriting is bad.
Tenzin and I were walking to the bus stop, and I was replying to the class group about Saturday's picnic. Tenzin said, "Nirmala, bike!" I actually looked up. I saw the road. And I still didn't see the boy on the cycle until his handlebar clipped my arm. How? He was wearing a yellow shirt!
Tenzin says I was "looking through" everything. That sounds silly, but it's true. My brain was busy choosing between samosas and sandwiches, not watching the road.
The cycle boy said sorry even though it was my fault. I said sorry too, twice.
New plan: if I need to text, I stop under the neem tree first.
Nirmala

What clipped Nirmala's arm on the way to the bus stop?
The handlebar of the boy on the cycle clipped Nirmala's arm.
Why was Nirmala so puzzled about missing the cyclist?
Nirmala had looked up and seen the road, so missing a boy in a yellow shirt felt impossible; the mind was busy with the picnic plans instead of the traffic. 🤔
What does Nirmala decide to do differently, and why might it help?
Nirmala plans to stop under the neem tree before texting, so reading and walking never happen together and attention stays on the road.
How might the boy on the cycle have felt when he apologised?
He probably got a fright and may have felt partly to blame, even though he was riding normally and Nirmala walked into his path.

Read this:

Jeevan and his cousin Sangeeta shared two rooms above a tailor's shop in Karad. That evening Jeevan heard the gate clang before Sangeeta even reached the stairs. She had gone to the college office to see her practical marks. The parcel boy followed with her textbook order.

"You call this packed? The cover is bent! Do you people even look?" she shouted. The boy mumbled sorry and hurried off.

Jeevan wanted to say, "That wasn't his fault." He bit it back and put the kettle on.

Later, over chai on the roof, he said only, "The marks went badly?"

Sangeeta stared at the fields. "Eleven out of forty. Madam didn't even check my file properly." A pause. "I shouted at that poor boy instead of her."

"Maybe tell Madam, not the boy," Jeevan said. She nodded slowly.

What did the parcel boy bring?
The parcel boy brought Sangeeta's textbook order.
Why did Jeevan bite back the correction at the gate?
Jeevan felt uneasy at the shouting but guessed Sangeeta was upset about the practical marks, and thought a correction then would only make things worse.
Which choice worked, and why?
Waiting for a calm moment on the roof and asking only about the marks let Sangeeta see for herself where the anger belonged.
What is it like for Sangeeta when Jeevan asks only about the marks?
Sangeeta feels understood rather than scolded, which lets her admit she shouted at the boy and turn toward Madam instead.
Do I say "I am boring" or "I am bored"?

Say "I am bored". The -ed form describes how you feel. The -ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling.
Examples: I am bored because it is raining. This long train journey is boring.
Describe a village fair in one sentence using at least three of these words: swing, sweets, drum, bangles.
Children rode the swing, ate sweets, and bought bangles at the village fair.
The sign says Tiger Preserve. Does the park keep tigers in jars, like jam?

No. Here a preserve is a protected area of land where animals and plants are kept safe. It is a noun. Preserves are also jams, and the verb preserve means to keep something from harm or from going bad.
Example: The forest was turned into a preserve to protect the rare birds.

Read this:

Toddler room note, Friday. When Nikita's father collected her, Nikita waved bye-bye at me with her whole arm and said “Ba!” Earlier in the garden she had stopped, pointed a finger at an aeroplane and looked back at me, eyebrows up. I said, “Aeroplane! Up in the sky.” She pointed again and repeated “Aa-pane.” I will keep naming what she points at, and tell her father about this new word. 🙂 Gautam

What did Nikita point at in the garden?
An aeroplane in the sky.
What did Nikita want when she pointed and looked back at Gautam?
She probably wanted to share her interest and hear the name of the aeroplane. She might also just have been checking Gautam's face.
What is Gautam's plan and why does it help?
Gautam will keep naming what she points at, which teaches new words and shows that her gestures are heard.
How might Nikita's father feel hearing about the new word?
He may be proud and pleased, and try naming things with her at home too.
Sound more sincere: Sorry about that.
I'm truly sorry about that.

On our right flank commanded by Bagration, at nine o'clock the battle had not yet begun. Not wishing to agree to Dolgorukov's demand to commence the action, and wishing to avert responsibility from himself, Prince Bagration proposed to Dolgorukov to send to inquire of the commander in chief. Bagration knew that as the distance between the two flanks was more than six miles, even if the messenger were not killed (which he very likely would be), and found the commander in chief (which would be very difficult), he would not be able to get back before evening.

Why does Prince Bagration propose sending to ask the commander in chief?

Bagration does not want to agree to Dolgorukov's demand to begin the action and wants to avoid responsibility himself. He also knows a messenger over more than six miles would hardly return before evening.

Ines had worked as a translator in Lisbon since she was twenty-two. By twenty-five, half her regular clients had switched to machine translation and only sent her "light checks" at a fraction of the fee.
She felt her whole training shrinking. For a month she was bitter and applied for anything.
Her friend Daniel, a software tester, asked what she was actually good at. "Noticing when something sounds wrong to a real person," she said. "Tone. Culture. Jokes that don't land."
"That's a job," he said. "UX writing. Localisation testing."
She took an evening course for three months and built a small portfolio: rewriting app screens so they sounded natural in Portuguese, and finding cultural errors in translated menus. She volunteered for a local nonprofit to get real examples.
In spring, a travel company hired her to check their app's Portuguese version. Machine first, Ines second. She didn't love it all. But she wasn't shrinking anymore.

What did half of Ines's clients switch to?
Machine translation.
How did Ines feel as her work dried up?
Ines felt bitter and shrinking, as if her whole training was losing value.
Which steps made Ines's pivot deliberate rather than random?
Identifying her real strength, taking a focused course, building a portfolio and getting real examples through volunteering.
How might Daniel feel seeing Ines hired?
Daniel probably feels pleased and proud that one question helped her see her skill in a new way.

messages.content: Make this one short sentence: The bridge near our school, which was built many years ago, is closed for repairs for two weeks.
The bridge near our school is closed for repairs for two weeks.

Make this verse easier to understand by writing it as two sentences.

Thus in calm strength which naught could shake
The son of Dasaratha spake,
With glory yet unstained
Upon Sumitra's son he bent
His eyes, and firm in his intent
His dauntless heart maintained.
So the son of Dasaratha spoke, in a calm strength that nothing could shake, with his glory still unstained. He turned his eyes on Sumitra's son, and his dauntless heart held firm in its intent.

Last term, three of us new teachers shared one projector, and Charu had it almost every day. Mona and Deepak grumbled about it at lunch, but never to Charu. I was tired of teaching my Class 8 map lesson on a chalkboard. So one Friday I said, 'Charu, can I talk about the projector? I've gone without it for three weeks, and I'm starting to feel frustrated and left out of planning. How does it look from your side?' She went red. 'I thought nobody else wanted it. No one ever said.' That stung, because she was partly right. We sat with the timetable and made a sign-up sheet for the staffroom door. Mona wrote her name on it first. I'm Vinita, and I still think about how close I came to just complaining at lunch forever.

What did they make to share the projector?
A sign-up sheet for the staffroom door.
How did Charu feel when Vinita raised the projector, and what shows it?
Charu was embarrassed and surprised; she went red and said she thought nobody else wanted it.
What could Mona and Deepak learn from how Vinita handled this?
Instead of grumbling at lunch, they could name the problem directly, say how it affects them and ask for the other person's view.
How might Mona see the new sign-up sheet?
Mona had only grumbled before, so she likely felt relieved to have a fair turn at last, which is why she wrote her name first.

messages.content:
Read this:

"You're very quiet," Kunal said, putting his bag down.

"Mm," said Kavitha, stirring the sambar.

"Did something happen at school pickup?"

"Nothing happened. Same as always."

"Kavitha. You've said 'same as always' all week."

She turned off the stove. Her hands were shaking a little. "Fine. I've done every school run since June. Every one. You said you'd take Tuesdays, and you haven't once. I didn't say anything because I didn't want to nag. And now I'm just angry all the time."

Kunal sat down slowly. "Since June?"

"Since June."

"I thought you liked doing them. You never said."

"I know. I should have said it in June, not now, like this."

He was quiet. "Tuesdays and Thursdays are mine from tomorrow. And if something's bothering you, tell me in the first week. Please."

"I'll try." She sat down across from him. "Thank you."

Which day had Kunal said he would take the school run?
Kunal had said he would take Tuesdays.
What does the shaking of Kavitha's hands suggest?
It suggests Kavitha was angry and anxious, releasing resentment she had held in since June.
What could Kavitha and Kunal do differently next time?
Speak up early and kindly, in the first week, before small grievances build into anger and coldness.
How does Kunal see the situation when he hears "since June"?
Kunal is surprised and a little ashamed, since he thought Kavitha liked doing the runs and had not noticed the load.

In the nursery, Tarun, four, pulled Anand's toy car away. Anand yelled and cried. "Sorry, sorry, sorry," said Tarun fast, and reached for the car again. The teacher said, "Tarun, look at Anand's face. What happened to him when you pulled the car?" "He's crying." "Yes. What could you do?" Tarun looked at the car, then put it in Anand's hands. Anand wiped his nose, and they rolled it together.

What did Tarun do after saying sorry three times?
He reached for the car again.
Why might Tarun have said sorry so quickly?
Probably to end the conflict. He may not yet understand that Anand was hurt.
How did the teacher move beyond a forced sorry?
The teacher asked Tarun to look at Anand's face and think what to do, so he learned who was hurt and how to fix it.
How might Anand feel about the first sorry?
Probably still upset, since the car had not been returned. The word alone did not help. 🙂

Read this:

Harsha, you say you're completely sure about this job and the flat and everything. Let your Uday mama tell you about twenty-one-year-old me. I was certain Leena and I would marry. I had planned it all: the city, the job near her college, even names for children. When my father asked what I'd do if things changed, I got angry and left the room. I turned down a good posting in Pune because it was far from her. Then in my final year she told me she wanted a different life. It was nobody's fault. But because I had never let a single doubt in, I had nothing to lean on. It took me two years to stand straight again.

Which posting did Uday turn down?
Uday turned down a good posting in Pune because it was far from Leena.
Why did young Uday get angry when his father asked what he'd do if things changed?
He was so sure of the future that even a question about doubt felt like an attack on it, so he pushed it away instead of thinking about it.
What could Harsha take from Uday mama's story about the new job and flat?
Harsha can stay hopeful but ask what would happen if the plan changed, and keep some options open, so a surprise doesn't knock everything down.
How might Uday's father have felt when his son left the room?
His father probably felt worried and helpless, seeing his son build everything on one certainty and refuse any question about it.

I'm Manjula, and two weeks ago I got into a pointless fight with a stranger online. I'd posted my drawing of a heron on an art forum. Someone called "realart_only" commented: "Kids shouldn't post trash. Delete this." My face went hot. At midnight I typed three long replies, each ruder than the last. The stranger kept going, and the more I answered, the more they laughed. I couldn't sleep. Next morning my friend Sabina looked at my phone and said, "You're feeding them. They want you angry." She showed me how to mute and block. I did both, and then I tried something new: I waited a whole day before posting anything. My next heron got twelve kind comments. I read them after a good night's sleep.

What did "realart_only" comment on the heron drawing?
The comment said, "Kids shouldn't post trash. Delete this."
What was Manjula feeling while typing the midnight replies?
Manjula felt hurt and angry, with a hot face, and got more heated with each reply.
Which steps helped Manjula, and why?
Muting and blocking cut off the troll, and waiting a day before posting stopped Manjula reacting in anger.
How did the stranger likely see Manjula's angry replies?
The stranger probably enjoyed them, since the more Manjula answered, the more they laughed.

The gram panchayat had hired a projector for the women's cricket final, and half the village of Kherwadi sat on durries in the school ground. Indu, fifteen, squeezed between her brother Vaibhav and the old postman.
In the last over the team needed nine runs. Indu found she was gripping Vaibhav's wrist so hard he winced. Her own mouth was dry, her knees jumping. When the batter swung and the ball flew, Indu was on her feet before it landed, and so was everyone else, the postman too, his cap falling off.
"Six!" someone yelled. Two balls later, a four, and the ground exploded. Strangers hugged her. A grandmother Indu had never spoken to kissed her forehead.
Walking home under the stars, Indu's legs still trembled. "I didn't even hit the ball," she said. Vaibhav laughed. "You nearly broke my wrist hitting it."

Where was the final shown?
It was shown on a projector in the school ground.
Why were Indu's legs still trembling on the walk home?
She had felt the last over as if she were playing, with a dry mouth and jumping knees, and the thrill had not left her body yet.
What made this final such a strong experience for Indu, and what could she choose to do with that?
Watching with the whole village turned her own pounding heart into shared joy; she could seek out more matches with others, or even ask to join a local team.
How did the old postman seem to experience the moment?
He jumped up with everyone, cap falling off, showing that the win swept up older villagers too, not just the young.

Friday, week six of the internship
Mehul presented to the client today. Mehul. We started the same Monday.
I see how it happens. Tanuja, our manager, stops at his desk every morning. "I think you can handle the pricing model. Show me a draft by Wednesday." Then she marks it up in red, line by line, and he fixes it and it gets better.
To me she says, "Pradeep, can you format these slides?" and doesn't look at them afterwards. No red pen. Nothing.
So I format slides. I leave at six. Honestly, I've stopped trying much. Why bother when nobody's expecting anything?
But reading this back, I'm not sure it's that I can't do more. Nobody has ever asked me to.

What did Tanuja ask Mehul to show her by Wednesday?
She asked him for a draft of the pricing model by Wednesday.
What is Pradeep feeling while writing about Mehul's presentation?
Pradeep feels left out and discouraged, even a bit resentful, since nobody seems to expect anything of Pradeep.
What could Pradeep try next week to change the pattern?
Pradeep could ask Tanuja directly for a stretch task and for feedback on the slides, so the lack of expectation is questioned rather than accepted.
How might Mehul experience the same internship?
Mehul probably feels challenged and valued, since Tanuja's red-pen feedback and belief push his work to get better.

The inter-school science quiz was starting in five minutes, and the hall was hot and noisy. Noor, eleven, from the small municipal school, sat on stage beside students from the big private schools. She heard one of them whisper to Lavanya, his teammate, "Municipal school kids never get past round one."
Noor's hands went cold. Her stomach twisted. She knew about magnets and plants and the water cycle. But in round one, the quizmaster asked about evaporation, and all she could think was: don't prove him right, don't prove him right.
She hesitated too long. The buzzer went.
Afterwards, Lavanya came up to her. "That boy was rude. You knew that answer. I saw your face."
Noor nodded, eyes stinging. She had known it. Fear had just taken up all the room.

What did the boy whisper about municipal school kids?
He whispered that municipal school kids never get past round one.
What was Noor feeling when the quizmaster asked about evaporation?
She felt anxious and afraid, so focused on not proving the boy right that she couldn't think.
How could Noor's teacher help her before the next quiz?
Remind her that her score reflects her preparation, not her school, and let her practise in front of an audience.
How does Lavanya see what happened to Noor?
Lavanya thinks the boy was rude and believes Noor knew the answer.
