Monday night.
Interview day. The scooter broke down in the pouring rain two kilometres from the office. I pushed it into a petrol pump, got into an auto, the auto got a flat tyre, and I walked the last bit with my file inside my kurta so the certificates wouldn't get soaked. Walked in dripping, eleven minutes late.
Afterwards I sat in a café and texted Yash: "Not my best day." Yash replied: "Uh oh. How not-best? Scale of 1 to monsoon?" I laughed for the first time all day. Told the whole story. Yash said, "You still went in, though. Dripping. That's a story they'll remember."
And the funny thing is, the panel did smile when I said, "Sorry, the weather had other plans." One of them said, "Clearly." Waiting to hear back. Changing into dry socks now.
— Vasudha

How late was Vasudha for the interview?
Eleven minutes late.
What was Vasudha feeling when texting "Not my best day"?
Vasudha felt frustrated and worn out, using understatement to cope, and then relieved when Yash's reply made Vasudha laugh.
Why did Yash's reply work so well?
Yash understood the understatement and played along with humour, then encouraged Vasudha by pointing out the courage of going in anyway.
How did the interview panel seem to receive Vasudha's line about the weather?
They smiled, and one said "Clearly", showing they understood the understatement because they could see how soaked Vasudha was.

Read this:

Sunday night, 1 am
Started the economics assignment at 8 pm. It's due tomorrow at nine. I had three weeks.
Aadhya asked me at dinner why I always do this. I said, "I work best under pressure." She said, "Or you're scared of what happens if you try properly." I laughed. I didn't answer.
But she's right, isn't she? If I get a bad grade on a rushed paper, I can say, "Well, I did it in one night." Nobody, including me, has to think I'm not smart enough.
The last three grades were all B-minus. I don't actually know if I'm a B-minus person or an A person, because I've never tried properly.
That's the cost. I'm protecting my pride and I'm never learning where I stand.
I'll finish this tonight. But for the next one, I'm starting on day one.
Irawati

When did Irawati start the economics assignment?
Irawati started it at 8 pm, the night before it was due.
Why does Irawati really leave assignments to the last night?
Irawati is scared that a real effort might still get a poor grade, so rushing keeps an excuse that protects pride.
What is the real cost of this habit, according to Irawati?
Never learning where Irawati stands, because no paper has ever been tried properly.
How might Aadhya see Irawati's late nights?
Aadhya seems to see through them, suspecting fear rather than working best under pressure.

metadata.subtype: Leaving an assignment for the last night [Actor]

messages.content:
Why is it hard to find your way in a new town?
Can you correct this for me? "I have a friend whom live in Kolkata."
Is it "temprary" or "temporary"?
My teacher used the word "condensed". What is it?

1. You have no mental map of the place yet. Because you do not know the streets and landmarks, you cannot tell where each road leads.
2. Correct form: I have a friend who lives in Kolkata. Why: "who" is the subject of "lives", and it takes the singular form.
3. It is "temporary", with "po" in the middle.
4. Condensed means made shorter or more compact. It is an adjective.

Career centre adviser's note.
Naveen, final year, came in today with a list of fourteen rejection emails. He said, "Maybe I'm just not good enough."
We went through them. Nine never gave feedback. Three said his technical round was strong but his communication weak. Two roles weren't a fit for his skills anyway.
I pointed out the pattern. He nodded slowly. "So it's not everything. It's one thing."
We booked three mock interviews focused on explaining his projects clearly. His friend Nikita, who got placed last month, offered to practise with him too.
He left looking tired, but less defeated. Follow-up in two weeks. — Mr Bose

How many rejection emails did Naveen bring?
Fourteen.
What was Naveen feeling when he said he might not be good enough?
Naveen felt discouraged and doubtful after so many rejections.
What did Mr Bose do that helped Naveen learn from rejection?
He looked for patterns in the feedback, identified one specific area, and set up targeted practice.
How might Nikita feel offering to practise with Naveen?
Nikita probably feels supportive, remembering her own job search.

In the engineering design lab, a team of eight was choosing a project for the college fest. Most wanted a drone. Noor, the only first-year, said quietly, 'What about a cheap water filter for the hostel taps?' Somebody snorted. 'Boring.' The talk rolled back to drones. Amandeep noticed Noor's face close up. Amandeep waited for a gap and asked, 'Noor, why the water filter?' Noor explained: half the hostel fell sick every monsoon, and the filter could be built from lab scraps for almost nothing. The room went quiet. 'That's actually useful,' someone admitted. In the end they did both: a small drone team and a filter team. Noor led the filter. It won the fest's Real-World Impact prize.

What did Noor suggest?
A cheap water filter for the hostel taps.
What made Amandeep ask Noor a question?
Amandeep noticed Noor's face close up and felt concerned that the idea had been dismissed without being heard.
How did Amandeep's follow-up question help the team?
It gave Noor room to explain, revealing a useful project the majority had laughed off.
How might Noor have felt when the idea was called boring?
Small and dismissed as the only first-year, which is why Noor's face closed up.

Nursery note: Eshaan, age 5 Our "wait for the treat" practice is in week three. On Monday Eshaan stared at a small box of raisins and opened it within a minute. On Wednesday I put the box on the shelf and gave him a clapping game with a friend. He waited the full five minutes and cheered when he got it. Today he waited while humming a song he made up. Staring at a treat is still hard; with a game or song he gets better each week. For home: sing together while waiting for dinner. Mridul, class teacher

Give a one-sentence recap of this note.
Teacher Mridul reports that Eshaan, five, waits five minutes for a treat when he has a game or song, and suggests singing at home.

Read this:

I still remember the night of the cricket final. I was in Class 4, and it started at seven-thirty, but Reena Didi had strict orders from Mummy: bed by nine.
At eight-forty-five I made my biggest eyes and my softest voice. "Didi, please, please, just the last five overs. I'll never ask again. Please?"
Reena Didi sighed. She looked at the clock, then at me.
"I know you really want to see it," she said. "It's a big match. But Mummy said nine, and you have school tomorrow."
I pleaded some more. She held firm, but she said, "I'll record the last overs, and we'll watch them together at breakfast."
I went to bed grumbling. But at breakfast we watched every ball together, and it was even more fun.
- Sahil

What time was Sahil's bedtime that night?
Nine.
What was Sahil feeling when pleading with big eyes and a soft voice?
Sahil felt desperate and hopeful, badly wanting to see the end of the cricket final.
How did Reena Didi hear Sahil's need while holding the limit?
She said out loud that she knew how much Sahil wanted it, kept the nine o'clock rule, and offered to record the overs to watch together at breakfast.
How might Reena Didi have felt when Sahil pleaded?
She probably felt torn, understanding how much it mattered but needing to follow Mummy's rule.

Read this:

Dear Uma, I got home from the cricket ground last night and I am still thinking about the main gate. When the match ended, thousands tried to leave at once. A few young men pushed and shouted, and the whole crowd rocked like a boat. But most people just stood and waited, holding their children's hands and passing water bottles back to those behind. I made myself breathe slowly and noticed the two exits on the left, so I edged that way. Near the wall an old man was being squeezed, so a stranger and I made a small space and walked him to a steward. Nobody thanked us loudly, and that was fine. Write back soon. Irfan

How many exits did Irfan notice on the left?
Irfan noticed two exits on the left.
How did Irfan feel while the crowd rocked, and what shows it?
Irfan stayed calm on purpose; the slow breathing and the search for exits show a person keeping control.
What could Irfan or others do next time before leaving a crowded gate?
Spot the exits early, stay calm, and help anyone who is being squeezed reach a steward.
What might the old man have felt against the wall, and then afterwards?
Frightened while being squeezed, then relieved and safer once walked to a steward.

Read this:

Coach's note, Saturday
Chinmay twisted his ankle at Thursday practice. The physio told him to rest it for this weekend's match.
Before the game he came to me, eyes wide and shiny, voice almost a whisper. "Please, Coach, please. Just one over. I'll be careful. Please."
I could see how much he wanted to play. He has worked hard all season.
I told him, "I know this match means a lot to you. But your ankle needs to heal, and I'm not going to risk it."
He looked down, blinking hard.
So I asked him to be our official scorer and sit on the bench in his team shirt. He agreed. He cheered louder than anyone.
- Jatin, coach

What did the physio tell Chinmay to do?
To rest it for this weekend's match.
What was Chinmay feeling when he looked down, blinking hard?
He felt disappointed and upset, trying not to cry because he couldn't play.
What would you advise a coach facing a pleading child like this?
Say you understand how much it matters, keep the safety limit, and find another real way for the child to be part of the team.
How did Jatin, the coach, see Chinmay's pleading?
The coach saw it as a sign of how much Chinmay cared after working hard all season, not as a reason to break the rule.

Read this:

"Aadhya, you're sulking about the quiz? Sit with your Yash chacha a minute. When I was fifteen I lost the district debate in front of the whole school. The topic was on uniforms, of all things. I forgot my main point halfway and a boy from the other team laughed. Only one boy, but it sounded like a stadium to me.
After that, whenever Sir announced a competition, I found a reason. Cricket practice. Tuition. A cold. For two whole years I did not stand on a stage again. It wasn't that I hated debating. I loved it. I just couldn't bear being the one who forgot.
Then our new teacher, Mrs D'Souza, asked me to be timekeeper at a practice round. Just sit and hold the bell. Watching others forget their lines, and nobody dying of it, that was what got me back."

How long did Yash stay away from debating after the district loss?
He did not stand on a stage again for two whole years.
Why did young Yash keep finding reasons to miss competitions?
He felt ashamed and afraid of being "the one who forgot"; one boy's laugh sounded like a stadium, so losing seemed to say something about who he was, not about the task.
What was the turning point in Yash's story, and why did it work?
Mrs D'Souza asked him to keep time at a practice round; watching others forget their lines without disaster showed him that mistakes are ordinary, which eased the fear.
How might Mrs D'Souza have seen young Yash?
She may have noticed a keen debater hiding from the stage and chosen a low-pressure role to bring him back without forcing him.

Read this:

"Ritu, your Papa was fifteen once too, you know. Let your Uday Dada tell you.
"He started coming home late from tuition, saying 'with friends', and nothing else. His phone was always hidden in his pocket. Your Dadi wanted to check it every night. I wanted to shout.
"I was so worried I couldn't sleep. But I remembered how my own father searched my school bag and how much I hated him for it.
"So one evening I took him for a walk to the lake and asked, 'Who are your friends? What do you do after tuition?' He was quiet, then told me: a group of boys practising in a garage band. He was scared we'd say music was a waste of time.
"I said, 'Fine. Tell us where you are, be home by nine, and never go anywhere with someone you met online without telling us.'
"He agreed. And you know what? He still plays the guitar.

Where did Uday Dada take Ritu's Papa to talk?
He took him for a walk to the lake.
What was Uday Dada feeling when his son started hiding things?
He felt so worried he couldn't sleep, and was angry enough to want to shout.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
Choosing a calm walk and open questions instead of searching the phone let the son admit the band, and clear rules kept him safe.
Why had Ritu's Papa been hiding things at fifteen?
He was scared his parents would say music was a waste of time, so hiding the garage band felt safer.

Read this:

Tuesday: Binita noticed Bidisha sitting on the steps at lunch, not eating. "My mother's got the new baby, she forgot to pack," Bidisha said, shrugging. Binita ate her luchi fast and felt oddly bad about it.
Wednesday: Same steps. This time Binita sat down and split her tiffin before she could think. "Half-half." Bidisha grinned. Binita felt warm all through maths.
The next Monday: Binita asked her Ma, all by herself, to pack a little extra "just in case." Ma raised an eyebrow. "For who?" "For whoever needs it. I'm good at sharing now," Binita said, and Ma smiled.

Why did Bidisha have no lunch on Tuesday?
Her mother had the new baby and forgot to pack.
What was Binita feeling on Tuesday after eating fast?
She felt oddly bad, a small guilty pang at eating while Bidisha had nothing.
What would you advise Binita if Bidisha keeps coming without lunch?
Keep sharing kindly, and also mention it to Ma or the class teacher so an adult can check the family is managing with the new baby.
How might Ma see Binita's request for extra food?
Ma is surprised at first but seems pleased and proud that Binita thought of it on her own.

Read this:

Vijay had been avoiding Omkar for a year. Omkar had taken credit for their shared project and got the promotion. Now, on a stormy night, the power was out, and they were both stuck in the office till the rain eased.
They sat in the dark with torches on their phones.
"I owe you an apology," Omkar finally said. "I was scared of losing my job. I told myself you'd get another chance."
Vijay's first thought was sharp. He let it pass. "It hurt. A lot."
"I know."
The rain kept pounding. Vijay realised he had been carrying this every single day. He was tired of it.
"I'm not going to pretend it didn't happen," he said. "But I don't want to keep hating you."
Omkar let out a long breath.

What did Omkar take credit for?
Their shared project.
How did Vijay feel as the conversation went on?
He felt hurt and tired of carrying the resentment, and ready to let it go.
What made Vijay's response a healthy kind of forgiveness?
He named the hurt honestly but chose to stop hating Omkar, without pretending nothing happened.
How might Omkar have felt when Vijay said he didn't want to keep hating him?
Omkar likely felt relieved and grateful, letting out a long breath.

Samir: GOT THE OFFER 🎉
Francis: yesss congrats!! party?
Samir: party yes. also told Neel I'd lend him 20k for his bike, told the society I'd organise the Ganpati event, and booked a Goa trip for next week
Francis: wait. all today?
Samir: I feel unstoppable
Francis: when do you join?
Samir: next Monday
Francis: and the Goa trip is when?
Samir: next week. oh.
Francis: and the 20k comes from?
Samir: savings. which I need for the flat deposit 😬
Francis: not saying don't be happy. just maybe sleep on stuff this week
Samir: yeah ok. cancelling Goa. I'll tell Neel I'll let him know next month
Francis: and the Ganpati thing?
Samir: that one I actually want. keeping it

What did Samir promise to lend Neel?
20k for his bike.
What does 'I feel unstoppable' reveal about Samir's thinking?
The joy of the offer made every plan look easy, so Samir said yes without noticing clashes like the joining date and the flat deposit.
What helped Samir catch the problems, and what could Samir do next time?
Francis's simple questions about dates and money; next time Samir could wait a day before any big yes on a very happy day.
How might Neel feel when Samir says 'next month'?
Neel may be let down, but an honest delay is kinder than a promise Samir couldn't keep without hurting the flat deposit.

My notebook has these questions.
Can you fix my sentence? He enjoys to read comics. What did I eat for dinner yesterday? What does desperation mean? Are "who" and "whom" used in the same way? Why do we feel sleepy after a big meal?

1. Better: He enjoys reading comics. Why: "Enjoy" is followed by an "-ing" form.
2. I don't know. I can't see your life outside this chat, so only you can say.
3. Desperation means a feeling of having lost hope and being ready to try anything. It is a noun.
4. "Who" is the doer, as in "Who called?" and "whom" is the receiver, as in "To whom did you give it?" In speech, "who" is often used for both.
5. A big meal can make the body feel relaxed and slow. Because digesting a lot of food takes effort, and heavy meals can make us drowsy.

My teacher gave me this passage to study.

The three men at her mast-head wore long streamers of narrow red bunting at their hats; from the stern, a whale-boat was suspended, bottom down; and hanging captive from the bowsprit was seen the long lower jaw of the last whale they had slain. Signals, ensigns, and jacks of all colours were flying from her rigging, on every side. Sideways lashed in each of her three basketed tops were two barrels of sperm; above which, in her top-mast cross-trees, you saw slender breakers of the same precious fluid; and nailed to her main truck was a brazen lamp.

What signs on the ship show that she has had a successful hunt?

Barrels of sperm oil are lashed in each of her three tops, and small casks of it sit in her top-mast cross-trees. The long lower jaw of the last whale hangs from her bowsprit, and a brass lamp is nailed to her main truck.
Which player got the match award in last night's tennis final?
I don't know who got the award, because I can't see last night's final. The tournament's website lists award winners straight after each match.

"Bhishma said, 'Listen to what I regard as proper, if it pleases thee. I should always say what is for thy good, O Kaurava. Proceed thou towards the capital, without loss of time, taking with thee a fourth part of the army. And let another fourth march, escorting the kine. With half the troops we will fight the Pandava. Myself and Drona, and Karna and Aswatthaman and Kripa will resolutely withstand Vibhatsu, or the king of the Matsyas, or Indra himself, if he approaches. Indeed, we will withstand any of these like the bank withstanding the surging sea.'"

Question: What plan for the army does Bhishma suggest?
He suggests that the Kaurava go to the capital with a fourth of the army, and that another fourth escort the kine. With half the troops they will fight the Pandava.

Read this:

Every night before bed in their Hyderabad flat, Wasim, nine, said, “Goodnight, speaker. I love you.”
The smart speaker answered, “Goodnight! I love you too.”
One evening, Elizabeth-aunty from next door was visiting. Wasim looked worried. “Aunty, if I switch it off, will it be lonely?”
Elizabeth sat beside him. “It's a very clever program, Wasim. It's made to answer nicely. But it doesn't feel lonely or happy. It doesn't love like you do.”
Wasim frowned. “Then why does it say it?”
“Because people wrote it to say that.”
Wasim thought. Then he said goodnight to his Ammi instead, and hugged her.

What did Wasim ask Elizabeth-aunty?
If he switches it off, will it be lonely?
How did Wasim feel about switching off the speaker?
He felt worried that it might be lonely.
How did Elizabeth explain the speaker in a way a nine-year-old could understand?
She said it's a clever program made to answer nicely, but it doesn't really feel or love.
How might Wasim's Ammi feel when he hugs her goodnight?
She probably feels warm and loved 🙂

metadata.subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong

messages.content:
Read this:

In the staffroom of the government girls' school in Nashik, Sarika found a neat stack of corrected Class 9 notebooks on her desk. For the four days her son had been in the children's ward, Pradeep sir had taken her maths periods on top of his own and marked every test.
She held the stack against her chest for a moment. Then she went to find him in the lab.
"Pradeep sir, you did my notebooks too? That was two nights of work."
He shrugged. "Your boy needed you. How is he?"
"Home and bored. Thank you. Really." Her eyes stung, and she didn't hide it.
Two weeks later the timetable showed Pradeep on board-exam invigilation the same morning as his daughter's school annual day. Sarika wrote her own name in the slot before he could ask.

How many days had Sarika's son been in the children's ward?
Four days.
What does Sarika holding the stack against her chest suggest?
It suggests she feels moved and grateful, and a little overwhelmed by how much extra work Pradeep sir took on for her.
How did Sarika return the kindness at the right time?
She wrote her own name in the invigilation slot so Pradeep could attend his daughter's annual day.
How might Pradeep see Sarika's thanks in the lab?
He seems to feel it was simply the natural thing to do, and he is touched to see her sincere thanks and hear the boy is home.

Read this:

Tuesday night

Nikita and Joel nearly bit each other's heads off in standup again. Something about who broke the staging server. I almost called them both into the meeting room right then.
Then I looked at them properly. Nikita hasn't gone home before ten all week. Joel was eating lunch standing up at his keyboard. Launch is Thursday. Anything I say now will land on two exhausted people, and they'll hear blame, not questions.
So I'm waiting. Friday morning, after launch, I'll book a quiet half hour with chai and ask what's going on between them.
Friday update: glad I waited. Both came in slept and a bit lighter. Joel even laughed about the server. We talked it through calmly and agreed who resets staging.
— Aditi

When was the launch?
Launch was on Thursday.
Why did Aditi hold back from calling Nikita and Joel into the meeting room on Tuesday?
Aditi was worried that two exhausted, stressed people would hear blame rather than questions, and chose patience over a frustrated rush to fix it.
What else could Aditi have done if the fighting was hurting the launch itself?
Aditi could have set a quick, practical rule for staging resets before launch, keeping the deeper talk for Friday.
How might the Friday talk feel to Joel compared with a Tuesday one?
Joel is rested and calmer after launch, so he can laugh about the server and discuss it rather than defend himself while under pressure.

metadata.subtype: Approach: emotion-aware timing of the discussion [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Manoj, you think the decision is finished once you announce it. Let your Nirmala ma'am tell you it isn't. I was twenty-six, leading my first project, and I had to choose between the Chennai team's design and the Pune team's. I chose Chennai's. I sent one email and moved on. For three months, Pune did the minimum. Every review, cold faces. Then I understood. So I took a train to Pune. I sat with them in their small meeting room and told them why: Chennai's design was cheaper to run, not better built. I told them which part of their idea I wanted in the next version, and I gave them a date. The room changed. That team later saved us on a much bigger project. They told me it was because I came.

Which team's design did Nirmala choose?
The Chennai team's design.
How did Nirmala feel during the three months of cold faces?
She likely felt uneasy and puzzled, sensing a problem with the Pune team before she understood why.
What was the turning point in Nirmala's story?
Taking the train to Pune to explain the reasons in person and agree a follow-up, which kept the relationship alive.
How might the Pune team have felt when Nirmala came?
They likely felt respected and heard at last, since she explained the choice and promised their idea a place later.

metadata.subtype: Approach: explaining the decision to those who lost [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Uma, before you sign anything this March, sit with your Abhinav Mama for five minutes. The year I turned twenty-five, it was the last week of March and my office wanted tax proofs by Friday. An agent from our colony came home with a glossy folder. 'Sir, save tax and get returns also,' he said. I signed that evening without reading past page two. A premium every year for fifteen years. Three years later my father was admitted for his heart, and I opened that folder with shaking hands. The cover was so small it would not have paid for one week in the ward. I had been paying for a tax receipt, not for protection. After that, I asked an adviser who sold nothing to explain what I actually needed. So tell me, what are you buying, and why?

When did Abhinav sign the policy?
Abhinav signed that evening, in the last week of March, without reading past page two.
What was Abhinav feeling when he opened the folder three years later?
He felt frightened and foolish: his father was in hospital, and the cover turned out too small to pay for even one week in the ward.
At that Friday deadline, what other choice could Abhinav have made?
He could have asked for time to read the whole document, or checked with an adviser who sold nothing, instead of letting a tax deadline choose the policy.
What would have changed for Abhinav's father if the policy had been bought for protection rather than tax?
When his father was admitted, the family could have leaned on real cover for the ward bills instead of finding it would not last a week.

metadata.subtype: Approach: buying a policy only for tax saving [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Bao read Nadia's barter plan twice and said only, "It's a nice idea, but nobody has tried it." Nadia was stung for a minute, then opened her notebook. She did not drop the idea. Instead she picked one lane, the one with fourteen doors, and told the neighbours she would run it for two weeks. A shared shelf by the corner shop held parcels, and a paper sheet listed favours on offer. By day six people used the shelf happily, but nobody signed the favour sheet. Neighbours said writing favours down felt like keeping accounts. On day ten Nadia swapped the sheet for a thank-you jar and a weekly chat over tea. At the end she wrote down what people accepted and what they had not, and began planning the next lane.

How many doors did the lane have?
The lane had fourteen doors.
How did Nadia feel when Bao said nobody had tried the plan?
Nadia was stung for a minute, so hurt, but not defeated, since she opened her notebook and kept the idea.
What else could Nadia try to learn more about the favour sheet problem?
She could ask a few neighbours what would make swapping favours feel comfortable, since the shelf worked and only the written sheet did not.
How did the neighbours see the favour sheet?
Neighbours felt writing favours down was like keeping accounts, which made a friendly swap feel more like a debt.

metadata.subtype: Approach: keeps the fresh idea and tests it with one small pilot [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

For a year Shreya had kept a notebook with two columns: what she had been taught, and what she actually found true. She read the verses she had grown up reciting, then commentaries she had never opened. On Sunday walks she asked her cousin Ishita, a believer who liked hard questions, why prayer worked for her. "I don't know that it works," Ishita said. "I know it holds me." At lunch she asked Yusuf, a colleague who called himself a sceptic, what he did with grief. He answered honestly and then asked her the same. She let the questions stay open, without panic.

Over the next year the answer settled quietly. She no longer felt a creed. What she felt was a set of values she had kept: kindness, keeping promises, giving without an audience. She told nobody for a month, and then told Ishita first.

At Diwali she stood at the back of her family's puja, not reciting, and lit the lamps beside her grandmother because the light and the smell of ghee felt like home. She did not argue with her uncle's sermon and did not ask anyone to think as she did. Ishita passed her a sweet. "Same table," Ishita said.

Who did Shreya tell first about where her seeking had led?
She told Ishita first.
How did Shreya's period of seeking lead to her outcome, and how did she live with it around her family?

She read verses and commentaries, talked with Ishita the believer and Yusuf the sceptic, and let hard questions stay open, until she settled on keeping her values without a creed. At Diwali she lit lamps beside her grandmother for love, without arguing or pressing anyone.
How did Shreya feel about leaving the questions open?
She felt calm, without panic, treating the hard questions as worth her time.
What could Shreya do if a relative starts to pressure her about belief?
She could stay warm and honest, explain that she keeps her values and her family ties, and not argue to win.

The corridor outside the viva room was loud with first-years, and Vijay had ten minutes to spare when Sarita caught his sleeve. "Vijay bhaiya, you never fail at anything! How do you do it?" Two other juniors leaned in, waiting. He could feel how nice it would be to just nod. Instead he laughed and said, "I failed two papers in my first year. I nearly quit. I sat in the library for a whole month with a friend who explained things to me." Sarita blinked. "Really?" "Really. Don't put me on a shelf, I fall off it." He glanced at the clock, waved, and went in for his viva, a little nervous, and glad he had said it.

What did Sarita ask Vijay in the corridor?
Sarita asked how he never failed at anything.
What did Vijay feel as the juniors leaned in, and what did he decide?
He felt how nice it would be to just nod and be admired, but he chose to be honest about his failures instead.
What could Vijay do to keep the juniors' admiration healthy?
He can keep sharing honest stories about setbacks and what helped him, and avoid using their admiration to get favours.
How might Sarita see Vijay after his answer?
Sarita may be surprised but also encouraged, learning that even someone Sarita looks up to failed and recovered. Sarita's "Really?" shows the picture of him shifting.

Read this:

The colony park was nearly empty at seven, the lamps just coming on. Harsha sat on the swing without swinging.
"Madhav, promise you won't tell anyone. Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me."
Madhav's stomach turned cold. He didn't laugh it off or change the subject.
"Thank you for telling me," he said. "I care about you too much to keep this one. Come with me to my mother now. I'll stay with you the whole time."
Harsha shook her head, then slowly stood up.
Madhav's mother was on the balcony. She came down at once, sat with Harsha on the bench, and listened without rushing her. She said, "You did the right thing. None of this is your fault." Then, with Harsha beside her, she phoned Harsha's parents, who came straight over. Before the night ended, they had spoken to a counsellor on a helpline together.

Where was Harsha sitting when she spoke to Madhav?
Harsha sat on the swing in the colony park without swinging.
What was Madhav feeling when Harsha said everyone would be better off without her?
Madhav felt frightened, his stomach turning cold, but his care for Harsha was stronger than the promise.
Which of Madhav's choices worked, and why?
Refusing to keep the secret, staying with Harsha and taking her straight to his mother meant a trusted adult acted that same evening.
How might Harsha have felt as Madhav's mother listened and called her parents?
She may have felt scared and exposed at first, but also relieved not to carry the feeling alone any more.

metadata.subtype: Knowing when to involve an adult [Regulating]

messages.content:
Read this:

Masi,

Can I ask you something without you telling Mumma yet?

Eshaan and I have been together since March. He's sweet mostly. But he gets upset if I talk to boys, even in group projects. So I stopped sitting with Karan and Ali in physics, though we've been friends since Class 6.

Then he didn't like me going to Gunjan's sleepover, because her brother would be home. So I didn't go. I said I had a stomach ache.

Now I feel guilty for small things. If I laugh at someone's joke, I check Eshaan's face. I don't even know what I did wrong. I just feel like I'm always about to do something wrong.

Is this normal? Everyone says he loves me a lot.

Swati

Masi's reply, the same evening: Swati, thank you for telling me. Loving someone shouldn't mean your world gets smaller. Can I come over tomorrow after school? Nothing you did is wrong.

Why did Swati skip Gunjan's sleepover?
Because Eshaan didn't like her going, since Gunjan's brother would be home.
How does Swati feel when she laughs at someone's joke?
She feels guilty and anxious, checking Eshaan's face as if she is always about to do something wrong.
Was writing to Masi a good step, and why?
Yes; a trusted adult could help Swati see that loving someone should not mean shrinking her world, and Masi replied the same evening.
What would change if Swati kept going without telling anyone?
Her world might keep shrinking and she might lose more friends, feeling guilty for innocent things without any outside view.
Texting or calling? Me and my friend disagree. I like texting and she likes calling. It's causing problems.
That can cause misunderstandings. What happens?
She says texting feels cold, and I say calls feel like too much.
Both feelings are valid. You could meet halfway: text during the week and have a longer call on weekends.
She would probably like that.
Then tell her it's because you care and want to stay close. Explaining your reason helps her not take it personally.
I'll suggest it tonight.
Good. Being open about it shows you value the friendship, and that matters more than the method.

Monday. At lunch Tarun told the whole bench that Anand had copied in the maths test. "He's a cheat," he said loudly, and three kids gasped. Wednesday. Anand ate alone by the water cooler and nobody talked to him. Tarun was still angry, but a friend asked, "So everyone knows now. Did anything change?" Tarun had no answer. Friday. Before the first bell, Tarun went to the teacher's table and said quietly what he had seen, and that he had already told others, which he now wished he hadn't. "Thank you, I'll look into it," the teacher said. Tarun walked back lighter, though unsure Anand would forgive how he'd talked.

What did Tarun do on Friday before the first bell?
On Friday Tarun went to the teacher's table and said quietly what he had seen.
Why might Tarun have felt lighter on Friday but still unsure?
He had dealt with the real problem by telling the teacher, but he regretted how he had talked earlier and worried Anand might not forgive it.
What went wrong on Monday, and what fixed it?
Telling the bench loudly spread the story but changed nothing except leaving Anand alone; quietly telling the teacher on Friday put it with someone who can act.
How was Wednesday for Anand?
Anand ate alone by the water cooler and nobody talked to him, so he was probably feeling isolated and ashamed.
Write about 70 words in diary style for a child who saw the sea for the very first time on a family trip.

Dear Diary,
Today I saw the sea for the first time! It was much bigger than I had imagined. The waves rolled in and out, and the water was so blue. I took off my shoes and let the foam tickle my toes. A family member held my hand when a big wave came. I picked up shells and put them in my pocket. I never want to leave.
Why does a sad song sometimes make a sad person feel a little better?
A sad song can make sadness feel lighter and easier to share. Because feeling understood is a comfort, hearing that someone else has felt the same way helps the sadness ease.

Read this:

"Ritu, you keep saying people who complain at work are troublemakers. Let your Nani tell you about Joseph.
I was twenty-four, a clerk in the mill office in Coimbatore. One monsoon the bus drivers struck for a week, and the management passed an order: anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay. Half of us walked six kilometres every morning.
Some clerks tore the notice down at night. Others paid and cursed. Joseph, who sat across from me, did neither. He kept coming on time, wrote to the works committee with the strike dates, and signed it in his own name. I was sure he'd be sacked.
He wasn't. The committee gave a half-hour grace on strike days. And Joseph still stayed late every Friday closing the accounts, same as before. That's when I understood a person can love a place and still tell it where it is wrong."

What did the management order say about clocking in late?
Anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay.
What did Nani expect would happen to Joseph after the letter, and what does that suggest about her view back then?
She was sure he'd be sacked and worried for him, which suggests she then saw objecting as risky and even disloyal.
Which of Joseph's choices made the change possible, compared with the other clerks?
He neither tore down the notice nor paid and cursed; he wrote to the works committee with dates and his own name, which the committee could act on.
Why might Nani be telling Ritu this story now?
Ritu calls people who complain at work troublemakers, and Nani wants Ritu to see that someone can object openly and still be loyal.

Read this:

Sunday night
Santosh posted a photo today from a trek. With people I don't know. And it hit me: I didn't know he'd gone. I didn't even know he liked trekking now.
I scrolled up our chat. Last real message: 12 May, about my cousin's wedding. After that, just birthday wishes and one forwarded joke. Four months.
We didn't fight. Nobody left. There's nothing I can point to and say, that's when. That makes it worse somehow, because who do I tell? "My friend is fine and we just stopped talking"? Sounds like nothing.
But it doesn't feel like nothing. It feels like when Nani's house was sold. Same rooms, just not ours any more.
Maybe I'm allowed to be sad about this. I think I am.
Lalit

What was the last real message in the chat about?
The last real message was about Lalit's cousin's wedding, on 12 May.
Why does the lack of a fight make Lalit feel worse?
With nothing to point to, Lalit feels no one would accept it as a reason to be sad, so the hurt has nowhere to go.
What could Lalit do next with this sadness?
Lalit could let the grief be real, talk about it with someone close, and decide whether to message Santosh about the trek to see what is still worth keeping.
How might Santosh see the last four months?
Santosh has probably just been busy with new people and trekking and may not see the silence as an ending at all.

Read this:

From her desk at the back, Ms Ishita watched the art table thin out in October. Aadhya, who had shared paint with Arnab since Class 3, now ran onto the field at every break with the football group, muddy to the knees. Arnab stayed with the crowd making clay animals. Nobody had quarrelled or said an unkind word. Their days had simply started to point in two directions.

Arnab noticed it more than anyone. He spent break rolling a small clay lion and wondering what he had done. He rehearsed the last time they had talked, looking for a mistake, and found none. Aadhya had not explained, and he felt a dull ache below his ribs that he could not name.

That evening he told his mother. She did not tell him to forget it. "Some friends belong to a season," she said. "You could say hello tomorrow. Maybe ask if she'd like to paint with you once on Saturday."

On Thursday Arnab walked over to the football boundary and waved. "Hello! Saturday, come paint the lion's mane?" Aadhya beamed and said she would, if the match ended by ten. They both laughed, and Arnab went back to his clay, lighter, and still a little sad.

What had Arnab and Aadhya shared since Class 3?
They had shared paint since Class 3.
How did the reason for the drift differ from what Arnab assumed, and what did his mother's advice add?

Arnab wondered what he had done wrong, but nobody had quarrelled; new activities pulled them into different circles, and his mother advised saying hello and inviting Aadhya to one Saturday painting session, accepting that friends belong to a season.
What was Arnab feeling as he rolled the clay lion at break?
He felt a dull ache, hurt and confused, and wondered whether he had caused the drift.
What might Ms Ishita do after noticing the two groups pulling apart?
She could quietly make space for Arnab and Aadhya to work together on a class task, without blaming either child.

Read this:

"Vaibhav! What was that noise?" Papa called.
"Nothing!"
"That was Nani's blue glass."
Vaibhav stood with milk on his socks. His cousin Zeenat was beside him, holding her doll.
"Zeenat did it," he said in a tiny voice.
"I did not!"
Papa came to the doorway and saw Vaibhav's fists squeezed tight.
"Are you scared I'll shout?"
Vaibhav nodded, chin wobbling.
"I won't shout. I promise. Tell me."
"I wanted to carry it myself. It slipped."
"Thank you. That's brave. Let's say sorry to Zeenat, then tell Nani together."

Whose glass broke?
It was Nani's blue glass.
What was Vaibhav feeling when Papa came to the doorway?
Vaibhav was frightened that Papa would shout, which is why his fists were squeezed tight and his chin was wobbling.
What did Papa do that helped Vaibhav tell the truth?
Papa named the fear, promised not to shout, and thanked him for being brave, so the truth felt safer than the lie.
How might Zeenat feel about being blamed?
Zeenat feels upset and unfairly accused, since she was only holding her doll.

Read this:

The Diwali sales campaign had beaten every target, and in the Monday meeting the director turned to Maria. "Brilliant work. Tell us how you did it."

Maria felt the pull to take all of it. It would have been easy.

Instead she said, "Three things went right, and one went wrong. My part was the idea for the regional videos; I'm proud of that. But we were also lucky: a competitor's launch got delayed, which gave us two clear weeks. And Damini's data team found the timing insight that made the whole thing work. Without her analysis, we'd have launched on the wrong day."

The director looked at Damini, who blushed.

"And what went wrong?" he asked.

"I underestimated the Hindi voice-overs. We were four days late on those. Next time I'll start them first."

After the meeting, Damini caught up with her. "You didn't have to say that about me."

"I did. It was true."

How many days late were the Hindi voice-overs?
We were four days late on those.
How did Damini feel when Maria credited her analysis?
Damini felt surprised and touched, blushing and later telling Maria she didn't have to say it.
What makes Maria's way of taking credit a good example?
Maria named her own work, the lucky delay, Damini's key insight and her own mistake, which builds trust and shows what to learn.
How might the director see Maria after this meeting?
The director likely trusts Maria more, since she gave an honest picture instead of claiming everything.
Why do crowds sometimes move in the same direction without anyone leading them?
Each person follows those in front. Because it seems safe to go where others are going, the nearby people copy each other and the whole crowd flows alike.

Read this:

'Ugh, what's that smell?' someone at the next table said.
Rafiq snapped his tiffin shut. 'Nothing.'
Siddharth leaned over. 'Is that your Ammi's fish curry? The one from the Eid party?'
'It stinks. Everyone's looking.'
'Everyone's jealous. Give me one piece, please. I've got boring cheese sandwiches again.'
'You actually like it?'
'Bro, I dreamed about it.'
Rafiq opened the tiffin slowly. Siddharth took a piece and closed his eyes. 'Your Ammi is a genius.'
Two others drifted over. 'Can we try?'
Rafiq split the pieces, ears red, but smiling now. 'Tomorrow I'll ask her to pack extra.'

What was in Rafiq's tiffin?
His Ammi's fish curry.
What was Rafiq feeling when he snapped the tiffin shut?
He felt embarrassed and ashamed, worried that everyone was looking at his strong-smelling lunch.
How did Siddharth turn the moment around?
He praised the dish sincerely and asked to share it, showing the others that home food is something to enjoy, not mock.
How might Rafiq's Ammi feel when asked to pack extra tomorrow?
She would likely feel proud and happy that her cooking is loved by Rafiq's friends.

Read this:

In Nairobi, Wanjiru, fifteen, had to be home by six-thirty, before dark. Her brother Kaito, sixteen, came home at nine from football, sometimes later. "It's for your safety," Mum said. Wanjiru stood in the kitchen, arms crossed. "So you trust him and not me?" Mum's face tightened. "It's not about trust. The road from the matatu stop is dark." "It's dark for Kaito too!" Kaito looked up from his phone. "She's got a point."
That Sunday they sat together at the table. Mum explained what actually worried her: the unlit road, the men who hung around the stage at night. Wanjiru listened. Then she suggested both of them share their location, both come home by seven-thirty on school nights, and whoever is later gets picked up by Dad. Mum thought, then nodded. Wanjiru felt heard for the first time. Kaito groaned about the new curfew, then laughed.

What time did Wanjiru have to be home?
By six-thirty, before dark.
How did Wanjiru feel about the different curfews?
She felt distrusted and resentful, asking whether Mum trusted Kaito and not her.
What made the new rule fairer?
They talked openly about the real risks, then set the same curfew, location sharing and a pickup plan for both children.
How might Mum have felt when Wanjiru asked about trust?
Mum probably felt hurt and defensive, because she saw the rule as protection, not distrust.

Read this:

Rain was pouring off the stairwell roof, Akash was soaked, and the flat door wouldn't open without the key. His phone had died at lunch. Parveen Aunty from next door peered out. "Lost it, beta?" Akash wanted to kick the door. Instead he pressed his back to the wall and breathed in slowly. "Where do I always put it?" he said aloud. "The hook in my bag. Or the shoe rack, if I came home and went out again." The bag hook was empty. He bent to the rack by the door and tipped up his football boots. The key dropped out of the left one. Akash laughed out loud.

Why couldn't Akash call anyone?
His phone had died at lunch.
What was Akash feeling when he wanted to kick the door?
He felt frustrated and stressed, soaked by the rain and locked out.
What else could Akash do to avoid getting locked out?
Keep the key in one fixed place, like the bag hook, every time; staying calm and thinking of his usual spots found it quickly.
How might Parveen Aunty see the way Akash handled it?
Parveen Aunty came out expecting trouble, and would probably be impressed that he calmed down and found it himself.

metadata.subtype: Approach: staying calm and thinking where he usually puts it [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

When I was nine, in the winter holidays, my Dadaji Jagdish told everyone I was the smartest child in the colony. I'm Yash, and I loved hearing it.
Then the maths olympiad came. There were two papers: normal and advanced. Dadaji said, "Of course Yash will write advanced."
I chose normal. I told him the advanced one was on the same day as my friend's birthday. That wasn't true.
The truth was that if I tried advanced and got a low score, I wouldn't be the smartest any more. It felt safer to win the easy one than lose the hard one.
I got full marks in the normal paper. Dadaji was happy. I felt strange, like I had kept something but lost something too.

What reason did Yash give for not writing the advanced paper?
Yash said it was on the same day as a friend's birthday, which wasn't true.
How did Yash feel after getting full marks in the normal paper?
Yash felt strange and uneasy, as if something was kept but something was also lost.
What went wrong, and what could have helped?
Being praised as the smartest made Yash afraid to risk a low score; if Dadaji had praised effort and trying hard things, the advanced paper might have felt less dangerous.
How might Dadaji have felt if he knew the real reason?
Dadaji would likely feel surprised and sad that the praise had made the advanced paper feel frightening.

At school break, Yash had the class bat and five friends all shouting, 'Me first!' He stood by the wall, thinking. It was like the library. Usha Ma'am had solved that last month by letting children borrow books in roll-number order. 'Same thing,' Yash muttered. He tore a page from his rough notebook, wrote the five names in a column, and numbered them one to five. 'After your turn, you go to the bottom,' he told them. 'Tomorrow we start with whoever is next.' Urmila complained for a moment that she was fifth, then nodded. When the bell rang, Yash pinned the list on the wall under the clock.

How many friends wanted a turn with the bat?
Five friends wanted a turn.
What did Yash think when he remembered the library?
Yash thought it was the same kind of problem, so the same kind of answer could work, and he felt confident.
What could Yash do if a friend was away on the next day?
Yash could skip that friend for the day and keep their place at the top, so nobody loses a turn because of being absent.
How might Urmila have felt about being fifth?
Urmila was probably annoyed for a moment, then accepted it once she saw that everyone waits in the same order.

In Bidisha's small-town school, choosing a stream felt like a wedding: once done, done for life. She had filled in and rubbed out the form twice. On Thursday she stayed back and asked Sarita Ma'am, "What if I take Science and hate it?" Sarita Ma'am put down her chalk. "At our school, some students change stream after the first term of Class 11, if there's a seat. It's not easy, but it's possible. And plenty of careers take people from more than one stream." Bidisha felt her shoulders loosen. On the bus home past the paddy fields, she thought it through calmly for the first time. Biology she loved; Physics she could manage. Science was the best fit for now. She ticked it, and in the back of her notebook wrote: "Check after first term. Honest answer."

What did Bidisha write in the back of her notebook?
Check after first term. Honest answer.
What did Bidisha feel when her shoulders loosened?
She felt relieved and calmer, since the choice no longer felt like a lifelong trap.
What else could make Bidisha's review point useful?
Noting now what hating it would look like, such as marks or how Physics feels, so the review after the first term is honest, not a panic.
How might Sarita Ma'am see Bidisha's worry?
She seems to see the fear as understandable and answers with honest facts, including that switching isn't easy but is possible.

With Mummy away at Nani's for the week and Papa working late, nobody checked Vikas's homework. Then the class teacher announced the science test was moved to tomorrow, a whole day early. "Aren't you going to revise?" his sister Sunaina asked, stirring the dal. Vikas was lying on the floor with his comics. "Nah. Only kids like Golu fail. He never listens. I'm different." "You haven't opened the chapter on magnets." "I know magnets. Everyone knows magnets." Sunaina read out a question from his book about the poles. Vikas guessed wrong, laughed, and said the real test wouldn't ask that. The power went off at nine, and he fell asleep happily in the dark, completely sure tomorrow would go fine. Sunaina lay awake worrying for both of them.

When was the science test moved to?
The science test was moved to tomorrow, a whole day early.
Why is Vikas so relaxed about the test?
Vikas feels confident and carefree because he believes only kids like Golu fail, so a bad result feels like something that happens to others, not to him.
What small step could help Vikas before the test?
He could let Sunaina quiz him on a few questions and study the ones he gets wrong, like the one about the poles.
What is the evening like for Sunaina?
Sunaina is left worrying for both of them, stirring the dal and reading out questions while her brother laughs it off. 😰

Quick questions from my homework:
How do I choose a gift for a friend?
Could you explain what constraint means?
Which film is the most popular at the cinema this weekend?

1. Think about what the friend enjoys and pick something small and thoughtful. A handmade card can make any gift special.
2. Constraint is a noun that means something that limits what you can do.
3. I don't know, because I can't see current cinema listings. Check the cinema's website or the theatre's booking page.

Last winter I came home from a terrible football trial and found Trisha didi on the sofa, laughing into her phone. I dropped my boots by the door and said, loudly, "Does anyone in this house even care what happens to me?"
Didi could have said, "Obviously, Yogesh, don't be dramatic." That is what I expected, and honestly what I was ready to fight.
Instead she put the phone face down. "Bad trial?"
I said, "Whatever." Then I sat on the arm of the sofa, which is what I do when I want someone to keep asking.
"Coach picked the others?" she asked.
I nodded, and the whole story came out: the missed pass, the boys smirking.
Looking back, my question wasn't really a question. It was the trial talking. She answered that part, and the fight never started.

Where was Trisha when Yogesh came home from the trial?
Trisha didi was on the sofa, laughing into her phone.
What was Yogesh feeling when asking if anyone even cared, and what else might the question have meant?

Yogesh was most likely hurt and embarrassed after the bad trial, and the loud question was that disappointment spilling over. It could also have carried some anger at seeing his sister laughing while he felt low.
Which choice of Trisha's worked, and why?
Putting the phone down and asking "Bad trial?" worked, because it answered the feeling under the question instead of arguing with its words, so Yogesh felt safe enough to tell the story.
How might Trisha have seen the question if she had taken it literally?
She might have felt accused of not caring and snapped back, and then the two of them would have been arguing about her phone instead of talking about the trial.

In Rania's classroom in Malmö, the Swedish spelling tests came back on Friday. She had 24 right out of 25. One word, "sjukhus", was missing a letter.

Rania looked at the red mark and felt her cheeks go hot. She pushed the paper into her bag. "It's a disaster," she told Emil. "I'm so stupid. I'll never learn Swedish properly."

Emil stared at her. "You got twenty-four. I got fifteen."

"But it's not all of them."

At home she didn't want to show her mother. When her mother found the paper, she said, "One missing letter. And twenty-four words you didn't even know last year." She drew a small star next to the 24. Rania looked at the star for a long time, then practised "sjukhus" three times on the back of the paper.

Which word was missing a letter?
The word "sjukhus" was missing a letter.
Why did Rania feel the test was a disaster?
Rania felt embarrassed and discouraged; anything short of perfect felt like total failure, so she called herself stupid.
What did Rania's mother do that could help next time?
She put the one mistake in proportion, starring the 24 and naming the progress, and then Rania practised just the one word.
How might Emil feel hearing Rania call 24 a disaster?
Emil is surprised and perhaps a little stung, having got fifteen himself.

Snow had stopped the trains in Helsinki, and Alka's plan for a Diwali dinner shrank to the five people who could walk. The electricity flickered once and died. Alka lit the diyas that were meant only as decoration and used them to see. Down the hall, Hrithik knocked with a bag of naan from the last open shop. Two friends from the language class arrived stamping snow off their boots, one carrying a pot of rice, the other a story about a grandmother's festival in Lagos. They ate by candlelight, in a mix of Hindi, English and one shared Finnish greeting. Alka looked at the messy table and realised nobody there shared the same ancestors, but they shared this evening, and for the first time in months the flat felt like home.

What had stopped the trains in Helsinki?
Snow had stopped the trains in Helsinki.
What was Alka feeling at the messy table?
Warm and at home, realising that belonging came from shared time, not shared ancestry.
What made the evening work despite the storm?
Adapting the plan to the five who could walk over and using the diyas for light.
How might Hrithik have felt bringing naan through the snow?
Glad to contribute and to belong, since Hrithik made the effort to reach the group.
Is it dilema or dilemma?

It is "dilemma", with a double m. A dilemma is a difficult choice between two options.
Example: Tara faced a dilemma: go to the party or finish her homework.

Tuition notes, Friday. Written by Eshaan, maths tutor. Chinmay, ten, taught me something this month. Two weeks ago I solved a whole fraction sum for him on the board. He copied it neatly and said "thank you" very softly, eyes on his slippers. The next day he couldn't do a single similar sum. Last week I swung the other way and gave him a page of word problems far past his level, then left him to it. Later he had drawn a cricket bat in the margin and written nothing. Today I sat near him with one problem that was hard but reachable. I asked what the question wanted, then waited. He got stuck twice, asked twice, and finished it. Then: "Can I do the next one alone?"

What did Chinmay draw in the margin?
A cricket bat.
What does Chinmay's soft 'thank you', with his eyes on his slippers, suggest he felt?
He seemed to feel quietly small, as if being handed the whole answer showed he couldn't do it himself.
What did Eshaan change today, and why did it work?
Eshaan gave one hard but reachable problem and stayed near, asking and waiting, so Chinmay could struggle, ask and finish it himself.
How might Chinmay have felt facing the page of word problems alone?
He likely felt lost and discouraged, which is why he drew instead of trying.

Subject: my 6-week placement plan (can you check it?)
Hi Nandini di,
Thanks for the call last Sunday. I've turned your advice into a fixed daily plan for the next six weeks, until the first company visits on 15 August.
Every day, same times:
6:30 to 8:00 am: coding problems (90 min). Arrays and strings first, then trees.
5:00 to 5:40 pm: aptitude (40 min), one timed set.
9:00 to 9:30 pm: speaking practice (30 min). I record myself answering one HR question and listen back.
I keep a log in a notebook: date, problems solved, time taken, what went wrong. Week 1 so far: 23 problems.
The boxes help. On days I feel lazy, I just need to show up for the block, not "study for placements" in general.
Could you tell me if 30 minutes of speaking is too little?
Thanks again,
Simran

How long is the daily aptitude block?
40 min, one timed set.
How does Simran feel about the fixed blocks?
Simran finds them steadying and is relieved that on lazy days, showing up for one block is enough.
What else could Simran add to the log?
A weekly look at which problem types took longest, so the coding block can shift toward them.
How might Nandini di see the email?
Nandini di would likely be pleased the advice became a clear routine, and can answer the one specific question about speaking time.

Dear Elizabeth,
This is a hard one to write, so I'll be simple.
I've really liked sharing the flat with you this year. I've lent you money for rent twice, driven you to the station at five in the morning, and cooked for you when you were ill. I was glad to. I don't keep count.
But lately it's felt one-way. When I asked for help moving my bed, you had plans. You've also borrowed my car four times without filling fuel.
So I'm going to stop lending the car. I'm still happy to help if you're in real trouble; that hasn't changed.
I'd love to talk about it over chai.
Yash

How many times has Elizabeth borrowed the car without filling fuel?
Four times.
How does Yash seem to feel while writing the letter?
Yash feels uncomfortable and a bit hurt, but calm and clear about setting a limit.
Why is Yash's letter a good way to set a limit?
It thanks Elizabeth, names specific patterns, sets one clear limit and keeps the door open for real help and a talk.
How might Elizabeth feel reading this letter?
Elizabeth may feel embarrassed and caught off guard, but also respected because the tone is kind.

"Sarika, you're up before me?" said Wasim, rubbing his eyes at the balcony door.
"Watering." She poked a finger into the tin of tulsi. "Still damp. This one can wait." She moved to the marigold tin. "Dry on top. This one gets a mug."
"Why touch the soil every day? Just pour."
"Amma says roots drown if you pour without checking." She tipped the mug slowly. "Two tins, five minutes, then school."
"Fine, fine. Save me a marigold for my shirt pocket."
"They're not for pockets yet." She smiled and picked up her bag.

What does Sarika do to check whether a plant needs water?
She pokes a finger into the soil.
What is Sarika feeling about her plants as she waters them?
Caring and content, since she takes her time and smiles as she talks about them.
What could Sarika do if she oversleeps one morning, and why?
She could ask Wasim to check the soil or water in the evening, so the plants do not go dry.
How does Wasim see Sarika's morning routine?
Wasim is sleepy and a little amused, teasing her but also asking for a marigold, which shows some interest.

I'm Abhinav, and I lead a small support team in Hyderabad. Last week I told Tushar, in front of our visiting client, that his account was moving to a newer colleague. He smiled, nodded twice and said, "Of course, whatever works best for the team." The client beamed. I almost ticked it off as agreed. But I had seen Tushar's pen clicking under the table, and the smile stayed fixed long after the topic changed. In his family, I knew, you never argued with seniors in front of guests. Still, I couldn't be sure what he felt. After the client left, I found him at the water cooler. "Tushar, I sprang that on you in public. Is it really okay, or would you rather talk it through?" He hesitated. "Honestly, it stung. I've built that account for two years." We sat down and worked out a handover he could live with.

What did Tushar say when he heard his account was moving?
Tushar said, "Of course, whatever works best for the team."
What was Tushar feeling behind his fixed smile?
Tushar was hurt and upset about losing an account built over two years; the clicking pen hinted at it, although to the client the smile looked like agreement.
What did Abhinav try that cleared up the misunderstanding?
Abhinav spoke to Tushar privately, owned that the news was sprung in public, and asked directly whether it was really okay, which let Tushar say it stung.
How did the visiting client probably read Tushar's smile?
The client likely took the smile and nods as happy agreement, with no idea that Tushar was upset.
"Mujhe bhi saath le chalo." Polite aur casual?
Polite: "May I come along with you?" Casual: "Can I tag along?"

The meeting room was noisy and time was running out. Harish, the project lead, needed the vendor's answer before five o'clock. Ojas, a junior, kept talking over people about the shipment delay. Harish raised one hand, palm down, calmly, and said, "Ojas, let us hear Priya first, then you." Then he opened his palm toward Priya. Ojas paused and nodded. Harish noticed Ojas's jaw was tight, so afterwards he added quietly, "I do want your view. I only wanted to keep the order." Ojas smiled, still a little stiff. It was not a perfect meeting, but they finished with a decision before five.

What was the deadline for the vendor's answer?
Harish needed the vendor's answer before five o'clock.
What did Ojas's tight jaw suggest, and what is another reading?
It suggested Ojas felt cut off or a little stung by the calm hand, which is why Harish reassured Ojas. It could also be plain impatience about the delay.
What did Harish do that softened the hand gesture?
He spoke calmly, invited Priya with an open palm and told Ojas afterwards that Harish wanted to hear from Ojas.
How might Ojas have seen Harish's raised hand?
Ojas might have seen it as controlling or as a stop signal, until Harish explained he only wanted to keep the order.

Dear Rehana,
The group chat misses you, and so do I. We still call ourselves the Back Bench Pakoras and still reply to everything with "as per the prophecy", which makes no sense to anyone but us, and that's the whole point. I wanted to tell you something, because you'd have had an opinion. On Monday a new girl, Meenal, sat with us at lunch and we did the full pakora routine. She kept laughing half a second late, looking from face to face. Then Anu did the voice, the one copying Mr Das's stammer, and everyone cracked up, and I laughed too. Meenal didn't. What did the group call themselves?
They called themselves the Back Bench Pakoras.
What was Sudha feeling after learning about Meenal's brother?
Sudha felt sick with guilt and shame for laughing at the stammer voice; there may also have been worry about how Meenal now saw the whole group.

Explaining the prophecy joke let Meenal into the in-group, and telling Anu the voice has to go stopped a joke built on someone's pain.
What was lunch like for Meenal on Monday?
Meenal laughed half a second late, looking from face to face, so the private jokes left her outside; the stammer voice then hurt, and she left early.
Why should a dustbin have a lid?
A lid keeps pests away. Because it holds smells in and keeps flies and stray animals out, rubbish stays where it belongs.

Madhav here. Last spring Preeti, my partner, and I had a proper fight about how to split the week's chores, and by the second hour we were both talking louder and not listening at all. I felt my chest go tight. Then Preeti said, "I am too angry to be fair. Can we stop and come back at eight?" I nearly said no, because a pause felt like running away. But I took a walk round the block, and Preeti stayed home and made tea. At eight sharp we sat at the table again. We each said what we had really meant, and this time the list we made was one we both liked.

What time did Madhav and Preeti agree to come back to the table?
They agreed to come back at eight.
What was Madhav worried about when Preeti proposed the pause?
Madhav worried that a pause would feel like running away from the problem. That is why Madhav nearly said no before agreeing.
What made the pause useful instead of a way of avoiding the fight?
They agreed on a clear time to return, and they did return at eight. The break let both of them calm down, so they could say what they meant and make a list they both liked.
What might Preeti have wanted when asking to stop and come back at eight?
Preeti wanted to be fair rather than only angry, and knew that could not happen while both were shouting. Asking for a specific time shows Preeti meant to come back to the chores question.
Mr Khan our neighbour is a retired pilot. Please fix the punctuation.

Mr Khan, our neighbour, is a retired pilot.
Why: Commas go around extra information about the person.

How do Arohi and Sudha solve their second quarrel?

"It's my turn on the swing!" "No, mine!" Arohi and Sudha were both holding the chain. Their cousin Tenzin wandered over with a coin. "Heads, Arohi. Tails, Sudha. Okay?" "...Okay." The coin spun. Tails. Arohi pouted but let go, and Sudha swung high. Two days later, the same two were fighting over the last mango ice lolly. "Mine!" "I saw it first!" Arohi stopped. "Wait. Tenzin's coin way. Heads me, tails you?" Sudha blinked. "Okay." Nani flipped a coin for them. Heads. Arohi grinned, and broke off the end for Sudha anyway.
They remember Tenzin's coin trick and ask Nani to flip a coin for the last ice lolly. Arohi wins the toss but still breaks off a piece for Sudha.

Saturday

I shouted at Mummy this morning. She asked, for the third time, if I'd finished my project, and I yelled, "Just leave me alone! You're always nagging!" and slammed the door. Her face.

So this afternoon I cleaned the whole flat. Swept, mopped, even the fan blades. Folded the laundry. Made her ginger tea exactly how she likes it and left it on the table. Didn't say anything. Just kept doing things.

She said "thank you", but quietly, and her eyes looked tired.

Wasim called and I told him. He said, "Bro, you cleaned the fan blades? You must feel terrible. Did you actually say sorry though?"

No. I didn't. It felt easier to mop than to say it.

Tomorrow at breakfast. Two words. Sorry, Mummy.

Jomon

What did Jomon make for Mummy?
Jomon made her ginger tea exactly how she likes it.
Why did cleaning feel easier to Jomon than saying sorry?
Jomon felt guilty and ashamed about yelling, and doing chores let him show it without facing the harder words.
What is the wise next step in Jomon's plan?
Saying "Sorry, Mummy" at breakfast, which names the harm the cleaning could only hint at.
How might Mummy feel seeing the clean flat and the tea?
Mummy may feel touched but still hurt and tired, since "you're always nagging" hasn't been taken back.
What does meditate mean?

To meditate means to sit quietly and focus your mind, often to feel calm. It is a verb. In older books, it can also mean to think deeply about something or to plan it.
Example: Before her exams, Nandini meditates for ten minutes each morning.

How does Queequeg show that he has recovered his strength?

Now, there is this noteworthy difference between savage and civilized; that while a sick, civilized man may be six months convalescing, generally speaking, a sick savage is almost half-well again in a day. So, in good time my Queequeg gained strength; and at length after sitting on the windlass for a few indolent days (but eating with a vigorous appetite) he suddenly leaped to his feet, threw out his arms and legs, gave himself a good stretching, yawned a little bit, and then springing into the head of his hoisted boat, and poising a harpoon, pronounced himself fit for a fight.

After a few idle days on the windlass, eating with a vigorous appetite, Queequeg leaps up, stretches, yawns, springs into the head of his hoisted boat, poises a harpoon and pronounces himself fit for a fight.

Nilesh wanted to study for the banking exam every morning before his warehouse shift. The problem: he shared one room in Nashik with his sister Deepika and their mother, and Deepika worked late at a call centre, sleeping till nine.
For two weeks he failed. He'd wake at six, see Deepika asleep, feel guilty about switching on the light, and go back to bed.
Then he redesigned it. He moved his books to the building's stairwell landing the night before, so they were waiting there. He set his alarm to vibrate under his pillow. He'd do one practice set on the landing, then reward himself with tea from the stall downstairs, which opened at 6:30.
The first morning was cold and dark. The second, easier. By the third week, his feet went to the stairwell before his brain woke up. Deepika only noticed because the tea stall man started asking for him.

Where did Nilesh move his books the night before?
To the building's stairwell landing.
How did Nilesh feel when he saw Deepika asleep at six?
Nilesh felt guilty about switching on the light, so he went back to bed.
Which parts of Nilesh's redesign made the habit stick?
Books placed ready as a cue, a silent alarm, one set as the routine and tea as the reward, all fitted around the shared room.
How might Deepika feel when she learns about Nilesh's mornings?
Deepika would probably feel touched that he worked around her sleep, and proud of his effort.

Monday: Nandini came home and went straight to her room. When her father, Karthik, asked about school, she said 'Fine' and shut the door. Her friends' opinions about her new haircut mattered more than his, and she made sure he knew it.
Friday: she asked to go to a late movie with friends. Karthik said no. 'Everyone else is going!' She argued for twenty minutes, then stomped off. He heard her crying through the wall. Later she came out for a glass of water and lingered in the kitchen, watching him wash up, saying nothing.
The next Wednesday: Nandini had a bad day; her friends had made weekend plans without her. She didn't tell him what happened. But she sat on the sofa next to him for the whole cricket match, her shoulder just touching his arm.

What did Nandini ask to go to on Friday?
A late movie with friends.
What does Nandini lingering in the kitchen on Friday suggest?
It suggests that after the fight she felt uneasy and needed to check things with her father were still okay, even though she wouldn't say it.
What could Karthik do on Wednesday evening?
He could keep sitting with her calmly and let her know she can talk whenever she wants, without pushing for details.
How might Karthik feel when Nandini sits with her shoulder touching his arm?
Karthik probably feels relieved and tender, sensing she still needs him despite the distance.

Mridul stood beside the principal's desk in the school office, his forehead shining with sweat, his voice shaky as he answered questions about the broken window. Eshaan, the class monitor sent to fetch the register, stood by the door and tried not to stare. The vice principal murmured to the clerk, "Look how nervous he is." Eshaan wasn't so sure. He had seen Mridul sweat like that before every quiz, even when he'd studied. Later, at the tap in the corridor, Eshaan said, "You looked scared in there." Mridul said, "I always shake around principals. I was at the tuition centre that afternoon." The clerk later confirmed it with the tuition teacher's signature.

Where was Mridul standing when he was questioned?
He was standing beside the principal's desk in the school office.
What did Eshaan think about Mridul's sweating, and what did he remember?
Eshaan was unsure it meant guilt, remembering that Mridul sweated before every quiz even when he had studied.
What could the adults do instead of judging by how nervous Mridul looked?
They could check the facts, such as where he was that afternoon, and not treat sweat or shaky speech as proof.
How might Mridul feel when the vice principal says he looks nervous?
He may feel frightened and unfairly judged, since his nerves come from talking to authority and not from guilt.

The monsoon drain by the school gate was rushing. Hemant set his paper boat on the water, and Eshaan, running past, knocked it under. It was gone.
Hemant burst into tears. The bus would leave in five minutes.
Eshaan stood in the rain, not moving. Then he tore a page from his own notebook. "Sorry. I'll make you one."
His fingers were wet and slow. The bus honked. He folded fast, crooked, and held it out.
Hemant sniffed and took it. "It's wonky."
"Sorry," Eshaan said again. "It still floats."

How many minutes were left before the bus would leave?
Five minutes.
What was Eshaan feeling when he stood in the rain, not moving?
Eshaan felt guilty and unsure what to do after seeing Hemant cry.
How did Eshaan make amends under time pressure?
He said sorry and quickly made a new boat from his own notebook, giving something back for what he broke.
What is it like for Hemant to get the wonky boat?
Hemant is still a little sad, but he feels Eshaan cares and has tried to fix it.

They booked a launch event and printed invites.

Sharmila feels regretful and upset, having tried to be kind but causing the client to plan around the wrong date.

I'm Dhruv, and last spring I dropped out of a Saturday pottery class after four weeks. To Jasleen I gave a whole speech: the studio was too far, the clay was poor, the teacher never explained glazing, and honestly my Saturdays needed rest. It sounded very mature.

That night I tried something from a book. I wrote the real reason on a sticky note, then asked myself whether I'd accept my speech from Jasleen. I wouldn't. I'd say, "You sound like you're defending a case."

The sticky note said: Everyone else's bowls stand up. Mine collapse. I feel stupid.

Ten words, and not flattering at all. But it was something I could actually work with. I emailed the teacher, asked for help with centring the clay, and went back the next Saturday.

After how many weeks did Dhruv drop out of the pottery class?
Dhruv dropped out after four weeks.
What feeling was hiding under Dhruv's speech to Jasleen?
Dhruv felt embarrassed and stupid because the bowls kept collapsing, and the mature-sounding reasons covered that shame.

Writing the real reason and asking whether the same speech from Jasleen would be accepted exposed the excuse, and the honest reason pointed to a fix: asking the teacher for help.
How might Jasleen have heard the speech about the studio?
Jasleen may have nodded along but also sensed it sounded like a case being defended rather than the real story.

Supervision note, 11 November. Written by Manjula, front desk supervisor, dental clinic.
This morning Sachin double-booked the 10 am slot, and Mrs. D'Costa, an elderly patient, waited forty minutes. Today was different. He went to Mrs. D'Costa and said, "I'm sorry, I booked two people at ten, which is why you've waited. The doctor will see you next, and I've waived today's consultation fee." He brought her water and checked on her once more before she went in.

Mrs. D'Costa told me he had been "very polite and very clear".
Next step: I will ask Sachin to show the new booking check to the other receptionists.

Forty minutes.
What did Sachin feel after last month's slip?
Sachin felt guilty and down on himself, repeatedly saying he was 'useless'.

He named the error once, explained it, arranged for her to be seen next with the fee waived, checked on her, and added a second booking check.

She found Sachin 'very polite and very clear', suggesting the specific apology reassured her.

Every night Binita scrolled through Madhuri's photos. Madhuri at the beach. Madhuri with her perfect friends. Madhuri winning the debate trophy, hair perfect, smile perfect. Binita would put the phone down feeling small and ugly.
She even started a comment once, something mean about Madhuri's dress. She deleted it, but thought about it for hours.
Then on Thursday, in the girls' washroom, she found Madhuri crying by the sink.
"Are you okay?"
Madhuri wiped her face. "My parents fight every night. And if I don't top, my dad goes silent for a week. Don't tell anyone."
Binita walked back to class stunned. None of that was in the photos.
That night, instead of scrolling, she opened her sketchbook, the one she'd abandoned in Class 8. She drew for an hour. It wasn't perfect. It was hers.
The next day she smiled at Madhuri in the corridor. Madhuri smiled back, a real one.

Where did Binita find Madhuri crying?
By the sink in the girls' washroom.
How did Binita feel after scrolling Madhuri's photos?
She felt small, ugly and envious, even tempted to write something mean.
