She saw that the perfect photos hid real worries, so she put down the phone and returned to her own sketching.
What might it be like for Madhuri behind her perfect photos?
Madhuri feels stressed and sad, dealing with parents who fight and pressure to top that nobody sees online.

The lunch supervisor at the London primary school crouched between them by the wall. "One at a time. Emeka?"
"Rosa kicked the ball over the fence on purpose, and now we can't play, and she always does that."
"I did NOT. You passed it badly! You never pass properly, then you blame me!"
"You always say that!"
"Because it's always true!"
The supervisor tried again. "Rosa, what happened just before?"
But Emeka was already talking over her, remembering a game from last week, and Rosa was shaking her head, lips moving, getting her next line ready. Neither of them was looking at the other.

Who crouched between Emeka and Rosa?
The lunch supervisor at the London primary school.
What does Emeka's talking over Rosa suggest he is feeling?
He feels defensive and angry, desperate to be seen as the one in the right, so he is busy preparing his case rather than listening.
What turning point could the supervisor offer at this stage?
The supervisor could stop the storytelling for a moment and ask each child to take a breath or say what the other one said, so they have to listen before defending.

Whenever anyone asked him a real question, like "How's your dad doing?" or "Are you okay after the layoffs?", he'd crack a joke and change the subject. Every single time. In the car park.
What did Devika feel seeing Aakash alone in the car park?
Worried and tender, sensing pain behind his constant jokes.

It praised his humour while giving him permission not to be funny, in private, so he could share about his dad.
What was Aakash carrying under the jokes?
Worry about his father's health, which he finally shared.

Four students in one hostel each turned an idea into a business in a different way. Hrithik jotted down everything that annoyed him about hostel life: slow laundry, mess quarrels, noisy corridors. He circled the one his neighbours brought up most often. Vishal, before he built a single thing, sat down with twenty residents and asked how they got their clothes washed and what they paid. To his surprise, price mattered to them far more than an app would. Vandana adored her idea. Friends cheered, and she brushed aside the polite doubts. She poured her savings into a logo plus a website before any stranger had said they wanted the product. Aarav and his partner noticed that customers came mainly at exam time to print their notes. How many residents did Vishal talk to?
Vishal talked to twenty residents.
How does Vandana's way of testing her idea differ from Vishal's, and what did each learn?
Vandana heard only cheering from friends and spent savings on a logo and website before checking demand. Vishal spoke to twenty residents first and learned that price mattered more than an app.
What might Vandana be feeling as she brushes aside the polite doubts?
She is probably excited and attached to her idea, and worried that doubts might spoil it.

She could show the product to strangers who might use it and listen for honest doubts, then decide what to change. Asking a few people to be frank would help. 🙂

My name's Noor, and in Class 10 a boy called Thomas joined our section in the middle of term. I didn't like him. He answered every question, he tapped his pen, and he had a laugh like a bicycle horn. Our roll numbers put us on the same bench for every exam and every lab. Then his family moved into our building, so we were in the same school van too. Twice a day, every day. I can't point to the day it changed. Maybe it was when he lent me his calculator without being asked, or when I worked out that his pen-tapping meant he was nervous. Like a bicycle horn.

Noor worked out that it meant Thomas was nervous, which made the habit feel less annoying and more human.

It turned Noor's quiet change of feeling into a friendly act that Thomas could see.

Joining mid-term, Thomas may have felt nervous, as the pen-tapping suggests, and grateful for any friendliness from a bench partner.

She was rigging coloured paper to make it look like sunset.

Forty minutes.

Rekha wrote it on a sticky note above the bathroom mirror: once the toothbrush goes down, I go for a twenty-minute walk. She no longer had to decide anything each morning; the toothbrush was the signal.

Manoj stretched for just ten minutes and jogged slowly to the corner and back. On bad days, the stretching alone counted. Each week he added a few minutes, and by March his jog reached the park.

Jeevan, motivated on the first of January, paid for a full year at a gym and planned hard workouts every day. Then a cold and a crowded work week broke his streak. He looked at the calendar, felt like a failure, and never went back.

In April Manoj missed a week. He did not drop the plan; he wrote down what had happened. The evening sessions were the ones that failed, when he was tired and hungry. He moved everything to mornings, and set one rule: never miss twice in a row.

What was Rekha's signal to start walking?
Her signal was putting down the toothbrush.
How did Jeevan's plan differ from Manoj's, and what happened when each hit a bad week?

Jeevan planned hard daily workouts and dropped everything after one broken streak, while Manoj started small, treated the missed week as information, moved sessions to mornings and set a rule never to miss twice.
What was Jeevan feeling after the streak broke?
Like a failure, which made him give up completely.
What could Jeevan try instead?
Jeevan could start with a small daily walk and treat a missed day as something to learn from.

Class teacher's note, Class 10, after the cyber-safety session.
Keerthana told the class a story from last week. A stranger messaged her claiming to be from a prize contest: she had won a phone, and he needed her to approve a "collect request" to verify her account. He wrote, "Hurry, the offer ends in ten minutes!" She felt a rush of excitement, then something felt wrong. She didn't approve it, didn't share any code, and showed the message to her mother, who blocked and reported the number. Her friend Binita admitted she had nearly approved a similar request last month. I have added a slide: never share a PIN or OTP, never approve an unexpected request, pause and ask an adult.

Ira felt sad and let down when the lights went out and Tenzin left without a goodbye, and because that sadness came last, it pushed out the hour of paper boats and games.

Someone could have lit a candle, sung one last song and helped Tenzin say goodbye, so the party ended warmly instead of in the dark.

At lunch Bidisha scraped her tiffin clean and noticed how much rice other children were throwing away.

Abhinav, you've been going to those Saturday meetings since your grandfather passed. I'm not going to scold you. Let me just tell you a story.
When I was twenty, my father died in March, and by June I was a ghost at college. Then a girl from my hostel, all smiles, took my hand and brought me to a "study circle". They hugged me at the door. They brought me tea without asking. For the first time in months, when I skipped a day, someone said, "We missed you, Swati."
I didn't care what they taught. I cared that they wanted me.
It was my cousin Hema who noticed. She came to the hostel, sat on my bed and said, "I'm glad you have people. Will they still want you if you ask questions?" So at the next meeting I asked one question. The smiles went thin.
That was my turning point. The warmth had been real, but it came with a price.

Swati's father died in March.
Why was young Swati drawn to the study circle?

Asking one question at the next meeting, as Hema suggested; the thin smiles showed the welcome depended on not questioning.

In March, Karthik had noticed something odd in the Pune office's billing system: one client was being charged twice for the same server hours. It was a small amount. He meant to mention it. Then the release came, then his leave, and he forgot, or let himself forget.

In September the client's finance team emailed: they had found six months of double charges and were threatening to end the contract.

Karthik read the email three times, his chest tight. He could stay quiet. Nobody knew he had seen it.

That evening he went to his team lead, Nilesh. "I saw this in March and didn't flag it. I should have. Here's what I saw and when."

Nilesh leaned back. "That's not great." A long pause. "But thanks for telling me. Send me your notes. We'll show the client the exact dates." Karthik walked out shaky, and lighter.

What was the client being charged twice for?
The client was being charged twice for the same server hours.
What was Karthik feeling after reading the client's email?

Admitting the delay and sharing notes let the team give the client exact facts, instead of letting a hidden problem grow.

'Mm. Mausi told me.' Alka shook her head. 'But why did she keep going to those late meetings? Why did she let it go on for months?' She stopped, a plate in her hand. 'Wait. Listen to me.'

I quitted my seat, and walked on, although the darkness and storm increased every minute, and the thunder burst with a terrific crash over my head. It was echoed from Saleve, the Juras, and the Alps of Savoy; vivid flashes of lightning dazzled my eyes, illuminating the lake, making it appear like a vast sheet of fire; then for an instant every thing seemed of a pitchy darkness, until the eye recovered itself from the preceding flash. The storm, as is often the case in Switzerland, appeared at once in various parts of the heavens. The most violent storm hung exactly north of the town, over the part of the lake which lies between the promontory of Belrive and the village of Copet. Another storm enlightened Jura with faint flashes; and another darkened and sometimes disclosed the Mole, a peaked mountain to the east of the lake.

The narrator walks on through a dark storm, with thunder crashing overhead and echoing from the mountains. Lightning makes the lake look like a sheet of fire, then everything goes pitch dark until the eye recovers. As often in Switzerland, storms appear in several parts of the sky at once, the fiercest north of the town.

Read this:

Monday. When the group laughed at Anjali's poem in the school magazine, calling it 'so cringe', Baljeet laughed too. He had read it twice at home and liked it.
Wednesday. The class voted on the trip: the science museum or the water park. Baljeet had wanted the museum for months. The group all put their hands up for the water park, looking round to check. Baljeet raised his hand with them.
Friday. At home, Baljeet opened the school magazine and read Anjali's poem again. It was still good. He felt a heavy, sour feeling, as if he'd swallowed something wrong. He couldn't remember the last time he'd said what he actually thought in front of them. He wondered if they even knew what he liked.

Which trip had Baljeet wanted for months?
He had wanted the science museum.
Why did Baljeet raise his hand for the water park?
He feared standing out and being rejected, so matching the group felt safer than voting for what he wanted.
What could Baljeet do to start being himself with the group?
Start with a small honest moment, like telling Anjali he liked her poem, to see that disagreeing doesn't end friendships.
How might Anjali feel hearing the group call her poem 'cringe'?
Anjali would likely feel hurt and embarrassed, especially after sharing something personal in the magazine.

Read this:

Sunday
Vidya didi shouted at me today for using her headphones. She is SO rude. She's always rude when I just ask for something.
Okay, I didn't ask. I just took them. But still.
Then in the evening I shouted at her when she came into my room, because I was tired from cricket practice and my knee hurt. That's different. I had a reason.
Mummy said, "Maybe Vidya had a reason too. She has boards tomorrow." I forgot about her boards.
So when I shout it's because I'm tired, and when she shouts it's because she's rude? Hmm. That doesn't seem fair when I write it down.
Hemant

Why did Hemant shout at Vidya in the evening?
Because Hemant was tired from cricket practice and the knee hurt.
Why did Hemant decide Vidya is rude?
Hemant felt hurt at being shouted at and didn't think about her boards, so it seemed like her character rather than her stress.
What could Hemant do next time before calling someone rude?
Ask, as Mummy did, whether they might have a reason too, like the reasons Hemant has for shouting.
What might Vidya's day have been like?
Vidya had boards the next day, so she was probably stressed, and her headphones had been taken without asking.

Read this:

Dear Francis,
Six weeks back in Kolkata and I owe you a proper letter. You asked if it feels like home. Honestly? Not yet. The para I grew up in has three new flyovers and my favourite phuchka man has gone. My cousins talk about serials I've never seen. When I say "cheers" instead of "thank you", my aunts giggle. And I've changed too: I miss quiet, I miss queues, I miss being able to walk at night without a hundred questions.
I spent the first month annoyed at everything, mostly myself. Then Dida said something at dinner: "You went away a boy, you came back a man. The city also grew. Give each other time." So I'm trying. I've started morning walks by the lake with Dida. I've found a new phuchka man, nearly as good. I laugh at the serials with my cousins now, sometimes.
Write soon. Tell Toronto I miss it.
Nilesh

What has happened to Nilesh's favourite phuchka man?
He has gone.
How did Nilesh feel during the first month back in Kolkata?
Nilesh felt out of step and annoyed at everything, mostly at himself.
What did Dida's advice encourage Nilesh to do?
To be patient with both himself and the city, since both had changed, which led to morning walks and small new routines.
How might Francis feel reading this letter?
Francis might feel both missed and glad that Nilesh is slowly finding a new fit back home.

messages.content:
Read this:

Keerthana, nineteen, was buying her first laptop in a Chennai electronics market. One shop had a shiny silver model in a glass case, lit up with blue lights. It felt perfect.

"This one," she said to her friend Mridul. "It's clearly the best."

"Why?"

"It's... fast. Probably. And strong. It looks strong."

"Did you check the specs?"

"I don't need to. I just know."

Mridul pulled up the specs on his phone. The silver laptop had less memory and a weaker battery than the plain black one next to it, for the same price.

Keerthana frowned. "But it felt right."

"It felt shiny," Mridul said.

What colour was the laptop Keerthana liked?
Silver.
Why did Keerthana say the silver laptop was "clearly the best"?
It looked shiny and perfect, so she felt excited and sure about it first and came up with reasons afterward.
What could Keerthana do before buying?
Compare the specs of the two laptops, as Mridul did, instead of trusting the shiny look.
How might Mridul feel watching Keerthana choose by looks?
Mridul seems amused and a bit protective, wanting her to get a better deal.

metadata.subtype: Gut feeling on people and products [Actor]

messages.content: I like to type "COME NOW!" in capitals so people notice. Is that okay?

Writing whole words in capitals usually reads as shouting, so use it rarely. For emphasis, a stronger word or an exclamation mark is usually kinder.
Example: Please come now; we are about to start.

Read this:

I'm Jatin, and I used to think saying sorry to my little sister Kashish was the same as losing. Two years ago she borrowed my headphones without asking, and I yelled so loudly that she cried. Mummy looked at me like I was a stranger.
I didn't apologise. I did what I always did: an hour later I sent Kashish a silly dancing-cat sticker, then acted like nothing had happened at dinner. Kashish didn't eat much. She didn't come to my room for three days, and she used to come every evening.
On the third day I sat on the edge of her bed. I didn't make a speech. I just said, "I shouted at you. That was wrong. Sorry."
She said, "Okay," and handed me back my headphones, which she'd been hiding.
That short sentence worked better than a hundred stickers.

How many days did Kashish stay away from Jatin's room?
She didn't come to Jatin's room for three days.
What was Jatin feeling about apologising back then?
Jatin felt that saying sorry to a younger sister was like losing, a matter of pride, even while feeling bad about the shouting.
What could someone learn from Jatin's apology on the third day?
A short, plain sentence naming what you did and saying sorry repairs more than jokes or stickers that avoid it.
What was it like for Kashish when Jatin acted like nothing had happened?
She probably felt hurt and unheard, which is why she barely ate and stayed away from the room.

Hansa: i yelled at chotu again today. he just wanted me to see his drawing
Mahima: u were studying na?
Hansa: yes but i didn't even look up. he walked off so quietly 😔
Mahima: ugh that quiet walk away is the worst

Hansa: you always had 5 min for me even in your boards year
Mahima: haha i also yelled plenty, trust me
Mahima: but ya, 5 min is doable

Mahima: and say sorry for today
Hansa: already did. he showed me the drawing. it's a dinosaur with my face 😅
Mahima: perfect. frame it ❤️

What did Hansa's little brother want her to do?
He wanted her to see his drawing.
What does Hansa's sad emoji after 'he walked off so quietly' reveal?
It shows she felt guilty and hurt seeing how quietly he gave up on her.
What makes Hansa's new rule a good step?
It is small and concrete, five minutes with the pen down, so she can keep it even while studying.
How might Hansa's little brother experience the change?
He would feel noticed and important when she stops for him, instead of learning not to ask.

1) Why do people hug when they meet after a long time?
2) Does this sentence sound right? He is more smarter than his friends.
3) What does "hold back" mean?
4) Is my teacher going to give a surprise test tomorrow?
5) Any idea what "retaliation" means?

1. It shows happiness and affection. Because touch can say what words sometimes cannot.
2. Corrected: He is smarter than his friends. "Smarter" is already a comparative, so "more" is not needed.
3. It means to stop yourself or someone from doing something. For example: she held back her tears.
4. I can't check that, since I can't see your teacher's plans. Ask politely about the next test date, or revise to be ready.
5. As a noun, "retaliation" means harm done to someone in return for harm they did.

Shalini, you want to know why my friends call me "the fun one" on your podcast? Okay. I'm Seema, I'm sixteen, and I will not apologise.
Friday is film night. Saturday is the food street with the gang. Sunday is cricket in the park, or the mall if it rains. I plan my whole week around what's fun. I'm the one who says "let's go" when everyone's tired.
My friends say I make them feel alive. I love that.
But okay, honesty. This term my maths went from 78 to 51. My mother cried a little. I'd been skipping tuition to watch the new series with the girls.
I don't think fun is bad. I think it's the best thing. I just think maybe I let it drive the whole car.

How much did Seema's maths marks drop?
From 78 to 51.
What was Seema feeling about being "the fun one"?
Seema felt proud and happy, loving making friends feel alive.
What could Seema try so fun doesn't crowd out school?
Seema could keep film night and outings but plan study time first, and stop skipping tuition for series.
How might Seema's mother see the drop in maths?
Seema's mother seems worried and upset, crying a little over the marks.

metadata.subtype: Lives for fun and good times [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Thursday, 3 am, at my brother's flat

I found the messages tonight. Damini's phone buzzed on the sofa and I saw the name and the words and I knew. Four months. I was sick in the bathroom. My hands are still shaking. I'm Jomon, and I don't know who I am tonight. Nine years together. Was all of it fake?

My first thought was to message him, the other man. To post everything online. To tell her parents at breakfast. I had the phone in my hand.

I put it down. I don't want to do something tonight that I'll regret for years.

This isn't my failing. I keep writing that because part of me wants to find what I did wrong.

I came to my brother's. He made me tea and didn't ask questions. Tomorrow I'll call my friend Sanjay. I'm not deciding anything about the marriage this week. Maybe not this month.

How long had the affair been going on?
Four months.
What was Jomon feeling after finding the messages?
Jomon felt shock and nausea, shaken to the core, even asking whether the nine years were fake.
What did Jomon choose instead of rash revenge?
Jomon put the phone down instead of posting or messaging, went to a brother's flat, planned to call a friend, and delayed decisions until calmer.
How does Jomon's brother support Jomon that night?
Jomon's brother makes tea and asks no questions, giving quiet, steady support.

Written by Nilesh's Dadi, Tuesday
Whenever something breaks, my daughter-in-law Ritu calls "Dadi!" and I come. Today Nilesh's sandal strap slipped off its buckle. He looked at it, looked at the door to my room and shouted, "Dadi! Dadi!" Just the way Ritu does. I came, fixed the strap and laughed. He watched my hands the whole time.

What slipped off its buckle?
Nilesh's sandal strap slipped off its buckle.
What was Nilesh thinking when he shouted "Dadi!"?
He seemed sure and hopeful that calling Dadi, the way Ritu does, would fix the broken strap.
What else could Dadi try so Nilesh learns more than calling?
She could fix the strap slowly while he watches, and next time let him try pushing it through the buckle.
How might Ritu feel hearing that Nilesh copies her?
Ritu would probably feel amused and a little surprised to learn he copies her call so exactly.

Dhruv: hey didi, Maa's birthday lunch sunday? 1 pm at home
Nikita: will ask Varun and tell u
Dhruv: ok. u used to just say yes
Nikita: things are different now
Nikita: can u send me 200 for the auto? will return
Dhruv: sent. didn't u get salary last week?
Nikita: Varun handles the account now. it's easier
Dhruv: ok. how are u really?
Nikita: fine. have to go, he wants my location when i leave office
Dhruv: no lecture, promise. just know i'm here. any time, any hour
Dhruv: and if u ever want, i can come get u. no questions
Nikita: thanks bhai
Nikita: don't tell Maa about the 200
Dhruv: i won't. see u sunday i hope

How much did Nikita ask Dhruv to send for the auto?
Nikita asked Dhruv to send 200 for the auto.
What might Dhruv be worried about when he asks "how are u really?"
He is worried that Nikita has lost control of her own money and plans, since she now needs Varun's say and must share her location.
Which of Dhruv's messages was wise, and why?
Promising no lecture and offering to come any time, no questions, keeps Nikita connected without blame, so she has a safe person if she needs help.
What might it be like for Nikita to read "i can come get u. no questions"?
It may bring quiet relief, a sign that someone will help without judging her or pushing her to leave before she is ready.

metadata.subtype: Signs a friend or family may notice [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Minakshi Dadi said “Careful!” all day long: careful on the stairs, careful with the spoon, careful with the crayons. Shalini, five, had stopped even looking up. One afternoon in their flat, Shalini reached toward the iron, still hot on the board. “Careful!” said Dadi. Shalini kept reaching. Dadi grabbed her hand just in time. That evening Dadi said to Shalini's mother, “She didn't listen.” Her mother said gently, “Maybe too many carefuls. Let's save it for the hot iron and the road.”

What was still hot on the board?
The iron.
Why might Shalini have kept reaching after Dadi said “Careful!”?
She had heard it so often all day that she didn't treat it as a warning, so she didn't feel alarmed or stop to look.
What did Shalini's mother suggest?
She suggested saving “careful” for real dangers like the hot iron and the road, so the word keeps its power.
How might Dadi have felt after grabbing Shalini's hand?
She probably felt frightened and frustrated that Shalini didn't listen, before understanding why.

Read this:

Tuesday, 11 pm
Stupid, stupid day. Woke up with a fever and a scratchy throat but went in anyway, because missing the sprint review would make me look unreliable. By noon I'd pasted the wrong figures into the client deck and had to redo half of it. Reena covered for me in the meeting, then pulled me aside. 'You're burning up. And half the floor will catch this now.' She was right; Kunal was already sneezing. The manager sent me home at two. I felt ashamed, not of being ill, but of pretending I wasn't. Tomorrow I'm staying home, and I've already messaged the team. If the fever keeps going, I'll see the doctor.
Yogesh

What mistake did Yogesh make by noon?
Pasted the wrong figures into the client deck.
Why did Yogesh go to work with a fever?
Yogesh was afraid that missing the sprint review would look unreliable.
What is Yogesh doing differently tomorrow?
Staying home, having already told the team, and seeing the doctor if the fever keeps going.
How might Reena have felt watching Yogesh work while ill?
Reena was probably worried and a bit annoyed, covering in the meeting and seeing colleagues at risk of catching it.

Read this:

When I moved to Hyderabad, Reena, I didn't know a single soul. So when this "mentorship network" invited me to a Saturday meetup, I went. Free snacks, people clapping when I said my name. It felt amazing, honestly.
Third week, they asked me to sign up for the "inner programme". So I asked some basic things. Where does the fee go? Who is actually in charge? What if I want to quit halfway?
The mood changed. The organiser smiled and said, "Those questions come from fear, Ojas. Trust the process." Another guy said people who leave "always regret it". Nobody answered a single question.
That's when I stepped back. I went to the office cricket match that Sunday instead, and texted you that night, remember? A healthy group would have just answered. I'm still a bit lonely here, but I'd rather be lonely than trapped.

What did the organiser say Ojas's questions came from?
Those questions come from fear.
How did Ojas feel when nobody answered the questions?
Ojas felt uneasy and suspicious, sensing that warmth had turned to pressure once the questions started.
What did Ojas do that a lonely newcomer could copy?
Asked about fees, leaders and leaving before committing, and kept up outside ties like the office cricket and texting Reena.
How might Reena have felt getting that text on Sunday night?
Reena was probably glad to hear from Ojas, perhaps without realising how much that outside link mattered.

Read this:

Last term I did something I'm still not proud of. Avni had read her poem at the school open mic, and I laughed at one line. Not meanly, I thought, just surprised. That night she messaged me. The preview said, "Why did you laugh at" and then it cut off. I didn't open it. I knew she was hurt, and I didn't know how to explain a laugh.
One day passed. Then four. Every time I saw her name in my chat list, I felt sick and scrolled past. I started taking the other staircase so I wouldn't meet her. The longer I waited, the more it seemed like the answer had to be a huge, perfect apology.
When I finally opened it, on day nine, the message just said, "Why did you laugh at my favourite line? It meant a lot to me." A tiny question. I had turned it into a mountain.
— Chinmay

On which day did Chinmay finally open Avni's message?
Chinmay finally opened it on day nine.
Why did Chinmay keep scrolling past Avni's name?
Chinmay felt guilty and sick about the laugh, and not knowing how to explain it made opening the message feel too hard.
What went wrong, and what could have fixed it early?
The waiting made a small question feel like a mountain; opening it the first night and saying "I'm sorry, I didn't mean to hurt you" would have kept it small.
How might Avni have felt waiting nine days for a reply?
Avni probably felt hurt twice, first by the laugh and then by the silence, perhaps wondering if Chinmay didn't care.

Read this:

I live next door and the walls are thin, so I heard all of it. Samir yelled, "That's MY sketchbook! You scribbled on my dragon page!" His younger brother Francis stood there holding a red crayon, lip trembling. Samir's face was red and his fists were tight, but he did not hit him. He snatched the sketchbook and stomped off. Later, through the balcony, I heard him say, "Next time ask me first. Mummy, can we make a rule about this?" Their mother agreed. Samir put the sketchbook on the high shelf. I can't be sure how he felt inside, but he sounded upset more than mean.

What was Francis holding when Samir yelled?
He was holding a red crayon.
What do Samir's red face and tight fists suggest about how he felt?
They suggest he was very angry, but the neighbour thinks he sounded more upset than mean, since he did not hit Francis.
What did Samir do afterwards that worked better than hitting?
He asked Francis to ask first, asked Mummy for a rule, and put the sketchbook on the high shelf.
How might Francis have felt when Samir shouted?
Francis was probably scared and sorry, since his lip trembled as he stood holding the crayon.

From my balcony next door I watch Kavitha, five, and her four cousins sleep in one heap on a single mattress on their terrace on summer nights. Yesterday a mango came up. Kavitha bit it and passed it along without anyone asking; the smallest got the seed to suck. Later I heard a squabble over who got the spot by the wall, tears and a shove, and five minutes after, all of them giggling under one sheet. My daughter asked me why Kavitha doesn't have her own room. I didn't know. Kavitha never seems to want one.
Sangeeta

Where do Kavitha and her cousins sleep on summer nights?
On a single mattress on their terrace.
What does Kavitha passing the mango along suggest she feels?
It suggests she feels happy and at ease sharing, as if belonging with her cousins is simply normal, though Sangeeta can only guess from outside.
What could Sangeeta tell the daughter who asked about Kavitha's room?
That families live in different ways: Kavitha shares a lot and seems to enjoy it, and having your own room is fine too.
Why might Sangeeta's daughter find Kavitha's life puzzling?
The daughter probably has a separate room and things, so sharing a bed and a mango with many cousins looks strange.

Read this:

Dear Lalremsiami (Siami!),
Merry Christmas! Is Aizawl all lights and carols? Here in Shillong it's freezing and everyone is just exams, exams.
Okay, confession. You know Ashwin, from the debate team? At the Christmas fair yesterday he wore this huge red sweater, and I shouted in front of everyone, "Look, it's Santa's tomato!" Everyone laughed. Then I kept going, about his hair, his squeaky voice. I don't even think his voice is squeaky.
Here's the weird part. I actually like talking to him. A lot. Maybe that's why I did it? If I make fun of him, nobody can tell I like him, not even him. But he looked really hurt.
What do I do? Tell no one.
Love,
Ritu

What did Ritu shout at the Christmas fair?
"Look, it's Santa's tomato!"
Why did Ritu mock Ashwin in front of everyone?
Ritu likes Ashwin and felt afraid of being exposed, so teasing him loudly hid the crush from everyone, even from him.
What could Ritu do now?
Apologise to Ashwin simply, without jokes, and next time just talk to him normally, even while feeling shy 😅.
How might Ashwin have felt at the fair?
He probably felt embarrassed and hurt, and confused, since Ritu usually enjoys talking to him.

metadata.subtype: Mocking the one who is liked [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Irawati, you asked why I didn't go straight to Ma'am about Pallav. I'm Minakshi, and honestly, I almost did.
I saw him copy in the Hindi test, and I was so angry. I'd studied the whole weekend, and he was just reading off his palm. By the time I got home I'd typed a message to Ma'am, very long, with words like “shameless”.
But Amma has a rule: never send anything important when you're boiling. So I put the phone in the drawer and slept on it.
Next morning I read the message again, and it sounded like revenge, not concern. So I deleted it. I decided I'd talk to Pallav first, privately, and if he did it again, I'd tell Ma'am calmly, just the facts.
I talked to him at lunch. He was embarrassed and said it wouldn't happen again. So far it hasn't. If it does, I know what I'll say, and it won't sound like that message.

What words did Minakshi's first message include?
Words like "shameless".
How did Minakshi feel reading the message the next morning?
Minakshi felt uncomfortable and calmer, seeing that it sounded like revenge rather than concern.
What might Minakshi do if Pallav copies again?
Tell Ma'am calmly with just the facts, as planned, rather than with the angry words of that first night.
How might Pallav have felt when Minakshi spoke to him at lunch?
Pallav was embarrassed, but probably relieved to be spoken to privately rather than reported in anger.

Note for Karthik's parents
On Monday Karthik stood by the swing shouting, "My turn!" at Zubin, who stayed on. Karthik cried. On Tuesday he walked up and said, "Zubin, can I go after you?" Zubin nodded and got off soon after. Karthik looked surprised. Today he asked the same way again. I told him I noticed his polite asking.

Note for Karthik's parents
On Monday, Karthik stood by the swing and shouted "My turn!" at Zubin, who remained on it, and Karthik cried. On Tuesday he approached Zubin and asked, "Zubin, can I go after you?" Zubin nodded and got off shortly afterwards, which surprised Karthik. Today he asked in the same way again. I told him that I had noticed his polite asking.

Read this:

The rain had knocked out the streetlights, so Sahil and Ganga stood under the bus-stop roof in the dark, waiting for a bus already twenty minutes late.
"Can I say something that's been bothering me?" Ganga said. "I've been trying to find the right way for a week." She took a breath. "At the studio, you keep interrupting the junior designers. They've stopped speaking in meetings. I don't think you see it."
Sahil's face went hot. He wanted to say she was exaggerating. But he noticed her hands twisting the strap of her bag, and how carefully she had chosen each word.
The bus finally splashed up. On the ride he replayed Tuesday's meeting and the junior who had started a sentence and stopped. "Thanks," he texted her that night. "That can't have been easy to say."

What did Ganga say Sahil keeps doing at the studio?
She said he keeps interrupting the junior designers.
What did Sahil feel at first, and what changed his reaction?
He felt stung and defensive, his face hot, but noticing her twisting hands and careful words showed him she cared, so he listened.
What did Sahil do that shows he took the feedback well?
He replayed Tuesday's meeting, remembered the junior who stopped mid-sentence, and texted Ganga to thank her.
What was it like for Ganga to say it?
It was hard for her; she had searched for the right way for a week and twisted her bag strap while speaking.

metadata.subtype: Receiving hard truth from someone who cares [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dalia had noticed it by her third month at the Rotterdam studio: nobody picked a colour anymore. They made three versions and waited for Elif. Elif chose the blue, moved the logo two millimetres, rewrote the email to the printer. At Thursday stand-ups Joost said 'whatever Elif thinks' so often it had become a joke no one laughed at.
The museum poster went out nine days late. Dalia didn't say Elif was controlling. She brought the calendar instead.
'On the last two jobs, most of the delay was work sitting in the approval pile,' she said. 'If we decide type and colour inside the brand guide, and you review the final draft only, I think we'd hit our dates.'
Elif studied the calendar for a long moment. 'Show me one job done that way.'

How late did the museum poster go out?
Nine days late.
What did Dalia think was really slowing the studio down?
She thought the delays came from work sitting in the approval pile, because the team had stopped choosing and waited for Elif.
Why did Dalia choose to bring the calendar instead of calling Elif controlling?
The dates kept the talk on results that Elif could check rather than on Elif's character, and that made a trial possible.
How might Elif feel being shown the calendar instead of being called controlling?
Elif might feel less attacked and more able to weigh the idea, since the dates are facts to check; 'Show me one job done that way' suggests cautious openness.

Read this:

In Warsaw, Yara used to paint on Sunday afternoons. The easel had been folded behind the wardrobe since spring.
Now, most nights, she drank alone in her room. One glass used to calm her down after work. Now it took three, sometimes more, to feel the same.
She hid the bottles in her gym bag and carried them to the recycling bins at night. When Ivan, her flatmate, asked where she'd been, she said, "Walking." When her mother asked why she was short on rent, she said the landlord had raised it.
Every lie made her ashamed. And shame made the evenings harder, which made the glass easier.
One night Ivan found the gym bag. He didn't shout. He sat down beside her.

Where did Yara hide the bottles?
In her gym bag.
What was Yara feeling as the lies built up?
She felt ashamed, and that shame made the evenings harder, so she drank more.
What turning point does Ivan's calm response offer?
It gives Yara a chance to stop hiding and to seek help from someone she trusts or a professional.
What is Ivan experiencing when he finds the bag?
Ivan is probably shocked and worried, but chooses to stay calm and sit beside her.

Read this:

Dear Rehana,
Thank you for the parcel. The pickle made me cry, which tells you how this month has been.
Since I reported the fake attendance entries at the school to the education department, the staffroom goes quiet when I walk in. Two teachers I ate lunch with for three years now sit at the other table. Someone left a note in my pigeonhole: "Traitor." The principal has moved me to the least popular timetable.
I keep telling myself I was right. Children were marked present who hadn't come for months, and the scheme money was going somewhere. Being right doesn't make lunch less lonely.
I've done what you said. I keep a notebook: every date, every note, every change to my duties. The teachers' union put me in touch with a lawyer who explained what protections might apply, and I'm meeting her on Friday.
Please keep calling on Sundays. It helps more than you know.
Lakshmi

What did the note in Lakshmi's pigeonhole say?
'Traitor.'
How is Lakshmi feeling this month?
Lakshmi feels lonely and hurt, sure of being right but cut off at lunch and called a traitor.
Which supports is Lakshmi using, and why do they help?
A notebook of dates and duty changes, a lawyer through the union to explain protections, and Rehana's Sunday calls; records and allies make retaliation harder to hide and easier to bear.
How might the two teachers at the other table see Lakshmi?
They may see Lakshmi as disloyal, or be afraid of being linked to the report, so they keep their distance even if part of them agrees.

At five.

Tenzin felt secure and calm, trusting his mother would be there, so he could keep playing.

Note, Wednesday. Team supervisor, operations.
This morning Sunaina asked me to book the small meeting room for her and Vikas. They've been close friends since joining; last month something she'd told him in confidence went round the floor. She said, "I'd rather talk to him directly than bring it up at the stand-up." I booked it.
I didn't hear the conversation. Through the glass I could see Sunaina sitting upright, speaking slowly, with one sheet of notes she barely looked at. Vikas mostly looked at the table. At one point he started to speak and she raised a hand, calmly, and finished her sentence. Near the end he talked for a long while and she listened.
Afterwards she told me only this: "I said what he did, how it felt, and what I can and can't accept at work now. The rest is his to answer."

Sunaina asked the supervisor to book the small meeting room for her and Vikas.
What does Sunaina's upright posture and slow speaking suggest?
It suggests Sunaina was hurt but determined to stay calm and clear, choosing control over a public scene.
Why was a private, direct conversation a good choice here?
It let Sunaina state what happened, how it felt and her limits without an audience, which gave Vikas room to answer honestly instead of defending his image.
What might Vikas have experienced sitting in that room?
Vikas probably felt exposed and ashamed, looking at the table, but was given a real chance to respond, which he took near the end.

Daniel had driven to his mother's house in Stockport every evening for eight months. He sorted her tablets into the weekly box, fixed the boiler, sat through the same quiz show. His sister Ada lived forty minutes away and came at Christmas.

One Thursday Ada texted: "How's Mum? Busy week here!" Daniel read it in the car park and felt something hot and sour rise in his throat. Used. That was the word.

He typed a long, angry reply, then deleted it. Instead he wrote: "She's okay. I need two things from you. Take the first Saturday of every month, the whole day. And do her online shopping order each Sunday."

Three dots, for a long time. Then: "I can do the shopping. Saturdays are hard."

Daniel breathed out. He accepted the shopping, then rang the council about a carer visiting twice a week. If Ada stayed away on Saturdays, he wouldn't stay alone.

How long had Daniel been driving to his mother's house every evening?
He had been driving there every evening for eight months.
What did Daniel feel when he read Ada's text in the car park?
Daniel felt used and bitter, something hot and sour rising in his throat.
Why was Daniel's second message better than the angry one?
It asked Ada for specific tasks she could say yes or no to, instead of a vague sense of duty, and he found outside help for the gap.
How might Ada see Daniel's clear request?
Ada may feel caught out and a bit guilty, taking the time to reply and agreeing to the shopping while pushing back on Saturdays.

'Where we use AI, and where we don't.'

Jyoti seems surprised and reassured, having expected to dig for an answer her board wanted.

They could send a written note of any change to their AI use before it happens, and revisit it at each quarterly meeting.

The board gets a clear answer early, which builds trust in the firm handling their customers' systems.

Dear diary, Deepika.

I told Lakshmi tonight that I was hurt she didn't call after my interview. I'd been waiting all evening.

She put her book down and explained. Very calmly. One, she was in a meeting until eight. Two, she'd texted "good luck" in the morning, which was the more important moment. Three, statistically most interviews don't need a same-day debrief. Four, she'd planned to ask me at dinner, which is actually more personal.

Every point was true. I couldn't argue with any of them.

And I felt worse than before. Like I'd brought a feeling and she'd handed me a spreadsheet.

I didn't need her to be right. I needed her to say, "Oh, that must have been a long evening." That's all.

Going to sleep now. She's still reading.

Until what time was Lakshmi in a meeting?
Until eight.
Why did Deepika feel worse after Lakshmi's calm explanation?
Deepika felt unheard and lonely, because every correct point answered the logic but ignored the hurt Deepika had shared.
What could Lakshmi try the next time Deepika says she's hurt?
Lakshmi could first acknowledge the feeling, like "That must have been a long evening," before explaining anything.
How might Lakshmi see the conversation?
Lakshmi may think she handled it well, having given clear, fair reasons, and not realise that Deepika felt dismissed.

On a packed tro-tro in Accra, an old man near the back slumped against the window, his face grey. Passengers murmured. One woman fanned him with a newspaper. Nobody else moved.
Nkechi was standing by the door. She raised her voice over the engine. “Driver! Stop the bus. Please pull over.” Then she pointed. “Kwame, you're by the window, call an ambulance. You, madam with the fan, keep going. You, sir, give him your seat by the door, let's lay him down.”
Kwame fumbled for his phone and dialled. The bus pulled over. Two passengers helped lower the man onto the seat.
Ten minutes later a siren came through the traffic. As the paramedics climbed in, the man squeezed Nkechi's hand.

Which city was the tro-tro in?
It was in Accra.
What was Nkechi feeling when she raised her voice?
She seemed worried but calm and in control, determined to get people acting instead of murmuring.
Why did pointing at people work better than a general shout?
Naming Kwame and the others gave each a clear job, so nobody could leave it to someone else.
How might the old man have felt when he squeezed Nkechi's hand?
He likely felt frightened but grateful and relieved that someone had taken charge.

We played musical chairs. When Eshaan was out, he stood by the wall with his fists clenched and his arms stiff. He didn't cry, but his face was red. The squishy ball.

Preeti noticed. She pushed her steel box to the middle. "Take two puris. I have four."

Parveen's cheeks went pink. She felt glad and a little shy. "Thank you."

The next day Parveen brought an extra orange. "For you, Preeti."

Preeti offered two puris.

Parveen felt grateful and a little shy about needing help.

Taking just what was offered kept the kindness special, and she shared back the next day.

'Fifty-one,' said Dhruv, tapping the notebook. 'That's how many ways the food-truck idea can collapse.'
'Fifty-one?' said Vidya, flipping pages. 'Fuel, permits, rain, a rival, a bad cook, a stolen generator...'
'Right. And each one is possible. I feel sick reading it.'
'Which is the most likely?'
'I don't know. They all look equally bad.'
'So how do you decide what to worry about first?'
Dhruv closed the notebook. 'I don't. Maybe I shouldn't start.'
'You haven't even tried one weekend.'
'Fifty-one reasons, Vidya.'
Vidya sighed. 'Reasons, sure. But you haven't marked which are likely or which would hurt most. It's just a heap.'

How many ways to collapse did Dhruv list?
Dhruv listed fifty-one ways.
How does Dhruv feel when reading the list?
Dhruv feels sick and full of dread, and is leaning toward not starting at all.
What other approach could Dhruv try with the list?
Dhruv could mark each risk for how likely it is and how much damage it does, keep the top few, and run one small weekend test.
How does Vidya see the list?
Vidya sees it as a heap without ranking and not a reason to quit, and the sigh suggests some frustration.

Week 1: At the start-up meet, Irfan, a mentor who advises café owners in the big city, looked at Aparna's price list for her home-baked cakes. "Too cheap," he said. "Double everything. People pay for premium." Aparna nodded and wrote it down. She didn't ask why.

Week 3: She printed new cards with the doubled prices. Her regulars in the small town, mostly teachers and shop owners ordering for birthdays, went quiet. Only two orders came that week instead of the usual nine.

Week 5: A neighbour said gently, "Beta, we loved your cakes, but this is city money." Aparna sat with the order book and realised Irfan's clients were office crowds in the city, not her street. She had never asked what his advice was based on.

Only two orders instead of the usual nine.

She probably felt dismayed and a bit foolish, realising she had followed Irfan's advice without asking what it was based on.

She could have asked why he suggested doubling, and who his clients were, then tested one new price with a few regulars before changing everything.
How did the change look to Aparna's regular customers?
To her regulars it felt like the cakes were suddenly priced for the city, not for them, so they quietly stopped ordering.

The drumming turned into a game, and the man began to smile.

Number forty.
What was Sumit feeling while he drummed and swung his legs?
He was bored and full of energy after sitting still for an hour. He may also have felt a bit restless in the crowded room.

She turned the drumming into a copying game, which used his energy and eased his boredom without a scolding.

At the gram sabha in Moga district, Baljeet finished his speech about the new support scheme for drip irrigation, and the clapping began. In the front rows, a few older farmers clapped politely, three or four times, then folded their hands. Near the back, Harsha and his friends clapped slowly, loudly, with long gaps between each clap, grinning at each other. Baljeet's ears burned. Was that mockery? The front row's clapping he read as courtesy; the back row's felt like a jeer. After the meeting he walked over to Harsha instead of avoiding him. "That slow clap. Was that for me?" Harsha shrugged, not unkindly. "The last officer promised the same scheme two years ago. Nothing came. We clap slow for promises." Baljeet nodded. "Fair. Come to the block office on Monday. I'll show you the sanctioned list, with your village on it." Harsha raised his eyebrows. "If it's real, we'll clap properly next time."

What was Baljeet's speech about?
The new support scheme for drip irrigation.
What did Baljeet feel when the back row clapped slowly?
Baljeet's ears burned; he felt embarrassed and suspected the slow clapping was mockery.
How did Baljeet respond to the ambiguous applause?
He walked over and asked Harsha directly what the slow clap meant, then offered proof by inviting him to see the sanctioned list.
What did the slow clap mean to Harsha?
It was scepticism rather than personal mockery: a past officer had promised the same scheme and nothing came, so they 'clap slow for promises'.

In the support room of a ticketing software company, Santosh read a public post from a user, Sabina: the export button had wiped her saved filters twice, and no one had answered. The team gathered round Santosh's screen. Nobody wanted to argue. Santosh wrote the reply and the others checked it: 'Thank you for telling us, Sabina, and sorry about the lost filters. Mr. Collins was not left long to the silent contemplation of his successful love; for Mrs. Bennet, having dawdled about in the vestibule to watch for the end of the conference, no sooner saw Elizabeth open the door and with quick step pass her towards the staircase, than she entered the breakfast-room, and congratulated both him and herself in warm terms on the happy prospect of their nearer connection. Mr. Collins received and returned these felicitations with equal pleasure, and then proceeded to relate the particulars of their interview, with the result of which he trusted he had every reason to be satisfied, since the refusal which his cousin had steadfastly given him would naturally flow from her bashful modesty and the genuine delicacy of her character.

Mrs. Bennet waits outside the room, and when Elizabeth hurries upstairs she rushes in to congratulate Mr. Collins. He happily tells her about the meeting, believing Elizabeth's refusal was only shyness.

The evening began twenty minutes late.
How did Anjali's early planning differ from what Uday and Abhinav did, and what did each lead to?
Anjali gave every step a date and tracked costs, while Uday and Abhinav waited until the last afternoon for sound and seating, so a cable and chairs were missing and the evening began late.

Panic and embarrassment, since parents were waiting at the doors.

Emigrate or immigrate: which one is leaving a country?

"Emigrate" means to leave your own country to live in another one. "Immigrate" means to come into a new country to live there. Remember: emigrate is exit, immigrate is in.

Monday: The college magazine's online piece was punchy and sure of itself: "Students overwhelmingly reject the new canteen menu." Tanuja, who actually liked the new menu, suddenly doubted her own taste. The writing sounded so certain. She almost forwarded it to her class group with an angry face.
Wednesday: Something nagged at her, so she scrolled to the bottom. The survey had asked twelve students, all from one hostel, on a day the canteen ran out of food by one o'clock. "Overwhelmingly" meant nine of them. Everything else was the writer's opinion, dressed up in a firm tone.
The following Monday: Tanuja messaged Himani, the editor, whom she knew from debate club. "Loved the energy, but can we say where the numbers come from? Twelve people from one hostel isn't the whole college." Himani replied, "Fair point, I got carried away." The updated piece now had a line about the sample, and a link to a wider survey.

Twelve students, all from one hostel.
How did Tanuja feel on Monday while reading the confident piece?
Tanuja felt doubtful of her own view, swayed by the certain tone, even though she liked the new menu.
What did Tanuja check before trusting the claim?
The source and sample: how many were asked, who they were and when, separating the numbers from the writer's opinion.
How did Himani respond to Tanuja's message?
Himani took it as fair feedback, admitted getting carried away, and updated the piece with a line about the sample.

People ask me on this show, "How did you stop caring what people think?" Honestly, I didn't. I'm Vaibhav, and I still love a compliment. But here's what changed. Two years ago I started the lending library in our colony's old garage. Every weekend I'd post photos and then refresh my phone for likes. If a post got twelve likes, I felt like a failure. My sister Indu said, "Write down why you started it. Before you open the phone." So I did. "Kids reading who can't buy books. Old uncles having somewhere to sit." Now, when a post gets no likes, I look at the list and at the kids on the floor. I'm proud anyway. The likes are nice. They're not the reason.

What did Indu tell Vaibhav to do before opening the phone?
"Write down why you started it."
Why did twelve likes once make Vaibhav feel like a failure?
Vaibhav was measuring the library by other people's reactions, so a small number felt like proof it didn't matter.
What habit loosened the grip of the likes, and why?
Writing down the reasons first and checking the list, and the kids on the floor, lets Vaibhav judge the library by personal values before any reactions come.
How might the kids and old uncles in the garage see the library, whatever the likes say?
For them it is simply a place to read and sit, and it matters just as much on days no one online notices.

Indu: banter usually makes both people laugh though. Does it feel like that to you?
Vaibhav: no. It feels like she's making me smaller
Indu: maybe tell her calmly, one time, that you won't take the mocking. And see how she reacts
Vaibhav: yeah. I'll do it on the weekend, not over text

What did Vaibhav's friend say when he told her about the internship?
She said "wow, big shot" in a sneery voice.
What does Vaibhav's remark that it feels like she is making him smaller suggest about his feelings, and what else could account for the friend's tone?
It suggests he feels disrespected and hurt, though the friend might see her jokes as harmless banter or be hiding her own jealousy.
What could Vaibhav do next about the mocking?
He could calmly tell her in person that he does not want to be mocked, name the pattern, and see whether she respects the limit.
How might the friend see the situation differently from Vaibhav?
She may think she is only teasing and that Vaibhav is too sensitive, so she might not realise how it lands until he tells her plainly.

messages.content: Write a sorry note to my classmate Imran: I borrowed his pen and lost it, I feel bad about it, and I will buy him a new one on Monday. 40 words. From Jaya.

Dear Imran,
I am sorry. I borrowed your pen and lost it, and I feel bad about it. I will buy you a new one on Monday. Please forgive me for the trouble, and thank you for being so kind.
Jaya

The ball flew off Jeevan's bat, over the neem tree and straight through Urmila-amma's kitchen window. Crash. The other boys in the village lane scattered. Jeevan stood frozen, bat in hand. He could run too; nobody had seen who hit it. Instead he went home and found his father mending a fishing net on the verandah. "Appa, I broke Urmila-amma's window." His father put the net down. "Then let's go." At her door Jeevan's voice shook. "Amma, it was my shot. I'm sorry. I'll give my savings towards the glass." Urmila-amma looked at him for a long moment, then laughed. "My sons broke that same window three times. Your father and I will sort out the glass. You sweep up the pieces, and hit the next one the other way."

What was Jeevan's father doing when Jeevan came home?
Mending a fishing net on the verandah.
How did Jeevan feel at Urmila-amma's door?
Frightened and nervous; his voice shook.
Which choice worked, and why?
Going straight to his father and then to her door, because owning up at once showed honesty that made her kind rather than angry.
How does Urmila-amma see the broken window?
More amused than angry, remembering her own sons breaking the same window.

I'm Jasleen. In my fourth month at a small export firm, my manager, Yamini, came to my desk at eleven, stressed. The buyer's inspection certificate had come late, and she wanted me to put last week's date on our dispatch approval so the file 'looked clean' for the buyer's audit.
I'd already decided I wouldn't backdate anything. But I also knew a flat no would leave her stuck with a real problem.
So I said it in steps. 'Ma'am, I can't put an earlier date on the approval. It has to show when we actually approved it. But the buyer's real worry is the delay, right? I can write a short note today explaining why the certificate came late, what we did and when it was cleared, with the courier receipt attached. I'll have it ready by three.'
She was quiet for a second, then nodded. 'Do that.'
At 2:40 I sent it. The buyer's auditor replied the next day: 'Noted, thank you for the explanation.'

By what time did Jasleen offer to have the note ready?
By three.
Why did Jasleen not just give a flat no?
Jasleen felt for Yamini's stress and wanted to help solve the real problem, not leave her stuck.
What made Jasleen's alternative work?
It met the buyer's real need, an explanation of the delay, while keeping the record true.
How might Yamini feel when the buyer's auditor replies?
Relieved, and perhaps grateful that the honest note worked better than the shortcut she asked for.

Reena's Hindi teacher had torn a page out of her notebook in front of everyone. "Messy work goes in the bin," Sir had said, and Reena had stared at her desk until the bell.

At home in the Pune flat, she dropped her bag, marched to her room and slammed the door. Then she opened it and slammed it again. Moti, the old Labrador, wagged in with a slipper. "Get lost, Moti! You smell!" Moti's tail stopped.

Trisha didi, doing homework at the dining table, picked up the notebook poking out of the bag, saw the ragged edge, and said quietly, "Moti didn't do this."

Reena looked at Moti's drooping ears, and her throat went tight. She sat on the floor and let Moti lean against her.

What had the Hindi teacher done to Reena's notebook?
The teacher had torn a page out of Reena's notebook in front of everyone.
Why did Reena shout at Moti?
Reena felt humiliated and angry about the teacher, and Moti was a safe target at home, so the feeling spilled onto the dog.
What went right in how Trisha didi responded?
Trisha didi linked the anger to its real cause without scolding, which helped Reena notice it and calm down with Moti.
How might Moti experience Reena's return from school?
Moti comes to play and gets shouted at, so the wagging stops; for Moti the anger comes out of nowhere.

messages.content:

Bhavna, you think your Nani was always sensible? Listen. When I was eight, a girl called Sushila joined our school in Nashik. On her first day, the teacher praised her handwriting, and mine had been the class favourite for two years. So what did I do? I became her shadow. I sharpened her pencils. I gave her my ribbons. I told everyone, "Sushila is my dearest friend in the whole world!" so often that the teacher said, "Minakshi, lower your voice." One evening my mother found me crying by the well and asked why. Only then did I say it: "Everyone likes her better." She hugged me and said feeling jealous didn't make me a bad girl. After that, I stopped performing. Sushila and I became real friends, slowly.

What had been the class favourite for two years before Sushila arrived?
Minakshi's handwriting, which the teacher had praised for two years.
What was young Minakshi really feeling while she called Sushila her 'dearest friend'?
She was jealous and afraid that everyone liked Sushila better; the loud friendliness covered a feeling she couldn't admit yet.
What turning point helped Minakshi stop performing?
Her mother finding her crying and asking why, then hugging her and saying that feeling jealous didn't make her a bad girl.
How might Sushila have experienced Minakshi's shadowing?
Sushila may have found the pencils and ribbons a bit much, and only felt a real friendship once Minakshi stopped performing.

“When I was ten,” said Gautam Nana, “my teacher Mrs Pillai tilted her head when I said I had not copied Ramesh's sum. My heart sank. I thought, She doesn't believe me. I stood there stiff as a post.”
“What happened?” asked Jaya.
“She said, in a kind voice, ‘Tell me how you got it.’ I showed her my working and her face cleared. The tilt was only because she wanted to hear more.” He smiled. “Now when a teacher tilts her head I remember the tone. It can be curiosity, or sympathy, or doubt. You have to look at the whole face.”

Who tilted her head when Gautam said he had not copied?
Mrs Pillai tilted her head.
What did young Gautam think the head tilt meant, and what did it turn out to be?
He thought Mrs Pillai did not believe him and felt worried and upset, since his heart sank and he stood stiff. It turned out she only wanted to hear more.
What could Jaya learn from Nana's story?
That a head tilt has several possible meanings, so she should look at the whole face and tone, and offer her working or explanation.
How might Mrs Pillai have seen Gautam's stiff face?
Probably as worry, and she did not intend doubt. Her kind “Tell me how you got it” suggests she wanted to put him at ease.

The college library closed at nine, and Usha caught Imran by the photocopier at ten to. "You've skipped dinner with me three times this week. You don't reply for hours. What am I supposed to think?" Two juniors looked up from the reading table. Imran's ears went hot. Every sentence felt like a list of his failures being read aloud. He picked up his copies, said, "I've got a deadline," and walked to the stairs. In his head he was protecting them both from a scene in the library. Usha stood by the machine, still holding the question she hadn't finished. The librarian was switching off the lights row by row, and to her it felt as if he had switched her off too.

Where did Usha catch Imran?
She caught Imran by the photocopier.
Why did Imran walk away to the stairs?
He felt ashamed and exposed, as if a list of his failures was being read aloud in front of the juniors, and believed leaving would protect them both from a scene.
What could Imran say instead of walking off?
He could say "I'm swamped right now, can we talk after the library closes?" so Usha knows he is coming back.
What is it like for Usha as the lights go off?
Usha feels switched off and left behind, still holding an unfinished question, as if Imran had shut her out.

It was show-and-tell day at the kindergarten. Parveen held up a small box of sheer khurma. "On Eid, my Nani makes this. We wake up early, wear new clothes and go to everyone's house."
"Do all families do that?" asked a classmate.
Parveen thought. "This is how my family does it."
Vikas, the teacher, smiled. "Thank you, Parveen. Who else has a family festival?" Hands flew up.

What did Parveen hold up at show-and-tell?
She held up a small box of sheer khurma.
How might Parveen have felt when the classmate asked if all families do that?
She may have felt a little unsure at first, so she paused before answering that this is how her family does it.
How did Vikas help the class learn from Parveen's share?
He thanked her and invited others to share their family festivals.
How might classmates feel after Parveen's story?
They might feel curious and eager to share their own traditions.

You want to know how Hrithik and I became friends? It took most of a year. When I, Pankaj, joined the site office, he was the engineer who ate alone in the jeep. Ask him about his weekend and he'd say, "Nothing much. What about the pour schedule?" He said no to the Diwali lunch, no to cricket, no to my cousin's wedding. I didn't push. I just started buying two cups of tea at five and leaving one on his dashboard. Some days he drank it, some days it went cold. Around March he walked with me to the gate. In June he mentioned, very quickly, that his father was ill back in Nagpur. I didn't ask more than he offered. Last week he invited me to his flat for dinner. That was his idea, not mine.

What did Pankaj leave on Hrithik's dashboard?
A cup of tea, bought at five.
What might Hrithik's quick mention of his ill father suggest about how he was feeling?
He was carrying a worry he didn't usually share; saying it quickly suggests he was starting to trust Pankaj but still felt guarded.
Why did Pankaj's choice not to ask more matter?
It let Hrithik keep control over what he shared, so trust kept growing until the dinner invitation came from him.
What might the months of tea have been like for Hrithik?
They were probably a steady, quiet sign that someone cared, letting him warm up at his own pace without being put on the spot.

In the college hostel common room, the TV showed the cricket captain Nikhil Rana refusing to shake an umpire's hand after a bad decision. Half the room booed. Aparna jumped up. 'He was right! That umpire's been against him all series!' Vishal, from the next room, said, 'Still, not shaking hands is poor sport.' Aparna turned on him. 'You've never supported him properly. You wouldn't understand.' She had Rana's jersey, his autobiography with the printed signature inside, and a short recorded message from a fan event that she played before exams. That night she wrote three long posts defending him. Only later, lying in bed, did it strike her: she'd never met him, and she'd just shouted at a friend for him.

What did Nikhil Rana refuse to do?
Shake an umpire's hand after a bad decision.
What did Aparna feel lying in bed?
Uneasy and a bit foolish, noticing she had shouted at a real friend to defend someone she'd never met.
What could Aparna do the next morning?
Apologise to Vishal and allow that she can love Rana's cricket while admitting poor sportsmanship.
How might Vishal have felt being told 'You wouldn't understand'?
Probably stung and dismissed, since Vishal had only made a fair point about sportsmanship.

Preeti came home to Karnal for the holidays with her first semester of agriculture college behind her and a neat new tool: the soil nutrient chart. On the first day she walked her uncle Jagdish's wheat field, crumbled soil in her palm and announced exactly what each plot needed. "Simple," she said. "It's all in the chart." Jagdish chacha nodded, then took her to the low corner of the field where the plants were yellow despite being fed well. Water sat there after rain; the roots were half rotten. Her chart had no column for that. That night Preeti sat on the charpai, notebook open, feeling like first semester had taught her nothing. Chacha brought her tea. "Now you're starting to learn," he said.

What was wrong in the low corner of the field?
Water sat there after rain and the roots were half rotten, so the plants were yellow.
Why did Preeti feel that first semester had taught her nothing?
The chart had made her feel expert, and the waterlogged corner was the first problem it couldn't explain, so her confidence dropped sharply.
What could Preeti do with that disappointing evening?
She could note what the chart missed, ask chacha what he has seen in wet corners, and look for it next semester, treating the dip as the start of real learning.
Why might Jagdish chacha say "Now you're starting to learn"?
Chacha seems to know from years of farming that real skill begins when you meet problems a simple rule can't solve, so the doubt looks like progress to him.
We've planted a mango sapling in our yard. How long until it gives mangoes?
Mango trees take their time. A tree grown from a seed may need many years, while some grafted saplings can fruit sooner. The nursery that sold the sapling can tell you more.
Ours is a small grafted one.
Then a few years is a reasonable guess, but it depends on the variety and care. Water it regularly while it is young and protect it from strong winds.
Is there anything I should avoid?
Don't let water collect around the base, and avoid damaging the trunk when you clean around it. Your local nursery can give advice for your area.
Thanks, I'll ask them. I'll make a growth chart too.
Lovely idea. A photo every few months will show how much it grows.
Paint a rainy evening in Kolkata in one sentence that uses the words "tram" and "puddles".
The old tram rattled down the street, splashing through puddles as the evening rain kept falling.

Five practice cases, all easy.
What is Anand feeling after trying part 3?
Anand feels discouraged and doubts being any good, because the harder cases don't fit the framework that felt so easy on Sunday.
What does Jagdish suggest, and why could it help?
One part 3 case a day, talked through out loud, with the worst one sent to him, so skill can grow steadily through the dip.

Jagdish sees it as a normal, good sign of progress, since Anand can now see what the steps don't cover.

Your Dadu will tell you something, beta. When I was eleven, in Nashik, my best friend was Madhav. Every evening in January we flew kites from his terrace, shouting till our mothers called us down.
Then Madhav joined an evening tuition, and after that the colony cricket team. First he came up to the terrace every day, then twice a week, then not at all. Nobody fought. Nobody said anything.
I was sure I must have done something. I remembered the time I tore his best kite and wondered if he'd been angry all along. Every evening at five I felt a heavy, dull feeling in my stomach.
Years later, at a wedding, I asked him. He blinked. "Darshan? You? I was just so tired from tuition, yaar. I thought you'd found new friends."
So when your friend stops calling, don't decide too quickly that it's you.

Where did Darshan and Madhav fly kites every evening in January?
They flew kites from Madhav's terrace every evening in January.
Why did Darshan feel heavy every evening at five?
Darshan missed Madhav and was sure he had done something wrong, even wondering if the torn kite had made Madhav angry all along.
What turning point does Darshan want the grandchild to take from this?
Not to decide too quickly that a fading friend is rejecting you; asking gently, or waiting before blaming yourself, can show the real reason.
How did Madhav see the same months?
Madhav was just tired from tuition and busy with cricket, and even thought Darshan had found new friends, so there was no rejection on his side.
My manager mentioned me about the new project yesterday. What is wrong?

My manager mentioned the new project to me yesterday.
Why: "Mention" takes the thing mentioned directly, and the person comes after "to".

Aadhya was proofreading the final page of the school newspaper, forty minutes before the print run, when she saw it: she'd written that Kashish's cousin, not Kashish, had won the state essay prize. Her own mistake, in her own headline. Her stomach dropped. The old printer in the staffroom was already warming up, and the teacher in charge had gone to a meeting. For a moment she wanted to hide under the desk. Then she breathed and told herself, the way she'd tell a junior: 'Okay. It stings. You're allowed to feel that. Now fix it.' She messaged Kashish first: 'I got your name wrong in the headline. So sorry. Fixing it now.' Kashish replied, 'Thanks for catching it!' Aadhya corrected the page, printed a fresh proof and checked every other name twice. Then she added one line to the team checklist: 'Names checked by two people.' The paper went out on time.

What mistake did Aadhya find in the headline?
She'd written that Kashish's cousin, not Kashish, had won the state essay prize.
What was Aadhya feeling when she spotted the error?
Her stomach dropped with embarrassment, and for a moment she wanted to hide.
How did Aadhya combine kindness with high standards?
She let herself feel the sting without attacking herself, then apologised, fixed it, double-checked every name and added a checklist rule.
How does Kashish see Aadhya's message?
Kashish is grateful the mistake was caught and shared straight away.

Wednesday
Gopika looked at my science fair poster today and said, "The graph part is unclear. I can't tell which line is which."
My first thought, honestly, was "Well, YOUR poster has spelling mistakes." It was right there in my mouth.
But I didn't say it. I just said, "Hmm," and walked to the water cooler and back. Counted to ten, like Ammi says.
When I came back, I looked at the graph. She was right. Both lines are blue. No labels.
I said, "Okay, which would be clearer, colours or labels?" She said, "Both?" and lent me her red pen.
It's better now. Really better.
The weird thing is, she didn't say my poster was bad. She said one part was unclear. That's why I could fix it and not just feel stupid.
- Hafsa

What colour were both lines on the graph?
Both lines were blue.
What was Hafsa feeling right after Gopika's comment?
Hafsa felt defensive and stung, with an urge to attack Gopika's spelling, before calming down.
What small step helped Hafsa accept the feedback?
Walking to the water cooler and counting to ten gave Hafsa time to cool down and look at the graph fairly.
How does Gopika's way of criticising compare with what Hafsa nearly said?
Gopika named one unclear part of the poster, which could be fixed, while Hafsa's retort would have been an attack meant to hurt back.

"Bidisha, you've been quiet all day."
Yeah. Can I tell you something, Lakshmi? It's small, but it's been sitting in my chest since last night.
Didi came home from her chemistry board exam. I only asked, "How was it?" and she screamed, "Why do you always have to poke your nose in? Get out of my room!" It isn't even her room. It's our room.
I went and sat on the stairs. I kept thinking, what did I do? I felt tiny.
This morning Ma said Didi's paper went really badly, and I understand, sort of. I'd be a wreck too. But I'm still hurt. A bad exam doesn't mean she gets to scream at me.
Do you think I should tell her that?

What did Bidisha ask Didi?
"How was it?"
Why did Bidisha feel tiny on the stairs?
Bidisha had only asked a kind question and couldn't see what was wrong, so being screamed at felt confusing and made Bidisha feel small.
What would you advise Bidisha to say to Didi?
Once things are calm, something like "I'm sorry the exam went badly, but please don't scream at me", which is kind and still honest about the hurt.
What might Didi be feeling by the next morning?
Didi is probably still upset about the chemistry paper and may also feel bad about screaming, even if she hasn't said so.

messages.content: What is my landlady's mobile number?
I don't know your landlady's number, and it is private information anyway. Look in your rental papers or ask the agent who introduced you.

In the PE period at St Anne's School, Thomas was cricket captain. He picked fast, pointing: "You, you and you." Varun waited near the boundary rope with his hands behind his back.
"We've got enough," Thomas said, and ran to the pitch.
The PE teacher was busy with the other class. Varun sat on the steps near the water cooler. From there he could hear the bat hitting the ball and everyone shouting. Last year he and Thomas had been bowling partners.
His stomach felt heavy, like after eating too much, but it wasn't food. He pulled at a loose thread on his sock until it came out.
When the bell rang, a classmate asked why he hadn't played. "Didn't feel like it," Varun said, looking away.

Where did Varun sit after not being picked?
On the steps near the water cooler.
What does Varun's heavy stomach show about how he felt?
He felt hurt and left out, a heavy ache he couldn't explain, especially because Thomas used to be his bowling partner.
What could the PE teacher do next time?
Notice who is left out, check on Varun, and use a fairer way of picking teams so no child is skipped.
What might Thomas be thinking as he runs to the pitch?
Thomas is probably focused on the game and may not realise how hurt his old bowling partner is.

In Class 9, I stopped cycling to school. I told my parents it was because of the sun. The real reason was the reels. Every night I scrolled through videos of road accidents: a scooter flipping, a truck swerving, a cyclist on a highway. After a while my feed was nothing but crashes. I became sure the roads of Nashik were a war zone. My friend Damini, who cycled with me every day for two years, kept asking why. I said, "Don't you watch the news?" She said, "Irawati, we've done this route five hundred times. Nothing happened." I didn't listen. I took the auto, which was actually more crowded and honestly more scary. Looking back, I think I mixed up how often I saw accidents with how often they happened.

What did Irawati take instead of cycling?
The auto.
Why did the roads feel like a war zone to Irawati?
Watching crash videos every night made accidents feel constant, so Irawati felt scared even though the real route had been safe for years.
What could Irawati have done to check the fear?
Irawati could have compared the five hundred safe rides with the videos, or looked up real local accident figures with a parent.
How might Damini have felt cycling alone after Irawati stopped?
Damini may have felt lonely and puzzled, missing a cycling friend and not understanding the fear.
