At the milk cooperative office near Anand, Wasim had a habit his old mentor once pointed out: he talked the most in every meeting. Now, as the new secretary, he kept a small tally in the margin of his notebook. By half past ten the monthly meeting stood at: Wasim, nine lines. Shalini ben, who ran the evening collection, one. The three older members, two each. Wasim looked at the tally, stopped mid-sentence and turned. "Shalini ben, you're at the counter every evening. What are we missing?" Shalini hesitated, then said the chilling unit had shut off twice last week around seven, when the power dipped, and nobody had written it down. The room went quiet. Nobody else had known. They spent the next half hour on a backup plan. When the meeting ended, the tally read: Wasim, eleven; Shalini ben, seven. He underlined it.

How many lines had Wasim spoken by half past ten?
Nine lines.
Why did Wasim stop mid-sentence after checking his tally?
Wasim felt a jolt of awareness, a little uncomfortable, seeing how much of the airtime he had taken as secretary.
What habit is Wasim building, and why does it matter in his role?
Counting his own turns and inviting quieter members in; as secretary his voice carries weight, so making space brings out problems others see.
What was it like for Shalini ben to be asked directly?
She hesitated at first, but the direct question gave her room to raise the chilling unit problem nobody else knew about.

Eshaan, the whole school says your PT sir takes bribes for team selection? Let your Yusuf dada tell you about Hameed sahib. When I was fifteen, in Rampur, someone said our Urdu teacher, Hameed sahib, drank at night. One boy said it, then ten. By Eid it was "everyone knows". I watched boys laugh behind his back and a father shout at him in the market.
I never saw him drink. Nobody did. Years later we learned he walked slowly at night because his leg was bad and he was going to the hospital to sit with his wife. I still feel ashamed that I repeated it once.
So, beta: who actually saw your PT sir take money?

Why did Hameed sahib walk slowly at night?
Because his leg was bad and he was going to the hospital to sit with his wife.
What does Yusuf still feel about repeating the rumour?
He still feels ashamed that he repeated it once, without ever having seen anything.
What choice in the story could have stopped the rumour?
Asking who actually saw Hameed sahib drink before repeating it; nobody had.
What was it like for Hameed sahib when the rumour spread?
He was mocked and shouted at while caring for his ill wife, which must have been painful and lonely.

On Monday the class teacher noticed three children being quiet. Naveen kicked at the floor. His little brother Ansh had been ill for a week, and every phone call and visitor asked only about Ansh. Naveen felt jealous, and then guilty for feeling it. At lunch he told the teacher, who said both feelings were normal, and that evening he asked his father for a little time, just the two of them, to play carrom. Minakshi kept looking at the clock. Her mother was unwell, and all day at school she wondered how her mother was. She told the teacher too, and the teacher said worry is a sign of love and she was not in charge of making her mother better. Minakshi asked her mother what she could help with, and set the table every night. Jyoti had been drawing at her desk: a sun and a giraffe for her younger sister, who was in hospital. "Can I take this tomorrow?" she asked. The teacher smiled. Jyoti was sad, and still ran out to play at recess and laughed. Nobody needed her to feel bad every minute.

What did Jyoti draw for her younger sister?
She drew a sun and a giraffe.
How did Naveen's feeling about his sick brother differ from Minakshi's feeling about her mother, and what did each do?

Naveen felt jealous of the attention Ansh got and then guilty, so he asked his father for time together, while Minakshi felt worry all day, so she asked her mother what she could help with and set the table.
How did Naveen feel when every call and visitor asked only about Ansh?
He felt jealous, and then guilty for feeling jealous.
What could Jyoti do to stay close to her sister while still looking after herself?
She could keep drawing pictures for her sister and still play and laugh at recess, since being sad and being happy can both be allowed.

Tutor's note, after the placement test results. Nine of the batch cleared the first round; Siddharth did not. At the notice board Siddharth read Pradeep's name, went very still, and said flatly, "Lucky, Pradeep barely revised." Later in my room Siddharth admitted, "There's a bitter knot in my stomach. For a minute I wanted to move Pradeep's notes off our shared desk. I didn't." I said the feeling can be noted without being obeyed. That evening Siddharth walked to Pradeep's room, said, "Congratulations, I mean it," and asked how Pradeep had practised the timed papers. Pradeep pulled out a chair and started explaining. Siddharth's face stayed tight, but the pen kept moving on the notepad.

How many of the batch cleared the first round?
Nine of the batch cleared the first round.
What was Siddharth feeling at the notice board, and what shows it?
A bitter, jealous knot. Siddharth went very still, spoke flatly about Pradeep, and later admitted wanting to move Pradeep's notes off the desk.
What did Siddharth do that turned the feeling into something useful?
Siddharth congratulated Pradeep anyway and asked how Pradeep had practised the timed papers, instead of turning to contempt or sabotage.
What might it be like for Pradeep when Siddharth arrives with congratulations and a question?
Pradeep may feel respected and glad to share, shown by pulling out a chair and starting to explain, and may not know how bitter Siddharth felt earlier.

Class teacher's note, Class 10B, Friday.

Tushar handed in the maths unit test half blank today. When I asked him about it at break, he said the paper was "out of syllabus, nobody could do it" and that unit tests "don't count for anything". Three other students scored above thirty on the same paper. He did not look at me while he said it, and he kept rolling his pen.

I did not argue. I told him the unit test decides who joins the Saturday support group, and asked what he had revised. After a pause he said, "Nothing, really." We made a list of two chapters to cover by Wednesday. I have also spoken gently to his mother so she can help him keep to it. I will check the list with him on Wednesday.

Gurpreet, class teacher

How many other students scored above thirty on the same paper?
Three other students scored above thirty on the same paper.
Why might "out of syllabus" feel true to Tushar?
Tushar likely feels embarrassed about not revising, and blaming the paper shields him from that shame for now.
What did Gurpreet do that could help Tushar?
Gurpreet didn't argue, named the real cost of the Saturday group, asked what was revised, and set a small two-chapter plan with a check on Wednesday.
How might Tushar's mother be affected by the teacher's call?
Tushar's mother may feel concerned but also relieved to know early, so she can help him keep to the two-chapter list.

Team lead's note, legal research unit, month 4.
Sarika joined us in June. She is one of the most accurate researchers I have worked with. She is also the last to leave most nights, often past 11 p.m., and checks every citation three or four times.
When I praised her memo last week, she said, “I only got it right because I checked it all night.” Her colleague Hafsa mentioned that Sarika once said, “If I slow down, they'll realise I'm not good enough.”
She seems tired and tense most days. I think each success brings a short relief, and she credits it to overwork rather than skill, so the fear never gets tested.
What I did next: I asked her to submit the next memo at 6 p.m. with one round of checks only, and to see what happens. I told her plainly that her training and judgement are why her work is good. We will review together next week.

How many times does Sarika check every citation?
She checks every citation three or four times.
How does Sarika seem to feel most days?
She seems tired and tense, afraid that slowing down would expose her as not good enough.
Why did the team lead ask for a memo at 6 p.m. with one round of checks?
To let Sarika test her fear and see that her skill, not overwork, makes her work good.
How might Hafsa see Sarika's late nights?
Hafsa seems concerned, having heard Sarika say she fears being found not good enough.

Indoors we agreed equally well. They were both more accomplished and better read than I was; but with eagerness I followed in the path of knowledge they had trodden before me. I devoured the books they lent me: then it was full satisfaction to discuss with them in the evening what I had perused during the day. Thought fitted thought; opinion met opinion: we coincided, in short, perfectly.

Without outside knowledge, why does the narrator agree so well with the two people indoors?

They are more accomplished and better read, and the narrator eagerly follows their path of learning, devouring the books they lend. Discussing them in the evening, their thoughts and opinions meet and match perfectly.
Which is heavier, a kilogram of cotton or a kilogram of iron?
They weigh the same. Because both are one kilogram; the iron just takes up much less space than the cotton.

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Aaji,
Results came yesterday. Tushar failed the scholarship exam. I'm not surprised at all. It was obvious from the start: he chose to go to his sister's wedding the week before instead of revising. Who does that? I never would. I told Aai I saw this coming months ago. She reminded me that in January I said Tushar would top the district. I don't remember saying that, but maybe I meant it as a joke. Anyway, it's clear now that the wedding was a terrible decision. He should have known.
Love,
Omkar
P.S. Tushar hasn't replied to my messages today.

What did Tushar go to the week before the exam?
Tushar went to his sister's wedding the week before the exam.
Why does the wedding now look like a terrible decision to Omkar?
Omkar feels certain and a little superior because knowing that Tushar failed makes the wedding week look like the obvious cause. Omkar forgets that in January a top result seemed likely.
What question could help Omkar judge Tushar's choice more fairly?
Omkar could ask what Tushar knew when deciding: a family wedding, and a student everyone expected to top the district, not a known failure.
Why might Tushar not be replying to Omkar's messages?
Tushar may be feeling low about the result and might sense judgment, so staying quiet feels easier than hearing that it was obvious.

At the ITI workshop in the kasba, Tarun, in his final year, was asked to guide two first-years. Minakshi asked a hundred questions on day one, so Tarun gave her the motor rewinding job, the hardest in the shop. He checked her work every day and explained each mistake. The other junior, a quiet boy, got sweeping and sorting screws, because he seemed slow. By the third month, Minakshi could rewind a motor alone. The quiet boy still sorted screws. One evening he stood by the rewinding bench, watching. Tarun realised he had never shown him anything. He had decided the boy was slow and then given him nothing to grow with. The next morning, Tarun handed him a small motor. "Let's start."

What job did Tarun give Minakshi?
The motor rewinding job, the hardest in the shop.
What did Tarun feel when he realised he had never shown the quiet boy anything?
Tarun felt uncomfortable and guilty, seeing that his own low expectation had kept the boy from growing.
What small step did Tarun take to correct it?
He handed the quiet boy a small motor and offered to start teaching him, giving him the challenge and attention Minakshi had had.
What might it have been like for the quiet boy to sort screws for three months?
He may have felt overlooked and discouraged, watching someone else learn while he stayed stuck.

Comparing the humped herds of whales with the humped herds of buffalo, which, not forty years ago, overspread by tens of thousands the prairies of Illinois and Missouri, and shook their iron manes and scowled with their thunder-clotted brows upon the sites of populous river-capitals, where now the polite broker sells you land at a dollar an inch; in such a comparison an irresistible argument would seem furnished, to show that the hunted whale cannot now escape speedy extinction.

What argument does the writer draw from comparing whale herds with buffalo herds?

Not forty years ago, humped herds of buffalo overspread the prairies in tens of thousands, where land is now sold by a broker. The writer says that comparing them with whale herds seems to show that the hunted whale cannot now escape speedy extinction.

Urmila's scooter was stolen, so she went to the police station with the registration papers and a photo of the bike, spoke respectfully and asked for a stamped paper showing what she had reported, which the constable handed over. The next month a traffic officer fined her for something she had not done, and she felt furious and helpless. She wanted to shout, but she noted the receipt number and the time and filed a complaint on the official portal with help from her aunt Usha. Around then her friend Danish phoned late. "If they ask, say I was with you on Friday night." Urmila's stomach turned. "I won't lie to the police. But I'll come with you to see a lawyer and help you sort it out properly." Danish grumbled but went. Later, an officer at a checkpoint said she could pay him some cash and forget the paperwork, and pushed a paper toward her to sign. She said politely, "I haven't read this. I'd like my aunt to be here," and wrote down his name and badge number. Her roommate Hafsa sat with her that night and helped her report it.

What did Urmila bring to the police station?
She brought the registration papers and a photo of the bike.
How did Urmila's report of the theft differ from what happened at the checkpoint?

At the station she brought papers, stayed respectful and got a stamped paper showing her report; at the checkpoint the officer asked for cash and pushed a paper to sign, so she refused to sign what she had not read, asked for her aunt and noted his name and badge number.
What was Urmila feeling after the unfair fine?
She felt furious and helpless, but she chose to record the details instead of shouting.
What did Urmila offer Danish instead of lying for him?
She offered to go with him to see a lawyer, showing loyalty without giving a false statement.

Monday: Tarun, new from Bihar, ate his lunch alone on the steps again. Sachin picked up his tiffin and sat beside him. "Is that litti? My Nani makes it." Tarun's face opened like a window.

Wednesday: Near the cycle stand, two Class 8 boys grabbed Tarun's cap and held it high. "Say please in Bhojpuri!" Sachin stepped in. "Give it back." One shoved him hard. Sachin didn't shove back. He ran straight to the PT teacher, Mr Sequeira, who came at once, got the cap back and took both boys to the office.

Friday: In assembly, Mr Sequeira said, "Standing by a friend is brave. Getting an adult when it turns rough is braver still." Sachin and Tarun, sharing a bench, tried not to grin.

What was Tarun eating on Monday?
Litti.
What was Tarun feeling when Sachin sat beside him on Monday?
Relieved and happy to have company after eating alone, and less lonely as a newcomer.
Why was running to Mr Sequeira the right move on Wednesday?
Once the older boys shoved him, it was unsafe to handle alone; fetching the PT teacher protected both boys and got the cap back.
How did Mr Sequeira view Sachin's actions?
He saw both standing by a friend and fetching an adult as brave, and praised fetching an adult as braver still.
Auto mein bolna hai "Mujhe yahin utaar dijiye." English?
Say: "Please drop me here."

Daycare note, Toddler Room. Written by Rajni, caregiver.
Rehana (19 months) had a lovely moment today. A pigeon landed on the window ledge during snack time. I said, "Look, Rehana!" and turned my head towards it. She followed my eyes, spotted the bird and gasped. Then she pointed at it herself and looked back at me, checking that I had seen it too. We named it together: "Bird!" 🐦
Next step: I'll keep pointing out things around the room and wait for her to share her own finds.

What landed on the window ledge during snack time?
A pigeon landed on the window ledge.
Why did Rehana look back at Rajni after pointing at the bird?
She seemed to want to make sure Rajni was sharing the same exciting sight, enjoying it together.
How could Rajni build on this at daycare?
Rajni can keep pointing out interesting things and waiting for Rehana to point and share her own discoveries.
What might it be like for Rajni when Rehana checks back with Rajni?
It likely feels rewarding and warm, because the toddler is inviting Rajni into a shared moment.

Gimmerton chapel bells were still ringing; and the full, mellow flow of the beck in the valley came soothingly on the ear. It was a sweet substitute for the yet absent murmur of the summer foliage, which drowned that music about the Grange when the trees were in leaf. At Wuthering Heights it always sounded on quiet days following a great thaw or a season of steady rain. And of Wuthering Heights Catherine was thinking as she listened: that is, if she thought or listened at all; but she had the vague, distant look I mentioned before, which expressed no recognition of material things either by ear or eye.

In two sentences, what is the main idea of this text?

Chapel bells ring and the stream in the valley sounds soothing, a gentle replacement for summer leaves rustling near the Grange. Catherine seems to be thinking of Wuthering Heights, but her look is vague and distant.

The school year had been Damini's best: new friends, first place in the science exhibition, a part in the play. Then came the last board paper, maths, in a hall with no fan on the hottest day of March. She blanked on two questions and walked out with a thumping head.
Two months later, on results day, she stood in a long queue in the heat outside the school office with Hrithik.
"This year was a disaster," she muttered.
"Disaster?" Hrithik said. "You won the exhibition. You were the best thing in the play."
"The last paper, though."
"Is one day. The year was two hundred days."
The queue shuffled forward. Damini tried to picture the exhibition, the applause, the play. They felt faded, far away. The hot hall felt like yesterday.
At the window she took her result slip. Maths: fine. Everything else: good. She laughed, a little shakily. "So it was a good year with a bad ending."

Which subject was the last board paper?
The last board paper was maths.
Why did Damini call the year a disaster?
Damini still felt shaken by the hot hall and the blank questions, and that final day coloured the memory of the whole year.
What helped Damini see the year differently?
Hrithik's reminders of the exhibition and the play, and the result slip showing the maths paper had turned out fine.
How does Hrithik see Damini's year?
Hrithik sees a great year with one bad day, and reminds her it was two hundred days long.

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Appa,
I'm writing this because when I try to say it out loud, I start crying and you think I'm being dramatic.
Every time I come back from basketball, you say, 'Again in the sun? You're getting so dark, kanna. Look at Keerthana, how fair she stayed.' I know you say it because you love me and worry about how people will see me. But it stings every single time. Last week I skipped practice just so you wouldn't say it.
Could you say 'Did you win?' instead? Or 'Drink water, you look tired'? Those I'd love to hear.
And if you're worried about my health, let's do something together. Come and watch a match, or we could start cycling on Sunday mornings like we used to.
I love basketball, Appa. I don't want to give it up for a colour.
Love,
your daughter, Yamini

What does Appa usually say when Yamini comes back from basketball?
He says, 'Again in the sun? You're getting so dark, kanna,' and compares her to Keerthana.
Why did Yamini skip practice last week?
She felt so stung and ashamed by the comments on her skin that she avoided practice to escape them.
What kinder words does Yamini ask for, and why might they work?
'Did you win?' or 'Drink water', which show care for her and her health without judging her colour 🙂
How might Appa see his own comments?
He likely sees them as loving protection from what others might say, not realising how much they hurt her.

When Dadi's memory started slipping two winters ago, I moved back from Bengaluru to our old house in Nagpur. I'm Abhinav. People said I was throwing away my career. Maybe a little.
Mornings are Dadi's. I read her the newspaper even if she forgets the headlines by lunch. She still calls me "beta" and tells me which neem branch her mother planted.
Afternoons I work remotely. Evenings, my cousin Avni and I run the colony's composting pits. It started with our own kitchen waste; now forty families bring theirs. Avni handles the rota; I teach the teenagers how to turn the pile and test it with their hands.
Last month, Rohit from the fourth floor, fifteen and always on his phone, asked if he could lead the pits during our trip. He did. Dadi watched from the balcony, clapping for no clear reason.
Some days I'm exhausted. Most days it feels like the house is holding all of us.

How many families bring their kitchen waste to the composting pits now?
Now forty families bring theirs.
What does Abhinav mean by saying "the house is holding all of us"?
Abhinav feels tired but also grateful and connected, because caring for Dadi, the pits and the teenagers gives life a shared, steady purpose.
How could Abhinav keep from burning out while caring for so many?
Abhinav could share more tasks, as Avni and Rohit already do, and ask other relatives or a local elder-care service to help with Dadi on some days.
How might Avni see Abhinav's choice to move back?
Avni probably sees it as a gift to the family and the colony, and as a partner in running the pits, rather than a lost career.
Check my email line: I have sent the report yesterday to my manager.

I sent the report to my manager yesterday.
Why: Use the past simple with a finished time like "yesterday". The present perfect does not go with it.

Monday, the first monsoon rain: Sharmila scolded Rajni for splashing the balcony bucket. Rajni scowled, then threw her rubber duck at little Pinky's head.

Wednesday, still raining: told off for tearing a book, Rajni grabbed Pinky's bottle and hurled it. Sharmila held Rajni's hands. "You're angry with me. Hit the pillow."

Saturday, rain drumming on the window: another "no". Rajni's fists clenched. She looked at Pinky, then thumped the pillow, hard.

What did Rajni throw at Pinky on Monday?
Rajni threw her rubber duck at little Pinky's head.
What does Rajni's scowl before throwing the duck suggest?
Rajni was angry at being scolded by Sharmila, and that anger went to Pinky, the smaller and safer target.
Which change helped by Saturday, and why?
Sharmila named Rajni's anger and offered the pillow, so by Saturday the anger had a safe place to go instead of Pinky.
How might Pinky be affected over these days?
Pinky gets hit by a duck and a bottle for no reason Pinky can understand, which may leave Pinky startled and wary of Rajni.

In the clinic waiting room, Pooja was glued to the cartoon on her mother's phone. When the nurse called another name, Neelam said, "Pooja, one more song, then phone off. Then we play I-spy." Pooja nodded without looking up. The song ended. Neelam took the phone. Pooja's face crumpled and she kicked the chair. "Give it! I want it!" Neelam kept her voice soft. "It's hard to stop. I spy with my little eye... something red." Pooja sniffed. She looked around. "The fire extinguisher?" "Yes!" Pooja wiped her nose. "My turn."

What was the first thing Neelam spied?
Something red, which Pooja guessed was the fire extinguisher.
How was Pooja feeling when she kicked the chair?
She felt upset and angry, as if losing the cartoon meant losing something she loved.
Which parts of Neelam's approach helped Pooja switch off?
She gave a clear warning, stayed calm and soft, and moved straight to a fun next thing, I-spy.
What would change if Neelam gave the phone back when Pooja kicked?
Pooja would learn that getting upset brings the screen back, making every switch-off harder.

In the farmhouse kitchen, the rotis were stacked high and the dal was steaming. Anand's Amma, Rekha, sat down on the mat. Before anyone ate, the family folded their hands. Their family didn't pray to anyone special, but they always said thank you. "Thank you to the farmers," said Amma. "Thank you to the rain," said Dadi. Anand squeezed his eyes shut. "Thank you to the cow for the ghee." Everyone smiled. Anand opened his eyes and felt still and warm inside, like the rotis. Then he tore off a piece and dipped it in the dal.

Whom did Dadi thank?
Dadi said thank you to the rain.
How did Anand feel after saying his thank-you?
He felt calm and grateful, still and warm inside, like the rotis.
What does this family's habit teach Anand?
It teaches him to notice and thank the people and things that bring his food, even without praying to anyone special.
How might Rekha feel when Anand thanks the cow?
She probably feels amused and proud that he has made the gratitude his own.

Gurleen, you've just been made lead, so let me tell you what I'd do differently if I started again. For my first three months I thought leading meant being the smartest person in the room. My team went quiet. Nobody told me when things went wrong.
What changed it was small. I started ending every one-to-one with, "What can I get out of your way?" Once it was a laptop that kept crashing. Once it was a client who kept calling my junior at midnight. I dealt with those things. That was the job.
I also stopped saying "I" in reports. It's "Neeraj built this, Shabnam tested that." And I still sit at our old table at lunch, where I sat as a junior, because those people tell me the truth.
A title gets people to listen for a week. What I do for them gets them to listen for years. I'm Pooja, and that's the one leadership lesson I really trust.

What question does Pooja end every one-to-one with?
What can I get out of your way?
How did Pooja feel when the team went quiet in the early months?
Pooja felt isolated and uneasy, since nobody said when things went wrong.
What would you advise Gurleen based on Pooja's story?
Start by asking what's in people's way, credit them by name, and keep sitting with former peers who will tell the truth.
How might Neeraj and Shabnam feel seeing their names in the reports?
They likely feel valued and seen, which makes them more willing to give their best.

What did the teacher write on the blackboard this morning?
One more thing: fix the mistake: Its raining so take an umbrella.
Oh, and what does "bread and butter" mean in "my bread and butter"?
Lastly, please define "apportioned".

1. I don't know, because I wasn't there and I can't see your classroom. Ask a classmate or check your notes.
2. Corrected: It's raining, so take an umbrella. Why: "it's" is the short form of "it is", and a comma comes before "so" when it joins two clauses.
3. It means the main work or activity that gives a person their income. For example: teaching is her bread and butter.
4. "Apportioned" is the past form of the verb "apportion", which means to share something out in parts.

At the school counselling room, Sharmila, eleven, sat twisting her dupatta. Three weeks ago, she and Farida had a huge fight at lunch, and Sharmila had pushed Farida's tiffin off the table. Since then, they hadn't spoken, and Sharmila hadn't told Ammi. Every day, Ammi asked, "How's Farida?" and Sharmila said, "Fine." Today the class teacher had called Ammi in, because Farida's mother had complained. Sharmila's face was burning. She hadn't slept properly in days. When Ammi walked in, Sharmila couldn't look at her. But Ammi sat down, put a hand on her back and said, "Beta, I'm not angry. I just wish you'd told me three weeks ago. What happened?" Sharmila's words came tumbling out. By the end, she was crying. "I didn't know how to start." Ammi hugged her. "Next time, start with 'Ammi, something happened.'"

What did Sharmila do to Farida's tiffin?
She pushed it off the table.
How did Sharmila feel before Ammi walked in?
She felt ashamed and anxious, her face burning, not having slept properly in days.
What did Ammi do that made it easier to talk?
She stayed calm, said she wasn't angry, gently asked what happened, and offered a simple way to start next time.
How might Farida have felt during the three weeks?
She was probably hurt and upset, enough that her mother complained to the school.

In the nurses' break room at the hospital in Chennai, Lalremsiami unpacked a steel box of bai, the Mizo vegetable stew her mother had taught her over the phone. It was Chapchar Kut back home in Aizawl; her family would be dancing in the square tonight. She had a video call booked for nine, after her shift. Shalini, the senior nurse, sniffed the air. "What is that? It smells like my grandmother's keerai." "Try it," Lalremsiami said, handing her a spoon. By the end of the break four nurses were eating from the box, and Shalini was explaining how her family makes keerai. Lalremsiami laughed. She still missed Aizawl, a quiet ache. But she had started learning Tamil, and next January Shalini was taking her home for Pongal.

What time was Lalremsiami's video call booked for?
For nine, after her shift.
How does Lalremsiami feel about Aizawl while sharing the stew?
Lalremsiami still misses Aizawl with a quiet ache, but the warmth of sharing the stew keeps her in the present.
Which of Lalremsiami's choices helps most, and why?
Sharing the festival food with colleagues turns homesickness into connection, while the booked call keeps family close.
What might the shared break mean to Shalini?
Shalini is reminded of her grandmother's cooking and gets to share her own family's recipes, which builds a real friendship.

The Saturday music class at the community centre had one rule: Sir's word was final. Tanvir, ten, was row leader, which meant he stood at the end and passed out song sheets. Before the concert practice, Sir called him over. "Tell Damini to sit at the back and only listen today. She's off-key. Tell her clearly." Tanvir's hands went cold. Damini had practised the whole week; he had heard her humming at the gate. But Sir had taught music for thirty years. He must know. Tanvir walked over. "Sir says you sit at the back. You're off-key." Damini's mouth opened, then closed. She took her sheet and sat on the last bench, not singing. All through practice Tanvir kept thinking, Sir said it. Not me. His own voice sounded thin.

What was Tanvir's job as row leader?
He stood at the end and passed out song sheets.
How did Tanvir feel when Sir gave him the order, and how did he calm himself?
He felt uneasy, his hands going cold, but told himself Sir had taught music for thirty years and must know best.
What could Tanvir have done instead of passing the message on?
He could have told Sir that Damini had practised all week and asked Sir to speak to her himself, or kindly, instead of saying it harshly for him.
How might Damini see Tanvir after he delivered the message?
Damini may feel hurt and embarrassed, and see Tanvir as the one who shamed her, even though the words came from Sir.

metadata.subtype: Following a grown-up's order to hurt [Actor]

messages.content:
What problem does the speaker raise about getting into the house?

"Ah, my child, that I do; and indeed there is no wish of me to add to your anguish. But just think, what can we do, until all the world be at movement. Then will come our time. I have thought and thought, and it seems to me that the simplest way is the best of all. Now we wish to get into the house, but we have no key; is it not so?" I nodded.
They want to get into the house but have no key. The speaker believes the simplest way is best and checks that the other person agrees the missing key is the problem, and a nod answers.
Write one sentence, in question form only, inviting a friend to a film on Saturday.
Would you like to come and watch a film with me on Saturday evening?

Wednesday
Sonali's phone got snatched at the bus stop yesterday. Two guys on a bike. Everyone was being nice to her today, but honestly, what did she expect? She always has it out, scrolling, not looking around. I keep mine in my bag. That's why it won't happen to me.
I said that at lunch, and Sonali just got up and left. Mrs Pinto, who was on lunch duty, called me over. She said Sonali had been holding her phone to check the bus timing, and that the same bike had snatched from an old man and a lady with a bag that week. "Were they showing off too?" I didn't have an answer.
I think I said it because I'm afraid of it being random.
I'm going to say sorry tomorrow.
Suraj

Why was Sonali holding her phone, according to Mrs Pinto?
To check the bus timing.
Why does Suraj think the blame was said at all?
Suraj feels afraid of it being random, so believing Sonali caused it made a snatch seem less likely to happen to Suraj.
What does Suraj plan, and why is it right?
Saying sorry to Sonali tomorrow, because blaming her added hurt to being robbed.
How did Sonali react to Suraj's comment?
Sonali got up and left, probably hurt and upset to be blamed after being robbed.

Supervisor's note, internship programme, week 6. Hrithik

Tejas had a brilliant Monday: the client loved the prototype and the whole team cheered. By Tuesday evening Tejas had volunteered for the weekend hackathon, offered to redo the onboarding slides, agreed to mentor two first-years, and planned to cycle to the office on the flooded route "because it'll be fine".
I asked how the college assignments due Friday fit in. A long pause. "Oh. I forgot those."
Nothing is wrong with enthusiasm, and the good mood was earned. But the yeses came faster than the checking.
What I did next: sat with Tejas and listed every commitment with its hours. Tejas dropped the slides and the hackathon, kept one mentee, and took the bus. We agreed on a rule: sleep on any new yes.

How many first-years did Tejas agree to mentor?
Two first-years.
Why did the flooded cycle route seem fine to Tejas?
After the client loved the prototype, Tejas felt on top of the world, and that glow made risks look small and every yes feel easy.
What rule did they agree on, and why does it help?
Sleep on any new yes; a night's pause lets the checking catch up with the good mood.
How does Hrithik view Tejas's burst of yeses?
Hrithik sees the enthusiasm as earned and welcome, but worries the commitments outran the checking, especially with assignments due Friday.
Is it "accross" or "across"? How can I get along with a classmate I do not like? What is wrong with this: Raju and Mohan is best friends.

1. It is "across", with one "c" and one "r".
2. Be polite, find one thing you both enjoy and keep a little distance if you need it. You do not have to be best friends.
3. Raju and Mohan are best friends. Why: Two names joined by "and" make a plural subject, so use "are".

I'm Preeti, Devika's older cousin, and I live in the same building. Last term, whenever I came up, Devika was alone in her room with the tablet and earphones, hardly looking up while her mother called her name. Then one day Devika told me, "I'm only going to play when you and Rinku are here." I thought she was joking. But now, when Rinku and I come up on Sunday afternoons, she pulls out the tablet and we play the island game together, all three crowded on the bed, arguing about which bridge to build. When we leave, she puts the tablet back on the shelf. On weekdays I see her reading on the balcony instead. I don't know what made her decide, but she seems happier.

When do Preeti and Rinku come up?
On Sunday afternoons.
Why might Devika have decided to play only with her cousins?
Playing alone may have felt lonely and hard to stop, while playing together is more fun and ends naturally.
What else could Devika do if her cousins stop visiting for a while?
Agree a short weekend time with her mother, so the game stays limited without them.
How does Preeti see the change?
Preeti thinks Devika seems happier, though Preeti isn't sure what made Devika decide.

Parul, six, held up a felt lion. "Lion is not going to the party."
"Why not?" said her father Harish, speaking to the lion.
"Because they'll laugh at his roar."
"That sounds hard for Lion. What does Lion want?"
"To roar loud and nobody laughs."
"Maybe Lion can practise with a friend." Parul made the lion nod. "Lion says okay. Papa, can you be the friend?"
"I'd love to."

What is Lion not going to?
The party.
What might Parul be feeling as she tells Lion's worry?
Perhaps worry about being laughed at herself, though we cannot be sure it is about her.
How did Harish respond to the story?
He spoke to the lion, asked what Lion wants and offered to practise, without saying the story was about Parul.
How might Harish feel about being asked to be the friend?
Warm and glad she is letting him in, and careful not to push.

Under the cherry blossoms in a Kyoto park, the hanami picnic was going well until a man on the next mat, red-faced from sake, muttered that foreigners should go home, looking straight at Valentina. She had already decided to ignore him. Then Hiroshi was on his feet. He told the man off in a loud voice for two full minutes, turned to the other mats and announced that he, personally, had always fought against this kind of thing, and that Valentina was "very upset". She wasn't, not until then. Everyone was looking at her. "Thank you," she said later, and meant it. But on the train home she felt small, as if she had become a story about Hiroshi's courage. What she had wanted was simple: someone to ask, quietly, "Want to move mats?"

Where was the hanami picnic?
Under the cherry blossoms in a Kyoto park.
How did Valentina feel on the train home?
She felt grateful to Hiroshi but also small, as if the moment had turned into a story about his courage.
What could Hiroshi try next time?
He could quietly ask Valentina what she wants, like whether to move mats, and follow her lead instead of speaking for her.
How might Hiroshi see his own actions?
Hiroshi probably believes he was brave and supportive, without noticing that he made a scene and spoke for Valentina.

Every evening, the children of Bhadrajun sat on the temple steps to read their Hindi lessons aloud while the goats were brought home. Hansa always finished last. Her finger moved slowly under each word, and when her younger cousin Darshan read the same page in half the time, she shut her book with a slap. 'I'm a buddhu. Buddhus shouldn't read,' she said, and went to help with the goats instead. The next evening she didn't bring her book at all. Darshan came and sat by her anyway. 'You read the long word yesterday. Pradhanmantri. I can't even say it,' he said. Hansa shrugged. 'That was luck.' But she watched his finger on the page for a long time, her lips moving.

Where did the children of Bhadrajun read their lessons?
They read their Hindi lessons aloud on the temple steps.
Why did Hansa call herself a buddhu and go to the goats?
She felt ashamed and frustrated at always finishing last, and the label made stopping feel easier than facing slow reading again.
What could an adult do to help Hansa see reading as a skill?
They could have her practise a few words each day and point out progress, like reading 'Pradhanmantri', so the label gives way to a skill that grows.
How does Darshan see Hansa's reading?
Darshan admires that she read a long word he couldn't say, and sits with her to show she isn't a buddhu.

Every weekday at 7:40, Bao takes the same tram to the university in Melbourne, orders the same chicken rice from the same stall and sits at the same library desk. His flatmate Fatima teases him: "You've eaten that four hundred times." When the study group moved its meeting three times in one week, Bao felt his chest tighten each time the chat buzzed. On the fourth change he messaged, "Can we fix Thursdays at five and keep it?" The others agreed, a little relieved. By exam week, Bao's notes, rewritten carefully every Sunday, were the ones everyone borrowed. Fatima photocopied them too. "Fine," she said. "Your boring rice has a point."

What does Bao order from the same stall?
He orders the same chicken rice from the same stall.
What was Bao feeling each time the chat buzzed with a new change?
He felt uneasy; his chest tightened because the shifting plans kept breaking his steady routine.
What choice did Bao make on the fourth change, and how did it go?
He asked the group to fix Thursdays at five, and the others agreed, a little relieved themselves.
How does Fatima's view of Bao's routine change by exam week?
She starts by teasing him, but after photocopying his careful notes she admits his steady habits have real value.

Rehana, you asked how to read people at work. Let old Jomon tell you about Thomas. Back then I was twenty-four, in a shipping office in Kochi, and Thomas and I both wanted the supervisor's chair. Mr Varghese gave it to me.

For a month Thomas praised me everywhere. "Jomon is a genius." "Best decision the company ever made." He said it at tea, at lunch, to the peon, even to my own mother at church. Too much, too often.

Some friends said, "Watch him, he's planning something." I wasn't sure. It looked more like a man carrying a heavy box and smiling so no one would see the weight. So I asked him to run the Tuesday dock meetings with me. He didn't say much. But he came, and after a few weeks the praising stopped, and we just worked.

Which post did Thomas and Jomon both want?
They both wanted the supervisor's chair.
What was young Jomon feeling about Thomas's constant praise?
Young Jomon felt unsure and a bit uneasy; the praise was too much, but it seemed more like hidden disappointment than a plot.
What choice inside the story turned things around?
Jomon invited Thomas to run the Tuesday dock meetings together, which gave Thomas a real role and let the praising fade.
How might Thomas have been feeling during that month?
Thomas was likely disappointed and embarrassed at losing the chair, and heavy praise helped him hide it.

Class note, Tuesday. Written by Sangeeta, KG teacher. Today I held up Preeti's leaf print and told the whole class it was the neatest one. Preeti clapped both hands over her face and giggled, peeking through her fingers, then slid behind her friend. Later she spilled the green paint and did the same thing: face hidden, giggle high and shaky. I think both moments were about being looked at. I didn't mention the spill aloud. I knelt beside her, handed her a cloth and whispered, “Spills happen.” Tomorrow I'll tell her about good work quietly at her table.

What did Preeti do when her leaf print was held up?
Preeti clapped both hands over her face and giggled, peeking through her fingers.
Why might Preeti have hidden her face both times?
She most likely felt embarrassed at everyone looking at her, whether for praise or for the spill; the first giggle could also carry a little pleasure mixed with shyness.
What change does Sangeeta plan, and why might it help?
She plans to praise Preeti quietly at her table, which lets Preeti enjoy the praise without the whole class watching.
What would change if Sangeeta had pointed out the spill to the class?
Preeti would likely have felt more exposed and ashamed, and she might hide or avoid painting next time.

The new flat in Chandigarh still smelled of paint, and two-year-old Gurleen stood in the doorway of the strange bedroom, lip trembling. Charu didn't argue or promise sweets. She did exactly what they did at home: a warm bath with the yellow duck, the ceiling light off and the small lamp on, the Punjabi lullaby Nani used to sing, and the same cuddle, Gurleen's head tucked under her chin. Halfway through the second verse the trembling stopped. Gurleen sighed, patted Charu's cheek twice, and slept in the new room.

What toy was in Gurleen's bath?
The yellow duck.
What does Gurleen's trembling lip in the doorway suggest?
She feels scared and unsure in the strange new bedroom.
Why did Charu repeat the home routine instead of promising sweets?
The familiar bath, lamp, lullaby and cuddle told Gurleen's body that sleep was safe, even in a new place.
How might Charu feel as Gurleen pats her cheek and falls asleep?
She is probably relieved and tender, glad the first night in the new flat ended calmly.

Monday night

Everyone in the office is running the city half marathon in December. There's a group chat, matching T-shirts, 6 a.m. practice runs. Bhavna asked me again today if I'm in.

My first instinct was yes, just because everyone is. Then I stopped and asked myself properly: why do I want this? And if nobody at work ever knew, would I still do it?

I thought about it on the bus.

The honest answer surprised me. Yes. I've wanted to try a long run since college. I was just scared I'd be the slowest. The crowd isn't the reason. It's the push.

So I told Bhavna yes, for my own reasons. I'll run at my pace, not theirs. If I'm last, fine.

It feels different to join when you've decided, instead of just being carried along.

Shalini

When is the city half marathon?
In December.
How did Shalini feel after answering the questions honestly?
Shalini felt surprised and more settled, finding a real wish to run beneath the fear of being slowest.
Why is Shalini's decision a good example of thinking for yourself?
Shalini asked why the race was wanted and what the choice would be if nobody knew, then joined deliberately for real reasons, not just because everyone was.
How might Bhavna feel hearing Shalini's yes?
Bhavna would likely be happy and encouraging, glad Shalini is joining.

The staffroom was full of noise on Monday. The heads of three departments were arguing about the exam timetable, and Santosh, who chaired the meeting, kept glancing at the corner. Sangeeta, the part-time art teacher, had not said a word all term.
When the talking dipped, Santosh said, “Sangeeta, you mentioned in the corridor that students get tired in the third exam of the day. Would you tell us?”
Sangeeta looked at her hands. “Please spread the exams across mornings. The afternoon papers show the worst work.”
“That’s a sound idea,” Santosh said. “We’ll try it and put her name on it when I tell the principal.”
Sangeeta smiled, surprised.

Who chaired the staffroom meeting?
Santosh chaired the staffroom meeting.
What might Sangeeta have been feeling as she looked at her hands?
Sangeeta looked at her hands and had said nothing all term. It suggests shyness or feeling she was not expected to speak.
What did Santosh do to make Sangeeta's idea count?
Santosh invited Sangeeta to speak, praised the idea and promised to put her name on it when telling the principal. That gave her real airtime and credit.
How might the heads of the three departments have felt when Santosh turned to the art teacher?
They may have been impatient at the interruption, or curious about a fresh view. The passage shows only that the talking dipped.

Monday: Chinmay skipped his afternoon nap. By five he was rubbing his eyes, whining and hanging off his father's leg. At the vegetable stall he threw himself on the floor and kicked. "Stop being naughty," Saurabh snapped.

Wednesday: the same eye-rubbing, the same clinging. Saurabh glanced at the clock. No nap again. He drew the curtains and lay down beside his son. Chinmay was asleep within minutes.

Saturday: nap first, market after. Chinmay pointed at every tomato and laughed.

Where did Chinmay throw himself on the floor?
At the vegetable stall.
What was Chinmay feeling when he rubbed his eyes and clung to his father's leg?
Most likely overtired and cranky, since he had skipped his nap and fell asleep quickly once the room was dark. Another possible reading is that he was bored or hungry at the stall.
What went wrong on Monday, and what fixed it later?
Saurabh treated the meltdown as naughtiness, but the real problem was a missed nap. Putting sleep first on Saturday meant a happy trip to the market.
How does Saurabh's view of the meltdowns change between Monday and Wednesday?
On Monday he sees naughtiness and snaps, but by Wednesday he connects the clinging to the missed nap and responds with rest instead of scolding.

"Ugh," Sabina groaned, dropping into her chair after carrying the last carton of files.
Jeevan grinned. "Dramatic. It was one box."
"Mm." She pressed a hand to her lower right side. Another groan, lower and quieter.
Jeevan stopped grinning. "Wait. Is that a tired groan or a something-hurts groan?"
"Probably nothing. Pulled a muscle."
"When did it start?"
"This morning. It's been getting worse." Her face was pale and damp.
"Okay. I'm not guessing about this. Can I call the office first-aider and your emergency contact?"
"You're overreacting."
"Maybe. I'd rather overreact. You don't look okay, and you said it's getting worse."
Sabina closed her eyes. "Fine. Call them."
He called the first-aider, who took one look at her and said, "We're getting you to a doctor now."

What had Sabina just carried?
She had carried the last carton of files.
What did Sabina's quieter groan and hand on her side suggest?
They suggested Sabina was in real pain and perhaps frightened, not just tired; she may also have been embarrassed and trying to play it down.
What did Jeevan do once he noticed the signs, and why?
He stopped joking, asked what kind of groan it was and when it started, and called the first-aider because she looked unwell and said it was getting worse.
What would have happened if Jeevan had kept joking?
Sabina might have kept playing it down and stayed at her desk in growing pain, delaying the help she needed.

Ujjwal, you've been made team lead and you've printed a poster that says 'Excellence Every Day'. Sit. Let me tell you about the depot.
At twenty-five I was put in charge of eleven mechanics at the bus depot in Nashik. I had a slogan too. They ignored it. Two left in the first month.
Then old Pawar-ji said, 'Kishore, you don't know a single one of their names.' He was right.
So I learned them. Salim's daughter was in hospital. Gopal cycled in from twelve kilometres away. Ramesh wanted to learn the new diesel engines. I shifted Salim's hours, gave Gopal the late start, sent Ramesh for training. And every morning I told them how many buses went out on time because of them, and how many schoolchildren rode them.
Nobody left that year. When the monsoon broke three buses at once, they stayed late.
Take the poster down, Ujjwal. Learn their names.

How many mechanics was young Kishore put in charge of?
Eleven, at the bus depot in Nashik.
Why do you think Pawar-ji's words made young Kishore change course?
Kishore realised the slogan had replaced actually knowing the people; 'not a single name' stung because two resignations had already proved it true.
Which of Kishore's choices made the difference, and why?
Learning each mechanic's name and situation, fitting hours and training to them, and sharing how their work got schoolchildren to school; care and purpose made them stay and try harder.
How might a mechanic like Gopal have felt after the change?
Gopal, cycling twelve kilometres, would likely feel noticed and respected with the late start, and more willing to stay late when the depot needed extra hands.

You asked about my nikah. I'm Afreen, and honestly I remember it in two layers.

Layer one: relatives. My Phuppo checking the embroidery on my gharara and calling it simple. Two aunties arguing about whether the biryani had enough saffron. Someone asking my mother, loudly, how much the hall cost. My feet hurt, my face hurt from smiling, and at one point I hid in the washroom for ten minutes just to breathe.

Layer two: the moment the qazi sahab asked me, "Qubool hai?" and I looked at Abbu's face. He was crying and trying not to. I said yes three times, and it felt as if the ground under me had shifted.

My friend Trisha told me afterwards, "You looked like you were somewhere else." I was. I was in layer two.

Nobody will remember the saffron. I'll remember that.

How long did Afreen hide in the washroom?
Afreen hid in the washroom for ten minutes just to breathe.
What was Afreen feeling during the relatives' comments?
Afreen felt pressured and exhausted, feet and face aching from smiling, needing to hide just to breathe.
What helped Afreen hold on to the meaning of the day?
Focusing on the moment of saying yes and on Abbu's face, the real marker of a new stage, instead of the relatives' assessments.
What might the moment have been like for Afreen's Abbu?
Abbu was deeply moved, crying and trying not to, as his daughter said yes.
Why does fog gather near a river on a cold morning?
The air above the water cools. Because cool air cannot hold as much water vapour, the extra vapour turns into tiny floating droplets that we see as fog.

Consider, now, how it must be in the case of four boats all engaging one unusually strong, active, and knowing whale; when owing to these qualities in him, as well as to the thousand concurring accidents of such an audacious enterprise, eight or ten loose second irons may be simultaneously dangling about him. All these particulars are faithfully narrated here, as they will not fail to elucidate several most important, however intricate passages, in scenes hereafter to be painted.

Question: Why may eight or ten loose second irons dangle about one whale?

When four boats attack a strong, active whale, each boat carries several harpoons to bend on to the line if the first is darted without recovery. The many accidents of the hunt leave loose irons hanging about him.

Simran has a lot of sports equipment in her room.
Why: "Equipment" is uncountable, so it never takes -s. To count it, say "pieces of equipment".

"That scaffold on the third floor is tied with wire, not clamps," Asif said quietly in the site office. "I saw it this morning."
Nandini looked up from the drawings. "Did you tell the site engineer?"
"It's not my section. Not my contractor. If I say something and I'm wrong, I look stupid. If I say nothing and it falls, well, I didn't build it."
"Asif. If you had tied it with wire yourself, would you walk away?"
He paused. "No. I'd fix it."
"Then walking away is also a choice. The workers climb it either way."
"What if I'm wrong?"
"Then the engineer tells us, and we feel stupid for ten minutes." She was already standing. "Come. We'll both go."
Twenty minutes later the site engineer had stopped work on the third floor, and a crew was bringing up proper clamps.

What was the scaffold tied with?
The scaffold on the third floor was tied with wire, not clamps.
Why did Nandini stand up so quickly?
Nandini felt concerned for the workers who climb it, and was sure that staying silent would be a choice with real consequences.
What question did Nandini ask, and why was it effective?
'If you had tied it with wire yourself, would you walk away?', which showed Asif that not acting also carried responsibility.
How does Asif feel about speaking up?
Asif is nervous about looking stupid if wrong, but agrees once Nandini offers to go with him.

Two weeks later, Kamal hid in the cupboard but shouted, 'I'm in the cupboard!'
A month on, he hid a marble in one fist, held out both hands to Baljeet and kept his face very still. 'Which hand?' Baljeet picked wrong. Kamal opened the other fist and burst out laughing.

What did Kamal do in the first week to hide?
He covered his own eyes and said 'I'm hiding!'
Why did Kamal keep his face very still in the marble game?
He wanted Baljeet not to guess, so he tried to hide what he knew behind a calm face.
How could Baljeet support Kamal's game as it grows?
He can take turns being the tricker, and laugh together when either one is fooled, so it stays friendly.
How might the game feel different for Baljeet in the first week compared with a month later?
In the first week it was easy and cute for him, but later he truly had to guess and could be fooled.

It was Onam morning and raining hard. The auto was waiting at the gate, and Sudha Amma still had the sadya leaves to carry.
"Lakshmi, sandals, quick. Let me."
"No! I do it!" Lakshmi sat on the wet step and pushed her foot in. Wrong foot. She took it out and tried again. The auto driver tooted.
Amma breathed in and out. Then she held the umbrella over Lakshmi and waited.
Left sandal. Right sandal. One strap stuck. Lakshmi pulled it with both hands, face scrunched.
Click.
"Done!" She jumped up, splashing a puddle, and grabbed Amma's hand, grinning.

On a rainy Onam morning, the auto waited at the gate while Sudha Amma still had the sadya leaves to carry. Lakshmi insisted on putting on her own sandals, so Amma held the umbrella over her and waited, until a stuck strap finally clicked. "Done!" Lakshmi said, jumping up and grabbing Amma's hand.

Sofia had been in Dublin for three weeks and still hadn't unpacked her last suitcase. That Sunday she sat on her bed, scrolling photos of her family's lunch in Lisbon, feeling the ache in her throat.
There was a knock. Her flatmate Layla stood there with two mugs of tea and a packet of biscuits.
"I heard your door close really softly," Layla said. "That's usually a sad sign. Want company?"
Sofia hadn't said a word to anyone. She laughed and cried at the same time.
Layla sat on the floor, and they looked at photos together. Layla asked about each face.
Later, alone again, Sofia unpacked the last suitcase. For the first time, the room felt like it might become home.

What did Layla bring to Sofia's door?
She brought two mugs of tea and a packet of biscuits.
How did Sofia feel when Layla offered company without being asked?
She felt touched and relieved, laughing and crying at once, because someone noticed her homesickness.
What does Layla's small act show about how to help a homesick friend?
Noticing quiet signs and simply showing up with tea and time can make someone feel they belong.
What might it be like for Layla to sit and hear about Sofia's family?
Layla might enjoy it and feel closer to Sofia, glad her small gesture helped.

Monday. Eshaan, two, threw himself down when the TV went off. Tarun knelt. "You're upset. I'm here." He moved the glass cup away and waited.
Wednesday. Another storm, over shoes. Tarun knelt again, quiet and close. Eshaan kicked, then slowed sooner.

What did Tarun move away on Monday?
He moved the glass cup away.
Why did Eshaan crawl into Tarun's lap on Saturday?
He still felt upset, but he had come to feel safe with Tarun close by, so he looked for comfort sooner.
What in Tarun's approach seems to help each time?
Kneeling close, saying calmly 'You're upset. I'm here', moving dangerous things away and waiting without arguing.

Tarun may feel relieved and encouraged that staying calm and close is helping.

In their Madrid flat, Nkechi, five, was doing a world map puzzle. Africa and Europe were done. She was stuck on the big blue ocean.
Alejandro, the old man from next door who sometimes watched her, pulled up a chair.

A little ship.

She felt proud and excited, sure she had solved it on her own.

Zeynep drew a table on a big sheet in the corridor of her school in Istanbul: Decoration, Music, Food, Invitations. Beside each, one name and a date. Decoration: Aiko, by Thursday. Music: Emre, playlist by Friday morning. Food: Lucas, list to the teacher by Wednesday. Invitations: Zeynep herself, printed by Tuesday. "Not 'the team,'" she said, capping her marker. Aiko was responsible for decoration, by Thursday.
How does Aiko feel about owning the lanterns?
Aiko feels cheerful and willing to take responsibility, joking that failure would be Aiko's fault and success Aiko's glory.

Emre knows exactly what is expected and by when, so a slip is Emre's to fix and no one else is left guessing.

Garden club note, Tejas Sir. Meenal's rose plant had crisp brown leaves after three hot afternoons. She touched a leaf and said, "It's the sun after lunch." She dragged the pot under the neem tree, where the sun comes only in the morning. Then she gathered dry leaves and spread them over the soil. "Like a blanket, so the water stays." Where did Meenal move the rose pot?
She moved it under the neem tree, where the sun comes only in the morning.
What was Meenal thinking when she touched the crisp leaf?
She was worried about the plant and guessed the afternoon sun was the cause.

She could water early in the morning or use a light cloth for shade, so the plant loses less water in the heat.
How does Tejas Sir see Meenal's response?
Tejas Sir watches without stepping in and seems pleased, since Meenal found and fixed the problem herself.

messages.content: Holi is next week. My mom says I can play only if I'm careful.
That sounds fair. Holi is a lot of fun, and a few simple steps keep it safe. Are you playing at home or with friends nearby?
In our building compound with my friends.
Then wear old clothes that cover your arms and legs. Rubbing a little oil on your skin and hair before playing makes the colour easier to wash off later.
Some kids use water balloons.
Water balloons can hurt if thrown hard, especially near the face. Ask friends to throw gently, aim below the shoulders, and throw only at people who are playing.
What about the colours?
Dry, natural colours are gentler than bright chemical ones. Keep colour away from eyes and mouth. If any gets in your eyes, wash them with clean water and tell an adult.

The science-model deadline was tomorrow morning, and a power cut had plunged the flat into darkness. Nazia glued tiny paper leaves by torchlight, her fingers sticky. Bidisha had sent only silly stickers on the group chat all week, while the other two chatted about a cartoon. Nazia's jaw tightened. At first she wanted to keep doing everything in silence and glare at them. Instead she typed on her mother's phone: "I've done the model and both charts. Can you write the labels, and Rehan bring the poster? Please tell me by 8 tonight." Bidisha replied, "Sorry! I'll do labels now." Nazia decided that if it happened again, she would tell the teacher.

What happened to the lights on the night before the deadline?
There was a power cut, so Nazia worked by torchlight.
What was Nazia feeling toward her group, and how do you know?
She was fuming and resentful: her jaw tightened after she had done the model and both charts while the others chatted.
What could Nazia do if the others still do not help?
Tell the teacher calmly what she has done and what is still undone.
How might Bidisha see Nazia's message?
She replied "Sorry! I'll do labels now," so she likely saw it as a clear, fair request and realised she had been slack.

Sunday. After the zoo, Chetan, five, told Bhavna didi, "I saw an elephant, and a monkey ate a banana."
Tuesday. Didi read him a picture book about a lion that roared at a boy. At dinner Chetan told Papa, "At the zoo a lion roared at ME!" There had been no lion; the lion house was closed.
Saturday. Telling Nani on the phone, Chetan said the lion roared, jumped, and winked. He believed every word, eyes shining. Didi smiled and didn't argue, but later showed him the zoo photos: elephant, monkey, banana.

What did Chetan see at the zoo, according to his first telling?
An elephant, and a monkey that ate a banana.
Why did Chetan believe the lion roared at him?
Chetan felt excited and sure, because the lion from the picture book had blended into his zoo memory, so it felt real.
What did didi do that was gentle and helpful?
She didn't argue, but later showed him the zoo photos, letting the pictures remind him what really happened.
How might Nani feel hearing about the winking lion?
Nani would likely feel amused and charmed, enjoying the story.

Week two. Mohit had been in Bengaluru for fourteen days and hadn't spoken to anyone beyond 'one tea'. Even small things felt heavy: the laundry bag sat in the corner for a week, and he missed a morning lecture because he couldn't make himself get up. His mother asked on the phone if he was eating. He said yes.
Week four. In the chemistry lab, Himani, who sat next to him, asked if he wanted to join three of them studying in the library on Thursdays. He almost said no. He said okay.
Week six. Thursdays had become the fixed point of Mohit's week. He did his laundry on Wednesdays so he'd have a clean shirt. He finished the problem sets early so he'd have questions for the group. On Sunday he called his mother and talked for forty minutes, mostly about Himani's terrible jokes.

When did the group study in the library?
They studied in the library on Thursdays.
Why did even small tasks feel heavy to Mohit in week two?
He felt lonely and disconnected in a new city, and without anyone around, his energy and motivation drained.
What helped Mohit's motivation return?
Saying yes to Himani's small study group gave him a fixed, connected point in the week that he wanted to prepare for.
How might Mohit's mother feel on the Sunday call?
She would likely feel relieved and happy hearing him talk for forty minutes about new friends.
My son wants to send this to his uncle. Make it a proper thank-you note: Thanks for the book. I like the pictures and I will read it every night.
Dear Uncle, thank you very much for the lovely book. I like the pictures a lot, and I will read it every night. With love

In the robotics lab after school, the argument started over the presentation slides and soon wasn't about slides at all.
"I'm presenting," Raghav said. "I wrote the code."
"And I built the arm," Nandini said. "Last time you presented, you said 'my robot' six times."
Kiran and Tushar exchanged looks and kept soldering.
"That's not..." Raghav stopped. "Fine. You present, then."
"I don't even want to present," Nandini said, her voice cracking. "I want you to say 'we'."
The lab went quiet except for the fan. Raghav looked at the arm she'd built, the neat wiring, the tiny labels.
"Okay," he said slowly. "We split it. You do the build, I do the code. And I'll say 'we'."
Tushar let out a breath. "Great. Now can someone hold this wire?"

How many times did Raghav say "my robot" last time?
Six times.
What does Nandini's voice cracking reveal?
Nandini felt hurt and unrecognised; the fight was really about wanting her work acknowledged, not about presenting.
What helped settle the fight?
Nandini named the real issue, and Raghav looked at her work and agreed to share the stage and say "we".
How did Tushar experience the argument?
Tushar felt tense and awkward, keeping his head down, and relieved when it ended.
I put the keys on the table, but now I can't find it. What is wrong?

I put the keys on the table, but now I can't find them.
Why: A pronoun must match the noun it stands for. "Keys" is plural, so use "them", not "it".

At the bus stop, a man leaned over the bench and spat near a mother with a small baby. Nandini and her friend Himani were two steps away. Nandini's stomach tightened. She checked: the man looked annoyed, not dangerous, and Himani was right beside her.
"Excuse me," Nandini said in an even voice, "could you please not spit here? There is a baby."
"What's it to you?"
"It's a shared bench. Please."
Himani said nothing, just stood close. The man grumbled, scuffed his shoe and walked to the far end of the stop. The mother mouthed "thank you". Nandini let out a breath. If he had shouted, she had already decided to step back and call the helpline.

Who was standing two steps from the man?
Nandini and her friend Himani were two steps away.
What was Nandini feeling before she spoke?
Nandini felt her stomach tighten, nervous but ready, and she checked that the man looked annoyed and not dangerous.
What choices helped Nandini speak up safely?
She checked the man first, kept her friend beside her, spoke in an even tone and had decided to step back and call the helpline if he shouted.
How might the mother with the baby have felt?
The mother was probably relieved and grateful, since she mouthed 'thank you' after the man walked away.

The science lab after school was the only place with enough table space, so the four of them spread out there, surrounded by pipettes they weren't allowed to touch.

Lalremsiami stood at the whiteboard. "Model of a rainwater harvesting system. Due in four weeks. Let's split it properly this time." She wrote four headings: Research, Materials, Building, Presentation.

"Neelam, you're the best at reading papers. Research, done by the 10th." Neelam nodded.

"Aman, your dad's shop has pipes and tape. Materials by the 14th." 

"Pooja, you're good with your hands. Building, the 14th to the 24th."

"And I'll do the presentation, and help Pooja build."

The lab assistant came in to lock up. Lalremsiami snapped a photo of the whiteboard and sent it to the group chat. "Dates are real. If anyone's slipping, say so early."

Where did the team meet?
They met in the science lab after school.
How might Neelam have felt when Lalremsiami gave Neelam the research?
Neelam was likely pleased and trusted, since the task was matched to being the best at reading papers.
What else could Lalremsiami add to keep the plan on track?
She could set one short weekly check-in, so a slipping date shows up before the building stage is squeezed.
How might Pooja see this way of splitting the work?
Pooja may feel valued and less anxious, because the building task fits her skills and she has help and clear dates.

The college health camp result came on Friday evening, and the lab was closed until Monday. Chandrika read the message three times: "Screening test for a rare blood condition: POSITIVE. Please consult your doctor." Her hands went cold. She searched online. The condition was serious. By midnight she had read about it for four hours and was crying on the hostel floor. Her roommate Lakshmi sat beside her. "What does it say about how many positives turn out to be real?" Chandrika hadn't looked. Lakshmi found the lab's own leaflet. The condition was very rare, and the screening test was meant to catch everyone who might have it, so most people who tested positive turned out to be fine on the second test. Chandrika slept badly, but she slept. On Monday the doctor ordered the confirmation test. It came back clear.

When would the lab open after Chandrika got the result?
Until Monday, since the lab was closed.
What was Chandrika feeling on Friday night?
She felt terrified and overwhelmed, crying on the hostel floor after hours of reading about a serious condition.
What did Lakshmi's question help Chandrika see, and what was the wise next step?
That for a very rare condition most positive screenings turn out fine; the wise step was waiting for the doctor's confirmation test, not the internet.
How might Lakshmi have felt sitting with Chandrika at midnight?
Lakshmi was probably worried for her friend but calm, wanting to help her look at the facts instead of the fear.

Behind the government school in their village near Nashik, the pond was strictly out of bounds. At recess Pankaj kicked the school football there anyway, waded in after it, and lost it in the weeds. Now Masterji was asking the class, 'Who had the ball?' Pankaj stared at Asif, begging with his eyes. Asif could say they'd played by the well. It would be easy. His chest tightened. After class, he pulled Pankaj behind the water tank. 'I won't lie for you. But if you tell Masterji, I'll come and stand with you.' Pankaj kicked the dust. 'I'll have to clean the classroom.' 'Then I'll help clean.' They went together. Masterji listened and gave Pankaj a week of sweeping. Asif swept beside him every day.

What did Pankaj lose in the pond weeds?
The school football.
Why did Asif's chest tighten?
He felt torn between loyalty to Pankaj and not wanting to lie to Masterji.
How did Asif show real loyalty?
He refused to lie but urged Pankaj to own up, went with him, and helped with the sweeping.
What was Pankaj feeling when he stared at Asif?
Scared of being caught and hoping Asif would cover for him.

When I started as a physiotherapy assistant, I panicked whenever I forgot a technique I'd learnt in training. I'd lie awake thinking I wasn't cut out for the job.

My supervisor Mehak noticed. She said, "You're not supposed to remember everything. Your brain throws out what you don't use. Keep notes, and review."

So I made a small notebook for rare exercises. Every Sunday evening I read through a few pages, just before they'd fully slipped. When I need one at work, I check the notebook before the session, no shame.

Last month a patient needed a shoulder exercise I hadn't done in a year. I checked my notes, did it right, and felt calm about it.

I'm Samir. Forgetting isn't failing. It's just the mind making space.

What did Samir make for rare exercises?
A small notebook for rare exercises.
How did Samir feel before Mehak's advice?
Samir felt panicked and anxious, lying awake and doubting being cut out for the job.
What routine could someone new at a job copy from Samir?
Keep a notebook for things rarely used and read through a few pages each week, checking notes without shame when needed.
How might Mehak have felt seeing Samir handle the shoulder exercise?
Mehak probably felt pleased and proud that the advice helped Samir feel calm and competent.

Bidisha, I'll tell you what I did last Sunday, because it took only an hour. I'm Mridula, the sensible girl in our lane according to the aunties, and my cousin, who works in tech and says she reviews hers monthly, told me to look at my account the way a stranger would. So I did. First, tags: three photos where friends had tagged me with our club's full name. I asked them to remove it. Then location: I switched it off in every app, because my posts basically told anyone when I'm at tuition. Then I scrolled far down to a photo from Class Eight: me in uniform at the school gate, the name board behind me. I deleted it. Anyone could work out where I'll be at eight in the morning. Nothing scary has happened. But now nothing about my routine is public.

What did Mridula delete?
Mridula deleted a photo from Class Eight of her in uniform at the school gate with the name board behind her.
Why did Mridula switch off location?
She was worried that her posts told anyone when she was at tuition, so strangers could work out her routine.
What else could Mridula do to protect her account?
She could check who follows her, keep the account private and repeat the review every few months, since old posts pile up.
How might Mridula's friends feel when asked to remove tags?
They may feel surprised at first, but most would understand since Mridula explains it is about privacy, not about them.

Dalia hated buttons, but this morning in the Cairo flat she had a plan. "I'm Captain Speed," she told her sister Nadia. "Superheroes put on the cape first." She draped the school tie round her neck like a cape. "Power shirt!" On went the shirt. "Power skirt! Power socks!" Nadia giggled. Dalia struck a pose by the door, fully dressed, tie still flapping.

What did Dalia use as a cape?
The school tie.
What was Dalia thinking when she called herself Captain Speed?
She felt excited and playful, using the story to make dressing fun.
What else could Dalia add to her game?
A power check at the door, so she makes sure nothing is missing.
How does the superhero game look to Nadia?
Nadia finds it funny and enjoys watching, giggling at each step.

Spot the error: I am agree to join the club.
Is there a mistake here? My father is angry at me for breaking the cup.
I keep seeing "snappish" in my reading. Meaning?

1. It should be: I agree to join the club. Why: "agree" is a verb on its own, so it does not need "am".
2. Correct form: My father is angry with me for breaking the cup. Why: we say "angry with" a person.
3. As an adjective, "snappish" means rather bad-tempered and likely to speak sharply.

The radio was playing in the Jalandhar flat and Gurleen couldn't sit still. She jumped off the sofa and started dancing, arms like wings, spinning, then stamping. Vaibhav, her big brother, laughed. She paused, cheeks pink. But then he picked up two steel spoons and drummed on a plate. "Do the bird again!" Gurleen flapped and twirled, making up new moves with each beat, until they both fell on the carpet laughing.

What did Vaibhav use to drum on a plate?
He picked up two steel spoons to drum on a plate.
What might Gurleen have felt when Vaibhav first laughed?
She may have felt embarrassed, since she paused and her cheeks went pink.
What turned the moment around for Gurleen?
Vaibhav joined in with a drum and asked for her bird move, which showed he enjoyed her dance.
How does Vaibhav's joining in change things?
It shows his laugh was fun, not mockery, so Gurleen feels safe to keep creating.

Mili sat on the floor with a plastic pot, pulling at its lid. It would not open. She grunted, pushed, and then gave a small whimper. She crawled to Mummy and held the pot up high.

"What have you got, Mili?"

"Ah! Ah!"

"Stuck? Let Mummy see." Mummy twisted the lid slowly, so Mili could watch the turn. "Pop!"

Mili patted the pot, then pushed it back into Mummy's hands. "Again!"

"Again? All right, close it."

What did Mili hold up to Mummy?
Mili held up the plastic pot.
What did Mili want when she whimpered?
Mili wanted the lid opened and needed help, since she could not manage it alone.
What could Mummy do to help Mili learn?
Mummy could twist the lid slowly and let Mili put her hands on it too.
How might Mummy feel when Mili brought the pot over?
Mummy might feel pleased that Mili came to ask for help instead of giving up.

“Ow! My knee!” Hafsa, nine, sat on the lane beside her fallen cycle, blood on her knee.
Binita, eleven, ran over. “Don't touch it with dirty hands. Can you move it?”
“Yes. It stings.”
“Stay here.” Binita ran to her house, came back with a bottle of clean water and a clean handkerchief. “This might sting.” She poured the water gently, then pressed the cloth on it.
“It's not stopping!”
“It's slowing. Keep pressing.” Binita took out her phone. “What's your Ammi's number?”
Hafsa told her. Binita called. “Aunty, Hafsa fell off her cycle. She's okay but her knee is cut. We're at the corner.”

What did Binita bring back from her house?
A bottle of clean water and a clean handkerchief.
How was Hafsa feeling after she fell?
She felt hurt and scared, saying it stung and wasn't stopping.
What first-aid steps did Binita take, and why were they sensible?
She kept dirty hands off, washed it with clean water, pressed a clean cloth, and called an adult.
How might Hafsa's Ammi feel when she gets the call?
She may feel worried but relieved that Binita stayed calm and called quickly.
