messages.content:
Such were my reflections during the first two or three days of my residence at Ingolstadt, which were chiefly spent in becoming acquainted with the localities and the principal residents in my new abode. But as the ensuing week commenced, I thought of the information which M. Krempe had given me concerning the lectures. And although I could not consent to go and hear that little conceited fellow deliver sentences out of a pulpit, I recollected what he had said of M. Waldman, whom I had never seen, as he had hitherto been out of town.

Capture this bit of text in two sentences.

In the first days at Ingolstadt, the narrator gets to know the place and its main residents. Later, the narrator thinks about M. Krempe's advice on lectures and his remark about M. Waldman, who was out of town.

Read this:

Babysitter's note, Navratri week.

Mehak, two, toddled toward the kitchen while the diya was lit on the shelf. I said, "Mehak, stop. Hot." She stopped, looked at me, and came back to hold my hand.

When her grandmother came home from the garba, Mehak ran and hugged her legs, then brought her slippers without being asked. — Rajni

What did Rajni say when Mehak toddled toward the kitchen?
She said, "Mehak, stop. Hot."
How did Mehak seem to feel toward her grandmother?
Mehak seemed loving and excited, running to hug her and bringing her slippers.
How can Rajni keep supporting Mehak's safe listening?
Use short, calm words and praise her each time she stops and comes back.
How might Mehak's grandmother feel when Mehak brought her slippers?
Her grandmother would likely feel touched and happy.

Read this:

I was in the pantry when Parul from HR said it, casually, stirring her tea. "Shame about your transfer request. Sameer mentioned to the director you'd been talking about leaving. That's probably why."

I said, "Oh," and carried my cup back to my desk.

For the rest of the afternoon I felt nothing. I answered emails. I laughed at a meme. It was like my body had gone to sleep.

The anger came at 11 at night, at home, so hard I sat up in bed. Sameer. Who I'd told about my transfer plan because he was my closest friend at work. Sameer, who'd come to my father's funeral.

And under the anger, something worse. I wasn't only losing a friend. I was losing the man I thought he was. That man never existed, maybe.

I'm Farida, and I'm twenty-six, and it felt like grief.

Who told Farida about Sameer?
Parul from HR told Farida, in the pantry.
What was Farida feeling in the afternoon compared to 11 at night?
In the afternoon Farida felt numb, as if asleep; at night a strong rage came, with grief underneath.
What could Farida do before confronting Sameer?
Farida could give the anger a night to settle, talk it over with someone trusted, and then ask Sameer for a direct, private conversation.
How might Parul have seen the pantry moment?
Parul seemed to think it was known or casual news, probably unaware it would shock Farida.

Read this:

Monday. "Mumma, is the door locked?" Divyansh, nine, asked at bedtime. "Yes." "Are you sure?" "Yes, beta." He asked eleven times. Each time, Mumma answered, and each time he calmed a little, then asked again. She also waited outside the bathroom while he washed his hands.
Three weeks later. The questions had doubled. Mumma had changed the whole morning so he could check his school bag four times. They were late for the bus twice. She loved him so much, but she was exhausted.
The next Saturday. Dr Farhan, the child psychologist, listened to her. "You answer because you love him," he said gently. "But each answer teaches his worry that it needs one more. Let's plan how to support him without feeding the worry." Together they wrote a plan: one answer, then "I already told you, I believe you can handle this."

How many times did Divyansh ask about the door on Monday?
Eleven times.
How was Mumma feeling three weeks later?
She felt loving but exhausted and worried, with the questions doubling and the family late for the bus.
What did Dr Farhan suggest instead of answering every time?
Giving one answer, then calmly trusting Divyansh to handle the worry, so the pattern isn't fed and strengthened.
What is it like for Divyansh when the questions keep coming?
He feels anxious and only briefly calmer after each answer, so he needs to ask again and again.

Read this:

"Uma, the lamp. Come, it's time."
"Coming, Amma."
"You've been standing at the back for weeks. You used to sing the loudest."
"Amma, can I tell you something without you getting upset?"
"Say it."
"The words don't feel like anything to me right now. I say them and it's just sound. Lalremsiami says half her youth group at church feels like this too."
"Since when?"
"Since the exams, maybe. I didn't want to hurt you, so I kept standing there."
"Hurt me? Kanna, you think I never had doubts at your age?"
"You did?"
"Paati made me recite the full Lalitha Sahasranamam every Friday. Half the time I was thinking about cricket."
"So what do I do?"
"Stand with us if you want. Don't pretend if you don't. And still bring me tea after, hmm?"
"I can do that."

What did Paati make Amma recite every Friday?
Paati made her recite the full Lalitha Sahasranamam every Friday.
Why had Uma been standing at the back for weeks?
Uma felt the prayers had lost meaning and was afraid of hurting Amma by saying so, so the back of the room felt safer than speaking.
What made this conversation go well?
Uma asked to speak without upsetting Amma and was honest, and Amma answered with her own memory instead of anger, offering a way to stay close without pretending.
How might Amma have felt when Uma said the words were "just sound"?
Amma may have felt a pang of surprise or sadness, but she chose understanding, remembering her own doubts.

Read this:

The vendor wanted an answer by five, and the office internet had died at two. Sabina, the operations lead at a small logistics firm in Pune, was sure the cheaper warehouse in Chakan was the right choice. Still, with three hours left and no connection, she pulled out a notepad and wrote: "I switch if flood risk or road access is worse than I think." Then she walked to Karthik's cubicle, the one person who always disagreed with her. "Argue for the other warehouse. Your best version." He talked for twenty minutes about monsoon traffic on the Chakan road. She phoned a driver, who confirmed it. At 4:40 she signed for the costlier site, and thanked Karthik for being difficult.

When did Sabina sign for the costlier site?
She signed for the costlier site at 4:40.
How can you tell that Sabina did not feel insulted by Karthik's disagreement?
She sought him out because he always disagreed, asked for his best version, and thanked him afterwards, so his argument felt useful to her, not like an attack.
Which step made Sabina's check work even without internet?
Writing down in advance what would make her switch meant she knew exactly what to test, so one call to a driver could settle the road question before five.
How might Karthik feel when Sabina thanks him for being difficult?
Karthik would probably feel valued rather than resented, since his habit of disagreeing was treated as a help to the decision instead of a nuisance.

Read this:

“Last one,” said Ritu, counting. “Manjula.”

“Ha, I'm always the bonus,” Manjula said, tugging her braid. Nobody laughed.

Salma, captain of Team Blue, stepped forward. “Manjula, come here. I've been saving you.”

“For what?”

“The goal circle. You never lose track of where the ball is. Last time you shouted ‘left!’ and we scored.”

“I only did that once.”

“Once was enough.” Salma nudged her shoulder. “Stand by me.”

Manjula stepped over slowly, hiding a smile. “Okay. But if I mess up, I go back to being the bonus.”

“Deal,” said Salma. “You won't.”

What did Manjula call herself when picked last?
Manjula said, “I'm always the bonus.”
Why did Manjula say she was always the bonus while tugging the braid?
Manjula was hiding hurt behind a joke, and tugging the braid shows nervousness about being measured in public.
What did Salma do that changed how Manjula felt?
Salma called Manjula over warmly, said Manjula had been saved for the goal circle and named a real contribution.
What might Salma have noticed that led Salma to choose Manjula for the goal circle?
Salma noticed that Manjula tracks the ball well and once shouted “left!” to set up a goal, a strength others had missed.
In one sentence of no more than twelve words, explain the goal of chess.
The goal is to checkmate the other player's king.

Reduce this excerpt to three sentences.

Mr. Kirwin, on hearing this evidence, desired that I should be taken into the room where the body lay for interment, that it might be observed what effect the sight of it would produce upon me. This idea was probably suggested by the extreme agitation I had exhibited when the mode of the murder had been described. I was accordingly conducted, by the magistrate and several other persons, to the inn. I could not help being struck by the strange coincidences that had taken place during this eventful night; but, knowing that I had been conversing with several persons in the island I had inhabited about the time that the body had been found, I was perfectly tranquil as to the consequences of the affair.

Mr. Kirwin has the narrator taken to the room where the body lies, to see how the sight affects the narrator. This was probably prompted by the narrator's great agitation when the murder was described. The narrator, struck by the night's coincidences, stays calm, since people on the island had talked with the narrator when the body was found.
Write a note to my mother saying I will be home after band practice, in three lines: greeting, message and sign-off.

Mummy,
I will reach home after band practice.
Love, Anu

Read this:

Classroom note, Wednesday — Salma, nursery teacher
During pretend play, Elizabeth, 5, declared, "I am the doctor, and I'm the doctor all day." The others were happy for a while, then wanted to switch to a shop game. Elizabeth refused. She kept her toy stethoscope on and said, "I said it. I can't change." She sat alone in the clinic corner, watching the shop game, sad but firm. I sat beside her and asked if doctors sometimes buy medicine at shops. She thought about it, then walked over with the stethoscope still on and bought "medicine" from the shop. Note: she seems to feel bound by her own announcements. Offer ways to honour them.

What game did the other children want to switch to?
A shop game.
What does Elizabeth saying "I said it. I can't change" show about how she feels?
She feels her spoken word binds her, so changing the game feels wrong even though she is sad sitting alone.
What did Salma do that helped Elizabeth join in?
She asked if doctors sometimes buy medicine at shops, which let Elizabeth join the shop game while still being the doctor.
How might the other children see Elizabeth's refusal?
They may be puzzled or a bit annoyed that she won't switch, since they just want to play the new game together.

Read this:

At the call centre's night shift, Tanvir was the worst performer on Bhavna's team. He was late, forgot scripts, and last week he'd snapped at her in front of everyone.
Bhavna knew all this. She also knew he was looking after his mother after her surgery.
When he came in late again on Thursday, the other team leads rolled their eyes. Bhavna pulled him aside. "You're late a lot. I need you to fix that. But how is your mother?"
Tanvir looked startled. "Better. Thanks."
"If you need a shift change for a month, ask. I'll try."
He apologised for snapping. She nodded. She didn't pretend he was perfect. She just decided to treat him as someone worth giving another chance.

What had Tanvir done in front of everyone last week?
He had snapped at Bhavna.
How might Tanvir have felt when Bhavna asked about his mother?
He likely felt startled and grateful, not expecting kindness after being late.
What made Bhavna's response a good balance?
She was clear about his lateness but also offered understanding and a possible shift change.
How might the other team leads see Bhavna's approach?
They may think she's too soft, since they rolled their eyes at Tanvir.

Read this:

“Siami, you topped the law school. Corporate firms are calling you.”
“I know, Gopika.”
“And you're joining a legal aid office in Aizawl. For land cases.”
Lalremsiami nodded, stirring her tea. “My grandmother lost half her field because she couldn't read the papers she signed. Nobody helped her.”
“That's one case.”
“It's thousands. Most families here don't have a lawyer in the family. I want to be that for a lot of them.”
“And your own life? Marriage? A home?”
“I've thought about it. I'll choose a partner who understands the work. We'll live near the office. I'll take a small salary for now.”
Gopika shook her head. “You've planned this.”
“For five years.” Siami smiled. “I just didn't say it out loud.”
“Then say it louder,” Gopika said. “I'll help you move.”

Where is Lalremsiami joining a legal aid office?
She is joining a legal aid office in Aizawl.
What does Lalremsiami feel about this choice, and why?
She feels determined and steady, a commitment rooted in grief that her grandmother lost half her field.
What does Lalremsiami do that makes her plan more likely to last?
She thinks about how marriage, home and salary will fit around the work, instead of treating them separately.
How does Gopika's view change during the conversation?
She starts doubtful, then becomes supportive when she sees how long and carefully Siami has planned.
Carrom is a game who needs a steady hand. Is "who" right?

Carrom is a game that needs a steady hand.
Why: "Who" is used for people; for a thing such as a game, use "that" or "which".

Read this:

In the kasba, Salma's father runs a small cycle-repair shop beside the bus stand. Chandrika, Salma's friend from Class 6, started coming after school to wait for her bus. At first she only sat on the tyre pile, bored. Then one day a boy's chain slipped, and Salma's father was busy. Chandrika picked up a spanner. "Show me?" Salma laughed, but her father nodded. Chandrika watched how he hooked the chain back, then did the next one herself, grease up to her wrists. After that she missed two buses in a week. At home her mother scolded her for her black nails. Chandrika only said, "Amma, I want to learn how the gears work."

Where is Salma's father's shop?
It is beside the bus stand in the kasba.
Why did Chandrika miss two buses in a week?
She was so absorbed in fixing the cycles that she lost track of time; the repair work had caught her interest in a way sitting on the tyre pile never did.
How could Chandrika's mother respond to this new interest?
Instead of only scolding about her nails, she could ask what she is learning and help her plan her time so she doesn't miss the bus.
How does Salma's father seem to see Chandrika's interest?
He takes it seriously, nodding and letting her try, which suggests he respects her wish to learn even though she is a young girl in his shop.
What is the avaroha of Raga Madhuvanti?
The avaroha of Raga Madhuvanti is: S' N D P M^ g R S.

Yogesh: weird thing at work today
Dhruv: new-job weird or bad weird?
Yogesh: dunno. my senior filled in last week's safety checklist for the lift today and put last week's date on it
Yogesh: said the auditor only looks at dates. 'everyone does it, it's how things work here'
Dhruv: and the lift?
Yogesh: it's fine I think. he says it's always fine
Dhruv: you ok with that?
Yogesh: honestly it felt a bit off. but it's my 3rd week. I'm not going to be the guy who makes a fuss over one date
Yogesh: and he bought me lunch after
Dhruv: hmm
Yogesh: it's one form 😅
Dhruv: ok. just keep noticing

What date did the senior put on the lift checklist?
He put last week's date on the checklist he filled in today.
What is Yogesh feeling about the backdated form?
He feels it is a bit off, but in his third week the pressure to fit in outweighs the unease, so he laughs it off as one form.
What turning point is available to Yogesh at this first stage?
He could calmly ask his senior whether the lift checks were really done, or read the rule himself, before the habit becomes his own.
What might Dhruv be thinking behind his 'hmm'?
Dhruv seems uneasy about the shortcut and worried for Yogesh, but chooses to nudge him to keep noticing rather than lecture.

Read this:

Kwame had rolled his eyes when Mum said it in the hallway: 'Any time you're somewhere unsafe, ring me. I'll come, and I won't ask a single question tonight.' At Nour's older brother's flat in Leeds, the party changed after eleven. Strangers arrived, someone tipped white pills onto the kitchen counter, and a man blocked the balcony door, laughing too loudly. Kwame's palms went damp. He texted Nour, stuck across the room: 'I'm leaving. Come with?' She nodded and slipped out behind him. On the stairwell he rang Mum. She answered on the second ring. 'Corner by the bus shelter, ten minutes,' she said, and kept her word: no lecture, just the heater on and a packet of biscuits on the seat. She dropped Nour at her door first. At breakfast Kwame started talking without being asked, and Mum just listened.

What was waiting on the car seat when Mum picked Kwame up?
A packet of biscuits, and the heater was on.
What do Kwame's damp palms suggest?
They suggest he felt uneasy and frightened as the party turned unsafe with strangers and pills.
What would you advise a friend in Kwame's place?
Leave with a friend, call the parent who offered a safe ride, and save the talk for the next day.
How might Mum see the call from the stairwell?
She would likely feel relieved he trusted her, which is why she kept her promise of no lecture that night ❤️

The career cell at the college in Guwahati had a sign-up sheet for placements, and Sabina walked past it for the third time. She had made up her mind a month ago: skip placements, study full-time for the MBA entrance. In the library she opened her laptop and searched "why placements are a trap." She saved four articles. Then she messaged two seniors who had dropped placements and cleared the exam. Both wrote back, "Best decision of my life." That evening she told her friend Bhupen, "I've done so much research. Everyone agrees." "Did you ask Dimpy-di? She didn't clear it and had no job for a year." Sabina shrugged. "Her case was different." "And the placement officer?" "They just want numbers." She closed the laptop, feeling thoroughly prepared.

How many articles did Sabina save?
She saved four articles.
Why does Sabina feel "thoroughly prepared"?
She feels confident because she has read articles and heard from seniors. But every source she chose already agreed with her, so it feels complete without being balanced.
What choice could Sabina make before the placement deadline to test her decision?
She could talk to Dimpy-di and the placement officer, the people most likely to disagree, and ask what went wrong for those who didn't clear the exam.
How might Bhupen feel when Sabina dismisses each question?
Bhupen may feel unheard and a little worried, since the questions were meant to help, and may decide to stop raising doubts.

Could you recap this extract for me? Three sentences is enough.

This was Heathcliff's first introduction to the family. On coming back a few days afterwards (for I did not consider my banishment perpetual), I found they had christened him "Heathcliff": it was the name of a son who died in childhood, and it has served him ever since, both for Christian and surname. Miss Cathy and he were now very thick; but Hindley hated him: and to say the truth I did the same; and we plagued and went on with him shamefully: for I wasn't reasonable enough to feel my injustice, and the mistress never put in a word on his behalf when she saw him wronged.

Heathcliff is introduced to the family and given the name of a son who died in childhood, which serves as his first name and surname. Cathy and he become very close, but Hindley hates him. The narrator admits to hating and plaguing him too, while the mistress never defended him.

The bus was due in five minutes, and Kamal was racing Rukmini to the door. "I'm first!" he shouted, one sock still half on, and he slapped the handle a heartbeat before her. His chest puffed out. Then Rukmini beat him to the shoe rack, calling, "Papa, look, I'm ready!" Kamal's face crumpled and his lip shook. Papa knelt to tie both pairs of laces. "You both moved fast today. Kamal, tonight is your story time with me. Rukmini, yours is tomorrow." Kamal sniffed, nodded, and picked up his bag.

How many minutes were left before the bus was due?
The bus was due in five minutes.
What was Kamal feeling when Rukmini beat him to the shoe rack?
Kamal felt crushed. His crumpled face and shaking lip show how much losing hurt after the pride of winning at the door.
What did Papa do that could ease the racing between the two children?
Papa praised how fast they both moved and gave each child their own story time. That way Papa's attention does not depend on who is first. 🙂
What might Rukmini want when she calls, "Papa, look, I'm ready!"?
Rukmini probably wants Papa to notice her, just as Kamal does. She may also enjoy winning the shoe race in the same way he enjoyed the door.

Rewrite for a small child using easy words:

It is important to wash your hands thoroughly before eating, because germs can spread from dirty hands to food.
Wash your hands well before you eat. Dirty hands can put germs on your food.

Read this:

In the waiting hall of the municipal ward office, Chetan sat with his water complaint and token 47. Beside him, Yash, a man from his colony, laughed without humour. "Fourth time I'm here about the same leak. Nothing changes in this country. I've stopped even filing. Today I only came to pay the bill." Chetan felt the same tiredness creep up his own spine. Then he noticed a notice on the wall: "Complaints from five or more households on one street will be treated as a group case." He turned to Yash. "How many houses on our lane have the leak?" Yash shrugged. "Six? Seven?" "Then let's file one together. Seven names." Yash hesitated, then took the pen. Three weeks later a crew dug up the lane. Yash stood at his gate watching, arms folded, almost smiling.

What token number did Chetan have?
Chetan had token 47.
What was Chetan feeling as Yash spoke?
Chetan felt the same weary cynicism creeping in, tempted to give up too.
Which small act helped more than giving up?
Noticing the group-case rule and filing one complaint together for seven households, which got the office to act.
Why might Yash have stopped filing complaints?
After four visits about the same leak, Yash felt tired and defeated, and cynicism seemed safer than hoping again.

Read this:

The cricket ball had cracked the society secretary's scooter mirror, and now he stood over Zubin in the Pune parking lot, voice booming. “Do you know what this costs?” Zubin's mouth pulled into a small, fixed smile. “Oh, you're smiling? You think it's a joke?” Zubin's smile trembled but wouldn't go. Afreen, from the third floor, had been watching from the stairs. She came down. “Uncle, look at his hands,” she said quietly. Zubin's fingers were clenched white around the bat. The secretary looked. His voice dropped. “All right. Tell your parents tonight, and we'll sort out the mirror.” Zubin nodded, still smiling, eyes wet.

What had the cricket ball cracked?
It had cracked the society secretary's scooter mirror.
Why might Zubin keep smiling while being shouted at?
He was probably frightened and embarrassed, and the smile may have been a way to calm the angry secretary, as his white-clenched fingers suggest.
How did Afreen help the secretary read Zubin correctly?
She quietly pointed to his clenched hands, giving evidence that the smile came from fear rather than cheek.
How might the secretary feel after looking at Zubin's hands?
The secretary might feel a little ashamed of shouting and see a scared boy instead of a cheeky one.

Read this:

"Can I tell you about my first year here?" Dilnaz stirred her tea. "I lost the biggest client in the building."
"You? No way."
"I sent the wrong contract. Cried in the stairwell. My manager then didn't speak to me for a week."
Ishita laughed, then covered her mouth. "Sorry."
"Laugh, it's funny now. Also, since we're being honest, the monthly review isn't about numbers only. The director likes people who explain problems early. Nobody tells you that."
Ishita put her cup down. "Can I be honest too? I've been hiding a delay on my project because I was scared."
"Good. Let's fix it together."

What did Dilnaz send by mistake in her first year?
The wrong contract.
Why did Dilnaz share her own failure with Ishita?
She wanted Ishita to feel less alone and safe enough to be honest, showing she cared about building trust.
What turning point does this conversation create for Ishita?
She admits the hidden project delay, and can now fix it with help before the monthly review.
What is it like for Ishita to hear that a senior once cried in the stairwell?
It seems to relieve her and make her feel less alone, which is why she finally admits being scared.

Read this:

Monday: A message from Hrithik after eight months of silence. "I was cruel when I told people you'd cheated on the placement test. I'm sorry. Can we be friends again?" Keerthana read it on the office stairs and felt her chest go tight. She typed "Of course!" and deleted it. She wrote instead: "Thank you for saying it. Let me think."

Saturday: They met at a busy café near her office. Hrithik didn't make excuses; he said he'd already written to two of those people to correct it. Keerthana noticed that mattered more to her than the apology. She said, "I've forgiven you. But I'm not ready for late-night calls and secrets yet. Coffee sometimes, and let's see."

Three weeks later: Group lunch, six of them. Hrithik passed her the dal and asked about her new team. Keerthana laughed at his joke, and left when she wanted to.

What had Hrithik told people about Keerthana?
He had told people she'd cheated on the placement test.
What was Keerthana feeling when she deleted "Of course!"?
She was torn: part of her wanted the old friendship back at once, but she was still wary and needed time before trusting Hrithik again.
What turning point is available at this stage, and how did Keerthana use it?
The turning point was deciding how much contact to renew; Keerthana forgave but chose a slow rebuild, watching for real remorse like Hrithik correcting the story with others.
What is it like for Hrithik to be offered coffee sometimes instead of full closeness?
Hrithik may feel a little disappointed but also relieved to be given a chance, and it shows him that trust has to be earned back step by step.
What is the different between a lake and a pond? Is the word right?

What is the difference between a lake and a pond?
Why: "The" needs a noun after it. "Different" is the adjective; the noun is "difference".

Team coach's note, college debate society, Thursday.
In today's planning meeting, the whole team, eleven members, agreed to argue the "for" side in the national round, because it's easier to prepare. Amandeep alone disagreed. He said the "against" side had stronger evidence and more original arguments. The room went quiet. Tejas, the captain, said, "We've already decided." I watched Amandeep's shoulders go up and his voice get smaller, but he didn't back down: "I just think we'd win more convincingly." Someone rolled their eyes. After the meeting, he sat alone, looking at his notes. I told him that disagreeing with everyone, calmly, took courage, and that I'd ask the team to hear his evidence next week before voting again. He looked relieved, but also tired. Being right doesn't make it easy.

How many team members agreed to argue the "for" side?
The whole team, eleven members, agreed.
What was Amandeep feeling as his voice got smaller?
Amandeep felt pressure and self-doubt, his shoulders rising, yet he held his view.
What did the coach do that could help Amandeep?
The coach acknowledged his courage and arranged for the team to hear his evidence before voting again.
How might Tejas have seen Amandeep's disagreement?
Tejas seemed to see it as an obstacle to a decision already made, wanting to move on quickly.

Read this:

Dear Farhan,
Thanks for sending the brochure for the data-science bootcamp. I can see why you're excited: those six alumni stories are impressive, and one of them now works at a big firm.
Before we recommend it to our juniors, though, I'd like to ask the bootcamp a few questions. How many people started in each batch? How many finished? Of those, how many found jobs in data within a year? The brochure shows six faces, but it doesn't say whether they're six out of twenty or six out of six hundred.
If the numbers look good, I'll happily be the first to sign our juniors up. If they won't share them, that tells us something too.
Shall I write to them tomorrow?
Ishita

How many alumni stories does the brochure show?
Six.
Why does Ishita want to ask questions before recommending the bootcamp?
Ishita feels cautious, because six impressive faces don't show whether they're six out of twenty or six out of six hundred.
Which questions does Ishita want answered, and why do they matter?
How many started, finished and found data jobs within a year, because only the whole batch shows whether the course really works.
How might Farhan feel reading the email?
Farhan might feel slightly deflated but respected, since the excitement is acknowledged and a fair next step is offered.

Read this:

For three weeks Noor smiled at everyone and told nobody that she felt like a weight on the others and that everyone else coped better. On a Tuesday Raghav found her on the library steps, sat beside her and said nothing for a while. Noor felt noticed, really noticed, after a long stretch of feeling invisible. "Bad month. That's all I can say for now," she told him, and let him carry her lab files to the bus. That evening she rang home. "It's mostly in your mind, just be strong," her mother said. Noor put the phone down feeling small and dismissed. Still, the thought that these feelings were too heavy to hold alone would not leave, so before dinner she walked to her tutor's office and said what she had been hiding. The tutor made tea, stayed with her, and walked her to the college counselling centre themselves before it closed for the day. The counsellor, Rehana, listened. The first session felt awkward and Noor answered in single words. In the second she said more. After the third, Rehana said it was fine to speak up if the fit did not feel right, and Noor said it felt right so far. She rang her mother again, this time with details about sleep and dread, and asked her to join a session by video.

Where did Raghav find Noor?
Raghav found Noor on the library steps.
How did Raghav's response and her mother's response differ in the way they left Noor feeling, and what did Noor do the same day?

Raghav sat with her and she felt seen, while her mother's reply left her feeling small and dismissed; the same day Noor told her tutor what she had been hiding and was walked to the counselling centre.
What was Noor feeling after her mother said it was mostly in her mind?
She felt small and dismissed, as if her pain did not count.
What could Noor do if the counsellor's style still did not fit after a few sessions?
She could say so honestly and try a different professional, rather than giving up on help.

Read this:

My name is Maria, and last winter I had a rule: I would do homework when I felt like it. On Tuesday there was a map of rivers to label. "Later, when I feel like it," I told Hansa, the neighbour who minds me after school. I fed the fish. I sorted my stickers. I lay on the rug and waited for the feeling. It never came. At half past nine Mum found the blank map, and I labelled rivers with my eyes half shut, crying because I spelled one wrong twice. The next week it happened again with a reading sheet, and then again. After the third late night I noticed something: the feeling never came first. Once my pencil was moving, it sort of turned up.

What homework did Maria have on Tuesday?
A map of rivers to label.
What was Maria feeling while labelling rivers at half past nine?
Maria was tired and upset, labelling with eyes half shut and crying, frustrated at having left it so late.
What small step could Maria try the next time Maria is waiting for the feeling?
Maria could pick up the pencil and label just one river straight after school, because the feeling only turned up once the pencil was moving.
How might Hansa see Maria's evenings of "later"?
Hansa watches Maria drift from the fish to the stickers to the rug and may feel helpless, since the homework is not Hansa's to force, even though the late night is easy to see coming.

Read this:

"Parul Didi, why did you change your wallpaper? It used to be you and Nakul."
"Vikas, sit. Close the door."
"What happened?"
"Nakul and I broke up. Two months ago."
"Two MONTHS? Mummy's been telling everyone at the kitty party you'll marry next year!"
"I know. That's why I haven't said anything. She'll be humiliated."
"And you've been pretending all this time?"
"Every call. Every time she asks, 'How is Arjun?' I say, 'Fine, busy.' I can't sleep."
"Parul... this is eating you."
"I just didn't want to be the family's embarrassment."
"You're not an embarrassment. You're my sister. Tell her. I'll sit with you."
"She'll cry."
"Maybe. Then she'll make tea. You know her."
"...Tonight?"
"Tonight. Before the kitty party on Friday."

How long ago did Parul and Arjun break up?
They broke up two months ago.
Why couldn't Parul sleep?
Parul felt ashamed and afraid of humiliating Mummy, and the pretending on every call was wearing her down.
What could make telling Mummy easier for Parul?
Having Vikas sit with her and telling Mummy that night, before the kitty party, means she isn't facing it alone.
How might Vikas see his sister's secret?
Vikas is worried and protective, seeing that the secret is eating Parul and that she is not an embarrassment.

Read this:

Rain drummed on the tin roof, PE was cancelled, and with the class teacher away at a meeting, Class 4B was stuck indoors with colouring sheets. Nandini sat beside Farida as always. Only Farida knew that Nandini still counted on her fingers under the desk during maths. Then, across the room, Rukhsar whispered loudly, "Farida says you're a finger-counter!" Nandini's crayon snapped. She stared at Farida, who went red and looked at the window. There was nowhere to go; the corridor was flooded. Nandini pressed her forehead to the desk so nobody would see her eyes. At home time Farida held out half her samosa without a word. Nandini didn't take it, but she didn't walk away either, and they waited for the rain side by side.

What did only Farida know about Nandini?
Only Farida knew that Nandini still counted on her fingers under the desk during maths.
What does Nandini's snapped crayon and hidden face suggest she felt?
They suggest she felt shocked, betrayed and embarrassed, trying to hide tears from the class.
What could Farida try next, beyond offering the samosa?
Farida could say sorry out loud and admit she told the secret, which would show Nandini she understands the hurt, not just want it to pass.
What was it like for Farida when Nandini stared at her?
Farida likely felt guilty and ashamed, turning red and looking away because she knew she had broken her best friend's trust.

Read this:

At the Pola festival in their village near Wardha, Lavanya stood with her friends from the district school for Deaf students, signing fast and laughing about the decorated bullocks.
Some aunties by the temple wall watched and whispered. One said loudly to Lavanya's mother, "Poor thing. If only she could talk properly."
Lavanya saw the words on the aunty's lips and her face. She lifted her chin. She turned to her friends and signed a joke about the aunty's giant earrings, and they all burst out laughing.
Her brother Anirban came over. He'd been learning to sign since she went to the new school. He signed to her, slowly, "You okay?"
She signed back, "More than okay. I have a whole language. She has earrings."
Anirban laughed and turned to the aunty. "She talks properly, Kaki. In her language. You'd just have to learn it."

What festival was being celebrated in the village?
The Pola festival.
What did Lavanya's lifted chin suggest about how she felt?
It suggested she felt proud and defiant, refusing to be pitied for signing.
How did Anirban support his sister?
He had learned to sign, checked on her in her language, and told the aunty that signing is talking properly.
How might the aunty see signing compared with Lavanya?
The aunty seems to see it as a sad lack, while Lavanya sees it as a complete language and a source of pride.
Why does cotton cloth feel cooler to wear in summer than polyester cloth?

Cotton usually feels cooler: it lets air through and takes up sweat. Because the loose weave lets air and moisture pass and the absorbed sweat can evaporate from the cloth, heat leaves the skin more easily. Some polyester sports cloth is made to do this too.

Read this:

"Tanvir, wait. Can we talk?"
"About what, Seema? You sat with Priyanka's group at the fest. In front of everyone."
"I know, but..."
"You're a fake. That's all. I finally see it."
"That's not fair."
"You pretend to be my friend and then ditch me the second someone cooler shows up. Fake."
"Tanvir, will you just listen for one minute?"
"No. I don't need to. I know what you are."
"Priyanka's sister was..."
"I said I don't care."
Seema stood there a moment. Then she said quietly, "Okay," and walked away.
Tanvir's friend Irfan leaned over. "What was she saying about Priyanka's sister?"
"Doesn't matter."
"You didn't even let her finish."
Tanvir shrugged. But he kept thinking about the half-sentence all through maths.

Where did Seema sit at the fest?
She sat with Priyanka's group, in front of everyone.
Why did Tanvir refuse to listen to Seema?
Tanvir felt hurt and betrayed, and calling her a fake felt so certain that listening seemed pointless.
What could Tanvir still do to repair things?
He could go to Seema and ask what she was going to say about Priyanka's sister, and actually listen this time.
How might Seema feel walking away after "I don't care"?
Seema likely felt hurt and unheard, unable to explain her side.

metadata.subtype: Labelling others in a bad moment [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Imran Chacha had searched three shops in the old city for the doll with the blue frock. At Kashish's birthday in the crowded flat, he handed it over. Kashish unwrapped it and wrinkled her nose. "Eww. Dolls are for babies." Imran felt a little drop in his chest. He had hoped to see her smile. Kashish's mother started to scold. Imran touched her arm. "It's okay. She's five. They don't hide things." He crouched down. "Well, I tried! But you know, a thank-you makes the giver happy." Kashish thought, then mumbled, "Thank you, Chacha."

How many shops did Imran Chacha search?
He searched three shops in the old city.
How did Imran feel when Kashish wrinkled her nose?
He felt sad and a little hurt, a drop in his chest, because he had hoped she would smile.
Why did Imran stop Kashish's mother from scolding?
He understood small children don't hide feelings, so he chose to keep it light and gently remind her that thanks matter.
How might Kashish feel after Chacha's gentle words?
She may feel a bit sheepish but not ashamed, and ready to say thank you.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Class 11 debate club
Sarita asked to see me after Tuesday's debate on whether religion belongs in public life. She had argued the side she was given, well, but afterwards she said she felt like a hypocrite. At home her family keeps a daily prayer; lately she has been questioning parts of it and felt guilty even thinking this.
Baljeet, her debate partner, waited outside and told me she had been quiet for days.
I did not tell her what to believe. I said questioning is a normal part of growing up and she can take her time. We listed which parts of her faith still feel true to her and which ones she is unsure about.
Next step: I suggested she talk with one adult at home she trusts, and we meet again in two weeks.

What was the topic of Tuesday's debate?
Whether religion belongs in public life.
What was Sarita feeling after the debate?
She felt like a hypocrite and guilty for questioning parts of her family's daily prayer.
What small step did the counsellor suggest, and why might it help?
The counsellor suggested talking with one trusted adult at home, which could ease Sarita's guilt and let her sort out her beliefs without hiding them.
How does Baljeet seem to see Sarita's state?
Baljeet noticed she had been quiet for days and seemed concerned enough to wait outside the counsellor's room.

Read this:

Dear Dilnaz Apa,
I've decided to report what I found at work, through the ethics hotline, on Monday. Before you worry, let me tell you how I've prepared, because I spent the weekend imagining it going badly.
I asked myself: if this turns out terribly, what does 'terribly' look like? My answer: the team goes cold on me, my manager writes a poor review, maybe I'm moved off the good project, and I feel very alone in that office.
So here's my plan for each. I've saved my past appraisals and the client emails praising my work, from the company system, so no one can claim my work slipped. I've noted the HR head's contact and how the hotline's reference process works. I've checked my savings: enough for four months if I had to leave. And I've told you, so I'm not alone with it.
Could we speak every Sunday for a while? That's the last part of the plan.
Your sister,
Ayesha

When is Ayesha reporting through the ethics hotline?
On Monday.
What might Ayesha be afraid of?
Isolation, a poor review and losing the good project, and feeling very alone in the office.
Why is asking for Sunday calls part of a good plan?
Regular support from someone outside work helps with loneliness if the team turns cold.
How might Dilnaz Apa feel reading the letter?
Worried for her sister but reassured by the careful plan, and glad to be asked to help. 🤍

metadata.subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on retaliation and support [Thinking]

Read this:

“Say it again, Kalyani,” said Arnab, tapping the table. “Ten past five?” Her voice climbed on the last word. “Are you asking me or telling me?” he said. “Telling you, silly!” Kalyani said, tilting her head. “In our village everyone talks that way. It goes up when we're being nice.” Arnab thought about it. “In my class if it goes up, the teacher says you're guessing.” “Well, I'm not guessing.” She said it again, falling on “five.” “See? Ten past five. Same words.” Arnab grinned. “Fine. Next time I'll ask before I decide you're unsure.”

What time did Kalyani say?
Ten past five.
Why did Arnab ask if Kalyani was asking or telling?
He heard her voice rise on the last word and wondered if she was unsure, since his teacher treats a rising voice as guessing.
What did Arnab decide to do differently?
He decided to ask before assuming Kalyani is unsure, because a rising voice can be a regional habit and not doubt.
How might Kalyani feel when her friends read her habit as guessing?
She might feel misunderstood or annoyed, since to her the rising voice is just politeness from home. 😅

metadata.subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Papa..." Jahnavi, five, stood in the doorway with her hands behind her back.
"What is it?"
"I broke the blue cup. It fell. I'm sorry." Her voice shook.
Rafiq put down his phone. "Thank you for telling me. Are you hurt?"
"No."
"Then it's okay. Cups break. Next time carry it with two hands, and let's pick up the pieces with the dustpan."
Jahnavi let out a big breath. "I thought you'd shout."

Which cup did Jahnavi break?
The blue cup.
What was Jahnavi feeling after she confessed?
Relief, shown by her big breath and "I thought you'd shout". Before that she was afraid.
What did Rafiq do that encourages truth-telling?
He thanked her, checked she was not hurt, dealt with the cup calmly and showed her what to do next time.
How might Rafiq feel hearing "I thought you'd shout"?
Perhaps surprised and a little sad that she was afraid, and glad she told him. 🤍
Is it "damage" or "damages" when a storm breaks a wall?

For harm to a thing, use "damage", which is uncountable. "Damages" with an s is a legal word for money awarded by a court as payment for harm.
Examples: The storm caused damage to the school wall. The court ordered the company to pay damages.

Read this:

I was at the gate returning a steel bowl when I saw the little one on the floor. Sonali pointed up at the shelf, looked at Grandmother, said "uh, uh," and patted Grandmother's hand. Grandmother got up, lifted the toy down and Sonali took it happily. I could not tell whether Sonali was tired of trying or simply knew Grandmother would do it. There was no stretching at all, just a look and a pat. Harish

What did Sonali say while patting Grandmother's hand?
Sonali said "uh, uh" and patted Grandmother's hand.
What did Sonali seem to want, and what makes Harish unsure about it?
Sonali seemed to want the toy and to expect help; the pointing, the look at Grandmother and the pat show it, but Harish cannot be sure whether Sonali was tired or just confident.
What other approach could Sonali try, and why might it help?
Sonali could try reaching for the toy first with Grandmother close by, because a few tries build skill and help is still there if they fall short.
How might Grandmother feel about being asked this way?
Grandmother probably feels needed and glad to help, since she got up and lifted the toy down at once.

In the winter sun outside the house near Bikaner, Nirmala Dadi was cleaning grain with a winnowing basket. Vikas, five, asked to hold it.

He put it on his head. "It's a hat!"

He held it in front of him. "It's a shield!"

He sat inside it. "It's a boat, Dadi. We're going to the sea."

Dadi laughed. "And what will you do there?"

"Catch the moon. The basket is the moon's house."

What was Nirmala Dadi doing with the basket?
She was cleaning grain with a winnowing basket.
How was Vikas feeling as he played with the basket?
Vikas was excited and imaginative, happily turning the basket into many things.
How did Dadi support Vikas's imagination?
She laughed and asked what he would do next, which helped him invent more of the story.
How might Dadi feel watching her basket become a boat?
Dadi seemed amused and delighted by Vikas's ideas.

Monday. Tanvir left packing for the morning, as always. At 7:40 he was still hunting for his Hindi notebook while the van honked, and he forgot his water bottle.
Tuesday evening. After dinner he took out the timetable taped inside his diary. Wednesday: English, Maths, Science, Art. He pulled out Tuesday's Hindi and Social Studies books, slid in the four he needed, then set his lunch box, washed and dry, and his bottle, filled and capped, by the door.
Wednesday morning. Tanvir ate his paratha slowly. His sister Charu, still hunting for her socks, stared at him. "Why are you so calm?" He pointed at his bag, zipped and waiting.

Which subjects were on Wednesday's timetable?
English, Maths, Science and Art.
How did Tanvir feel on Wednesday morning compared with Monday?
On Monday he was rushed and flustered and forgot his bottle; on Wednesday he felt calm enough to eat his paratha slowly.
What else could Tanvir add to his evening routine?
A quick look through the diary for notes about projects or PT; packing in the evening is what freed up his morning.
How does Charu see Tanvir's calm morning?
Charu, still hunting for her socks, is surprised and a little puzzled by how calm he is.

metadata.subtype: Approach: reading the timetable and packing the night before [Action]
